Nine-Month Novena in Preparation for the Centennial of the Fatima Apparitions

NINE-MONTH NOVENA IN PREPARATION FOR THE CENTENNIAL OF THE FATIMA APPARITIONS July 31, 2016 Dear Fathers, Brothers, and Friends, Between the 13 th of May and the 13 th of October in 1917 the six apparitions at Fatima —with its message of repentance, comfort, warning, and singular protection— took place. In May of next year, we will celebrate the 100 th anniversary of this memorable event which has left a deep mark not only on the Church of the twentieth century, but also on Marian devotion, on the Christian conscience, and even on the actions of some Popes (pilgrimages to her shrine, the revelation of the secrets announced by the Blessed Virgin Mary to Venerable Sr. Lucia and to Blessed Jacinta and Blessed Francisco, as well as the consecration of the world to Mary’s Immaculate Heart). As is known, the prayers of our Mother, and those intentions that She asked the Church to pray for —the world and some countries in particular (Russia)— were decisive in the events of the end of the last century, in a special way in the fall of Soviet empire, one of the most anti-Christian em-pires in whole history. Ours is a time full of lights and shadows, of hopes and of the predication of future storms, of political uncertainties and doctrinal confusion, some of them unlike ever before. Today, as in so many crucial moments, we need the particular intervention of this protective Mother and a new triumph of her Immaculate Heart. Once again the Church goes through history “amid the persecutions of the world and the consolations of God” (St. Augustine), and many hearts are troubled by anxiety and uncertainty. The proximity of the next celebration is a special opportunity to call upon our Mother with all of our strength. A unique way to prepare for the centennial of her protecting providential help is with a novena, though not of days, but of months. Beginning in August, which starts tomorrow, we have exactly nine months before next May. That is why, from the General House of the Institute, we want to guide and make our own initiative that was presented to us by Father Miguel Angel Fuentes. It is the following: without overloading the regular activities with which we already express our Marian devotion, but rather by ordering and emphasizing them, we can make this work of preparation an opportunity to express a distinctive Marian devotion that should characterize us on account of our fourth vow of Marian slavery. Our proposal consists in joining together these nine months by devoting each one of them to exalt one of the main privileges of Mary and performing some activities, of which some are listed below, as well as all those you would like to add (recitation of the Rosary in community or in family, a continuous recitation of the Rosary on some occasions, pilgrimages to her shrines, etc.). This is an invitation for everyone: priests, men and women religious, and the lay people of our Third Order, who would like to join us in this choral prayer, ample in its dimension, just like the expansion of our Religious Family, and long-lasting, like the upcoming nine months. However, at the same time, it is a free and spontaneous response of all who wish to accept it. The privileges that we should keep in mind in each of the months are the following (all of them can be found in the work of Antonio Royo Marin, The Virgin Mary , or in any of the good treatises on the Blessed Virgin Mary, all of which are easily found online): 1st. August: Mary’s Predestination 2nd. September: The Immaculate Conception 3rd. October: Mary’s Perpetual Virginity 4th. November: Divine Motherhood 5th. December: Spiritual Motherhood 6th. January: Marian Co-redemption 7th. February: Mary Mediatrix of All Graces 8th. March: The Assumption of Mary into Heaven 9th. April: Mary Queen of the Universe In each of these months several activities could be performed. 1. To celebrate all Saturday Masses in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary as the liturgy allows. 2. To preach on the Blessed Virgin Mary at least two Saturdays each month, if possible on the privilege to which the month is dedicated. 3. Offering all the rosaries that will be prayed during these months for the triumph of the Immaculate Heart of Mary over the dangers that the Church goes through in our time and asking for a special protection for persecuted Chris-tians—in a singular way those in the Middle East—and for our Religious Family and vocations. 4. Offering the Saturday hour of adoration or that of the first Saturdays in atonement for the offenses committed against the Immaculate Heart of Mary. “Have pity on the Heart of your Most Holy Mother. It is covered with thorns with which ungrateful men pierce it at every moment, and there is no one to remove them with an act of reparation” (Words of the Infant Jesus to Sr. Lucia on December 10 th , 1925). 5. To fulfill monthly with the conditions that the Church requires to obtain indulgences: confession, communion, and prayers for the Pope. 6. This could be a good opportunity to renew and promote the consecration to Mary according to of St. Louis de Montfort’s method among the Third Order members and the laity in general, with the 33 days of preparation indicated by the saint. Father Miguel Fuentes has offered to put some devotional thoughts regarding the corresponding Marian privilege into writing each month which will be sent out via email. As it can be seen from the above, the intentions of this novena are essentially threefold: 1. To ask for the triumph of the Immaculate Heart of Mary over the dan-gers that the Church goes through in our time. 2. To request a special protection for persecuted Christians, in a singular way for those in the Middle East. 3. To intercede for our Religious Family and for vocations. The novena should begin during the month of August this year, 2016, simply by letting everyone know that it is happening and beginning with that which can be done from day one: we must keep those intentions which are being offered as part of the novena in mind, as well as the prayers for the intentions already indicated, to which everyone can add more, if desired. The Superiors of each Province and House will then suggest other activities that can be per-formed. From what has been said above, the reading of and meditation on some classic books on Mary, such as the works of St. Louis de Montfort, St. Alphon-sus Liguori, Roschini, Antonio Royo Marin (the explanation of the aforementioned privileges can be taken from his work The Virgin Mary ), and others, is also recommended. We thank Fr. Miguel Angel Fuentes for having taken the initiative to make this nine-month novena and we wish you all a very fruitful preparation to celebrate the 100 th anniversary of the apparitions of Our Lady at Cova da Iria in 2017.
Consecration to The Sacred Heart of Jesus

CONSECRATION TO THE SACRED HEART OF JESUS August 31 st , 2016. Dear Fathers, Brothers, and Seminarians, As you all know, by God’s grace, at the closing Mass of the past General Chapter, and as result of a unanimous decision of the Chapter Fathers, we consecrated the Institute to the Sacred Heart of Jesus. Said consecration was made by the “enthronement” of His image, accompanied by the corresponding prayers, in the church of St. Bartholomew the Apostle at the Institute’s seminary in Mon-tefiascone (Italy). For us it is an act of great significance and of profound spiritual meaning, a pledge of many fruits of holiness, mutual union and concord, and apostolic fruit-fulness for the members of the Institute. With this consecration, by the sheer grace of God and His mercy, we have just been following what the Pontiffs have insistently recommended in recent years with specific documents, establishing this devotion throughout the Church not as simply another devotion, but as one essential to the Catholic faith. This is because devotion to the Sacred Heart is nothing other than devotion to the Person of the Redeemer, in whose love con-sists all the perfection of Christian life and of the consecrated life 1 . At the same time, we cannot fail to see that in recent times this devotion has gained a new momentum since the institution of the feast of Divine Mercy on the Sunday of the Octave of Easter for the universal Church, and this because Divine Mercy is nothing other than the manifestation of the infinite love of the Heart of Christ 2 . Through this Circular Letter I would like to exhort everyone to delve more deeply into the meaning of this consecration and devotion, while establishing that in each Province and in each community of the Institute the same consecration or enthronement be made during the current Jubilee Year of Mercy declared by Pope Francis. For the future, we also establish that whenever a new community of the Institute is erected, the enthronement of the image of the Sacred Heart is to be made with due solemnity. 1. Meaning of this Consecration Although here I cannot explain the entire significance of this devotion, I offer a brief summary. The consecration of people, houses, jurisdictions, and of the Institute itself to the Sacred Heart of Jesus has as its final end the worship of the Person of the Divine Redeemer, seeking to love Him with all our heart, with all our strength, with all our mind, and all our soul (cf. Mt 22:37), which is the same as the end of our religious consecration, as well as to repair for the offenses committed against Him, which is also identified with the sacrifice and holocaust of our own religious life 3 . Thus Pope Pius XII stated that the devotion to the Sacred Heart is the devotion to the Person of Jesus, but particularly to its triple love for us: the love He has for us as God, in union with the Father and the Holy Spirit; the love of His most holy human will, full of grace; and His sensible love, perfectly ordered in Him, and which is like the external revelation, with its authentically human traces, of His most tender and infinite mercy 4 . Such devotion would be in vain if it did not entail a corresponding reply on our part, which is precisely what our Lord complained about to St. Margaret Mary: “Behold the Heart which has so loved men that it has spared nothing . . . and in return, I receive only ingratitude.” In this same sense Pope Leo XIII teaches: “There is in the Sacred Heart, the symbol and express image of the infinite love of Jesus Christ which moves us to love in return” 5 . Furthermore, the enthronement also means setting Jesus on a symbolic throne by which the father of the family (the superior of the house or jurisdiction) cedes to Christ all his powers of government and by doing so, he professes Jesus’ absolute kingship over himself, over the other members of the house, their people and apostolates, and over the house itself. Therefore, said consecration must not remain a mere outward sign. It should imply the desire to unite oneself more and more to our Savior, identifying oneself with Him as His members who seek the perfection of charity and mystical transformation, which is the end of our religious consecration, and seeking to bring to fulfillment in us the consequences of our baptism by which we were incorporated into Christ. This devotion, then, entails not simply a partial identification with Christ, but rather one that has the characteristic of totality and, therefore, perfect identification with Him 6 . To identify oneself with Him and to transform oneself into Him also means to immolate oneself with Him in reparation for our own sins and the sins of all our brothers through the holocaust of our religious life. In fact, reparation is an essential element of this devotion, as the Lord deigned to reveal to Saint Margaret Mary. 2. Benefits Promised by the Sacred Heart to Institutes that Consecrate Themselves to Him There are four main benefits promised to the Institutes that render special devotion to the Heart of Christ, as stated by Saint Margaret 7 . 1st. To preserve the primitive fervor of the Institute: “These fruits of life and health [that the devotion to the Heart of Jesus will bring] will renew us in the primitive spirit of our holy vocation.” Elsewhere she says: “Satan wanted to throw up their anger by destroying the spirit [of our Institute], and hereby ruin it. But I think it will not achieve its intent, if we want, according to the intentions of our holy Father [St. Francis de Sales], to use the means he gives us [this devotion] to restore to the first vigor the spirit of our holy vocation, living according to the maxims of the Sacred Heart of Our Lord Jesus Christ.” In a letter to her spir- itual director, no longer only in reference to her order, but to all orders in general, she writes: “Above all do all you can so that religious people may em- brace [this devotion], because they will draw from it so many favors that it will not be necessary any other remedy to restore the original fervor and the most exact regularity in the less observant Communities.” 2nd. Achieving the ends of the Institute: This follows from the renewal of the Insti- tute’s primitive fervor. Recalling a vision in which the Most Blessed Virgin Mary gave the devotion to the Heart of Jesus to the Order of the Visitation and to the Society of Jesus, the saint says: “In proportion as they give Him pleasure, this Divine Heart, source of blessings and graces, will shower them so abun- dantly on the works of their ministry that they will produce fruits far beyond their labors and expectations. And, this, too, for their own personal salvation and perfection.” 3rd. Union of charity among the members: In a letter, after listing several promises to religious communities, Saint Margaret Mary adds: “What great blessings and graces He intends to shower on this dear Institute, especially on houses that procure great honor and glory for Him, if we are faithful in removing what He gives us understand is impedingthe pleasure He wants to take in pouring forth sweet unction of His charity in all these communities in general, and on each 4th. Strength and unity in front of the dangers of division and external attacks: The saint says, “I am sure that our holy Founder, fearing that the foundations of his edifice will begin to crack, had asked for a support able to defend it. He was given the devotion to the Heart of Jesus as the means to repair the cracks of the edifice and to serve him as the defense against the attacks of his enemies, and as the support so that it may not succumb in the future.” “I cannot help adding a word about what happened on the Feast of our Holy Founder. He gave me to understand that there was no more efficacious means of making reparation for the faults committed in his Institute than to introduce the devotion to the Sa- cred Heart, and in it He wants this remedy applied.” “I think His Sacred Heart is one of the most efficacious means for raising it up after it has fallen. It will be an impregnable fortress for the Institute against the attacks the enemy will continually level against it. Satan will try to overthrow it by false spirit of pride and ambition which he wants to introduce in place of the spirit of humility and simplicity, which are the foundation of the whole edifice. I am sure our holy Founder desires and asks that this devotion be introduced into the Institute, for he knows how efficacious it will be.” 3. Promises Made to Those who will Honor Him by this Devotion In addition to these promises made to religious communities, the Lord re-vealed to St. Margaret Mary other promises for the people who honor Him by this devotion. Well known to all are the promises about the efficacy of this devotion concerning the personal sanctification of those who practice it, but I think it is good to mention them within this context 8 : 1st. I will give them all the graces necessary for their state of life. 2nd. I will give peace in their families. 3rd. I will console them in all their troubles. 4th. I will be their refuge in life and especially in death. 5th. I will abundantly bless all their undertakings. 6th. Sinners shall find in my Heart the source and an infinite ocean of mercy. 7th. Tepid souls shall become fervent. 8th. Fervent souls shall rise speedily to great perfection. 9th. I will bless those places wherein the image of My Sacred Heart shall be exposed 10th. I will give to priests the power to touch the most hardened hearts. 11th. Persons who propagate this devotion shall have their names eternally written in my Heart. 12th. In the excess of the mercy of my Heart, I promise you that my all powerful love will grant to all those who will receive Communion on the First Fridays, for nine consecutive months, the grace of final repentance: they will not die in my displeasure, nor without receiving the sacraments; and my Heart will be their secure refuge in that last hour 9 . 4. Properly Prepare for the Consecration It is apparent to all that the goods promised by the Divine Redeemer to individuals and communities who honor his Sacred Heart are invaluable and infinite. However, the acquisition of these goods will depend largely on our interior dispositions. So I want to encourage you to properly prepare for the act of consecration in each of our houses and jurisdictions, by means of an appropriate previous catechesis, for example, using the Good Nights or sermons, and by holding a Triduum or a preparatory Novena. The most important papal documents on the subject can be very useful for sermons, since they are both brief as well as very substantial and rich, especially Pius XII’s Encyclical Letter Haurietis aquas 10 . * * * * Dear all, I think the act of consecration done at the end of the General Chapter will bear much fruit, especially in terms of personal sanctification and spiritual embellishment of the Institute. It is up to each one of us to be faithful to our religious consecration, and therefore, to use this admirable means that the Lord Himself has revealed repeatedly to distinguished saints and that He Himself wanted to propagate in his Church through His vicars, the holy Pontiffs. Likewise, do not forget that we are in the Jubilee Year of Mercy, a year of special graces, not only to gain indulgences, but also in order to atone for our sins, to obtain forgiveness and mutual reconciliation where it is lacking, as well as to restore peace and concord wherever is necessary. Let us take advantage, then, of the treasure of the infinite merits of Christ that the Church makes available to us at this precious time so that we may grow in the love of Jesus Christ, which is the main cause and end of our consecrated life. May the Blessed Virgin Mary, of whom we are slaves of love, help us. We ask her, the “Hodegetria,” She who shows the Way, that She may reveal her Son to us, that she may form us like Him in the divine mold of her virginal womb, and that she may bless all our efforts towards our sanctification and make fruitful all our apostolic works. Saint José Gabriel Brochero and the Spiritual Exercises

SAINT JOSÉ GABRIEL BROCHERO AND THE SPIRITUAL EXERCISES September 30th, 2016. Dear Fathers, Brothers, and Seminarians: This coming 16 th of October, the Holy Father will raise the Argentine priest José Gabriel del Rosario Brochero (1840-1914) to the honors of the altar. Brochero was a distinguished preacher of the Spiritual Exercises of Saint Ignatius of Loyola, and Saint John Paul II called him “the Curé of Ars of Argentina.” 1 In addition to filling us with happiness, his canonization is wrapped with a particular importance for us, since, as an Institute, we want to “accomplish [the] evangelization of the culture by sanctifying people individually. This will be done preferably by using the Spiritual Exercises according to the method and spirit of Saint Ignatius of Loyola.” 2 For this reason, it seemed opportune for me to remind all the members of the religious family of the importance that the apostolate of the Spiritual Exercises has as an efficacious means for the preaching of the Word of God and their “irreplaceable value . . . for the renewal of Christian life.” 3 1. The Example of Fr. Brochero 4 José Gabriel del Rosario Brochero was ordained a priest on November 4 th , 1866, at the age of 26. In December of 1869, at the young age of 29, he was named pastor of the vast parish of San Alberto, in the west of the province of Córdoba (Argentina), with a territory of 4,336 square kilometers of steep mountains and inhospitable paths. The population of little over 10,000 inhabitants lived in remote areas, without roads or schools, entirely in isolation because of the Sierras Grandes, which tower over 2,000 meters high. There, in the midst of the moral and material poverty of his parish, suffering from the unwarranted criticisms and misunderstandings of other priests and the indifference of authorities, the merciful heart 5 of this heroic priest urged the preaching of the Spiritual Exercises for his rough and simple people. His faith and conviction in the miraculous fruits of holiness 6 from the Spiritual Exercises—which he had known as a seminarian—were so strong that he did not hesitate to throw himself completely into this apostolic endeavor. Hence, he would say: “The priest who has scarce pity for sinners is only half a priest. These vestments I wear are not what make me a priest; if I don’t have charity in my heart, I am not even a Christian.” Far from being scared at the difficulties or making excuses because of the lack of support, he wrote in one of his letters: “I trust in God and in the Virgin Most Pure,” and in this way, this man of faith bore witness that being a pastor and being a missionary are one same reality. His biographers recount that he would put together caravans that would surpass over 500 people, in order to undertake a journey of more than 200 kilometers (which required three days journey on mule) in order to withdraw from the world for nine days where he would teach them to conquer themselves and to order their lives according to God. At the end of the Exercises, he would bid them farewell, telling them: “Well, now go on and be on guard against offending God by returning to your old ways. The priest has already done his part so that you might be saved if you want. But, if anyone insists on being condemned, may a thousand devils carry him off.” 7 Years later, Fr. Brochero himself, together with parishioners, built his own House for the Exercises, and God—who does not let Himself be outdone in generosity—hurried to reward him with abundant blessings. The story is told that his happiness was so great when the foundations were laid for the House of the Exer-cises that he himself wanted to lay the first stone and, foreseeing hell’s opposition against the building from which he awaited so many fruits, he threw it with exu-berance, as if he was crushing the head of a serpent with it, and exclaimed: “Devil, you’re done for!” The house was opened in 1877 with groups of over 700 people. The following year, the exercitants grew to 4,000, and ultimately more than 40,000 people made the Exercises in the House during the parochial ministry of Fr. Brochero. Moreover, since the House’s opening until the present no fewer than 100,000 people have “taken” the Exercises in that house, 8 spiritually renewing themselves (Fr. Brochero called the Spiritual Exercises “bathes for the soul”). It’s worth mentioning that as soon as the construction of the House for the Exercises was finished, Fr. Brochero brought a religious community—the Hand-maids of the Sacred Heart of Jesus—to look after it. Eager to fulfill an old dream, he also built a school for girls (cared for by the same sisters) and a residence for priests. In his inexhaustible missionary zeal, and in an effort to bring his beloved parishioners out of the poverty in which they were found, he built more than 200 kilometers of roads, several churches, founded towns, and planned a railway branch line that would unite Valle de Traslasierra with Villa Dolores y Soto. “Abandoned by everyone but not by God,” he used to say. Setting aside the misunderstandings of his peers because he preached the Ex-ercises to the men and women of the mountains, who were simple, suspicious, and often illiterate, he recommended to the priests that sometimes came to help him: “The more sinful, or more rough, or more rude my parishioners, the more sweetness and friendliness they must be treated with in the confessional, from the pulpit, and in daily contact.” Convinced that the “parish must produce faithful people who are able to make the seed of the Gospel blossom in the place where they are,” “Cura Brochero preached to, confessed, directed, and helped the participants, dedicating himself entirely to them.” 9 He would often say: “I would be happy if God would take me from this earth seated hearing confessions and preaching the Gospel.” Authentically Ignatian in his preaching, the holy priest invited all to serve under Christ’s standard. He would tell the exercitants: “Jesus invites to follow Him and to place yourself under His standard with a most pleasant manner and with the sweetest words. Our health and our life, the strength of our heart, the joy of our spirit, and the hope of heaven is in the Cross.” At last, when he was diagnosed with the terrible sickness of leprosy, which he contracted through his care of and companionship with, even to the point of shar-ing his mate , a man ill with the same illness, Brochero could see how many of those in whom he had trusted had abandoned him, frightened by his awful infirmity, and how he was left with his sister Aurora for his only companion. On February 2 nd , 1908, at the age of 68, almost blind and deaf, Brochero gave up his parish, impossible as it was for him to care for it. With admirable resignation, he embraced the heavy cross with which God wanted to test his arduous old age, and his last years were an eloquent lesson of tried virtue. Both his leprosy and agonizing solitude revealed in an unexpected way the fruitfulness of his surrender as a priest. While he was already sick, he was heard to say: “I am very content with what God has done with me with regard to my sight, and I give Him great thanks on account of it. When I could serve humanity, my senses remained healthy and robust. Today, now that I cannot, one of the senses has been rendered useless. It is a great favor that God our Lord has done me in freeing me entirely from the active life and leaving me the task for seeking my end and of praying for men of the past, present, and those who will come until the end of the world.” Our Founder calls our attention to the following point: “His life of faith was fed by the Spiritual Exercises of Saint Ignatius, daily Mass, even during his long trips and on his sick bed, his rosary, and the breviary that he carried at his waist and that he prayed daily. ‘He lived by faith,’ noted one witness. From there arose his great pastoral charity and his death on the cross. In it he found his support and strength in his long illness and, thanks to it, before he died he could say, ‘I trust in God’s mercy.’” 10 He died, a blind leper, on January 26 th , 1914, at the age of 74. 2. Spiritual Exercises in Order to Evangelize “The preaching of the Ignatian Spiritual Exercises in our parishes is a characteristic proper to the Institute. The way in which said Exercises strengthen the life of the parish by means of the strengthening of the spiritual life of the faithful has been proven.” 11 For this reason, “we must enthusiastically return to this practice, which has given so many fruits of holiness,” 12 and which constitutes one of the preferential apostolates of our Institute. 13 In this sense, Blessed Paul VI wrote: “We know that the most effective preaching is precisely that of the Spiritual Exercises. . . . We must spread this foundation of salvation and of spiritual energy; we must make it accessible to all classes of people.” 14 Our spiritual father, Saint John Paul II, exhorts us: “I hope that… priests, religious, and lay people continue being faithful to this experience [of the Spiritual Exercises] and that they give them increase.” 15 For this reason, dear brothers in the Incarnate Word, by means of this circular letter I want to exhort you all to renew your fervor for the preaching of the Spiritual Exercises, that each one should take this as your own responsibility, each one col-laborating with what corresponds to him. 16 I implore you not only to preach the holy Exercises, but also to do everything to organize them, even at the cost of great sacrifices, making use of the help of the lay members of our Third Order and of the Sisters Servants of the Lord, who can be of great help. God will not cease to bless the efforts that are made so that He can reign in souls! We, too, like Saint Fr. Brochero, have offered ourselves totally to “our Lord, the Eternal King,” whose “will [it is] to conquer the whole world.” 17 Hence, we must not spare any sacrifice in carrying out this magnificent apostolate. This “should bring us to know the Ex-ercises deeply, to prepare ourselves to preach them fruitfully, 18 and to have the necessary dispositions so as not to miss any opportunity to preach them.” 19 It turns out to be of great importance to know how to adapt the Exercises to all classes of exercitants and to promote them “so that all parts of the world take advantage of the benefits” of the Exercises, making use of “new methods for evangelization, as the use of the Internet can be, also for the preaching of the Spiritual Exercises” 20 according to the language of the place, and also seeking—in the measure that it is possible—to have an adequate and proper place dedicated to the preaching of the Exercises, even though many times this entails great sacrifices and, in short, it might be a cross. It is from this same cross that innumerable blessings for our souls, for our Institute, and for the universal Church are born, as the great work of Saint Cura Brochero shows. Among the most valuable and outstanding fruits we can include: the efficacious influence that they have on the holiness of people, the numerous conversions, the great number of vocations to the path of perfection that are decided during the Exercises, the grace of perseverance, and more. All of these are fruits that promote an authentic and profound renewal of the Christian life, in this way collaborating in the establishment of Christ’s reign. Therefore, may our desire always be to know how to take advantage of this precious instrument in order to carry out the new evangelization, which is “a ‘fascinating adventure,’ one that is ‘arduous and exciting, that summons all of us together.” 21 In this context, I cannot help but mention another great grace for the nation of Argentina and for the universal Church that has recently taken place. I refer to the beatification of María Antonia de la Paz y Figueroa, Mama Antula , that heroic woman who was a great apostle of the Spiritual Exercises of Saint Ignatius, above all after the expulsion of the Jesuits from the Americas. 22 She also founded the House of Exercises in Buenos Aires (which still operates), fighting against innumerable misunderstandings and difficulties as a result of her sex, the era, and from certain ecclesial spheres. The strength and apostolic drive of this apparently frail female figure of holiness should move us to put into place the means and to know how to discomfort ourselves so that the greatest possible number of souls might benefit from that spiritual bath which are the Exercises. 23 For this reason, I raise with all fervor my prayer to our Lord that, on the occasion of the canonization of Saint Cura Brochero, the ardor might be renewed and the efforts and initiatives intensified that are directed towards promoting, improving, and increasing the opportunities for preaching the Spiritual Exercises of Saint Ignatius as a most appropriate means for the evangelization of the culture, that is, as a means to transform the world from within through the influence of grace. This is because, as the saint said so well, the Exercises help to “encourage man here on the earth, but with his sight fixed on heaven.” In a special way, I urgently recommend that Provincial Superiors put into place the means so that the priests of the Institute might make their knowledge of the Exercises of Saint Ignatius more profound, and that the preaching of those Exercises to all classes of exercitants might be increased. To neglect this aspect of our apostolate or to not properly encourage it would be an offense to our specific purpose and to our mission in the Church, who awaits from us the exercise of the apostolates proper to our charism. May the new saint José Gabriel del Rosario Brochero intercede for our beloved Institute and obtain for us the grace of a total, permanent, and happy surrender in the exercise of our priesthood, and the immense grace of preaching authentically Ignatian Exercises everywhere, and this for the glory of God alone and the good of many souls. Wishing you a beautiful feast for the canonization of Blessed José Gabriel del Rosario Brochero, I greet you in Christ, the Incarnate Word, and His Most Holy Mother. The 300 th Anniversary of the death of St. Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort

THE 300 TH ANNIVERSARY OF THE DEATH OF ST. LOUIS-MARIE GRIGNION DE MONTFORT October 10, 2016. Dear Fathers, Brothers, and Seminarians, In Article 4 of our Constitutions, which deals with the proper charism of our Institute, we profess to be essentially missionaries and Marian 1 and that we desire to work “in supreme docility to the Holy Spirit and according to the example of the Virgin Mary,” 2 to make “a fourth vow of slavery to Mary according to the spirituality of Saint Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort… [which will] secure her indispensable help in perpetuating the Incarnation in all things.” 3 Such an affirmation becomes an essential and non-negotiable element for our Institute. And as such, as our founder, Fr. Buela, clearly points out, it is something “that cannot be lost without serious damage to our charism.” In addition, it becomes “a perennial source of supernatural fruitfulness for our small Religious Family.” 4 Both aspects are of great importance. It is such that our spirituality “that longs to be of the Incarnate Word” 5 is “marked with a special prominence” 6 because of our consecration to Mary “‘in maternal slavery of love’ according to the admirable method taught by St. Louis Grignion de Montfort” 7 in professing our fourth vow, “so as to “marianize” our whole life.” 8 This is what we say in the fundamental code of our spirituality: “Not Jesus or Mary; not Mary or Jesus. Neither Jesus without Mary; nor Mary without Jesus. Neither only Jesus, but also Mary; not only Mary, but also Jesus. Always Jesus and Mary; always Mary and Jesus. To Mary through Jesus: Behold, your mother! (Jn 19:27). To Jesus through Mary: Do whatever he tells you (Jn 2:5). First Jesus, the God man; then Mary, the Mother of God. He, the Head; She, the Neck; we, the Body. Everything through Jesus and through Mary; with Jesus and with Mary; in Jesus and in Mary; for Jesus and for Mary. In short, simply: Jesus and Mary; Mary and Jesus. And through Christ, to the Father, in the Holy Spirit.” 9 For this reason, in a particular way during the year 2016 in which is com-memorated the 300 th anniversary of the death of that gigantic apostle of the Mother of God who was St. Louis Grignion de Montfort, I wanted by means of this circular letter to put forth for the consideration of all, in the first place the magnificent example that we are given by the “authentic apostle of the last times,” 10 as well as to say something about the great obligation that we have as religious of the Incarnate Word to live with the same spirit with which he lived, which is in “total surrender to Mary so as to better serve Jesus Christ.” 11 1. St. Louis Marie, an apostle formed by Mary The soul of St. Louis Marie was deeply marked by the word ‘more!’…St. Louis Marie was authentically magnanimous because he ‘directed his soul to great acts’ 12 concerning himself with great things… “carrying out great works in all virtue.” 13 Be it for his ardent missionary zeal 14 , for his wise and enflamed preaching 15 , his preference for the poor 16 , for the prolific spiritual legacy that he left in his writings 17 , or for his “ardent love for Christ” 18 , the life of this “apostle of the Divine Truth,” as Pius XII called him, is exemplar, no matter under which aspect you consider it. Nevertheless, above all else, “as the two poles of the life and apostolate of Montfort” emerge his passion for “the Cross of Jesus and the Mother of Jesus.” 19 In the first place and in a brief way, I wanted to recall in this anniversary and in this Circular Letter certain events of his life which set him apart under the august title of a true son of Mary, of whom he gloried to belong as her slave. While he was still a seminarian, in the midst of a time which “placed opposition between Marian devotion and the worship due to God and the Incarnate Word, Jesus Christ,” 20 his devotion to the Blessed Mother found a favorable environment to grow and take root in the small Seminary of St. Sulpice, where the saint totally dedicated himself to the practices of Marian devotion. “Sensible to the objections of his fellow seminarians-who reproached him for making of the Blessed Virgin a divinity, or for recalling or loving the Mother more than the Son,” he was concerned with giving theological foundations to his “innate love of Mary” 21 , although always far from leaving aside his devotions. So, after having read all of the books of the Seminary Library which dealt with the Blessed Virgin Mary, and with great conviction, he proposed to the Superior General of St. Sulpice to change the formula of “slaves of Mary’ for that of “Slaves of Jesus in Mary.” In this way St. John Paul II affirmed “St. Louis Marie surprises us above all by his Theocentric spirituality…the person of Christ dominates his thought.” 22 And this, because he understood that “If then we are establishing sound devotion to our Blessed Lady, it is only in order to establish devotion to our Lord more perfectly, by providing a smooth but certain way of reaching Jesus Christ.” 23 June 5, 1700, at 27 years of age, he is ordained a priest. In his 16 years of priestly ministry he always carried with him the desire to lead a “hidden life” and “to go in a humble and simple way to teach catechism to the poor in country places and to arouse in sinners a devotion to our Blessed Lady.” 24 And from the beginning he dreamt of founding for this purpose “a small company of good priests who would exercise this ministry gathered under the standard and the protection of the Blessed Virgin.” 25 St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort “in a particular way, showed his greatness of soul amidst tribulations and difficulties, which were great and numerous.” 26 He always continued onwards trusting that which he reminded his sister of: “There is an unshakeable truth, a divine and eternal axiom, as true as the existence of one God…‘Seek first the kingdom of God and his justice and all the rest will be added unto you.’ 27 If you fulfil the first part of this declaration, God, who is infinitely faithful, will carry out the second; i.e. if you serve God and his holy Mother faithfully you will want for nothing in this world or the next.” 28 This is why St. John Paul II said: “Poor among the poor, profoundly inte-grated into the Church despite the lack of understanding he had to face, St Louis-Marie adopted as his motto these simple words: “God Alone”. He sang: “God alone is my tenderness, God alone is my support, God alone is my every good, my life and my wealth” 29 . His love for God was total. It was with God and for God that he went towards other people and walked the roads of the mission. Constantly aware of the presence of Jesus and Mary, his entire being was a witness to the theological virtue of charity which he desired to share with everyone. His deeds and his words had only one aim, to call people to conversion and to motivate them to live for God.” 30 “A Gospel wayfarer inflamed by the love of Jesus and of his holy Mother, he knew how to touch the hearts of the crowds, and how to make them love the Redeeming Christ, contemplated on the Cross,” 31 he dedicated himself with great zeal to the predication of popular missions. Although his works endend in apparent failure, “he was a missionary of extraordinary range and influence.” 32 The priestly ideal of St. Louis Marie can be deduced from what he himself asked of the Incarnate Word in his Prayer for Missionaries : “priests who are free with the freedom that comes from you, detached from everything,” “in bondage to your love and your will,” “with the Cross for their staff and the Rosary for their sling,” “men always available,” “true children of Mary,” “true servants of the Blessed Virgin who, …will range far and wide, with the holy Gospel issuing from their mouths like a bright and burning flame, and the Rosary in their hands…[who with] their authentic devotion to Mary…will crush the head of the serpent wherever they go…” 33 Certainly, as St. John Paul II well said, “He lived in complete fidelity to this vocation.” 34 The great secret of this Saint and the very source of his apostolic drive to win souls for Jesus Christ was, without a doubt, his devotion to the Blessed Virgin. Convinced that “through the Blessed Virgin Mary that Jesus came into the world, and it is also through her that he must reign in the world,” 35 he wrote Treatise on True Devotion to the Blessed Virgin . In which writing, he proposes the Total Consecration to Jesus through Mary in condition of total slaves of Mary, as a most efficacious way to achieve holiness, following the footsteps of Jesus Christ who subjected himself completely by becoming flesh in her womb. He himself explains is as he writes: “Mary is the great mould of God. No godly feature is missing from this mould. Everyone who casts himself into it and allows himself to be moulded will acquire every feature of Jesus Christ, true God.” 36 He also adds: “She is a holy place, a holy of holies, in which saints are formed and moulded.” 37 He exhorted all to enter into the spirit of the consecration, which is not reduced to mere external practices, but which rather implies being “completely possessed and governed by the spirit of Mary,” 38 and in the end “may be expressed in four words, doing everything through Mary, with Mary, in Mary, and for Mary, in order to do it more perfectly through Jesus, with Jesus, in Jesus, and for Jesus.” 39 In the last years of his life, during which he was tireless in his missionary initiatives, he founded free schools for boys and girls, as well as the Company of Mary and the Daughters of Wisdom. 40 April 28, 1716, with his soul bathed in humility, after having fought for some time with the infernal enemy, he was heard to have said: “It is useless for you to attack me. I am between Jesus and Mary. Thanks be to God and the Virgin. I have come to the end of my path: I will sin no more.” 41 He only had 16 years of priestly ministry and was only 43 years old. 2. Our responsibility to live in this spirit We, “by the grace of God, by inspiration of the Virgin , consecrate ourselves to her with a fourth vow according to the writings and spirit of St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort.” 42 This fourth vow 43 -for us as religious of the Incarnate Word—implies on the one hand, surrendering to the Mother of God with great valiance, all that we are, all that we have, “as well as everything we shall acquire in the future in the order of nature, of grace, and of glory in heaven. This we do without any reservation…And we give for all eternity without claiming or expecting, in return for our offering and our service, any other reward than the honour of belonging to our Lord through Mary and in Mary.” 44 Everything, absolutely, we place in her hands because we recognize ourselves as her slaves of love. And on the other hand, this consecration by means of a vow implies that it “is our desire, our explicit intention to marianize our entire lives, which means, doing all things through Mary, with Mary, in Mary, and for Mary, so as to do all through Jesus, with Jesus, in Jesus, and for Jesus…entering into the mysterious current of life which was brought to us by our Heavenly Mother, and with her to learn to give glory to our Heavenly Father by the grace of the Holy Spirit.” 45 This goes to say that the total consecration to Jesus through Mary is a “beautiful plan of life,” and it grants us religious the most perfect way of living the evangelical counsels. For, “consecrating oneself to the Virgin means allow-ing oneself to be brought by her to the Heart of Christ so that Christ may be formed in us. 46 ” 47 In such a way that the consecration “should accompany us during our entire lives,” 48 deepening evermore the sense of our consecration and the practical con-sequences that it has in the lives of each ony of us in the different circumstances in which we find ourselves. Particularly by the study and reading of the beautiful book Treatise of True Devotion to the Blessed Virgin 49 and “renewing as many times as necessary, even several times a day, our consecration. By doing such, we learn each time more to belong entirely to Mary, and so we may be ever more entirely of Jesus.” St. Louis Marie pointed out: “It is not enough to give ourselves just once as a slave to Jesus through Mary; nor is it enough to renew that consecration once a month or once a week…The chief difficulty is to enter into its spirit, which requires an interior dependence on Mary, and effectively becoming her slave and the slave of Jesus through her.” 50 Because “we would not be devout children if we do not know how to imitate the virtues of the Mother.” 51 Let us then be “apostles of the Congregation, ‘apostles of Mary,’” 52 following the eloquente example given us by Saint John Paul II, the Spiritual Father of our Religious Family. For Marian devotion is an essential part of evangelization. Let us follow, the splendid motion of St. Louis Marie: “Since we have given ourselves completely to her service, it is only right that we should do everything for her… Like every good servant and slave we must not remain idle, but, rely-ing on her protection, we should undertake and carry out great things for our noble Queen.” 53 For this reason, I encourage you to put into practice the various initiatives which are inspired by our love for the Blessed Virgin, especially those which are directed to honor, to promote, and to spread the Total Consecration so as to increase the number of those truly devoted to the Mother of the Incarnate Word, thus extending the Kingdom of Christ. Although there is great variety and value among the different apostolates which our religious throughout the world carry out to this end, I wanted to share with you all something that—by the grace of God—we did in our parish Our Lady of Peace , in California. It could be of some motivation and help to some of you. With the help of some of our laity we planned a program to invite people to total consecraton to Jesus through Mary following the method set forth by St. Louis Marie. 54 After an introductory talk, which we usually gave on the Saturday previous to the feast of St. John Paul II, we gave them materials to carry out the prayers and daily practices of piety. Five other talks followed, which we gave in English and Spanish, with the help of the sisters. Thirty-three days before the consecration, which usually took place on the feast of Christ the King, at the end of the daily mid-day Mass for those who were able to attend, we prayed the pre-paratory prayer for the Consecration. We thought that we might attract a few hundred people from our parish. The fact was that the first year, around 3,000 people consecrated themselves, and the next year 4,000 more. Together with the help of our parishioners, we made a website 55 , which can be used to register and get access to the conferences given and the material distributed (in English and Spanish). Such an initiative has become for many of the parishioners a concrete apostolate which they carry out with great enthusiasm and generosity. As a matter of fact, they themselves also offer to all our missionaries that which would be necessary, be it help or materials to carry forth this apostolate of Total Consecration in other parts of the world. 56 Another valiant initiative, directed towards revitalizing the spirit of our Consecration under the form of our vow, was carried out recently by the Province “Our Lady of Loreto” (Italy), following the directives of St. Louis Marie, doing one-month preparation to renew annually the total consecration to the Blessed Virgin. And so, my dear brothers, may the Blessed Virgin continue to bless our beloved Religious Family with true sons of Mary who have “a courageous faith which inspires…to undertake and carry out without hesitation great things for God and the salvation of souls.” 57 Notes 1 Cf. Advent and Christmas

“Do not be afraid. Look, I bring you news of great joy... Today in the town of David a Savior has been born to you; he is Christ the Lord.” (Lc 2:10-11) November 27, 2016 Dear Priests, Brothers, and Seminarians, With great joy and deep affection, I greet all of you in this month of December, the month in which we prepare ourselves to celebrate the consoling mystery of Christmas: God has desired to dwell among us to bring us joy and peace. The Incarnate Word! Unfathomable mystery which at once transcends and envelops us, surpasses and penetrates us. “Christmas: this is paradise!” 1 St. Anthony of Padua would say. When, over two thousand years ago, the Most Holy Virgin gave birth to her Son, happiness itself became flesh. This means that God fulfilled his promise, as the “proof that God has heard our cry.” 2 This happiness came in the flesh so that he may be contemplated, be embraced, be treasured in the depths of hearts and to illuminate the entire reality of man. This happiness is Jesus, the Word made flesh. For this reason, the birth of the Incarnate Word represents an invitation for all men to rediscover, to renew, and to strengthen one time more in our souls the immeasurable joy of the truth about God and the truth about man, knowing that God, in his ineffable love, is the Emmanuel—God with us—who has desired to share our history so as to transform it and to make us participants of the divine life. And the Word became flesh (Jn 1:14). God became a child and in that very instant love united the eternal to history 3 . Celebrating Christmas means making present the mystery of our salvation, because “the Incarnation of the Son of God is an event which occurred within history, while at the same time transcending history 4 ” for, all “that the Son of God did and taught for the world's reconciliation, we not only know as a matter of past history, but appreciate in the power of their present effect.” 5 Namely, the words which were addressed to the shepherds that night are directed to each one of us and to our religious family—whatever the circumstances of our life may be. “Do not be afraid. Look, I bring you news of great joy... Today in the town of David a Savior has been born to you; he is Christ the Lord.” (Lc 2:10-11) Let us implore the grace to always see that Light which burns still today in the night of the world and which can only be seen by the simple eyes of faith, by the meek and humble hearts of those who await the Savior. The light which in-vites each one of us to open our souls so as to “let ourselves be totally transformed by the One who took on our flesh.” 6 It is my desire, by means of this circular letter, to encourage each of you to live this time with special dedication, singular intensity and spiritual determination, not letting any single occasion offered to us go to waste (be it in the liturgy, personal or community prayer, practices of piety, or works of mercy). May we, by the “experience” of these most holy mysteries, obtain the fulfillment of our end of “making each person ‘like a new Incarnation of the Word.’” 7 In a special way, I would also like to ask the superiors of the various levels that they make the effort on their part so that the precious times of Advent and Christmas may be particularly emphasized in our communities, our apostolates, in our souls and in the souls that have been entrusted to us. As it is with all of the mysteries of the life of the Savior, but in a more tangible way with that of Christmas, there are three elements that are linked, for we can say that the one derives from the other, and that one is contained in the other. He who assumes the first, necessarily obtains the second and arrives to the third. This is an evangelical law, or better yet “the evangelical law,” because it derives directly from the paschal mystery of Our Lord. He who lives the virtues of self-denial obtains the grace of the precious pearl (cf. Mt 13:46), the treasure of the Cross; 8 and the one who is granted the Cross, obtains happiness and eternal life. This is the spirit of the Blessed! of the Beatitudes (Cf Mt 5:3-12) to which we want to testify, because the world can neither be transfigured nor offered to God without this Spirit 9 . 1. The Virtues of Self-Denial You will find a babe wrapped in swaddling cloths and lying in a manger 10 . The first Christmas Eve, Bethlehem seemed like heaven. In the words of St. John Chrysostom, “This day He Who is, is Born; and He Who is, becomes what He was not. For when He was God, He became man; yet not departing from the Godhead that is His. Nor yet by any loss of divinity became He man, nor through increase became He God from man; but being the Word He became flesh, His nature, because of impassability, remaining unchanged.” 11 In this way, Christmas becomes a “mystery of love” 12 which is revealed in the abysmal self-denial of the Son of God. How can one not tremble upon pondering the fact that God goes “from transcendent to immanent, from powerful to weak, from majestic to humble, from immortal to mortal, from infinite to finite, from most pure Spirit to material flesh, from eternal to temporal, from impassible to passible, from immense to small, from limitless to limited, from all-embracing to servant, from rich to poor, from Lord to slave, from King to subject, ‘from eternal life to death here in time.’ 13 ” 14 In one way, we can say then, that Christmas hides the humility of God, and it calls us, religious of the Incarnate Word who long “to radically live the demands of the Incarnation, and the Cross,” 15 to live as the shepherds: with a great spirit of faith, and with a deep humility and simplicity. “Only those who are open to love are enveloped in the light of Christmas. So it was on that night in Bethlehem, and so it is today.” 16 The virtues of self-denial that we so strongly desire to live 17 shine forth in the mystery of Christmas. The Evangelist continues saying that “the shepherds said to one another, ‘Let us go over to Bethlehem and see this thing that has happened, which the Lord has made known to us.’ And they went with haste” (Lk 2:15-16). What did they see? They saw a Child who was in need of care, dependent in all things, and even weak. Contem-plating this Child they adored Him who neither heaven or earth can contain. They never imagined that they would have seen Omnipotence wrapped in swad- dling clothes, Salvation lying in a manger. No one would ever have suspected that God coming to this earth would ever be so helpless. 18 Nevertheless, it is the faith-filled man that is able to recognize in Him Wisdom because he is foolish, Power because he is weakness, and the Infinite, Immense, and Eternal God, because he is little—hence only the humble man understands the meaning of the Incarnation. 19 It is my prayer and my fervent desire that God grant us, by means of his Most Holy Mother, the grace to be genuinely and profoundly humble so as to contemplate in the tender heart of the Child Jesus, the Heart of this God who “wants to be our ‘joy’, our ‘salvation’ our ‘hope’ our ‘happiness’, and our ‘Sovereign one.’” 20 In this way, witnessing such colossal humility, we may be moved to “practice the virtues of self-denial: humility, poverty, suffering, obedience, self-surrender, mercy and charity to all men.” 21 “More succinctly, we simply want to take up our cross,” 22 as our Savior did. Learning to “love like Him…to serve like Him, unto death. To be just, patient, meek, humble, to sacrifice ourselves, to carry the cross: the cross of our daily life, the cross which is the fulfillment of the law of God, the cross which is the fulfillment of the duties of our state of life, the cross which is bearing my defects and the defects of those around me.” 23 In a word, to testify with our lives that we profess “Never the Cross without Jesus, nor Jesus without the Cross.” 24 2. The Cross There was no place for them in the inn. 25 The example of St. Joseph and the Blessed Virgin before the fact that there was no place for them in the inn (Lk 2:7), should call us to have a providential outlook on life 26 keeping in mind the truth that God in his wise Providence makes certain means work together for certain ends. In this way he obtained glory and fruitfulness bringing together the cross. And so, “if the cross is the condition for salvation, and tribulation is the way, then suffering some sort of tribulation is a proof that one has not lost the way, but rather that he is on the right path.” 27 The Gospel texts point out very clearly that the Prince of Peace (Is 9:5) was born in the miserable and cold grotto of Bethlehem so as to give his life on Golgotha so that love might reign on earth. “Every other person who ever came into this world came into it to live. He came into it to die.” 28 That is why it is true that “the Word became flesh to be able to go to the cross, and the cross is possible because Christ became Incarnate.” 29 “If there were no Cross, there would have been no crib; if there had been no nails, there would have been no straw.” 30 For this reason, the Cross was always there from the beginning and cast its shadow back towards his birth, 31 teaching us resoundingly and silently that all the graces that God wants to give to us must necessarily pass through the cross. It is as if He were not able to teach the lesson of the cross as a ransom for sins, if He himself had not first learned it from his very birth. The newborn Incarnate Word laying in a manger “was already bearing His Cross—the only cross a Babe could bear, a cross of poverty, exile, and limitation,” 32 thus defying our ambition with his poverty, our pride with his humiliation, our eagerness for security with his needs. In this way he taught all with his Divine loving pedagogy that the power of God does not admit hin-drances. Even if he is wrapped in swaddling clothes, weak and seated on the lap of his Mother, He upholds the universe with his hand. This is one of the realities of Christmas that cannot be as something distant to us as religious of the Incarnate Word, who desire to be “another humanity of Christ” 33 living “radically…the demands of the Incarnation, the Cross, the Sermon on the Mount, and the Last Supper.” 34 He became flesh to die, he became flesh to suffer. The Cross was the precious means to show us his love and to grant us his salvation. It is “upon the cross,” as ignominious as this may be, where we “should find the greatest motive for glory,” because the cross is nothing other than “the glory of the Love disposed to all” 35 as is so clearly demonstrated in the mystery of Christmas. All of the saints confirm this doctrine. Blessed Paolo Manna, for example, would say to his missionaries: “None of us should be surprised if there is suffering in the mission, even if in our days in some missions there is extraordinary suffering. This means that everything is going well. If there is suffering, there is redemption.” Then, he went on to insist with words that are very enlightening to the situation which our religious family is living (as it has lived, and will continue to live if we are faithful to God). He said to them, and I implore you to pay attention to these words: “Courage! If the Institute suffers, it means that it is strong and pleasing to the Lord, it means that it is useful for the glory of God and the good of the Church...and even more so, we have every right to await with all confidence that the final victory will one day be ours.” 36 The mystery of Christmas teaches us to have a wise gaze towards the vicissitudes of our history. We must never fear in the face of sufferings, but rather know how to rejoice in them, whether they be sufferings on a personal level, or those of the Religious Family. In the face of calumnies, humiliations, contempt, and discrediting, even those coming from those from whom we least expect them, we must think about how Christ, the Incarnate Word, the Child of Bethlehem, has passed through them before we did. The Institute does not become ugly because of these trials, but rather becomes more beautiful in the midst of them. That is why today I want to repeat to you again the phrase of the Blessed, who was the Superior General of the PIME: “Courage! If the Institute suffers, it means that it is strong and pleasing to the Lord, it means that it is useful for the glory of God and the good of the Church...and even more so, we have every right to await with all confidence that the final victory will one day be ours.” This truth is not only a conviction, it is a law, contained in the very heart of the mystery of Christmas. Regarding this, our Founder wrote: “God is often where it seems like he cannot be, as he was in a stable, a place which humanly speaking seems as though it were the least fitting place for God to be born.” And so, we must ask the Mother of God “to teach us as well to discover God in the difficult circumstances.” Knowing how to rejoice supernaturally and bear fruit in those places where the Divine Providence in his merciful design has brought us. Because, “there, in that trial, in that difficulty, in that suffering, there is God; and if one knew how to have eyes of faith as the shepherds had, and as the Magi had, one would realize that many times God is in those places where it seems impossible for him to be.” “How many times in our lives has God proposed ways for us that are unbelievable! We have had to walk by ways which are superior to those ways we had imagined, because the thoughts of God are much greater, much higher, much more transcendent than our thoughts, the thoughts of men.” 37 How can we not be grateful for the innumerable blessings and graces that we have received as a Religious Family by means of the trials and difficulties that we have needed to overcome; graces which maybe we would never have received by other means! St. Paul, in his unrivaled hymn to the Philippians (1:12-2:4) in which he magnificently speaks of the Incarnation of the Word, invites us to know well these truths. The verses 27-30 are particularly enlightening for what we are speaking about, because it is there that he teaches us and encourages us to continue always onwards not frightened in anything by your opponents (v.28) because the prize is great and God has granted to you that for the sake of Christ you should not only believe in him but also suffer for his sake (v.29). Acting always according to the fortitude of true religious of the Incarnate Word, that in the face of crosses manifest a manner of life … worthy of the gospel of Christ , standing firm in one spirit, with one mind striving side by side for the faith of the gospel . (cf. v.27). 3. Glory Be not afraid, I bring you good news of a great joy 38 The manger, as it always happens with suffering, is also the precursor to happiness and glory. Our Saint John Paul II said “Christmas is a mystery of joy!” 39 Yes! Because the encounter of the humility of God and with his Cross, fills us with joy and from there springs forth feasting. Joy that is born from “knowing that God is not distant but close, not indifferent but compassionate, not aloof but a merciful Father who follows us lovingly with respect for our freedom.” 40 This joy which is “spiritual and supernatural,” 41 should be “an essential element in our Religious Family,” 42 and should be lived “even in the midst of the difficulties along the way, whether they be human or spiritual, as well as amidst the daily sorrows.” 43 Since Pope Benedict XVI so aptly put it: “God is good, and he is the supreme power above all powers… he is the most important thing, ultimately the one truly important thing.” 44 The invitation to joy that the angel brought to the shepherds is also an invitation for us: I bring you good news of a great joy which will come to all the people , accompanied by an exhortation to overcome all fear: Be not afraid! (Lk 2:10). As they were moved by a holy joy to go in haste—even in the middle of the night— to go adore the God Child, so let us sacrifice ourselves to bring to all men “the salvation which comes from the fullness of the happiness of God,” 45 going even “to work in the most difficult places – those where no one else wants to go,” 46 with the indestructible peace of soul knowing that we are infinitely loved by God. Contemplating the example of the shepherds after the decisive encounter with the Incarnate Word and his Most Holy Mother , the words of Blessed Paul VI come to mind: “Let us preserve the delightful and comforting joy of evange-lizing, even when it is in tears that we must sow… [with] an interior enthusiasm that nobody and nothing can quench. May it be the great joy of our consecrated lives.” 47 I think now of our religious that are sick, of those who live in situations of war, in those who fight in the midst of great adversities and those who in all parts make great efforts to give witness that to you is born…a Savior (Lk 2:11). May our lives also radiate with the fervor of those “who have first received the joy of Christ, and who are willing to risk their lives so that the kingdom may be proclaimed and the Church established in the midst of the world.” 48 My dear brothers: it is my most sincere desire that the birth of Christ may be for all a consoling caress to our souls that livens our trust and instills joy, and that these may become strength for apostolic action. Then, as the shepherds who returned, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen (Lk 2:20), we too may go out to the world grateful to God—especially for having become a Gift for us—as well as for the countless graces and blessings that from overflowing hands he pours out onto our dear Religious Family, in our souls, and in the souls entrusted to us, in this way bearing all things nobly 49 . In this Christmas, may the Virgin dispose all things according to her wisdom and maternal tenderness so that the Incarnate Word may find in the purity of our souls and in the fraternity of our communities a crib where he may be born, to radiate the peace and joy which he came to bring to the world. Be assured that I will have all of you very much present during the Christ-mas Eve Mass and during the Octave of Christmas. Finally, wishing you a holy and happy Christmas, as well as abundant bless-ings for the New Year which will begin shortly, I greet you in the Incarnate Word and in his Most Holy Mother. Notes 1 Cf.
