God’s unconditional ones

“God’s unconditional ones” 1 Formula of monthly renewal of vows “The soul that has attachment to anything…, will not reach the freedom of divine union” 2 , wrote St. John of the Cross. And what he wrote is exactly what he himself practiced and what he tried so eagerly to instill in his dealings with souls. For that is the Christian vocation of the new man 3 , a vocation to freedom, since for freedom Christ has set us free 4 . Therefore, and as could not be otherwise, the whole aspiration of our spirituality is directed entirely to the conquest of freedom. Precisely because “authentic freedom is identified with holiness, with the New Law, with the Christian faith, with charity; it is the freedom… of the children of God 5 ” 6 . For that is why the Son of God became incarnate: to free those who through fear of death were subject to bondage all their life 7 , as the apostle St. Paul says. Hence, then, what is proper to the members of the Institute of the Incarnate Word is “to live in the freedom of the children of God, who do not let themselves be enslaved: neither under the elements of the world 8 ; nor under the letter that kills 9 ; nor under the spirit of the world 10 ; because we must not submit to the yoke of slavery… (otherwise) Christ would be of no benefit to us” 11 . Since “slavery can have no part with freedom” 12 . Consequently, our Constitutions make manifest the call to the conquest of spiritual poverty or nakedness when they say that in our Institute “the fourth degree of poverty can be practiced more intensely, thus conquering total detachment , not only from material goods—the proper object of the virtue of poverty—but from everything that is not God Himself, which presupposes the perfection of charity and complete and consummate holiness” 13 , which, as we have said before, is identified with freedom of spirit and is the path to union with God. Given that we, as members of the Institute, are exhorted to form ourselves according to the magisterium of that great master of the spiritual life who was St. John of the Cross, since his teachings are “a limpid fountain of the Christian sense and of the spirit of the Church”—as Pius XI proclaimed when he honored him with the doctorate—we wish to present in these few lines the example of life and the wise teaching of the Mystical Doctor in order to attain “this noble good of the soul, so necessary for serving God, which is freedom of spirit” 14 . 1. Freedom of spirit St. John of the Cross was a religious of the Carmelite Order for 28 years (1563-1591), although he lived only 23 years in the Discalced Carmel (1568-1591). In any case, we must say that even before becoming a religious, but especially during all those years and in not a few circumstances, he showed that the struggle to attain the authentic freedom we have been speaking of is the business of our life. ▪ He decides to become a Carmelite On finishing his studies at the College of the Society of Jesus, at 21 years of age, Juan de Yepes was “sought after by all, loved and wanted by many religious orders, for his virtue and the signs of holiness he gave” 15 . And although he was sought after by the Benedictines of San Bartolomé, the Dominicans of San Andrés, the Franciscans of Santa Clara, the Calced Trinitarians of La Concepción, the Premonstratensians of San Saturnino, and the very Jesuits with whom he had studied, he set all those offers aside and chose to enter the Carmelite Order 16 . His brother Francisco de Yepes testifies: “He took refuge in what was safest and, determining to enter religion, set his eyes on that of Carmel, and so he went very secretly to the Carmelite convent of Santa Ana in this town (Medina), where he asked for the habit, and the prior and friars gave it to him at once with great joy” 17 . He showed thereby that self-giving to God—who calls souls by the free initiative of His love 18 —also demands a free response on the part of the religious; and so, turning a deaf ear to the solicitations of the other religious orders, he wished “to correspond freely and generously with the prompting and grace of the Holy Spirit” 19 to God’s call, and entered the Carmelite Order. That same act of freedom implicit in his entry into the Carmelites he maintained explicitly throughout his whole religious life, as we shall now see. ▪ He leaves the Carmelite Order of the mitigated rule Thus, for example, after having made profession as Fray Juan de Santo Matía, he was somewhat disillusioned with his Order and was tempted to go to the Carthusians. St. Teresa herself tells it: “I praised Our Lord, and on speaking with him, I was very pleased with him, and learned from him that he too wanted to go to the Carthusians” 20 . It is she herself who, in that same conversation, convinces him “to wait until the Lord gave them a monastery, and [of] the great good it would be, if he was to better himself, to do so within his own Order, and how much more he would serve the Lord. He gave me his word to do so, provided it did not take long ” 21 . Let us underline here the freedom of spirit of Fray Juan who, although he consents to the foundress’s proposal, sets her the condition “that it not take long” 22 . For freedom of spirit asks for docility and promptness in carrying out what the Holy Spirit asks; that is why our Proper Law not in vain warns us that “slow calculations are foreign to the grace of the Holy Spirit” 23 . And so, on November 28, 1568, the renewal of Carmel officially began in Duruelo (Ávila), Fray Juan adopting from then on the name of Fray Juan de la Cruz—John of the Cross. ▪ Lordship over men The Directory of Spirituality teaches: “to the extent that the religious gives himself generously to the service of Jesus Christ, the only King who deserves to be served, he acquires an effective, though spiritual, kingship over men, even over those who have power and authority, and even over those who abuse it. For they take upon themselves the burden of their sins and their sorrows, through a humble and serving love that goes as far as the sacrifice of oneself” 24 . Accordingly, with the same freedom with which Fray Juan de Santo Matía decided to leave the Carmelite Order of the mitigated rule to begin the discalced reform, with that same freedom he let himself be subjected and submitted to various torments and vexations after measures were taken against the Discalced at the General Chapter of the Order held in Piacenza on May 21, 1575; but he did not draw back from his purpose, that is, he did not give up remaining firmly and faithfully a Discalced Carmelite. That is how he suffered his first imprisonment: simply for being discalced. For some Calced religious, taking advantage of the climate of hostility against the Discalced, took justice into their own hands, as was the case of the prior of Ávila, Fr. Valdemoro, who took John of the Cross and his companion Fray Francisco de los Apóstoles prisoner and locked them up in the convent of Medina del Campo. They left there by order of the nuncio Ormaneto. One cannot forget the dignified and noble behavior of St. John of the Cross when, years later, Fr. Diego de Cárdenas, provincial of the Calced Carmelites of Andalusia, along with other religious accompanying him, came to Baeza to make the canonical visitation of the College where John was rector. The provincial was bringing a vexatious brief (something like a decree of reprimand) for the Discalced. The fact is that before the visitation began, the ordinary ecclesiastical court appeared and imprisoned the provincial and his companions. Fray Juan de la Cruz presented himself before the ecclesiastical judge who held them prisoner and begged him to release them. And the judge did so. Once they were out of prison, he took them to his College, prepared a banquet for them and sent them off in great peace. That is how the saints take ‘revenge’! For Cárdenas had forgotten that he no longer had any jurisdiction over the Discalced 25 . The second imprisonment that St. John of the Cross suffered took place on the night of December 2 to 3, 1577. “The crime” of which they accused him is unknown to this day . What is certain is that they gave him the treatment prescribed in the Constitutions for “those guilty of the crime of rebellion,” and so he spent a little more than eight months in the conventual prison of Toledo. Some argue that very probably the reason for his imprisonment was that he was judged an accomplice in the rebellion of the nuns of the Incarnation when they elected St. Teresa as prioress against the instruction and command of the provincial who presided over the election. Others think that perhaps it was the fact that he was living outside the convent, in the little house of La Torrecilla 26 , while both John of the Cross and his companion Germán de San Matías were conventuals of Mancera. In any case, that does not concern us here. What we do want to point out is the princely spirit with which the holy religious conducted himself during the time he was in captivity, suffering not a few vexations: the daily disciplines, the narrowness and extreme poverty of the cell, the meager diet to which he was subjected, which was meant rather to finish off his health than to keep him alive, the darkness, the intense heat and the penetrating cold, the “torment [of] the lice,” the impossibility of saying Mass, the merciless reprimands to make him abdicate his principles and his discalced way of life, etc. Even so, every day when they brought him down to the refectory to administer the discipline to him, the other friars marveled that John of the Cross remained so solid and unbreakable and that he gave no sign whatsoever that he was going to change. Indeed, as time went by, seeing him ever more invincible in enduring, suffering and keeping silent, the Calced contemptuously called him a “silent file” ( lima sorda ), because that is what one calls a file that is dulled with lead and makes little or no noise when it files. For those who behave as lords, however reduced they may find themselves, stand out above the rest by their self-possession and by holding honor as dear as life 27 . However, that ‘ill-treatment’ did not afflict him as much as hearing his jailers say that the Reform of the Order had its days numbered. Fray Juan never bore a grudge against the prior of that convent who caused him so much suffering. “This is how he behaved in matters concerning his neighbors; and so he suffered the trials God sent him, without admitting human relief or consolation” 28 , testified Ana de Jesús, a Discalced Carmelite in Segovia. Indeed, he himself, as one who had endured the file and abandonment on the part of superiors, would later write in the second precaution against the devil—which our Constitutions 29 make their own: “never look upon the superior with any less regard than upon God, whoever the superior may be, for you hold him in His place. And so watch with great vigilance that you do not look at his temperament, nor his manner, nor his appearance, nor other ways he has of proceeding ; for you will do yourself so much harm that you will come to change obedience from divine into human, moving or not moving only because of the ways you see visibly in the superior, and not for the invisible God, whom you serve in him. And your obedience will be vain, or all the more fruitless the more you grow heavy because of the superior’s unfavorable temperament, or light because of his good temperament” 30 . ▪ Lordship over oneself In our Proper Law we read that the religious exercises a certain dominion over himself “to the extent that man triumphs over sin, masters the incitements of the flesh, and governs his soul and body. The religious, to the extent that he fully subjects his soul to God, arrives at a state of indifference and detachment toward the things of the world, which does not mean impotence but, on the contrary, a masterful and free will, capable of dedicating itself to things without letting itself be dominated by them” 31 . An example of this is the following episode in the life of St. John of the Cross. Knowing the spiritual stature of St. John of the Cross and the lordship he possessed, it is laughable to read that his captors in the conventual prison of Toledo wanted to ‘buy’ him by offering him a good library, a good cell, a priorship and even a gold cross. Faced with such an offer, Fray Juan de la Cruz answers categorically: “He who seeks Christ naked has no need of gold jewels” 32 . And so later he would write in his second Precaution against the world that “it is necessary […] to abhor every manner of possessing, and let [your soul] have no care about it: not about food, not about clothing nor any other created thing, nor about tomorrow, employing that care in something higher, which is in seeking the kingdom of God, that is, in not failing God; for the rest, as His Majesty says, will be added to us 33 , since He who takes care of the beasts will not forget you” 34 . And with that same lordship which goes hand in hand with forgetting everything that is not God for the love of God, he escaped from prison. For, according to what some witnesses state, “after having commended this to our Lord for some days, [Fray Juan] felt in his soul a great impulse to go, that our Lord would help him.” And so he did. Certainly the painful experience of prison marked Fray Juan de la Cruz deeply and taught him the science of the cross: “God did well; for, after all, abandonment is a file, and suffering darkness is for great light” 35 . Because, “What does he know who does not know how to suffer for Christ?” 36 ; “The purest suffering brings and carries with it the purest understanding” 37 . That same science of the cross and freedom of spirit is what he transmitted to all the souls with whom he dealt, whether religious or lay people. Indeed, most of his subjects highlight his admirable talks, with which he encouraged them to be perfect and taught them that, in order to climb to perfection, they were to want neither goods of earth nor of heaven, but only to want and seek nothing but to seek and want in all things the glory and honor of God. And they say that those who dealt with him most made the most progress 38 . His subjects recount that “he had no things to which he could be attached. And he sought this same thing in his religious, even in things of devotion, insofar as they were curiosity, teaching them to keep their spirit free, and not to feed it on trifles” 39 . And he gave them this example: “For it is all the same to me whether a bird is tied by a thin thread or a thick one, because, even if it is thin, it will be as tied to it as to the thick one, as long as it does not break it to fly” 40 . Likewise, in his frequent conversations with the religious he “insisted on faith and nakedness and detachment from creatures. And ‘that in prayer we should not have our spirit measured out and determined to ascend to God by one path, but should leave ourselves in His hands, according to the spirit with which His Majesty might visit us; and that we should rejoice greatly in dryness, wanting nothing but God’s pleasure’” 41 . St. John of the Cross was a man with the spirit of a prince, one of those who “have set a style in their conduct” 42 , and therefore what he taught others he first demanded of himself. For example: the freedom of spirit of this man is striking with regard to what the rule prescribed concerning prayer in common. In the Constitutions of Fr. Gracián, 1576, it says: “prayer will be in choir, all being together.” In the Constitutions of Alcalá, 1581, the following is prescribed in the clearest and most detailed way: “Prayer shall be held in choir, where, the brothers being together, the Antiphon Veni, Sancte Spiritus and the prayer Deus, qui corda fidelium shall be begun. And then there shall be a little reading from some devout book that may be matter for meditation. And when it is finished, all shall remain praying in silence until the hour is over…” 43 . If we had no testimony to the contrary, we would believe that John of the Cross had observed what the rule prescribed to the letter and with exemplary scrupulousness. However, his subjects recount how he would go out into the countryside to pray and had them do the same, and they did so with great devotion and quiet. Thus the aforementioned freedom of spirit of Fray Juan is shown: he safeguards prayer in common, but interprets broadly the place in which it was to be made. He was also supremely free in his practice of charity. That is why in the first precaution against the world he advises: “toward all persons have equality of love and equality of forgetfulness” 44 , and he certainly gave proof of it. Thus, for example, when María de la Cruz 45 —a Discalced Carmelite nun whom the saint held in great esteem—fell ill, without caring about ‘what people would say,’ Fray Juan “divided the poor food they gave him in the convent of Granada and sent some of it” to the monastery of the Discalced nuns, something the sick nun prized and kept as a relic and as a thing come from heaven. Likewise, they recount that a very needy old woman usually came to the door of the convent to ask for food and that, if she ever failed to come, he would send two religious to find out why and to take her whatever she needed 46 . One more example: when Fray Juan de la Cruz was prior of Granada, contrary to what some might think of as ‘favoritism,’ he did not hesitate to call his brother Francisco de Yepes, an expert in masonry, to give him some work; he paid his travel expenses, and Francisco lived with them for some months in the convent 47 . For St. John of the Cross was one of those men capable of giving things that no one requires and of abstaining from things that no one forbids 48 . Even more admirable is the indifference and detachment the saint displays when, at the General Chapter of the Discalced in Madrid (1591), even though he was the first general definitor (what for us would be vicar general), “they afflicted him greatly” 49 because John of the Cross expressed himself about the matters being dealt with in the Chapter 50 “in the way he always did, not like some who in the conclave, before Doria—the superior—, applauded his decrees and outside murmured against them” 51 . For he greatly lamented that “in chapters no one objects, but everything is granted and they go along with it, each one only looking to get his own bite; whereby the common good suffers gravely and the vice of ambition is bred, [and he said that this] had to be denounced, without fraternal correction, as a pernicious vice opposed to the universal good” 52 . In accordance with this, and rather than betray his conscience, he spoke out with great vehemence, for he had nothing to do with the “law of whim that guides many ignorant men who pride themselves on being clever” (as the Quixote says). This earned him, at that very chapter, being given a patent to go to Mexico and being left without office. So it was that, in view of preparing his departure for the Indies 53 , he went off to the solitude of La Peñuela. Thus was fulfilled the fervent petition he had so often made to God: “I only desire that death find me in a remote place, far from all dealings with men, without brothers in the habit to direct; without joys to console me, and tormented by every kind of sorrow and pain. I have wanted God to test me as a servant, after He has tested in labor the tenacity of my character; I have wanted Him to visit me in sickness, as He has tried me in health and strength; I have wanted Him to try me with disgrace, as He has done with the good name I have had before my enemies. Deign, Lord, to crown with martyrdom the head of Your unworthy servant” 54 . ▪ Lordship over the world Our Proper Law says that our religious are to exercise lordship over the world in two ways: one of them, collaborating with the world of creation through work and with the world of redemption through the apostolate 55 . St. John of the Cross was tireless in his labor, for he was a man skilled in many fields. His spiritual work of directing souls, his handling of the pen, his gifts for government, his skill in prose and art, did not cancel him out in other areas such as material works, laying floors, putting up partition walls, etc. Thus, for example, when he was already Definitor General, we can say that he built the ‘generalate house’—even while entangled in a thousand concerns of government. For he himself took charge of drawing up the plans, which included the present church and the square cloister. Pablo de Santa María, an eyewitness, recounts: “Father Fray Juan de la Cruz was very affable and cheerful with everyone, and austere and penitent with himself; and in the harshest part of winter and with much snow he went with nothing on his feet to the quarry where the stone was extracted, to be overseer of the laborers, and with it snowing and hailing on his uncovered bald head, he seemed to set everyone on fire. And many days, being of advanced age, he ate at one in the afternoon having had no breakfast but the Most Blessed Sacrament, so that he seemed more of bronze than of flesh” 56 . Another of the brothers employed in this work also affirms that when they went to work in the morning they already had their tools prepared (laid out), and it was as if someone had gotten their work ahead for them and they had gained half a day. But he was also a man lavish in his apostolates: now with the nuns, now with families, now with the children he catechized, now with the gentlemen, now with the young people in the colleges where he was, now with those he met in his path in the street, now with all kinds of clerics who came to consult him. Likewise, when John of the Cross was at the College of Baeza, in order to be able to attend fully to the people who came to confession, he changed the timetable so that they made the two hours of prayer early in the morning, in order to be free and attend to the people throughout the day. Another of the ways of exercising lordship over the world, our Proper Law affirms, is “by rejecting the world, whether out of loyalty to the world itself, which must be held as a means and not as an end, or out of loyalty to God, resisting the concupiscences, temptations and sins of the world; being independent in the face of the maxims, mockery and persecutions of the world, depending only on our upright conscience illuminated by faith; ready for martyrdom out of loyalty to God, which constitutes the full and total rejection of the evil world” 57 . When John of the Cross was prior in Granada, the vicar provincial, Diego de la Trinidad, turned up there and began to pressure and pester Fray Juan, telling him that as superior he had to visit the authorities of the city, principally the president and judges of the Audiencia. And he said this, reproaching him that “if he did not visit the important people of the city, he could not sustain his convent.” Obedience calls. Fray Juan calls Jerónimo de la Cruz and tells him: “Let your reverence take your cloak, for they say we must make visits.” They go down to the city and make their visit to the president of the Audiencia, during which Fray Juan tells him that if they had not visited them before, it was in order to fulfill the obligation of religious recollection. The president answered them that they should go on fulfilling their duty to our Lord in that way, and that in fact they themselves hardly had time to rest, giving them to understand that they were not at fault for not visiting them. The moral: the saint draws it immediately, for “on leaving, he said to me [says Fray Jerónimo de la Cruz]: ‘Our Lord has made it clear to us that He does not want us to fulfill courtesies with men in the world, since there are so many who take care of that, but to be with His Majesty alone.’ And we went straight back to the convent. And I do not remember seeing him make another courtesy visit.” That is to say, he did it once, as the superior commanded him, but against all human respect he did not do it again. We have already mentioned the vexations Fray Juan de la Cruz suffered for being faithful to his vocation as a Discalced Carmelite, and how much he had to endure to remain free and independent in the face of the maxims, mockery and persecutions of the world, not caring that because of this he was left without office or that his honor was trampled by the most infamous persecution. But we have not said with what eagerness St. John of the Cross very ordinarily told his religious “that the honors of the world were to be fled like the devil, because they were all full of poison” 58 . And at the same time as he told them this, he gave them an example of it, for “he was a great enemy of outward show and of being considered a saint, nor did he like others to make such a demonstration.” Proof of this was when Diego Evangelista 59 brought a defamatory process against the saint to discredit him, going as far as the convents to make inquiries—wanting to prove that he had had base habits 60 —and becoming very angry when he could not get to hear what he wanted. Many religious wrote to Fray Juan de la Cruz urging him to complain to the vicar general and the definitory about those inquiries and to give an account of himself, but the saint ‘answered all with great serenity that he was a worm, and that therefore no one did him any wrong, and that whatever his Creator disposed in his regard, it was for him to embrace it for His love and nothing else’ 61 . Such was the spiritual nakedness of Fray Juan de la Cruz that this same man who, being at prayer, in answer to Christ’s question: ‘ Fray Juan, ask Me for whatever you wish, and I will grant it to you, for this service you have done Me ’ 62 , is capable of answering: ‘Lord, what I want You to give me is trials to suffer for You, and that I be despised and held of little account’; is the same who later writes with great nobility of soul: “Love greatly those who contradict you and do not love you, for in this way love is begotten in the breast where there is none, as God does with us, who loves so that we may love Him by means of the love He has for us” 63 . “That is to have a princely spirit ; [that] is to direct the soul toward great acts… [that] is to be concerned with great things… it is to accomplish great works in every virtue. [That] is to be noble” 64 . “For to love is to labor to strip and denude oneself for God of all that is not God” 65 . In such a way that we do not care at all about the esteem and good opinion of men, about bodily health and strength, about the posts or offices that may be given to us or taken from us, about the prosperous or adverse events that may befall us, about dying young or old 66 . “Whence it is clearly seen that not only must the soul go unencumbered of everything that comes from the side of creatures, but also of everything that comes from the side of its spirit it must walk dispossessed and annihilated” 67 . For in order to conquer freedom of spirit, one must work so that the heart is not held back by any human thing 68 . Since, as the Mystical Doctor writes: When you dwell upon something, you cease to cast yourself upon the all. For to come wholly to the all you must deny yourself wholly in all. And when you come to possess it wholly, you must possess it wanting nothing. For if you wish to have something in all, you do not have your treasure purely in God 69 . In this sense the saint affirms with complete conviction: “happy the soul that loves, for it holds God as its prisoner, surrendered to all that it may wish” 70 ; for that is why he says: when you come to possess it wholly, you must possess it wanting nothing . That is why our Constitutions exhort us in a fatherly way “to love all that God wants us to love, without being slaves of our affections for creatures, that is, to love without chaining ourselves, to possess without being held captive, to use without selfish enjoyment, to preserve complete independence, to seek in all and through all the glory of God” 71 . 2. The teaching of St. John of the Cross on freedom of spirit We could almost say that the teaching of St. John of the Cross consists in disposing the soul to conquer freedom of spirit and to consolidate it therein. Without attempting in the least to make an exhaustive analysis of his very abundant doctrine, we give here only a few brushstrokes that we consider of great help so that the heart may not go about in base things 72 and may rise to the summit of the Mount of perfection, where the saint says: “Here there is no longer any path, for for the just man there is no law” 73 . Let us begin by saying that this great Master of the faith teaches that “the soul will not be able to reach the true freedom of spirit which is attained in its divine union” 74 if it submits to other things that are not God and His Divine Will, that is, if it lives attached. And the saint insists on this: “the soul that has attachment to anything…, will not reach the freedom of divine union” 75 . Simply “because slavery can have no part with freedom, which cannot dwell in a heart subject to desires, because that is the heart of a slave, but in a free heart, because it is the heart of a son” 76 . From this it follows: a) That if there is not this true evangelical renunciation—detachment from creatures—neither is there any setting out on the way toward union with God. For no one will find the new life if he is not willing to walk in the denial of himself. But if one goes by the way of denying and losing one’s own life, following the Incarnate Word, then one will not only find true life, but will enjoy many benefits that are drawn from denial: interior peace, poverty of spirit, and the hundredfold of true possession of God and of all that one has previously denied oneself. It is here that the dark nights, the active and passive purifications through which we must pass 77 , take on their full meaning, because it is they that prepare us “to remain in the supreme nakedness and freedom of spirit that are required in order to reach divine union” 78 . b) Every attachment—whatever it may be—implies slavery. This is contrary to the doctrine of Christ, for, as we have already said: for freedom Christ has set us free 79 . The condition, then, for arriving at true freedom of spirit is to overcome the slavery to which the appetites subject whoever lets himself be guided by them. “For until the appetites are lulled to sleep by mortification in sensuality, and sensuality itself is at rest from them, so that it wages no war on the spirit, the soul does not go forth into true freedom, to enjoy union with its Beloved” 80 . And why do we say that it is slavery? The Mystical Doctor explains it: because “the affection and attachment that the soul has for the creature makes the soul equal to the creature, and the greater the affection, the more it makes it equal and similar, because love creates likeness between the one who loves and what is loved. […] And so, he who loves a creature remains as low as that creature, and in a certain way lower; because love not only makes equal, but even subjects the lover to what he loves. And hence it is that, by the very fact that the soul loves something, it becomes incapable of pure union with God and of transformation in Him” 81 . St. John of the Cross gives us examples so as to make us see it even more clearly, saying: “All the beauty of creatures, compared with the infinite beauty of God, is supreme ugliness […]. And so the soul that is attached to the beauty of any creature is supremely ugly before God; and therefore this ugly soul will not be able to be transformed into the beauty that is God. And all the grace and charm of creatures, compared with the grace of God, is supreme gracelessness and supreme insipidity; and therefore the soul that is captivated by the graces and charm of creatures is supremely graceless and insipid in the eyes of God. And all the goodness of the creatures of the world, compared with the infinite goodness of God, can be called wickedness. […] therefore the soul that sets its heart on the goods of the world is supremely wicked before God. And all the wisdom of the world and human skill , compared with the infinite wisdom of God, is pure and supreme ignorance. […] Therefore every soul that would make much of all its knowledge and skill in order to come to be united with the wisdom of God is supremely ignorant before God, and will remain very far from it. And all the lordship and freedom of the world , compared with the freedom and lordship of the spirit of God, is supreme slavery, anguish and captivity. Therefore the soul that falls in love with positions of superiority, or other such offices, and with the liberties of its appetite, is held and treated before God not as a son, but as a base slave and captive, for not having wished to take up His holy doctrine, in which He teaches us that whoever would be greater, let him be lesser, and whoever would be lesser, let him be the greater 82 . And all the delights and sweetness of the will in all the things of the world, compared with all the delights that God is, are supreme pain, torment and bitterness. And so he who sets his heart on them is held before God as worthy of supreme pain, torment and bitterness. All the riches and glory of all created things , compared with the riches that God is, are supreme poverty and misery. And so the soul that loves and possesses them is supremely poor and miserable before God” 83 . With this the saint wants to make us see that “the appetites and gratifications, as with snares, ensnare the soul and hold it back [so] that it does not go forth from itself into the freedom of the love of God” 84 . But also that the nights, although they darken the spirit and the senses, do so only to give it light on all things; and although the night humbles a person and makes him miserable, it is only to exalt and raise him up; and although it impoverishes him and empties him of all possession and natural affection, it is only so that he may divinely reach out to enjoy and taste all things above and below, being, with freedom of spirit, universal in all 85 . c) The conquest of this freedom is a source of lordship over all things. It is worth noting how the saint contrasts this lordship with that of any kingdom or lordship of the world when he says that temporal lordship and temporal freedom “before God are neither kingdom nor freedom” 86 . That is why the radicalness of the freedom that our Proper Law and St. John of the Cross propose to us is that of interior freedom, since that is the spirit of our Institute: “to live fully the freedom of the children of God” 87 . “From the negative point of view, it is liberation from sin and from the appetites that enslave man. Positively, it is the capacity for self-mastery and decision in view of one’s own personal fulfillment, which obviously takes place in communion with God, for which man has been created and positively ordered. On it the Mystical Doctor bases freedom of spirit, making it coincide with divine union” 88 . Indeed, at the summit of the Mount of perfection, where this union is attained, he writes these significant words, which our Proper Law quotes in the paragraph where it speaks of freedom: “Here there is no longer any path, for for the just man there is no law” 89 . That is to say, this freedom is not only “ libertas a malo ,” but fundamentally “ libertas ad bonum .” It is to pass from the slavery of sin to the service of God, from the old man to the new. Although it is defined as the passage from one servitude to another 90 , paradoxically true freedom lies in it 91 . That is why it is not surprising that our Proper Law has included martyrdom when speaking about lordship and inviting us to be “ready for martyrdom out of loyalty to God, which constitutes the full and total rejection of the evil world” 92 ; and when it affirms immediately afterward that “the greatest grace that God can grant to our tiny Religious Family is persecution” 93 . For the soul that knows itself called to be deiform 94 must not fear to walk along the narrow path that leads to union with God, for which it is necessary to go “naked of everything, wanting nothing” 95 , which consists, says St. John of the Cross, in “knowing how to deny oneself in earnest, outwardly and inwardly, giving oneself to suffering for Christ and annihilating oneself in everything, because by exercising oneself in this, all the rest and more than that is accomplished and found in it. And if there is a failing in this exercise, which is the sum and the root of the virtues, all those other ways are beating about the bush and making no progress , even if one has considerations and communications as lofty as the angels’” 96 . That is why the Constitutions , quoting the Mystic of Fontiveros, urge us vividly to the “nothing, nothing, even to leaving one’s skin and all the rest for Christ” 97 . Therefore the desire of that martyr who said must grow to giant proportions in our breast: “Let fire, the cross, packs of wild beasts, lacerations, amputations, the wrenching of bones, the severing of limbs, the crushing of my whole body, all the cruel torments of the devil come upon me, provided only that this serves me to attain Christ” 98 . That is to say, one must know how to renounce, how to sacrifice whatever must be sacrificed, but not compromise in anything our march toward the conquest of freedom. Rather, one must truly resolve to walk along “the way of perfection in all humility and detachment within and without, not with a childish spirit, but with a robust will” 99 . Putting all one’s effort into denying oneself, “knowing that this is to follow Christ” 100 , and “if at any time anyone, whether a superior or anyone else,” warns the Master of the faith, “should urge upon you some lax doctrine, even if he confirms it with miracles, do not believe or embrace it; but rather more penance and more detachment from all things; and do not seek Christ without the Cross” 101 . That is to be “God’s unconditional ones” 102 ; that is “to prefer nothing to His love” 103 . And that, and no other, “must be the priestly attitude of every member of our small Religious Family. […] An attitude in which one must live permanently, without diminutions or retractions, without reservations or conditions, without subterfuges or delays, without retreats or slowness. As much in the commitments of the inner life as in high historical undertakings: [because] whoever is not capable of setting fire to his ships when he lands is not capable of building empires” 104 . In this way, the path of freedom is the path of “nothing” that leads to the all: “to come to possess everything, desire to possess nothing in anything” 105 . After renouncing all things, the soul has them all with it and enjoys them with freedom of spirit: “Stripped of every manner of natural affection,” it can now “commune freely, with breadth of spirit, with divine Wisdom, in which, through its purity, it tastes all the savors of all things with a certain eminence of excellence” 106 . And all this without the sensitive part coming to hinder it 107 . The saint expresses this very beautifully in his Canticle , when the Bride (who is the soul) has now attained union with the Divine Bridegroom and hears His voice without anyone disturbing her, in breadth of spirit: “free of all temporal disturbances and changes, and stripped and purged of the imperfections, hardships and mists both of sense and of spirit, she feels a new springtime in freedom and breadth and joy of spirit” 108 . That is why this “happy freedom, desired by all” 109 of which we have been speaking “is a good that contains within itself all the goods of the world; it is a great lordship” 110 . To attain it and live it in fullness is our program. So that what is proper to the members of the Institute of the Incarnate Word is to subject themselves to Christ, to His Divine Will, because in this lies true freedom and the fullness of our happiness; and we want to do so following the path that Christ Himself followed, which was none other than that of the cross. In such a way that, even if they made us lords of all the created things of this world, and even if they threatened us with the loss of bodily life 111 , and all our works came to nothing, we must have the manliness to make the “formal decision not to make pacts, not to compromise, not to capitulate, not to negotiate, not to concede, nor to strike deals with the spirit of the world” 112 , since otherwise we would be failing God and would ourselves suffer great slavery and misery. The watchword is simple: “Show by the depth of your convictions and by the consistency of your actions that Jesus Christ is our contemporary” 113 . How? By removing from oneself “totally whatever is repugnant to and does not conform with the divine will” 114 , until one is “dissolved into nothing” 115 , until one becomes “fools for Christ” 116 , which in the language of St. John of the Cross is the fullest “freedom of spirit” 117 . They will drag us here and there, they will laugh at us and take us for dull, backward and even feeble-minded; nevertheless, we must know how to bless those who curse us and laugh along with those who laugh at us and mock us, like children who do not understand; and even when we are beaten, persecuted and martyred, we must give thanks to God who found us worthy 118 . Understood in this way, to be God’s unconditional ones is to make effective the “offering of greater worth” 119 that we make each year in the Spiritual Exercises. “It is to be noble. It is to be men of heart. Men who have something for themselves and for others. They are those born to command. They are those capable of punishing themselves and of punishing. They are those who have set a style in their conduct. They are those who ask not for freedom but for hierarchy. They are those who set themselves laws and keep them… They are those who hold honor as dear as life. Those who, because they possess themselves, can give themselves. They are those who know at every instant the things for which one must die. Those capable of giving things that no one requires and of abstaining from things that no one forbids. They are those who always consider themselves beginners: […] never ceasing to aspire to a holier and more perfect life, never stopping” 120 . And for a more complete idea of freedom of spirit, let us conclude with those words that St. John of the Cross places on the lips of God the Father: “ behold my Son, subject to me and subjected by my love, and afflicted ” 121 ; that is the image of true freedom. For so great and sublime a conquest we are not alone; we count on the extraordinary help of the Most Blessed Virgin Mary, because no one more than she “is totally oriented toward God, and the closer we draw to her, the more intimately she unites us to Him” 122 . “I personally believe,” said St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort, “that no one can attain an intimate union with Our Lord and a perfect fidelity to the Holy Spirit without a very close union with the Most Blessed Virgin and a true dependence on her help” 123 . That is why he recommended that we renew our consecration to Mary every day. “And the more you repeat it,” he said, “the sooner you will be sanctified and will arrive at union with Jesus Christ. A union that always follows union with Mary, since the spirit of Mary is the spirit of Jesus” 124 . May the Incarnate Word, who found His freedom in letting Himself be enclosed in the womb of Most Holy Mary, find us each day “more the slaves” of so very sweet a Mother. The ministry of divine mercy

“The ministry of divine mercy” 1 God reconciled us to Himself through Christ and entrusted to us the ministry of reconciliation 2 . The words of the Apostle are especially challenging to us, to whom, as priests, belongs the sublime exercise of the ministry of divine mercy. “Never as in this time has man had such need of mercy,” St. John Paul the Great said already in the ’80s. It is in this same sense that Pope Francis reminded us in his Apostolic Letter Misericordia et misera : “The Sacrament of Reconciliation needs to find again its central place in Christian life; for this, priests are needed who place their lives at the service of the ministry of reconciliation 3 , so that no one who has sincerely repented may be prevented from approaching the love of the Father, who awaits his return, and so that all may be offered the possibility of experiencing the liberating power of forgiveness” 4 . That is why to speak of the priesthood implies speaking of the care of souls, and to speak of priests is to speak of men who by the sacrament of Orders have been called to be “living and effective signs of the mercy of God” 5 , knowing themselves to be “the first to be forgiven” 6 . 1. The assiduous pastoral practice of confession 7 As members of the Institute of the Incarnate Word we are called in a particular way to evangelize the culture. “But how does one evangelize a culture? How does one help the work of the Holy Spirit among men? One begins by evangelizing people , since culture is produced by people and is forged by the quality of their relationships with one another and with God. Thus, the first step is to evangelize, as Jesus did, calling each one by name to conversion ” 8 . A conversion that implies the vital need to be united to Christ through an intense Eucharistic life and to be continually renewed through the reception of the sacrament of Reconciliation. Understood in this way, the mission of the Institute is the same as that of the Church, that is, “to lead men to conversion to God, to ‘full and sincere adherence to Christ and His Gospel through faith’ 9 , which must tend toward the worthy reception of the sacraments” 10 . From which it follows that the reception of the sacrament of Confession constitutes a special help—or, better said, an indispensable one—when it comes to evangelizing the culture. Indeed, we are convinced that “mercy is indispensable for the spiritual progress of each soul, as well as for human, civil and social progress” 11 , and therefore we consider that our mission is effective if, as John Paul II said, it “moves to conversion, that is, to a return to the truth and to the friendship of God, those who had lost faith and grace through sin; if it calls routine Christians to a more perfect life; if it sets souls on fire; if it convinces people to live the beatitudes; if it awakens priestly and religious vocations” 12 . It is striking that we should have to remind ourselves and reaffirm to ourselves and to others these truths in our time, when it often seems that a veil is drawn over the founding and fundamental mission of the Church in the world. For its part, the apostolate of the confessional is explicitly highlighted by our Proper Law in a forceful way when it says: “our priests and the whole Institute of the Incarnate Word should be known for the assiduous pastoral practice of confession […] Let people know that everywhere there are priests of our Religious Family, they will always be able to find a ‘spiritual father’” 13 . The Exhortation Reconciliatio et Paenitentia , written by the Spiritual Father of our Religious Family, maintains that “the Son of God, coming as the Lamb who takes away and takes upon Himself the sin of the world 14 , appears as the one who has the power both to judge 15 and to forgive sins 16 , and who has come not to condemn, but to forgive and save 17 ” 18 . And this power that Jesus has to forgive sins He conferred on the Apostles and their successors, responsible for continuing His work of evangelization and redemption. From this the greatness of the figure of the minister of Penance becomes evident, who must act in Persona Christi as “brother of man 19 , merciful high priest, faithful and compassionate 20 , shepherd determined to seek the lost sheep 21 , physician who heals and comforts 22 , sole master who teaches the truth and points out the ways of God 23 , judge of the living and the dead 24 , who judges according to the truth and not according to appearances 25 ” 26 . Now, the assiduous pastoral practice of Confession requires on our part great pastoral charity and great mercy in order to bring relief to the souls entrusted to our care. Confession is often spoken of as the “tribunal of penance,” and that is not wrong, because Penance has something of a tribunal about it, and the priest is the judge. But Penance is much more than that. “Unlike purely human tribunals, it is more an instrument of mercy than an instrument of justice. That is why it is also called the sacrament of Reconciliation. In absolving, the priest frees the penitent from the sin that held him prisoner. In the confessional, besides being judges, we must be fathers, teachers, physicians—in a word, true shepherds of the little sheep placed at our feet. We must consider the circumstances, background and psychology of the penitent; have the heart of a father, of the good Samaritan who cauterizes the wounds inflicted by the robbers. If God has waited, showing infinite patience, by what right do we, who are also sinners just like the one before us, flare up at the penitent, or treat him with bitterness of spirit?” 27 . And where does a priest learn mercy? He learns it from the deep conviction that God did not treat us as we deserved 28 , said Venerable Archbishop Fulton Sheen. The exercise of the sublime office of hearing confessions takes on for us, priests of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, certain particular features that our Proper Law especially underlines, echoing the abundant treasure of the Magisterium of the Church, and which it is always fitting to keep in mind if we do not want to betray our identity and mission in the Mystical Body of the Church. Let us pay attention: “The maximum availability of priests for confession must be something characteristic of our parishes, also making sure that there are always one or more confessors during Holy Mass. Other priests from outside the parish should also be invited to hear confessions, and where possible and fitting, a permanent confession center should be set up” 29 . Our Proper Law repeats something very similar elsewhere, declaring that the “apostolate toward sinners will be exercised in a particular way in the administration of the sacrament of reconciliation, being always available at any moment to hear confessions” 30 . This maximum availability asks of us that we be always available for so high a ministry, and not only during “confession hours.” But it is also true that this availability must be made visible to people. One of the ways in which this availability on the part of IVE priests to hear confessions can be made visible to souls is what St. Manuel González called ‘early-morning worship’: “A church open from very early, at least an hour before the work of the town begins, with a priest who is the first to come in and the last to leave, and who waits seated in the confessional, and this in a constant and fixed way , is a church that cannot be long in seeing itself well attended.[…] A priest seated in his confessional from before sunrise, determined not to tire or grow bored with the solitude, will not be long in seeing Samaritan women and men arrive to ask him for the water that springs up to eternal life” 31 . “How are we to foster among our parishioners, especially busy ones, daily meditation at a fixed time, frequent confession and spiritual direction, if we do not give them, at a fixed and early hour, an open church and Tabernacle and a confessor at their disposal?” 32 . A holy suggestion to keep in mind both in the parishes of the most remote villages and in those set in the great cities. This disposition is also shown when it comes to attending to the sick promptly (without delay), which so often calls for the sacrament of divine mercy. “Illness makes it possible for many sick people to approach the Sacraments for the first time; that is why our solicitude will be very important, working with their family, and especially when the family opposes the Sacraments of Penance and Anointing for fear of the fright this may cause the patient” 33 . It is an act of true love to comfort the sick with the sacraments, especially Confession, the Anointing of the sick, and the viaticum of the Eucharist—the last, before they see God beyond the sacramental signs. That is why the Polish Pope insistently recommended to priests: “Always be diligent and fervent in the administration of these sacraments of mercy, sparing neither energy nor time, deeply aware that ‘the Church lives an authentic life when she professes and proclaims mercy—the most stupendous attribute of the Creator and of the Redeemer—and when she brings people close to the sources of the Savior’s mercy, of which she is the trustee and dispenser’ 34 ” 35 . Moreover, on the occasion of popular missions, one must not be remiss in dedicating one day of the mission to be “a penitential day, on which confessions are heard all day long . Strictly speaking, it is ideal for one missionary father always to remain at the mission center and for the people to know that he is at their disposal from the first day of the mission” 36 . Persuaded of the importance of the life of grace and of the immense value of the sacrament of confession, we can affirm that most of our pastoral activities should include this availability for confession. We have learned this countless times from the beginning: for example, alongside our processions there were always priests with the purple stole, praying the rosary, whose mere presence was a silent but eloquent call to reconciliation with God for the people taking part in or watching the procession; the same happens in our camps, in gatherings with young people, with families, in the oratories, where there must never be lacking the priest who waits patiently, ready to hear confessions. Given the special circumstances we are going through because of the pandemic, how edifying and praiseworthy has been the example of several of our members who, even at the risk of becoming infected themselves, with all courage and priestly spirit went to the sick to hear their confession and bring them the last sacraments. That is the true mettle of a priest of the Incarnate Word! One who “does not flinch at any difficulty, nor shrink back before any obstacle!” 37 . From what has been said so far we can conclude that every priest of the Institute must devote a generous part of his time to the ministry of the sacrament of Penance—which the grace of God will make fruitful—and to instructing souls about the value and importance of this sacrament for the Christian life; which brings us to the second characteristic of the exercise of this ministry highlighted in the documents of our Institute. “It seems very fitting that priests preach about the marvelous benefits of frequent confession” 38 . In this regard the Directory of Preaching of the Word specifies—following the teachings of St. Alphonsus Maria de Liguori 39 —that when choosing the subject matter of preaching, the priests of the Institute must “take care to choose those that in a special way move people to abhor sin and to love God” 40 ; “… the love Jesus Christ has for us, the love we owe Him, and the trust we must always have in His mercy when we want to amend our lives” 41 ; “… the means of remaining in the grace of God, such as fleeing dangerous occasions and bad company, frequenting the sacraments…” 42 ; “… bad confessions made by concealing sins out of shame” 43 , etc. That is why the Constitutions point out that people (including our own members, and especially those in formation) must be helped to “discover the beauty and joy of the sacrament of penance, in a world that has lost the sense of sin and of divine mercy” 44 . “Striving to possess the due knowledge and keeping up to date in moral questions ” 45 . For the members of the Institute “knowledge of the due moral science is indispensable ” 46 , and this on a twofold account: both for exercising the ministry of reconciliation 47 and also “for fulfilling the purpose of our Institute of evangelizing cultures, which presupposes ordering them so that they help man to attain his end, and therefore a discernment of their morality, since morality is the transcendental relation of what is human toward the ultimate end” 48 . That is why all “priests must have knowledge of spiritual theology and must exercise themselves in the discernment of spirits” 49 . For priests are “educators in the faith, formers of consciences, guides of souls, so as to enable each Christian to develop his personal vocation” 50 ; that is why it is fitting, and very much so , to prepare oneself well—remotely and proximately—for the administration of the sacrament of Confession. In Reconciliatio et Paenitentia we read that for the effective fulfillment of the ministry of Confession the priest “must also have a serious and careful preparation, not fragmentary but integral and harmonious , in the various branches of theology, in pedagogy and in psychology, in the methodology of dialogue and, above all, in a living and communicative knowledge of the Word of God. But it is even more necessary that he live an intense and genuine spiritual life. In order to guide others along the path of Christian perfection, the minister of Penance must first travel this path himself and, more by deeds than by long speeches , give proof of real experience of lived prayer, of the practice of the theological and moral evangelical virtues, of faithful obedience to the will of God, of love for the Church and of docility to her Magisterium” 51 . Of the great confessor St. Leopold Mandić it is said that “he had taken very seriously his preparation for carrying out so delicate a ministry, not only by studying thoroughly dogmatic theology, law, moral theology, ascetical and mystical theology during the period of his studies prior to the priesthood, but afterward he continued to apply himself very seriously to this kind of study throughout his whole life. His preferred authors were St. Augustine, St. Thomas and St. Alphonsus Maria de Liguori; along with them he always had at hand other modern authors […]. He also attached great importance to the encyclicals of the Popes, since, as he used to say, in them one finds the easiest and surest way to resolve the most difficult questions, even from the point of view of moral casuistry” 52 . It is particularly recommended to us that, in our effort to acquire knowledge and exercise ourselves in the discernment of spirits, prayer, the study of Sacred Scripture, of the writings of the Fathers, of the great Theologians and of the Mystics, one’s own experience of the spiritual life, as well as familiarity with and deep knowledge of the Rules for the discernment of spirits of St. Ignatius of Loyola 53 , should all occupy a preponderant place. “Do not cease to study and pray, so as to be equal to the ministry of reconciling man with God, a faculty so unheard-of that it made people exclaim in astonishment: Who can forgive sins but God alone? ” 54 . Finally, and above all, following the example of Christ, we must exercise this precious ministry of Confession showing a heart of true mercy 55 . “The priest has to live a truly heroic mercy. […] A heroic mercy that must be shown in a particular way in the exercise of that great sacrament of mercy which is confession, which involves hours and hours and is very tiring. At some point it can become a boring thing for the priest who for so many years has been hearing more or less the same things, give or take, with some small addition. One must have that disposition which only a merciful heart gives” 56 . St. Alphonsus, Patron of confessors, merited this title because from the first years of his priesthood he heard a great many confessions, above all during spiritual exercises and popular missions, acquiring in this field an incomparable experience. In his Praxis confessarii he indicates the conditions for the exercise of this ars artium —as he liked to define it, following the example of St. Gregory the Great—to be fruitful: “The confessor cannot consider himself satisfied with a holiness limited to the mere state of grace, but must feel himself filled with charity, meekness and prudence” 57 . “Thanks to these virtues,” commented St. John Paul II, “the confessor will be able to become a minister of divine charity, exercising the far from easy task of father, physician, teacher and judge. As a father , he will welcome penitents with sincere love, showing greater understanding to those who have sinned more, and then he will send them off with words imbued with mercy, so as to encourage them to return to the path of Christian life 58 . As a physician , he must prudently diagnose the roots of the evil and suggest to the penitent the appropriate therapy, thanks to which he may live in accordance with the dignity and responsibility of a person created in the image of God 59 . As a teacher , he will seek to know the law of God thoroughly, deepening its various aspects through the study of moral theology, so as not to give the penitent personal options, but what the magisterium of the Church authentically teaches 60 . As a judge , finally, he is to practice equity. It is necessary that the priest always judge according to the truth, and not according to appearances, taking care to make the penitent understand that in the fatherly heart of God there is room for him too” 61 . In imitation of the Incarnate Word we must have, in all our pastoral endeavors, that patience and that kindness of which the Lord Himself has left us an example, having come not to judge, but to save 62 . “Like Christ, be uncompromising with evil, but merciful with persons. In whatever difficulties they may have, the faithful must find in your words and in your shepherds’ hearts the echo of the voice of the Redeemer, meek and humble of heart 63 ” 64 , said St. John Paul II. Fulton Sheen tells of a woman who, after thirty years, decided to go to confession. The confessor, a priest who in thirty years had not made his meditation before Mass, barked the following question at her: ‘How is it possible that you have been away from the Church for thirty years?’ To which the woman replied: ‘Because thirty years ago I met a priest just like you.’ “The depth of our compassion is the measure of our apostolic success” 65 , the venerable American archbishop concluded. “Many times the priest is very busy, but he has to learn to occupy himself with the principal things of the ministry, not with accidental or secondary things. Souls need to speak with the priest and need to tell him their concerns, because the priest is also a physician of souls” 66 . Finally, but no less importantly, let us say that if in the recent past, and even more in the present, there is something like a crisis of the sacrament of Confession, we must recognize that among the many factors that may have contributed to this situation, a lack of enthusiasm or availability for the exercise of so demanding and delicate a ministry not infrequently has a negative influence. Therefore, if the pastoral work of the Institute is to be in every sphere “with grit,” enthusiastic and proactive, it must also be so when it comes to carrying out with firmness and conviction the apostolate of the reconciliation of man with God. In this sense, “the sacrament must be celebrated in the best possible way and in the liturgically prescribed forms, so that it may preserve its full character as a celebration of Divine Mercy” 67 . In this sense it is important that the minister fulfill his obligation well. His capacity to welcome, to listen, to dialogue, and his constant availability, are essential elements for the ministry of reconciliation to manifest all its value. The faithful proclamation, never reticent, of the radical demands of the word of God must always be accompanied by great understanding and delicacy, in imitation of Jesus’ manner with sinners” 68 . 2. Personal experience of the sacrament of Reconciliation It has always been the teaching of the Church that through priests is shown the mercy of God, who forgives sins in the sacrament of Penance. And although the administration of the sacrament of forgiveness is “without doubt the most difficult and delicate, the most tiring and demanding, it is also one of the most beautiful and consoling ministries of the Priest” 69 . “Be, therefore,” John Paul II said to priests and religious, “the first to receive this sacrament frequently, with authentic faith and devotion” 70 . For in order to be faithful and to fulfill adequately our ministry of sanctifying, our personal experience of the sacrament of reconciliation, through frequent confession, is indispensable. Since the joyful experience of being forgiven by Christ nourishes the desire to offer His forgiveness to others 71 . That is why, “for our tiny Religious Family the holy sacrament of Reconciliation or Penance occupies a most important place in the spiritual life, so much so that we consider it advisable to receive it weekly” 72 . That has been and continues to be normal practice according to our way of living religious life in the Institute. And our Proper Law exhorts us in a fatherly way to “have devotion to frequent confession” 73 , listing the “many fruits that follow from it: ‘…genuine self-knowledge is increased, Christian humility grows, bad habits are uprooted, spiritual lukewarmness and indolence are resisted, the conscience is purified, the will is strengthened, a salutary direction of consciences is obtained, and grace is increased by virtue of the sacrament’” 74 . That is to say, in the same way that availability is asked for in administering the sacrament of Confession, assiduity in receiving it is also asked of our members, so that Christ may constantly purify our hearts, making His ministers less unworthy of the mysteries they celebrate 75 . It is worth noting that the Liturgy, very aptly, in the Roman Canon calls priests “sinners”: “ To us, also, your sinful servants …” 76 . Priests carry a treasure in earthen vessels 77 . That is why it is important “to protect it and care for it, through daily prayer, through the celebration of Holy Mass and through frequent reception of the sacrament of Penance” 78 , the Spiritual Father of our Religious Family assured us. Our members must never underestimate the importance of the sacrament of Penance, together with that of the Eucharist, for strengthening the soul for the time of trial. “Who does not see that the priest, constituted by God as minister of Christ’s reconciliation, is called to be the first to experience in himself the gift of reconciliation, making it operative in his own life? We are persuaded that it is not possible to propose the message of reconciliation to others if we are not capable of living its saving power in ourselves. In a Church called to renew herself, priests must go before their brothers by their example and their life. From this personal appreciation of the sacrament of penance as the royal road of purification and growth in faith there will also come to you a further appreciation of the immeasurable gift the Lord has given you in choosing you as His priests, to forgive sins in His name” 79 . The priest who is familiar with the Lord in prayer is the one who has the clearest awareness of being a sinner, even if he had never committed a mortal sin in his life. That is why, in his first Letter to Priests for Holy Thursday 1979 , John Paul II insisted to them: “To be converted means to return to the very grace of our vocation, to meditate on the immense goodness and infinite love of Christ, who has addressed each one of us and, calling us by name, has said: Follow me . To be converted means to give an account at every moment of our service, of our zeal, of our fidelity, before the Lord of our hearts, so that we may be ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God 80 . To be converted means also to give an account of our negligences and sins, of our cowardice, of our lack of faith and hope, of thinking only ‘in a human way’ and not ‘in a divine way’.” The priestly vocation is a special vocation to holiness, so that, acting in the person of Christ, priests may sanctify others. Thus, then, as ministers of the sacraments, priests bring the gift of salvation to the people of God and nourish them with the divine life that they themselves have received from Christ. Now, the challenge of presenting Christ demands constant conversion. “The priest,” says Fulton Sheen, “who has been crucified and has borne his passion with patience will always be a merciful priest. If outside one confessional on a Saturday there is a long line of penitents and at the other confessional there are one or two penitents, it is time for that priest [at the latter confessional] to ask himself some questions. Holiness attracts penitents. Because the attraction of such priests is that of Christ” 81 . If for all the members of the Institute it will always be of enormous spiritual benefit to consider oneself a sinner, how much more so for the ministers of the sacred mysteries, who need continual conversion. St. Joseph Cafasso said: “To be an exemplary priest, the judgment of the world is not enough. A priest can be reputed a saint and not be one before God. A third of the virtues proper to a cleric are enough for him to be considered a saint, but the Lord does not recognize him as such unless he strives with all his strength to flee not only mortal sin, but also venial fault and the appearance of guilt” 82 . It is this clear awareness that we are sinners that must lead His ministers to be men of mercy. With great realism the venerable American archbishop wrote: “Every time his knees bend in confession, the priest admits that he has had something to do with the Crucifixion of our Lord, and when his feet move, like worms, coming out from beneath the curtain of the confessional, he rises from the dead. God did not choose angels to be His priest-victims, because they would not have understood what human weakness is. He chose instead fragile vessels who know, in their very weakness, the hope of being strong again that burns in the heart of a believer. In hearing the confessions of others, a priest sees more empty tombs than those the sun of the First Easter lit up in Jerusalem. When he himself goes to confession, his spirit feels the sweet indifference that comes from faith. If I die, I shall be with Christ; if I live, Christ will be with me ” 83 . “There are priests,” said St. Joseph Cafasso, “who go to confession, when they can, in hiding, in secret: they seem afraid that people will know they go to confession. Why so much mystery on our part when we go to confession? Will the faithful perhaps cease to esteem us if they see us frequenting such a sacrament?” 84 . Quite the contrary, the saint considered it a good example for people to see a priest go to confession. The vast majority of the members of the Institute have the grace of living with another priest of the Institute or at least near others. Whatever the case, our Proper Law emphasizes that the “confession of the members to one another is an excellent manifestation of the exquisite charity that must reign in the community” 85 , and points out that “every priest of the Institute of the Incarnate Word should have as an absolute apostolic priority attention and availability toward his brothers in religious life. That is why fostering visits—especially to those who are farthest away and most isolated—and being generous with one’s own time toward one’s brothers in the priesthood and religious life is one of the clearest manifestations of the exquisite charity that our Family wants to live” 86 . These visits to the priests who are farthest away, even if they involve long hours of travel only to be there for an hour or two and then set out again on the journey back, are something we have grown up seeing our elders do, and they should not be lost; rather, it is a precious example that we priests of the Institute should pass on to future generations. In a word: let us love this sacrament, let us cooperate through our availability in giving it the central place in Christian life that the Holy Father asks of us, and let us receive it often ourselves. * * * * * Let us conclude with the words of Reconciliatio et paenitentia , which, although written 36 years ago now, remains as relevant as it was then: “ Be all of one mind…, not returning evil for evil…, be zealous for what is good 87 . […] For it is better to suffer for doing good, if such is the will of God, than for doing evil 88 . This watchword is imbued with the words Peter had heard from Jesus Himself, and with ideas that were part of His joyful good news : the new commandment of mutual love; the desire for and commitment to unity; the beatitudes of mercy and of patience in persecution for the sake of justice; returning good for evil; the forgiveness of offenses; love of enemies. In these words and ideas is the original and transcendent synthesis of Christian ethics or, better and more profoundly, of the spirituality of the New Covenant in Jesus Christ” 89 . We entrust to the Father, rich in mercy; to the Son of God, made man as our redeemer and reconciler; and to the Holy Spirit, source of unity and peace, the pastoral ministry of reconciliation that the Institute carries out throughout the world, and which is so intrinsically united to our specific end. May Most Holy Mary, in whom the reconciliation of man with God was accomplished by Christ, increase our appreciation of the need for and importance of the Sacrament of Penance 90 and inspire in us an enthusiastic pastoral ministry in this regard. Likewise, let us ask Our Lady for the grace to know how to recognize that the sacrament of Confession is also a help, a guidance and a medicine for priestly life 91 .
