Priestly lordship

“Priestly lordship” “Let them live to the full Christian and priestly kingship and lordship” Constitutions, 214 “We want to form priestly souls and priests who are not ‘tributaries’ 1 ” 2 , our Proper Law declares with all firmness and clarity. What does it mean to be a tributary? Our documents also explain it to us: “A tributary […] is one who acknowledges the lordship that another has over him and pays something as a manifestation of it. Tributary means: ‘to offer or show veneration as a proof of gratitude or veneration (…) it is one who subordinates himself – unduly – to temporal powers, to cultural fashions, to the spirit of the world, as though they were the ultimate end instead of God” 3 . Understood in this way, when the priest is a tributary he becomes a vassal who hands something over to his master in recognition of his lordship. And as the Mystical Doctor of Fontiveros, St. John of the Cross, magnificently explained: “thus, he who loves a creature remains as low as that creature, and, in some way, lower ; for love not only makes equal, but even subjects the lover to what he loves” 4 and all “temporal lordship and temporal freedom before God is neither kingdom nor freedom” 5 . 1. Tributaries: incapable of coherence Let us give more concrete examples, since historically various forms of tributarism have occurred on the part of some members of the Church. To illustrate: “Within the Protestant movement this became very evident, because they had to pay for the concessions they made to the temporal power in order to triumph in their rebellion against the Church. Thus they became subject to the prince, who took the opportunity to seize the riches of the Catholic Church and the consciences of his subjects” 6 . But more recently still, “the progressives who attempt to reconcile their supposed Catholic faith with modern ideologies are tributaries. Supposed Catholic faith, because one who adheres to principles and norms that are not in keeping with the faith and tradition of the Church is not Catholic; nor is one who tries to subject the Church to the civil power” 7 . That is why those are also tributaries who, in their eagerness to attract vocations, propose an ‘attenuated’ style of life, to the point of accommodating themselves to a worldly model of life that sets aside the radicalness of the beauty and worth of following Christ Crucified. Or those who take away the strength and solidity of the doctrinal formation they offer, diluting it to adapt it to passing doctrines, or rather, embracing a doctrine that “escapes all classification and has only one distinctive and characteristic note, which is the note of perfect and absolute incoherence ” 8 and which seems rather to worship dilogy 9 , ambiguity, multiplicity of meanings, equivocation and amphibology 10 . Such people are scandalized, considering that ‘it is not normal’ for an Institute to flourish in vocations precisely because it offers a “witness to the Transcendent,” because of its austerity and manner of life, because of the spiritual atmosphere and serene joy lived in its communities, because of its fervor in apostolic works, because of the solidity of its formation rooted in the most absolute fidelity to the Tradition of the Church and to the teachings of the Pontifical Magisterium—when vocations are precisely a concrete proof of the goodness of God, and the works of religious who live in communion with the legitimate Pastors and are faithful to their vocation in the Church are a manifestation of the kingdom of peace that the Lord has promised us and won for us by his cross and resurrection. Those also behave as tributaries who make use of “pretexts” to “oppose evangelization,” as St. John Paul II taught with clear-sightedness: “Nor are there lacking internal difficulties within the People of God, and these are certainly the most painful. My predecessor Paul VI pointed out, in the first place, «the lack of fervor, all the more serious because it comes from within. This lack of fervor is manifested in fatigue and disenchantment, in accommodation to the surroundings and in lack of interest, and above all in lack of joy and hope» 11 . Great obstacles to the Church's missionary activity are also the past and present divisions among Christians 12 , the de-Christianization of Christian countries, the decrease in vocations to the apostolate, and the counter-witness of faithful who do not follow the example of Christ in their lives. But one of the most serious reasons for the lack of interest in the missionary commitment is the indifferentist mentality, unfortunately widespread even among Christians, often rooted in incorrect theological conceptions and marked by a religious relativism that ends up thinking that «one religion is as good as another». We can add—as the same Pontiff said—that there are also «pretexts which seem to oppose evangelization. The most insidious of these are certainly those for whose justification people wish to employ certain teachings of the Council»” 13 . In the same way, those are tributaries who try to distort prescriptions of Canon Law, or of the Proper Law, seeking to safeguard their own comfort, and thereby making true once again that “internal difficulties within the People of God are certainly the most painful” 14 . Do they perhaps not realize that “those who await Christ are still an immense number” 15 and that “there is no mission without missionaries” 16 and that there will be no missionaries if there is no one to send them? No less tributaries are those who criticize what is in fact being done for evangelization: they criticize now the lack of means, now the shortage of missionaries, now the ‘quality’ of the work; they criticize everything, forgetting that God is the Author of the mission. Without making the proper distinctions they are criticizing God and opposing, in vain, the plans of God, but God laughs at them 17 . One last example: those are tributaries who consider it rash to undertake works trusting in Divine Providence. And out of fear of lacking what is necessary, or out of hunger for material securities, they hand over their works to civil organizations or to the State, corrupting Catholic institutions and abandoning the reality of trust in Divine Providence 18 . Such people forget that “bodily danger does not threaten those who, with the intention of following Christ, abandon all their things, entrusting themselves to Divine Providence” 19 . We, not only as priests and members of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, but also as simple Christians, have “not only the right and the duty, but also the satisfaction and the honor of confessing the sublime lordship of God over things and over men” 20 . That is why we are told explicitly: “The priest must not be a tributary by reason of his investiture and his ministry. He must transmit the truth of God, even at the cost of his blood. He must transmit the holiness of God, accepting to be a sign of contradiction. He must transmit the will of God even to giving his life for the sheep” 21 . Let it be well understood that being a tributary implies in some way losing one's Christian identity, which makes one let oneself be carried along by worldliness and give in to the discourse of whoever proposes renouncing the existential recognition of God's lordship over all things, over society and its intermediate bodies, to the point of becoming incapable of coherence . The Holy Father Francis warned us of this with marked emphasis when he said: “worldliness destroys our Christian identity, leads us to a double life—the one that is appearance and the one that is real—and takes you away from God” 22 . That is why our Proper Law continues to teach: “The priest (and every Christian) is a man of two kingdoms: he is a citizen of the Kingdom of God and a citizen of the kingdom of the earth. When the priest becomes a tributary, he becomes a traitor twice over: he betrays the Kingdom of Heaven and he betrays the kingdom of the earth, because he does not give the latter what it demands of him, which is the truth and the freedom that come only from the Kingdom of God” 23 . Indeed, the Christian and priestly lordship asked of the members of the Institute demands—out of loyalty to the world and out of loyalty to God—that we be “independent in the face of the maxims, mockery and persecutions of the world, depending only on our upright conscience illuminated by faith; ready for martyrdom out of loyalty to God, which constitutes the full and total rejection of the evil world” 24 . Hence what belongs to us is subjection and “generous self-giving to the service of Jesus Christ, the only King who deserves to be served” 25 , in order thus to attain “an effective kingship, though spiritual, over men, even over those who have power and authority, and even over those who abuse it” 26 . To act otherwise is to be tributaries, and to be tributaries is a counter-witness, an incoherence. Why do we say this? Because “every counter-witness, every incoherence between how values or ideals are expressed and how they are actually lived, every seeking of oneself and not of the Kingdom of God and his justice 27 , every falsification of the word of God 28 ” 29 involves some pact, some compromise, some capitulation, negotiation, concession or deal with the spirit of the world. In this sense “hypocrites live on ‘appearances.’ And like ‘soap bubbles’ they hide the truth from God, from others and from themselves, displaying a ‘holy-card face’ to ‘put make-up on holiness’”; “they make themselves look righteous, good,” and they often do this to win the applause of the world, to promote themselves and—if not that—out of some financial interest… ‘they are hypocrites’” 30 . Hence we say that tributarism, besides being an incoherence, is a counter-witness. Throughout the short existence of our Institute many, “under color of zeal” 31 and “under the cloak of virtue” 32 , have objected to, criticized, obstructed, ridiculed, accused without reason, prohibited and even, it would seem, set out to ‘dynamite’ 33 the small work of our Institute. These hypocritical persons—inside and outside the congregation—are those who “ always accuse others but have not learned the wisdom of accusing themselves” 34 . For hypocrisy has the attraction of not saying things clearly; the fascination of the lie, of appearances, is a spirit of revolt and confusion which, “in plain language, means the spirit of understanding things backwards” 35 . This hypocrisy sows division, and the Gospel is full of examples. One of them is that of the Pharisee and the publican: The Pharisee, standing upright, prayed in his heart in this way: ‘O God, I thank you that I am not like other men, who are thieves, adulterers, nor like that publican there’ 36 . Immediately the Pharisee declares his distance: that publican there , he says mockingly . For the hypocrite tries to finish off—or at least to denigrate as much as he can—the one whose virtue, holiness or good works make him uncomfortable; the radicalness of the other shakes him, and in his attempt he only makes his own meager virtue and twisted interests stand out all the more. Another beautiful passage of Sacred Scripture teaches us the hatred of the wicked against the just man: “ Let us lay traps for the just man, because he annoys us and opposes our way of acting; he reproaches us for our transgressions of the Law and rebukes us for our faults against the teaching we received. […]He is a living reproach against our way of thinking and his mere presence is unbearable to us, because he leads a life unlike that of others… For if the just man is the son of God, He will protect him and deliver him from the hands of his enemies ” 37 . A passage that is applied to Christ: Let us put him to the test with insults and torments, to know his temper and try his patience . Let us condemn him to a shameful death, since he claims that God will visit him ” 38 . Pope Francis comments: “This prophecy is very detailed; the plan of action of these wicked people is one detail after another, let us spare nothing, let us test him with violence and torment, and let us put his spirit of endurance to the test… let us lay snares for him, let us set traps for him, [to see] whether he falls… This is not a simple aversion; there is no wicked plan of action—certainly—of one party against another: this is something else. This is called fury : the devil is always behind all fury, he tries to destroy and spares no means. […] What does the devil do? He rages . Always. Behind all fury is the devil, to destroy the work of God ” 39 . Deceiving themselves in their hypocrisy, and in their purpose of finishing off that person, that Institution that challenges their way of living, the tributaries carry on the “little daily lynching , [the one] that tries to condemn people, to create a bad reputation…, to discard them, to condemn them: the little daily lynching of gossip that creates an opinion ; […]and with that ‘it is said that’ an opinion is created in order to finish off a person. […] And in our Christian institutions we have seen so many daily lynchings that were born of gossip.” In fact, “gossip is also a form of fury” 40 . We know well that “even before having begun our Congregation—on March 25, 1984—we already had people opposing us, and not just in any way, but with rage .” How many threatening voices were raised throughout all these years with pitiful calumnies: that we were more Lefebvrist than Lefebvre—they told us—, that we were disobedient to the Pope, closed to dialogue, without sensus ecclesiae … and how many unfounded accusations: that we do things without permission, that there is no selection and that is why we have many vocations (or if not, they accuse us of ‘brainwashing’ them), that we have many foundations because in some cases religious are sent alone… With what heavy-handedness they have wanted to ‘change’ us, they have wanted to ‘convince’ us of the contrary: change this, write this, sign here and your problems are over… with what cunning ‘factions’ have been formed to orchestrate perverse machinations and to obstruct noble projects, pastoral initiatives, decisions of government, and to carry off some good people in the revolt… It should not astonish us that, almost exclusively, these attacks come from consecrated persons. “This is a sickness of the Church ,” says the Holy Father, “a sickness that arises from a worldly way of thinking and feeling that makes itself the interpreter of the law” 41 . That is why we dare to say that behind all these accusations there is a nihilistic indignation, like that of one who seeks annihilation. The confrontation is, in its ultimate foundation, theological. One who gives radical, explicit—positive and negative—witness to Jesus Christ, our Lord, cannot fail to be attacked. That is, one who gives witness to the light that came into the world; and the darkness continues to hate the light for the same reasons: and men loved darkness rather than light because their works were evil 42 . Jesus prophesied it: they have hated me, they will hate you too 43 ; St. Paul says it: all who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution 44 . Almost every page of the Gospel teaches it, in which the Lord himself calls blessed those who suffer for his sake 45 . We would like here to recall once again that for “persecution to be blessed it must, without fail, meet two requirements: that we be ‘reviled for Christ's sake,’ and that ‘what is said against us be false’ 46 ; and we must take great care not to turn our troubles over and over, entertaining ourselves with delicate complacency in them, or falling into ‘that Luciferian belief that we are something great ’ 47 , that we are suffering a great deal” 48 . That is why, and within this framework, we would like to warn that one must be very careful not to fall into the error of settling in one's heart that whoever contradicts us is persecuting our virtue, or has little experience of spiritual things, or is envious, or has similar faults, in order thereby to excuse ourselves from receiving correction from anyone. There have been many who, tempted by vainglory or moved by who knows what passion, pretended that they were persecuted for their virtue and did not understand that it was not so, but rather for their ‘worldliness’; and “believing themselves to be something great”—since according to them they were persecuted for their virtue—they secretly went on nourishing in their hearts an idol of their own self-esteem, and although sporadically they seemed to humble themselves in their thoughts and words, in reality these were not humiliations made before the Majesty of God with holy fear of offending him, but before the secret and disguised idol they had made of themselves. May it not happen to us as it did to them, who dressed self-love in virtuous garments and then wanted to be adored. And if anyone did not adore their statue, they then judged him to be a persecutor of their virtue or contrary to their law. For they made their own tastes, their criteria, their conduct ‘the rule of virtue.’ So much so that everything that departed from that, they condemned and despised and even strove relentlessly to destroy. St. Peter Julian Eymard came to affirm concerning them: “Bear in mind that all who abandoned their vocation did not esteem the rule, to which they wished to add or from which they wished to take away. Jesus Christ rejects them , because he does not want two laws, nor wills contrary to his own, indicated to the founder” 49 . We must open our eyes and “not let ourselves be weakened by the spirit of the world, and live coherently, without giving in and without compromises.” Pressures, being taken aside by someone who tries to convince you by offering you a comfortable solution, uncertain situations, the risk of being caught up in gossip, the risk of losing everything and of our works coming to nothing, the risk of exposing oneself to unpleasant consequences, demotions, persecutions—all of this is always on the horizon. That is why we must feel as our own, and very intimately, the exhortation of St. John Paul II who told us: “Show by the depth of your convictions and by the coherence of your conduct that Jesus Christ is our contemporary” 50 . St. Alphonsus Maria de Liguori already said that “whoever wishes to be glorified with the saints of Heaven needs, like them, to suffer on earth, for none of them was loved and well treated by the world, but all were persecuted and despised, so that the words of the Apostle himself were verified: All who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus will be persecuted ” 51 . 2. Firm in our convictions If it is said of tributaries that they are ‘incapable of coherence,’ what is asked of us, so as not to be such, is precisely coherence , avoiding all false duality, as one dimension of fidelity. “To live in accordance with what one believes. To adjust one's own life to the object of one's adherence. To accept misunderstandings and persecutions rather than permit ruptures between what one lives and what one believes: that is coherence. And it is, perhaps, the innermost core of fidelity” 52 . For this implies being aware of one's own identity and manifesting it, with complete respect, but without hesitation or fear. “But all fidelity must pass the most demanding test: that of duration. Therefore, another dimension of the fidelity asked of us is constancy . It is easy to be coherent for a day or a few days. What is difficult and important is to be coherent all one's life. It is easy to be coherent in the hour of exaltation, when everything is ‘going well,’ but it is difficult to be so in the hour of tribulation. However, only a coherence that lasts throughout one's whole life can be called fidelity. Our Lady's fiat at the Annunciation found its fullness in the silent fiat she repeated at the foot of the cross. To be faithful is not to betray in the darkness what one accepted in public” 53 . What is asked of us is a coherence that is not ephemeral, but constant and persevering. To belong to the Church, to belong to the Institute, to serve the Church, to be faithful to the charism received is today something very demanding. Perhaps it may not cost the shedding of blood, but it may cost contempt, indifference, insults, marginalization and even prison. The danger of fear, of weariness, of insecurity is then easy and frequent. But we must not let ourselves be overcome by these temptations. We must not let the vigor and spiritual energy of our being “of the Incarnate Word” and servants of his Church fade away. “The tributary priest is an aberrant being who has ceased to be salt and has ceased to be light, and like salt that has lost its savor: It is no longer good for anything but to be thrown out and trampled underfoot by men 54 ” 55 . Far be it from us to be such. For each of the members of the Institute has been called to be an imitator of the Incarnate Word, in whom “everything is transparency, authenticity, sincerity, coherence and truth” 56 . We must be firmly planted in that conviction. We must show nobility of soul, fidelity to our own conscience, acceptance of the merciful designs of God—individually speaking and as an Institute—which of course also includes its risks, but convinced that these are things worth dying for. To behave otherwise, that is, to depart at any point from that transparency , authenticity , sincerity , coherence and truth , is a departure from the Ideal and—to a greater or lesser degree—will also be a betrayal of one's own conscience, of Truth itself, of the vocation received and of the principles that were instilled in us. Our convictions tell us that “in our spirituality we must never dialectically separate teaching from action, nor action from teaching. We must always unite integrity of doctrine with uprightness of life, orthodoxy and orthopraxis” 57 . It is also our “most firm conviction that only in the strictest fidelity to the doctrine of Jesus as understood in the Church is the strongest, most living, fresh and graceful originality to be found” 58 . These are all expressions of the Proper Law. We are convinced, moreover, that “truth contemplated makes one teach with conviction and—according to its degree of theological certainty—with an authority that is nothing other than a participation in the authority of Christ” 59 , and that, therefore, “to teach one's own doctrines, to demand undue assent, to emphasize the accidental, to have a doubtful attitude about everything, to remain in insinuations or approximations, to problematize the simplest things, to obscure what is clear and not clarify what is obscure, to seek oneself […] to be padded with filler instead of sober, opaque instead of transparent, confused instead of precise, […] to stir up the waters so that others will think they are deep… is not to have the spirit of Christ who said: Let your word be yes, yes; no, no; anything beyond this comes from the evil one 60 ” 61 . We are convinced of the immense value that the apostolate has for the life of the Church 62 and “that the best way to carry out an effective apostolate is in the closest union with the Incarnate Word and in love for souls to the point of the heroism of unreserved self-giving” 63 . And that is why we go to the mission with the impetus of the saints 64 , trusting only in the Providence of God 65 . We are convinced that in the “spirit bequeathed by the Founder and in the fulfillment of the Constitutions , that is, in the patrimony of the Institute, are contained the riches that the Holy Spirit has granted it for the good of the Church” 66 . Therefore, to the extent that we offer the world a radical witness of Christ Crucified—in contradiction with the spirit of worldliness—we will be able to say that our collaboration in the cause of evangelization is effective, because only thus will we be fit for the Master 67 , since we will be living “to the full Christian and priestly kingship and lordship” 68 . That is why a moment of crisis is a moment of choice; it is a moment that places us before the decisions we must make. In those moments the Incarnate Word could also ask us, as he asked his apostles: Do you also wish to go away? 69 . “In my homeland there is a saying: ‘Don't change horses in the middle of the river,’” the Holy Father commented; “in times of crisis, one must be very firm in the conviction of faith . Those who left ‘changed horses’; they looked for another teacher who was not so ‘hard,’ as they said to Him. In times of crisis we have perseverance, silence; staying where we are, standing firm. This is not the moment to make changes. It is the moment of fidelity, of fidelity to God, of fidelity to the things [decisions] we have made before. […] May the Lord give us the strength, in moments of crisis, not to sell out the faith ” 70 . To make it even clearer, it seems important to us, then, to highlight the contrast that the Proper Law draws in two of its paragraphs regarding the great disparity between being a tributary and not being one, and to point out the fruits that follow from each: The Directory of Spirituality 293 identifies the characteristics of the ‘tributary’ The Directory of Works of Mercy 249 establishes the parameters for not being one Counter-witness The priest must not be a tributary by reason of his investiture and his ministry Incoherence between how values or ideals are expressed and how they are actually lived He must transmit the holiness of God accepting to be a sign of contradiction. Seeking oneself and not the Kingdom of God and his justice He must transmit the will of God even to giving his life for the sheep Falsification of the Word of God He must transmit the truth of God, even at the cost of his blood. From being a tributary follows the fruit of barrenness: “they are often strong obstacles for those who feel the call of Christ: come, follow me …” 71 ; moreover, it seeks to break apart, it sows division. From not being one follows precisely the fruit of fruitfulness, since these religious “by their example spur many to welcome into their hearts the charism of vocation” 72 ; in addition to the fruit of unity: “A profound understanding of the charism leads to a clear vision of one's own identity, around which it is easier to create unity and communion” 73 . The choice is ours. If we are truly to be coherent so as not to be tributaries, then we must, “even at the cost of renunciations and sacrifices, always seek the truth and never sell it or conceal it out of a desire to please men , to astonish, or out of originality or a desire to make a show ” 74 . For “there can be no unity at the expense of truth” 75 . Indeed, an attack on unity is “both obsequiousness and servility, which sacrifice truth and one's own conscience in an attempt to maintain a false peace, not to cross a friend, to avoid some problem or, at times, to gain an advantage through silence or applause” 76 . That is why the cohesion of all the members, always resting on the truth, becomes imperative. All “the good and the evil of the Institute concern everyone equally” 77 , Blessed Giuseppe Allamano told his own, and the same applies to us. That is why the Proper Law tells us: “that in our communities, which must be a unity among persons, a body full of members who think , no one should behave like a closed and solitary whole, like a self-sufficient nomad, but rather we must learn to act as the parts or members of a whole” 78 . We will have many difficulties, we will have defects and weaknesses to spare, but if we remain united, each giving a coherent witness from his own place, contributing not criticisms, not fictitious plans, but practical solutions, initiatives in keeping with our spiritual patrimony, giving ourselves fully to the mission in total forgetfulness of self, God will preserve his work, the work of the Institute. “Do not let yourselves be deceived by gusts of wind that pass and sweep everything away” 79 , said our Spiritual Father. Let us defend with complete freedom of spirit the great good of unity that tributarism and hypocrisy seek to break apart; let us work in unity of purpose, making of our communities, of each province and of all the provinces among themselves one heart and one soul 80 . No matter how many deadly blows they launch against us, how many lynchings by gossip they organize around us, with how many incoherences they strive to accuse us, with how much fury they try to see us disappear, let us persevere in a “perfect spirit of union and personal self-giving” 81 , solid around the charism. That is, living it without cuts, guarding it jealously, deepening it and developing it over time, in homogeneous continuity, whatever the historical circumstances may be 82 . And all this in the most absolute fidelity to the Church our Mother. It would be a grave error to want to level our charism or make it uniform according to pastoral needs polarized around a one-sided objective 83 , or worse still, to want to modify it to please some ‘worldly criterion.’ What is properly ours is that, with the dignity and nobility of soul that a coherent life gives, we bear unequivocal witness that the Word was made flesh , even though many may come wanting to ‘buy us off’ by telling us: “be a little more normal, like other people, sensible…” We must never tire of insisting on the fact that “it redounds to the good of the Church herself that institutes have their own particular character and function” 84 , and for that reason we must always strive diligently to preserve the place that Divine Providence has assigned us in that same Church, of which we are honored to be sons, responding as far as we are able to the new needs that arise in the Church, without ever departing from our patrimony and sound traditions. Our respect must be the greatest for the riches that have been bequeathed to us in the charism, as it was conceived, and which have been approved by the legitimate Authority of the Church. Let us be persuaded that “union is life and confrontation is death; for where there is union there is virtue, and in confrontation there is only disorder and sin; for where there is union there is vigor, prosperity and progress, while discord leads to weakness, to decline, to nothingness. […] Unity strengthens families” 85 . And “if union in a religious family is a powerful evangelical witness, division among brothers is a stumbling block to evangelization” 86 . That is why, in a certain way, everything comes down to our personal fidelity. A fidelity that implies, in the first place, the search for the Will of God. For there can be no fidelity if, instead of seeking the Will of God, I seek to follow my own. A fidelity that also implies—besides the coherence and constancy we have already mentioned—taking a stand and accepting the risks that must come with it. Let us not be naïve: we will not lack crosses, nor does God want us to lack them. Strength and courage are needed to live the identity of a religious, and of a religious of our beloved congregation of the Incarnate Word, without compromises, without a double life. But we need even more fortitude in times of greater combat, a combat that God permits in order to purify the soul and raise it to the highest summits of heroism—as may be the case when an entire Institute is shaken and tossed about by the storm so as to reveal all the beauty of the patience, fidelity and submission of its members. You know it well: “fortitude is a firm disposition of soul to bear courageously any kind of evil, even the worst and most prolonged” 87 . That is why fortitude “always requires a certain overcoming of human weakness and, above all, of fear. For by nature we men spontaneously fear danger, unpleasantness and suffering. […] Fear sometimes robs us of courage when we are in the midst of a climate of threat, oppression or persecution. Thus those men have special courage who are capable of crossing the so-called fear barrier in order to bear witness to truth and justice . To reach such fortitude we must in a certain way ‘go beyond’ our own limits and ‘surpass’ ourselves, running the ‘risk’ of finding ourselves in an unknown situation, the risk of being frowned upon, the risk of exposing ourselves to unpleasant consequences, to calumnies, to demotions, to material losses and even to prison or persecutions. To attain such fortitude, one must be sustained by a great love for the truth and for the good to which one gives oneself . Let us understand it well: the virtue of fortitude walks at the same pace as the capacity for self-sacrifice ” 88 . “This is the resounding idea: to sacrifice oneself . That is how history is directed, even silently and hiddenly” 89 , even if it costs us our lives. That is why, all of you, listen well: We need strong men! For the truly just man is only the one who has the virtue of fortitude. Let us ask God for all the members, present ones and future generations, the gift of Fortitude, so that when we lack the strength to surpass ourselves with a view to higher values such as truth, justice, vocation, this “gift from on high” may make each one of us a strong man and may whisper within us at the opportune moment: Take courage! 90 . The importance of the life of prayer in a religious of the IVE

“The irreplaceable importance of the life of prayer” Cf. Constitutions , 40 The Directory of Spirituality , quoting St. John of the Cross, says: “Let those, then, who are active, who think to encircle the world with their preaching and exterior works, take note here that they would profit the Church much more, and please God much more, if they spent even half the time in being with God in prayer” 1 . The capital importance of prayer in the religious, priestly and missionary life of the members of the Institute of the Incarnate Word follows not only from the universal end for which God has called us together—namely, “to seek the glory of God and the salvation of souls” 2 —but also from its specific end, which is “to inculturate the Gospel” 3 . But even more notably, the irreplaceable importance of the life of prayer 4 follows from our spirituality centered on the mystery of the Incarnation, within which our consecrated life is framed; as well as from “our particular way of imitating the Incarnate God starting from the mystery of the Transfiguration” 5 ; since both mysteries—the Incarnation and the Transfiguration—were events of prayer. Therefore, one cannot be a religious, priest or monk of the Incarnate Word without being a man of prayer who seeks “familiarity with the Word made flesh” 6 whom he aims to imitate. That is more important than any other service we can render to the Church. And in this sense the Second Vatican Council said that religious should “seek God before all else and him alone” and “join contemplation with apostolic love” 7 . The Proper Law adds, moreover, a connotation derived from the demands proper to the religious state, mentioning “the urgency of unceasing prayer and contemplation, and the awareness of the need for the active and passive purifications of sense and spirit” 8 . Indeed, given the missionary character of our Institute, we must admit that the proclamation of the Gospel presupposes that strength, courage and hope are obtained through the life of prayer, for it is especially in prayer that God communicates numerous spiritual graces, which not only serve as spiritual nourishment for the missionary, but there, in turn, he receives what he will later transmit to souls. That is why Blessed Paolo Manna, that great formator of missionaries, said: “The Missionary who wishes to live and remain at the height of his vocation must nourish himself constantly on this spirit of faith, enlightening and inflaming himself with meditation […] He must receive from God, whose instrument he is, through continual prayer, the grace he needs for his ministry, and without which he can do nothing with regard to the eternal salvation of his own soul and of those he went to evangelize” 9 . In this regard, the life of prayer in our Institute involves four ‘dimensions,’ namely: personal and communal, liturgical and private; and it constitutes a fundamental element of primary demand in our spiritual formation. 1. Private Prayer Succinctly, the Proper Law sets down the following maxim: “The missionary must be a ‘contemplative in action’” 10 . For “our spiritual commerce lies in doing our works well, and our holiness in doing them according to the rule. Perfection consists in doing them with a spirit of prayer ” 11 , St. Peter Julian Eymard told his own. That is, “it is not enough to have forms of prayer (set times, ways, pious exercises…); rather, it is a matter of attaining a prayerful attitude (like the soul sinking its depths into God)” 12 . Achieving this prayerful attitude is fundamental for the religious of the Incarnate Word—whether seminarian, brother, priest or monk—to progressively attain holiness 13 . Prayer must permeate all our acts. This is what the Mystical Doctor pointed out to a religious: “try to be continual in prayer, and in the midst of bodily exercises do not leave it. Whether you eat, drink, or speak or deal with lay people, or do anything else, always go about desiring God and attaching your heart to him, which is something very necessary for interior solitude” 14 . Hence, from their entrance into religious life, our candidates are encouraged “to know and experience the authentic meaning of Christian prayer, as a living and personal encounter with the Father through the Only-begotten Son under the action of the Spirit” 15 . It is there that the seminarians and novices of the Institute learn to become familiar with his Person and plan of salvation, in order to make it their ideal of life and the inspiration of all their youthful enthusiasm 16 . Now, for this living and personal encounter with the One and Triune God, in Jesus Christ, silence is necessary as the indispensable spiritual atmosphere for perceiving the presence of God and letting oneself be conquered by it 17 . “Another indispensable means for acquiring the spirit of prayer is to attend ‘diligently to the exercises of piety recommended by the holy custom of the Church’ 18 , taking care that ‘spiritual formation not be placed in these alone, nor cultivate only religious affection’ 19 ” 20 . Among the numerous exercises of piety that Holy Mother Church provides us, our rule prescribes (though without being restricted to these alone): “the daily recitation of the Holy Rosary and the Angelus, the Way of the Cross, the wearing of the scapular, etc.” 21 . And intrinsically linked to our spirituality and mission is the beloved presence of Our Lady, which flows over the whole sphere of our spiritual life and, to tell the truth, over our whole life: whether in the celebration of Mass, or in the hymn to Our Lady at the end of events or of eutrapelia, or in the missions, etc. All the devotional practices mentioned above “have their meaning insofar as they are ordered to having a solid spiritual life; that is, [so that the members] live ‘according to the model of the Gospel,’ are grounded in the practice of the theological virtues, ‘in faith, in hope and in charity,’ acquire ‘the spirit of prayer,’ and thus may ‘strengthen and defend their vocation, obtain solidity in the other virtues and grow in zeal to win all men for Christ’ 22 ” 23 . 2. Personal Prayer From the beginning it has been a practice of the discipline of the Institute to have “the exposition and adoration of the Blessed Sacrament for one hour daily” 24 , since “a while of true adoration has more value and spiritual fruit than the most intense activity, even if it were apostolic activity itself” 25 . That great promoter of Eucharistic adoration—especially among his brother priests—Ven. Archbishop Fulton Sheen insisted that it must be “an hour” (stressing thereby that it was not to be cut short): “the holy hour is grounded in Christ and in Scripture” […] “Why an hour? Because our Lord asked for it so. And our Lord made few requests during his life” 26 . And he added that Eucharistic adoration should be made every day: because our crosses are daily, not once a week; because children, the sick, the missions, families, the dying need our intercession every day 27 ; because the enemy does not rest 28 . Moreover, the venerable archbishop said that faithfulness in keeping the hour of adoration with perseverance and fidelity throughout one's priestly life is a sign that the priest is a true victim. Of the members of the Institute, by reason of our specific vocation, besides the daily hour of adoration, there is asked: “assiduous and prolonged adoration of the Eucharist” 29 , “as well as perpetual adoration in each Province and distributively in each house, since to adore the Blessed Sacrament is ‘the most excellent act […] it is the most just act’” 30 . Such a demand follows from what our Constitutions declare in their first lines, saying that it is our intention “to give the ‘witness that the world cannot be transformed and offered to God without the spirit of the beatitudes’ 31 ” 32 . For we will give this witness of the Gospel beatitudes only if we enter deeply into the contemplation of the word, into intimacy with Christ, and into community life as service and self-giving. Intimate dealings with Christ are, for every Christian and even more for us, like the air we breathe to stay alive. To refuse air is to die. To forget prayer, to let oneself be dragged along by the routine that cools the affection of God's nearness, is also to die 33 . We now mention three ‘additional’ reasons, besides those already known, that Venerable Fulton Sheen gives for not failing to make the hour of adoration: ▪ The hour of adoration combats priestly weariness We must admit, the North American archbishop affirmed, that “as in a marriage, after some years in the priesthood the sensitivity of love is lost. Therefore we must pay closer attention to the things we have heard, lest we drift away , as the Letter to the Hebrews says 34 . Our souls are lost not only because we do evil things, but also because we are negligent in doing good things: we bury the talent, we do not walk the extra mile, we pass by the wounded man the Samaritan helped. How often in the Gospel condemnation follows precisely from not doing: you did not give me to eat, you did not give me to drink, you did not welcome me, you did not visit me …” 35 . That is why he proposed the hour of adoration as a means of combating priestly weariness. How many times have we witnessed this very thing: contemplating Christ in the Eucharist, as Model and as Strength, how many of our missionaries in remote places where fraternal consolation hardly reaches, experiencing the weariness proper to unconditional self-giving to the mission, keep the robustness and freshness of their self-giving unaltered, ready to give even more. We have the enormous privilege of having in our houses the Divine Presence of our Lord, and therefore a greater responsibility to adore him and keep him company. However, two main reasons are often put forward to excuse negligence in making adoration, namely: lack of time and lack of willpower (to overcome laziness or tiredness). “We say we have no time. How many hours do we spend on things that scatter us? The excuses we sometimes make are as foolish as those given in the Gospel to that king for not attending the banquet: I have bought a field and I have to go and see it (imagine, he bought it without seeing it); I have bought five yoke of oxen and I am on my way to ‘try them out’; I have just gotten married… and so why don't you bring your wife too? And so we argue that we have no time…” 36 . In response to that first ‘excuse’ for not making the hour of adoration, the Spiritual Father of our Religious Family, speaking once to priests, told them: “The increase of work in the Lord's vineyard, precisely when the number of laborers is decreasing, can make us forget that we have been called above all to be with the Lord, to listen to his word, to contemplate his face. The contemplative dimension is inseparable from the mission, because, according to the famous definition of St. Thomas, also taken up by the Council, the mission is essentially ‘ contemplata aliis tradere’ , to hand on to others what we have first long contemplated. Hence the need for long spaces of prayer, of recollection, of adoration […] As consecrated persons we must not only pray, we must be a living prayer. One could also say we must pray while apparently not praying. We must pray while apparently not having time to pray, but we must pray. It is another paradox. Humanly, this is something impossible. How can one pray while not praying? But St. Paul tells us: the spirit prays in us , and then the matter turns out somewhat differently” 37 . “The second real reason for not making adoration is our weakness of will. We live in an age in which our will collapses under emotion; we have no determination. How many have abandoned the self-discipline that is the condition for our priestly victimhood. We become like children: not more than a second must pass between our demands and their satisfaction. How do we overcome the excuse of apathy? By taking control of a segment of time, of one hour, and redeeming it. It is for our Lord, it is for the Church, it is for the world, not for me. We must kill acedia by displacing it with a new love. We cannot expel our vices all at once, but we can hem them in by deepening our love for Christ” 38 . ▪ The hour of adoration is a sign of our victimhood in the work of redemption Because it incorporates us into the intercessory work of Christ. We are bound to humanity, to the nations, to the missions, to our homeland, to our diocese, to our parish, to our Institute, to our friends and to our enemies. Our priesthood-victimhood commits us to intercede for them and for their salvation. The agony of Christ continues in marriages going through difficulties, in young people who have lost their purity, in religious who are tempted, in the children of addicted parents, in the abandoned elderly, in defections… The hour of adoration of the Blessed Sacrament allows us to practice an eminent act of charity, since “we adore our God and Lord with all our mind, all our heart, all our soul and with all our strength, and in adoring him we also practice perfect charity toward our neighbor, praying for him and imploring on his behalf the graces and mercies of the Savior” 39 . That is why another motivation for the hour of adoration is also that of reparation. The Proper Law says it explicitly: we “adore Jesus Christ for those who do not adore him, who abandon him, forget him, despise him and offend him” 40 . “To be a priest,” said John Paul II, “means to be a mediator between God and men, in the Mediator par excellence who is Christ. Jesus was able to carry out his mission thanks to his total union with the Father, because he was one with Him […] In order to be able to continue the mission of Christ effectively, the priest too must in some way have already arrived where he wishes to lead others: he arrives there through assiduous contemplation of the mystery of God, nourished by the study of Scripture […] Fidelity to the times and means of personal prayer contributes to sanctifying the priest and leading him to an experience of the mysterious and fascinating presence of the living God, enabling him to act powerfully upon the human environment around him” 41 . ▪ Finally, the hour of adoration is necessary as a form of authentic prayer No one is unaware that our world is incredibly fast. To that must be added the noise that drowns out the voice of conscience. We live in a world where activity kills the knowledge of oneself and of God that contemplation brings. And precisely for that reason, today more than ever, “the priest and the religious must live in intimacy with their Master and strive to become saints as the rule asks, in order to be available to the intuitions of the Holy Spirit and respond better to the calls of the world. The life of prayer—St. John Paul II warns—does not distance one from men; on the contrary, it helps one to perceive more deeply their fundamental needs, which only Christ can reveal to us” 42 . It is true “that it is not easy, especially today when the pace of life has become frenetic and occupations absorb us to such a great extent. But we must be convinced—the Pope continued—that the moment of prayer is precisely when the unity of the priest with his own faithful is strongest, the moment when he is ‘most present’ and his ministry is most effective” 43 . We must not forget what the Constitutions warn us of in this regard: “For us pastoral work is a cross, not a reason for escapism; that is why we must never fall into sterile activism: ‘activity for the Lord must not make us forget Him who is the Lord of activity’” 44 . Moreover—and this we would like to underline—the level of pastoral and apostolic yield will always be in proportion to the measure of our fidelity to Christ according to the commitments assumed in our profession of vows, a fidelity that rests on union with God through prayer and the sacraments in order to maintain the life of grace. If there were not a perfect balance between our life with God and the activities carried out in the service of others, not only the work of evangelization would be compromised, but also our personal condition as evangelized. Prayer is the soul of our work for the Kingdom. “The priest must be insatiably hungry for God” 45 . For “the priest is the man of God, the one who belongs to God and makes people think of God…” 46 . The people who have been entrusted to us seek the solidity of the doctrine of the faith, absolute values, and that Absolute is God. That is why we must respond to this request by speaking of Him, communicating Him and Him alone. That is the greatness of our mission, and to carry it out fully we must nourish that faith and strengthen it every day in prayer. St. John Paul II said that priests must be the “professionals of faith,” and that for this assiduous prayer is necessary, living our days at a rhythm of prayer. In this sense, “ recollection is absolutely necessary in order to draw profit from what one does; otherwise, we are left with those sorts of oases [of intermittent acts] which are the spiritual practices, but outside of them, everything is arid. When, afterwards, we cannot keep our minds fixed on God, it is enough to refer our actions to him and everything becomes prayer. In this consists the spirit of prayer, which helps the interior life greatly. A missionary must be able to maintain recollection anywhere; to know how to pass from study or work to prayer; to remain united to God with a permanent, or at least frequent, lifting up of the heart; in short, to work with great diligence and, at the same time, to pray. If you do not have this spirit, you will never be good missionaries. You may believe you are, but in reality you are not. Happy are you if you always try to advance in the interior life, with the spirit of recollection and prayer!” 47 , said Blessed Allamano. Benedict XV wrote in the encyclical Humani generis redemptionem : “The salvation of souls is not achieved by many words, nor by learned disquisitions, nor by fervent perorations. And if a preacher bases his preaching on these means, he is nothing more than a sounding brass or a clanging cymbal 48 . What really makes the human word capable of helping souls is the grace of God” 49 . And the grace of God is obtained through prayer and through a life in conformity with his supreme directives. On the other hand, none of our members should be unaware that, just as the life of prayer has an irreplaceable importance, so too there is a great “need for the active and passive purifications of sense and spirit” 50 . When the soul passes through the “cure of the night,” it must not abandon prayer on that account; quite the contrary, it must remain in patience and persevere in it. For, as St. John of the Cross says, “very foolish would be the one who, lacking spiritual sweetness and delight, should think that for that reason God is lacking to him, and, when he had it, should rejoice and delight, thinking that for that reason he had God. And more foolish still would he be if he went about seeking this sweetness in God and rejoiced and lingered in it” 51 . 3. Communal prayer Complementary to personal and private prayer is communal prayer. “The words of the Lord, pray always without losing heart 52 , apply both to personal and to communal prayer 53 . Both require fidelity and perseverance. Both are supernatural means that help the growth of community life and will certainly help to overcome, in a creative and prudent way, the difficulties proper to some communities, such as the diversity of tasks and therefore of schedules, the absorbing overload of work and the various forms of tiredness” 54 . In our Institute, communal prayer includes, besides daily Mass, adoration of the Blessed Sacrament and the recitation of the Liturgy of the Hours, the weekly penitential liturgy and the sacrament of reconciliation 55 , whenever possible and pastoral needs permit. “Prayer in common is the response to and the basis of all community life. It starts from the contemplation of the mystery of God, great and sublime, from wonder at his presence, at work in the most significant moments of our religious families as well as in the humble daily reality of our communities. The religious community, as a response to the Lord's pressing invitation watch and pray 56 , must be vigilant and take the time necessary to care for the quality of its life. Sometimes the day of religious who ‘have no time’ runs the risk of being too busy and anxious, and for that very reason may end up tiring and exhausting them” 57 . 4. Liturgical prayer “Most valuable in this regard is liturgical prayer. In no one may the conviction weaken that community is built up starting from the Liturgy, above all from the celebration of the Eucharist, of the other sacraments and of the common recitation of the Liturgy of the Hours” 58 . In this sense, the priests of our Religious Family are asked to celebrate Holy Mass daily and, barring pastoral commitments, to try to concelebrate as often as possible. Likewise, a moment of the day must be found for communal Eucharistic adoration 59 . And, thirdly, “all due importance must also be given to the pious and devout recitation of the Liturgy of the Hours […] Ordinarily the major hours of the Office should be recited in community” 60 , the Proper Law establishes. ▪ On the Liturgy of the Hours Regarding the recitation of the Breviary, it is important to highlight the “pious and devout recitation” mentioned above. That is, at no time should it be hurried or unthinking, like someone who instead of reading ‘scans’ the page and does not think about what he is saying. It must be a moment of true prayer, of asking God, of praising him with the very words with which He wants us to ask him and praise him. They are words of the Holy Spirit! In such a way that, together with Eucharistic adoration, the recitation of the Liturgy of the Hours may help to cultivate and maintain throughout the whole day the spirit of prayer of which we spoke at the beginning. The recitation of the Breviary must truly be a “source of piety and nourishment for personal prayer” 61 . Archbishop Fulton Sheen, however, writes with great realism in his autobiography: “Few priests like vocal prayer. It is a fact. This is not because priests are not men of prayer. It is because their prayers are sighs, aspirations and inspirations. […] They have few petitions. Rarely do they make a novena for something they need; they ask people to make them. […] And few want to admit that they are bored with something they are supposed to like. The Breviary belongs to that category. Priests are expected to rave with love for the Breviary, but many of us are like those people who go to an opera for the sake of appearances but neither enjoy it nor understand it. […] Perhaps the Breviary was meant to be difficult for any average priest. Could it not be like the wrestling between Jacob and God? If we look at it from this point of view, it may still be a struggle, but it would fall into the category of prolonged and unceasing intercession. For we would be praying it as our Lord prayed in the Garden of Olives, like the friend who kept knocking on the door at night asking for a piece of bread, like the widow who never ceased her pleas before the judge. Importuning is not relaxing in dreams, but sustained work” 62 . “The Liturgy of the Hours is the sanctification of the day,” says the Laudis Canticum of St. Paul VI. That is why it is important that, before or after Mass, this be the first thing we do, that we make sure of it. Blessed Joseph Allamano, for his part, told his own: “Let us observe the indications of the Church with regard to the time for praying the Liturgy of the Hours. Having a lot of work must not lead us to postpone it. Prayed in good time, it is a sweet burden. As for the place, if possible, pray it in the church, which is the house destined for prayer. The Liturgy of the Hours is the most excellent prayer after the Mass. May praising God be one of our principal occupations, as it will be for all eternity!” 63 . We must add, moreover, that “the Liturgy of the Hours, like the other liturgical actions, is not a private action, but belongs to the whole body of the Church, manifests it and influences it” 64 . In such a way that each time we take up the Breviary to pray, we take up the millions of unbelievers in this world, the persecuted churches, the most distant missions, the thousands of Catholics in the world who do not regularly have a priest where they live, the thousands of priests in the world who must carry out their ministry covertly, etc., so that our prayer becomes a missionary work. Archbishop Fulton Sheen even offers us some practical recommendations for praying the Breviary 65 : To pray it, as far as possible, before the Blessed Sacrament. A practice that also allows us to gain the corresponding indulgences. To notice that most of the psalms confront us with two figures: the Sufferer and the King. That helps us to interpret the psalms better. To have recourse to the Holy Spirit during the recitation of the Breviary. Not necessarily with a formal prayer, but as a gesture asking for help to do it well, with understanding, unhurriedly. To offer certain Hours of the Liturgy for certain intentions. Let us say, finally, that the Breviary is not a yoke and a burden; rather, it is an obligation, but an obligation of love. If the priest is selfish, the recitation of the Liturgy becomes merely an obligation; if the priest is a person aware that it is the prayer of the Church, that obligation carries love contained within it; if the priest is a victim, love turns that obligation into such ardor that he feels no obligation at all. ▪ On Holy Mass One of the great loves of every member of the Institute is the Eucharist 66 . In accordance with this, we read in our Constitutions : The principal thing, the most important thing we must do each day, is to take part in the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass 67 . “We must be characterized by the importance that must be given to the celebration of Holy Mass, as well as by the reverent way of celebrating it” 68 , we read in one of the acts of the 2007 General Chapter, which points to this very thing as an element attached to the non-negotiable charism. That is why it can never be sufficiently stressed that it belongs to us “to be masters of the ars celebrandi , and to our major seminarians, our brothers, etc., to strive for their part to live the ars participandi in the most perfect way” 69 . “It must be kept in mind that the celebration of the Mass is a thermometer of the priestly life” 70 . So much so that one can say that “a priest is worth as much as his Eucharistic life is worth; his Mass above all. Mass without love, a sterile priest: fervent Mass, a priest who conquers souls. Eucharistic devotion neglected and without love, a slack priesthood, even more, a priesthood in danger” 71 . The Eucharist, St. Leonard Murialdo recalled, is not a rite to be performed but a mystery to be lived 72 . And if this is a mystery to be lived, then we must not forget that our “style of liturgical celebrations as part of our charism [consists in] celebrations in which the Word becomes incarnate and in which he appears—sacramentally—Incarnate, in which the principal presence and action of the principal Priest 73 is always highlighted, in which it is perceived that the essential attitude of the secondary priest is the prayerful attitude —proper to one who knows himself to be a mere instrument, and a deficient instrument, subordinate to the principal cause and subject to its ends—, in which all the visible elements contribute to the splendid knowledge of the Invisible” 74 . Concretely: “our liturgical celebrations must be exemplary: ‘in their rites, in their spiritual and pastoral tone, and in the fidelity due both to the prescriptions and texts of the liturgical books and to the norms issued by the Holy See and the Episcopal Conferences’” 75 . * * * * * In short, to pray is necessary in order to live well. Whoever prays responds to his vocation and is faithful to it. A priest of the Incarnate Word will never be able to be “another Christ” for men if he is not first a “man of God.” That is why we must feel as personally addressed to us the exhortation of the Spiritual Father of our Religious Family, who said: “Learn to pray! …so that you may become ‘masters’ of prayer and may also teach those entrusted to you to pray!” 76 . For, being contemplatives of the Incarnate Word, we will draw strength from the mystery we contemplate to prolong generously “the Incarnation in all reality” 77 . Consequently, all of us members of the Institute must not only respect the prescribed times of prayer, but also know how to find time to be alone with God, listening in silence to what He has to tell us. For prayer allows us in a certain way to place ourselves within the dimensions of God, inserting ourselves humbly but courageously into the very heart of God, from which we must “not want to leave” 78 . We must be souls of prayer , souls of the Eucharist 79 . Wherever we carry out our mission, our spiritual mission is the same everywhere: to illuminate with the “resplendent light that dawns from on high” all those who “dwell in darkness and in the shadow of death” 80 . This is truly our mission, whether we are priests in a parish in one of the great cities or serve a small rural community; whether we carry out our activity as pastors, chaplains, teachers, assisting in a home, or have been sidelined for reasons of health. “To pray is to acknowledge that Christ is risen and deserves unconditional dedication” 81 . In other words: “Take care of your life of prayer and goodness, so as to be exemplary ministers and bearers of joy and serenity to all! Cultivate intimacy with Christ through a sincere and deep interior life, always remembering that your mission is to be witnesses of the supernatural and heralds of Christ to the men of our time, who are becoming ever more aware, even when appearances may sometimes suggest the contrary, of the call of God and their need for him” 82 . Let us not forget that one must love prayer in order to be zealous apostles of the kingdom of God. […] One must find the time to pray ‘well,’ since from the heart immersed in God springs the spiritual energy for an effective apostolate 83 . We conclude by paraphrasing the Mystic of Fontiveros, who wrote in a letter to one of his directees: “Do not let the soul cling to anything; for, as long as prayer is not lacking, God will take care of its affairs, since it belongs to no other master, nor ever shall” 84 .
