For the Kingdom of Heaven

For the Kingdom of Heaven 1 Constitutions , 257 Every year we members of the Institute of the Incarnate Word make the Spiritual Exercises of St. Ignatius of Loyola, in which the Spanish saint “invites us to the great conquest of holiness” 2 . During the ‘second week’ of these Exercises we are given the opportunity to make the contemplation of the “call of the King” 3 , since the Christian life is not the mere adherence to a doctrine, but the following and accompanying of a Person. There we hear, like a refrain, the question “What must I do for Christ?” 4 , which denotes the singularly ‘practical’ tone of the call and of the consequent following of Christ. For, as St. Ignatius rightly points out, “ love ought to be put more in deeds than in words ” 5 . Hence the importance of constantly renewing the dispositions of magnanimity and generosity in our adherence to the will of the King. This certainly includes returning often to the first fruits and freshness of that call which Christ one day made personally to each one of us, and once again resolutely pronouncing our yes to the Beloved. At the same time, it includes ‘making more room’ in our life, in our souls, in our heart, so that God may reign in us. 1. Jesus Christ is King The Directory of Spirituality says: “The Lord is King of all humanity in the strict, literal and proper sense, since He received from the Father authority, power and the kingdom 6 ; that is why He is King of kings and Lord of lords 7 . As you know, the foundation of this kingship is fourfold: In the first place, it belongs to Him because He is God, the Incarnate Word, and thus St. Cyril of Alexandria says: “Christ holds dominion over all creatures, not seized by force nor taken for any other reason, but by His very essence and nature” 8 ; in the second place, it belongs to Him by virtue of the Redemption, by right of conquest, since He bought us with His blood: You were not ransomed… with perishable gold or silver, but with the precious blood of Christ 9 ; in the third place, because He is Head of the Church, by the fullness of grace: full of grace and truth 10 ; in the fourth place, by right of inheritance: whom He appointed heir of all things 11 . His royal authority includes the fullness of the threefold power: legislative, judicial and executive” 12 . Moreover, “the scope of His kingship is twofold, personal and social. He reigns over minds because He is the Truth, ‘and men must receive the truth from Him with obedience’ 13 ; He reigns over wills because He is Goodness, ‘in such a way that He inflames us toward the noblest things’ 14 ; and He reigns over hearts because He is Love. And He also reigns socially, since ‘there is no difference between individuals and civil society, because individuals, united in society, are no less under the power of Christ than each one of them is separately. He is the source of private and public well-being’ 15 ” 16 . “Certainly His is not a temporal or earthly kingdom: my Kingdom is not of this world 17 ; rather it is an eternal Kingdom: His Kingdom will have no end 18 , and it is universal: all power in heaven and on earth was given to Him 19 ; a Kingdom of truth and life, of holiness and grace, of justice, love and peace 20 ” 21 . 2. An effective kingship Now, having freely heard the Lord’s call to follow Him wherever He goes: “ whoever wishes to come with me ” 22 , we have accepted to be with Him, because we want to be steeped in His presence and to become, little by little, “other Christs” 23 . That is, we religious have embraced “the form of life which Jesus, the supreme consecrated one and missionary of the Father for His Kingdom, embraced and proposed to the disciples who followed Him” 24 . This implies −as we were saying earlier− that Christ must reign in our lives, and that is nothing other than “to prefer nothing to Christ” 25 . For “it is clear −teaches St. John of the Cross− that the more one fixed one’s eyes on the king’s servants and paid attention to them, the less notice one took of the king and the less one esteemed him; […] for the more one sets [one’s eyes] on the servants, the more one takes away from one’s lord; and then such a one did not judge very highly of the king, since the servants seem to him to be something in the presence of the king, his lord. So it happens to the soul with regard to its God when it pays heed to the said creatures” 26 . In this sense, “the religious state […] reveals in a special way the superiority of the Kingdom over all created things, and its radical demands. It also shows all men the extraordinary greatness of the power of Christ the King and the infinite efficacy of the Holy Spirit, who works wonders in His Church” 27 . Many of you will know the story of St. Rafael Arnáiz Barón (1911-1938), a Trappist monk, whose monastic life was interrupted three times because of his illness (diabetes). Rafael had just asked the abbot to be allowed to return to the monastery for the third time. And this would be the last. Then one day in November 1937 he wrote a letter to Brother Tescelino −who had been his infirmarian at the Trappist monastery− telling him that Father Abbot had told him he could return to the monastery whenever he wished… but that he should think it over carefully and not be hasty, because they now had no infirmarian (since Brother Tescelino had been called up for military service). Then Rafael reflects: “Humanly speaking, it is very prudent, don’t you think? But what am I to do? Well, look, this is how I think about it; let’s see what you think. Suppose you are at home sick, surrounded by care and attention, almost crippled, useless…, unable to fend for yourself, in a word. But one day you saw Jesus pass beneath your window. […] If you saw that Jesus was calling you and giving you a place in His retinue, and He looked at you with those divine eyes radiating love, tenderness, forgiveness, and said to you: Why do you not follow me? … What would you do? Would you perhaps answer Him… Lord, I would follow You if You gave me an infirmarian…, if You gave me the means to follow You in comfort and without danger to my health… I would follow You if I were healthy and strong enough to fend for myself…? No, […] surely you would have said to Him: I am coming, Lord; my ailments do not matter to me, nor death, nor eating, nor sleeping … If You will have me, I am coming. If You wish, You can heal me… It does not matter to me that the road by which You lead me is difficult, steep and full of thorns. It does not matter to me if You want me to die with You on a cross […]. I am given prudent warnings… But what is all that worth beside the gaze of a God like Jesus of Galilee, who offers you a place in heaven, and an eternal love? Nothing, brother… not even suffering until the end of the world is worth giving up following Jesus” 28 . Likewise, each one of us −certainly assisted by the grace of God− has answered our Lord’s call, leaving everything behind to follow Him. This is the radicalness that is required if we are to love the Incarnate Word with an undivided love. For ours has been, and must continue to be, “the choice of a greater and undivided love for Christ and His Church” 29 . That is what enables us “to offer a ‘privileged witness of a constant search for God and an absolute dedication to the growth of His Kingdom” 30 . This is something we should keep very much in mind, above all when poverty is felt more harshly, when health does not keep pace with apostolic zeal, when we are criticized in spite of our dedication, when loneliness becomes heavier, when divine help seems to have run out for us, when the temptations to make a pact with the world grow gigantic. In other words, our consecration implies –in fact– a life of lordship. A religious of the Incarnate Word must exercise this life of lordship: Over himself : to the extent that he triumphs over sin, masters the incentives of the flesh, and governs his soul and body. The religious, to the extent that he fully submits his soul to God, arrives at a state of indifference and detachment from the things of the world, which gives him a masterful and free will, capable of dedicating himself to things without letting himself be dominated by them 31 . Over men : to the extent that the religious gives himself generously to the service of Jesus Christ, the only King who deserves to be served , he acquires an effective, though spiritual, kingship over men, even over those who have power and authority, and even over those who abuse it. For they take upon themselves the burden of their sins and their sorrows, through a humble and serviceable love that goes as far as the sacrifice of oneself 32 . Over the world : this happens in two ways, namely: 1) by collaborating with the world of creation through work and with the world of redemption through the apostolate. For this kingship to be effective, it will be necessary that, together with dedication to things, there be at the same time a detachment and disengagement from them; 2) by rejecting the world, whether out of loyalty to the world itself, which must be held as a means and not as an end, or out of loyalty to God, resisting the concupiscences, temptations and sins of the world; being independent in the face of the maxims, mockery and persecutions of the world, depending only on our upright conscience enlightened by faith; ready for martyrdom out of loyalty to God, which constitutes the full and total rejection of the evil world 33 . Over the devil : our Proper Law says: “We need religious convinced not only that by the grace of God they have power to resist the devil, but also to be able to exorcise him” 34 . We must be convinced that we have been “consecrated for the Kingdom” and, therefore, we are true religious insofar as we are totally consecrated to the service of God, offering ourselves to Him as a holocaust 35 . This is achieved through the faithful and constant practice of the religious vows. Indeed, the Magisterium of the Church teaches that “the vocation of consecrated persons to seek first the Kingdom of God is, first and foremost, a call to complete conversion, in self-renunciation, in order to live fully for the Lord” 36 . Therefore, it is our oblation through obedience, poverty and chastity that makes our existence “a living memorial of Jesus’ way of living and acting as the Word made flesh 37 , in relation to the Father and in relation to men” 38 , and an effective contribution to the reign of Christ. 3. I make my oblation 39 Christ’s invitation “whoever wishes to come with me” brings with it “to labor with me,” and St. Ignatius puts the reason for this on the lips of Christ: “so that, following me in suffering, he may also follow me in glory” 40 . And although we have already said it many times and it is known to all, we believe it is worth mentioning again that the following of Christ “is not the promise of easy successes. It promises no one a comfortable life. It is demanding. And at the same time it is a Great Promise: the promise of eternal life for man, subject to the law of death; the promise of victory, through faith […]. To find life, one must lose life; to be born, one must die; to be saved, one must take up the Cross” 41 . Our consecration is synonymous with holocaust, with oblation. Said in a more Ignatian tone, this would be equivalent to saying that our consecration to the kingdom of Christ “entails the acceptance of spiritual combat” 42 . That is why it seems possible to us to draw a parallel between St. Ignatius’ prayer of oblation of the kingdom and our formula of religious profession, which it is always worthwhile to explore more deeply. It is remarkable how the two correspond in a way that fills us with wonder; let us see: Oblation of the kingdom 43 Formula of consecration in the IVE 44 Eternal Lord of all things For love of the Father, first origin and supreme end of consecrated life; of Christ, who calls us to His intimacy; of the Holy Spirit, who disposes the soul to welcome His inspirations. Our consecration has its origin in God’s initiative, and it is toward God Himself that we tend, for “for the glory of the Most Holy Trinity, the greater manifestation of the Incarnate Word and the honor of the Church founded by Christ” 45 we have embraced this state of life which “imitates more closely … that form of life which the Son of God chose when He came into the world…” 46 with the sole “end of seeking God alone” 47 . In this way, our religious life, insofar as it promotes a transfigured existence through the practice of the evangelical counsels, becomes a manifestation of God and a confessio Trinitatis , that is, one of the concrete traces that the Trinity leaves in history 48 . “Concretely, chastity is the reflection of the infinite love that unites the three divine Persons; poverty is the expression of the total gift of self that the three divine Persons make to one another; obedience is the reflection in history of the loving correspondence proper to the three divine Persons” 49 . Thus, then, starting from a transfigured existence, we wish to participate in the life of the Trinity and to confess the love that saves 50 . Indeed, our formula of profession 51 and the very Constitutions 52 that govern our particular style of sanctification and apostolate begin with a Trinitarian invocation and end with one; because the beginning and the end of our consecration is none other than “God alone” 53 . And just as St. Ignatius begins by saying: “Eternal Lord of all things,” our Constitutions begin by saying: “We confess that God is the Lord and Father of all things, the beginning and end of them all,” and all of them we wish “to restore, entirely, in Christ” 54 , since that is precisely “to prolong the Incarnation in all things” 55 . That is why we understand that the practice of our religious vows is a “manifestation of the giving of oneself to God with an undivided heart 56 and a reflection of the infinite love that unites us to Him” 57 . This requires a “holy familiarity with the Word made flesh” 58 and being formed in a profound intimacy with God 59 , which disposes our soul to welcome His inspirations 60 , “so that we may belong more and more to Christ, and therefore to His Mystical Body, since if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ 61 ” 62 . In this way, our “religious consecration becomes an image of the Trinity: ‘it is a proclamation of what the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit, accomplishes with His love, His goodness and His beauty… That is why its first objective is to make visible the marvels that God works in the frail humanity of those who are called’ 63 ” 64 . In other words: “We embrace this state of life in order to be able more easily to give ourselves to divine things, attaining eternal beatitude with greater security and, finally, to dedicate ourselves with greater freedom to the work of leading others to the Kingdom of heaven” 65 , in such a way that our consecration “must be useful to our neighbor insofar as it is a living witness of supernatural realities” 66 . Oblation of the kingdom Formula of consecration in the IVE I make my oblation, with Your favor and help I, N.N., freely make to God the oblation of my whole being […] “Consecration is the basis of religious life. By affirming this, the Church places first the initiative of God and the transforming relationship with Him which religious life involves. Consecration is a divine action. God calls a person and sets him or her apart for a particular dedication to Himself. At the same time, He offers the grace to respond, so that consecration is expressed, on the part of the human person, in a profound and free self-surrender” 67 , as the Magisterium of the Church teaches. Now, this “consecration to God of the religious life is a total consecration, which ‘requires, according to St. Gregory, consecrating to God ‘one’s whole life’” 68 , which can only be carried out by means of the vow, since we do not possess our whole life all at once, in one moment. By means of the vow man freely renounces ‘the very freedom to abstain from what pertains to divine service’” 69 . That is why our Constitutions make explicit that our oblation consists principally in the fulfillment of the three vows of chastity, poverty and obedience, impelled by charity 70 . And therefore, religious profession constitutes a true holocaust of oneself, since by virtue of the vows one gives to God everything one has, reserving nothing: by the vow of chastity, the good proper to the body; by the vow of poverty, external things; and the goods of the soul by the vow of obedience 71 . This consecration truly embraces one’s entire life, and that is why we say “of my whole being.” For this reason we can say that “religious life consists essentially in the three vows of poverty, chastity and obedience 72 , by which one gives to God external goods, the right to form a family, and freedom, which is what man holds most dear. So that absolutely nothing is left to the religious. St. Thomas teaches that ‘those are called religious par excellence who consecrate themselves totally to the service of God , offering themselves to Him as a holocaust . […] In the holocaust the victim offered to God is immolated. Immolation implies the total destruction of the victim in honor of God. The religious immolates himself to God as a holocaust, following Christ poor, virgin and obedient unto death on a cross” 73 . “But rather than of a destruction, we should speak of a positive transformation. The religious gives everything in order to attain the perfect charity that will make him possess God intimately and fully” 74 . So, “it is a matter of giving everything, but not as an end in itself, rather in order to be free of all the impediments that could draw one away from perfect charity 75 , and therefore with a view to a more intimate consecration to God and a new and special dedication to the service of God and to the saving mission of the Church” 76 . What is more, our formula of profession explicitly mentions that we make the oblation of our whole being “freely”: Freely we have chosen to be among the eunuchs who have made themselves so for the sake of the Kingdom of Heaven (Mt 19:12) 77 . Freely we have chosen poverty in order to proclaim “the Absolute of God, who is our only wealth” 78 . Freely we choose to be obedient and to submit our own will to legitimate Superiors, who take the place of God when they command something according to the Constitutions 79 , imitating in this Jesus Christ, who became obedient unto death, even death on a cross 80 . Therefore, “the evangelical counsels of chastity, poverty and obedience, lived by Christ and embraced out of love for Him, appear as a path to the full realization of the person in opposition to dehumanization; they proclaim the freedom of the children of God and the joy of living according to the evangelical beatitudes” 81 . Far from being a renunciation that impoverishes, they rather enrich us because they free us “from the impediments that could draw us away from the fervor of charity and the perfection of divine worship, consecrating us more intimately to the service of God” 82 , so as to come to possess God intimately and fully 83 . Put another way, we have chosen to belong totally to the Incarnate Word, and that makes us joyfully free. And freely we have consented to belong to Him, making the oblation of our whole being 84 through the practice of the evangelical counsels according to the “evangelical path traced out in the Constitutions of the Institute of the Incarnate Word” 85 , because we are convinced that, as the Mystical Doctor says, “the immense goods of God do not fit nor fall except into an empty and solitary heart” 86 . Oblation of the kingdom Formula of consecration in the IVE before Your infinite goodness, and before Your glorious Mother, and all the holy men and women of the heavenly court, […] Therefore, before God our Lord and all His saints , […] I ask the intercession of Our Lady , of the Twelve Apostles and of the other patron saints , […] Our formula of profession takes on full solemnity as we present ourselves “before God our Lord and all His saints” and invoke the intercession of “Our Lady, the Twelve Apostles and the other patron saints.” And this is so because the oblation we make is at once a historical and a supernatural reality, in such a way that both the profession and the very practice of the vows become a reality that transcends the earthly plane, moving us to practice the virtues of transcendence: faith, hope and charity 87 . Moreover, it gives our consecration a stamp and a luster that distinguishes us from other religious, namely, the great veneration for the Mother of the Incarnate Word and for the saints, masterpieces of God, in whom we honor God Himself 88 . It seems fitting to me to affirm that, since our spirituality is anchored in the mystery of the Incarnation to the point that we can say that it “derives from the Person of the Word and of His Mother” 89 , Marian devotion is inherent to our consecration, and without it our consecration cannot be understood, for we say that we are “ essentially missionary and Marian” 90 . That is why we raise our prayers to the Mother of God, that she may obtain for us the grace “to attain this disposition of supreme, total and unrestricted docility to the Holy Spirit” 91 “in order to claim for Jesus Christ the lordship of all that is authentically human” 92 . So that our consecration may manifest “a lordship over all things, together with a most free will, ready to please God alone” 93 . And from the Virgin Mother we hope to obtain all the help necessary to fulfill the honorable duty of “prolonging the Incarnation in all things” 94 . Consequently, our consecration is framed by, impregnated with, and diffusive of devotion to Mary Most Holy, its “natural consequence being to marianize one’s whole life” 95 . Our Lady then becomes “the model that guides ‘all our intentions, actions and operations’ 96 ” 97 and is, moreover, the end toward which our acts are directed, the object that draws our heart, and the motive of the labors we undertake 98 . Thus, then, if our consecration implies the oblation of our whole being to the Incarnate Word, we wish to make that offering −“in order to serve Jesus Christ better” 99 − through the hands of Mary Most Holy, “so that she may dispose of everything according to her good pleasure 100 , certain that through Mary, Mother of the Incarnate Word, we are to go to Him, and that she is to make of us ‘great saints’ 101 ” 102 . Furthermore, the veneration of the saints – as “the best members of the Mystical Body of Christ and the greatest and most complete fruit of the Incarnation and the Redemption” 103 −, the study of their wise doctrine, the riches with which they adorned the work of the Church, their heroic virtues and examples of life, their intercession before the throne of God “impel us to seek the city that is to come… perfect union with Christ, that is, holiness” 104 . “They constantly commend to us heaven, eternal life, the reward of merits, God! […] spurring whole generations on to the heroism of following Jesus Christ” 105 . For this reason our self-giving to Christ finds in the saints inspiration, help and wise doctrine, so that we may reach the heaven they have already reached. Oblation of the kingdom Formula of consecration in the IVE that I want and desire, and it is my deliberate determination, provided only it be Your greater service and praise, I pledge all my strength not to shy away from the missionary adventure, to inculturate the Gospel in the diversity of all cultures, to prolong the Incarnation of the Word “in every man, in the whole man and in all the manifestations of man,” assuming all that is authentically human, to be like another humanity of Christ, to carry out with greater perfection the service of God and of men . And this is so, simply because “ love ought to be put more in deeds than in words ” 106 . To “pledge all one’s strength” is to “resolve in earnest” 107 to imitate Christ in His suffering, of which St. John of the Cross speaks and which our Proper Law expresses in various ways: “We want to imitate Jesus Christ as perfectly as possible” 108 ; “firmly resolved to attain holiness… with ‘a great and very determined determination not to stop until reaching it (holiness)’ ” 109 , etc. For religious consecration in this Institute implies the closer imitation of the mystery of the Incarnate Word and of the attitudes it entails 110 , which brings with it the demand for conversion and holiness, for a transfigured existence, for contemplating and bearing witness to the transfigured face of Christ 111 . The Incarnate Word offered Himself to the Father without restriction; He made Himself an oblation as a victim, immolated Himself in expiation, gave Himself without reserve, and that is precisely what the priestly attitude of every member of our small Religious Family must be 112 . Therefore, all of us members of the Institute seek to perfect ourselves “by being in Christ ‘an eternal offering to God’ 113 , ‘a living and perfect victim for the praise of His glory’ 114 . For that is the priestly attitude proper to the ‘third class of men’ of the Spiritual Exercises of St. Ignatius of Loyola 115 . And we wish to live permanently in that attitude, without diminutions or retractions, without reservations or conditions, without subterfuges or delays, without retreats or sluggishness. Both in the undertakings of the inner life and in high historical undertakings” 116 . Thus, then, since “in institutes dedicated to the apostolate there is no path of holiness, nor of profession of the evangelical counsels, nor of life dedicated to God and His service, that is not intrinsically linked to the service of the Church and of the world 117 ; all our missionary and apostolic work is founded on the conviction that He must reign 118 . Now, in this work of the apostolate, the first place is held by the witness of life, since “one is a missionary above all by what one is… before being one by what one says or does” 119 , and that is for us the “first and irreplaceable form of mission” 120 , so that the charity of Christ may shine forth among the faithful 121 . In this sense, “all the members of our Institute must not only fulfill with the greatest possible perfection the evangelical counsels and the self-giving to Jesus through Mary, but also ‘order their life according to the Proper Law of the Institute and thus strive to attain the perfection of their state’ 122 ” 123 . Nevertheless, not only through our consecration but also through our apostolic labor we seek to associate ourselves with the work of redemption and with the spreading of the kingdom of God 124 , transfiguring the world from within with the power of the Beatitudes. Confessing that Jesus Christ is true God and true man, who in His one divine person unites both natures, we are in the world without being of the world, and we assume in Christ everything human, since “what is not assumed is not redeemed” 125 . Consequently, our sublime endeavor is “to ‘assume’ cultures, purifying them and elevating them starting from Christ and His Gospel, understood ‘in the Church’” 126 , and we wish to do this “even in the most difficult situations and under the most adverse conditions” 127 . The Word assumed human nature, granting it the dignity of His divine person. In the same way, this assumption of the whole reality of men and their cultures “is only real when it truly transforms what is human in Christ, elevating it, dignifying it, perfecting it. What is left only on the human level has only apparently been assumed” 128 . So, in all our missionary work we are guided by the principle which says “that true inculturation is from within and consists, ultimately, in a renewal of life under the influence of grace” 129 . At the same time, we are convinced that “it is the task of consecrated life to spread the Kingdom of Christ to the most distant regions, to the growing multitude of those who do not know Christ. For this reason also “it urges us to work in the most difficult places (those where no one wants to go)” 130 . What is more, far from regarding pastoral work as a means of escapism, which has led some to fall into activism, for us missionary labor is a cross and, as such, unites us more closely to Christ. Indeed, the interior source of our apostolate is, and we wish it always to be, our ever deeper communion with the pastoral charity of Jesus Christ 131 . Contrary to what some think, we are persuaded that “mission strengthens consecrated life, gives it renewed enthusiasm and new motivations, and stimulates its fidelity” 132 , since the act by which one loves God and the act by which one loves one’s neighbor are specifically the same 133 . “For all these reasons the members of our Religious Family must collaborate with all enthusiasm in missionary work 134 , making the gift of themselves to God out of love for so many men and women of our time who do not know Jesus Christ, and who seem to be pleading like that Macedonian: Come over to Macedonia and help us 135 ” 136 . The zeal of our members for the establishment of the Kingdom of God and the salvation of men becomes the best proof of an authentically lived self-giving 137 . Oblation of the kingdom Formula of consecration in the IVE to imitate You in bearing all injuries and all reproach and all poverty, actual as well as spiritual, […] so that my life may be a living memorial of Jesus’ way of living and acting , the Word made flesh (cf. Jn 1:14), before the Father and before men. […] I vow to live forever chaste, for the Kingdom of Heaven, poor, showing that God is man’s only true wealth, and obedient, unto death on a cross, in order to follow more intimately the Incarnate Word in His chastity, poverty and obedience These words of our consecration –so profound and so rich in content– point us to the very reason for religious profession, namely: to bring the consecration of Baptism to its fullness and to represent perpetually in the Church that form of life which the Son of God chose when He became incarnate 138 . Therefore, if earlier we said that our religious profession was an image of the Trinity, now we must say that it is at the same time Christocentric, since our vocation implies “an adherence that enables us to conform our whole existence to Christ, through the practice of the evangelical counsels as the most radical way of living the Gospel and following Christ” 139 . And although “this applies to every religious, ‘with much greater reason it falls to us to live this reality as religious of the Family of the Incarnate Word’ 140 . For this reason, even though it is essential to every religious, we want it not to go unnoticed in our lives. Even more, we want this Christocentric stamp to be branded with fire upon us and upon our apostolate of evangelizing the culture. Since this reality of being other Christs is central to our spirituality” 141 . That is why “we want to imitate Jesus Christ as perfectly as possible, since He teaches us: I have given you an example 142 , and St. Paul exhorts: Have the same sentiments as Christ Jesus had… 143 , so that we may be the good fragrance of Christ 144 , ambassadors for Christ 145 … of the mystery of the Gospel 146 , a letter of Christ 147 , clothed with Christ 148 , firmly convinced that we are predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son 149 , reproducing Him 150 , becoming like Him 151 , being configured to Him 152 , knowing that we reflect the very image 153 of the Only Son of God” 154 . In a few words: “If we are religious, it is in order to imitate the Incarnate Word, chaste, poor, obedient and son of Mary” 155 . Each one of us members of the Institute knows that we are called to be united to God by the the practice of perfect charity, and by the profession of the three vows we seek to remove at the root all the obstacles that could prevent us from reaching the perfection of charity. These obstacles, as our Proper Law clearly teaches, “can be three: the love of external goods, which is destroyed by the vow of poverty; the desire for sensible pleasures, above all carnal ones, which is destroyed by the vow of chastity; and, finally, the disorder of the human will, which is remedied by the vow of obedience” 156 . Consequently, if the evangelical counsels essentially constitute religious life, charity is its soul and its most intimate reason for being; it is its end. Through the practice of evangelical poverty, we members of the Institute of the Incarnate Word seek to imitate Christ poor: “poor in His birth, poorer in His life and poorest on the cross” 157 , until we come to win total detachment, not only from material goods but from everything that is not God Himself, which presupposes the perfection of charity and complete and consummate holiness. As St. John of the Cross says, “to love is to strip oneself, for God, of all that is not God” 158 . Through the practice of consecrated chastity we offer God the holocaust of our body and of all our natural affections, which implies a preferential choice of exclusive love for God. Our longing is to live a victorious, triumphant chastity, as a longed-for and joyful sacrifice in order to obtain intimate union with God in that spiritual and virginal marriage which characterizes consecrated life, in which the heart is not stifled, but given, made sacred 159 . Furthermore, and most especially, following the example of the Incarnate Word, we members of the Institute give ourselves totally to God through the vow of obedience, by which we wish to make a gift of our will 160 . “Man can offer nothing better to God than the submission of his own will to another for the love of God” 161 , teaches St. Thomas Aquinas. Therefore, in imitation of the Incarnate Word, who became obedient unto death, even death on a cross 162 –by which He redeemed and sanctified men– we seek to live obedience by cooperating with Christ in the salvation of our neighbor, that is, by participating in the Redemption of Christ. Oblation of the kingdom Formula of consecration in the IVE should Your most holy majesty wish to choose and receive me into such a life and state. May the love and grace of the Most Holy Trinity help me to be faithful in the work that He has begun Finally, let us say that “religious life is a following of Christ, but not in just any way, ‘but with the purpose of not turning back. That is why our Lord said: No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the Kingdom of God 163 . And it is with that firm purpose of following Christ that we make the vows’” 164 . But being aware of the sublimity of such an undertaking and of the miseries and weaknesses that afflict us, we not only ask for the intercession of Our Lady and the saints, but we ask God Himself to help us to be faithful in the work He has begun 165 . In the name of the Church and of the Institute, the one who receives the profession of religious vows acknowledges the religious’ explicit desire for total conformity with Christ, the Incarnate Word 166 . A desire that must be made effective and in which one must persevere precisely “for a more abundant holiness of the Church” 167 and the spreading of the kingdom of God. * * * * * The path that leads to holiness, the conquest of the kingdom, entails, then, the acceptance of spiritual combat. “The transformation of the world and the building of the kingdom of Christ, a kingdom of justice and peace, can only be accomplished by the grace and the power of God’s love in us. Only love can transform hearts… The only violence that leads to the building of the kingdom of Christ is the sacrifice and service born of love” 168 . That is why the resounding idea continues to be: to sacrifice oneself. This is how history is steered, even silently and hiddenly 169 . “Faith in the Incarnation”

Have faith in the Incarnation! 1 St. John Paul II Just a few days ago we began Advent, a time in which we devote ourselves –as our Directory of Spirituality teaches us– “in a special way to prayer, to the practice of charity and piety, to denying oneself, to fulfilling better the duties of one’s state, etc.” 2 , as a preparation for the commemoration of the event that inaugurated the Christian era: the birth of Jesus. It can be very illuminating during this time to note that in the first reading that we will read at the Christmas Eve (or Midnight) Mass, we will hear the Prophet Isaiah speak to us of a people that walked in darkness … [that bore a] heavy yoke, and whose shoulders were struck by a rod 3 . And he will also tell us that it was that people, with all its darkness and its pain, that on that first Christmas saw a great light, and its joy was made great 4 . So it is: to a depressed, despairing and distrustful world, God came 5 . And He came to order men and the world according to God, to order not only their hearts and their souls but also their business affairs, their family life, their governments and everything human. This reminds us of that phrase of our Proper Law which we have read and heard so many times and which in this context takes on lofty relevance: “what is not assumed is not redeemed” 6 . That is why our beloved St. John Paul II, quoting the Prologue of the Gospel of St. John, which we will read this Christmas, said: “The Word became flesh, and made his dwelling among us 7 . In saying became flesh, the evangelist wishes to allude to human nature, not only in its mortal condition, but also in its totality. Everything that is human, except sin, was assumed by the Son of God. The Incarnation is the fruit of an immense love, which moved God to want to share fully in our human condition” 8 . So we can say that God solved the social, political, family and economic problems of the world not by promulgating a new economic system; He did not do it by showing us a mountain of papers with the results of His research, revealing new aspects of the problem; nor did He do it with wars. He saved the world from its evils by being born as a Child in the insignificant village of Bethlehem, assuming everything human. If we look closely, that apparently trivial incident, so common and so ordinary, which tells how the owners of the inn turned away the Holy Family, simply telling them that there was no room for them in the inn, is the event that turned the order of the world upside down and the solution that gave it its peace. How many times have we also read that the Virgin Mother sought refuge in a manger and laid the newborn Child on the ground of this world. Well then, that Child, in taking that immense leap from the heavenly life down to the abyss of human existence, like another Samson shook the pillars of the world from their very root, pulled down the building that was already collapsing, and built the Temple of the living God where men will once again be able to sing, because they have found their God. That is the Good News that we are called to proclaim to the ends of the earth. 1. In Christ, human time was filled with eternity But someone may ask: what does the birth of God as a Child have to do with the social, political and economic conditions of His time and of our time? What relationship can there be between the Child lying on the straw of a manger and Caesar on his golden throne? The answer is this: the birth of the Son of God in the flesh was the introduction of a new life into the historical world order; it was the proclamation to the world that the rebuilding of society has to do with its spiritual regeneration; that nations can be saved only when men are reborn to God as God was born that night for men. And this cannot leave us indifferent, we who are members of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, called as we have been to “launch ourselves boldly to restore all things in Christ” 9 . In becoming man, God enters into the created order, becomes part of its history in an entirely new way, draws near to us and gives us a strength that comes from on high. Our Proper Law has, in this regard, a phrase of St. John Paul II that says: “God was never so close to man −and man was never so close to God− as precisely at that moment” 10 . Let us note, then, that “the fact that the Word of God became man brought about a fundamental change in the very condition of time. We can say that, in Christ, human time was filled with eternity. It is a transformation that affects the destiny of all humanity, since ‘the Son of God, by his incarnation, has united himself in some way with every man’ 11 . [For] He came to offer everyone a share in His divine life. [And] The gift of this life entails a share in His eternity” 12 . That is, “the Savior… willed to become the Son of Man so that we might become children of God” 13 . That is the true meaning of Christmas. Jesus became man to make us sharers in His divine life and then in His eternal glory. That is why Christ is born as a Child: to teach us that liberation from all the economic, social and political chaos can be achieved only by a birth. The birth of Christ in souls. Since what is proper to us is “to restore, integrally, all things in Christ” 14 , it seems necessary to emphasize once again that the “Gospel must also penetrate, purify and transform the economic, social and political order” 15 . At the time of Christ’s birth, humanity was weary; it was mentally and spiritually exhausted; for four thousand years it had been carrying out the experiment of humanism, and it found itself like a sick man who cannot cure himself. It was in a state like that of our world, which since the days of the Renaissance has tried to build a civilization upon the self-sufficiency of man without God. How long it takes us men to recognize that humanity, left thus to itself, sinks and becomes little more than a beast. We have sufficient proof that people of an advanced culture can end up becoming a savage culture… (it is enough to watch the news on one of these evenings). Without supernatural help, society goes from bad to worse until its deterioration becomes universal. It is the law of man without God: not evolution but regression; just as it is the law of the sunflower without the sun. Humanity left to itself cannot even tie its own shoelaces. With all the knowledge that man has nowadays about chemistry, about genetics… we cannot make a human life in a laboratory, because we lack the life-giving principle which is the soul, which comes only from God. Life is not a push from below, but a gift from above. It is not the result of man’s necessary ascent, but of God’s descent. It is not “progress”; it is the fruit of the Incarnation. Therefore, like that world into which Christ was born, today’s world also needs not a mixture of old retouched ideas, not a new economic system, not a new financial system: it needs a New Birth. It needs the irruption into its order of a new life and a new spirit, which only God can give. We cannot give ourselves that New Birth, in the same way that none of us can be born again naturally. If we are to be reborn to this new life, the principle of regeneration must come from heaven, and that is precisely the meaning of the Incarnation: the introduction into the world, at the level of human life, of the Life of God, who came not to judge the world but to save it. And that is why we say that the Incarnate Word solved our problems by being born as a Child, because the regeneration of society has to do with being born, being born to the life of grace and growing according to it. In this sense, the Incarnation is not something of the past. How can God belong to the past? The Incarnation is taking place now 16 . For what God did to His individual human nature –which He took from the Blessed Virgin Mary– is what He wishes to do, to no lesser degree, to every human nature in the world; that is, to make us sharers in the divine life. The Incarnate Word, who from all eternity willed to be born in Bethlehem on that cold Christmas night, wants us and all the men and women who walk this world to be born into the eternity of our Heavenly Father, made new creatures, possessed by the new life of His grace and members of His Kingdom. The same divine life that came into the world two thousand twenty years ago must once again permeate the course of the world. And unless it is reborn to that new life, the world will perish. That is why we affirm once again that today, as yesterday, “the correct understanding of the adorable mystery of the Incarnation of the Word is also the keystone for understanding and building the whole human temporal order, its culture and its civilization. To confess the authentic and integral human condition of Jesus, assumed by the eternal Word of God, makes it possible ‘to recover the dimension of the divine in every earthly reality’ 17 ” 18 . This is the truth that must drive us to mission. We must never forget that we “confess the One Master and Lord, Our Jesus Christ 19 , and that in Him is contained a reference to all creatures. […] [Which means that He] is the point of union and meeting place of God and man; of the eschatological and of the incarnate; of sidereal distances and of the millimeter. Therefore, nothing escapes Christ: neither space travel, nor the world of electronics and computers, of the most current science or of the most perfected technology, nor recent discoveries, nor the family, work, culture, the economic-political sphere, etc.” 20 . Evangelizing in “the modern areopagi” 21 is not simply a metaphor; it is our task to make it a reality. In writing these paragraphs it seems inevitable to recall the ardent request that St. John Paul II made to us in the inaugural address of his pontificate: “Open, open wide still more, the doors to Christ! Open to His saving power the boundaries of States, economic and political systems, the vast fields of culture, of civilization and of development. Do not be afraid!” 22 . Likewise, how timely and relevant it is to recall the fatherly exhortation he made in 1984 to some religious, which seems to be addressed especially to us here and now: “Have faith in the Incarnation! The nearness of the Christmas feasts moves me to highlight this fundamental program of your religious life […] To have faith in the Incarnation means first of all to believe firmly in Divine Providence. For God has concretely manifested His love for humanity by entering into it as Man and as Savior. St. John writes: in this is love, not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as expiation for our sins 23 . Many events of present-day life shock and disturb us; the ‘Christian anthropology’ based on the concept of the ‘human person’ created by God, redeemed by Christ, enlightened by the Church, responsible for his acts for eternity, stands in opposition to the immanentist and historicist anthropology with no relation whatsoever to Revelation. […] But with all this, the commemoration of Christmas once again highlights, and continues to highlight, that the Word became flesh to enlighten humanity about its true destiny and about the presence of divine love in the vicissitudes of history. Humility is needed to accept and live this reality. To have faith in the Incarnation also means to love man, whoever he may be, as a creature of God. The very fact that God willed to become man clearly shows how much He loves, esteems and values him. […] And finally, to have faith in the Incarnation means to come to the aid of souls in order to save them. For it was for this that He was born in the grotto of Bethlehem and died on the cross” 24 . That is why the call to subject everything human to our Lord is inescapable, and not to “leave anything untried so that the love of Christ may have supreme primacy in the Church and in society” 25 : since He is the only one who brings men into communion with God, ‘it is necessary that all of human culture be filled with the Gospel’ 26 . There lies the most important and fundamental role that our little Religious Family is called to play. “Christmas is the divine light that gives value and meaning to the life of persons and to the history of humanity,” said the Spiritual Father of the Institute. That is why spending our lives in multiplying Christmases must be the purpose of our priesthood. For it is so that God may be born anew in the hearts of so many men and so many women who still do not know Christ, or who perhaps, knowing Him, are not consistent with it, that the sacrament of Holy Orders has been conferred on us. Evangelization, the preaching of the Good News, belongs to each one of us personally, in spite of our littleness, the lack of means and adverse circumstances. The watchword of this Christmas continues to be to contemplate our life with the eyes of God, full of trust and love. Jesus was born in the poverty of Bethlehem to embrace all of our humanity. Jesus comes back to us this year too, to renew the hidden marvel of the salvation offered to all men and to the whole man. His grace works silently in the intimacy of each soul, because salvation is essentially a dialogue of faith and love with Christ, adored in the mystery of the Incarnation. Let us accept this mystery as the true gift of Christmas and let us be, in turn, magnanimous distributors of this Gift, so that through our self-giving the ideals −the only ones that console− of a life spent in faith, in charity, in goodness, in holiness may triumph, today as always. And this brings us to the next point: 2. Bringing the mystery of Christmas to the people St. John of the Cross wrote that “the works of the Incarnation of the Word and the mysteries of faith; which, being greater works of God and containing in themselves a greater love than those of creatures, produce in the soul a greater effect of love” 27 . St. John Paul II, for his part, imbued no doubt with the doctrine of St. John of the Cross, did not hesitate to affirm that “in the Incarnation, more than in any other work, the glory of God is revealed” 28 . Therefore, bringing to all peoples the light of the truth of God made Man, who has been given to us as “brother, companion and master, price and reward” 29 , is not only an excellent way of giving glory to God, but is the very purpose of evangelization and, certainly, one of the most effective pastoral practices, or rather, “the pastoral practice.” The Holy Father explains: “Man cannot live without love. He is called to love God and neighbor, but in order to love truly he must have the certainty that God loves him” 30 . And for this there is nothing better than the mystery of the newborn Son of God who asks for our love, “through which we spontaneously learn to enter into His feelings, into His thought and into His will: let us learn to live with Him and also to practice with Him the humility of renunciation, which is an essential part of love” 31 . That is the “greater effect of love” that we want to achieve. What is more eloquent for souls “than the tenderness of God: God who looks at us with eyes full of affection, who accepts our misery, God in love with our littleness” 32 . 3. An altogether singular example Before mentioning the different activities that our Proper Law proposes to us during the Christmas season, I would like to mention, as an altogether singular example for us, how St. John Paul II lived Christmas, for he lived it as a time of particular spiritual intensity. For we consider that his example, so human and at the same time so supernatural, can be replicated with a certain ease in our lives, in our communities, in our missions, given its simplicity. Let us see: His devotion to the mystery of Christmas goes back to his childhood, and he describes it very succinctly but beautifully in a letter addressed to children: “When, many years ago, I was a child like you, I too lived the serene atmosphere of Christmas, and on seeing the star of Bethlehem shine I would run to the Nativity scene with my friends to remember what happened in Palestine 2000 years ago. We children expressed our joy above all with songs. How beautiful and moving are the carols which, in the tradition of each people, are sung around the Nativity scene! What deep feelings they contain and, above all, how much joy and tenderness they express toward the divine Child who came into the world on Christmas Eve! The days that follow the birth of Jesus are also days of celebration: thus, eight days later, we remember that, according to the tradition of the Old Testament, a name was given to the Child, calling Him Jesus” 33 . Those who spent Christmas with the Holy Father testify 34 how much he liked this time of year and how he longed for the coming of Christmas. They say that he always wanted to celebrate it in a family atmosphere, according to the Polish tradition; that is why he generally invited all those who shared his daily life with him, the sisters who worked in his house and the secretaries. He also invited some of his old friends from Krakow along with their families. On Christmas night, John Paul II would begin by lighting a candle and placing it in the window. They say that he began this tradition in 1981, when General Jaruzelski declared martial law in Poland; and the Pope wanted to symbolize with that candle his closeness to his persecuted fellow citizens. Once this was done, a passage from the Gospel was read, and only after that did the dinner begin, at which, of course, traditional Polish dishes were served. After dinner, carols were sung. Those who lived with him testify that he liked singing very much, and during the Christmas season he did so every night from December 24 to January 6. John Paul II also liked the Christmas tree, and very much so. It was he who began the tradition of setting up a monumental Nativity scene next to a giant Christmas tree in St. Peter’s Square. Not content with this, he also liked to decorate his apartment with the little trees from the Polish mountains of Zakopane that were sent to him, and in the hallway during the Christmas season there was always a Nativity scene, “because there is no Christmas without a Nativity scene,” he used to say. What is more, “in the Christmas period the stable with the manger occupies a central place in the Church” 35 , the Holy Father put in writing. Now, under the Christmas tree there were no presents −following the Polish tradition− in which presents are given on December 6, the day of St. Nicholas. So on that day, “St. Nicholas came into the refectory, announced by bells. It was one of the sisters dressed up as the ‘Saint of presents.’ I don’t know if I should tell you this,” said one of his secretaries −now Archbishop Mieczyslaw Mokrzycki− and he continued: “To tell the truth, in my first year in the papal household I was surprised, because it seemed to me a children’s party and we were all quite grown up. But it really moved me a great deal to see how much the Pope loved us, and also because I understood that in those moments he was remembering his childhood in Wadowice” 36 . “At that point, ‘St. Nicholas’ had something to say to each person present there before handing out the presents. Little things: pastries, fruit, a scarf, a shirt, gloves. We joked and we laughed. And so it always was, every year, until the end, until December 2004” 37 . This little testimony lets us glimpse, along with the simplicity of heart of the Holy Pope, the care and importance he gave to every detail of Christmas as a family, as if wanting to make others perceive −in a tangible way− God’s love for each one of them personally. Moved surely by the same intention, it is no minor detail to recall the fact that in 1959, as a bishop, he celebrated Christmas in the open air in Nowa Huta, the so-called ‘model workers’ city’ on the outskirts of Krakow, the first city in the history of Poland deliberately built without a church. Likewise, throughout the length and breadth of his whole pontificate, but especially at Christmas, St. John Paul II strove to make “the unheard-of tenderness of God, which is offered to all men and which is admirably manifested in the Child of Bethlehem” 38 reach everyone. He wanted to infect everyone with the Christmas spirit. Thus, for example, when he visited New York in October 1995, before thousands of people in Central Park, the Pope who had loved Christmas since he was a child suddenly set aside the text he had prepared and began to speak about one of his favorite Polish carols, which he then began, spontaneously, to sing. The crowd applauded with delight, to which the Pope responded by saying: “And to think that you don’t even know Polish” 39 , and the people applauded even more vigorously. Then he said: “That is a hymn that moves us deeply by reminding us that Jesus, the Son of God, was born of Mary, born to sanctify us and to make us adopted sons and daughters of God. It is a hymn to the creative power of the Holy Spirit. It is a song to help us not to be afraid. If I speak of Christmas it is because in less than five years we will reach the end of the Second Millennium, two thousand years since the birth of Christ on that first Christmas night in Bethlehem. We must let the Holy Spirit prepare us for this important event, which is another significant stage of His passage through history and of our pilgrimage of faith” 40 . 4. Our way of celebrating Christmas Similarly, and under the guidance of the Polish pope, each of the members of the Institute, imbued with faith in the mystery of the Incarnation and with great apostolic enthusiasm 41 and priestly self-giving 42 , must not only personally live the Christmas season in all its spiritual depth and with festive joy 43 , but must also strive to transmit, spread and form others in the spirit proper to Christmas; even through the humblest expressions of popular sensibility, such as setting up a good Nativity scene, decorating a beautiful Christmas tree, promoting the participation of as many as possible in the ‘living Nativity,’ organizing pilgrimages to the Nativity scenes in the various churches or homes of the faithful, singing carols or holding Christmas concerts, etc. All these expressions of popular piety help people grasp intuitively 44 : – the value of the ‘spirituality of gift,’ proper to Christmas: a child is born to us, a son is given to us 45 , a gift that is the expression of the infinite love of God, who so loved the world that He gave us His only Son 46 ; – the message of solidarity that the event of Christmas entails: solidarity above all with sinful man, for whom, in Jesus, God became man for us men and for our salvation; solidarity with the poor, because the Son of God, though He was rich, became poor to enrich us by His poverty 47 ; – the sacred value of life and the wonderful event that takes place in every woman’s giving birth, because through Mary’s giving birth the Word of life came to men and became visible 48 ; – the value of messianic joy and peace, the deep aspirations of men of all times: the Angels announce to the shepherds that the Savior of the world, the Prince of peace, has been born 49 , and express the wish for peace on earth to men whom God loves 50 ; – the atmosphere of simplicity and poverty, of humility and trust in God, that surrounds the events of the birth of the Child Jesus. And so, in a simple way, all these practices of piety help to safeguard the memory of our Lord’s earthly coming, and keep the strong religious tradition linked to Christmas from becoming fertile ground for consumerism or for the infiltration of neo-paganism 51 . Our Proper Law, for its part, though briefly, lists several activities which are not only expected to be carried out in our houses of formation or in our parishes, but which it wishes to see fostered and enriched as much as possible −whenever pastoral prudence allows− making room for apostolic creativity to give rise to other activities that awaken in souls the desired “holy familiarity with the Word made flesh” 52 . The Directory of Parishes, for example, mentions that the Christmas Vigil should be solemnized 53 , and it may very well be preceded by a Christmas novena, since this is one of the high points of parish pastoral work 54 . Likewise, it stresses that this season should be made the most of, and with that in view it must be carefully prepared 55 The Directory of Works of Mercy points out, in addition, that “it would be praiseworthy to foster the works of mercy among our laity. Such as the pious tradition of clothing a poor child on Christmas Day in memory of the Child of Bethlehem, or a whole family on the day of the Holy Family” 56 . Charity toward the poor who come looking for food should not be forgotten when preparing Christmas dinner 57 , and this not only in the missions but also in the houses of formation. The Directory of Minor Seminaries says, in turn, that one of the hobbies it would be nice for the minor seminarians to learn is various techniques for building Nativity scenes 58 . Elsewhere, the creation of an Association of Christmas Nativity Scenes is also suggested, to take charge of promoting, spreading and awarding prizes to the public and family Nativity scenes made in a parish 59 . On the other hand, the Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy issued by the Congregation for Divine Worship and the Discipline of the Sacraments during the pontificate of John Paul II suggests things that may very well enrich the activities already being carried out, or that can begin to be put into practice, whether at the community or parish level as appropriate 60 ; for example: → During Advent The Directory points out the tradition of the Advent wreath, which is customary above all in Germanic countries and in North America, and has become a symbol of Advent in Christian homes. The Advent wreath consists of four candles on a wreath of green branches, which are lit progressively, Sunday after Sunday, until the solemnity of Christmas. It is a remembrance of the various stages of the history of salvation before Christ and a symbol of the prophetic light that gradually illumined the night of waiting, until the dawn of the Sun of justice 61 . It is good to make it, and to make it well, explaining the value of these traditions both to the faithful and to the religious of our communities. Likewise, mention is made of Advent processions, which are a proclamation through the streets of the city of the coming birth of the Savior (the ‘clear star’ in some places in Italy), or else representations of the journey of Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem and their search for a welcoming place for the birth of Jesus (known as the ‘posadas’ in the Spanish and Latin American tradition). Or likewise the novenas held at dawn in some of our missions, such as in the Philippines (known as Simbang Gabi), Guyana, etc. → For Christmas Eve: In the time between First Vespers of Christmas and the Midnight Eucharistic celebration, together with the tradition of Christmas carols, which are very powerful instruments for transmitting the Christmas message of joy and peace, popular piety proposes some of its expressions of prayer, differing from country to country, which it is fitting to value and, where necessary, to harmonize with the celebrations of the Liturgy. These may include, for example: – “living Nativity scenes,” and the inauguration of the household Nativity scene, which can provide an occasion of prayer for the whole family: a prayer that includes the reading of the account of the birth of Jesus according to St. Luke, in which the typical Christmas songs resound and supplications and praises are raised, above all those of the children, the protagonists of this family gathering; – the inauguration of the Christmas tree. This too lends itself to an act of family prayer similar to the previous one. – Christmas dinner. The Christian family which every day, according to tradition, blesses the table and gives thanks to the Lord for the gift of food, will carry out this gesture with greater intensity and attention at Christmas dinner, in which the firmness and the joy of family bonds are manifested in all their strength. The Church also wishes that all the faithful take part on the night of December 24, if possible, in the Office of Readings, as an immediate preparation for the celebration of the Midnight Eucharist. Where this is not done, it may be fitting to prepare a vigil with songs, readings and elements of popular piety, drawing inspiration from that office. At Midnight Mass, which has great liturgical meaning and enjoys popular esteem, the following may be highlighted: – at the beginning of Mass, the chanting of the proclamation of the birth of the Lord, with the formula of the Roman Martyrology; – the prayer of the faithful, which should take on a truly universal character, even, where appropriate, with the use of several languages as a sign; and in the presentation of the gifts at the offertory there will always be a concrete remembrance of the poor; – at the end of the celebration, the faithful may kiss the image of the Child Jesus, and it may be placed in the Nativity scene set up in the church or in some nearby place. It is also important to give people catechetical instruction about the possibility of gaining plenary indulgences during the Urbi et orbi blessing imparted by the Pope, which must be accompanied by confession and communion on the part of whoever receives it with faith and devotion, even through television, radio or the internet. I would like to add a word about Christmas songs, the carols, which should fill this whole season. It is beautiful for us to foster these songs, in the liturgy, in families, in parish groups, in Christmas processions, etc. May we religious be instruments for maintaining, enriching and increasing these beautiful traditions. → The Feast of the Holy Family For the Feast of the Holy Family (Sunday within the octave of Christmas), our parishes should encourage the whole family to take part together in the Eucharist on that day. And it would be very meaningful for the family to entrust itself anew to the patronage of the Holy Family of Nazareth, for the blessing of children to take place, or for marriage promises to be renewed. In several of our jurisdictions, this day is also used for us religious to gather with the tertiaries to celebrate the Christmas season “as a family,” which has already become a beautiful tradition. → December 31 It is customary to have prolonged exposition of the Blessed Sacrament, which offers both religious and faithful an occasion for a time of prayer, preferably in silence; and the singing of the Te Deum, as a communal expression of praise and thanksgiving for the benefits obtained from God in the course of the year that is about to end. In some places, above all in monastic communities, on the night of December 31 a prayer vigil takes place, which usually concludes with the celebration of the Eucharist. This vigil should be encouraged, and its celebration must be in harmony with the liturgical content of the Octave of Christmas, lived not only as a justified reaction to the carelessness and dissipation with which society lives the passage from one year to another, but as a vigilant offering to the Lord of the first fruits of the new year. → The Solemnity of Mary, Mother of God In the West, January 1 is a day for exchanging greetings: it is the beginning of the civil year. The faithful are caught up in the festive atmosphere of the beginning of the year and exchange wishes of “Happy New Year” with everyone. However, it is good to know how to give this custom a Christian meaning, and make of it almost an expression of piety. The faithful know that “the new year” is under the lordship of Christ, and that is why, in exchanging greetings and good wishes, they place it, implicitly or explicitly, under the dominion of Christ, to whom belong the days and the eternal ages 62 . Connected with this awareness is the rather widespread custom of singing on January 1 the hymn Veni, creator Spiritus, so that the Spirit of the Lord may direct the thoughts and actions of each and every one of the faithful and of Christian communities throughout the whole year. In addition, on that day, since 1967, the “World Day of Peace” has been celebrated. In short, much more could be said, but what is important is that we all live Christmas as it should be lived: in a Christian way, as a family, and with festive joy. How much our world needs all this! It is our honorable office to permeate culture with the truth of Christmas: “The only-begotten Son of God, wishing that we too might be sharers in His divinity, assumed our human nature, so that, having become man, He might make men gods” 63 , that is, sharers by grace in the divine nature. And it is imperative to implore heaven that this divine life which makes souls fruitful may descend upon souls –as the dew descends each morning upon the field. A holy Christmas! and a holy year!, which is the same as wishing you everything, everything good in the life here below that may serve, or at least not hinder, the gaining of everything good in the life beyond, which is the true life. And since wishes, if they are not turned into works or prayers, are of no use, let us turn our wishes into supplications to the Incarnate Word and His Most Holy Mother for one another. May the simplicity and tenderness of the Child in Bethlehem make its nest in your hearts and spread to your communities and, better still, to the whole world, thanks to you. A very happy and holy Christmas! Notes 1 To the religious of the Hospitaller Order of St. John of God in Rome (23/12/1984). 2 Directory of Spirituality, 103 3 Cf. Is 9:2; 4. 4 Cf.
