“Truth on social networks”

This Word is truly the Truth 1 Directory of Spirituality , 54 “Social networks exponentially amplify gossip and idle talk, to the point that we do not know what is true, no matter what the subject may be” 2 . This sentence, which belongs to Tristan Harris 3 , gives us in some way a glimpse of the dictatorship of relativism reigning in modern culture. Harris argues that “technology is degrading our capacity for attention, our relationships, our courtesy, our community, our habits, our differences, our critical thinking […] our mental health, our creativity, our intimacy, our self-esteem, our productivity, our common ground, our shared truth, our attention, our systems of government, nations, our values. The great problem with technology −he continues− is that it is degrading human beings” 4 . This problem has not escaped the Pontiffs of our time, including Pope Francis himself, who in his latest encyclical Fratelli tutti speaks of “a degradation: a ‘leveling down’ by way of a superficial and negotiated consensus” 5 , due, among other things, to “a feverish exchange of opinions on social networks, often directed by media information that is not always reliable . They are merely monologues that proceed in parallel, perhaps imposing themselves on the attention of others by their loud or aggressive tones . But monologues commit no one, to the point that their contents are frequently opportunistic and contradictory” 6 and they become mere “spreaders of confusion and lies” 7 . St. John Paul II already warned us of the same thing two decades ago: “Media culture has been progressively penetrated by a typically postmodern sense in which the only absolute truth admitted is the nonexistence of absolute truth or, if it did exist, it would be inaccessible to human reason and therefore irrelevant. With such a perspective, what matters is not the truth but ‘the story’; if something is newsworthy or entertaining, the temptation to set aside considerations of truth becomes almost always irresistible” 8 . Likewise, Pope Francis speaks of “the illusion of communication” through social media, in which “everything is to be shown, and each individual [or Institution] becomes the object of gazes that pry, strip bare and spread abroad, frequently anonymously. [Where] respect for the other is shattered” 9 under the false excuse of “a suitable form of group care” 10 or under the cloak of a “false community mystique” 11 , when in reality these are associations against someone whom they consider an enemy 12 . That is why, now that we are close to the celebration of the Incarnation of the Word − Way, Truth and Life 13 − , recognizing that we are called to an absolute and total love of the truth, to work so that the principles of the Gospel may effectively influence the life of men, and to combat error with all our strength, in the midst of a world that believes that error has the same rights among men as the truth, it has seemed fitting to us to devote these pages to developing (even if briefly) the fact that the noble office of being “servants of the Truth” 14 most often brings with it the opposition of the world; for have we perhaps forgotten that our Lord called Satan, the prince of this world, the father of lies 15 ? As everyone is aware, many institutions and members of the Church who work actively in spreading the Gospel, among them our Institute, are constantly and unjustly slandered, defamed and misrepresented on today’s online services by cowardly minds who unscrupulously write without knowing what they are doing 16 , and speak and pronounce on what they do not know. But it is precisely full adherence to the truth that the Word became flesh that makes man free, and its proclamation from the housetops of this world 17 is the cause for which it is worth suffering every difficulty in order to faithfully fulfill the mission that has been entrusted to us. 1. Modern totalitarianism Let us begin by quoting here a “memorable” text of St. John Paul II: “If there is no transcendent truth, in obedience to which man achieves his full identity, then there is no sure principle for guaranteeing just relations between people […] If one does not acknowledge transcendent truth, then the force of power takes over, and each person tends to make full use of the means at his disposal in order to impose his own interests or his own opinion, with no regard for the rights of others. […] The root of modern totalitarianism, therefore, is to be found in the denial of the transcendent dignity of the human person, who as the visible image of the invisible God” 18 . That is why, when “the logic of being is replaced by the ‘logic of power’ and science and technology are withdrawn from the service of man (through leveling) and subordinated to ever-increasing productive efficiency, spiritual autonomies are no longer admitted” 19 and totalitarianism is established. This is what is currently happening because of technocracy, for which “greatness” is miserable opulence and its end is well-being; it is, then, a satanic inversion of the very concept of well-being, which makes men slaves of the “standard of living” and feeds everything that is vanity. And since in such a world the understanding of being is an unbearable scandal, it hates the intellect, as all tyrannies do. “What is happening to us today” −points out Pope Francis− “and dragging us into a perverse and empty logic, is that ethics and politics are being assimilated to physics. Good and evil no longer exist in themselves; there is only a calculus of benefits and burdens. As a result of the displacement of moral reasoning, the law is no longer seen as reflecting a fundamental notion of justice but as mirroring the dominant ideas. Here we enter into a degradation : a ‘leveling down’ by way of a superficial and negotiated consensus. In the end, the logic of force prevails” 20 . In this context, and so that we may better grasp the reality of modern totalitarianism and realize that it is not a mere philosophical disquisition, it seems worthwhile to us to bring up here the opinion of those very people who were involved from within in the social networks that the whole world uses today. Tristan Harris himself, the former Google employee we quoted at the beginning, admits: “The classic saying is: ‘If you’re not paying for the product, then you are the product .’ A lot of people think, you know, ‘Oh, well, Google is just a search box and Facebook is just a place to see what my friends are doing and look at their photos.’ But what they don’t realize is that they [Google and Facebook] are competing for your attention. […] You know, Facebook, Snapchat, Twitter, Instagram, YouTube, companies like these have a business model that consists in keeping people hooked on the screen. […] It is a for-profit business model of disinformation . You make money to the extent that you allow messages to reach anyone at the best price without any kind of regulation” 21 . Sandy Parakilas, a former Facebook employee, for his part maintains: “We have created a system that leans toward false information . Not because we want to, but because false information makes companies more money than the truth . The truth is boring ” 22 . People from this milieu also speak of AI (artificial intelligence) as what is currently driving the world. By the term ‘artificial intelligence’ they mean computers (machines) that imitate cognitive functions such as ‘learning’ and ‘problem-solving ability’. “In these companies like Google there are immense rooms, some of them underground, some of them underwater, just of computers. Tons and tons of computers, as far as the eye can see. They are all deeply interconnected with one another and run extremely complicated programs, sending information back and forth to one another all the time. They run many different programs, for many different products, on those same machines. Some of those things could be described as simple algorithms, while others could be described as algorithms so complicated that they could be called intelligence” 23 , says Justin Rosenstein 24 . Such mega-computers operate with algorithms according to some definition of success. If a company wants to sell something (a product, a form of government, a religion, an idea, a cultural model, etc.), it builds the algorithm according to that definition of success (which generally has a commercial or political interest), which in the vast majority of cases will result in a gain (of money). Every day the computer itself ‘learns’ how to sell more and better: which ads to show, in what order, which video to recommend, etc. (and it does this differently with each person) so that the person spends more and more time entertained with that product (or idea) until he finally buys it or consents to it. To do this, AI needs a great deal of information about us, and it certainly takes care to collect it. Thus, for example, a person who reads a newspaper online, or receives the news in his email, or watches some program on YouTube may come to believe that everyone thinks the same as he does, simply because the opinions he reads and the videos YouTube recommends to him are precisely similar to the ones he looks for, the news is generally of the kind he usually reads, etc.; and so the temptation grows to accept something he does not even know to be true (because the distinction between truth and illusion is distorted), and critical thinking is nullified, as he thinks something is true simply because there is a ‘manufactured consensus’ given by the number of views of a video, or the number of comments, etc., with the result, not infrequently, that something completely false goes ‘viral’. Not long ago a politician in the United States said: “We are a nation of people who have isolated ourselves so as to watch only the channels that tell us we are right” 25 . And when one has reached that point, one is easily manipulated, because in reality one is choosing to see only the options that YouTube, Google, etc. show one. Another example: Facebook tells people ‘choose your friends’, but people do not realize that Facebook has already chosen them for them, since it presents to them only those whom the computer ‘thinks’ might interest them. All this has serious cultural, psychological, political, sociological consequences, etc., as is to be expected 26 . A former Facebook investor said: “If everyone is entitled to their own facts, there is really no need for mutual agreement, no need for people to come together. In fact, there is no need for people to interact. [However,] We need… to share some of the reality we understand” 27 . That is why in 2009 Pope Benedict XVI had warned: “Life is not a mere succession of facts and experiences; rather it is a search for truth, goodness and beauty. Our decisions and the exercise of our freedom are directed toward these ends, and in them −truth, goodness and beauty− we find happiness and joy. We must not let ourselves be deceived by those who merely seek consumers in a market of undifferentiated possibilities, where choice itself is presented as the good, novelty is confused with beauty, and subjective experience supplants truth” 28 . For her part, Cathy O’Neil 29 maintains that unfortunately “we are allowing the technologists to frame this as a problem they are prepared to solve… That is a lie. People talk about AI (artificial intelligence) as if it knew the truth. AI will not solve these problems. AI cannot solve the problem of false news ( fake news ). Google (she is referring to its computers) does not have the option of saying, ‘Oh, is this a conspiracy? Is this true?’ Because they do not know what the truth is… They have no indicator of truth that is better than a click” 30 . These few examples serve to show how “technocracy does not admit the criticisms of the intellect nor critical thinking (replaced by ‘team research’); nor, at bottom, does it admit any dialogue at all, because it admits it only in one direction (with those who are inside the ‘system’); for the true opponent there is no room except aggressive silence, typical of dogmatic intransigence ‘against all knowledge that does not have external experience as its origin and calculation based on data as its result’” 31 . “Reading (which makes one think) is replaced by the ‘civilization’ of the image, by that stupefying hammering of images that admits ‘dialogue’ in only one direction. This tyranny is in truth ashamed of the tradition of the West and wages an offensive against six essential factors: Against authority, in whose empty place it sets up an insidious form of authoritarianism (at the same time as it ‘speaks’ against it); Against the environment; Against feelings; Against every moral principle; Against imagination; and Against political ideologies themselves, in pursuit of union-industrial power. This reduction of everything to itself leads technocracy, by means of ‘rational planning’, to the destruction of the landscape and of the sense of nature at the hands of ‘technicians’ and ‘experts’ 32 . They are precisely the ones who first spoke of the problem of ‘pollution’ (caused by themselves) without noticing what Sciacca calls the ‘pollution of consciences’, which is its main and true cause” 33 . Sadly, this leads not only to the destruction of the natural habitat but also of the urban habitat (“all together and each one shut up in his isolation”) as well as of the political-social habitat; to “de-theologization,” which runs parallel to “depoliticization”: a politics without politicians who think or thinkers who think about politics, whose “democratic character” works like this: first, the plans are foreseen, drawn up and carried out according to technocratic criteria, the only one with the power of decision; then, the working and consuming “masses” are persuaded by propaganda and advertising; finally, once the persuasion has been carried out, the plans are submitted to the “democratic consultation that gives ‘consensus’” 34 . Thus everything is integrated into the system: “democratized” education (the learning machine is already foreseen), the confusion of language as a sign of the loss of the exercise of thinking 35 and, finally, the worldwide technological “organization,” the great totalitarian tyranny, above communism, liberalism and the Church conceived as a Christianity without faith or sense of the supernatural. […] Cultural impiety is, therefore, the most terrible totalitarianism, as an expression of the nihilation of Being. It would be naive to think that this technocratic totalitarianism exists only in the so-called “people’s democracies” or communist ones, for, as is evident given the massive reach of the media, it also exists in the so-called “Western democracies,” where men are instruments of production for consumption. “The true ‘product’ of this process is the uncultured man, though ‘armed with the most developed technology’ and at the same time capable, out of hatred, of destroying the whole world of culture; it is thus a sort of uneducated ‘uncivil’ man who ‘has only the appearances of civilization, but barbarous customs and laws: civilization falls into incivility’; the right to be well informed is violated daily by the so-called ‘social communication media’ and true anti-democracy slips into populism, because ‘populism is the great enemy of the education of the people, if to educate oneself is to mean to raise oneself up’ (to perfect oneself as a man); there does not and cannot exist a ‘collective’ culture (which is the opposite of culture) nor truly cultural tasks in ‘teams’ or ‘cooperatives’ of ‘thinkers’; and so, through the abuse of these media (cinema, television, social networks, websites, apps), a culture of the image, a substitute for the book… murders the word and thought,’ condemning children (and future men) to ‘chronic infantilism, which is what the civilization of well-being and technology, the anti-culture, looks toward” 36 . That is why a contemporary author said that we are heading “toward a dark age with so many interplanetary voyages and other marvels of measurement, all rational calculations without intellect –whose sign is limit– all technical elaboration and manipulation of empirical and verifiable data for social well-being, but without love, which is the sign of the sacred; an age that will taste to the very bottom all the uncivilized misery of man without truth and without God , extreme spiritual destitution” 37 . Technocratic cultural impiety also presupposes, as we have just noted, religious impiety, because that “organization” is considered the end of all religions; at bottom, it is considered the “earthly fulfillment of the messianic promises” 38 . In such an immanent and horizontal society there is room only for a worldly, “new” and, above all, de-Hellenized “Christianity,” since the existence of a transcendent God is not a Christian problem but a Greek one; God died with Christ and, therefore, Christianity “frees itself from God” 39 ; what is more, this vertical fall of the Church includes the de-Romanization of Christianity (the death of the “Church”-institution), and thus the Church can turn to the building of Babylon, the impious society 40 . In the first case, “ a ‘de-Hellenized’ Christianity is a Christianity that has renounced the logos or the natural light of truth and, with it, being, and therefore it is impossible for it to receive Christ as supernatural Logos ” 41 . Without a metaphysics of being (without logos) it is not possible to elaborate dogmatic theology, nor even positive theology, and biblical theology is denatured 42 . Such, then, is the first picture of religious impiety, which presupposes the loss of being and, therefore, the loss of respect (piety) for everything; in other words, impiety is “the absence of respect for every thing, institution and value” 43 . Thus the spirit of the world as world imposes itself. “Hence this immense technocratic totalitarianism, in relation to the Church, advocates, first, the integration of the Church into technocratic society within the shared horizon of a welfare society, thus perfectly accomplishing ‘the Enlightenment and neo-Enlightenment continuity between liberalism, communism and modernism”; secondly, the distortion of the Second Vatican Council so as ‘to prevent the awakening of faith within the welfare society’ 44 ” 45 . Pope Benedict XVI denounced a few years ago: “Darkness truly threatens man because, yes, he can see and examine tangible, material things, but not where the world is going and where it comes from. Where our own life is going. What is good and what is evil. The darkness concerning God and his values is the real threat to our existence and to the world in general. If God and values, the difference between good and evil, remain in darkness, then all the other illuminations that give us such incredible power are not only progress, but at the same time also threats that put us, and the world, in danger. […] In material things we know and can do so much, but what goes beyond this, God and the good, we no longer manage to identify” 46 . The question then arises: What is to be done? “We must get used to unmasking the various ways in which the truth is manipulated, distorted and concealed in public and private spheres. What we call ‘truth’ is not only the spreading of facts carried out by journalism . It is above all the search for the most solid foundations that lie behind our choices and also behind our laws. This presupposes accepting that human intelligence can go beyond the conveniences of the moment and grasp some truths that do not change, that were true before us and will always be so” 47 . “That is why faith, which shows us the light of God, is the true illumination ; it is an irruption of God’s light into our world, an opening of our eyes to the true light” 48 . In this sense, it seems essential to us to recall the role of the missions ad gentes carried out also through media of every kind, since these can play an essential role in the work of evangelization and in making available to people the truths and values on which human dignity rests and by which it is perfected, together with the values of transcendence. The presence of the Church in the media is, in fact, an important aspect of the inculturation of the Gospel required by the new evangelization to which the Holy Spirit is calling the Church throughout the world 49 . And we are convinced that Christ, our Divine Redeemer, is the Good News, ever perennial, which can and must be preached through the various means of communication so as to be heard by the whole world. 2. I am the light of the world 50 Let us place ourselves, then, in that Gospel passage which sets us in the city of Jerusalem, during the feast of Tabernacles, and let us contemplate the Incarnate Word. As soon as Jesus appears on the scene, the crowds look for him, though not before muttering a great deal about Him (the evangelist points out to us), since some said ‘he is a good man’ while others said ‘No! he leads the people astray’ 51 . Nevertheless, having gone up to the Temple, Jesus declares to his hearers that his doctrine is the doctrine of God who sent him and of whom He is the Son. In the court of the Temple, there were probably, very near Him, some sumptuous hangings from which hung two lamps that spread their light over the Temple. Our Lord sat there, between those immense lamps that lit up the faces of friends and enemies alike, and at the threshold of the Holy of Holies, He who is thrice Holy proclaimed that the Light of God had come to enlighten men who walked in darkness: I am the Light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life 52 . There was no error in his words. He did not say that he was like the light; he did not say that he was like those lamps that lit up the darkness; he did not say that he was the light of some people and not of others; but that he was the very Light itself, which is identified with the Truth and which enlightens every man who comes into this world. To say such a thing, Jesus had to know all things. Yet his audience did not remember having seen him in any of the great schools of Jerusalem, nor having seen him seated at the feet of Gamaliel. Then those who heard him −common people, Pharisees, Levites− looked at one another until they ended up asking him: Who are you? They were astonished to hear him say that his Truth was the Light of the world and that he possessed it from all eternity: You are from below, I am from above. You are of this world, I am not of this world. […] If you remain faithful to my word, you will truly be my disciples: you will know the truth and the truth will make you free 53 . His hearers, not grasping the great truth that the Incarnate Word was the Light of the world, asked: Are you perhaps greater than our father Abraham, who died? 54 . Our Lord’s answer was nothing other than an affirmation of his eternity: Abraham, your father, thrilled with joy, hoping to see my Day: he saw it and was filled with gladness. The Jews said to him: ‘You are not yet fifty years old, and you have seen Abraham?’ Jesus answered: ‘I assure you, before Abraham was born, I Am’ 55 . In saying “I Am,” Yahweh, Jesus identifies himself with the Light, equal to the Truth; that is, he identifies himself with God. That was his battle cry to an erring world, an alarm that rang out for the slaves who were to be set free in the name of the one Truth that makes man free. But just as the noonday sun is too strong for weak eyes, so the Light of the world was too bright for those minds accustomed only to the light of a candle. That is why, in their fury against Him who claimed to be the only Truth of this world, the Light of Life, uncreated Wisdom, the people took up stones to stone him 56 . But at the very moment when the arms of those who sought to stone him drew back for the swing of the sling, Christ hid himself 57 proving once more that He was the Truth, for the Truth hides itself from those who seek to kill it and do not seek it with simplicity and humility of heart. Of them the Holy Father said: “There are people […] who cannot live in the light because they are accustomed to darkness. The light dazzles them; they cannot see. They are human bats: they only know how to move about at night. […] But the worst thing is that the eyes, the eyes of the soul, from living so much in darkness grow so used to it that they end up not knowing what light is. They lose the sense of light because they grow more accustomed to darkness” 58 . “What scandalizes people about Jesus is his nature as God incarnate. And as with Him, so with us too ‘they set traps for us in life’” 59 . And just as Christ suffered opposition, rejection, and even death for bearing witness to the Truth, so must his followers suffer. The Incarnate Word does not deceive us; he told us clearly: They will hand you over to the sanhedrins, and you will be scourged in the synagogues, and you will appear before governors and kings because of Me, to bear witness before them… you will be hated because of my name 60 . That is why, with wise insight, Ven. Archbishop Fulton Sheen said: “To be tolerated [or accepted] is sometimes a sign of weakness; and to be persecuted, a compliment. The mediocre survive. The person who is persecuted shows that his belief is taken seriously and that the cause he defends must be eliminated if evil is to triumph. It is true that the wicked are persecuted, but they do not fall within the beatitude, for as St. Paul says: if I hand over my body to be burned, but have not charity, it profits me nothing 61 . A martyr must die for his faith, not for his property, not for his good name, not for his party. Numerous are the martyrs who are the architects of their own martyrdom, but they have no place in the ranks of those to whom the Kingdom of heaven was promised for carrying the cross on their shoulders” 62 . What we mean by this is that, although many –even “religious people” 63 − are bent on destroying us, and attack us by becoming “part of networks of verbal violence through the internet and the various forums or spaces of digital exchange, even in Catholic media where defamation and slander tend to be treated as normal, where all ethics and respect for the good name of others seems to be left aside 64 , our task continues to be to bear witness −in a luminous and singular way 65 − to the inescapable truth that the Word became flesh… full of grace and truth 66 . Now then, consider any other ‘master,’ philosopher, spiritual guru, great thinker, moralist or preacher who has walked upon this earth, no matter which. None identified himself with the truth. They may have said ‘I will show you the way,’ but none said as our Lord did: I am the Way . They may have said: ‘I will tell you how to possess the truth or how to discover the light,’ but none said as our Lord did: I am the Truth; I am the Light of the world . Many may have promised a life that dies no more, but none said as our Lord did: I am the Life . All pointed to an ideal outside themselves. In the case of our Lord, He is the Ideal with a capital letter. There is no system outside Him. His most adorable Person is the system. There is no way outside his Way, no truth outside his Truth, no life outside his Life. There is nothing outside or beyond the Incarnate Word, for in Him all the paths and truths scattered throughout the world find their center and their source, to such a degree that Christ could affirm with all authority: Without me you can do nothing 67 . Which is as much as to say: ‘you will be able to buy and sell without Me, you will be able to enlarge your buildings and increase your possessions without Me, you will be able to build ships and create incredibly powerful technologies, but you will not be able to take a single step toward the Ideal, which is the divine Life, without Me, because I am the Life . You cannot even go to the Father without Me, because the Father and I are One 68 . “The Incarnate Word governs the whole law of relations of the supernatural and the natural order, but He also governs what, within the latter, must be ordered, without unhealthy dialectic and against every false monism” 69 . That is why the Constitutions tell us very clearly: “Our Lord, [is the] Way we must follow and [the] example we must imitate” 70 and the truth we must proclaim. Even when they contradict us or seek to undermine what we have barely managed to raise up with so much sacrifice, even in the midst of the harshest poverty and in spite of our great miseries. Christ, true God and true Man, is and must always be the platform from which we launch ourselves boldly to restore all things 71 . That is our noble mission, for God wants all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth 72 , recognizing that Christ himself, who sends us on mission, at the same time promises us his divine help: I will be with you always, until the end of the world 73 . To act otherwise would be not only to live far from reality but to betray the very purpose for which God has raised up the Institute. Without the Incarnation of the Word the foundation of our faith is lacking, and without faith, our life collapses. It is true that, as St. John Paul II pointed out, “the world of the media can sometimes seem an environment as unfavorable to evangelization as the pagan world was in the time of the Apostles. But just as the first witnesses of the Good News did not withdraw when they met hostility, neither must the followers of Christ do so today. The cry of St. Paul still resounds among us: Woe to me if I do not proclaim the Gospel! 74 ” 75 . “In a particular way −the Constitutions point out, and we have grown up in religious life hearing it− it is urgent to exercise the apostolate in the so-called ‘modern areopagi.’ Among these new environments is, first of all, the world of communication, on which the work of evangelization of modern culture largely depends , since ‘it is unifying humanity and turning it into a ‘global village’… that is why [the media] are the chief means of information and formation… The new generations, above all, are growing up in a world conditioned by these media ” 76 . Social networks belong to those modern areopagi of which our Proper Law speaks. And although, as we said at the beginning, many use these platforms to spread lies and sow confusion, they are nonetheless a valid means for proclaiming the truth. In this regard Pope Benedict XVI affirmed: “These technologies are a true gift to humanity and therefore we must ensure that their benefits are placed at the service of all human beings and all communities” 77 , and after speaking of the “extraordinary potential of the new technologies” 78 he exhorted Catholics “to bring the witness of their faith to the digital world” 79 . For just as “in the early days of the Church, the Apostles and their disciples brought the Good News of Jesus to the Greco-Roman world. Just as then evangelization, in order to bear fruit, needed an attentive understanding of the culture and customs of those pagan peoples, so as to touch their minds and hearts, so also now the proclamation of Christ in the world of the new technologies requires a profound knowledge of them in order to use them appropriately. To you […] belongs in a particular way the task of evangelizing this ‘digital continent.’ Take up with enthusiasm the proclamation of the Gospel to your contemporaries. […] The most valuable gift you can offer them is to share with them the ‘good news’ of a God who became man, suffered, died and rose to save humanity” 80 . We would not like to go on without mentioning that, by the grace of God, the Institute uses these media in various parts of the world to promote the cause of Christ and its work of evangelization. Nevertheless, in our view, there is much still left for us to conquer in terms of quality in the presentation of the message and of pedagogy when presenting topics that are in themselves very profound. * * * * * Jesus, the Incarnate Word, is the Light of God that “makes encounter possible. It makes communication possible. It makes knowledge possible, access to reality, to truth” 81 . Therefore, for us it will always be a duty and a privilege to proclaim the truth, the glorious truth about human life and human destiny revealed in the Word made flesh. That is why we religious of the Incarnate Word must affirm not only with our lips, but with the witness of our life and with our works of apostolate, that the “ Word is truly the Truth ” 82 . For “everything in Him is transparency, authenticity, sincerity, coherence, truth: I am… the Truth 83 […] In Him there is nothing empty, hollow, or not hypostatically assumed. There is nothing of varnish or shell. Nothing feigned or camouflaged. Nothing of lies, falsehood, insecurity, concealment or hypocrisy. He is One Alone 84 –the Word– in two distinct natures, both perfect, whole and hypostatically united” 85 . Today and always let us raise high the standard of “ Our One Master and Lord Jesus Christ 86 , in whom is contained a reference to all creatures. [For] Christ is the point of union and meeting of the comprehensor and the wayfarer; of the Master 87 and the slave 88 ; of the century and the second; of the universe and the atom; of the from now on of salvation and the until now of the promises; of the not yet of what we hope for and the already accomplished; he is the point of union and meeting of God and man; of the eschatological and the incarnate; of sidereal distances and the millimeter. That is why nothing escapes Christ: neither space travel, nor the world of electronics and computers, of the most current science or the most perfected technology, nor recent discoveries, nor the family, work, culture, the economic-political sphere, etc.” 89 . Let us ourselves learn, and teach others, to follow the wise counsel of St. Ignatius of Antioch: “Stop your ears when you hear anyone speak of anything that does not have Christ Jesus as its foundation…” 90 and let us not cease “to attempt everything so that the love of Christ may have supreme primacy in the Church and in society” 91 . Yes, it is true, the preaching of the Word made flesh is a scandal that brings with it the persecution of the world. But it is well to remember: every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ come in the flesh is of God; and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not of God; this is the spirit of the Antichrist, which you have heard is coming, and now is already in the world 92 . Let us not be deaf to the anguished appeal that the Incarnate Word makes to us from the Cross: “I am the Light, and you do not look at me. I am the Way, and you do not follow me. I am the Truth, and you do not believe me. I am the Life, and you do not seek me. I am the Master, and you do not listen to me. I am the Lord, and you do not obey me. I am your best Friend, and you do not love me. If you are unhappy, do not blame me” 93 . Let us quench the thirst for God and relieve the spiritual destitution of men with the clear and courageous preaching that the Word became flesh and made his dwelling among us… full of grace and truth 94 . Our joy must be spiritual and supernatural

Directory of Consecrated Life , 392 “Our world is growing old with so much seriousness… the priest today has the mission of keeping the universe transparent and so preserving humor” 1 , wrote the Venerable Archbishop Fulton Sheen. In a few days we are going to celebrate, together with Christians throughout the whole world, the mystery of the Resurrection of our Lord, a mystery from which springs “an element that must be essential in our spirituality ” 2 : joy. What joy are we speaking of? We are not referring here to “the consumerist and individualistic joy so present in some cultural experiences today. For consumerism only bloats the heart; it can offer occasional and passing pleasures, but not joy” 3 . Our Proper Law tells us that “our joy must be spiritual and supernatural” 4 . That is why we would like to devote this space to developing, at least in its most outstanding features, what it means that our joy must be spiritual and supernatural. May these pages be a heartfelt tribute to so many of our religious who in many places, and carrying out very varied offices, live in constant joy, keeping alive the memory of the benefits of our Lord, and who in spite of their weariness, limitations, trials and failures live joyfully because they are close to Christ and useful to the Church. But most especially may these pages go to all those who, because of the fruitlessness of their apostolic labors, the various spiritual torments and dense solitudes, are wavering, discouraged and ready to surrender to sadness. May God be pleased to make use of these lines to console them and so that serene joy may return to their souls. 1. Joy Joy can be natural or spiritual. Natural joy is, for example, that of the young religious whose soul has not yet experienced the trials of missionary disillusionment; or the joy of health, when all food tastes good; it is the joy of success after a battle won, or it is the joy of affection when one feels loved, and “feeling loved always produces consolation and joy” 5 . All these ‘natural’ joys are intensified and raised onto a more lasting and deeper foundation by spiritual joys. In general, we could say that “spiritual joy is serenity of temperament amid the changing situations of life, like that of a mountain when a storm sweeps over it. That is why a man who does not have his soul rooted in the Divine blows every problem out of proportion. He cannot apply his full potential to anything because he is worried about many things” 6 . More than a passing attitude, spiritual joy is rather a habit, and being more permanent, it makes difficult things easier to bear. In other words, this spiritual joy to which we are referring can be experienced both in prosperity and in adversity. In prosperity it consists not in the goods that are enjoyed, but in the goods that are hoped for; not in the pleasures that are experienced but in the promise of those in which we believe even without having seen them. Goods may abound, but those we hope for are of the kind that neither moth nor rust destroys, nor thieves can seize. It is the joy experienced even in adversity in knowing that the Divine Master died on the cross as the condition for his Resurrection 7 . That is why our Proper Law says that “the splendid fact that Christ is risen must lead us to live… with immense joy” 8 . And from this follows one of the characteristic features of ‘our joy.’ The joy of the missionary, of the religious, of the monk of the Incarnate Word is intimately related to the Paschal Mystery of Christ, that is, to our Redemption. Our joy is spiritual precisely because “ it is born of the contemplation of the mysteries of the Life of Christ , in particular of his Incarnation and his Resurrection” 9 . Let us therefore acknowledge that spiritual joy finds its source, is nourished and is preserved in prayer, in familiarity with the Incarnate Word 10 . Contemplation of the Incarnation “By the Incarnation of the Word the immortality of happiness is made credible” 11 , says St. Augustine. Jesus by his birth brought a “new vision” to the world and to men. Only if we are humble can we contemplate in the Child lying in the manger, in the Word made flesh, divine Omnipotence, infinite Joy 12 . But, as we say, for this one must be humble, become little and enter into the divine game of not taking oneself seriously, of not thinking oneself too central, so as to be able to become by grace what He is by nature 13 . Consequently, one must rise to the joyful forgetfulness of self 14 . “The birth of the Incarnate Word urges us, among other things, to live in joy, the fruit of the Holy Spirit and a consequence of the Incarnation, as the angel announced to the shepherds: I bring you good news, a great joy that is for all the people (Lk 2:10); it is the joy of the Virgin Mary, ‘cause of our joy’” 15 . The Directory of Contemplative Life develops this point very beautifully, saying: “In the Incarnation of the Word one can already perceive a certain loving and eternal ‘game’ that only God could carry out: – man had aspired to become like God 16 through sin; through the Incarnation God becomes man 17 to save him and raise him, by grace, to his divine level. – Man sinned by claiming ‘to be an adult,’ knowing good and evil; God, the Eternal Wisdom, in becoming incarnate ‘becomes a babbling child’ so that man may attain his maturity in Christ 18 . – Man, wanting to run the adventure of his autonomy, asked God for his share of the inheritance 19 , and ended up feeding pigs 20 ; God, being rich, became poor to enrich him with his poverty 21 ” 22 . That is why our joy −as far as we come to understand it− also has to do with becoming like children (which −let us clarify− has nothing to do with the infantilism that makes people who have reached biological maturity display psychological attitudes proper to childhood). Spiritual childhood restores joy to our lives because it makes us humble and, for that very reason, makes us recognize that we need Redemption. God laughs at those who think themselves ‘wise’ because they flaunt some academic title, or at those who think themselves ‘something’ because they hold some important post, or at those who think they ‘need nothing’ because they have a few things. The Incarnation of the Word teaches us to live according to criteria very different from these, and particularly us, who make religious profession and want to confess with courage and fortitude our faith in Christ. Because, in the end, living joyfully is a question of faith. “If a priest loses faith, he loses joy. To the extent that his faith increases, his joy increases, to the point of the folly of the cross” 23 . Let no one deceive himself –says the apostle– If anyone among you thinks he is wise in this age, let him become a fool so as to become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness to God 24 . That is the logic of the Incarnation, which our Proper Law describes very eloquently: “The folly of the cross consists in living the beatitudes. Blessed are the fools for Christ! They will be carried from here to there, they will be laughed at and taken for clumsy, backward and even feeble-minded: theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven. Blessed are the fools for Christ! For they have emptied themselves and stand before God in all their guilelessness. Blessed are these fools for Christ! No wisdom of the world will ever be able to deceive them. It is the folly of love without limits or measure. It is to bless those who curse us 25 , it is not to repay evil for evil (Rom 12:17). When the world says of us: Look at the fools! stones are thrown at them and they kiss the hand that throws them; people laugh at them and mock them, and they laugh too, like children who do not understand; they are struck, persecuted and martyred, but they give thanks to God who found them worthy. When the world says that, it is a sign that we are on the right path” 26 . The mystery of the Incarnation puts us in contact with Christ emptied, with Christ the Victim, whom we must imitate. But just as Christ knew how to bear every pain, every humiliation, and even death for love of us, so we too must know how to see in those same things the opportunity to return to Christ love for love. “If we do not learn to be victims with the Victim, all our sufferings are useless” 27 . But suffering is overcome by loving and by finding in it a new way of serving others. And that service is transformed into spiritual joy, which allows us, in spite of the trials and obstacles of this life, not to lose heart and always to keep going forward. Ours is to be priests always victims, but in spirit always victorious. Let us be imitators of Jesus, who, in place of the joy that was set before him, endured the cross, disregarding its shame 28 . It is faith that gives us the courage to overcome defeats, which in the end, in the light of the Incarnation and Resurrection of Christ, are only apparent defeats. For our victory over the world is precisely our faith in the Son of God who, incarnate, has come into the world 29 . When Jesus Christ, the Incarnate Word, passed by, all the people rejoiced 30 . In the same way we, missionaries of the Incarnate Word who make religious profession so that our life may be a living memorial of the way of existing and acting of Jesus, the Word made flesh 31 , must strive to radiate the joy of Christ 32 . Ours is not just any joy; it is spiritual and it is supernatural, and for that very reason it cannot be contained; that is why our motto is “to live in crystal-clear and contagious joy” 33 . It is true that “there are hard moments, times of the cross, but nothing can destroy supernatural joy, which ‘adapts and changes, but it always endures, even as a flicker of light born of our personal certainty that, when everything is said and done, we are infinitely loved’ 34 . It is an inner security , a hope-filled serenity that offers a spiritual satisfaction incomprehensible by worldly standards” 35 . The kenosis of the Lord in his Incarnation and in his Passion makes us see the mysterious relationship between renunciation and inner joy, between sacrifice and breadth of heart, between discipline and spiritual freedom 36 . Let us not be pessimists: Let us rejoice even in our sufferings 37 ! To help us in this, and almost in passing, our Proper Law gives us the following provision: “It is fitting that the priest […] desire and rejoice to visit and adore Christ sacramentally present in the Eucharist” 38 . Contemplation of the Resurrection “There is no greater reason for joy –says our Proper Law– than the Resurrection of the Lord, because his triumph is our triumph, his victory is our victory. The Paschal Mystery is the manifestation par excellence of God’s love for men: he loved them to the end 39 . That is why in this mystery we must rejoice, and our joy must be permanent ” 40 . Now, for our joy to be permanent, besides keeping our gaze firmly fixed on the Incarnate Word, we must have a good sense of humor, so outstanding, for example, in St. Thomas More, who said: “Happy are those who know how to laugh at themselves, for they will never stop being amused,” or in St. Philip Neri, whom our Proper Law quotes with the following phrase: “‘melancholy is the eighth capital sin’ 41 ” 42 , or in the Blessed martyr Miguel Agustín Pro, in whom “neither sufferings, nor serious illnesses, nor exhausting ministerial activity, often carried out in painful and dangerous circumstances, could stifle the radiant and communicative joy that was born of his love for Christ and that no one could take from him” 43 , and he ended his life as he had always lived it: generously, with joy, giving everything and keeping nothing for himself. “The priest cannot take this world too seriously. We are pilgrims, not tourists. The Kingdom of God is not the Secular City” 44 , said Fulton Sheen. That is why, aware that we are pilgrims, we must have our hearts set on God and learn to have a providential view of life , knowing how to look upon everything as coming from Him who does not forget even a little sparrow… and has counted even the hairs of our head 45 . And “in saying all things it means all events, prosperous or adverse, what concerns the good of the soul, the goods of fortune, reputation, all the conditions of human life, all the interior states through which we pass, even faults and sins themselves” 46 . For this reason, if our joy is to be permanent, it cannot be worldly . “Worldliness is always sad, because if we lose the ball of this world, we feel miserable. The holier we are, the less sad we are. And if nowadays there are sad priests, it is not because ‘the world is full of problems’ –when has it ever been without problems?–, it is because the priest has lost the transparency of faith” 47 , in the sense that he has lost that capacity to see the providence of God in the events of this world and of his own life in particular. That is why we say that our joy is supernatural. Now, it is true that “in every community there are various categories of souls. Some live joyfully and radiate around them the holy joy they enjoy. Not the merely sensible joy, which may depend on temperament, but the interior joy that is a prelude to eternal happiness. Others do not enjoy it; within they are troubled, restless, unhappy. Why this difference? Because, in the first case, whoever seeks God in all things always finds Him, in every place, and with God acquires the supreme good and the happiness that is not lost. In the second case, on the other hand, the soul clings to creatures, feeds self-love, and in seeking itself heads toward emptiness, and this cannot content it. It will give itself entirely to exterior occupation, but that distraction will be illusory and insufficient; it will find distraction, but not consolation, and will feel its life to be heavy and hard to bear” 48 . How much we must guard ourselves against falling into the temptation of being the uptight priest : “all seriousness, always distant, inaccessible, tense, who does not know how to laugh, to whom every healthy recreation seems frivolity, for whom an ill-sounding word is a grave sin, for whom eutrapelia seems not to be a virtue, who for looking at the tree forgets the forest, and tends to make storms in a glass of water” 49 . Or into the temptation of being a bad-tempered priest : “always impatient, sullen, who is approachable only when he is in a good mood, and becomes sterile, sees everything as black, is not a celibate but an old bachelor, and in fact does not know that a milligram of grace weighs more than all the sins of the world, even these raised to the nth power” 50 . “Serene joy is the outward expression of a balanced spiritual interior life” 51 . Quite the contrary, we must try each day to have a positive and hopeful spirit and, without losing realism, know how to take things with a certain sense of humor, being grateful and not overly complicated. This attitude, this supernatural view of things, this detachment from earthly things is, according to Fulton Sheen, the vestibule of mysticism 52 . As priests we must learn to spiritualize, sacramentalize and ennoble everything in this world and make it into prayer, that is, raise everything to God and unite ourselves voluntarily with Him in everything, through the active exercise of faith, hope and charity. Note that no occupation is so lowly that it cannot be spiritualized, no suffering so hard that it cannot be ennobled. We must develop in ourselves that capacity which does not let the many occasions that daily life gives us slip by without making them into prayer or drawing from them a divine lesson. That is why, with a certain humor, our Proper Law places us before this situation: “it urges us to work in the most difficult places (those where no one wants to go) and when it is no longer possible to continue there, after praying about it for a night before Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament, to ask the bishop to send us to a worse place” 53 . So that even in such a situation, we may know where to find calm, recover the supernatural sense of things and respond with even greater self-giving, without losing heart. The Passion, Death and Resurrection of our Lord raise us above our precariousness and our situations, so often miserable, to the supernatural plane. Fulton Sheen said: “If an act of contrition had to be translated into a facial expression, it would be a smile… If one does not know that one is wounded, one can never rejoice at being healed” 54 . It is in this sense that our Proper Law exhorts us “to rediscover […] the beauty and joy of the sacrament of Penance” 55 as an occasion to experience “the consoling joy of forgiveness” 56 . What joy is more crystal-clear than that of a clean conscience! What is more, we can say that the Resurrection of Christ is a cause of rejoicing not only for the Lord but also for the redeemed, since it allows us to make our own the words of the psalm: Then our mouth was filled with laughter and our lips with shouts of joy 57 . One day St. John Paul II, speaking to priests and religious in Copenhagen, told them (and today he wants to repeat it to us): “God has not called us only to a life of sacrifice and renunciation, but also to a life of intimate joy and fulfillment” 58 . That too is important to keep in mind. For at times the project of sanctification or ‘evangelical perfection’ is identified one-sidedly or exclusively with self-denial and the cross, renunciation and purification. There is no doubt: following Christ requires all that as the first condition of the disciple, and it is also important to accept it and embrace it, for these are basic guidelines of the one Gospel. However, unfortunately we sometimes reduce holiness to that alone, when in reality the active and passive nights serve to dispose us so that the divine action may reach its fullness: union with God, infinite Joy. And that must not be forgotten. 2. Distinctive characteristics Let us now single out some distinctive features of the joy that must characterize us, and our specific way of living it and manifesting it in the Institute. ▪ Our very consecration as religious must be a source of joy ; that, in the first place. For the profession of our vows proclaims “the joy of living according to the evangelical beatitudes” 59 . And for those of us who are already priests, “our [priestly] identity, our true dignity, must be especially the source of our joy and the certainty of our life” 60 . ▪ Lived in community : Consequently, this spiritual and supernatural joy of which we have been speaking must also be lived and manifested in community. “Fraternal love multiplies our capacity for joy, since it makes us capable of rejoicing in the good of others: Rejoice with those who rejoice 61 ” 62 . For joy is “a fruit of the Holy Spirit and an effect of charity, and therefore we must try, by every means , that ‘no one be disturbed or saddened in the house of God.’ For this it is absolutely indispensable to live fraternal charity ” 63 . Which is a rule for superiors and subjects alike. How many religious live discouraged or sad because of disagreements among themselves! We must be careful about this, because a fraternity without joy is a fraternity that is dying out, and very soon its members will be tempted to look elsewhere for what they cannot find at home… 64 . On the contrary, joy in religious arouses an enormous attraction toward religious life; it is a source of new vocations and a support for perseverance 65 . Our Proper Law is clear: “Every community of our little Religious Family must live that spirit of healthy recreation and contagious joy, which are founded on the fulfillment of religious duties and on always considering that ‘God is the first served’ 66 ” 67 . Now, “only he truly rejoices who rejoices in love: ‘where charity rejoices, there is festivity’ 68 . And this because every feast implies an existential richness that in turn is born of a renunciation , for there can be no time for a feast unless something is renounced. And this renunciation implies love, for there is no renunciation where there is no love 69 ” 70 . And from this follows the following practical note for living joy as a religious of the Incarnate Word. Namely: ▪ “ To live in a climate of festive joy ” 71 : This is one of the characteristics of our joy, closely related to the previous note. For “our communities must show how the love of Christ drives away even the shadow of sadness” 72 . Indeed, our Proper Law, in a fatherly way, commands us “to foster even outwardly an atmosphere of joy ” 73 . And it emphasizes: “It is very important to cultivate this joy in the religious community: excessive work can extinguish it, exaggerated zeal for some causes can make one forget it, constantly questioning one’s own identity and one’s own future can overshadow it…” 74 . Therefore, one must “know how to rejoice together , allow oneself personal and communal moments of relaxation, step back from one’s own work from time to time, rejoice in the joys of one’s brother, pay solicitous attention to the needs of brothers and sisters, give oneself generously to apostolic work, face situations with mercy, go out to meet the future with the hope of always and everywhere finding the Lord: all this nourishes serenity, peace and joy , and becomes strength for apostolic action. The path is difficult, but possible in Christ: Joyful in hope, strong in tribulation, persevering in prayer 75 ” 76 . We must always be clear that our way of living in community implies living “as a true family in Christ, with signs of deference, and bearing one another’s burdens” 77 ; “helping, encouraging or spiritually enkindling one another” 78 . This also implies accepting with kindness the defects, real or apparent, of others, even when they bother us, and gladly accepting all the sacrifices imposed by living together with those whose mentality and temperament do not fully agree with our own way of seeing and judging 79 . From this follows the next note for practicing joy according to the spirituality of our Institute. ▪ To live in an affectionate and joyful family climate : whether in the minor or major seminary, in a contemplative monastery or in a small community dedicated to the mission, the religious, the seminarian, the priest must love his companions as true brothers and his Superiors as true fathers 80 . In this sense our Proper Law, condescending to our weaknesses and with great pedagogy, exhorts us, telling us that “to foster the practice of charity in the joyful mutual help that is born of the contemplation and love of God, and which can be summed up in the oratorian spirit 81 , it is important to celebrate duly the solemnities of the liturgical year, promoting participation in the liturgy of the mysteries of Christ and of the Church, as well as the proper feasts of the Congregation and of the Seminary, prepared by means of novenas or triduums, especially the Octave of Easter, Sundays, and the feasts of the Apostles and of Our Lady 82 . All this is achieved by solemnizing and actively participating in the liturgy, and also by means of rest , joy and fitting celebrations ” 83 . “Likewise it will help –to the extent possible– to set aside certain solemnities or feasts for gathering with the other communities of the Religious Family that are in the Province” 84 . It is important to know how to ‘invest’ in everything that contributes to that spirit of a festive family climate, as we are explicitly told: the religious “must have spiritual joy but also manifest it ” 85 . “Everything must contribute to joy” 86 . At times people tend to think that manifestations of joy are reserved for the youngest, who have not yet been ‘hardened’ by the sufferings of the mission; or else, others think that because religious are older they no longer have fun. Not infrequently those who think this way believe that joy is merely ‘horsing around.’ The truth is that for each age there is a way of having fun and of expressing that joy. Let us pay attention to what our Proper Law points out to us: “The presence of elderly persons in communities can be very positive. An elderly religious who does not let himself be overcome by the ailments and limits of age, but keeps joy, love and hope alive, is a support of incalculable value for the young” 87 . As time goes by and –by the grace of God– in various communities of our Institute we come to have religious of ‘the youngest’ and of ‘the oldest’ together, we must know how to tap the potential of wisdom and experience of the latter, but they too must know that they are called to practice, in keeping with their age, the virtue of eutrapelia, which is the next characteristic note of our joy. ▪ Eutrapelia : “Recreation and rest in common are of the highest importance. We call this by the name of the virtue to which they belong: eutrapelia ” 88 . “The soul, like the body, grows tired and must rest. The rest of the soul is delight, so that this must be the remedy against the weariness of the soul, interrupting the tension of the spirit. Hence it is necessary to procure this rest for the soul by means of games and festivities, whose moderation belongs to the virtue of eutrapelia, practiced in times of recreation” 89 . “St. Thomas wisely says that no one has the right to be burdensome to others ” 90 . Therefore, the virtue of eutrapelia is not a synonym for the religious who makes everyone else the object of his jokes, or for the religious who thinks he is a comedian and makes himself the object of the jokes of others. Eutrapelia “has as its object to regulate games and amusements according to the right order of reason” 91 . Opposed to this virtue is foolish mirth , which gives itself over to illicit amusements, whether by reason of their very object or for lack of the due circumstances of time, place or person; and also opposed to this virtue is the excessive austerity of those who neither want to take recreation themselves nor let others do so. “It is in eutrapelia that generosity is seen and good spirit is verified; not in amusement in itself, which may be the fruit of human enthusiasm, but insofar as it is supernatural joy, which can exist even in the company of trials or interior dryness” 92 . Our Proper Law also fittingly points out that “there is no fixed or obligatory measure for taking part in the eutrapelias, but it is certain that the more charity one puts into it, the more of God’s goods one will receive; and it can be verified that those who are most generous in times of joy are those who are most productive in their other activities” 93 . Fulton Sheen said that there is no group in the world with more humor than priests at their recreations –we could say– the “Pro” gatherings of priests. And in a few lines –and with no little irony– he exemplifies the healthy joy that must reign in them: “the well-meant jokes that immediately deflate the puffed-up, the endless stories about bishops, mother superiors and parishioners make laughter reign at every gathering. [There] no talent is defended, no achievements are rewarded, but neither are the losers allowed to get depressed. Only about one thing does one never laugh, and that is the salvation of a soul. […] Since faith reigns at those gatherings, and therefore sound judgment, our opinions are ‘always correct.’ If we say that ‘such-and-such a priest is a madman,’ that priest is a madman. Individual opinion is often absurd, but when faith reigns: where two or three are gathered in My name, there am I in their midst 94 ” 95 . ▪ To rejoice in Christ proclaimed : that is, in apostolic work. “The characteristic of every authentic missionary life is the inner joy that comes from faith” 96 . It is important to recall what our documents say about religious brothers, but which applies well to any of the members: “Through work the religious brother brings great help to the community, especially if he knows how to find in work a source of joy . In work he can see the progress of his abilities, the development of his personality and the perfecting of his physical and spiritual qualities. Joy, moreover, comes from service , according to the saying of our Lord quoted by St. Paul: There is greater happiness in giving than in receiving (Acts 20:35)” 97 . “The idle man will never taste the joys of a well-earned rest, for work is pleasant also because it is afterward rewarded with rest” 98 . How edifying is the example of the religious of the Institute devoted to the sublime and at the same time demanding office of evangelization in countries at war, or amid great privations and trials, who, surpassing themselves, know how to transform suffering into self-giving and service, and keep the joy of evangelizing, even when they must sow in tears. Truly their example spurs us on, gladdens us exceedingly and stimulates us to greater self-giving. ▪ Lived even in poverty : We members of the Institute are commanded “to accept with joy, for the love of God, privations, even in necessary things , for the sake of holy poverty” 99 . Many of us who remember the first years of the Institute, or who were present at the beginnings of some mission, know –not from hearsay– the needs we went through, and yet the common denominator was the immense joy we enjoyed, to the point that shortages seemed to us a reason for greater joy and became anecdotes. That is why we think we are not mistaken when we say that joy is deeply related to poverty of spirit. “For the poor in spirit is more constant and joyful in want, because he has placed his all in nothing at all, and so finds in everything breadth of heart” 100 . In other words: “There are no worries about this world for one who wants to have nothing in it; for his wealth is God” 101 . ***** In short, let us not seek another path to the deep and serene joy of religious life, for there is none other than this: active and responsible abandonment for the sake of the will of God. The difficulties, the crosses that will never be lacking “nor does God want them to be lacking” 102 , must not diminish our joy. For in life “there is only one sadness, that of not being saints” 103 . The rejoice in the Lord always 104 is something theological: it is the fruit of a continual friendship with the Incarnate Word and of letting oneself be guided by his Spirit, one of whose fruits is joy 105 . Now that together with the whole Church we rejoice in the Resurrection of our Lord, let us remember that our spirituality is also that of the “Gloria” and of the “Magnificat” 106 , and let us take up again with vigor our struggle for holiness; let us advance with renewed enthusiasm in our mission so that our witness of hope in the resurrection may be credible 107 . Let us never lose heart. In the midst of the insecurity of situations, of the helplessness that is a file for the soul, of the scarcity of resources of every kind, of the perplexities that try to halt our march, we must not look back, nor must we ‘shrink back.’ Jesus gives us an assurance: You will be sad, but your sadness will turn into joy . […] I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you 108 . I have spoken to you of this so that my joy may be in you, and your joy may be complete 109 . Today the Church needs our witness of joy. Let us raise our prayers so that the recognition of our limits and weaknesses, and our Christian acceptance of challenges, may become an occasion to experience the power of God and the extraordinary riches of his grace. The Risen One is beside us and repeats to us once again: Do not be afraid! 110 Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your heart… it is I myself 111 . May the Blessed Virgin, Mother of the Risen One and Cause of our joy, make us witnesses of the joy of Christ who lives forever. This Easter we greet you with the customary greeting of Don Bosco, the Saint of grace and joy: Be joyful! Notes 1 Cf. Those Mysterious Priests , ch. 15.
