“Our badge of honor: our belonging to the Church”

Our badge of honor: our belonging to the Church Cf. Directory of Spirituality , 227 In one of their first paragraphs our Constitutions declare that “ we want to be founded on Jesus Christ… because the rock is Christ 1 and no one can lay any other foundation 2 . We want to love and serve Jesus Christ, and to make Him loved and served: His Body and His Spirit. Both the physical Body of Christ in the Eucharist, and the Mystical Body of Christ, which is the Church, formed by ourselves who, through holiness of life, must become ‘other Christs’, and by all men in whom we see Christ Himself, especially the poor, sinners and enemies. We want to be ‘like another humanity of His’ 3 , we want to be chalices filled with Christ that pour out His superabundance upon others, we want to show with our lives that Christ lives. And the Spirit of Christ, because He is the soul of the Church and because if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ 4 ” 5 . With this succession of “we want,” they make clear what the foundation of our Religious Family of the Incarnate Word is. In full agreement and continuity with the above, the Directory of Spirituality states without hesitation that “ we want to know nothing outside of Her” 6 , that is, nothing outside the Church, since “Christ Himself is Incarnate in His Body, the Church” 7 . And we fervently desire that “our belonging to Her, through faith and Baptism, may always be our badge of honor ” 8 . In this month of May, in which the liturgy providentially sets before us the celebration of the Christ of the Quebrada, a date so significant for us since it is the day of the foundational grace, and a few weeks later the Solemnity of Pentecost, it seems to us that it may be of spiritual benefit for all the members of the Institute to contemplate once again the mystical Life of the Incarnate Word , that is, “the marvel of the Church, Body of Christ, nourished by the Word of God, One, Holy, Catholic –missionary and ecumenical–, Apostolic, enriched by and resting upon the three white things” 9 . A Church which, moreover, is the one who “by her authority, accepts and approves” 10 the charism of an Institute precisely “for the building up of the Body of Christ” 11 . It is our desire that the reading of these considerations may help to deepen and increase our faith in the mystical Life of the Incarnate Word, as we asked in the novena in preparation for the Annunciation of the Lord; and at the same time, that it may serve to delve more and more deeply into the beautiful texts that our law contains on this subject. 1. Christ, Head of the Church As could not be otherwise, already in the first lines of our Constitutions we confess “Christ who ‘remains in the Catholic Church governed by the successor of Peter and the Bishops in communion with him’” 12 . Likewise “we confess the preeminence of Christ, even as man, over all creation. A primacy that Christ has over the souls and over the bodies of the members of His Mystical Body and also over all men of all times –He is Head of all– even of those not predestined, who will cease to be potential members of the Body of Christ only when they leave this world” 13 . And without delay, the Directory of Spirituality goes on to say: “We confess that Christ is Head of the Church 14 and of all men 15 , and that He has over all a threefold primacy: of order, of perfection and of power. He has priority of order , since by His nearness to God His grace is the highest and the first, though not in time; for all who receive grace receive it in relation to His: Those whom He foreknew He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He might be the firstborn among many brothers 16 . He has priority of perfection , because He possesses the fullness of all graces: We have seen Him… full of grace and truth 17 . He has priority in power , since He has all power to communicate grace and glory to all the members of His Body: From His fullness we have all received, grace upon grace 18 ” 19 . According to this last point, we could say that Christ also has primacy in interior influence. It is a physical, intimate, vital, mystical influence, analogically comparable to the influence of the vine upon its branches. From which it follows that “absolutely the whole humanity of Christ, His body and His soul, has an influence on all the men and women of the world and on their bodies and souls, and in all times. All, because they belong to the Mystical Body, in fact ( in act ) or as a possibility ( in potency ), even the unbaptized, or pagans, or sinners, or… All! receive the influence of Christ, by means of actual graces. Neither the devil nor the Antichrist is the head of the wicked, properly speaking, since they can in no way exercise an interior influence. They exercise only an exterior influence: by means of temptations, bad examples, or infestations, or suggestions or possessions. Insofar as man freely wills to turn away from God through sin, he submits himself to the power of the devil. And only in this improper sense can the devil be called the head of the wicked” 20 . And because of this threefold primacy of the Incarnate Word as Head of the Church, which is His Body, “the Church founded upon the rock cannot be destroyed” 21 . His Mystical Body will suffer wounds; there will be ‘scandals,’ just as He was a stone of stumbling, because if the human nature of Christ suffered rejection and ‘apparent defeat,’ why expect His Mystical Body to be exempt from it? Archbishop Fulton Sheen wrote in one of his books: “If He allowed thirst, pain and a death sentence to affect His physical Body, why would He not allow mystical and moral weaknesses such as loss of faith, sin, scandals, heresies, schisms and sacrileges to affect His Mystical Body? When all these things happen, it does not mean that the Mystical Body of the Church is not Divine in its innermost nature, any more than the Crucifixion of our Lord meant that Christ was not of divine nature” 22 . “The presence of the Holy Spirit in the Church means that she, although marked by the sin of her members, is preserved from defection” 23 . St. John Paul II explained that the words of our Lord: Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it 24 “attest to Jesus’ will to build His Church, with an essential reference to the specific mission and power that He, in due time, will confer on Simon.” “The word rock –the Pope went on to say– expresses a permanent, subsisting being; consequently, it applies to the person [of Peter], rather than to an act of his, which is necessarily passing. The duration of the Church is bound to the rock . The Peter-Church relationship repeats in itself the bond between the Church and Christ. Jesus, in fact, says: ‘ My Church.’ This means that the Church will always be the Church of Christ , the Church that belongs to Christ. She does not become the Church of Peter , but, as the Church of Christ, she is built upon Peter , who is Kephas in the name and by virtue of Christ” 25 . In the face of the ups and downs of time and circumstances, we must always keep in mind that “our Lord is the Founder, the Head, the Sustainer and the Savior of this Mystical Body” 26 . Knowing how to give glory to God by trusting without limits in His Providence, which disposes all things for the good of those who love God 27 , and believing with unshakable firmness that even the most adverse events, those most opposed to our natural outlook, are ordered by God for our good, even if we do not understand His designs and do not know the end to which He wishes to lead us 28 . Our proper law devotes many pages to developing the very profound theological theme of the mystical Life of the Incarnate Word, since from it spring principles essential to our spirituality. It is not our intention now to transcribe all that is said there –although we do warmly recommend reading it 29 – but rather we would like to point out some of those elements rooted in faith in the mystery of the mystical Life of Christ which have to do with our consecrated life and particular mission; since it was the Holy Spirit who granted a singular grace to our Founder so that through him our Religious Family might contribute to the building up of the Church according to its own particular way of living the religious life and the apostolate 30 . 2. Badge of honor All the members of the Institute must be very clear that “just as the Word assumed a human nature to fulfill the plan of salvation, so, to prolong that plan throughout the ages, He chooses other human natures so that salvation may reach all men of all times. The Church is Jesus Christ continued, spread abroad and communicated; she is like the prolongation of the redemptive Incarnation, continuing the threefold office: prophetic, priestly and royal” 31 . Together with this, it is imperative to remember that our belonging to the Church, not only through Baptism but also through faith , must be our badge of honor. That is to say, we must stand out for our filial love and obedience to our Holy Mother the Church. For it could not be otherwise, since faith in the Church is unfailingly united to faith in the mystery of the Incarnate Word. “For one cannot separate the Church from Christ, nor Christ from the Church” 32 . We know well that the Holy Spirit, after the Resurrection and Ascension of Jesus into heaven, was sent to the Church 33 precisely on the day of Pentecost. “Therefore the Holy Spirit is a gift given by God to the Church: you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit 34 , a gift that at the same time gives her life […] and gives her life to such a degree that He is rightly called ‘the Soul of the Church’” 35 . The Holy Spirit, then, plays a fundamental, essential, constitutive role in the Church. He is the source of the Church’s unity and the source of holiness; He is the pledge of eternal life: the Spirit of the promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance 36 ; He is the one who helps us, since the Spirit comes to the aid of our weakness, for we do not know how to pray as we ought, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings 37 ; He is the one who enriches the Church with the diversity of His gifts: all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each one as He wills 38 . Note that “the Holy Spirit dwells in the Church, not as a guest who remains, in any case, a stranger, but as the soul that transforms the community into a holy temple of God 39 and continually assimilates it to Himself by means of His specific gift, which is charity 40 ” 41 . For this reason, our proper law paternally exhorts us to ask “the Lord always to grant us His Holy Spirit, and docility to Him, so that we may belong more and more to Christ, and hence to His Mystical Body, since if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ 42 ” 43 . “The hierarchical and at the same time mystical, visible and spiritual, earthly and heavenly, canonical and charismatic, human and divine reality [of the Church], by a profound analogy ‘is compared to the Mystery of the Incarnate Word’ 44 , since ‘Christ Himself is Incarnate in His Body, the Church’ 45 . Therefore, we who are honored to call ourselves religious ‘of the Incarnate Word,’ would most gravely betray our charism if we did not work to have an authentic ecclesial spirituality, one that incorporates us fully into the Church of the Incarnate Word” 46 . Therefore, we not only confess our faith in the Church as the manifestation of the Mystical Life of the Incarnate Word in time, but we seek to stand out for our belonging to Her with our whole life. To look no further, our very consecration cannot be understood except in the Church , and for this reason “we desire to live in a state that ‘more closely imitates and perpetually represents in the Church that form of life which the Son of God chose when He came into the world…’” 47 . Thus “moved by charity… we want to live more and more for Christ and His Body, which is the Church” 48 . The existence of our Institute and what guides its action is precisely its vital relationship with the Church, as our proper law clearly expresses throughout all its documents. Here we shall only point out some of the elements that make this evident: ▪ We are convinced that “only in the most absolute fidelity to the Holy Spirit can one skillfully wield the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God 49 . Our poor breath is fruitful and irresistible only if it is in communication with the wind of Pentecost” 50 . And for this reason we cannot conceive of the reading of Sacred Scripture except as done ‘ in the Church ’ 51 , for which we consider absolutely necessary the strictest fidelity to the supreme Magisterium of the Church of all times, the proximate norm of faith 52 . Indeed, for us “the Word of God must be ‘deepened in the Church’ 53 , that is, with the same Spirit in which it was written 54 ; only when understood in this way does the Word of God become the strength of our Institute 55 . Hence the formation we impart to those in formation “‘is based and built above all on the study of sacred doctrine and theology’ 56 , which proceeds from faith and seeks to lead to it, as the Magisterium of the Church and Catholic theologians have always taught” 57 . Moreover, “the teachings of the Pastoral Constitution on the Church in the Modern World Gaudium et spes of the Second Vatican Council, the Apostolic Exhortations Evangelii nuntiandi and Catechesi tradendae , the address of Pope St. John Paul II to UNESCO and others on the same subject, the Puebla Document , the Encyclical Letter Slavorum Apostoli , the Encyclical Letter Redemptoris missio , the Post-Synodal Apostolic Exhortation Pastores dabo vobis , n. 55, c; and all the future directives, guidelines and teachings of the ordinary Magisterium of the Church that may be given concerning the specific end of our little Religious Family” 58 constitute our rule of work in order to make a real contribution to the mission entrusted to us. For this reason we do not merely say it, but we take care and make it our concern “to be men docile to the great discipline of the Church, expressed in the Code of Canon Law , in all the other ecclesial norms and laws, and docile to the particular discipline of our Institute” 59 . ▪ In turn, our Constitutions point out that “the spirit of our Religious Family wants to be none other than the Holy Spirit , and if it degenerates into another, from now on and from wherever we may be, we pledge our supplication that the Lord may blot it out from the face of the Church” 60 . All the members of the Institute –whether brothers, seminarians, priests, monks, novices– form in the Church one and the same Congregation, regardless of their place of origin or the place where they are on mission, of how many years they have been in religious life, of the academic degrees they may or may not have, of the offices they hold, etc. We all have the same rule, the same charism, the same spiritual patrimony; we all have the same mission, that is, “to work, in utmost docility to the Holy Spirit and within the imprint of Mary, in order to claim for Jesus Christ all that is authentically human, even in the most difficult situations and in the most adverse conditions” 61 . For this reason an intense fraternal love must unite us, today and always, in our vocation. The Holy Spirit, “Soul of the Church,” is a spirit of charity, and our proper law sets out countless provisions so that we may live according to that spirit as an integral and essential part of our fidelity to the charism and to the very vocation received within the Church. For example, we are told, and here we would like to emphasize it, that “we must strive, by every means, that ‘no one be disturbed or saddened in the house of God’ 62 . For this it is absolutely indispensable to live fraternal charity : ‘That is: let them consider others more worthy 63 ; let them bear with boundless patience one another’s weaknesses, both of body and of spirit; let them strive with all their effort to obey one another; let all seek the good of others rather than their own; let them put into practice a sincere fraternal love; let them live always in the fear and love of God; let them love their Abbot [Superior] with sincere and humble charity; let them prefer absolutely nothing to Christ, and may He bring us all together to eternal life’ 64 ” 65 . Without charity toward our brothers, whether they be peers, subjects or superiors, our confession of faith in the mystical Life of the Incarnate Word, which is prolonged in every soul in grace, is of no use whatsoever. However much such a person may have read all the documents of the Magisterium, however many years he may spend as a missionary in distant countries or sacrifice himself in the silence of the cloister, however much he may call himself a most obedient son of the Church, however much he may call himself very faithful to the charism of the Institute and appear outwardly to follow all its rules… Because whoever says he loves God and does not love his brothers is a liar 66 . What is more, such a person “even if he is with us in body, does not belong to our spiritual family” 67 , since he betrays or departs gravely from the spirit of our Religious Family, which is the Holy Spirit, the Spirit of Charity. ▪ Being “essentially missionaries” 68 , we members of the Institute, as faithful sons of the Church, are dedicated by vocation to the spreading of the Gospel. The Holy Spirit is the one who guides our discernment of reality so as to interpret the signs of the times and know how to respond with the zeal of the saints 69 to the missionary needs of the Church today. What is more, “we will carry out all our missionary undertakings in communion with the Church , aware that it belongs to the missionary Dicastery to direct and coordinate throughout the world the work of the Evangelization of peoples and missionary cooperation” 70 . In view of this, our major Seminaries prepare future priests by the Church and for the Church 71 : therefore, the pastoral formation of the candidates strives to make them know and live the ecclesial dimensions 72 , inviting them to open their minds and hearts, and to make themselves available for every opportunity offered them to proclaim the Gospel 73 . This formation also seeks to ensure that all our candidates are ready to be sent to preach the Gospel in any part of the world 74 and to “take an interest ‘not only in the particular Church… but also in the universal Church’” 75 . Because we are “convinced that the missionary dimension of ecclesial life is not something that depends simply on personal generosity, but belongs to the very nature of the Church 76 and of the ministerial priesthood” 77 , we give great importance to our seminarians being filled “with so Catholic a spirit that they grow accustomed to going beyond the limits of their own diocese or nation or rite and to helping meet the needs of the whole Church, ready to preach the Gospel everywhere” 78 . Proof of this is that our missionaries dedicate all their strength to the service of the great work of establishing and extending the kingdom of Christ in the world, and are today found in 44 countries carrying out a great variety of apostolic works. And since “the love of God, of the Church and of souls imposes on us the apostolic work of vocations” 79 , because the matter of vocations “affects the whole Church in one of her fundamental marks, which is her apostolicity” 80 , at present we can give thanks to God that, in the course of our short history as a religious and missionary Institute, He has blessed us with numerous native vocations from the places where we are on mission and even from countries where we are not yet present. In fact, our numerous vocations in formation come from 45 different countries. For as St. John Paul II rightly said: “Vocations to the priesthood and to consecrated life are a sure sign of the vitality of a Church” 81 . Deo gratias ! ▪ The mystical Life of the Incarnate Word is enriched by and rests upon the three white things 82 : the Eucharist, the Blessed Virgin Mary and the Pope. “The Church is the Body of Christ. This means that the Eucharist , in which the Lord gives His Body and transforms us into one Body 83 , is the place where the Church permanently expresses herself in her most essential form” 84 . In this sense, our proper law points out that “the oneness and indivisibility of the Eucharistic Body of the Lord implies the oneness and indivisibility of His Mystical Body. From each Eucharist arises the self-giving to the Lord by being inserted into His one and undivided Body” 85 . Consequently, by the spirit of faith that animates us and that has been handed down to us, we have as our motto “with Peter and under Peter” 86 . For “the unity of the Eucharist and the unity of the Episcopate… are not independent roots of the unity of the Church because, by institution of Christ Himself, Eucharist and Episcopate are essentially linked realities 87 ” 88 . This being so, we always find the deepest foundation of our unity as a Religious Family in the Eucharist 89 . The Eucharist is one of our great loves; it is the principal thing, the most important thing we must do each day 90 . A sign of this is the great importance and the great care we put into the celebration of Holy Mass in our religious and missionary communities, since wherever we go the Sunday Eucharist especially is central 91 . From there flows our pastoral ministry of holiness as the source and means for establishing a truly Christian culture. ▪ “Because the Church is the ‘universal Sacrament of salvation’ 92 , she is open to the missionary and ecumenical dynamic, and not turned in on herself, since she has been sent to proclaim and bear witness to, to make present and to extend the mystery of communion that constitutes her; to gather all people and all things in Christ 93 . For this reason, in the image of the Church, our little Religious Family never wants to be turned in on itself, but open like the arms of Christ on the Cross, whose arms were wrenched out of joint from opening them so wide in love” 94 . Consequently, all the members of the Institute make their own the ecumenical cause of the Church, for it is our determination “to work with all our strength to build up our life in union with the legitimate Pastors, and most especially with a heartfelt adherence to the Bishop of Rome, thus showing forth the one Church: – So that all Christians may come to perfect unity, that the promise and prophecy of the Lord may be fulfilled: There will be one flock and one Shepherd (Jn 10:16), and that His prayer may bear fruit: Father, that they all may be one (Jn 17:21). This is the ecumenical work. – So that all men may confess the adorable Name of the Lord Jesus, fulfilling His commandment: Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature (Mk 16:15). This is the missionary work. Not forgetting that: ‘it is truth, more than anything, that builds unity: the communion of minds easily becomes a union of hearts…’ 95 ” 96 . It is our mission, therefore, to remain “open to every particle of truth wherever it may be found” 97 in order to discover “the seeds of the Word,” with joy and respect, so as to seek to awaken in men a more ardent desire for truth and charity 98 . Without forgetting that there are countless men and women who have not yet heard the Name of Jesus and to whom the immense gift of salvation has not yet been offered, each day we must devote ourselves to the explicit proclamation of Jesus as Lord, without which there can be no true evangelization. At the same time, inculturation and interreligious dialogue play an important role in several places where we are present; there our missionaries, in full communion with the Church of Christ, bring the truth of the redemption that God accomplished in Jesus. Let us add here that a serious and open dialogue with cultures and religions should not be considered as opposed to the mission ad gentes , but as “part of the evangelizing mission of the Church” 99 . This requires on the part of our missionaries serious personal preparation, mature gifts of discernment, and fidelity to the indispensable criteria of doctrinal orthodoxy, moral integrity and ecclesial communion 100 . “It must never be forgotten that dialogue can deepen and purify the Catholic faith, but it cannot change it” 101 , since “the unity that ecumenism seeks not only cannot do without the truth, but is unity in the very truth” 102 . ▪ Our Constitutions state that the Mystical Body of Christ, which is the Church, [is] formed by ourselves who, through holiness of life, must become ‘other Christs’ 103 . It is therefore natural that our proper law should exhort us to be formed in virtue according to “the doctrine of the great masters of the spiritual life… and of all the saints of all times whom the Church proposes as exemplars so that we may imitate their virtues. In such a way that, by following the Pope in doctrine and the saints in life, we shall never go wrong, since the Pope cannot err in the teachings of faith and morals, nor did the saints err in the practice of the virtues” 104 . Moreover, the Blessed Virgin , most eminent member of the Mystical Body of Christ, is another of our great loves because of “her union with Christ and with the Church. Because she begot us, the members, together with the Head. Because she was given to us as Mother” 105 . For “one cannot speak of the Church unless Mary is present… The Marian dimension is essential to the one Church of Christ, just as the Eucharistic dimension and the Petrine dimension are essential to it” 106 . Indeed, Mary is for us the model of ecclesial communion and the image and beginning of the Church 107 , and we firmly believe that, just as she was in the midst of the Apostles, so she is in our midst and in the midst of the Church of all times 108 . Likewise, in our task of proclaiming the Gospel, from the very beginnings of the Institute we have been taught always to do so “with the fervor and enthusiasm of the saints, even in moments of difficulty and persecution in a de-Christianized and atheistic world” 109 . Because “the saints are a most eloquent sign of the vitality of the Church; they have always transformed the world. They have been the true reformers of the world and of the Church. They are the best members of the Mystical Body of Christ. They are the greatest and most complete fruit of the Incarnation and the Redemption. The saints have been the outstanding witnesses and protectors of the divine Tradition of the Church, that is, they recall and transmit with their lives the very breath of the Church. They have known how to overcome all the obstacles that stood against Evangelization, and therefore they are models to follow and to whom we must turn in the work of Evangelization” 110 . ▪ “Our third great love [is and] must always be the white figure of the Pope : ‘Where Peter is, there is the Church’” 111 . For we understand that “the idea of a Body of Churches calls for the existence of a Head of the Churches, which is precisely the Church of Rome” 112 . Thus, then, we members of the Institute, wherever we may be, strive to give “witness of a firm and convinced communion in filial relationship with the Pope, perpetual and visible center of unity of the universal Church, and with the bishop, ‘visible principle and foundation of unity’ in the particular Church, and in the ‘mutual esteem among all forms of apostolate in the Church’” 113 . Consequently, “we make our own the teaching of St. Ignatius of Loyola: ‘To be right in everything, we must always hold that the white I see, I will believe to be black, if the hierarchical Church so determines’ 114 ” 115 . Because “to be with the Pope in everything means to be with God in everything; to love Jesus Christ and to love the Pope is the same love” 116 , since “… to love the Pope, to love the Church, is to love Jesus Christ” 117 . Persuaded that “the Pope must be loved on the cross; and whoever does not love him on the cross does not truly love him” 118 , our proper law makes its own the expression of St. Luigi Orione, who says: “We must annihilate ourselves at the feet of the Church and of the Superiors and obey out of love for Christ and be like doormats… let no one ever surpass us in filial obedience, in deference and love for the Pope and the Bishops, whom the Holy Spirit has placed to govern the Church of God” 119 . 3. To enrich His one Church From Pentecost to our own day, the Holy Spirit pours out His gifts in a great multiplicity of forms in order to enrich with them His one Church, which, in her varied beauty, unfolds in history the unsearchable riches of Christ 120 . In any case, it is always a divine gift, fundamentally one, even within the multiplicity and variety of the spiritual gifts, or charisms, granted to persons and communities 121 . Among the immensity of gifts with which God is pleased to adorn His Church are the charisms granted to men and women destined to found ecclesial works and especially religious institutes, which receive their character from the charisms of their founders, live and act under their influence and, to the extent of their fidelity, receive new gifts 122 , as St. John Paul II explained. In fact, the Council observes that “the Church willingly received and approved with her authority” the religious families 123 ; for it belongs to her above all not to quench the Spirit, but to test everything and hold fast to what is good 124 . That “is the reason why the Church defends and supports the proper character of the various religious institutes” 125 . Hence “a true religious keeps faith with and shows great love not only for the gift of religious life but also for his own institute, which includes in a particular way “the mind and purpose of the Founder” 126 and the Constitutions ” 127 , since ultimately it is a matter of being faithful to the gift of God and to His Church, which has raised up our Religious Family for a specific ecclesial service: the evangelization of culture. Since the Church canonically erected our Institute and approved its Constitutions on that May 8, 2004, there is a particular reciprocal bond between the two, for from that moment our Institute became part of the spiritual and apostolic patrimony of the Church 128 . For this reason, as we draw very near to celebrating the day of the foundational grace, and within the ecclesial context we have been discussing, it seems fitting to us to quote once again that paternal warning which the Spiritual Father of our Institute gave us, saying: “at times one finds today a prejudice according to which the ‘differences’ that characterize and distinguish religious institutes from one another should be eliminated. Each institute must take care to maintain its own ‘physiognomy,’ the specific character of its own reason for being, which has exercised an attraction, which has given rise to vocations and particular attitudes, giving a public witness worthy of esteem. It is naive and presumptuous to believe, in the end, that each institute must be the same as all the others by practicing a general love of God and neighbor. Whoever thought this way would forget an essential aspect of the Mystical Body: the heterogeneity of its constitution, the pluralism of models in which the vitality of the spirit that animates it is manifested, the transcendent human and divine perfection of Christ, its Head, which can only be imitated according to the innumerable resources of the soul animated by grace” 129 . Aware of the great importance of our specific vocation, both for our Religious Family and for the whole Church, let us come to know, deepen, live with conviction and transmit the proper spirituality of the Institute to the whole Church. ***** As we said at the beginning, this month of May that we begin today is strewn with dates very significant for our Institute: May 3, the day of the foundational grace; May 8, the solemnity of Our Lady of Luján –Queen of the Institute–; and May 23, the solemnity of Pentecost, the day on which the Church was born. All of them invite us to pause and celebrate the gift that the Holy Spirit has granted to our Institute in relation to the growing needs of the Church and of the world. Let us know how to recognize in the magnificent charism and spiritual patrimony of our Institute one of the clearest signs of divine generosity, which has inspired and continues to spur the generosity of so many souls. We must truly rejoice at this fact, since it shows that among men the sense of service to the kingdom of God and to the growth of the Church is broadening and deepening. Let us have confidence in the One who has called us, the Incarnate Word Himself, Head of the Church. He has entrusted to us the wonderful gift of this special vocation for the sake of the whole Church, so that we may go and bear fruit, fruit that will last 130 . Let us have confidence in God who is able to make us abound copiously, far more than we ask or think, by the power at work within us; to Him be glory in the Church and in Christ Jesus, in all generations, for ever and ever. Amen 131 . May Mary Most Holy, Mother of the Church, whom we will celebrate with great solemnity this coming May 8, always bless and protect the life of our Institute. Through her intercession may the Lord grant us His Holy Spirit, and docility to Him, so that we may belong more and more to Christ 132 , and hence to His Mystical Body, and may we “sing forever the mercies of God” 133 . Guardians of the spirit

Dear Monks: On the very happy occasion of the 30th anniversary of the founding of the Contemplative Branch of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, I wish to convey to you, in my own name and in that of the entire Religious Family of the Incarnate Word, our most sincere appreciation and our very best wishes to all the religious of contemplative life scattered throughout the world. Truly, our whole Religious Family joins gladly in the common hymn of praise and gratitude to the Lord for the gift He has given to our Institute and, in fact, to His whole Church in the Contemplative Branch of the Institute of the Incarnate Word. The pages of this commemorative magazine for the thirtieth anniversary of contemplative life in our Institute, which I have the pleasure of presenting today, do nothing other than illustrate the importance and the very significant role that you carry out in ecclesial service for the benefit of all the members of the people of God, and the spiritual enrichment you bring to our Institute. 1. An eminent role Indeed, in the decree Perfectae Caritatis , the Second Vatican Council did not limit itself to affirming that contemplatives still retain today their meaning and a fully valid foundation; it said that the place they occupy in the Mystical Body is “eminent” 1 . It is undeniable that the demands of evangelization today are many and urgent. But we would be mistaken if, starting from the observation of even urgent apostolic needs, we were to judge a form of life dedicated exclusively to contemplation as outdated. That is why our Constitutions say: “the best way to carry out an effective apostolate is the closest union with the Incarnate Word” 2 , which constitutes the principal end of the monk 3 and through which you contribute effectively to the apostolic activity not only of the Institute but of the whole Church 4 . Looking back over these 30 years, it is consoling to think that precisely in these times, when the needs of evangelization are greater, our monks have had a qualified expansion. In this fact there is an indication from the Spirit that reminds all of us, frequently tempted by the allure of efficiency, of the supremacy of supernatural means over merely human ones. Indeed, how eloquent for all is your witness—the witness of our monks—who, “renouncing everything and aiming directly at the End” 5 , tell us that “God is all and must be all in all” 6 . 2. Guardians of the spirit If the Magisterium recognizes in contemplatives “the glory of the Church and a wellspring of heavenly graces” 7 , you are no less so for us. For our monks are—as our Proper Law explicitly states—“key pieces of the apostolic endeavor of our Institute” 8 , of “the greatest importance” 9 , since they are “magnets of God’s grace and lightning rods of His wrath” 10 , who occupy a “preferential place in our Institute” 11 . From this also follows the most important mission that has been entrusted to you: “to be at the vanguard of our Institute and to be the guardians of its spirit” 12 . You know well that our beloved Religious Family has not been immune to difficulties and that it advances “like a pilgrim amid the persecutions of the world” 13 and the contradictions of good people 14 . But it seems to me that we too can see applied to ourselves the words of St. John Paul II when he said: “In a not-so-distant historical period, it was almost feared that your orders would be suppressed, but the fidelity of the monks of that time, sustained by divine help and by the protection of Most Holy Mary , enabled them to overcome the trial and not die” 15 . Therefore, with great confidence I turn to you, the noble souls of our contemplatives, to entrust to the ardor of your charity this great mission, which I would like you always to keep very much in mind: the safeguarding of the charism of our Institute depends in no small measure on you, on your fidelity, on your joyful acceptance of the demands of silent immolation, on the intensity with which you live our proper spirituality. In a word: much depends on your configuration to Christ the Victim 16 . Be tenaciously faithful to the patrimony of the Institute, to the evangelical intention of our Founder, and by your example “spur many to welcome the charism of the vocation into their hearts” 17 . And thus, “bearing the weaknesses of many, without faltering before flattery or threats, and remaining above the ups and downs of fortune or failure, keep your soul always ready to accept death, if necessary, for the good of the Institute in the service of Jesus Christ” 18 . May your fidelity—of which this anniversary speaks to us so persuasively—be today and always the consoling bulwark of protection for our Institute. And may your prayers and sacrifices be the fortification that silently rises around us to keep us solidly united, founded on the Rock that is Christ 19 . May the “communal witness of poverty and fraternal charity itself” 20 of our monasteries make them beacons of joy that enlighten all the members. May tender devotion to the Mother of Christ, which silently interweaves prayers and sacrifices offered as caresses to this Blessed Mother, be the mantle that wraps us when the storm rages and that preserves in all of us “spiritual fervor, the joy of evangelizing, even when we must sow in tears” 21 . Persevere always in your mission of being vigilant sentinels of the Absolute , in constant prayer with God, so as to present to Him “the joys and the hopes, the griefs and the anxieties” 22 of our beloved Institute, and thus open the floodgates through which may pour forth that torrent of graces we so greatly need “to to prolong the Incarnation in all things” 23 . In other words: be always faithful to your vocation; zealously preserve the gift that has been given to you and make it bear fruit. We expect much of you! Finally: To you who, by your particular consecration, carry forward the whole work of the Institute 24 , who extend our apostolic works with a mysterious fruitfulness 25 , and who by your hidden immolation enrich the whole Church with most abundant fruits of holiness 26 , I want to say in the name of our whole Religious Family: Thank you so very much! And “thanks be to God, who endowed you with so faithful a heart… Let these works shine before men; let them see them, celebrate them, and glorify the Father who is in heaven” 27 . Invoking upon all of you the maternal protection of Mary, I wish you, in the name of the whole Institute, a great abundance of blessings and great fruitfulness in vocations. A very happy anniversary! “The indispensables”

The ‘indispensables ’, “absolutely” and “totally” Cf. Constitutions, 17 , 95, 174 and 210; Directory of Spirituality 37 When reading our Proper Law, especially its principal documents, that is, the Constitutions and the Directory of Spirituality , it is striking that the word indispensable is mentioned five times. And on two of those occasions the Proper Law also adds the adverbs “absolutely” 1 and “totally” 2 . The Royal Spanish Academy defines “indispensable” as the adjective applied to a thing or person that one cannot do without; that which is necessary, which is obligatory 3 . In this sense, both in the Constitutions and in the Directory of Spirituality we read: “We wish to manifest our love and gratitude to the Blessed Virgin, and at the same time obtain her indispensable help to prolong the Incarnation in all things, by making a fourth vow of Marian slavery according to St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort” 4 . “With regard to joy, as a fruit of the Holy Spirit and an effect of charity, we must strive by every means that ‘no one be disturbed or saddened in the house of God’ 5 . For this it is totally indispensable to live fraternal charity…” 6 . “… charity is indispensable to evangelize the culture, both as the end of the agent and as the end of the work. Otherwise, ‘the civilization of love’ will not be attained 7 ” 8 . “He became incarnate so that we might have life and have it abundantly (Jn 10:10). To have that life in Christ Jesus (1 Cor 15:21-22) it is absolutely indispensable to be united to His Person, to have His Spirit, to assimilate His doctrine, to frequent His sacraments, to imitate His examples, to love His Mother tenderly, to be in perfect communion with His Hierarchical Church through its twofold bond, namely: through one same faith and one same charity, and through the government of one alone over all: Peter” 9 . “We must always remember that for persecution to be blessed it must, indispensably , meet two requirements: that we be ‘reviled for the sake of Christ,’ and that what is said against us be false’ 10 ; and we must take great care not to turn over and over our troubles, dwelling on them with delicate self-indulgence, or falling into ‘that Luciferian belief that we are something great,’ that we are suffering a great deal” 11 . Each of these paragraphs, with its own particular nuance, highlights precisely that which is essential, vital, irreplaceable to us—that is, indispensable —if we are to carry out with growing “perfection the service of God and of men” 12 , which is the same as saying “a true service to the Church” 13 . In light of the force of these texts, it becomes telling to delve into that without which we would not be living our vocation to the full, and whose absence would be greatly detrimental to the work of the Institute. 1. Absolutely indispensable We would like to begin by developing what the Constitutions , in number 210, define as absolutely indispensable , the expression underscoring the essential character of what follows. The first thing mentioned there is precisely the end of the Christian life: “ to be united to His Person ,” that is, to be united to Christ. In this lies “the true greatness of the Christian and religious vocation: union with God” 14 . Indeed, it is for this that we became religious, to this that we consecrated our lives, and that is why the Directory of Consecrated Life , quoting the Magisterium of the Church, points out: “The religious who consecrates himself to God in a particular way, seeking union with God through the practice of perfect charity, must do so through Christ , with Christ and in Christ . He is called to be united to God in Christ and to imitate more closely and represent perpetually in the Church ‘that form of life which the Son of God took up when He came into this world to do the will of the Father, and which He proposed to the disciples who followed Him’ 15 ” 16 . What is more, “if this applies to every religious, ‘all the more reason must we live this reality as religious of the Family of the Incarnate Word’ 17 ” 18 . The tireless search for union with God is essential to every religious and must be so for us. Moreover, this Christocentric imprint must be branded into us and into our apostolate of evangelizing the culture. That is why the “reality of being other Christs is central in our spirituality” 19 . Our Proper Law expresses it magnificently in a line that should become the banner we hold aloft every day: “If we are religious, it is in order to imitate the Incarnate Word, chaste, poor, obedient and son of Mary” 20 . Now, religious life as the following of Christ in order to attain the perfection of charity “is only to be lived within the framework of one’s own institute: ‘Growing conformity to Christ is brought about in accordance with the charism and norms of the institute to which the religious belongs . Each institute has its own spirit, character, purpose and tradition, and it is by conforming to them that the religious grows in his union with Christ ’ 21 ” 22 . For this reason the Mystical Doctor St. John of the Cross, in his Counsels to a Religious on How to Reach Perfection , writes: “In no way should you wish to know things, but only how you will better serve God and better keep the things of your institute” 23 . For this it is necessary to know in depth the spirit of the founder and the sound traditions of the Institute, to be ‘specialists’ in the Proper Law and to draw from it the criteria of discernment for one’s own action and conduct; it is also necessary to know the writings of the founder and to grow fond of what is our own, of the ideals and holy interests of the Institute. Each member of the Institute must make the non-negotiable elements his own, interiorize them and live them as such. For precisely what is so well explained and developed in each of those elements is what God has called us to live; it is for this that God has gathered us from so many countries and from such diverse cultures, and it is to this very thing that we committed ourselves before God and men when we made our religious profession. For do we not say that we consecrate ourselves in poverty, chastity and obedience “according to the evangelical way traced out in the Constitutions of the Institute of the Incarnate Word 24 ”? That is why it is indispensable that “all the members of our Institute not only fulfill with the greatest possible perfection the evangelical counsels and the self-giving to Jesus through Mary, but also ‘order their life according to the Proper Law of the Institute and thus strive to attain the perfection of their state’” 25 . For, in the end, in all these elements we have just mentioned we have the concrete expression of the path we must follow toward union with the Incarnate Word. It is very important to bear this in mind because there is no lack of religious who nourish themselves on a foreign spirituality, which may be very good—excellent—for religious of that other congregation, but it is not ours and it is not what God wants for us. That must be clear. Throughout the length and breadth of our Proper Law and the abundant treasure of the Institute’s patrimony, we find a whole range of guidelines that converge precisely on union with God. Among them we would like to highlight a few: – Prayer : it is in prayer—vocal or mental—that the soul finds a favorable means of uniting itself to God, and it is there that it finds that familiarity with the Incarnate Word 26 which is so fundamental for one who calls himself His religious. That is why each document of our Proper Law, with paternal insistence, addresses to us the call to “unceasing prayer and contemplation” 27 , since it is in prayer that the soul gradually puts on the “purity, taste and will” 28 of our Lord. Blessed Giuseppe Allamano used to say to his religious: “If there is piety, there is union with God, and everything else comes in addition, because the Lord gives us the graces we need when we pray well” 29 . And along the same lines Blessed Paolo Manna wrote: “without prayer there is no union with God, and without union with God there is no stability in the good” 30 . Likewise, and within the sphere of the life of prayer, silence is a privileged means for union with God: “Silence is a need of the soul, to manifest in the deepest way that, in the presence of God, there is nothing more to say” 31 . It is a means to attain union with God and, therefore, it should lead to the summit of prayer. – The practice of the religious vows : for these “contribute not a little to purity of heart and spiritual freedom, continually stir up the fervor of charity and […] are able to make the Christian more like the kind of virginal and poor life that Christ the Lord chose for Himself and that His Mother, the Virgin, embraced” 32 . Therefore, if the specific end of the Institute consists in attaining the perfection of charity, “by the practice of the evangelical counsels ‘charity toward God and toward neighbor is singularly fostered” 33 . Consequently, “the evangelical counsels have an eschatological meaning and, in particular, consecrated celibacy announces the life of the hereafter and union with Christ the Bridegroom; poverty provides a treasure in heaven; the commitment of obedience opens the way to the possession of the perfect freedom of the children of God in conformity with the will of the heavenly Father” 34 . All of which is wonderfully expressed in the very formula of the religious vows: “… chaste , for the Kingdom of Heaven, poor , manifesting that God is man’s only true wealth, and obedient , unto death on a cross, in order to follow more intimately the Incarnate Word in His chastity, poverty and obedience” 35 . – Apostolate or work itself, whatever it may be, is conducive to union with God: since “all apostolic activity must be animated by union with Christ, toward which religious cannot fail to tend by virtue of their profession” 36 . “The apostolate being a supernatural reality—fully theological—its fruitfulness depends on union with God and with the Church” 37 . In turn, “identifying ourselves with Christ must lead us to act as He did, of whom it is said that He has done all things well 38 ” 39 ; “bearing the weight of work in union with Jesus” 40 . – The cross in our lives: that is, sufferings. Like a refrain, this must resound in the depths of our soul: “neither Jesus without the Cross, nor the Cross without Jesus” 41 . Both are indispensable in our life; that is why we must learn to profit from the crosses God sends us, which always come accompanied by the intimate and real companionship of the Incarnate Word. The Directory of Spirituality tells us so splendidly: “All the co-redemptive efficacy of our sufferings depends on their union with the Cross, and in the measure and degree of that union. […] No pain is redemptive unless it is united to the Passion of Christ. If we do not learn to be victims with the Victim, all our sufferings are useless” 42 . That is why “one must live dying” 43 . “This is the secret of all supernatural fruitfulness! Everything lies in knowing how to die! That is the great science!” 44 . And to encourage us to suffer in union with Christ it tells us: “Nothing attracts divine benevolence as much as suffering” 45 . So fundamental is the cross in our lives that our Proper Law takes as its own the statement of the Mystical Doctor of Fontiveros, who says: “If… anyone should try to persuade you… of a doctrine of laxity and greater relief, do not believe it or embrace it, even if it be confirmed by miracles, but rather penance and more penance and detachment from all things; and never, if you wish to come to possess Christ, seek Him without the cross ” 46 . – The help of Most Holy Mary , for no one was united to God as she was, in being espoused to the Holy Spirit and bearing the Word of God in her most pure womb. She is “the proximate end, the mysterious center and the easy means for going to Christ” 47 . Each member of the Institute must learn to depend “totally and in every way on God through Mary” 48 if he wishes to attain union with God, since for us there is no smoother, easier or shorter way to go to God than “through Mary, with Mary, in Mary and for Mary” 49 . Without this, we could not say that we are essentially Marian 50 . All these things, when well lived, practiced conscientiously and with conviction, bring with them certain attitudes, ways of proceeding, and criteria for undertaking or setting aside apostolic endeavors, which must gradually transform us from within into ‘other Christs.’ Our Spiritual Father St. John Paul II expressed it beautifully and with great power of synthesis as follows: “The truth of consecrated life as union with Christ in divine charity is expressed in certain fundamental attitudes, which must grow throughout one’s whole life. Broadly speaking, they can be summarized thus: the desire to transmit to all the love that comes from God through the heart of Christ, and, therefore, the universality of a love that does not stop before the barriers that human selfishness raises in the name of race, nation, cultural tradition, social or religious condition, etc.; an effort of benevolence and esteem toward all, and especially toward those whom one humanly tends to neglect or despise most; the manifestation of a special solidarity with the poor, the persecuted or those who are victims of injustice; solicitude to help those who suffer most, such as, at present, the many handicapped, the abandoned, the exiled, etc.; the witness of a humble and meek heart, which refuses to condemn, renounces all violence and all revenge, and forgives with joy; the will to foster reconciliation everywhere and to see that the evangelical gift of peace is welcomed; generous dedication to every apostolic initiative that tends to spread the light of Christ and to bring salvation to humanity; assiduous prayer according to the great intentions of the Holy Father and of the Church” 51 . It is likewise absolutely indispensable “ to have the Spirit of Christ and to assimilate His doctrine .” This is so, purely and simply, because the Spirit of Christ, that is, the Holy Spirit, is the spirit of our Religious Family 52 . “By the proper charism of the Institute,” say our Constitutions , “without coercion of any kind, scrupulously respecting consciences, promoting healthy pluralism, leading to the full living of the freedom of the children of God 53 , because where the Holy Spirit is, there is freedom 54 ” 55 . Consequently, it is vital to employ the means to keep the soul constantly ready for whatever God may dispose 56 . Inexorably united to docility to the Holy Spirit is the assiduous reading, “deepened within the Church” 57 , of Sacred Scripture, which must always be “the soul of our soul, of our spirituality, theology, preaching, catechesis and pastoral work” 58 , because it is there that the doctrine of Christ , as understood in the Church, is found 59 . Put in a few words: “Only one who is totally faithful to the doctrine of Christ can be an effective apostle” 60 . It is not surprising, then, that one of the non-negotiable elements attached to the charism is precisely docility to the Magisterium of the Church, and that our members be formed in the “strictest fidelity to the supreme Magisterium of the Church of all times” 61 , solidly instructed in a sound theology—which “proceeds from faith and seeks to lead to faith—” 62 , built upon “a profound knowledge of the philosophy of being” 63 . The Constitutions also point out that it is absolutely indispensable for each member of the Institute “ to frequent His sacraments, to imitate His examples .” And regarding this we find abundant provisions in our Proper Law, which not only prescribe and encourage us toward the fruitful reception of the sacraments—making sacramental life an essential part of the discipline of the Institute—but also make it central when it comes to mission. “Authentic evangelization must lead to and culminate in the worthy reception of the sacraments, for through them the grace of the Holy Spirit is ordinarily communicated” 64 . Indeed, several of our documents develop, from different points of view, the sacramental life both for the members and for the faithful in our missions. It is natural, then, that Eucharistic devotion and the worthy celebration of Holy Mass, as the liturgical act par excellence of the mystery of the Redemption, should be another of the non-negotiable elements. Regarding the imitation of the examples of Christ , we have already said something above. Let us add here that “if every Christian should pass through this earth in imitation of the Incarnate God, all the more reason must we live this reality as religious of the family ‘of the Incarnate Word.’ And not only must we ourselves live the life of Christ, seeking God in all things, but we must spread the life of Christ in others, and inform with it the cultures of men in order to elevate man” 65 . With various expressions our Proper Law insistently stresses how indispensable it is for us “to be ‘other Christs,’ to be ‘like a new incarnation of the Word,’ ‘like another humanity of His,’ so that the Father may see in us ‘nothing but the beloved Son’ 66 ” 67 . In fact, this is the very thing we have committed ourselves to under vow, when we say that we wish “to follow more intimately the Incarnate Word” so that our “life may be a living memorial of the way of existing and acting of Jesus, the Word made flesh 68 , before the Father and before men” 69 . All our documents are nothing but an unfolding of guidelines, attitudes, criteria, explanations, etc., on how best to imitate the Incarnate Word. Truly, in our spirituality—if it is to be serious, as we want it to be—the imitation of Christ is irreplaceable. “ To love His Mother tenderly .” We have said it and we wish to emphasize it: love for the Mother of the Savior, devotion to the Blessed Virgin—which must be great, tender and constant 70 —is indispensable in the life of every member of the Institute. For ours is a consecration in slavery of love to the Mother of God. And as such we must “invoke her, greet her, think of her, speak of her, honor her, glorify her, commend ourselves to her, rejoice and suffer with her, work, pray and rest with her” 71 . For this reason, from our entrance into the Institute, we can say that our formation is “a school of filial and profound love for the Blessed Virgin Mary” 72 . She is, moreover, not only the Model and protection of our consecrated life 73 but also our Model as missionaries 74 , since it is from her that we learn everything, particularly “docility and promptness in carrying out what the Holy Spirit asks” 75 and, truth be told, her “help is indispensable to us to prolong the Incarnation in all things” 76 . For this reason, one cannot belong to the Incarnate Word without at the same time belonging to the Mother of the Incarnate Word. Finally, the paragraph of the Constitutions we have been developing ends by saying that it is absolutely indispensable “ to be in perfect communion with His Hierarchical Church through its twofold bond, namely: through one same faith and one same charity, and through the government of one alone over all: Peter .” This is so because the Institute was born in the Catholic Church, and is of the Catholic Church and for the Catholic Church; therefore, all of us members of the Institute of the Incarnate Word are formed and work for the building up of the one Church of Christ. In this sense, we read in the Directory of Spirituality that “to love Jesus Christ and to love the Pope is one and the same love” 77 , since “… to love the Pope, to love the Church, is to love Jesus Christ” 78 . That is why “our motto is ‘with Peter and under Peter’” 79 . For it could not be otherwise, since “in the very spirit of the Institute of the Incarnate Word we find the foundation of our love and fidelity to the Church—of an authentic ecclesial spirituality—for ‘Christ Himself is Incarnate in His Body, the Church’ 80 ; and in every man, because ‘Christ mysteriously identifies Himself with every man […] ‘in Him we are christs and Christ’ 81 ” 82 . And, furthermore, as true devotees of the Blessed Virgin Mary, who is the model of ecclesial communion 83 , we cannot but tend toward the unity of the universal Church. Since perfect communion with His Church is thus indispensable for each one of us and for the work of the Institute, we strive “to achieve, through prayer, penance, study, dialogue and collaboration, full communion in the unity of the Church ‘which Christ bestowed on His Church from the beginning, and which we believe subsists indefectibly in the Catholic Church and hope will grow until the consummation of the ages’ 84 ” 85 . From this follow, as indispensable, our fidelity to the Magisterium of the Church, our unfailing love for the figure of the Holy Father, the embracing of the cause of ecumenism, and the carrying forward, with the zeal of the saints, of the missionary work on behalf of the Church, with the sole objective that Christ may reign. 2. Charity is indispensable In this second point we would like to treat, albeit very briefly, what the Constitutions say in numbers 17 and 174, which point to charity as indispensable—that is, cardinal and capital—for our evangelizing task, if we are to carry it out fruitfully and joyfully. Quoting the words of St. Paul VI, our Proper Law says: “… charity is indispensable to evangelize the culture, both as the end of the agent and as the end of the work. Otherwise, ‘the civilization of love’ will not be attained 86 ” 87 . For “to love God by manifesting it in concrete love for our brothers is the only possible way of loving God, as Jesus Christ taught us” 88 ; that is why “our Religious Family, as another prolongation of the Incarnation of the Word, ‘in order to incarnate Him in all that is human,’ humbly dedicates itself to achieving this through the works of mercy” 89 , spiritual and corporal. In this sense we are convinced, and it has been our experience over the years, that the specific and singular end of the Institute is in absolute harmony with the spiritual works of mercy, and that it is these which most spread the good 90 . However, since “love of God and love of neighbor merge with each other: [for] in the humblest we find Jesus Himself and in Jesus we find God” 91 , and because, furthermore, our Redeemer did so, we also dedicate ourselves to the corporal works of mercy 92 , especially with the disabled and the poorest. That is, it is our preferential option to serve those who find themselves in a situation of greater weakness and, therefore, of graver need 93 , since “charity toward the poor […]; care for the sick and those who suffer, contribute significantly to the mission of the Church” 94 . Hence we consider the members of the Institute who work in this kind of apostolate as “key pieces of the apostolic endeavor of the Institute” 95 . Our Proper Law indicates that it is, then, the works of mercy “that, by giving concrete witness of charity, will win many men for the kingdom of Christ, giving glory to God and saving many souls, thus fulfilling our universal end and also the specific end of our religious family” 96 . Our Institute having been conceived as missionary—with active and contemplative members—we must say that mission itself is already a work of charity and that the works of charity themselves form an “essential part of the mission of the Church” 97 . Consequently, “together with the proclamation of the Word and the administration of the sacraments, the service of charity also forms part of the essential spheres of evangelization” 98 . “The advantages that the works of mercy have for the concrete realization of the charism of the Institute are manifest, above all in countries where the explicit proclamation of the Gospel is forbidden and the only way to do it is through the silent witness of the religious. In Muslim countries, for example, it may become the only means of evangelization. But it also allows, in places where one can preach with the word, to corroborate with deeds what is proclaimed” 99 . “For this reason, among the variety of apostolates of our Institutes, a preferential place must be reserved for charitable work, which is an essential component of the evangelizing mission of the Church and an indispensable element for the evangelization of culture” 100 . For, as Pope Benedict said, this “remains the royal road for evangelization” 101 . It is understood, then, that the works of mercy or charitable activities, whatever they may be, are indispensable to our missionary task and a non-negotiable element attached to the charism of the Institute. But we must say that paragraph 174 of the Constitutions which we have quoted, immediately after emphasizing that “we must give priority to the care of the poor, the sick and the needy of every kind” because the charity of Christ urges us 102 , exhorts us to practice “charity concretely, as a witness, in the first place, to all the members of our Institutes that ‘charity, charity alone, will save the world; blessed are those who have the grace of being victims of charity!’ 103 ”. “In this work of apostolate, in which ‘one is a missionary above all because of what one is… before being one because of what one says or does’ 104 , the first place is held by the witness of life, ‘the first and irreplaceable form of mission’ 105 , so that the charity of Christ may shine forth among the faithful 106 ” 107 . If this witness of charity is lacking among the members of one’s own Family, not only is the message preached not credible, but many are prevented from embracing it, to the great detriment of the missionary work that has been entrusted to us. This “practice of charity is manifested in the attitude of service to others: in imitation of the Incarnate Word who, by His gesture of washing the feet of His disciples, revealed to us the depth of God’s love for man: in Him, God Himself places Himself at the service of men! Thus giving us an example that our religious life is fully realized in self-offering love, of concrete and generous service” 108 . “If in mission lands the religious communities are truly such, and in them there is an effort to live fraternal charity intensely with each and every one of their members 109 , then much fruit may be expected. If, on the contrary, a missionary does not know how to live with his peers, is ignorant of the fundamental principles of dialogue, does not practice fraternal charity de facto , and makes everything revolve around himself, in that community a good share of energy will have to be spent merely in bearing with the weak brother” 110 . There are many who call themselves very faithful to the Institute because they have been in it for many years, because they quote some phrases of the Proper Law with a certain ease, because they hold or have held some important office, because they occasionally take part in some celebration—without realizing that “it is not enough to take part in some meeting or festivity to be fully a religious” 111 –, etc., and yet, at the same time, they allow themselves serious faults against charity. Among them, “the one that is sometimes committed with the least remorse is murmuring” 112 . Our Proper Law calls these religious “‘ two-faced men ,’ because they sow confusion among many who live in peace 113 ” 114 , and they do not realize that they are attacking concord, the union of the brothers of one same Family and the peace of the community, spreading sadness—so often the fruit of an evil spirit and of unjust comments—thus squandering the basic foundation of their consecration in this beloved Institute, which is precisely love and service of Christ, “both of the physical Body of Christ in the Eucharist and of the Mystical Body of Christ, which is the Church, formed by ourselves… and by all men” 115 , among whom are the members of the Institute. We must be ready to die for one another, to defend the Institute with all its non-negotiable elements, to guard firmly the very rich patrimony that has been bequeathed to us: that is why whoever adopts an attitude, so often a comfortable one, and does not fight for the interests of the Institute or to keep the banner of our ideals held high… such a one has, in some way, already deserted. Have we not read that each one should have “the soul ready to accept death, if necessary, for the good of the Institute in the service of Jesus Christ” 116 ? Let us understand this well: if we do not practice charity concretely with the members of the Institute, we are straying from the path of perfection to which God has called us. “The missionary is the man of charity” 117 , and without charity we are not missionaries, and we do not even reach the level of a ‘good Christian.’ The apostle St. Paul told us so: Though I were to speak all the languages of men and of angels, if I do not have love, I am like a resounding bell or a clanging cymbal. Though I had the gift of prophecy and knew all mysteries and all knowledge, though I had all faith, a faith able to move mountains, if I do not have love, I am nothing. Though I were to distribute all my goods to feed the poor and hand over my body to the flames, if I do not have love, it profits me nothing 118 . One may know many languages, have much learning, have published books and given countless lectures; one may know the whole world, have friends of some influence, have considerable personal gifts and abundant means for the apostolate, but once again… if I do not have charity, all of that profits me nothing. “This is the reason why we must nourish fraternal charity 119 in our religious communities. It is true that there will always be difficulties, because we are creatures, fallible, and therefore we can fail. But these difficulties are borne, they are resolved. That is why the lack of charity and, specifically, murmuring in fraternal life, comes from a lack of understanding, or from not wanting to understand, the commandment of love in an exquisite way. Would that it could be said of the members of the Institute of the Incarnate Word what was said of the first Christians: See how they love one another!” 120 . And if anyone thinks these are sugary words for beginners, let him read what the Constitutions themselves say on the matter: “And let no one think that this is a utopia, for we have often already heard similar expressions. We must have the firm resolve always to safeguard charity, even though there may be false brethren 121 , who slip in to spy on the freedom we have in Christ Jesus 122 , who seem to be with us, but who are not of us 123 . Charity will never die! 124 ” 125 . All our members should always keep in mind the counsels of St. Benedict: “Let them be first to honor one another. Let them bear with the greatest patience one another’s weaknesses, whether of body or of character; let them vie with one another in obedience; let no one seek what he judges useful for himself, but rather what is useful for others; let them practice fraternal charity chastely; let them fear God with love; let them love their Abbot with sincere and humble affection, and let them prefer absolutely nothing to Christ, and may He bring us to Eternal Life” 126 . Without the practice of charity there is no joy. For “only he truly rejoices who rejoices in love” 127 . Therefore, the greater our fidelity to these indispensables , the more vehemently we will be tending toward perfection, the broader and more creative our charity will be, the more disinterested our sacrifice, the better we will fulfill our end as religious of the Incarnate Word, the greater our joy will be, and we will be in the fullness of our grace. * * * Perhaps we will be persecuted for all this, in which case we must give thanks to God who has found us worthy, and reread the indispensable requirements for persecution to be blessed 128 , taking great care not to turn over and over our troubles, dwelling on them with delicate self-indulgence, or falling into ‘that Luciferian belief that we are something great,’ that we are suffering a great deal 129 . May the Most Holy Virgin, Mother of the Incarnate Word and our Mother, who knows our interior struggles and our needs, when the storm rages, repeat to us with a maternal accent the do whatever He tells you 130 that she said to the servants at that wedding, and may the water of our frailty and weakness be changed into the wine of her strength.
