God, a provident Father

After increasing the number of seminarians from 42 to 147 in eight years, and that of minor seminarians from 200 to 500 in four seminaries; after providing ongoing formation to the priests of six dioceses of the metropolitan Church of Hue; after developing and intensifying the formation of young people and laity in the diocese of Nhatrang (Vietnam), the then bishop of that diocese, Francis Xavier van Thuan, was named by St. Paul VI coadjutor archbishop of Saigon. However, nine months after arriving there he was arrested by the communists and sent to a “re-education camp”—a euphemism they used for the word prison—where he remained from 1975 to 1988, suffering the “harshest captivity” 1 . Of those 13 years, he spent 9 in isolation, alone with two guards, something he himself describes as “a mental torture, in absolute emptiness, without work, walking around the cell from morning until half past nine at night so as not to be destroyed by arthrosis, at the edge of madness” 2 . He was then 48 years old. Certainly his was an extreme case; nevertheless, it is common for many good men and women to suffer moral evils through no fault of their own. That is why, as could happen to any one of us and in fact does happen to us when the things for which we fought so arduously are destroyed from one day to the next, Bishop van Thuan was tempted, and more than tempted, he was tormented by the fact that, being 48 years old, having worked eight years as a bishop, having acquired much pastoral experience, etc., he now found himself isolated, inactive, separated from his people. How many times throughout our history—at the level of the Institute, but also personally—have we had to leave unfinished a program or a project that was well planned, well organized; how many times have activities that we set in motion with great enthusiasm been obstructed; apostolates or projects of great scope have become minor activities; how many times, seeking to do good, have we been calumniated, persecuted, threatened… Nevertheless, we too, like Bishop van Thuan, must learn to “choose God and not the works of God” 3 , who disposes all things for our greater benefit. God grants us today to begin a new year. And so it might seem strange to speak of such an experience, when the whole world is planning the new year with optimism, but frequently without including God in its projects. For our part, it is not that we do not have projects, it is not that we do not have goals to reach, nor old challenges to keep facing, but it is no less true that divine providence has merciful designs for us that do not always coincide with our plans. This does not mean that this providential intervention of God must always be adverse; on the contrary, it is always positive and seeks to smooth the way for us, even when those situations do not please us and seem to us bad and very unfavorable. For this reason, it has seemed to us that it may be very healthy for our souls to take into account in ‘our planning’ that master coordinate, which in reality is the central axis on which hang the various variables that make up the interweaving of the many events of our daily life. So that, far from beginning the year with a pessimistic view of reality, we wish to offer a brief reflection on the special and merciful divine providence that is manifested even when bad things happen to the good and good things to the wicked, since, as St. John of the Cross says, “His Majesty having so ordained it, it is what is most fitting for us all” 4 . 1. The “hidden treasures” of divine providence It happens to not a few Christians that, even while they profess their faith in divine providence and strive with all their effort to give the best of themselves to do something good, for themselves or for others, they see their efforts despised and the work of their hands vanish before their eyes. Thus not a few are faced with the reality, for example, that their businesses went to ruin; that even having married and given everything, their family ends up divided; that the mission which cost them so many sacrifices has been closed, or an illness has taken them away from the apostolate; or simply that those from whom they expected help have betrayed them. Hence the reality of evil and suffering, present in so many forms in human life, constitutes for many—even religious—the principal difficulty in accepting the truth of divine providence (and we say accept in the sense of assimilating it interiorly and not simply of giving intellectual assent to a truth). Echoing this reality, St. John Paul II stated in one of his audiences: “In some cases, this difficulty takes on a radical form, when God is even accused of the evil and suffering present in the world, to the point of rejecting the very truth of God and of His existence (that is, to the point of atheism). In a less radical and yet disquieting way, this difficulty is expressed in so many critical questions that man poses to God. Doubt, questioning and even protest arise from the difficulty of reconciling the truth of divine providence, of God’s fatherly solicitude toward the created world, with the reality of evil and suffering experienced in various forms by men” 5 . On the other hand, every year we make the Spiritual Exercises and every year, therefore, we meditate on the Principle and Foundation : “Man is created to praise, reverence and serve God our Lord, and by this means to save his soul; and the other things on the face of the earth are created for man, and that they may help him in pursuing the end for which he is created . From this it follows that man is to use them as much as they help him toward his end, and ought to rid himself of them as much as they hinder him from it. For this reason it is necessary to make ourselves indifferent to all created things, in all that is granted to the liberty of our free will and is not forbidden to it; in such a way that we, for our part, do not want health more than sickness, riches more than poverty, honor more than dishonor, a long life more than a short one, and so in all the rest; desiring and choosing only what most leads us to the end for which we are created” 6 . St. Ignatius calls it the Principle and Foundation of his Spiritual Exercises, but it is also the most fundamental truth about the existence of man and divine providence. St. John Paul II expressed this when he said: “ Faith in divine providence is intimately linked with the basic conception of human existence, that is, with the meaning of man’s life . Man can face his existence in an essentially different way when he has the certainty that he is not under the dominion of a blind destiny ( fatum ), but depends on Someone who is his Creator and Father. For this reason, faith in divine providence, inscribed in the first words of the Apostles’ Creed, ‘I believe in God the Father almighty,’ frees human existence from the various forms of fatalistic thinking ” 7 . Nevertheless, it sometimes happens that under pressure or in difficult circumstances we forget this, or we accept these words as mere abstract principles of the spiritual life without their becoming an integral part of our daily life. That is, we do not take them on in a vital way. That is why in this first point we would like to bring up what the Magisterium of the Church and her illustrious Doctor, St. Thomas Aquinas, teach on this so fundamental topic. On the one hand, none of us is unaware that the truth of divine providence is present throughout all of Revelation. Even more, we can say that it “permeates all of Revelation ” 8 . Likewise, it is found from the beginning, as a fundamental truth of the faith, in the ordinary Magisterium of the Church, although only the First Vatican Council pronounced on it within the framework of the solemn dogmatic Constitution De fide catholica , in connection with the truth about creation. Here are the words of Vatican I: “God preserves all that He has created and directs it with His providence, ‘reaching from end to end mightily and governing all things with goodness’ 9 . ‘All things are naked before His eyes’ 10 , even what takes place through the free initiative of creatures.” Following in the footsteps of the constant tradition of the Church’s teaching, it is also deduced from the texts of the Second Vatican Council that God is the one who “cares for all with fatherly solicitude” 11 , and in particular “for the human race” 12 . A manifestation of this solicitude is also the “divine law, eternal, objective and universal, by which God orders, directs and governs the whole world and the ways of the human community according to the design of His wisdom and His love” 13 . “Man… does not in fact exist except through the love of God, who created him, and through the love of God, who preserves him. And he can only be said to live in the fullness of truth when he freely acknowledges that love and entrusts himself entirely to his Creator ” 14 . In the Summa Theologica , I, q. 22, the Angelic Doctor treats of the providence of God. We shall not transcribe everything explained there—although we strongly recommend reading it 15 —but shall simply confine ourselves to offering the basic concepts that will serve us as guidelines for approaching this topic. What in God is called providence is the plan of the order of things toward their ends 16 . All beings are subject to divine providence, and not only as a whole, but also in particular 17 . Providence comprises two things: the plan of the order of the beings provided for toward their end, and the execution of this order, called “government.” As to the first, God provides immediately for all things, because in His intellect He has the plan of them all, even of the least, and because to whatever causes He entrusted some effect He gave sufficient activity to produce it, for which it is indispensable that He should know beforehand, in its proper plan, the order of such effects. As to the second, divine providence makes use of intermediaries, for it governs lower beings by means of higher ones , not because its power is insufficient, but because its goodness is so great that it communicates to creatures themselves the prerogative of causality 18 . It is an effect of divine providence not only that anything whatever should happen, but that it should happen in a necessary or a contingent way; and therefore what divine providence disposes to happen infallibly and necessarily happens infallibly and necessarily , and what is in the plan of divine providence to happen contingently happens contingently 19 . Now, the suffering that arises from the many experiences of evil, especially when it is without fault, leads man to pose those difficult and dramatic questions which are at times an accusation, at other times a challenge, or a cry of rejection of God and His providence. In some way these questions could be summed up thus: “How can evil and suffering be reconciled with the fatherly solicitude, full of love, that Jesus Christ attributes to God in the Gospel? How can they be reconciled with the transcendent wisdom of the Creator? And in an even more dialectical way: in the face of all the experience of evil there is in the world, especially in the face of the suffering of the innocent, can we say that God does not will evil? And if He wills it, how can we believe that God is love , and all the more so that this love cannot but be omnipotent?” 20 . The affliction or suffering of the good—if it is without fault—is what seems to stand in opposition to divine providence. Faced with these questions, we too, like Job, experience how difficult it is to give an answer. That is why, with humility before the mystery 21 , we seek the answer in the Word of God, which the Holy Spirit made fruitful with the truth 22 . Thus in the Old Testament we find the affirmation: … but wickedness does not prevail over wisdom . Wisdom reaches mightily from one end to the other and governs all things gently 23 . We see, then, that in the face of the manifold experiences of evil and suffering in the world, the Old Testament already bore witness to the primacy of the Wisdom and goodness of God, of His divine providence. This attitude is outlined and developed in the Book of Job, which is entirely devoted to the theme of evil and pain seen as a trial, at times a tremendous one, for the just man, but overcome with the certainty, laboriously attained, that God is good. St. Thomas Aquinas in his Expositio super Job ad litteram states the following: “After most men had affirmed the opinion that natural things did not happen by chance but by providence, because of the order that clearly appears in them, a doubt arose among most men about the acts of man, that is, whether human affairs developed by chance or by causality, whether they were governed by some kind of providence or higher order. This doubt was nourished especially because no sure order is apparent in human events. For good things do not always happen to the good, nor bad things to the bad. On the other hand, bad things do not always befall the good, nor good things the wicked, but good and evil fall indiscriminately upon the good and the wicked . This fact especially moved the hearts of men to hold the opinion that human affairs are not governed by divine providence. Some said that human affairs proceed by chance except insofar as they are governed by human providence and counsel; others attribute their outcome to a fatalism governed by the heavens. This idea causes great harm to humanity . For if divine providence is denied, no reverence or true fear of God will remain among men. Every man can well weigh how great the propensity to vice and the lack of desire for virtue that follow from this idea will be. For nothing so draws men back from evil things and induces them to good as much as the fear and love of God. For this reason, the first and principal aim of those who had sought wisdom inspired by the spirit of God for the instruction of others was to remove this opinion from the hearts of men. So… the Book of Job… is directed to this: to show that human affairs are ruled by divine providence … […] The affliction of the just is what seems especially to impugn divine providence in human affairs. For although at first sight it may seem irrational and contrary to providence that good things sometimes happen to bad men, this can be excused in one way or another by divine compassion. But that the just should be afflicted without cause seems to undermine the foundation of providence entirely. Thus the varied and grievous afflictions of a certain just man named Job, perfect in all his virtues, are proposed as a kind of theme for the question that is to be discussed” 24 . In the Christian spiritual tradition Job symbolizes resigned suffering, the trusting acceptance of pain. That is why ‘Holy Job’ is the archetype and paradigm of Christian patience. Moreover, he is, according to scholars, “the best typical and tropological figure of passive purification” 25 , for he passes through all the stages of the dark purification: from the physical trial—nakedness, abandonment by friends, loss of goods—to the heartrending cry of the afflicted and humiliated soul that “roars and bellows” 26 . And this purifying night has the meaning of a means with respect to the end, which is to arrive at union with God. That is why we must know how to recognize that whatever ‘our night’ may be, it is “ a night that conceals the hopes of the light of day ” 27 . This being so, the affirmation of Sacred Scripture, wickedness does not prevail over wisdom 28 , strengthens our conviction that, in the providential plan of the Creator regarding the world, evil is ultimately subordinated to good . And it is very important always to bear this in mind. Our Proper Law reminds us of this very thing when it exhorts us to give glory to God by trusting without limits in His providence, telling us: “that all things work together for the good of those who love God 29 . In saying all things , it excepts nothing. Therefore, here are included all events, prosperous or adverse, what concerns the good of the soul, the goods of fortune, reputation, all the conditions of human life (family, studies, talents, etc.), all the interior states through which we pass (delights, joys, privations, dryness, displeasures, tedium, temptations, etc.), even faults and sins themselves. Everything, absolutely everything. In saying work together for the good , it is understood that they cooperate, contribute, happen for our spiritual good. One must have this vision and not that of the carnal or worldly man. One must see everything in the light of the loving designs of the providence of God, which only the spiritual man discovers: the spiritual man judges all things 30 . We must believe with unshakable firmness that even the most adverse events, those most opposed to our natural outlook, are ordained by God for our good, even though we do not understand His designs and do not know the end to which He wishes to lead us. But for our part, we must fulfill a condition for this to come about. That is why it adds of those who love God , that is, those whose will is united and submissive to that of God, who seek above all the interests and the glory of God, who are ready to sacrifice everything without reserve, persuaded that nothing is so advantageous as to abandon oneself into the hands of God in everything it may please Him to ordain, as Jesus gave us to understand: if anyone serves me, the Father will honor him 31 . He alone knows everything, even our soul, feelings, character, the secret springs that must be moved to bring us to heaven, the effects that this or that thing will produce in us, and He has all means at His disposal” 32 . Moreover, in the context of the integral truth about divine providence, and for a better understanding, it is necessary to bear in mind the following statements: “God does not will evil as such” and “God permits evil.” Concerning which St. John Paul II explains: “Regarding the first, it is fitting to recall the words of the Book of Wisdom: … God did not make death, nor does He rejoice in the destruction of the living. For He created all things that they might exist 33 . As for the permission of evil in the physical order , for example, in the face of the fact that material beings (among them also the human body) are corruptible and undergo death, it must be said that this belongs to the structure of these creatures. On the other hand, the unlimited continuance of every individual bodily being would be hardly conceivable in the present state of the material world. We can, then, understand that, if God did not create death , as the Book of Wisdom affirms, He nevertheless permits it with a view to the overall good of the material cosmos . But if it is a question of moral evil , that is, of sin and guilt in their various forms and consequences, even in the physical order, this evil God decidedly and absolutely does not will . Moral evil is radically contrary to the will of God. If this evil is present in the history of man and of the world, and at times in a totally oppressive form, if in a certain sense it has its own history, it is only permitted by divine providence , because God wills that there be freedom in the created world. The existence of created freedom (and consequently of man, and even the existence of pure spirits such as the angels, of whom we shall speak on another occasion) is indispensable for that fullness of good which God wills to bring about in creation. The existence of free beings is for Him a more important and fundamental value than the fact that those beings abuse their own freedom against the Creator and that, for this reason, freedom can lead to moral evil” 34 . That is why our Proper Law, with a fatherly accent, calls us to offer with our lives—with all their vicissitudes and particular circumstances—“an unceasing worship to divine providence,” having “the certainty that ‘bodily danger does not threaten those who, with the intention of following Christ, abandon all their things, entrusting themselves to divine providence’ 35 . That Father full of goodness who takes care of the birds and the flowers of the field 36 will not abandon those who give themselves to Him with such confidence” 37 . Undoubtedly reason and revelation greatly enlighten us concerning the mystery of divine providence which, while not willing evil, tolerates it in view of a greater good. However, the definitive light can only come from the victorious Cross of Christ. The Spiritual Father of our Religious Family develops this masterfully in a series of catecheses, saying: For “in the eternal plan of God and in His providential action in the history of man, all evil , and especially moral evil—sin— is subjected to the good of redemption and salvation precisely through the Cross and Resurrection of Christ. It can be affirmed that, in Him, God draws good out of evil . He draws it, in a certain sense, from the very evil that sin implies, which was the cause of the suffering of the immaculate Lamb and of His terrible death on the Cross as an innocent victim for the sins of the world. That is why in the liturgy of the Easter Vigil we exclaim: ‘ felix culpa ’ 38 ” 39 . “Thus, to the question of how to reconcile evil and suffering in the world with the truth of divine providence, no definitive answer can be offered without reference to Christ . Indeed, on the one hand Christ—the Incarnate Word—confirms with His own life—in poverty, humiliation and toil—and especially with His passion and death, that God is at man’s side in his suffering ; even more, that He Himself takes upon Himself the manifold suffering of man’s earthly existence. Jesus reveals at the same time that this suffering possesses a redemptive and salvific value and power , that in it is prepared that imperishable inheritance of which St. Peter speaks in his first Letter: the inheritance that is reserved for us in heaven 40 . The truth of providence thus acquires, through “the power and the wisdom” of the Cross of Christ, its definitive eschatological meaning. The definitive answer to the question about the presence of evil and suffering in man’s earthly existence is offered by divine Revelation in the perspective of ‘predestination in Christ,’ that is, in the perspective of man’s vocation to eternal life , to participation in the life of God Himself. This is precisely the answer that Christ has offered, confirming it with His Cross and with His Resurrection. In this way, everything, even the evil and suffering present in the created world, and especially in the history of man, is subjected to that inscrutable wisdom , about which St. Paul exclaims, as if transfigured: O the depth of the riches, of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! How inscrutable are His judgments and unfathomable His ways…! 41 . In the whole salvific context, it is in fact the wisdom against which wickedness cannot prevail 42 ” 43 . That is why what we have been saying—although, as we have said, we shall treat it on another occasion—applies also to the action of the demons, who are mere creatures and cannot escape the causality of God, the First Universal Cause of all being and acting. They, much to their regret, end up fulfilling the plan of God, who disposes all things for the good of those who love Him 44 . And the more they rage against the works of God and against Christians, even to causing them martyrdom, the more they contribute to the sanctification of the elect and to the spread of the Kingdom of God. That is why Tertullian said that “the blood of martyrs is the seed of new Christians.” 2. Some practical counsels of the saints It is well known that the saints also suffered and were purified in the crucible of the sorrows that befell them so often ‘unjustly,’ while they were totally innocent. Now, since the saints were not mistaken in the practice of the virtues 45 , it is fitting to learn from them to complete what is lacking in the Passion of Christ 46 with an affective… effective… and afflictive reparation… for our own benefit and that of the whole Mystical Body, as is asked of each one of us 47 . So that, if at some time everything should crumble and everything for which we fought and which we so defended should seem ruined; if the things we plan to do should come to face threats and we should find ourselves wrapped in moral evils and suffer the crushing weight of humiliation and calumny; if the question “what to do when nothing seems to make sense?” knocks at the door of our souls; let our answer be: it is time to believe. It is time to exercise our faith. It is time to cling still more to God. It is time to live with confidence the folly of the Cross, which consists in living the beatitudes 48 . It is the time to live “the folly of love without limits or measure, by which we are to bless those who curse us, without returning evil for evil 49 ” 50 . It is the time to strive to acquire the wisdom of the Cross, by which the world will not be able to deceive us 51 . The apostolic writings are full of precisely this wisdom, to help us, when we are afflicted, to recognize the passing of the grace of God. Thus St. Peter writes to the Christians of the first generation: Rejoice in this, even though now you must be saddened a little, in various temptations 52 . And he adds: so that your faith, tested, more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire, may be found worthy of praise, glory and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ 53 . These last words refer to the Old Testament, and especially to the book of Sirach, in which we read: For gold is tested in the fire , and men pleasing to God in the crucible of humiliation 54 . That is why the Apostle, taking up the same theme of trial, continues in his Letter: Rather, rejoice insofar as you share in the sufferings of Christ, so that at the revelation of His glory you may exult in His joy 55 . In an analogous way the Apostle James expresses himself when he exhorts Christians to face trials with joy and patience: Consider it the greatest joy, my brothers, to find yourselves surrounded by various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith produces patience. But let patience be accompanied by perfect works, so that you may be perfect and complete 56 . Lastly, St. Paul in the Letter to the Romans, after comparing human sufferings to “ labor pains ,” adds: Now, we know that God makes all things work together for the good of those who love Him… 57 , and further on, Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, anguish, persecution, hunger, nakedness, danger, the sword? 58 , finally concluding: For I am persuaded that neither death nor life… nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God (manifested) in Christ Jesus, our Lord 59 . That is why we must learn to see, together with the fatherhood of God, which is manifested through divine providence, the pedagogy of God: You suffer for the sake of your correction. God is treating you as sons; for what son is there whom his father does not correct (educate)…? God, looking to our benefit, corrects us to make us sharers in His holiness 60 . Thus, then, seen with the eyes of faith, suffering, although it may present itself as the darkest aspect of our earthly destiny, allows the mystery of divine providence , contained in the revelation of Christ, and in a special way in His Cross and in His Resurrection, to shine through for us. The saints of all times had this truth of divine providence firmly settled in their souls. And so when things were not going well, when they saw their plans seriously altered and the fruits of their efforts lying on the ground, when they were insulted and driven out of towns (even, in some cases, by the bishops of the dioceses), when they were not allowed to preach, when they were falsely accused, even when they were threatened with death and led to the scaffold, they were not disturbed, they did not lose their calm, they forgave their enemies and even rejoiced. We, like every Christian, are not exempt from those trials, and therefore, if any of this should happen to us, we must do ourselves the favor of praying . Not a prayer that tells God the things He has to do about the injustices we suffer and the sufferings that lacerate us. God already knows what He has to do. Rather, ours must be a prayer that nails us even more to our center, namely, God Himself—who for us was nailed to the Cross 61 —and reaffirms us in the knowledge that we are in His hands, striving, as St. John of the Cross says, “to keep the heart in peace,” letting “no event of this world disquiet” us; for “consider that everything must come to an end” 62 . The Mystical Doctor had the truth about the fatherly solicitude of our Lord so deeply imbued in his soul that in the most arduous combats he did not see his confidence diminished; quite the contrary, it grew in proportion to the trials he faced. And he counseled this very thing to souls, as is seen, for example, in the letter to Doña Juana de Pedraza: “All of it is knockings 63 and blows upon the soul so as to love more , which bring about more prayer and spiritual sighs to God, so that He may fulfill what the soul asks of Him. I already told you that there was no reason to be disquieted over those little things, but to do what you have been commanded, and, when they prevent you, obedience, and let me know, for God will provide what is best . Those who love God, He Himself takes care of their affairs, without their being anxious about them ” 64 . And in another letter he counsels a Carmelite nun something that all of us can practice: “When some unpleasantness and displeasure comes to you, remember Christ crucified, and be silent. Live in faith and hope, even if it be in darkness, for in that darkness God protects the soul. Cast your care upon God, for He cares for you; nor will He forget you. Do not think that He leaves you alone, for that would be to wrong Him” 65 . Moreover, let us bear in mind that the truth about divine providence is also closely united to the truth of the kingdom of God , and for this reason the words spoken by the Incarnate Word in His teaching on providence have a fundamental importance: Seek first the kingdom of God and His justice… and all these things will be given you besides 66 . The truth concerning divine providence, that is, the transcendent government of God over the created world, becomes comprehensible in the light of the truth about the kingdom of God , about that kingdom which God planned from all eternity to bring about in the created world thanks to predestination in Christ , who was begotten before every creature 67 . That is why it is common doctrine among the saints to exhort the faithful to live poverty of spirit as the fundamental disposition for preparing oneself to receive the divine gift. Indeed, this is how our life “becomes an unceasing worship of divine providence” 68 . The Mystic of Fontiveros recommends this very thing, for example: “ preserve the spirit of poverty and contempt of everything … wishing to be content with God alone. And know that you will not have or feel more needs than those to which you wish to subject your heart; for the poor in spirit is more constant and joyful in want , because he has placed his all in nothing at all, and so finds in everything breadth of heart” 69 . For his part, St. John of Ávila, Doctor of the Church, in the same line as St. John of the Cross, also invites us to see the adverse events that God permits to happen to us as moments of special purification for the good of our soul. Thus the Doctor of Ávila writes with a wise pen to a married woman whose son had suffered a misfortune: “Our Lord… takes care to send us some tribulations so that we may see our weakness, and be undeceived if we thought ourselves strong, and see the fortitude God gives us to suffer them joyfully, and know how powerful His hand is, which places virtue in such weak vessels, and how good He is, since He makes us gain from evils ” 70 . And then he shows her how God, through these sufferings, “cleanses [us of] our faults and fashions crowns for us in heaven; and the thanks given to God in these tribulations are a Christian and sweet music in His ears. I say Christian, because to give Him thanks in consolations belongs to everyone, but in tribulations only to good Christians” 71 . Therefore, the Saint of Ávila goes on to say, those events that are adverse to us, painful, and not seldom very sorrowful, must not disturb us, nor must we consider them punishment, “because Christian truth confesses that nothing comes by chance, but all things under the providence of God ; and as something from His hand let your grace take what has happened. And although you take it from His hand, look at His heart, and you will find that He sent this with great love, although in the hand it may seem severity. God truly loves us, although at times He conceals His love and pretends to go far away, not because He forgets us, for He has sworn, saying: If I forget you, may my right hand wither, and may my tongue cleave to my palate if I do not remember you 72 . Certainly, He who has us written on His hands 73 , and at great cost to Himself, fulfills it just as He says it; but He withdraws so that we may sigh for Him and hunger may disquiet us, so that afterwards the bread that sustains heaven and earth may taste better to us” 74 . So, even though for the moment it may seem that everything is coming to an end and everything is very toilsome for us, St. John of Ávila says: “in truth, whoever sees a little will find that there is no other joy or rest than that the will of God be fulfilled in us; and true consolation is to rejoice in the will of God, even if it leaves us disconsolate. And if it seems to us that these desolations come from our lukewarmness (which is what usually distresses many), I say, after having looked at it, that it is better to bear one’s fault with calm evenness of heart and good confidence in the divine mercy than, in order to kill the fly (as they say) that is stinging my forehead, to give myself a blow that kills me. Not all who are to go to heaven have to be equal; nor must we despair because we are not among the best or even the middling ; but give thanks to our Lord because He gave us hope of salvation through His clemency. And it is fitting to gladden the heart in this and to thank God for it , so that He may not take from us, as from ingrates, what He has given us, and so we fall into hell because God did not make us among the best in heaven. Believe me that this matter of the peace of heart that the perfect have is not given because of discontent or blows of the fist, but God gives it to whom, and how, and when it pleases Him ” 75 . St. John Paul II taught something similar, inviting souls not to be disquieted if for the moment it seems to them that they cannot bear with a resigned spirit, or find consolation in, the events that are adverse to them, or if they even experience interior and at times also exterior complaints about the ‘injustices,’ mistreatment, etc. that they suffer. For “ gradually ,” the Holy Father stated, “and with the help of faith nourished by prayer, one discovers the true meaning of the suffering that each one experiences in his own life. It is a discovery that depends on the word of divine revelation and on the ‘ word of the Cross ’ 76 of Christ, which is the power and the wisdom of God 77 ” 78 . The Master of Ávila continues, giving us the following counsel: “Let us not fail to do what we can and to have good confidence in God , in whom we must place ourselves so wholeheartedly that we do not dare to pass sentence even on ourselves as to how we are faring 79 ; but, trusting in Him , let us run with joy the course of His commandments and of His footsteps, and hope that He will reward our good deeds and pardon our evil ones, so that for the one and the other we may praise and bless Him forever and ever” 80 . And St. John of the Cross could well add at this point what he wrote in a letter to one of his directees: “But all is brief, for all lasts only until the knife is raised, and then Isaac remains alive, with the promise of a multiplied offspring 81 ” 82 . For this reason the need becomes evident to “ask for the grace of the science of the Cross and of the joy of the Cross, which are attained only in the school of Jesus Christ” 83 , as our Proper Law expressly points out to us. For “if in the present economy of salvation the Passion of Christ was necessary, our suffering will also be necessary. If there were another way to go to heaven, Jesus Christ would have followed it and, what is more, would have taught it. But it is not so; Christ went by the royal road of the Holy Cross and taught us to go by it” 84 . This very thing, although in other words, is what the Master of Ávila tried to make a bishop of Córdoba (Spain) understand when he went to preside over a provincial council held in Toledo (1565), and which it is well for the health of our soul to keep in mind as we begin this year: “Let not your lordship think to persuade anyone to reform if he himself does not go reformed. Nor let him think that his embassy is to be fruitful by other means than those which Jesus Christ, by the ordinance of His Father , took to fulfill His own. For if there were other more fitting ones, neither would divine wisdom have been ignorant of them nor would His providence have failed to ordain them instead ; for since, with such deliberation, and though they were so costly to His own Son, He ordained the ones we know, it is great temerity for the servant and attendant to wish to flee the means the Son took and to esteem his own carnal wisdom more than that of God. Let your lordship raise his eyes to the Son of God placed on a Cross, naked and crucified, and strive to strip himself of the world and of the flesh, and of blood, greed and honor, and of himself, so that he may thus be wholly like Jesus Christ and his embassy may be effective and fruitful. Let him die to everything and he will live to God, and will be the cause of others living; because, if he does not do this, he will lose himself and the others, for the word of Christ our Lord cannot fail: Nisi granum frumenti 85 , etc.” 86 . Lastly, St. John of Ávila recommends the reading of Sacred Scripture, since from it “one will draw great joy , founded on the mercy of God; one will draw contentment and patience in the labors and sorrows that may come, considering that, if not a leaf on the tree stirs without the will of God, neither will those labors have come without His providence ; and so, considering that the one who sends them is his God, who died for him, he will understand that it must be something that is fitting for his salvation. He will also have long-suffering in the petitions he makes to God when He does not grant them in the way he asks, understanding that He who gave him His own life will give him what is less, if it is fitting for him. And so he will see that He, as supremely wise, seeing things to come, understands that this is not fitting for him or that, if it is fitting, it is not for that moment, for which reason His mercy delays it” 87 . ***** That is why the time of trial, whatever it may be, is the time to prepare oneself to experience true joy , as St. Francis of Assisi calls the supernatural acceptance of the merciful designs of divine providence over us. You will remember that chapter of The Little Flowers when the saint answers Brother Leo: “When we arrive at St. Mary of the Angels, soaked by the rain and frozen by the cold and covered with mud and afflicted with hunger, and we knock at the door of the place, and the porter comes angrily and says to us: ‘Who are you?’ And when we say: ‘We are two of your brothers.’ And he answers: ‘You lie; you are two rascals who go about the world deceiving people and stealing the alms of the poor; get out of here’; and he does not open to us and makes us stay outside, in the midst of the snow, the rain and the cold, and hungry, until nightfall; then, if we bear so much injury, so much cruelty and so many insults patiently, without being disturbed and without murmuring against him, thinking humbly and charitably that that porter truly knows us and that God makes him speak against us , oh, Brother Leo!, in this will be true joy . And if we persevere in knocking at the door and he comes out disturbed and, as if we were troublesome scoundrels, drives us away with abuse and with blows, saying: ‘Off with you, most vile little thieves; go to the hospital, for here you will neither eat nor lodge,’ and we bear it patiently and with joy and with love, Brother Leo, write that in this there will be perfect joy. And if, driven by hunger, by the cold and by the night, we knock again and call and beg for the love of God, with great weeping, that he open to us and let us in, and he, scandalized, says: ‘These are troublesome rascals; I will give them the pay they deserve,’ and he comes out with a knotted stick and, seizing us by the hood, throws us to the ground on the snow and beats us hard; if then we suffer all these things with joy, thinking of the sufferings of the blessed Christ, which we must suffer for His love, oh, Brother Leo!, write, here perfect joy will be found; but attend to the conclusion, Brother Leo: above all the graces and gifts of the Holy Spirit that Christ grants to His friends is that of conquering oneself and willingly bearing sufferings, injuries, reproaches and contempt for His love ; for we cannot glory in the other gifts, because they are not ours but God’s; whence the Apostle says: What do you have that you have not received from God? And if you have received it, why do you glory as if it were your own? But in the Cross of tribulation and affliction we can glory, because this is ours, and for this the Apostle says: I do not wish to glory except in the Cross of Our Lord Jesus Christ ” 88 . Now at the dawn of this new year we entrust ourselves to Most Holy Mary, Mother of Divine Providence, so that she who, like no one else, abandoned herself to God, may grant us to face this 2022, with all its graces and with all its trials, entirely abandoned to the will of good pleasure of our good God 89 . With gratitude, let us advance confidently along the level path of the Divine Will, striving to fulfill completely what He asks of us, according to the circumstances He disposes, and at the time He requires it, which will always be what is best. The self-destruction of the Church

“The self-destruction of the Church” St. Paul VI 1 G. K. Chesterton once said: “There is one thing in the world that never makes progress, and that is the idea of progress.” By this he meant that unless we have a fixed concept of what progress really is, we will never know whether we are making any advance. Unfortunately, there are many who, instead of working to attain an ideal, change it , and call that progress. In that way, one could never know whether one is progressing from Buenos Aires toward Rome if one identifies Rome with New York. Only when the goal is fixed and definitive can we say that we have a target to aim at and the energy needed to shoot our arrow toward that target. It often happens that man loses sight of the goal and concentrates on what is merely transitory and earthly, and tries to derive some pleasure from it. We see it in daily life. They are the ones who delight in turning the pages of a book but never finish reading the story; the ones who take brushes in hand but never finish the painting; the ones who travel the seas but never reach a port. And this can also happen to religious, to priests, and of course it can also happen at the ecclesial level, which very often translates into Christian progressivism. That is why, when in 1980 St. John Paul II addressed the French Bishops’ Conference, he warned them: “It is not at all strange that in this ‘post-conciliar’ stage there have also developed, with considerable intensity, certain interpretations of Vatican II that do not correspond to its authentic Magisterium. I am referring to the two well-known tendencies: ‘ progressivism ’ and ‘integrism.’ The former are always impatient to adapt even the content of the faith, Christian ethics, the liturgy and ecclesial organization to changes in mentality, to the demands of the ‘world,’ without taking sufficiently into account not only the common sense of the faithful, who feel disoriented, but also what is essential in the faith already defined: the roots of the Church, her centuries-old experience, the norms necessary for her fidelity, her unity, her universality. They are obsessed with ‘moving forward,’ but toward what ‘progress,’ in the end? The others—pointing out certain abuses which we are evidently the first to reprove and correct—harden their position, stopping at a particular period of the Church, at a particular level of theological formulation or liturgical expression which they regard as absolute, without penetrating sufficiently into its deep meaning, without considering the totality of history and its legitimate development, frightened by new questions, without admitting, in the end, that the Spirit of God continues to act today in the Church, with her Pastors united to the Successor of Peter” 2 . Pope St. Pius X had already warned of this same thing in 1907 in his Encyclical Pascendi , in order to rebuke and unmask the doctrine of what was later called modernism and, more recently, progressivism . Wishing to expose this most dangerous and tangled doctrine and present it to the Church, he called it, quite simply, “the synthesis of all heresies” 3 , or, as it is also said, “the sewer of all heresies.” As such, it does not let itself be easily understood—nor does it wish to be—and it attacks the Church and our faith from very different flanks, seeking to fill her with confusion by its doctrine, as perverse as it is slippery, because “more than a system, it is a confusion” 4 , even though all who raise the progressive banner “without exception, wish to be and to pass for doctors in the Church” 5 , as St. Pius X said. Founded on an immanentist philosophy, progressivism presents itself as a continuation of the Gnosticism of the first years of the Church, which in recent times has gathered more and more strength, as the great Pope St. John Paul II said: “It must be admitted realistically, and with deep and anguished sensitivity, that Christians today, in large part, feel lost, confused, perplexed and even disillusioned; ideas contrary to the truth revealed and always taught have been scattered by the handful; true and proper heresies have been spread in the dogmatic and moral field, creating doubts, confusions, rebellions; even the liturgy has been manipulated; immersed in intellectual and moral ‘relativism,’ and therefore in permissiveness, Christians are tempted by atheism, by agnosticism, by a vaguely moralistic illuminism, by a sociological Christianity without defined dogmas and without objective morality” 6 . Fr. Alfredo Sáenz, for his part, stated: “in recent times, especially from the end of the last century, something unheard-of occurred, namely that this ‘worldly’ world penetrated with its criteria into the very interior of the Church, mainly through modernism and the subsequent progressivism, to the point that [St.] Paul VI could speak in dramatic terms of a ‘self-demolition of the Church’” 7 . Indeed, progressivism remains very much latent in the Church today, since its promoters “hide in the very bosom of the Church, being enemies all the more harmful the less openly declared they are” 8 , seeking to distort her nature and to confuse the faithful. That is why our duty is to know it more deeply in order to unmask it better, and thus to defend the Mystical Body of Christ and protect souls, so as not to be unfaithful to the most sacred of our duties, which is to be servants of the Truth 9 . St. Paul VI said, with brilliant analysis: “Everyone knows how the Church is immersed in humanity, forms part of it; from it come her members, from it she draws precious treasures of culture, and how she suffers its historical vicissitudes and also contributes to its successes. Now, everyone likewise knows that humanity in this time is on the path of great transformations, upheavals and advances, which profoundly change not only its outward forms of life but also its ways of thinking. Its thought, its culture, its spirit are being intimately modified, both by scientific, technical and social progress and by the currents of philosophical and political thought that invade and pervade it. All of this, like the waves of a sea, engulfs and shakes the Church herself: the minds of the men who entrust themselves to her are strongly influenced by the climate of the temporal world, so much so that a danger, as it were, of vertigo, of bewilderment, of aberration, can shake her very solidity and induce many to follow the strangest ideas, imagining as though the Church ought to deny herself and embrace entirely new and unthought-of forms of life. Thus, for example, the modernist phenomenon—which still surfaces in various attempts at expressions foreign to the authentic reality of the Catholic religion—was it not precisely a similar episode of the predominance of psychological-cultural tendencies, proper to the profane world, over the faithful and genuine expression of the doctrine and norm of the Church of Christ? Now, we believe that in order to immunize ourselves against such a danger, ever imminent and manifold, coming from many sides, a good and obvious remedy is to deepen the Church’s awareness of what she truly is, according to the mind of Christ contained in Scripture and in Tradition, and interpreted and developed by genuine ecclesiastical teaching, which is, as we know, enlightened and guided by the Holy Spirit, who is always ready, when we ask Him and when we listen to Him, to give unfailing fulfillment to the promise of Christ: The Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and will remind you of all that I have said to you (Jn 14:26)” 10 . 1. The great storm Historically, and as Fr. Julio Meinvielle demonstrates well and at length in one of his masterworks 11 , progressivism is a continuation of what is known as the Jewish Kabbalah 12 , which is nothing other than the culpable perversion of the primordial tradition originating with our first parents, and of the revelation given to the patriarchs, owing to the chosen people’s continual contact with idolatrous peoples. Our Lord alludes to this perverted tradition or secret gnosis when He says to the Pharisees and scribes: You nullify the commandment of God in order to keep your tradition […] making void the word of God through this tradition that you hand on; and you do many other such things 13 . After the Incarnation of the Word of God, the Redemption and the founding of the Church, this Kabbalah also penetrates nascent Christianity, thus giving rise to Christian Gnosticism , which affirms a fundamental ontological monism that ends up flowing into absolute pantheism. It gives evil a positive consistency and a dynamic force, and places within man the very origin of his salvation, in such a way that he needs no savior and no grace. This Christian Gnosticism took on different names and survived thanks to many philosophers, theologians and writers who, with heterodox doctrines, opposed what the Magisterium of the Church taught and authentic Christian philosophy and theology, represented most perfectly in St. Thomas Aquinas. Now, at the end of the nineteenth century, this Christian Gnosticism appears more vigorously under the name of modernism , carried forward by a throng of intellectuals who were consumed with the intention of ruining the Church 14 , seeking to change her doctrine from within and by means of confusion. Modernism , against which St. Pius X struck forcefully, could be summed up as the effort to accommodate the Catholic faith to the requirements of the world; that is, to make the Church of Jesus Christ bend and conform, in complete submission, to the wishes and whims of the course of history, on the sole argument that history is the manifestation of God. “The subjectivist, immanentist and evolutionist currents that infected the modern mentality were infiltrating Catholic intellectual circles, giving rise in exegesis, in the history of dogma and of the Church, in philosophy and theology, to a new interpretation of Christianity which, in actual fact, altered it fundamentally and thereby destroyed it” 15 . Modernism wanted to destroy the divine nature of the Church and turn her into a merely human entity at the service of modern history. That is why we do not fear to affirm that “at bottom, the ‘modernists’ of yesterday and today have in common the method presupposed by philosophical immanentism; but, as Lortz says, modernism is not so much a system of heretical doctrine as a heretical way of thinking 16 ” 17 . Thus it was that men like Félicité Lamennais devised strange ways and arguments to accommodate themselves to the world, betraying the Church and their own consciences. Nevertheless, as we have rightly been taught: “if modern civilization involves the absolute autonomy of man before God, it is abundantly clear that the Church cannot be reconciled with it” 18 . It is fitting to note that St. Pius X in a certain way foresaw the later development of modernism, which today has arrived at nihilism on the theoretical level (insofar as such a thing is possible) and at ‘absolute’ relativism on the practical level. Whichever form of immanentism (empiricist, rationalist, materialist, historicist, sentimentalist, scientistic, progressive in the sense of the Enlightenment) is taken as the method and as the basic philosophy for Theology, it will have the same conclusion: the elimination of the very possibility of supernatural Revelation and the denial of mystery. And that, for the Catholic Church, would mean the elimination of the revealed deposit and, therefore, death through her reduction to the sphere of the world 19 . Lately, thanks to many authors of the Nouvelle Théologie 20 , and with greater tenacity after the Second Vatican Council, this Christian Gnosticism presents itself under the name of progressivism and strives eagerly to subject the Church both to Marxist ideology and communism and to liberalism, denying a Christian social order 21 . Today, it is this progressivism that is the great storm the Church must face for the salvation of souls. 2. Confused mixture Being the gnosis that it is, progressivism presents itself as a confused mixture : “a concoction of supernatural and natural, a fusion of faith and reason, a spurious combination of Christ and Caesar, a confusion of theology with philosophy or sociology or psychology” 22 . What is more, contemporary progressivism , having taken on the essence of Marxism—which is dialectics—has no qualms about affirming and denying diametrically opposed things, or contradicting itself, because it does not seek the truth but rather to accommodate itself to the age. Pius XII had already underlined this characteristic: “These new opinions are not always proposed in the same order, with the same clarity or in the same terms, nor always with full unanimity of views among themselves; and in fact, what some teach today more covertly, with certain precautions and distinctions, others more daring will spread tomorrow openly and without limits” 23 . Progressivism also presents itself as an inversion , which is the fruit of that mania for making dialectics out of everything. “Instead of God, man… instead of love of God, love of neighbor… instead of a message of salvation, a social message… instead of the Cross, openness to the world… instead of absolute truth, the truth of the times” 24 . They do not know how to harmonize things that are apparently opposed, because they have never meditated on the mystery of the Incarnate Word. They subvert reality and turn it upside down, because they never manage to have a correct appraisal of things. “It is seeking first the things that are added and then, if there is time and desire left, the Kingdom of God” 25 . Progressivism is also characterized by dissolution . Since its strategy is confusion, it seeks to dissolve the truths of the faith and the Catholic religion itself, stripping them of their philosophical and historical foundations and always calling them into question, arrogating to itself the right to doubt the dogmas and the faith handed down by the Apostles and protected by the Magisterium. Thus they present false ‘salvations’ which, although they bear the name Christian , are nothing but disguised ways of allying oneself with the spirit of the world. They dissolve, in turn, the whole supernatural order into the natural, stripping it of its value and justification. They postulate an “absolute independence between the spiritual and the temporal,” “in such a way that it authorizes acting in the temporal sphere without concerns of a spiritual kind” 26 . Likewise, the Holy Pope declared with all his force: “They go about crying out that the government of the Church must be reformed in all its aspects, but chiefly in the disciplinary and dogmatic, and therefore that it must be harmonized inwardly and outwardly with what they call the modern conscience , which tends entirely toward democracy; for which reason, the lower clergy and the laity themselves must be granted a certain share in government, and authority, which is too concentrated and centralized, must be distributed. […] They likewise claim that the influence of ecclesiastical government in political and social affairs must be modified, so that, while separating itself from civil ordinances, it nevertheless adapts itself to them in order to imbue them with its spirit. […] In morals, that the active virtues must be placed before the passive ones, and that the former must be practiced in preference to the latter. […] There are, finally, some who, gladly following their Protestant masters, desire that sacred celibacy be abolished in the priesthood. What, then, remains intact in the Church that must not be reformed by them and according to their opinions?” 27 . 3. Inevitable consequences and immediate causes Dr. Alberto Caturelli, in an article prepared on the occasion of the 100th anniversary of the Encyclical Pascendi , points out that “philosophical, scientific and historical immanentism, which they arbitrarily postulate as having a knowable object, in contrast to faith, whose subject they deem unknowable, is the source of all errors and all rebellions” 28 . St. Pius X had already pointed out the inevitable consequences of this erroneous way of thinking, which leads to atheism and to the denial of all religion as the result of pure symbolism. “The proximate and immediate cause [of this evil] is, without doubt, the perversion of the intellect” 29 . If we ask about the motivations or personal causes that lead someone to think in that way, the Holy Father pointed out two fundamental ones: pride (“puffed up with the haughty name of science” 30 ) and, simultaneously, the vice opposed to the virtue of studiousness, which is curiosity in the sense of a vicious pursuit of the new (“under the impulse of a bold and unbridled love of novelties” 31 ), not of objective truth. In the case of Theology both vices are aggravated, because man sets himself up as the supreme norm 32 . If we ask “about the immediate causes , two emerge with invincible evidence: a) ignorance : this is not a common ignorance but a profound one (if it can be so described), an ignorance that can affect many ‘learned men’ who teach in Seminaries and Ecclesiastical Universities without real adherence to the Magisterium and with contempt for metaphysical realism; St. Pius X says: ‘All the moderns, without exception, who wish to be and to pass for doctors in the Church, although they extol modern philosophy with grandiloquent words and despise scholasticism, did not embrace the former (…) except because their complete ignorance of the latter deprived them of the arguments necessary to distinguish confusion of ideas and to refute sophisms’ 33 . b) The other cause is contained in the first, for it is none other than hatred of the scholastic method . These self-appointed ‘holders’ of a ‘parallel magisterium’ reject ‘the scholastic method of philosophizing, the authority and tradition of the Fathers, the ecclesiastical magisterium’ (…) ‘They generally ridicule and despise scholastic philosophy and theology’ 34 . In 1907 [as in 2022] all those who defend orthodoxy and fight for the Church are victims of ‘the conspiracy of silence’ 35 ; this way of proceeding against Catholics, says St. Pius X, ‘is all the more odious because at the same time they exalt without any moderation, with perpetual praise, all those who agree with them; the books of these men, the Pontiff concludes, full of novelties throughout, they receive with great admiration and applause…’ 36 ” 37 . Moreover, “if the Church condemns one of them, not only do they unite to praise him in public and by every means, but they go so far as to pay him almost the veneration due to a martyr for the truth” 38 . “Had St. Pius X lived today, he could have verified that what he denounced then has now attained a certain absoluteness. The windows of Catholic bookstores are full of books by Boff, Küng, Gutiérrez, Rahner, Moltmann and many others; precisely because they have been ‘censured’ by the Holy See they are good business… they sell… they sell a lot. In Pascendi , the Pope denounced the permeation of seminaries and congresses, journals, newspapers and religious orders” 39 . 4. Its attacks As has been said, progressivism is a conglomerate of all heresies 40 , and therefore there is no aspect or truth of our faith that it does not attack or seek to destroy. Beginning by destroying the preambles of faith, and in league with the philosophy of immanence , it takes away from reason its capacity to know reality objectively. “The essence of progressivism lies in its considering reality to be one-dimensional ; that is, despite words to the contrary, progressivism pushes toward a monism, and full progressivism is an absolute monism , which, in rejecting transcendence, affirms absolute immanence and entails a false concept of God” 41 . And as a consequence of this, progressivism denies the capacity of human reason to transcend creation and know its Creator, because for them God is nothing more than the world, and there is no distinction between being by essence and being by participation. Such is the real situation of the world, and they want to make us believe that today a ‘Theology without God’ is needed because that is the ‘maturity’ of the Christian. And if we want the world to listen to the Christian message—the progressives maintain—we must start from that ‘maturity’ (which takes on the situation of the atheistic world) and inaugurate a new exegesis… That is why progressivism is also a bitter enemy of the historicity of Sacred Scripture , often considering it a mere myth or a fanciful creation of certain communities, thus stripping Divine Revelation and the Person of Our Lord of all historical value, and calling into question the truthfulness of His very words contained in the Gospels. “It sinks the revealed datum into history and only into history. Archaeology and other disciplines placed at the service of the new exegesis acquire here an inordinate importance” 42 . What is more, for progressivism , Christ is not God as the Church has understood Him and as the Holy Fathers and the Holy Doctors have so aptly explained, among whom St. Thomas Aquinas stands out: the Ipsum Esse Subsistens , transcendent and purely spiritual, personal, free, provident and creator. Christ is nothing more than a human person in whom the presence of God was found in a more particular and evident way, thus denying the hypostatic union of the human and divine natures in the Second Person, the Son, a union that is by assumption. Consequently, Christ is not the Savior of the human race, but simply an example or motivation. Man saves himself by acting according to his nature in the total decision about himself. Thus the theologian Karl Rahner affirmed in his doctrine of anonymous Christianity . Once this outlandish assertion is accepted, all the sacraments collapse, as does the Church herself, her saving mission and her task of baptizing all nations. If man does not need the sacraments to be saved, then the Church becomes no less than a simple humanitarian organization and not the ark of salvation, being left completely secularized. From here, the progressive mind reinterprets everything, from the Eucharist , as a mere symbolic and commemorative celebration—speaking of transignification or transfinalization instead of transubstantiation—that has nothing actual or sacrificial about it, to the spiritual life of man and his search for God, even denying the existence of Heaven and Hell, or gratuitously asserting that at the end of time all men will be saved, because, according to them: “God is good and punishes no one” 43 . Traditional morality is replaced by a situation ethics, which ends up endorsing the most outrageous aberrations and sins, even intrinsically evil acts, such as the homosexual act. They even go so far as to speak of homosexuality as licit and willed by God. But at the same time, many trivialities are branded as sinful, such as a simple neglect of nature or indifference toward supposed climate change. They are champions of a severe justice and at the same time preachers of a false mercy: “In the temporal order they want justice without mercy, and in the supernatural order mercy without justice, thus exposing themselves to attaining neither justice on earth nor mercy in heaven” 44 . They speak of the priesthood as if it were not a sacrament instituted by Jesus Christ and constitutive of the hierarchy of the Church, but rather they assert that all Christians are priests in the same way. Thus they want to introduce female priesthood, and with the excuse of not falling into the Scylla of clericalism they fall into the Charybdis of the trivialization of Holy Orders. They detest vocations to the priesthood and to consecrated life, promote almost exclusively the lay vocation, and are appalled that some congregations have many vocations—as if that were something bad! The liturgy is also a victim of progressivism , for countless stupidities, abuses and deformations are introduced into it under the excuse of making it more entertaining or accessible to the people, or they turn it into an instrument and propaganda for anti-Christian ideologies. The false principle of “vital immanence” can go much further. This vital immanence postulates that human reason is rigorously enclosed within the circle of “phenomena,” and it closes off all natural access to God and all supernatural access to external revelation, thus leading to agnosticism. It makes faith depend on some phenomenon, even if this lies in the field of science and history. That is why the phenomenon itself is disfigured, being attributed a reality it does not have 45 . For the progressives “it is enough,” Dr. Caturelli states, “to accept or postulate the non-existence of propositions with a content of truth in order to conclude in the most radical relativism that invades the world today. It is not only a matter of academic circles; relativism (each one has ‘his’ truth and no one has ‘the’ truth) has penetrated not only science and ‘Theology’ (encyclicals are only the Pope’s ‘opinion’ and are debatable) but social life, all public manifestations, family life and politics” 46 . 5. The remedies St. Pius X recognized with great clarity that the principle of immanence was the common nerve of the errors he denounced at that time. We can say that it continues to be so for the problems that afflict us today. It has been said since ancient times that there is no “new” heresy. That is true. In progressivism there is a stubborn effort to “return” to the old man , transferring salvation to the world; but the only thing new is Christ, the Incarnate Word; therefore all errors and heresies are old, even if they wear a mask of “novelty.” What remedies did the Holy Father propose in 1907? Among others that the Pope sets out in the encyclical, we mention the following: “In the first place, then, with regard to studies, we will and definitively command that scholastic philosophy be made the foundation of sacred studies” 47 . So that no doubts remain, he adds: “The main thing to note is that, when we prescribe that scholastic philosophy be followed, we understand chiefly that which St. Thomas Aquinas taught,” and he warns: “departing from the Doctor of Aquino, especially in metaphysical questions, will never fail to be of great harm” 48 . “With this foundation of philosophy thus laid, let the theological edifice be built with great diligence” 49 . On the other hand, he exhorts the promotion of “the study of Theology, so that clerics may leave the seminaries filled with great esteem and love for it and may always regard it as their favorite study” 50 . He also advocates the study of secular disciplines, provided it is not to the detriment of sacred studies. Finally, he mentions some practical measures regarding the choice of “the rectors and teachers of seminaries or of Catholic Universities,” saying that if “they are in any way imbued with modernism [progressivism], they are to be removed without any consideration from the office, whether of governing or of teaching, and if they already exercise it, they are to be dismissed” 51 . * * * Progressivism , in short, in its many manifestations and facets, seeks quite simply to destroy the transcendent God, the God of the Gospels and of our Catholic faith. “Progressivism—liberal or Marxist, bourgeois or revolutionary—does not work so that the public and social life of peoples may be subordinated to God as to its ultimate end, because ‘its’ god is no longer transcendent; if every vulgarity is possible in ‘its’ liturgies, it is because ‘its’ god is not majesty itself; if they have questioned every truth of the faith and doubted every miracle or prophecy in Scripture, it is because ‘their’ god is not almighty; if they are fruitful in doubts and in sterile certainties, it is because ‘their’ god is not infinite truth” 52 . And having removed God from their midst, they have put man in His place, making gods of themselves, believing themselves to be the center of history, of theology and of salvation. Hence one speaks only of the rights of man, and little or nothing of the rights of God. They do not want Him present in society, whether communist, capitalist or of any kind whatever. Nor do they speak of making Him known in non-Christian countries, and they do not want to preach Him anew in the nations of ancient Christian tradition. Because of this progressivism, this reigning atheism, many today regard the modern world as ‘without hope.’ In truth, at times it seems like a long Good Friday in which everything divine seems to have failed. Perhaps never as now has the future seemed so unpredictable. People seem to suffer from an anguished sense of desolation. However, there is neither need nor room for such hopelessness. The world seemed as desolate before, when it crucified Christ, as it is now, and yet it rose again to the freshness of a new Christian civilization. The same can happen now, as it has already happened at least a dozen times since the coming of Christ. Yet one must realize that the modern ideal is not exactly goodness, but success. And such an ideal makes penance incredibly difficult. It is true that paganism before Christ also sinned, but the sin of modern paganism has the serious aggravating circumstance of having betrayed an ideal that the pagans did not have, namely, Christ. And that is why “progressivism” cannot be considered progress, because it has replaced the eternal Ideal with the temporal world and its maxims. Therefore, humanity will not rise again to peace and happiness through political and economic remedies, even though these too are necessary, but fundamentally through the spiritual regeneration of hearts and souls, through conversion—or return—to Christ, the only peace and happiness of man. That is why St. Pius X said on assuming the See of Peter: “If we are asked for a motto that expresses Our will, we will always present this one alone: to restore all things in Christ 53 ” 54 . This is the task that falls particularly to us as members of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, who have been called to “assume” cultures, purifying them and elevating them on the basis of Christ and His Gospel, understood “in the Church.” Therefore, analogously to the mystery of the Incarnation, it must be an assumption; that is, there must be an action and a passion that express the becoming and not only the final result, and that refer distinctly to each of the terms, that of departure and that of arrival. A mere union is not enough for us, nor is merely putting a nominalist label on reality so that it may truly be ruled by Christ. “Being in the world” only makes sense for us when it depends on “not being of the world.” Only thus can one truly be salt of the earth and light of the world 55 . Otherwise we would become salt that has lost its savor and a light under the bushel basket 56 . “Not being tributaries” 57 continues to be our watchword. In this sense, the doctrine that is received and imparted is of capital importance. Without it, which is the very expression of the Word made flesh, it is not possible to restore all things in Christ.
