The feast of the Presentation of the Child Jesus is also a feast of the Mother

Rome, Italy, February 2, 2018. Feast of the Presentation of the Lord “The feast of the Presentation of the Child Jesus is also a feast of the Mother” St. John Paul II, February 2, 1990 Dear Fathers, Brothers, Seminarians and Novices: The mystery of the Presentation of the Lord leads us to turn our gaze to His Most Holy Mother, who carries Him in her arms, sheltered by her most tender Heart, to be presented in the temple forty days after His birth. In this way, the Most Holy Virgin also becomes a figure of all the mothers who throughout history –including our own dear mothers– continue to offer their sons and daughters to the Heavenly Father, associating them with the one oblation of Christ, the cause and model of all consecration in the Church 1 . This mystery of the life of Christ, which speaks to us of our vocation as consecrated persons as a most exalted heavenly favor, as an eternal and most merciful election on the part of God the Father, also speaks of the divine election of our mothers to be, precisely, mothers of a consecrated person, whether he be a priest, brother, missionary or monk. They “came forth from the heart of God” 2 to be our mothers! Which is the same as saying, to be “the supreme consolation in this valley of tears.” That is why this letter is in some way also addressed to them: to your mothers, and I ask you, please, to be so kind as to pass it on to them, if you think it fitting. First of all, I wish with all my heart to express a most particular gratitude to all the mothers of the priests, brothers, novices, monks and seminarians of our dear Institute, for each of them having been a providential instrument in our fulfillment of the Will of God, and for the unconditional accompaniment they offer us with their constant prayer and service, which speaks so clearly of their boundless love. May a special and heartfelt thanksgiving also rise to our Lord for all the mothers who have already departed for heaven and who from there now fully contemplate the splendor of the Priesthood of Christ, in which we –their sons– have come to share. To all of them –among whom is my own most beloved mother– who from heaven continue to intercede for us in a unique and, mysteriously, much more effective way: infinite thanks! Likewise, I would like to take advantage of this feast, which “is also a feast of the Mother” 3 , to dedicate a few simple words to give expression to the lasting affection and heartfelt homage that we, the sons, owe to our mothers. For a mother, in a special way, is everything to a person (and I believe that we religious live this reality more fully and more beautifully than other children do). Because to a great extent, everything one is, one’s way of being, of thinking, of believing, all the good one has, one owes principally to one’s mother. Who could doubt that our mothers’ contribution to our lives has been decisive! That is why I dare to say that, among all human relationships, there is none that can equal this one. For as St. John Paul II taught, “although both of them together are parents of their child, the mother is the special ‘part’ and the more qualified one” 4 . For every time a child is born, a mother is born as well, and the relationship established between the two is unique, most intimate, unrepeatable and eternal, since no other future relationship, however deep it may be, nor the most tortuous circumstances, nor the most humiliating human weaknesses, not even death itself, will ever be able to erase the sacred bond between mother and child. For a child, his mother will always be his mother, and for a mother, her child will always be her child. A mother is, in some way, like our Providence on earth in the first years of life, our firmest support in the following years of childhood, our most tender and loyal friend in youth, and our most inseparable and unconditional companion throughout our whole life (and even when she is no longer among us). A good mother is a blessing from God and the supreme consolation that has been given to us in this valley of tears. She shows us the way when we go astray. She lifts us up when we fall. She encourages us when we are downcast. She sweetens life on earth and, as if by magic, turns thorns into roses. God conveys to the world the consolation of love through the soul of a mother. That is why a mother’s love knows no bounds. She can generously renounce her own interests and suffer with a smile on her lips because she loves; she is capable of renouncing, out of love for her child, all the grandeurs of the earth. She devotes her life to fighting for her children and rejoices to see them happy. That is why for a child there is no place in the world, however beautiful it may be, like this one: his mother’s heart. There is no creature in this life to whom we are more closely united than the heart and soul of our mother. It is said of the Heart of Our Lady and that of Our Lord that they beat in unison, and one author says that this happens with all mothers, with the difference that in that beating it is always the mother who sets the rhythm, and that is why she always knows or senses what is happening in her child’s heart. Who has not experienced this? That is why Hebrew women would counsel one another, saying that making the decision to have a child is of crucial importance: “it is to decide forever that your heart will walk outside your body”; and the proverb says that “whoever takes a child by the hand, in the end, takes the heart of a mother.” Therefore, it happens with good mothers as with the saints: the work she accomplishes in us is so great that all that remains is to praise God for the gift of having given her to us, because she has been, is, and will continue to be, even when she is no longer here with us, the image of God’s providence and love on this earth. The mother is the heart of the family; it is the mother who in a certain way creates and constitutes the home and protects its unity. Who has not seen this? Around her, everything is ordered and unified, everything is harmonized and develops. That is why, when a mother departs, nothing is ever the same. She weaves the bonds among everyone; she sends the children toward the father and the father toward the children. The mother is in a particular way the one who listens, consoles, encourages, forgives, reconciles and gives each one his place. She spreads the balm of love and tenderness over all family relationships. She is constantly concerned for each one and does not rest until all are content. How many of us can say of our mothers –to whom God Himself has entrusted us 5 – that they have been and are the precious gift through which we are given to see how full of love Divine Providence is! For they, considering “good example as their first mission” 6 , “with their maternal fiat (‘be it done unto me’)” 7 taught us that there is no greater happiness than doing the Will of God. And in the shelter of the sanctuary of their hearts they taught us that what is most noble, pure and complete is generous self-giving, without conditions, without time limits, a limitless self-giving even to the point of forgetting oneself out of love. That is why our mothers will always be the most luminous brushstroke that God set down in the book of our lives, and the most tender caress through which we came to know the fatherly gentleness of God. Therefore, any one of us, wherever he may be, cherishing his good mother in his heart, can say with St. John of God: “God has deposited the treasure of His love on earth in three chests: in the Eucharist, in Confession, and in my mother’s heart.” Before so excellent a gift, all that remains is to praise God and burst forth in thanksgiving to Him who has been pleased to give us our mothers as the most tangible proof we have of the riches of His kindness. Let us acknowledge with gratitude, and for the great consolation of our souls, that we will always have the hearts of our mothers beating in our own bodies, and that wherever we go we will not cease to experience that wave of love and sweetness with which maternal gazes are wont to bathe their children. Thanks to our mothers, all of us will always find in a corner of our hearts that ray of hope which inspires us, consoles us and encourages us to sacrificial love, such as theirs is. That is why our gratitude to our mothers will always be eternal. ***** Together with this gratitude, I also wish to extend an invitation to you: it is the “40 Hours Project.” St. Angela Merici used to say that “mothers, even if they had a thousand children, would always carry each one of them engraved in their hearts, and would never forget any of them, because their love is exceedingly genuine” 8 . That is why I know beforehand that they will accept the proposal. The 40 Hours Project goes back to 1881 when, in Lu Monferrato –a town in Italy which today has some 1,500 inhabitants– a group of mothers, moved by that genuine love of which we were speaking and with a great spirit of Christian faith, decided to join together to adore Christ in the Blessed Sacrament, praying for vocations to the priesthood and to consecrated life, and every first Sunday of the month they received Communion, offering it for the same intention. The fact is that our Lord more than answered the trusting prayers of those fervent and loving mothers, to the point that 323 vocations can be counted, missionaries in 36 countries (all of them persevering by the grace of God), arising from that tiny village. Inspired by the great example of faith and love of these mothers, a group of ‘our mothers’ have embraced the same initiative, which today I would like to extend to all our mothers. They unite for 40 continuous hours on the 14th , 15th and 16th of each month, each offering one hour of prayer, preferably before the Blessed Sacrament, to pray for the increase , perseverance and holiness of priestly and religious vocations for our Institute. St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort affirmed that “when we pray in common, the prayer of each person becomes the prayer of the whole assembly, and all together form but one prayer” 9 and that “a person who prays the Rosary alone has the merit of only one Rosary, but if he prays it with thirty persons, he acquires the merit of thirty rosaries” 10 . It seems to me that what is said of the Rosary may well be said also of adoration of the Blessed Sacrament. That is why I want to invite all our mothers to join together in praying for us, their sons, the sons of the Family of the Incarnate Word. For this purpose we have created a website, www.40horas.org , where they can register to pray at the time most convenient for them on the assigned days. The site is available in six of the main languages spoken by our religious, and it is our intention that in the future it will be available in a few more (it will be a way of seeing how many mothers in the different parts of the world join this project of praying for vocations). I understand that many of our mothers are already elderly, or work, or have no church nearby, or bear in their bodies the precious cross of illness that keeps them in bed. This invitation is for them too! For these mothers can also offer their hour of work, the rosaries they silently pray bead by bead while the rest of the family sleeps, and all the sufferings of body or soul, for these, their dear sons of the Incarnate Word, scattered across the five continents. And to make this call even broader and more inclusive, I also address personally all the Sisters “Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará,” all the women of our Third Order, all the female relatives of our religious, our sisters, all our ‘mothers of the heart’ who have adopted us as their sons and who are so numerous in our missions, and, finally, all women, especially those who desire that God bless their family with a vocation to the priesthood or to consecrated life, to join this magnificent project of faith and charity, which God will know how to reward a hundredfold 11 . Now, since our beautiful Religious Family is present in places where access to the internet is still something ‘uncommon,’ and since on the other hand we know that many women would like to join this project, we have thought that the most fitting thing would be for the religious who come from those places or who are missionaries there to ‘register’ them themselves on the website mentioned above, so that as many as possible may join in the holy mission of imploring the Lord of the harvest 12 to send more laborers, and to deign to grant the grace of perseverance and holiness of life to those who are already working so that He may reign 13 . We are more than 800 members in the Institute of the Incarnate Word: what an enormous consolation it would be to know that there are more than 800 souls who, with the generosity and boundless love characteristic of the maternal heart, implore such excellent graces from heaven, collaborating almost imperceptibly –an attitude so typical of mothers– in the thrilling adventure of bringing the love of Christ to countless souls. “Jesus always kept His divine Mother with Him: they were never separated from one another” 14 . May we never lack mothers who accompany their sons with ardent and constant prayer, which brings so much consolation in this life. To the Most Holy Virgin, who became the Mother of our Light at the cost of the great sacrifice of her Son and of the maternal sacrifice of her heart, I entrust all of you and your mothers, as well as the fruits of this noble initiative. Ad maiora natus sum

“Ad maiora natus sum” St. Stanislaus Kostka Pope St. John Paul I, speaking from the balcony of St. Peter’s Basilica on the day after his election, recalled, among other things, that in the conclave on August 26, when it was already becoming clear that he himself was to be the one elected, the cardinals beside him whispered in his ear: Courage! Very likely this was the word he needed at that moment, and it remained engraved on his heart, since he recalled it right away the following day. So we too, like any Christian, need to hear this word of encouragement from time to time, above all when situations come upon us that require a “robust will” 1 . Naturally, it is not only the soldier who exposes himself to the risk of losing his life in a war to defend his homeland who is brave. It is well known that in time of peace, too, we need fortitude. Thus did St. Charles Borromeo, for example, who during the plague in Milan continued to exercise his pastoral ministry among the inhabitants of that city with great courage. Or St. John of the Cross, whom, when he was imprisoned in Toledo, they wanted to ‘buy’ by offering him a good library, a good cell, a priorate and even a golden cross. But he answered categorically: “He who seeks Christ stripped bare has no need of golden jewels” 2 . In the same way, how many times throughout history and today have we seen countless religious, priests and missionaries who, so as not to ‘sell themselves’ –even when they were promised advantageous ways out–, so as not to renounce their principles, so as not to let their freedom be trampled, in other words, so as not to be tributaries 3 , have known how to stand firm, with great courage and great fortitude, even in spite of the many threats they suffered and the consequences that such a decision held in store for them. That is why it is not only on battlefields that we must look for brave men. Each one of us, as members of this dear Institute, but even more by the simple fact of being Christians, has received the noble office of “confessing the faith of Christ with courage and fortitude” 4 . But this office, common to every Christian, takes on special connotations and even greater relevance in the case of religious. Why? Because our condition as religious requires a radical and total self-giving, because ours “must be a courageous and clear witness” 5 to the message of Christ, which, if authentic, must necessarily contradict the world, and “misunderstandings, rejections, persecutions” 6 are bound to come upon us… and, therefore, all of this requires greater courage. At this point, then, we would like to recall the example of St. Stanislaus Kostka, Patron of youth, whose tomb is in the church of Sant’Andrea al Quirinale in Rome. There this Saint, by nature very sensitive and frail, and yet very courageous, ended his life at 18 years of age. Fortitude led him, who came from a noble family, to choose to be poor following the example of Christ, and to place himself exclusively at His service. And although he faced great opposition in his surroundings, with great love and great firmness at the same time he succeeded in carrying out his resolve, summed up in the motto “ Ad maiora natus sum ” (I was born for greater things). He arrived at the Jesuit novitiate after making the journey from Vienna to Rome on foot, fleeing from those who were following him and wanted to dissuade him from his purpose by force 7 . We too “were born for greater things,” and we must know how to overcome the fear that comes upon us in situations of threat, of silent but ill-intentioned persecution, when we expose ourselves to the risk of unpleasant consequences, of suffering even greater insults, and even in the face of the possible loss of material goods or of going to prison. We were born for greater things! 1. A letter of St. John of Ávila This is the very thing St. John of Ávila sought to persuade the religious preacher Fr. Alonso de Vergara, O.P., of in a letter 8 that he wrote to him consoling him for a persecution that had arisen against him. And this letter seems to us so full of value, because of the wise doctrine it contains, and so fitting for those of us who have been called to serve the Truth 9 , that we shall quote some parts of it and offer some commentary, in the hope that the reflective reading of these pages may impress even more deeply on our hearts that the resounding idea continues to be: to sacrifice oneself! 10 , because we were born for greater things! A short time before, Fr. Alonso de Vergara had written a missive to the Doctor of Ávila, but in a tone quite opposite to that of the letter to which we are going to refer. In that first letter –to which St. John of Ávila had not replied– the Dominican preacher was consoled, and in this one that we are now going to consider, he is extremely desolate. That is why the first lines the Saint writes to him say: “ To anyone who wished to know what man is when God helps him and lavishes gifts on him, I would show a letter that your grace sent me some days ago; and to anyone who wished to know the weakness of man when he goes on his own, I would show this one that you have now sent me .” The same happens to us, and that is why, as we have been taught, we must apply to ourselves the rules of discernment of St. Ignatius that we have so often preached to others: “7th rule: let one who is in desolation consider how the Lord has left him in trial in his natural powers, so that he may resist the various agitations and temptations of the enemy; for he can do so with the divine help, which always remains to him, even though he does not clearly feel it; because the Lord has withdrawn from him his great fervor, abundant love and intense grace, while leaving him sufficient grace for eternal salvation” 11 . And that other one which says: “8th rule: let one who is in desolation strive to remain in patience, which is contrary to the vexations that come upon him, and let him think that he will soon be consoled, taking diligent measures against such desolation” 12 . “ Oh, God help me […]! What a great abyss of miseries man is, and how few things knock him down, and how quickly he changes, like thin ash before a great wind! […] Your reverence asks me whether I think you are alive or whether I count you among the dead, since I do not write to you. I answer that I do not forget you; but I was keeping my letter for this time, because at the other time it was not needed .” How great a truth the Saint has spoken here: what a great abyss of miseries man is, and how few things knock him down, and how quickly he changes, like thin ash before a great wind! We must accept that we are weak, that we are “nothing but sin,” as St. Catherine of Siena used to say, which requires humility on our part. How many religious are cast down by an ill-sounding word that has been said to them, by an apostolic failure –even having taken every precaution for the good outcome of the undertaking–, by a permission that has been denied them, by the many undeserved criticisms they receive from the very souls they shepherd, by the lack of support –on the part of superiors, of peers, of subjects–, etc. In short, all we can do is confess: how few things knock us down! That is why it is good to keep in mind the wise warning that our Proper Law gives us, this time through the pen of St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort: “Be very careful! Do not go believing –like proud and conceited devout people– that your crosses are great, that they are proof of your fidelity and a testimony of a singular love of God for you. This deceit of spiritual pride is very subtle and ingenious, but full of poison. Think rather that your pride and delicacy lead you to regard straws as beams, pinpricks as wounds, mice as elephants, a little word carried off by the wind –in reality a mere nothing– as an atrocious insult and a cruel abandonment… that delighted turning over and over of your own ills, that Luciferian belief that you are of great worth, etc.” 13 . The Saint then continues with the answer he was reserving for this moment, and begins by pointing out to him that he is not alone, invoking for this purpose the example of St. Anthony: “ St. Anthony complained to our Lord because during the battle he did not see our Lord, and [He] answered him that He was there. But He was watching how he fought, in order to make him reign 14 .” And immediately afterward he makes him see how trials, difficulties, the things that humble us, ‘are part of the program,’ are in some way inherent to our condition as Christians and are like the insignia of the religious and priestly state, and therefore one must not be frightened by them; that is why he makes him reflect thus: “ Did your reverence think you would never have to walk alone, without a baby-walker and without another’s hand leading you by yours? And how, father, were you to learn to walk? Was it all to be eating children’s food, pap and milk? And how were you to become a perfect man? Oh, my father, if it were not that I see your reverence distressed, how gladly, hearing you complain and tremble, I would laugh, like one who hears a child crying and trembling because they have frightened him with a straw lion! ” Does not the same thing happen to us? We see the name of the Institute outraged in a headline, we clearly realize that obstacles are placed in our way at every step, we are publicly wronged –always, of course, under the guise of good– and the temptation may come to us to be frightened, to want to flee, to be cast down or to lose heart. Do we not realize? The Master of Ávila tells us: “ if your reverence, by the strength of God, has died to what worldly people adore, and this before their very eyes, are you astonished that they want to stone you? They adore honor, one’s own judgment, one’s own spirit, duplicity, lukewarmness, self-love, self-reliance 15 and other similar idols they have made, which Moses –which spiritually means ‘the law of God’– calls abominable, senseless and most hideous things; but your reverence, who by the great mercy of our Lord lives as with your own lord, [that is,] with our God, and have truly adored not the vain idols of the world, which can give no good or salvation at all, but Him who with very great reason deserves to be adored. What wonder is it that there should be strife where there is such diversity of opinions and ends? But this strife is stirred up by the children of strife and suffered by the children of peace; the former biting like dogs, and the latter suffering and praying and loving like lambs; but, with the favor of God, the lambs will conquer the dogs, and even the wolves, for that is why God sent them, as lambs among wolves ” 16 . Why, then, are we amazed if we suffer setbacks because we are not “tributaries” 17 , if we do not mix the human with the divine –which is a kind of mixture with which no Christian understanding should clothe itself 18 –, if we treasure and defend the Constitutions and the sound traditions that form our own patrimony 19 , which is exactly what the Church herself has sanctioned as being ‘according to God and the Gospel.’ Why are we surprised that we are attacked if, when we have taken a firm position regarding the truth, those who prefer to ride the waves of popularity rather than dare to refute the triumphant error of the moment for fear of making enemies shout against us and look on us with scorn? Why are we surprised if, being poor and undertaking our humble works trusting only in Divine Providence, the rich and powerful look on us with suspicion? “ What wonder is it that there should be strife where there is such diversity of opinions and ends? ” It is for us, as St. John of Ávila says, to be children of peace, to suffer, pray and love like lambs, because they are the ones who will conquer. The Saint then recalls the example of the people of the city of Gibeon, who had made a pact with Joshua, and how “ five kings allied themselves to fight against them 20 ; because it seemed to them a great loss to lose so great and royal a city, and that this favor and people should be added to Joshua, their enemy. And so have the demons and worldly people done with your reverence, seeing you give yourself to Jesus Christ. […] They already smell the strength God has given you to wound hearts with the word of God, and they weep a double lament for what they lose and Jesus Christ gains. Hence the contradiction in everything and from everyone; hence the combat of the five who join together as one, and with one voice say what they say and do what they do .” We have heard the same from those who lament and are even appalled that we have vocations, and many vocations by the grace of God; so they begin to say that there is no selection, that we brainwash them, that we recruit them with tricks; they look on scandalized at the fact that our religious, even with the bare minimum of means, undertake great works or launch out to do missionary work in places where no one wants to go, and so, “all magnanimity seems to them pride, all heroism seems to them extremism, all generosity seems to them exaggeration” 21 , and they obstruct everything with false arguments. Hence the contradiction in everything; hence the combat of those who join together and with one voice say what they say and do what they do. But this too is ‘part of the program,’ and St. John of Ávila points it out to us with great realism: “ Is your reverence perhaps the first to be afflicted because he went over to Christ? Or will you be the first to be abandoned among those who suffer for Christ? Do you not see, my father, that the cause for which we are persecuted is not ours, but God’s? Do you not see that His honor is at stake in it? Tell me: why did you formerly have so many at peace with you and now so many opponents? Without any doubt the cause has been that your reverence has shown yourself to be on the side of Jesus Christ. For what king would there be who would not take it as a very great insult that, merely because someone had offered himself to him as a servant, and he had received him, there should be someone who despised and persecuted him? Is it not, perhaps, to despise and dishonor the king to persecute one who wishes to serve him, only because he came to live with him? Does this not concern the king? Is it not his affair? It is, certainly. And that is why David said: Awake, Lord, and defend Your cause. Look, Lord, and remember the affronts that this insolent and ignorant people does to You every day 22 . It is God’s cause, and they are God’s dishonors, those that are done to the servants of God; just as it is God’s honor and His cause when we do good to His little ones 23 and honor them .” In a few words: we signed up for this, and therefore persecutions –whatever they may be, and from whomever they may come– should not seem extraordinary to us. Cervantes already said it: “if they bark, Sancho, it is a sign that we are riding on.” On the other hand, we are not the only ones who suffer, nor those who suffer most, nor the first nor the last who will suffer for the cause of Christ. That is why, instead of grumbling and becoming downcast, we must learn to see in this the great favor God is granting us: that of imitating Him better 24 and of giving Him great glory whenever “what is said against us is false” 25 . But at the same time, we must “take great care not to turn our ills over and over” 26 . God Himself will defend His cause. St. John of Ávila exhorts the preacher, cast down by intense and continual persecutions, not to fear, reminding him of what the Levite said “ comforting the people of Judah, who were going up to war ”: Thus says the Lord to you: Do not fear or be dismayed before this so great multitude; for the battle is not yours but God’s 27 . “ And, therefore, –the Master of Ávila continues– it will not be you who fight, but only wait with confidence, and you will see the help of the Lord upon you 28 .” St. John of the Cross said something similar in one of his letters: “But, because it is fitting that we should not lack the cross, as our Beloved did not, even unto the death of love, He orders our passions in the love of what we most love, so that we may make greater sacrifices and be of greater worth. But all is brief, for all lasts only until the knife is raised, and then Isaac remains alive, with the promise of a multiplied offspring 29 ” 30 . And therefore, at times it is a matter of knowing how to wait patiently for God to do His work, without anguish in trying to solve a situation that is out of our hands, that is, that does not depend on us, without wearing ourselves out and being overwhelmed in defending ourselves. On this point, there is a text of St. Thomas Aquinas, in his Commentary on the Gospel of St. Matthew , in which he asks why Jesus remained silent before the High Priest. Perhaps it is a text that many of you know, but we consider it fitting to point it out again as a criterion for knowing how to conduct ourselves in similar situations. The Angelic Doctor answers: “He did so for three reasons. First, to teach us to be cautious; for He knew that whatever He said, they would use it to slander Him; and in such cases, before those who lay snares for us, we must be silent, as is said in Ps 39[38]:2: I said to myself: ‘I will guard my ways, so as not to sin with my tongue; I will put a bridle on my mouth while the wicked man is before me’ . Another reason: that it was not the moment to teach, but to endure patiently, and thus is fulfilled what Is 53:7 says: he was oppressed and he humbled himself and did not open his mouth. Like a lamb led to the slaughter, and like a sheep that is mute before its shearers, he too did not open his mouth. The third reason: to teach us constancy when someone unjustly accuses us of something, as is said in Is 51:7-8: lend me your ear, you who know what is just, people who are mindful of my law. Do not fear the insults of men, and do not be dismayed by their outrages; for the moth will eat them like a garment, and the worm will eat them like wool. But my justice will be forever, and my salvation for generation upon generation ” 31 . Now, it is true that many times those who persecute us, or assail us with their outrages, sometimes seem not to realize the harm they do, and even think they are acting according to God. Pay attention to the answer that St. John of Ávila, with a wise pen, has left imprinted in this letter we have been quoting: “ And if those who persecute think they do not offend God in it, what does this take away from my confidence, since the servants of God are expressly warned that they will be persecuted by people who believe they are rendering a great service 32 in persecuting them? They suffer for God and because they drew near to God; and the persecution is against God. If the persecutors think otherwise, perhaps they lessen their guilt somewhat, but not our crown; and if they, deceived, think they are serving God, we, undeceived, know that we are serving God .” Fr. Alonso de Vergara then complains that a certain person “carries and brings back” distorted information to a third party, which apparently brought him no small number of crosses. St. John of Ávila, a theologian of great depth and a true humanist, answers not as a spectator detached from the scene, but as one who knows the pain that slander causes, since he himself went to prison in 1531 because of a sermon of his that was misunderstood: “ What do you care, father, about the opinions of blind men, since it is certified that the doctrine you preach is from God, and that the manner in which you preach it is from God, as appears from the fruit; and that the spirit you have received is from God, since it has made you keep the law of God and has freed you from the law of sin…? Let your reverence see that Wisdom admonishes you not to think little of the knowledge our Lord has given you 33 , nor to let yourself be carried away or overcome, having that knowledge; rather, dare with it to despise the vain idols; and find yourself so rich with the hidden treasure God has shown you that you do not consider it a loss to lose all you had in order to obtain it. Do not esteem God so little that you would wish to give little for Him, since God esteemed you so much that He did not wish to give less than Himself for you. You were loved on a cross; love on a cross. You cost Christ dearly, and He who won you gave birth to you with groans; do not wish to offer the Lord sacrifices that cost you no toil and pain in your sensuality .” Do you realize? If we did not preach the last things, if we were not Thomists, if we did not denounce progressivism, if instead of elevating cultures with the values of the Gospel we offered only technical solutions, if we fed ourselves and not the sheep; if instead of preaching the Truth we negotiated with it, trimmed it, avoided it, do you think they would attack us? No. We would be doing exactly what the world wants us to do. But we do not do it, and, by the grace of God –in spite of our misery–, our apostolates bear fruit: it is enough to see the numerous vocations, many of them coming from countries that lament the crisis of the local Church, the 101 priests that the Institute has given to the Church in these last 6 years, all that which is “ certified to be from God ” and which is what the world and its henchmen attack and persecute and obstruct and want to put an end to once and for all. That is why, aware that we carry this treasure in earthen vessels 34 , we must not let ourselves be overcome, we must not cease to proclaim that the Word became flesh 35 , even when the world laughs at us and throws stones at us and curses us 36 . We must not let ourselves be swayed by what others say about us in trying to make us give up our purpose. What does it matter! We were born for greater things! “ What greater honor, my father, than to suffer for Christ! True glory […]. Blessed is he for whom the reason he is mistreated is that he serves God and does not wish to give in to the vain entreaties and opinions of men. This is a business of love, and love is a manner or kind of war, and cowards are not admitted here, whom God commanded to be dismissed from among the men of war 37 .” For as our Proper Law says: “love that is not born of the Cross of Christ is weak” 38 . But it is also true that when one “sees himself denigrated among his own” 39 , when those who ought to defend us are precisely those who insult us, when those who ought to listen to us are those who turn a deaf ear to our appeals, when it is those in whom we hoped to find protection who reject us and cast us out, who is there, however virtuous he may be, who does not complain at least interiorly? But notice what this giant of good spirit points out: “ Why do you complain, father, of the words and esteem of men and the judgments of the blind? See that your witness is in heaven, watching you to see how you do 40 , who is to be the judge of proof and, upon proof, approves your doctrine and work. Well, if He vouches for you, what does it matter if all the rest condemn you? 41 . It matters little and is nothing that men without God condemn us in this life 42 . Let your reverence count it as nothing that such base and miserable judgments condemn you. What heed is to be paid to people who will grow old like everyday clothes 43 and will be eaten by moths 44 ? ” Do we not meditate every year on the Principle and Foundation, where we read: “that we should not, for our part, want honor more than dishonor 45 ? “ Why tremble or faint over such small things, when our great Lord suffered such grave things for love of us and is to give us such abundant rewards here and there for our labors .” How can we not recall at this point that comforting phrase that our Proper Law places on the lips of our Most Sweet Savior: “I, your defender: why do you fear adversaries?” 46 . We have been called to share in the labors of our Lord Jesus Christ; we say that “we want to imitate Him until we can truly say to others: Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ 47 , it is no longer I who live, it is Christ who lives in me 48 ” 49 . Now, have we fought to the point of shedding blood 50 ? The truth is that we are not yet companions and equals in labors with the Apostle, who said: I die every day 51 . “Can your reverence count persecutions, affronts, stonings, scourgings, prisons that you have undergone for Jesus Christ with St. Paul? 52 . Why are you so delicate a soldier, and why do you show yourself so weak, fighting on the side of Jesus Christ 53 and having as your captain this Lord, to whom His Father gave a person and a countenance firmer than diamonds and flint 54 , so that no affronts, no insults, no blows could make Him turn back from what He had begun? Come, then, sir, let us leave this heaviness and weakness that holds us in its grip, and let us run with patience to the war that is set before us, always looking to Jesus Christ to take courage, who, just as He is the author of our faith, will carry it to its end and perfect it in us .” Note that the Master of Ávila does not deny how arduous the struggle is, but he also warns us that as long as we persevere patiently in the struggle that God Himself prophesied to us as real – you will weep and lament 55 ; in the world you will suffer tribulation 56 – no less real is the reward He promised us. “ He commands you to carry the cross, He promises you an eternal reward; and if it is a hard word to suffer temptations with Him, it is most sweet to sit at His table with Him in His kingdom 57 . Oh father, and why should we go and sit at that table of the persecuted, the dishonored, the saints, the tempted and those put to the sword 58 , having ourselves suffered nothing? […] Let us bring something to glory in; let us bring some feat of love for our true Lover, so that our love may not be of word alone. Let us trample this viper of tribulation and press on, preparing ourselves for greater things ”; because we were born for greater things! The Saint then goes on to advise: “ Offer, father, your life and honor into the hands of the Crucified, and make a gift of it to Him, for He will keep it safe, as He has done for others: I know whom I have believed , says St. Paul 59 . And it did not go badly for him. What is suffered is little and momentary 60 ; and to whomever it seems great, it is because he is small in love and has false weights. Let him grow and he will eat, for this is food for the grown 61 . And even if His help is delayed, He will come and calm the sea .” “ Our Lord has wished to test you, not to abandon you; the mother has hidden behind the curtain and is listening to the child cry, who cannot bear to be without her; but she will come out, for her heart will not let her bear it, and she will take the child in her arms and give him milk, and he will be so happy that he will forget his past troubles, as if they had never happened. And many of those who now persecute you will follow you, according to the promise of our Lord Jesus Christ: Those who murmured against you will come to you 62 .” But at the same time Master John of Ávila warns that if the persecuted one were to turn back because of the persecution he suffers, he will be gravely accused on the day of judgment, especially by the persecutors, who will say to him: “ ‘If we persecuted you, we did not have knowledge; but you, who had it, would have done well not to abandon it; for if we had known what you knew, we would not have abandoned it because of the persecution of those who did not know it. You harmed yourself and us, because, if you had persevered in virtue, we would have come to the knowledge of it.’ And that is why, my father, –St. John of Ávila goes on to say– you must take strength in the Lord, and believe most certainly [that], if you persevere, et per Christum abundat tribulatio tua, ita per Ipsum abundabit consolatio tua 63 , and that the Lord will repay you with the gain of souls for what you lose in those other things in the eyes of worldly people .” Persecution suffered over a long time, and the wearing down –humanly speaking– of physical strength through missionary labor, can take a toll on the missionary spirit. That is why, in the last paragraphs of the letter, in a tone that is always very human and compassionate, St. John of Ávila recommends to Fr. Alonso de Vergara some things that we too can put into practice if God ever grants us the favor of being able to suffer something for Him. First recommendation: “ a trip to Escalaceli or some similar place, where you might have time for yourself alone for a few days .” Our Proper Law, for its part, also has the same suggestion: “particularly when they see that a missionary has slackened in his spirit or shows signs of a certain weariness. A few months in another community or carrying out other activities, under the guidance and supervision of a qualified Superior, can restore to the missionary the spirit and strength that have perhaps been spent in apostolic battles” 64 . Second suggestion: “ and if this is not enough, I would like you to have the company of Father Fray Luis .” Our Directory also recommends that the missionary, during that time of prolonged rest , have the opportunity, whenever possible, to turn more easily to the company of good friends 65 . St. John of Ávila’s third practical recommendation: the reading of Sacred Scripture. “ To you –the Lord Himself says– it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God, but to the others in parables 66 . Who are these ‘you’? To you, my disciples, who do not live gladly in this world and despise it, afflicted for my sake, made the refuse of this world 67 . […] And without this, reading is of no profit at all. It seems to me that, by reading St. John and St. Paul and Isaiah, they will soon come to know the Scripture […] I do not know what more to tell you, father, except that you should read these; and when you do not understand them, consult some holy interpreter on them, and especially read St. Augustine, Against the Pelagians and against others of that sect; and set a crucifix before you and understand Him in everything, because He is everything and all of them preach Him. Pray and meditate and study .” In this sense our Proper Law says that the time of rest “is not a time in which ‘nothing is done,’ but one in which the missionary can recover his physical energies, take up again his intellectual work, perhaps somewhat neglected, give witness of his missionary life, etc.” 68 The Master of Ávila ends his letter to the persecuted preacher by telling him: “ And do not weary yourself in standing up for yourself or in giving many excuses for your innocence, because the Lord says: You shall keep silent, and the Lord will fight for you 69 .” 2. Great confidence St. John of Ávila was, according to Pope Benedict XVI, a promoter of “a spirituality of trust” 70 . Our Proper Law does the same throughout all its documents, exhorting us to have “total confidence” 71 in the Incarnate Word. In times of greater trial, and if we do not want to offend Christ, it is very fitting to cling to His goodness and trust in His infinite mercy. We would be very blind if, after so very many benefits that God has granted us, individually speaking and at the level of the Institute, we did not love the Incarnate Word with complete surrender, and our weakness would be very great if, after so many mercies as we have experienced, we did not trust in Him. All the goods that God has been pleased to grant us are means to stir us to love Him more and, at the same time, a call to strive to trust more; because if God has given us all the goods He has given us in the past, has called us to follow Him more closely and has put us –so to speak– on this course, He will also grant us to finish it, because “God will take care of His estate, for it belongs to no other owner” 72 and the Owner “will not abandon those who give themselves to Him with such confidence” 73 . Now that we are beginning Lent, let us take the opportunity to devote ourselves to meditating unhurriedly and deeply on the Passion of our Lord, for that is where the infinite goodness of the Father is manifested, who “handed Him over for all of us; [and] from which there must spring up in us a limitless confidence in the overflowing generosity of the Father: How will He not give us all things with Him? 74 ” 75 . Christ suffered and died out of love for us! That is why let us say with the Master of Ávila: “let every doubt, then, go far away, every faintness of heart and every distrust; for as great as is the power of His Passion, so great are our merits, since it is ours, for He gave it to us. There I presume and trust, and there I mock my enemies; there I make my petitions to the Father, offering Him the Son; from there I pay what I owe, and have more than enough left over. And although my sorrows are many, there I find greater remedy and cause for joy than I find in myself cause for sadness” 76 . We do God a great wrong if we do not trust fully in Him. St. John of Ávila would say: “we are worse than brutes!” Do we perhaps not believe that He will give us everything, and even more than we ask, after all He has already given us? “Shall we not believe that You will defend those whom You drew out of hell? Will You not feed those whom You took as children? Will You not teach the way to those whom, being astray, You set upon it? Will You not give what they ask for Your service to those to whom You gave many things when they were outside Your service, and, when they were offending, You defended them, and when they were fleeing from You, You followed them and brought them to Yourself, and cleansed them and gave them Your spirit, and filled their souls with joys, giving them the kiss of peace? And why all this? Surely so that they may believe that, since through Christ You reconciled them to Yourself when they were enemies, You will all the better keep them through Christ now that they are friends” 77 . We must stamp on our hearts an immense confidence in God, even when we do not feel the sweetness of consolations. “ Do we feel weak? Let us hope in God, and we will be strong. Do we not know what we must do? Let us trust in God, and light will be given to us, as Isaiah says: If anyone has walked in darkness and has no light, let him hope in the name of the Lord and lean upon his God 78 ; and elsewhere it is written: Those who trust in the Lord will understand the truth 79 . Are we in tribulations? Let us hope in God, and we will be delivered, as God says through David: He hoped in me and I will deliver him 80 . In these words we must note that God asks no other merit in order to deliver us than to hope ” 81 . “Oh souls created for these grandeurs and called to them! What are you doing? With what are you amusing yourselves? Your aspirations are lowliness and your possessions miseries. Oh miserable blindness of the eyes of your soul, for you are blind to so much light and deaf to such great voices, not seeing that, while you seek grandeur and glory, you remain miserable and lowly, made ignorant and unworthy of such great goods!” 82 . We were born for greater things! * * * * * We need strong men, brave men! Let us persevere steadfastly in the struggle. Let us strive to keep our hearts in peace, without letting any event of this world disquiet us, since everything is to come to an end 83 . If we place all our love in Christ, there we will find peace even in the midst of the cruelest affronts, since He is the foundation of everything: all things were created through Him and for Him… all things hold together in Him 84 . For this reason our Proper Law affirms that “peace must be sought within, not outside, filling ourselves with useless worries and filling our hearts with resentment against everything around us, because the peace of our soul does not depend on the disappearance of exterior obstacles, but of attachment to sin” 85 . And if at times we feel the file of abandonment more harshly, we must remember that Christ is watching how we fight in order one day to make us reign. May the Virgin Mother, who persevered immovable at the foot of the Cross, obtain for us the grace to persevere bravely and in peace, even though the storms grow fiercer, because we know in Whom we have trusted. May the company of our ever-loving and solicitous Mother fill us with great courage and always remind us that the sufferings of the present time are nothing compared with the glory that is to be revealed in us 86 . Come, then! We were born for greater things! The little shepherd

“We must have a very great devotion to the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ: ‘Everything is in the Passion. It is there that the science of the saints is learned’ 1 ” 2 , our Proper Law points out. And it also gives us the noble watchword of “wanting to know nothing except Jesus Christ and Jesus Christ crucified 3 ” 4 , since it is precisely the mystery of Christ’s self-emptying in His Passion –the supreme priestly act– 5 that is the chair from which we learn the sublime science of dying in order to live, of being buried in order to rise, of suffering in order to rejoice, of losing one’s life in order to find it, of humbling oneself in order to be exalted, of sacrificing oneself in order to be fulfilled, of submitting oneself in order to be free. So much so that we can say that “the language of the Cross teaches us that, in strict truth, reality is different from what it appears to be. For the Cross changes the meaning of things. It authentically teaches us to transignify them, since in reality the Cross gives them another end; the Cross transfinalizes reality” 6 . But so that this devotion does not remain an idyll or an abstract consideration, our Proper Law also urges us to make this practice “concrete in the knowledge and love of the Gospel accounts of the Passion 7 , in the theology of the Passion and Redemption, in the contemplation of the holy places of Jerusalem, of crucifixes, of the Way of the Cross, of the beautiful texts of the Imitation of Christ on this subject, of the Eucharist, the perpetuation of the Passion and Cross and second act of the one drama of the Redemption, of the Cross in our life, so well taught in the Circular Letter to the Friends of the Cross of St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort, and, finally, in fervor to bring the grace of the Redemption to all of reality” 8 . For the Christian, and very especially for religious, the Passion is an inexhaustible source of wisdom and is a guide and model for our whole life. That is why St. Peter Claver used to say: “The only book one needs to read is the Passion” 9 . And the great St. Thomas writes: “Whoever wishes to lead a perfect life need do nothing other than despise what Christ despised on the Cross, and love what Christ loved on the Cross” 10 . For his part, St. John of the Cross also “invites us to contemplate the mystery of the Cross of Christ, as he habitually did, in the poem ‘ El Pastorcico ’ [The Little Shepherd]” 11 , a poem that describes “Christ who suffers for the soul” 12 . It is a precious, very singular text that, in a poetic and mystical way, describes the centrality of the heart of Christ and of His immeasurable love for souls with singular beauty and depth. In the midst of the Lenten season, and as we prepare to begin in a few days the celebration of the Great Week of Christendom, we believe that a weighed and reflective consideration of the profound and regal doctrine about the Crucified contained in those concise 20 lines from the pen of St. John of the Cross can be of great profit for our souls, “to nail in the heart Him who was nailed to the Cross for us” 13 , as the great St. Augustine beautifully said. 1. The Crucified in the spiritual striving of the poet Before devoting ourselves to considering the poem, we would like to point out that Christ Crucified was the model to which the poet 14 St. John of the Cross sought to conform himself all his life, he who from his childhood learned to read himself and to read the events of his life in the key of the Cross. Fray Diego de la Concepción, who was prior at La Peñuela when Fray John of the Cross, on his way to Mexico, stayed there and fell ill with the erysipelas from which he died, went to visit him in Úbeda when the saint was already very gravely ill. He says in a letter that when five wounds opened in the saint’s foot, he and those who accompanied him heard him remark: “Many thanks I give You, my Lord Jesus Christ, that the five wounds Your Majesty had in Your feet, hands and side, You have wished to give me in this one foot. Where did I merit so great a favor?” Regarding this, Fray Diego comments: “Although his pains were so great, he did not complain, but bore it all with great patience” 15 . Thus we see how in his daily life and “in the life of faith, the mystery of the Cross of Christ was a habitual reference and rule of life” 16 . And that is the very thing the Mystical Doctor recommended to all souls, as numerous testimonies corroborate, among them that of Mother Francisca de la Madre de Dios, who always carried with her some little notes with certain counsels the Saint had given her: “Crucifiedinteriorly and exteriorly with Christ. She will live in this life with fullness and satisfaction of her soul, possessing it in her patience 17 ” 18 . “Let Christ Crucified be enough for her, and with Him let her suffer and rest, and for Him let her annihilate herself in all things exterior and interior” 19 . “Let her love trials greatly and think little of them, in order to find favor with the Bridegroom, who did not hesitate to die for her” 20 . “Let her have fortitude of heart against all things that would move her toward what is not God, and let her be a friend of the Passion of Christ. He who does not seek the Cross of Christ does not seek the glory of Christ” 21 . Likewise, all the friars who went about and lived with Fray John of the Cross knew his consistent conduct and attested to it in his Dictámenes . “He used to say that two things serve the soul as wings to rise to union with God, namely, affective compassion for the death of Christ and for one’s neighbors; and that when the soul is lingering in compassion for the Cross and Passion of the Lord, it should remember that on it He was alone in working our redemption, as it is written: Torcular calcavi solus 22 (Is 63:3). From this it will draw, and there will be offered to it, most profitable considerations and thoughts” 23 . The letters he wrote while suffering the harshest persecution say as much, a period that corresponds –according to some 24 – to the “moment” of the composition of the Pastorcico . To the Carmelite nuns of Beas he wrote: “Serve God, my beloved daughters in Christ, following His footsteps of mortification in all patience, in all silence and in every desire to suffer, becoming executioners of your own satisfactions, mortifying yourselves if perchance something remains to die that hinders the interior resurrection of the Spirit, who dwells in your souls” 25 . The Saint, placed upon the Cross by the chapter of Madrid in 1591, writes by way of farewell to Mother Ana de Jesús: “… occupy yourself in exercising the virtues of mortification and patience, desiring to become in suffering somewhat like this great God of ours, humbled and crucified; for this life, if it is not for imitating Him, is not good” 26 . Since, then, “John of the Cross is a master and model by his life and his writings” 27 , we consider that the assiduous reading of his works and attentive consideration of the example of his life is not only of very great profit for assimilating the doctrine of the Cross, the foundation stone of our spirituality 28 , but also shows us “the necessity of the Cross in our lives” 29 . For as our Proper Law asks of us: “Jesus is loved and served on the Cross and crucified with Him, and in no other way” 30 . 2. The poem 31 A little shepherd 32 Other songs in a divine sense (by the same author) about Christ and the soul. A little shepherd, alone, is in grief, a stranger to pleasure and contentment, his thoughts all set upon his shepherdess, and his breast by love most sorely wounded. He does not weep because love has wounded him, for it does not pain him to see himself so afflicted, though in his heart he is wounded; but he weeps to think that he is forgotten. For only at the thought that he is forgotten by his fair shepherdess, with great grief he lets himself be ill-treated in a foreign land, his breast by love most sorely wounded. And the little shepherd says: Ah, wretched is the one who has gone away from my love and does not wish to enjoy my presence, and my breast for love of her most sorely wounded! And after a long while he has climbed up upon a tree, where he opened his fair arms, and dead he has remained, hanging by them, his breast by love most sorely wounded. El Pastorcico tells in a few, shattering lines what the Night of Christ is. In this poem St. John of the Cross speaks of a profound aspect of the mystery of the kenosis , the same one St. Paul describes and to which our Proper Law refers so abundantly: Have the same sentiments as Christ Jesus. He, though He was of divine condition, did not regard this equality with God as something to be jealously guarded: on the contrary, He emptied Himself, taking the condition of a slave and becoming like men. And appearing in human form, He humbled Himself to the point of accepting, out of obedience, death, even death on a Cross. That is why God exalted Him and gave Him the Name that is above every name 33 . “The three allegorical elements of the song, shepherd, shepherdess and tree, represent Christ, the soul, and the tree of the Cross” 34 . According to scholars of the subject, “the imitation and following of Christ, which [St. John of the Cross] teaches at the beginning of the Ascent , he simplifies in this poem. It is the image and the permanent appeal of the supreme Humility of God, inviting the soul to the encounter with Him, there on the Cross” 35 . St. Edith Stein comments in her Science of the Cross that “in the Song of the Pastorcico the sentiments of the soul are not expressed directly. The poet grasped an image and expresses it artistically. ‘He sees Christ Crucified and hears the complaint He addresses to souls and how He weeps to think that He is forgotten.’ With this theme he composes a pastoral poem so much to the taste of his time, as he did in grander style in the Canticle . If for the latter he drew inspiration from the Song of Songs, for the former he thought of the Good Shepherd who gives his life for his sheep (Jn 10). And is not the shepherd’s complaint to his elusive shepherdess an echo of that plaintive call of Christ when He wept over Jerusalem? (Mt 23-37). The refrain, ‘ his breast by love most sorely wounded ,’ is the key to the state of his soul” 36 . 1.A little shepherd, alone, is in grief, a stranger to pleasure and contentment, his thoughts all set upon his shepherdess, and his breast by love most sorely wounded . The first stanza recreates the setting for us and situates us. The poem is in itself, from the beginning, an invitation to tenderness and gratitude: the little shepherd is alone . It is his solitude, that of God and that of the Sufferer. God is by nature the Holy One, without likeness, impenetrable in His judgments. That is why He is the ‘stranger’ and, of necessity, upon becoming incarnate, He must feel Himself “in a foreign land” (v. 10). It is interesting to note the detail of St. John of the Cross in personifying Christ as the Pastorcico . Fray Luis de León, in his work De los Nombres de Cristo , points out that “the life of the Shepherd is innocent, and peaceful, and delightful, and the condition of his state is inclined to love; and his task is to govern, giving pasture and adapting his governance to the particular conditions of each one; and being wholly for those he governs, he provides them with all they need, always directing his work to this, which is to make a flock and a fold. The genius and qualities of this Shepherd, in a thousand ways and details, reveal and make manifest the loving heart He has, to whose greatness no tongue or praise can attain; because, besides the fact that all His works are love […] the affection, the tenderness of heart, the solicitude and loving care, and the ardor and intensity of will with which He always does these same works of love, exceed all that can be imagined. There is no mother so solicitous, nor spouse so gentle, nor heart of love so tender and won over, nor any title of friendship so joined to steadfastness, that equals Him or comes near to Him” 37 . Christ, though He was of divine condition 38 , lets Himself be seen and treated in history as one in grief [ penado ]. This word has a double sense which better explains the solitude of the divine Sufferer . One meaning places Him in a Penitentiary , which is a prison of the highest category because of the crimes punished there. The other sense is the one that expresses the sentence , with its consequences, for which He is there, suffering His penalty and awaiting a final judgment. He feels Himself blamed and condemned to pay, out of obedience to the Father , the debts of all men. The pleasure and contentment of His divine nature are strange to Him here, and although He Himself is a stranger among men, He nevertheless thinks of them, moved by His love: his thoughts all set upon his shepherdess . How much beauty there is in this line! For what most aggravates His situation is loving and seeking His shepherdess (the soul) where she is not and ought to be; it is the cruelest drama for a lover, for He is not willing to see Himself defeated by lack of love. And that is why St. John of the Cross teaches that “if the soul seeks God, much more does her Beloved seek her” 39 . It is the absence of the shepherdess that causes his breast by love most sorely wounded. This line, and his breast by love most sorely wounded , which is repeated with very slight variations as the ending of all the other stanzas except the second, wants to make us notice the sorrowful and painful aspect of the heart of the Pastorcico , dwelling in the breast of love , the Tabernacle of merciful love, which sets out toward Calvary. All the stanzas point to the same point of observation and expectation. 2.He does not weep because love has wounded him, for it does not pain him to see himself so afflicted, though in his heart he is wounded; but he weeps to think that he is forgotten. We can say that this second stanza solemnly proclaims the profound drama. Here the Pastorcico lets us hear his wounded heart, which, moreover, weeps , is stricken , afflicted , wounded and forgotten . With one brushstroke the Mystical author has summed up for us all the dimensions of Christ’s redemptive suffering. The most apparent, the one that outwardly tends to impress us most and represents all of them, is weeping. And he gives us the reason why He weeps: to think that he is forgotten by his shepherdess. His physical sufferings do not seem to be the principal causes of His sorrow; rather, it is the forgetfulness of His shepherdess that makes Him truly, deeply grieved. To see that God, in His human nature, weeps for us is impressively moving and convincing. Thus St. John of the Cross reveals the sorrowing Divine Heart of our Lord so that we may experience that, in its sorrow, that Heart tenderly caresses, and is maternal in its way of loving, of bearing, of waiting, of nourishing, of forgiving its forgetful and rebellious children. This Heart, so wounded, dwelling in the breast of love, cries out to us that only a paternal-maternal heart is capable of thinking, of measuring distances and absences, of feeling and weeping the immense sorrow that the forgetfulness of men causes God… But instead of dwelling at length on the reason for His grief, He concentrates the whole reservoir of His tears as the supreme expression of sorrow, saying: He does not weep because love has wounded him, … but he weeps to think that he is forgotten. 3.For only at the thought that he is forgotten by his fair shepherdess, with great grief he lets himself be ill-treated in a foreign land, his breast by love most sorely wounded. This is exactly His “great grief”: only at the thought that he is forgotten , and that is the reason why he lets himself be ill-treated in a foreign land . That great grief is what provokes the sorrowful weeping that Christ could not conceal in the Garden of Olives nor while expiring on the Cross. That is why, only at the thought that he is forgotten by his fair shepherdess , He takes upon Himself all the sufferings, servitudes, poverty, humiliations, outrages, pains, injustices, calumnies, deaths… of all men, women and children, religious, priests, missionaries, monks, brothers, novices… slaves in their prisons of selfishness, of all that ill-treatment means, so long as He may recover so lamentable a loss, and He goes about with his breast by love most sorely wounded. How can one contemplate His Heart dwelling in the breast by love so sorely wounded and not dissolve in tears and compassion for Christ in His Passion! At the beginning we quoted a thought of St. Peter Claver, a great devotee of the Passion of our Lord. It is told of him that, when “night came, before going to bed he would sit on the bed, with a chair beside him and the book of the Passion open on it. At times he would kneel to read it, and he would read a verse and begin to weep. On other nights he would get up and, with a Cross on his shoulders, go to the chapel and stop before the Tabernacle to pray and weep. Truly for him the Passion was not something distant, something remote, but something present, living, vital, current, of now, of this moment; as it is, mysteriously and sacramentally, in the Mass. If what is happening today in religious life is happening, if what is happening in priestly life is happening, it is because what our Lord suffered in the Passion has fallen out of the consideration of the consecrated soul. The Way of the Cross hangs on the walls, but what consecrated soul is attuned to what is represented on the walls?” 40 . 4.And the little shepherd says: Ah, wretched is the one who has gone away from my love and does not wish to enjoy my presence, and my breast for love of her most sorely wounded! This fourth stanza is like the Gospel condensed. And the little shepherd says… It is the Word. His office is to say, to repeat, to warn, to alert, to keep watch, to break open all roads and directions, to become the wayside cross at every crossroads, to forestall the risks and dangers of going astray. For the soul’s absence through sin multiplies exponentially the possibilities of evil. That is why He says: Ah, wretched is the one who has gone away from my love and does not wish to enjoy my presence! The Pastorcico laments that the wayward soul cannot enjoy the happiness that Divine Love has destined for her, and that is why He goes about with his breast for love of her most sorely wounded. 5.And after a long while he has climbed up upon a tree, where he opened his fair arms, and dead he has remained, hanging by them, his breast by love most sorely wounded. And after a long while… how long has this adorable Pastorcico been waiting for the return of his fair shepherdess ? That is why the expression after a long while denotes infinite patience, unhurried waiting, constant and not intermittent love, an expectation without reproach. It also shows that it is God who decides His Hour and ours, the hour of Calvary and the hour of the encounter. For as our Proper Law says: “He alone knows everything, even our soul, our feelings, our character, the secret springs that must be moved to bring us to heaven, the effects that this or that thing will produce in us, and He has all means at His disposal” 41 . That is why it seems to us that this while , a rather long one, consists of the spaces of forgetfulness, of absences and of delays that we men interpose to the offer the Pastorcico makes us from the Cross. The tree, where he opened his fair arms, is none other than the tree of the Cross, where the Divine Lover continues to wait for His fair shepherdess with arms open and fastened to the tree, in order one day to ‘absorb’ her “powerfully and strongly in the abyssal 42 embrace of His sweetness” 43 . From beginning to end, the Pastorcico invites the soul to rest in its center: the breast of the Beloved, where the Good of all goods dwells; until one day His shepherdess recognizes “that infinite knowledge and that hidden secret, what peace, what love, what silence is in that divine breast…!” 44 and falls overcome on her knees to say to Him: “Who will be able to free himself from lowly ways and limits if You do not lift him up to Yourself in purity of love, my God? How will man, begotten and reared in lowliness, rise up to You, if You do not lift him up, Lord, with the hand that made him?” 45 . In His infinite Mercy and ineffable love, the Pastorcico seeks, invites and waits for the soul, his fair shepherdess , without reproaching her for her follies, her ingratitude, her rebuffs, her forgetfulness, but appealing to the soul to contemplate his breast by love most sorely wounded , as if telling the soul to have compassion on Him, that by consoling Him she will be infinitely happy and “will see how exalted a knowledge it is that God teaches there –in that divine breast–” 46 . Hence our Constitutions declare plainly that our office is to weep for Jesus Christ 47 and, so as not to cause our God grief, they exhort us that “the memory and remembrance of Him should never depart from our hearts. With this, sleep should come, and of this they should dream while sleeping. The heart always melted in love of Him, and the memory occupied with nothing other than Him” 48 . The Pastorcico , in His solitude of love and sorrow, tries to bring about the encounter with His shepherdess. That is why St. John of the Cross makes solitude the condition, the setting and a specific note of His love. This solitude from every creature (in the sense of detachment) is the guardian key of intimacy. It is the inescapable invitation to enter into the mystery. That is why he writes: “By love alone , which at this time burns…; it is what guides and moves the soul then and makes her fly to her God by the road of solitude ” 49 . It is in the “sounding solitude” and in the “divine tranquility” that [God] communicates Himself and unites Himself to the soul 50 . The reason is that love is the unity of two alone, who wish to communicate with each other alone; and “because the Beloved is found only alone , in solitude” 51 . Only the soul that is alone can “come to the delights of the embrace of union with God” 52 , an embrace that has the property of hiding the soul within itself, where the soul sees itself so secret when it sees itself raised above every temporal creature 53 ; and once that embrace has taken place, says St. John of the Cross, it places the soul “in the veins of the science of love” 54 , which is none other than the science of the Cross. 3. The school of the Cross The Cross, in its most eloquent silence, speaks with a special power. St. Paul says that Jesus taught him this science of the Cross: …my power is shown perfect in weakness. Therefore, most gladly will I continue to glory above all in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me. That is why I take pleasure in my weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions and in distresses suffered for Christ; for when I am weak, then it is that I am strong (2 Cor 12:9-10). In the encounter with Christ Crucified, contemplating the figure of that Pastorcico who, having climbed up upon a tree, opened his fair arms , and embracing the breast of love so afflicted and so wounded, we cannot help but imitate Him and effectively desire to become ourselves an image of Christ laden with the Cross and crucified, and, conformed to His Cross, to let ourselves be shaped by Him. That is why the Saint of Fontiveros recommended: “If you wish to be perfect, follow Christ to Calvary and the tomb” 55 . This demand becomes even more imperative if we ponder that we who have been called to be “other Christs” will one day be judged according to that same pattern. Fray Luis de León says: “If it belongs to the shepherd to serve in lowliness, to live in a despised garb, not to be adored and served, accustomed to the dress of his sheep and clothed in their lowliness, and if his skin served to win his flock, by this pattern must all those be cut who have received the mission of shepherds. Even so, Christ the Shepherd surpasses them in having come down from heaven to seek man as pasture and, above all, in that Jesus died for the good of his flock, which no other shepherd did, and that, to snatch us from between the teeth of the wolf, he allowed the wolves to make him their prey” 56 . For this reason, St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort, in his Letter to the Friends of the Cross , which our Proper Law recommends that we read 57 , tells the “disciples of a crucified God” that the science of the Cross “must be learned in practice, in the school of Jesus crucified” 58 . And he goes on to say: “Train yourselves, then, in this supereminent science, under the guidance of so excellent a Master. Thus you will come to master all the sciences, since this one contains them all in the highest degree. It constitutes our natural and supernatural philosophy, our divine and mysterious theology. It is our philosopher’s stone which, thanks to patience, will change the most ordinary metals into precious ones; the most atrocious pains into delights; poverty into riches; and the deepest humiliations into glory. Whichever of you knows best how to carry his Cross, even if he is illiterate, is the wisest of all. […] Rejoice, then, you poor unlettered one…! If you know how to suffer with joy, you know more than any doctor who does not know how to suffer as well as you do! 59 ” 60 . To train ourselves in this science, besides the contemplation of the mystery of Christ in His Passion, the Eucharist is a concrete moment during the day in which we can learn a little more of the science of the Cross. “There Christ makes Himself a victim, under species not His own, perpetuating the sacrifice of the Cross. There we offer Him as Victim to the Father, and we offer ourselves as victims together with Him. There, in receiving Him in Communion, we participate intimately in His sacrifice, making ourselves victims, eucharistically, with Him. That is why there is nothing like daily Mass for knowing Jesus better and for being set aflame with His love” 61 . Finally, “we never know the Cross better than when some sorrow, some suffering, some persecution strikes us. It is the moment to experience, in some way, what Jesus experienced in His Passion and on His Cross” 62 . And that is why the very Cross that is suffered becomes a cause of joy: I overflow with joy in all tribulations 63 . ***** Man’s “return,” so sought after by Christ, involves numerous attempts, always being once again at the beginning. Since it is a matter of love, is there anything more fickle and fragile than the human heart? The Pastorcico was willing to reckon with this. His shepherdess will continue to be fair , even though she leaves Him alone. The true return to Him will begin when the soul recognizes its disordered appetites and affections and “resolves to submit to carrying this Cross, which is truly to resolve to want to find and bear hardship in all things for God” 64 . For as the Holy Doctor teaches, and of this he wants to persuade us, “this road to God does not consist in a multiplicity of considerations, nor methods, nor manners, nor delights (although this, in its way, is necessary for beginners), but in one thing alone that is necessary, which is to know how truly to deny oneself, exteriorly and interiorly, giving oneself to suffering for Christ and to annihilating oneself in everything; because, by exercising oneself in this, all the rest and more than it is accomplished and found in it. And if there is a lack in this exercise, which is the sum and root of the virtues, all those other ways are a beating about the bush and making no progress, even if one has considerations and communications as lofty as the angels. For progress is not found except in imitating Christ, who is the way and the truth and the life, and no one comes to the Father except through Him ” 65 . Christian mortification, to which the Church invites us especially in the season of Lent, is figuratively night ; subjectively (united to that of Christ), it is death ; but objectively and in its outcome it is resurrection . The whole process is directed toward the ‘Pasch of the embrace’ –not in a sensible sense– but of the mystical embrace that forms part of God’s plan and that is none other than the radiant goal of union with God. The Pastorcico , who has remained with His arms open, fastened to the tree of the Cross, speaks to us of the longing He has for this embrace. It is the image of a divine waiting, of God’s hope-filled offer to man. Who is there who, after contemplating the Pastorcico , does not turn toward Him, does not feel himself committed? From the Cross hangs the Savior of the world! From the tree of the Cross hangs Christ with his breast by love most sorely wounded! Wherever we may go, or wherever the reading of this writing may find us, let us embrace the Cross that God has been pleased to send us, and let us count on the fact that the definitive triumph always belongs to Jesus crucified and to those crucified with Him. May the Holy Virgin, who at the foot of the Cross experienced this reality, obtain for us from her Only Son the grace, today and always, of wanting to know nothing except Jesus Christ crucified 66 . A very fruitful Lent and a very happy Easter!
