Our Lady of Luján, Mother of the vocations of the IVE

This coming May 8 the Church throughout the world will celebrate the World Day of Prayer for Vocations, which will happily coincide with the beautiful feast of our Most Holy Mother, Our Lady of Luján, and with the 5th anniversary of our offering of the Golden Rose “in perpetual testimony of our love and gratitude for the vocations that She sends to our Religious Family… and as a pledge of confidence for the many that through her intercession we hope to conceive” 1 . How much we have to thank Our Lady for! From the last General Chapter (July 2016) until the present, our small Institute has given the Church 103 priests! for the greater glory of God. That is a very great grace for the Institute. Just to grasp the scale of the blessing this represents, let us consider that there are very important dioceses that have had no priestly ordinations, or very few, in the last 10 or 20 years; the same unfortunately happens with religious congregations of great prestige and tradition. Moreover, today we have 503 vocations in formation 2 , of which only 16% are Argentine vocations and 84% come from other countries 3 , which speaks of the fruitfulness with which God has been pleased to crown the evangelizing efforts of our missionaries throughout the length and breadth of this world, so that the message of Christ may reach more effectively the heart of each of its cultures. Likewise, we consider it no minor detail that Our Lady of Luján has sent the Institute vocations coming from the same family. For double family ties –by blood and by the spirit– not only contribute to the unity and cohesion of the Institute, but are an important apostolic witness for other families and, to tell the truth, for other Christians. Therefore, in view of celebrating next May 8 the World Day of Prayer for Vocations within the setting of the Solemnity of the Most Pure Conception of Luján, we would like to address in these lines the priority commitment of each member of the Institute to promote vocations, and one of the means of promoting vocations, which is precisely “family ministry, which is of itself vocational” 4 . 1. A priority commitment “Because Christ is one, we want to work with all our strength… So that all men may confess the adorable Name of the Lord Jesus, fulfilling his commandment: Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature 5 ” 6 . Now, without enough laborers for the harvest , it will not be possible for us to carry out Christ’s mandate – Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature 7 – which is the very reason for the existence and mission of the Institute in history, nor to renew each day the Eucharistic sacrifice – Do this in memory of me 8 – “because without a priest there can be no Eucharistic sacrifice” 9 . At the same time, it is well known to all that every vocation is a gift of God and, like all gifts that come from God, they arrive through many human mediations: parents, educators, pastors, some good Catholic friend, etc. But certainly, the first who must feel involved in vocational ministry are those who are themselves called to the ministerial priesthood. And if this is true for all priests, it is doubly so for the members of the Institute, since it is an “integral element of our spirituality to know how to call, teach, direct, accompany and select priestly, diaconal, religious, missionary and secular vocations” 10 , a task that none of the members of the Institute can evade. Even more: “the pastoral care of vocations is intrinsic to the end of the evangelization of culture and to the charism of the Institute, since the evangelical counsels are an integral part of the message of salvation and those who follow them especially manifest the ‘eschatological character of the Church’ 11 , being the adornment of the Bride of Christ” 12 . Up to here, nothing new. We know this. However, it is easy to become lethargic or to give priority to some other kind of ministry –perhaps of more immediate fruit– rather than to vocational ministry. And how are priestly and religious vocations promoted? We know very well that at the basis of all vocational ministry, as Our Lord Jesus Christ taught, lies authentic and persevering prayer asking for more laborers for the harvest 13 ; nevertheless, our Proper Law explicitly points out to us a necessary and consequent means: “through the faithful and joyful witness of consecrated life” 14 . It is what St. Paul expresses when he says: I beg you to walk as befits the vocation to which you have been called 15 . “Conduct that corresponds to the vocation,” says St. John Paul II, “makes new vocations spring up. This consistent conduct constitutes, as it were, the permanent basis of prayer; it prepares it, and prayer is like its development; reciprocally, prayer continually calls for such behavior” 16 . Therefore, before the hundreds of projects we can carry out with a view to vocational ministry, the first, together with prayer, is that of priestly and religious witness . We cannot ignore that our life is always a significant presence beside young people: it encourages or discourages, it awakens the desire for God or constitutes an obstacle to following Him. That is why consistent and joyful witness represents the first vocational proposal within reach of any of our members. If we truly give a joyful witness of serving Christ “carrying out our proper apostolates with competence and generosity” 17 , if we are capable of radiating hope because of the faith that dwells in our breast despite all the weariness of the struggle, if we truly give ourselves to souls without neglecting prayer, how can we doubt that vocations will arise around us? The vocations that God has sent us through Our Lady of Luján from countries with a Christian minority such as Tajikistan, the Gaza Strip, Egypt; or from places where the presence of the Institute is scarce, as in Papua New Guinea, or nonexistent, as in Sri Lanka, India, Guatemala, Slovakia, etc., prove that prayer united to the witness of a consistent life always bears fruit where God wills and as God wills. Nevertheless, none of us is unaware, however few years of religious life he may have, that missionaries are lacking in the outskirts of the great cities, in rural areas, among the inhabitants of the high mountain regions and in the immensity of the jungle. There is a lack of priests to devote themselves to the young, to families, to the elderly and sick, to workers, to intellectuals, to professionals and to the uneducated, to artists, to the rich and to the poor, to those of our own homeland and to immigrants… It is our experience that a greater number of priests and religious is urgently needed in parishes, in parish groups, in schools and universities, in factories, and in so many other fields… we can even say “that the ends of the earth, to which the Gospel must reach, are drawing ever farther away” 18 . This lack of laborers for the harvest already constituted a challenge for Jesus himself in Gospel times. His example allows us to understand that the too-small number of consecrated persons is a situation inherent to the condition of the Church and of the world, and not merely an accidental fact due to present circumstances. However, the Incarnate Word, moved with compassion for the multitudes, gave them his teaching because He saw that they were weary and downcast, like sheep without a shepherd 19 , but He wanted his disciples also to take part in the solution, inviting them above all to pray 20 . We too can and must influence the number of vocations through prayer. Sometimes when we say that we must pray for vocations we often think it is a general intention; however, we judge it fitting that there should not be lacking frequent and explicit prayer for vocations, especially for our Institute. Nor is it any less important to invite others to pray –as is in fact already done in various places through the “40 Hours Project” or the “priestly Thursdays” or the “rosary for vocations”– because we must be aware that vocations will not be able to take the step by their own strength, and for this reason they must be stimulated with prayer, accompanied and sustained, understanding that a vocation is a true gift that comes from heaven. We highlight here the preponderant role of the contemplatives of the Institute, since the abundance and quality of priestly, contemplative, missionary and consecrated vocations for the Institute depends in no small degree on generous and joyful fidelity to the contemplative life. It is moving to think that our Lord has willed to associate the precious gift of vocations for his Church with the joined hands of a monk and his silent immolation. Together with this, it is almost evident that vocational ministry requires closeness to young people, without which the witness of consecrated life cannot be given. And many of them are searching for a meaning to their lives. That is why we must be lavish in inviting them to collaborate in our pastoral activities: to take part in our Masses, in the feasts of the Institute, to help in the homes, to volunteer in the various missions of the Institute, to take part in popular missions, to help in organizing Spiritual Exercises, oratories or any other apostolic activity; to invite them to be catechists, to take part in the Voices of the Word, to consecrate themselves to Jesus through Mary, to make Spiritual Exercises themselves, to invite them to camps, etc. In short, our Institute, by the grace of God, has countless opportunities and a great variety of activities to involve others in the cause of Christ, and to a great extent it depends on us how much room we give them. It is also, and has always been, an option in our Institute to invite young people to share our religious life, taking the precautions that each case requires. Did not Christ say to Andrew and John: come and you will see 21 ? Let it be well understood that vocational ministry cannot be exhausted in occasional and extraordinary initiatives –such as the “ come and see ” or the “ open house ” events organized by the houses of formation– but must be one of the constant concerns of the ministry of each of the priests of the Institute. Always –unless the superior disposes otherwise– the doors of our houses can be opened to young people; they can be invited to eat pizza on Fridays with the other members of the community, to go on an outing or a pilgrimage; in short, the occasions are countless. Far be it from our members the temptation to say “I’m past that sort of thing,” “there are already the seminary people who do apostolate with young people,” “it’s not my job because I’m in a Hogarcito,” “I’m a contemplative,” “the young people here are into other things,” “I’m alone in my parish,” or some similar excuse. To all who think this way we answer with what St. John Paul II said to some contemplatives, but which we judge applies also to those in active life: “Young people today are animated by great ideals and, if they see consistent men, witnesses of the Gospel, they follow them with enthusiasm. To propose to today’s world the practice of the life hidden in Christ means to reaffirm the value of humility, of poverty, of interior freedom. The world, which deep down is thirsty for these virtues, wants to see upright men who practice them with everyday heroism, moved by the awareness of loving and serving their brothers through this witness” 22 . And that concerns us all. Moreover, at some moment God puts each of us in contact with a young man “made of good timber” to whom we can explicitly propose the consideration of the priestly vocation. How many of us entered the Institute because a priest had the courage and insight to propose the vocation to us with enthusiasm. We must not be pessimistic, resigned or timid in speaking of vocations. That was not the example we received. Without doubt the seed of the vocation is in the hearts of many young people and is simply waiting for a favorable occasion to germinate. “To seek vocations is also to propose them: ‘with passion and discretion’ 23 ” 24 , says our Proper Law. Let us also note that our Proper Law affirms that in vocational ministry “the best energies must be invested” 25 . And when we say the best energies we are referring to the quality of the time we devote to vocational ministry –it is essential to be available to young people–; to the generosity with which we use all means –even financial ones– to seek, sustain and accompany vocations; to dedication to study and personal preparation in order to be able to give young people good formation, so that we ourselves may know how to discern well, etc. All, and very especially pastors, must conceive of vocational ministry as an obligatory dimension of the overall pastoral plan. “In pastoral action it must never be forgotten that to educate in the faith also means to develop the vocational dynamism proper to Christian life. To be a Christian is, of itself, a vocation, a call: the highest and strongest vocation, and the basis of every specific following within the ecclesial community” 26 . That is why the Directory of Parishes pointedly says: “Let it be remembered that vocations will be the sign of a parish’s maturity 27 , and that vocational work must become a pastoral priority , knowing how to foster them with generosity and to let go of them when they decide to follow Jesus Christ more closely” 28 . In this sense, it seems necessary to us to make special mention of the parish, which always has a decisive role with regard to priestly and religious vocations. The parish is where young people in fact live their Christian experience; in it they hear the message of Christ and are inserted into the life of grace; it is also in the parish that they come into contact with our priests, brothers, sisters, seminarians and even occasionally with our monks. In this regard, the importance of the witness and good example of each of them is evident, as the normal instrument of God’s call to a more generous service. It is imperative “to reactivate an intense pastoral action which, starting from the Christian vocation in general and from an enthusiastic youth ministry, may give the Church the servants she needs” 29 . In addition to all the means already mentioned, in our Institute we have the precious resource of the festive Oratory , which should not be lacking in any IVE parish. For “the Oratory is an incipient source of vocations” 30 and very probably “the only form of complete Christian education accessible to great masses of young people” 31 . An element of great importance also when it comes to awakening vocations is community witness . Experience has shown us that it is often the example of a religious , of a priest, that contributes decisively to the realization of a vocation to the priesthood or to consecrated life. Similarly, the community witness of fidelity and joy arouses an enormous attraction toward religious life and is, definitively, a source of new vocations and a support for perseverance 32 . In other words, “religious communities cannot attract young people except through a collective witness of authentic consecration, lived in the joy of personal self-giving to Christ and to the brethren” 33 . How many times young people have approached us simply because of this witness of joy, because they have seen us give ourselves generously to apostolic work in the missions ad gentes , or simply because they met us while climbing some mountain or on some other community outing. For this reason it continues to be very important to cultivate joy in the religious community 34 . Finally, we must highlight the importance of family ministry as one of the means of promoting vocations. Our Proper Law points this out in several of its documents, and it is what we will address in the second point. 2. Family ministry is of itself vocational The Directory of the Third Order , quoting St. John Paul II, says: “The family, the domestic Church, is the first field in which God cultivates vocations. For this reason it is necessary to understand that a correct and careful family ministry is, by itself, a vocational ministry” 35 . Indeed, “God has willed to bless us, from the very beginnings of our Institutes, with large families of sound human and Christian formation, from which numerous vocations to consecrated life or to the priesthood have sprung” 36 . And while this has been so since the beginning, we have all seen it in the recent priestly ordinations. Therefore, a careful dedication to family ministry, and to the Third Order in particular, ensures the life of our Religious Family, preparing the ground and hearts for the call of the Incarnate Word 37 . The family is one of the turning points of culture 38 and, therefore, family ministry concerns us all: not only the one in charge of the Third Order, not only the one who is a pastor, not only the one who is a priest, not only the specialists 39 , but all, because we are all members of this Institute whose charism has as its first field of action “to prolong Christ in families” 40 . Having said this, let us now turn to the close relationship that exists between families and the priestly and religious vocation. The Spiritual Father of our Religious Family, in a message for the World Day of Prayer for Vocations, wrote the following: “The family, to the extent that it becomes aware of this genuine vocation [apostolic vocation through the sacrament of matrimony] and responds to it, the family in which one learns to live meekness, justice, mercy, chastity, peace, purity of heart, becomes what St. John Chrysostom, in other words, calls the domestic church , that is, the place in which Jesus Christ lives and works the salvation of men and the growth of the kingdom of God” 41 . To help this come about, and so that families may truly be helped and instructed in fulfilling their own duties and Christian life may be fostered within families, pastoral work is necessary. That is why, among the very varied means and opportunities that God gives us to carry out this apostolate, our Proper Law exhorts us to visit families as an occasion to share in family concerns, to pour out upon them the superabundance of Christ through the timely word, and to correct them paternally if they stray from good conduct 42 . It must be acknowledged that God has often made use of this contact on our part with families to call many priestly and religious vocations. Indeed, not a few members of the Institute themselves considered the vocation or simply drew close to the Religious Family through these visits to families –families of the parish, of the Third Order, of the catechism children, of the school students, of benefactors, of the young people of the Oratory, etc. Visits to families remain an ever-current apostolate in our Institute that should not be neglected. “The task of Christian parents,” John Paul II goes on to say, “is very important and delicate, because they are called to prepare, cultivate and defend the vocations that God awakens in their family. They must, therefore, enrich themselves and their family with spiritual and moral values” 43 . But if there is no one to offer them these values, to teach them or remind them of them, how do we expect that tomorrow the vocations that may arise in that family will not be stifled? And do we still dare to be surprised and even complain if families let themselves be swept along by the consumerism, hedonism or secularism that disturb and hinder the realization of God’s plan, if we ourselves do not exhort them to the contrary? If we do not form parents in generosity toward God when He calls one of their children, and even to ask, for the good of the Church, the inestimable gift of a vocation for their children, are we amazed that vocations do not arise from our parishes, from our missions, from our jurisdictions? With great sorrow John Paul the Great wrote: “How can children, left morally orphaned, without educators or models, grow in esteem for human and Christian values? How can the seeds of vocation that the Holy Spirit continues to place in the hearts of the young generations develop in such a climate?” 44 . St. Manuel González already said it: “it is not that vocations are lacking, but that Christian homes are lacking, which are the ovens that give warmth, atmosphere and life to the vocations that God gives” 45 . We must become aware that the family is the privileged place for authentic vocational growth. It is for this reason that we say that “vocational ministry finds its first and natural setting in the family. Parents, in fact, must know how to welcome as a grace the gift that God gives them in calling one of their children to the priesthood or to consecrated life. Such a grace is asked for in prayer, and it is positively welcomed when children are educated to understand all the richness and joy of consecrating oneself to God” 46 . This requires forming families in the knowledge of this important aspect of their mission, which makes necessary a ministry directed toward spouses knowing themselves to be cooperators in the mission of the Church, creating a family climate of faith, charity and prayer that leads the children to be available and to accept God’s plan for the life of each one. In this sense it is important that we know the problems families face so as to be able to instruct spouses, through the proclamation of the Word of God, in their specific responsibilities, so that, well formed in the faith, they may know how to accompany their children, possibly called, to give themselves to God without reserve. In fact, it is through the apostolate we carry out with families that many children have found the support of their parents to be able to realize their vocation. “Parents who accept with feelings of gratitude and joy the call of one of their sons or daughters to the special consecration for the kingdom of heaven […] discover with amazement that, thanks to the sacred vocation of their children, the gift of their love has been multiplied beyond limited human dimensions” 47 . How many times has it happened to us that the parents of other religious men or women receive us as if we were their own children; how many times they themselves have told us that with their son’s entrance into the seminary or their daughter’s into the convent “the family has grown bigger” … and how beautiful that it should be so. From this also follows the important duty of gratitude and exquisite charity that we owe not only to our own parents but to the parents of the other religious, especially those who do not see their children so often, who are older, who are going through various hardships and who belong to our parishes, to our jurisdictions, etc. 3. Mother of the Lord and our Mother An example that somewhat illustrates the priestly attitude in vocational ministry is given to us by St. Luigi Orione. He himself puts it in writing in a letter he wrote from Tortona to a married couple who were friends and benefactors of his, on the vigil of the liturgical feast of the Assumption in 1927. Speaking of this Marian feast he writes with great tenderness and subtlety: “Just to think of Our Lady, of the most sweet Mother of God and our Mother, the spirit grows calm, the mind becomes serene; in speaking of Our Lady joy spreads, it is like a wave of most gentle spiritual peace, and in invoking her courage is restored and life returns to me, the highest life!” 48 . Then he adds with great insight: “ Happy the parents who offer their children into the hands of the Mother of the Lord! ” 49 . Then the saint continues, giving news concerning new vocations of sisters and future priests: “Tomorrow morning, at 5:30, I will sing Holy Mass in the humble little house of San Bernardino and then I will give the habit of Perpetual Adorers of Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament to four blind women who have already been with us for years. Then I leave for Villa Moffa near Bra, to give the religious habit tomorrow afternoon to some young men… Then, in a few months, Rag. Adriano Callegari will also enter. Out of him, the hand of God will make good cloth” 50 . Then with complete naturalness and courage he poses the question: “ And you, will you give me one of your children? I will not keep him for myself; I will give him at once to Our Lady, and he will be the consolation, the glory, the blessing of your family” 51 . Trusting devotion to Our Lady, the promotion of vocations and the courage to propose the vocation –things of which St. Luigi Orione gives us an example– should be corollaries of our vocational ministry. Tender and trusting devotion to the Blessed Virgin is truly a bulwark and an incentive in our priestly ministry, especially when it comes to awakening vocations. And so it has been from the beginning. Our Founder used to say: “I am convinced of it, and I attribute to the intercession of Our Lady of Luján the vocations that God gives us.” Regarding the role of Most Holy Mary in awakening, welcoming, accompanying and sustaining vocations of special consecration, we would like to point out a few elements. Our Institute, being “essentially missionary and Marian” 52 , and because of our particular way of living our consecration to Christ through consecration in slavery to Most Holy Mary, has in devotion to Our Lady a special quality that wins over many souls. Thus, many of our members became interested in the Institute precisely because of our deep Marian devotion; others Our Lady brought to us on the occasion of some Marian feast or a visit to some Marian shrine; others through taking part in the groups of consecration to Our Lady, etc. By this we mean that the Marian stamp with which we must live and carry out our apostolate is –undoubtedly– something we cannot fail to take into account when it comes to vocational ministry. Mary’s maternal presence must be present in awakening and guiding the vocations that God has destined for our Institute. In the apostolic exhortation Vita Consecrata we read: “All vocations are inspired by the contemplation of Christ crucified; in it they have their origin” 53 . Now, at the foot of the Cross stands the Mother. She is the one who shows souls the shortest and easiest way to give themselves to Christ. That is why in our Institute every vocational apostolate is also essentially Marian. Moreover, trusting recourse in prayer to the Mother of God, who keeps nothing for herself and busily cares for us, will always provide for the needs of the family and will send abundant vocations to our Institute in due time, as in fact she has already been doing, if we remain intimately united to her. Even more, if in our priestly ministry, after having guided a vocation toward God, we want it to persevere, St. Alphonsus Mary de Liguori recommends: “let the visit to the Most Blessed Sacrament and to Most Holy Mary be made without fail every day” 54 . If at the same time these vocations are faithfully Marian, Our Lady will make of them “great saints… because only this singular and miraculous Virgin can accomplish, in union with the Holy Spirit, excellent and extraordinary things” 55 Finally, if devotion to Our Lady is promoted “with grit” among Christian families, defined as the first seminary and irreplaceable reserve of vocations 56 , there will be fostered among the children the welcoming of the Lord’s call, their generous response and their joyful perseverance, and, on the part of the parents, a generous acceptance of God’s will. We are convinced that the ever-growing number of vocations that God has been pleased to grant us in these last years is a special proof of the maternal and ever-solicitous presence of Our Lady of Luján in the history of the Institute. And to her we must always cling. ***** Before concluding, a word of sincere appreciation to all the parents –living and deceased– of our religious for their generous self-giving and their unequaled contribution to the cause of Christ. St. John Paul II already said it: “the cultivation of the missionary vocation in their sons and daughters will be, on the part of parents, the best collaboration with the divine call” 57 . “Always be holily proud that the Lord has called someone of your family to follow Him closely. But continue each day to accompany him with prayer, so that his commitment of consecration may always be persevering and fervent” 58 . Know that your support through prayer, and the understanding, help and love you give us, are of incalculable value for our missionaries. Now, to finish, we would like to include an extract from the book Un sueño pastoral by St. Manuel González concerning the topic we have been addressing. The saint says: “Ordinarily, when this point [vocations] is spoken of, all eyes are fixed on the pastor, and the only point of agreement is how much he can foster vocations through his constant vigilance and zealous work of selecting, educating and preserving those who may become or already are seminarians. That is most certainly true. But it is no less true that the secret of the effectiveness of the pastor’s action must not be a secret belonging exclusively to him, but to all priests. Observe in general the qualities of those pastors who are skillful hunters and fosterers of vocations. You can sum them all up in this one: he is a priest conscious of his dignity. A worthy priest . There lies the secret. He may not be an eloquent orator, nor a brilliant writer, nor a first-rate intellect, nor a prodigy of extraordinary things. It does not matter. It will be enough for him to live and present himself to his people as befits a priest. Meek and affable in his dealings. Respectful toward those above without servility. Approachable to those below without vulgarity. Always found when sought in his church, at the bedside of his sick, in the children’s school or in his house, and never in the club, nor in taverns, nor in the gatherings of the powerful or of the idle. Generous without squandering. Studious and fond of learning without arrogance, as well as ready to teach without envious rivalry. Immovable as a rock before tyrants. Soft as wax toward one who commands him in the name of God or asks him for charity. A child with children. Sick with the sick. Weak with the weak. Joyful with those who laugh and sad with those who weep. And, in sum, made all things to all men , to win all for Jesus Christ. This is the secret, and if you will let me say it, the great secret of attracting men to the priesthood. Place anywhere a priest, whether a pastor or not, who conducts himself with this awareness of his dignity, and I pledge you my word –and neither God nor logic will let me fail– that not much time will pass before shoots have sprung up around that tree. A worthy clergy is the best and most effective populator of a seminary. A worldly clergy, forgetful of its dignity, is condemned by God, by logic and by the moral sense, to the most shameful sterility . Hard is the punishment, truly, but as inevitable and just as it is hard” 59 . To the Pure and Clean Conception of Luján our most humble gratitude for each and every one of the vocations she has been pleased to send to the Institute. May she, Virgin Mother of the Incarnate Word, help us “to be able to discover and guide so many vocations that we could fill all the good seminaries and novitiates of the whole world” 60 ; may the young people who come into contact with us, drawn by the beauty and gentleness of this Most Holy Mother, be docile to the call of Christ; and may parents, contemplating and imitating the assiduous prayer of the Holy Family, be sure guides for their children toward spiritual and eternal goods. Grant us, Holy Virgin of Luján, Mother of vocations 61 , to be able to see in our days too the wonders of the mysterious action of the Holy Spirit, who calls multitudes of souls to make them witnesses of the beatitudes. Virgin of Luján, you are now and always all our hope. The grace of combat

Without enemies 1 You say you have no enemies? What a pity, my friend! That is a poor thing to boast of. Whoever has joined in the struggle of duty, which the valiant endure, is bound to have made enemies! If you have none at all, the work you have done is slight. You have struck no traitor from behind, you have snatched the cup from no perjured lips, you have never changed evil into good, you have been a coward in the struggle! It is said that Margaret Thatcher kept this poem on her desk. This detail of the former British prime minister’s life recently came to light when, in a contemporary film series, she recites this poem to Queen Elizabeth II after the latter expressed her concern that the government was making enemies for itself with the reforms it was pushing forward. Beyond the media popularity the poem enjoys today because of internet television, and beyond the prime minister who recited it, the verses express a truth, namely the fact that the mediocre, preferring to ride the waves of popularity and to spare themselves every kind of inconvenience, choose to negotiate with the spirit of the world and its henchmen. The valiant, on the other hand, that is, those who have dirtied their hands in the struggle of just duty, are the ones who reap enemies: “If you have none at all, the work you have done is slight.” That is why being accepted just like that, without any opposition, is often a sign of mediocrity (or of cowardice, in the poet’s language), whereas being persecuted is a compliment. It is in this sense that the Venerable Archbishop Fulton Sheen said that our “persecutors pay us the beautiful tribute of hostility; they pay us the fine compliment of opposition” 2 . It is the mystery of persecution. A mystery which, when that persecution is unjust or is for Christ, involves one of the Gospel beatitudes. 1. Blessed are those persecuted for the sake of justice That is why one day the adorable lips of our Lord pronounced these profound words: Blessed are those who are persecuted for the sake of justice, for theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven 3 . “For Matthew, for his readers and hearers, the expression those persecuted for the sake of justice had a prophetic meaning. For them it was an advance allusion the Lord had made to the situation of the Church in which they were living. It had become a persecuted Church, persecuted for the sake of justice . In the language of the Old Testament, ‘ justice ’ expresses fidelity to the Torah , fidelity to the word of God, as the prophets had always demanded. It is a matter of persevering on the straight path indicated by God, whose core is formed by the Ten Commandments. In the New Testament, the concept equivalent to that of justice in the Old Testament is that of faith : the believer is the ‘ just man ,’ the one who follows the ways of God 4 . For faith is walking with Christ, in whom the whole Law is fulfilled; it unites us to the justice of Christ himself” 5 . These persecuted ones of whom Christ speaks, explains Pope Benedict XVI, “are those who live by the justice of God, by faith. Since man’s aspiration always tends to emancipate itself from the will of God and to follow only itself, faith will always appear as something that stands opposed to the ‘world’ –to the dominant powers of each moment– and that is why there will be persecution for the sake of justice in every period of history . […] In her lack of power and in her suffering, the Church is aware that she finds herself where the Kingdom of God is arriving” 6 . That is why we who follow Christ will never be popular nor, so to speak, comfortable, since nonconformity with evil is a form of resistance that the world cannot bear, because the spirit of the world demands collaborationism 7 ; it asks you to work hand in hand with it, in a sort of “single way of thinking.” And this happens even to religious and churchmen when they become worldly, for these, rather than suffering persecution, are normally the ones who carry it out. It happened to Jesus! Let us suppose for a moment that our Religious Family no longer had any external difficulty, any persecution. That would certainly be very pleasant, but it could at the same time be a sign that our salt has lost its savor and our flame has gone out. For this reason, as our Proper Law very well says, “the greatest grace that God can grant to our tiny Religious Family [is] that of persecution” 8 . We must realize that “the world, which so dislikes zeal for the kingdom of God, hated Christ first. It was his zeal that led Him to the Cross. The world loves the indifferent, the mediocre, the ordinary, the good-natured, but it hates two kinds of people: those who are truly good and those who are truly bad. […] Some go to the cross because they are very good in contrast with the majority or with the system; others go to the cross because they are very bad. And since the world hates in the same way in which it hated Christ, it hates the one who is zealous for the cause of Christ because he reproaches the world for its mediocrity; but it also hates the wicked, as it hated the thieves crucified on either side of Christ, because they were a nuisance to its self-complacency. Do you see? The good go to death because they are good; the wicked go to death because they are wicked; the mediocre survive . The mediocre are those who “settle in,” who try to occupy posts for which they are not fit, who covet and abuse power and unscrupulously wield it against those who want to do things well. In the words of our Lord: The world cannot hate you; but Me it hates, because I testify against it that its works are evil 9 . And if this was true of our Lord, it must also be true of us. The servant is not greater than his Master ” 10 . That is why those who slander us or attack us unjustly do nothing but confess that they take our purpose seriously and that –if evil wants to triumph– they must eliminate the cause we defend. The same thing happened to Jesus with his worldly contemporaries; here lies the theological foundation of persecution: If the world hates you, you know that it hated Me before you. If you were of the world, the world would love its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you. Remember the word that I said to you: ‘ A servant is not greater than his master’… But all this they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know the One who sent Me. If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin 11 . That is why persecution is the law of the Church –as Fr. Castellani rightly pointed out–; it is the burden we must carry, and today we must look it in the face. Throughout history persecution of the good has always been present; not that all Christians have been persecuted, certainly. Not, for example, Christians in name only, who not only do not suffer but at times even serve the ungodly as useful idiots. For as St. Paul said: all who want to live piously in Christ Jesus will be persecuted 12 . He did not say “all the baptized”; he said: all who want to live piously 13 . Just by way of illustration, let us mention the martyrdom of the Apostles, who were martyred in different parts of the world, followed by the ten bloody persecutions in Rome, in which thousands of Christians of every condition were put to death, almost always with refined and terrible tortures. Also the countless persecutions that still today assail the good. To the point that at times it seems that “Jesus here on earth grants us as Christians only one right: the right to persecution and to the curses of men” 14 . But internal persecution also exists. To go no further, as we were saying, it is the one Christ himself suffered at the hands of Judas. That is why He warned us: And a man’s enemies will be those of his own household 15 , a stealthy and treacherous persecution of which St. Paul himself complained when he said that he went through dangers among false brethren 16 . And very probably that is the worst kind of persecution, because it is full of hypocrisy and not infrequently of cruelty. St. Peter Julian Eymard expressed it thus: “There is above all one kind of pain that makes one suffer, and that is the persecutions and slanders of [supposedly] devout persons. Nothing wounds so deeply, because their [supposed] virtue gives grounds for believing that they must be right and that it is God himself who is angry. He permits that at times the [apparently] best do not look kindly on one and persecute him , despite his innocence, in order to purify him better ” 17 . And, therefore, it is nonetheless a grace. If in our eagerness to remain faithful to the will of God expressed in our Constitutions 18 unfounded attacks come upon us, blessed be God! Because “this Cross prepares for us an eternal weight of incalculable glory ” 19 . Sometimes we complain because our persecutors or “false brethren” harass us with false accusations, in the same way that they accused Christ, calling Him a glutton and a drunkard 20 . Sometimes we protest because some people question everything we do, not because they want an answer, but precisely because they do not want one; but careful! not without first telling us that they want to hear our opinion, that they are interested in hearing our view. In the face of all these machinations, deep down we must know how to say: blessed be God! If we did not pray, if we had a lax formation, if we had a light spirituality instead of a serious (though not “rigid”) spirituality, if we had no vocations, if we did not defend the charism of the Institute tooth and nail, if we were subservient, they would never harass us. They would leave us completely in peace. In any case, one may validly ask: why so much opposition? To which the Venerable Fulton Sheen answers: “They ridicule you and harass you because you have something they do not have, and because your faith is a reproach to their wickedness. In the depths of their souls they would like to have your peace; they would like to have your certainty instead of their doubts; your joy instead of their fears, your trust in God instead of their confusion. They envy you and what you have, but they want all of that at their price, not at Christ’s price. In a word, they want your faith, but without the Cross” 21 . To the point that without meaning to they seem to fulfill the psalm that says: they repay me evil for good because I strive for what is good 22 . “In former times a person’s character was known by the people who loved him; nowadays character is better known by those who hate him” 23 , Fulton Sheen affirmed. Thus, having enemies in some way declares to the world that the one persecuted for the sake of justice possesses a princely spirit , for such men “are those who know at every instant the things for which one must die” 24 , “they do not ask for freedom but for hierarchy” 25 and “they feel honor as they feel life” 26 . And since all these values clash with the spirit of the world, the world seeks to eliminate them; that is why they seek to divide and scatter us. Now, we would not be realistic if we said that the attacks cause us no grief. But we must be convinced in faith that God draws good out of evil and therefore that the most adverse events contribute to our good. They will serve, with God’s favor, for personal growth and the growth of the Institute, and as badges of the good fight. Let us hear the advice that St. Peter Julian Eymard gave to some religious sisters: “God permits the saints to be slandered, despised and persecuted. And since the Lord was too, it is an honor for you to be so” 27 . Thus, for example, St. John of the Cross was envied by Diego Evangelista, who had once felt humiliated by a correction from the saint. It was to a great extent this resentful friar who set in motion the last great persecution suffered by the Mystic of Fontiveros. St. Mary Mackillop was excommunicated by the bishop after being accused of insubordination; and so many, many, many other examples we could cite. Fulton Sheen himself, who had millions of followers on television, who had converted thousands of souls, under whose leadership the office of Propaganda Fide raised great sums for the missions, was falsely accused of embezzling funds. Another example: Blessed Marie Anne Blondin, the foundress and superior general of the Sisters of St. Anne, was greatly persecuted by the chaplain assigned to the community, who, exercising dictatorial control over it, had elections called for a new superior, not without first warning Marie Anne not to accept any position of authority even if she were elected by the sisters. She spent the rest of her days doing domestic work; she did not even appear on the lists of the sisters. And St. Joseph Calasanz. And St. Josemaría Escrivá de Balaguer. And St. Pio of Pietrelcina… The list is endless. That was the road the saints followed, strewn with stones and intricate accusations, in constant conflict with their enemies, who breathed cruelty upon them; but all of this served them to purify their faith and unite themselves more to God. With that attitude of noble gallantry we must not only accept but face the tribulations that God is pleased to send us, or at least permits. Disloyal gossip, slander, false judgments: all are born, in one way or another, of envy. In this sense, the venerable American archbishop points out: “every word born of envy is based on a false judgment about our own moral superiority. Sitting in judgment makes us feel as though we are above those being judged and that we are more just and more innocent than they” 28 . That is why accusing others is a way of saying “I am not like them,” or like saying “they have robbed me of what is mine.” In this way “envy becomes a total denial of justice and of love. And so a cynicism develops in individuals that destroys all moral values, because to bring others to ruin (stripping them of all good reputation, for example) is ultimately to bring oneself to ruin” 29 . There are churchmen who envy someone for having many vocations, and so they speak ill, they criticize… And one may well ask whether this is not precisely what they lack. In other words: those who speak ill of others with slander often, in the end, speak ill of themselves. When envy takes root in a group of people it produces such a deception and such a lie that it makes the group extend a welcoming hand to anyone who dissents, for example from a religious congregation –regardless of his record, as long as he joins the attack– until he becomes powerful enough and, therefore, bothersome; then they expel him because he no longer serves their cause. We have seen it many times! Fulton Sheen therefore advises that “since envy is so rampant in today’s world, it is extremely good advice not to believe 99% of the twisted assertions we hear about others. Think how much the good thief had to discount from what the others were saying in order to arrive at the truth. He had to distrust the judgment of four envious judges, set aside the mockery of the elders and scribes of the temple, turn a deaf ear to the blasphemous slanders of the curious onlookers, and dismiss the envious mockery of the bad thief, who was willing to lose his soul in exchange for keeping his nimble fingers to commit more thefts. Realize that it is very likely that there is a bit of jealousy, a bit of envy behind every sharp comment and every stinging whisper we hear our neighbor say. And for those who are unjustly attacked, let it be a consolation to know that it is physically impossible for someone to get ahead of us if he is always behind us kicking us ” 30 . 2. Christ had enemies Christ had enemies. The Sadducees and the Pharisees, Judas and the Sanhedrin, Rome and the priests of the Temple, Pilate and Herod –all these, who were in a certain enmity among themselves– united in great hostility to confront Christ. Let us speak of the Pharisees. Fr. Castellani says that the whole biography of Jesus as man can be summed up in this formula: “ He was the Messiah and He fought against the Pharisees ” 31 . Without the Pharisees the story of Christ would not be the same, just as the history of the Church would not be the same. Pharisaism is religious pride: it is the subtlest and most dangerous corruption of the greatest truth, the truth that religious values come first. But the moment we claim them for ourselves, we lose them; the moment we make our own what is God’s, it ceases to belong to anyone, if it does not become the property of the devil. The Pharisee is the man of practice and of will. It is true that the Pharisee is not like other men; only he is not better, as he believes, but worse. Christ called them hypocrites 32 , for they are those who say, but do not do 33 . We could say with St. Paul that the Pharisees, enemies of Jesus, are those who, boasting of being wise, became fools 34 . Hypocrite, in itself, means being an actor; but whoever continually behaves as an actor runs the risk of becoming a fraud, for concern with appearances goes hand in hand with unconcern for what one really is. That attitude ends up leading to blindness and absurdity . They deceive others, beginning by deceiving themselves. And in their blindness they can even go so far as to speak out against and deplore Pharisaism itself, deceiving still more those who lend them an ear. According to Fr. Castellani, Pharisaism “is a radically irreligious, and even antireligious, attitude that appears religious” 35 . Because hypocrites live on appearances, they know how to put on a holy-card face, they make themselves look just 36 , they make themselves up as good 37 , they repeat to you ad nauseam that they want to help you, they present themselves with a ‘savior’ attitude and, as if they were masters of all contingencies, they assure you a future full of sunshine if you agree with them and join them… only, mind you, until they come out ‘apparently’ victorious, because when you are no longer useful to them they discard you. To them apply the words of the psalm that says they are workers of iniquity, who speak peace to their neighbor and plot evil in their heart 38 . To achieve his aim the Pharisee uses the hypocrite’s technique 39 : he flatters you, makes you believe he loves you, deceives you with his ‘pious ways’ of proceeding, but deep down acts with bad intention, since he hides a secret ambition. Several centuries ago St. John of the Cross already noted this way of proceeding when he said: “The Calced are touched by the vice of ambition, and so everything they do they color and tint with goodness, so that they are incorrigible…”, about which Fr. Castellani comments: “Ambition in religious, which at times becomes for them a stronger passion than lust in lay people, is one of the finest parts of Pharisaism: To love the first places … to love the vain honor that men give ” 40 . It becomes for them “a way of life” 41 . That is why Pharisaism is a hundred times worse than any other vice. For Pharisaism is a spiritual vice , that is, it is diabolical, since corruptions of the spirit are worse than corruptions of the flesh. Thus Christ said to St. Catherine of Siena: “That is why I assure you that if all the other sins they have committed were placed on one side and this one alone on the other, this one would weigh more than the others” 42 . For Pharisaism is like a compendium of all the spiritual vices: avarice, ambition, vainglory, pride, obstinacy, hardness of heart, cruelty, which has come to empty out diabolically from within the three theological virtues, thus constituting the sin against the Holy Spirit. […] But the flower of Pharisaism is cruelty: stealthy, cautious, slow, prudent and subterranean cruelty, putting to death while believing one is offering service to God . Everything is done in silence, in the dark, by means of cover-ups and complicated schemes, behind a curtain of feigned goodness and evangelical spirit. But “hypocrisy destroys, hypocrisy kills; it kills persons, it even tears out a person’s personality and soul. It kills communities. When there are hypocrites [‘false brethren’] in a community there is a great danger there, there is a very ugly danger” 43 . It can even go so far as to decide on “the illegal, cruel and iniquitous death of a man,” Fr. Castellani points out, which “is resolved in meetings where the Law is invoked with the texts in hand, in grave religious conclaves, dialogues, phrases in which almost nothing speaks but Sacred Scripture and the most sacred words that exist on earth are used. Truly I tell you that, if a dead man raised to life came to testify, you would not believe him 44 ” 45 . And since for the Pharisee anything goes, “all means are good as long as they are stealthy: slander, bribery, fraud, distortion, false testimony, threats” 46 , dropping into their speeches the names of great personalities, as one who boasts of the backing he receives from them and of the impunity they believe they enjoy. “Caiaphas killed Christ with a summary of the prophecy of Isaiah and with the dogma of the Redemption. Is it not expedient that one man should die for the welfare of a whole people ? 47 . If we look closely at the case of Christ, for example, He was judged a heretic for breaking the Sabbath, and therefore his fate was sealed. Afterward there would come in succession, as anger and envy at his successes grew, the labels of madman, magician, possessed by the devil, and then blasphemer, seditious, and finally conspirator against Caesar. As we said above: anything goes. It is an accusation that keeps growing as time passes, without the accused being asked for a defense or explanations; on the contrary, every defense he gives becomes a new charge. The process is secret. When the judges intervene in public, it is no longer an accusation but a sentence. They make slanderous assertions and try to catch the accused in a slip in order to make the slander stick 48 . That is why the Pharisees secretly rejoice in the slow fermentation of slander among the people. That was the drama of Christ. Thus the Savior died. All his meekness, all his most adorable sweetness, his benefits, his tears, his Precious Blood, his warnings, his prophetic threats were to shatter against the hardness of heart of the Pharisees. That continues to be the drama of his Church. Christ himself complained to St. Catherine of Siena about the wounds that this movement of internal persecution in the Church caused his Mystical Body: “I told you that they wounded Me, and it is the truth. Inwardly they persecute Me as they can. Not that I in Myself can receive any injury or be wounded by them, but they act like a stone which, when thrown, is not received but turns back against the one who throws it. Thus those wounded by their offenses, those who cast forth the pestilence, cannot harm Me; rather the poisoned arrow of guilt turns back against them. It deprives them of grace in this life, as they lose the fruit of the blood, and at the last moment, if they do not amend with holy confession and contrition of heart, they come to eternal damnation, separated from Me and bound to the devil. […] By this bond, the persecutors of the blood find themselves united with others, and, as members bound to the devil, they have taken up the office of devils. […] This bond is knotted with pride and one’s own reputation , with servile fear, for they lose grace out of fear of losing their positions . These bonds bear the seal of darkness, because they know into how many evils and miseries they have fallen and make others fall. […] O dearest daughter! Grieve infinitely to see such blindness and misery in those who, like you, have been washed in the blood and were nourished and grew up on that blood at the breasts of holy Church. Now, like rebels, out of fear and under the pretext of correcting the vices of my ministers – whom I have forbidden anyone to touch – they have turned away from these breasts. […] The worst of it is that, under the cloak of the defects of my ministers, they want to shelter and cover up their own , and they do not consider that there is no cloak that can keep Me from seeing them. They can hide from the eyes of creatures, but not from Me, from whom neither present things nor anything else is hidden. One of the reasons why the wretched men of the world do not amend is that in reality they do not believe with a living faith that I see them; for if they truly believed that I see their vices and that every vice is punished, just as every good work is rewarded, they would not do so much evil, but would correct themselves of what they have done and humbly implore my mercy. […] No persecution must be carried out on account of any sin seen in the ministers of the blood ” 49 . It is clear that Pharisaism is not a thing of the past; we find it also in our own days, because it is a specific vice and a grave disease of the true religion 50 . “The chair of Moses is still the chair of Moses. We must do what they say without doing what they do; and say a number of things that they keep silent about, which must be said, and which will make them leap like vipers: bear witness to the truth ” 51 . “If over the course of the centuries an enormous mass of sufferings, and even of blood, had not been rendered by other christs in resisting the Pharisee, the Church would not exist today. Pharisaism is the greatest evil that exists on earth” 52 . And today, far more than yesterday, “we need someone to remind these modern Pilates that there is another Power up above” 53 . 3. What is to be done? We do not intend here to give a recipe for a solution. But one thing is evidently clear: we must not be Pharisees. Lest it happen to us as it did to those who were on Calvary, but on the wrong side. They devoted a great part of their time and energy to the study and observance of the Law and, nevertheless, they missed the Messiah. We must be persons of integrity, free, not subservient 54 , and conduct ourselves through this life, in whatever circumstances Providence disposes, always with a princely spirit 55 . These are times of intense struggle; that is why we must have our priorities in order and remain loyal even if we are wounded in battle. These are magnificent times to be faithful to the Incarnate Word, to his Church and to the Institute in which we have consecrated our life both to the Lord and to the Church, which is to say the same thing. It must be noted that if ever there was an innocent person who had the right to protest against an injustice, it was our Lord. And yet He forgave. He ignored the insults to his Person. Did not the Incarnate Word preach meekness? Must we not practice it? Certainly, to see ourselves attacked, when it is unjust, grieves us. Certainly, to recognize our enemies in those very people who should be our friends causes pain and brings a great feeling of abandonment. Of course, to see some of the ‘brothers’ secretly ally themselves to fight against their own Family is unpleasant, fills one with helplessness, and wounds deeply. But at the same time, the lesson is clear: pain does not make us better 56 ; it makes us fit to bear even worse things. Who has not experienced in moments of intense suffering the feeling that we cannot hold out one more minute? But that minute passes and we realize that we are touching new layers of endurance. Nevertheless, pain never becomes pleasant. But we must keep going forward, with our gaze fixed on heaven, where the Reward with a capital R awaits us. Everything depends on whether we unite our pain to Him who, for the joy set before Him, endured the Cross, disregarding its shame 57 . And ultimately we must rejoice if they persecute us. Because if our faith must be “perfected by persecutions” 58 , these will only serve to wound our pride, but not our mettle; they will cauterize our arrogance, but will not stain our soul, since the very insult on the part of the world is the consecration of our goodness 59 . We know that praying for those who nail us to the Cross is not of this world. But that is precisely the point: our faith is not worldly; our faith turns the values of the world completely upside down. We know that loving our enemies is not according to “common sense,” because loving our enemies would mean hating ourselves (according to what the world thinks); but that is the intent of Christianity. Very often our executioners are our allies; those who crucify us are our greatest benefactors. Thus St. Thomas More wrote in the margin of his breviary when he was imprisoned in the Tower of London: “Grant me the grace, good Lord… to fix my mind firmly on You and not to weigh the words that come out of the mouths of men; to be content to be alone… to be glad in tribulations… to consider that my enemies are my best friends , because Joseph’s brothers could not have benefited him as much by their love and goodwill as they did by their malice and hatred” 60 . It is the attitude of thoroughgoing Christians of all times, who with holy pride died at the hands of their enemies for the glory of God and of his Church. Let us think, for example, of the martyr Tomás de la Mora, killed on August 15, 1927 in the city of Colima, Mexico, a victim of the persecution unleashed by President Plutarco Calles. Tomás, who had been a seminarian, wrote a year earlier: “ We must no longer ask God to stop the persecution, but that in every Catholic there may be a hero as in the times of Nero .” After being arrested for the sole crime of being a Christian, and having learned his sentence, he asked that it be carried out immediately: “The delay bothers me,” he said. On seeing the tree where Benito Juárez had once rested 61 , he asked the head of the escort to be hanged there: “This,” he said, “is a place of ignominy; hang me here so that this place of curse may be changed into a blessing.” With a cry of “Viva Cristo Rey!” he was hoisted up at midnight on a Saturday. He was only 18 years old. To have this fortitude and strength of soul we must at the same time pray, and pray much, asking to remain faithful, keeping our conscience intact and persevering in the holy vocation God has granted us. And pray also for our Institute, as St. Peter Julian, for example, prayed for the Blessed Sacrament Fathers: “Keep away from your Eucharistic family false, deceitful and impure vocations; never allow this poor and humble family to fall into the hands of a proud man, an ambitious man, or any hard and wrathful man. Do not hand over to unclean and perverse beasts the souls that confess You and hope in You. Preserve your Eucharistic family from all scandal, keep it virgin of every vice, free from all worldly servitude, a stranger to the world, so that it may place all its joy in serving You holily and freely, in peace and tranquility” 62 . And when the struggle grows even fiercer we can put into practice the advice St. John of Ávila gave to a lady: “It is not fitting, madam, to lose heart because of the greatness of the enemies, nor because of their cunning, nor because of the torments they inflict; for you will be all the more acceptable to your Lord the more persevering you are in greater torments for Him. We must stay on the Cross until we give up our spirit to the Father; and while alive we must not come down from it, however much scholars and Pharisees tell us to come down and that profit will follow from coming down , as they said to the Lord 63 . The Cross was taken up for Him, and He has helped you carry it until now; and if at times it is so heavy that it makes you fall to your knees, so it did to our Lord too; and He will not be surprised that our weakness should kneel, since his great strength knelt; which He willed to do so that the weak might not lose heart when, under the weight of their labors, it sometimes seems to them that, being unable to bear so much, they are bogged down in sadness and as if with some lack of confidence, and without the joy in suffering that they had at other times. The Lord well knows our clay, well knows our stain, for we carry it written on our forehead before Him; He is not surprised at our weaknesses, and He loves our humble confession of our fault more than our conceit about our righteousness 64 . Moreover, we must “pray much for the Church of Jesus Christ, so tried and so persecuted, that God may defend her from her enemies, who at the same time are her own children , and that He may touch their hearts, convert them and lead them, humble and penitent, to the foot of the throne of mercy and justice” 65 . And when the hours grow dark and the file of abandonment makes itself felt even more strongly, let us make room for confidence. Every act of confidence implies that one cannot see. If we saw, if we had certainty, there would be no room for confidence. Now, to trust in God means to cling to the truth that his designs are good and holy, not because we see it clearly, but in spite of all appearances to the contrary 66 . It is the practice of the theological virtue of hope, which looks to the omnipotence, to the infinite goodness of God, to his providence! This attitude of soul is fundamental in Christian life and is part of that non-negotiable element attached to the charism which must characterize us and which we call ‘having a providential view of life.’ All tribulations, down to their smallest details, are woven into the fabric of that mantle of holiness which God wishes to grant to us who believe in Him. Let us be “ready to sacrifice everything without reserve, persuaded that nothing is so advantageous as to abandon oneself into the hands of God in all that He is pleased to ordain” 67 . And, finally, let us give thanks to God, who has found us worthy to suffer something for his Kingdom. In this month in which we celebrate the Solemnity of the Sacred Heart of Jesus, let us nestle in our soul the thought that “the Heart of Jesus guards us… to defend us from our enemies, like a mother who, to save her child from a danger, clasps him to her heart, so that the child cannot be wounded without the mother also being struck” 68 . May the Virgin Mother shelter us all, united, under her mantle and lead us to a safe harbor. She is our hope, because she is the Mother of the One who is Hope.
