To the pastors of the IVE

“The Institute of the Incarnate Word will undertake the apostolates most conducive to the inculturation of the Gospel,” we read in no. 169 of the Constitutions . Therefore, “in response to the requests of bishops, the direction of parishes may be accepted, preferably in mission areas or areas of greater need” 1 . Thus today the Institute serves some 110 parishes throughout the world, some of them shrines 2 , others cathedrals 3 , some in the midst of great cities such as New York or Hong Kong, others in more rural areas such as those in Scotland or Bolivia, some located in residential areas such as the parish in Australia, others in the middle of the jungle, such as the parish the Institute serves in Wagina (Solomon Islands). This means that the immense majority of the more than 400 priests of the Institute are dedicated –in one way or another– to parish ministry, whether as pastors, parochial vicars, members of the community attached to a parish, or occasionally collaborating with the preaching of triduums, novenas, patronal feasts, confessions, etc., that take place in some parish. Wishing, then, to prolong the redemptive work of Christ himself 4 , according to our proper charism of inculturating the Gospel in the diversity of all cultures 5 , the Institute gives the parish apostolate “great importance” 6 and “preference” 7 –since it is one of the principal “places” where the Institute can exercise its specific charism 8 – and we consider it a privileged setting for the encounter with the message of Christ 9 . That is why we would like to take this opportunity to highlight the characteristics that, according to our proper charism, must shine forth both in the priest dedicated to parish ministry and in the IVE parish itself, if we wish to contribute effectively “to enriching the universal Church” 10 . Needless to say, the reading of the Directory of Parishes is highly recommended in this matter; though very brief, it sheds much light on the practice of parish ministry. Before beginning to address these two points, and by way of introduction, we would like to define what we understand by a parish. “The word ‘parish’ comes from the Greek para (= near) and oikos (= house), meaning a group of houses or also a group of neighboring inhabitants. Etymologically it means neighborhood, in which Jesus Christ is the principal Neighbor. Others derive the word ‘parish’ from the Greek parojeo (= to transport) or from the Greek parechō (= to supply). Both fit very well with the office of the pastor, who dwells in the midst of his parishioners to supply them with sound doctrine, the sacraments, etc. In fact, three things are understood when speaking of a parish 11 : 1st The body of the faithful who are under the jurisdiction of the pastor. 2nd The church where he exercises his functions. 3rd The portion of the territory of the diocese” 12 . St. John Paul II once affirmed that “it could be said that the parish is a family of families , since the life of the parish is intimately bound up both with the vigor and with the weakness, or with the needs, of the families that make it up” 13 . And all those families that make up a given Catholic parish are gathered together precisely by their faith in Jesus Christ. In the book of the Acts of the Apostles we read the following about the life of the first Christians: They devoted themselves assiduously to the teaching of the apostles, to communion, to the breaking of bread and to the prayers 14 . Therefore, instruction in the faith of the Apostles, the building up of a living community, the celebration of the Eucharist and the other sacraments, and the life of prayer constitute the essential elements of the life of every parish 15 . In this sense, every parish is founded on a theological reality, and that theological reality is Jesus in the Eucharist. “Without Eucharistic worship as its beating heart, the parish becomes sterile” 16 . We therefore consider it fitting to make this clarification explicit: “the parish is not principally the building, nor the institutions, nor the canonical aspect, nor the territory, nor charitable works, nor paperwork. Principally it is the theological reality of being a Eucharistic community . It will also be, but secondarily , the church building, the institutions, the canonical aspect, the territory, help for the poor, and the minimal and indispensable procedures proper to an organized society” 17 . 1. The IVE pastor Naturally, when a bishop entrusts a parish to the Institute, he does not entrust it to a religious considered individually but to the Institute as such. Therefore, it is a matter of the presence of the Institute in a diocese and not of religious considered individually 18 . So we say that when a parish is entrusted to the Institute, “in a certain sense it becomes a religious parish [of the IVE], inasmuch as in such a parish the Institute expresses its proper charism and proper apostolate, even while subject to the bishop” 19 . Thus, an IVE pastor must shape the parish according to the charism and spirituality of the Institute 20 . For this it is imperative that the pastor be steeped in the charism of the Institute and show great fidelity to it, including the sound traditions that form part of the Institute’s patrimony 21 . Our Proper Law abounds in details about community life and the government of the community of religious in a parish for its harmonious functioning, but we will not deal with that now. We refer the reader to the Directory of Parishes , 8-40. We likewise leave aside consideration of those human aptitudes that so greatly facilitate pastoral work, such as organizational ability, friendliness and good humor, facility for languages, gifts as an educator and catechist, foresight and personal initiative. Here, rather, we want to speak of the characteristic virtues that should stand out in the conduct of a priest especially dedicated to parish ministry. ▪ Charity Like every priest, whoever holds the office of pastor is called to reflect the fatherhood of God in daily life. Not for nothing is the name most frequently given us by the sensus fidelium precisely that of father, and parish ministry offers the right setting to exercise spiritual fatherhood with great fruit through the concrete exercise of charity. That is why it is not surprising that the first virtue that must stand out in an IVE pastor is charity, since “charity is indispensable for evangelizing the culture” 22 . For, in imitation of the Incarnate Word who came not to be served but to serve 23 , a pastor is expected to be the first to serve others, sharing with the souls entrusted to him their problems and difficulties. It is interesting to note that our Proper Law specifically states how this charity is to be manifested according to the kind of sheep he is given to shepherd. Thus, for example, it says that he must lavish “charity on the sick , especially the dying, solicitously strengthening them with the administration of the sacraments and commending their soul to God” 24 ; that an IVE pastor “will always treat with particular diligence the poor , the afflicted, those who are alone, emigrants or those who suffer special difficulties” 25 ; that “he must go to the utmost in charity and kindness ” 26 with those weak in faith , imitating Christ: He will not quarrel nor cry out… the bruised reed he will not break and the smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory 27 . He must be affable with all who come to his parish 28 , with those who enter “the parish office, with each family that receives his visit” 29 , etc. Given that the great majority of our parishes are in difficult places (many in places where no one wants to go), where poverty, whether material or spiritual, is the normal setting in which our parishioners’ lives unfold, it seems good to us to recall that “we should be deeply ashamed if ever, straying from the path of concrete charity toward the poor, we stopped attending to them in order to devote our attention only to those sick people, students, etc., who can repay us materially” 30 . We must beware of the temptation to think that “all the poor who knock at your door are freeloaders” 31 . This virtue, which should stand out in priests dedicated to parish ministry, makes evident the need for “the whole formation of candidates for the priesthood to be directed toward preparing them in a specific way to communicate the charity of Christ, the Good Shepherd” 32 . ▪ Patience One of the virtues most necessary for parish ministry is certainly patience. That is why our Proper Law warns: “if we do not have patience with the parishioners, then nothing will hold the sheep back and they will go off after false shepherds, because the shepherds God had given them fed themselves” 33 . And it adds: “in contrast to a ministry of high-handedness, we prefer that of Jesus Christ” 34 . This is the patience asked of an IVE pastor in dealing, for example, with those who doubt in the faith, so as to “answer with patience and clarity the objections they raise” 35 , or with those weak in faith, since “more than once this kind of faithful end up drifting away from the Church of Christ not only because of their weakened faith but above all because of the impatience of the shepherd” 36 . St. Manuel González, speaking of the circumstances in which the office of pastor is exercised today, said: “It is true that they could not be worse” 37 . And in one stroke he illustrates some of those situations that not infrequently test the priest’s patience: “The priest who, as the fruit of a life of sacrifices and bitterness, reaps a church almost always empty; five percent, perhaps, of the faithful fulfilling the Easter and Sunday precept; most of the sick dying impenitent or, at most, with the conditional holy oil; the very men he has favored with jobs, favors or alms turning their faces away so as not to greet him; even those who frequent the church bored, as like as not; and, to cap and crown it all, his works, the best ones, those done with the best intention, misinterpreted or slandered. The priest, I repeat, who sees all this truly needs all the heroism of a martyr to rise each day with a smiling face, a hopeful heart and a spirit tranquil enough to go on plowing his furrow without losing heart and without falling” 38 . We must not insist on deceiving ourselves; we must admit that the priest, as a man, is made of the same clay as the children of Adam. And long and sad experience shows that it is a rather fragile and brittle clay. We know, because sacred theology teaches it, that without a most special privilege of grace no one can be exempt from each and every venial sin, and Sacred Scripture says that the just man falls seven times a day. Nevertheless, we can work to modify our character and diminish the number of our faults, and even rid them of their habitual character. But without ever forgetting that, to know what a man is capable of, one must always reckon with the fact that he has a character that some will like and others will not, and faults that will sometimes make him fall short and at other times overshoot 39 . That is why St. John Paul II, addressing a group of priests in the city of Prato, emphasized that, if “patience in apostolic work has always been necessary, [it is] all the more so in our times. Patience –the Holy Father clarified– does not mean acquiescence to error, passive tolerance, timid and inert coexistence, giving in to equivocation and ambiguity. Patience means acceptance of the designs of Providence, which respects the times and ways of maturation of each individual and of peoples. To have patience means to eliminate irritations, exasperations, annoyances and also frustrations, demoralization, weariness, in order to commit oneself to the fulfillment of one’s own mission with tireless dedication , in humility and in silence, always with consistency and promptness” 40 . ▪ Zeal Our Proper Law says it clearly: “the minister of God… will have a tireless zeal for souls, a spirit of sacrifice” 41 . In a well-known sermon St. Alphonsus Mary de Liguori declares that it is “the obligation of all priests to have zeal for souls.” It is said: “There are many priests and there are few; many in name, but few in their works,” and St. Alphonsus adds: “The world is full of priests, but those who strive to be true priests are few, that is, to fulfill the office and dignity of the priest, which is to save souls” 42 . Let it be well understood that the great charism of religious and priestly life is generous love for Christ and for the members of his Body. That love is expressed in service and consummated in sacrifice. Therefore, the readiness for self-giving will be proportional to love, and when love is perfect, the sacrifice is complete 43 . Hence what is proper to us is to be ready to stake our lives so that others may have life and hope 44 , and to try with “healthy creativity” 45 –and without losing heart– to create opportunities to reach all the souls entrusted to us in our priestly ministry. No excuses that ‘one is alone,’ that ‘one has no means’ or that ‘one lacks support’… a priest of the Incarnate Word must “be moved by the impulses of zeal” 46 . What is proper to us is “to be impatient to preach the Word in every form… We must seek out the sheep , use the method of dialogue, of witness and of solidarity, correct sinners, teach doctrine – faith comes through hearing 47 –, visit the sick, bring souls to the sacrament of Reconciliation” 48 . In a word, we must work industriously for the cause of Christ. It is fitting here to recall that the priestly program, especially in our Institute, which is missionary by nature, “implies availability” 49 . Far from us be those “priests who, on the slightest excuse, so as not to expose themselves to a bit of work or out of fear of some illness, neglect helping souls. St. Charles Borromeo said that the pastor who wants to adopt every kind of comfort and use whatever he can to favor his bodily health will never be able to fulfill his obligations well. And he added that the pastor should never go to bed except after three attacks of fever” 50 . At the same time we must remember the wise maxim of St. Manuel González, which guards us against occasional discouragement, and be convinced “that we can and must work with all our might to convert souls, because that is our part . But we must not be troubled if they are not converted, because that is the part of God and of the souls themselves” 51 . ▪ Faith The pastor must bear witness to the faith as a priest, that is, be a channel of grace to communicate divine life through the worthy celebration of the divine mysteries, the administration of the sacraments and, in particular, of the sacrament of reconciliation. We must be men of faith. Without faith religious and priestly life makes no sense. We must be men of integral faith, so that, on hearing us, all may unmistakably recognize the Word of God. Christ alone is the light of men that shines in the darkness 52 . God placed this light in the hands of the Church, which with the assistance of the Holy Spirit faithfully preserves and transmits it. Therefore, a clear expression of that faith is sincere and trusting adherence to all the doctrine of the authentic magisterium of the Church, of which our preaching and our catechesis must be an echo. Let everyone always remember: Faith is strengthened by giving it! 53 . Finally, our Proper Law, reminding us that pastoral ministry is a Cross, adds the following to these characteristics that must stand out in the priest dedicated to parish ministry: “mercy, prudence, presence of mind, tranquility of soul, the ability to overcome the repugnance that certain illnesses can cause, spiritual fortitude in the face of the dangers that may arise in the fulfillment of his ministry and, finally, availability to all” 54 . 2. The IVE parish As we said earlier, the parishes entrusted to the Institute become, so to speak, religious parishes 55 , since, although the exercise of the apostolate as such is subject to the authority of the bishop, we must exercise our own mode of apostolate, which is in keeping with the character and nature of our religious Institute 56 . We must bear in mind that the bishop has called us to his diocese precisely to do that: our apostolates, in our own way and style. For this we received the canonical mission on the day of the canonical erection of our Institute. That is, we were sent by the Church to carry out our apostolates in the name of that same Church. Our Institute has a charism to maintain and promote in the Church, which implies that the religious must remain faithful to their own identity and their own patrimony, at the service of the whole Church, without identifying with, losing themselves in or letting themselves be absorbed by a particular Church; and, on the other hand, they must work within it and in fidelity and obedience to the legitimate pastors 57 . How sad it is when one visits an IVE parish and hardly notices any difference from the neighboring diocesan parish! All this means that parishes constitute for the members of the Institute “a special setting for the exercise of some of our specific apostolates,” and, therefore, these must be given preference, since they in fact shape a style of our own. Regarding these apostolates, our Proper Law specifies and emphasizes that ours must be an “enthusiastic ministry” 58 , not a drowsy one; “incisive” 59 , not bureaucratic; “one of proposal” 60 , not of cancelling at the slightest obstacle. Allow us, then, to refer now to these specific apostolates. ▪ The Eucharistic celebration : The liturgical celebration, particularly the Eucharistic celebration, must be the center of the parish community of the faithful 61 . That is why it is necessary that priests dedicated to ministry in parishes take as a personal obligation the task of teaching the faithful to receive the Eucharist devoutly, “through serious liturgical formation , so that they may understand the meaning of the symbols they celebrate and take an active part in the celebrations” 62 . ▪ To this end, our Proper Law invites pastors to “ organize teams dedicated to the preparation of the various celebrations: commentators, lectors, those in charge of the collection, organists and those responsible for liturgical music, choirs, those in charge of the sacristy and the church, groups of altar servers” 63 , etc. And although Sunday will be the central day of the week for the whole parish 64 , it is also foreseen that there be great and solemn celebrations on occasions such as “Holy Week, novenas and patronal feasts, first communions and confirmations, popular missions” 65 , Christmas, the Easter Vigil and Pentecost 66 . It will then be the pastor’s task to promote these celebrations energetically and well in advance if he wants the greatest possible number of people to attend 67 , besides preparing them well . St. Alberto Hurtado already said it in one of his poems: “improvising on principle” is one of the sins of the man of action 68 . That is why Sunday Mass must be well prepared, because for many the preservation and nourishment of their faith is tied to participation in that Eucharistic celebration. Moreover, Eucharistic adoration cannot be lacking in an IVE parish. An important detail that is sometimes forgotten is this exhortation found in our Constitutions : “In a special way, according to the place, let the churches be kept open , and if there are dangers, let some kind of surveillance be prudently arranged; but, except in truly grave and insoluble circumstances, let the People of God be able to approach Jesus present in the Tabernacle with ease” 69 . How sad it is to see churches open only at Mass time, and one hardly even notices that they are open because the door has merely been unlocked, but the doors remain closed when they should be wide open (so that people know it is open); and, worse still, inside everything is gloomy and dark, because on the excuse that it uses a lot of electricity only a few lights are turned on during the celebration of Mass! We mention, moreover, that the Instruction Redempitionis Sacramentum specifies that “it is the right of the community of the faithful that, above all in the Sunday celebration, there should be suitable and fitting sacred music, according to custom, and that the altar, the vestments and the sacred linens should always , according to the norms, shine forth in their dignity, nobility and cleanliness” 70 . This will give the church and its worship an attractiveness that will very soon turn into an increase in the devotion of the priest himself and of his faithful. St. Manuel González further warns that “lack of punctuality in Holy Mass or in services is often sufficient cause to leave a church deserted… A fixed schedule for parish functions not only attracts the faithful, but is even a good example of order and seriousness given to Christian families” 71 . ▪ Catechesis, both of children and of adults. It must have priority among parish apostolates –of every parish, not only of those served by us. But it falls to us to carry out this apostolate very conscientiously also according to our Proper Law, which says clearly 72 that we want to devote ourselves “in a special way… to the preaching of the Word of God… in all its forms. In the study and teaching of Sacred Scripture… Catechesis…” 73 , sharing in the prophetic function of Christ 74 . Therefore, “as a Congregation we must always keep in mind the words of the Holy Father to religious: ‘I exhort you with all my heart, you who by virtue of religious consecration must be all the more available to serve the Church, to prepare yourselves as well as possible for the catechetical task… May communities dedicate the utmost of their abilities and possibilities to the specific work of catechesis!’” 75 . ▪ The work of the Spiritual Exercises : “The preaching of the Ignatian Spiritual Exercises in our parishes is a characteristic proper to the Institute. The way in which these Exercises strengthen parish life through the strengthening of the spiritual life of the faithful has been proven. All priests assigned to parish ministry must regard the holding of the Exercises as their own responsibility and collaborate in whatever falls to them. It is fitting that in every parish there be a committee to support the organization and coordination of the Exercises” 76 . The varied reality of our parishes perhaps makes the preaching of the Spiritual Exercises more difficult in some cases, but that does not mean that our priests are exempt from preaching them, or that our parishioners cannot make them, since with the various adaptations that are stipulated 77 they can be put within reach of all , so that “ all the faithful may enjoy the benefit that the life of prayer brings” 78 . That is why it is to be desired that in all our parishes the pastors not only actively promote the Spiritual Exercises, but strive to send people from their parish to the Exercises organized at the provincial level, and that they themselves preach Exercises in their parishes or invite other priests to do so on those days of the year when it is easiest for the faithful to attend, making them accessible to the greatest possible number of people. There should be no IVE parish in which the catechists, married couples, young people and members of the Third Order do not make the Exercises annually. After the administration of the sacraments, this should be a priority apostolate for the pastor. For, as our Constitutions establish, “the Institute shall undertake the evangelization of culture through the sanctification of individual persons, which will be done preferably by the preaching of Spiritual Exercises according to the method and spirit of St. Ignatius of Loyola, and, in addition, by spiritual direction” 79 . ▪ Confessions : “The utmost availability of priests for confession must be a hallmark of our parishes, also seeing to it that there are always one or more confessors during Holy Mass” 80 . Likewise, the Directory of Parishes insists in another paragraph that the “apostolate toward sinners will be exercised in a particular way in the administration of the sacrament of reconciliation, being always available at any moment to hear confessions, striving to possess the requisite knowledge and keeping up to date on moral questions and, above all, after the example of Christ, showing a heart of true mercy” 81 . It may happen that some of our parishes occasionally have only one priest, which makes the desired availability difficult; nevertheless, our Proper Law makes the following provision to be borne in mind: “Other priests from outside the parish should also be invited to hear confessions, and where possible and fitting, let a permanent confession center be set up” 82 . The holy and experienced bishop of Málaga affirmed: “A priest seated in his confessional from before sunrise, resolved not to grow tired or bored with the solitude, will not have to wait long before he sees Samaritan women and Samaritan men arrive to ask him for the water that springs up to eternal life” 83 . Because “a priest seated in his confessional from very early, even if he has no penitents to confess the whole morning, or until very late, is always a sweet and overpowering violence upon the Heart of Jesus, that He may pour out extraordinary graces” 84 . Something to bear in mind. ▪ Preaching : “The pastor and the assisting priests will see to it that ‘the Word of God is proclaimed in its entirety to those living in the parish’ 85 , instructing the lay faithful ‘in the truths of the faith, above all through the homily’ 86 ” 87 . Therefore, although canon law establishes “the homily which is to be given on Sundays and holy days of obligation” 88 , our priests will also strive to give a brief homily every day 89 , which must be conscientiously prepared and in some cases even rehearsed. The parish is the center of religious instruction; therefore, the pastor has the grave duty to complete with catechism the religious instruction received in the family, to spread the Word of God through popular missions, through ordinary preaching, through talks given to the various groups of the parish, etc., seeking that its members give authentic witness to Jesus Christ as living and active members of his Mystical Body, teaching them to order their family and working life according to God, and to be integrated with the universal Church through participatory, missionary, solidary and ecumenical attitudes 90 . St. Manuel González gives some advice regarding daily preaching that may be useful to us: “by parish preaching is meant simple preaching, without shouting or dramatic theatrical effects, and above all lasting ten minutes . Time and habit take away from the pastor’s preaching the appeal of novelty, and it bores or drives away novelty-seeking faithful, that is true. But it is also true that what it loses in appeal for these, it gains in authority, prestige and appreciation among good parishioners, above all if it is brief and heartfelt preaching. Brevity avoids weariness; heartfeltness produces interest and strengthens bonds. The priest who preaches daily need not worry about the danger of ‘exhausting the subject matter,’ since at most what he will repeat will be ideas, and it is good that these be repeated so that they are not forgotten and are put into practice” 91 . At the same time, it is expected that in our parishes “‘initiatives that promote the evangelical spirit, and everything that concerns social justice’ will be fostered” 92 : with the poor, seeking to alleviate their situation, promoting a ministry of charity 93 ; and with the rich, fostering in them detachment, a sense of justice, and mercy toward the weakest 94 . On our part, “justice will be exercised in visiting homes, in caring for the sick, in affability toward those who come to the parish, in patience with those who do not understand the things of God. These will be our weapons” 95 . In turn, it is recommended that all our parishes, especially those where the faith is more deeply rooted, include “ missionary animation as a primary element of ordinary ministry, both in associations and in groups, especially youth groups” 96 ; since “the parish must beget faithful capable of making the seed of the Gospel germinate in the environment in which they live” 97 . That is why the pastor and the other priests of the community must strive “by every possible means, also with the collaboration of the faithful, so that the Gospel message may reach likewise those who have stopped practicing or do not profess the true faith” 98 . In this regard the Directory of Parishes reminds us several times of the relevance, excellence and effectiveness of popular missions. Many other apostolates proper to us could be mentioned here, which for lack of space we will not address. Care of the sick must be a priority, as it is one of the pillars of all parish ministry; but since we are speaking of our parishes, this presentation would be incomplete if we did not mention these last two, albeit briefly: ▪ Oratory : “Let every superior see to it that a festive Oratory is organized in his parish, school, house and other works of his jurisdiction, considering that this work is one of the most important of all those entrusted to him” 99 . Therefore, the festive Oratory should not be lacking in any IVE parish, however small and poor it may be. Let it be our longing “that many, very many children and young people frequent the Oratory and love it; and even that a work such as this may multiply and prosper where it already exists or arise where it does not yet exist, next to every parish ” 100 . The Oratory is moreover an incipient source of vocations because, being a school of service , where one learns to work selflessly for the community, for the little ones and the poor, it becomes a privileged path for the birth and growth of authentic vocations to the priesthood and to consecrated and missionary life, as well as of solid lay vocations, married or not, based on the gift of self in the service of others 101 . “Let it be remembered that vocations will be the sign of a parish’s maturity 102 , and that vocational work must become a pastoral priority 103 , knowing how to foster them with generosity and to let go of them when they decide to follow Jesus Christ more closely” 104 . ▪ Third Order : because “the parish is a privileged place for the insertion and apostolate of the Third Order” 105 , in all IVE parishes “efforts will be made to foster the establishment and growth of the Secular Third Order of the Religious Family of the Incarnate Word, seeking –as far as possible– its incorporation into or participation in the life of the parish and of the local religious community” 106 . Moreover, it is more than desirable that in all our parishes the work the Institute carries out in the world be known; that people know of our devotion to Our Lady of Luján, of our fourth Marian vow, of our love and veneration for St. John Paul II; that they be persuaded by our conduct of the non-negotiables ; and that little by little, according to the makeup of the parish, our “sound traditions” become customary among them. How much good it does when, whenever possible , the faithful of our parishes take part in the feasts organized by the Religious Family, or when the parish itself hosts one of these feasts! What a great boost to the faith of young people and children when they take part in the camps, the youth days, the courses for university students organized by the Religious Family! The same may be said of when they attend ordinations and clothing ceremonies. How many blessings it draws down upon our parishioners when they take part in popular missions, in volunteer work in the works of the Institute; when they are benefactors of our missionaries or of our members in houses of formation! In short, by the grace of God, in our Institute we have opportunities to spare to promote and instill the charism among the faithful of our parishes and to contribute greatly to enriching the local Church. Not a little depends on the love the pastor has for the Institute and on his good will and magnanimity in doing good to others 107 . *** We want to end with the ardent watchword that St. Manuel González gave to his priests: “Most beloved priests, you who sit in the first stalls of the Cathedral as well as you who shepherd the remote village, receive and keep in your hearts this single word that I give you as a watchword for this hour, so full of confusions that inflame and of pessimisms that cow and depress; in this hour, I know not whether of funereal sunsets or of mysterious dawns: Fulfill your ministry . In the name of Jesus Christ who chose and appointed you, of Mother Church who needs you, of society which in the end will miss you, of the paralyzed souls who cry out for the man who will make them walk, of the little ones who ask for bread, of your own interests, spiritual and even earthly… Do your duty! The whole duty, that of justice and that of charity ! And afterward… Wait in peace!” 108 . “Remain at your posts, even if the solitude and silence of abandonment surround you; let your mouth not cease to open to speak of the Gospel, even if no one hears you, and let your hands not cease to stretch out to offer with one the Eucharist that nourishes souls, and with the other the piece of bread of your poverty that sustains the body, even if they meet no mouths or hands to receive it from you. Let your feet not cease to move in order to go, as the Master commanded, always to go , even if thorns are strewn along your path and not even a pair of friendly eyes meets your gaze… Remain at your posts , come what may; for at the very least you give glory to the heavenly Father who sends you; you lessen and delay, without any doubt, the triumph of evil; and you give an example, the example the world so greatly needs at this moment, that battles are won not by deserting duty but by fulfilling it” 109 . The attraction of and longing for divine beauty

That all men may discover the attraction and the longing for divine beauty Cf. Constitutions , 254 , 257 One of our fundamental commitments, which can at times go unnoticed or not be understood in all its fullness and potential, is the one contained precisely in our formula of profession, in which we say that we make an oblation to God of our entire self so that “all men may discover the attraction and the longing for divine beauty” 1 . A succinct phrase in which is implicit the challenging and, at the same time, thrilling task of “knowing how to call, teach, direct, accompany and select priestly, diaconal, religious, missionary and secular vocations” 2 . As we are only a few days away from celebrating the luminous mystery of the Transfiguration of the Lord, this solemnity seems to remind us once again that the icon of the transfigured face of Christ continues even today to exercise a powerful attraction over countless souls, and that it is our unavoidable task to rekindle with great strength, above all in young people, that deep longing for God, thus creating the proper setting for vocations to spring up as a generous response. 1. Urgency It is nothing new that “the vocational problem constitutes the fundamental urgency of the Church” 3 and, therefore, it is so for our Institute as well, because the subject of vocations “affects the whole Church in one of her fundamental marks, which is her apostolicity” 4 . For vocations are “a proof of her spiritual vitality and the very condition of that vitality. They are the condition of her mission and of her development” 5 . Truly, “the problem of vocations is an authentic challenge that directly questions Institutes, but which concerns the whole Church” 6 . In this sense, we understand that what is said in terms of vocations about the vitality and development of the Church refers not only to the universal Church, but also to each of the particular Churches and, analogously, also to our Institute. Since “vocational ministry” –as the Magisterium of the Church defines it very well– “is the mission of the Church ‘intended to care for the birth, discernment and accompaniment of vocations, especially vocations to the priesthood’ 7 ” 8 ; in that definition we recognize the “urgent” call “to strive, through explicit proclamation and suitable catechesis, to foster in those called to consecrated life the free, but prompt and generous, response that makes the grace of vocation operative” 9 . This urgency becomes even more pressing, above all if one hears that “the annual average of persons who leave religious life is more than 3,000 people, about 10 a day; which represents 0.3% of all consecrated life” 10 . Aware that vocations are not the fruit of spontaneous generation nor of an activism that relies only on human means, vocational ministry has been central to the mission of the Institute. Simply because we understand that, although each vocation is a gift of God, like all His gifts, they come through human mediations. By the grace of God, we can rejoice that the Institute has many vocations in formation (about 500) coming from some 50 different countries, which not only enrich the life of our Religious Family in the various jurisdictions and particular Churches, but are a sign of the vitality of religious life in our Institute, as well as the result of the faithful and devoted ministry of its members. However, this does not mean that the commitment to raising up and accompanying vocations to the priesthood and to consecrated life has come to an end. Our Proper Law points this out to us explicitly: “we would like God to give us the gift of being able to discover and guide so many vocations that we could fill all the good seminaries and novitiates of the whole world” 11 . Today as yesterday “the call of Christ: come and follow me ” 12 remains current and, therefore, our requirement remains current of a “work with vocations that is active , constant , full of drive and vitality , committed and urged on by the charity of Christ 13 , and necessarily opposed to a mentality of ‘ordinary administration or bureaucratic slowness’ 14 , which negligently waits for vocations to knock at the door. For God, by grace, sows the seeds of vocation with full hands 15 ” 16 . In a world that so frequently seeks fulfillment in material comforts and in the manipulation of power, in a world that strives to seek happiness without a clear reference to God, we members of the Institute of the Incarnate Word must be like signposts pointing to higher values, showing our contemporaries that we are ambassadors of Him who proclaimed the true ‘newness’ of life they are seeking when, on the summit of the Mount, He raised the standard of the Beatitudes. That is why the Spiritual Father of our Religious Family insisted with great emphasis that priests and religious –monks, brothers, seminarians– be concerned with raising up priestly vocations and forming them 17 , and that they dedicate themselves to the marvelous work of vocational ministry “with passion and discretion” 18 . This, although it is the task of all priests –religious or not, contemplative or not– and of all consecrated persons in general, is imperative and “indispensable” 19 for us, since the ministry of vocations “is intrinsic to the end of the evangelization of culture and to the charism of the Institute” 20 . Therefore, no member of the Institute can remain indifferent or claim that it is not his concern to pray for this intention and to raise up vocations of special consecration. Indeed, whoever does not do something, however small, for vocational ministry will never be able to enjoy that “most abundant apostolic and vocational fruitfulness” 21 to which we aspire, and his contribution to the cause of evangelization would be gravely restricted, however much apostolic zeal he may have in other areas. Here we highlight the preponderant role that the contemplatives of the Institute have in this regard, who have as their very special mission to pray for “the increase in quantity and quality of priestly and religious vocations” 22 , and on whose generous and joyful fidelity depends in large part the abundance and quality of vocations for the Institute and the whole Church. 2. A leap in quality Now, if from the members of the Institute is expected “a ministry of proposal, an incisive ministry” 23 in all areas of the apostolate, with how much greater reason do these qualifiers apply to vocational ministry which, as is well known, is a pastoral priority 24 and an “obligatory dimension” 25 of every pastoral plan. This is the concern not only of those ‘in charge’ in the various jurisdictions, but it must be considered one of the primary objectives of the Institute, and all the members must feel involved in it. For those ‘in charge’ will fulfill their mission all the more effectively the more all the members –according to their abilities and offices– help to make their own the commitment to increase the priests and consecrated persons that the Church needs today. The decline in vocations, or the abandonment by many consecrated persons that we mentioned earlier, led St. John Paul II long ago to ask himself: “What is the cause?” 26 . Among the various reasons he enumerates, we list the following: “It is likely that the cultural changes of our time provide a certain explanation, but it is also necessary to think of the process of secularization that affects religious life. And there is also a form of presence in the world that leads slowly but inexorably to the suppression of every specific and perceptible aspect of religious life. This specific character consists in being a ‘sign of contradiction,’ not against man but against what is inhuman in contemporary society; not against the modern human universe, but in order to save it. […] At times concern for a poorly understood human development or for community well-being, and the existence of a certain bourgeois comfort , have weakened the search for the one thing necessary which must constitute the witness of religious life” 27 . “The vocational crisis must not be attributed principally to a lack of generosity on the part of young people, but rather to the fact that a prophetic sign of the presence of God, which is precisely the first dimension of religious life, is not sufficiently perceived in religious life” 28 . “The proposals that tend to ‘ laicize ’ the ministry and priestly life, to replace ‘sacramental’ ministers with other ‘ministries,’ judging that they respond better to today’s pastoral demands, and also to deprive the religious vocation of the character of prophetic witness to the kingdom, orienting it exclusively toward functions of social animation or even of directly political commitment” 29 . If religious/priests “ do not bear witness to the Transcendent […] if they are not a sign of what lies beyond this world and its transience, and of what is much higher –divine and eschatological realities–, they will not be able to exercise an authentic attraction to religious life on young people” 30 . The spread of “ erroneous opinions about the value of consecrated life, which produce perplexity and disorientation especially among young people” 31 . The fact that priests/religious make “ rereadings of the Gospel according to the times, conforming themselves to everything the world asks for” 32 . For these reasons, and given the historical and cultural circumstances of our world and the particular circumstances the Church is going through, we feel compelled to make a leap in quality in the vocational ministry of the Institute. For without enough laborers for the harvest , it will not be possible for us to make a reality of Christ’s command: Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature 33 (which is the very reason for our existence and mission in the Church), nor to renew each day the Eucharistic sacrifice: Do this in memory of me 34 . Therefore, the vocational ministry we are attempting is not exhausted in occasional or extraordinary initiatives, but aims to be a constant concern of all the members in all our apostolates. For notwithstanding the present difficulties, it is palpable that throughout the world there are young people more than eager and open to live an authentic Christian radicalism, to give themselves and dedicate themselves to selfless service of the poor, the sick, children, etc., and we must know how to see in the demands and desires of these young people a summons and even an opportunity for the mission of our Institute. How do we bring it about that “all men may discover the attraction and the longing for divine beauty” 35 ? That is what we will try to answer in the points that follow. 3. Attraction through fidelity The young people of our time have great need of the spiritual visibility and transparency of religious communities. Therefore, to the extent that we preserve the physiognomy of our Institute, and that each one of us is like an incarnation of its charism and spirit in the realities we are called to live, young people will feel especially attracted. This is what experience has shown us: very often, the example of a religious man or woman acts in a decisive way in the vocational orientation of a young person, who discovers in that religious’s fidelity, in the joy that springs from “preferring nothing to Christ” 36 , the concrete realization of an ideal of life. We have heard it so many times: example draws others along. In this sense our Proper Law points out that “religious institutes must maintain a firm and clear sense of their own identity and mission” 37 . The more fervent the members of the Institute are in practicing with conviction the non-negotiables attached to the charism, in living faithfully the religious vows according to the spirit of the Institute, and in carrying out all our proper apostolates with zeal and in union with the Incarnate Word, in communion with the pastors and with a full ecclesial sense, the more inevitable will be –barring divine permission– a flourishing of vocations for the Institute and the whole Church. In other words, we consider that the example is decisive of “religious and priests who serenely live their vocation day by day, faithful to the commitments they have made, humble and hidden builders of the Kingdom of God, from whose words, behavior and life radiates the luminous joy of the choice they made… it is precisely they… who by their example will spur many to welcome into their hearts the charism of vocation” 38 . By preaching with good example young people are led to embrace a life of total consecration and service, because it is only possible to beget new vocations spiritually when one lives “firm and faithful to the call, to the vocation, above any other claim of this earth” 39 . And we are convinced that the consistent witness of Christ represents in itself a vocational proposal. Consequently, as our Proper Law expresses very well: “every counter-witness, every inconsistency between how values or ideals are expressed and how they are actually lived, every seeking of oneself and not of the Kingdom of God and His justice 40 , every falsification of the Word of God 41 , “are frequently strong obstacles for those who feel the call of Christ: come and follow me …” 42 . 4. Attraction through the radicalism of the Gospel “Today young people need to see living examples of those who, leaving everything, have embraced as their ideal the life according to the evangelical counsels” 43 , said St. John Paul II. That is, they need to see priests and religious of the Incarnate Word who accept with joy, for the love of God, privations even in necessary things 44 ; who are ready to live “the radicalism of the self-emptying of Christ and of His condition as a servant” 45 ; who, by dying to the world, are “ready for martyrdom out of loyalty to God, which constitutes the full and total rejection of the evil world” 46 ; who are ready to leave their family to become part of the Family of the Incarnate Word; in short, who live in “a process of continual conversion” 47 , “resolved to attain holiness” 48 . Let it be well understood that it is real sincerity in the radical following of the Incarnate Word that will continue to attract vocations to our Institute, since young people are seeking precisely that evangelical radicality. To the extent that young people get to know us more closely and see us as generous followers of Christ and radical in the choice we have made –given that our way of life offers no material rewards nor accommodates itself to the models of the world– they will be strongly attracted to Christ’s firm and thrilling challenge to leave everything to follow Him. Far be it from us to make adaptations in our way of life or spirituality that are born of laxity or lead to it. That would not only mean the loss of the spirit of the Institute, but it would be a bleeding wound for our mission in the Church and a regrettably effective way of driving away new vocations. 5. Attraction through joy Our Proper Law already says it: the “witness of joy arouses an enormous attraction toward religious life, it is a source of new vocations and a support for perseverance” 49 . For it is through a collective witness of authentic consecration, lived in the joy of personal self-giving to Christ and to others, that young people feel attracted. Note that priests, deacons, contemplatives, brothers, novices, seminarians, all of us, absolutely all, have a special responsibility in awakening and sustaining vocations. If we give a joyful witness of serving Christ; if we spread hope through the faith that animates us, even in spite of the weariness of the apostolate and of the struggle; if we are truly given over to souls and are capable of teaching others to pray, how can we doubt that vocations will arise around us? Has that not been the experience of many of us? If we are “sad and discouraged, impatient or anxious” 50 religious, bad-tempered or irascible, we will do little or nothing to encourage young people to embrace the call to special consecration. We must be aware that our witness as religious “encourages or discourages, arouses the desire for God or constitutes an obstacle to following Him” 51 . Seeing us, young people must perceive that “God does not call only to a life of sacrifice and renunciation, but also to a life of intimate joy and fullness” 52 . We must be persuaded that young people are in search of an Absolute that a good number of adults and even some religious are incapable of revealing to them. That is why our mission toward them is indispensable; they hope that we will prepare them for a life worth living and that we will put them in contact with the Transfigured Christ and His Gospel that does not pass away. Therefore, it is necessary to make every possible effort so that young people come to place Christ at the center of their search and to follow docilely His eventual call. 6. Attraction through fraternal charity Community life is an inseparable element of religious life in our Institute and is for us a great richness thanks to the benefit of the complementarity of gifts. The simple austerity of our lives united to ardent fraternal charity anchored in the interior richness of obedience is one of the conditions for vocations to flourish everywhere in a world dominated by consumerism and selfishness 53 . That is why there is asked of each member of the Institute “a new and determined evangelical witness of self-denial and sobriety, a style of fraternal life inspired by criteria of simplicity and hospitality” 54 . But also and above all, the practice of “fraternal charity, as in a true family ” 55 , since without any doubt young people feel attracted by the discovery of communities united in charity. We want to highlight here the great value that the practice of hospitality has as a means of raising up vocations. Let us remember, then, that “in our houses, provided it does not gravely affect the internal order of the house and the area of cloister of the religious is respected” 56 , the practice of this work of mercy is very desirable. For “not infrequently have we observed that this work of mercy has led many souls to friendship with God through conversion or to discover their vocation of consecration to the Lord” 57 . St. John Paul II already said it, and it seems to us worth emphasizing: “Do you want a key to apostolic fruitfulness? Live unity, the source of great apostolic strength 58 . In fraternal communion lies, in fact, the guarantee of the presence of Christ and of His Spirit, for putting your responsibilities into practice, following the rules of your institutes. The Church needs the example and witness of religious who live evangelical fraternity. […] The young people who knock at your doors wish to find an ecclesial life characterized by fervor in prayer, by a family spirit, by apostolic commitment. […] Be capable of welcoming them and guiding them, carefully cultivating new vocations, the search for which must be one of your principal concerns ” 59 . Therefore, the more community spirit there is among the members of the Institute, the more effective our ministry will be. Where there are living communities, where the members live together fraternally, that is where there are more vocations. 7. Attraction through service to the poor Our task, as has been well expressed in our Constitutions , “is to love and serve, and to make Jesus Christ loved and served… especially [in] the poor” 60 . That is why we are commanded “to give priority to the care of the poor, the sick and the needy of every kind… concretely practicing charity” 61 . Let us open the doors of our missions to young people so that they can collaborate in our activities: parish catechesis, care of the poor, oratories, popular missions, volunteer work, home visits, etc. Let us give them the opportunity to give themselves and dedicate themselves to the selfless service of the poor, of the little ones, of the needy and the sick 62 . How enriching is the experience of the many young people who have been able to collaborate as volunteers in the various homes the Institute runs, in the popular missions accompanying the religious or helping in whatever way, or assisting in simple parish tasks. In fact, several of our own discovered their vocation precisely after such an experience. Therefore, it is desirable that young people be increasingly involved in our apostolates and that they perceive up close the religious’s forgetfulness of self for the spiritual good of his neighbor. For witness remains the most convincing force of attraction at our disposal. The idea is that, seeing our good works , young people may follow in our footsteps for the glory of our Father who is in heaven 63 . 8. Attraction through solid formation Young people today, as yesterday, seek the certainty of the truth that does not pass away. They want to give their life to the Lord, not to have it squandered. That is why our Proper Law points out that “without good formation God does not bless with an abundance of vocations” 64 . This implies that “intense efforts must be made to foster vocations and to procure the best priestly formation possible in the seminaries” 65 . At present the Institute has about 250 major seminarians under the care of some 35 formators, not counting the itinerant professors who often visit the seminaries, procuring the best possible formation, according to the norms of the Church in force, as the mission entrusted to us in the Church requires. Likewise, some 215 priests already hold an academic degree obtained at pontifical universities and there are about 30 more studying to obtain one (that is, more than half of the priest members have some academic degree-level preparation), which in a certain way implies an investment by the Institute in vocational ministry. For we are convinced that vocational ministry also presupposes and needs a careful and concrete follow-up of vocations. And this requires that each of the priests especially prepare himself spiritually, theologically and pedagogically, in an ongoing way, for this important ecclesial mission 66 . 9. Attraction through prayer “The ‘center of all vocational ministry’ is prayer” 67 , our Proper Law points out. Jesus made it clearly understood in the Gospel. When calling the disciples to send them throughout the world, He urges them above all to look on high : Pray, therefore, the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest 68 . “The vocational pedagogy –affirmed St. John Paul the Great– that the Lord uses shows that a ministry unbalanced toward action and promotional initiatives runs the risk of proving ineffective and without prospects, because every vocation is, above all, a gift of God” 69 . “Seeing a priest make his meditation before Mass does more for an altar boy’s vocation than thousands of vocational propaganda pamphlets” 70 , wrote Fulton Sheen. That is why today more than ever we must be promoters and drivers of a great movement of prayer , counteracting the wind of secularism that pushes us to give priority to human means, to efficiency-mindedness and to a pragmatic approach to life. What a blessing it would be if the faithful of our parishes and “the key pieces of the apostolic endeavor of our Institute” 71 –that is: the monastic communities, the sick, the religious brothers– as well as the families of the Third Order and those who suffer, were to raise to God every day a fervent prayer for vocations. Let us take the time to exhort others to pray; let us create spaces of prayer for vocations, especially before the Most Blessed Sacrament of the Altar or with a Rosary in hand. 10. To the young people of the Voices of the Word In the first place, we want to thank you for your generous commitment to spreading the Gospel in the different spheres of daily life. But, in addition, today we want to make you our confidants and tell you that a symphony of many voices is needed to express the one Word 72 across the vast horizon of this world. For this it is first necessary to remove from the ears of the soul the noises that often prevent one from catching the divine voice 73 , in order to give Jesus room in the heart and let oneself be seduced by the Eternal One, as the prophet Jeremiah said: You have seduced me, Lord…; You were stronger than I, and You prevailed 74 . “Let yourselves be fascinated by the Incarnate Word, the Infinite One who appeared among us in a visible and imitable form. Let yourselves be drawn by His example, which has changed the history of the world and directed it toward an exultant goal. Let yourselves be loved by the charity of the Holy Spirit, who wants to turn your eyes away from earthly models, in order to begin in you the life of the new man, created according to God in justice and true holiness 75 . Fall in love with Jesus Christ, so as to live His very life, so that our world may have life in the light of the Gospel” 76 . Today “there is a lack of workers for the Gospel on the outskirts of the great metropolises, in rural areas, among the inhabitants of the heights of the Andes, [in the Russian steppes, in the African deserts, in remote islands] and in the immensity of the jungles. There is a lack of servants of the good news who will dedicate themselves to young people, to families, to the elderly and the sick, to workers, to intellectuals, to the builders of a society, as well as to the poorest and most marginalized. The presence of a greater number of priests and religious is urgently needed in parishes, in apostolic movements, in basic ecclesial communities, in schools and universities, and in so many other fields […]. On the other hand, looking at the wide horizons of the universal mission entrusted to the Church, there is also a lack of men and women missionaries who will go beyond the borders, to proclaim to the world the unsearchable riches of Christ ” 77 . In a word: the Church needs today more than ever “radical and total self-giving, new and courageous impulses” 78 . Take heart “to discern the will of God through familiarity with the Word of God, read and studied in the Church, under the guidance of her legitimate Pastors” 79 . Do your best to make the Spiritual Exercises every year, which is one of the most qualified means for ordering one’s life according to God and, accordingly, in many cases, for discerning the divine plan for one’s life. Seek spiritual direction frequently. Take part whenever you can in the popular missions or in the volunteer opportunities the Institute offers. It is an enriching experience from every point of view. And at all times, be men and women of prayer. Finally, let this be an explicit invitation addressed not to the Voices of the Word as a group, but to each one of you, whatever country you may be in and whatever the circumstances of your life at the present moment. It is the invitation to put out into the deep 80 , taking seriously, thoroughly, the demands of the Gospel: go, sell all that you have … 81 so as to be ambassadors for Christ 82 , reproducing Him, becoming like Him, being configured to Him according to the charism of the Institute. “Consider the immensity of this world,” Blessed Paolo Manna used to tell young people and newly ordained priests, “do not be one of those who see nothing beyond the narrow limits of their own country. There is a great part of the world about which no one thinks because it lies asleep in error and sin. […] Go, then, you who have wept when you contemplated the Blood of Christ poured out in abundance and apparently with little result… Go to the missions and apply the merits of this Most Precious Blood to the countless souls who have no one to make them sharers in such blessings. Save them and console the Heart of Jesus, which desires nothing more than that. Go with a pure heart burning with charity, you whose love –you say– is without limits, go to the mission. […] Go to the mission, chosen soul who are nourished by the graces of the Eucharist, soul who desire nothing more than to spend yourself for the love of God. Go to the mission. […] Enlist to go to the mission, you who like to work. […] You whose sins have been forgiven, consecrate yourself for the rest of your life to the work of the apostolate among the pagans, thereby making reparation for a youth spent, perhaps, far from God. […] If God really calls you, do not be afraid, go to the mission, keeping in mind the promise that the workers of the last hour will receive the same pay as those who worked from the first. […] Let those who until now have resisted the voice of the Lord now say: ‘Yes, I will be a missionary. / I will not resist God’s call a moment longer. I will not hinder God’s great plan to save all men. I will not deprive the Church of my humble services. I will not postpone the promptings of my conscience to generosity; I will be a missionary. / I wish to contribute with all my strength and with my very life, if it were necessary, to extending the kingdom of Jesus. I wish to immolate myself to promote His glory and to procure salvation for so many needy souls who perhaps await the Savior in me.’ What joy there will be in heaven if any of you makes such a decision!” 83 . ***** Let all the members of the Institute remember that “in these times of few vocations, those who do not have them often consider it a sin to have many vocations, and mercilessly attack those who have them. That is why one must know how to be holily determined not to tolerate anything that could impede them. For this one must be ready even for martyrdom, if it were necessary, knowing how to maintain an unshakable firmness in order to be faithful to God, who is the Author of every vocation and the one principally interested in their flourishing. In other words, one must not place obstacles to the work of God” 84 . We must be convinced that the exemplary character of our religious life by virtue of our proper charism, the spiritual atmosphere of our communities, the austerity and manner of life, the solid and sure formation that prepares candidates to ‘bite into reality,’ and fervor in the works of the apostolate will be a cause of edification for the whole Church and will attract to our beloved Institute ever more numerous vocations of generous young people, who aspire not to mediocrity in the following of Christ, but to radicalism in their consecration to Him. We entrust to Our Lady of Luján, Queen of the Institute and Mother of vocations, all the young people of the world, as well as the pastoral work of all our members on behalf of vocations of special consecration. May the sweetness of this Kind Mother draw young people to her Immaculate Heart so that they may understand with her the beauty and joy that await them if the Incarnate Word calls them to His intimacy, to make them witnesses of His Love and to render them capable of gladdening the Church with their consecration.
