From my previous experience, although in primary school it can be positive, it usually is not so in secondary school” 124 . – No graduation trip at the end of secondary school: “From the beginning we said that in our schools there would be no so-called graduation trip , which is usually a ‘trip of sins.’ Instead we would make a great act of love and gratitude to Jesus Christ for the formation received, by doing mission work in humble places such as the backwoods of Santiago del Estero” 125 . Worthy of mention is that our Founder launched the Humanities High School with practically nothing. Some of the seminarians of that time went to teach classes, others were proctors, etc. In short, what could be done was done. That is why Fr. Buela points out that ours is perhaps “the first school built by the teachers themselves, because with what the seminarians were paid, the walls of the High School were paid for” 126 . But that was a great experience, since the “Humanities High School also turned out to be an arena for the seminarians, where they could teach, and so what Aristotle says was fulfilled, that ‘only he knows who is able to teach.’ The Humanities High School was also a very great grace from God for the Major Seminary as well” 127 . That remains a very desirable experience for all the present and future seminarians of the Institute. Printing press and publications From the beginning Fr. Buela wanted the seminarians to be proficient in everything having to do with printing and the spreading of the good press. He tirelessly repeated that in the field of the intellectual apostolate one had to give priority to “publications, since what is written remains and spreads more widely” 128 . Thus arose the journal Diálogo , the Vox Verbi Bulletin, the magazine Ave María , etc. The journal Diálogo , published since 1992, was born and developed as an apostolate of the major Seminary under the direct supervision and direction of Fr. Buela. He himself took care of naming the journal, and he had a very clear idea of its objectives, which he naturally conveyed to the seminarians who worked at the printing press, but in fact to everyone, since those who did not work at the press suddenly found themselves distributing the journal. Fr. Buela’s attention to detail in everything concerning the journal showed the importance he gave to such an apostolate. There is the anecdote of when a seminarian showed him a draft of the cover design that included some dashes or flourishes on both sides of the journal’s title. Fr. Buela immediately said that those flourishes should be removed. Moreover, he tirelessly wrote articles for the journal 129 . Once again, this apostolate involved significant expenses for the Seminary. And yet the best means and the best human capital were devoted to that undertaking. To the point that Cardinal Quarracino, after receiving a copy of the journal, wrote a letter to the Founder in which, among other things, he says: “It seems that with your journal you have overcome two difficulties: the laziness about writing proper to Latin Americans and, of course, to Argentines; and the financial difficulty, because I can imagine the outlay that each issue of ‘Diálogo’ means. Here is a modest contribution of mine” 130 . But this apostolate was not to remain confined to the houses of formation; rather, “even as part of the good press,” Fr. Buela said, “if circumstances permit, one can try to set up a parish printing press . Don Bosco used to repeat: ‘First a printing press, then a great printing press, and then many printing presses…’” 131 . Oratory Our Proper Law establishes that “every Superior should see to it that a festive Oratory is organized in his parish, school, house and other works of his jurisdiction, considering that this work is one of the most important of all those entrusted to him” 132 . That is why Fr. Buela added: “In our Directory of Oratories what it is about is well treated. It must be read, explained and implemented ” 133 . “The ‘oratorian spirit’ is the Oratory in the broad sense; it is the spirit that must be present in our families, in our communities, in the major and minor seminaries, the schools, retreats, camps, study trips or pilgrimages, outings, conferences, congresses, poetry contests, etc. All our activities and pastoral works must be imbued with this oratorian spirit ” 134 . If there is one thing that characterized Fr. Buela, it was his festive spirit or, as his own brother described him: “he was a homo festivus .” Preparation of sermons Certainly the seminarians who are preparing for the care of souls must know that they are to beget spiritual children through the word 135 . Therefore, it is imperative −and Fr. Buela gave great importance to the subject− to prepare sermons well. “Parishioners,” he said, “love it when the pastor prepares his sermons ; they listen to them gladly and with great spiritual profit. And they are supremely bored when the priest habitually does not prepare his sermons” 136 . For this reason, he asked the priests of the Institute “ not to be boring . We are tired of humdrum clerics who bore people with their singsong of failed functionaries, of mere administrators, of ecclesiastical bureaucrats” 137 . Instead, he exhorted them “to know how to be poets, that is, to know how to bring to light the non-trivial dimension of existence. […] Let them be, therefore, creative , that is, not mere repeaters of known things, of things even badly said, of things that have no force because they are repeated wearily. […] Let them be original , not in order to repeat foolish novelties, which in the end are nothing more than ancient heresies, but let them know how to lead to the authentic origins [that is, to God]” 138 . “The preparation, let us say proximate, should begin on Sunday afternoon, reading the readings of the following Sunday and bearing in mind the particular topic chosen. (It may have happened, or may yet happen, that some notable event occurs that makes it preferable to choose another topic). In the remaining days the sermon is gradually written” 139 . In this regard Fr. Buela said that it was “important to read the beginning of St. Alphonsus’s work Sermones abreviados para todas las Dominicas del año , arranged so as to serve in missions and spiritual exercises” 140 , although in his view “the great work on this subject is that of Fray Luis de Granada, Retórica Eclesiástica ” 141 . He was a great promoter of Courses in rhetoric among our members; he had Fray Luis de Granada’s book digitized and ordered that our own edition of it be published. At the same time, he himself began the classes in oratory and its exercises. To evaluate whether or not the sermon had been understood, he had the following irrefutable criterion: “If one learns that the parishioners were talking about the sermon at lunch, it is a sign that they understood it” 142 . Ecumenical Conference “Pastoral zeal and charity must also extend to the members of non-Catholic Christian Churches and communities. For this purpose, an ecumenical formation is necessary…” 143 . Fr. Buela himself, with the help of other IVE priests, organized at the major Seminary “Mary, Mother of the Incarnate Word” the 1 st Ecumenical Conference in San Rafael. Care of the poor We would say that the care of the poor arose almost simultaneously with the beginning of the Institute. It was a work very dear to our Founder, and he stressed the “importance of concrete charity when speaking of the subject of the poor” 144 and of the Hogarcitos in the pastoral formation of the seminarians. In fact, food began to be given to the poor daily as soon as the seminary at La Finca began to operate. Using the text of Mt 25:34-45, where we read ‘ Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty, or a stranger or naked, or sick or in prison, and did not help you? He [Christ] will answer them: ‘Truly I tell you: what you did not do for one of these, the least, you did not do for me either ’; Fr. Buela taught that that is why “in our Homes, at the foot of the cross, a sign is placed that says: ‘This is how to love’ and also: ‘Look, it is I!’ , for it is Jesus Christ who speaks, referring to our guests. That is what we aim to do with the Hogarcitos for persons with special needs or with any need, orphans, elderly people without help, parents of priests or of women religious, etc.” 145 . “If the Princes of the Apostles, Peter and Paul, were Christ’s poor, how could we refuse to help the one who comes to us with some need? And to help them, as far as possible, as if they were Christ Himself ” 146 . That is the way a member of the IVE cares for the poor, the sick, the elderly, orphans, etc.: as if they were Christ. And he said it with “the conviction that only charity, as St. Luigi Orione said, will save the world” 147 . Fr. Buela strongly emphasized that charity must be concrete . Because “holiness consists in love lived concretely. And our neighbor needs bread, a home, clothing, a word, our time so as to confide to us his problems and his torments. […] Love of neighbor, too, needs the gift of the heart. Is it really necessary to love God with all one’s heart and one’s neighbor only with one’s head?” 148 . In this sense, he suggested “that in every parish there should be a Hogarcito, because ministry with the poor obliges us to concrete charity, against which there is no arguing, and it is an irrefutable form of charity. It is always a ministry loved by the people” 149 . And he insisted, “I know from experience that when we care for God’s poor, He always helps us generously. […] Having the poor with us, no Parish would be dying. In some cases, as in countries with a Muslim majority, it is almost the only visible and possible apostolate” 150 . As we mentioned earlier, it was Fr. Buela who promoted the festive dinner for the poor who habitually came to our houses and for others who wished to join for the occasion. It was prepared like a party, with food somewhat better than what was usually served. The seminarians themselves cooked and waited on the tables; some were assigned to sit among the guests in order to do apostolate, others prepared a campfire, etc. And so, concretely, the seminarians learned to practice charity with the poor: by serving. Apostolate of presence Concretely, so as not to shy away from the missionary adventure, our Founder stressed that “there must be young priests ready −for example− to be custodians of the holy places. There must be young priests who have that disposition, which is a disposition for martyrdom ” 151 . For they will not know churches full of parishioners and, very probably, will not be able “to know popular missions with all their fruits” 152 if they are on mission in a place where the Christian population is a minority, and in a time of persecution because Christians are regarded as second-class; and even more so in a highly conflictive situation due to Muslim fundamentalism 153 . Likewise, he would announce to all the priests and seminarians, as if it were a grand event, whenever he received a request for a foundation in some emblematic place: Chad, Sudan, China, Papua New Guinea, Tajikistan, etc. And so he kept feeding the thirst for souls, the missionary drive that must stand out in every member of the IVE, and he prepared them for a magnanimous self-giving in places that were in fact very difficult. He taught the seminarians to be ready to go anywhere, and that is how several offered themselves for China, Equatorial Guinea, Australia, Rwanda, the Czech Republic, Russia, etc. It is told that when the letter arrived from the bishop requesting a foundation in Chad, and after Fr. Buela had announced it to the whole Seminary body, he placed the bishop’s letter in the hands of Our Lady of Sorrows in the Seminary church. The next day, when the seminarians came in for Mass, they found the Virgin holding the letter. However, in some cases −because of how challenging or dangerous the situation was−, Fr. Buela advised “the apostolate that has been called ‘of presence.’ [Because] an authentically Christian presence means the witness of charity, which is a most effective way of preaching the Gospel” 154 . Those who are preparing for mission in our houses of formation must be convinced of this. A markedly Marian imprint From the moment our candidates set foot in the novitiate −as the sound traditions of our Institute attest, which are replicated in the houses of the IVE whatever the language, the culture, the country, the years of religious life, etc.− all learn to love Our Lady with filial and trusting devotion: whether with the kiss on Our Lady’s mantle, the song to Our Lady at the end of recreation, the renewal of the consecration to Most Holy Mary before the final blessing at Mass, the daily praying of the rosary, etc. And this same filial love and true devotion to the Mother of God is manifested whatever the form of apostolate to which the members are devoted: with the dawn rosary in the popular missions, in the Marian processions with the corresponding decoration of the float that carries the image, the invocation of Mary in the peroratio of a sermon, teaching children to pray the Hail Mary and to bring flowers to Our Lady in the Oratory, the promotion of consecration to Mary according to the method of St. Louis Mary Grignion de Montfort, the celebration of Marian feasts with all solemnity, pilgrimages to the shrines of Our Lady, and so many other apostolic practices inherited from our Founder which today are connatural to our pastoral style and which should not be lost; rather, they should always be practiced with new fervor. It is the testimony of those who were seminarians and formators at the time when the Founder lived at the Finca that “if there was one thing that was omnipresent in the Seminary, it was the maternal care of Our Lady and Fr. Buela with his great love for her. That was constantly perceived, and so we learned it, connaturally.” In this regard Fr. Buela reminded us “that in the Constitutions it says that ‘for the suitable formation of the seminarians [and women religious] they must be taught to value and to love [ … ] the Most Blessed Virgin and the saints as intercessors and models of life [ … ].’ Let us bear in mind that progressivism even today continues to vilify, in one way or another, the cult of the saints. Among us that must never happen . We must love and honor the saints, and invoke their protection, especially that of those we have as protectors or patrons. They are our brothers in the faith, who have already reached the goal and who, therefore, can help us; that is why we must relate to them” 155 . And if that is said of the saints, how much more of the Queen of all saints. Apostolate with women religious and the laity It is certainly a grace and an enormous advantage to be able to count on the support of women religious and of the laity −men and women− for carrying out our apostolates. For the consecrated woman enters places where we [priests] cannot enter. […] The feminine presence does great things in the pastoral ministry of the Church, and in fact a very great pastoral complementarity can come about” 156 . Our Proper Law says the same about the laity, since they can “take and carry Christ to the most distant, most hidden places, where priests cannot reach or enter, evangelize cultures from their deepest, most intimate core, bringing reality under the lordship of the Lord, inculturating the Gospel in the most remote corners of human life” 157 . It is important, therefore, that the seminarians learn to work with them. The seminarians must be taught to “exercise great prudence in dealing with women” 158 . “‘But, Father −you will tell me−, we women are not bad…’ Certainly. And certainly we −so we have been taught− must see a woman as we see our mother, as we see our sister, as we see the Most Blessed Virgin. Yes, sir, but one must be prudent, cutting off familiarities in good time. But one must also know that there are women who are not good, who are bad women and who seek out the priest in order to ruin him. A priest ran into a former seminary classmate who had abandoned the priesthood, in a bar in the Flores area, and the man said to him: ‘Look, all I can tell you is: go and tell the cardinal that there are women here, paid by Freemasonry, who go looking for priests, even in the confessional.’ Even so, one must know that sometimes the more dangerous ones are those who pretend to be ‘good’” 159 . “Between a holy woman and a holy man, a wall of stone and mortar,” Fr. Buela used to point out to his own in a fatherly way. Care of family members “We have the particularity that, instead of setting aside our natural family, we draw it into our Congregation. Great friendships even form among them. In short, they help us in every way” 160 . “Hence the importance of including families in the Institute of the Incarnate Word: for us it is a great joy when the fathers and mothers of our men and women religious visit us, because it is as if they were our own relatives. We have founded a home for the care of the relatives of priests, seminarians, sisters… who need it” 161 . “It is what the fourth commandment of the law of God teaches: to honor, respect, obey −while one lives in one’s parents’ home… it ceases with the emancipation of the children− love and serve one’s parents in their needs, when the children are grown. And analogously, one’s brothers and sisters, grandparents, pastors, catechists, teachers, friends…” 162 . It goes without saying how much respect, esteem and consideration he had for his own relatives and for the relatives of our members. And he instilled that same attitude in the other members of the Institute. Thus, for example, once the parents of a seminarian traveled from another province to visit him at the seminary, in such a way that one of the days of the visit coincided with the seminarian’s apostolate day. He went to consult Fr. Buela: ‘Do I go to the apostolate and leave my parents here? Or do I look after my parents and miss the apostolate?’ To which the Father answered with complete simplicity: “these days your apostolate is your family.” Internet For Fr. Buela the internet or, as he himself says, “the new world of cyberspace” 163 represented a “call to the great adventure of using its potential to proclaim the Gospel message” 164 . He realized the “magnificent opportunities for evangelization” that the use of the internet entailed if “it is used competently and with a clear awareness of its strengths and weaknesses” 165 . Fr. Buela was very aware that at present it was necessary to work in the areopagus of the media of communication with due precautions. We already mentioned earlier how from the beginning he wanted computing to be used as an instrument of apostolate. Our Founder was the great originator and promoter of the Spiritual Exercises website. Moreover, we were perhaps among the first religious in San Rafael to have a system of communication with the whole world from El Nihuil, with the “BBS” system that was brought from the USA on the occasion of the ’94 chapter. Help to diocesan priests A special note of charity, one that speaks of the nobility of his soul, was his great interest in helping priests, even diocesan ones. For he considered it “of great importance that all priests, diocesan or religious, help one another” 166 . In this sense he recommended: “Do not forget… hospitality; cultivate beneficence and the sharing of goods; be especially solicitous for the sick, the afflicted, those overburdened with work, those who are alone, exiled from their homeland, victims of persecution; [feel yourselves] especially obliged toward those who suffer difficulties; to those who have failed in some respect, show fraternal charity and magnanimity, praying for them to God unceasingly, and show yourselves continually to be true brothers and friends to them” 167 . How many times have we witnessed our Founder’s great example of priestly fraternal charity toward diocesan priests or priests belonging to other orders. An example of that concrete charity is the case −almost emblematic, we might say− of the elderly Fr. Victorino Ortego, whom Fr. Buela personally invited to live in the major Seminary, and in fact he lived 15 years among our members. But many other diocesan priests of San Rafael also benefited from his generous fraternal charity, for example, when −given the poverty there was in Argentina at that time− Fr. Buela offered them some Mass intentions. That is, he asked them to pray for the Congregation and gave them a stipend for it. Indeed, there was a chart of the diocesan clergy of San Rafael on which were counted the Mass intentions given to each one, in order to keep track that they did not lack what was necessary to live. Another example of his solicitude for the good of priests is shown by the fact that when Fr. Buela learned that in Ukraine there were many married clergy close to the Institute (some of them even members of the Third Order), he took care that they would not lack what was necessary, given that they also had to support their families. But above all he encouraged them to go to mission places, especially eastern Ukraine, near Russia. Some went, and Fr. Buela supported them with Mass intentions and other monthly aid. Prefects Fr. Buela wanted the major seminarians, “preferably from the Theology years” 168 and, “if possible, [with] one of them a deacon” 169 , to have the experience of serving as prefects during formation. Although the prefects are not formators, Fr. Buela wanted some to have the experience of working side by side, so to speak, with the Superior of the house of formation, not only to organize some activities, to watch over the discipline of the minor seminarians or the novices, and even −in some cases− “to act as an older brother” 170 , but also so that they might learn criteria, the way the formation of young men is carried out in the Institute, so that they might better understand the difficult task of governing, etc. ***** By way of conclusion it seems to us more than fitting to quote here the words of the Founder about the formation he longs for those who are preparing to be priests and missionaries in our Institute. “Well then, we have the aspiration −I do not know whether we will achieve it, but we have the desire− to form young priests who throw down the gauntlet to the Antichrist , that is, who are not only good but who, in addition, pick a fight with evil in the name of Jesus Christ. How can that be achieved? I think it must be with three principal things. The first thing necessary to form priests who throw down the gauntlet to the Antichrist is: Striving for them to be ‘self-motivated.’ It is absolutely necessary to form authentically free priests, not ones who use freedom as an excuse to fall into licentiousness, but who live according to the ‘freedom of the children of God’ (cf. Rom 8:21). Not so that they may be foolish rebels as the world wants them, but so that they may be rebels against the spirit of the world in order to be faithful to God […]. For this it is necessary to teach future priests to think . Nothing is achieved with knowledge held together by pins. Nothing is achieved with a kind of philosophical blah-blah learned by heart as if it were a catechism of first notions. We must form young men who make the effort and have the courage to think, even at the risk of being mistaken, because it is less serious to be mistaken than to be deprived of what distinguishes and constitutes man as such, which is his thinking. […] The second thing necessary to form priests who throw down the gauntlet to the Antichrist is: Forming them so that they are ready to lay down their lives for the sheep. They will be shepherds and they must be so in the image of the Good Shepherd . The Good Shepherd knows his sheep, calls them by name, goes ahead of them; The Good Shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (Jn 10:11). He is not like the hireling shepherd who sees the wolf coming and abandons the sheep, and who lives off their wool, their milk, their meat. He uses the sheep for his own profit, without caring for their good. Today we are fed up with so much nominalist pastoral ministry , desk-bound ministry. Fruitless, sterile, and with the sterility of the incapable. With schools, teacher-training colleges, novitiates, seminaries and universities that are Catholic only in name, in the little sign at the entrance. Because there is no one who lays down his life for the sheep. Never as now have so many meetings of shepherds been seen, such that if Christ came now He would not find us united, but He would certainly find us meeting. Unfortunately, as experience shows: ‘when the shepherds meet, the sheep dies,’ as the Spanish proverb wisely says. It is difficult to form shepherds ready to lay down their lives for the sheep, but the promise of Jesus Christ and the power of the Holy Spirit are at stake. The third thing necessary to form priests who throw down the gauntlet to the Antichrist is: That they be men of deep prayer. Today, more than before, it is absolutely necessary that the priest be a man of true prayer. Only personal contact with the One and Triune God can save him from the trivialization of his priestly life and even from the loss of his priestly identity. The priest who prays is saved; the priest who does not pray is damned. In a particular way he must be the man of Eucharistic prayer. At Mass, acting in persona Christi , he transubstantiates the bread and wine into the Body and Blood of the Lord, thus perpetuating the sacrifice of the cross on our altars. The Mass is the heart of the Catholic priesthood. No other action, not even the most exalted, can be compared to it. It is the most important thing of the day, so much so that the true priest divides the day in two: before Mass, preparing for it, and after Mass, giving thanks for it” 171 . “If the seminaries still fail to form priests of great human, spiritual, intellectual and pastoral stature, if we settle for mediocrities that are even very far from the aurea mediocritas , if every means is used to have young men without lucidity and without courage, if we do not succeed in forming young priests who are poets, contemplatives and warriors, who have a metaphysical intelligence and know how to grasp beauty so as to be capable of dialoguing with and refuting modern culture in what it has that is anti-Christian, when even ‘the traditionalist sector of the clergy,’ which ‘has remained sound in its cultural formation but without the vigor to take a position in the face of modern culture,’ has been sterile in evangelizing the culture” 172 . May Most Holy Mary, always available for the service of her Divine Son and of men for God’s sake, obtain for us the grace of giving the Church shepherds after the Heart of Christ, that is, tireless evangelizers. To the Seminarians of the Seminary of San Rafael, 2017

Talk to the Seminarians of the Mother Mary of the Incarnate Word Seminary [Exordium] Dear all: Since this talk is addressed especially to you, seminarians, I want to tell you that I am very happy to be among you. It gives me great joy to see how Christ’s call bears fruit in your souls. And for that reason I cannot –we cannot– fail to thank the Incarnate Word for the gift of your vocation for our beloved Institute. How can one not rejoice, having before one the promise of future priests, of future missionaries with whom God blesses us? That, first of all. Now then, for this meeting here with you, I thought it would be very profitable to reflect on the importance of our intellectual formation as part of that ‘configuration with Christ’ to which we are called and to which we solemnly committed ourselves on the day of our religious profession. The secret of our formation lies in configuration with Christ. The Venerable Servant of God, Archbishop Fulton Sheen, used to say: “seminarians usually say: ‘I am studying for the priesthood.’ But how often does the seminarian say, or even think: ‘I am studying to be a Priest-Victim’?… And yet, that is precisely what we do. That is what you are doing here in these years of Seminary. And within this process of configuration with Christ, the seminary offers an irreplaceable help, because it is here that the foundations of the future ministry are laid. It is necessary that you, and all those who are in the houses of formation preparing to carry out great works for the glory of God in the missions to which they will be sent, have a very clear grasp of the doctrine of Our Lord, the Truth planted in the mind and in the heart, so as not to be deceived by vain fantasies. The Church and the people expect missionary priests to possess a fervent devotion to the truth 1 . A truth that must be transmitted even at the cost of renunciations and sacrifices, bearing witness to the Truth with one’s own life. Our beloved John Paul II wrote in his book “Rise, Let Us Be on Our Way!”: “One cannot turn one’s back on the truth, stop proclaiming it, hide it […] One must bear witness to the truth, even at the price of being persecuted, even at the cost of one’s blood” 2 . 1. The importance of good formation That is why it seems to me that it is always worthwhile to reflect on the importance of our formation; for it is a reality, a fact, that many aspects of what we will do in the future as religious and missionaries, in the various posts where God calls us to serve Him –whether in the cloister or in mission lands–, will be marked in some way by the seriousness, the integrity, the solidity and the depth of the formation imparted in our classrooms. Because our intellectual formation is imparted with a marked pastoral perspective and “with the intention of disposing them –you, seminarians– to carry out in the future, and competently, the ministries proper to a pastor: preaching, catechesis, teaching, counsel, spiritual direction, the wise discernment of God’s will in the lives of men, etc. This pastoral dimension of study certainly requires particular attention to the problems of today’s world. For the priest must be sensitive to all that happens around him, to the cultural movements of his age, to the currents of thought. Only thus will he be able to illuminate, from Christian revelation, the problems that concern man, bringing the truth that comes from Jesus Christ” 3 . That is why on this occasion I would like briefly to highlight the great importance for our times, because of the heavenly fruits it produces, of the study of the doctrine of St. Thomas, which in the words of Pope Urban V is “true and Catholic” 4 and which “has over all others –added Innocent VI– propriety of words, order in its matters, truth in its judgments, in such a way that those who follow it will never be seen to stray from the path of truth, and whoever attacks it will always be suspected of error” 5 . A doctrine that becomes key when it comes to evangelizing the modern world, and that appears more necessary and timely than ever for the times in which we are given to live. 2. The world we are called to evangelize The world in which we live… The Venerable Servant of God, Archbishop Fulton Sheen, in the prologue of his book “ Religion Without God ” describes with clairvoyance the religious panorama we face today: the religious panorama of the contemporary world. He says there, for example, that in today’s world “the word ‘God’ is still used by certain thinkers, but it is emptied of all its content and becomes diluted and diffuse so that it may be adapted to signify any idea, however volatile, or any kind of insubstantial fantasy”. He characterizes modern thought as a thought in which “God has been dethroned, the heavens have been abandoned and man has been put in the place of God[…]”. Thus the Venerable Archbishop formulated the very thing that our Cornelio Fabro would later denounce systematically and brilliantly in his studies, in his courses and in his books: that is, the primacy of immanence and its baneful consequence, atheism, a world without God. Msgr. Fulton Sheen continues his “description” of our world, saying that: “the problems that once centered on God are now solved in terms of man, and those that once referred to man are now merged with the whole universe. […] God is humanized, and man naturalized. Physical science […] comes to tell us what God is and what man is.” And he goes on to say: “Man now not only imagines himself to be God, but really believes he is beginning to become so. And thus man, raised to this state they call ‘supernatural’, has no need of a redeemer; just as in the natural state he has no need of God. As a result of this philosophy of self-sufficiency there arises the bizarre phenomenon proper to our times, of a religion without God and a Christianity without Jesus Christ”. The general principle implicit in all this is ultimately the denial of the transcendent and the affirmation of the immanent 6 . From which follow the nefarious errors we must live alongside. And thus –says Fr. Alfredo Sáenz– preeminence is given “instead of to God, to man… instead of to the love of God, to love of neighbor… instead of a message of salvation, [one speaks of] a social message… instead of the Cross, of openness to the world… instead of absolute truth, of the truth of the times” 7 , “faith is dissolved into the rational, the sacred becomes profane” 8 , and so there is an attempt to accommodate the Church to the modern world, to group Catholicism with Protestantism; in the end theology and philosophy are confused with sociology and psychology 9 , and there is no longer talk of the slavery of sin, of the reality of hell, etc., all of which is consistent with immanence , since thus, under these presuppositions, as Fr. Cornelio Fabro said, “without hell, existence becomes a picnic” 10 . 3. Our preparation to evangelize the world in which we live Our Proper Law says that it is to this world that God sends us as lambs in the midst of wolves in order to transform “the wolves themselves into lambs” 11 ; to seek and to know how to identify the “seeds of the Word” through which the Holy Spirit continues to act in the heart of man 12 . To be the salt and light of the world 13 . This magnificent undertaking requires of us –who are essentially missionaries– a competent philosophical preparation, which above all gives us “a solid and coherent knowledge of man, of the world and of God” 14 , for it represents “an indispensable help for deepening the understanding of the faith and communicating the truth of the Gospel to all those who do not yet know it” 15 . It is in this sense that our Constitutions stress the urgency of its study 16 , since it is sound philosophy, the metaphysics of being, that gives us a “certainty of the truth”, and “without it there is no basis for a total personal self-giving to Jesus and to the Church, since ‘if one is not sure of the truth, how can we stake our own life and have the strength to challenge seriously the lives of others?’” 17 In our intellectual formation we must imbue ourselves with the Truth, which is nothing other than conforming our mind to the mind, to the criteria of judgment, of the Incarnate Word Himself, and which is a most important part of our ‘configuration with Christ’. From there, “we must proclaim the Gospel with the fervor and enthusiasm of the saints, even in moments of difficulty and persecution in a de-Christianized and atheistic world” 18 , says the Directory of Missions Ad Gentes . And here we see how our intellectual formation has the very greatest importance as preparation for being a Priest-Victim. Therefore, let us strive to acquire what our Proper Law –using an expression of Fr. Cornelio Fabro– calls “essential Thomism”. In such a way that, well imbued with the doctrine of the Angelic Doctor, we may be capable of thinking from him; and, “from him, enter into dialogue and debate with contemporary problems and thinkers” –as our specific end asks of us and our Proper Law commands us–. Only thus will we be able to discern what corresponds to the Gospel, so as to accept it, and what does not, so as to reject it. This obviously entails an active judgment on human thought and on Thomism itself in relation to modern thought 19 . It is not enough to know ‘something’, just like that, superficially. “The lack of an authentically metaphysical intelligence renders pastors of souls incapable of knowing reality, of making precise diagnoses and applying the appropriate remedies. And from there are born formalistic or essentialist ‘spiritualities’ and ‘pastoral approaches’, without grip and without biting into reality. […] To avoid that, a metaphysics with grip is needed, one that bites into reality” 20 . That is why today we are asked that, taking into account the philosophical investigations of modern times, especially those that most influence the life of nations and the progress of the sciences, we come to know well the character of the age in which we are given to live, so as to be prepared for dialogue with our contemporaries 21 . And in this way to seek the solution of human problems in the light of Revelation; and to know how to apply eternal truths to the changing condition of human affairs, and of course, to communicate them in an appropriate way to the souls entrusted to us 22 . That is why today, in what is the Mother House of our beloved Congregation, I would like, by way of conclusion, to quote the wise counsel given in our Directory of Intellectual Formation : “Without the discipline and habit of study, the future priest will not be able to be the wise man according to the Gospel who, in season and out of season, exhorts with the word of God, convinces with the truth and frees from error. The priest is called to be a teacher of the Christian faith and, therefore, must be capable of giving a reason for the faith he preaches and teaches. Dedication to study must be undertaken with this pastoral perspective ” 23 . That is why I told you at the beginning that many aspects of all that we do in the future depend -with the help of God’s grace- on the seriousness, solidity and depth of our formation. The philosophy of St. Thomas is the philosophy of being, that is, of the ‘ actus essendi’ , whose transcendental value is the most direct path for rising to the knowledge of subsistent Being and Pure Act, which is God. And only by rediscovering in its fullness being and the first principles of being and of thinking can man validly ascend to Subsistent Being Itself, his beginning and end, and the supreme guarantor of his inalienable freedom. Let us remember that each one of us is a disciple of Him who one day presented Himself to the disciples saying I am 24 . So we too must be priests, religious and missionaries of ‘being’. This implies: “being pioneers, ready to take the first steps for Christ, to commit oneself totally to God, trusting in His Word, in His power and in His mercy. It also implies being men of transcendence, not confined or trapped in the temporal by the principle of immanence, but rather knowing how to rise through created things, so as to reach also beyond the limited horizons of this world” 25 . It implies launching oneself – with a genuinely Catholic spirit – to help in the needs of the whole Church with a spirit ready to kindle the light of the Gospel everywhere. 26 Let us then implore on this day the Mother of the Incarnate Word, Patroness of this beloved Seminary, for the grace to know how to make the most, with resolute spirit and great fidelity, of all the time we dedicate to our formation. May the Mother of God, who is Teacher by the holiness of her example, educate us with maternal wisdom to configure our lives to that of the Incarnate Word. Thank you very much! May God bless you all. “The Theological Virtues in Relation to the Threefold Priestly Function”

Conference for the Seminarians of the “St. Vitalian, Pope” Seminary April 20, 2018 [Introduction] I thank the Father Rector for the invitation and all of you for allowing me to spend this day with you, which is truly very consoling for me. At Holy Mass a moment ago we were saying how preparation for the priesthood necessarily implies a configuration to Christ the Priest, which is brought about through the practice and purification of the theological virtues. All of which implies “living according to an infused reality.” For once the glorious day arrives when you are ordained priests, from then on you will be “representatives of Christ the head, charged by Christ himself with continuing his presence and saving work in the Church and in the world with his threefold office of sanctifying, teaching and shepherding” 1 . That is why the Second Vatican Council, in its decree Optatam Totius , says that the preparation of seminarians “must aim at the formation of true shepherds of souls, after the example of our Lord Jesus Christ, priest, teacher and shepherd” 2 . So, if you will allow me, I would like to make here a concrete application of the theological virtues in relation to the threefold priestly function of sanctifying, teaching and shepherding. For the office of sanctifying oneself is directly related to the theological virtue of charity, the office of teaching to that of faith, and likewise the office of shepherding to the virtue of hope. And in this way to highlight even more the importance of the exercise of our theological life in the soul in correspondence with our priestly vocation. 1. Sanctifying – The theological virtue of Charity Our Constitutions point out as our specific end the attainment of the perfection of charity 3 . And if this applies to any religious of the Institute, whether lay brother, monk or novice, all the more does it apply to those who are preparing for the august priestly ministry. Because, once again, do not the Constitutions also tell us that “the priest is the man of charity” 4 ? The Magisterium of the Church affirms: “‘The new evangelization needs new evangelizers, and these are the priests who commit themselves to living their priesthood as a specific path toward holiness’ 5 . But already now it is of fundamental importance that each one discover every day the absolute necessity of his personal holiness. Therefore, it is imperative that “the spiritual formation of the future priest include the practice of charity, which is the bond of perfection” 6 . “In particular a preferential love for the poor, in whom Christ is present in a special way, and a merciful love full of compassion for sinners” 7 . You already have this; it is a matter, then, of knowing how to make the most of that opportunity –with all its crosses, difficulties, and also great spiritual joys– to sanctify oneself and imitate Christ. Because if we do all that we do but do not have charity, what good is it to us? Look, this is so important that St. Gregory warns: “he who does not have charity toward another must absolutely not exercise the ministry of preaching” 8 . A charity that should lead us to be able to say together with St. Paul: Although we could have imposed our authority as apostles of Christ, we were gentle among you, like a mother who tenderly cares for her children 9 ; the love of a father ready to give his life for his children: So, loving you, we wanted to share with you not only the Gospel of God but even our very selves, because you had become very dear to us 10 ” 11 . “Such is the love that the Lord expects of every preacher of the Gospel, of every builder of the Church,” the Directory of Missions Ad Gentes very aptly points out 12 . We do not perform a job like civil servants, we do not climb the ranks; we are called to serve like Christ himself, who became a servant. That is why ours “is not command, nor honors, but total self-giving to the service of God and to pastoral ministry” 13 . We must be driven by love 14 , by the theological virtue of charity, which goes beyond natural aims and self-satisfaction; simply because supernatural love is sacrificial, as Ven. Archbishop Fulton Sheen used to say. It is, then, a love that knows how to rise above one’s own tastes, that knows how “to renounce oneself for the good of others” 15 , that knows how to conform one’s own will to the Will of God and knows how to see in those things which seem bad and adverse to our nature and which give no pleasure, what is best for the soul, because God so orders it, who wills our good and only our good, and because it recognizes that it is always more profitable to go on annihilating oneself 16 , as St. John of the Cross says. But above all, this supernatural love does not go about seeking consolation or pleasure, either in God or in anything else; rather, all its care is directed to seeing how it can give God some pleasure and serve him in something 17 . A sign of this love will be to dedicate oneself without reserve and without looking back to the proclamation of Jesus Christ 18 . Without high-handedness, without arrogance, without trampling over others, but rather kindly, and always with courage, with enthusiasm and very great fatherly patience; all of it wrapped in serene joy. Blessed Paolo Manna told his religious, and today I want to tell you here: “what most often opens the way to the faith is not the eloquence and erudition of the Missionary but his charity. A Missionary may be as learned as you like; if he is harsh, cold, dry and reserved, if he does not deign to deal with children, with savages, he will not do much good. The pariah, the poor Chinese, and whatever souls stand before us are better attracted by goodness than by the prestige of authority and of preaching. Even though conversions take place for one of these reasons, it is afterward always the personal goodness of the Missionary that wins the heart and attaches the convert to the faith and to Jesus Christ, whose superhuman image he sees in the missionary” 19 . We have to understand that only the charity of Christ will save the world. It is not our programs, it is not our methods, it is not our wisdom; it is only the charity of Christ that will save the world. In a thousand ways our Proper Law exemplifies and specifies this practice of charity –which, if you agree, it would be good, very good!, to devote yourselves to reading carefully. Today I would simply like to emphasize two of them: the celebration of the Eucharist (where precisely the source of this supernatural charity we have been speaking of is found) and our charity particularly toward those whom –generally speaking– we will always have at our side: our brother priests. Regarding the Eucharist: always remember that the principal reason for the ordained priesthood is the celebration of the Eucharist. The priest is in a certain sense “by it and for it” 20 . If the Eucharist does not become the center and root of your lives, you will never be able to fulfill yourselves fully as priests, and you will go about seeking loves and consolations in empty and cracked cisterns 21 . No work we carry out as priests is as important as the Mass. Indeed, the celebration of the Eucharist is the best way of serving our brothers and sisters in the world, because it is the source and center of the dynamism of their lives. How crucial it is, therefore, for our happiness and for a fruitful ministry, that we cultivate a deep love for the Eucharist. Now, during your time in the seminary, through the theological study of the nature of the eucharistic mystery and a good knowledge of the liturgical norms, so as to prepare yourselves well to promote a full, conscious and active participation in the liturgy. Our Proper Law itself says it several times: “the celebration of the Eucharist is of essential importance in the spiritual formation of seminarians” 22 ; and it must be “the center of the life of the Seminary” 23 , because that is the fountain from which we drink the charity of the Incarnate Word, which is what gives us strength for daily self-giving, now and later in priestly life. Bear in mind also that the “worthy celebration of Holy Mass” 24 is one of the non-negotiable elements attached to our charism. Therefore, you must prepare yourselves as men who are going to be masters of the ars celebrandi , because it is there that one learns to love God more, offering oneself unblemished to God 25 . Notice that all “the other sacraments, as well as all ecclesiastical ministries and works of the apostolate, are closely bound up with the Holy Eucharist and are directed toward it. For in the Most Holy Eucharist is contained the whole spiritual good of the Church, namely, Christ himself” 26 . The Eucharist is like the source and summit of all evangelization, and from it ardent love for souls is nourished. In the Eucharist one understands that every participation in the priesthood of Christ has a universal dimension, and our readiness to go and proclaim him to all nations 27 keeps growing wider . That is why today I also want to make a request of you: “May love for Christ present in the Eucharist grow, thanks to our apostolic work.” Regarding our charity toward our brother priests: our Proper Law commands this of us when it says that among priests there must be an intimate fraternity, which “must be shown in spontaneous and willing mutual help, spiritual as well as material, pastoral as well as personal…” 28 . “Our brothers in the presbyterate must also be a privileged object of the priest’s pastoral charity. To help them materially and spiritually, to make confession and spiritual direction delicately easy for them, to make the path of service pleasant for them, to be close to them in every need, to accompany them with fraternal solicitude in any difficulty, in old age, in sickness…”. 2. Teaching – The theological virtue of Faith The Directory of Major Seminaries says it clearly: “Before the mystery of the ministerial priesthood, intimately united to the mystery of Christ and of the Church, there remains only the response of faith. Without it nothing is understood” 29 . “Only the man of faith can understand the reality of the priesthood and what pertains to the priesthood” 30 . Hence the mystery of the Catholic priesthood can only be discovered with a deeply contemplative attitude, with a contemplation made life, and with the study of theology made contemplation. That is why it is so important that you acquire a great supernatural sense of your existence, that you nourish this faith, strengthen it every day and defend it. You must be “professionals of the faith; the specialists of God” 31 , as John Paul the Great called priests. As future priests you must know that you have been called to be teachers of the faith, and therefore you must be able, already now, to give an account of the faith that you will preach and teach. This highlights the importance of study, aimed not only at the acquisition of knowledge, but as a complementary part of our vocation. Faith must become the “new criterion for judging and evaluating people and things, events and problems” 32 . Therefore, one must not be content with a number of ideas pinned loosely in one’s head, but must have well-founded truths, by which one lives and for which one is capable of giving one’s life if necessary; one must be well and solidly formed in right thinking. In this one must demand the utmost of oneself; one cannot improvise, one cannot neglect intellectual formation. To do so would be to be negligent in pastoral work and to betray the commitment made to Christ. Because without the discipline and habit of study, the future priest will not be able to be the wise man according to the Gospel who, in season and out of season, exhorts with the word of God, convinces with the truth and frees from error. Souls hope to have solid certainties, words that do not pass away, absolute values. God is the only certainty; He is the Absolute who has manifested himself in the Incarnate Word. Now pay attention to this: our Proper Law points out that you must be formed in such a way that you “are forewarned especially against the errors of ‘theological progressivism,’ which seeks a false understanding of the faith through a lack of criticism and discernment in the face of modern philosophies and through the assimilation of the principle of immanence” 33 . Hence it is imperative that you, our seminarians, make the most of the richness of the formation offered to you, which allows you “to know the mystery of Christ, while at the same time preparing you so that, God willing, you may be able to proclaim the Gospel” 34 with complete fidelity. St. John Bosco used to say: “after piety, what must be most recommended is study” 35 , because every hour of study has repercussions tomorrow in the apostolate. Here we see, then, that dedication to study must always be undertaken with a pastoral perspective, which can never be dissociated from the problems of today’s world. The Magisterium of the Church and our Proper Law itself repeat it to us over and over: it is indispensable for evangelizing the culture 36 that “the priest be sensitive to all that happens around him, to the cultural movements of the age, to the currents of thought. Only thus will the problems that concern man be illuminated by Christian revelation, bringing the truth that comes from Jesus Christ” 37 . This is what we mean, in a few words, by “biting into reality.” To evangelize means, in fact, to proclaim and spread, by all the honest and suitable means available, the contents of the revealed truths (Trinitarian and Christological faith; the meaning of the dogma of creation; the eschatological truths; the doctrine on the Church, on man; the teaching of faith on the sacraments and the other means of salvation; etc.). And it also means, at the same time, teaching how to translate those truths into concrete life, into witness and missionary commitment 38 . We must, then, undertake with all enthusiasm and all solicitude the wonderful “work of ‘intellectual charity’ through a permanent and patient catechesis on the fundamental truths of Catholic faith and morals and their influence on the spiritual life” 39 , in imitation of Christ the Teacher. St. Gregory affirmed that the priest is especially appointed by God to teach the right way to him who has gone astray; and that is why St. Leo adds that the priest who does not point out to the faithful their straying shows that he himself has gone astray”. From which it follows that the office of teaching, the task of preaching, is unavoidable for the priest. And if this is true for every priest, it is even more so for us as members of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, who are commanded “to be impatient to preach the Word in every form ” 40 . “Faith comes from the message, and the message consists in speaking of Christ, says St. Paul. So you must be fervent and diligent in acquiring a profound knowledge of the Word of God, as it is lived and proclaimed in the Church. And if you want your preaching tomorrow to bear fruit in the lives of those whom you will serve, you must cultivate in mind and heart a real interior adherence to the Magisterium of the Church” 41 . Notice that without faith we do not even set out on mission; without faith our strength fails and we want to skimp on our self-giving, or one may even wish to abandon the mission post; without faith we can fall into the temptation of carrying out our offices or the mission itself as earthly business is carried out, that is, with exclusively human outlooks and methods: relying too much on earthly means and on our own skill and energy, setting aside trust in Divine Providence. On the other hand, he who has faith not only commits himself to going to the most difficult assignments 42 but does not complain about doing mission in the most difficult situations and under the most adverse conditions 43 . What is more, he remains faithful even “without being able to have a tabernacle and an image of Our Lady,” or having to spend some time alone, and even so he has apostolic initiatives! For that, my dear seminarians, faith is needed! So, if you want to live and remain at the height of your vocation, you must constantly nourish yourselves with this spirit of faith, being enlightened and set on fire by meditation on Scripture and by praying well. We are instruments of God, and from Him we must receive, through continual prayer and the reception of the sacraments, the grace we need for our ministry, without which we can do nothing with regard to the eternal salvation of our souls and of those entrusted to us. Consequently, “an aspect, certainly not secondary, of the priest’s mission is that of being teachers of prayer” 44 . From this it follows that an intellectual knowledge of Christ alone is not enough: one must learn from Him! One must bear witness to the faith we profess! Hence the task of becoming familiar with his Divine Person and his plan of salvation is unavoidable; one must be steeped in the very sentiments of Christ, and in some way evangelize oneself by acquiring his criteria of judgment. Jesus Christ must be the center of our thoughts, the theme of our words, and everyone must recognize that He is the reason for our life. And if the Incarnate Word is the object of our love, every initiative must draw its vigor from Him. Each one of us must embrace the ideal of the Incarnate Word as life itself, in such a way that if we were to fall dead, we would die embracing Him. That is why these years of doctrinal preparation must also find nourishment in a solid spiritual life 45 . Blessed Paolo Manna has some masterly lines on this, which, if you will allow me, I would like to share with you today. He says: “The missionary is par excellence a man of faith: he is born of faith, he lives by faith, for it he works gladly, suffers gladly, suffers and dies. The Missionary who is not this is, at most, an apprentice of the apostolate” 46 . And he goes on to say: “the fervor of a Missionary’s life, his controlled, wise, industrious, tireless activity, his unalterable joy and his perseverance in work, even amid privations, calamities and difficulties, are always the result of a life of faith . If faith grows dim, zeal too diminishes in intensity; then, even in the strongest, weariness and depression appear, and one may come even to despair and the loss of one’s vocation. If the Missionary lives by faith, then he is great, he is sublime, he is divine; the Church and souls can hope for everything from him; no labor, no difficulty frightens him, no heroism is beyond his strength; if the spirit of faith in him is languid and weak, he will bustle about, he will nevertheless work, but his toils will profit him little or nothing, and the poor success of his half-hearted works will increase his distrust and depression” 47 . I told you so in a circular letter: “Without faith, no one sacrifices himself willingly in the missions. It is through faith, through deep convictions and great love for the Incarnate Word, that the heroic deeds of the Cross are then carried out” 48 . 3. Shepherding – The theological virtue of hope There is a phrase in our Proper Law that I particularly love, because, speaking of us as missionaries, it says: “People are needed who will present the fatherly face of God and the motherly face of the Church, who will stake their lives so that others may have life and hope ” 49 . This phrase condenses, so to speak, what we have been talking about until now, but it also adds that note of eternity: hope. So characteristic of our Lord’s style of shepherding… instilling hope, encouraging, raising people above natural outlooks. We as missionary priests are sent into a world anguished and oppressed by thousands of problems, but right there, in those circumstances which so often pull toward pessimism, we must give our lives to proclaim the ‘Good News’ and bear witness with our own lives that we have found true hope in Christ 50 . That is why everything we do, everything we suffer, must be wrapped in that special grace which is the victorious hope that Christ won for us. An author, in one of his definitions of the priesthood, says that “the priest is a beacon of hope in the midst of so much darkness and storm” 51 . You here now in the Seminary are preparing yourselves “specifically to communicate the charity of Christ, the Good Shepherd” 52 , “who watches over, shepherds and evangelizes; who knows how to suffer in silence and knows how to give his life for his sheep” 53 . That is the goal of the whole formative process with a view to priestly ordination: to form shepherds of souls 54 , full communion with the pastoral charity of Jesus Christ 55 . Or as our Constitutions magnificently say: “to form for the Catholic Church priests according to the heart of Christ” 56 . This tells us plainly that “pastoral work cannot be reduced, even in the best of cases, to a competent science or a truly technical practice.” “To be formed for the priesthood is to learn primarily from the pastoral charity of Christ; it is to prepare oneself, out of love for Christ, to shepherd his flock” 57 . And that is why “the virtues related to others” must be required of you, that is, that ‘they not be arrogant or quarrelsome, but affable, hospitable, sincere in their words and in their heart, prudent and discreet, generous and available for service, capable of personally offering and of fostering in everyone loyal and fraternal relationships, ready to understand, forgive and console” 58 . That on the one hand. But on the other hand you must also “take on your responsibilities in a conscious and mature way, form the interior habit of evaluating problems and establishing priorities and the means of solving them, always grounded in clear motivations of faith and according to the theological requirements of pastoral work itself” 59 . How consoling it is to see a religious who lives moved by pastoral charity as the total gift of himself for the salvation of others 60 , who has apostolic zeal, who manages things in such a way that no one leaves him without being persuaded that he truly seeks the supernatural good of his soul, who is lavish in pastoral initiatives, and who, amid difficulties, knows how to maintain serene trust in God, which undoubtedly springs from the hope that beats in his soul! At this point I would like to cite the example of Fr. Ciszek –an American Jesuit priest– because it seems to me that his experience sums up in some way all that I would like to tell you on this point, especially when hope is tested. As a seminarian, Fr. Ciszek volunteered to go to the Russian missions after Pope Pius XI wrote a special letter to the Jesuits telling them that he had opened a seminary to prepare young priests for the mission in Russia. After he was ordained they did not send him to Russia, but to Poland. He was there when the Germans invaded the country in 1939 and during the deportation that followed. Fr. Ciszek, passing himself off as a laborer, went with the refugees in the hope of being able to serve them spiritually. But soon the Soviet secret police discovered him and sent him to prison. He spent 5 years imprisoned in Lubyanka; afterward he was sentenced to 15 years of forced labor in the prison camps of Siberia. They put him to work in outdoor construction in extreme arctic cold, and he also worked in coal mines, poorly clothed, poorly fed and housed in miserable conditions in barracks fenced with barbed wire. He himself bears witness to how men died, especially those who abandoned hope. When the 15 years were over, he went on living in small Siberian towns, because he could not leave Siberia nor even go to the main cities of Russia. So he worked as a mechanic and at other trades of that kind, until the American government exchanged him –in 1963– for two Russian spies. Regarding his experience in Lubyanka, and after recounting the inhuman situation in which he lived and the injustice of having been imprisoned without reason, and detailing how in prison he was despised precisely for being a priest, he writes –pay attention–: “No situation is without value or meaning in divine providence. It is a very human temptation to feel frustrated by circumstances, to feel overwhelmed and helpless before the established order, whether it be a prison, or the Soviet system as a whole, or this whole oppressive and rotten world! In the worst circumstances imaginable, man is still man, endowed with a free will, and God is always ready to help him with his grace. What is more, God expects him to act in those circumstances, in that situation, as He wants him to act. Because those situations, those people, those places and those things too are what God wills for him at that moment. It may not be in his power to change the ‘system,’ just as it was not in mine to change the conditions of the prison, but that is no excuse for failing to act. Many men feel frustrated, or discouraged, or even defeated when they find themselves facing a situation or an evil against which they can do little. Poverty, social injustice, hatred and resentment, war, corruption and the oppressive bureaucracy of institutions (and each of us could add something to the list): all of it can generate a bitter frustration and, at times, a feeling of utter hopelessness. But God does not expect any man to change the world by himself, to put an end to all evils or cure all diseases. What He does expect of him is that he act as He wants him to in the circumstances arranged by his will and his providence . To act in this way he will not lack the help of divine grace. The feeling of hopelessness that we all experience in circumstances like these is really born of our tendency to bring too much of our self into the picture. […] We tend to concentrate on ourselves, to think about what we can or cannot do, and we forget God, his will and his providence. God, however, never forgets the importance of each one, his dignity and his worth, and the role He asks us to play in the work of providence. To God, every individual is equally important at every moment. We do matter to Him. But He also expects each of us to accept, as coming from his hands, the daily situations He sends us, and to act as He wants us to act, with the grace He grants us for it” 61 . Consider that the man who writes this was deprived of all external support: of his family, of his fellow Jesuits, of the visible Church… not even his basic needs were minimally met. That is the hope we must have, an invincible hope, which neither the most adverse situations nor the most lacerating trials can succeed in bending. “In life there are no difficulties, there are only circumstances. God guides everything, and He guides everything well. There is nothing to do but abandon oneself, and serve at every moment as far as possible” 62 . That is the hope we must have! Trust in Jesus even in your discouragements, even when body or spirit are reduced to helplessness and refuse to cooperate. Keep your trust fixed on God, for He looks upon you with ineffable love. It is true that at times God is pleased to multiply difficulties; He halts us and nails us down in helplessness. One would like to, but one cannot. But when one takes a step and prays, God comes and gives wings to keep moving forward 63 . So: take heart! Jesus does not deceive us. He is God-with-us, the faithful love that does not abandon us and that knows how to transform our nights into dawns of hope. Always trust in Him and distrust yourselves; a grace I wish you now and always. Much more could be said on this point, but it would make this even longer. [Conclusion] Simply, as a final thought, I want to leave you a piece of advice from the book “ Sacerdotes para siempre” . “One must begin by purifying oneself before purifying others; one must be instructed in order to be able to instruct; one must become light in order to illuminate, draw near to God in order to draw others near to Him, become holy in order to sanctify” 64 . This takes concrete form in the pursuit of a deep unity of life, which leads the priest –the seminarian, we could say here– to strive to be, to live and to serve as another Christ in all the circumstances of life. The faithful of the parish, or those who take part in the various pastoral activities, see –they observe!– and hear –they listen!– not only when the Word of God is preached, but also when the various liturgical acts are celebrated, in particular Holy Mass; when they are received in the parish office, where they hope to be attended to with cordiality and kindness; 65 when they see the priest eating or resting, and are edified by his example of sobriety and temperance; when they go to look for him at his house, and rejoice at the priestly simplicity and poverty in which he lives; 66 when they see him neatly wearing his own habit, when they talk with him, even about unimportant things, and feel comforted on finding his supernatural outlook, his tact and the human refinement with which he treats even the humblest people, with authentic priestly nobility. ‘The grace and charity of the altar thus spread to the ambo, to the confessional, to the parish archive, to the school, to youth activities, to homes and to the streets, to hospitals, to means of transport and to the media of social communication, wherever the priest has the opportunity to carry out his task as shepherd: in every case it is his Mass that extends itself, it is his spiritual union with Christ, Priest and Victim, that leads him to be –as St. Ignatius of Antioch said– the wheat of God, that he may be found the pure bread of Christ , 67 for the good of his brothers 68 . It only remains for me to encourage you in this race to reach Christ. Realize that He has already reached you first. Let yourselves be formed by Him. Love without reserve the Church, our beloved Institute and our Most Holy Mother. May She, the Mother of Christ the Priest, educate you with her maternal love, so that in you may be formed the true image of her Son. To the most pure Virgin I commend each one of you very specially, individually, with all your needs, with all your longings. May Our Lady always keep you. I wish you this with all my affection. Thank you very much for your attention. May God bless you and make you holy missionary priests. Truly, thank you. Notes 1 Directory of Major Seminaries , 2; op. cit. Optatam Totius , Preface. 2 Cf.
