Talk to the Members of the Third Order in Argentina

First of all, I would like to tell you that it is a great joy for me to be among you, to see so many faces that are familiar to me and, in short, to be able to thank you in person for everything you do for us. Even if my words fall short, know that everything you do is a great help and an extremely important contribution to our missionary work. And without a doubt it is a very edifying example of charity that you always give us St. John Paul II said that the “believer widens the borders of his charity, showing concern for those who are far away as well as for those who are near; praying for the missions and for missionary vocations, following their activities with interest and, when they return, welcoming them with that same joy with which the first Christian communities heard from the apostles the marvels that God had worked through their preaching” 1 . Well, know that many… very many of our religious bear witness that this is precisely what the members of the Third Order in Argentina do. And in their name, and personally as well, truly, I thank you infinitely. And a ‘double thank you’ to those who have ‘made a greater offering’ and have offered their children to God to work for the spread of his Kingdom. I see here present many parents and relatives of our religious. It is truly a great joy to have you here. One feels at home with family, because that is in reality what we are, isn’t it? As the Directory of the Third Order says: “a single family, united by the same faith, the same ends, the same mission, the same charism, the same character and the same spirit” 2 . Introduction Today, if you will allow me, I would like to speak to you about the special dignity and mission entrusted to you, lay people of the Third Order of the Incarnate Word, in the Church and in our religious family. These are perhaps very well-known and very elementary points, but, after all, it is always good to recall them, since they are also, in the end, very profound realities. St. Peter says that Christians are a royal priesthood, a holy nation (1 Pet 2:9). All Christians, incorporated into Christ and into his Church through baptism, are consecrated to God. They are called to profess the faith they have received. Moreover, as all of you know, through the sacrament of confirmation you have also been endowed by the Holy Spirit with a special strength to be witnesses of Christ and sharers in his saving mission. Therefore each one of you is, consequently, an extraordinary work of the grace of God and is called to the highest summits of holiness. At times it can happen that lay people do not fully appreciate the dignity and vocation that is proper to them as lay people. Each one of you, members of the Third Order of the Institute, is called to become holy and to sanctify the whole world from within your own lay condition 3 . This implies that you are called to play a very important role in the evangelization of the world. Yes, you, the lay people of the Third Order of the Incarnate Word, are a chosen race, a holy priesthood , called also to be the salt of the earth and the light of the world . Your specific vocation and mission consists in manifesting the Gospel in your lives and, therefore, in introducing the Gospel, like leaven, into the reality of the world in which you live and work. That is why the Proper Law says that our tertiaries must seek “to order temporal affairs according to God 4 , restoring all things in Jesus Christ 5 , making Christ manifest to others, primarily through the witness of life, the radiance of faith, hope and charity, illuminating the temporal realities with which it is closely bound up” 6 . The great forces that shape the world (politics, the media, science, technology, culture, education, industry) are precisely the areas in which you are especially competent to exercise your mission. You know well that if these forces are led by people who are true disciples of Christ and, at the same time, fully competent in secular knowledge and science, then the world will certainly be transformed from within by the redeeming power of Christ 7 . In this sense, it is good that you become aware that your role in the mission is of such importance that the mission could never be properly carried out without you. Inculturating the Gospel “We must bring it about that Christ reigns in the whole world, in all cultures and in the hearts of men” 8 , –that is the commitment you have taken on as Tertiaries: to work with all your strength to inculturate the Gospel 9 –. So it is good to remember that “in order not to go astray in this task so proper to us, one must know, study and go deeper into the Social Doctrine of the Church,” and that is why it is “indispensable that this doctrine be assimilated and brought into social reality in the forms and to the extent that circumstances permit or demand,” whether in the education of one’s children, or at work, in whatever environment one moves in (and if one no longer works, or is sick, or whatever it may be, well, then to pray and to know how to offer one’s sufferings and daily routine so that the kingdom of Christ may spread). I know that there are many among you who are very committed to the decidedly Christian task of permeating society with the leaven of the Gospel. In this sense, the Directory of the Third Order says explicitly: “We must never forget that we must transform reality from within , evangelizing the culture and not culturizing the Gospel ; everything that is redeemable must be used for good” 10 . Means In this regard, what does this ‘from within’ mean? Mainly it means through an “ authentic witness of Christian life ,” which unfailingly implies a life of grace. It implies that our tertiaries “speak and act by example, that they be known by others for the effective practice of the Christian virtues, [simply] because they carry Jesus and Mary in their blood, and know that words move, but examples draw ” 11 . That is to say, there must be consistency of life between the faith one professes and the way one lives. It is not enough to have a son or daughter who is a religious; each one of you has to pray and become holy and go to confession. You cannot imagine the strength and encouragement toward holiness that the example you give represents for others, even for the religious themselves. How many of ours find in the silent sacrifice of their parents, in the supernatural outlook of their mother, in the self-denial of their sister or brother, a concrete encouragement to practice virtue, to persevere in hard times, to dispose themselves magnanimously to carry out a work simply because they learned it from their father; to be compassionate before the needs of others because that was the example they received from their parents… Always keep that in mind. What you do has effects that go beyond the limits of the home, of work, of the little room you clean or in which you study… they are examples that have an impact on the lives of many. If not, think of the example of St. Thérèse’s parents. Two years ago, in October 2015, the Pope canonized them. In her autobiography the saint –today Patroness of the Missions, Doctor of the Church, and the greatest saint of modern times 12 – wrote: “As I had nothing but good examples around me, I naturally wanted to follow them.” St. Thérèse’s father was a watchmaker and her mother a lacemaker. So that you may see the magnitude and the lasting effects of the authentic witness of Christian life. And on the other hand, there are also the concrete works of apostolate , in which I know so many of you are involved and for which we will never thank you enough… I think of those who help so much in the hogarcitos, during the youth days, the camps, the spiritual exercises; those who, according to their various abilities, give invaluable collaboration to our Religious Family; the many of you who support these works with your prayers and sacrifices and material donations too… All these things, concrete apostolates carried out in union with God, while giving at every moment, whatever environment one finds oneself in, a consistent witness of Christian life, are a contribution, an effective collaboration in the cause of Christ, which is to illuminate every man, the whole man and all human realities with the light of the Gospel in one’s own environment. To achieve this end, I would like to point out to you… really, more than anything, to remind you in a specific and concrete way of some means in which the members of our Third Order should distinguish themselves and which they should make use of. There are nine, and all are taken from the Magisterium of the Second Vatican Council: (And, if you allow me, I would like to develop these points very briefly following the Magisterium of the Church, interspersing it with some texts from our Directory of the Third Order). 1. The laity do not exercise hierarchical religious activities, but they participate directly in the liturgy of the Church « Holy Mother Church earnestly desires that all the faithful be led to that full, conscious and active participation in liturgical celebrations which is demanded by the very nature of the liturgy, and to which the Christian people, a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a purchased people (1 Pet 2:9; 2:45), have a right and an obligation by reason of their baptism » 13 . Therefore, participation in Holy Mass in an ever more conscious and fruitful way is essential, « because it is the primary and indispensable source from which the faithful are to derive the true Christian spirit » 14 . 2. The laity, through their sanctification, impress a Christian character on all the activities of their life If each one of you sanctifies his life as belonging to the Church, the Mystical Body of Christ, requires of him, he also sanctifies all the activities of his life, and life itself, private and public 15 , said Pope Pius XII. 3. Each one of you, by virtue of being a lay person, can and must exercise the common apostolate As we already mentioned before: « The apostolate of the laity is a participation in the saving mission of the Church itself, an apostolate to which all are commissioned by the Lord himself through baptism and confirmation. And the sacraments, especially the Holy Eucharist, communicate and nourish that love toward God and toward men which is the soul of the entire apostolate » 16 . That is why the Directory says: “the laity, ‘moved by the charity that comes from Christ, do good’ 17 .” Because love of Christ cannot be separated from love of neighbor. « The laity are especially called to make the Church present and operative in those places and circumstances where only through them can she become the salt of the earth. Thus every lay person, by virtue of the gifts bestowed upon him, is at once a witness and a living instrument of the mission of the Church herself, according to the measure of Christ’s gift (Eph 4:7) » 18 . Now, it is important to keep in mind that “within the love of God, and also as the basis of all apostolic action, the tertiary must stand out for the faithful and perfect fulfillment of the duties of his state. It is impossible to build any apostolic work unless it is founded on one’s first obligations, faithfully and legitimately fulfilled” 19 . 4. The laity, by virtue of the apostolate, can exercise the mandated apostolate of Catholic Action « Besides this apostolate, which pertains to absolutely all Christians, the laity can also be called in various ways to a more immediate cooperation with the apostolate of the Hierarchy, like those men and women who helped the apostle Paul in evangelization, laboring much in the Lord (cf. Phil 4:3; Rom 16:3ff). Furthermore, they have the capacity to be appointed by the Hierarchy to certain ecclesiastical offices. Which they are to carry out for a spiritual purpose » 20 . 5. The laity must sanctify or Christianize, immediately and directly, married and family life « In it –in married and family life– the apostolate of the laity finds an opportunity for exercise and an excellent school if the Christian religion permeates the whole organization of life and transforms it more each day. Here the spouses have their own vocation: to be witnesses of faith and of Christ’s love to one another and to their children. The Christian family loudly proclaims both the present virtues of the kingdom of God and the hope of a blessed life. Thus by its example and its witness it convicts the world of sin and enlightens those who seek the truth » 21 . The Directory of the Third Order abounds in examples and guidelines that can serve very well as a guide as to how to Christianize married and family life. I will simply mention a few examples: forming oneself in a Christian way, knowing, loving and proclaiming the doctrine of the Church 22 ; forming families that are true apostolic nuclei, that foster works of charity, that help other married couples in need 23 , for example; seeking a solid Catholic education for one’s children, and many other examples that you yourselves can add… 6. The laity must sanctify and Christianize, directly and immediately, economic life in its various aspects a) the use of private property; b) the management of small, medium and large enterprises in the agricultural, commercial and industrial sectors; c) efficiency and the meaning of work; d) the exercise of the various professions Vatican II strongly points out the need for the lay person to fully assume his responsibility as one baptized, that is to say, his condition as a sharer « in the priestly, prophetic and kingly office of Jesus Christ », so that, just as through Jesus Christ, the great Prophet, the Kingdom of the Father was proclaimed, so too, « through the laity », « the power of the Gospel may shine forth in daily, family and social life » 24 . Each one must do with zeal what he has to do in his chosen profession, “in order afterwards to face, with competence and in a spirit of evangelical detachment, the burden and the joys of the social responsibilities toward which Providence may direct them” 25 , for which there is undoubtedly need of a serious spiritual life, which makes them see what they do as a collaboration for the kingdom of Christ, so as to discern what the Will of God is, etc. 7. The laity must sanctify and Christianize, directly and immediately, the different manifestations of culture a) letters; b) education; c) the arts; d) the experimental sciences; e) technology; f) the sciences of the spirit; g) philosophy Lumen Gentium says: « Even in secular occupations they must help one another toward a holier life, in such a way that the world may be permeated with the spirit of Christ and may more effectively attain its end in justice, in charity and in peace. In the fulfillment of this universal duty, the laity hold the most prominent place. Therefore, by their competence in secular affairs and by their activity, elevated from within by the grace of Christ, let them contribute effectively so that created goods, in accordance with the design of the Creator and the enlightenment of His Word, may be promoted by human labor, technology and civil culture for the benefit of all men without exception; may be more fittingly distributed among them; and may in their own way lead to universal progress in human and Christian freedom. Thus Christ, through the members of the Church, will increasingly illumine the whole of human society with His saving light » 26 . « Likewise, let the laity coordinate their forces to remedy the structures and conditions of the world when they incite to sin, so that all these things may be conformed to the norms of justice and may favor rather than hinder the practice of the virtues. By acting in this way, they will imbue culture and human works with moral value. By this manner of acting, the field of the world is at the same time better prepared for the sowing of the divine word, and the doors through which to bring the message of peace into the world are opened wider to the Church » 27 . I know there are many among you who already do this. Know that you are a source of pride for us, and I encourage you to keep doing it. 8. The laity must sanctify and Christianize, directly and immediately, civic and political activities, at the municipal, civic, national and international levels Our Directory , quoting St. John Paul II, says: “the lay faithful can in no way abdicate their participation in politics; that is, in the many different economic, social, legislative, administrative and cultural activities which are intended to promote the common good organically and institutionally… the lay faithful must promote a widespread educational effort, aimed at overcoming the prevailing culture of selfishness, hatred, revenge and enmity, and at developing the culture of solidarity at every level” 28 . 9. The laity must have as the direct and immediate mission of their lay state the Consecration of the World to Jesus Christ « For those whom He intimately joins to His life and mission, He also makes sharers in His priestly office, so that they may offer spiritual worship for the glory of God and the salvation of men. Therefore the laity, as consecrated to Christ and anointed by the Holy Spirit, are marvelously called and equipped so that ever more abundant fruits of the Spirit may be produced in them. For all their works, their prayers and apostolic initiatives, their married and family life, their daily work, their rest of soul and body, if they are done in the Spirit, and even the very trials of life if they are patiently borne, become spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ (cf. 1 Pet 2:5), which in the celebration of the Eucharist are most devoutly offered to the Father together with the oblation of the Lord’s body. In this way the laity too, as worshippers acting in a holy manner everywhere, consecrate the world itself to God » 29 . And to conclude and to clarify the depth of this consecration of the world to God, nothing is more fitting than the words of Paul VI on August 18, 1965 30 : « The development of modern culture has recognized the legitimate and just distinction between the various fields of human activity, giving to each of them a relative autonomy, demanded by the constitutive principles and ends of each field, so that each science, profession and art has its relative independence, which separates it from the properly religious sphere and confers on it a certain “laicism” which, rightly understood, the Christian is the first to respect, without confusing, as they say, the sacred with the profane. But wherever this field of activity concerns man, considered in his integrity, that is, in accordance with his supreme end, all can and must honor and be honored by the religious light that illumines that supreme end and makes its attainment possible. So that where activity becomes moral, it must be referred to the central pole of life, which is God, and whom Christ reveals to us and guides us to attain. And all of life, even when profane, provided it is upright, can be Christian. Does not St. Paul teach us to refer everything to the Lord: “Whether you eat, drink, or do anything else, do all for the glory of God?” (1 Cor 10:31)». Manner: evangelizing the culture and not culturalizing the Gospel Now then, the Directory specifically clarifies that this inculturation of the Gospel must be done—and it uses this expression— by evangelizing the culture and not by culturalizing the Gospel . What does this mean? What must we keep in mind in this regard? What must we guard against? Well then: 1. From the very fact that Jesus Christ became man without ceasing to be God, we must learn to be in the world 31 , «without being of the world» 32 . We must go to the world to convert it and not to blend into it. We must go to the culture and to the cultures of man not to be converted into them, but to heal them and elevate them with the power of the Gospel, doing, analogously, what Christ did: «He suppressed what was diabolical, assumed what was human and communicated to it what was divine» 33 . 2. It also means that, just as Christ became like us in all things except sin (Heb 4:15), sin, error, and all their derivatives cannot be assumed. That is to say, without conversion reconciliation is impossible; without renouncing evil there is no redemption. There can be no unity at the expense of truth. There is no holiness without purity of soul: «holiness means purity» 34 . 3. On the other hand, only what has dignity or necessity can be assumed. Neither the inhuman, nor the anti-human, nor the subhuman can be assumed. The irrational, the absurd and all their derivatives cannot be assumed. 4. But nothing that is authentically human should be rejected, since Christ assumed an integral human nature. We must assume everything human—that is, all the elements of truth and goodness present in cultures—since «what was not assumed was not redeemed either» 35 , and the human that is not assumed «becomes a new idol with an old malice» 36 . 5. And this assuming of the human must not be merely apparent, but real. This assumption is only real when it truly transforms the human in Christ, elevating it, dignifying it, perfecting it. What is left only at the human level has only apparently been assumed. 6. In a particular way, what has been said applies to the evangelization of culture, where we must always be firm in our Catholic identity and know how to discern and dialogue with those whom we have to evangelize. Without ever forgetting that «true inculturation is from within: and it consists, ultimately, in a renewal of life under the influence of grace» 37 . Indeed, the Lord Jesus sent His disciples to proclaim the Gospel to the whole world and to baptize all nations (cf. Mk 16:15-16; Mt 28:18-20; also Lk 24:46-48; Jn 17:18; 20:21; Acts 1:8). 7. Furthermore, the Directory of the Third Order says: “With a disinterested love of God, in a specific way, the lay members of the Incarnate Word will distinguish themselves by their help to priests and to men and women religious, who are the representatives of God on earth, those placed by God to direct the Church, being ever ready to serve and collaborate, so that they may always find in these lay people hands ready to collaborate in the great enterprise of evangelization” 38 . That is to say, this is one of the channels through which you too can evangelize the culture. Farewell Well, that is more or less what I wanted to tell you. And to conclude, I wanted to come back to something I told you at the beginning: that we are “a single family, united not only by the same faith, but by the same ends, the same mission, the same charism, the same character and the same spirit”. The spiritual union among us, between the religious and our dear members of the Third Order, rightly understood, is very deep and bears unforeseeable fruits for the life of our institutes and of the Church. You are for us a great potential, a treasure! A very great help, in every sense. Let us always remain united, founded on the Incarnate Word and always faithful to Him. Above all, let us have immense confidence in the merits of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the power of His death and resurrection. And let us always remain joyful and always at peace, in the Incarnate Word, because truth prevails over lies, good over evil, peace over war, mercy over vengeance, and the Most Holy Virgin of Luján, the Woman Clothed with the Sun, radiates her grace over our nation, over each one of our families, over each one of her missionary children. To Her I entrust all of you, and I also commend myself to your prayers. Thank you very much for coming! May God bless you! — Notes 1 Redemporis Missio , 77. 2 5. 3 Cf. Rege O Maria

Today, the Religious Family of the Incarnate Word wants to say [to the world]: Rege O Maria! Because our spirituality is that of the “Hail Mary” and of the “Angelus” 1 ; Because our hymn is that of the kenosis 2 and the “Gloria” resounds in our souls when we call her “Mother”; Because in her fiat and in her magnificat our religious life finds the model for the self-giving of our own life 3 : Rege O Maria! Because our identity is to be “essentially missionary and Marian” 4 and Mary, “the first Missionary after her Son Jesus Christ” 5 , is the eminent model to follow in our task of inculturating the Gospel 6 ; Because the Mother of God, like a tower girded with strong defenses, is the safeguard of our faith and strengthens the bonds of communion among her children; Because She was, by divine election, the ally in the struggle against sin and its consequences 7 and her irreconcilable enmity with the evil enemy will have no end: Rege O Maria! Because no greater consolation has been given us in this valley of tears than to be able to say “that the treasure of God, in which He has placed what is most precious to Him, is also ours” 8 ; Because we want to thank God for His countless benefits and to obtain new ones through the Suppliant Omnipotence of Mary; Because the Mother of the Incarnate Word and our Mother is the image and fulfillment of the Kingdom of God, and she calls us to it and awaits us in it; For all this and much more, it springs from us as a natural impulse of the soul to say: Rege O Maria! And just as in times past legions of men and women united under one same standard to defeat enemies and win triumphs for their king, today we, the members of the Religious Family of the Incarnate Word, from the four corners of the earth, have united under the sky-blue and white standard of the Pure and Immaculate Conception of Luján, represented in the sign of the scapular we have just received, in order to manifest our irrevocable belonging to the Most Blessed Virgin Mary and our most absolute and radical commitment to work without reserve for the reign of Jesus Christ through His most holy Mother, according to the mission of the Religious Family of the Incarnate Word, which is none other than “to bring to fulfillment the consequences of the Incarnation of the Word” 9 . The scapular that from today we wear on our breast is the sign of our “covenant” and reciprocal communion with the Mother of God. And just as the great ones of the world consider it an honor that other men should wear their insignia, so we trust that Most Holy Mary will look with pleasure upon us, her devoted children, wearing her scapular as a clear and courageous testimony that we are consecrated to her service. That is our badge of honor, and it is in this sublime office that we wish to stand out. But the scapular is not only the sign of our covenant; it is also the mold in which we want to learn the most absolute availability to the will of the Father, so as to be transformed into what God wants us to be: other Christs 10 ; and it is also a shield and bulwark while “we go on pilgrimage amid the persecutions of the world and the consolations of God” 11 , according to those words of St. Augustine: “Oh! How powerful and strong we are before Jesus Christ when we are armed with the merits and intercession of the worthy Mother of God, who lovingly overcame the Almighty!” 12 . So then, if the scapular of Our Lady of Luján is our standard, our mold, our shield and bulwark, “to marianize life” 13 is our program of life. To marianize is something more than invoking Our Lady; it is to copy the style of Most Holy Mary, her constant yes, her sentiments; it is to incorporate into our existence all that the spirit of Most Holy Mary is and contains. “All for Jesus and for Mary; with Jesus and with Mary; in Jesus and in Mary; for the sake of Jesus and of Mary” 14 . That is the “fundamental code” of our spirituality. It is the precious pearl that we must treasure, guard, know how to transmit to the peoples and bequeath to those who will come after us. Let us realize that “the congregation will always live within the Immaculate Heart of Mary if each one of us is capable of making others see that not only by our words but by our deeds we belong to Her” 15 . Let us rejoice, then, and celebrate! For that is the fitting response of a lover to whom what he loves has fallen by lot 16 . And to us God has granted the honorable privilege of being slaves of Mary. Listen well, all of you: May wearing the scapular close to our heart enliven our hope, because in the same way that God “looked upon” our Mother the Virgin Mary and did “great things” in Her, displaying His power, we trust that He will do the same with us, His children of the Religious Family of the Incarnate Word, who give everything through the hands of His Holy Mother; and that is why we can hope with certain hope that our Lord will scatter the proud, cast down the mighty, fill the hungry, exalt the lowly and protect His servants, forever 17 . Therefore: “Oh! you, whoever you are [and wherever you may find yourself; with all your limitations and miseries, with all your successes and failures, with all your triumphs and battles, with all your virtues and sins] …look to the Star, call upon Mary. […] May her name never depart from your lips, never leave your heart; and to obtain the help of her intercession, do not neglect the examples of her life. Following her, you will not go astray; praying to her, you will not despair; thinking of Her, you will avoid all error. If She upholds you, you will not fall; if She protects you, you will have nothing to fear; if She guides you, you will not grow weary; if She is favorable to you, you will reach the goal. And thus you will verify, by your own experience, how rightly it was said: “ And the name of the Virgin was Mary ” 18 . Come on! Take heart! For we belong to Our Lady and Our Lady is ours. Introductory Letter to the IVE Meeting

Let us give each other our hand and walk together toward the Heavenly Homeland 1 Directory of the Third Order, 119 My dear members of the Third Order and friends: Welcome to you all! Blessed be God who grants us this joyful meeting with you, the lay people and friends of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, who have come from more than 30 different countries! Immense is the joy of being able to welcome you and to express to you personally our appreciation and gratitude for your magnificent contribution to the cause of Christ. Our meeting is made more significant by the fact that we are here in Rome, the seat of the Vicar of Christ on earth, as “a single Family, united by the same faith, the same ends, the same mission, the same charism, the same character and the same spirit” 2 . This represents an unparalleled occasion to bear witness together to our perfect communion with the Church and to confess that our motto is “with Peter and under Peter” 3 and that we have no greater aspiration than that of serving the spread of the Kingdom of Christ 4 . You –who have chosen to be the leaven that renews humanity from within– are the answer of God, who is always close to men, to the innumerable needs of evangelization of this world, and an irreplaceable support for the mission of our Institute. Because what is ours is to bring the Incarnate Word to all men, to permeate the values of society with the fragrance of Christ, to transform the hearts of men with His adorable Presence, to undertake epic works for His cause; it is to make the love of Christ reign in families, it is to kindle the burning lamp of the truth of the Incarnate Word in the four corners of this world, even in the most difficult situations and in the most adverse conditions. And it is you, the courageous and consistent witnesses of the duty and mission of the evangelization of cultures, who help us to bring Christ to the most distant places; to bring reality under the lordship of the Lord, inculturating the Gospel in the most hidden recesses of human life. The collaboration of all of you, tertiaries and friends, in all our missions represents a most important and effective help so that the mission entrusted to us within the Church may expand and reach those most hidden places and spheres of society (proper to lay life) which it would be very difficult for us to reach otherwise. I assure you that your help in our missions is vital. Without a doubt these are days of special blessings for everyone. It is my fervent prayer for each one that this first international meeting of the members of the Third Order and friends of the IVE may increase the family spirit among us and serve as an incentive so that, on returning to your countries, you may continue working with great dedication to “order temporal affairs according to God 5 ” 6 , knowing that you are not alone in the mission but have a whole Religious Family that supports you and expects great things of you. Because believe me, on committed lay people like you “depends in great part the extension of the Kingdom of God and the mission of our Religious Family in the world” 7 . For the close union of forces is the only thing that avails to achieve fully all the ends of the apostolate of our Institute and to protect its goods effectively 8 . As Don Orione said to his own: “let us give each other our hand and walk together toward the Heavenly Homeland. Let us edify one another with mutual good example” 9 . I encourage you with all my heart to continue bearing witness to Christ, the Incarnate Word, always and everywhere. I could not conclude without first expressing my deep and heartfelt gratitude to all those who organized this event: priests, religious, Servant Sisters, benefactors, and of course, once again: our dear lay people and friends. I thank all of you for the great effort you have made to come. I ask you kindly, on returning to your homes, to bring my words of encouragement and very great appreciation to all the members of the Third Order who were unable to come, and my most sincere thanks for their support of our missions. Invoking upon each one the protection of Mary, Queen of Apostles and Star of the new evangelization, I wish you every good in time and in eternity. Lectio Brevis for the Opening of the 2022 Academic Year

The necessary path of the metaphysical element Cf. John Paul II, Fides et Ratio , 83 [Introduction] Without a doubt “culture is a fundamental dimension of the person and of human communities. [And] since culture is the result of the life and activity of a human group, the persons who belong to that group are formed, to a great extent , by the culture in which they live. As persons and societies change, so too does culture change with them. When culture is transformed, it likewise transforms persons and societies” 1 . Each one of the religious who are here, I and each one of you, has been called by God to the sublime and, more than ever, urgent task of evangelizing the culture. For this, “it is essential to know sufficiently today’s culture in its main lines of thought and orientations” 2 in order to be able to refute effectively the errors of our time 3 and to make our proposal from the Gospel. Hence the great importance for us of attending the Lectio Brevis as the inaugural act of the sustained effort we must make throughout the whole year to study, sparing neither means nor effort 4 for it, given the great bearing it has on evangelization; since study is one of the principal means by which we prepare ourselves for a fruitful and effective dialogue with the men of our time, as the apostolic ministry 5 entrusted to us demands. In this identifying of the lines of thought and orientations of the humanity of our time, the Venerable Archbishop Fulton Sheen, in the prologue of his book “ Religion Without God ”, maintains that nowadays 6 “there is an evident contempt for all that was best in the culture and in the tradition we inherited”. And in this same sense Gaudium et spes does not hesitate to affirm that: “the conditions of life of modern man, from the social and cultural point of view, have undergone a profound change, such that one can speak of a new age of human history” 7 . In which the “modern world appears at once powerful and weak, capable of the best and the worst” 8 . We perceive this in innumerable symptoms: it is enough to go downtown one day and observe people’s behavior, to look even at the behavior of children and young people in our parishes, to read some political speech in the newspaper, to pay attention to the debate on laws in some countries… it is evident that our world is deteriorating in aspects that are vital. The Archbishop emeritus of Philadelphia, Archbishop Chaput, wrote in an article something that seems to me to sum up these symptoms in some way: “we live in a disenchanted world, which means a world remade by human hands, rationalized and technocratic. It is a world without transcendence. In this world, we ‘protect’ ourselves from the inconvenience of God, from His demands and His invitations, by walling ourselves off from Him. God, for example, we do not mention in polite conversation. Religious convictions are held to be difficult or awkward at best, and dangerous at worst. What happens to human reason in the absence of any reference to God is predictable. Its horizons become low. It becomes the tool of the modern sciences. […] Man is reduced to a physical animal who solves his problems through technology, politics and economics. Culture becomes an empty shell. The spirit is stifled by the deep questions about justice, friendship, fidelity, worship, existence, God, beauty. […] Our modern universities usually avoid God as a serious subject of study. Without God, or at least without some sense of a higher order, the dignity of the person is little more than folklore, the residue of pre-Darwinian beliefs. God and the soul are in exile. And that is”, concludes the Archbishop, “because classical philosophy is in exile, to the detriment of genuine learning” 9 . The genius of Fulton Sheen said something similar: “What traditional thought called transcendent (but not in Kant’s sense), our contemporaries regard as extrinsic ; and the extrinsic is considered a threat to freedom of thought and to the freedom to think; as something that stands between us and ‘our power’ to procure our salvation by ourselves” 10 , and so one ends up adopting an attitude of complete indifference toward the truth; man is no longer interested either in what lies beyond him, or in what is above him, or in what is superior to him. Indeed, we see ad nauseam the notorious distrust of reason and of the human capacity to grasp the truth; even the very concept of truth is called into question. There are those who say that truth is constructed culturally for the management of the masses and that so-called “absolute truths” are nothing more than the product of a culture at a given moment of time and place, and therefore subject to criticism and change 11 . (To affirm such a thing “is the same as saying that something is true at three in the afternoon but false at half past four, and the same as saying that two apples plus two apples are four apples on a Monday, but not on a Friday” 12 ). At the same time, each person is urged to develop an autonomous vision of himself, different from that of others; each has his ‘own truth’. It is the culture of “ It’s all about me ” or “ the me-culture ”. This leads inevitably to a culture of simultaneous selfishness “in which everyone thinks, more or less, the same thing, which is what the media repeat daily, ad nauseam, the media being under the dictatorship of the ‘givers of meaning’” 13 . According to the Scottish philosopher Alasdair MacIntayre 14 , our society today is regulated by what he calls the ‘morality of emotivism’ 15 , by which man implicitly places feelings above prudent judgment (it is the “just do it” we see, for example, in Nike advertisements), ‘sincerity’ above facts, and so, in the name of being ‘authentic’ –though in a worldly and even perverse sense– man does not care about the great harm he may cause to others and even to himself; what is more, he takes pride in it 16 (in fact, ‘authenticity’ in quotation marks is one of the arguments used by the agenda of gender ideology). “Life is no longer appreciated or loved; that is why a certain culture of death advances, with its bitter fruits: abortion and euthanasia. The body and human sexuality are not rightly valued or loved; from this derives the degradation of sex, which is manifested in a wave of moral confusion, infidelity and pornographic violence” 17 …If one stops to think about it, modern man has manufactured a world of sex without children, a world where one can generate (and even design) a new life without there being any contact between its progenitors. All this that we have been saying is what our Proper Law synthesizes when it says that man, “intoxicated by the prodigious conquests of an unrestrainable scientific-technical development, and fascinated above all by the most ancient and ever new temptation of wanting to become like God (cf. Gen 3:5) through the use of a freedom without limits, forgets God, considers Him without meaning for his own existence, rejects Him, and sets himself to adore the most diverse ‘idols’” 18 . Faced with these symptoms, what is the diagnosis? Our beloved St. John Paul II, with clairvoyant vision, does not hesitate to affirm: “We live in a time characterized, in its own way, by the rejection of the Incarnation” 19 , because of ancient errors that do not die, but remain dormant for a time and then reappear in other forms 20 , and which we identify as the two great evils of gnosticism and of the philosophy of immanence (other great evils derive from these postulates, such as, for example, neo-Pelagianism in morals and neo-Arianism in dogmatics). Gnosticism is ancient; immanence is modern. And these are the two main points into which I am going to divide this conference. 1. Gnosticism In the first place, gnosticism. Gnosticism is a syncretism, which is why it is often difficult to detect. Nevertheless, gnosticism claims to give a worldview of God, of man and of the world. It is “the knowledge of what we are and of what we have become; of the place from which we come and of that into which we have fallen; of the goal toward which we hasten and from which we have been rescued; of the nature of our birth and of our rebirth” 21 . It is not a particular religion, but rather takes elements from different religions to form a kind of mosaic. What is more, it avoids taking sides or opposing any religion and culture. A first misunderstanding that should be dispelled: gnosticism is not the same as gnosis. We are speaking in the context of biblical revelation, Mosaic and especially Christian. There exists a Christian gnosis clearly different from gnosticism, even Christian gnosticism. When one speaks of Christian gnosis, one refers to that knowledge of God and of His mysteries which the ancient authors describe as the higher ideal of the perfect Christian and which they distinguish from simple faith. Christianity –and the Jewish religion that preceded it– is a knowledge ; the knowledge of a secret or revelation , which is God’s design to save man. In a particular way, this Christian gnosis would be fully and systematically elaborated, in large part against the gnostic heresy, by Clement of Alexandria and Origen. The Origenist tradition remains alive in Gregory of Nyssa and Evagrius Ponticus. But there is always a grave danger. That danger is gnosticism, which John Paul the Great defined as “that attitude of the spirit which, in the name of a profound knowledge of God, ends up distorting His Word, replacing it with words that are merely human” 22 . That is why we can say that gnosticism is a corruption of the Christian gnosis we were speaking of a moment ago. Now notice that the same Pope warned us: “Gnosis has never disappeared from the sphere of Christianity, but has always lived alongside it, sometimes in the form of philosophical currents, more often in religious or para-religious modes, with a decided, though at times undeclared divergence from what is essentially Christian” 23 . “Are we not seeing today the strange resurgence of gnosis and esoteric beliefs together with ancient pantheism and old paganism? Men have abandoned the fountains of living water , as the Prophet already said, and have gone to empty cisterns ” 24 . And even before him, the Holy Pope Paul VI denounced: “We do not accept the attitude of those who seem to ignore the living tradition of the Church, even the Gospel itself, spiritual realities, the divinity of Christ, His Resurrection or the Eucharist, practically emptying them of content and thus creating a new gnosis” 25 . These are –says John Paul II– those who with “bold denials that touch the very heart of the Catholic faith, such as, for example, the lack or at least the uncertainty, regarding Christ, of His clear identity as Son of God, and many other vital points of the Creed” 26 . They are those who make a concoction of the natural and the supernatural, confuse psychology with spirituality 27 , “want to accommodate the Church to the world”, etc. “Hence progressivism, [for example] being a gnosis, is compelled to fall into religious syncretism or irenicism or false ecumenism, in which all doctrinal distinctions disappear, even revealed ones” 28 . “It is a kind of mixture with which no Christian understanding should clothe itself” 29 , says our Directory of Spirituality . The decisive point is the following: Why is legitimate gnosis so easily transformed into gnosticism? 30 It is because of human pride, the same pride that brought evil into the world in Genesis and that makes reason grow proud and believe itself self-sufficient, and therefore resist the authentic truth of God and His decisive redemptive work. For we observe, admirably, in the great thinkers who study these subjects, that the decisive and determining point is found before the mystery of the Cross of Christ; on its acceptance or rejection everything is at stake, for the truth is at stake. Let us see it. God reveals Himself, reveals His intimate mysteries, and also reveals many things that, because of the weakness of the human intellect, are mysterious to man. Man responds by accepting, assimilating, knowing divine revelation. It is the response of faith. “Faith alone makes it possible to penetrate the mystery, favoring its coherent understanding” 31 , says Fides et Ratio . We are beings made for the Truth. And that is why we are beings unlimited in our desires. However, we experience many limitations, and one of them is the limit of our reason because of “its finiteness before the infinite mystery of God” 32 . That is why, after experiencing the limit of our understanding, it is necessary to accept that we need help from on high. Accepting that help demands “the humility of reason before the mystery” 33 , against which man can certainly rebel. Here gnosticism and the resistance of reason reappear. The Hebrew people, for example, witnessed innumerable divine interventions in their favor. In many of them God made it very clear that it was His arm and not weapons that gave the victory, a victory for which the people had to give thanks in humility. But many of them fell into the temptation of gnosticism, also called Kabbalah: an attempt to dominate and instrumentalize the divine powers in a magical way. Something very similar happens in modern times. To illustrate it, Fulton Sheen uses a passage from the Prophet Isaiah, who, referring to the ancient idols, said: The carpenter takes measurements with the line, marks out the shape with the stylus, works it with the chisel and draws it with the compass; he gives it the figure of a man and the beauty of a human being, that it may dwell in his house. Indeed, he cut down some cedar, or took a holm oak and an oak which he had let grow among the trees of the forest, or planted a fir which the rain then made grow. Man uses them to make fire, takes them to warm himself and also kindles them to bake bread. But, besides, he makes a god of them and prostrates himself before it; he makes an idol and worships it 34 . The modern idolater –says Fulton Sheen– does not go to the forest, but enters the laboratory, and there, with the help of scientific concepts, he fashions the kind of God he will afterwards worship. This is the fatality of a philosophy that no longer speaks of God, but of the idea of God”. […] “If God were only an idea, there would be very little difference between the ancient idolatry and the new, for the ancient idols were the work of the hands of men and the modern idols are created by their intelligence” 35 . So far Fulton Sheen. This temptation to the “kabbalah” or to the “idolatry” of gnosticism is not absent in many who claim to be Christians, as we said before. In fact, Paul VI himself goes so far as to say: “We are in a gnostic age. And this is the battle: against the cerebrations of gnosis” 36 . A few years ago we celebrated the 20th anniversary of the magnificent Encyclical Fides et Ratio (which is the true Magna Carta on this subject), where we read a phrase that can give us the answer to the question of why one falls into this: “the Cross can give reason the ultimate answer” 37 that man seeks. Nevertheless, the Cross is precisely and at the same time the central point that challenges all philosophy [and that presents the great challenge for our understanding]. At this point every attempt to reduce the saving plan of the Father to pure human logic is doomed to failure. For what God wishes to accomplish, the mere wisdom of the wise man is no longer possible; rather, a decisive step is required to welcome a radical newness: God chose rather what is foolish in the world to confound the wise […]. What is low and despised in the world God has chosen; what is not, to reduce to nothing what is 38 . And this is for many men, for many Christians –even today– a scandal (though they do not admit it conceptually). The wisdom of man refuses to see in his own weakness the precondition of his strength; in the face of which St. Paul does not hesitate to affirm: the preaching of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing; but to those who are being saved – to us – it is the power of God . (…) It pleased God to save those who believe through the foolishness of preaching. Thus, while Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom, we preach Christ crucified, a scandal to Jews, foolishness to Gentiles 39 . Man cannot manage to understand how death can be a source of life and love, but to reveal the mystery of His design of salvation God has chosen precisely what reason considers folly and scandal . In imitation of the Incarnate Word, reason too must pass through this difficult self-emptying of the cross, a self-emptying which nevertheless does not destroy it but is able to strengthen it: its knowledge is transformed into “affective” knowledge, in which God comes even to be “experienced” more than merely known. It is the “ Crede, ut intelligas ” of St. Augustine, who knew gnosticism from within but knew how to make use of humility, this being the vehicle that freed him from gnosticism; and it was then that his reason, thus humbled, began to be raised up to become the Eagle of Hippo and the beacon of the Christian West. That is why, if we make an in-depth analysis, we see that it is in the truth of the preaching of, and authentic penetration into, the mystery of the Cross that contemporary problems are finally centered. For from its rejection or acceptance follows either the rise or the collapse of contemporary gnosticism (as it was with that of all times). That is why the words of John Paul the Great in Fides et Ratio are particularly illuminating –and with this I wish to finish this first point–: “The wisdom of the Cross, then, surpasses every cultural limit that one might wish to impose on it and obliges one to open oneself to the universality of the truth of which it is the bearer. What a great challenge is presented to our reason, and what profit it obtains if it does not give up! Philosophy, which by itself is capable of recognizing man’s ceaseless self-transcendence toward the truth, can, aided by faith, open itself to welcome in the folly of the Cross the authentic critique of those who believe they possess the truth, imprisoning it in the recesses of their system. The relationship between faith and philosophy finds in the preaching of Christ crucified and risen the reef on which it can be shipwrecked, but beyond which it can flow into the boundless ocean of truth. Here the boundary between reason and faith becomes evident, but the space in which both can meet also becomes clear” 40 . 2. Immanence Let us now say something about the philosophy of immanence. Our Directory of Evangelization of Culture affirms: Man is essentially a religious being, for which reason the transcendent dimension constitutes the heart of culture. ‘Every culture is an effort of reflection on the mystery of the world and in particular of man: it is a way of expressing the transcendent dimension of human life. The heart of every culture is constituted by its approach to the greatest of mysteries: the mystery of God’ 41 . The great cultural challenge of today lies in the sphere of man’s openness to truth and to the good, ultimately to transcendence and to the mystery of God. [Since] the “ontological” dependence of man in relation to God is the ultimate foundation of the full development of human freedom and life, as well as of respect for the dignity and life of every human being. That is why the central place in every culture is occupied by the attitude that man takes before the mystery of God 42 ” 43 . However, we are not afraid to affirm that the most impressive cultural phenomenon of this age is precisely atheism, especially practical atheism. Gaudim et spes , in fact, says that “it is one of the gravest phenomena of our time” 44 . This practical atheism is the one about which John Paul II warned us in his apostolic exhortation Ecclesia in Europa when he said: today “European culture gives the impression of a ‘silent apostasy’ on the part of self-sufficient man, who lives as if God did not exist” 45 . And we have seen it reflected to some extent also in the symptoms we mentioned at the beginning, in all cultures, not only in Europe. This atheism is the logical consequence of the principle of immanence, hence its gravity, since the principle of immanence , by remaining in mental being, does not reach extra-mental being, and cannot, therefore, validly ascend to the Principle of all beings, to the Supreme Being. That is why Pope Pius X calls the philosophy of immanence: “An infinite heap of sophisms, with which all religion is cracked and destroyed!” 46 So, if earlier we said that gnosticism is a syncretism, now we must say that the philosophy of immanence presents itself as radically concentrated in a single principle: intra-mental being, the cogito . Unlike ‘classical naturalist atheism’, in which there was as it were a lowering and a materialization of man by placing him on the same ontological level as matter, modern atheism implies a divinization of man, that is, the elevation of man to the cogito , that is, the reduction of the actuation of being to the actuation of the cogito . That is why Fabro can add that “this positivity of the new atheism is expressed in the ambitious epithet of ‘humanism’ which the atheists of the modern age claim, especially from Feuerbach on”. The latter goes so far as to affirm, for example: “God is nothing but humanity” 47 , and that is why one even speaks of the “ drama of atheist humanism ” 48 . That is to say: modern thought sets up thought, the cogito , as a creative source. Hence, God is not necessary. That is: “The man who ‘makes’ God, in his head, then denies Him”. Thought suffices to create the world. If the reality of the world is not independent of and prior to thought, there is no need either to seek the explanation of that worldly reality and of thought. Consequently, God does not exist. The principle of immanence implies atheism. Its three principal historical moments can be identified in the philosophies of Descartes, Spinoza and Hegel. a) Descartes introduces the principle of immanence as the first principle of philosophy: “ Cogito ergo sum ”. God is reduced to a mere content of human consciousness. God is no longer Creator, nor does He give Himself in the mystery of the Incarnation and the Redemption; He is only an idea freely elaborated by human thought. Consequently, the foundations of the “philosophy of evil” crumble. For evil, in its realist sense, can exist only in relation to the good and, in particular, to God, the supreme Good […]. But if man by himself, without God, can decide what is good and what is evil, he can also decide, for example, that a certain group of human beings be annihilated 49 . Think of the communist regimes, think of abortion, and of all the other forms of infringing the law of God that emanate from this conception. b) Spinoza introduces metaphysical immanence. For him, God is identified with the world of created things. The creature being divine, man too is divine, and he remains united to the divinity. The immanence of God in man is changed into the immanence of man in God. c) Hegel constructs a philosophy that becomes, as it were, the most complete form of modern thought, the theoretical and most systematic expression of the principle of immanence. He goes so far as to affirm: “Without the world, God is not God”. This is what our Proper Law –quoting Cornelio Fabro four times in a row– defines as contemporary nihilism-atheism 50 , which is radical atheism as the denial of the transcendent, of the existence of ‘a metaphysical world that transcends the sensible world’ 51 , causing “the human spirit, closed in on itself, no longer to open itself to the real –to the act of being– and, therefore, to God, and so it becomes incapable of expressing the truth and of grounding freedom” 52 . Unfortunately, says a contemporary author, “it is now noticeable that the fascination with Hegel is gaining ground not only in the Protestant camp, but also in the Catholic camp” 53 . That is why I would like to mention at least two examples that show the application of these principles in the Catholic milieu: The first example is “the dialectic that has also entered the Catholic world regarding the historical Christ and the Christ of faith. In the end it turns out to be something Hegelian, because for that whole line of thought the real historical Christ is of no interest; what matters is the idea one has of Christ, which is eternal, which is present in our soul beyond its historical exemplifications” 54 . John Paul the Great in Redemptoris Missio says, word for word: “It is contrary to the Christian faith to introduce any separation between the Word and Jesus Christ. St. John clearly affirms that the Word, who was in the beginning with God , is the same who became flesh 55 . Jesus is the Incarnate Word, a single and inseparable person: one cannot separate Jesus from Christ, nor speak of a ‘Jesus of history’ who would be different from the ‘Christ of faith’. The Church knows and confesses Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God 56 . Christ is none other than Jesus of Nazareth, and He is the Word of God made man for the salvation of all” 57 . Crystal clear. The second example corresponds to progressivism, which considers that reality has a one-dimensional character, that is, it pushes toward a monism; and full progressivism is an absolute monism, which in its rejection of transcendence affirms absolute immanence and which entails a false concept of God 58 . Cornelio Fabro very aptly warns: “The God of theological progressivism is the reflected image of progressivist confusion: a God of softness and weakness, a God of unconcern and sufficiency. No trace of the God who is a consuming fire, before whom the heavens are not pure, who did not spare His only Son the ‘chalice’ of the Passion” 59 . As it seems to us, there are two implications that necessarily enter into progressivism, since it is a one-dimensional and immanentist conception of reality in which the natural, the profane, the worldly, the rational, the temporal, the secular are exalted… at the expense of the supernatural, the sacred, the interior life, faith, the eternal, the religious, God (it is the denial of the supernatural and the exaltation of the natural): On the one hand, the deification of man , not by grace or by the merits of Christ or by the work of the Church, but by himself, by his own power, without subordinating himself to anything or anyone. Christ, Son of God consubstantial with the Father and Savior of the world, is superfluous; the ‘institutional Church’, as distinct from the world –‘In her alone is salvation’– is superfluous; sanctifying grace –according to Trent the ‘ única formalis causa ’ (Dz. 799) of justification– is superfluous, and the sacraments are superfluous. Nothing is needed that comes from above and from outside: Man redeems himself. On the other hand, progressivist monism implies an immanent character. Since Church and world are one and the same, there is no “outside” the Church; everything is “inside”. Hence progressivists do not feel compelled to leave the Church. What is more, knowing the formative power of the Church over minds, they seek not to be singled out by the hierarchy as enemies of the Church. So as not to be thrown out, they are always ready to camouflage themselves. 3. Remedy We said at the beginning that “culture is the activity that man carries out in order to perfect himself” 60 . But it is evident from all that has been said that not everything man does truly contributes to his perfection, and therefore not all his activities are truly “culture”. That is why not every philosophical reflection grounds a true human culture, since there are many currents of thought very widespread today –such as these two we have seen today– whose errors lead to the distortion of any culture that rests on them 61 . Both gnosticism and the philosophy of immanence, and so many other currents of thought, show the need to ground culture in a true metaphysics, which can be none other than the metaphysics of being . For it is the metaphysics of being, and only the metaphysics of being, that can restore to man the true place he occupies in society and give the true foundations on which man must build his culture 62 . And this is so because it is the philosophy of being that allows full and comprehensive openness to all of reality, overcoming every limit and making it possible to reach Him who perfects all things 63 . The philosophies we have described, and all those not grounded in the act of being, are far from satisfying man’s deepest aspirations. They are far from providing man with “an absolute capable of giving an answer and meaning to all his searching. Something that is ultimate and the foundation of all else. (…) Hypotheses may be fascinating, but they do not satisfy” 64 . For there are many systems that speak of God, that affirm the existence of God, but it is not the God we men need and whom the Christian faith proclaims 65 . Archbishop Chaput, in the same article I mentioned earlier, recounts how “he sometimes hears parishioners complain about some priests because of the content of their homilies. They say they are glad to be exhorted to generosity and kindness, but they hunger to have the substance of the faith, its mysteries and its doctrines, presented to them in a way accessible to them. These homilies are not easy to make –the Archbishop comments–. But they are impossible to make if we do not have a credible theology, one that has been informed by the strong philosophical tradition that is at the heart of the Church and is the patrimony of the Church” 66 ; he is clearly referring to the perennial philosophy of the Aquinate. For it is “from a philosophy of being that man can find his true foundation, which is being; he can [moreover] find his ultimate end, which is Being by Essence, and he can also find his ground, which is freedom. In this way he will be able to discover the true cultural values. For ultimately all cultural values –of science, of art, of laws and customs, etc.– as objective expressions of beauty, truth and goodness, are grounded in the act of being 67 . We, the members of this beloved Religious Family of the Incarnate Word, will be able, on the pastoral level, to offer a positive and effective response to the great challenges and even dramas of ‘postmodern’ man, principally starting from the metaphysical level, through the philosophy of being 68 . * * * [Conclusion] That is why –and with this I am now finishing– we are asked “not to settle for a superficial knowledge of philosophy and theology, incapable of understanding in all its depth the drama of contemporary atheism and therefore incapable of remedying it” 69 . It is incumbent upon us, because of the mission we have received, to have a strong cultural formation that takes a stand before modern culture 70 . A “metaphysics with grip” is needed, one that bites into reality. Pay attention to what John Paul II says: “If I insist so much on the metaphysical element, it is because I am convinced that it is the necessary path for overcoming the situation of crisis that affects large sectors of philosophy today and thus for correcting certain erroneous forms of behavior widespread in our society ”. A verbatim quotation from the Directory of Major Seminaries , 315. For a philosophy in which the truth of Christ shines forth represents an effective contribution to the true and at the same time worldwide ethics that humanity needs today. The present age has an urgent need of Jesus Christ. The needs of the new evangelization are enormous, and we cannot evade the challenging call Christ makes to us to go into all the world proclaiming the Gospel . Let us always remember it: Our pastoral work must tirelessly propose Jesus Christ, the Incarnate Word, the fullness of all authentically human life and culture 71 . “A task that belongs not only to specialists but to all ” 72 , and for which there is need –I repeat– of a solid philosophical formation, since in pastoral life we must all face the demands of the contemporary world and examine the causes of certain behaviors in order to give them an adequate response. “The basis for building a true civilization is to collaborate with all our strength so that ‘an authentic sense of man may prevail in the world, not enclosed in a narrow anthropocentrism, but open to God’” 73 . This basis is the Rock 74 itself, that is, the very mystery of Jesus Christ, the Incarnate Word. And He is the model from which our spirituality and our pastoral work derive at their root 75 .
