The devil you do not know (2)

“The devil you do not know” Part II We publish here the second part of the Conference published in April. Here we present the first strategy that the devil ordinarily uses in his way of acting, which is deception . Later we will go on to set out the other three strategies. For this whole work we draw on the excellent book by Louis J. Cameli, The Devil You Know Not , which we follow freely to a large extent in developing the argument. [The translation from the English original is ours]. His strategies: the ordinary work of the devil Let us now see concretely what the common strategies of the enemy of our souls are. We can identify four of them: deception , division , diverting or distracting the soul from its purpose (from its objective, in short: from the end for which it was created) and finally, discouragement . Today we will speak of the first of them: Deception – Jesus says: He (the devil) was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he utters a lie, he speaks from what is his own, because he is a liar and the father of lies 1 . The devil inverts reality, that is, he turns things around, he presents them upside down. And then he proceeds to present that “inversion of things” as a “truth come from God.” In other words: he lies. Very often that lie has to do with promises which, of course, he will not keep, nor does he want to keep, either now or ever. The devil uses very deceptive promises to tempt us, to derail us. That is nothing new. It has been so since Adam and Eve: The serpent said to the woman: ‘No, you will not die . God knows very well that when you eat of that tree, your eyes will be opened and you will be like gods , knowing good and evil.’ There the lie worked. You will remember that well-known temptation of Jesus, steeped in deceptive promises, with which the devil had no success at all. It is in the Gospel of St. Matthew: The devil then took him to a very high mountain; from there he showed him all the kingdoms of the world in all their splendor, and said to him: ‘ I will give you all this , if you fall down and worship me.’ Jesus answered him: ‘Begone, Satan, for it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve.’ Then the devil left him, and angels came to minister to him” 2 . Notice how all these promises are rooted in the future. The devil seems to say: ‘there is something further ahead that I can assure you you are going to like and that will suit you really well.’ Promises about the future, positive results guaranteed, the promise that it will be a “ suffering free ” experience, consequences controlled or controllable… all these things are quite attractive. One feels much better knowing how things are going to turn out, even when that feeling is based on something improbable and, definitively, false. One feels much better moving forward having some kind of control over things and circumstances than walking only in trust and hope, without any control over what is going to happen. That is why the first lesson here is to realize that very often the devil's deception is joined to a promise that has to do with the future. That must alert us and put us on guard when we look toward the future, when we make plans or when we are daydreaming about what ‘could be.’ Listen to what C. S. Lewis says in “ The Screwtape Letters ”: “Nearly all vices are rooted in the Future. Gratitude looks to the Past and love to the Present; fear, avarice, lust and ambition look ahead.” All this means that we expose ourselves to being deceived when we want to anticipate what is going to happen. The deceptions can be about various things, of course: “how happy I'm going to be when I no longer live with this one and live with that one”; “how great it's going to be when I work in such and such a diocese”; some imagine ‘all that they will do’ and ‘all that they are going to enjoy’ if they leave the Institute, if they are promoted to some office that gives them ‘renown’; they imagine how secure and satisfied they are going to be if they are assigned this mission and taken out of where they are, if they are sent another superior, if suddenly the Institute did not have ‘the drawbacks’ it has… There are also other assurances about the future, equally deceptive, which falsely promise to hide what we prefer to keep secret. The desire to maintain privacy in one's life has an absolutely positive tone. We think of privacy as a form of legitimate reserve that keeps for oneself what would otherwise be something discourteous or rude in front of others. Although an earlier age might have equated privacy with refinement, today privacy has a less attractive aspect. For many, privacy means blocking off parts of their life that they simply want to keep in reserve, generally because they are not exactly proud of their actions or because they fear that these actions may have negative repercussions and disrupt their way of life. There are many things that people in general prefer to block off: the use of pornography, the propensity to take things from work that do not belong to them, etc. But it happens to us too: we want to hide that we have the regular habit of ignoring requests for help, that we have bad thoughts, that we accept ‘credit’ for things we do not do, that deep in our heart—and even though we do not want to admit it—we harbor a certain ‘hope of glory,’ of being vindicated… And where does the devil come into these private matters? The devil is active in various ways. Blocking off or bracketing areas of our life in order to keep them hidden, and not seeking help or a solution, is a deception that belongs in a notable way to the evil one. St. Ignatius describes this phenomenon very well in rule of discernment number 13, which is found in [326] of the book of the Exercises and which you know very well: [Our enemy] acts like a false lover in wanting to remain secret and not be discovered ; for just as the false man who, speaking with evil intent, solicits the daughter of a good father or the wife of a good husband, wants his words and insinuations to be kept secret; and the contrary displeases him greatly, when the daughter reveals to her father or the wife to her husband his vain words and perverse intention, because he easily infers that he will not be able to succeed in the undertaking he has begun; in the same way, when the enemy of human nature brings his wiles and insinuations to the just soul, he wants and desires that they be received and kept in secret; but it weighs heavily on him when the soul reveals them to its good confessor or to another spiritual person who knows his deceits and malice: because he infers that, his deceits being laid bare, he will not be able to succeed with the wicked plan he had begun. That is the strategy of deceptive concealment, to which the devil adds the promise (again deceptive) of mitigating the evil he offers as a temptation. The promise is simply that the evil will not be known by others, and the mitigation is that ‘in reality it does not matter much in this case.’ The promise is false and the mitigation is false. If it were advantageous for the devil that our fault be known, of course he will make it known! On top of that he can falsify, confuse others, scandalize, and make the person who is exposed become engulfed in intense sorrows of depression. This is exactly the case with the stories of sexual abuse of minors by priests. What seemed to be sealed forever, out of public view and a closed case, through personal shame and institutional connivance (collusion), at a certain point ‘that secret’ came to the surface and quickly, and in some cases forcibly, caused confusion among people about the Church, provoking scandal after scandal. That shameful truth, now public, unleashed waves of destructive depression among the perpetrators, the victims, and countless good souls in the Church. The mitigation promised by the devil, “it really doesn't matter much,” in this case of clerical sexual abuse, but also in other instances in which the devil hides evil, is clearly revealed as false. Whether the evil is public or apparently private and hidden, it has an impact and exacts a price. The truth is that we are so interrelated with others and so interdependent that we can never ‘isolate’ ourselves completely from the rest of humanity, nor from the impact of others on our life and of our impact on the lives of others. To put it in a few words: the devil does not keep his promises because he is the Liar. Identifying this reality, however, does not automatically free us from the influence of the one who habitually inverts the truth and seeks to entrap us with his distortions. We are vulnerable to this and therefore we must be alert. Another aspect of the strategy of deception on the part of the Liar with a capital L: the devil deceives us by entangling us in all sorts of complexities. Be careful: this has nothing to do with something that is in itself difficult to understand. Since I am not a mathematician, I may find it very difficult to understand number theory and graphs and things of that kind. By this I mean that there does exist a difficulty that is inherent in the subject matter, which is studied precisely because it has an intelligibility, a capacity to be known and understood with the appropriate tools. In the case that now concerns us, what the devil tries to do, through the complicatedness of his presentation, of his logic, of his argumentation, is to hide a very simple truth. He seeks to confuse us and to hide the fundamental truth from us. All those complicated tangles are related to deception and have to do with the free choice to complicate things so that they may remain obscure and, in the end, part of the deception. In this one sees the hand of the devil: intelligence joined to a malicious will. The devil is more than capable of bringing confusing complexities into our lives and trying to hide the truth about who we are and about the call God has made to us. Various layers are superimposed, for example, questioning our motivations, raising worries about how others perceive us or what they think of our projects, setting before us aaall the possible difficulties we might come across… all this serves only to block us or at least to make us stumble on our way, injecting deception by means of complications. And he uses this strategy especially when it comes to projects that are going to do a great deal of good; a concrete example is when it comes to works of mercy or when many souls are going to benefit. We must open our eyes and realize that the devil is a sworn enemy of the plain and simple truth. Precisely because it is plain and simple, the truth will be known and will be the path that leads us to God, who is the Truth, and the devil does not want that. The enemy—listen carefully—will always be interested in hiding the truth by entangling it in complexities that do not allow us to see it, or use it, or even speak of it. That the devil is a liar and his task is to deceive is also shown in expressiveness. In fact, a style of expressiveness in language (loquacity) and in gesture can be masking deeper realities. Put another way: that a person is loquacious, exceedingly expressive, is no guarantee that he is revealing an interior truth. The devil can use this for deceptive purposes. And one of the most interesting ‘circumstances’ is that he uses it to hide a religious truth or one that has to do with religion. The devil can, and in fact does, orchestrate religious observances, not for a positive end, of course. How many times have we seen that the devil uses intense expressions of religiosity that have little or nothing to do with an interiorized and genuine faith. How much fanaticism some priests can show regarding certain religious practices, but afterwards they fail in charity and, without any pastoral tact, ridicule, criticize, get angry when someone does not do as they like, which greatly contradicts the interior faith that must animate us. The devil's deceptive tactic includes, then, a pernicious encouragement of religious practices as purely external observances without a corresponding interior commitment. Another area in which the devil uses the tactic of deception is the ambiguity of sexual relationships. We are not speaking here of lust, which clearly speaks the language of selfishness. The more subtle attraction, and the direction in which the devil is wont to lead souls, is to make them think that they have an apparently intimate relationship, or at least that is how it appears outwardly. This is the case of those who cohabit. They are not promiscuous, and therefore they do not see themselves as lustful. They believe they are experiencing great intimacy, but such an assessment is based only on the external, on the physical. In reality, that physical closeness neither represents nor expresses a deeper intimacy, because it lacks the full commitment to be faithful and to lead a life in communion; that relationship remains confined only to the provisional and limited. And so we see in this example how an external expression replaces the truth of the substance. Another manifestation of the strategy of deception turns out to be: “information instead of truth.” We live in a world driven by information ( information-driven society ). It is obvious: just think of the computers that store and process such an enormous amount of information divided into millions of little pieces. Information well handled is a marvel: business is done more efficiently, schedules are better synchronized, people have the possibility of being more in communication with others. Now, the truth of our lives is not tied to little pieces of information that can be shuffled (as cards are shuffled) and dealt out in different directions. The truth of our life is manifested in our identity, which is stable, and began when we were born and accompanies us throughout our whole life until our last breath. And that truth of our lives is manifested in our freedom. A freedom that allows us not only to choose, but to give ourselves to others out of love (or not to do so) and to affirm our existence as a gift received (or not to do so). The truth that makes us free leads us to truth itself, to a truth beyond our imagination, a transcendent truth that is grounded in the Truth with a capital T. And that is God. Information that supplants the truth or ignores the guidance of the truth is deceptive and dangerous. When all those little pieces of information mask the truth, disfiguring it, things take on a dangerous color, and that is the devil's terrain. We see it in so many who show themselves on Facebook or on “ Talk shows ,” presenting themselves in a way that does not correspond to real life. They offer information about themselves, but not the truth about themselves. They tell you the country they live in, what they do, how old they are, their particular interests… but the truth about the person never emerges from those little pieces of information. And you will be saying to yourselves: ‘Well, Father, but we neither have a personal Facebook page nor go around checking other people's Facebooks .’ Perfect. However, notice how this also affects us in another sphere. The devil can easily, and for his own convenience, use the confusion between information about persons and the truth about those same persons to sow seeds of discord and even of great antagonism. How many times have we heard things said about other religious, and then he is sent to the community where one is, and right from the start one has a certain mistrust of that person, or underestimates him, or even avoids him… and worse if they are superiors, because one does not even take the time to get to know the person, gravely wounding that priest in some cases and even causing great division and turmoil in the community. St. John of the Cross has a magnificent teaching about this in his first precaution against the world: “Think nothing of them [of the other religious/priests], deal with nothing of theirs, neither good nor bad… and if you do not observe this, you will not know how to be a religious, nor will you be able to reach holy recollection or free yourself from imperfections.” And further on he says: “The third precaution is very necessary so that you may know how to guard yourself in the convent from all harm regarding the religious; and many, by not observing it, not only lost the peace and good of their soul, but came, and ordinarily come, to fall into great evils and sins. It is this: that you guard with all care against setting your thought, and still less your word, on what happens in the community; what it is or has been, nor on any religious in particular, not on his character, not on his manner, not on his affairs, however grave they may be, neither under the color of zeal nor of remedy, except to the one to whom it rightly belongs, saying it at the proper time; and never be scandalized or amazed at things you see or come to know, striving to keep your soul in forgetfulness of all that . For if you want to look at anything, even if you live among angels, many things will seem to you not good, because you do not understand their substance (it is our keeping hold of that little piece of information which does not tell me the whole truth about that person). […] So that you may understand that, even if you live among devils, God wants you to live among them in such a way that you do not even turn the head of your thought toward their affairs, but leave them entirely, striving to keep your soul pure and whole in God, without a thought of this or that hindering you. And for this, take it as certain that in convents and communities there will never be lacking something to stumble over, since there are never lacking devils who try to bring down the saints, and God permits it in order to exercise and test them. And if you do not guard yourself, as has been said, as if you were not in the house, you will not know how to be a religious, however much you do, nor reach holy nakedness and recollection, nor free yourself from the harms that are in this; because if you do not do so, however good your aim and zeal, the devil will catch you in one thing or another, and you are well caught already when you give room to distracting the soul in anything of this” 3 . Another manifestation of this strategy of deception that the tempter uses is to use lies and deceptions as remedies for pain. The devil leads souls to lie either to avoid suffering or to find relief in their suffering. There are thousands of examples, and they can range from the smallest to the greatest: like women who lie about their age as a way of coping with the fact that they are growing old and all that this entails; or they can be terribly greater, like the lie of an entire government. But we religious also fall into this trap: like the one who lies about his achievements to relieve himself of the pain of disappointments and lack of self-esteem. Like the one who exaggerates his ‘spiritual sufferings’ to console himself with the thought that he is advancing through the nights of the soul, when in reality those sufferings are due to his lukewarmness. And it sometimes happens that we spend more energy trying to twist the truth, to accommodate it to our liking, than in trying to accept or resolve a difficult reality. The devil strives to instill in us, by suggestion, the idea of an “easier” way instead of the truth, to make us believe that lying is a more attractive option. How many times—even with religious—has he made them think that it is better to lie, even if there are painful consequences, because the raw truth, just as it is, is even more painful. And even worse, the devil makes us believe that the lie works, that is, that we can create another version of reality or soften the real circumstances of our life. That in itself is false! In the long run, lies do not work! Lies are fictitious constructions of reality. How many religious ‘pretend’ to be one thing before their superiors only to obtain an office of greater importance, to be sent to one place or another, or before their spiritual directors to obtain this or that permission, to obtain approval… and afterwards they themselves cannot cope with what they obtained from their superiors! Because they built on air, on soap bubbles, because they do not have the solidity that comes from the truth. At some point, my dear friends, all that has been built on fallacies will come crashing to the ground. And there is no lack of religious who lie to ‘protect’ themselves. Listen carefully: the lie protects no one! Neither oneself nor others. The devil's deception lies in the fact that he always offers the lie as a remedy for suffering. He makes us follow an incredible logic of convenience, until he convinces us that it will be easier this way. And that is the real temptation, the real offer. Without doubt, the possibility of sparing ourselves some pain captures our attention and makes us doubly vulnerable to the devil's suggestions. And another thing about this is that the devil's most effective attacks are not direct, but oblique and evasive; those are the ones that work best. Another criterion for identifying the presence of the evil one and his deceptions is that the presence of Christ is always marked by love and truth. The absence of love, and of its correlative, which is truth, is a clear sign of the enemy. Where love is lacking, truth is lacking. On the other hand, truth—whatever that truth may be—cut off from love ceases to be truth and becomes an apparent truth or pure deception. St. Edith Stein expresses this very well, giving us this great advice: “do not accept anything as truth if it lacks love, and do not accept as love anything that lacks truth; one without the other becomes a destructive lie.” Something to keep in mind, isn't it? Sometimes we ourselves say to someone, “I'm going to give you my honest opinion,” and we do it without any hesitation, without charity, without any concern for how what we say is going to affect that person. Perhaps I am giving reliable information, but information that is also debatable, that is based on what I see externally and may be deceptive and not really true. This kind of “honest feedback ” insinuates that what I say defines the person. It insinuates that your identity, what you are worth, your place in the world is reduced to what I present to you in my very narrow understanding. If someone is told: “look, your sermon was a disaster, people were falling asleep,” perhaps he will never want to preach again. If that ever happens to you, realize that this information that is thrown at me like that, and that falls on me like a bucket of cold water, does not define me as a person . Part of the devil's deception is to make the part look as if it were the whole. Losing a match is not losing the championship! At an even more personal level, I cannot, in my eagerness to be truthful, say to someone, “you're in a bad way,” because I saw him cry and then carry on through life as if nothing had happened. That can be crushing for the soul. Very probably that person already knows that he is in a bad way. The question is what I do to help that person. The Jew who was lying on the road and was helped by the Samaritan already knew that he was in a bad way and that if no one helped him he was going to die there. There was no need for anyone to tell him. What was needed was for someone to help him get better, to recover. And that is where charity comes in. Do you see? Truth always goes together with charity; otherwise it becomes cruelty. And if it catches someone at a bad moment, it can be deadly. Think of the case in which a doctor tells a patient that the results of the biopsy were not good, that he has stage-four cancer and that the chances of a cure are minimal or nonexistent. The doctor is a specialist in the field, and routinely reports this type of news to his patients. To bear the emotional burden that this kind of news implies, the physician abstracts himself from the human context and simply reports the facts, what they found in the examination. It does not matter to him whether the patient has children or not, whether he is a newly ordained priest, or whether he is young or old. Obviously there is no loving concern or solicitude on the part of the doctor for the whole person, and that is why the patient receives the news as decisive, as if what now defines him is the cancer he suffers from. And that is not true! That is disconnecting the illness from the rest of the picture and keeping only that little piece. Is that clear? I think we realize that the work of the father of lies in our lives is not only ordinary (in the sense of routine) but extraordinary, because of how intricate and refined it can become and also because of the scale of his work. What we have considered here in no way represents the totality of the manifestations of his strategy of deception, but it helps us to be alert to the work of the enemy in our lives. Now, everyone here knows that one cannot speak of the devil without speaking of the victory of Jesus Christ over the devil in all his forms. In Christ, who is the Way, the Truth and the Life, we find the hope and confidence to keep going forward. In Him we find the specific means and the grace we need to free ourselves from the stratagems of deception that we may encounter. Notes 1 Jn 8:44. 2 Mt 4:8-11. 3 The Precautions , third precaution against the world.
The devil you know not (3)

“The devil you know not” Part III We continue with the publication of the Conference, following Louis J. Cameli’s book The Devil You Know Not . We have discussed the first strategy the devil uses, which is deception , and today we will speak of the second strategy: Division – But Jesus, knowing their thoughts, said to them: “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and house falls upon house. And if Satan is divided against himself, how will his kingdom stand? For—as you say—I cast out demons by the power of Beelzebul (Lk 11:17-18). A second strategy of the devil is precisely to cause division. The devil tries at all costs to cause division and disunity. For his efforts are aimed at working directly against the heart of our redemption in Christ, which is precisely our reconciliation and our participation in communion with the unity of the Trinity. All the attacks of the devil that have to do with division represent the counterpoint to the work of Jesus Christ: healing, reconciliation, union. For all of us, who are on the way to union with God, which is the unity for which Christ prayed at the Last Supper (“ that they may all be one” ), it is decisive that we know and be alert to the ways in which the enemy will try to undermine this unity. And we will try to see this at the different levels of our life: personal, interpersonal, social and spiritual. Personal : as we struggle with “what-we-are-and-what-we-are-not,” the devil tries to stir up waves of discouragement (another great strategy that we will see in another talk). It is easy to become discouraged when one is trying interiorly to put all the pieces together and make something coherent of one’s life. We have all had moments of discouragement, with their ever-present companion, which is the temptation to stop trying ( to stop trying ). There we already begin to see a little of the devil’s basic strategy. He will try by every means to paralyze us in what concerns the project of giving unity to our life, of making what I say agree with what I think, of making the way I act a consequence of the faith I carry in my soul—in a word: while I try to be coherent. Generally, discouragement is quite effective in this regard. But he can also make us think that it is completely out of our reach ( way beyond our reach ), like the one who realizes that he is light-years away from holiness and therefore stops even trying. In others he instills fear, because he presents to them as something ghostly the “truly determining oneself” of which St. John of the Cross speaks. They do not even want to look at the book of the “ Dark Night .” And yes, fear can easily make us retreat. The devil can also suggest that we compare ourselves with others, usually with the plan of making us overestimate the progress of others and underestimate our own: “Look how patient this one is… and I still get angry over nothing”; “How impressive! What a gift this one has for discernment, and it takes me years, and on top of that most of the time I get it wrong”; and so on, thousands of examples. What all those thoughts do is stop us abruptly. Others he makes impatient, because they think that holiness is like that, a straight ladder to heaven, where one only advances upward, and since he experiences that this is not his case he becomes agitated, gets angry… and then what does he do? He stops trying. Again and again, the devil’s plan is that we stop trying to reach holiness. And the easiest way is by making us draw back from the self-giving we have made of ourselves. A mistake. A grave mistake. The devil always tries to put an end to every possibility of self-giving and of self-donation to God and, for God, to our neighbor. St. Isaac Jogues, a few months before his death, wrote a letter in which he said: “Although I am wretched in the extreme and have made bad use of the graces God has given me in this country, I do not lose heart . God still takes the trouble to help me to be better and gives me new opportunities to be better. […] My hope is in God, who really does not need my achievements to accomplish His designs. All we need is to try to be faithful to Him and not ruin His work with our miseries.” That is the spirit. Now, in order to give ourselves we must first possess ourselves. Our Constitutions say it: “We want to form authentically free men, masters of themselves, who by possessing themselves can give themselves totally ” 1 . This possessing oneself means that there must be unity, integrity and coherence in our life. I am not a priest only when I celebrate Mass, and afterwards a parish lad who goes off to the gym. I am not saying that going to the gym is wrong, but that at every moment I am a priest and therefore I must keep the conduct proper to a priest (in custody of the eyes, in the way I dress, in what I listen to while I work out, in the attention—always moderated by temperance—that I give to the care of the body, etc). Obviously none of us here wants to be the devil’s plaything and fall into his traps. So what are the means we have to put all the pieces of our life together and offer them to God? In the first place, coherence of life implies engaging in a process of change. It is what we call ongoing conversion. Our Proper Law is very clear on this: “A religious who is not willing to go through the second and the third conversion, or who does nothing concrete to achieve it, even though he is with us in body, does not belong to our spiritual family” 2 . Word for word. And then the usual: the ascetical practices that all of you know: the discipline of denying oneself in order to be freer and more purified of the attachments that hang on us. Fasting, the penitential practices we learned in the novitiate and that are still in force, the examination of conscience that explores how we have failed to fulfill God’s will and makes us aware of the ways in which God’s grace is active in our life. Spiritual direction—honest, serious, supernatural—which presents one’s experiences to the director so that he may help to identify the way in which God is leading him and working his sanctification. And of course, prayer. That is essential, and without it everything else we do will fall to the ground. Now notice that all these means have as their ‘objective,’ if you will, to lead us to knowledge of ourselves. This self-knowledge leads us to order the pieces of our life in a coherent way, that is, according to God’s plan. Knowledge of oneself is key to self-acceptance, which is in turn key to our self-giving to God. At the interpersonal level: that is, division among ourselves. It is undeniable: divisions among men exist, with greater or lesser consequences. That is sad and at times it breaks your heart. Now, we must not blame the devil for all divisions. Each of us on our own can separate himself from the group and steadily maintain that separation. Nevertheless, one of the devil’s main works is to cause division, setting some against others. Certainly the devil can tempt us directly to separate ourselves from others, or he can exploit the divisions that we ourselves have caused. In either case, division is certainly one of the devil’s priorities. On the other hand, it must be clear that unity among us is something willed by God and that our final destiny is union with God Himself. Anything that moves us in any direction other than that is clearly not from God. The devil can use a variety of situations to create divisions and separations. For example, the promise of something better can draw us away or separate us from those who deserve our most loyal union. Like those who pursued studies paid for by their Institute at expensive universities, published books, traveled the world… and, for the promise of a paid job in a diocese, with the illusion of a ‘very good’ relationship with the bishop, and who knows what other motivations, separated from their Institute and ended badly. The promise of something better really is tempting—above all if one is going through ‘low moments,’ through times of desolation, through community difficulties, etc.—which can lead to painful and devastating divisions and separations, as happens so many times in cases of adultery or in the abandonment of friends. Another springboard for separation and division is the feelings of anger, resentment and contempt that we may have toward other people. The story of Judas is an example of this process. First he gets angry because ‘they wasted the perfume’; Our Lord “rebukes” him by praising the woman’s gesture, and there resentment enters him; and finally he despises Christ by betraying Him, separating himself from Him and from the other disciples. Not infrequently, when we feel contempt for others, when their behavior exasperates us, we distance ourselves from those people and do everything to avoid them. Yet one more motive that can cause separation is fear. At times we are afraid to show ourselves friends of others because of the potential consequences this may bring us. A classic example is Peter’s denial. I need not go into detail. But the story of the incredible separation of Peter, one of the apostles closest to Our Lord, in the decisive hour, shows how powerful the fear of what might happen to us can be, to the point of separating ourselves, ‘to save ourselves,’ at least momentarily, from those who deserve our fullest adherence, who have given us so much, etc. 3 . Likewise, greed can be another of the causes that lead to the separation of people. Not only financial greed, as when someone says “there isn’t enough here for you and me,” and so the married couple separates to seek their fortune separately. But it can also be greed for other goods: like the religious who “separates himself” from the others because he wants attention only for himself, or an apostolate only for himself; and it is also true that some simply separate themselves from the Institute out of greed for goods… because they believe that with a cross on their shoulders (the discomforts associated with poverty, misunderstandings with their superiors, the harshness of the mission… and a long etcetera) they will get nowhere. A division on a larger scale is the division that money, power, status, and invoking religion to force domination bring with them. It is precisely forgetfulness of the principle and foundation, but at a more universal level, and it is almost literally the following of the earthly king. Schlier’s book “ Principados y Potestades ” describes very well how Satan exerts his influence to twist God’s plan in an almost universal context. It says: “He begins to exercise his power above all in the general spirit of the world, in the spirit of an age and in public life, as well as in the spirit of a people, of a country, etc. This spirit, in which «the age of this world» holds sway, is not a loose spirit suspended in the air, but is breathed in by men and through them is taken up into their institutions, in one circumstance or another. It also becomes condensed in particular situations. Thus it comes to be a historically intense and powerful spirit, from which no individual can escape. Man is ruled by this spirit, and it presents itself to him as self-evident. To act, think or say anything against it is nonsense, when it is not even unjust and criminal. In it life and all other things are carried on. And «in it» one thinks: just as this spirit presents things to us, with all the concepts and valuations proper to its presentation. The prince of this world, by means of the atmosphere he dominates, makes the world and existence itself, the things, the relationships and situations of this world, appear as his own and as he understands them.” The counterpoint to the devil’s work of division is the reconciliation and unity that the Incarnate Word brought us. The most direct and solid affirmation of this unifying work of Christ is in the Letter to the Ephesians: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. For Christ is our peace; He has united the two peoples into one, breaking down the wall of enmity that separated them , and abolishing in His own flesh the Law with its commandments and ordinances. Thus He created out of the two peoples one single new Man in His own person, making peace, and reconciled them to God in one single Body, through the cross, destroying the enmity in His person. And He came to proclaim the Good News of peace, peace to you who were far off, and peace also to those who were near. For through Christ we all without distinction have access to the Father in one same Spirit. Therefore you are no longer strangers and guests, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God. You are built upon the apostles and the prophets, who are the foundations, while the cornerstone is Jesus Christ Himself. In Him the whole building, well joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. Clearly, the victory of Christ with His peace and His unity rises above all of Satan’s attempts to divide and separate us interiorly, among ourselves and at a universal level. Notes 1 200. 2 Directory of Spirituality , 42. 3 The opposite example is shown by the wife in the film “ A Hidden Life ” when her husband is about to be condemned to death because he refused to take part in the war by killing innocent people. She says to him: “I love you. Whatever you decide I am with you always.”
The devil you know not (4)

“The devil you know not” Part IV Today we are going to present the third strategy the devil uses, which is diversion (in the two previous conferences we spoke of deception and of division ), always using as our basis Louis J. Cameli’s book The Devil You Know Not . Diversion : I would like to begin speaking of this third strategy of Satan by reading a passage from the book of Exodus: When the people saw that Moses delayed in coming down from the mountain, they gathered around Aaron and said to him: ‘Make us a God who will go before us, for we do not know what has happened to Moses, that man who brought us out of Egypt.’ Aaron answered them: ‘Take off the gold rings that your wives, your sons and your daughters wear in their ears, and bring them here.’ So all of them took off their earrings and gave them to Aaron. He received the gold, worked it with a chisel and made a calf of molten metal. Then they said: ‘This is your God, Israel, who brought you out of Egypt.’ Seeing this, Aaron built an altar before the statue and announced in a loud voice: ‘Tomorrow there will be a feast in honor of the Lord.’ And the next morning, very early, they offered holocausts and communion sacrifices. Then the people sat down to eat and drink, and afterwards rose up to amuse themselves. The Lord said to Moses: ‘Go down at once, for your people, whom you brought out of Egypt, have become corrupt. They have quickly turned aside from the way I had pointed out to them, and have made themselves a calf of molten metal.’ Then they bowed down before it, offered sacrifices to it and cried out: ‘This is your God, Israel, who brought you out of Egypt’ 1 . Undoubtedly the devil wants our ruin; he wants us too to suffer his situation, that is, enmity with God. We have already seen how he employs deception and suggestion to divide us. Now we will see how he strives to divert us from the path pointed out by God, in the same way that he diverted the people of Israel, who were on their way to a free land, drawing them away from the worship of the one God. Idolatry, in fact, represents one of the main forms of diversion the devil employs. And now we will also see others that the devil uses with great effectiveness to derail us on our way to God. Pay attention: the aim of the tactic of diversion is simply to make us lose focus , that is, the center of our attention, namely: Jesus Christ; and also to make us lose the meaning of our life and the end toward which we are walking; it really derails us, draws us aside, makes us miss the mark, diverts us from our mission (or at least he tries to by every means). So, while deception and division can at times become dramatic, with a more explicit manifestation, so to speak, diversion normally operates subtly. And in truth, it may take us some time to realize that we are being led in another direction or that we have been going astray for a long time. The basic remedy for this diversion is simply the disposition to be attentive and focused on what God wants of us, and to cling to Christ, who always shows us how to remain faithful and how to live in accordance with the end we are aiming at. Let us now look at some of the manifestations of these strategies of the devil in our lives. Diversion by becoming absorbed in a task, in an office . At first sight, becoming absorbed in the task that falls to us may seem like “staying on track,” that is, like a way of aiming at the end toward which we are heading. But in fact, being absorbed in a task that has been given to us does not mean that we have correctly understood the direction we must take. Being absorbed in a task can block our attention from the purpose par excellence, which is union with God, and toward which we must orient ourselves beyond the intense demands our office makes on us. Mind you, it is not that what keeps us busy is bad, but at times it may take away from us the attention and energy that we ought to use in being transfigured into Christ. A classic example is that of Martha and Mary. What Jesus says to Martha He says to us: what occupies us—and occupies our time, our energies, our attention—may not be what ought to occupy us. How many priests spend their time listening to little videos by political commentators, reading the newspapers of the USA, of Europe, of Argentina… and obviously, since out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, the only topic of conversation they have is that… If only they would spend all that time and energy reading something for ongoing formation, calling the loneliest parishioners, those who are sick, to see if they need anything; thinking about what they can do to reach souls… Do you see? Many other examples could be given: the one who spends his time climbing mountains with young people and it seems that his whole priestly life is just organizing outings; the one who spends more time busy with ‘administrative’ tasks of the parish than in contact with souls; the one who thinks that instead of being a pastor he is the head of a construction company, and instead of pastoral activities has only building initiatives; or, on the contrary, the one who gives an excessive importance to the care of souls, or to his spiritual life (and spends his time shut up in his room reading) and forgets that the church is falling to pieces on him, that it is dirty, that for months there has been a burnt-out bulb in the sanctuary that needs changing, that the sound system does not work and a new one must be obtained…; or the one who concentrates only on the liturgy but neglects the catechetical preparation that this liturgy requires, and both he and the people end up dissatisfied with the mess that results… The point is that being wrapped up, concentrating excessively on one activity, can make us stray from the path on which God wants us to walk. The story of Martha and Mary illustrates, it seems to me, how subtle and how powerful this strategy can be, which uses self-absorption, our being absorbed in an activity, to draw us away from what we ought to do. Notice that Martha is doing something good, very good: serving. Her moral uprightness is beyond question. Notice also that she is striving to achieve something of great worth: to serve Our Lord. Now, one small detail: doing a good thing that really involves something of great worth, and moreover doing it in such a way that it ‘shows’ that I do it better than others, is really a powerful temptation to become wrapped up in it, and it works with many souls. Other things, which may be much more important, run the risk of being easily eclipsed. I leave it there for you to think about. Another of the ways in which this strategy of diversion can be identified is, in a certain way, the opposite of the previous one, that is, by disdain for the activity that has been entrusted to us. It may happen that we are absolutely certain of the direction we must follow and the goal we must reach. We know exactly what we are supposed to do, or if you want it more clearly: what we are obliged to do. But at the same time we are repelled by the idea of having to do it and having to walk that path. The devil, who is very cunning, takes advantage of some thought of ours, of a lack of ‘liking,’ of some hidden laziness, and fixes us on something negative, making us despise what we have to do, as if it lowered us… The classic example is the story of the prophet Jonah. God entrusts him with an important mission: Set out at once for Nineveh, the great city, and cry out against it, for its wickedness has come up before me 2 . But instead of doing what God asks of him, Jonah set out to flee to Tarshish, away from the presence of the Lord 3 . Literally. Eventually he goes to Nineveh, fulfills his mission, the Ninevites repent and God forgives them. Nevertheless, Jonah was extremely displeased that God had forgiven them, and he considered them contemptible people. This contempt he had for them was so strong that it diverted him from fulfilling the mission God had entrusted to him. He knew very well what his mission was, but the thought that he was among lowly, rough, poor people made him turn aside from the mission for which God had chosen him. Many times the same thing happens to us: we think we are among ‘savages,’ that they are ignorant people who will never understand, etc., and we do not teach them, we do not catechize them, and on top of that we excuse ourselves by saying: “ah, it’s because in my parish there are no nuns”: then you teach them! Something similar happens to others regarding their place of mission: that it is a place of punishment, that they sent me here so I wouldn’t bother anyone… “am I not good for something better?”, some ask themselves… And watch out, because thinking that way, that same questioning, that dissatisfaction, that disdain can then be carried over to the vocation itself: “I didn’t become a priest to look after the disabled”; “my thing is teaching and here I am…, they send me to a parish I don’t like, in the middle of the city…”. Conclusion: so I leave. Such men forget that our calling “is not command or honors, but total self-giving to the service of God and to the pastoral ministry” 4 , and that implies any work, among whatever people, and for as long as God wills. To act otherwise is to set aside the charism of the Institute, which commands us to work in the most difficult situations and in the most adverse conditions 5 . What is more, the Constitutions also say that we must “Gladly accept, and even ask for, the lowliest offices, the most difficult assignments…” 6 “those where no one wants to go” 7 . Notice that this strategy of diversion is particularly ‘successful’ in the Church, and the best of missions can be ruined by it. At times one sees so much mess in the Church, so many problems, so many injustices, that really the little, the very little one does seems no longer to make sense: what for?! Thank goodness St. Ignatius did not get caught up in that thought, otherwise the Counter-Reformation would not have happened. Another way in which this strategy of diversion presents itself: diversion means aiming a little bit to the side instead of at the center. But that slight deviation can, in the long run, make one deviate seriously from the initial starting point. Generally the way the enemy operates, according to this strategy, is to begin with a clear and noble mission, but then, by means of temptations, he gradually moves you in a very different, even opposite, direction. If that happens, the original vision we had is corrupted and one ends up turned in on oneself. St. Anthony the Abbot had a temptation of this kind. St. Athanasius tells it: “But the devil, who hates and envies what is good, could not bear to see such resolution in a young man, and tried by every means to do what he had done with so many others. First of all, he tried to draw him away from the discipline, whispering to him the memory of his wealth, the care of his sister, the claims of his kin, the love of money, the love of glory, the various pleasures of the table and other relaxations of life, and lastly the difficulty of virtue and of the labor to attain it; he also worked on him with thoughts of the infirmity of his body and the length of the trials. In a word, he raised in his mind a great cloud of debate, wishing to draw him away from the purpose on which he had settled.” The devil tries to do the same with us. Note that this strategy takes advantage of our psychology to maximize the power of temptations. On the one hand, it takes advantage of our inclination to have “human securities,” especially in what concerns material things (that I have health insurance, that I know what is going to happen from now until next Easter, that I can have a car at my disposal, that the superior supports me in ‘my projects,’ etc.). At another level of temptations, it awakens in me a certain nostalgia for the things I have left behind: “ah, when I was in Guyana… I did what I wanted, the people were wonderful!”; “ah, when I lived with so-and-so… it was fantastic.” And at a third level these temptations trigger a temptation that is in some way more dangerous than the previous ones: discouragement. Now, listen carefully: at all those levels at which temptation operates there is a central and very powerful message that the devil wants to suggest to us: all resistance is impossible . Only clinging to Christ tooth and nail is effective in fighting against this temptation and finally overcoming it. This kind of temptation, if one does not know how to overcome it, can have a devastating effect on the one who suffers it. The power of the temptation derives from the total reversal of what the person was initially seeking, from the discouraging fact that this reversal still feels like a real possibility, and—what is most significant—from the sense of total loneliness that accompanies the temptation. Only in the solace of Christ’s presence can that crushing loneliness find relief. An even more common way of diversion is by means of distraction. There is a military strategy that says that to check the advance of an army one has to destroy its communications command. Because if they cannot communicate with one another, they will surely fall. Similarly, if the devil can make us stray from our path toward union with God, it will be precisely by interrupting our communication with God, that is, our prayer. We are not speaking here of the common distractions that occur in our daily prayer. But of those distractions that come to us from anxieties or fears about the future, from the slights and offenses we have suffered at the hands of others, from comparing our situation with that of others, and from thinking about the pleasures of the present moment. Regarding fears and anxieties, let us say that they are like a fixed feature of human nature. Now, if we realize that we keep going around in the same circles of worry again and again, it is because we are stuck (stagnant) within the perimeter of “unnecessary anxiety.” Why worry any more about what I cannot solve! When these anxieties plague my prayer life, they have simply diverted me from contact with the Incarnate Word, in whom my future rests. I have to realize that this bombardment of worries (perhaps very legitimate ones) prevents me from contact with Our Lord, who is precisely our surest source of security. The other distraction that can draw us away from our path is turning over and over within ourselves the offenses we have received. How many religious spend their hour of adoration opening and reopening the wounds they have received. It is true: being offended, being treated with disrespect, being criticized or falsely accused knocks us down. Now, if for whatever reason one cannot resolve that offense, that wound can fester and reappear at some other moment of difficulty. And with it return all the feelings of anger, of resentment, of not wanting to cross paths with that person again, etc. These thoughts invade many religious especially during the time of prayer, as perhaps some of you have experienced. Now, if that is the case, how is it resolved? Simply with prayer and trust in God as the avenger of the wrongs done to me. And of course, by learning to forgive and by being humble. Those are the two means by which we can break the spell of the distraction that resentment causes us and that diverts us from contact with God in prayer. The third kind of distraction is comparing my situation with that of another with respect to who we are and what we have. This is a dangerous temptation because it makes us fix our eyes on others. In most cases it makes us envious: envy of the other because they gave him the parish or the mission I wanted; envy because the other was asked to go and preach who knows where and they never send me; envy because the superior always does what the other tells him and never what I tell him; envy because all the books the other writes get published and mine don’t; envy because they send the other someone to help him, and I have been asking for ages and am still waiting… Envy is infectious and can invade the way we think about and judge things, people, situations, and it can greatly influence our behavior. And in this sense it can mean a great diversion from our path. Other times—though perhaps not so common among us, but it certainly can happen and does happen, albeit covertly—it is making the comparison the Pharisee made in the temple: “I thank you, Lord, that I am not like these people: thieves, adulterers, or even like that tax collector” 8 . Pay attention: one cannot move forward if one is constantly looking off to the sides. The last form of distraction is becoming absorbed in momentary consolation. Enjoying something is not forbidden, but drowning in it can certainly divert me from the path. As happened to the rich man Dives in the Gospel of Luke. We know the story. The rich man was so absorbed in the world of his own satisfactions that he did not even notice the presence of Lazarus. He was shut up in himself and so he strayed from the path of compassion. Another way in which this strategy of diversion manifests itself (among several others we could mention) is straying precisely by remaining conservative—not in the sense of religious orthodoxy, but in the sense of remaining fixed in one’s quirks, in one’s habits, in one’s ways of doing things, which make one averse to everything that is new or that moves us toward a range of new possibilities, and divert us from the mission God has entrusted to us. The example that comes to mind now is technology, the whole world of social media today. If the pastor has an aversion to technology, preaches all the time about its excesses but never about its good uses and the benefit of using them well, such a man is stuck in the past. I have known some who do not allow their students computers, because they have to learn to write. Fantastic! But tomorrow they also have to go out to work, and if they do not know how to use a computer, what are they going to do? There are others who are professors—for years—and who argue that, because the doctrine of St. Thomas Aquinas has not changed, they keep teaching the same classes in the same way they have been doing for the last 30 years. Don’t even mention to them using a PowerPoint, incorporating some teaching technique… They are excellent and very solid in their doctrine, but they don’t connect, because they are stuck in the past and do not know how to present the material in a way that responds to the sociocultural idiosyncrasy of the students. And that way, what culture are they going to evangelize? When God says through the mouth of Jeremiah: amend your conduct and your deeds 9 , it means: “you have to change what you have been doing. You have to go in a new direction.” Obviously this does not apply to everything, but to those things that precisely do not allow me to advance in the direction in which I have to advance. It is also somewhat what Christ says in the parable of the talents regarding the one who buried the only talent he received—why? Because he was afraid. They choose a “safer path” and so they do not advance, because they are attached to their “old securities.” ‘No, it’s that I have this sermon that I preached when I was at the top of the mountain, and it was excellent, it came out really well.” Yes, my dear, but now you are in New York City. Do you follow? The man in the parable does not advance because he opted for the ‘conservative,’ and therefore unproductive (in the sense we have been mentioning). Some act this way because they are comfort-seekers (in which case the temptation does not come from the devil but from ourselves), but many times (and this is indeed from the devil) out of fear. Another way of ‘being conservative,’ in the pejorative sense it has here, can be seen in St. Paul’s Letter to the Galatians. You will remember when the converts from Judaism insisted to the Galatians, who were converts from paganism, on the necessity of circumcision. Those who came from Judaism clung inflexibly to the past they had inherited, to the rituals, to the laws, and placing their security in those things drew them away from Christ and emptied the faith the Galatians had received. By remaining “fixed” in the past they cannot embrace the new that comes to them through Jesus Christ. One last way the devil tries to divert us is by means of relativism. The opposite of the previous one. Practical relativism holds that everything is on an equal footing and that nothing matters in particular. There is no stable truth, so there is no solid foundation, and therefore there is no correct or appropriate direction. Watch out! For this can also happen to us, even though we are re-vaccinated against progressivism and relativism. In fact, there has been someone out there who had even written a book about progressivism and ended up a relativist on certain matters of religious life. In a religious context, relativism is like a practice of atheism, or it suggests that if God exists He does not care much how one acts or what decisions one makes. It is what Psalm 10 expresses when it says: the wicked man exclaims in the height of his arrogance: ‘There is no God who will call me to account.’ This is all he thinks 10 . And a little further on it says: ‘God forgets; He turns away His face and never sees anything’ 11 . And so one who formerly ‘loved’ the Institute and who made his perpetual vows thinks that God forgets him, and even ends up becoming an enemy of the Institute. One who formerly deplored religious who indulged in luxuries himself chooses a diocese where he earns a good salary and is full of human securities. And one wonders: how is it that you changed the whole set of values you used to have? God does not act that way. The truth is stable. In short, the devil finds a way, and one can freely cooperate with him in derailing oneself. Another example of how this relativism also represents a temptation for us religious appears in something the prophet Isaiah expresses very well. ‘Why do we fast and you do not see it, humble ourselves and you do not acknowledge it?’ 12 . How many times we complain: “but I’m doing everything right! I pray, I do penance, I put my heart into the apostolate, I humble myself and go and speak with so-and-so, and still things go badly for me, still they correct me, still they criticize me…”. And of course, as a practical corollary of these musings comes the thought that no matter what I do, it seems God does not care. One way to resist this ‘relativism’ is to plant oneself securely in Jesus Christ. God sees it! Do we not say that God is Omniscient? As St. John Newman says: “ He knows what he is about .” God knows what He is doing; I am the one who does not know. Clinging to Christ and orienting myself toward Him establishes me in the truth beyond all the ‘variables’ and factors that may influence my life. To sum up: on this Ascent of the Mount of perfection, as St. John of the Cross himself warns, and as you can see in the traditional drawing made by the saint himself, there is the risk of straying. These are the two paths that veer off to the right or to the left and that definitely do not end in union with God (one because it seeks the goods of heaven and the other because it seeks the goods of earth). The only straight path is that of nothing, nothing, nothing, which seeks only—as we have been saying in these Exercises—the glory and honor of God. Let us realize that walking on the path of the Ascent of the Mount is not the same as having arrived, and therefore I am inevitably going to encounter difficulties and a great many challenges. That is why the words of St. Peter suit us very well as a call to be realistic: Be sober and always alert, because your enemy, the devil, prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in the faith 13 . What, then, must we do to “resist firmly,” as St. Peter says, and not stray? First of all, we must exercise ourselves regularly in being vigilant, and the best thing for that is the examination of conscience. We have to examine ourselves, review our life in the light of God’s will, of His Word. And at the same time as we do that, we have to pray to the Holy Spirit to keep us in fruition with the will of the Incarnate Word. We must not take that for granted simply because we are priests. The Letter to the Hebrews expresses this perseverance in our ‘attachment’ to the path undertaken in the company of Jesus Christ, saying: Therefore, since we are surrounded by a true cloud of witnesses, let us strip ourselves of everything that hinders us, especially of sin, which always besets us , and let us run resolutely the contest that lies before us. Let us fix our gaze on the pioneer and perfecter of our faith, on Jesus , who, instead of the joy that was offered Him, endured the Cross, disregarding its shame, and is now seated at the right of the throne of God 14 . This running resolutely that St. Paul mentions implies great trust, not in ourselves but in God, who began the good work and will bring it to completion 15 .
