To Be Perfect-Ten Nuns – Part 2

To Be Perfect-Ten Nuns Part 2 6. Maternal Attitude Acting that must always be accompanied by maternal unction. This maternal attitude in dealing with souls, which must be especially characteristic of you as superiors, is something John Paul II –in one way or another– always reminded the superiors of. Thus, for example, in 1987 he told them that it was the primary responsibility of the superiors to assume the “daily maternal function of spiritual animation of consecrated souls. Here is the primary role of your service –he reminded them–: no one can replace you in the fulfillment of this mission, which invites you to be welcoming and full of affection toward the persons entrusted to you” 1 . Your Directory of Consecrated Life is quite extensive on this subject (and it should be a subject of constant study for all, but especially for those who serve as superiors in the Institute) because it is what “defines the essence and the function of the woman religious in the Church” 2 . There we find expressions such as “to consume their lives serving” 3 , “they would never forget any [of their daughters], because their love is exceedingly authentic” 4 , and the constant invitation to find in the Most Blessed Virgin Mary their most perfect model of a spiritual mother 5 . And “if she is truly a mother,” says Fr. Buela, “she has to do everything a mother does.” Which implies a whoooole bouquet of virtues and a long list of tasks. You know this better than I do! I will be frank with you: I do not intend to give you a lesson on what a superior-mother should be, but I do want to tell you with John Paul II that this motherhood must be according to the example of the best of mothers: Most Holy Mary; who gave us the most perfect “example of that maternal love with which all those must be animated who, in the apostolic mission of the Church, cooperate in the regeneration of men” 6 , and which therefore makes these mothers “strong, gentle, intrepid, always sacrificed because they are consecrated, sometimes tired, and yet always generous” 7 , said the Pope. Once, also speaking of spiritual motherhood, John Paul II quoted a writing of St. Edith Stein in which she details precisely what this mother's love consists in. It reads: “To give oneself to God, totally forgetful of self, not taking one's own individual life into account in order to leave room for the life of God: here is the deep motive, the beginning and the end of religious life. The more perfectly this is realized, the richer the divine life that fills the soul. But this divine life is love; overflowing love, which has no limits and which gives itself freely; love that bends mercifully toward every need; love that heals the sick and awakens to spiritual life what was dead; love that protects, defends, nourishes, teaches and forms; love that grieves with the grieving and rejoices with the one who is glad; that is ready for the service of each one in order to fulfill the design willed by the Father; in a word: the love of the divine Heart” 8 . That is the maternal love expected of you. This love has nothing to do with the spirit of the “vinegary nun” 9 , as Fr. Buela calls her, or with the nun who in her dealings is “wrathful, impatient, angry, harsh, who talks much and vainly, who is a muddler and a schemer” 10 ; nor is it the attitude of the superior who only pays attention to the nuns who smile at her and agree with everything she says. Her solicitude is for all the sisters under her care and, to tell the truth, for all the members of the Religious Family. That is why it is of capital importance to nourish supernatural charity and to know that this spiritual motherhood must be exercised as “an apostolic service” 11 . All the superiors, from the first to the last, should be an example in the exercise of this spiritual motherhood toward the sisters and toward the members of the IVE, whoever they may be: seminarians, chaplain, professor, novice… it does not matter; we are all members of the same family and you are the ‘mothers’. Your Directory of Consecrated Life has a paragraph that ours does not have, but which I consider it fitting to quote here, since we are speaking of spiritual motherhood, which is ultimately an exercise of charity and requires a certain formation. A paragraph that should be kept in mind when selecting future superiors. The text says the following: “A religious who does not order her affectivity, who seeks to be loved by others in a selfish way, who wants to be the center of attraction and, rather than serving, seeks her own comfort and to be served, who takes possession of her neighbors, not only seeking affection in a disordered way but wanting to exercise her dominion proudly –worse still if it is a matter of superiors–, who shows favoritism, surrounding herself with obsequious people even though they are evidently not the most suitable or the best, but only those who flatter and never contradict, who cannot bear the slightest slight or correction –even when she is right–, etc.,” 12 cannot be a superior. It would be a disaster, “even if she fulfills perfectly –which will be quite rare– all the ‘material’ observances of religious life” 13 . And the same Directory says: “it would be a living lie.” Watch out for that!: external observance does not necessarily imply capability for command, much less having the maternal spirit that must prevail in a superior. The Proper Law defines a superior as one who has “the spirit of a mother, has patience in dealing with others and in bearing their defects, must be just in reproving and punishing faults, have confidence and also hope of their amendment, and above all must have the exquisite charity that seeks only the good of her subjects” 14 . “Now, in order to obtain sisters adorned with these qualities, it is of great importance to have superiors of good judgment at the head of the Institute –says St. John Bosco–; superiors who thoroughly possess, and themselves practice, the virtues they must instill in the sisters. It is necessary –the saint goes on to say– that the superiors love all without distinction…; but to this patient and kind charity they must join a certain firmness of character which, when there is need, knows how to prevent abuses and the non-observance of the Constitutions without the least violence, but also without human respect” 15 . I end this point with a short quotation from Don Orione speaking of the charity that must animate all religious-mothers: “Charity has nothing arbitrary, nothing hard about it; it finds its happiness in spreading and radiating around itself goodness, sweetness, kindness; one thing it desires: to immolate itself in order to bring about the happiness and salvation of others, for the glory of God” 16 . Truly, it is my wish for all the Servants, present and future, that they exercise their spiritual motherhood in that spirit. 7. Exercise of authority Intrinsically associated with this theme of spiritual motherhood comes the exercise of authority on the part of the superiors. Which is of the first importance, says John Paul II. And so he goes on to say: “The exercise of authority, with a spirit of service and love for all the sisters, is a vital subject, even though it is difficult and demands no little courage and dedication. The superior has the duty to help the religious so that she may fulfill her vocation ever more perfectly. The superior cannot evade this obligation, which is certainly arduous but indispensable. The fulfillment of this duty demands constant prayer, reflection, consultation, but also courageous decisions, with awareness of one's own responsibility before God, before the Church and before the religious themselves who expect this service. Weakness, like authoritarianism, constitutes deviations equally harmful to the good of souls and to the proclamation of the Kingdom” 17 . That is why the Proper Law defines the office of governing as a sacred office 18 , as a Cross 19 , and ultimately as a service 20 . Our Founder has bequeathed to us by example and by word a very rich patrimony from which to learn the way authority is exercised in our Institute, and all the superiors of the SSVM must be fluent in the knowledge of this doctrine. “The system of government there must be,” says Fr. Buela, “is an evangelical system, proper to a family, where the superior, man or woman, is not a despot, is not a dictator, is not a sergeant. That is a mockery of the Gospel and of Jesus Christ. Yes, we have the religious vows, but according to the Gospel. We must not imitate formal, external types of obedience that are carried out in other spheres” 21 . “There does not exist in the Catholic Church a military-type system of government; that does not exist, it must not exist. We are the ‘family of God’, says St. Paul” 22 . Hence the Proper Law affirms that the exercise of authority in our Institute “must be above all fraternal and spiritual, and must know how to involve the sisters in the decision-making process through dialogue; nevertheless, the last word belongs to authority, to whom it also belongs to see that the decisions taken are observed” 23 . Regarding the exercise of authority as service, Fr. Buela goes on to say: “Those who have responsibilities in the community [such as those who are superiors] must flee the temptation to consider themselves ‘great’ and to make their authority felt. The first must make himself the last; the great, small; the leader, servant” 24 . This means that one must “govern subjects as children of God; and those who are superiors must project onto their subjects the same charity with which God loves them as daughters” 25 ; it means “showing veneration for the human person, specifically for their subjects, based on the dignity of every person” 26 (because there may be superiors who claim this veneration only for themselves, and then instead of daughters they have a retinue that waits on them). Moreover, this office requires knowing how “to listen willingly” –without hurry, placing oneself within the other person's frame of thought 27 – and fundamentally “to decide and command what must be done” 28 . But very principally it also implies “promoting voluntary obedience, encouraging willingness in obedience, submissive freedom” 29 . Therefore, all the superiors of the Institute of the Servants must be masters (pay attention to what I am telling you), “ masters of Don Bosco's preventive system ”, which is so well explained in the Directory of Oratories . Why? Because the oratorian spirit is the embodiment of our spirituality and therefore must be lived in all our houses, not only in the houses of formation, not only in the Hogarcitos, but in every community of sisters. There one finds concrete and excellent guidelines on how authority is exercised in our Religious Family. How can there be superiors who have never read it? Look, there the superiors are taught “always to show themselves as mothers”, “to try to make themselves loved rather than feared”, “to foster trust between subjects and superiors”, “to show a liking for what the subjects like”, “to promote that family spirit by which ‘familiarity leads to affection and affection leads to trust’”, and so we could go on with a long list that would make life easier for all. Few things bother subjects as much as the superior who is distant, haughty, who never lowers herself to them, who seems to govern ‘sitting behind a desk’ and never mingles with the tasks of her daughters. Do you want the sisters to talk with you, to open their hearts to you, to obey you promptly? The secret lies in familiarity and trust, which is not obtained except in closeness to the other person, in an attitude of service on your part –in fact and in deed– (genuine and not only in word). So if a sister asks to see you, you must immediately make arrangements for that to happen within the possible limits of time and space, never limiting yourselves to closeness by WhatsApp (not that it is wrong; I only say that one must not limit oneself to that). If the sisters perceive you as inaccessible, if to speak with you one has to ask for an appointment a week in advance (or more), if they write you an email and with luck you answer within a month, if the dialogue between you and the sisters is restricted ‘solely and exclusively’ to the canonical visitation, if you do not know how to make the others co-responsible by sharing with them what you know about the Institute or about the missions, if you never ask them whether they need something or how you can help them, if they speak with you and within a minute or two the rest of the community knows what you talked about, if they hear you criticize other religious (something that should not happen)… all that, sisters, uproots –I would say at the root– the trust and familiarity that ought to exist between you. And it sows such discredit with respect to authority that it can hardly be remedied some day, with the great harm this entails for religious life. I know, and I am well aware, that it is not easy in our day to fulfill this mission of superiors. We have just said that it is a Cross. That is why, making the words of John Paul II my own, I encourage you not to abdicate your duty and the exercise of authority; to exercise it with a deep sense of the responsibility that falls upon you before God and before the sisters. With all understanding and fraternity, do not give up practicing, when necessary, patient correction, so that the life of the sisters may fulfill the purpose of religious consecration. These inescapable difficulties of your mission are part of your own vocational self-giving 30 . Without realizing it, you are forming the future superiors, those who one day will govern the Institute. Do not fail to keep it in mind. 8. Formation In the Conclusions of your last General Chapter are recorded the many advances that have been made with regard to the Formation of the sisters, and from the length of the treatment, the importance this has in the Institute becomes evident. One must continue in that direction. In all the areas and stages that a thorough formation embraces, according to the identity and mission of the Institute. Now I simply wanted to mention to you just two little things St. John Paul II says on this subject: The formation of the formators. A formation oriented toward “biting into reality”. Regarding the first, John Paul the Great affirmed: I hope that the institutes that receive numerous candidates (as is your case, by the grace of God) will prepare the formators who will accompany them with competence, patience and effectiveness throughout their initial and ongoing formation 31 . About this effectiveness, it seems important to me to point out that it is imperative that those who serve as formators be fully imbued with the spirit of the Congregation. It is in this sense that the Proper Law says: “The formation of formators has a priority character 32 . [It is necessary that the] formators be capable of ‘forming young people of great spirit, who know how to transmit to the new generations of our Religious Family the charism that the Holy Spirit granted to the founder’ 33 ” 34 . And therefore all the formators must be united in one same spirit and tend to one same end 35 . Remember that the future of the Institute depends fundamentally on the formation given to the members in the times of preparation 36 . And in that we must know how to invest our best energies and resources. Sometimes one falls into the error of choosing formators who are only pleasant to deal with, but who have great failings as regards knowledge of the spirit of the Institute (perhaps because they are very new, perhaps because they were not seasoned in an apostolic mission, perhaps because that is what they learned…). Other times they are versed in the Magisterium of the Church and in doctrine, but they too do not know the patrimony of the Institute thoroughly. Other times they are so harsh and distant that they make any learning unbearable, or they are so attached ‘to what is their own’ that they make assimilation difficult for the candidate who is of another culture. I mean, I know it is not easy, but one must seek a balance between the human virtues required for such an office together with doctrinal formation and a thorough knowledge of the patrimony of the Institute. Regarding the second, that is, formation oriented toward “biting into reality”, it is something key for us. And as you well know, it belongs to one of the non-negotiable elements attached to the charism and therefore must be emphasized in the formation given in our houses. In this sense, the first thing is to conform our life to that of the Incarnate Word. That is clear. But this formation also aims to form women capable of facing reality with a supernatural vision, in order to transform it according to the spirit of the Incarnate Word and according to the mode of the Incarnation, that is: assuming the cultures that must be evangelized 37 . And, faithful to the mystery of the Incarnate Word, to undertake evangelization without diluting faith into the rational, without turning the sacred into the profane, without falling into insubstantial spiritualities, without accepting any dualistic and Manichean view of reality, nor that which considers reality to have a one-dimensional character 38 . Hence the importance we give to Thomistic formation, and how important it is that the sisters learn St. Thomas not as a catechism, but that they be taught to think. A formation that must not be restricted to the years of initial formation, but must extend even to ongoing formation –as I believe is already done in several provinces– and that enables them to give a positive response to the current problems from the point of view of the Gospel. That is why our Spiritual Father pointed out the need for a serious and authentic updating on the part of the religious in the various doctrinal fields, overcoming the dangers of superficiality and emotionalism. It is necessary, therefore, to watch attentively over the various means of renewal and orientation (books, newspapers, magazines, courses of study, etc.), so as not to let oneself be confused by false ideas nor lead the persons one deals with along mistaken paths. Every family [and every person] desires the truth from one who is consecrated to God; be, then, faithful and happy to be able to proclaim it and bear witness to it 39 . 9. Vocational ministry One cannot “be a perfect-ten nun” and not work for vocations. That is why another of St. John Paul II's requests to the major superiors refers precisely to vocational ministry. “Governing is a cross; true power is vocations” 40 , says the Directory of Government . How much is done at the level of the General Government and in the Provinces for vocational ministry? And when I say vocations I do not mean only vocations to consecrated life, but also priestly vocations. I know that in many places they hold open-house days or come and see events, as the format is known in some places, by which young women are invited to spend one or several days at the convent and get to know a little more about the Institute. And that is very good! One must keep on doing it, and ever better and with greater quality. But that is not the only means. The Proper Law speaks of “reactivating an intense pastoral action… of an enthusiastic youth ministry [which] gives the Church the servants she needs” 41 . If Fr. Buela says that every parish should have a good oratory, analogously every convent should at least have a group of children, of young people, etc. –whenever possible, of course; if you work in a home for the elderly, the thing will be more difficult– but something can and must always be done for vocations. I think I once told this in a circular letter, but I will tell it to you again now. I do not know if you know the story of Blessed Jordan of Saxony, a Dominican. Only three years after entering religious life he replaced his Founder and became Superior General of the whole Community. And he remained in this office for 15 years, until his death in 1237. During his term 249 houses of the Congregation were founded and six new provinces of religious were made. Now, think about it: you have to have people to send to all those houses. And the fact is that they say Jordan of Saxony had great influence among university students. One of his early biographers, a companion of his, says: “The religious houses where Father Jordan lived looked like beehives, because of the many young men who entered to become religious, and the many who went out from there to be superiors of other religious houses. That is why, on arriving at a convent, he would order many religious habits to be made, trusting that God would send him very numerous vocations, and so it happened to him everywhere.” Father Jordan not only went to the universities to find very well-educated young men to become religious, but he also went to the countryside and to the working-class neighborhoods to invite healthy lads, even if they were unlettered, to enter the community. And this earned him the accusation that he was receiving people who were not going to bring glory to his Congregation. I tell you this first because of the importance of the university apostolate as a source of vocations, but also to point out what the Conclusions of your Chapter in 2016 say, namely: “to be very careful not to place obstacles to vocations, being on the contrary very patient in giving the necessary time , bearing in mind that the selection of the candidate, although it must be serious, must nevertheless be progressive, not being too demanding at the beginning, as we have always been advised, seeking the middle ground: ‘ the selection must be serious but one must also have mercy ’ (cf. annex Conclusions Chapter 2010)” 42 . Certainly there will be no lack of those who say that because you have many vocations ‘there is a lack of discernment there’ or that ‘it is not normal’, setting limits to Divine Providence and setting themselves up as counselors of God, who is the one who calls them. Do not let that discourage you from continuing to do all you can for vocations. Each of you must feel responsible for vocational ministry, and you must pass this on to the sisters when you return to your countries, proposing concrete initiatives, among which the promotion of the Spiritual Exercises cannot be lacking. But also always remember that the “center of all vocational ministry” is prayer. In how many Provinces is the apostolate of the 40 Hours still not promoted as it should be? By this I do not mean that you do not pray for vocations, but that it is always a matter of doing more and better for the cause of Christ, using all the means within reach. Become promoters of the apostolate of the 40 Hours. And you yourselves, whenever you can, offer at least one of those 40 Hours for vocations in your Province. John Paul II told the superiors: “Pray without ceasing for religious vocations: [so that] the ideal of consecrated life, an immense and gratuitous gift of God, may exercise an ever greater attraction on numerous young women oriented toward the highest and noblest achievements” 43 . Finally, Fr. Buela also says: the great secret of vocational flourishing is the Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, the only one who has words of eternal life (Jn 6:68). Which must not be lacking in our proclamation. 10. Model: Most Holy Mary Lastly, and as it could not be otherwise, again and again the Holy Pontiff exhorted women religious to find in the Mother of the Incarnate Word the Ideal Model of what a consecrated woman should be. And so already in ’87 he told them: “In carrying out your apostolic mission, you have the model of the figure of Mary, … May you discover in her, ever more deeply, the model of your consecration to God and, at the same time, that of your apostolic commitment in the service of your brothers and sisters” 44 . Note that John Paul II points to Mary as a model 1) of religious consecration and 2) of service. Regarding Mary as a model of religious consecration, the Directory of Consecrated Life has a section devoted to the subject. There it is mentioned how Our Lady is the perfect model of consecration that all of us –and very especially you, mothers– must contemplate and imitate. Because the Mother of God is “the obedient Virgin”, “the contemplative woman”, “the missionary”, “the only one sensitive to the needs at Cana; the firm witness at the foot of the Cross; the center of unity who held together the newborn Church in its expectation of the Holy Spirit” 45 . But Most Holy Mary is also pointed out to us as the Model (with a capital letter) of spousal love and of maternal love, so imperatively necessary for a woman religious. For to be a religious implies being a spouse of Christ, and if she is to be a spouse of Christ she must embrace the same life of poverty and virginity as Christ, which means also assuming Mary's kind of life 46 . Our Mother in Heaven is truly the star that shines as a model of virtue before the whole community of the elect 47 And with those virtues of the Mother, says the Holy Pope Paul VI, “the children will adorn themselves, who with steadfast purpose contemplate her example in order to reproduce it in their own lives” 48 . What, then, are those virtues that must stand out with special splendor in women religious? Paul VI also mentions them in his apostolic exhortation Marialis Cultus : “faith and the docile acceptance of the word of God; generous obedience; simple humility; solicitous charity; reflective wisdom; piety toward God, prompt in the fulfillment of religious duties, grateful for the gifts received, which she offers in the temple, which prays in the apostolic community; fortitude in exile, in suffering; poverty borne with dignity and trust in the Lord; vigilant care for the Son, from the humility of the crib to the ignominy of the Cross; delicate forethought; virginal purity; strong and chaste spousal love 49 . Nothing is more inconsistent with this Model than the religious (or the superior, if you like) who is not obedient, or rather who obeys “depending on who commands or what is commanded” 50 , or “who obeys amid murmuring and complaint, and the ‘spirit of opposition’, or simply as a display of the servility and pharisaical obedience that animates her 51 . Nothing is further from the Model of consecration that is Most Holy Mary than the religious/the superior who is neither humble nor simple and who often conducts herself with arrogance, or does everything to be seen, so that people may have ‘a good opinion’ of her (in our Argentine way we would say: ‘she does it to make sure of her post’). Those also contradict this magnificent Model of consecration who are not grateful but demand everything (or think that “everything is owed to them”), who, far from possessing that reflective wisdom the Pope mentions, are impulsive, govern and make decisions according to the mood they are in that day. Have you noticed that the Most Blessed Virgin is also the Model of that vigilant care one must have for all the children? Not only for this one or that one ‘because later I need her to help me with something’, but for all, including the priests. And this to such a point that, in imitation of Most Holy Mary, women religious, and above all if they are superiors, must exercise that virtue which the Pope mentions almost at the end and which is delicate forethought (in English it is her delicate forethought ). It means that she anticipates, foresees in advance what the needs of her son/daughter will be, which implies putting herself in his place and, with great forgetfulness of self, knowing how to arrange the means, anticipating with the timely word, and so… doing those strokes of genius that mothers do that make one say: “I was just thinking about how I was going to manage and …” “or that was exactly what I needed …”, etc. Because Our Lady's maternal love is “a concrete love, which is not limited to words of understanding, but commits itself personally to authentic assistance” 52 . That is why Our Lady is also the Model of service “to the ignominy of the Cross”. The image of the Most Blessed Virgin at the foot of the Cross –as Fr. Buela explains– “must remind you not only of the why, but of the place, the function and the mission of the Servants ” 53 . “May the Virgin Mary help you to love, at the cost of any sacrifice, even to the point of heroism, as so many of your sisters have known how to do. May her presence be for each of you guidance and help.” Never forget that our spirituality wishes to be especially marked, with special prominence 54 , by our devotion to the Mother of God. Always have recourse to her. Distinguish yourselves by your devotion to Our Lady. And encourage and sustain the vocations entrusted to you, after the example of Mary, by the generosity of her fiat. Know that Our Lady is not only your model but also your Mother. And therefore a sure recourse in need, a source of strength in moments of difficulty and danger, and the greatest thing we have in this valley of tears. * * * In short, as I told you at the beginning, I believe that these 10 points, if they are maintained, if they are made life in each of you and in the jurisdictions in your charge, will be decisive in the life of the Institute. Much is at stake and it is very important that you remain thoroughly and genuinely firm in the principles that have guided the Institute from its origins. The key word here is fidelity: fidelity to God, fidelity to the charism and patrimony of the Institute, fidelity to the Church that has approved it; all of which is ultimately also fidelity to oneself. These are times of trial, and blessed be God that it is so! “For it is fitting that we not lack the Cross, as our Beloved did not” 55 . And because the Cross is absolutely and definitively part of the program. Did not the Founder tell you so in one of the first sermons preached to the Servants? “The Cross on which are the Lord and the Virgin of Matará constitutes a most beautiful program of life which those who take pride in bearing that name must strive to attain, with the grace of God, which is never lacking if one does what must be done . To project to the new generations the high ideals expressed in this Cross must be a renewed endeavor of each and every member of our Religious Family through the ages, so that the Gospel of Jesus Christ may resound in every corner of the earth: Go into all the world and preach the Gospel (Mk 16:15)” 56 . One last anecdote: one day, after a clothing ceremony at which he had handed out many crucifixes, St. John Bosco gave a talk to the Daughters of Mary Help of Christians, among whom were many superiors and directresses. On that occasion he gave them some advice which I believe is very fitting for you too. St. John Bosco told them: “let us all seek to carry, not the cross we would want, but the one the holy will of God assigns us [as may be the office you hold and in the present circumstances the Religious Family is going through]. Let each of us carry it cheerfully, thinking that as the years pass, so does the cross. […] Yes, daughters, let each of us carry our own cross with love and not lean it on others. Let each one say to herself: ‘Certainly I am a cross for others, just as others are often a cross for me; but I want to carry my cross by myself, and I must not be a cross for others’. […] This applies especially to you, teachers and directresses, who are directly occupied with the salvation of your neighbor. […] Perhaps you work a great deal and, in spite of everything, do not succeed in making others content. Always work for the glory of God, and always carry your cross well, because that is how it pleases the Lord. Certainly there will be thorns, but thorns that in time will be changed into flowers that will last for all eternity […] Do good, do good works. Toil, all of you work hard and always for the Lord with good will. Yes. Do not waste time. Do all the good you can. You will never regret it” 57 . “Let each one, therefore, fulfill the office entrusted to him; but let him fulfill it with zeal, with humility and trust in God, and let him not lose heart if he must make some painful sacrifice. Let it serve him as consolation to think that his labors will redound to the benefit of that congregation to which we have consecrated ourselves” 58 . When one thus contemplates at a glance these 10 points that John Paul II pointed out, and examines oneself personally and also how one is carrying out the sacred office entrusted to one, not infrequently one realizes that we are unprofitable servants ; but we must never be discouraged, nor retreat, nor come down one point with respect to the ideals and holy interests of the Institute. “Have confidence in Jesus even in your discouragements, even when your body or your spirit is reduced to powerlessness and refuses to help you. Say then: I do not rely on myself, my God, but on you, and in you I can do all things if you help me. I have nothing, and I can do almost nothing, but even so, I am going to begin. You will finish. –And, having said this, set to work; do the little you can, and God will take care of the rest. God is pleased to multiply difficulties; he halts and nails one down in powerlessness. One would like to, but one cannot. It ends in an agony […]. But when one takes a step praying and invoking, God comes, gives wings of love, and you will be amazed to see how you fly with freedom and grace. Come now! our Lord is yours; go to him with confidence. Exercise yourselves in confidence. Always trust in him and distrust yourselves: a grace I wish you for today and for always” 59 . Finally, all that remains is for me to give you much encouragement and wish you, as always, all the best. May Our Lady always protect you and bless you abundantly. On the Prayer Life of the Priest – Part I

Our Directory of Spirituality , quoting the Mystical Doctor, says: “Let those, then, who are very active, who think to encircle the world with their preaching and exterior works, take note here that they would bring much more profit to the Church and be much more pleasing to God if they spent even half the time in being with God in prayer” 1 . They say that when St. John of the Cross was free from other occupations he would be found in a little corner of his cell, or commonly in the choir before the Blessed Sacrament. They say that most of the siesta hours in summer, and two or three hours of the night in winter, he spent in prayer in the church or in the choir. And the Saint recommended that same spirit of prayer to other religious: “try to be continual in prayer, and in the midst of bodily exercises do not leave it. Whether you eat, drink, or speak or deal with lay people, or do anything else, always go about desiring God and attaching your heart to him, which is a very necessary thing for interior solitude” 2 . That is what we are going to treat now: prayer. Only for reasons of simplicity and order we will divide this talk into four points: Mental prayer Liturgical prayer The most excellent prayer, which is Holy Mass Marian devotion 1. Mental prayer “In doing our works well lies our spiritual commerce, and in doing them according to the rule, our holiness. Perfection consists in doing them with a spirit of prayer.” Who said this? St. Peter Julian Eymard, founder of the Blessed Sacrament Fathers. Definitely, that is the idea. Prayer must permeate all our acts. As St. John of the Cross was also just saying: …whether you drink, eat, or deal with lay people, you must always have your mind and heart on God alone. As you well know, part of the discipline of our Institute is “the exposition and adoration of the Blessed Sacrament for one hour daily” 3 , because we are aware that “a while of true adoration has more value and spiritual fruit than the most intense activity, even if it were apostolic activity itself” 4 . That must always be kept in mind and must be guarded very carefully. Fulton Sheen, as you perhaps already know, was a great apostle of Eucharistic adoration. He himself made it daily. To tell the truth, in his time Eucharistic adoration was not something so common, and that is why he insisted a great deal, above all to priests and to those preparing for the priesthood, that they devote an hour to adoration daily. Then some objected to him that an hour a day was very difficult. So he told them that what is done once a week is an interruption in the week, that an hour of adoration once a week never becomes a habit, that an hour a week is not a gift that shows a very deep love. Because: What mother is content to see her son only once a week? What wife is content to see her husband once a week? Love is not intermittent. Adoration must be done every day, he said, because our crosses are daily, not once a week; because the children, the sick, the missions, the families, the dying need our intercession every day 5 ; because the enemy does not rest 6 . We have the ease and the grace that in our communities and in most of our parishes Eucharistic adoration is daily and something ‘familiar’. Nevertheless, there is always the risk of not doing it with the excuse that one is ‘very busy’, has to travel, is on vacation, is alone for a while, and who knows what else. Not to mention interior dryness, tiredness, ‘meetings’, soccer matches, the siesta, our own lukewarmness and a host of other things that are always trying to make us set adoration aside. Fulton Sheen himself affirms that the hour of adoration faithfully kept throughout priestly life is a sign that the priest is a true victim . I do not remember where I read it, but he tells how many times he had to get up earlier in order to make his adoration, and sometimes that meant very few hours of sleep, but he made his hour of adoration all the same. And elsewhere he tells that once, being in Paris, he had two hours between trains, so he went to the Church of Saint-Roch to make his holy hour. And he says that although there are not even ten days in a whole year on which he sleeps during the day, that day was one of them, because he was utterly exhausted. He says he sat down at about two in the afternoon (he was too tired to kneel) and fell asleep. He slept soundly until three in the afternoon. On waking, he says, he asked our Lord: Did I make the hour of adoration? (as if he had not even noticed) and he says Christ answered him: Yes, that is how the apostles made their first hour of adoration. The point is that thus, tiredness and all, between trips or before trips, at home or away from it, he would look for an adoration chapel and there make his hour of adoration, but he did not fail to make it. A temptation that is always there. You know very well all the reasons why it is more than fitting to make adoration. Here I would like to add or specify some others, besides the principal reason, which was that the Incarnate Word himself asked his priests, the apostles, to do it: Watch one hour with me . The hour of adoration combats priestly weariness . As in a marriage, after some years in the priesthood one loses the sensitivity of love. Therefore we must pay closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away , as the Letter to the Hebrews says 7 . Our souls are lost not only because we do evil things, but also because we are negligent in doing good things: we bury the talent, we do not walk the extra mile, we pass by the wounded man the Samaritan helped. How often in the gospel condemnation follows precisely upon not doing: you did not give me to eat, you did not give me to drink, you did not welcome me, you did not visit me 8 … We who have the enormous privilege not only of being priests but of having in our houses the Divine Presence of our Lord, how much greater is our responsibility to adore him and keep him company. If I ask you: How many retreats have you made in your life? Ten? Twenty? Forty? How many resolutions made in all those retreats have you kept? There it gets more difficult. Perhaps many of those retreats were like those congresses held about health: everyone wants health but no one makes a concrete proposal. Eucharistic adoration is something concrete, a practical resolution that helps me confront the apathy and decline that corrode our souls. Usually the main reasons why we give up the hour of adoration are: 1. Time; 2. The weakness of our will. We say we do not have time. How much time do we spend reading the newspaper on the internet, or watching a match, or going to the gym, or watching stupid little videos on YouTube? But we are intelligent, so sometimes the excuses take on a more religious tint: ‘I have to plan the mission’, ‘I have to prepare a sermon’, ‘the novices are coming to the parish’, ‘today I have to teach six hours of class’… The excuses we sometimes give are as silly as the ones given in the gospel to that king for not attending the banquet: I have bought a field and I must go and see it (imagine, he bought it without seeing it); I have bought five yoke of oxen and I am on my way to ‘try them out’; I have just gotten married, well then, why don't you bring your wife too?! And so we argue that we have no time, which leads us to the second real reason for not making adoration, which is the weakness of our will. We live in an age in which our will collapses under emotion; we have no determination. How many have abandoned the self-discipline that is the condition for our priestly victimhood. We become like children: not a second must pass between our demands and their satisfaction. How, then, do we overcome the excuse of time and apathy? By taking control of a segment of time, of one hour, and redeeming it. It is for our Lord, it is for the Church, it is for the world, not for me. Period. We must kill acedia by displacing it with a new love. We cannot expel our vices all at once, but we can hem them in by deepening our love for Christ. The hour of adoration is a sign of our victimhood in the work of redemption . Because it incorporates us into the intercessory work of Christ. We are bound to humanity, to the nations, to the missions, to our homeland, to our diocese, to our parish, to our Institute, to our friends and to our enemies. Our victim-priesthood commits us to intercede for them and for their salvation. Perhaps one of the cruelest words a priest can say to those who suffer is ‘Pray.’ Are we not their intercessors? We must pray for them and with Right there. The agony of Christ continues in marriages going through difficulties, in girls who have lost their purity, in religious who are tempted, in children of addicted parents, in abandoned elderly people, in priests who have lost their faith, in enemies who fight against us with malice, in catechists who teach everything but Christ, in defections… That is why another motivation for the hour of adoration is also that of reparation. The Proper Law says it explicitly: we “adore Jesus Christ for those who do not adore him, who abandon him, forget him, despise him and offend him” 9 . How many of my adorations do I offer for that intention of reparation? Lastly, the hour of adoration is necessary as a form of authentic prayer . Our world is incredibly fast. The other day I had to prepare a talk on technology. Do you know what happens in one minute of internet? I will give you some figures so you can realize the speed of the age in which we live. For example: in one minute, Netflix users watch 694,444 hours of video. 277,777 posts are made on Instagram. Every minute YouTube users watch 4,500,000 videos. 511,200 tweets are sent. 188,000,000 emails are sent. Every minute more than 18 million text messages are sent. Skype users make 231,840 calls. 55,140 photos are uploaded to Instagram. 4,497,420 searches are made on Google. Every minute 1,389 bookings are made on Airbnb. 9,772 Uber rides are taken. Every 60 seconds 390,000 apps are downloaded. We are included in all those numbers, eh? Add to that the noise that drowns out the voice of conscience; get on a train and see how many do not have earphones: most do. We live in a world where activity kills the knowledge of oneself and of God that contemplation brings. Even in many seminaries, in many communities, there is a sort of fragmentation of spiritual exercises, that is, now we do adoration, at noon we pray the Angelus, at night I pray Compline, done. But the spirit of prayer that ought to be present throughout the whole day is lacking. Fulton Sheen says: hell is full of clocks, and so is our priestly life. And he proposed as a solution making an uninterrupted hour of adoration, an hour that begins along with the day, early in the silence of the morning, and is prolonged throughout the day . Being faithful to that hour of adoration and not letting anything interfere with it is definitely, he says, a sign of our victimhood with Christ. God has not called us to lead the penitential life of the anchorites, but our hour of adoration is our sacrifice united to that of Christ. Many of you, I know for a fact, make it with great fidelity: Congratulations! Because the pastoral work you are doing proves that you have first been in familiar converse with the Incarnate Word. And that must be maintained with all fidelity. In one of his books Sheen recounted the following: “I know a priest who has never failed to make his hour of adoration in 54 years. His daily petition is to drop dead in the presence of the Blessed Sacrament on a Saturday, on a feast of our Lady. He is not sure the Lord will grant it to him after having asked for that grace for so long, but he always says that if the Lord does not grant it, he will be ashamed when he sees him.” He was speaking of himself. He died on Sunday, December 9, 1979, the day after the solemnity of the Immaculate Conception. This past year (2019) marked 40 years since his death, and since December 8 fell on a Sunday it was moved to December 9. It seemed that God was fulfilling his wish. So far we have spoken of the formal hour of adoration, which is part of our rule and which we must not neglect. An hour of prayer that we must prolong throughout the whole day, however busy we may be. We must live as if clothed with the spirit of prayer. We pray in the morning, at night and several times throughout the day; but these are acts of prayer, not habits that form the spirit of prayer. Why, after so many days, months, years of performing these acts of piety, are we still so far from perfection? And we do not say this only out of humility, but starting from reality. The answer can only be this: either we do not do them well, or we do not try to profit from them. “Recollection is absolutely necessary in order to profit from what one does; otherwise we are left with those kinds of oases [of intermittent acts] that are the spiritual practices, but outside of them, everything is arid. When, afterwards, we cannot keep our mind fixed on God, it is enough to refer our actions to him and everything becomes prayer. In this consists the spirit of prayer, which helps the interior life a great deal. A missionary must be able to maintain recollection in any place; to know how to pass from study or work to prayer; to remain united to God with a permanent, or at least frequent, elevation of the heart; in short, to work with great dedication and, at the same time, to pray. If you do not have this spirit, you will never be good missionaries. You may believe you are, but in reality you are not. Happy are you if you always try to advance in the interior life, with the spirit of recollection and prayer!” 10 , said Blessed Allamano. If we maintain this spirit of prayer, of recollection, it becomes not only easier to discern the will of God, but also to safeguard oneself against a host of temptations and dangers. I give you as an example St. John of the Cross, who was a man of well-settled categories and demanded of himself what he taught others. He said: “ What does it profit you to give God one thing if he asks you for another? Consider what God will want and do it, for in this way you will satisfy your heart better than with that to which you are inclined” 11 . That is, faced with one task or another, having discerned the will of God, the saint immediately did what was asked of him and knew how to leave contemplation for adobe bricks, spiritual direction for the broom, poetry in order to attend with all attention and patience to some poor man who knocked at the door. All of which was possible because he lived in the spirit of prayer. And we must do the same “so that we may proceed from the lesser to the greater and from the more exterior to the more interior, until we reach the intimate recollection where the soul is united with God” 12 . It is no news that priestly life, missionary life, is strewn with great graces but also with great trials and much work. “Hence the need for long periods of prayer, of concentration, of adoration; the need for an assiduous and meditated reading of the word of God; the need for a contemplative and therefore calm and relaxed rhythm in the celebration of the Eucharist and of the Liturgy of the Hours; the need for silence as an indispensable condition for achieving a deep communion and thus making our whole life a prayer. As consecrated persons we must not only pray, we must be a living prayer . One could also say: we must pray while apparently not praying. We must pray while apparently not having time to pray, but we must pray. It is another paradox [of our priestly life]. Humanly this is impossible. How can one pray while not praying? But St. Paul says that the Spirit prays in us , and then the matter turns out somewhat differently…” 13 . This was said by our beloved John Paul the Great. To be a living prayer… to pray while apparently not praying… because the Spirit prays in us . That is what I would like to refer to now. To those unspoken, silent prayers; to the prayers made of our crosses and labors. The unspoken prayers of the priest: Since we as priests are not free from the infirmities of our fallen nature, notwithstanding our sublime call to the priesthood, Sacred Scripture often calls us to pray. But the truth is that many times we are not exactly very inclined to pray. And we forget the role that only the Holy Spirit plays in our sanctification. Bad habits, acedia, lukewarmness, tiredness, all of that, as we have just said, can conspire to prevent us from raising the level of our prayer. But even in those cases the Holy Spirit, who is God, can enlighten the darkest soul and purify it thoroughly. The same happens with good souls, with souls who make spiritual exercises, who make an effort but are not completely detached. We must realize that the Holy Spirit is not indifferent to the obstacles created by man's carnal nature. And just as a nurse gently lifts the patient from his bed, so too the Holy Spirit sustains the priest in his weakness, and “puts him under cure so that he may obtain his health” 14 . How many times our soul, plunged in spiritual nights, in the midst of deep afflictions, of painful anguish, rather than speaking to Christ lets out a groan . That is a good sign, a sign that one is making progress in the spiritual life. According to St. John of the Cross it is passing from the dark night of sense to the dark night of the spirit. Let me explain: That passage the saint speaks of is marked principally by three well-defined characteristics in our prayer: The first is seeing in oneself that one can no longer meditate or reason discursively with the imagination, nor take delight in it as one used to before; rather one now finds dryness in what before used to engage the senses and yield juice 15 . The second is when one sees that one has no desire at all to fix the imagination or the senses on other particular things, exterior or interior 16 . The third and surest is if the soul delights in being alone with loving attention to God , without particular consideration, in interior peace and quiet and rest, and without acts and exercises of the faculties, memory, understanding and will −at least discursive ones, which means going from one thing to another− but only with the general loving attention and knowledge we speak of, without particular understanding and without understanding about what. The saint clarifies that these three signs must be present together for one to be able to be sure that one should venture to leave the state of meditation and of sense and enter that of contemplation and of the spirit. It has nothing to do with the distractions that so often assail us, nor with the lukewarmness that feels distaste for spiritual things −because here “neither does it find consolation in created things” − nor does it have to do with the melancholy that sometimes gets into the heart and does not let us think of anything, or makes us not feel like thinking about it 17 . It is what in Sanjuanist language is called the night of sense, which in prayer is seen manifested by these three signs: Lack of savor in spiritual things . Not finding pleasure or consolation in the things of God implies, as we have said, “not finding it in created things either.” And that is proof that the dryness or apparent tedium does not come from sins or imperfections. There is, moreover, a painful solicitude and care about the things of God . There is a sort of constant thinking about God and that one is not serving him as one ought, and that instead of advancing one is going backward, on seeing the lack of spiritual pleasure. They are eminently spiritual crosses. We must say, for the peace of the soul passing through this night, that the dryness and lack of savor do not proceed from lukewarmness or slackness, because in fact this soul “has with it an ordinary solicitude to serve God”, but it seems to it that it is not achieving it, that it is not doing it. And in reality the cause of this dryness is that God is transferring the goods of sense to the spirit, and since the senses and natural strength are not capable of them, they remain fasting, dry and empty 18 . But without realizing it this soul goes on strong and more solicitous in its care not to fail God. What is the attitude to have in these cases? The saint explains it very well: to know how to be quiet , unconcerned about any interior or exterior work, without solicitude to do anything there, [because] then in that unconcern and idleness they will delicately feel that interior refreshment 19 . What he means here is not to be troubled, to let God do his work: because “if it wants to work with its faculties, it rather hinders the work that God is doing in it than helps it” 20 . That is why he says further on that we must persevere in patience, trust in God 21 and be content with a loving and calm attentiveness to God , and remain without care and without effort and without desire to taste him or feel him; because all these pretensions disquiet and distract the soul from the calm quiet and gentle idleness of the contemplation that is given here 22 . I would like to emphasize that loving attentiveness to God. St. John of the Cross mentions that at first this loving attentiveness is not much noticed, but later, “the more the soul grows accustomed to letting itself be calmed, the more that loving general knowledge of God will always grow in it and be felt, which it enjoys more than all things, because it causes it peace, rest, savor and delight without labor” 23 . Perhaps it was for this reason that he wrote that beautiful saying: “O sweetest love of God, so little known! He who has found its veins is at rest” 24 . As if denoting the repose and refreshment the soul finds in that loving attentiveness to God. Let us say it plainly: This loving attentiveness is when the soul places itself before God in an act of confused, loving, peaceful and calm knowledge, to drink wisdom and love of God, practically without doing anything other than remaining in quiet. That is when the soul passes to contemplation. In which one must apply the Sanjuanist principle that here “to enter upon the way is to leave one's own way” 25 . Know that the moment will come when no effort at all is necessary to maintain this attitude: “when the soul feels itself being placed in silence and listening, even the exercise of loving attentiveness… the soul must forget , so that it may remain free for what the Lord then wants of it. For that loving attentiveness it should use only when it does not feel itself placed in solitude or interior idleness or forgetfulness or spiritual listening, which, so that it may understand it, whenever it occurs, comes with a certain peaceful calm and interior absorption” 26 . Notice how the Master of faith uses the principle of tanto-cuanto (insofar as): “that loving attentiveness it should use only when it does not feel itself placed in solitude or interior idleness or forgetfulness or spiritual listening”, for we must be detached even from that. Then comes the groan. One reads in the Spiritual Canticle : “And so the peace and tranquility and satisfaction of heart which the soul can reach in this life is not enough for it to cease having a groan within itself, though peaceful and not painful, in the hope of what is lacking. For the groan is annexed to hope; like the one the Apostle 27 said he and the others had, though perfect, saying: We ourselves, who have the first fruits of the spirit, groan within ourselves, awaiting the adoption of sons of God . This groan, then, the soul has here within itself in its enamored heart; for where love wounds, there is the groan of the wound, crying out ever in the feeling of absence, especially when, having tasted some sweet and delightful communication of the Bridegroom, and he having gone away, it is left suddenly alone and dry” 28 . Once the soul has passed from discursive meditation to contemplation, that does not mean that the work is already finished and that from now on everything is sweet and rose-colored. Here too the soul must undergo its purification. I do not know how familiar you are with the Sanjuanist writings, but as soon as one begins to read his major works, especially the Night and the Ascent , one realizes that the saint establishes a sort of parallel between night and contemplation. But one must not identify night with contemplation, because contemplation also occurs in forms that do not produce night (in the purgative sense of the word). You will have read or heard it said: “the night of contemplation” 29 or “night of purgative contemplation” 30 or “this night, which we say is contemplation” 31 , underlining that it is night because it is contemplation. For darkness is a characteristic note of contemplation during a certain period on the mystical or spiritual way, but it is not coextensive with it. I mean that one can speak of contemplation, for example, in the unitive life, or of the “now clear and beatific contemplation” of the blessed, and in so many periods in which contemplation is experienced luminously and delightfully. But here we will speak very briefly of this contemplation in the purgative sense, of the night of contemplation. We must say that this night of purgative contemplation disposes the soul for union with God 32 . It is important to keep that in mind ( don’t panic ). But we must also add that this night of contemplation has two principal effects on our soul: to purge and to illumine 33 . The well-known definition of contemplation is the one that says: “this dark night is an inflowing of God into the soul…” 34 and therefore, although it is “secret” 35 and “loving” 36 , it is also defined as “dark”, “gloomy and horrible” 37 or painful at the same time. Such a paradox gives the night of contemplation some characteristics of its own. Pay attention: “for two reasons this divine Wisdom is not only night and darkness for the soul, but also pain and torment: the first is because of the height of the divine Wisdom, which exceeds the capacity of the soul, and in this way it is darkness to it; the second, because of the soul's lowliness and impurity, and in this way it is painful and afflicting to it, and also dark.” So it must be said that, since the light of divine Wisdom is so great and supernatural, it deprives and darkens the act of natural intelligence. That is why one speaks of the night of contemplation, because it is dark , and as dark as darkness itself. Is that clear? The pain comes, says St. John of the Cross, not from the side of God's inflowing, for there is nothing on his part that could cause pain, but the cause is the weakness and imperfection that the soul then has, and its contrary dispositions for receiving the divine communications 38 . Are you following me? That is, in the light of God the soul discovers its miseries, and indeed they are greater than it thought. The soul realizes how it clashes, so to speak, with the holiness of God. “It brings out its ugliness and makes it black and dark, and so it appears worse than before and uglier and more abominable than it used to be […] it seems clear to it that it is in a bad state, that it is not only in such a state for God to see it, but for him to abhor it, and that he already abhors it” 39 , as St. John says in the Night . The suffering is terrible. And what is suffered in prayer is prolonged in the common fabric of life. The uncertainty, the bewilderment, the discouragement, the immense abandonment the soul experiences is unspeakable. In fact, it is one of the most horrendous and tempestuous trials of the purgation of the night of contemplation. “To find no consolation or support in any doctrine or spiritual master”; one may have read St. John of the Cross from top to bottom, have the holiest spiritual director, but that does not exempt one from that great desolation, because, as the Proper Law says, only God knows “the secret springs that must be moved to bring us to heaven” 40 . Even more: “the soul is so absorbed and immersed in that feeling of evils in which it sees its miseries so clearly” that others try to console it without feeling what it feels, and “instead of consolation, it rather receives new pain, it seeming to it that that is not the remedy for its ill, and in truth it is so. Because until the Lord finishes purging it in the way he wishes to do, no means or remedy serves it or profits it for its pain.” It feels “as if in a dungeon, bound hand and foot, without being able to move or see, or feel any favor from above or below” 41 . In a certain way everything comes down to the violent confrontation of two contraries: God with his purity and man with his misery. And all of this, as we were saying, is manifested in daily life: As an immense pain over one's own impurity : the soul knows that “it is not worthy of God nor of any creature” 42 . Pain over its own natural, moral and spiritual weakness : it feels as “if it were under an immense burden; it is suffering and agonizing so much that it would take dying as a relief and a bargain” 43 . It experiences pains like the shadow and groans of death through the clash of its own misery with God. It feels itself being undone, feels itself without God and punished, and cast off and unworthy of him 44 . It also has pain because of the profound emptiness and extreme poverty in which it sees itself . It is a very great suffering that brings great anguish to the soul 45 . In fact it feels as if it were coming to an end, so acute are the sufferings. But God, in his merciful and fatherly pedagogy, sends us relief; otherwise we would succumb. So, after all this we have mentioned, there follows an interpolation of reliefs 46 in which the soul experiences peace and gentleness, and it even seems to it to be a sign of health and that its trials are over, but that sensation lasts only a short time, and the so sudden change in the soul even causes amazement in spiritual directors. But St. John of the Cross and other authors based on him say that the purgation, if it is to be radical, lasts “some years” 47 , and so after the calm the storm rages again, perhaps more intensely than before. And sometimes the pains are so many that the afflictions and straits they experience “pierce the soul in the sudden remembrance of the evils in which it sees itself, with the uncertainty of the remedy” 48 –‘there is no solution to any of this’, it constantly repeats to itself− and to that evil is added the memory of past prosperity. Abandonment on the part of creatures is particularly painful, especially if it is a matter of friends, but it is necessary so that the soul may be purified in solitude, dryness and emptiness. However, there is something that afflicts and desolates the soul even more, and that is not being able “to raise its affection and mind to God or to pray to him” 49 , thinking that there is a cloud in front and that its prayer does not reach him. If at some time it does pray to him, “it is so without strength and without juice that it seems to it that God neither hears it nor pays any attention to it” 50 . And it thinks that it is lost and its blessings finished forever 51 . In short, the interior combat is so great “that it brings into the spirit a pain and groan so deep that it causes it strong spiritual roarings and bellowings, sometimes uttering them with the mouth, and dissolving into tears when there is strength and power to be able to do so, though this relief is seldom given” 52 . You see, then, how that groan, those interior crosses so great, so deep, how those heartfelt tears are also prayer. I knew a soul who, experiencing this inability to raise the mind to God or to pray to him, would rest her head on the joined hands of an image of Our Lady and interiorly, with that gesture, say to her: pray for me, my Mother. The Mystical Doctor strongly recommends: “to persevere with patience and humility” 53 , knowing that “abandonment is a file, and suffering darkness is for great light” 54 . Since “the immense goods of God do not fit nor fall except into an empty and solitary heart, that is why the Lord wants you so, because he loves you well , well alone , wishing himself to be all your company” 55 , as the saint wrote to one of his directees. We must not lose sight of the goods that await us: “Deep is this war and combat, because the peace it awaits must be very deep ; and the spiritual pain is intimate and delicate, because the love it is to possess must also be very intimate and refined ; for the more intimate and finished the work is to be and remain , the more intimate, careful and pure must be the labor, and the stronger , the more solid the building” 56 . On the Prayer Life of the Priest – Part II

Liturgical prayer We now pass to the liturgical prayer of a priest of the Incarnate Word. Our friend Fulton Sheen writes with great realism in his autobiography: “Few priests like vocal prayer. That is a fact. This is not because priests are not men of prayer. It is because their prayers are sighs, aspirations and inspirations. […] They have few petitions. It is rare that they make a novena for something they need; they ask the people to make it. […] And few want to admit that they are bored with something they are supposed to like. The breviary belongs to that category. Priests are expected to rave with love for the breviary, but many of us are like those people who, to keep up appearances, go to an opera but neither enjoy it nor understand it. […] Perhaps the breviary was supposed to be difficult for any average priest. Could it not be like the wrestling between Jacob and God? If we see it from this point of view, it may still be a struggle, but it would fall into the category of prolonged and unceasing intercession. Because we would be praying it as our Lord prayed in the garden of olives, like the friend who kept knocking at the door in the night asking for a piece of bread, like the widow who did not cease her pleas before the judge. Importuning is not relaxing in a daydream, but sustained work” 1 . The following is prescribed for us: “One must also give all the importance it has to the pious and devout praying of the Liturgy of the Hours, formerly known as the Divine Office or Breviary. To this end it will help, among other things, to study Laudis Canticum 2 . Also its importance as preparation for and prolongation of Holy Mass 3 . Ordinarily the major hours of the Office should be prayed in community” 4 . It is important to highlight the matter of pious and devout praying, which is in no way hurried or unaware, like one who, instead of reading, ‘scans’ the page and does not think about what he is saying. It must be a moment of true prayer, of asking God, of praising him with the very words with which he wants us to ask him and praise him. They are words of the Holy Spirit! In such a way that, together with Eucharistic adoration, the praying of the Liturgy of the Hours may help to cultivate and maintain throughout the whole day the spirit of prayer we spoke of at the beginning. The praying of the breviary must truly be “a source of piety and nourishment for personal prayer” 5 . “The Liturgy of the Hours is the sanctification of the day,” says St. Paul VI's Laudis Canticum . That is why it is important that, before or after Mass, it be the first thing we do, that we make sure of it. Blessed Joseph Allamano told his own: “Let us observe the indications of the Church regarding the time for praying the Liturgy of the Hours. Having a lot of work must not lead us to postpone it. Prayed in good time, it is a sweet burden. As for the place, if possible, pray it in the church, which is the house destined for prayer. The Liturgy of the Hours is the most excellent prayer after the Mass. May praising God be one of our principal occupations, as it will be for all eternity! 6 That must be a practical resolution we must make. To set ourselves a schedule for praying the hours and keep it strictly. I also think it helps to have a ‘plan B’ in case of travel, or of some particular circumstance that affects the original plan. But it should always be one of the first things we do in the day. Under another heading we must also say that “the Liturgy of the Hours, like the other liturgical actions, is not a private action, but belongs to the whole body of the Church, manifests it and has an effect upon it” 7 . So that each time we take up the breviary to pray we take with us the billions of unbelievers there are in this world, the persecuted churches, the most distant missions, the thousands of Catholics in the world who do not regularly have a priest in their villages, the thousands of priests in the world who carry out their ministry “ undercovered ”, etc. When St. John of the Cross was imprisoned in Toledo, in that tiny cell with a minimal little window through which very little light came in, they say that in order to pray his breviary he would climb up on a little stool to be able to see. How many priests like that there must be in the world… We advance in holiness with the breviary. Sometimes we expect too much from the breviary, but once we realize that we are not parrots repeating words, but that our prayer is the same song the angels sing in heaven before the throne of God in the name of the whole Mystical Body of Christ and of the world, then it becomes easier. Above all for those who pray in a language other than their mother tongue, one must know that perhaps we do not understand everything we are saying, but God does understand it. A moment ago we were saying that the words of the psalms are the Holy Spirit's. Well then, it is the same Holy Spirit who can make our recitation of the Liturgy of the Hours something fruitful. Some practical recommendations for praying the breviary 8 : Pray it, as far as possible, before the Blessed Sacrament. A practice which, moreover, gains us a plenary indulgence. Notice that most of the psalms confront us with two figures: the Sufferer and the King. That helps us interpret the psalms better. Have recourse to the Holy Spirit during the recitation of the breviary. Not necessarily with a formal prayer, but as a gesture asking for help to do it well, with understanding, unhurriedly. Offer certain hours of the liturgy for certain intentions. Realize, if we have not done so yet, that one cannot properly pray the breviary with the computer in front of one and the email inbox open, or with music on, and reading WhatsApp messages at the same time. Finally, let us say that the breviary is not a yoke and a burden; rather it is an obligation, but an obligation of love. If the priest is selfish, the praying of the liturgy becomes only an obligation; if the priest is a person aware that it is the prayer of the Church, that obligation brings love contained within it; if the priest is a victim, love turns that obligation into such ardor that he feels no obligation at all.
