On the Prayer Life of the Priest – Part III

The most excellent prayer, which is Holy Mass One of the great loves of every member of the Institute is the Eucharist 1 . In accordance with this, we read in our Constitutions : The principal thing, the most important thing we must do each day, is to participate in the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass 2 and, in our case, to celebrate it. “We must be characterized by the importance that must be given to the celebration of Holy Mass, as well as by the reverent way of celebrating it” 3 , as one reads in one of the acts of the General Chapter of 2007, which points to this very thing as a non-negotiable element attached to the charism. That is why one can never insist enough on the fact that it falls to us “to be masters of the ars celebrandi , and to our major seminarians, our brothers, etc., to strive on their part to live the ars participandi in the most perfect way” 4 . “It must be borne in mind that the celebration of the Mass is a thermometer of priestly life” 5 . To such a point that it can be said that “a priest is worth as much as his Eucharistic life is worth; his Mass above all. A Mass without love, a sterile priest; a fervent Mass, a priest who conquers souls. A neglected Eucharistic devotion without love, a slack priesthood, even more, one in danger” 6 . The Eucharist, St. Leonardo Murialdo recalled, is not a rite to be performed but a mystery to be lived 7 . And if this is a mystery to be lived, then we must not forget that our “style of liturgical celebrations as part of our charism [consists of] celebrations in which the Word becomes incarnate and in which he appears –sacramentally– Incarnate, in which the principal presence and action of the principal Priest 8 is always highlighted, in which it is perceived that the essential attitude of the secondary priest is the prayerful attitude –proper to one who knows himself to be a mere instrument, and a deficient instrument, subordinate to the principal cause and subject to its ends–, in which all the visible elements contribute to the splendorous knowledge of the Invisible 9 . Concretely: “our liturgical celebrations must be exemplary: ‘in their rites, in their spiritual and pastoral tone, and in the fidelity due both to the prescriptions and texts of the liturgical books and to the norms issued by the Holy See and the Episcopal Conferences’” 10 . St. John of the Cross, with a bit of humor, will tell those who want to impose special rules on the priest for the Eucharistic celebration to leave “the mode and manner of saying Mass to the priest whom the Church has there in her place, for he has instruction from her as to how he must do it. And let them not want to use new means, as if they knew more than the Holy Spirit and his Church” 11 . Therefore, all of us priests of the Institute must strive so that the liturgy of our Masses may be cathedral-like without formalism, beautiful without affectation, solemn without pomposity, austere yet full, faithful to the rubrics yet creative, with the maximum participation and developing to the maximum all the possibilities the liturgy itself offers, particularly in the chants and sacred music 12 . We must celebrate Mass “with unction without affectation, with solemnity without bombast, with fidelity without lacking healthy creativity, with piety without pietism, with the awareness that the one who does the principal work is Jesus Christ –the principal Priest–, being transparent of him and not an opaque membrane that prevents people from transcending to him” 13 . How many there are who think they are the principal actors of the Mass! “What supernatural vision does the priest have who turns the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass into a kind of show in which he is the protagonist?” 14 I find the following statement of the Proper Law supremely true: liturgical celebrations will generally be what the celebrant wants them to be and what he himself is. That is why it falls to him to take care of all the details so that the celebration may be as it should 15 . That is why I would like to recall what the Proper Law says, for example, about some details regarding words and gestures in the Mass. It reads: “The visible elements have great importance in the liturgy. The word must have its rhythm, neither fast nor slow, neither a grating voice nor a lifeless one ; it must be spoken with expression, without theatricality , with sincerity, clarity, precision, originality, unction” 16 . The same applies to the liturgical proclamation of the Word of God, which must first be venerated and interiorized by us so that it may then reach the faithful as a true light and a strength for the present moment 17 . – Liturgical gestures must be full, not unnecessarily repetitive, orderly, human, not those of automatons. They must not be omitted. The quality of our celebrations must be cared for down to the details: careless, slack, unprepared, hasty, verbose, anodyne 18 , insipid celebrations… weaken the faith of the participants 19 ” 20 . – Likewise some particular elements are specified, such as: a) giving room to contemplative silence : “… silence occupies an indispensable place in the liturgy, when it is well prepared; it allows each one to develop in his heart the spiritual dialogue with the Lord 21 ; b) that the signs speak for themselves . Silence is favored when fire is fire and not an electric lamp; when the candle can melt and drip instead of being a wick fed by a flammable liquid; flowers should give off perfume, open and wither, and that is better than their being artificially eternal; that the liturgical space allow for the dynamism of the liturgical action; that the ambo be the worthy place in which to set the Word of God; that the chair show forth the one who acts in the person of Christ the Priest; that the altar speak for itself and that everything be directed toward it, because the sacrifice has been the price of our souls; that the vestments be worthy; that they make it possible to distinguish the priest from the people and even the principal celebrant from the concelebrants 22 . c) Finally, proximate and remote preparation is absolutely necessary for the liturgical celebration in general and especially for our daily Mass. In fact, the day should be divided in two: one part of preparation, the other of thanksgiving. There is nothing more important in our Christian life. When one celebrates or participates in the Mass, the day is already won 23 . – Moreover, it is always characteristic of our Masses to give Communion with hosts consecrated at that same Mass and to offer Communion under both species whenever possible and permitted 24 . – To take care of the singing, because it too is a “necessary or integral part of the solemn liturgy” 25 . I mean, all these little things are details, and much of all this is perhaps already being done, but they are details that always help us to improve and to go deeper into the mystery we celebrate, to pay more attention to it, to do it with more unction, so as not to fall into monotony either, so as not to lose the sense of the mystery we celebrate. And I also believe they shed light when it comes to making concrete resolutions for an ever better and more fruitful celebration of Holy Mass. Notes 1 Cf. Humility

NATURE What, then, is humility? Although it may not seem so to us, this virtue consists in the right consideration of what we are; that is why St. Thomas defines it as the virtue that inclines us to restrain the disordered appetite for our own excellence, giving us a just knowledge of our littleness and misery before God. A just knowledge, neither more nor less: what we really are. That is why, when we contemplate the considerations the saints made in order to foster it, we must understand, strictly speaking, that it is not that they were exaggerating, but rather that they were the ones who understood the truth of the creature before the Creator. St. Francis Borgia devoted two hours of meditation each day to self-knowledge and self-contempt, because he had learned that he must never cease to consider his miseries; and so, even before these examples, how much the knowledge of our pride ought to grow. St. Bernard: It is a true knowledge by which one knows oneself and holds oneself in low esteem . That is why the best definition is the well-known formula of St. Teresa: humility is walking in truth . Man, St. Thomas said, can be summed up in two things: what he has from God, and what he has from himself; from God he has everything that pertains to goodness and perfection, since, as we know, all created goodness or perfection is a participation in the divine and uncreated; and from himself −he says− he has only imperfection and defect. This is what we are, this is what we contribute to the work of God: imperfection and defect; and this is no exaggeration, it is the plain truth. Hence St. Augustine says in the Soliloquies : “ If there is any good, small or great, it comes from You, for from us nothing but evil can proceed ,” and elsewhere: “ Whoever counts his own merits, what does he do but count Your gifts? ” That is why to be humble is to be wise, because it is to consider the truth about man. Whoever does not understand that he is misery and nothingness −said St. Teresa− understands nothing and lives in a lie; and further on she will say: “ if humility is not considered, all is lost .” In order to learn, we must always repeat that prayer of St. Augustine: “May I know myself and may I know You ”; which is what St. Francis of Assisi always asked of God: “ Who are You and who am I?” , because he was amazed at the greatness and goodness he saw in God, and at the same time at the unworthiness and misery he discovered in himself. This is why the saints humbled themselves to the very depths: the more they knew God, the poorer and the more full of defects they saw themselves. The proud, by the very fact of being deprived of light, lose the enormous grace that God grants to the humble, that is, the grace of recognizing their lowliness and their truth. The holy man, however many virtues he may have, will always have to recognize, first, that he possesses all those goods because God has given them to him, what do you have that you have not received 1 ; and second, that all those created gifts are nothing beside the majesty of God; created gifts are like grains of dust before the infinite perfection of God. EXCELLENCE Now, despite its greatness, humility is not the greatest of all the virtues. Above it are the theological virtues, the intellectual virtues, and even justice. But St. Thomas calls it the fundamental virtue, because it lays the foundations for the moral edifice. That is why it is an indispensable virtue, the greatest remedy against pride. A man who neglects to practice it may as well renounce the life of heaven right now. God resists the proud and gives his grace to the humble 2 , says the apostle St. James. The whole edifice of the virtues has holy humility as its foundation. That is why without humility one cannot take a single step in the spiritual life. God is the supreme Truth, and He cannot tolerate anyone voluntarily placing himself outside of it. St. Augustine said: “ there is no higher way than the way of charity, but only the humble set foot upon it .” The higher the edifice of the spiritual life that we wish to raise with the grace of God, the deeper must be the foundations of humility upon which it is to be built. Let us listen to some texts of St. Teresa: And since this whole edifice is founded on humility, the closer one has come to God, the further this virtue must advance, and if not, all is lost. This whole foundation of prayer is founded on humility, and the more a soul lowers itself in prayer, the more God raises it up. I do not remember His having granted me any very signal favor except when I was undone at seeing myself so wretched. And if they do not resolve upon this, have no fear that they will make much progress, because, as I have said, the foundation of this whole edifice is humility, and if this is not very genuine, the Lord, even for your own good, will not wish to raise it very high, lest it all come crashing to the ground. If all this is true for any Christian, it is all the more so for us religious. According to St. Bernard, the more elevated one is in dignity −as is the case with religious− the more humble one must be; otherwise, should he fall into sin, his fall will be all the deeper for being hurled from a higher place. That is why St. Augustine said: placed in the most sublime office, you need a more excellent humility . And before that our Lord had declared: Let the greatest among you become as the least 3 . More than anyone, we must follow the examples of Our Lord, the humble one par excellence, practicing all the degrees. THE PRACTICE OF HUMILITY The saints speak of the degrees of humility in different ways. For St. Anselm it is necessary to recognize oneself as worthy of contempt , to grieve over it , to confess it simply, to persuade others of it , to bear patiently being told so, to bear patiently being treated as vile, and to rejoice in it . The substance of humility −said St. Thomas of Villanova− is the definitive death of our self-love. There are four things, says St. Alphonsus, that we must strive for in order to be truly humble, not in name but in reality. 1° To abhor pride : it is the queen and mother of all vices and sins, because it is the root and beginning of all of them. It was the sin of the angels and the sin of the first man. Pride is the prelude to great ruin 4 , says the book of Proverbs. St. Gregory says: “ pride is a seedbed of impurities, because the flesh hurls into hell those whom haughtiness exalts” . In itself the devil does not fear the proud; St. Joseph Calasanz, speaking of the proud priest, said that “ he is in the hands of the devil like a ball that he throws and casts to the ground whenever he pleases .” St. Thomas points out four forms of it: (1) attributing to oneself the goods one has received from God, (2) believing that we have received them on account of our own merits, (3) boasting of goods one does not possess, and (4) wishing to appear as the sole possessor of such goods, with contempt for others. 2° Not to glory in the good one has done : St. Jerome says that the highest mountains are the most battered by the gales; that is why the more sublime our ministry, the more exposed we are to the attacks of vainglory… ”. “ How many religious, for lack of humility −says St. Alphonsus− for lack of humility fell miserably over the precipice. They rose to the point of working miracles, and afterwards ambition made them fall into heresy .” The spiritual man dominated by pride is in himself a thief, who steals not material goods but spiritual ones, because he steals the glory of God. That is why St. Francis of Assisi said: “Lord, if You grant me any good, keep it for me Yourself, lest I steal it from You .” That is why St. Paul writes to the Corinthians: by the grace of God I am what I am 5 ; and so for him, by ourselves we cannot do a good work, nor even have a good thought. Hence it would always be a necessity to say We are unprofitable servants , we have done what we had to do 6 . For everything we do is nothing if we consider that it is for a God who deserves infinite love and who has suffered so much for love of us. “ Who would not laugh at the clouds -says St. Bernard- if they boasted of the rain they pour down? ” Each time St. Teresa did some good, she praised God for it, saying that all that good came from Him. St. Gregory said: “ he who does many works of virtue, but without humility, is like one who throws dust into the wind .” 3° To remain in distrust of oneself : If God does not help us, we cannot preserve His grace: Unless the Lord guards the city, in vain do the watchmen keep vigil 7 . Let us never expect the fruit of our labor except from the hands of God. Indeed, what proportion is there between our efforts and the conversion of a sinner? Good works are more God's than ours; the rest is just talk. Without Him it is not that we can do little, but that we can do nothing. If we cannot conceive a thought by ourselves, how much less can we accomplish a good work. That is why the key here and always is to place ourselves in His hands: let us recognize our uselessness in order to become useful. And when some great work is imposed on us, let us not lose confidence by looking at our incapacity, but let us trust in God, who tells us in Exodus: I will be with your mouth and with his, and I will teach you what you must do 8 . The humble, trusting in God, work with His divine arm, and that is why they obtain from God what they desire. 4° To accept humiliations : In order to acquire humility we need to accept the humiliations that come to us from God or from men, and to repeat with Job: I had sinned and perverted what was right, yet he has not given me what I deserved 9 . That is true humility: to know that we are contemptible because of our sins. And to be so in truth. There are those who consider themselves the most deserving of contempt; but when they are corrected in something, right then and there they boil over like scalded milk. HUMILITY AND MAGNANIMITY But, as Chesterton often points out, Christianity is the doctrine of admirable paradoxes. We say that we must humble ourselves to the point of contempt, that this is the truth of man; but precisely in that lowering of ourselves our greatness is found; that is why whoever humbles himself will be exalted. That is why St. Augustine points out that “ God is on high: if you exalt yourself, He flees and hides from you; if you humble yourself, He comes down to you .” God hears only the prayers of the humble, of those who give themselves to Him with all their heart. When St. Jerome speaks of the humility of St. Paul, he says: “ He attained glory by fleeing from it; for just as the shadow follows the one who flees from it, so glory follows the one who despises it and withdraws from the one who seeks it .” And this is so because, necessarily, when we empty ourselves of ourselves, when we scrape away from ourselves what hinders our progress —which is our very selves— it is at that moment that we are filled with God. That is why St. John of the Cross says: “When he comes to be reduced to nothing, which will be the highest humility, the spiritual union between the soul and God will be accomplished ” 10 . And furthermore, because when we let ourselves be led by the Spirit of God, we have the power of God at our disposal. And that is why we launch ourselves into great undertakings, toward great honors, because we can do all things in Him who strengthens us 11 . That is why, always, as St. Teresa said, “ love your littleness .” Albino Luciani wrote: Humility goes hand in hand with magnanimity. To be good is something great and beautiful, but difficult and arduous. So that the spirit may not aspire to great things in an immoderate way, there is humility. So that it may not lose heart before difficulties, there is magnanimity. I think of St. Paul: contempt, scourgings, pressures do not depress this magnanimous man; ecstasies, revelations, applause do not exalt this humble man. Humble when he writes I am the least of the apostles. Magnanimous when he declares I can do all things in Him who strengthens me. Humble, but for that very reason he knows how to fight when the time comes : are they Jews? so am I… are they ministers of Christ? I speak like a madman, but I am more. He places himself beneath everyone, and that is why in his duties he lets himself be bent by nothing and by no one. The waves dash the ships in which he travels against the reefs; serpents bite him; pagans, Jews, false Christians expel and persecute him; he is beaten with rods and thrown into prison; he is made to die each day; they think they have frightened him, annihilated him, and he reappears fresh and full of vigor to assure us: I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities, nor things present nor things to come, nor spiritual powers, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will ever be able to separate us from the love of God, made manifest in Christ Jesus, our Lord . Therefore let us always live in this holy spirit of humility, and we will do enormous works. God chose what is weak in the world to combat what is strong, so that no mortal might glory in the presence of God, since Christ, for the conversion of the world, did not wish to choose the powerful or the wise but humble and unlettered fishermen who, far from trusting in their own strength, placed all their trust in God. St. Gregory said: “Nothing is difficult for the humble.” All this has a special bearing on us, religious of the Incarnate Word. We must imitate with all our strength Jesus Christ in His hidden life, in His hidden life, in His passion, in His resurrection, His humility in the Eucharist; and let us ask Mary, the most perfect model of humility, who always lived in the attitude of a poor handmaid of the Lord, Ecce Ancilla Domini, who scarcely speaks, draws attention to herself in nothing, devotes herself to the tasks proper to a woman in the poor little house of Nazareth, who appears on Calvary as Mother of the ‘Great Failure,’ and who lives obscure and unknown under the care of St. John after the Ascension of the Lord, and who works no miracle — let us ask her to teach us that science which she lived from her conception, which is that of being humble, so that we may say with Her: My soul proclaims the greatness of the Lord, for he has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid 12 . Three kinds of humility

Points preached during a spiritual exercise corresponding to numbers [164-168] of the book of the Spiritual Exercises According to paragraphs [164-168] of the book of the Spiritual Exercises [Introduction] In order to gather and concentrate into a single beam all the rays of light that have shone from the Principle and Foundation up to now, St. Ignatius presents us with a luminous beacon to guide and orient us when the time comes to make the election. The beacon is none other than the consideration he calls the “three kinds of humility” [164-168], which is what we are now going to consider. The saint wants this consideration to be made “before entering upon the elections,” “considering it at intervals throughout the whole day, and likewise making the colloquies” [164]. The purpose of this contemplation is none other than “to seek and find the divine will in the disposition of one's life” 1 . This is a meditation that aims not only at the intellect or the will but at both, so as to fix firmly in the soul what the message of the standard of Jesus Christ is: the cross. Unlike the previous contemplations, no fixed hour is indicated, nor are all the preludes that are ordinary in prayer prescribed. Nevertheless, we must keep the preparatory prayer, which is always the same: [46] Prayer. The preparatory prayer is to ask grace of God our Lord, that all my intentions, actions and operations may be ordered purely to the service and praise of His Divine Majesty. And we must keep the first prelude: [150] 1st prelude. The first prelude is the history. This we will find between numbers [165] and [167] of the book of the Exercises. 1. Three kinds of humility St. Ignatius presents us with three kinds of humility. All three are good, but each represents different kinds of dispositions (that is, how much I let God work in my soul), and therefore some bear more fruits of holiness than others. Now, it is important to understand that these fruits we are speaking of are not exterior things, but are principally interior. It is not a matter here of saying: well, I am a nun; if I become superior general I bore much fruit; or, I am a local superior; if I become provincial superior I bore much fruit; or, if I was a subject all my life I bore no fruit. Nor is it a matter of thinking that because one spent one's whole life as a subject one is super-humble, and that if one had to serve as superior one is not. The fruits of faith are not measured that way; they are measured by the degree of holiness. So it is a matter here not only of realizing what my interior dispositions are, but of determining myself to improve in order to order my life according to the divine will. Placing our intellect and will at the service of God with great courage and generosity, as we said at the beginning of these exercises; with “a great and very determined determination” 2 to want nothing else but what is of greater service to God; taking care that “the eye of our intention” 3 be simple, be upright, that there be no passion that might divert my election. That I may be capable of sacrificing whatever must be sacrificed, of renouncing whatever must be renounced for the glory of God, seeking in all things to do the will of God. [165] 1st humility. The first kind of humility is necessary for eternal salvation, namely, that I so lower and so humble myself, as much as is possible for me, that in all things I obey the law of God our Lord, in such a way that even if they made me lord of all created things in this world, or for the sake of my own temporal life, I would not deliberate about breaking a commandment, whether divine or human, that binds me under mortal sin. This kind of humility, St. Ignatius says, is necessary for eternal salvation. It is characteristic of those who keep away from evil by every means. That is, not only from mortal sin, but from venial sin, and who fight against their imperfections. So to speak, they are the ones who strive to diminish the voluntariness and the number of daily imperfections, of the small infidelities to the will of God into which we fall day after day (give examples). That is, they are souls who are concerned with correcting, or with effectively combating, their own defects. They are the ones who, with the will of the third class of men, have decided to walk the way of perfection. Notice that St. Ignatius says that they are those who obey the law of God in everything, in such a way that even if they made them lords of all created things in this world and even if they threatened them with losing their bodily life, such persons have made the “formal decision not to make pacts, not to compromise, not to capitulate, not to negotiate, not to concede, nor to make deals with the spirit of the world” 4 . They are those who, as long as they are allowed, are determined to do every good with fervor, to fulfill their office completely; even when they are criticized, even when their intentions are misinterpreted, they want to do good, to act according to the will of God, because otherwise, they understand, they would fail God. [166] 2nd humility. The 2nd is more perfect humility than the first, namely, if I find myself at such a point that I do not want or incline more to having riches than poverty, to wanting honor than dishonor, to desiring a long life than a short one, provided it be equally for the service of God our Lord and the salvation of my soul; and, with this, that not for all creation, nor even if they were to take my life, would I deliberate about committing a venial sin. These are souls who, besides having left sin and correcting their defects, seek to practice generously the virtues of self-annihilation, namely: “humility, justice, sacrifice, poverty, suffering, obedience, merciful love…, in a word, to take up the cross” 5 . Such persons have conscientiously applied themselves to embracing spiritual poverty; they have truly determined to submit themselves to the divine will, and “they live as if there were nothing in this world but God and it (the soul)” 6 . In such a way that neither “for all creation nor even if they were to take its life” would they consent to the slightest infidelity or offense against God. Our Constitutions describe them, saying that they are those who have “uprightness and severity, so as to act solely seeking to please God, together with kindness and meekness, so that all may perceive that he acts moved by charity; likewise, there shine in them magnanimity and fortitude, to begin great works in the service of God and to persevere to the end in carrying them out, bearing the weaknesses of many, without faltering before flattery or threats and remaining above the ups and downs of fortune or failure, having the soul ready to receive death, if necessary, for the good of the Institute in the service of Jesus Christ ” 7 . [167] 3rd humility. The 3rd is most perfect humility, namely, when, including the first and second, and the praise and glory of the Divine Majesty being equal, in order to imitate and be more actually like Christ our Lord, I want and choose poverty with Christ poor rather than riches, reproaches with Christ filled with them rather than honors, and I desire more to be esteemed as worthless and a fool for Christ, who was first held to be such, than to be thought wise or prudent in this world. This degree of humility is most perfect. In the words of St. John of the Cross it is “the highest humility” 8 , which is precisely “to be reduced to nothing” 9 , which he identifies with “freedom of spirit” 10 . This is the nun who preaches the gospel without many words; who, when she speaks of suffering, knows what it is to suffer; who, when she speaks of renunciation, knows what it is to renounce; who, when she speaks of martyrdom, knows what martyrdom is; and when she speaks of the love of God −blessed is she− knows what love is. This degree of humility makes a person coherent between what she preaches and what she does. These are the ones who truly fulfill that exhortation of St. John Paul II which our Proper Law does not hesitate to make its own and which says: “ Demonstrate by the depth of your convictions and by the coherence of your conduct that Jesus Christ is our contemporary” 11 . You see, then, that it is not a matter of having only deep convictions or of only carrying out exterior works; both things go together and are a demonstration of the faith and charity that animate them. Those who possess this third degree of humility are the ones who dispose themselves for what is most perfect, because they have removed from themselves “completely whatever is repugnant to and not in conformity with the divine will” 12 . But not only that; they even want and choose poverty, reproaches, and even becoming “fools for Christ” 13 . Those who have this third degree of humility “will be led here and there, they will be laughed at and held to be dull, backward and even feeble-minded; nevertheless, they will know how to bless those who curse them and will laugh along with those who laugh at them and mock them like children who do not understand, and even when they are beaten, persecuted and martyred, they will give thanks to God who found them worthy” 14 . That is, they are not content with the holiness attained, with doing good, but have desires for greater holiness, for heroic holiness. They always seek what is most perfect; they are the ones who truly make “offerings of greater worth.” They are “God's unconditionals,” unconditional in their self-giving, in sacrificing whatever it may be, in serving God in whatever it may be and as God wills. An Irish Jesuit priest wrote during his spiritual exercises something that seems to me can very well be applied to women religious too. It goes like this: “God wants me not to be content with the life of a mediocre religious; He wants me to wage incessant war on myself, on my passions, inclinations, bad habits, to subdue and break my will, to mortify it in all things. For this I must strive to cut away every comfort from my life, to choose what is hard, to go against my natural inclination and to renounce the life of self-pleasing I have led until now. The motive for doing so is the immense, deep and true love of the Heart of Jesus for me. Will I be able to do this for five, ten, twenty years? Will I be able to lead such a long crucified life? Jesus asks me only to do it for this day, which passes so quickly, and with it the memory of the small suffering and mortification endured. Once it has passed, it is over. But the reward is eternal.” This and no other is the humility asked of us; it is the humility proper to the true missionary of the Religious Family of the Incarnate Word; because it is solid, because it remains unchangeable before the ups and downs of fortune or failure; because it seeks to do the will of God in everything, whether in the most adverse circumstances or in the most favorable. 2. Third kind of humility This virtue of humility, while it is essential for every Christian, is of capital importance for women religious. I would say that it is inherent to the condition of a religious. To the point that one cannot be a religious and not be humble. Because women religious have consecrated their lives to serving God and neighbor. If they do not serve, then there is a great contradiction between what they believe they are and what they are in reality. Being haughty, seeking to stand out, not serving others (and of course for this they look for a thousand pretexts), promoting oneself among others by boasting of EVERYTHING one does –to the point that they seem never to have read that phrase of the gospel that says: do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing –, wanting to have the last word in everything, never consulting, “commanding imperiously” 15 , as St. John of the Cross says (meaning with pride, with high-handedness), and thousands more examples we could cite, take us away from, or at least put in great danger, the humility that must characterize us and that must characterize you especially. A Carmelite, Ana de Jesús Lobera, who was a directee of St. John of the Cross, bears witness to the saint's humility. It is a very short example, but it can serve to illustrate what we have been saying. The Carmelite nun says: “I also remember that once, when he was present, I began to praise him before some persons of rank, and I began to say that he had been prior or subprior of a certain convent, and he ‘brought up, with greater salt [with greater emphasis], that in that very place he had been the cook. As if fleeing from vainglory and humbling himself’” 16 . Do you see where this is going? You must not think too highly of yourself. “Those who have responsibilities in the community must flee from the temptation of considering themselves ‘great’ and of making their authority felt” 17 . “The humble one is the one who hides in his own nothingness and knows how to abandon himself to God” 18 : that is how the saint categorically defines the humble person. Something to bear in mind. On the other hand, notice that the expression “third kind of humility” appears explicitly in three of the four books written for you, and the word “humility” appears eighty times in those same works. If we take into account our Proper Law, in the Constitutions and the Directory of Spirituality alone the words humility/humble appear some thirty-five times. What do you think? Is this topic of humility important or not? “The third degree of humility is to set out really to attain perfection, that is, to embrace the Cross: ‘Nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing, nothing. And on the Mount nothing,’ in order to reach the Supreme Good, which is God” 19 . Notice that Father says to set out really , not in a utopian way, not when I make my perpetual vows, not when I celebrate 50 years of perpetual vows, but here and now: really; in spite of my crises, in spite of my spiritual dramas, in spite of whatever… It is a determining of oneself here and now, in these exercises, not in next year's, not when I get a better spiritual director, or when I am sent to another assignment. But here and now, as I am, whatever the state of my soul, to set out. And the first step is simply to be humble. To know and acknowledge our misery. And to be ready to renounce those things, those ways, those places that make me feel so comfortable; those people who make me feel loved, valued, who consult me; those tastes, those offices that give me so much security; those defects to which I cling so much and which so often hold me back, take me away, or distract me from the summit I must reach. It also means continuing to do good, even though others envy me, criticize me, whether I feel like it or not; without becoming sad because others push me a little to one side, without engaging in the thankless task of keeping count of how much I do and how much others do… to embrace the cross, to know how to abandon oneself to God. Now, I want it to be well understood that the self-denial to which St. John of the Cross invites us in his works, and Christ above all in his gospel, is not a denying oneself for the sake of denying oneself; it does not consist in programming a life of mortification –as if it were a matter of drawing up a fixture list of the penance you are going to do each day– but of opting totally ( radically ) for Jesus Christ. Is that clear? I suppose that by now you will have realized this, but I mention it anyway: climbing that summit, reaching the highest humility, is a matter of time and effort, as is acquiring any virtue or habit. The concrete way to proceed –the Saint advises– is to accept the nothingness of one's own being before God 20 , that is, “not only holding one's own things as nothing, but with very little satisfaction in oneself” 21 . From there springs the sincere desire to be taught and guided by others 22 . And he also says that it is a sure sign of true humility to accept one's own limitations and imperfections. Humble souls, “in the imperfections into which they see themselves fall, bear with themselves in humility, and with gentleness of spirit and loving fear of God” hope in Him 23 . They are those who hold others to be better and do not think themselves ‘something’ because of the things they do or are entrusted to do, or because of the academic achievements they have had, because, since they are humble, they know how much God deserves and how little is all that they do for Him. Humble souls do not think themselves anyone's teachers, because they never think they get anything right; so they ask for advice, they ask for help, they let themselves be taught, they consult… Nor do they go around noticing whether others do or do not do things, as if keeping count of what the other sister does and what she herself does. The humble sister does not despair over mistreatment either, over the lack of esteem of the other sisters or of the superiors; her world does not come crashing down if she suffers some injustice, if she receives some insult… Now the one who is not humble, says the saint of Fontiveros, would like “to teach everything, and even when it seems they are being taught something, they themselves take the words out of the teacher's mouth as though they already knew it” 24 ; I do not know whether you have ever come across someone like that. “Also some of these, the saint goes on to say, make little of their faults, and at other times become overly sad at seeing themselves fall into them, thinking that they should already be saints, and they become angry with themselves with impatience, which is another imperfection.” “Sometimes too, when their spiritual masters do not approve of their spirit and way of proceeding (because they want their things to be esteemed and praised), they judge that they do not understand them, or that they are not spiritual, since they neither approve of it nor go along with it. And so they then desire and try to deal with someone else who suits their taste.” “In general they are enemies of praising others and friends of being praised, and sometimes they even seek it.” The Saint treats all this in the first book of the Dark Night . Hence St. John of the Cross says that “whoever trusts in himself is worse than the devil” 25 . True humility is intimately linked to self-knowledge and has its concrete expression in spiritual nakedness, which leads straight to the exercise of charity 26 . In this regard, Fr. Segundo Llorente, a Jesuit, missionary in Alaska, in some talks he gave to Carmelite nuns about this “setting out really” (or concrete practice of spiritual nakedness), told them that “when you do not know what to confess, be sure that you fail in the following”; there are four things, pay attention: 1st. «Practically contenting oneself with mediocrity in the spiritual life», that is, not aiming higher, not aspiring to more, not wanting to distinguish myself more in the service of God, not loving God with all the strength I ought, not supernaturalizing everything I do as I should… and not doing all that amounts to contenting oneself with mediocrity in the spiritual life, all right? 2nd. «Interior irreverences in dealing with God». Everyone falls there, don't they? Because if we really realized, fully realized, whom we are dealing with in Holy Mass or in communion and those things… well, we would be, like… trembling with emotion, in a state of trembling tenderness before God… and instead, we take it for granted and go yawning to communion… Well, not yawning, but we go carelessly, thinking about So-and-so or What's-his-name, or thinking about who knows what, instead of thinking what we ought to think; so that is what is called interior irreverence; outwardly we are very prim and proper, very pretty indeed… inwardly we are off wool-gathering in the hills, aren't we? Now you have two accusations. 3rd. «Failing in interior silence». Do you know what it is to fail in interior silence? We fail in interior silence when we have frivolous thoughts, silly thoughts, vain thoughts, thoughts about the past, thoughts of when we went to school, of that time we fell into the river, of that time we went out dancing…, and through lack of interior silence God our Lord does not speak to us as He would like to speak to us, because He finds us busy… He wants to speak to us, but we are busy. What are we busy with? Well, with those thoughts.” Silence is not a minor topic; our Proper Law gives it great importance. And here comes the interesting part, pay attention: 4th. «Worrying uselessly about things that are none of my concern». Because you are not dead yet… Are you dead already? You haven't died yet, have you?… To die, 1st, you must want it, you have to want it… 2nd, you go to the church… and you begin to die to everything. You die: to your homeland , because if they send you to Alaska, or send you to Tanzania or to Canada, you are ready to leave Italy, aren't you? Well then, you die to your homeland. And to those who have already been a long time in this or another country we can also say: ‘you are ready to leave your mission country, aren't you?’ you die to your language . [Several here died to their own language long ago] If they send you abroad you have to learn another language. Are you ready to learn another language? Japanese or Arabic or English or something like that? Are you ready to sacrifice Spanish?… Each one of these deaths is a formidable blow to the head of selfishness, eh?… you die to your family , which means that you must be completely detached. You must love your family very much, eh?, but you must leave it, all right? Some are terrified of going to a remote mission place because they will be far from their family. What kind of missionary is that? then you die to your own will . Why, that is very easy, says Fr. Llorente, and in a couple of lines he puts into practice the doctrine of St. John of the Cross on humility that we have just mentioned. He says: “Look, all you have to do is the following: never do anything because you like it, never fail to do anything because you dislike it. Do it because that is the will of God the Father; everything you do, you do to please God, and with that you no longer have a will of your own. Well, what things does God want?… He wants all the things the Rule commands; God wants that; the virtues, the practice of the virtues, God wants that; silence, union with God. What is it that God wants?… Well, the soul develops a kind of radar to see, even if there is a very thick fog at an enormous distance, even if it is the darkest night, with which it sees the heavens coming from afar; it already sees coming from a thousand kilometers away what offends God and what pleases God… eh? You do things to please God . Everything you do, you do because God wants it; you go to bed because God wants it, you eat because God wants it. You do everything for the glory of God, and when death comes to you, you say: I am dying because God wants it… I live because God wants me to live… and if you fall ill, you say: because God wants it, like that… And when you supernaturalize everything, when you do everything, since you have done it for the glory of God, you have died to your own will… It is not impossible, is it? Well then, get to work… then you die to companionship . You are here with the sisters God brings you, not with those you would have wanted to have. But there are times when you get a superior who is favorable to you, or a sister who is truly like your sister, or a chaplain or spiritual director or parish priest who is truly a father to you or with whom you work very well; now, if God takes you away from those people, well then, die to the consolation of good company too. you die to spiritual consolations . You cling to the consolations God gives you. To the tears He gives you, cling tightly to them, and if God takes them away from you, if God wants you to go through those purifications, nights of sense and night of the spirit, do not complain, eh? And say to the Lord: Lord, if you reprove me, you are loving me… The more arid and dry I am, the more you love me. That way, with that, the aridity is easier to get through… When the devil persuades you that you are already damned, that these are the trials of the purification of the spirit, say to the Lord: here Satan does nothing but tell me that I am damned, but I do not believe him… You say it to Him, eh? And so with that you are now stripped of everything and dead to everything… Ah, of course! There is reputation ; you must die to reputation. It makes no difference to you whether you are abbess or cook, does it? One office is the same to you as another, isn't it?… Are you not yet dead to offices?… reputation, occupations, companions, your own will, your language, your homeland, your family and spiritual consolations… to all that you must die. And when you have died to this, then you are dead. And then afterwards you get up dead and start walking dead. Is that clear?… Until after three or four days you rise again… and once you rise again… die again! Do you know how many times you have to die and rise again? Seventy times seven!… And if death catches you dying and rising, dying and rising, you are like the Lord, who was on the way to Calvary, which is death, and there: Come, blessed of my Father … And that's it… St. John of the Cross says –Fr. Llorente goes on– that God draws such souls with such force, and the souls draw on God with such force, that the flesh can no longer hold the soul and the soul goes out, and that is dying of love… And those souls no longer pass through purgatory, because they are already purified by the love of God. And they do not pass through judgment, because they are already judged beforehand and approved. Well, that gave me a lot of light… When I find myself in some difficulty or some setback comes along, or a snub or something, I say: Well, what does all that matter to me, if I am going to die of love?… What difference does it make to me… whether I drown, or die in the hospital, or die in bed, whether it snows, whether it is cold, whether I miss the train or don't miss it; what difference does it make to me, if I am to die of love? What difference does it make to me! Perhaps it may help you” 27 . [ Peroration] That is why now, when you go to the meditation, let each one think about what it is she must die to in order to be more humble. And make the decision, or renew the decision, to live according to the third class of men and according to the third kind of humility. Ask God and Our Lady for great desires for reproaches and contempt in order to imitate Jesus more! Say with Blessed Mary of Jesus Crucified: “If I do not taste your sufferings, O my Jesus, I live sad and sorrowful. Wound me, then, for I have already given you my soul. And if you do me this good, my God, I will see clearly that you love me well” 28 . [ Colloquies] In this case St. Ignatius recommends with singular emphasis in note [168]: [168] Note. Thus, for one who desires to attain this third humility, it is very profitable to make the three colloquies of the classes of men already mentioned, asking that our Lord be pleased to choose him for this third, greater and better humility, in order more to imitate and serve Him, if it be equal or greater service and praise to His Divine Majesty. These are the ones found in [147] of the book of the Exercises. [ Examen of the meditation] We must not omit making the examen of the meditation for the space of fifteen minutes, as the holy Jesuit recommends. Notes 1 Fr. The law of the Incarnation is a law of suffering

SOLEMNITY OF THE INCARNATION The end of the Incarnation according to St. John [Exordium] The words of the Archangel St. Gabriel to the Blessed Virgin Mary that we have just heard are striking, among so many riches, because they contain various elements that speak of the kingship of Christ (it was in fact one of the prophecies about the Messiah who was to come, that he would be King). And so we read: He will be great and will be called Son of the Most High; the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his reign there will be no end 1 . Reading the Gospel of St. John, we notice that these words find a particular echo in another passage of the Gospel, which also speaks to us of Christ as King and of his reign, and it is to this passage that I want to refer in today’s homily. It is a verse known as “the end of the Incarnation” according to St. John. Scholars say that the evangelist St. John used the Greek verb γένναω ( to be born ) only once in his whole work and spoke only once of the “birth” of Jesus; this is found in Jn 18:37, our verse. Both texts (that of the Annunciation and this one of St. John) highlight, on the one hand, the transcendence of the kingdom of God, which is founded on the fact that it does not derive from a merely human initiative, but from the plan, the design and the will of God himself. And, on the other hand, they tell us plainly that Jesus Christ is the one who makes it present and brings it about in the world, through his Incarnation. However, the reign of Christ (this too the texts make very clear, and we know it very well) is not as the world imagined it back then, nor even now –we might say– although more than twenty centuries have already passed. That is why today, when we have the happiness of gathering in this magnificent church of the abbey of Fossanova to celebrate the Solemnity of the Incarnation of the Word, an “event which –as the Constitutions say– is greater than the creation of the world and cannot be surpassed by any other” 2 , and which (also according to our Proper Law) is for us the sun of our faith, the starting point of our history, the pledge of our hopes, the motive that glorifies all our sorrows, what drives us in our missionary task, and the tremendous fact that links our life with immortality, I would like us to ponder a little the uniqueness of this text. In our Constitutions we have the following sentence, which is somewhat mysterious or mystical, and which says: “The law of the Incarnation is a law of suffering” 3 . Perhaps in no text of the Gospel are those realities found so closely united as in this one. The text of Jn 18:37 is a profound expression and, if you like, disconnected in itself; but read in the light of the context in which it unfolds, of the solemnity of the account and of the magnitude of what is taking place, it makes us return to it again and again. 1. The Dialogue between Jesus and Pilate As we well know, the dialogue between Jesus and Pilate inside the Praetorium is a marvel of the fourth Gospel. It is an extremely graphic text and a remarkable literary production, so much so that it seems written as if it were the script of a theatrical scene. It is a text that represents a singular peak in the story of the Passion. After this episode, we could say (following St. Thomas), the definitive road toward the cross will begin. Jesus will be scourged and reviled; a crown of thorns will be pressed onto his head, a red cloak and a reed scepter will even be put on him in mockery, and he will be brutally humiliated before the whole crowd in the Ecce Homo (marking in a graphic way, as it were, the contrast between the two kingdoms, that of Jesus and that of the world). From then on the physical sufferings in the Passion will go constantly in cresendo until ending on the cross, in St. John’s consummatum est (19:30). The episode with the procurator Pontius Pilate, as we know, has two moments: one public, before the people and the Sanhedrin (probably even Caiaphas was there, as St. John tells us); and the other in private ( he had Jesus called aside , in the praetorium, because he had serious doubts about the charge on which he was being condemned), and it is this one that interests us now. – There is first a dialogue of questions: Then Pilate went back into the praetorium and called Jesus and said to him: “Are you the king of the Jews?” Jesus answered: “Do you say this on your own, or have others told you about me?” Pilate answered: “Am I a Jew? Your own people and the chief priests have handed you over to me. What have you done?” (Jn 18:33-34). – And finally there are affirmations. Two, specifically: The first of them refers to the nature of his Kingdom: My Kingdom is not of this world. If my Kingdom were of this world, my followers would have fought so that I would not be handed over to the Jews; but my Kingdom is not from here 4 . This affirmation or confession of Jesus probably placed Pilate in a strange situation: the accused was claiming kingship and a kingdom ( basileia ). But on the other hand he was affirming that it was a kingship and a kingdom of an altogether particular kind: no one fights for this reign, it is not a violent kingdom, it has no legion at its disposal. Therefore, he would have thought, it did not represent a threat to the Roman order, and this perhaps reassured Pilate. The kingdom of Christ is not domineering: the Son of God became incarnate and came into this world when crimes were great, and yet he told us: those who take up the sword will die by the sword 5 ; He came into this world when men would have proclaimed him king immediately if he had improved their political or economic situation, and yet he said: My kingdom is not of this world . He came into this world, accustomed to judging temporal power by appearances, and to this world he said: Take up your cross and follow me 6 . Then there is the second affirmation Our Lord makes, in which he highlights the relationship between the king, the kingdom and the subjects who make it up (and it is the text that interests us, Jn 18:37): Pilate therefore said to him: “So you are a king?” Jesus answered: “You say it: I am a king.” “For this I was born and for this I came into the world, to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice” 7 . The verse is strong, for, on the one hand, it places Truth as an essential, definitive and distinctive constituent of the kingdom he came to establish in this world; and, on the other, it declares that it is the cause (or the end) of the Incarnation: for this I was born… for this I came into the world . It even seems like an unexpected affirmation (Pilate asks him whether he is a king, and He responds with this explanation of his affirmation that he is a king). If we look closely, we have: First, a reference to the king: Yes, as you say, I am a king (obviously of the kingdom he has just described). Second, there is a reference to the kingdom: For this I was born and for this I came into the world: to bear witness to the truth (it is a kingdom established in the truth). Finally, in third place, a reference to the subjects of that king. It is an important sentence: Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice . Everyone who accepts the truth and abides in it belongs to his kingdom. Pope Benedict XVI explains it this way: “Throughout the interrogation Pilate introduces another term coming from his world and normally linked with the word ‘kingship’: power, authority ( exousía ). Dominion requires power; indeed, it defines it. As we see, with these words Jesus has created an absolutely new concept of kingship and of kingdom, and he sets it before Pilate, the representative of classical power on earth.” And he asks: “What must Pilate think? What must we think of this concept of kingdom and kingship? Is it something unreal, a daydream we can do without? Or does it perhaps concern us in some way?” But there is something more, the Pope says: “Alongside this, however, with the clear delimitation of the idea of kingdom (no one fights, earthly powerlessness), Jesus has introduced a positive concept to make understandable the essence and particular character of the power of this kingship: truth . And this is what is important.” Certainly Christ’s answer must have surprised (or unsettled) the Roman procurator. That is why it has been said that in this verse of “the end of the Incarnation” two unquestionable realities are taught to us: It teaches us that truth is the end of the Incarnation… he came into the world to manifest it… to bear witness to it. For this I was born… for this I came into the world. It teaches us that, ultimately, the search for truth, adherence to it and preaching it are the most important things in this life: everyone who is of the truth hears my voice. Impressive and simple at the same time: Jesus Christ is king, he came to bear witness to the truth, and whoever adheres to the truth is the one who forms part of his kingdom. For this Truth (with a capital letter) it is worth leaving behind everything that is most precious to man. If their kingdoms are different, this affirmation implies in a certain way that adherence to this truth entails ‘not getting along with the world’ and being scourged and crucified by it (as we see if we read on about what Pilate does with the Truth). “The law of the Incarnation is a law of suffering” 8 . There are many who assent to these words outwardly, but few are those who are willing to suffer as much as necessary for adherence to this Truth. That is why our Proper Law, in a fatherly and farsighted way, already warned us, telling us to guard against “sacrificing the truth and one’s own conscience in an attempt to maintain a false peace, not to cross a friend, to avoid some problem or, at times, to gain advantage through silence or applause. [Because] Those who do such things resemble those Jews who believed in Him, but because of the Pharisees did not confess him, fearing to be put out of the synagogue, for they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God 9 ” 10 . Today, the day of the Incarnation of the Lord, it is fitting to remember that on the day of our religious profession we committed ourselves to the sublime office of being servants of the truth 11 , and to “always seek the glory of God, the ultimate end of the whole universe; in a particular way, in the search for, investigation, proclamation and celebration of the truth” 12 , when we solemnly said that we want “all men to discover the attraction of and the longing for divine beauty” 13 . 2. The perennial question The text of the dialogue with Pilate ends in a sublime way… it lets us understand that the procurator grasped, in a certain way, the foundational character of Jesus’ affirmation; and he then asks his question not about the accusations presented, but about the foundation: What is truth? What is known as “the perennial question,” or the inevitable and inescapable question of life. A question that was addressed –no less– to the one who had just said for this I came into the world, to bear witness to the truth . What is truth? Does truth exist? Does it make sense to speak of objective truth (based on the object… on reality)? Can one speak of absolute truth? The outcome of the scene is incredible: Pilate does not wait, does not listen, does not seek… he simply goes outside, explains that there is nothing serious against this man, and watches as the people and their rulers reject the truth by choosing Barabbas. What does he do then? He goes back inside and orders the crucifixion of the one who had said he was the witness to the truth … of the one who had said I am the truth . Astonishing! 3. The world we live in Let us notice that there is a very great and eloquent parallel between the attitude of Pilate and the attitude of the contemporary world, with which we must dialogue and to which we too –because we follow Jesus Christ– have the obligation to offer the witness to the truth . There is a very great contrast between the attitude of those who profess faith in the Truth of the Incarnation and the attitude of the world before the very mystery of truth incarnate. Not for nothing had our Lord, before the affirmation to which we are referring, said that his kingdom was not of this world … that it was totally different from the kingdoms of this world. For, like Pilate, modern man also asks the question: what is truth … but, like Pilate, with his evasive attitude he trivializes what is fundamental and foundational. Just like Pilate, man today realizes the transcendence of the question, the importance it has, but once he has formulated it, he falls into a skeptical and relativistic attitude. It seems that the basic observation is that truth does not exist… or if it exists, we do not know whether we can attain it. Both end up blinded before the Truth in person who stands in front of them; and how many today, like Pilate yesterday, order the truth to be scourged and finally crucified. This is an image to remember (that of Pilate sending Jesus… the Truth… to be crucified); for we must be forewarned: to be witnesses to the truth implies the violent persecution of the world. That is what happened to our Lord, and the disciple is not above his master (Lk 6:40). This is the world we face: – Not long ago the Barna Research Group in the United States asked Americans Pilate’s same question in the following form: “Does absolute truth exist?” The result of the survey was the following: 66% of adults answered that they believe that “there is no such thing as absolute truth .” What is more, the most common statement among the answers was that “different people can define truth in conflicting ways and still be right at the same time.” They then asked the same question of younger people (between 18 and 25 years old), and the result was that 72% stated that one cannot speak of absolute truth . – Another example: at Harvard University a series of numerous random interviews were conducted among various students with the same question, “Is it possible to speak of the existence of truth?”; more explicitly, the question was framed as follows: “Is there a truth that can remain stable across times and cultures?” The answers obtained were summarized in the following four statements, the report says: 1. “Truth is found in whatever you believe, whatever that may be”; 2. “There is no absolute truth”; 3. “In case there were an absolute truth, there is no way we could know which it is”; 4. “People who believe that absolute truth exists are dangerous people.” It is easy to see that all these statements are illogical and contradictory; nevertheless, we know well that they are what make up the dominant way of thinking. Pope Benedict XVI has described this reality as a dictatorship, as despotic thinking, as “the dictatorship of relativism.” That is how it is, and we see it constantly. For many thinkers (leaders, rulers) of today, truth depends on the outlook not only of a culture but of whatever one wants to impose. The dominant way of thinking does not always consider a statement true by taking care to ascertain its correspondence with reality. Adecuatio rei et intellectus : that is not the criterion. A true statement is nothing but the statement that a person, a culture, a situation or a convenience causes to be considered true. And this is the criterion that is applied. A poet named Steve Turner wrote a parody of this modern view of reality, which he called “I believe” ( Creed ). And in one part, sarcastically, known as the “creed of modern man,” he says (in our rendering): “I believe that every man must find the truth, whichever is good for him / reality will then have to adapt to it. / The universe, if necessary, will readjust itself / and history, if necessary, will be altered. / I believe there is no absolute truth / except the absolute truth that there is no absolute truth. / I believe in the rejection of creeds, / and in the flowering of individual thought.” This poet also says that to the question “Can man live without God?” or “Can man live without an absolute truth?” the modern world answers: “we all know very well that the answer is NO… but we will keep trying anyway.” If the existence of Truth is denied, or if it is sent to be scourged as Pilate did, everything becomes relative and everything is irrelevant; and the only thing that counts is the thinking of whoever wants to impose himself, regardless of whether it has any relation to reality or not. If there are no absolute truths, there is no right and no correct. It is as Fr. Richard John Neuhaus (the founder and editor of First Things ) said: “when truth is absent, the one who has power is the only one who matters in society” ( in the absence of truth, power is the only game in town ). Pope Benedict XVI affirmed it: “What is truth? Pilate was not the only one who set this question aside as insoluble and, for his purposes, impracticable. Today too it is considered bothersome, both in political struggle and in discussion about the shaping of law. But without truth, man ultimately loses the meaning of his life, leaving the field open to the strongest.” The modern world thinks that in this way it can do “basically whatever each one feels like” and thus believe itself “free,” forgetting that the founding principle of authentic freedom is truth. The truth will make you free , says our Lord in St. John. 4. The perennial truth Finally, the following. Before this reality… before these statistics… before the reigning relativism and skepticism… we may well ask ourselves: What is our answer? What is our attitude? What are we going to say to modern man? To young people who basically do not believe that truth can be reached? Well then, our answer is basically what we celebrate today with so much devotion and solemnity. Our answer is: the Word became flesh … It is a clear and firm answer. We believe that in this mystery is found the answer and the solution to all the problems and questions of contemporary man and of man of all times. The Word became flesh and came to bear witness to the truth . For this he was born and for this he came into the world. He showed us the Truth, He taught it to us and He explained it to us, and He gave us conclusive proofs of the truthfulness of his testimony. Since then there is no other possible option, there is no other answer… neither for us nor for the world… only united to Him can we find the way out and the solution, because everyone who is of the truth hears my voice. Quid est veritas? We say it to the modern world, we say it to Pilate: Truth is God and Jesus Christ. Truth is the Incarnate Word. And the Word of God became flesh, and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, full of grace and full of truth (Jn 1:14) I am the way, I am the truth and I am the life (Jn 14:6) I speak the truth (Jn 8:45) That is why St. Paul’s recommendation to the first Christians was the following: if indeed you have heard him and have been taught by him, according to the truth that is in Jesus… put off the old man … and put on the new man, created according to God in the justice and holiness of truth 14 . [Peroratio] During the novena that we finished praying yesterday, we went day by day meditating on and asking for the immeasurable grace of our faith in the Incarnation of the Word. For we know that in that faith is found the answer to everything, the solution to all the problems of our existence; there is found the peace and the life of the soul. That is why, yes –let us say it once more– our answer is and will always be that of St. John’s prologue: the Word became flesh and we have seen his glory, full of grace and truth… for the law was given to us through Moses, but truth came to us through Jesus Christ. Even more: truth is our end on this earth, for “we commit all our strength to inculturate the Gospel, that is, to prolong the Incarnation [of the Word] in every man, in the whole man and in all the manifestations of man” 15 ; it is our spirit , for “we consider that our spirituality must be profoundly marked by all the aspects of the mystery of the Incarnation” 16 ; it is what we set before ourselves when we say that we want “to live with all radicality the demands of the Incarnation” 17 ; because ultimately this is our mission : “the mission received from the founder and sanctioned by the Church is to bring to fullness the consequences of the Incarnation of the Word, which is the compendium and root of all goods” 18 . May the Blessed Virgin always watch over and protect our faith in the fact that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.
