Through the Incarnation of the Word

the immortality of bliss becomes credible [Exordium] We are gathered here to celebrate the most important solemnity of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, which, truth be told, is the primordial and fundamental truth that the Second Person of the Trinity became man. And therefore this occasion is most solemn for the whole Catholic Church. Since we who are here are religious of the Religious Family of the Incarnate Word, some members of the Third Order, the young people of the Voices of the Word, and very dear friends of our Institutes, it seemed to me that it would be good, since we are in the intimacy of our family, to reflect on a sentence that appears twice in the principal documents of our Proper Law, which are the Constitutions and the Directory of Spirituality , and which in turn the Directory of the Third Order repeats precisely. The sentence is this: “Grounded in the mystery of the Incarnation, wrought by the Spirit in the Virgin Mary, we must always sing the mercies of God 1 because ‘ through the Incarnation of the Word the immortality of bliss becomes credible ’ 2 ; we must have a clear awareness that without Jesus Christ we can do nothing 3 , and we must strive with all our strength always to advance in virtue” 4 . Let us explain a little what this means. 1. Grounded in the mystery of the Incarnation, wrought by the Spirit in the Virgin Mary As you know, Jesus in His first coming became incarnate in the most pure womb of the Virgin Mary by the work and grace of the Holy Spirit. The Latin text says: et Verbum caro factum est , hence the initials you see on the coat of arms of the Institute, which mean: and the Word became flesh 5 . Grounded, or rather, anchored in this mystery, we as a Religious Family want “to launch ourselves boldly to restore all things in Christ 6 ” 7 , that is, to make Christ reign, first in our souls, and then in other souls and in the whole world, that is, in culture, in families, in education, in the means of social communication and among men of thought… in everything 8 . Now, although “the work of the Incarnation is common to the three divine Persons, it is attributed specifically to the Holy Spirit” 9 , and this for three reasons: 1) because its cause is the supreme love of God: God so loved the world that He gave His Only-begotten Son 10 , says the Gospel of John; 2) because the human nature was not assumed by its own merit, but by grace alone, which is attributed to the Holy Spirit; and 3) because Jesus Christ is the only Holy One and Son of God; that is why the Gospel of Luke says: what will be born of you will be Holy, He will be called Son of God 11 . And what does this have to do with us? someone might ask. Well, this has several implications for us, not only for religious but also for you. In the first place it should lead us “to act moved by the Holy Spirit, being supremely docile to Him” 12 . For which three things are necessary; pay attention: “ Attention to the inspirations of the Holy Spirit, for which one must work against habitual dissipation, lack of mortification and disordered affections” 13 . “ Discernment of spirits in order to accept and second the motions of the Holy Spirit and reject those of the evil spirit” 14 . “ Docility and promptness in carrying out what the Holy Spirit asks, because slow calculations are foreign to the grace of the Holy Spirit’ 15 ” 16 . This “being grounded in the mystery of the Incarnation” also implies living the evangelical beatitudes 17 , which is what the Incarnate Word came to teach us; that is, we must be poor in spirit, meek, merciful, pure of heart… And finally, it also follows from this mystery that, just as Our Lady “gave her ‘yes’ as a slave” 18 and then the Word took the form of a slave, being made in the likeness of men 19 in her most pure womb, so we too make a vow of slavery to Our Lady 20 . Are you following me? The second part of the sentence says: 2. We must always sing the mercies of God And why sing? Because “song springs from joy, and, if we look at it closely, it is born of love: acting is proper to love. Whoever, then, knows how to love the new life that Christ came to bring us by making us children of God, also knows how to sing the new song” 21 . For it is in the Incarnation of the Word that the Mercy of God is most plainly manifested. In fact, one of the invocations of the litany of Divine Mercy honors God by saying: “Divine Mercy, descending to earth in the Person of the Incarnate Word, I trust in you.” That is why it is proper to us, listen well, “to praise and give thanks, to sing and rejoice in God, Mighty, Holy, Merciful, Savior and Faithful” 22 , “even in the most difficult situations and in the most adverse conditions” 23 . St. John of Avila, a Spanish saint and Doctor of the Church, understood this very well, for he said: “If we let His heart do what it wants for us, everything would be showing us mercy, because showing mercy is proper to Him; if He punishes, He punishes as though forced, and against His nature: He does not afflict willingly, nor gladly grieve the children of men 24 . When God brings someone low, He does not do it from His heart, but as though forced; like a father who sees his son being bad, he punishes him with love, and it is the son who makes him punish him” 25 . Therefore, the man, the woman, the young person, the religious sister who lives consistently with her Catholic faith will never cease to sing the infinite mercy of God: I will sing forever the mercies of God 26 , says the psalm. And this brings us to the third part of the sentence of the Proper Law, which says, quoting St. Augustine: 3. Through the Incarnation of the Word the immortality of bliss becomes credible First of all we must clarify what bliss St. Augustine is speaking of here. It is true bliss, the bliss we are to enjoy in eternal life, in heaven, the endless happiness that the Son of God won for us by His death and resurrection. That is why the Saint of Hippo says that “if all men desire to be happy, and this is their sincere desire, they must without doubt want to be immortal; otherwise they could not be blessed” 27 . For the happiness to which we refer here is not an earthly happiness, in danger of being lost at any moment, limited, intermittent −happy at times, unhappy at times−, nominal, happy only in appearance but without being true, deep and completely full. Nevertheless, how much we men strive to be happy “according to the world,” or in this ephemeral world. In the face of this, another Spanish Doctor of the Church, St. John of the Cross, tells us (and it is worth listening to this attentively): “ all the delights and pleasures of the will in all the things of the world, compared with all the delights that God is, are supreme pain, torment and bitterness. And so, whoever sets his heart on them is held before God as deserving of supreme pain, torment and bitterness. And thus he will not be able to come to the delights of the embrace of union with God [that is, where bliss is immortal], being himself deserving of pain and bitterness” 28 . That is also why Our Lady said to St. Bernadette: “I do not promise to make you happy in this world, but in the next.” For man to live fully happy, it is necessary that he live. But in this earthly and miserable life we are passing through, and therefore any ‘happiness’ is passing, and even if it lasted a hundred years it must end with this life. The Incarnate Word has won for us eternal life, true life, where we will experience the delights of the embrace with God. Because, to put it in a few words, “life cannot be truly happy unless it is eternal” 29 . Now, the Son of God by nature became son of man out of compassion, out of mercy for us, the children of men −because that is what the words the Word became flesh and dwelt among us , men, mean−, in such a way that by His grace we may be made children of God −and therefore co-heirs with Christ 30 − and may one day dwell in God, in whom and through whom alone we can be blessed and sharers in His immortality. To convince us of this truth, the Son of God became a sharer in our mortality, says St. Augustine 31 . That is why on this beautiful solemnity the Proper Law invites us to think: What is more fitting to revive our hope, so often weighed down, submerged in the heaviness of our existence, so often bewildered, than for God to show us His high esteem and the immense love He has for us? Is there a more luminous and convincing proof than this infinite condescension of the Son of God, good without change , who, remaining in Himself what He was (God) and taking from us what He was not (human nature), became one of us, and took upon Himself our sins, without having committed any fault Himself; so that, believing in the excess of His love and hoping against all hope, He might grant us, out of pure liberality, His gifts without any merit of ours? 32 . That is why all the afflictions we may have in this life, the dark nights and the perplexities that God permits us to go through, the losses in our families, the very heavy loneliness, the criticisms we have to suffer, poverty itself, illness, the collapse of our plans, our very miseries and sins… all of this is lost like a drop in the ocean before the immense mystery of the Incarnation of the Son of God, who came to give us immortal bliss, the bliss that does not end, that is full, that is immense and cannot be contained. That is why the Apostle said: the sufferings of the present time are nothing compared with the glory that is to be revealed in us 33 . Whatever crosses we may suffer, we must know that they are preparing for us an eternal weight of incalculable glory 34 . Contemplating one day the immense mystery of love that we celebrate today, and which identifies us as members of this Religious Family, St. John of the Cross said: “O souls created for these grandeurs and called to them! What are you doing? With what are you occupying yourselves? Your aims are base things and your possessions miseries. O wretched blindness of the eyes of your soul, since you are blind to so much light and deaf to such great voices, not seeing that, while you seek grandeur and glory, you remain miserable and base, made ignorant and unworthy of so many goods!” 35 . Which means: how is it that we occupy ourselves with base things, with the glitter of this world, and set our heart on miseries, if we have been called to immense bliss… to heaven itself, where we will be transformed into the very beauty of God 36 and will be inebriated with love, hidden forever in the most adorable breast 37 of Christ, the Son of God. The Incarnation of the Word tells us that our place is in heaven, in the very Heart of Christ, where all delights are found. “And one must not hold it to be impossible that the soul should be capable of so lofty a thing” 38 , St. John of the Cross goes on to say, because precisely “so that it might come to this, [God] created it in His image and likeness 39 .” That is why the Proper Law goes on to say: 4. We must have a clear awareness that without Jesus Christ we can do nothing 40 , and we must strive with all our strength always to advance in virtue That is the message of the Incarnation of the Word for each of the members of this Religious Family, here or wherever they may be, whether religious or lay, contemplative or apostolic, and whatever the field of mission Providence has assigned them. Because ours is “to be another Incarnation of the Word” 41 , imitating the Incarnate Word in earnest ; working not for ephemeral or passing things, but for ‘the most divine work among the divine,’ which is the eternal salvation of souls and the glorious resurrection of bodies 42 , and striving to attain the perfection of our state 43 . ***** [Peroratio] Therefore, on this day we ask the Mother of the Incarnate Word for the grace always to keep our eyes fixed on the heaven that her Divine Son won for us, and that, whatever the circumstances of our pilgrimage, she may help us always to sing, with our lives more than with words, the song of the new man, which only new men can learn, renewed from their former condition by the work of grace and already belonging to the New Testament, which is the Kingdom of Heaven 44 . A happy feast of the Incarnation of the Word to all! Notes 1 Cf. Ps 89:1. 2 St. Augustine, De Trinitate , XIII, 9. 3 Cf. Our spirituality must be that of the hymn of the kenosis

[Exordium] In our Directory of Spirituality we read: “We could say that our spirituality must be that of the hymn of the Kenosis” 1 , referring to the text of Philippians 2:6-7: He, who was of divine condition, did not consider this equality with God something to be jealously guarded: on the contrary, He emptied Himself, taking the condition of a servant and becoming like men. And in an even more challenging way we read in another place of our Proper Law that what is properly ours is “to imitate Christ in the self-emptying of His Incarnation” 2 . Perhaps that is also what makes our point of focus, as members of this Religious Family, the text of the kenosis, given that we are called to replicate in our lives the example of the Incarnate Word and to prolong the Incarnation 3 . 1. The self-emptying of the Word There is no way to weigh justly what the self-emptying of Christ means. Some used the example of toads to explain the self-emptying of the Word in the Incarnation 4 . Others, like Fulton Sheen, use that of dogs. The idea is the same. Sheen says 5 , after narrating a whole hypothetical case in which we had to lower ourselves to live like dogs in order to save them, that the humiliation is twofold. First, in assuming the body of a dog, it is as if that man had decided to confine himself to the limits of a canine body. He could speak, but he only barks. He could reason and count the stars, but he is only guided by instinct and would have his snout fixed to the ground. The second humiliation would be that this man would have to spend the rest of his life with dogs, knowing that he is a million times better than the dogs. He would always have to run with them. The futility of his life among dogs would be incredibly degrading. And in the end, the dogs would turn against you and tear you to pieces. And one would think that the humility of such a man is very great, because of his spirit of poverty, of sacrifice, of service, of love for dogs, by the fact of having become canine. “However, says one author, that self-emptying would be within the order of creatures, within finitude; it would be the passage from a higher creature to a lower creature. This is not, even remotely, the case of the Incarnation, in which the self-emptying is that of an entire infinite God who assumes a finite nature. This is abysmal. It is an infinite self-emptying and an infinite abasement . One is not in the same order as in the hypothesis we were speaking of; rather, in this reality there is a lowering from the order of the Creator to the order of the creature. Therefore, abysmal too is the example of the virtues that Jesus Christ teaches us by His Incarnation: abysmal is His humility, His poverty, His obedience, His sacrifice, His patience, His sorrow, His service and His love for man. It makes one shudder to think of it ! From transcendent to immanent, from powerful to weak, from majestic to humble, from immortal to mortal, from infinite to finite, from most pure Spirit to material flesh, from eternal to temporal, from impassible to passible, from immense to small, from unlimited to limited, from all-powerful to servant, from rich to poor, from Lord to slave, from King to subject, ‘from eternal life to temporal death’ 6 . And all that, without ceasing to be God! It is an abysmal self-emptying!” 7 . God became a servant and lived with servant men (slaves). 2. Implications Now then, notice that we have been called to be other Christs 8 , to imitate −as we said before− Christ in the self-emptying of His Incarnation” 9 . Therefore, it is fitting to ask: What are the implications of the kenosis of the Son of God for us who are called to be priest-victims, or priests of the Incarnate Word? Fulton Sheen answered – As priest, it will imply the emptying of oneself in order to be filled with holiness; – As victim, it will imply that one empties oneself in the service of others. It is the challenge of our vocation. This kenosis in a priest of the Incarnate Word is manifested specifically in two resolutions: Humility : because the measure of the increase of the Spirit of Christ in the soul is in direct relation to the decrease of self-love, of one’s own judgment, of attachments, etc. 10 The other is the emptying of oneself , which also comes in direct proportion to compassion toward others. The less emphasis there is on the ego, the more care and the more attention there is toward one’s neighbor. Our Founder says this same thing in these words: “The priest, like Christ… is a man who possesses nothing, because he possesses Him who is everything and is possessed by Him who emptied Himself, who made Himself nothing” 11 . The more the religious or the priest empties himself of his own plans in order to carry out God’s plan, of his comfort in order to sacrifice himself for Christ, when he empties himself of that excessive desire to be appreciated, to be praised, to be taken into account, to be consulted, to be preferred to others, he ceases to be bound hand and foot by anxiety. As the humiliation of Christ becomes his model, then even the very sufferings he endures become part of the interior joy and of the service they offer outwardly. 3. Look at Him also made man 12 Our Constitutions have in number 7 that marvelous paragraph that we know almost by heart: “We want to found ourselves on Jesus Christ, who has come in the flesh (1 Jn 4:2), and on Christ alone, and Christ always, and Christ in everything, and Christ in everyone, and Christ All.” Those very brief lines of our Proper Law, which so explicitly refer to the mystery of the Incarnation, have an immense depth, and I think they are of great fruit for our spiritual and priestly life. It is clear that it is to Him that we must look, it is to Him that we must return again and again, and to Him alone. St. John of the Cross has a chapter in his book of the Ascent in which he speaks precisely of this, and it is where he speaks of Christ as the All of the heavenly Father. Thus the saint says that “in giving us [the Father], as He gave us His Son, who is His one Word −and He has no other−, He spoke everything to us together and at once in this single Word, and He has nothing more to say” 13 . “What God formerly spoke to our fathers through the prophets in many ways and in many manners, now at last, in these days, He has spoken to us in the Son all at once . By which the Apostle gives us to understand that God has become as it were mute and has nothing more to say, because what He used to speak in parts to the prophets He has now spoken in its entirety, giving us the All, who is His Son ” 14 . Christ is the definitive Word, the one and best Word of the Father. A present, a gift that has been given to us. This being so, says the Mystical Doctor, “anyone who would now wish to question God, or desire some vision or revelation, would not only be acting foolishly , but would be offending God , by not fixing his eyes entirely on Christ, without wanting any other thing or novelty” 15 . With which he is already telling us that precisely what must be done is to fix our eyes firmly on the Incarnate Word and realize the Treasure we have in Him. Then he places on the lips of the Heavenly Father the following: “If I have already spoken all things to you in my Word, who is my Son, and I have no other, what can I now answer or reveal to you that would be more than that? Fix your eyes on Him alone , because in Him I have said and revealed everything to you, and you will find in Him even more than what you ask for and desire ” 16 . This should be applied to everything in our life, whatever the circumstance in which we may find ourselves, whatever our anxiety and whatever our uncertainty or need; to all He answers: “He is all my speech and answer, and He is all my vision and all my revelation. Which I have already spoken, answered, manifested and revealed to you, giving Him to you as brother, companion and master, price and reward ” 17 . I cannot extend myself much on this now, but we can mention how healthy it is for the soul to think of the Incarnate Word as our brother, as our companion, as our master, as our price and as our reward… And the Heavenly Father goes on to say: “If [still] you would wish me to answer you some word of consolation, look at my Son, subject to me and bound by my love, and afflicted, and you will see how many He answers you. […] look at Him also made man , and you will find in that more than you think […] [Because] in Christ dwells bodily all the fullness of divinity ” 18 . Look at Him also made man , look at Him emptied, look at Him suffering the same pains as, and even greater than, those you are going through, look at Him forgotten, look at His Heart saturated with ingratitude, look at Him with arms outstretched to embrace you… look at Him also made man , because in Him dwells the fullness of divinity , that is, all rest, all goodness, all sweetness, everything, and the only thing that gives true satiety to the soul, even if everything else is lacking. [Peroratio] Each one of us, by being a member of the Institute and by being a priest, is called to “prolong the Incarnation.” That is our specific end 19 , our apostolate 20 , our charism 21 , our vocation. For that, we must first prolong the Incarnation in ourselves. The Virgin Mother gave God a human nature through which He taught, governed and sanctified. Each time we genuinely renew our consecration to Jesus Christ (through Our Lady, as is also “what is ours”), we give Christ our human nature so that He may analogously use our priesthood to continue His teaching, His governing, His sanctifying work. I conclude once more, so that it may be engraved on our souls: what is properly ours is “to imitate Christ in the self-emptying of His Incarnation.” It is a great grace, almost unsurpassable if we see who we are, and one that we must always implore from our Lord; that is why we can conclude by asking for this grace by means of “the prayer of the soul in love” of the mystical doctor of Fontiveros. Lord God, my beloved! If You still remember my sins, so as not to do what I keep asking of You, do Your will in them, my God, for that is what I most desire, and exercise Your goodness and mercy, and You will be known in them. And if You are waiting for my works, so as by that means to grant my request, give them to me Yourself and work them in me, and the pains You would wish to accept, and let it be done. And if You are not waiting for my works, what are You waiting for, my most clement Lord? Why do You delay? For if, after all, it must be grace and mercy that I ask of You in Your Son, take my little mite, since You want it, and give me this good, since You also want it. Who will be able to free himself from base ways and limits if You do not lift him up to Yourself in purity of love, my God? How will man, begotten and raised in lowliness, rise up to You, if You do not lift him up, Lord, with the hand that made him? You will not take from me, my God, what You once gave me in Your only Son Jesus Christ, in whom You gave me all that I desire. Therefore I will rejoice that You will not delay if I hope. Let us remember what our Proper Law says: other congregations will shine for their renown, for their great influence, for the magnificence of their works. We only want –and this has always been our declared intention– to stand out by imitation in the kenosis of the Incarnate Word 22 , by configuring ourselves to His style 23 , by passing through this world doing good 24 and bearing witness to the Truth 25 . That is why our passion must be “to ‘assume’ cultures, purify them and elevate them on the basis of Christ and His Gospel, understood ‘in the Church’ 26 ” 27 . This is and this has always been our intention, our goal. Even when they contradict us or persecute us, even in the midst of the harshest poverty and in spite of our great miseries. Because our faith and our trust are fixed on Him who said: Whoever acknowledges me before men, I too will acknowledge before my heavenly Father 28 ; yes, in the world you will have tribulations, but do not fear: I have overcome the world 29 I will be with you always, until the end of the world 30 . May God our Lord and His Most Holy Mother grant us the grace always to have before our eyes the mystery of the Incarnate Word that we celebrate today. May it be so. Notes 1 Cf. Unlimited confidence in the Virgin of Luján

The Crown, the Mantle and the Moon at the Feet of Our Lady of Luján [Exordium] Dear brothers, I would like first of all to thank God for this beautiful gift of providence, that we can be here together as a Religious Family around our Mother, the Virgin of Luján. To honor and express our love for her who is the “excellent masterpiece of the Most High” 1 , the “paradise of God” 2 , as St. Louis Marie called her, and who is, at the same time… our Mother! Our Directory of Spirituality says “that we were conceived in the most pure womb of Mary, and that is why she is our true and proper spiritual Mother” 3 . What is more, it clearly states: “We were born from the womb of the Virgin, in the manner of a body united to its head” 4 , the Head who is Christ, the Incarnate Word. That is why we say with all propriety that she is our Mother and that there is between us and the Most Holy Virgin a most intimate union, like that of a mother with her child, who expects everything from her, to whom he entrusts everything. And as our Mother, the Virgin of Luján is in fact wholly devoted to the good of our souls, whether in the physical or material order, but above all in the spiritual order. I would like, then, on this day, contemplating the beautiful image of the Most Pure and Immaculate Conception of Luján that we have here, to reflect together with you on the unlimited confidence we must have in the Most Holy Virgin, as true children of so blessed a Mother. And I would like to do so, if you will allow me, by looking at three elements that adorn her image: the crown, the mantle and the moon at her feet. 1. Crown The original imperial crown of the Virgin of Luján was blessed by Pope Leo XIII and placed upon the precious brow of our Mother on a day like today, exactly 130 years ago, this being the first coronation of an image of Our Lady in America 5 . We can say that today we are also celebrating that event. The Virgin of Luján is Queen. For Christ himself crowned his most worthy Mother with a crown of twelve stars and raised her upon a royal throne, establishing her as Queen and Lady of all creation. And if she is Queen, she is Queen of the Angels, of the Apostles, of the Martyrs, of the Virgins, of all the Saints, of families, and therefore also of our Religious Family. In fact, our Founder consecrated our Institutes and the Third Order to her 6 . But let us not forget that, although she is Queen, she is a Queen all sweetness and clemency, inclined to do us not only good, but only good and the greatest good, to all and always. And that is why our dear St. John Paul II says: “The title of Queen does not replace that of Mother: her queenship is a corollary of her particular maternal mission , and simply expresses the power conferred on her to carry out that mission” 7 . So, even amid crosses, persecution, setbacks of any kind, when human strength fails, and even under the weight of “our faults and sins, no one –that is, none of us– should distrust the mercy of God” 8 , because Mary is Mother and Queen of Mercy. And if she is Queen and Mother, her power is immense. Hence we say that before the Most Holy Queen the powers of the principalities of this world vanish, adversities, however threatening they may be, wane, and the greatest sorrows and crosses are sweetened. How many miracles the Virgin of Luján has worked to convince us of her formidable power! And although they are many, I would like to bring here the example that Fr. Salvaire himself, a French Lazarist missionary, recounts about himself. He says that it happened at the end of 1875, on the Argentine pampas, when he was 28 years old. There the Indians took him prisoner and were going to execute him because they accused him of having brought the plague of smallpox to those lands. Surrounded by the Indians, who rode in circles around him with lances in hand, he only prayed and promised Our Lady –before whom he had prayed in an oratory before beginning his mission– that if he was saved he would devote his life to raising a shrine to her and spreading her devotion. It was then that a young man appeared from the midst of the throng and interceded with the chief to set him free. And so, miraculously saved by the intercession of the Virgin of Luján, this holy priest built the Basilica in her honor (the first Gothic church in pointed-arch style in Argentina), wrote a magnificent two-volume book with the history of Our Lady, and it was he himself who petitioned the papal blessing of the crown for our Mother. It is good to recall this event today, as we celebrate one more anniversary of the coronation. And so this example –like so many others we could cite here– shows us how all of us will find a ray of hope in a corner of our heart whenever we invoke the help of Mary. May contemplating the crown of our Mother always remind us of the sovereign power of the Queen of Mercy! 2. Sky-Blue and White Mantle And this leads me to speak to you about the second element that adorns the Virgin of Luján, and that is her mantle. Because “according to Spanish custom, from the earliest times she was dressed in garments. And since she is the Immaculate Conception, the attire is a white tunic and a sky-blue mantle” 9 . This mantle of Our Lady is like the wings of the hen under which the chicks take shelter. And it must always remind us that, as a good Mother, she wants all of us in her lap, united under her mantle, close to her Most Pure Heart, so united to the fountain of Life born on Golgotha. That is why everything that causes division or dispersion, or hinders union, saddens her greatly. What mother is happy if one of her children is missing? Ah!… But if one should come to be missing, with what solicitude this Good Mother goes out in search of her children! And with a thousand delicate touches and motherly tones she tries to draw him close again. An example of this very thing is the fact that, already from the time when the Black Manuel took care of the Virgin of Luján, many times at dawn he would find her covered with dew, and at other times with her mantle full of burrs and dust and some mud 10 , because she went out during the nights in search of her children to rescue them from their vices, or to draw near in the hardship of one of them, to free them from some danger or to help them die well. For she herself wants to lavish her care upon them and to feed them and defend them and give them everything they need. What is more, she does not allow anyone to leave her side disconsolate or to feel less loved. And so the saints of all times have seen in the mantle of the Mother of God an eloquent sign of her maternal protection, of sure defense against all evils, of shelter against the snares of evil. St. Alphonsus said: “Let us run to this divine Mother, let us take refuge under her mantle, and she will save us” 11 . St. John Paul II affirmed: “Mary, glorified in heaven […] continues to be Mother of all men, […] until the end of the ages. In the light of the divine glory, she contemplates all and each one of her children, in all and in each of the moments of their existence” 12 . The Virgin of Luján loves us as much as her power, and her power has no limits, because she is the Suppliant Omnipotence; and so she follows us with her tender gaze wherever we go and extends to all of us the mantle of her tenderness, which shelters us from the cold of loneliness, protects us from the heat of the passions, serves as our refuge against the evil one, and soothes the sorrows of this life. How many times in our short history as a Religious Family have we experienced the sure help of the Virgin of Luján, who has even made us progress in everything! The same –I am sure– each of us can say in a most personal way: How many times Our Lady has saved us from imminent dangers, has brought us out of extremely difficult situations, and, even more, has granted us favors before we asked her for them! How fitting, then, is the beautiful custom that our elders taught us of kissing the mantle of Our Lady, which is at once an invoking of her protection and a grateful response to so much affection. That is why: “Let no one [of us] lose heart! Let no one be led astray in moments of difficulty and of eventual defeats! Let no one be overcome by the temptation that efforts are useless!” 13 . The colors of the mantle of our Blessed Mother must make us raise our gaze to heaven, where one day we hope, as our whole reward, to embrace her for all eternity. Her sky-blue mantle reminds us that heaven is the goal. Let us then always keep present and firmly rooted in our mind and heart that we have a Mother who watches over us and always accompanies us and who desires –even more than we do– to give us every good. Protected under the shield of her mantle, we have nothing to fear. That is why our confidence in the Mother of Heaven must be unlimited, unshakable, unbreakable. Knowing that she does not remain distant, but becomes fully involved and follows step by step every detail of our lives. 3. Moon Finally, at the feet of the Holy Image there is a silver crescent moon, “because she is Mediatrix between Christ –the Sun– and the Church –the Moon.” And if she is our Mediatrix, then she is a “sign of sure hope” 14 . Pope Benedict XVI explained that “the Most Holy Virgin Mary has the moon at her feet, an image of death and mortality, because she has left death behind and is completely clothed with life, the life of her Risen Son. And so the Virgin Mary is a sign of the victory of love, of the goodness of God, giving our world the hope it needs” 15 . We, members of the Church, who journey as pilgrims “amid the consolations of God and the persecutions of the world” in order to bring the Incarnate Word to men, have in the Virgin of Luján our Mother, who unceasingly implores for us before the throne of God the gifts of salvation 16 . That is why, although the Church suffers her setbacks, she always comes out victorious 17 –Pope Benedict affirmed–, since through the most powerful intercession of the Mother, there cannot triumph over those who entrust themselves to her, even “in spite of their poor strength, in spite of their littleness, in spite of their weakness, either the Evil One or those who belong to the Evil One. It is a prayer of the Mother and, therefore, it is a prayer that the Son is, so to speak, obliged to hear” 18 . And Our Lady certainly does hear prayers! Look around you. Each of us is the living confirmation and the palpable proof that the Virgin of Luján hears prayers. Was it not to her that Fr. Buela asked for the grace to be able to accompany many vocations? See what an attentive and generous Mother Our Lady is! So, if Our Lady is not only our Queen and Mother, but also our powerful Intercessor, why be afraid? St. John Paul II, when he visited Argentina, referred to the Virgin of Luján, calling her the “Virgin of Hope” 19 , through whom “salvation and the hope of a new world came to us” 20 . This image of the Virgin of Luján, present in our communities, in all our missions, in countries so distant and in cultures so diverse, helps us to fix in our soul this reality, which undoubtedly strengthens our hope: that of the “certainty of the maternal protection of Our Lady” wherever we go and whatever the circumstances, whether speaking individually or as an Institute. Her presence among us seems to say to us: “Am I not here, I who am your Mother?” That is why, today and always, “now and in the future,” “she is all our hope because she is the Mother of the One who is ‘our hope’” 21 . [Peroration] St. John Bosco wrote to one of his missionaries who was somewhat discouraged, saying: “We must work! Think of dying on the field of labor as a good soldier of Christ. Am I good for nothing? I can do all things in Him who strengthens me . Are there thorns? With the thorns turned into flowers, the angels will weave a crown for you in heaven. Are the times difficult? They always were, but God never failed with his help. Christ is the same yesterday and today” 22 . And we know that this help comes to us unfailingly through the virginal hands of Most Holy Mary. That is why let us always go forward, always doing good, without being intimidated, confident in the help and protection of Mary. And the same saint, on another occasion, “in 1862 confided to Don Cagliero: ‘Such sad times are upon us that we need precisely for Our Lady to help us preserve the Christian faith.’ And St. John Paul II, reflecting precisely on Don Bosco's saying, commented: “[These] are grave and serious words that we too can repeat today, consolidating ever more our love and our confidence in Mary. Trust in Mary. Entrust your activities and concerns to her maternal care each day.” 23 And that is exactly what we want to do: To her we entrust all the activities, all our missions and all the concerns of our Religious Family. In a particular way, to her we entrust the religious who today will make their perpetual vows, making a total offering of their life to Jesus, through his Mother. May this always be our attitude: that of unrestricted confidence and of an immense and tender love for the Mother of God. We ask the Virgin of Luján to obtain for us this grace from her Son. And we also ask it through the intercession of the Spiritual Father of Our Religious Family, our dear St. John Paul II. She is part of our history!

Homily on the Solemnity of Our Lady of Luján Dear Religious Family: This beautiful day in May on which we celebrate Our Lady of Luján, the Queen of the Institute, is an altogether special day, a day of grace. A day that speaks to us of the constant manifestations of tenderness and maternal care, of the special intercession, of the great condescension that this most Kind Mother has shown and continues to show us, and which has brought so much consolation to our missionary hearts. It is a day on which there shines forth more brightly how the Virgin of the sky-blue mantle, crowned with twelve stars, has been pleased to interweave her history with ours, and keeps us safe between her joined hands, in the warmth of her Immaculate Heart. In truth, this love story of the Blessed Virgin began to be woven on that first May 8, 1630, when, with that first miracle –the miracle of the cart– the Most Pure Conception chose to remain by the Luján River in Argentina to be the Mother, Queen, Lady and Patroness, first of all, of the Argentine people. Who would have thought that today, almost 400 years later, hundreds of her children would have set out to the four corners of the earth, carrying her image everywhere to make her the magnificent guardian of all our missions! And no longer only children of the Argentine people, but also of many other peoples from among whom the Lord has raised up vocations for our Religious Family! God willing, we will continue going to all nations , as her Son commanded us (cf. Mt 28:19-20), always bringing Her, too, to the whole world. Truly, all of us, the members and the tertiaries of this Religious Family, of such different origins, nationalities, races and cultures, are, one by one, her children, and in Her we were born. We can truly say of our Mother of Luján what Scripture says of Jerusalem, that she is Mother of all peoples: This is the City the Lord founded upon the holy Mountains! The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob. Glorious things are said of you, City of God: ‘I will count Egypt and Babylon among those who know me; Philistines, Tyrians and Ethiopians, all were born in her.’ Thus will it be said of Zion: ‘This one, and that one too, were born in her, and the Most High himself has founded her.’ When he registers the peoples, the Lord will write: ‘This one was born in her.’ And all will sing as they dance: ‘All my springs of life are in you’ 1 . This most Sweet Mother has proven to us more than enough how much she loves us, and how many times she has made us experience her preference and special affection for this, our little Religious Family, which is honored to have her as Patroness. To highlight how significant and providential this May 8 is, and to stir up our trust in Her even more, and as an encouragement to our hope, I wish to mention some anniversaries that fall this year and which, like links along one and the same history, make “manifest the dominion and maternal providence that Mary has over all things” 2 , because they form, as it were, a golden chain that keeps us anchored at the feet of this magnificent Queen, captivated by love. In the first place, this year marks 385 years since the first chapel was erected to guard and honor the most sweet image of the Virgin of Luján. In that place this Compassionate Mother welcomed “the numerous pilgrims who came there, drawn by the graces that She dispensed to her devotees” 3 . Certainly that chapel was very rustic and small, but from there the holy image worked unceasing wonders in countless souls. How can we not see in this anniversary a most gentle and providential coincidence, when we think of the shrine that we wish to offer her today in her honor in Tajikistan –a country that has had her as Patroness for 18 years–! A shrine that we trust will be –as that first chapel was– “an oasis in the desert of this life, a beacon of light” 4 that enlightens minds with the Truth that saves. A house from which this Exalted Queen and Mother may form and forge true apostles of hers, Marian apostles. Missionaries who, like this “great evangelizer of culture” 5 , love what is their own while remaining open to universal values, without exaggerated particularisms, without incomprehensible insularity 6 . By the merciful design of the same Incarnate Word, also providentially, this year marks 320 years since the death of Black Manuel –a slave native to Africa– who was consecrated to serving the Blessed Virgin for more than 40 years in Luján. He would proudly say: “I belong to the Virgin and no one else,” and he acknowledged “that he had no other master to serve but the Most Holy Virgin.” I think, then, of these three brothers of ours: two from Argentina and one from Egypt (from North Africa), who today are going to consecrate themselves perpetually to God by means of the three religious vows and who, “in order to do so better” 7 , will consecrate themselves in perpetuity in maternal slavery of love to this most Merciful Mother, so that “She may dispose of everything according to her good pleasure” 8 . What better feast to give oneself totally to Her as religious of the Institute than that of Mary of Luján, our Mother and Patroness! And what better place than this magnificent basilica of St. Mary Major, the first dedicated to Mary Mother of God in the West! Moreover, contemplating the example of Black Manuel, who “applied himself with such solicitude to the worship of this Divine Lady, to the point that he never left her Image without light” 9 , I think of the offering of the men’s monastery in Papua New Guinea and of the women’s monastery in Tajikistan , which today we will joyfully offer to our Mother. So that our monks and contemplative sisters, with their silent holocaust, may be there like that votive lamp that burned unceasingly at the feet of the Virgin of Luján, to thank her forever for the vocations that She herself begets for our Religious Family, and to beg her unceasingly that new vocations may spring up everywhere, ready to embrace the most noble apostolic undertaking that going to the emblematic missions implies, in order “to make Jesus Christ loved and served” 10 . Great and generous souls who understand that true “worship consists in making one’s own life an offering to God” 11 , as Black Manuel himself teaches us, and in an eminent way the Blessed Virgin herself with her blessed fiat (Lk 1:38). Finally, it has been 33 years since that year of 1985 when, “with the approval of the Bishop, Msgr. León Kruk, the first group of our members founded, on February 22 of that year in San Rafael, Argentina, the first house of the Institute which, by common agreement, came to be called “Villa de Luján” and which today houses the Major Seminary “Mary, Mother of the Incarnate Word,” the largest Major Seminary of the Institute 12 , and which has given to the Church, as we said at the beginning, hundreds of missionaries scattered throughout the world. We also wish to say, to the honor of this kind Mother, that one year after the offering of the Golden Rose that we made in this very place, our beloved Institute has had a notable increase in vocations, perhaps counting today more vocations than ever before in its history. All of this certainly thanks to the immeasurable intercession and condescension of our Queen and Mother, the Virgin of Luján. In the face of all this, how can we not make our own the cry of St. Paul, who said to us in the second reading we heard today!: Blessed be God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every kind of spiritual good in the heavens, and has chosen us in him, before the creation of the world, to be holy and blameless in his presence, through love 13 . And truly, how many are the gifts with which God has blessed us in Christ! But among the most eminent gifts is certainly the gift of his Most Holy Mother, as the Incarnate Word himself told us in the Gospel we heard a few minutes ago: Here is your mother 14 . So, for all that we have just mentioned and for many more things that remain unsaid, our devotion and love for the Virgin of Luján cannot be reduced to just one day or one year, for example, only to this May 8. She is part of our history as a Religious Family! She is an integral part of our spirituality! She is the very depth of the soul of every religious of the Incarnate Word! She is the Mother who gathers us in a tender embrace from very different nations to whisper in our ear: Do whatever He tells you 15 . She is the ribbon that binds, as in a bouquet, the countless blessings that God sends us. Through Her the doors of the world are opened to us so that we may go and evangelize. …But let us be aware that love is repaid with love… Let us be Apostles of Mary 16 , that is, let Her be “the end toward which our acts are directed, the object that captivates our hearts and the motive of the works we undertake” 17 . And let us be apostles in imitation of Mary, that is: “carrying out the things of God promptly 18 ; serving our neighbor, like Her, even in the simplest tasks” 19 ; founding “all our apostolic enthusiasm” on her Son, the Incarnate God. In such a way that our whole existence may become an offering in thanksgiving and a pledge of the true and perpetual love that we render her. [Peroratio] Let us ask, then, on this day, the grace for all the members of our Religious Family “that the Blessed Virgin may be the model, the guide, the form of all our acts” 20 , and that, as our Proper Law says, She may make of us “great saints” 21 . We ask her this in this Holy Mass. Notes 1 Ps 87. 2 Constitutions , 83 . 3 Cf. Fr. Sermon on the Solitude of Our Lady

[Exordium] Our Proper Law teaches that “Everything is in the Passion. It is there that the science of the saints is learned” 1 . The Passion is, par excellence, the work of Jesus Christ, the work of the Incarnate Word. You did not want offerings or sacrifices, but you have given me a body; holocausts and sacrifices for sin did not please you. Then I said: ‘Behold, I come to do your will, O God’ (Heb 10:5-7). Fr. La Palma teaches that“The Passion of our Lord, from whatever side we look at it, whether from the side of the person who suffers, or of the things He suffers, or of the end for which He suffers them, is the highest and most divine thing that has happened since God created the world, nor will its like happen until the world’s end” 2 . That is why St. Paul of the Cross, quoted in our Proper Law, tells us: “ Everything is in the Passion ” 3 . However, the mystery of Jesus Christ has not been fully considered or understood unless, indissolubly united to it, we consider the mystery of the Mother, His Mother, whom we can also properly call “ our ” Mother, by virtue of that wonderful transformation wrought on the day of sorrow. Precisely that most intimate union with Christ –which culminates at the foot of the Cross– and the motherhood which at that moment She assumes toward us are the first reason why our Proper Law tells us that the Virgin Mary must be one of our great loves: “Because of her union with Christ and with the Church. Because she begot us, the members, together with the Head. Because she was given to us as Mother when she stood at the foot of the Cross: Behold your son (Jn 19:26)” 4 . In this sermon on the solitude of the Blessed Virgin, in which our gaze and imagination turn to the afternoon of Good Friday and to the events of Golgotha, I would like to set before our consideration and contemplation three moments of the Friday of the Passion. And it seems important to me here to consider this whole drama from another angle, from that other great focal point of Golgotha: Standing by the Cross of Jesus is his Mother (Jn 19:25) . To see how this profound sorrow of Our Lady was offered in union with the sacrifice of her most adorable Son out of love for us , so that She might cooperate in the great work of the Redemption; all of which should fill us with confidence and increase in us fervor in our devotion to Her whose slaves of love we are, and to whom we can have recourse, confident in her intercession for us 5 . The Blessed Virgin is the second figure in importance in this drama, and so we will now consider these three moments, which are like three paintings, but seen this time not from the mystical side of the Redeemer but from the point of view of the Co-redemptrix. 1. Mary at the foot of the Cross At the foot of the Cross, standing, as an image of faith, w ith her soul pierced by the sevenfold sword, stood the Virgin Mary. By the Cross of her Son stood his Mother, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene (Jn 19:25).It is a spectacle at once dramatic and marvelous. Let us leave aside, since they are now behind us, all the central parts of the drama: the nails, the agony, the seven last words (among which was the third, in which His Mother became our Mother), the mockery of the Jews, the weeping of Magdalene. Longinus, with terrible fierceness, has just struck the final blow: the lance, and has pierced the open side of the Savior, from which flowed blood and water (Jn 19:34) . Christ has died, the drama is consummated; the blood begins to clot, breathing can no longer be felt, and the body grows cold… icy. Wondrous is the spectacle that now presents itself to our eyes. That Jesus who preached life, who brought a new life to this earth, is dead, though at His side someone still lives, and it is His Mother, bathed in tears. She weeps, she contemplates, and she redeems. Many wondrous things were happening in Jerusalem. Darkness would still be covering the earth; the earthquake that had been felt would still be stamped on the faces of the inhabitants of Jerusalem; in the distance one would hear the clamor of the Jews on learning that the veil of the temple had been torn from top to bottom, with all that this meant; the people were going back beating their breasts (Lk 23:48) . Yet someone remained. All the rest mattered little. Mary was still at the foot of the Cross. How edifying this image is! The Co-redemptrix was fulfilling her mission to the utmost, and in the absence of her Son, with her heart shattered by all that had happened, she remained standing, as if it were now She who bore on her shoulders the whole drama of the Redemption. Here the solitude of Mary begins. The union of Christ and His Mother was most intimate. Christ was dead, His blood clotted; little that was divine or royal could be perceived in Him. The death of Our Lady on the day of the Passion was spiritual, but it was a death as real as the death of her Son. She won for us with her tears what Jesus won for us with His blood. Her heart was pierced not by the two-edged sword but by the sevenfold sword. As members of this Religious Family in which we wish to imitate Jesus Christ as perfectly as possible “until we can truly say to others, Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Cor 11:1), it is no longer I who live, it is Christ who lives in me (Gal 2:20)” 6 , we too must die with Christ, like His Most Holy Mother, to the point of completing in the flesh –as the Apostle Paul teaches– what is lacking in the Passion of Christ (Col 1:24). “The sacrifice of oneself, following the example of Christ and united to Him, is most efficacious for cooperating in the redemption of the human race” 7 . “If in the present economy of salvation the Passion of Christ was necessary, our suffering will also be necessary. If there were another way to go to heaven, Jesus Christ would have followed it and, what is more, He would have taught it” 8 . It is true that, as our Directory of Spirituality teaches, we “add nothing substantial to the sacrifice of Christ, but in the order of operation we complete it in some way. In His sacrifice Christ the head offered to the Father His own sufferings and those of all the members of His Mystical Body; He took upon Himself not only the sins of all men, but all their sufferings; these were sufferings that His members would have to suffer for love of Him; they would be persecuted because they served Him 9 ” 10 . By the grace of God we too can be “co-redeemers,” provided we unite our sufferings to those of Christ: “All the co-redemptive efficacy of our sufferings depends on their union with the Cross, and is in the measure and degree of that union” 11 . Let us see the sublime way in which Our Lady immolates herself together with her Son, so as to follow her example and cooperate with our humble service in this magnificent work of the Redemption. 2. The Pietà Mary’s inmost being is pierced with new sorrow by the hammers that unnail Jesus from the high Cross. Nicodemus gives the nails to the Virgin, so that they may go from the body of her Son to crucify her soul. The ceremony of the deposition begins; Christ is taken down from the Cross; they begin to unnail the completely disfigured body, a “holy skein,” as Lope de Vega calls it in one of his poems. The body of the Savior hung lifeless on the Cross… at anyone’s mercy. But above all it belonged to His Mother. She alone had given Him that by means of which Jesus had accomplished His Redemption; She alone made it possible for Jesus to exist; She alone made Him the new Adam. Joseph of Arimathea arrived; immediately afterward came Nicodemus. These two men took part in this claim of Mary: Nicodemus, the secret disciple of Jesus, and Joseph of Arimathea, who gave up his new tomb for Him. The latter had asked Pilate for the body of our Lord, and Pilate granted it to him. The wealth, rank and position of these two men were notable; one of them had heard the crucified One speak of how one day He would be lifted up (Jn 3:14); the other came from the land of weeping, from the place of Rachel’s tomb. Centuries before, Isaiah had prophesied that our Lord would be rich in his death (Is 53:9); now He is handed over to the rich Joseph of Arimathea. These two men, after they took our Lord down from the Cross, after unnailing Him and removing the crown of thorns, laid Him in the arms of His Most Holy Mother. Death. The Pietà. Christ dead, or stronger still, God dead in His human nature at the hands of merciless men. “When Adam was driven out of Paradise, after the punishment of labor had been imposed on him, he wandered in search of the food he had to earn by the sweat of his brow. Once, during his search, he came upon the lifeless body of his son Abel. Then he lifted him up, put him on his shoulders and laid him on Eve’s knees. However much Adam and Eve spoke to their son Abel, he did not answer. Never in all his life had he been so silent. They lifted his hand, but it fell limp upon his mother’s body. Never had he acted like this. They looked into his eyes, and they were cold, glassy, mysteriously elusive. His parents had never seen him like this, so passive and unfeeling. Then they asked themselves what had happened, but they could find no answer, until they remembered the words: Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for when you eat of it you shall surely die (Gen 2:16-17). That, Abel’s, was the first death in the world.” “Centuries passed, and Christ, the new Abel, was condemned to death by His brothers of the race of Cain, poisoned with jealousy. The life that had come forth from the infinite depths was preparing to return to the Father’s house. The new Abel too was laid on the knees of the new Eve. This was the death of Death! When the tragic moment came to fulfillment, Mary, weeping, must have thought she had returned to Bethlehem. The head crowned with thorns, which knew not where to lay itself except on the wood of the Cross, would seem in Mary’s vision to be that little head she pressed to her bosom in the days of Bethlehem. Those eyes, which on closing had darkened the sun and the moon, would be for Her those little eyes that gazed at her from among the straw of the manger crib. The lifeless feet, pierced by the nails, would be for Her those of the Child before whom gold, frankincense and myrrh were laid. The lips, now disfigured and reddened with blood, would again be for Her those full lips which long ago, in that distant Bethlehem, had been nourished by the Eucharist of her body. The hands that now could hold nothing but a wound would seem again the small hands of the Child who in Bethlehem could not even reach the necks of the cattle. The embrace at the foot of the Cross would recall the embrace beside the manger. In that sad hour of death, which often makes us think of birth, it would seem to Mary that she had returned once more to Bethlehem.” “Let us pray to her, then: No, Mary, Bethlehem has not come back! This is not the manger, but the Cross; here there is not a birth but a death; this is not a day on which one rejoices gladly with shepherds, but the moment of a death in the company of thieves. No, it is not Bethlehem, it is Calvary.” Nicodemus and Joseph anointed the body with a hundred pounds of myrrh and spices, and wrapped it in the whitest linen. In the place where he was crucified there was a garden (Jn 19:41). In that garden was the tomb in which no one had ever been buried ( ibidem ).There the Savior was laid. And an enormous rock hid Him from His Mother’s eyes. In the Pietà, at least she held Him in her arms, but now not even that. Mary was completely alone. Without Christ living and without Christ dead. 3. The Solitude of the Blessed Virgin Mary Look and see if there is any sorrow like my sorrow (Lam 1:12) Grown pale, the roses of your anguished lips; withered, the purple lilies of your tearful cheeks; Remembering the joyful hours long gone in Bethlehem, with no consolation now, and no good to fill her solitude… See her, where she comes, daughters of Jerusalem! The return begins. What Jeremiah had lamented centuries before was being fulfilled: How lonely sits the city! How sad is she who lived so joyfully in this life with her Son! The Lady of the nations has become like a widow! (Lam 1:1).They begin to go toward the upper room; Our Lady went almost by force; her body was moving away from the tomb, but her heart remained within it. They take her to the Cenacle, where Jesus Christ celebrated the Passover the night before. Those streets of Jerusalem were walked by the Mother of the Savior, sad, anguished and alone. “O wounded woman! Alone and forsaken, what will you do? With whom will you console yourself? To whom will you tell your sorrows? What heart is strong enough to keep you from fainting, having lost such a Son and having seen with your own eyes Him suffer so many torments, and so blamelessly!” The Virgin alone weeps for the death of Christ, weeps for the solitude of the world. Without a spouse, because Joseph was held captive by death, without a father, because He hides, without a son, because He is dead “Bethlehem is Jesus as you, His sinless Mother, knew how to give Him to the world. Calvary is Jesus as the sinful world knew how to give Him back to you. Something has come between your giving Him beside a manger and His being given back to you beside a Cross: what has come between is my sins. Mary, this is not your hour, but mine: my hour of malice and of sin. If I had not sinned, death would not now be beating its dark wings over His body of clotted blood; if I were not full of pride, the crown of thorns would never have been woven, because He suffered in my place; if I had been less rebellious in running the long road that leads to destruction, His feet would never have been pierced with the nails; if I had been more docile to His Shepherd’s voice calling me so as not to let me fall among the thorns and thistles, His lips would never have been so deformed; if I had been more faithful, His cheeks would never have been dishonored by the kiss of Judas. Mary, I find myself between the birth and the redeeming death. When you embraced Him in the Pietà, He was not white as when He came from the Father, but red because He comes from me. The last drops of blood have already fallen from the chalice of the Redemption, staining the wood of the Cross and reddening the rocks that split apart in horror. Mary, my Mother, intercede with your divine Son for the forgiveness of the sins that have changed your Bethlehem into a Calvary. Ask Him, Mary, in these anguished moments o f solitude, to grant us the grace not to crucify Him anymore and not to pierce your heart anymore with seven swords. Mary, implore your dead Son that I may live. Jesus has died, Mary, and He has died for me!” Let us too die, so as to be able to “nail in our hearts Him who for us was nailed to the Cross” 12 . We must “die totally to our own self,” aspiring to that perfect imitation of Our Lord which is only “achieved through perennial labor. It is a matter of dying in order to live : you have died and your life is hidden with Christ in God (Col 3:3). The life of Christ was a continual death, whose last act and consummation was the Cross” 13 . “The science of the Cross and of the joy of the Cross is attained only in the school of Jesus Christ” 14 . [Peroration] May the Blessed Virgin teach us how to remain at the foot of that Cross. The Incarnate Word has told us that only those who persevere to the end will be saved. But perseverance is often very difficult. Few of us are willing to remain at the foot of the Cross for three full hours until the Crucifixion is finished. Most of us are deserters of Calvary, half-crucified souls, impatient to sit down when we are not nailed to a Cross. Many of us make firm resolutions in the morning, but few of us keep them until the end of the day. The soul of the Mother of Jesus does not falter, because the soul of her Son did not falter. He kept His promise. He finished the work that was given Him. And His Mother herself remained standing to the end on that day of sacrifice. And there she is to help us, and to Her we must go with confidence, as our Proper Law encourages us, to ask her for “fortitude in moments of trial, because she remains a t t he foot of the C r oss of each of her children” 15 . May Our Lady intercede for us, then, and obtain for us the grace to remain three full hours on Golgotha, so that when our life has ended, we may pray with Him and with Her: ‘I have finished the work you gave me. Now, my God, take me down and raise me to everlasting union with You.’ Let us ask fervently for the grace of the science of the Cross, of the joy of the Cross.
