Ecce venio… ecce Mater

30 th priestly anniversary [Exordium] My dear friends: I have the grace of being able to celebrate this Holy Mass with all of you in this beautiful church dedicated to the Immaculate Heart of Mary on the day on which I celebrate the 30th anniversary of my priestly ordination. I want to thank very especially Fr. José for allowing me to celebrate this Mass, and all of you for having come to share this day and to thank God and Our Lady for this very great grace He has granted me of being a priest of the Incarnate Word. Since I was ordained a priest, I must say that my life, and especially my whole priesthood, has been intimately intertwined with our Most Holy Mother, whom I learned to love and honor from early childhood, thanks to my parents and very especially to my mother. That is why I wanted, in this homily and at the feet of this beautiful image of the Immaculate Heart of Mary that presides over our church, to speak of her, the mother of priests. 1. The mother I see here among you many who are mothers of families, and many others whom I call ‘mothers of the heart,’ who, although they have no children of their own, devote themselves to others with an exquisite maternal love from which I have not infrequently benefited (as is the case with the sisters). The reality of a mother on this earth is an immeasurable gift… Mothers are the supreme consolation that God has given us in this valley of tears… I believe the mystery of a mother is so intimate and profound that on this earth not even they realize the greatness of this vocation. For the mother, in a special way, is everything to us (and I believe that we religious live this reality in a fuller and more beautiful way than other children). Because in large part, everything one is, one’s way of being, of thinking, of believing, everything good one has, one owes principally to one’s mother. Who could doubt that our mothers’ contribution to our lives has been decisive! That is why I dare to say that, among all human relationships, there is none that can equal this one. Because, as St. John Paul II taught, “although parenthood belongs to both the father and the mother, the mother is the special and more qualified ‘part.’” For every time a child is born, a mother is also born, and the relationship established between them is unique, most intimate, unrepeatable and eternal, since no other future relationship, however deep it may be, nor the most tortuous circumstances, nor the most humiliating human weaknesses, not even death itself, will ever be able to erase the sacred bond between mother and child. For a child, his mother will always be his mother, and for a mother, her child will always be her child. The mother is, in some way, like our Providence on earth in the first years of life, our firmest support in the following years of childhood, our most tender and most loyal friend in youth, and our most inseparable and unconditional companion throughout our whole life (and even when she is no longer among us). A good mother is a blessing from God and the supreme consolation that has been given to us in this valley of tears. She shows us the way when we go astray. She lifts us up when we fall. She encourages us when we are downcast. She sweetens life on earth and magically turns thorns into roses. God conveys to the world the consolation of love through the soul of the mother. That is why a mother’s love has no boundaries. She can renounce her own interests generously and suffer with a smile on her lips because she loves; she is capable of renouncing, for love of her child, all the grandeurs of the earth. She dedicates her life to fighting for her children and rejoices to see them happy. That is why, for a child, there is no place in the world, however beautiful, like this one: his mother’s heart. There is no creature in this life to whom we are more united than to the heart and soul of our mother. It is said of the Heart of Our Lady and that of Our Lord that they beat in unison, and one author says that this happens with all mothers, with the difference that in that beating it is the mother who always sets the rhythm, and that is why she always knows or senses what is happening in her child’s heart. Who has not experienced this? That is why Hebrew women would counsel one another that making the decision to have a child is of crucial importance: “it is deciding forever that your heart will walk outside your body”; and the proverb says that “whoever takes a child by the hand, in the end, takes a mother’s heart.” That is why it happens with good mothers as with the saints: the work she does with us is so great that all that remains is to praise God for the gift of having given her to us, because she has been, is, and will continue to be, even when she is no longer here with us, the image of the providence and love of God on this earth. The mother is the heart of the family; it is the mother who in a certain way creates and constitutes the home and protects its unity. Who has not seen this? Around her, everything is ordered and unified, everything is harmonized and grows. That is why, when a mother departs, nothing is ever the same. She weaves the bonds among everyone, sends the children toward the father and the father toward the children. The mother is in a particular way the one who listens, consoles, encourages, forgives, reconciles and gives each one his place. She spreads the balm of love and tenderness over all family relationships. She has a constant concern for each one and does not rest until all are content. How many of us can say of our mothers –whom God Himself has entrusted to us– that they have been and are the precious gift through which we are given to see how full of love Divine Providence is! For they, considering “good example as their first mission,” “with their maternal fiat (‘be it done unto me’),” taught us that there is no greater happiness than doing the Will of God. And in the shelter of the sanctuary of their hearts they taught us that what is most noble, pure and full is generous self-giving, without conditions, without time limits, limitless self-giving to the point of forgetting oneself out of love. That is why our mothers will always be the most luminous brushstroke that God set upon the book of our lives and the most tender caress through which we came to know the paternal gentleness of God. Therefore, any one of us, wherever he may be, as he caresses his good mother with his heart, can say with St. John of God: “God has deposited the treasure of His love on earth in three coffers: in the Eucharist, in Confession and in my mother’s heart.” St. Angela Merici said that “mothers, even if they had a thousand children, would always carry each one of them engraved on their hearts, and would never forget any of them, because their love is exceedingly genuine.” * * * Now, if we say this of our earthly mothers, how much more must we say of the Mother of God, who is Mother of Jesus the High Priest and of all priests. Who could measure the length, the height and the depth of the love contained in that Immaculate maternal Heart? And even more so in relation to priests St. Manuel González, a Spanish saint, said: “The fire of the sun, reinforced by the fires of all the suns of creation, is not even a pale imitation 1 of the fire of love accumulated in the heart of the priestly Mother … Love of the Mother of God, who can measure you? Love of the mother of the priesthood, who will dare to count your degrees?” 2 . And yet, how much she had to suffer! For all Christians, but particularly for us, the Most Holy Virgin is everything. Who can doubt that, given the perfect communion of spirit and heart that always exists between good mothers and good children, and in a most excellent way between that Mother and that Son, the scene of Gethsemane had two settings: the garden where the Son sweated drops of blood, and the hidden dwelling where the Mother wept drops from her heart; and that the sacrifice of His heart and of His affection for the Son had as its echo the sacrifice of the heart and of the affection of the Mother? From the sacrifice of the Immaculate Heart of Mary, Mother of priests, all Christians, but especially we priests, must learn to love as the Mother does, even those who outrage her Son, and to shed tears for the salvation of their souls, and even to sacrifice ourselves like her, who, without altering the serenity of her countenance, lets herself be called upon by them. 2. My priestly chasuble I was ordained a priest on a day like today in 1993, and from that moment I took it as settled that Our Lady would be everything to me. That I would live for her and would try to die next to her. That if I was with her, whatever happened, I would always be safe, consoled and, in the end, happy (as happens with our mothers). That is why I chose that the image of Our Lady should be very present on my ordination chasuble, which is the one I am wearing now. On the front and on the back. Ecce venio Where do these words come from? Ecce venio ut faciam Deus voluntatem tuam . They are taken from the letter to the Hebrews, and do you know what? They represent the offering that Jesus made upon entering this world. It is the priestly consecration of our Lord upon entering this world; it was the beginning of His priesthood, and I wanted that to be my priestly motto: that I might always do the will of God on this earth, whatever it might cost, whatever I might suffer, and that I might always try to live with Jesus. But to do so I also knew that I needed the help of the Most Holy Virgin; hence the image of the Annunciation, when the ecce venido of our Lord was united to the fiat of our mother. Fiat michi secundum verbum tuum , be it done unto me according to your word. May that be the model of my life, that of the Mother; I asked Jesus to have the same sentiments as He and my Father had in order to fulfill His will. Such was the beginning of the Savior; so too did the Most Holy Virgin begin her mission as Mother of the Redeemer; and so I too wanted to begin my priesthood. Ecce Mater On the front I placed an image of Our Lady of Sorrows; it is the Virgin of the Macarena, venerated in Spain, where my grandparents came from before emigrating to Argentina. She is a Sorrowful Virgin, or better said, serenely sorrowful. It was at the foot of the cross that Our Lady, as the model of a priestly mother, standing beside her Son, won for us with her tears what Jesus was winning for us with His blood. It was Our Lady of Sorrows who was given to us as mother: Ecce Mater… ecce mater tuam… She, in her sorrow, was saving us, and in a particular way, in being given to the apostle John, she was granted the grace of co-redeeming the world. That is the model: her offering of her life and of all that one does and suffers for the salvation of souls. At my first Mass, on the 10th in the afternoon (it was a Sunday), a priest preached the first Mass for me and spoke to me about this, something I will never forget… And I always thought that this would have to happen, and so I should always be very close to Our Lady of Sorrows. That is how it is: every priest must go through this, and this is the sublime degree of our vocation. The holy bishop Manuel González teaches: “Think that many times you will have to go to Gethsemane, many times in the course of your ministerial life! And there, look, think about what you are going to give and what you are going to receive… You: your clean, upright, unmeasured affection, your work, your word, your talent, your sweat, your money, your comfort, everything that is yours… yourself; all of you! And what are you going to receive? A handful of faithful, generous, loyal souls, but few… very few indeed. Around you?… The same ones who were around the Master,” the bishop goes on to say: “ Good people who soon tire and fall asleep, or who are frightened even sooner and flee. Friends who sell or deny… Around these, or mixed in with them, the envious , the ambitious , the Pilates , who do not protect the one unjustly persecuted, those who spit, scourge and slander. And afterward, or in the midst of it all, the cross! And to carry it and face them all, a frail man, a rebellious flesh and a heart of clay!” 3 . That is the sacrifice of the priest’s heart in imitation of his Master. However, just as Christ in the garden of Gethsemane was consoled by an angel, so in the Gethsemane of our priestly life, and beside the altar where our priestly heart is immolated −what joy!−, it is not an angel, but the very Mother of the Incarnate Word who, with her Heart in her hand, helps us to say: Ecce venio! Which means: Here I am, I come to do your will 4 , and which is my priestly motto, taken from the Letter to the Hebrews. [Looking at the image] My Mother, give the heart of this your priest son, in his hours of Gethsemane, strength to love much and give much, expecting nothing! With a sacrificed heart! Because, as St. John of the Cross teaches: the one in love [with God], the more wounded he is, the more he is repaid 5 . Now, taking advantage of the fact that we are here as among very dear friends: first, I want to thank you very much for having welcomed me so well −as if we were family− when I arrived at the parish, and I also want to express my gratitude for all the support and prayers you have given me since I arrived. But at the same time I would like, if you will allow me, to express a wish to you. 3. A wish Providentially we are here in this beautiful church dedicated to Mary. God could have taken us to other parishes, but He wished to place us under the patronage of her Immaculate Heart (which is also a Sorrowful Virgin; look at that pierced heart). And we cannot fail to see in this a special design of mercy on the part of our Lord. But at the same time, the honorable duty of loving our Mother tenderly, of giving her consolations, not sorrows. That is why my wish, which is at the same time my prayer, is that you love the Most Holy Virgin very much, tenderly and trustingly . I know that you already love her very much. But at times I fear that our devotion to Our Lady may be intermittent: we remember her only now and then, or only on her feast, or we pray the Rosary only once in a while. Our Lady wants you to be entirely hers. And, like every mother, she wants you always beside her, every day; in every circumstance, be always Mary’s. And may you become apostles of Mary, that is, may your true and heartfelt devotion to the Mother of God radiate that silent influence on other souls that makes them want to be devoted to Mary as well. I have always liked to watch the interaction between mothers and their children. Have you noticed what mothers do with their little children before sending them off to school? They wash their faces, comb their hair, prepare a snack for them to take, and they may forget many things. But one thing they do not forget before parting: to plant a kiss on their forehead; and the children run off to catch the bus or go into the school while the mother watches them go, bathed in the waves of a gaze that is all affection and satisfaction. In the same way, how happy it would make me if every day the Virgin Mary saw you set off to your work, to school, to the club, to a gathering of friends, but not before passing in front of her Image to give her a kiss or make the sign of the cross, and to commend yourselves to her with a prayer. With what satisfaction and affection our Mother would look at you. But it does not end there. Because that would be a purely external devotion if it were not accompanied by a sincere interior life, nourished by the sacraments, which has charity toward others and which every day silently tells its rosary beads. For that is doing everything with Mary. How much the Most Holy Virgin will bless those souls, those homes, those parishes! And that, in the end, is what I wish for you: that you may have the greatest consolation in this valley of tears, which is to live and die embracing this Immaculate Heart that loves us so much. [Peroratio] Allow me now to turn this sermon into a prayer to Our Lady: Receive, Most Holy Mother, my fiat , now as a prayer, now as an act of faith in doubt, as an act of hope in fear, and always as an act of love. Fiat! I am in your hands, my Mother! Suffering, exalted, humbled, useful for something or useless to all, I will always love you and I will always be yours, Beloved Mother! No one will separate me from you! In joys and in sorrows I will always be your son. Lonely and unknown like the flower of the desert, wandering like the bird without a nest, always, always, my Lady and most sweet love of my soul, from my lips will come your submissive answer to God’s plan: Fiat! Be it done unto me according to your word! Present my offering before the throne of your Son and grant me the grace to live and die saying: ecce venio , like Jesus, the Incarnate Word. So be it! The Presentation in the Temple

Homily preached on the occasion of the Feast of the Presentation of the Child Jesus in the Temple The sacred liturgy on the feast of the Presentation raises us to consider the sufferings of Christ and of Mary. It is the feast of consecration, in which the offering of Christ is made, and it is interesting to see how the offering of Christ takes place by means of suffering. With every step the Savior took, the cross became more evident. The presentation of the Child Jesus and the prophecy of Simeon open the sorrowful portico of the life of the Most Blessed Virgin. As soon as Mary presents to God an offering worthy of Him, she immediately receives the reward of an unspeakable sorrow for her whole life, because it is a fixed thought of the Lord that the sufferings of this world should be the roots of the graces of the next. That is why the saints rejoice in suffering, becoming like Christ. From this moment everything was sorrow for Mary: time, because it shortened the distance to Calvary; the sight of the Child, which reminded her of it; the sight of the fields and the city, which always brought to her mind something related to the Passion. The Most Blessed Virgin had to carry out her tasks always under this affliction. And if she was able to do so, it is because she always had Jesus present. Thus St. Teresa affirms it, saying: “The Lord said this to me another day: Do you think, daughter, that merit lies in enjoyment? It lies only in working and in suffering and in loving … You see My whole life full of suffering, and only on Mount Tabor will you have heard of My joy. Do not think, when you see My Mother holding Me in her arms, that she enjoyed those consolations without grave torments. From the time Simeon spoke those words to her, My Father gave her clear light to see what I was to suffer …”. There Mary understood better all that she would have to suffer. Perhaps there all the sufferings she had endured at the birth of Christ began to become clear to her. The immensity of Mary’s sorrow and the promptness with which she accepts her oblation show the holiness of our Mother, for God proportions tribulations to the strength necessary to bear them. There is something that is always said when speaking of the sufferings of Jesus and Mary, and it is that such is the union between the two that every suffering was increased by the fact that one suffered for the other. And this is so because each suffered for the suffering of the other; more still, each suffered because the other suffered on account of his or her sufferings. St. Bernard said, referring to Mary at the foot of the cross: The same pain that filled the heart of Mary set the heart of Jesus ablaze with bitterness; and he has Our Lady say: I was there seeing Him and He was seeing me, and He suffered more for me than for Himself. It is interesting, but on this day the Church marks the day of religious life, because it is the day on which the offering of Christ by Mary is celebrated. And if in all the acts of our life we must look to Christ as our model, according to that saying of St. Thomas that the actions of Christ are our example, with much greater reason in this mystery in which the consecration of religious life is represented. The consecration of Christ and Mary was by means of suffering. Simeon says: My eyes have seen the salvation , but then he adds: a sword will pierce your heart. Salvation and sorrow are intimately united, in such a way that they cannot be separated. If we want to make the same offering as Christ, we must also know how to consecrate ourselves through suffering and sorrow. Like Jesus and Mary, we consecrate ourselves for salvation, to suffer. This is how salvation is worked. St. Paul tells the Ephesians: Therefore I beg you not to lose heart in your many sufferings, as I suffer for you, for all these tribulations are for your glory . This suffering is the path that God has chosen for all His saints, even for the greatest persons who ever walked this earth: Jesus and Mary. St. Ignatius himself in the Spiritual Exercises says: “I will look and consider what Our Lady and St. Joseph are doing, how they set out on the road, how they suffer a thousand trials so that the Lord may be born … and die at last on the cross, and all this for me .” For the dying of Christ was a consequence from the instant He was conceived; the sorrows of Mary are a consequence of that fiat of the Incarnation. This is the glory of the saints and of the imitators of Christ. Without doubt the reason why Mary suffered was that God willed the Mother and the Son to be alike in everything, and that, since this Virgin was the most perfect of the perfect, she should not fail to share in the greatest glory of the Holy One of holies. And because the greatest glory of this Lord was to have suffered so many sorrows out of obedience to the Father, it was not right that His Most Holy Mother should lack a share in this glory. On this day let us ask God to have it in our hearts to consecrate ourselves to God by the same means by which Jesus and Mary offered themselves, that is, through sorrow; let us ask to have the longing that St. Bernard had: “ But what do we offer, brothers, or what do we give back to Him for all the good things He has done for us? She offered for us the most precious Victim she had, being unable to give a more precious one; let us too do what we can, offering Him the best we have, which is certainly ourselves. He offered Himself; who are you, that you hesitate to offer yourself? Oh, if I had the happiness that so great a Majesty would deign to receive my offering! …It is better for me, and much more useful and glorious, to offer myself to You than to keep myself for myself .” And if one day the path of suffering seems difficult to us, we must repeat the invocation of St. Bernard: Look to the star, call upon Mary !
Evangelization requires holiness

Homily on the occasion of the celebration in honor of St. John Paul II [Exordium] Dear all in the Incarnate Word, we are gathered here in this magnificent Basilica of St. Peter, beneath whose vaults lie the sacred relics of St. Peter, the first Pope; those of some of the apostles; those of glorious martyrs and those of an admirable succession of Supreme Pontiffs. Here too, in this majestic reliquary, rest the remains (and this is particularly significant for us, being the reason that has brought us together here today) of one who was among the most illustrious Pontiffs of the Church: our dear St. John Paul II. These very walls –a symbol of the Catholic Church and of the Primacy of Peter– which rise up as silent witnesses of the countless demonstrations and teachings of holiness of the successor of St. Peter whom we celebrate today, give us the fitting setting in which to contemplate the eloquent example of love and self-giving to the Church that God was pleased to offer us in the person of St. John Paul II. That is why I would like to reflect with you, -among the many aspects of his fruitful life that could be mentioned- on the holy Pope’s love for the Church, referring to three notes which, although common to many Roman Pontiffs, in some way characterized and distinguished the Papacy of John Paul II from all the others, whether by their heroism or by their magnitude. – I refer in the first place, as the first note, to the universal missionary spirit with which he exercised his Petrine ministry; – in the second place, as the second note, his tireless dedication to preserving and increasing the unity of the Church , the priority task of every successor of Peter; – and finally, in the third place, as the third note, the unconquerable fortitude and courage with which he himself carried out these tasks, giving us a magnanimous and joyful witness and example of love for the Cross of the Lord. For love for the Church implies love for Jesus, and love for His Cross is an inescapable condition of love for Jesus. It was this witness that encouraged all of us and so many others -and continues to encourage us- to act in the same way… to try to imitate him… to have him as a model of what we are and what we do. All these elements are, also, fundamental principles of our spirituality and of our mission as consecrated persons, members of the Religious Family of the Incarnate Word. 1. Universal Missionary John Paul II understood from the very first moment that the call to be Successor of Peter was a call to a universal mission, simply because the church is universal. He said so himself on a day like today, 39 years ago now, when in the homily for the inauguration of his pontificate he stated: “Today, a new Bishop ascends the Roman Chair of Peter, a Bishop full of trembling, conscious of his unworthiness. And how could one not tremble before the greatness of such a call and before the universal mission of this Roman See!” 1 . St. John Paul II recognized as implicit in his call to be Universal Shepherd the call to “act in the name of Christ and in harmony with him in the whole vast human area in which Jesus willed that his Gospel be preached and the saving truth proclaimed, [that is, in] the whole world.” 2 And that is exactly what he did. He was a tireless evangelizer… a tenacious missionary… an indefatigable lover and spreader of the truth. His universal solicitude embraces not only geography, but also his immense Magisterium. We could say that there is hardly any aspect of theology and of human, ecclesial and social life that St. John Paul II did not address in his almost 27 years of pontificate with his 14 Encyclicals, 15 Apostolic Exhortations, 45 Apostolic Letters, with the promulgation of the Catechism of the Catholic Church, with the reform of the Code of Canon Law and of the Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches, with his countless speeches, homilies, letters and books. He was, without a doubt, a planetary missionary. His 104 apostolic journeys outside Italy, and the 146 within this country 3 , and his visits to almost all the parishes of the diocese of Rome bear witness to his immense desire to reach –in imitation, we say it analogically, of the Incarnate Word Himself– “all Christians and the whole world” 4 , fulfilling so fully the mission entrusted by Christ to the Apostles: make disciples of all nations 5 . He recognized himself as a “sign of the presence of Christ in the world. And this is a presence –he wrote– that goes out to meet people wherever they may be ; it calls them by name, encourages them, comforts them with the proclamation of the Good News and gathers them around the same Table” 6 . And wherever he went, that is precisely what he did. It is always very striking, as we remember him, to see the vivid awareness he had of the universal mission… to the ends of the earth. John Paul II showed us and taught us a tireless missionary spirit, for he exercised his Petrine ministry -as he liked to repeat- moved by the sollicitudo omnium Ecclesiarum and devoting all his energies “to being a sign of the great Friend (with a capital F) of all of us” 7 , as he once told priests and religious. “The Church must be tireless in this mission received from Christ, -these are his words- she must be humble and courageous, like Christ himself and like his Apostles. She cannot lose heart even in the face of dissent, protests or any kind of accusation […] The Church cannot cease to proclaim the Gospel” 8 . How magnificently his example rises before us, missionary religious, the example of this man who knew no limits in loving and serving Christ… because Christ himself loved us to the end 9 ! And Christ himself told us: I have given you an example, so that you also may do as I have done to you 10 . All his wealth consisted in giving himself to the Word 11 in his “Mystical Body, which is the Church” 12 . In this resolve he showed himself to be well grounded, giving us a supreme example. John Paul II insistently repeated that evangelization requires holiness, and holiness requires nourishing the spiritual life 13 . That is why every day he devoted a long time to prayer. And so, both in Rome and during his apostolic journeys, he prayed a great deal: besides Mass, he recited the breviary, prayed the Rosary, made his hour of adoration -on Thursdays he made an additional hour of adoration-, and prayed the Way of the Cross on Fridays. He often spent long hours during the night in the shelter of the Heart of Christ in the Eucharist. Thus he would present himself in prayer “before Mary and Joseph and ask them for help [to] build, together with them and with all those whom God entrusted to him, the house for the Son of God: his holy Church” 14 , as he so beautifully confessed in one of his books. Many bear witness, and many of us have seen and verified it, to how prayer was the driving force of John Paul II’s existence. Those who were his closest collaborators state that John Paul II “prayed for the whole Church. But not in an abstract way. He used to speak of the ‘geography of prayer’ and he had an atlas of the world on his desk; every day he would turn the pages and choose a country or a diocese to pray for. This universal solicitude was also manifested in the numerous meetings with bishops from all over the world, whom he would invite to lunch when they passed through Rome, so as to be able to talk with them about the situation of the Church in each place. After many years of pontificate, –those close to him recount– he knew very well both the strengths and the weaknesses not only of the dioceses but also of their pastors” 15 and he prayed with greater insistence. In short, his example as a “universal missionary,” which we wish to evoke today, is without a doubt for us, who want “to be as another humanity of Christ, in order to carry out with greater perfection the service of God and of men” 16 , a beacon of light, a guiding star, a constant stimulus for our religious and missionary life. 2. The unity of the Church The second characteristic note of John Paul II’s self-giving and love for the Church is, in my view, the great zeal with which he devoted himself to promoting her unity. He knew how to awaken in so many places a lively sense of communion with him and, through his person, with all the believers of the Church spread throughout the whole world 17 . He was a man with a great capacity for inclusion 18 , Pope Benedict XVI wrote of him. He considered it his own duty to fight for the cause of the unity of the Church, and with great courage he carried out the charge that Christ himself entrusted to Peter 19 , and he encouraged others to join in the endeavor to achieve the union willed and explicitly asked for by Christ. “Christ calls all his disciples to unity!” 20 , he said forcefully. “Division ‘openly and clearly contradicts the will of Christ, is a scandal to the world and harms the most holy cause of preaching the Gospel to every creature’” 21 , he wrote in his most beautiful Encyclical Letter Ut Unum Sint . A unity that is built -he said- above all on the truth. A unity that he fostered not only among Christians of other churches and ecclesial communities, but also by strengthening the bonds of unity within the Catholic Church herself. In this regard, I would like to read you a paragraph from a message he addressed to priests and religious in 1982. It read: “the communion of minds easily becomes union of hearts, a convergence of efforts for the same cause. A kingdom divided against itself cannot stand . A divided apostolate annihilates itself. And we know that it will be divided if it yields to the temptation of an exclusivism contrary to the rightful diversity of gifts and charisms, or to the temptation of isolation, losing interest in or closing itself off from the work of others, without fitting into common pastoral programs or plans. […] The union of forces of the workers of evangelization requires understanding; and this in turn will only be achieved through authentic dialogue” 22 . John Paul II taught us that the essential identity that Christ has given to his Church is precisely the Eucharist, which is the ‘memorial’ of the Lord, and this of course is stronger than all the divisions introduced by men. The most genuine essence of the Church, that is, what is proper to her, is not division but unity 23 , and that unity is caused as its proper effect by the Eucharist. That is why for us too the cause of the unity of the Church is our own cause, which begins with the firm union of each one of us to the Incarnate Word and among ourselves through mutual love 24 . 3. Fortitude Finally, the Holy Father, whom we so often saw clinging to the cross, gave us proof of his immeasurable love for the Church through his sufferings which, united to the tribulation of Christ, he bore with heroic fortitude. St. John Paul II was without a doubt a man of suffering, but of a suffering borne with dignity, with heroism and with joy. He himself said -he said it repeatedly- that he had placed his life under the sign of the cross 25 . Certainly, over the centuries there were many Pontiffs who served the Church with unfailing fortitude in the faith. Nevertheless, among all of them, the Polish pope shone in a particular way. And this is seen in “the primacy he gave to faith throughout his whole life and in all his activity, to a courageous and fearless faith, a faith refined in difficulties, ready to respond generously to every call of God” 26 . For he knew that the “ Follow me which he had accepted, hearing the voice of Christ in the call of the Church, also carried with it the Whoever seeks to keep his life will lose it; and whoever loses it will keep it alive ” 27 . We know well, as he himself stated, that engraved upon his soul were the words that Cardinal Stefan Wyszyński addressed to him at his episcopal ordination: “you have the duty to act not only through the word and liturgical service, but also through the offering of suffering. […] Lack of fortitude is the beginning of defeat. Can [one] go on being an apostle? For an apostle, the witness given to the Truth is essential! And that always requires fortitude. […] The greatest fault of the apostle is fear. Lack of faith in the power of the Master awakens fear; and fear oppresses the heart and tightens the throat. The apostle then stops professing his faith. Is he still an apostle? The disciples who abandoned the Master increased the courage of the executioners.” How firmly these words remained engraved in the Polish Pope! So much so that already in his first homily he told the whole world: “Do not be afraid to welcome Christ and to accept his power! … Do not be afraid of Christ!” John Paul II was convinced that “one cannot turn one’s back on the truth, cease to proclaim it, hide it, even if it is a difficult truth whose revelation brings great pain with it: You will know the truth and the truth will set you free (Jn 8:32). This is our task and, at the same time, our support! -he said-. […] One must bear witness to the truth, even at the price of being persecuted, even at the cost of one’s blood, as Christ himself did” 28 . And so, without denying the difficulties and the crosses that the proclamation of and fidelity to the Incarnate Word entail, he exhorted us: “Go everywhere with confidence […] know how to speak the word that gives light, because it comes from God with the power of the Spirit of Jesus. Never lose heart in the face of difficulties. Humbly take your share of the Church’s toil” 29 . And with an extraordinary spirit of faith and long experience in the crucible of tribulations, this most worthy successor of Peter, even though he himself was immersed in sufferings, knew how to instill courage in everyone. And so he told us: “Surely we will encounter difficulties [in our life and in our apostolate]. There is nothing extraordinary about that. They are part of the life of faith. Sometimes the trials are light, at other times very difficult and even dramatic. In the trial we may feel alone, but divine grace, the grace of a victorious faith, never abandons us. That is why we can hope to overcome victoriously any trial, even the most difficult” 30 . This was his message, this was his example, and this continues to be the hope he sought to awaken in everyone: “The presence of evil is always accompanied by the presence of good, of grace. […] There is no evil from which God cannot draw a greater good. There is no suffering that cannot be turned into a path that leads to Him. […] All suffering exists in the world to awaken in us love, which is the gift of oneself in generous and disinterested service of others. In love, which has its source in the Heart of Jesus, lies the hope for the future of the world” 31 . [Peroratio] Dear all: I would like to conclude by recalling the words that John Paul II himself wrote in a poem dedicated to St. Stanislaus, and this place, this basilica, would seem to be the most fitting place to do so: “ The Church is always outliving me, she is the ground of my life, and its summit; the Church […] is the Sacrament of my existence unfolded in God, who is my Father .” May his example of love and unconditional self-giving in the service of the Church transform us, as it did him, into “other Christs.” With heartfelt supplication we commend today to our St. John Paul II, in a very special way, our dear Religious Family, our missions and our religious so that, moved by the magnanimous and heroic example of this Holy Pope, we may go forth with generous zeal and resolute self-giving to serve our Mother the Church without limits of horizons, being builders of unity and persevering with unshakable firmness in the faith, giving everywhere consistent witness to the truth. And through his intercession we also ask this grace of the Mother of the Incarnate Word, of whom the Great Pope was a tender and devoted son and slave. The heroism of St. John Paul II

Memorial of St. John Paul II [Exordium] Dear all in the Incarnate Word, we are gathered here in this magnificent Basilica of St. Peter, whose walls rise as silent witnesses of the innumerable demonstrations and teachings of holiness of the successor of St. Peter whom we celebrate today. I am referring to our beloved Spiritual Father, His Holiness John Paul II. This celebration is of special importance for our Religious Family, not only because we are celebrating the “great missionary of the twentieth century,” who “knew how to write with his life a sublime epic deed” and governed the Universal Church with constant solicitude and heroic generosity, but also because “his magisterium animates the fundamental aspects of [our] charism,” making it a “fruitful source from which we quench our thirst for fidelity to the Lord.” That is why this occasion fills our soul with great joy. The Gospel we have just heard ends with the irresistible invitation of Our Lord: Follow me! 1 , after St. Peter’s threefold affirmation of love, and after the Incarnate Word had announced to him his martyrdom. This reminds us that the condition of a true apostle is the cross, because, as Christ himself teaches us: the good Shepherd gives his life for the sheep 2 . These words serve as the perfect frame for contemplating the life of this man -a priest- who “died as he had always lived, animated by the indomitable courage of faith, abandoning himself to God and entrusting himself to Most Holy Mary” 3 , giving himself to the very end. Today the figure of St. John Paul II rises before us “with the strength of a giant” 4 as a “model and powerful intercessor of the good Shepherd, and invites us to follow in his footsteps and his loving self-giving without limits” 5 . And I would like to emphasize these words: “without limits,” because in them are summed up the “consistency of his faith, the radicalism of his Christian life and the desire for holiness that he continually manifested” 6 . An author says that “God sends to each age the saint who excels in the virtue the world most needs” 7 . John Paul II was “a man of colossal virtues,” a “hero of the seven seas.” And all his biographers remind us that Karol Wojtyła was “a gift from God” in one of the darkest moments of the twentieth century. That is why today I would like us to reflect together on the marvelous invitation to heroism that his example and his words set before us. 1. Heroic forgetfulness of self St. Thomas Aquinas points out that “virtue consists in following or imitating God” 8 . And that “man must raise himself beyond his natural life toward the divine life,” following the command of our Lord: Be perfect as your heavenly father is perfect . And of this St. John Paul II gave us an eloquent example from his youth. It is well known that when he had just begun his university studies, with the Nazis in power in his native Poland promoting a regime of terror in the country, he showed heroic courage by joining the clandestine seminary run by the Cardinal of Kraków. For he was convinced that “vocation is a divine initiative,” and it was the Incarnate Word who whispered in the depths of his soul the Follow me that we have just heard in the Gospel. When he asked to enter the seminary, the rector told him: “I accept you, but not even your mother must know that you are studying here” 9 . So he studied on his own from the manuals he received from his professors and, as he himself recounts, “I studied theology in secret” 10 while “I worked in the factory” 11 , which required exquisite discipline. But far from becoming discouraged, he studied with heroic enthusiasm in the midst of work and of the dangers to which he was exposed because of it. Later he reflected on this, saying: “That was the situation then. Even so I managed to keep going” 12 . That is why once this great connoisseur of the human heart told us with great ardor: “Do not be discouraged! You are not alone in walking the way [of the cross]. Jesus walks with you” 13 . “Do not be afraid to welcome Christ and to accept his power” 14 . “Always look upward: look to Christ, who is at once the author, the giver and the absolute exemplar of the priesthood. From Him you will obtain the satisfaction and the joy of following Him and serving Him in souls. Look upward –and he encouraged everyone to recall the words of St. John XXIII, who wrote in his Journal –: ‘I must always convince myself of this great truth: Jesus wants from me […] not just a mediocre virtue, but the highest: He is not content with me until I make myself, or at least strive with all my strength to make myself, a saint’ 15 ” 16 . St. John Paul II was deeply persuaded that holiness “is not a kind of extraordinary life, practiced only by a few ‘geniuses’ of holiness” 17 ; that is why he exhorted everyone to live life to the full, with heroism, with unlimited trust in the Goodness of God the Father, telling us: “We are not the sum of our weaknesses and our failures; on the contrary, we are the sum of the Father’s love for us and of our real capacity to become the image of his Son” 18 , that is, to become saints. And so, on one occasion he told seminarians: “The discipline of seminary life must be valued not only as an effective defense of common life and charity, but as a necessary part of the whole formation, in order to acquire self-mastery , because it is in this way that one forges the dispositions of soul that are of the greatest use for the ordered and fruitful activity of the Church” 19 , that is, to die and bear fruit. “It is in the atmosphere of recollection created by seminary discipline that those attitudes so desirable in a priest develop interiorly, such as joyful obedience, generosity and self-sacrifice ” 20 . You see, then, how St. John Paul II understood that the capacity to give ourselves even to the point of heroism is already formed in the seminary, in the house of formation. It is in the seminary that one learns -he said- the “habit of forgetfulness of self” 21 , which is, the Holy Father added, “an indispensable condition for loving truly and caring only for the interests of Christ” 22 . And so, even in the midst of the communist tyranny that soon replaced the Nazi regime, and already ordained a priest, he showed with new ardor his priestly mettle and courage when, in the face of harassment by the regime, of unjust criticism, of the threat of severe punishment, he carried on his priestly work with great fortitude, devoting himself to the formation of young people in the great Catholic spiritual and theological tradition. He spared no effort to bring the Gospel of Christ to all men, without claiming anything for himself. He gave us the example of an incisive, enthusiastic pastoral work; not one of waiting, but of proposing 23 . Convinced that “pastorally speaking there is nothing more effective than total death to one’s own self” 24 . He kept very much in mind that on the day of his ordination he had prostrated himself on the ground. This “is a sign -he said- of the total gift of oneself to Christ, who, in order to fulfill his priestly mission, emptied himself of his rank and took the condition of a slave […]. And so, acting like any other man, he lowered himself even to submitting to death, and death on a cross ” 25 . Karol Wojtyła understood his priesthood “as a self-giving marked by total commitment” 26 . So much so that, already as Successor of Peter and after having suffered the assassination attempt here in St. Peter’s Square in 1981, after a long hospitalization and convalescence, he intensified his pastoral commitments with heroic generosity . Because “to become a personal witness of the Good Shepherd,” whom one must “love with all one’s soul and all one’s heart, so that this love may be the norm and the driving force of all our actions,” the Holy Father affirmed, “renunciation and mortification are indispensable” 27 . With these sentiments of heroism, of love to the extreme, with full awareness of the radicality of his call to be a “servant of the power of Christ” 28 -as he identified himself- beat the heart of our beloved St. John Paul II, called the Great, and Spiritual Father of our Religious Family. How much his example enlightens us! Of this self-giving of the Holy Father to the end and without cutting corners, Pope Emeritus Benedict XVI also bore witness when, speaking of his predecessor, he said: “The Holy Father was a priest to the end, because he offered his life to God for his sheep and for the entire human family, in a daily self-giving in the service of the Church and above all in the harsh trials of the last months” 29 . 2. Heroic fidelity Like all the saints, John Paul II did not admit a half-hearted following of Christ, but on the contrary invited everyone to a heroic fidelity , to the point of complete configuration with our Lord, the Good Shepherd. “We have consecrated our life to Christ, who loved us first and who, as a good shepherd, sacrificed his own life for us.” That is why he considered it a duty of loyalty to Christ that “we too, pastors of the Church,” be “the first to commit ourselves to responding to this love by being faithful, keeping the commandments and offering our life daily for the friends of our Lord” 30 . Especially to us –consecrated persons– he taught on one occasion: “To understand what it means to be faithful, we must look to Christ, the faithful Witness 31 , the Son who learned obedience through what he suffered 32 ; to Jesus who said: I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me 33 .” And he added: “We look to Jesus, not only to see and contemplate his fidelity to the Father in spite of all difficulties 34 , but also to learn from Him the means he used in order to be faithful: especially prayer and abandonment to the will of God 35 ” 36 . Because ‑as he himself explained with great emphasis on one of his pastoral visits-: “[It is] necessary that the heroic become normal, everyday, and that the normal, everyday, become heroic” 37 . And so he encouraged everyone, saying: “Remember that in the final analysis perseverance in fidelity is a proof not of human courage and strength, but of the efficacy of the grace of Christ. Therefore, if we are to persevere, we must be men of prayer who, through the Eucharist, the Liturgy of the Hours and personal encounters with Christ, find the courage and the grace to be faithful. Let us trust, then, remembering the words of St. Paul: I can do all things in Him who strengthens me 38 ” 39 . With what force the words he spoke at the beginning of his pontificate resound now: “Do not be afraid! Open the doors to Christ!” 40 , inviting us all to heroism, to live with the spirit of a prince. Our Lord in today’s Gospel says to Peter: I assure you that when you were young you dressed yourself and went wherever you wanted. But when you are old, you will stretch out your arms, and another will bind you and take you where you do not want to go . Our beloved St. John Paul II –we all know it– never wanted to safeguard his own life, to keep it for himself; rather he gave himself without reserve, to the last moment, for Christ and for us. Thus we saw him, during the first years of his pontificate, go to the ends of the earth, as an “expression of his constant pastoral solicitude for all the Churches” 41 . But “during the last years, when the Lord gradually stripped him of everything, in order to assimilate him fully to himself; and when he could no longer travel, and then not even walk, and in the end not even speak, his gesture, his proclamation was reduced to the essential: to the gift of himself to the very end. His death was the culmination of a consistent witness of faith” 42 . And he knew how to walk heroically “the royal way of the cross,” discovering that in suffering, too, Christ was to be found, who once more repeated to him: Follow me! And so, raising high the banner of the Cross, he gave the Church perhaps “its most fruitful stage, the one with the greatest spiritual resources and greatest evangelizing efficacy, and even more, the one with the greatest apostolic projection onto the modern or postmodern world” 43 . [Peroratio] My dear brothers and sisters in the Incarnate Word: The example and magisterium of St. John Paul the Great rise before us and before those who will come after us –we who are honored to have him as Spiritual Father of our Religious Family– as a lighthouse from which shines the light that scatters the darkness, as a staff for our steps and as an invitation to heroism that compels us to follow him. Today from heaven St. John Paul II says to us all once again with great fervor -to those present here and to those in the most distant missions-: “Do not be afraid! Open, and open even wider, throw wide open the doors to Christ!” 44 . St. John Paul II was undoubtedly “a hero for all ages” 45 , and from Paradise he continues “pushing entire generations to the heroism of following Jesus Christ” 46 , and us too, and those who will come; that is why the words he spoke at what was to be his last World Youth Day seem especially addressed to us: “I still identify with your expectations and your hopes. […] Although I have lived through much darkness, under harsh totalitarian regimes, I have seen enough to be unshakably convinced that no difficulty , no fear is so great that it can completely stifle the hope that springs eternal in the hearts of the young. […] In the difficult moments of the Church’s history the duty of holiness becomes even more urgent . Holiness is not a matter of age. Holiness is living in the Holy Spirit” 47 . We ask this “Apostle formed by Mary” 48 , who now enjoys “a dignity that is in a certain way infinite” 49 and “is our intercessor and protector” 50 , to obtain for us through his intercession from the Incarnate Word the grace that, like him, we may know how “to direct the soul to great acts in every virtue; […] so that, possessing ourselves, we may know how to give ourselves, never ceasing to aspire to a holier and more perfect life, never stopping” 51 , “ready for martyrdom out of loyalty to God” 52 . And may he obtain for us from Most Holy Mary the grace to be always “ready to do great, heroic, even epic things for Christ and for his Church” 53 . These graces we ask of him in this Holy Mass. Homily on the day of St. John Paul II

The magisterium of St. John Paul II is inherent to our Proper Law Dear brothers, the celebration of the holy memorial of Pope St. John Paul II, Spiritual Father of our Religious Family, takes on a special significance in this place and at this moment through which our Institute is passing; all the more so since on this occasion, with this Holy Mass, the community of fathers who have been living for some time in this famous abbey is officially established, whose aim is to lay the foundations for the relaunching of the Center for Higher Studies. Moreover, the fact that we find ourselves in the very place where St. Thomas brought his life, and in a certain way his work, to its consummation makes this a unique and historic celebration. John Paul II himself called St. Thomas Aquinas the “apostle of truth” 1 , words that in a certain way summarize the mission that our Center for Higher Studies is to have and that it wants to instill in those who will teach and study in this house in the future. You will remember that a little more than a year ago we also gathered here to make a vow to St. Thomas, asking him to grant us the grace that today we joyfully see fulfilled (the testimony of this offering can be found in the commemorative plaque and the votive lamp located in the Chapel of the passing of the Holy Doctor to the Father’s House). 1. John Paul II, the IVE and its insertion in the Church I would like, first of all, to recall something that is known to all, and that is important, because in a certain way it defines us and explains why we celebrate this day in such a particular way: the Magisterium of St. John Paul II is absolutely inherent to the proper law of the Institute and “animates the fundamental aspects of the charism” 2 (these are the founder’s exact words). And so it is: we have this stamp that has marked us from our origins, fidelity to the Magisterium of St. John Paul II. And we can say that if it is true for each one of us –as St. John Paul II also taught– that “to belong to this beloved Religious Family also means to make its charism and its spirituality one’s own and to accept it as the framework in which our life offered to God unfolds” 3 “for the building up of the Church” 4 –, it is also true that each one of us, and our Institute as a whole, never considers itself an island among the other ecclesial communities, but rather “devotes itself in a particular way to the work of the Church in the world” 5 . Since “Christ Himself is Incarnate in His Body, the Church” 6 , we are aware that “we would most gravely betray our charism if we did not work to have an authentic ecclesial spirituality, one that incorporates us fully into the Church of the Incarnate Word. That is why our proper law expressly declares that we want to know nothing outside of Her” 7 . In such a way that there is fulfilled in us that saying of the one we remember today, our beloved St. John Paul II, who said: “love for the Church has been the origin of the rules and constitutions of religious families, which at times expressly declared the commitment of submission to ecclesial authority” 8 . Thus it is –as we can see, and as is reflected throughout the length and breadth of our whole proper law on innumerable occasions– that we always recognize in the Supreme Pontiff our first and supreme authority, to whom we profess not only obedience but also fidelity, filial submission, adherence and availability for the service of the universal Church 9 . But besides the fundamental documents of the Institute’s proper law, which on each of their pages repeat like a refrain that what is ours is and always has been “to love and serve, and to make Jesus Christ loved and served in His Mystical Body, which is the Church” 10 , there are also the fundamental elements attached to the charism, through which our Institute shows again and again, under the explicit guidance of the Second Vatican Council and of the magisterium of St. John Paul II, that we understand that “the path followed by the Church through the centuries is the sure path and that, therefore, it cannot be abandoned” 11 . As the Council itself wisely affirms: “It is for the very good of the Church that all Institutes have their own character and proper end. Therefore, the spirit and aims of the Founders, as well as sound traditions, must be known and faithfully preserved, for all of this constitutes the patrimony of each of the Institutes” 12 . Therefore, “the strictest fidelity to the supreme Magisterium of the Church of all times, the proximate norm of faith” 13 is an integral and constitutive part of our charism, of our mission and of our way of sanctification and apostolate; and it is also a mark of honor. Indeed, to act otherwise would not correspond to the spirit of our Institute, which always had and has as its sure criterion sentire Ecclesiam and sentire cum Ecclesia , acting in perfect communion with its pastors 14 ; nor would it fit within our apostolic mission as religious, since this can be nothing other than the building up and extension of the kingdom within the perspective of ecclesial unity 15 . This is so true that each of the non-negotiable elements attached to the charism not only is set out and developed with magisterial documents (particularly those of Pope John Paul II), but is a clear and explicit response to the requests made by the Council itself, seeking in everything to reflect “the doctrine of the Church as communion, proposed so emphatically by the Second Vatican Council” 16 , and thereby demonstrating our commitment to apply its teachings as faithfully as possible. 2. John Paul II, the IVE and its fidelity to St. Thomas In this context of love for Holy Church, the pillar and foundation of the truth 17 , it is not surprising that it is “our clear intention to follow St. Thomas Aquinas”, whom –in the words of John Paul II– the Second Vatican Council cites, making his doctrine its own 18 , and whose teachings “not without reason the Supreme Pontiffs and the Code of Canon Law itself 19 have taken up and made their own. [Moreover], the Second Vatican Council also prescribes, as we know, the study and teaching of the perennial patrimony of philosophy, a distinguished part of which is constituted by the thought of the Angelic Doctor” 20 . Thus, for example, the Second Vatican Council points out that “t he Church attends with solicitude to schools of higher learning, above all the Universities and Faculties, and those that depend on her she endeavors to organize in such a way that each discipline is cultivated according to its own principles, its own methods and its own freedom of scientific inquiry, so that the understanding attained of it may become deeper each day and, carefully taking into account the most recent research of contemporary progress, it may be perceived more profoundly how faith and reason tend toward the same truth, following in the footsteps of the doctors of the Church, above all of St. Thomas Aquinas” 21 .And elsewhere it determines that candidates for the priesthood should: L earn… to illustrate the mysteries of salvation as far as they can, and to understand them more deeply and observe their mutual relations by means of speculation, following the teachings of St. Thomas 22 .Whether some like it or not: to be faithful to the Council clearly means to be Thomists. Consequently, we could not take pride in being faithful to the Magisterium of the Church and to St. John Paul II, whom we remember and celebrate today with so much affection, if at the same time we did not strive to follow an element as fundamental for the proper formation of our candidates as the perennial doctrine of the Aquinate. Because, let us remember it once more, the “Church has proclaimed that the doctrine of St. Thomas is her own doctrine” 23 . And as the Council itself reminds us, “the mission of priests is not to teach their own wisdom, but the Word of God, and to invite all insistently to conversion and holiness” 24 . It is not possible to list all the reasons that have led the Magisterium to choose St. Thomas Aquinas as a sure guide in the theological and philosophical disciplines; but we can recall today three reasons that have been particularly highlighted in this regard by our beloved St. John Paul II: – The first is “the sincere and total adherence that [the Aquinate] always maintained to the Magisterium of the Church, to whose judgment he submitted all his works, during his life and at the moment of death” 25 . For indeed, he himself preferred “to the voice of the Doctors, and to his own voice, that of the universal Church, as if anticipating what Vatican II says: ‘The whole body of the faithful who have received the anointing of the Holy Spirit cannot err in believing’ 26 ; ‘When the Roman Pontiff or the Body of bishops together with him define a point of doctrine, they always do so in accordance with Revelation itself, to which all must adhere and conform 27 ” 28 . Secondly, because of his fidelity to the voice of the Word of God, transmitted by the Church. And, thirdly, without any doubt, and perhaps this is the preponderant reason, because he “laid down the principles of universal value that govern the relationship between reason and faith. Faith contains, says St. John Paul II, in a superior, different and eminent way, the values of human wisdom; for this reason it is impossible for reason to be at odds with faith, and if it is in disagreement, it is necessary to review and reconsider the conclusions of philosophy. In this sense faith itself becomes a precious help for philosophy” 29 . This is one of the reasons why the idea has arisen of naming our Center for Higher Studies, in this new stage, the Instituto Fides et Ratio , an institute that may be, in this context, a source for an authentic dialogue, from the standpoint of essential Thomism, with contemporary culture; so that, in this way, an authentic, genuine and lasting new evangelization may be carried out. That is why the same Holy Pontiff, in continuity with his predecessors and following the directives of the Second Vatican Council, named St. Thomas Aquinas “ Doctor Humanitatis ” –as he himself says– “because of his passionate dedication to the truth and the value of his anthropology and of his metaphysics”, and proposed him as a model of dialogue with the culture of our time 30 . And he added: “In the cultural conditions of our time it seems very opportune to develop ever more this part of Thomistic doctrine that deals with humanity, since his affirmations on the dignity of the human person and on the use of his reason, in perfect harmony with faith, make St. Thomas a teacher for our time” 31 . [Peroration] My dear all, St. John Paul II was a great promoter of the study and teaching of the Aquinate, as is shown by the fact that he was the first member of the International Society of Thomas Aquinas while still a Cardinal. Likewise, throughout his entire pontificate, he took care to keep alive the teaching of St. Thomas, so beautifully described and taught in his encyclical Fides et ratio , as well as in his many addresses, audiences and numerous documents. In fact, this document has always been considered the Magna Carta of our Center for Higher Studies. St. John Paul II constantly recommended to religious men, to seminarians, to priests, to religious women, the study and deepening of the theological and philosophical work of the Angelic Doctor. And so, for example, on one occasion he spoke these words that suit us so well: “You, more than others, must cultivate familiarity with the thought and writings of this peerless master, and renew and enrich his doctrine” 32 In this holy place, which Divine Providence chose as the fitting place for the passing of St. Thomas to his eternal espousal with the Truth, St. John Paul II says again to all of us: “The truth, like Jesus Christ, can be denied, persecuted, fought, wounded, martyred, crucified; but it always comes back to life and rises again, and it can never be torn from the human heart. St. Thomas placed all the strength of his genius at the exclusive service of the truth, behind which he seems to want to disappear, as if for fear of obstructing its brilliance, so that it, and not he, might shine in all its brightness” 33 . “I encourage [you] today… to become true disciples of St. Thomas, capable of facing the quaestiones disputatae , and of dialoguing with all who are far from the faith and from the Church…” 34 . I end with this sentence of St. John Paul the Great, which I would like to remain impressed on your minds and in your hearts. It says: “The founders knew how to incarnate the Gospel message in their time with courage and holiness. It is necessary that, faithful to the breath of the Spirit, their spiritual children carry on through time that witness, imitating their creativity with a mature fidelity to the charism of the origins, always attentive to the demands of the present moment” 35 . May these two outstanding non-negotiable elements of our charism, namely, fidelity to the Magisterium and the following of St. Thomas in his doctrine, shine with particular splendor in this Center for Higher Studies that we are relaunching. The Marian charism of St. John Paul II

Homily preached on the occasion of the 1 st centenary of the Birth of St. John Paul II We have the grace of celebrating the first centenary of the birth of our beloved St. John Paul II in this shrine dedicated to the Mother of God, where he himself, 42 years ago now, said: “I wanted to come here, to these mountains, to sing the Magnificat following in the footsteps of Mary” 1 . That is why today, in thanksgiving for his birth, we too have come here, to these mountains, to sing the Magnificat following in his footsteps. St. John Paul II was without any doubt a man of great soul, of magnanimous spirit, and that is why, upon being elected successor of Peter in 1978, to the question of Cardinal Jean Villot: “Do you accept the election?”, he answered: “In the obedience of faith before Christ my Lord, abandoning myself to the Mother of Christ and to the Church, and aware of the great difficulties, I accept” 2 . And seven days later he came here, to this Marian shrine which in his own words “attracted him in a special way” 3 . That gesture was the “first, humble response” 4 to God’s call: he came to pray to Our Lady. Because, as he himself said in this place, when man is “extremely burdened and harassed by the contingent conditions of daily life, by all that is temporal, by weakness, sin, dejection… Prayer gives meaning to the whole of life, at every moment and in every circumstance” 5 . Thus he began his pontificate, invoking the maternal help of Mary, and with her name on his lips he ended it. As Fr. Buela said: St. John Paul II “was great because he showed the Church the need to abandon oneself into the hands of the Most Blessed Virgin Mary , by his word and especially by his filial devotion to the Mother of God” 6 . Indeed, several authors maintain that Marian devotion was in many respects a particular charism of his pontificate, and that no Pontiff has promoted devotion to Our Lady as strongly and insistently as John Paul II 7 . This Marian charism showed itself very clearly in his life. Already as a child he was as if captivated by Our Lady, and after losing his mother, Emilia 8 , he would visit Most Holy Mary in his parish in Wadowice, where he also received the scapular. His childhood is dotted with pilgrimages to the shrines of Kalwaria and Jasna Gora, where he went with his father. And one cannot speak of Karol Wojtyla without saying that as a young worker he read the Treatise on True Devotion , and without highlighting the immense influence that reading had on the spiritual life of the one who would later be called the “Marian Pope.” This so filial and so authentic devotion of Karol Wojtyla to the Mother of God became evident to the eyes of the world in his Petrine mission, through his works and his gestures, in his Magisterium and in his heartfelt words. And it is to this that I wanted to dedicate this homily in his honor. On his gestures Proof of John Paul II’s love for the Mother of God is that of the 102 pastoral journeys he made outside Italy, most had as their high point his visit to some shrine of Our Lady. In fact, titles of Our Lady all over the world have seen him on his knees, have heard his expressions of affection, have received his petitions for the Church and the world. No Pope, before or after John Paul II, has made so many pilgrimages to Marian Shrines around the world, consecrating each country, each continent, each family and the whole Church to the Mother of God. Note that in just the first 5 years of his pontificate he consecrated to the Most Blessed Virgin Mexico, Poland, Ireland, the United States, Zaire, Ghana, Brazil, Germany, the Philippines and all of Asia, Nigeria, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, Argentina, Spain, Honduras and all of Central America, Haiti, France and Austria 9 . Of the 8 golden roses he gave as Vicar of Christ, 7 went to the Mother of Heaven: at the Shrine of Jasna Góra, Poland (1979); at the Shrine of Knock, Ireland (1979); to Our Lady of Luján, Argentina (1982); at the Shrine of Matka Boża Kalwaryjska, Poland (1987); to Our Lady of Evangelization in Lima, Peru (1988); to Our Lady of the Conception of Sameiro, Portugal (2003); and to Our Lady of Lourdes, France (2004). And the eighth rose he offered to the spouse of Our Lady, at St. Joseph’s Oratory in Quebec, Canada (2004). On the other hand, we cannot fail to mention the gift to Our Lady of Fatima of the bullet that pierced him in that attack of May 13, 1981. His Marian works Another fact that reveals to us the Marian imprint John Paul II wished to give the Church was his having declared 2 of the 3 Marian years there have been throughout the history of the Church: the first was declared by Pope Pius XII (1953-1954); the other 2 by Pope John Paul the Great: the first of them in 1987-1988; the second from 2002-2003, better known as the “Year of the Rosary” 10 . On the occasion of that first Marian year he published his sixth encyclical, Redemptoris Mater , on the Blessed Virgin Mary, and within the framework of the Year of the Rosary he published an apostolic letter, Rosarium Virginis Mariae , coinciding with the beginning of the twenty-fifth year of his pontificate. In that apostolic letter—as you know—he introduced the luminous mysteries of the rosary, after the mysteries of the rosary had remained ‘untouchable’ for almost a millennium. During that Marian year of ’87-’88 he visited all the most important Marian churches of Rome, and he frequently took advantage of the moment of the Angelus or the Regina Coeli to commemorate some title of Our Lady from some other part of the world. And so that we may see that his filial devotion to Mary reached even to the details: on December 7, 1981, he enthroned in St. Peter’s Square the mosaic of Mary, Mother of the Church, and on that occasion he said: “I am happy to inaugurate this testimony of our love and devotion, and I trust that she, with constant solicitude, will continue ‘caring for the brethren of her Son who still journey on earth surrounded by dangers and difficulties’ 11 , allowing our generation too to experience the invincible power of her maternal protection.” Likewise, you will remember when he handed over the Icon of the Mother of God of Kazan to Patriarch Alexy II, as his gift to the holy Russian Orthodox Church and to the whole Russian people, on August 28, 2004—one of John Paul II’s last public Marian gestures. Moreover, he renewed 5 times the consecration of Russia and the world to the Immaculate Heart according to the request of Our Lady at Fatima: The first was from his hospital bed on June 7, 1981, after suffering an assassination attempt, where in reality he makes an act of entrustment of the Church, of men and of peoples to Most Holy Mary 12 . The second was a repetition of the first on December 8 of the same year in the Piazza di Spagna 13 . The third was at Fatima on May 13, 1982, while he was on pilgrimage to thank Our Lady for having saved him from death the previous year. The fourth was during the Synod of 1983: the Holy Father repeated the consecration in essentially the same terms during Mass on October 17. And finally, as you know, on March 25, 1984, in St. Peter’s Square and before an image of Our Lady brought from Fatima especially for the occasion, in union with all the bishops of the world, he consecrated the world to the Immaculate Heart for the last time. Although ‘those who know’ say that only the acts of May 13, 1982 and of March 25, ’84 can be considered ‘official’ acts of consecration, and the others as preparation for those two 14 . On his Marian Magisterium In addition to the encyclical and apostolic letter we have just mentioned, John Paul II dedicated three years of general audiences—70 audiences, to be precise 15 —to imparting the most extensive Marian catechesis that any Pope had ever given in the whole history of the Church. He always concluded all his pontifical documents, his allocutions, homilies, addresses, etc. with a Marian invocation or by making a clear connection of the topic with the life of the Most Blessed Virgin. We could say that he wished to seal each topic by directing us to her who lived all these mysteries fully in communion with Christ. It is as if he had wished to sign each of his interventions with the presence of Our Lady. Just to give us an idea of the singular contribution made by the Marian magisterium of John Paul II, Cardinal Ratzinger, speaking of the encyclical Redemptoris Mater , said: “The Pope’s fundamental thesis is the following: the specific character of Mary’s mediation consists in the fact that it is a maternal intercession, ordered to an ever-new birth of Christ in the world […] It is true that the Second Vatican Council had already used the title of Mediatrix and had also spoken of Mary’s mediation. However, until now, this theme had not been set forth so extensively in any magisterial document. As regards content, the encyclical goes beyond what the Council already said, while keeping to its terminology. But the encyclical deepens the conciliar elements and gives them a new weight for theology and piety” 16 . So that, at a historical moment in the Church when many saw devotion to Mary as a need of the uneducated, of the simple, the Holy Spirit raised to the See of Peter a man of great human, spiritual and intellectual quality, who knew how to teach us all that kings as well as shepherds must prostrate themselves before Jesus, who is in the arms of His Mother. On his words His words revealed a Marian spirituality that was inwardly convinced, tender, constant and very holy. St. John Paul II was convinced that each person must learn to see himself in the words of the Master on the Cross: Behold your son; son, behold your Mother , and that these words, which were Christ’s testament, had to be welcomed—embraced, interiorized—by each soul, because that was the express desire of the Incarnate Word. That was decisive in his spirituality, I mean, the fact that he took on that filial love, letting Our Lady exercise her whole maternal mission. And that is precisely what he sought to transmit to all souls: a profound trust and filial love for Most Holy Mary. His Marian piety, so intimate, so tender and so theologically enriched, led John Paul II toward a Marian spirituality of profound trust. It is in this sense that at Czestochowa, during his first pilgrimage to Poland, he said: “ I am a man of great trust; here I learned to be so . I learned to be a man of profound trust here, in prayer and meditation before the great icon of Mary, the first disciple: Be it done to me according to your Word .” With what expressions of deep-rooted filial love he spoke of the Mother of God in order to lead souls to that same trust: “Icon of God’s tenderness—he called her—she shows herself attentive to the needs of others, eager to respond to them, and rich in compassion” 17 . He calls her a “sign of contradiction” by her association with her Son and at the same time a “sign of hope”; that is why he says: “The woman who is venerated as Queen of the Apostles without being placed within the hierarchical structure of the Church, and who nevertheless made all hierarchy possible because she gave to the world the Shepherd and Bishop of our souls. […] This is the Woman of history and of destinies!, the woman who encourages us today” 18 . Finally, and now to conclude, I would like to repeat those heartfelt words he addressed to young people at one of the last youth days, which suit us so well at this time. John Paul the Great said: “On the Cross, the Son can pour out His suffering into the heart of the Mother. Every child who suffers feels this need. […] Entrust yourselves to her with complete trust! […] Know, dear friends, that this mission is not easy. And it can even become impossible if you count only on yourselves. But what is impossible for men is possible for God 19 . The true disciples of Christ are aware of their own weakness. That is why they place all their trust in the grace of God, which they welcome with an undivided heart, convinced that without Him they can do nothing 20 . What characterizes them and distinguishes them from the rest of men is not their talents or natural dispositions. It is their firm determination to walk in the footsteps of Jesus ” 21 , holding the hand of Mary. ***** Everything for Jesus Christ through Mary. Thus he lived, thus he fulfilled his mission and thus he died, with the Totus Tuus on his lips and in his heart, this most worthy son of Mary. In his spiritual testament John Paul II, like another Christ on the cross, also wished, on leaving this world, to leave us in the hands of Mary: “Into these same maternal hands I leave everything and everyone with whom my life and my vocation have united me. Into these hands I leave above all the Church, as well as my nation and all humanity.” Through his intercession, may we too be worthy children of Mary and one day come to rest beside her heart. Deo gratias for the great gift of John Paul the Great!
