The religious example of St. John of the Cross

Feast of the Presentation of the Lord [Exordium] St. John Paul II used to say that although it is true that God has called each one of us individually, He has not called us to be alone, but to be part of a family. Today, on the feast of the Presentation of the Lord, we once again have the joy of celebrating the enormous and unmerited grace of being religious in a family which is our religious family of the Incarnate Word. This is where God has called us to work at stripping ourselves of all that is not God, in order to love Him and belong exclusively to Him 1 , according to a beautiful expression of St. John of the Cross in the Ascent of Mount Carmel quoted in our Constitutions. On this day and on this feast, I would like to propose for consideration some points of the great Mystical Doctor of Fontiveros on religious life, remembering that our Proper Law proposes to us the doctrine of St. John of the Cross as outstanding when it comes to forming “virtuous men” 2 . 1. St. John of the Cross, religious Of the total of 49 years that Friar John of the Cross lived (1542-1591), he was a religious for 28 years (at the age of many of us he had already completed his work and mission on this earth). Of those 28 years, he was a Discalced Carmelite for 23 3 , holding positions of authority in his Order for most of those years. While in Segovia, as Definitor General, he said something very interesting which perhaps many of us can repeat without the saint’s exaggeration; he said: “when I remember the foolish things I have done as a prelate [superior], my face turns red” 4 . Since he was there at the beginnings of the Carmelite Reform, it fell to him to build convents, to suffer the poverty of the beginnings, to revise the Constitutions , to carry out several foundations, to be superior and at the same time exercise many apostolates and study, to be present at the first Chapters –ordinary and extraordinary– of the Discalced, and to suffer in his own flesh the difficulties of his Order. With all the store of graces that this means. The Incarnate Word chose him as one of the “first stones,” and a very special first stone, since on “this stone” Our Lord planned to build the edifice of the Carmelite reform. That is why we must say that John of the Cross was not only a privileged recipient of the Teresian charism, but a great transmitter of it. What is more, he was an unequaled and enriching exponent of that same spirit which he received, going far beyond the letter of the rule, to the point that he was regarded by his subjects as an “example of all the virtues professed in the religious state” 5 . (What praise!) To look no further, another of the religious, speaking of his “rare and great” example, said that “the holy father lived with great perfection of life, and with the same great perfection life was lived in the convents that he had and had had in his charge” 6 . His secret lay in this: “the prelate ought to teach by deeds rather than by words” 7 . Because, as he himself wrote in the Flame : “As the master is, so will the disciple be, and as the father, so the son” 8 . So it was, then, that Friar John of the Cross resolved as very few have to put into practice that same counsel he gave to a religious: have “constancy in carrying out the things of your Religious Order and of obedience, without any human respect, but solely for God” 9 . 2. Some points on the understanding of religious life in St. John of the Cross How did St. John of the Cross understand religious consecration? I would like to point out some points from a study by Father Vicente Rodríguez, perhaps the greatest expert on the life and work of the Saint today, entitled “San Juan de la Cruz y su estilo de hacer comunidad” (St. John of the Cross and his style of building community). There are six, and they are the following. The essential thing that the saint always kept in mind can be found in a letter to one of the nuns of Beas, to whom he insistently says: “ you are not your own, but God’s ” 10 . That is, in the first place and succinctly, his idea: to be a religious is to belong completely to God. That is why further on in that same letter he makes it explicit: “God wants the religious to be a religious in such a way that he has finished with everything and that everything has finished for him ; because He himself is the one who wants to be his riches, consolation and delightful glory” 11 . A characteristic needed to achieve this essential aspect is constant determination . In his writings one often sees an insistence on this, as also happens in St. Teresa, and it is good to keep it in mind. We have come to religious life urged on –says the saint– “by holy desires and motives to leave the world and change our life or way, and serve God” 12 , “to walk imitating the model who is Christ” 13 . And for this there is required a “ perfect boldness and determination in works [which] few spiritual persons attain; because, although some engage in and practice this way of life, and some even consider themselves among those far along [that is, very advanced], they never quite lose themselves in certain points, either of the world or of nature, so as to do perfect and naked works for Christ , not looking at what people will say or how it will appear. […] They are still ashamed to confess Christ by their deeds before men; [and] having regard for things, they do not truly live in Christ” 14 . A particular characteristic of living his belonging to God is given by what some scholars of St. John of the Cross consider “the four means” for union with God. In the Counsels he gives to one who “would be a true religious and fulfill the state he has promised to God” 15 , St. John of the Cross recommends: resignation, mortification, the exercise of virtues, bodily and spiritual solitude ; as means “so that the heart may not be detained by any human thing” 16 . It is through the practice of these “four means” or “ways,” St. John of the Cross teaches, that the perfection of the religious state is attained, which is identified with true freedom, “the happy freedom desired by all” 17 , as he writes in his Dark Night . Love for his Institute and its rule . The same man who wrote to a religious: “In no way seek to know anything except only how you will better serve God and better keep the things of your institute” 18 , was the same who every Friday read the rule or had it read, fulfilling what his Constitutions commanded but going amply beyond it with the abundance and loftiness of the instructions he gave his religious. And so, what John of the Cross teaches in his books about the way of living and perfecting oneself in religious life, he himself embodied and encouraged from his post and activity as superior. Two great virtues stand out in the religious life of St. John of the Cross as the foundation on which he built charity, and these are: obedience and humility. – Devotion to obedience, which he recommends mainly in relation to the office entrusted, by way of examen. He taught that it is in the office given that the will of God is best manifested. With great vigor he instilled in his religious: “ Do not fail to do the office you have , and any other that obedience may command you, with all the solicitude possible and that may be necessary , but do it in such a way that no fault clings to you in it, because neither God nor obedience wants this” 19 . – Humility , he says, must be the present virtue, and on the other hand he also says it is the manly virtue. When his star began to decline at that Chapter of Valladolid in which he found himself caught up in cruel calumnies and was left without office and went off to the desert of La Peñuela, he wrote: “To go about losing and letting everyone get the better of us belongs to valiant spirits, to generous hearts” 20 , because “temporal lordship and freedom, before God, are neither kingdom nor freedom” 21 . Finally, one cannot live religious life well without possessing an authentic freedom of spirit . And so, although he demanded great fidelity to the rule, at the same time he never tied himself to the letter. There are many examples of this. His biographers recount that St. John of the Cross was more or less the soul of everything in his community, and it ran to the tune and rhythm of its superior. Nevertheless, even though he was very observant, the freedom of spirit of this man before what was prescribed is striking. Fr. Vicente gives an example concerning prayer in common. Gracián’s Constitutions said “prayer shall be in the choir with all together.” Some later Constitutions, approved even by John of the Cross himself, prescribe even the prayers that were to be said. Coming from St. John of the Cross, one would think that he would have observed them to the letter with exemplary scrupulousness. However, witnesses say that “he was seen solicitously seeking out secret places suitable for contemplation” 22 , and so for the prayer at the first hour of the night and for the morning prayer he would go outside the chapel, and sometimes he had his religious do the same in order to pray. In this way Friar John safeguards the prayer in common, but interprets broadly the matter of the place where it was to be made. Why? Because he warned that one must not be like those many who, “blinding themselves with the lowliness of the letter and not understanding its spirit and truth, took the life of their God and Lord” 23 . There are many examples like this in the life of the saint: for instance, he changed the prayer schedules so that he and his friars could hear more confessions; he got a reprimand from the provincial because, it was said, he did not visit lay people and it would be good for him to do so in order to obtain alms; he did it once and never went back, because he said he was wasting time and it was better for him to pray that God would provide what was necessary (and in fact it always was so); another time he was criticized because his friars ate meat; he did not care, because his subjects said they needed it and therefore it was just that he should believe them and give it to them; and so many other examples… [Peroratio] For our part, we must be persuaded of what our Directory of Spirituality says: that our consecration as religious “drives us to irresistible demands of sacrifice for love of Christ , which is at the same time an act of integral faith and total self-giving, with the formal decision not to make pacts, not to compromise, not to capitulate, not to negotiate, not to concede, nor to make deals with the spirit of the world” 24 . That is why, in spite of our miseries and sins and the irrefutable fact that the years go by and it seems that we fall ever shorter, we can ask Our Lord today to grant us the precious grace of being good religious, without being discouraged by our faults, miseries and inconstancies, convinced that God will grant it to us. Perhaps we can do so with that beautiful prayer composed by John of the Cross himself, which goes like this: Lord God, my beloved! If you still remember my sins so as not to do what I keep asking of you, do your will in them, my God, for that is what I most desire, and exercise your goodness and mercy and you will be known in them. And if you are waiting for my works in order to grant my request by that means, give them to me and work them in me, and the sufferings that you would accept, and let it be done. And if you are not waiting for my works, what are you waiting for, my most clement Lord? Why do you delay? For if, in the end, it is to be grace and mercy that I ask of you in your Son, take my little coin, since you want it, and give me this good, since you also want it. [ Who can free himself from lowly ways and limits if you do not lift him up to yourself in purity of love, my God? How will man, begotten and raised in lowliness, rise up to you, if you do not lift him up, Lord, with the hand that made him? ] You will not take from me, my God, what you once gave me in your only Son Jesus Christ, for in Him you gave me all that I desire. Therefore I will rejoice that you will not delay if I wait. Notes 1 Book 2, ch. 5, 7. Keeping our soul, ours

[Exordium] We are on the eve of the Solemnity of Mary, Mother of God, which is, on the one hand, the greatest title a human being could ever come to possess, and, on the other, the most fitting one with which we can honor the Blessed Virgin Mary, our mother. And it is providential to celebrate this feast during these days of Christmas, when we see in our nativity scenes the Mother wholly bent over to contemplate in her Son-God the marvelous mystery of the Incarnation. 1. The law of the Incarnation is a law of suffering Bishop Fulton Sheen liked to repeat that expression so typical of him: “all men are born to live, but Jesus, the Incarnate Word, is the only one who was born to die.” That was the principal business in which he was engaged from the day of his Birth. That was his goal. So much so that -as Fr. Faber beautifully says- “Calvary was not different from Bethlehem or Nazareth; it surpassed them in degree, but not in nature” 1 . That is why -Fr. Faber went on to say- the law of the Incarnation is a law of suffering . Our Lord was a man of sorrows from his Birth, and his Mother knew it… His Passion was not merely an event in his life but the end and the proper outcome befitting it 2 . That is why that tender, fragile and defenseless Child whom we contemplate today in Mary’s arms is the same one who will later tell us: Do not fear those who kill the body… fear rather him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna 3 . The whole life of the Incarnate Word was wrapped in those words. Words that, at bottom, reveal to us the supreme struggle of every life and also of every day: the struggle to persevere in the good, to preserve our spiritual freedom and with it our dignity. Today we come to the end of the year, with all the great graces we have received personally and as an Institute, and also with all the adversities and hardships that have befallen us, likewise personally and as an Institute. Why? Because that same law of the Incarnation “embraces us and surrounds us” –says Fr. Faber– until it conquers us absolutely or, if you prefer, in the words of St. John of the Cross: “until [we are] reduced to nothing” 4 , in such a way that we are not concerned about the esteem and good opinion of men, about little or much health and bodily strength, about the posts or offices that may be given to us or taken from us, about the prosperous or adverse events that may happen to us, about dying young or old 5 ; which “will be the supreme humility, [and] the spiritual union between the soul and God will be accomplished, which is the greatest and highest state that can be reached in this life” 6 . A path on which one advances only with the staff of the cross. That is why, in contemplating God made man 7 in the arms of his Most Sweet Mother on this last day of the year, when one ponders the prosperous and adverse events one has gone through and prepares to face –with the grace of God– another new year, it is fitting to think that we too must conquer that glory which the Incarnate Word has won for us, and that very probably, in order to attain that supreme freedom with the glorious Christ, we may have to suffer great hardships on this earth. “True freedom consists –said Fulton Sheen– in preserving our soul, ours ( keeping our soul, ours ), even if we have to lose the body, if necessary, in order to preserve it.” To each of us there frequently comes in life what Card. Newmann called “the supreme moment” of each day and of life; it is the moment of choosing between a temporal pleasure and eternal freedom. Choosing between following the “law of whim that guides many ignorant men who pride themselves on being shrewd” (as Don Quixote says) and in that way finding oneself ‘free’ of threats, or standing firm in one’s principles and convictions even to giving one’s life out of fidelity to the truth and to what we believe. 2. The sufferings of this life Let us notice that from the cradle the Incarnate Word subjected his tenderness and fragility to the harshness and discomforts of the manger; his infinite Wisdom and Majesty was surrounded by rough, poor men, held to be of no account; he surrendered his Omnipotence to the needs and hardships of a life made human; being Lord of the world, he had to flee before the malicious plans of Herod, who was seeking him to kill him. And so it was throughout his whole life, up to the supreme moment of his Passion and of Calvary, when the Incarnate Word submitted his Majesty to the supremacy of his enemies; he subjected his hands and his feet to the nails; he submitted his Body to the tomb; he let his good Name be subjugated to the mockery of his enemies; he let his Blood be poured out, making it captive to the lance; he allowed his comfort to be subjected to the plans of pain of his enemies; and his Life he handed over like a servant at their feet. But there is one thing he did not hand over, and that was his Soul; his Soul he kept free for himself. That he did not surrender, because he knew that if he preserved his freedom, he could recover everything he had already handed over into their hands. His enemies knew this, and up to the last moment they tried to make him surrender even his spirit by challenging his power: Come down from the cross and we will believe 8 . And the Incarnate Word did not do it. He refused to do the human thing in order to do the divine: and he remained on the cross. And by acting in that way, he preserved his soul for himself. One thing was untouchable in his life, and in reality in each of our lives: the soul. Our soul is the impregnable fortress of our character. And as long as we keep it ours, no one can snatch it from us, even if they snatch our life. “Freedom –teaches Fulton Sheen– is not the right to do whatever we feel like, but the right to do what we ought in order to attain the highest and noblest end of our nature, which is nothing other than the enjoyment of eternal happiness.” St. John of the Cross, when he saw his religious discouraged or weary of the struggle, would tell them: “Come now, sons, on to eternal life” 9 , for what is ours is “to go by the level road of the law of God and of the Church, and to live only in dark and true faith, and certain hope and entire charity, and to await our goods there , living here as pilgrims, poor, exiles, orphans, dry, without a road and without anything, awaiting everything there ” 10 . It is always very healthy for our souls to keep in mind what our true destiny is, the purpose of our life, the goal we pursue. With that in mind, we can tell whether or not we are advancing. Now, if because of adverse circumstances, because of the momentary pressure of the powerful, if because of seeking ourselves, preferring a more comfortable and pleasant existence, we constantly change our goal and give up the post God has entrusted to us, it would be nonsense to say that we are advancing, because we are going after the imperfections of our will. The Incarnate Word, our supreme Model, never lost sight of his goal, and precisely because he did not, he sacrificed everything else so as to be free and able to reach it. It is as happens on journeys: one gets rid of unnecessary things in order to travel more freely, more quickly. What is more: our Lord left everything, even his life. That is why we said at the beginning: the Incarnate Word was born to die. And so he did. From the sacrifice of his life in order to keep his spirit free, we must learn not to be intimidated by the sufferings, the trials and the great disappointments of this life. The temptation is always there that, forgetting our ideal, we concentrate not on saving our soul but on obtaining a ‘peaceful and comfortable life here on earth.’ Our Lord could have had all the angels and the whole created universe attend to his needs; he could simply have halted the course of the malicious plans of his persecutors… but that would have meant that the ideal of one day being seated at the right hand of his Father in his glory was secondary to immediate and temporal pleasure here on earth. And then the purpose of his life would have been less important than a moment of his life; then the freedom of his soul would have been secondary to the healing of his hands and his feet; then the noblest and most elevated part of himself –his soul– would have been the slave of the lowest and most corruptible part. And that is what we must avoid by every means. Because “what profit is there, and what is it worth before God, that which is not love of God? And this love is not perfect unless it is strong and discerning in purging joy from all things, placing it only in doing the will of God” 11 . God in his infinite mercy grants us another year precisely to save our soul and attain the glorious freedom of the children of God. The Crucifixion ended, but Christ remains. How many sorrows –trivial or quite profound– we have gone through in this year that ends today! But here we still are, by the grace of God, and perhaps even stronger than before. That is why we must never descend from the supreme ideal of our lives, which means the imitation of the Incarnate Word and the salvation of our souls. The temptation will always be strong, and temporal advantages will seem to us ever grander, ever more irresistible: we must be strong and remain masters of our soul. Without retreating a single step in our endeavor. Fulton Sheen asks: “Must wood submit to the fire so that we can draw with charcoal? Is death the condition of life? Is disciplined study the way to knowledge? Are long hours of tedious practice the road to performing good music? Must we lose our life in order to save it for eternity? Yes. The answer is yes.” Because the sufferings of this life are nothing compared with the eternal joys that await us 12 . Often, in the face of adversity, we find ourselves asking: why? Why does what happens to us happen? Or: how long? How is it possible? And things of that sort. And I have not found a more satisfying answer than the one St. John of the Cross puts in the mouth of God the Father in the Ascent of the Mount , where he says: “Fix your eyes on Him alone, because in Him I have spoken and revealed everything to you, and you will find in Him even more than what you ask and desire” 13 . And “if you wanted me to answer you with some word of consolation, look at my Son, subject to me and bound by my love, and afflicted , and you will see how many he answers you. […] Look at Him also made man and you will find in that more than you think, because in Christ dwells bodily all the fullness of the divinity ” 14 . And “He has been given to us as brother, companion and master, ransom and reward” 15 , with all the treasure of graces that each of these titles of Christ means for us. Have you stopped to think about that? We have been chosen as God’s trusted men, and He himself has placed us at the head of this, his Family. To bargain away his trust, his friendship, for an existence free of tensions, to assent to falsehoods merely to be free of pressures, would be to do him a great offense. God deliver us from such ‘freedoms.’ [Peroratio] Let us begin this new year contemplating God made man in the arms of his Mother, who is also our Mother. And let us give thanks to the Virgin, Queen and Mother of our Institute, for all the blessings (including the crosses) she has granted us during this year. And to Her, the Mother of God who keeps nothing for herself, let us entrust ourselves and the whole Family in this year that is now beginning. May Our Lady bless and protect you all. Easter Morning

Easter Morning 2019 Jn 20:1-9 [Exordium] Dear Brothers and Sisters in Christ, only once in the history of the world was a guard of soldiers posted before the tomb of a dead man. Only once in the annals of time has it been recorded that a stone was rolled in front of a sepulcher to keep a body from escaping, and that was on a Good Friday. And yet here, in all seriousness, after the Man has been struck in the face, crowned with thorns, scourged to the point that his flesh hung from Him like scarlet ribbons, [after they] made him carry a heavy beam (which had been carved by members of his own trade) and forced him to drag it through the streets of the city up a hill, and then he was hung on the wood with nails for three hours, pierced with a lance until blood and water came out, found dead and then buried under the stifling weight of a hundred pounds of aromatic spices; after all this, the chief priests and the Pharisees went to the Roman governor and asked him for authorization to seal the stone and post a guard . These precautions even seem humorous given the circumstances. Yet what deprives the scene of that note of foolishness is that his enemies were really afraid that He would rise. The request for a guard until “ the third day ” referred more to Christ’s words about his Resurrection than to the fear that the Apostles would steal the body and fake his ‘Resurrection.’ The enemies of Christ were expecting his Resurrection. The Pharisees called Christ an impostor , and yet they were afraid he was not one; they asked him to come down from the Cross and were half afraid that he actually would; they ridiculed his prophecy that he would rise on the third day, but they sealed the door of his tomb because they were afraid that he actually would rise; they laughed at Him mockingly when he said that no other sign would be given to that unbelieving generation but the sign of Jonah, and yet they asked that Roman soldiers guard the whale of the earth, lest it throw off its weight and leave him on the shores of eternity. [The enemies of Christ] were sure that he had been buried, and yet they were not sure that his life had been taken away; they were certain that He was in his tomb but uncertain that they could keep him there. What a strange mixture of belief and unbelief! They had nothing more to fear, but they were not going to take any chances; they had rid themselves of his Presence but feared that he might walk again; he was dead and yet he could live. This unusual mixture of skepticism and faith is serious proof that when men rebel against the Godhead, people experience that uncomfortable feeling that somehow God might still be in the world. They will always be certain that they have killed Christ, and yet they will guard his tomb. While they celebrate their sweeping victory, they still keep their eyes on their enemies, because when God is the enemy, men can never be sure that they have carried the day. Their fears were justified. The Resurrection was a fact. He said he would rise again. Resurrexit sicut dixit! But how? At the sound of trumpets? Walking with invisible steps that slipped past the Roman guard? No! At the point of the darkest shadow and in the deepest of silences they suddenly saw a figure , for an angel of the Lord came down from heaven, and approaching, rolled back the stone and sat upon it. His face shone like lightning, and his garment was white as snow. And for fear of him the guards trembled and became like dead men . (Mt 28:2-4) The soldiers would have been brave amid the turmoil of a battle, but when the angel appeared the guards trembled and became like dead men . (Mt 28:4). Then the angel, turning to the women, who were seeing all this better than brave soldiers, said to them: “Do not be afraid; I know that you are looking for Jesus, the Crucified. He is not here, for he has risen as he said. Come and see the place where he lay… Suddenly Jesus came to meet them and greeted them, saying: “Rejoice.” They came up to him and, clasping his feet, bowed down before him . (Mt 28:5-6;8-9) Since that first Good Friday, men must always fear that closed doors cannot shut in the Light of the world. Because when God is the enemy, men can never be sure that they have carried the day. Now we turn the lesson of Easter around: when man has lost his day, God returns to save him. Man lost his day in Eden when he succumbed to the temptation of Satan, and God promised him a redeemer to save him from sin. Man lost his day on a Good Friday when he crucified on the tree of ignominy the only truly Good thing ever to be seen on this earth, and God came back on an Easter day to save him from his own deceptions. It is a peculiar fact of history that man never seems to need God so much as when his own strength fails him; God does the most for us when, like Peter, we have worked through a whole long night and caught nothing. Our world is full of people who have lost the path; of souls whose sins have been psychoanalyzed many times but forgiven never; of bodies embittered by sorrow and never sweetened by the vision of the cross; of hearts that have chased after thousands of luxuries, only to be left completely disillusioned in the end; of poor people who think that riches will give them peace of mind; of desperate people who think a drink can make them forget. But for all these souls the message of Easter rings out: there is no reason to despair. The Resurrection was announced to Magdalene: a soul like ours. So not everything is lost. We need to realize that we have crucified the Only One who can save us. We need to discover, like the prodigal son, that there is no place like the Father’s house. We need to accept the grace of Christ’s Resurrection. This is the invitation of Easter: to live in the hope of the risen Christ! Peace awaits you in the service of the God who made you; Redemption awaits you in the Mass; Forgiveness calls you from the Confessional; Love [wants] you in the Eucharist. As Pope Francis reminded us: “Let us not flee from the Resurrection of Jesus; let us never declare ourselves dead, whatever happens.” ( Evangelii Gaudium , 3) Because that is the message of Easter day: the Resurrection of the Dead One, the Triumph of the Vanquished, the Finding of the Lost; the Rebirth of the Earth; the Awakening of Life; the Trumpet of the Resurrection is resounding over the land of the living. So, in conclusion, the thought I would leave you with is that no matter how hopeless things may seem, there is still hope, because Christ is the Resurrection and the Life. “No matter how dark things are, goodness rises up again and spreads,” said Pope Francis. He who can make snowflakes out of drops of dirty water, draw diamonds out of coal, and make saints out of Magdalenes, can also make you victorious if you confess Him, in his mystical life on earth, as the Christ, the Son of the Living God. May the joy of our faith in the Resurrection of the Lord be rekindled as a quiet but firm confidence, because the unchanging love of our Lord never ceases. Bring your hearts to complete salvation, because the great storms of the Redemption are flooding everything! Bring your lesser calvaries to the Great Calvary, because the via crucis is the via pacis. The way to peace is the cross. Take up your cross and follow me . Then, beneath the muffled thunder of battle, the victory cry of the King of kings and Lord of lords will sound, because when man has lost the day, God returns to give him the victory! [Peroratio] Dear Brothers and Sisters: on this Easter morning, each of us must pause before the empty tomb and meditate on the supreme miracle of the Resurrection of Christ. May the Blessed Virgin Mary, silent witness of this mystery, strengthen us in our personal adherence to Him who died and rose for us. May She be our teacher and our guide in faith; may She support us in moments of doubt and temptation; may She obtain for us that interior peace which no one can disturb, because it is rooted in the certainty that Christ has truly risen. On this beautiful Sunday morning, at the feet of our Blessed Mother, let us entrust our lives to the Mother of the Risen Christ, together with all our intentions and all our hopes. Let us ask her for the grace always to keep alive the hope and joy of this Easter morning, which reminds us that love has triumphed, that mercy has been victorious! Happy Easter to all!
Thomism is essential to our mission

[ Exordium ] 747 years ago, on the morning of Wednesday, March 7, 1274, St. Thomas Aquinas received extreme unction right here, in the Cistercian monastery of Fossanova. Since then the Saint of Aquino has been acclaimed by pontiffs, academics, religious and non-religious alike as the “Prince and Master of all the scholastic doctors” 1 , as the “model for teachers and model for students” 2 . For his doctrine has earned him the titles of “ Doctor Ecclesiae ” and “ Doctor Angelicus ” (both titles granted by St. Pius V); the title of “ Patronus caelestis studiorum optimorum ” (conferred by Pope Leo XIII), and he is the one whom the Church calls “ Doctor communis ” (Common Doctor). St. John Paul II more recently gave him the title of “ Doctor humanitatis ,” arguing that St. Thomas “was always ready to welcome the values of all cultures” 3 . And particularly today, when we are gathered as a Religious Family to honor our Holy Patron, I would like to speak of the importance of Thomistic doctrine when it comes to the evangelization of culture. 1. A non-negotiable element Many times, throughout the length and breadth of our Proper Law, we are exhorted to give the doctrine of St. Thomas a preferential place 4 , to be formed under his magisterium 5 in a profound way 6 , “to think starting from him, entering into dialogue and debate with contemporary problems and thinkers” 7 . And one may ask: why? To be formed according to the doctrine of St. Thomas is not mere devotion, although his virtues, the sublimity of his thought and the holiness of his life move us to devotion. Nor is it one option of ‘discipleship’ among so many others we might have chosen, although it is definitely a conscientious and very firm choice, for we have “the clear intention of following St. Thomas as the Church commands” 8 . Nor is it an accessory, temporary or decorative element simply ‘because it suits us well.’ The formation we give and receive, our way of doing apostolate, of living community life, and our spirituality are inherently and fully informed by Thomistic doctrine, which is −let us say it once again− “the doctrine most in conformity with the Magisterium of the Church” 9 and without which there can be no transformation of persons and therefore of cultures; much less can there be a perfecting of them 10 (so closely is St. Thomas bound to our charism). That is, we cannot fulfill the specific end for which God has raised up our little Religious Family in the Church, which is precisely: “to inculturate the Gospel in every man, in the whole man and in all the manifestations of man, in accordance with the teachings of the Magisterium of the Church” 11 , without being steeped in the philosophy of being 12 . For is not culture a specific mode of man’s ‘existing’ and ‘being’? Put in a few words, one cannot be a member of the Institute of the Incarnate Word and have as one’s charism “to make Jesus Christ Lord of all that is authentically human” 13 and of every “legitimate manifestation of human life” 14 in the strictest fidelity to the Magisterium of the Church 15 without embracing the “golden wisdom of St. Thomas” 16 . Precisely because of that “openness to the whole of reality in all its parts and dimensions, without reductions or particularisms (without absolutizing a particular aspect), as the intellect demands in the name of objective and integral truth concerning reality. This openness is also a significant distinguishing mark of the Christian faith, of which catholicity is the specific sign. This openness has its foundation and its source in the fact that the philosophy of St. Thomas is a philosophy of being, that is, of the ‘ actus essendi ,’ whose transcendental value is the most direct path for rising to the knowledge of subsistent Being and pure Act, which is God” 17 . That is why it is entirely logical that following Thomistic philosophy should be for us one of the non-negotiable elements attached to the charism, and that it should be for us a most vivid sign of fidelity to the truth and of fidelity to the voice of the Church (and of apostolic fruitfulness). That is why I believe it can be said with all rigor that anything that attempts to set aside, diminish, dilute or render “wavering and superficial” our Thomistic philosophical formation is nothing other than a departure from the charism, a betrayal of the truth and ultimately of the Church and of the cause of Christ. And it is important that every member of the Institute keep this very much in mind, whatever his mission, whether he is in formation, holds an office of government, or is a contemplative: We are Thomists because we belong to the Incarnate Word and devote ourselves to the evangelization of culture, and without the realism and objectivity of Thomistic philosophy our efforts are in vain, ineffective, or rather, they become paralyzed. 2. Genus humanum arte et ratione vivit 18 In this regard, I would like to point out the following: “St. Thomas, commenting on Aristotle, says that ‘the human race lives by its art and its reason’” 19 (I am quoting our Directory of Evangelization of Culture word for word). “Relying on these words, St. John Paul II affirmed that culture is a ‘characteristic of human life as such’ 20 ; ‘it is a specific mode of man’s ‘existing’ and ‘being’’; man alone –because he transcends matter by virtue of the life of his spirit– ‘is the only ontic subject of culture’ and is ‘also its only object and its end.’ That is, culture is of man, by man and for man. It embraces the whole activity of man, his intelligence and affectivity, his search for meaning, his customs and his ethical resources. Culture is so connatural to man that his nature does not attain its full expression except through culture. Therefore, ‘culture is that through which man, as man, becomes more human, ‘is’ more, has more access to ‘being’’” 21 . “Hence the irreplaceable importance of establishing the true foundations so as to be able, starting from them, to discern which manifestations of man are truly culture and which manifestations are not” 22 . This can only be achieved from a philosophy of being, which is what will allow man to find his true foundation , which is being, to find his ultimate end , which is Being by Essence, and also to find his depth , which is freedom. Thus he can discover the true cultural values. Because, in the final analysis, all cultural values –of science, of art, of laws and customs, etc.– as objective expressions of beauty, truth and goodness, are grounded in the act of being 23 . That is why we must realize that each one of us, and those who will come after us, will only be able to “offer a positive and effective response to the great challenges or even tragedies of ‘postmodern’ man principally starting from the metaphysical level, through the philosophy of being 24 . You know well that the great cultural challenge of today lies in the sphere of man’s openness to truth and to the good, and ultimately to transcendence and to the mystery of God. That is why the central point of every culture is occupied by the attitude man takes before the mystery of God 25 . [ Peroration ] That is why let no one who devotes himself to the evangelization of culture say ‘St. Thomas is not for me,” since Thomism is an integral part of our vocation; it is the bulwark that defends us from the errors that swarm in our society; it is the proof that we keep intact the spirit in which we were conceived and the best guarantee of our fidelity to the Church, Teacher of Truth. By vocation and by the mission we have received, it falls to us to have a strong cultural formation, one that takes a stand before modern culture 26 , a “metaphysics with grip,” that bites into reality. Today, in one of the rooms of this very abbey, more than seven centuries ago, the earthly existence of the one who was called “Luminary of the Church and of the whole world” 27 came to an end. Nevertheless it is necessary, and I would say urgent, “to propose anew the thought of the Angelic Doctor in order to recover a use of philosophy in keeping with the demands of faith” 28 , to “develop that part of Thomistic doctrine which deals with humanity, since his affirmations about the dignity of the human person and about the use of his reason, perfectly in accord with faith, make St. Thomas a supreme master for our time” 29 . Let us hold high the torch of the light of the Sun of Aquino 30 , who illumined the Church of God more than any other doctor 31 , and “let us illumine the darkness of the world like suns” 32 . May the words that were written long ago on the walls of this “cell” remind us of our “mission” in this place Occidit hic Thomas lux ut foret amplior Orbi et candelabru sic nova fossa foret Here Thomas died so as to become [from this place] the most splendid light of the world so that Fossanova might be the lampstand that holds up that light Editus ardeti locus et non fossa lucerna, hac igitur fossam quis neget esse novam? This place has been exalted so that this light may shine and not be hidden, so that who could deny that this pit is truly new? Almost fifty years ago the seventh centenary of the death of St. Thomas Aquinas was celebrated, and Pope St. Paul VI decided to visit the Thomistic sites; he wanted to make a personal pilgrimage but could not, because many people from the area came to meet him at the various places. He left by helicopter very early, from the summer residence of Castel Gandolfo, on September 14, 1974, and the first place where he stopped was here in Fossanova (there should be a plaque around here recalling where the Holy Father landed). He arrived here in the morning, celebrated Holy Mass (in the afternoon he would go by car to Aquino, where he would also celebrate Mass) and delivered a brief but heartfelt homily. There, among many very beautiful things, he said these words: “[In a place like this we cannot avoid] asking ourselves: why are we here?… Certainly it is not only to perform a gesture of religious veneration, as if, before the appearance of the Saint on the screen of our conscience, we did not bow, trembling and happy, before his great and hieratic figure. Rather, his figure, made present and alive by the communion of Saints, immediately provokes in us a bold question: Master Thomas, what lesson can you give us [today]? To us , in this brief and intense moment that is the present; to us , who are seven centuries removed from your school; to us , who are galvanized by modern culture; to us , who are proud of our scientific knowledge; to us , distracted by ‘the fascination of frivolity,’ the fascinatio nugacitatis ,of which the book of Wisdom speaks ( Wis 4:12). A fascination we experience today, giving prevalence to sense knowledge over intellectual and spiritual knowledge; a dizzying fascination or dizzying spell; to us , subjected to the anesthesia of antireligious secularism; to us , St. Thomas, before whom your figure grows greater, as philosopher and as theologian, on the horizon of a thought eager for certainty, for clarity, for depth, for reality; to us [Thomas], even if with only one word, what can you say?” And the holy Pope continues: “St. Thomas does not answer us now with words, although there are many that nevertheless come to our ears at this moment through his works. He answers us [nevertheless] with the reflection of his figure and of his teaching, from which we seem to hear a lesson that exhorts us [… that cries out]: faith… confidence…confidence,in the truth of Catholic religious thought, as it was defended, expounded and opened to the cognitive capacity of the human mind by him [himself, by St. Thomas Aquinas]” 33 . To these words follows, and to this is dedicated, the whole rest of the homily: to the confidence we must have in Thomism. There he says very beautiful words, of which I mention only a few: faith and confidence in St. Thomas: Because “his work stands attested in the history of thought, both philosophical and theological, as a synthesis of what other eminent masters before him studied and left as an inheritance to universal culture”; Because “he assimilated the treasure of the most significant knowledge of his time (a time incomparable for the breadth and acuteness of its speculative study); [because he not only assimilated it, but] he refined it with the most rigorous intellectualism, the Aristotelian… so as to bring it into harmony with our rigorous modern scientific mentality”; Because this thought, his thought, “he submitted without prejudice to the dialectical discussion of an honest and rigorous rationality”; and “therefore he opened it to every possible progressive acquisition, should it ever be called for by the discovery of a further truth.” Because his thought “helps us to resolve the conflict, so loudly proclaimed and radicalized in our time, between the two forms of knowledge available to the mind of the believer, faith and reason ( fides et ratio )”; Because he resolved everything “taking as his starting point the revealed word of God, sustained by reasonable motives of credibility, committing the human mind to study it with its own proper and original principles and methods, in such a way that the resulting theology may, without presumption and without superstition, reach a true and marvelous level of vera scientia Dei .” Faith, because St. Thomas is for us “one of the most authoritative and convincing witnesses to the providential existence of that magisterium, entrusted by Christ to His Church, which does not exclude the paths of knowledge, but opens them, rectifies them and defends them” [and which does not withhold the light of life-giving Truth for those initiated into the labors, the ascents and the acrobatics of thought, but offers it with humble and sublime catechesis to all those in the Church herself who recognize themselves as disciples, and reserves the revelation of the highest and most saving mysteries of the faith to the little ones, to the simple, to the poor, to the People unversed in difficult speculations, but docile and open to the ineffable dialogue of the Word of God]” 34 . It is this faith and this confidence in St. Thomas that we ask in this Holy Mass of our Lord (whom St. Thomas loved so much) through the intercession of the Blessed Virgin (whom he also loved greatly), Mother of the Incarnate Word, and through the intercession of the Angelic Doctor himself. St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort

[ Exordium ] «The Cross of Jesus and the Mother of Jesus were the two poles of his life and of his ministry. And that is why his life, so brief in itself, was at the same time so full. And that is the reason why his ministry, which covered only the Vendée, Poitou and Brittany and lasted barely twelve short years, has outlived him by more than two centuries and has spread through many countries. And that is because Divine Wisdom, that Wisdom to whose guidance he had entrusted himself, made all his labors fruitful and crowned all his activities, which were only apparently interrupted by death. The work was entirely God’s work, but it bears the seal of the one who was His faithful collaborator.» With these words Pope Pius XII spoke of St. Louis Marie in an address to the faithful on the day after he canonized him, July 20, 1947. As we well know, from the very beginning our way of living religious life included the «fourth vow of Marian slavery according to St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort,» as our Constitutions expressly state in number 17. What is more, he is the first saint named in the Constitutions 1 . It may also serve as a fact that his name is explicitly mentioned 4 times in the text of the Constitutions and 2 times in the Directory of Spirituality . His works are quoted some 12 times in those two very important documents of our Proper Law, but they are also quoted in another 6 directories 2 (at least). Even more, the only book by a saint that our Proper Law recommends must be read is precisely the Circular Letter to the Friends of the Cross 3 , written in his own hand by our beloved St. Louis Marie. I say this so as to give a sense of the importance of the celebration of this great Saint and of the significance his doctrine and his figure have for us. St. Louis Marie, said Pius XII in the homily of his canonization, «showed the world the true mettle of a priest of Christ… his life was short, but it was an incredibly active life, rich in (apostolic) fruits, despite being singularly turbulent.» That is why I wanted to take advantage of this sermon to highlight three great loves of St. Louis Marie which were –in my view– the driving forces of that magnificent work that God was pleased to accomplish through him: love of the Cross, love of the Blessed Virgin and love for the missions. 1. Love of the Cross During his life he not only experienced the Cross himself –such as his family’s financial difficulties in his childhood, his choleric temperament and his tendency to violence, which cost him so much to overcome, the difficult apprenticeship of common life in the seminary of Saint-Sulpice, the great difficulties he suffered in the various apostolates he undertook, the misunderstanding of his superiors, bishops, brother priests…– but it was also the doctrine he preached, because he understood that this was the doctrine of Christ. At every popular mission he preached he appeared holding a cross, and at the end of the mission he planted a cross. The Calvary of Pontchâteau, the Cross of Poitiers with the inscription «love of the Cross. Desire for crosses. Contempt. Sorrows. Outrages. Insults…», the Circular Letter to the Friends of the Cross itself: all this bears silent but eloquent witness to St. Louis Marie’s love of the Cross. During his life the Cross stretched out before him, tracing his path and giving an unsuspected dimension and extent to his struggles. Thus, for example, in one of his letters he writes to Sister Catherine of St. Bernard: «If you knew my crosses and humiliations in detail, I doubt you would be so eager to see me. In fact, I cannot arrive anywhere without making my best friends sharers in my cross, often in spite of me and in spite of themselves. (For) Anyone who defends me or declares himself in my favor has to suffer for it» 4 . And to this same nun he says in another letter: «your battles take place within yourself and are not seen outside your community. Mine, on the other hand, explode all over France» 5 . Love of the Cross and love of Incarnate Wisdom are one and the same, and that is why St. Louis Marie could not preach the one while leaving out the other. In that precious work, The Love of Eternal Wisdom , he wrote: «Incarnate Wisdom loved the Cross from His tenderest years… As soon as He entered the world, He received it from the hands of the Father in the womb of Mary. He placed it in His heart as sovereign… He espoused it with ineffable love in the Incarnation. He sought it and carried it with unspeakable joy throughout His whole life, which was a continual Cross, and, after having made so many efforts to reach it, He died on it on Calvary… (But) Let us not think that, after His death, Wisdom detached Himself from the Cross or rejected it in order to triumph better. Quite the contrary! He has united Himself and, as it were, incorporated Himself with it, in such a way that neither angel, nor man, nor any creature of heaven or earth can separate Him from the Cross. Their bond is indissoluble , and their covenant eternal . (Then he lets out that irrepressible cry from the depths of his soul): Never the Cross without Jesus, nor Jesus without the Cross !» 6 , a phrase which, as you know, our Directory of Spirituality makes its own 7 . That Cross, with Jesus Crucified upon it, was the driving force of his life. «I am espoused to Wisdom and to the Cross,» he writes to his mother 8 , «they are all my treasures, temporal and eternal, earthly and heavenly.» That is why the words he wrote in a letter to Sister Catherine take on such force here, so much so that it seems he is saying them to us today too: «Courage! … Carry your Cross well wherever you are. I will try to carry mine well with the help of divine grace. You and I, without lamenting or complaining, without grumbling or throwing the Cross far away, without making excuses or crying like children» 9 . 2. Love of the Blessed Virgin The second great love of the Saint, and the secret of his apostolic drive to win souls for Jesus Christ, was without doubt devotion to Mary Most Holy. Convinced that «it was through the Most Holy Virgin Mary that Jesus Christ came into the world, and it is also through Her that He must reign in the world» 10 , he wrote the Treatise on True Devotion to Mary , proposing to all the total consecration to Jesus through Mary, in the condition of a total slave of Mary, as a most effective means of attaining holiness, following in the footsteps of Jesus Christ, who subjected Himself completely to her when He became incarnate in her womb. Even more, St. Louis Marie understood devotion to Our Lady «as the best means and the most marvelous secret for acquiring and preserving divine Wisdom» 11 . He himself explains it when he writes: «Mary is the mold in which not a single feature of the divinity is lacking. Whoever casts himself into it and lets himself be molded will receive all the features of Jesus Christ, true God» 12 . And he adds: «Mary is a holy place. She is the Holy of holies, where saints are formed and molded» 13 . Into that same mold the holy missionary abandoned himself, making filial devotion to Our Lady the spring of living water that made all his activity fruitful and the reason for all his confidence. To that same filial abandonment in the lap of Mary Most Holy he invited all the faithful. The devotion to the Mother of God which he sets out so masterfully in his Treatise on True Devotion contains, the Saint says, «what for so many years he has taught in his missions, publicly and privately, with no little fruit» 14 . As for us, members of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, our rule exhorts us «to be apostles of Mary, giving ourselves to Her in the maternal slavery of love and doing everything “through Mary, with Mary, in Mary and for Mary”» 15 . And, of course, as apostles we too must pass through our nights –St. Louis Marie knows this well– and that is why he says with great realism: «it will be necessary to pass through dark nights , strange battles and agonies, steep mountains, sharp thorns and frightful deserts. But by the way of Mary one advances more gently and peacefully.» And he adds one of the phrases that, for me, is among the most consoling: « In Mary there is no night » 16 , because in Her there is no sin. And if a person wants to be devout and to live piously in Jesus Christ 17 and, consequently, to suffer persecution and carry his Cross every day (as we say we want to), he will never carry great crosses, or will not carry them joyfully and to the end, unless he professes a tender devotion to the Blessed Virgin, who is the sweetness of crosses » 18 . 3. Love for the missions And since whoever loves Jesus and Mary cannot remain passive, we can affirm that the third great love, which allowed him to channel those two great loves and was the propagator of St. Louis Marie’s magnificent work of evangelization, was the missions. Truly, this «wayfarer of the Gospel,» said John Paul II, «inflamed with love for Jesus and His holy Mother, knew how to reach the crowds and make them love Christ the Redeemer contemplated on the Cross» 19 , devoting himself with great zeal to preaching popular missions. And although «his works (ended) in apparent failure,» «he was a missionary of extraordinary radiance» 20 . St. Louis Marie preached missions in at least 27 towns in France; he was chaplain of the General Hospital of Poitiers, although he was later expelled from that diocese; he then offered himself for the service of another hospital, but he was dismissed from there too, and went to live in a ‘hovel’ (in fact under a staircase) on the rue du Pot-de-Fer; he founded the Congregation of the Daughters of Wisdom for the work of free schools, organized pilgrimages, founded the Company of Mary, was the author of several books, and practically at all times preached missions. This very town witnessed the last mission the Saint preached. That is why today we also celebrate the wonderful missionary example St. Louis Marie has given us. For we too have been called to undertake with «courageous faith and to bring to completion, without wavering, great things for God and for the salvation of souls» 21 . [ Peroration ] Consequently, we can say that the priestly ideal St. Louis Marie proposed to the world can be deduced from what he himself asked of the Incarnate Word in his Fervent Prayer for Missionaries , for he himself personified what he asked for there. And this is the grace we ask of him today for us priests who are here and for all the priests of the Institute: «priests free with the freedom [of Christ], detached from everything,» «slaves of His love and of His will» […] «with the staff of the Cross and the sling of the rosary in their hands,» «men always available,» «true children of Mary,» «true servants of the Blessed Virgin, who […] go everywhere with the burning torch of the holy Gospel in their mouths and the holy Rosary in their hands […] and who, by means of a true devotion to Mary […] crush, wherever they go, the head of the ancient serpent,» «priests wholly of fire» 22 . And united to St. Louis Marie, in this very significant celebration, let us make our own his fervent prayer to the Incarnate Word and say: «Remember your Congregation!» 23 ; «It is time to fulfill your promises!» 24 ; «so that we may form, under the standard of the Cross, an army with banners unfurled and well ordered, to attack the enemies of God in concert» 25 ; «who may guard your house, defend your glory and save your souls, so that there may be only one flock and one shepherd» 26 . We ask this of him in this Holy Mass. Homily for 25 years of presence in Tajikistan

25th anniversary of the Missio Sui Iuris in Tajikistan Dan 7:9-10.13-14 or Rev 12:7-12a / Ps 137:1-5 / Jn 1:47-51 I thank you, Lord, with all my heart; I will sing to you in the presence of the angels. I will bow down before your holy Temple. I will give thanks to your Name for your love and your faithfulness, for your promise has surpassed your renown . The words of the psalm we have heard today turn out to be providential for the occasion that brings us together, for the psalmist expresses our need to give glory to God and to burst into thanksgiving for the 25th anniversary of the creation of the missio sui iuris here in Tajikistan. An event that has remained indelibly linked to the history of our Institute. When St. John Paul II referred to the missio sui iuris , he said that a great hope had been kindled 1 and that this constituted “the beginning of a promising era of evangelization ” 2 . And truly, at the end of these first 25 years, we can see how the enormous labor of the missionaries of the Incarnate Word and of the religious sisters, who have done missionary work without letting themselves be overcome by obstacles −the difficulty of the language, the lack of resources, the small number of priests in the face of the many needs of the mission− has borne abundant fruit for the Catholic Church in this beloved country. Thus we see today a community fervent in faith and in love for Our Lady, children and young people fond of their parish, the inestimable gift of having the first priests born in this blessed nation (a grace for which we will never be grateful enough), the grace of having two parishes: one here in Dushanbe and another in Bokhtar; today we have the presence of religious sisters who, with a spirit of authentic ecclesial solidarity, have left their homeland to do missionary work in these lands, and for some time now we have also had a contemplative monastery that implores God’s help day and night for all the souls in the missio sui iuris . Truly, I believe we can say without fear of being mistaken that upon the sufferings, upon the prayers and arduous labors of the Tajik Christians and of their missionaries −those who are here now and those who are no longer here− this mission rises, in which the new life of the Christian community has flourished. That is why we say again with the psalmist: I thank you, Lord, with all my heart… your promise has surpassed your renown. 1. To the Tajik Catholic faithful I would now like to speak especially to you, the lay faithful. As you well know, this anniversary we celebrate today was preceded by many years of harsh pressure and great crosses during the years of the regime. How many Christians of those days would have wanted to see what you see today: a church with several priests, with religious sisters, with children and young people who receive the sacraments… and yet they did not see it. That is why this feast teaches all of us to trust a little more each day in divine Providence, which never abandons us, above all in the hour of trial. The faithfulness and mercy of God that we sang in the psalm are the foundation of all our trust and of all hope. This feast also speaks to us of the great power of the prayer of the humble, which ‘wrests’, we might say, the greatest gifts from the Heart of Christ. And God, for whom all things are easy because He is almighty, uses His power for mercy 3 and draws from the most difficult situations, and from great evils, great blessings, like this one we are celebrating today. Let us be certain that, however heavy and stormy the trials we must face may be, we will never be abandoned to ourselves, we will never fall out of the hands of the Lord, the hands that created us and that now continue to sustain us on the road of life. That is why, while I congratulate you for your daily faithfulness in keeping the flame of faith alive within your families, I invite you also to be bearers of that hope of which John Paul II spoke. This means being responsible for ensuring that this magnificent gift is not lost, but that the flame of faith remains lit and spreads to many more souls. And so that the flame of faith does not go out, you must feed it with good catechetical formation, with the prayerful reading of the Bible, with the reception of the sacraments. That will help you to persevere in bearing witness to Christ, to forgive offenses, to be generous in the service of God and neighbor, and in this way you will be collaborating effectively in the service of the new evangelization. Know that you are the hidden pillars of the Church, to whom Jesus Himself addresses words of consolation: You will be blessed in the kingdom of heaven 4 . I also see several young people and children here. Some years ago Fr. Orzu and Fr. Maxim were also sitting on that side. And now they are missionary priests, because they knew how to listen to the voice of Christ and they realized that He needed them to pass on to other kids the joy and peace they experienced when they were here in the parish. And it may be that today, too, God is looking among you for someone who wants to be generous and enthusiastic in drawing others to Him. My message for you, dear young people, is this: Trust in Christ! He will not disappoint your hopes or your plans; on the contrary, He will fill them with meaning and joy. Talk with Christ. Ask Him what He wants for you, especially when you receive Him in Communion or come to the church at some other time. But do not fail to do it. 2. To the missionaries of the IVE Now, if you will allow me, I would like to address the missionaries, especially the priests. Without any doubt this celebration could not be a reality without the generous commitment of all the missionary priests who have passed through this mission and who are in this mission. That is why, first of all, I want −in the name of the whole Institute− to thank you and congratulate you, because you represent here today all the missionaries who, with great joy, but also with crosses and sacrifices, strove not only to begin the mission but also to persevere in the effort undertaken. Some of you have already been many years in this mission, which is the same as saying that for many years you have had the privilege of serving the Church of Christ in Tajikistan, and you have seen it grow. Following Christ’s mandate, some have come from very far away, and little by little they have courageously faced the challenges of a mission that was just beginning and of a culture different from their own, and they have been cultivating the precious fruits that today we have the joy of celebrating. My message is this: always look to Christ, our sure hope, and serve Him “with the fervor and enthusiasm of the saints” 5 , as is proper to the members of the Institute. The Tajik people need you, because they need God, who is the fundamental reason for our lives. Therefore, be magnanimous and creative in launching apostolic initiatives that bring Christ and the Most Blessed Virgin to as many souls as possible. May this anniversary not mean simply a goal reached, the finishing point, but on the contrary, may it be simply the beginning of that new era of evangelization announced by John Paul the Great. I want to thank most especially Fr. Pedro López, superior of the missio , for his meritorious and acknowledged pastoral work, as well as all the priests present here for the service they render to Christ in the children and young people, in the sick and in families. It only remains for me to entrust you to the intercession of Our Lady of Luján, who definitely is the Star of evangelization in this nation, and no one has done as much as she for the evangelization of the culture 6 of the Tajik people. Into her motherly hands I place the constant work of the missionaries, their expectations and plans, so that she may guide them and sustain them in their daily apostolic effort. May they be encouraged by the example and intercession of St. John Paul II himself, who showed so much zeal and affection for the people of Tajikistan. In short, may this be a day of full celebration. For truly the Lord has done great things for us . Notes 1 Cf. Ecclesia in Asia , 9. 2 Meeting with the ordinaries of Central Asia (23/9/2001). 3 Cf.
