Mt 5:10. 5 Directory of Missions Ad Gentes , 143. 6 Cf. Directory of Spirituality , 308.
Teacher of humanity

[Exordium] Good afternoon, everyone! Thank you very much for the invitation to visit the school and to celebrate this holy Mass with all of you on this very special day. Who knows which saint we are celebrating today? Yes, excellent! St. Thomas Aquinas, an Italian saint, and truly a giant for the whole Church. Some time ago I visited the tomb of this great saint and doctor of the Church in Toulouse, in the church of the Jacobins. There, on a side altar, in a golden urn, are the mortal remains of this hero. I spent a good while praying at the foot of the tomb of St. Thomas, thanking him for having guided me since I was a kid. For when I was about 14 years old and in secondary school, like several of you here, I had the privilege of hearing from a priest the arguments that prove the existence of God, which St. Thomas had formulated in the 13th century. I don’t quite know why, but listening to those very rational proofs of the existence of God, something like a fire was kindled within me. They made me grasp the reality of God much better, and in some way that was where my desire to serve God, to order my life radically toward Him, was awakened. While I was praying at the tomb of this great “teacher of humanity” –as St. John Paul II called him– I was thinking about the importance St. Thomas Aquinas has for our time. And you might ask yourselves: what can a 13th-century Dominican teacher teach us? Several things… Truth comes from God First, Thomas Aquinas saw with total clarity that, since truth comes from God, there can never be a conflict between the information the sciences give us and the facts of revelation, that is, with what the Bible says. In St. Thomas’s time there were some defenders of the “double truth theory”, who said that ‘the truths’ of philosophy and science were in one category and ‘the truths’ of faith were in another. Therefore, according to this interpretation, one could hold two completely opposite truths as long as one was aware that they were two positions located in different compartments of the mind. According to this theory, one could say that God created man male and female and at the same time accept that there are more genders of persons, or even that they have no gender at all. Well, St. Thomas realized that this theory did not make much sense and that there cannot be two opposite truths about the same question, and he said so. The apparent conflict between science and religion (to use current terms) arises either from bad science or from bad religion, and it should motivate us to think more deeply. Consequently, we must not be afraid to approach the sciences: physics, mathematics, chemistry, biology, etc.; everything that is learned in the sciences should lead us to the contemplation of God’s work in the world. On the other hand, this thinking more deeply does not mean that each one must develop an autonomous vision of himself or of the world, different from that of others, where each one has his ‘own truth’, which is what unfortunately often happens, and then we hear people say: ‘that is your truth, I have mine’, and everything is called into question. And the worst thing is that these people think that by stating ‘ their truth’ they are authentic, when in reality they repeat ad nauseam what they have read on social media or seen on YouTube, or what has gone viral on TikTok, which has nothing original about it and is not necessarily true. The only final and satisfactory explanation for the existence of things Second , St. Thomas knew that the Creator God of the Bible is the only final and satisfactory explanation for the existence of the created things of this world; he called them ‘contingent things’. He was struck by the existence of all those things that do not have their reason for being in themselves. Clouds, trees, plants, animals, human beings, buildings like this one, the benches where you are sitting, planets, stars certainly exist, but they do not have to exist necessarily. This means that the being of these things can only be explained by the fact that there is a higher reality that gives them being. That Supreme Being is what St. Thomas called God. How important this is in the times we live in! You know that there are people who do not believe in God; they are called atheists, and they think that believing in God prevents people from acquiring scientific knowledge. In fact, some have gone so far as to say that God does not exist because He cannot be found in the material world, because, according to atheists, the material world is the only thing that exists. So they think that God is like a superstition, and in fact they ridicule people who are believers. And they live as if there were no life after death. The truth is that God is the reason why there is something rather than nothing, why there are rivers, animals, angels, mountains… everything. It was St. Thomas who, in his demonstration of the existence of God by the five ways, said that God is the first cause of everything that exists, and His creation is full of secondary causes that work every day; for example, the law of gravity, which keeps us from floating in space. God is the first cause and gravity is a secondary cause, which God designed for the order and stability of the universe. However, some atheist scientists say that the autonomy of nature (that plants grow by themselves in the forest, for example) implies that God does not have all power; moreover, it implies that God does not exist, they say. But that is not true. God does not cancel the activity of His creatures, but lets them act according to their nature and thus fulfill the end for which He created them. So the next time someone tries to make you fall into the trap of believing that God does not exist, you can use the wisdom of St. Thomas to defend our faith, which teaches that God is the first cause of all things, sustains them in their being, but at the same time transcends them. The destiny of the human being is God Third , St. Thomas Aquinas was profoundly humanistic. What does this mean? It means that, since God became man in Jesus, the destiny of the human being is union with God, that is, to share in the divine life of God. No other religion or philosophy or sociological theory has upheld so lofty and so worthy a goal for man. That is why, says the Master of Aquino, there is something inviolable about the human person. How important this teaching is when euthanasia is practiced (now, I don’t know if you knew this, but with a 3-D printer they have created a machine made to measure for the person, in which one lies down, presses a button and it kills you… and so one chooses the day and hour of one’s death, free of pain; that is something terrible, very contrary to our faith: life is sacred and God is the owner of life). In how many places, for example, what is called a ‘preventive war’ is practiced, which means that a country is attacked because it is believed that a military conflict, although not imminent, is inevitable and that delaying the attack would be a great risk. It is like killing for the sake of killing, just in case! And so a great many people die, many children are left orphans with no schools to go to, with nothing to eat… Our faith teaches us that life is sacred. [Peroration] You have the grace and the privilege of coming to this school, of having families who love you and care about you, the grace of being Christians, of getting up each day and making the sign of the cross on your foreheads, the grace of receiving a careful Christian education, of coming to Mass; that is why you must make the most of these years, this time of formation. The bones of St. Thomas are in that golden casket in Toulouse I told you about, but his mind and his spirit must inform the life of each one of you, so that you may be the voice the Church needs in the world. The patron of this school, Blessed Pier Giorgio Frassati, was very well aware of the tremendous importance of truth firmly supported by faith; that is why he said: “to live without faith, without a heritage to defend, without the continual struggle for the Truth, is not to live but merely to exist”. May the Virgin Mary, Seat of Wisdom, grant to all the students of this school, to all their teachers, volunteers, religious and the families of these children the grace to raise with firmness the banner of the Truth of the Incarnate Word, the courage to defend the sacredness of life, and the eloquence of the saint we celebrate today to proclaim with conviction the existence of our Lord and Creator. We ask for that grace now in the Mass.
The death of our father

Homily preached on May 30, 2023, at La Finca on the occasion of the burial of Fr. Buela [Exordium] Dear brothers and sisters, just as one day missionaries set out from San Rafael to the whole world to conquer souls for the kingdom of Christ, so today, from the four corners of the earth, those missionaries return, and many others come for the first time, to pay tribute to their father… to our beloved father and founder, Fr. Carlos Miguel Buela. In just a few hours, this soil of San Rafael will keep forever in its bosom the mortal remains of one who, like a seed cast into the furrow, knew how “to die to himself in everything so that his children might live” 1 . The death of a father –at least naturally speaking– leaves us all with a great sense of loss. But we grieve with hope; with the firm conviction that He who wept at the death of His friend Lazarus is the one who said: those who are like Me in suffering and contempt will also be like Me in glory 2 ; yes, you will have sorrows and labors in preaching My law, in doing all that I have commanded you, because great temptations and persecutions will rise up against you, but all this will be for you an occasion of great joy, which will make you forget all your past sorrows and sadness . And we know that the promises of the Lord are true and that God is not mocked. Joy and hope What is more, on this occasion, as you will already have seen during the funeral in Genoa and as we have experienced these days here in San Rafael, the joy is also irrepressible, and this allows us to verify, even in a tangible way, that the “surprising fruit of sufferings for the cause of the Lord is joy, in perfect harmony with the beatitudes” 3 , as the father wrote in “ El Señor es mi pastor .” And in this case, we rejoice because the father, after so many vicissitudes, persevered to the end, as a priest and as a religious of our religious family, and we can think that God in His infinite mercy has granted him the grace of infinite joy, of the treasure that does not corrode, which God Himself promised to those who fight the good fight. The father has already entered into “the Great Feast”… We rejoice, in short, because we trust in God that there has fallen to Fr. Buela’s lot that which he loved 4 and to which he dedicated his whole life: the Incarnate Word Himself, whom he contemplates from the arms of Most Holy Mary. Given the circumstances that God in His providence disposed, the father, who in his life was a great formator, has also left us great lessons with his death, and the first that leaps to the eye is −in my opinion− that, as he himself told us: “we must be men of invincible hope ; have an unrestricted trust in the power of Jesus Christ, who said: heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away . [We, Fr. Buela would say,] We must be men and women of invincible hope!” 5 . Many of us can testify that when the storms raged so fiercely that we could say with the psalmist: from where will my help come? 6 , we always found the father serene, with an attitude of imperturbable trust, and it seemed to us as if the trials we were going through, which we considered ‘tremendous,’ made no dent in him. But with that same attitude of trust in God he seemed to answer us and say to us with the psalmist: my help comes from the Lord, who made heaven and earth and He will not let my foot slip 7 . Later, leafing through the last book he wrote, we find the reason for this, for there he writes in his characteristic style: “in the face of the threats to dissolve us, not to carry out the priestly ordinations, etc.: I never worried about that. Never. I defined myself as ‘undaunted.’ That is, I suffered nothing. They were just poor men…” 8 . And I believe this is so because, as St. John of the Cross says: “the one whose spirit is detached is more content and joyful in want, because he has placed his all in nothing whatsoever, and finds in everything breadth of heart” 9 . So convinced was he that all this was the work of God alone that he said that this was the “reason why even in the greatest trials and in the most unjust diatribes (insults) I have consoled myself simply by shrugging my shoulders” 10 . That was Fr. Buela: with his gaze and his heart firmly grounded in the Incarnate Word. He always sought “to separate himself from the ‘pattern of this world,’ in order to insert himself into the will of God, entering into what pleased God, into what is good, into what is perfect” 11 . And elsewhere he writes: “I never took it upon myself to give God advice, nor to ask Him why He acted that way. He is God and He does what He wants” 12 . So it is that today he seems to want to teach us that in the face of trials and difficulties, which are never lacking, nor does God want them to be lacking −speaking individually and as an Institute−, we must never be troubled; we must not fear nor lose confidence, much less become discouraged or look back. On the contrary, we must be men and women of stout spirit in the midst of the hardships we have to suffer, because, as Fr. Buela has taught us by his example throughout his whole life and now by his death, “ the Providence of God [is] the only one that guides and governs history ” 13 . That is why the great word that sums up today the message I want to convey is: trust ! Unlimited trust and abandonment in our Lord, first of all; filial trust in our Blessed Mother, who is solicitous to help us; trust even in the greatest trials because, as we have seen in the life of our Founder, God sends them to us for our benefit. Trust in the immense treasure that God has granted us through the person of Fr. Buela, which is the legacy we must guard and make fruitful. 2. Trust! Only time will show us the historical moment we are living, with all its weight and all its influence on the future. But what we can affirm today is that it was a religious priest with the spirit of a prince who, docile to the grace of God, raised up this which today we call the Religious Family of the Incarnate Word , which is made up of religious who must be of princely spirit and noble soul 14 , for it is they who, with the favor of God and the indispensable help of Our Lady of Luján, will carry our beloved Institute forward. If we remain united and the ideal bequeathed to us by Fr. Buela beats fervently in our hearts, there is no mountain we cannot climb −even though there is much vertigo and much danger 15 −; there is no sea that the little boat of our Institute will not sail to accomplish great works for the inculturation of the Gospel 16 , even though the salt water of reproach and injustice splashes our faces. Because our place is and always will be “ out into the deep! , far from the shore and from dry land, far from merely human, calculating and cold thoughts” 17 . Let us never forget where our heart is, and where it must always be… our way of life and our natural habitat : out there in the deep, “ Duc in altum ! It is an invitation to accomplish great works, extraordinary undertakings, where there is much of adventure, of vertigo, of danger, where the waves toss the boat, the salt water splashes the face, the prow cuts its way for the first time, where there are no tracks and the only points of reference are the stars, where the keel is shaken by clashing whirlpools, the unfurled sails receive the fury of the wind, the masts creak… and the soul trembles… Out into the deep!, … where the water churns, the heart beats fast, where the soul knows heavenly inebriations and fascinating joys” 18 . Because ours is and will always be “to take seriously, thoroughly, the demands of the Gospel: go, sell all that you have … 19 ” 20 , and that is the longing that must beat in the heart of all those who are called to follow the Incarnate Word, the Supreme Captain, in our Institute, of all the members of our beloved Third Order and of our Sisters. Because ours is always, unfailingly, to give everything for God 21 , as our Founder has taught us so well. And just as in times past legions of men united under one standard to overcome enemies and win triumphs for their king, so we must remain united under the standard that bears the emblem of the Incarnation of the Word, holding fast to the patrimony that has been bequeathed to us, and work without reserve for the reign of Jesus Christ according to the specific charism of our Religious Family, which is nothing other than “to bring to fullness the consequences of the Incarnation of the Word” 22 , and which so often implies the self-emptying of Calvary 23 . If we remain united , committed to missionary work, and faithful to the spirit that has been bequeathed to us, to the spirit of the Institute, under the mantle of Our Lady, we will not bow before the spirit of the world; we will not break by distrusting God; we will not yield before the sharpest threats; we will not give up, even though the struggle be fierce; we will not surrender before the giant tyrants of the world; we will not draw back from our endeavor; rather, we will be honoring in truth, and not only in word, the memory of Fr. Buela and, most importantly, we will not disappoint our Lord. ***** [Peroratio] That is why today, paraphrasing St. Francis de Sales, we can hear Fr. Buela tell us with his usual candor and firmness: “Be firm in trust in the Providence of God, which, if it prepares crosses for us, will give us courage to bear them. […] Do not run ahead of the painful events of this life; arm yourselves with a perfect hope that, as they come, God, to whom they belong, will deliver you from them. He has protected you until now; hold fast to the hand of His Providence and He will assist you on every occasion and, if you cannot walk, He will carry you. What do you fear, since you all belong to God, who has assured us that all things will work for the good of those who love Him? Do not think about what will happen tomorrow, because the same Eternal Father who takes care of you today will do so tomorrow and always: He will give you no evil, and if He does, He will give you invincible courage to bear it” 24 . “Forward, always forward! Ave Maria and forward!” 25 . And let us never forget the “tremendous” words of Master John of Avila, which we have written in our spirit, in our constitutions, and which are part of our DNA; and which point out to us the treasure that has been given to us in exchange for the gift of our lives: it is the Ipsum Esse who says it to us: “I (am) your Father, because I am God; I your firstborn brother, because I am man. I am your payment and ransom: why do you fear debts, if you, through penance and Confession, ask to be released from them? I am your reconciliation: why do you fear wrath? I am the bond of your friendship: why do you fear God’s anger? I am your defender: why do you fear adversaries? I am your friend: why do you fear that you will lack anything I have, if you do not depart from Me? Yours is My Body and My Blood: why do you fear hunger? Yours is My heart: why do you fear being forgotten? Yours is My divinity: why do you fear miseries? And besides, yours are My angels to defend you; yours My saints to pray for you; yours My blessed Mother to be for you a caring and tender Mother; yours the earth, so that in it you may serve Me; yours heaven, because you will come to it; yours the demons and the hells, because you will trample them as slaves and as a prison; yours is life, because with it you win the life that never ends; yours the good pleasures, because you refer them to Me; yours the sufferings, because you suffer them for love of Me and for your own profit; yours the temptations, because they are merit and the cause of your eternal crown; yours is death, because it will be for you the nearest passage to life. And all this you have in Me and through Me; because I did not win it for Myself alone, nor do I wish to enjoy it alone; for when I took fellowship with you in the flesh, I took it so as to make you sharers in what I labored, fasted, ate, sweated and wept, and in My sorrows and deaths, if it is not prevented on your part. You are not poor, you who have so much wealth, unless you, by your bad life, knowingly choose to lose it!” 26 . To the Pure and Clean Conception of Luján we commend the soul of her beloved son, our dear Father, Carlos Miguel Buela. Amen. Notes 1 Cf. Constitutions , 121 . 2 Jesus to St. Faustina Kowalska. Cf. A milestone in the history of the IVE

The appointment of Fr. Teodoro Matsapula on May 8, the feast of Our Lady of Luján, as bishop of the Byzantine-rite Eparchy of Mukachevo in Ukraine, and his upcoming consecration on July 16, is without doubt a milestone in the history of the Institute. Considering that the Institute of the Incarnate Word was founded barely 40 years ago, and that it has been present in Ukraine for barely 30 years, the appointment of the first IVE bishop is indeed a most singular grace. And this divine gift becomes even more outstanding considering the trying situation the Institute is going through. This is therefore an event that cannot go unnoticed by us. Divine Providence has chosen us to be witnesses, and in some way sharers, of an immeasurable grace, for there is being fulfilled before our eyes −and with the favor of God− that fervent desire which our Founder left in writing in the Proper Law, namely, that of “being able to help our brothers of the Eastern Churches, who form part ‘of the undivided patrimony of the Universal Church’ 1 ” 2 ; a task he considered pressing, particularly for us, who have been called by a special vocation to evangelize the culture 3 . What a privileged position for this is that of a bishop! And what a great grace that God has chosen one of our own for that noble task. At the same time, this fact also demonstrates the capacity the Institute has had not to “fall into particularisms, reductionisms, partialities or one-sidedness that undermine the catholicity” 4 of the Church; and if we can truly say that “the Catholic Church breathes with two lungs” 5 , today we can also affirm that the Church herself, by having entrusted to one of our own the shepherding of the souls of an entire territory of the Byzantine Church in Ukraine, recognizes that our Institute also breathes with “two lungs, that is, the Eastern and the Western” 6 . For that has been “the ‘theological reason’ that has moved us from the beginning to send missionaries to Ukraine” 7 , since in that nation −and as he had learned from St. John Paul II− Fr. Buela saw “the hope that the Church in Europe may once again breathe with her two lungs, so that the whole continent may experience a new evangelization” 8 . Likewise, this simple fact is a tribute to the fully Catholic formation that Fr. Buela wanted for the Institute he founded, according to the will of the Incarnate Word, who wants to gather all into unity 9 and desires to form priests “in absolute and unrestricted ecclesial communion” 10 . With what pride Fr. Buela would look today upon Fr. Teodoro being anointed by the Holy Spirit “to continue His living mystery on behalf of the Church” 11 , especially in Ukraine. For with words of praise he said: “it is for us, members of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, a very great and providential grace to be in Ukraine, a historic people, a bridge between East and West” 12 ; “from where the faith and Christian civilization radiated into Eastern Europe” 13 . And how rewarded our Founder would see his efforts, seeing one of our own consecrated a Successor of the Apostles . “The state of the bishop,” the Proper Law points out, “is the most perfect of all, even more than the religious state; to him belongs the fullness of the priesthood; to him above all others, the spirit of faith, of wisdom and of fortitude… The bishop knows no enemies of his own; for him there are only children, and the littlest, the humblest, the most unhappy are dearest to him. For all he prays, for all he has words of eternal life, for all he goes up to the altar and offers the Blood of the spotless Lamb that takes away the sins of the world… The bishop is the Good Shepherd, who watches, feeds and evangelizes; who knows how to suffer in silence and knows how to give his life for his sheep” 14 . That, in brief, is what Fr. Buela longed for in one of our own who might become a bishop, and it is also what we ask today of the Incarnate Word, through the intercession of His Most Holy Mother, for the new bishop, above all: “the spirit of faith, of wisdom and of fortitude.” What a beautiful occasion this is, then, to celebrate from every corner of the earth not only the consecration of the first IVE bishop, but also the fact that “we are members of one single missionary Religious Family, and above all, we are children of the One, Holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church, which ‘breathes’ with two lungs: the Eastern and the Western” 15 . Let us raise our supplication to the Virgin Mary, whom the liturgy of St. Basil praises as most holy, spotless, blessed above all, glorious Lady, Mother of God and ever Virgin, Woman full of grace and joy of the whole universe 16 , and let us invoke the help of the heavenly patrons St. Basil and St. Josaphat, of St. John Chrysostom and St. Clement of Rome, and of the 27 Ukrainian martyrs, for the new bishop Teodoro Matsapula, so that his ecclesial service may bring “a new apostolic enthusiasm from the patrimony of holiness left by those exemplary disciples of Christ” 17 in Ukraine. May Most Holy Mary, Queen of the Apostles, who knew how to respond to the Angel’s announcement: be it done unto me according to your word 18 , always bless, protect and help Bishop Teodoro Matsapula, so that he may carry out his mission according to the style of the Incarnate Word. May she shine for him as a sign of sure hope and of consolation in the sacrificial office of pastoral government, which is, as Pope St. Gregory the Great said, “the art of arts.” For these intentions we members of the Institute pledge our prayers. On this occasion we also congratulate the whole Religious Family in Ukraine: the priests of the IVE on the 30th anniversary of the Institute’s presence in those lands, the mothers and sisters on the 25th anniversary of their mission, and the members of the Third Order on the 15th anniversary of their foundation there. Paraphrasing Pope Leo XIII, we say to them: “ When our order flourishes, the Church in Ukraine flourishes .” Let no one fail to recognize the wonders God works for us and the enormous graces that in His mercy He grants us to see before our eyes, in the midst of so many crosses and persecutions. May the consecration of Fr. Teodoro be celebrated throughout the world! Showing the value of the charism

Mt 16:24-28 We find ourselves here in the Co-Cathedral of Priverno, reliquary of one of the most precious relics of him who “espoused the Truth” 1 and under whose magisterium we wish to be formed 2 : St. Thomas Aquinas. And within this framework I would like to recall the enormous importance of the formation given in our houses in fidelity to the charism. A formation that from the beginning has been conceived as definitively Thomistic. St. John Paul II, in Vita Consecrata , teaches: “Formators […] must be persons expert in the ways that lead to God, so as to be capable of accompanying others on this journey […] but above all they will show the beauty of following the Lord and the value of the charism in which this following is made concrete” 3 . Instilling the charism Certainly it is a duty of all the members of the Institute to bear witness to and transmit the charism in all its purity, but it is especially incumbent on formators to instill in the members in formation “living the charism proper to the Institute” 4 . That is, to infuse with determination and by every means the charism and spirituality of our beloved Institute. This, in our particular case, implies forming the candidates according to the very rich patrimony of the Institute, with all the non-negotiable elements attached to the charism, in such a way that all may “be thoroughly imbued with the charism and its purpose” 5 , and that nothing and no one may erase from any of them the seal of our “particular style of sanctification and apostolate” 6 . This point is immovable for us. Each of the aspects of our formation, in all its stages and with all its nuances, is a non-negotiable whole. In all of them must shine forth the DNA of a religious of the Incarnate Word, magnificently described in number 231 of our Constitutions , which should be the great charter of presentation of each of our members. That on the one hand. A consistently Thomistic formation But also, if we are to be faithful to the charism received, which identifies us and manifests our reason for being in the Church, our formation must be consistently Thomistic. This is of capital importance. I insist: we “have received the immense grace of Thomism, of being inserted into the current of the perennial philosophy. And with it a great responsibility, that of forming a school ” 7 . Because, as our Proper Law very rightly says, “holy priests and religious who are metaphysicians are needed” 8 . Which is the same as saying priests and religious who work so that the public and social life of peoples may be subordinated to God as to its ultimate end, and who do not end up adapting Christianity to modern civilization. Priests and religious who do not dilute faith into the rational, nor turn the sacred into the profane; who do not transform theology into anthropology, nor dissolve the eternal into history. Rather, may they work for the Christianization of the world, not for the worldliness of Christianity. That is, may they evangelize the culture not nominally, but from within, under the influence of grace 9 , in such a way that it may be ruled by Christ. It is imperative that we form complete men, heroic, of firm convictions, with “a solid mentality of faith” 10 that enables them “to be servants of the Gospel and teachers of the people of God” 11 . Our formation has nothing to do with making our candidates mere commentators in whom confusion reigns between theology and philosophy, or sociology, or psychology, and who, “ignoring the living tradition of the Church… interpret in their own way the doctrine of the Church, even the Gospel itself, spiritual realities, the divinity of Christ, His Resurrection, or the Eucharist, practically emptying them of their content and thereby creating new forms of gnosis” 12 , as St. Paul VI said. By the mission we have received, it falls to us to have a strong cultural formation, one that takes a stand before modern culture 13 . For which, my dear friends, what is needed is a “metaphysics with grip,” one that bites into reality. And, in this sense, our formation cannot but be Thomistic. Our vocation as members of the Institute of the Incarnate Word “presupposes a firm Christian identity” 14 and the learning of a living Thomism. And this certainly brings with it the cross of which the Incarnate Word speaks to us today: Whoever wishes to come with me must deny himself, take up his cross and follow me. So that thiscross, which was inseparable from the Incarnate Word, is inseparable from our lives as members of this Institute. Far be it from us to be ashamed of it. That is why today we ask the Blessed Virgin for the grace to remain faithful in our “act of integral faith and total self-surrender [to Christ], with the formal decision not to make pacts, not to compromise, not to capitulate, not to negotiate, not to concede, nor to make deals with the spirit of the world” 15 , but rather to remain always firm on the Rock 16 from whom our spirituality and our pastoral work derive at their very root 17 . And may this always be the attitude in which all our members, present and future, are formed. Notes 1 Adolfo Tortolo, “ Tomás de Aquino el Santo ,” Mikael 5 (1974), 11-12. The first charity we must do is to ourselves

[Exordium] When I was thinking about this homily, I began rereading some books I have of Don Orione. One of them is a collection of letters he wrote to his priests for various reasons. I could speak to you about the excellence of the role of the apostolate you carry out in evangelizing the culture; I could tell you that there is no better witness to Christ than that which proclaims Christian charity with deeds and makes its witness irrefutable 1 ; I could tell you that the spiritual and corporal works of mercy are those most in harmony with the end of our Institute, and are those that most spread the good 2 , and that therefore everything you do here, the least service you render to any of those here, you render to the very Incarnate Word himself, and it will not go unrewarded… but you already know all that very well. It is not for nothing that you are called the key pieces 3 in the evangelizing work of the Institute. Then I found this piece of advice that Don Orione gives to his own, which seems to me could serve you as well, and it goes like this: “The first charity we must do is to ourselves: we have to pray more, I say it to myself, I say it to you, I say it to everyone: we must pray more, cultivate piety more, humility, dependence, docility of spirit, and the religious spirit” 4 . How important this is, isn’t it? Obviously this is true for all priests, which is why the saint says: “I say it to myself, I say it to you, I say it to everyone,” but very especially for those who, like you, are directly dedicated to attending to the needs of others, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Our Proper Law highlights something similar in the Directory of Works of Mercy , where it explicitly says that one “must attend to the needs of men, but never abandon or neglect the service of God through prayer” 5 . Why? Because “it is precisely prayer that will allow [you] to give yourselves better to the service of others; because prayer makes it possible to discover God in our neighbor” 6 . That is why it remains important not only to pray: to pray the liturgy of the hours, to make the daily adoration, to celebrate Mass, to pray the rosary… but, as Don Orione says: “to pray more, to cultivate piety more.” I know that there are few of you here, that you have a great deal of work, which at times can become exhausting; nevertheless, we must not forget that for us, as priests of the Incarnate Word, the life of prayer is essential, and the truth is that nothing “can make us forget that above all we have been called to be with God, to listen to his word, to contemplate his face” 7 . That is why St. John Paul II once spoke to religious about “the need for long periods of prayer, of recollection, of adoration,” and added: “as consecrated persons we must not only pray, we must be a living prayer. One could also say, we must pray while apparently not praying. We must pray while apparently not having time to pray, but we must pray. It is another paradox. Humanly speaking, this is something impossible. How can one pray without praying? But St. Paul tells us: the Spirit prays in us , and so the matter turns out somewhat differently” 8 . That is why recollection during the day is important. Of course, in case of extreme necessity, one must apply what St. Vincent de Paul teaches: “Service of the poor must be preferred to everything, and it must be rendered without delay. Therefore, if at the time of prayer some medicine or any kind of help must be brought to a poor person, go to him with a very tranquil mind and do what is fitting, offering it to God as a prolongation of prayer. And do not have any scruple or remorse of conscience if, in order to render some service to the poor, you have left prayer; to leave the presence of God for any of the reasons listed is no contempt of God, since it is for Him that we do it” 9 . St. Benedict Cottolengo taught something very similar to his own: “be tireless in the service of the least, without forgetting, at the same time, that prayer is our first work and the most important, because prayer gives life to the Little House” 10 . St. Paul of the Cross, for his part, said: “for the sick, one needs a mother or a saint,” referring to the great care and exquisite delicacy one must have in attending to them, as if each were one’s only sick child. Well, that charity of the priest springs from prayer, from the contemplation of the mystery of divine mercy 11 . And so, when the work in the hogarcitos is born of prayer, that is, when it is supernaturalized, it presents itself as a most beautiful account of the love of God, which manifests in a special way his merciful tenderness as physician of souls and of bodies. You know better than I, but it seems to me that service to the sick, to the poorest, is an intense experience of God, which constantly leads us to seek the help of Christ in prayer. In that way, even though the occasions for self-denial multiply day by day, you are being purified, you are growing in virtue, and that is, in a certain way, like a confirmation of the value of the charism of the Institute as a path toward the perfection of charity, which is what we have come to do in this life. Don Orione also points out the importance of practicing in our lives “humility, dependence, docility of spirit, and the religious spirit.” For there is no doubt that “service of one’s neighbor neither divides nor separates the religious from God” 12 . And that is why in another letter he tells them: “be assiduous together in the practices of common life, and do your work together, bearing one another’s burdens and each one putting up with the defects of the others for the love of Jesus Christ: always joyful in heart, in spirit, in words, and also with serenity on your face as in your expressions: content to serve God, always content in perfect joy in Domino, in prayer, in work, in recreation, at meals, always and in everything with joy and simplicity of heart, praising God and serving God. And the Lord will do the rest, and will multiply blessings upon your steps, and your number” 13 . [Peroratio] Now, to conclude, I would like to express to you from the heart our gratitude and great appreciation for all that you do here; know that it does not go unnoticed, and it is very edifying for everyone to see all that you do in the Home (I have seen photos 14 of the Easter camps, of the stations of the cross, of an outing with the kids to the park…). I am more than convinced that it is not easy, so, as Don Orione used to say: “Courage! and always forward! Ave Maria and forward! ” I truly congratulate you. Let us ask the Heart of Jesus in this Holy Mass that charity may always increase in your souls, allowing you to bear witness ever more faithfully and eloquently to the Divine Samaritan through a holy and fervent life, sustained by constant prayer and aided by the maternal hand of the Blessed Virgin. And we also ask Her to send vocations that have the courage to do good as you do. Notes 1 Directory of Works of Mercy , 75. 2 Cf. Christ is the model of our mission as priests

Homily on the occasion of the priestly jubilee of some members of the IVE [Exordium] On the occasion of our Priestly Jubilee, we have the grace of making a pilgrimage in this Land, which is Holy because the Incarnate Word dwelt in it. And particularly today, to us, missionary priests of the Incarnate Word –come from the four corners of the earth– God gives the grace of beginning this pilgrimage precisely here, in Nazareth, in the very town where the angel appeared to the Most Holy Virgin to ask her consent so that the Word might take from her body and her blood to become man; and when She pronounced her fiat , in this place the Word of God clothed himself with our flesh in her most pure womb. Et verbum caro factum est. And so, in this town, so small and so sublimely simple, the Incarnation of the Word took place; that mystery which identifies us and which is central in the mystery of God. It is that mystery which was present in God from all eternity and which becomes, in time, an event greater than the creation of the world, one that can never be surpassed by any other 1 . The grace of knowing the fact of the Incarnation and the grace of faith in the Incarnation is overwhelming. This is the event that sums up the very history of humanity and at the same time the history of each man and woman in particular (ours too)… this is the mystery that not only divides history in two, but also answers man’s great questions, being, as it were, his metaphysical center. Here, we could say, and only before this mystery, the human spirit finds rest… here everything becomes clear, everything is understood and everything turns into light… And the word was the light of men Here the Word became flesh, and that is why it is in this place that all the aspirations of the human being and of all creation are resolved: all things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made of all that has been made , says St. John, underscoring the centrality of the event. We priests have an altogether special share in that mystery. For in the Incarnation of the Word there “took place the sublime priestly consecration of Jesus Christ, since He was marked and anointed forever as High and Eternal Priest, sole Mediator between heaven and earth” 2 . And we, already 25 years ago by the grace of God, were ontologically configured to Christ, Teacher, Sanctifier and Shepherd of his People 3 , and this, too, forever. That is why being here makes us return, in some way, to the origins not only of the history of salvation but also to the very origin of the Catholic priesthood and of our priesthood. That is also why here, in this place, lies the mystery of our lives, of our own lives. It is here that we can understand more fully the mystery we carry in our hands and which we must live each day. For it is the place where the event occurred that has defined our existence and our earthly experience. How, then, are we to respond before such sublime realities? It is here, too, that we find the answer: the humility, the joyful docility, the genuine and serene obedience of the Virgin of Nazareth 4 , who, by pronouncing her fiat , gave the Word from her own human nature, through which He taught, governed and sanctified; these become the paradigm and the greatest model for our fidelity to that mystery of which we are continuators. Analogously, one day we too, like the Virgin at the Annunciation, were asked that question of entering into the central mystery of history: Would you give God your human nature? And by the great mercy of God we too pronounced our fiat , and God granted us the immense treasure of holy orders, which is the same as saying that God was pleased to clothe us with Christ 5 . This reality is ineffable for each one of us: our lives have been indelibly intertwined with the High and Eternal Priest, which inserts us specifically into the Trinitarian mystery 6 . God has chosen us to be priests of the Incarnate Word, for the sublime office of “prolonging the Incarnation in every man, in the whole man and in all the manifestations of man” 7 . That is our end, that is our charism, that is and must always be our commitment 8 . For this we were born and for this we live. That is to say, the same Word who one day, in this very place, assumed a human nature to fulfill the design of salvation, is the same incarnate God who has chosen our poor “human natures so that salvation may reach all men” 9 , making us his priests and thus continuing what He did: teaching, governing and sanctifying, by delegating to us “his threefold prophetic, priestly and royal function” 10 . That is why we can say that, analogously, the Incarnation continues to take place, and that it took place particularly in us when we were anointed as priests and became “living instruments of the Eternal Priest so as to be able to carry on, through time, his admirable work… Since every priest –as the Magisterium teaches– represents in his own way the person of Christ himself” 11 . That is why here today we can and must renew our commitment to the threefold priestly office of Christ that has been entrusted to us, so that we may be faithful and always true continuators of the Incarnation of the Word in time and in this portion of history in which Divine Providence has given us to live. 1. In such a way that our priesthood cannot be understood unless we teach Christ with our word and with our very life : He and his mysteries are always, directly or indirectly, the subject matter of our preaching and of our earthly existence. And just as the Virgin told the servants at the Wedding of Cana: Do whatever He tells you , so we too must proclaim the Gospel in such a way that those who hear us are able to “translate those truths into concrete life, into witness” 12 , into criteria for living. Therefore it falls to us to be thoroughly imbued with Christ, with his Truth. So that, the fire of his Truth burning first in us, we may radiate it to others. This takes concrete form in the pursuit of a deep unity of life that leads us to try to be, to live and to serve as another Christ in all the circumstances of life 13 . 2. Moreover, as priests we exercise the authority of Christ and must rule and feed his flock : Our Constitutions say it clearly and beautifully: our “destiny is not command or honors, but total self-giving to the service of God and to the pastoral ministry” 14 . And we will not find a better example of humility and service than that of the Virgin. “The Virgin gave her ‘yes,’ here in Nazareth, as a handmaid, and God looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid 15 , and it was then that the Word took the form of a slave , becoming like men 16 in her most pure womb” 17 . 3. Finally, as priests we must sanctify, and to do so we must be Victims with Christ : The Word of God became incarnate in the immaculate womb of the Virgin of Nazareth precisely in order to be able to be a Victim, to be able to immolate his humanity. And therefore the ministerial priesthood is a sacrificial priesthood. This is an inescapable condition. That is why there is usually much suffering in priestly life. This is our vocation: “sacrifice,” with all its consequences. The priest must spend his life letting himself be consumed, like Jesus in the Eucharist. In other words, “the vocation to the priesthood is a vocation to the Cross. It is a vocation to mystical dying, to spiritual dying, day by day… [to live] as men condemned to death … This is the priestly program!” 18 . [Peroratio] That is why, of the Most Holy Virgin, who joined herself with a maternal heart to the priestly sacrifice of her Son, lovingly consenting to the immolation of the Victim begotten in her womb, as a consequence of that fiat pronounced here in Nazareth, let us ask the grace that she take us into her hands and, in the shelter of her Mother’s Heart, conform our priesthood to the Priesthood of her Son, and give us the grace to persevere until death, proclaiming with our whole life that the Word became Flesh and dwelt among us. So be it. Notes 1 Cf. Constitutions , 3 . 2 Cf. Directory of Spirituality , 70. 3 Cf. Fr. Carlos Buela, IVE, Sacerdotes para Siempre , Part I, ch. 6.3. 4 Cf. Lk 1:26-27. 5 Cf. Gal 3:27. 6 Cf. What the world needs is intolerance

[Exordium] In the Gospel we have just heard, the evangelist mentions how, after the healing of the leper, as the fame of Christ spread more and more, the crowds came flocking in great numbers to hear Him and to be healed of their illnesses 1 .That is, Jesus devotes Himself to those who suffer, to those on the margins of society. He heals them and thus opens up for them the possibility of living and deciding together with others; He brings them into equality and fraternity. This, obviously, concerns all of us as well: Jesus shows all of us the direction of our action; He tells us how we must act. And since today too there are pathologies and deadly illnesses that infect our religion and our very reason, it is necessary that we too take on the responsibility of healing. What illnesses are these? For example, the destruction of the image of God because of hatred and fanaticism, the passion for novelty that forgets the truth, accepting everything ‘unfiltered’ in the eagerness to appear tolerant or ‘open-minded,’ raising the banner of equality where everything ends up being a shapeless mixture and one’s own identity is diluted. We must be careful about this, because none of us is exempt from it. G. K. Chesterton warned with his usual irony: “Do not be so open-minded that your brain falls out” 2 . “Merely being open-minded means nothing. The purpose of opening the mind is like that of opening the mouth: it is in order to close it again on something solid” 3 . That is why our task continues to be not to propose “technical solutions” to poverty, to the tragedy of racism still prevailing today in many countries, to the precarious health situation that affects so many places; rather, our “first contribution to the solution of social problems must be the proclamation of the truth about Christ, about the Church and about man, applying it to a concrete situation” 4 . This is what we call ‘biting into reality.’ “The social question and the Gospel are truly inseparable. If we give men only knowledge, skills, technical abilities and tools, we give them too little” 5 . Therefore, it is necessary to make Jesus Christ known, loved and believed in; hearts must be converted, so that there may also be progress in the social sphere, so that reconciliation may begin, so that injustices and the social scourges of drug addiction, adultery, etc. may be fought, truly confronting their deep causes and healing the sick with due attention and compassion. The world needs God. We need God. We do not impose our faith on anyone. That kind of proselytism is contrary to Christianity. But we must also say that faith can only develop in freedom. And it is to the freedom of men that we appeal, asking that it open itself to God, seek Him, listen to Him, let itself be healed. We do not disrespect other religions and cultures, we do not disrespect their faith, if we confess aloud and without half-measures the Incarnate Word, that God who opposed His suffering to violence, who in the face of evil and its power raised up His mercy. For Who is it that overcomes the world but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? 6 . What the world needs is intolerance 7 We can say then, with the Venerable Archbishop Fulton Sheen, that the world today does not suffer from intolerance, but from tolerance. Yes, listen carefully. Our world, our country and so many others are not suffering from a lack of tolerance, but from a lack of in tolerance. For people tolerate, as if it were nothing, the jumbling together of good and evil, of truth and error, of virtue and wickedness, of Christ and chaos. That is why we can say with Sheen: our country –present-day society– has not been invaded by intolerant people, but by the ‘open-minded’ 8 . Because if a man reaches a decision in an orderly way, discerning, guided by principles, just as any man makes up his bed every morning, then he is called ‘intolerant,’ a fanatic, ‘self-referential’; but if a man cannot make up his mind, and instead shows himself ambivalent before the options, he is called tolerant, open-minded. An intolerant man is one who refuses to accept a reason for anything; an open-minded man is one who accepts anything for a reason, provided it is not a good reason. It is true that there is a demand for precision, exactness and definition, but it is only a demand for scientific precision, not logical precision. This has produced a mental collapse, says F. Sheen, which shows itself in three ways : the tendency to settle problems not with arguments but with mere words, the willingness to accept without reservation anyone’s authority on the subject of religion, and, lastly, the love of novelty. The fact is that the truth of our holy religion has the right to be heard from the lips of qualified spokesmen , just as the science of physics or astronomy has the right to be heard through its qualified spokesmen [hence the urgent need for a solid formation]. Religion is a science, even though some turn it into a feeling. Religion has its principles, natural and revealed, which are more demanding in their logic than mathematics. But the false notion of tolerance has obscured this fact in the eyes of many who are extremely intolerant about the smallest details of life but extremely tolerant in their relations with God: they teach aberrations contrary to the faith, they commit grave injustices, everything good is suspect to them, all heroism seems to them extremism, etc . Another sign of the collapse of reason that has produced this strange mushroom of ‘open minds’ is the passion for novelty , as opposed to the love of truth. Truth is sacrificed for an epigram 9 , the Divinity of Christ for a headline in Monday morning’s newspaper. What is more, more than one ‘modern pastor’ is much less concerned with preaching Christ and Him crucified than with his popularity among the people. That lack of intellectual backbone makes men talk nonsense by the heap, and although we will not give examples here, it is enough to repeat what Chesterton said: “Those who abandon the tradition of truth do not escape into something called freedom. They only escape into something else that we call fashion.” That is why we very rarely see an accusing finger raised against the injustices that occur in the courts, against parents who favor and even encourage homosexuality in their children; no voice rings in the ears of the rich, saying with something of ‘intolerance’: It is not lawful for you to live with your brother’s wife . Rather we hear: “Friends, times are changing!” To believe in the existence of God, in the divinity of Christ, in the moral law, is considered a thing of the past. But, mind you, the latest thing in this new fashion of tolerance is what is considered the true , as if truth were a fashion, like a hat, instead of being a well-founded institution, like the head. Finally, this broadness of outlook makes us think that truth is novelty and that, therefore, ‘truth’ changes with the passing fancies of the moment. Like the chameleon that changes color to adapt itself to its surroundings, they claim that truth changes to adapt itself to the weaknesses and crookedness of the age. Pay attention: The nature of certain things is fixed, and none more so than the nature of truth. Truth may be challenged a thousand times, but that only shows that it is strong enough to survive a thousand assaults. For someone to say: ‘Some say this, some say that, therefore there is no truth,’ is as logical as it would have been for Columbus, hearing some say, ‘The earth is round,’ and others saying, ‘The earth is flat,’ to conclude: ‘Therefore, there is no earth.’ And just as a carpenter might get rid of his ruler and use each beam as a measuring rod, so too those who have cast aside the standard of objective truth have nothing left to measure by except the fashion of thought of the moment. The giddiness of novelty, the sentimental restlessness of an unstable mentality and the unnatural fear of a good dose of solid thinking all seem to combine to produce that little band of the tolerant who think there is no difference between God as Cause and God as a “mental projection”; or who put Christ and Buddha on the same level, or who then, in a sweeping overflow of their ‘already open minds,’ say not only that any ‘Christian’ sect is as good as another, but even that any religion in the whole world –whatever that religion may be– is as good as another, or that every religious institute must be the same as the others –and therefore forget its own identity– practicing a general love of God and neighbor. How many religious, carried away by an excessive desire for adaptability and spontaneity, in their eagerness to be ‘open-minded,’ to progress, to update themselves, have abandoned the characteristic features of their religious family so as to blend in with the others, and have left the works they were carrying out for fear of being branded ‘rigid and old-fashioned’ 10 . Meanwhile, any sensible man wonders how there can be progress without direction and how there can be direction without a fixed point. And because one speaks of a “fixed point,” they immediately say that one is backward, that such people are closed, when in reality they are beyond time, mentally and spiritually speaking. That is why, says Fulton Sheen, in the face of this false ‘open-mindedness,’ what the world needs is intolerance. The world seems to have completely lost the faculty of distinguishing between good and evil, right and wrong. There are some minds that believe intolerance is always wrong, because they make ‘intolerance’ mean hatred, intellectual narrowness or fanaticism. And they are the same ones who believe that tolerance is always right because, for them, it means ‘charity,’ being intelligent –precisely because ‘they are open-minded’– and having a good nature, which more often than not is falsely compassionate. What is tolerance? Tolerance is an attitude of reasoned patience toward evil and a restraint that keeps us from showing anger or inflicting punishment. But what is more important than the definition is the field of its application. The important point here is this: tolerance applies only to persons, but never to truth. Intolerance applies only to truth, but never to persons. Tolerance applies to those who err; intolerance to error. That is why today the society of the contemporary world does not suffer so much from intolerance, understood as fanaticism, but from tolerance, which is indifference toward truth and error, and that philosophical indifference which is interpreted as being open-minded. Do not misunderstand me: of course greater tolerance (in the good sense) is desirable, because one can never show too much charity to people who differ from us. In fact, our Lord Himself asked that “we love those who slander us,” because they are always persons, but He never told us to love slander. In accordance with the Spirit of Christ, the Church has always encouraged us to pray for all those who are outside the bosom of the Church and asks that the greatest charity be shown to them. Charity, then, must be shown to all persons and, in particular, to those who are outside the fold, who must be drawn or brought back by charity, so that there may be one flock and one Shepherd. Shall God, who does not look with an equally tolerant eye on all religions, perhaps be denied the name of ‘Wisdom’ and be called an ‘intolerant’ God? The Church identifies herself with Christ both in time and in principles. She began to reflect on her first principles, and the more she reflected, the more dogmas she developed. The Church never forgot those dogmas, but remembered them, and her remembering is what we call the Tradition of the Church. The dogmas of the Church, the truth preached by the Church throughout all these centuries, are like bricks, solid elements with which man can build, not like “religious experience,” which, like straw, is good only for burning. The Church has been and will always be intolerant with regard to the rights of God, because heresy, error and falsehood do not concern personal matters in which one may yield, but the very Divine Law itself, in which one must not yield. Truth is divine; the heretic is human. If due reparation is made, the Church will admit the heretic back into the bosom of her Wisdom, but never the heresy. What is right is right even if no one is in the right; and evil is evil even if everyone is mistaken. [Peroration] To conclude: The attitude of the Church toward the modern world on this important question can be better grasped by following the story of those two women in Solomon’s courtroom. Both claimed the child. The rightful mother insisted on having the whole child or nothing, because a child is like the truth: it cannot be divided without being ruined. The false mother, on the contrary, agreed to a compromise. She was willing to divide the baby, and the baby would have died because of that ‘broad-mindedness.’ We must perceive our mission in history and try to correspond to it. “It is important to say clearly in which God we believe and to profess with conviction the human face of God” 11 . What is needed is responsibility and concern for our salvation and for the salvation of the whole world. Let us be servants of the Truth, as our Proper Law asks of us: of the truth about God, of the truth about man and his mysterious destiny, of the truth about the world. A difficult truth that we must seek in the Word of God and of which we are neither the owners nor the arbiters, but the depositaries, the heirs, the servants 12 . Hence we must, even at the cost of renunciations and sacrifices, seek the Truth, form ourselves in the Truth, assimilate the Truth that we must transmit to others, without dissembling out of a desire to please others, to astonish, or to make an impression. Without obscuring the Truth through laziness in seeking it, or for the sake of comfort; rather, we must serve it without trampling on it. In this Mass we ask the Blessed Virgin for the grace to strip ourselves of the old man, which is like the leprosy we read about today in the Gospel, and instead to be clothed by Her with the purity, the tastes and the will of our Divine Savior. So be it. Notes 1 Cf. Lk 5:15. 2 “ Do not be so open-minded that your brains fall out .” 3 “ Merely having an open mind is nothing. Charity: the apostolic virtue par excellence

Perfect model of a consecrated woman [Exordium] Since we are essentially Marian 1 , and since our Proper Law has indicated in several of its documents the principal and preponderant role that the Virgin has in our spirituality and missionary activity, we cannot fail to consider and go deeper into the example of our Most Holy Mother. In fact, our Proper Law presents her to us as the “perfect model of a consecrated woman, whom every religious must always contemplate and imitate” 2 . That is why today I would like to highlight some aspects, or rather attitudes, of our Mother which, although they challenge every Christian, are –as I see it– essential in a Servant. 1. Service And the first attitude or quality that stands out in the Virgin is precisely that of service. Many times we have read in the Gospel that passage of the account of the Visitation that says: In those days, Mary set out for the hill country… 3 . The words of the Gospel account make us see with the eyes of the heart the young Virgin of Nazareth on her way to the town of Judah where her cousin lived, in order to offer her services. Analogously, each Servant sister, because she is a missionary –which is another essential aspect in us– is or will be sent to another town to offer her services. This implies availability, forgetfulness of self in order to serve the other, humility, zeal for souls… However, what strikes us above all in Mary is her attentiveness, full of tenderness , toward her elderly cousin. It is a concrete love , which is not limited to words of understanding but commits itself personally in authentic assistance. The Virgin does not simply give her cousin something that belongs to her; she gives herself , asking nothing in return. She has perfectly understood that the gift received from God, rather than a privilege , is a duty that commits her on behalf of others with the gratuitousness proper to love. That is why the quality that must stand out in each Servant sister must be precisely an attitude of service. If a sister does not serve others, she is of no use. It is a contradiction in terms. Because what is proper to every servant is precisely to serve, with humility, with concrete acts of service toward the members of her own community, toward the poor who come every day to the door of the convent, toward the priests and seminarians –members of our own Family– and of course toward the souls that have been entrusted to you. You must be convinced that you have consecrated your lives to the service of Jesus Christ, the Incarnate Word. That is not something abstract, a hazy idea, or something utopian; it becomes concrete “in humble service and generous self-giving, in the gratuitous gift of yourselves through a love to the extreme” 4 in the service of your neighbor. And saying gratuitous gift means without expecting reward, without expecting recognition, without expecting consolations, without demands… It is, moreover, a constant service; it is not something sporadic, but, following the example of Most Holy Mary, it is a self-giving that fills everything and every day. If a Servant says that she wants to be humble or thinks she is humble, but does not serve others, however many resolutions she makes and prayers she raises to heaven, she is beating around the bush. That is why, intrinsically associated with service, the virtue that must most distinguish the Servants is humility. And from this follows a second quality, which is: 2. Joy Every day at Vespers we pray the canticle of the Magnificat, which says: my soul proclaims the greatness of the Lord and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior, for he has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid . It is precisely from that availability for service, from knowing herself to be ‘handmaid of the Lord,’ that the joy of the Most Holy Virgin springs. Similarly, if each Servant is ready to proclaim her fiat to the will of God –without reluctance, without slowness, without reservations– then she will be able to proclaim her magnificat and live her consecration to the full. The joy of the Virgin springs from knowing herself looked upon by God, in spite of her lowliness 5 ; it springs from the ‘service’ she is able to render, thanks to the wonders that the Almighty works in her. It is interesting to note that the Magisterium of the Church says that “woman cannot find herself except by giving love to others” 6 , and therefore she will not find her joy, her fulfillment, except by giving herself. Which I –in my limited understanding– take to mean giving everything that love asks of us, with total availability, immediately, unconditionally, asking nothing in return, with joy and wishing that even more be asked of us. For this what is needed –among other things, and as I see it– is to ask for the grace of that maternal wisdom which instills an affection that foresees everything, so as to anticipate and satisfy the unspoken needs of our own; which carries charity down to the last detail; which makes of its hidden and silent service to its own a luminous and joyful sacrifice; which defends its own even with a glance; which knows how to spare them sorrow and toil; which receives with a strong heart the worries and annoyances that cloud their faces; which never keeps a tally of the things it has done for those it loves, because its happiness lies in giving itself “without measure, to the extreme, to exhaustion, to the end” 7 . Notice that after the Magnificat there followed those three months of service to her cousin Elizabeth, about which the Gospel says nothing. Or perhaps it tells us the most important thing: the good makes no noise ; the power of love is manifested in the serene discretion of daily service. And that is a great lesson for all of us, who so often seek offices and conspicuous apostolates that will win us human glory. The Virgin served in silence. 3. Intercession Finally, a third quality that we should see replicated in each Servant is that of being an intercessor. We see it in the dialogue between the Virgin and the Incarnate Word at the wedding at Cana. She is sensitive to the needs of others 8 and intercedes before Christ. She is the one who asks graces and favors from heaven for us. St. Louis Marie says that there is no grace of God that does not pass through the hands of Mary. That is why the Most Holy Virgin is the Woman who intercedes. Likewise, each Servant must implore with her sacrifices and prayers favors from heaven for all souls, especially for the Institute, for the whole Religious Family and of course for all souls. Our Proper Law tells us so explicitly: “we must have recourse to her merciful intercession” 9 and ask for all the graces we need to be faithful to our consecration 10 , as our formula of profession of vows says, a grace that must be asked not only for ourselves but for all the members of our Institutes. In this sense, one of the books of the Servants says that “it is fitting for the Servants… to direct everyone toward heaven by the example of their lives and by their intercession” 11 ; that is why you must pray for every grace for yourselves, for the Institute, for sinners… and especially now, when these are not easy times for the Church, is when we must ask the most. The intercession of Most Holy Mary does not fail. Because, as a good Mother, she is not distant from our concerns, our problems or our struggles; rather, with maternal solicitude she seeks to help us, protect us, defend us, give us what she knows is good for us to be happy in time and in eternity… That is why I invite and encourage you to pray fervently for our own, for our own Religious Family, that it may always remain united and rooted in the precious charism that has been bequeathed to us. And when some cross comes upon you, some sacrifice you must make –God willing– be so kind as to offer it –following the example of our Heavenly Mother– for the good of our Family. [Peroratio] In short, dear sisters, the exemplary holiness of the Virgin must always move us to raise our eyes toward her. That is why, in this Holy Mass, let us ask that the contemplation of the virtues of our Most Holy Mother –especially her readiness to serve, her joy and her dedication to intercessory prayer– may adorn our souls, and that we may reproduce them in concrete acts in daily life. For thus and only thus will we be behaving as true devoted children of the Virgin and fulfilling our purpose of being essentially Marian. May the Virgin bless you. Notes 1 Cf.
