On the 20th anniversary of the Fabro Project

20th ANNIVERSARY OF THE C. FABRO PROJECT [Exordium] As we celebrate today the 20th anniversary of the commendable work of those who began the Cornelio Fabro Cultural Project and of those who carry it on today, this occasion has dimensions that are in a certain way unprecedented, given the cultural, social and ecclesial context of the moment in which we live, and in some way it marks a milestone in the history of this small project, which began with the aim of making known the thought and person of Fr. Fabro (as the most profound and scientific connoisseur of St. Thomas Aquinas) and has become today the guardian of a great philosophical patrimony. That is why, in all honesty, with admiration and gratitude, I would like to congratulate all of you who in one way or another, over these years and in different countries, have been involved in such a significant and commendable apostolate! I would like, then, to devote this homily to highlighting the importance of the intellectual activity of our members as an ecclesial service. 1. Intellectual activity oriented to pastoral work The first thing that must be said is that pastoral activity and intellectual activity can never be set against each other as if they were two antagonistic things (unfortunately this is one of the great tragedies of the present moment in the Church of Jesus Christ). Both are complementary apostolic activities. What is more, both are necessary. One of the principal causes of the crisis in which the Church finds herself at present is precisely the lack of intellectual formation in the clergy and the false dialectic between pastoral work and study. The priest is formed intellectually, as that incomparable missionary St. Paul said, in order to bring every mind into homage to Christ 9 , and this is impossible to achieve without an adequate, strong intellectual and academic formation, capable of dialoguing with sound grounding and competence with contemporary culture. Without being imbued with the truth, without being solidly grounded in perennial philosophy, we might well ask ourselves: how will the priest of today be able to banish error and enlighten minds in a world which, in spite of countless signs of rejection of God, seeks Him by unexpected paths and painfully feels its need of Him 10 ? St. Paul VI asked this in Evangelii Nuntiandi. The world expects of us, yes, simplicity of life, a spirit of prayer, charity toward all… but it also expects, indeed demands, in a fundamental and preponderant way, the proclamation of the truth, clearly, challengingly and illuminatingly. And not only the world; for in the particular times of salvation history in which we are given to live, there is also in the Church a true need for the truth… for what is controversial to be clarified, for old errors swarming about under new labels to be unmasked, for the truth to be explicitly proclaimed, for authentic and traditional values to be safeguarded as is fitting, with the necessary renewal and relevance. Hence the importance of the Project whose twentieth anniversary we are celebrating. It is the intellectual apostolate, rightly understood, exercised through intellectual activities and among intellectuals (thinkers, men of science, researchers, etc.), that of itself exercises a sociocultural influence and an ecclesial service that is not only necessary but incomparable, irreplaceable… indispensable. In this sense, our Institute, born to evangelize the culture, has before it a field of action and a responsibility as great as the wide world. And although this is done in many ways, there must always be included, in a fundamental and primary way, the task of taking up and illuminating with the truth 11 even the most difficult or front-line fields, where there have been or are confrontations: at the crossroads of ideologies and in the social trenches, between the demands of man and the Christian message 12 ; it is there that our evangelizing action must reach. Hence we should all be aware of the place that this apostolate (of the Cornelio Fabro Cultural Project) must occupy within the whole of our commitments. Then the objection arises –widespread even among many members of the Church– that if we work in the intellectual field we run the risk of distancing ourselves from the real world and undervaluing the preference for the “urgent” apostolate among the poor, immigrants, care for the environment, etc., and for an active solidarity with the “voiceless.” Indeed, we will hardly be able to serve men (among them also the poor) if we have no contact with them and if we lack a minimum of experience of their life, or of the “smell of the sheep.” But let us not deceive ourselves: it is no less true that, precisely in order to promote justice and serve the poor, we must also direct our activity toward those who have responsibility or influence in the structures, or in what the Proper Law calls “the turning points of culture” 13 , among whom men of thought or ‘intellectuals’ have great social influence. We will be good servants in the social apostolate if we have a solid formation in the intellectual field; otherwise it will be very easy for us to go astray. We have seen this, and not just a few times. It is the men of thought, as you well know, who are “the principal ‘creators’ of culture, for they have an incisive influence on the behavior and cultural models of men and of societies. It is they, above all, who present to society ‘the criteria of judgment, the determining values, the points of interest, the lines of thought, the sources of inspiration and the models of life of humanity’ 14 ” 15 . Our Proper Law says this, and the Holy Pope Paul VI also said it. That is why the Spiritual Father of our Institute, St. John Paul the Great, said back in 1988: “Our time, marked by great and important sociocultural changes, urgently requires an evangelization of minds at all levels of knowledge . Therefore –the Pope goes on to say– without letting yourselves be influenced by any doubt, you must remain rigorously faithful to your charism” 16 (and I add) as well as to that bold sense of giving a convincing answer “starting from the metaphysics of being to the challenges that come from the various philosophical currents” 17 . The loneliness of modern man and the longing for an answer that gives meaning to existence must be a stimulus toward an ever more ardent and effective pastoral zeal. While today the greatest possible intellectual seriousness is required for any apostolic activity (without everything being reduced, evidently, to that), great pastoral sensitivity is also demanded. That is also why it is necessary that our intellectual activity reach “technological man, who places all his trust and all his interest in science and technology in order to attain the maximum well-being, and then finds himself empty” 18 ; that it root out the relativism that assaults consciences 19 ; that it reach the man who flaunts his unbelief; and that it also reach, why not, the churchman who strays from the purity of our faith, carried away by strange doctrines 20 , as the Apostle says. The intellectual apostolate can never and must never be confined within the walls of a library, but must be disseminated, must spread, since, as the Directory of Spirituality says: “the field of our action has no limits on its horizons” 21 , and that, I believe, is the great challenge for the future of the Fabro Project. So to speak, to “make it reach” … further and further… In a word, we must make the world a sharer in the great treasure that has been bequeathed to us. For so it is… the intellectual apostolate, rightly understood, is an apostolate with a clear and authentic ecclesial mission. Hence the urgency of having members dedicated to working on and spreading this project, which was designated at the last General Chapter as a “definitely priority” project 22 . And truly, in my humble understanding, I believe that the intellectual dimension inherent in our preferential apostolic options would not be respected if a significant number of members were not dedicated to working in an explicitly intellectual apostolate –speaking in general terms (as is being done at this time here in Fossanova)– and specifically in this project, as in any other project that promotes essential Thomism. Since that –as we know– is implied in one of the non-negotiable elements attached to our charism. I do not mean by this that the Institute should turn completely toward the intellectual, but it is undeniable that this occupies for us a relevant place when it comes to evangelizing the culture. From this follows the unconditional support that this type of apostolate deserves from us and from all the members of our Religious Family (and we must never tire of insisting on this, even if we meet with misunderstanding, even if we have to defend it and impose it); and the accompaniment that the religious employed in this task require. For it is understood and clear that those who dedicate themselves exclusively to the investigation of truth, to teaching and to dispelling the darkness of ignorance through the spreading of truth, are fulfilling a strictly pastoral office, and of the most qualified kind. 2. Learning, a requirement That is why our Proper Law says that this is not only the task of specialists or only of the members dedicated to working in the Fabro Project. It is something that concerns us all. All of us, as priests, having received from Christ the office and mission of teaching the Truth – teach all nations 23 – need “to be very attentive to the ‘signs of the times’ in order to enlighten souls at the time and moment they need it” 24 (this is a quotation from the Proper Law); that is why it is necessary to be formed not only sporadically, but permanently; what is more, the priest should be in a certain way a thinker, in order to discern the human vicissitudes that Providence disposes or permits, so as then to be able to preach well. Pope Pius XI in one of his encyclicals emphasized this very thing, saying that “the image of the Catholic priest would remain incomplete […] if we did not highlight another most important requirement that the Church demands of him: learning ” 25 . Nowadays we see how “without solid preparation, not a few priests are devoured by the world; and pastoral work itself ends up in shreds” 26 . That is why the Magisterium of the Church emphasizes that “it is necessary […] that the priest, even when already immersed in the overwhelming occupations of his holy ministry, and with his sights set on it , continue in the serious and deep study of theological subjects, increasing from day to day the sufficient store of learning acquired in the seminary with new treasures of sacred erudition that equip him more and more for preaching and for the direction of souls. He must, moreover, for the dignity of the ministry he carries out, and to win, as is fitting, the trust and esteem of the people, which serve so much for the greater fruitfulness of his pastoral labor, possess that store of knowledge , not precisely sacred, which is the common patrimony of the cultured persons of the time; that is, he must be a modern man , in the good sense of the word, as is the Church, who extends to all times, to all countries, and adapts herself to all of them; who blesses and encourages all sound initiatives and does not fear the advances, not even the boldest, of science, provided it is true science” 27 . “To evangelize the culture means to ‘make’ Christian culture, and this presupposes having culture” 28 . Without study, without knowledge of modern culture, dialogue with the world is impossible. That is why we have seen how, throughout history, the Church herself, after having preserved and saved the treasures of ancient culture, has shown us in her most illustrious Doctors how all human knowledge can contribute to the clarification and defense of the Catholic faith; among them stands out “the unsurpassed master Thomas Aquinas” 29 , whom Fr. Cornelio Fabro knew how to interpret so masterfully. That is why Fr. Fabro himself –priest and religious– presents himself to us on this anniversary as exemplary for his distinguished work in this privileged field on behalf of the Church. [ Peroratio] That is why I would like to encourage all of you, then, to continue with increased missionary zeal the magnificent work already being done. I believe that of all the apostolates the Institute carries out, perhaps the one that produces the most, tangibly and quantitatively speaking, is the Cornelio Fabro Cultural Project. For it is the apostolate that, under the guidance of the towering philosopher and theologian from Flumignano, engages like no other in an authentic dialogue with contemporary culture. “Christ, said Paul VI in a masterful phrase, made Himself contemporary to some men and spoke their language. Fidelity to Him requires that this contemporaneity continue” 30 . This, as I see it, is the great task carried out by the Cornelio Fabro Cultural Project, and it is, at the same time, the great challenge that lies before it. That is why, once again, we not only congratulate you, but we, the other members, are very grateful to you, and we wish you a future full of blessings and achievements for the cause of living Thomism. May Christ, through all of us and especially through the work of the Cornelio Fabro Cultural Project, become ever more contemporary to all men. May the Most Holy Virgin grant us this grace. Phariseeism

[Exordium] The whole biography of Jesus of Nazareth as man can be summed up in this formula: “He was the Messiah and He fought against the Pharisees” —or perhaps more briefly still: “He fought against the Pharisees.” That was the task Christ personally assigned Himself; that was His campaign 1 . The life of Christ was not an idyll but a drama, and there is no drama without an antagonist (without a villain in the story). Christ’s antagonist, the apparent victor , was Phariseeism. Without Phariseeism the whole history of Christ would have been different; and so would that of the entire world. His Church would not have been as it is now, and the universe would have followed another destiny, wholly unimaginable for us, with Israel as the head of the people of God, and not deicide and scattered. Without Phariseeism, Christ would not have died on the cross; but without Phariseeism fallen Humanity would not be this Humanity, nor would religion be religion. Phariseeism is the worm of religion; and after the fall of the First Man it is an unavoidable worm, for in this mortal life there is no fruit without its worm, nor any institution without its specific corruption. 1. Religious pride Phariseeism is religious pride . The moral portrait of the Pharisees that Christ paints in today’s Gospel is tremendous! To do all things in order to be seen by men; to broaden their phylacteries and lengthen their fringes (Mt 23:3); they are greedy for places of honor, for the first seats… they are of that generation that considers itself clean, yet is not washed of its filth (Prov 30:12). That is why Phariseeism is the subtlest and most dangerous corruption of the greatest truth: the truth that religious values come first. But the moment we claim them for ourselves, we lose them; the moment we make our own what belongs to God, it ceases to belong to anyone, if it does not become the property of the devil. The religious gesture, once one becomes self-conscious of it, turns into a grimace. The destiny of Jesus of Nazareth was to collide with Phariseeism; and once the collision occurred, the fight to the death followed inevitably. Christ came to fight against the false shepherds, against the wolves dressed as shepherds, those in sheepskin jackets. Humanity has never witnessed a sharper, more dangerous and more tragic conflict: living religion must live within dried-up religion without drying up or ceasing to be what it is, like a surge of sap that must move through a trunk turned to bark. This was the difficult and delicate work of Christ. The chair of Moses is still the chair of Moses. And as we heard in the Gospel: one must do what those seated in it say without doing what they do; and one must say a great many things that they keep silent about, which must be said, and which will make them leap up like vipers: “ to bear witness to the truth .” That must be done; and the other must not be omitted. 2. Spiritual vice Phariseeism is a spiritual vice , that is, a diabolical one, for the corruptions of the spirit are worse than the corruptions of the flesh. It is a compendium of all the spiritual vices—avarice, ambition, vainglory, pride, blindness, hardness of heart, cruelty—which has come to hollow out from within, diabolically, the three theological virtues, thus constituting the “sin against the Holy Spirit.” The deviations of the flesh are corruptions; but the deviations of the spirit are perversion. And why is it a sin against the Holy Spirit? Because the Pharisee sees himself as a holy man, a just man, almost divine, and therefore he sees all his actions as holy, just, divine. And in such a heart there is no room for the Holy Spirit to enter. That is why the words of the psalm apply to them: They have closed their heart with fat; arrogance speaks through their mouth [Ps 16(17):10]. Instinctively, the Pharisee smells out and hates true religiosity. He is its contrary, and contraries know each other. He feels certain that if he does not kill it, it will kill him. And that is why the Gospel says that the Pharisees went off and plotted how they might trap Him in some word (Mt 22:15). This whole drama unfolds in silence, in darkness, by means of cover-ups and intricate schemes. And every means is good, provided it is secret: calumny, bribery, fraud, distortion, false witness, threats. Such was the drama of Christ. Thus did the Savior die. All His meekness, all His gentleness, all His docility, His benefits, His prudence, His eloquence, His pleas, His tears, His withdrawals, His warnings, His imprecations, His prophetic threats, His artistic talent, His blood, His silent imploring as the Ecce Homo, were to shatter against the heart of the Pharisee, harder than stone. 3. Drama of Christ and His Church It is the drama of Christ and of His Church . If, in the course of the centuries, an enormous mass of suffering and even of blood had not been offered up by other christs in resisting the Pharisee, the Church would not be standing today. Does Phariseeism exist in the church today? Of course it does! But that is no excuse for leaving her or for not entering the bosom of the Catholic Church. Ven. Archbishop Fulton Sheen used to say: “[Jesus] came to place a prostitute higher than a Pharisee, the repentant thief higher than the high priest, and the prodigal son higher than his model brother. To all the frauds and pretenders who would claim they could never join the Church because His Church was not holy enough, I would ask: ‘How holy does the Church have to be before you will enter her?’ If the Church were as holy as they want her to be, they would never have been let in!” 2 . [Peroratio] None of us is exempt from falling into that spiritual vice. That is why it is supremely important to follow our Lord’s warning at the end of the Gospel we heard today: The greatest among you will be your servant. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted (Mt 23:12). Humility and the fear of God are the antidote to Phariseeism. Of Our Lady, the humble handmaid of the Lord, we ask these gifts in this Holy Mass: great humility and fear of God for ourselves and for all those in the Church who hold the office of shepherds of souls. Notes 1 In this sermon we quote freely from Fr. Leonardo Castellani, Cristo y los fariseos , prologue. 2 Ven. Fulton Sheen, The Life of Christ , ch. 21. [Translated from the English]
Our priorities in order

[Exordium] Insecurity and uncertainty are real facts of life. The very life of Christ begins with the Child in danger, and, truth be told, insecurity accompanied every step He took. If we read the Gospel from the first page to the last, we will not find a single time when Christ encourages us to nurture feelings of security. The message of Christ, as you well know, is that if one is trying to reach the end for which he was created, it is important that he realize that worldly security is an illusion. That is why, when God gives us a shake, it is important to have our priorities in order. Having decided that in these sermons I wanted to preach using examples of American saints, I came across a book that in several chapters describes various trials that our dear Fulton Sheen had to go through, and which certainly made him stagger and caused him great sorrow, but did not bring him down, precisely because he had his priorities well defined. Many of you may already know them, so I will mention, if you will, the most notable ones. 1. Trials Fulton Sheen went through as a bishop The greatest trials came upon Fulton Sheen −as you probably know− when he was already auxiliary bishop of New York. There he had several disputes with Cardinal Spellman. Spellman was the head of the richest diocese in the world and was used to getting his way. That is why some say that the clash between the most powerful and the most popular was something inevitable. On one of those occasions Cardinal Spellman insisted that Sheen, as director of the office of the Propagation of the Faith, reimburse him an enormous sum of money for powdered milk that Spellman had donated during the Korean conflict and that Propaganda Fide had distributed. Sheen refused. Because he knew that Spellman had received the milk as a donation, and so he reasoned that if the archdiocese had not paid anything, he did not have to reimburse anything. Spellman became furious and appealed to the Pope. They were fighting over powdered milk! The cardinal even tried to persuade the Pope to replace Fulton Sheen as head of the office of the Propagation of the Faith, and what is more, he offered Fulton Sheen a wealthy parish, which the latter flatly refused. Furthermore, Spellman launched three different investigations hoping to find something with which he could incriminate the auxiliary bishop, but he found nothing. Eventually the two appeared before Pope Pius XII, each presenting his case. But Fulton Sheen made a documented presentation of his, and, obviously, Spellman had not paid a cent for the milk. That meant that the cardinal had lied to the Pope and to Fulton Sheen. The Pope obviously sided with Fulton Sheen, and he remained head of Propaganda Fide. But the cardinal assured Sheen that he would make him pay for it: “it will take six months or ten years, but everyone is going to know who you are,” Spellman told Fulton Sheen. Years later Sheen would refer to this incident of the milk money as one of his crucifixions. They say that when the cardinal visited the Seminary in New York he told the seminarians that Sheen was “the most disobedient priest in the country” and that he did not want any of them to be like him. And over the years he kept coming down hard on him: traditionally Fulton Sheen preached on Good Friday from the most coveted pulpit, that of St. Patrick’s Cathedral in New York. Spellman decided that he would no longer do so, and so Sheen went to preach in New Jersey (another diocese). Later Sheen withdrew from television, and although he publicly said that he did so for “spiritual considerations,” many knew that it was the cardinal who forced him off television, even though his was the number one show in the ratings. Speaking of his struggles with the cardinal, he once said: “envy is the tribute the mediocre pay to genius.” It was during that time that Sheen wrote the Life of Christ −which I believe we have all read− because, as he himself explained, “during those days when my life was pressed against the cross, that is when I learned to know it and to love it more.” Many distanced themselves from Fulton Sheen because they did not want to risk becoming victims of the cardinal’s fury for being friends of the auxiliary bishop. A short time later Spellman exiled him from New York −some say so that he would stop overshadowing him− and made him bishop of Rochester. In his farewell sermon in St. Patrick’s Cathedral, in front of Spellman himself and some 3,000 faithful, Fulton Sheen began his sermon by thanking the cardinal, with his usual irony, “for those priestly intimacies that have united us forever.” 2. A petition against him Barely 15 months after becoming bishop he was already thinking of leaving, since in fact things were going rather badly for him. 125 priests of his diocese signed a petition against him. And that is how he later submitted his resignation and ceased to be bishop of Rochester after only 34 months. As he was leaving to take the plane to leave his diocese, he said to his vicar: “It used to be a glory to be a bishop. But nowadays I would not wish it even on my best friend.” Two weeks later he appeared on a television program and, without referring to Cardinal Spellman, said: “I would have gone far in the Church… but I did not want to pay the price.” The journalist asked him what that price was, and Fulton Sheen simply evaded the question, saying: “Well, I felt it would have been a lack of loyalty to my own principles and, I think, to Christian practice.” An upright man with his priorities very clear. When he moved to New York he told his niece: “I never thought I would end up washing dishes and making my own bed. It is not an unhappy adventure.” He distributed his vast library among various people and institutions and moved into an apartment that his family found for him. That is how this man went from being followed by multitudes, respected, admired… rubbing shoulders with the celebrities of the world and the great figures of the Church, with all the worldly securities that this entails, to being a poor priest living alone in a three-room apartment. But he lived and died with his head held high because he was not beholden to anyone. Everything was crumbling around him; those who before followed him and wanted his company now avoided him. His own cardinal went around everywhere running him down. Imagine how piercing the pain must have been that more than a hundred priests of his diocese asked that he leave… The sense of failure and frustration must have been immense. 3. We have a purpose in life And yet, this is the same man who wrote: “Very often the temptation will be very strong and the temporal advantages will seem grand to us” −for example, if one concentrates more on what is most immediate to him: the parish, study, preaching spiritual exercises, giving a little talk here or there… even one’s own province, simply because it is more gratifying, one sees immediate, tangible results, if you will−. “We have a purpose in life, but if we never stop to think why we are here, or where we are going, or what the purpose of our life is, we will end up changing our direction but we will not make progress. And what is worse, we will get stuck in those tiny, successive and incomplete destinations, only to end up completely lost. If a man who is lost in the forest had a distant point outside the forest to serve him as a reference, he could freely leave the forest or remain there. The same happens in life: if we have a fixed goal, we can make real progress toward that goal, but it would be complete stupidity to say that we are progressing (or doing things well) if we are constantly changing that goal. Our Lord on the Cross gave us an example of this: He left everything , even His own life, in order to run toward the goal. […] That is why we must NEVER step down from the supreme end and purpose of our life.” So far Fulton Sheen. This great man went through everything he went through, but they could not defeat him because he had his priorities in order, and thus he made history. [Peroratio] Mutatis mutandi , we, as religious of the Institute, and by the office that Providence has assigned us, have a goal, which in our case is to defend and guard the patrimony of the Institute, not to allow them to come and steal our candidates before our very eyes, to ensure unity among our own, to see to it that our ranks increase and do not decrease… That is the noble responsibility and the priority at this moment. It depends on us. If Fulton Sheen had shrunk back and had not stood firm against the leader of the richest diocese in the world, he would have ended up paying Spellman what he did not owe. If he had not had his priorities very clear, he would have left Propaganda Fide for a comfortable and wealthy parish, or he would have negotiated keeping quiet in order to continue with his television show. If he had let it go to his head, he would have clung to his office as bishop whether the priests liked it or not… but that was not the case. He was a man of a single purpose: to serve God, come what may. In one of his books he wrote −and with this I conclude−: “ We must do everything that is within our power to fulfill the will of God… but everything that is outside our power we must set aside and submit to His Holy Will. Note the difference, Sheen goes on to say, between within our power and outside our power . We must not be fatalists. Some things are under our control . What is wrong with fatalism is that it fails to recognize that, within certain limits, our will can affect the events of life . It would therefore be a grave error not to do the very best we can for the good of our brothers and the glory of God . It is the will of God that we men use our free will, subordinated to His Will, in order to be happy.” We ask the Virgin Mother for light to have our priorities very clear at this moment.
United by a higher cause

[Exordium] Chesterton used to say: “Real soldiers fight not because they hate what they have in front of them but because they love what lies behind them.” This was the case of many missionaries who one day left everything to embark on the marvelous enterprise of sowing the faith in distant lands. Many of them −as good soldiers of Christ− even gave their lives for what they rightly believed to be the greatest cause, the “most divine work among the divine” 1 , which is the salvation of souls. They took with them only the faith they had learned and, branded as with fire, the identity of religious of the congregation that had begotten them as such This was the case of the North American Martyrs: Jean de Brébeuf, Isaac Jogues, Gabriel Lalemant, Antoine Daniel, Charles Garnier, Noël Chabanel (six priests) and René Goupil and Jean de la Lande (brothers). All Jesuits, all with very strong personalities, very different from one another, with different preparation, some with more and others with fewer years of religious life, but all united by the same ideal: the greater glory of God, as good Jesuits. Incredible trials These men were not content to live side by side, like someone who shares a mission as if sharing an office −in fact they changed companions quite often−; rather, they strengthened one another as they made their way in the mission, and they fought together as good soldiers for the noble cause for which they had been chosen according to the providentially merciful designs of our Lord. To read their writings, their chronicles, their letters is to read a hymn of hope in the midst of incredible trials. If one thinks about it carefully, all the martyrs −and I believe these especially− proclaim to us the message of “not giving up,” of “not throwing in the towel,” even in the worst situations. This suits us very well, because the habitual setting in which the life of a member of the Institute must unfold includes precisely “the most difficult situations and the most adverse conditions” 2 . Sometimes we think that the martyrs were only witnesses of our faith, and indeed they were! But they also remind us that God draws good out of evil. The martyrs did not think that tortures or death itself were the most disastrous thing that could happen to them. On the contrary! They realized the unparalleled opportunity they had in each of those trials to give glory to God, to serve their Institute. That is why it is important to ponder their lives so as to put ours in true perspective. To make St. Jean de Brébeuf stop preaching, his torturers thrust a red-hot iron rod through his mouth down to his throat, cut off his nose, tore off his lips… With that same burning iron they gouged out his eyes and those of his companion (Gabriel Lalemant). In mockery, pretending a baptism, they poured boiling water over their heads, cut off their burnt skin in large pieces, and the Indians ate it in front of them. While they were still alive, they opened their chests, tore out their hearts and drank their blood. Brébeuf’s martyrdom lasted 3 hours. Lalemant’s, 15. Brébeuf was 52 years old, Lalemant 47. But greater was the love they had for what lay behind all that: God and the Society. An eminent favor St. Jean de Brébeuf has a magnificent letter that he wrote to his superior in France several years before his martyrdom, in which he tells him that perhaps they are close to martyrdom, but that he is not very sure that God is going to give him that grace; but that “be that as it may,” says this iron-willed Jesuit, “all our fathers await the resolution of this matter with great calm and a contented spirit. As for me, I can tell you in all sincerity that I have not yet had the slightest apprehension or fear of death for this cause (that of the salvation of souls). One thing we regret, and it is that these poor barbarians, through their own malice, close themselves to the Gospel and to the grace of God.” This is being said by a missionary who, after six years of apostolic work, had baptized only one adult. And he continues: “whatever conclusion they come to, and regardless of the treatment they give us, we will try, with the help of God, to bear it patiently for His service . It is truly an eminent favor that God does us in allowing us to bear something for His love. It is only now that we consider ourselves true members of the Society ” 3 . Because “real soldiers fight not because they hate what they have in front of them but because they love what lies behind them.” Again: the martyrs do not remind us that God can draw good out of evil. And although these Missionaries did not live to see it, their letters generated a quite singular enthusiasm in the Jesuit college in France, from which the missionaries for the foreign missions eventually came. These missionaries were ordinary men, so to speak; they had their failings, they had their miseries, they had their temperaments; some never adapted to mission life, as is the case of the martyr Noël Chabanel, who felt great repugnance for the food and the customs of the Indians; everything bothered him; in fact, he never learned the language, and this giant made a vow to remain among those Indians until death. And he died from an ax blow to the head by a ‘Christian’ Indian who betrayed him. Some of these missionaries were already worn out from so much daily struggle, so much self-denial, so many spiritual trials, so much perplexity before an uncertain future 4 , so much misery of their own and of others, and yet what makes it possible for us today to call them martyrs was the heroism with which they took upon their shoulders the cause for which they had been sent. They endured everything they endured, not for their own glory, not to say: ‘ah… I am invincible,’ but for the glory of God and of the Society. Because “ real soldiers fight not because they hate what they have in front of them but because they love what lies behind them .” Another of the martyrs, St. Isaac Jogues, wrote to another priest asking for prayers before leaving for New France. And he tells him: “I will have to live among those barbarians almost without freedom to pray, without Mass, without sacraments. I will be held responsible for each and every incident between the Iroquois and the French… What does it matter? My hope is in God , who has no need of my achievements for the accomplishment of His designs. All we need to do is try to be faithful and not spoil His work with our weaknesses.” That is the message. The greatest cause Throughout the whole pilgrimage through this valley of tears that the mission in New France meant, they encouraged one another, they gave each other courage, they forgot themselves in order to help the other. None of them expected to be spared from death. None expected heaven to open and an angel to come and rescue them from the midst of the drama they were living. But all of them hoped that God would be served by their lives and by their deaths. Men: what is happening to us is what had to happen to us for being faithful to our ideal, to our identity, to our mission. And perhaps only now can we consider ourselves true members of the Institute . We will probably die of what any ordinary person dies of: a heart attack, cancer, a car accident… what does it matter? Most of us will know that we are dying when we are dying. But we too have the same opportunity as the martyrs to give our life to God day by day, with all its demands, with all its trials, with all the attacks they may wish to perpetrate against us… The important thing is that “if one must keep watch, one keeps watch; if one must suffer, one suffers; if one must be humbled, one is humbled; if one must beg for alms, one begs; if one must fall ill, one falls ill; if one must die, one dies; but one dies in battle, with honor and with glory, with Christ and in the name of Christ and for the glory of Christ” 5 and the good of the Institute. Our capacity to accept suffering out of love for the Institute, out of love for the good itself, for truth, for justice, is what makes each one of us a man like these martyrs we have spoken about. Because when my well-being, my reputation, my health, my little job, “my little kiosk” −as Fr. Buela would say− is more important than the greatest cause that unites us, than the priority for which we must all fight together, then my life is a lie… because we came here to give our life for our brothers, as the Incarnate Word taught us. These men achieved what they achieved and persevered to the end because they remained united , because they fought it out together, because there was synergy between the gift of God and the commitment of each one 6 to move things forward . [Peroratio] We must succeed in taking on, with generosity and intelligence, the challenges that present themselves to us. Let us not be overcome by discouragement or weariness. Let us not, “because of the tree of difficulties, lose sight of the forest of things that are going well” 7 . Many of us sometimes feel that we are not going to be able to do it, and we feel like David before Goliath, but we must surpass our expectations. Like these martyrs, we must choose to rise above the average. If you allow me, I would now like to take advantage of this Eucharistic celebration to give thanks to God for each one of you, for the days past and for those to come! May God and the Blessed Virgin comfort you and give you all the encouragement you need to continue fulfilling that commitment, always demanding and so frequently accompanied by the sign of the cross, by a painful loneliness, and which demands on our part a profound sense of responsibility, a generosity without weaknesses or straying, a constant forgetfulness of self. May Our Lady of Luján, Mother of the Hope that does not disappoint, renew our vigor and assist us in our endeavor to do more and better for the cause of the Institute, which is none other than the cause of the Incarnate Word. Spiritual Writings and Biographical Sketches , p. 158. 4 Isaac Jogues wrote that he often could not hold back his tears, not so much because of the martyrdom of his companions as because of anxiety about the future. 5 St. Pedro Poveda. 6 Cf. Directory of Fraternal Life , 36. 7 Cf. Constitutions , 123 .
“He ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father”

It now falls to us to consider the mystery so consoling for us Christians, which is the mystery of the Ascension of the Lord. The Ascension is the fruit of His Passion After the Resurrection, Our Lord remained forty days with His disciples; during them Jesus prepared the nascent Church and strengthened it so that it might know how to bear His absence. At the end of those forty days, Christ led them all toward Bethany, a small village near Jerusalem; there the scene of the farewell would unfold, for there His Ascension into Heaven would take place. At that moment the event occurred: He raised those precious arms that bore the marks of the nails. That gesture would be the last memory of the Master that the apostles would keep. Those hands that now are raised so that afterwards, from heaven, they may descend toward the earth, bestowing unceasing blessings. Those hands that had been pierced by the nails of the cross—the moment had come for them to give their last blessing: While He was blessing them, He parted from them and was carried up into heaven 1 , says the Gospel of St. Luke. The Ascension took place on the Mount of Olives, at whose foot Bethany lies. To get there, He led His apostles through Bethany, which meant that He had to pass through the very place where Christ had suffered, for they crossed the Mount of Olives; from there Christ had wept when He saw Jerusalem, and it was from there, from a mount situated above the garden of twisted olive trees stained by the Blood of the Passion, from there that Christ manifested His supreme power by rising in body and soul to the Father who is in heaven. With this He taught us a great truth: that the Ascension and the glory of heaven were the fruit of that crucifixion. That in order to ascend to heaven, men must first face and bear the sufferings and crosses that present themselves to us on this earth, so as then to be able to enter thus into His glory. He had said, referring to Himself: It was necessary that the Messiah should suffer, so as thus to enter into His glory 2 . It is remarkable, but if He had been crowned on earth instead of ascending to heaven, the thoughts men would have conceived about Him would have remained confined to the earth. But the Ascension would cause the minds and hearts of men to rise above earthly things. It is sometimes hard to believe that precisely He, the Man of sorrows, acquainted with anguish and suffering, should now be in glory. It is hard to believe that He who had not wanted to come down from a cross could now go up to heaven. It is hard to believe that He who in the manger of Bethlehem had no strength to lift His arms should now raise them and rise with them to His Father’s house. The Ascension now dispelled all these doubts by bringing His human nature into an intimate and eternal communion with God. Men had mocked that human nature which He had assumed at His birth, when the soldiers blindfolded Him and asked Him to guess who was striking Him. They mocked Him as prophet; they mocked Him as king by putting a royal garment on Him and a reed for a scepter. Finally, they mocked Him as priest by challenging Him—He who was offering Himself as victim—to come down from the cross. But the vindication would be complete when He came in His justice, as judge of men, in the very human nature that He had taken from men. None of us who will be judged by God will be able to complain that God was ignorant of the trials to which we mortals are subjected. When He judges us, His very appearance will show that He has fought the same battles as men and suffered the same temptations as those who appear before the tribunal of divine justice. Triumphant wounds But there is something more important in the Ascension, and no less consoling, and it is what completes the phrase of the article of the Creed that falls to us today: He ascended into heaven, and is seated at the right hand of God the Father almighty. Another of the great reasons why Our Lord ascended to heaven in body and soul was so that He might plead, intercede before our Father with a human nature: He is true God, but He is also true man, and He can ask as a man, one with the rest of men. Now He can, by the mere fact of showing the wounds of His glory, not only as a trophy of victory but also as insignia of intercession. Before those triumphant wounds, through whose intercession all graces come to us. Christ, from the moment of the Ascension, is seated at the right hand of the Father; from there He intercedes for us. That is why we Christians must never cease to consider this truth: Christ lives in heaven, and it would be great folly to live as if He no longer existed. Our religion did not end on a Good Friday; rather, it triumphed with the victory of the resurrection, and with the Ascension it continues on its way toward its end, until the last of the elect enters the kingdom of heaven. That is why He can give us, and in fact does give us, if we ask Him faithfully, everything we need; and He knows well what we lack: no one like Him experienced that this life was a valley of tears, and He suffered the vicissitudes of the passion; He was like us in all things but sin: Having, then, a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let us remain steadfast in the faith. For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who has been made like us in all things but sin 3 . Christ ascended and there He waits for us, so that, following in His footsteps, we may arrive where He is, for, as He Himself said, I go up to prepare a place for you 4 , a place that awaits us and that none of us may leave empty. He had said in the Gospel of St. John: When I am lifted up from the earth I will draw all to myself 5 . Christ longs for us to reach that place; He watches over us and keeps us very much in mind. Sacred Scripture says: The eyes of God are fixed on His faithful 6 —fixed; that is, it is not that, being now in heaven with His mission finished, He is no longer interested in the things of earth; on the contrary, His priesthood is eternal and He wants to give us that glory which He won with so much effort on the Friday of the passion. If we live in accordance with this dogma of our faith, we will understand what a saint used to say: one thing is necessary, to reach heaven. All the sufferings and tribulations and troubles of this life die before one great truth: Christ has risen and is seated at the right hand of God 7 . That is why we must reach where He is; we may fail in many things, but in this we cannot fail. St. Alphonsus said: everything is little, not to say everything is nothing, so long as we gain paradise 8 . There all the problems of this life will come to an end. That is why, whatever may happen, when discouragement assails us, when sufferings and tribulations surround us, let us think of heaven, and let us think of Jesus Christ present in heaven; on Him our gaze must be fixed, because only there will we be happy, where, as the canon of the Mass says, God will wipe away the tears from our eyes, and there will be no more grief, nor pain, nor sadness , because we will arrive at the Father’s house, at the day without sunset, at the light that has no end, there where, as our Lord says in the Gospel, your sadness will be turned into joy 9 . As we contemplate today, in this novena to St. Cajetan, the mystery of the Ascension of the Lord, may God grant us the enormous grace of always living with our gaze fixed on heaven, and may we never give up in the struggle to get there, so that there may be fulfilled in us what Christ asked of the Father before the Passion: Father, I pray for them, that where I am, they also may be 10 . May the Most Blessed Virgin, who so many times after the Ascension must have fixed her eyes on the sky of Jerusalem, seeing her Son waiting for her with open arms, grant this grace to us all. Notes 1 Lk 24:51. 2 Cf. 24:26. 3 Heb 4:14-15. 4 Jn 14:2. 5 Jn 12:32. 6 Ps 32:18. 7 Cf. Rom 8:34. 8 Preparation for Eternity . 9 Jn 16:20. 10 Jn 17:24.
World Day of Prayer for the Missions

Dear brothers: Today, on this day, on this Sunday, we keep the World Mission Day. The Church therefore invites us today, once again, to consider the missionary vocation of the Catholic Church. This vocation is inscribed in the very moment of her institution: when Christ, after spending the whole night in prayer, chose the first twelve, that budding apostolic college had a single purpose: to send them out to preach. In the Gospels, Christ never tires of repeating that he has been sent to preach the good news, to announce the Kingdom of God, to bear witness to the Father, and so on, and he crowns it all by saying: as the Father has sent me, so I send you. There is no doubt: the Church was born with a missionary vocation; such are the last words of our Lord in the four Gospels, words that must be branded with fire on everyone who has a Catholic heart. Thus we read in the Gospel of Matthew, at the final farewell on the mount of the Ascension: “Go, teach all nations, … teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you … I will be with you until the end of time.” Mark is more explicit: “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature, … these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons, they will speak new tongues, they will take up serpents in their hands, and if they drink poison it will not harm them; they will lay their hands on the sick and these will be healed.” In St. Luke he told them that penance for the remission of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem. The last words that St. John gives us are also words of mission; they are Christ's desire before a heart that loves him: after the threefold confession of love, he says to Peter: “Feed my sheep.” Even the Acts of the Apostles, which narrate the beginnings of the Church, open by pointing out that Jesus ascended into heaven while charging his own: “And you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea, in Samaria and to the ends of the earth.” The Church was born for mission; mission is inscribed in the very essence of the Christian vocation: to be a Christian means to be a missionary; to be a Christian means to have a soul stirred by a longing for mission. This means having a Catholic spirit, a universal spirit: to the ends of the earth. 1. The salvation of souls To preach Christ, to carry the gospel to the ends of the earth; to make men share in the Life that comes from Him, to make men love God, the glory of God, the salvation of souls: here is the vocation of the Catholic Church. It is for this end that the Church forms priests in her seminaries; it is for this end that the Church sends her most dedicated and virtuous priests to the most inhospitable lands and countries. I think now of the priests and missionaries who suffer hardships, who endure hunger and privation, who are locked up in prisons and often subjected to torture for confessing Christ: “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to the whole creation.” There come to mind those two missionary priests in Sudan, in Khartoum (the capital), who, according to the latest report of the Congregation for the Evangelization of Peoples (the Roman congregation in charge of the missions, to which the collections of all the churches and chapels of all Christendom are sent on this day), are still being tortured so that they will confess to a crime they never committed; the priests who in Arab countries cannot make their names known; those who were imprisoned in Vietnam last month; those who in China are condemned to capital punishment if they do not answer to the national Church; and so many others who spend and wear out their lives, as St. Paul said, so that Christ may reign, so that Christ may conquer and so that Christ may command. It is for this end that so many men and women, leaving behind the pleasures and riches of this world, have dedicated their lives to the enclosure of monasteries to pray for the mission of the Church: “the salvation of souls” (St. Thérèse of Lisieux, Edith Stein). How much a soul is worth! When one reads the Gospel texts that lead Christ toward Jerusalem, one can penetrate into the heart of Christ and his love for souls: “I have a baptism of fire with which to be baptized, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished!” Before the Passion, at the moment of the institution of the Eucharist, we read: “having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.” A truly great work: Pseudo-Dionysius: “it is the most divine of all divine works.” St. John Chrysostom: “whoever converts a single soul pleases God more than if he were to give away all his goods. There is nothing dearer to God than the salvation of souls.” Clement of Alexandria: “it is so pleasing to God that one would say He has no greater desire than to see all men saved.” Our Lord to Fr. Colnado: “work for the conversion of sinners, for nothing is more pleasing to me.” The martyr St. Carpus said to his executioners: “Strike me again, for again I am ready to die for sinners.” St. Lawrence Justinian: “if you are concerned for the honor of God, you cannot seek it in any better way than by working for the salvation of souls.” St. Bernard: “In the eyes of God, one soul is worth more than the whole world.” This was the obsession of the saints: For St. Thérèse of Lisieux: “I desire only one thing: to make God loved.” St. Augustine: “If you love God, sweep everyone along toward divine love.” St. Alphonsus Maria: “Whoever truly loves God does all he can to move everyone to love Him.” St. Teresa said: “Whenever we read in the lives of the saints that they converted souls, it stirs in me much more devotion, more tenderness and more envy than all the martyrdoms they suffer; for this is the inclination Our Lord has given me, since it seems to me that He prizes one soul that, through His mercy, we might win for Him by our effort and prayer more than all the services we can render Him in this life.” Don Orione exclaimed: “Place me, Lord, at the mouth of hell, so that by your mercy I may close it.” For the saints this was something truly great: St. John Chrysostom: “I would wish to be regarded as an object of execration, provided that my subjects were converted.” St. Bonaventure: “I would undergo as many deaths as there are sinners in the world, so that they might be saved.” Of St. Cajetan it is said that “he died of grief at seeing the souls that were being lost.” 2. We and the missionary work Dear brothers, before such greatness we certainly cannot remain indifferent. We too, to the extent of our possibilities, must undertake the work of the salvation of souls, “the most divine of divine works,” and labor in our own surroundings so that those who are in contact with us may attain what the Fathers of the Church called “the grace of graces,” that is: “the grace of saving one's soul.” This is a great sign of predestination: St. Augustine said: “If you have saved a soul, you have predestined your own.” And St. James , in his letter: “ Know that whoever brings back a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins .” And may the universal mission of the Church never be indifferent or foreign to us, so that men may know Jesus Christ and the Life that comes from Him. May it not happen to us as to the one who had one talent and was rejected by our Lord because he did not make it bear fruit. According to St. Ambrose: “these are the ones who can work for the salvation of souls and do not do so.” And St. Augustine, to those who say that it is enough to save their own soul, says: “What are you saying? Do you not remember the servant who hid his talent?” May this day, on which the Church makes us recall our missionary vocation, serve to enkindle in us a thirst for souls. May we not incur the reproach of the angels at the Ascension of the Lord: “ Men of Galilee, why do you stand there looking up at heaven …?” May the Blessed Virgin make us aware of our vocation, and grant us a missionary heart, a Catholic heart. “Do not speak to me of finis terrae , a magic name that would close the path to every intention. A man of small ambition is he who would shut up his longings in so mean a word. As long as there remains one border of the earth that does not praise the One who came to save us, the earth has no end.”
To enjoy the wonderful exchange

Jn 1:1-18 – Preface of the Nativity III What existed from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have contemplated and our hands have touched concerning the Word of life (…) we proclaim to you 1 . My dear all, on this solemn day, on which we celebrate the birth of Christ, the Incarnate Word, we feel the truth, the power and the joy of these words of the apostle St. John. That God of whom no image must be made, because any image would only manage to diminish Him, and even to falsify Him, this God has made Himself visible in the One who is His true image, as St. Paul says (cf. 2 Cor 4:4; Col 1:15) 2 . This is the mystery of Christmas, which allows us to touch –so to speak– the humility of God. He who, as we said yesterday, has entered into human history and dwelt among us , in order to give us the capacity to become children of God, to be like Him. Each of the mysteries of Christ is not only a historical fact but contains special graces for the nourishment of our soul. What is that particular grace? The Church herself points it out to us in the collect we have just prayed: “… Grant us to share in the divine life of him who willed to share in our humanity .” A petition that touches us, the members of the Institute, very closely, since being configured to Him 3 , wanting “to be other Christs, is central to our spirituality” 4 . We are asking for the grace to share in that divinity to which our humanity was united. For in becoming incarnate God took our human nature and in exchange communicated to us a participation in his divine nature. This is the admirable exchange that God wants to make with us and with each and every man. That is why St. John of the Cross, in his Spiritual Canticle , asked the Lord: “assail my intellect with your divinity, giving it divine understanding, and my will, giving and communicating to it divine love, and my memory, with divine possession of glory” 5 . That is what we must strive for! That “God may bring us into his divine splendors by transformation of love” 6 . As He did that night with the shepherds. The Word who was in the beginning, with God 7 and through whom all things were made 8 invites us to be like Him. That is, to become like children, which is another way of saying to become humble. For this it is necessary to lay aside our false certainties, our intellectual pride, which so often prevents us from perceiving the nearness of God. We must get down, go spiritually on foot, so to speak, in order to be able to enter through the door of faith and find God, God who hides himself in the humility of a newborn child 9 . That going on foot, spiritually speaking, in order to enjoy to the full the wonderful exchange that God wants to make in each one of us, requires that one make progress in the practice of humility. Because only by being humble will we be saints 10 , that is, only by being humble will we imitate the Incarnate Word whom we contemplate today lying in a manger, surrounded by animals, in utter poverty, rejected by so many, and who, being so weak, is the very Infinite, Immense and Eternal God. In short, because only by being little can we discover something great, and only in that way can the meaning of the Incarnation be understood 11 . The humble, simple souls, little enough to see the greatness of God in the littleness of a Child, are therefore the only ones who will understand the reason for His visit. He came to this poor world to bring us a proposal; to tell us as only God could say: “You give me your humanity, and I will give you my Divinity; you give me your time, and I will give you my eternity; you give me your weary body, and I will give you my Redemption; you give me your withered heart, and I will give you Love; you give me your insignificance, and I will give you My All.” The world, so inclined to power, never seems to learn the paradox that, just as only the very little child discovers the greatness of what surrounds him, so only humble hearts will one day realize the greatness of God. You are not unaware that the world rejects this lesson. Why? Because it confuses littleness with weakness, the littleness of a child with childishness or immaturity, and humility with an inferiority complex. But that Child whom the angels adore 12 descended to the littleness of childhood as the first step toward his eternal triumph. And we must begin our eternal mission as He willed to begin His, that is, by the way of humility, which implies descending from our ignorant pride to the level at which we stand before His divine eyes. Jesus himself taught us: … Unless you turn and become like children you will not enter the kingdom of heaven 13 . To become like little children means nothing other than humility or sincerity of judgment about ourselves, an acknowledgment of the disproportion between our poor life and the eternal life before us, an acknowledgment of our weakness, our frailty, our sins, the poverty of all that we are doing now, and also of the power and the wisdom that are to be ours, provided that we are humble enough to kneel before this Child in a manger of straw and confess to Him that He is Our Lord, the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father 14 , our Life and Our All. Very particularly for us, this contemplation of Jesus in his birth, as we were saying a moment ago, must move us to practice the virtues of self-emptying 15 , among which humility is the first, and which our Proper Law translates “into the humility of a hidden life, into the acceptance of sufferings in order to complete in one’s own flesh what is lacking in the tribulations of Christ (Col 1:24), into silent sacrifice, into abandonment to the holy will of God, into serene fidelity even in the face of the decline of one’s strength and of one’s own influence” 16 . Something that is very proper to contemplative religious, since it is the fruit of the life of prayer 17 and of the true prayerful attitude that must permeate the whole life of the monk. That is why Fulton Sheen said that the closer we are to God, the more we become like children 18 , the more we become humble. Now, this humility of children is not simply a spiritual metaphor, nor is it a pious external pose. “To attain humility we must love and desire humiliations. Without that there can be no humility,” said Blessed Joseph Allamano. These humiliations may come to us from our own deficiencies, from our defeats or even from our mistakes, if not also from the ill will of our neighbor. Without this serene, even joyful acceptance of humiliations there is no authentic humility. But our calling is to imitate the Incarnate Word, and in order to enjoy to the full the wonderful exchange that God wants to make in each one of us, that is, to transform us into Him, it is necessary to practice humility actively and effectively. So that, by exercising ourselves along that path, we may attain the humility of the truly spiritual, which the mystical Doctor of Fontiveros describes as follows: “not only do they consider their own things as nothing, but they are very little satisfied with themselves; they regard all others as much better, and usually have a holy envy of them, with a desire to serve God as they do; because, the more fervor they have and the more works they do and the more delight they take in them, since they walk in humility, the more they know how much God deserves and how little is all that they do for him. And so great is what they would like to do for him out of charity and love that all they do seems nothing to them; and this loving care so urges, occupies and absorbs them that they never notice whether others do or do not do; and if they do notice, it is all, as I say, believing that all the others are much better than they. Hence, holding themselves in little esteem, they also want others to hold them in little esteem and to belittle and disparage their things. And even if others want to praise and esteem them, they can in no way believe it, and it seems strange to them that such good things should be said of them. These, with great tranquility and humility, have a great desire to be taught by anyone who can benefit them. Far from wanting to be anyone’s teachers, they are very ready to walk and set off on a path other than the one they are following, if they are ordered to, because they never think they are right in anything. They rejoice when others are praised; they only grieve that they do not serve God as those others do. They have no desire to speak of their own things, because they hold them in so little esteem that they are ashamed to tell them even to their spiritual masters, thinking that they are not things worth talking about. They are more eager to tell their faults and sins, or to have them known, than their virtues; and so they are more inclined to deal about their souls with those who think less of their things and their spirit. These will give the blood of their hearts to whoever serves God, and will help, as far as lies in them, so that He may be served. In the imperfections into which they see themselves fall, they bear with themselves with humility, and with meekness of spirit and loving fear of God, hoping in Him” 19 . On this beautiful Christmas morning, on which we celebrate the incalculable mystery of the humiliation of the Son of God, let us ask the Blessed Mother, who bent down to adore her Child-God, for the gift of humility, so that we may contemplate in the most tender breast of the Child Jesus the Heart of this God who “wants to be our ‘joy,’ our ‘salvation,’ our ‘hope,’ our ‘happiness,’ and our ‘only Sovereign’” 20 . May She teach us how to serve God, how to love God, how to pray to God.
