Directory of Contemplative Life , Appendix, 1: “a true prayerful attitude must be attained (like the soul sinking its depths into God), whose effects are very perceptible: love of the cross, authentic humility , love of corrections, patience in bearing injustices, acceptance of one’s own faults, longing for penance…”. 18 Cf. In the Fullness of Time , ch. 1. [Translated from the English] 19 St. John of the Cross, Dark Night , Book I, ch. 2, 1-8. 20 Cf. Fr. Carlos Buela, IVE, Ars Patris , Part III, Ch. 21.
A people who walked in darkness… have seen a great light

Homily preached to the monks of the Incarnate Word on the occasion of the feast of the Holy Family Homily in Getafe – St. Mother Maravillas December 30, 2018 Lk 2:41-52 Today we celebrate the beautiful feast of the Holy Family, which presents to us the sorrowful episode of the loss of the Child Jesus in the temple, which was, according to several authors, the greatest sorrow of the heart of the Mother of the Incarnate Word. The Gospel narrative allows us to imagine the life of the Holy Family in Nazareth, interrupted only by the obligations of religion, as we have just read: they used to go to Jerusalem every year for the feast of Passover . Jesus, Son of Mary, who at that time was surely 12 years old, walked at his Mother’s side. Let us think with how much tenderness the Virgin would contemplate her Son, and how each minute he would seem to her more beautiful than the moment before. After arriving at the gates of the city, the Holy Family went to the Temple for the celebration of the Passover, and there St. Joseph and the Virgin knelt on the steps of the temple with that Child before whom every knee must bend … When the feast was over and the crowds were returning to their homes, the men through one gate, the women through another, all gathered in one place to rest for the night, and it was then that Mary and Joseph realized that the Child Jesus was not with them. Imagine how terrible the grief of the Immaculate Heart of Mary was. The Virgin-Mother herself declares her affliction when she says: we have been looking for you, full of anguish. There were many sorrows in the world that night, but none like Hers. That is why an author says poetically: “If the stars had had a heart, they would not have shone that night.” How much anguish in the heart of that Mother! Our Lady seemed to be in darkness, as if she did not understand what the Lord was doing with Her. Yet she did not cease to seek Jesus, true God and true Man, who had gone away from Her. Perhaps never before had our Most Holy Mother realized how united her Heart was to that of her precious Son Jesus. Today, in this beautiful season of Christmas, we find ourselves, by the merciful design of God, celebrating this Holy Mass before the tomb of St. Mother Maravillas of Jesus. She too was the spiritual mother of countless souls, and she too had her heart fixed on the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus and on that of his Holy Mother, the Virgin Mary. Everyone knows of Mother Maravillas’ immense love for the Heart of Jesus. To look no further, the reason for the existence of the Carmel on the Cerro de los Ángeles was to satisfy the request that the Divine Heart made to her “with loud cries” to have a Carmel that would keep Him loving company. But great and tender too was Mother Maravillas’ devotion to the Mother of God, from whom she seems to have learned to love the Heart of Jesus so faithfully and so perfectly. For, like Most Holy Mary, she too made the will of God the axis of her life and lived totally abandoned to whatever his designs disposed for her. This is undoubtedly the fruit of her deep Marian devotion. She herself confessed: “I have taken the Most Holy Virgin as Mother in a most special way, and She is also the one in charge of preparing me, covering me and protecting me” (56: C-3193). In her letters, in her exhortations, in her conversations, she always repeated that the only important thing and the source of true happiness was to grow in the love of God, to please Him and to live attentive to his will, after the example of Mary: “How happy we are, truly wanting what He wants, and concerning ourselves with nothing but loving Him and saying yes to Him in everything!”; “She who most consoles our Christ,” she would tell her nuns, “will be the happiest”; “The greatest happiness on earth, which nothing can take away from us, consists in uniting oneself to God and fulfilling his will, loving Him and serving Him.” This love of God, which grew to gigantic proportions in the soul of Mother Maravillas as the years went by, can be said to have been the natural consequence of the deep and true love she professed for the Blessed Virgin, which led her silently and so quickly to the feet of the Heart of Jesus. She always liked to recall how great her joy was on learning that Carmel belongs entirely to Mary. Indeed, very frequently in her letters she called her convents “the houses of Our Lady” and said: “How can we live in her house, and please the Lord together with Her, without imitating her, as the Holy Mother desired? […]. It seemed to me that, since the Lord has me here now, I must strive for it, not only for myself, but so that this house may truly be the house of Our Lady: to be truly poor, sacrificed, humble, nothing” (28: C-101). You will also remember that episode when, in view of the difficulty she experienced in praying the fifteen mysteries of the rosary every day, she bound herself to it by a vow. This devotion to the Virgin Mary, so simple yet so deeply rooted in the heart of Mother Maravillas, is what –it seems to me– led her to love the Son of God so dauntlessly. That is why we, the religious of the Incarnate Word, are asked to have Mary as “the model, the guide and the form of all our acts” 1 . We are further bound to this by the most sweet duty acquired through the fourth vow that we one day professed to the Mother of God. Now, if devotion to Our Lady is common to every Christian, and therefore common to all religious, it must nevertheless be distinctive of all the monks of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, as the rule clearly specifies: “Every monk of the Institute of the Incarnate Word… must have a particular devotion to the Blessed Virgin” 2 , striving “to live to the full the ‘interior and true devotion’ of the slaves of Mary” 3 . And the Directory adds: “Because of his special configuration with Christ the Victim, the monk must seek strength in her in moments of trial, because she remains at the foot of the cross of each one of her children” 4 . I would like then, if you will allow me, to point out briefly three lessons that it seems to me we can learn from the sorrow of the Mother of God, which made her so close to us in our search for Him, using in this case some passages from the writings of Mother Maravillas. 1. To pray with reality. True prayer is born from the heart, from the present moment we are living, because prayer is precisely being honest and transparent before God. Each one of us occasionally passes through moments of darkness like the Blessed Virgin in the search for her Son, which often requires of us that ‘entering into patience’ of which the saints speak. Taught, certainly, by the Mother of God, St. Mother Maravillas wrote in a letter: “when the Lord does not wish to lift his hand, the consolation that creatures can give lasts but little, and there is nothing to do but, closing one’s eyes and always trusting and hoping against all hope, to throw oneself into the arms of the cross, where the arms of Christ are” 5 . 2. The sorrow of the Mother of the Incarnate Word also teaches us that the loss of Jesus, no matter how brief, is the greatest of evils. The magnitude of the Virgin’s grief is for us a visible way of grasping the magnitude of evil and of sin. Convinced of this, Mother Maravillas wrote: “To see souls, which have cost Him so much, being lost, is horrifying, and what a thing it is to give one’s life for them!” (34: C436). “Let us pray much that souls may return to God, and let us console Him for so much ingratitude, giving ourselves more and more to Him.” 3. And lastly, we see how in this event the Mother of the Redeemer, being physically separated from her Son, experienced our apparent separation from God when we pass through the nights of the soul. All that longing for God, all that spiritual melancholy for heaven, the Most Holy Virgin felt as her own because she did not have her little Redeemer. Therefore, an author says: She was suffering in reparation for all the souls who once had faith and lost it; for all those souls who once loved God and forgot Him; for all those hearts that once loved Him and today have abandoned Him. That is why we say to her: pray for us sinners. Hence St. Mother Maravillas said: “I ask the Most Holy Virgin to help me see things truly in her presence, so as to accuse myself of them and, purified and washed by her mercy, to begin what little life I have left, a new life in Him, with Him and through Him” (64: C-727). Lastly, and with this I conclude, from the Most Holy Virgin Mother Maravillas learned –and we must do the same– to say her fiat unconditionally. That is why she firmly affirmed: “Holiness is nothing other than our will united to God’s” (58: C-4403). “We shall see what the Lord wants. The truth is that we are happy. If the Lord were to ask us about this and about everything: about the moment of death, about which illness we would prefer to die of, about how we would like to be, etc., etc., we could only say to Him: ‘Lord, when You will, as You will, what You will; it is the only thing we want and desire,’ so all our desires are most completely fulfilled, for they are none other than his will” (59: C-2297). To the intercession of St. Mother Maravillas of Jesus we entrust the growth in us of that ‘attunement’ with the Mother of God, so that we may advance by leaps and bounds in holiness and one day rest in the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus, whom she loved so much. For this intention we continue praying in the Holy Mass. Notes 1 Constitutions , 19 . 2 Directory of Contemplative Life , 65. 3 Ibidem . 4 Ibidem . 5 Cartas de la Madre Maravillas , Antología epistolar de Sta. Maravillas de Jesús , Letter 48, To Doña Catalina Urquijo Vitorica, 18-6-1948.
Contemplatives of the Eucharist

Good Night Talk for the Monks of the Monastery “St. Michael the Archangel” – Brazil Contemplatives of the Eucharist 1 [ Exordium ] First of all, thank you very much for the invitation and the warm welcome. It is a pleasure to be here. How much this place has grown! Congratulations! I have titled this good night talk Contemplatives of the Eucharist , which is a phrase from the Directory of Contemplative Life . For if there is something that must characterize our monks, it is precisely that adoration of the Incarnate Word present truly, really and substantially in the Eucharist 2 , where one grows in familiarity with Him 3 day after day. And while it is true that this Eucharistic imprint is common to all the members of the Institute, the monks are (or must be) the adorers par excellence in our Institute. Now, I would like to point out that the ‘ of ’ in the phrase has a double meaning. On the one hand, it refers to contemplating the Eucharist, to being devoted to it as the holiest act we can perform 4 . But, on the other hand, the preposition can be interpreted as belonging or possession 5 . The contemplative becomes so attached to Christ in the Eucharist, goes about the monastery so recollected “so that dissipation may find no incentive” 6 , that whatever he does, his soul remains captivated by Christ, to the point that with great reason it can be said that this contemplative belongs to the Eucharist: Diego belongs to the Eucharist, José belongs to the Eucharist… And in this way he fulfills what our Constitutions say in number 209 (pay attention): “Jesus Christ, Son of God and of the Blessed Virgin, must be the center of all spiritual life : No one comes to the Father except through Me 7 . In the church, in the cloister, in the cell, in the refectory, in recreation, they must go about sighing for Jesus Christ. The song and the laughter of the members of our Religious Family must be to weep for Jesus Christ. This is their office . The sweeter the melody they sing in choir, the better they will manifest the deep and interior sigh of their souls longing for Jesus Christ. The memory and remembrance of Him must never depart from their hearts . With this, sleep must come, and of this they must dream while sleeping. The heart always melted in love of Him, and the memory occupied with nothing other than Him.” Interesting, isn’t it? How is this achieved? How do we bring it about that the memory and remembrance of Christ never depart from our hearts? By contemplating Christ in the Eucharist. By uniting oneself to the Eucharistic Christ. That is where the soul becomes steeped in the very sentiments of Christ, where it drinks of the divine Wisdom that God whispers in the silence of the soul, where it finds the Friend, to embrace Him and never let Him go. That is our noble office, says our Proper Law, but especially it is that of the monk of the Incarnate Word. You have been called to the service of the Most Blessed Sacrament, to serve the adorable person of Jesus Christ in the Most Blessed Sacrament. But the monk of the Incarnate Word must not be content with that alone; rather, carried along by a boundless love for Christ and by zeal for his glory, he must also strive to make all men love, adore and serve Him 8 , and that everywhere a throne may be raised to Him and faithful adorers gathered for Him 9 . This is so because if the monk “truly seeks God 10 , he must necessarily share in the ardent love of Christ for souls” 11 ; he cannot forget his neighbor 12 . And when we say neighbor, we do not refer only to the thousands of people in the world who do not yet know Christ, but very especially to the members of the Institute, “as the order of charity requires, according to which one must love –affectively and effectively– those who are closest more” 13 . And here, if you will allow me, I want to give you a threefold charge: Love the Congregation with a filial love; always defend it. Pray much for the Congregation when you contemplate the Incarnate Word in the Eucharist. Consider “that the graces a Congregation gives are never repaid as they deserve: we are always debtors to our mother. Each day’s labors are a small thing beside the debt, which is immense” 14 . To look no further, think of the immense gift God has given us in bringing us to this Religious Family to consecrate ourselves to Him, with all the means it gives us for our sanctification… In short, for all that the Congregation gives us, the only thing it asks of us in return –so to speak– is that we be faithful to its rule, to the charism, to the patrimony that has been bequeathed to us, to its sound traditions. St. Peter Julian Eymard told his own: “Keep, then, your rule, in order to preserve the life of your mother the Congregation” 15 . It is the same message I want to repeat to you. Just as in the Middle Ages, when the monasteries were the place where the cultural riches of the past were preserved 16 , so too may you today be the true guardians of the spirit 17 of our Institute. Be the faithful escort of the Incarnate Word. Notice that our Constitutions say that the spirit of our Religious Family, of our Institute, is identified with the Holy Spirit 18 . Now, that spirit is manifested or lives in a body, that is, through us. If we separate ourselves from that spirit, in some way we are departing from God (the Holy Spirit), from what He wants for us. And what happens to a body when it is separated from the spirit (from its soul)? It dies. That is why it is very important not only that we know this spirit well, but that we live it, that we do not depart from the spirit of our Institute in a single point, and that we know how to defend it with clear arguments, with courageous witness, and even with a look. Help our Congregation to expand . How? Well, the best way to do it –which is at the same time the best tribute of honor you can give to Christ in the Eucharist– is the loving practice of the rule. The faithful fulfillment of what is commanded of us not only greatly consoles Christ, but contributes to the prosperity of our Congregation and draws new members to it. And it is not enough to do what we are commanded; we must also perfect ourselves in what falls to us to do. The Congregation will be judged by us . If we are lax, if we have no apostolic zeal, if we are too bureaucratic or, on the contrary, totally disorganized, if we do not study seriously, if we chase after every novelty that comes along, people will think that this is what the Congregation is like. Conduct yourselves in such a way that those who see you may say: “there is a true religious of the Incarnate Word.” Lastly, always be generous and available 19 to achieve the end of the Institute, that is, the inculturation of the Gospel. May being contemplatives of the Eucharist lead you not to shy away from the missionary adventure, that is, not to refuse a priori this or that mission, to be capable of offering yourselves personally to collaborate in whatever is needed for the good of the Institute and the cause of Christ. [ Peroratio ] St. Peter Julian Eymard asked some religious while preaching the Spiritual Exercises to them: “What will make you saints? The rule, your religious rule, the rule of the congregation to which you belong. For you, holiness comes down to practicing it, because the rule is the will of God. […] What [God] wants to see in you is perfect religious of this Institute, and its living incarnation. In heaven you will be crowned, not as holy men, but as holy religious” 20 . And we could add: as holy religious of the Institute of the Incarnate Word. We cannot become saints except according to what God inspired in our Founder, which is set down in the Constitutions and in the Directories ; you know that very well. If any of you says that he loves Christ very much but does not love the Congregation, he is lying. Because, as our Proper Law says: a true religious keeps fidelity and shows a great love not only when he appreciates the gift of religious life but also when he loves and defends his own Institute, which includes in a particular way the founder and the Constitutions. Read it yourselves in the Directory of Consecrated Life 21 . That is why we must be forewarned, for there will be no lack of those who believe themselves called to reform the Founder and to do better than he did; but God blesses only the one he has chosen to found, and never those who oppose him 22 . We must be prepared for the hardest trials, and for that we must be firmly planted on the Rock that is Christ 23 , who lives among us in the Eucharist, from where every day He tells us: I am with you always, until the end of the age 24 . With the hymn to Our Lady, we ask Her to intercede for all of us, for the Institute, and I personally ask her to bless you always and to make you very holy. The heart in the body of the Church

[Exordium] Here, beside our common Mother, the Most Holy Virgin of Succor, I would like first of all to greet with great affection my dear brother priests, the religious men and women present here, and all the friends who have come to celebrate the happy anniversary of the presence of the monks of the Incarnate Word in this beloved monastery of “Our Lady of Succor” here, on “the island of eternal spring.” I want to tell you that it is a great joy for me to be able to celebrate this Eucharist with you. This is a privileged place of spirituality, and a true ‘capital of grace’ not only for the local Church –being the first men’s monastery in the diocese– but also for the whole Institute of the Incarnate Word and for the entire Church. That is why, within the framework of the celebration of another anniversary of the inauguration of the monastery –so beautifully built by the Jorge Dorta brothers: Don Juan, Don Hipólito and Don Vicente, on the graced lands of Güímar, and which they built with the purpose that it might be a point of reference for spirituality, prayer and expiation for sins– I would like to pause and ponder with you, if you allow me, the grace that a monastery signifies. One may well ask why the Jorge Dorta brothers wanted a contemplative monastery for men and not a parish, or a home for the elderly or for children, or any other work of mercy. Why a monastery? What is it that monks do that made them prefer a monastery above all the other works of piety they could have undertaken? That is what we will try to answer in this sermon. Someone may ask: 1. What is a monastery? And on this occasion we will answer this question by paraphrasing St. Luigi Orione and say that a monastery is like an “ oasis in the desert of this poor life , to which souls come like weary and wounded pilgrims, and often dying along the way” 1 . How many souls, how many of you here today, burdened by the trials of this life, have come to the doors of this monastery to find consolation, seeking rest to heal the spirit, and at the feet of the Most Holy Virgin of Succor have left the wounds of the heart… That is why we can also say that monasteries, and in particular this monastery dedicated to the Most Holy Virgin, “is a beacon of light that enlightens minds and recalls the truths of the Gospel.It is a center of radiation of divine mercyand of the maternal goodness of Mary. It is a source of spiritual elevation , of faith, of Christian morals for discouraged and weary souls. A monastery is also like a flame that shines upon the mountains , and moves hearts to lofty sentiments, to thoughts of heaven. In the dark gray of earthly life, a monastery is a lighthouse –like the one on the coast of Güímar– that guides the little boats of souls in danger toward the harbor of salvation” 2 . When the Lord Bishop Don Felipe Fernández García delivered the homily at the inauguration of the monastery, he said that “ a monastery … is like the heart in the body of the Church: an invisible organ but of primordial importance .” Because a “monastery represents the very intimacy of a Church, the heart, where the Spirit always groans and pleads for the needs of the whole community and where thanksgiving rises unceasingly for the Life that He gives us each day” 3 . A monastery is, then, something very singular in the life of the Church. Look around you. How can we fail to recognize, inscribed on the walls of this church, in the silence of the cloister, in the freshness and serenity of its gardens, the pure and iron-strong faith that motivated its construction and that continues to sustain this house of prayer and school of faith? I think you will agree with me if I say that it is here, in a monastery, that souls –with different states of life, at different stages of their spiritual life– find a fruitful space, far from daily concerns, to recollect themselves and recover spiritual vigor, to take up again the path of faith with greater ardor, and to seek, find and love Christ in the ordinary life of the family, of work, of school, in the midst of the world. Dear friends who have come today to celebrate these years of grace upon grace: may you too be the ones who draw others to come to the monastery to pray with the monks, to spend a day in silence before the Blessed Sacrament –that Physician of souls who works wonders in the serenity and silence of the soul that offers Him its friendship–; come yourselves and invite others to make the Spiritual Exercises, to consecrate themselves to Our Lady and, in short, to encounter God and be united to Him. Many of you come regularly to the monastery and will have seen the monks pray, work… and you have some idea of what contemplative life is, but perhaps few know what it means to be a monk of the Incarnate Word. And this leads us to answer in part the second question we asked at the beginning: 2. What does a monk of the Incarnate Word do? Well, “in imitation of the Word, who willed to live in the silence of Nazareth for thirty years, they consecrate themselves to Him in the contemplative state of life” 4 . That is to say, they consecrate their life to praying, to doing penance, to immolating themselves in the silence of the cloister to ask God for the conversion of sinners –above all of consecrated souls–, to praying for the intentions of the Holy Father, for the increase in quantity and quality of priestly and religious vocations, and for the perseverance of all the members of the Church 5 . Therefore, if, as we said a moment ago, a monastery is the house of God, “the monastery is the place which God guards 6 ; it is the dwelling of His singular presence. And its monastic community can be compared to Moses, who in prayer determines the outcome of Israel’s battles 7 , and to the watchman who keeps vigil in the night awaiting the dawn 8 ” 9 . That is why we say that they are at the vanguard of the missionary work. Did you know that the prayer of monks “serves as suffrage for the souls of the departed, strengthens the weak, heals the sick, frees the possessed, opens the doors of prisons, loosens the bonds of the innocent, forgives sins, wards off temptations, makes persecutions cease, consoles the downcast, delights the magnanimous, guides pilgrims, calms storms, feeds the poor, leads the rich onto the right path, raises up the fallen, sustains those who are about to fall, and makes those who are standing hold firm?” 10 . Because prayer is the only thing that has power over God. Contemplative monks are those who, with their silent immolation, in the observance of regular discipline, and above all, in the offering of prayers and sacrifices, in the divine office and in the worthy celebration of Holy Mass, open new paths so that the message of Christ may penetrate the hearts, the mentalities, the customs and the cultures of peoples. And that is why a monastery, and a contemplative community in a diocese, near your home, on this most beautiful island, is an honor for its Church, a torrent of heavenly graces and, listen well, a lightning rod against divine wrath. This is why the Jorge Dorta brothers built this monastery, as Don Hipólito explained well in a letter to his uncle, saying that they were building this monastery “as an expression of the value of prayer and of the dogma of the Communion of Saints” and, he added, that they wanted to offer to this “diocesan community the space of a vital need within it,” that is, a place where our Lord is adored, a place that is primarily a house of prayer. Hence the importance and preeminence of a monastery over all the other works of piety, which, although very important and very necessary, do not have the supremacy of a purely spiritual work through which all the others are obtained and bear fruit. Therefore this anniversary also invites us to see the merciful Providence of our Lord, who has willed to grace His Church of Nivaria with this immense capital of spiritual grace. And, we must also say it, it is for the Institute of the Incarnate Word a blessing, a singular privilege to form part of this magnificent history. 3. The Virgin of Succor Daily, in the silence and hiddenness of the cloister, the monks of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, with the profession of the evangelical counsels and their vow of Marian slavery, give themselves to the service of the Church in Güímar, so that in all hearts the name of God may be more fully praised and His Mother, the Most Holy Virgin of Succor, queen of these lands, may be loved more tenderly. Hence the devotion and trusting prayer that day after day our monks address to the Mother of God. For a monk of the Incarnate Word who does not love the Blessed Virgin tenderly and devoutly is inconceivable. Her help is indispensable for all of us, in every field. That is why at this point this sermon becomes a prayer in which I wish to entrust all of you, and those who will come after you, to the Blessed Virgin, with all your struggles, with all your needs, and whatever the vicissitudes of life you may be going through, that She may grant you her maternal protection and her heavenly succor. Mary is the Queen of heaven, close to God, but she is also the mother close to each one of us, who loves us and listens to us and is ready to give us her help. Always have recourse to Her, trust in Her. “If Mary protects you –said St. Bernard– you have nothing to fear; under her guidance, you will not know weariness; thanks to her favor, you will reach the goal” 11 . To her intercession we also entrust the souls of those who are no longer with us today, especially the Jorge Dorta brothers, illustrious founders of this monastery, and the souls of all who with great effort collaborated so that the first contemplative monastery for men in the history of this diocese might become a reality. And now, if you allow me, I would like to leave a final message to our dear monks, here in the Monastery of Our Lady of Succor: Know that to your prayers and to the holiness of your life this generous land of Nivaria is entrusted in a particular way, toward which you have responsibilities and duties. Contribute with the strength of your prayer to sustaining the local Church and gladden it with the fruits of loving faith. You have been called to bear witness here to the primacy of the charity of God. And as you know very well, witness means martyr, and the Church is faithful in martyrdom, in witness. Feel yourselves sharers in this mission especially when dryness and the nights of the soul make you suffer. May the Blessed Virgin, to whom you are so devoted, console you in your daily labors and nourish your hope. Be always faithful to your vocation; jealously guard and make fruitful the gift that has been granted to you. And as the Mystical Doctor, St. John of the Cross, said: see that the Lord “has taken you as first stones; so see what you must be, for as on the strongest the others are to be founded; take advantage of this first spirit that God gives in these beginnings to take up very anew the way of perfection in all humility and detachment within and without, not with a childish spirit, but with a robust will, wanting this Christ to cost you something” 12 . May Our Lady bless you, and may these first years of the monastery be only the beginning of many more anniversaries. To God and His Most Holy Mother we offer the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass in thanksgiving for the many gifts He has been pleased to bestow on His children in Güímar by planting His house here. Inauguration of the Monastery in Brazil

M k 13:33-37 [ Exordium] My dear all: it is with great joy in my soul that I celebrate this holy Mass with you on this precious first Sunday of Advent and in the setting of this magnificent occasion: the inauguration of the first monastery in the thriving Province of Nossa Senhora da Aparecida . Here in this place the petition that the prophet Isaiah made in the first reading seems to be fulfilled today: Oh, that you would rend the heavens and come down, making the mountains quake at your presence 1 . For what is a monastery if not a “sign of the presence of God in the world” 2 ? That is why special attention is deserved by the fact that today, here, through the work of the loving and most gentle Divine Fatherhood, God officially and publicly establishes a new house where the Incarnate Word himself is to be adored and served. What a great grace for our Religious Family! For this Province in particular and, truly, for the whole Church! For as an author said: “a Monastery is the power of God grafted onto the earth, like the Body of Jesus in the bread of the Eucharist and the Word in the womb of Mary. […] From there the power of the Spirit runs through the whole Body of the Church as in a second Incarnation” 3 . Analogously we can say that this monastery planted in these beautiful lands of Nossa Senhora da Aparecida comes to be like the Word, who in his immeasurable divine wisdom willed to enclose himself in the womb of Mary 4 in order to begin his redemptive mission from there. In the Gospel we have just read we heard our Lord compare himself to a man who goes on a journey, leaves his house and entrusts to each one what he is to do and charges the doorkeeper to keep watch , and then conclude with the final exhortation, telling us: so you too, keep watch. From these words of our Lord we can certainly deduce the lovingly vigilant attitude that must characterize all of us members of the Religious Family of the Incarnate Word. For are we not asked to put out into the deep , so as not to shy away from the missionary adventure, and to conduct ourselves in this life like fishermen, who are humble, hardworking men, who do not fear dangers, vigilant and patient in long night watches 5 ?. That is why, although the vigilance that Christ asks of us today in the Gospel is common to all the religious of the Incarnate Word, and even more, common to all Christians, it seems to me that we can also read in these same words the mission of these brothers of ours who are to devote themselves with tireless effort to giving “an outstanding witness to the majesty and charity of God, as well as to union in Christ” 6 , thus imitating “the Word who offered himself to the Father, silent and hidden, in the womb of Mary” 7 , in order to be true channels through which may descend the holiness that God wants to communicate to this nation and, why not, also to the whole Church and to the whole world. The Incarnate Word entrusts to each one what he is to do , and to our monks is entrusted – “ to be in the vanguard of all the apostolic works of the Institute” 8 . That is, that they go ahead with their prayers to implore with tender accents before the throne of God what the psalmist asked in the psalm we have just sung (heard): Lord, God of hosts, turn your eyes: look upon your vine and visit it, protect the stock planted by your hand, the shoot that you yourself cultivated . That is being in the vanguard! That is, keeping watch in prayer so that God may be pleased to make his vine bear fruit, the vine that his missionaries strive so hard to cultivate, and so that they themselves may not abandon it, discouraged by difficulties or cast down by failures. To be in the vanguard is to open new paths so that the message of Christ may penetrate hearts, families, the world of education, lines of thought, that is, the turning points of culture 9 , so that in all hearts the name of God may be more fully praised. That is why our monks play such an essential and important role in the Church, because they sustain the activity of our missionaries and of so many others who work on the many frontiers of evangelization. – Likewise, to them is also entrusted being “ guardians of the spirit of the Institute, showing to all the primacy of the love of God and the value of the mortifying virtues of silence, penance, obedience, sacrifice and oblative love” 10 . That is why the mission of our contemplatives is so inspiring, because it implies a “greater participation in and imitation of the radicalism of the self-emptying of the Word of God” 11 . A mission that necessarily entails “death like the grain of wheat, in order to see Christ in all things” 12 . How much humanity needs the witness of contemplative monks, to spur it to consider eternal and perennial values! How much it needs the serenity that you enjoy and that springs from intimate union with Christ! 13 . Look, our dear John Paul II once said: “In the history of evangelization, the destiny of an entire people was radically transformed for time and eternity because of the fidelity of someone who was faithful to his call to the end” 14 . So too, and I would like you to understand this well, I want to tell you that “God is counting on you; that He makes his plans, in a certain way, depending on your free collaboration, on the oblation of your lives and on the generosity with which you follow the inspirations that the Holy Spirit gives you in the depths of your hearts” 15 . Our blessed Catholic faith here in Brazil has been bound forever, according to God’s plan, to the fidelity of Frei Galvão –a man of peace and charity 16 – and of St. José de Anchieta –the apostle of Brazil–. But from now on we can also say that some aspects of God’s plan will be bound to your fidelity, to the fervor with which you say yes to the Word of God in your lives, to the genuineness with which you live the spirit of the Institute and according to the style 17 of the Incarnate Word. Always remember what the fidelity of these men has meant for Brazil and for the world, and be faithful, you too, to the mission that God entrusts to you as monks and missionaries of the Institute of the Incarnate Word here in these lands. May this monastery be like an oasis in the desert of this life … a beacon of light that enlightens minds and recalls the truths of the Gospel to all the weary souls who come to it. Always remember that you –our dear monks of the St. Michael the Archangel Monastery– are a focal point of the mercy of God and of the goodness of the Virgin Mary, and therefore it is your task to radiate that merciful fragrance upon all men. Make of this place what our Constitutions ask: “a magnet of God’s grace and a lightning rod of his wrath” 18 . Be, with your joyfully penitent, silent and hidden lives, those flames that shine in the darkness through the charity of Christ that burns in your souls. How much we need magnanimous souls who, with their sacrifices and prayers, rend that heaven so that the waters of grace and consolation –those that lead to eternal life– may flow upon our missions, upon our souls and upon those of so very many other souls who do not yet know Christ or live as if they did not know Him! That is why I would like to repeat to you the same words that the great mystic and doctor of the Church, St. John of the Cross, wrote to some nuns who had just founded a monastery in Córdoba, Spain, and which I believe fit this occasion well. He writes to the prioress so that she may pass them on to the other nuns, and he says: “Tell them, then, that our Lord has taken them as first stones , that they should consider what they ought to be, since the others are to be founded on them as on the strongest; that they take advantage of this first spirit that God gives in these beginnings to take up anew the way of perfection in all humility and detachment, within and without, not with a childish spirit but with a robust will ; let them pursue mortification and penance, wanting this Christ to cost them something, and not being like those who seek comfort and consolation, whether in God or outside him; but rather suffering in God, and outside him for him, in silence and hope and loving remembrance” 19 . [Peroratio] My dear all, dear Fr. Rossi, my brother priests, seminarians, novices, monks, dear mothers and sisters, I would not want to conclude without telling you, as St. Paul says in today’s second reading, that I continually thank God for the divine gifts he has granted you in Christ Jesus . I encourage you to keep working together and with great spirit because, as our Constitutions say, “in the [epic] task of evangelizing the culture, individual efforts or those of a single generation are not enough; rather, a great movement is needed that keeps growing in extent and depth” 20 . This is the resounding idea: to sacrifice oneself 21 !. May the foundation of this monastery here in the Province be a starting point for a new apostolic fruitfulness. May God bless you with many, very many vocations who wish to leave everything to give themselves to Him who is the All. May Most Holy Mary, Nossa Senhora da Aparecida , the first to welcome the Word in order to offer it to the world, make the communities of our Religious Family here in this blessed Brazilian nation burning centers of the new evangelization. To Her also I earnestly entrust each one of you. May Our Lady always protect you, make you ever more her own, and give you that caress in the soul that little ones need as an encouragement for their perseverance. To all of you I say, as the Spiritual Father of our Religious Family said when he visited Brazil back in the ’80s: “Pray, pray much for those who also pray, for those who cannot pray, for those who do not know how to pray and for those who do not want to pray.” And I too commend myself personally and very much to the prayers of all of you. Always count on mine. May Our Lady bless you. In the Name of the Father, and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Notes 1 Is 63:19. 2 Directory of Missions Ad Gentes , 97; op. cit. They are the honor of the Church and the torrent of heavenly graces

Directory of Contemplative Life , 172; op. cit. Perfectae Caritatis , 7 [Exordium] I have come very gladly to this beloved monastery to show you not only our esteem and affection, but also our deep gratitude for the prayers of all of you. That in the first place. Secondly, and given the expansion that the contemplative branch has had in these last years –consider that in 2016 the Institute had only 6 monasteries; by mid-2019 it had 11 monasteries, and at present there are 16– it seems important to me to highlight (although you already know this) the importance of contemplative life in mission lands. By the grace of God, today we can say that our contemplatives are on all 5 continents, since the monastery in Papua was founded. However, there are still 6 provinces, such as those of Peru, Russia, Ecuador, Northern Europe, Tanzania, and the delegation in Tajikistan, that do not yet have contemplatives. And besides, requests for the foundation of monasteries keep arriving: for example, there is a request to found the first male contemplative monastery in a diocese in Lithuania… Now of course, all this depends on what happens with us, but I wanted to tell you anyway so that you can help us pray. In these times men –and women– in the various parts of the world and in the diverse cultural contexts in which their lives unfold seek God with anguish, often seeking Him, as St. Paul would say, “groping, though He is not far from each one of us” 1 . And that is why it seems to me that we must see this expansion of the contemplative branch of the Institute among peoples so different in race, in mentality, in cultures, as a proof of the validity of the charism of the Institute and of the universality of the message we bring. It is indeed a providential fact that God leads our members to pray and do penance in places to which, if it were not for us, very probably no one else would go. Consider that we are in Turkey, in Papua, that we want to open a monastery in Iraq, another in Taiwan… believe me, there are not many who want to go to those places. But for the mission it is imperative to go. And certainly we would give great consolation to the Heart of Christ. Our proper law says it and today I want to repeat it to you: contemplatives “ are the honor of the Church and the torrent of heavenly graces ” 2 . The Second Vatican Council, for its part, in two of its documents – Lumen Gentium 3 and Perfectae Caritatis 4 – also praises the life of solitude with which you have chosen to follow more closely Christ praying on the mountain. And canon law also confirms this when it says that contemplatives “always have an outstanding part in the Mystical Body of Christ” 5 . Honor of the Church Why does it say that they are the honor of the Church ? Because Christ Himself has given us the example that the whole honor of love lies in loving, in giving oneself, in sacrificing oneself, and that is precisely what the monks of the IVE do. “ To live the life of the Eucharist –says St. Edith Stein– is to go out completely from the small circle of one’s own life and to grow into the infinity of the life of Christ” 6 . To live the life of the Eucharist is precisely the life of the contemplatives of the Incarnate Word. They are moreover the honor of the Church because you have chosen the better part and it will not be taken from you 7 . They are the honor of the Church because God has chosen them to consecrate them to honoring exclusively His adorable Person and His real and living presence among us. They are the honor of the Church because they dedicate themselves to honoring the sacramental state of the Savior, copying in their lives the virtues that Jesus practices in the Eucharist 8 . Torrent of heavenly graces But they are also a torrent of heavenly graces , or as the Directory of Spirituality says: “magnets of the grace of God” 9 . How many graces the contemplatives obtain for the mission, for our own missionaries, for the conversion of souls; how much the monks help the faith to take root in the various peoples; how much the prayer and sacrifice of the contemplative sustains the priest in his mission field, and how much it is needed that all this spread and multiply! The whole Church greatly needs the collaboration of the monks. That is why the most characteristic aspect of the apostolate of the monks continues to be the holocaust of yourselves hidden in penance, in the observance of monastic discipline according to the genuine spirit of the Institute and, above all, in the offering of prayers and sacrifices, both in the divine office and in the Holy Mass 10 . So then, the interior life of the monk, by virtue of his monastic profession, is not only a private exercise of spirituality, already in fact highly commendable, but is mission and ecclesial service for the benefit of all the members of the Mystical Body of Christ and, in reality, of all humanity. St. John Paul II, using a metaphor of St. Bernard, said that “just as the digestive system works for the benefit of the whole body, so the monks, by means of lectio divina and contemplation, assimilate the spiritual nourishment of the Word of God and of sacramental grace and transform it into vital juices for the benefit of all the members of the community” 11 . And that is why today, when so many people in the world are tossed about by confused intellectual currents, disturbed and thrown into spiritual crises by so many false spiritualities promoted everywhere, mainly by the media, there is great need not only of the prayer of contemplatives but of the example of the importance of the transcendent 12 . The recent canonization of St. Charles de Foucauld, the martyrdom of the monks of Tibhirine in Algeria 13 , the martyrdom of more than 70 contemplatives of various religious orders in Spain during the Spanish Civil War 14 , speak of how important the radical self-giving of the contemplative continues to be today when it comes to evangelization. [ Peroration] You see, a moment ago we mentioned the number of monasteries the Institute has today. Who would have thought that a handful of monks from here, from San Rafael, would carry contemplative life to the whole world! God has entrusted the whole wide world to your prayers and to your holiness of life. Let us take as addressed personally to us this longing of the Heart of the Incarnate Word expressed in the Directory of Spirituality , when, speaking of the monasteries, it says: Would that we could multiply them throughout the whole world! 15 . Let us ask in this Holy Mass that both you and all the contemplatives of the Institute throughout the world may contribute with the strength of prayer to sustaining the Church and gladdening her with the fruits of an ardent faith, and that all our monasteries may truly be “seedbeds of edification for the Christian people” 16 . The study of the religious

Study in the religious life The study of the religious, chiefly the knowledge of the truths of the faith together with the consequent penetration of them, is necessary for the formation of the religious. This is explicitly commanded in the legislation of the Church (CIC 587-589), where formation is required. Thus Pope Pius XII taught in his apostolic constitution Sedes sapientiae , addressed to the religious of the whole world: “Religious, whose principal obligation is the contemplation of divine things, seeking God alone and uniting themselves intimately with Him and transmitting these things to others, must remember that they can in no way carry out this most holy mission fittingly and fruitfully, nor rise to a lofty union with Christ, unless they possess in abundance that profound and ever-perfectible knowledge of God and of His mysteries which is acquired through sacred studies. “The first concern of religious superiors must be to watch over the solid and complete formation of the intellect, taking into account the natural development of the young and the distribution of studies. And although it is true that the same is not to be required of all religious nor of all orders, nevertheless it must never be forgotten that a thorough instruction in the subject of Religion and in the principles of Philosophy and Theology is absolutely incumbent upon all. Study in the religious of the IVE The words of the Magisterium—more could be cited—have greater force if we consider them in our own case, that is, as religious of the Incarnate Word, whose principal charism, which illuminates our religious life and reflects our longings, is the evangelization of culture. Indeed, we read in one of the directories: [14] “Every religious of the Incarnate Word knows that he must apply himself to the knowledge of the truth and to its transmission beyond the concrete place where he carries out his apostolate. He knows that in order to evangelize the culture he must devote himself thoroughly to this task” 1 . Why study? What is the principal end of our study? There are two, but one is merely a consequence of the first. We study in order better to know and love Jesus Christ, and in order better to make Jesus Christ known and loved. For a thing is loved insofar as it is known. “The supreme rule of religious life is the following of Christ 2 . And Christ is the supreme truth: I am the truth (Jn 14:ó). But to follow Christ as Truth means applying the intellect to know Him more, which will have to be something permanent in the disciple, for the riches found in Christ are inexhaustible. This is the foundation of the intellectual formation of monks” 3 . One could cite a great many texts, both from our Constitutions and from the directories, in which it is affirmed that all, to a greater or lesser degree, must apply themselves to study, at least as part of basic formation and of ongoing formation. In our Congregation, so to speak, no one is exempted from this: “The brothers shall make the Studentate, in which they will take some treatises of Philosophy and Theology, ‘attending to the needs of the Church and to the circumstances of men and of the times, as the end and character of the Institute require’ 4 . The religious brothers will continue their formation until perpetual profession, in the houses to which they are assigned and under the direct authority of the local Superior, and attention will be given to their ongoing formation” 5 . Study in the contemplative life of the IVE And this duty applies not only to those in the active life, nor only to priests who by their office will have to exercise intellectual activities, but evidently also to contemplatives: “The contemplative sisters of the Institute of the Servants must be firmly convinced of the ‘need for an initial and ongoing formation suited to the vocation and life of contemplative search for God in solitude and silence, in continual prayer and in intense penance,’ and that a formed and enlightened faith cooperates more with the end of the Institute” 6 . In the directories of monastic life this express will is particularly stressed, as is the fundamental importance of ongoing intellectual formation for monastic life, which finds its special vigor in relation to the spirituality proper to our religious family: “All the more so because of our particular spirituality in relation to our specific end, which ‘requires a faith enlightened by continual reflection that measures itself against the sources of the Church’s message, and a constant spiritual discernment sought in prayer’ 7 , that is, the special need of study and contemplation for the apostolate of evangelizing the culture” 8 . For: “Study will be useful for the contemplative life itself [as St. Thomas says]“directly, by assisting contemplation, that is, by enlightening the intellect…, indirectly, by removing the dangers of contemplation, that is, the errors which frequently occur in the contemplation of divine things for those who are ignorant of the Scriptures…” 9 . Likewise we read in the Directory of Monastic Life that “historically it was the monasteries that saved for humanity all that was most important of what the human spirit had produced through the centuries; becoming, moreover, sources of culture by teaching within their walls the works of the Fathers, those of pagan Greek and Latin authors, science and the liberal arts such as painting, music, etc. Therefore, in the monasteries cultural activities will be carried out which contribute to their proper end—union with God—and to the end of the Institute—the evangelization of culture— 10 . This will be regulated in each monastery” 11 . This requires, as we have already mentioned, “A formed and enlightened faith is necessary for the monk who is a priest and spiritual father, of whom St. Teresa said: see that he be learned’ 12 ” 13 . Therefore we must not neglect this fundamental aspect of our formation, so characteristic of our institute. Formation according to the measure of our possibilities and abilities. The virtue of studiousness Studiousness. It is the most specific virtue of the one who studies. Study implies above all a strong application of the soul to something, and this application is regulated by the virtue of studiousness. This virtue must be joined with three other virtues: The first and fundamental one, the virtue that informs all the acts of the other virtues and gives them, as it were, a new form, a new beauty, a new order. And this holds also for study: our study must be ordered by the love of God and by the love of neighbor. The Recognizing our limitations and possibilities is fundamental in the counsels of St. Thomas. Moreover, because without humility research engenders proud men and, worse still, intellectually proud men 14 . Study requires effort and therefore perseverance in that unceasing search for the truth, which must go together with humility, recognizing that all gifts come from God and must return to Him. Such study will be done in depth, avoiding a merely textbook-bound and formalistic study, in such a way that it helps the progress of faith and the increase of charity. The that is, the tenacity that keeps the student from falling prey to sloth, discouragement, apathy. It is the quality that crowns with success the undertakings begun. It is the quality that brings to completion the undertakings begun. Sloth, sensuality, pride, envy and the other vices are enemies of knowledge. It is necessary to practice the contrary virtues. This formation, which moreover must be ongoing, has a penitential aspect that counters the threefold concupiscence and therefore helps toward the fulfillment of the evangelical counsels themselves, “since it serves to avoid the lust of the flesh… to remove the desire for riches… (and) it is useful moreover as a lesson in obedience.” Moreover, only through persevering study can one attain Wisdom, with which all good things come. I rejoiced in all these goods, because Wisdom is the one who directs them, though I did not know that she was their mother 15 . Certainly the good practice of study will require effort and struggle. Vices There are two vices opposed to the right use of this virtue. As a moral virtue, one can sin against it both by defect and by excess. By defect, negligence 16 . That is, neglecting precisely this aspect of formation. That is, through negligence not forming oneself, not studying, not making the most of study time. Not fulfilling our duty to form ourselves. There can be many temptations of many kinds: such as sloth, loss of interest, excusing oneself with other duties, etc., etc. By excess, vain curiosity 17 , which is also a defect, no longer of the one who does not study but of the one who studies badly. Curiosity consists above all in devoting oneself to the study of purely superficial things, or else of important things but in disregard of one’s fundamental duties. Opposed to the virtue are both those who neglect the study required by the obligations of their state and profession, and those who devote themselves only to the study that satisfies their desires. The curious squander their real faculties. Practical helps for before, during and after study – Before , rectify the intention of doing it exclusively by and for the glory of God. There are four virtues that must influence intellectual work so that it may be completely sanctified: . studiousness, which is the most specific virtue of the one who studies; . religion, offering the hour of study as an act of praise to God; . obedience, studying as a duty of one’s state; . charity, turning the intellectual act into an act of love for God. – During study, it must possess the same qualities as prayer, since it is prayer. That is: worthily, attentively and devoutly. – After study one must give oneself to prayer. Let prayer prepare for study and study for prayer. Meditating before the tabernacle on what has been the object of our study. The counsel of St. Thomas: «do not cease to devote yourself to prayer. The true intellectual vocation is sustained by the spirit of prayer, which must not only precede and conclude intellectual work, but accompany it, permeate it and in some way constitute it: the work itself, especially when it is devoted to theological inquiry, is prayer. Since the object of theology is the truth, the living God and His plan of salvation revealed in Jesus Christ, the theologian is called to intensify his life of faith and always to unite scientific research and prayer. “For the saints, study was prayer and contemplation” 18 . Why, then, did some who apparently studied a great deal go astray? St. Augustine says: because “they did not know the way, your Word, by whom You made the things they number, the very ones who number them, the sense by which they perceive the things they number, and the mind by virtue of which they number them; […] they did not know this way, by which, descending from themselves, they might go down to Him and through Him ascend to Him; they did not know, I say, this way, and they thought themselves loftier and more radiant than the stars, and so they came tumbling to the ground, their foolish heart being darkened. They do not seek with a spirit of piety the Maker of the universe, and therefore they do not find Him … for it is vanity to make profession of these worldly things, but it is piety to confess You” 19 . Characteristics St. Thomas said in general terms: “the exercise of the moral virtues, by which the passions are mastered, is of the greatest importance for the acquisition of knowledge” 20 . Someone might say: ‘no, I don’t have the gifts, I’m no good.’ It is worth recalling the letter of St. Thomas to his disciple John, who asked him for advice on how to study better. His counsels do not deal above all with intellectual conditions but with human conditions. “Dearest: since you have asked me in what way you should devote yourself to study in order to acquire the treasure of knowledge, here is my advice: Do not wish to enter the sea all at once, but try to reach it by way of the rivers, because it is through the easier things that one must arrive at the more difficult ones. This, then, is my advice, which will serve you as a rule: – I want you to avoid useless talk. -Have purity of conscience. – Do not neglect prayer. – Love recollection – Be kind to everyone. – Do not be curious about the affairs of others. – Do not be overly familiar with anyone, because this breeds contempt and gives occasion to neglect study: – Avoid wandering about in all things. – Seek to imitate the example of upright persons; do not look at who it is that speaks, but retain all the good that he says. – Try to understand what you read and hear. – Clear up your doubts and fix in your memory all the good you hear, without regard to who says it. -Do not seek things beyond your capacity. By following these norms, you will put forth great branches and produce useful fruit wherever the Lord has destined you to live. By putting these counsels into practice you will be able to reach the goal to which you aspire.” Let us also recall here the example of St. Catherine of Siena, who, though illiterate, became a Doctor of the Church, and of St. Charles of Sezze, who, also illiterate, composed works of a most lofty spiritual tenor. May the Virgin Mary teach us to practice this virtue, so very important for religious life and fundamental for our spirituality, so that, according to our possibilities, we may devote ourselves to study in order to possess a profound knowledge of the Incarnate Word, for His greater glory. Homily for the Religious Brothers of the Incarnate Word 2018

Homily for the Religious Brothers of the Institute of the Incarnate Word – 2018 [Exordium] One of the great riches of our beloved Institute is certainly that of counting religious brothers among our members; that is, that you are part of our Religious Family, true religious, as much as any one of us. That is why I am very happy to be able to welcome you in the house of the Procura and to celebrate this Mass with you. Know that for me this meeting has a special importance, both in meaning and in affection. That is why I would like to take advantage of this sermon to develop briefly two points that the Capitular Fathers mentioned at the last Chapter regarding the religious brothers: 1) becoming aware of the gift and the specific character of the vocation of brother; 2) the contributions you are called to make to the mission of the Institute in the Church 1 . 1. The vocation of brother in the Institute St. Marcellin Champagnat said of the vocation of the coadjutor brothers in his order (and we can say the same): “the religious vocation is always an extraordinary grace. After baptism, it is the most excellent one God can grant to a soul. It is a sign of predestination, a second preference and election for the glory of heaven” 2 . You have been called to walk toward perfection by the way of the evangelical counsels, which one day you professed with a generous totality of commitment, and that is why you are called, and in fact are, religious in the full sense of the word. Because you have been chosen and consecrated by God for the excellent office of “loving and serving, and making Jesus Christ loved and served” 3 , as the Constitutions define our vocation as religious. And not to be just any religious, but religious of this magnificent Institute of the Incarnate Word, which in its manifold charity has seen in the vocation of the brothers a key piece 4 for the good of the Institute (the holiness of its members) and for evangelization. You, in fact, are called to the perfection of union with God –the perfection of charity–: that is your vocation! The same as that of the priest members of the Institute. But moreover, in fact, it is you and not we –the priests– who are called key pieces of the apostolic undertaking of the Institute. And that is because the Incarnate Word himself –always fascinated with the little and the humble– has seen in the vocation of brother a “greater participation in and imitation of the radicalism of his self-emptying, that by which, moved by love for men, He became an obedient servant unto death on the Cross to give his life for many 5 in order to transfigure the world 6 . Thus, for 33 years now 7 , our precious charism of evangelizing cultures has counted you among its most powerful allies. To the point that both you and we priests are indispensably associated in a single evangelizing vocation, namely, that “of claiming for Jesus Christ all that is authentically human, even in the most difficult situations and in the most adverse conditions” 8 ; each one, of course, in his own way. Notice that it is now unthinkable to carry forward such apostolic works as the Hogarcitos, for example, without your help. And how many of the Institute’s apostolates in the parishes, in the monasteries and in the various missions would be hampered or perhaps cut short without your help: I know that there is one who teaches Bible courses 9 , others who help with various works of service and hospitality in the missions, and we could mention several more examples… That is why our Proper Law affirms: “The coadjutor brothers participate in their own way in the pastoral solicitude of the [Institute]” 10 . And this way, it seems to me, is that of complementarity within the same religious life and under the same founding charism. So, on the one hand, there is the help with the apostolic activities of the Institute, which in itself is already a great thing. But in addition, I consider of capital importance and great value the contribution of the brothers to community life –made up mostly of priests– and the great evangelizing witness they give to others by it. For our Proper Law says that through “the fraternal life of the missionaries, that alone is already missionary work. Because there is no better witness than that of Christian charity” 11 . And elsewhere it says that “all the fruitfulness of religious life depends on the quality of fraternal life in common” 12 . Therefore, your role within community life is a very important factor for the mission and requires no small amount of work in virtue. John Paul the Great said: “I wish to remind all religious –brothers and priests– of their complementarity. To the religious priest, engaged in many pastoral activities, the brother recalls that religious life has a community dimension that he must not forget. To the brother, engaged in humble domestic work or in tasks of service, the priest recalls the apostolic dimension of what he does” 13 . Something we must always keep in mind. It also seems important to me to recognize the specific role and the great influence that the more experienced Religious Brothers can exercise over the younger brothers. All of which certainly redounds to the benefit of the whole Institute. Let us move on, then, to the second and last point of this sermon: 2. Contributions of the brothers to the mission of the Institute In a world accustomed to using words like “the greatest,” “super,” “ the top of the top ,” where it seems that value is given only to what is splendid, what is grand, what is most showy, works of service are undoubtedly of incalculable value for the mission and convey a very eloquent witness to the people who see them, and above all to those who benefit from your attentions: for they bring them the message of Christ, who said I have come to serve, not to be served , and who is the same one who promised that a glass of water will not go unrewarded . The splendid charism of our Institute has impelled us from the beginning not to shy away from the missionary adventure. But that is not something of the past, nor is it something that concerns only the youngest. I know that there are some among you here who long ago left their own country to go and put themselves at the service of peoples where the mission was just beginning (Guyana, Kazakhstan, Peru…), or who, even while remaining in their countries of origin, helped in the toilsome beginnings of several missions. Today, too, our Institute needs you, and very much. Because you continue to be “ co-responsible for the missionary activity ” 14 that has been entrusted to us. That is why the Capitular Fathers, speaking specifically of you, said that “there are many apostolates, including intellectual and teaching ones, to which you can devote yourselves with much fruit, after due preparation. There are also trades that you can learn and take on, and which will be a gift of Providence in any mission” 15 . So on this occasion I also wish to encourage you warmly to give an ever more vigorous impetus to the missionary commitment of each one at the service of the Institute and of the Church. The proclamation of the Gospel is more necessary today than ever. And many brothers are needed who, forgetful of themselves, wish to spend themselves for the good of others, to bring souls closer to God and God closer to souls. I also take this opportunity to exhort you to collaborate in vocations ministry, not only for the priestly life, but also and very especially for the life of a religious brother within the Institute. That is why you should not hesitate to propose this way of life as a religious brother of the Incarnate Word that makes you so happy. Through your enthusiasm, help others discover the joy of giving themselves totally to Christ in a religious community, in order to share better the gifts of God and to proclaim more forcefully the message of the Word who became flesh. [Peroratio] In short, what I would like to tell you is this: rekindle in yourselves the awareness and the joy of your state as consecrated persons, as religious brothers within this Institute of ours, with all the richness and breadth of the service you can render. Truly, much is expected of you… all the brothers of the Institute can and must play a most important role in the missionary work of the Institute; that is why you are called “key pieces.” Realize the special mission that God has entrusted to you in the life of the Church. Know how to make use of all the resources of your insight to grasp the needs of people, whether priests or ordinary people in the apostolate, in order then to try to respond with all the richness of your heart. From this also follows the need to form yourselves, so that the service you render may be ever more worthy of that Jesus whom you serve in each person. Always live content in the daily exercise of your tasks, because it is written that God loves a cheerful giver 16 . Let us ask the Most Holy Virgin, especially under the title of Our Lady of Luján, to obtain from her Son numerous and generous vocations of brothers for our Institute. And to Her we also entrust each one of you, so that she may be for each of you “the Virgin of the yes,” as St. John Paul II said, “the Virgin of fidelity and of total self-giving to the mission; and may She also be the Virgin of hope, which you must proclaim to all men, first making it a reality in your hearts” 17 . All this we ask of her as we continue praying in the Holy Mass. Notes 1 Cf. Intellectual formation of religious brothers

The Constitutions , speaking of the formation of the members, devote two paragraphs to the formation of the religious brothers. They are numbers 260 and 261. In the first of them they declare that “they will dedicate themselves to the service of the houses and to rendering spiritual services that do not require the sacramental grace of Holy Orders” 1 . And in the following number they describe in detail the intellectual formation of the religious brothers in the Institute. For example, they say that “they will take some treatises of Philosophy and Theology… [and that] they will continue their formation until perpetual profession, in the houses to which they are assigned and under the direct authority of the local Superior, [and then continue with] their ongoing formation” 2 . And I would like to dwell on this point. Because sometimes, even within our ranks, it is thought that the brothers do not study, or that they do not have intellectual capacity and that is why they are brothers; and even some brothers themselves think that because they are brothers they are exempt from ongoing formation or from a more demanding intellectual formation. The vocation of religious brother First of all, it must be said that the vocation to be a religious brother in the Institute of the Incarnate Word is something well defined. And like every vocation, it requires suitability, which “must be threefold: physical (and psychological), intellectual and moral (which implies having a right intention) 3 ” 4 , as is stated in our proper law. Therefore, the fact that someone is admitted into the Institute as a religious brother in no way means that he does not have the intellectual capacity necessary to carry out his vocation, which includes −as the Constitutions well describe− those aspects of study we have mentioned, since the brothers are not governed by different Constitutions 5 . And therefore, all the non-negotiable elements attached to the charism also apply to them, including the one that refers to the preferential study of the philosophy of St. Thomas, which will allow him a more effective way to bite into reality according to his vocation as a brother. So it is important, as the Capitular Fathers said at the last General Chapter, that all the members of the Institute become aware of the gift that the religious brothers are for the Institute, and of the specific character of this vocation, just as it is also important that the brothers themselves be aware of the contributions they are called to make to the mission of the Institute in the Church 6 . That on the one hand. The dignity of the religious brothers Secondly, it must be said that the vocation of brothers in our Religious Family “represents a differentiated participation in the mission of the institute, with services rendered in collaboration with those who exercise the priestly ministry, whether within the community or in the apostolic works” 7 . Now, this does not mean that they are “second-class” members. Quite the contrary. The Directory of Religious Brothers says it very clearly: “The brothers do not constitute a second order, but are true religious bound to the same perfection, and to exercise the identical apostolate that forms the essence of our Institute. Therefore, the one religious consecration and the identical apostolic mission are the foundation of the equality between the brother and the priest” 8 . Hence, the dignity of the brothers and the priests is equal, even though their tasks are different 9 . Each one contributes his service according to his vocation, whether priestly or as a brother, and the greatest respect must be shown for the voice of God, who calls whom He wills to the one or to the other. Moreover, both the Constitutions and the rest of our proper law acknowledge the religious brothers of our Institute as key pieces for its mission 10 . In fact, “in many areas [the religious brother] plays an irreplaceable role: [For] ‘There are things that neither priests nor clerics can do, and the brothers do them’, as Don Bosco used to say 11 ” 12 . Intellectual formation of the religious brothers And this very thing leads us to develop the third point, which is the intellectual formation of the religious brothers. Because a brother cannot be a key piece in the mission of the Institute if he is not prepared for the noble task of the evangelization of culture. To be a religious brother in the Institute of the Incarnate Word “requires an appropriate and integral formation: human, spiritual, theological, pastoral and professional” 13 . And elsewhere the Directory , citing the Constitutions , adds that the best guide for the formation of the brothers is the one followed for the formation of all the religious in the Institute, which embraces human, spiritual, intellectual and pastoral formation 14 . In this sense our proper law establishes that “the religious brothers need to form their intelligence. [Since] a ‘certainty of the truth’ is necessary, given only by a sound philosophy, founded on the objective reality of things, since ‘the intelligence… can reach what is ’ 15 ” 16 . So then, “the brothers, as far as they are able, must also have access to a philosophical and theological formation that allows them to face the challenges that ‘come from the values that dominate the globalized culture of our day’ 17 . And that is why it is established that they must do the Studentate, in which they will take some treatises of Philosophy and Theology” 18 . Furthermore, they must also study the Catechism of the Catholic Church because this gives them a complete and unified vision of the truths revealed by God in Jesus Christ and of the Church’s experience of faith; hence the twofold requirement of knowing all the Christian truths and knowing them in an organic way’ 19 ” 20 . All this forms part of the initial formation that they must then continue throughout their whole religious life with ongoing formation, which, as we know, never ends 21 . How is this ongoing formation carried out? Through “conferences, retreats, courses, exams, etc., but also through the month-long Spiritual Exercises, through pilgrimage to the Holy Land and to the great shrines of Christendom, etc. 22 . “But above all”, our proper law points out, the religious brother “must learn to let himself be formed by everyday life, by his own community and by his brothers and sisters, by the usual things, ordinary and extraordinary, by prayer and by apostolic weariness, in joy and in suffering, until the moment of death” 23 . In this way, initial formation is linked with ongoing formation, each one making himself available to let himself be formed every day of his life” 24 . That is why I would like to end with the following exhortation of the document Vita Consecrata , which our proper law makes its own. It says: “No one can be exempt from applying himself to his own human and religious growth; just as no one can presume on himself and lead his life with self-sufficiency. No phase of life can be considered so secure and fervent as to exclude every opportunity of being helped and thus being able to have greater guarantees of perseverance in fidelity, nor is there any age at which the complete maturity of the person can be considered concluded” 25 . May the Most Blessed Virgin, Model of every consecrated person, obtain for us the grace to make great use of all the means and occasions of formation that we have daily, in order “to make visible the wonders that God works in the fragile humanity of those who are called” 26 . I take this opportunity at the same time to thank all the religious brothers of the Institute −apostolic and contemplative− for the invaluable help they represent in so many of our missions, especially those in the most difficult and most remote places.
