“An invitation to accomplish great works”

We want to be ‘as another humanity [of the Word]’ 1 Good Night talk of October 5, 2017 at the Major Seminary in Argentina Dear Fathers, Brothers, dearest seminarians: Our Constitutions , in their general principles, already state in number 7 that we “want to be ‘as another humanity [of the Word],’ and we want to be chalices full of Christ that pour out his superabundance upon others, showing with our lives that Christ lives.” This wanting to be ‘as another humanity of the Word’ carries within itself an implicit call to the practice of apparently opposite virtues; for example, our Proper Law lists: justice and love, firmness and gentleness, fortitude and meekness, a holy anger and patience, purity and at the same time great affection, magnanimity and humility, prudence and courage, joy and penance 1 , “poverty and generous self-giving ” 2 , etc. In this good night talk it seemed to me that it might be profitable for everyone to dwell on two of them: magnanimity and generosity –not as abstract virtues or virtues isolated within our religious life– but in relation to the missionary zeal that must characterize every religious of the Incarnate Word throughout his whole life. Because without them, I find it very difficult for one not to shy away from the missionary adventure, as we once promised. Already in Christ’s very missionary mandate to his apostles, Go and teach all nations (Mt 28:19), throughout the whole world (Mk 16:15), there is a certain reference to these two virtues: go and teach , with all the effort that this implies, with all the renunciation that it entails –leaving one’s family, one’s own country, one’s own culture, one’s language…– with all the preparation it requires, and this without time limits, with generous self-giving day after day. In the words of our Directory of Spirituality , with a self-giving “without diminutions or retractions, without reservations or conditions, without subterfuges or delays, without retreats or sluggishness” 3 . In a word: with generosity. Also, on the other hand, Christ tells them to go and teach all nations and throughout the whole world , without exclusivisms and without exclusions 4 , without geographical limits, warning them against the temptation of “falling into particularisms, reductionisms, partialities or one-sidedness that would undermine catholicity” 5 . Rather to all men and everywhere, like this: with great spirit, with magnanimity. As the Incarnate Word Himself did and commanded us to do!: I have given you an example, so that you may do as I have done to you 6 , says our Lord . That is why our Proper Law emphatically invites us to “commit our whole life to manifesting Christ to the world, so that he may be acknowledged not only by the poor but also by the rich, not only by the ignorant but also by the wise, not only by those of our homeland but also by those of other peoples” 7 . And this, even though at times we may have to sow in tears 8 . Our dear Institute has been formed “to inculturate the Gospel in the diversity of all cultures , to prolong the Incarnation of the Word ‘in every man , in the whole man and in all the manifestations of man,’ assuming all that is authentically human, and so to carry out with greater perfection the service of God and of men,” as our formula of profession explicitly says 9 . This is the ideal that must beat in the heart of each one of our religious. We must not settle for less! To be a religious of the Incarnate Word “is an invitation to accomplish great works, extraordinary undertakings” 10 ; “it is to take seriously, thoroughly, the demands of the Gospel: go, sell all that you have… (Mt 19:21)” 11 , and to do so with the “zeal of the saints and martyrs, who gave everything for God” 12 . To be a religious of the Incarnate Word is –as our Proper Law says– “to dispose oneself to die, like the grain of wheat, in order to see Christ in all things” 13 . That is why being a religious of the Incarnate Word brings with it the missionary vocation –whether lived in the cloister or in mission lands– and therefore one must be ready to go to any point on earth where the preaching of the Gospel and the celebration of the Eucharist are needed. “Therefore, we make our own the ardent words of St. Luigi Orione –the Directory of Spirituality goes on to say–: ‘Whoever does not want to be an apostle, let him leave the Congregation: today, whoever is not an apostle of Jesus Christ and of the Church is an apostate’” 14 . Simply because the glory of God and the salvation of souls are at stake. And for that we must begin right now! Not wait for the one next to us to begin. Not wait until we make perpetual vows, but now! Each one has to strive to attain a “martyrial disposition.” Each one has to begin to live and vibrate in this spirit from the moment he sets foot in our houses. Because that must be the spirit breathed in each one of them. Each one has to raise high the standard of the Incarnate Word and be ready to do “heroic, even epic things for Christ and his Church” 15 . Beginning right now: As regards study, not being content with a number of ideas held together with pins, but rather having a firm knowledge of philosophy and theology that makes you capable of understanding in all its depth the drama of contemporary atheism and therefore capable of offering effective solutions 16 . As regards the spiritual life, being ready to pass through the active and passive purifications of sense and of spirit 17 . Being men of a manly discipline 18 . And as St. John of the Cross says: “to want this Christ to cost us something” 19 . In pastoral matters: “in the likeness of the Incarnate and crucified Word we must have a ‘thirst for souls’” 20 . And spend and be spent , and want to persevere in this way to the end, as we have always been taught so much. And in everything, to move with an intrepid faith, a faith that spares no effort to bring the Gospel of Jesus Christ to as many people as it can. Without asking for anything more. That is incisive, enthusiastic pastoral work; that is ‘to bite into reality.’ There is a whole world to be remade in Christ. Two thirds of the world have not yet heard of Christ, and there are others who know Him so little! That is why that paragraph of our Constitutions where we read the charism is so beautiful, so inspiring; it says: “By the proper charism of the Institute, all its members must work , in supreme docility to the Holy Spirit and within the imprint of Mary, in order to make all that is authentically human the domain of Jesus Christ, even in the most difficult situations and in the most adverse conditions ” 21 . To call oneself a ‘religious of the Incarnate Word’ and to “back down” (to retreat) in the face of difficulties, trials, obstacles; to abandon what one has undertaken because of the ‘contradictions of the good’; to be afraid to take on apostolates because of the greatness of the work or out of fear of sacrifice, and so many other human limits that we sometimes set for ourselves, is to go back on one’s word; it is a contradiction. Because, as we have just said: God thought of us so that we all might work even in the most difficult situations and in the most adverse conditions ” 22 . There, in those situations, is where the priestly mettle 23 that must be forged right now is shown. Difficulties, the cross, the cruelest persecutions, loneliness… are part of the program. None of that can diminish or dim the missionary impulse that must be ever more alive in our souls. Because to be a missionary is precisely to be totally ready “to let oneself be sacrificed joyfully in order to make Jesus Christ known, loved and served among the peoples of the unbelievers” 24 , said that great formator of missionaries, Blessed Paolo Manna. From our being religious and from our very charism ‘of the Incarnate Word’ follows the incompatibility of mediocrity with our spirit. “The mediocre man shelters under a false balance, considers himself ‘middle of the road’; all magnanimity seems to him pride, all heroism seems to him extremism, all generosity seems to him exaggeration; he makes everything mediocre: whether retreats, camps, popular missions, catechesis, his own spiritual life, etc.” 25 Pettiness has nothing to do with our spirit: like that of the one who sows so stingily, “doing as little as possible with the excuse of not falling into activism, or because the times are bad, or because the family does not form as it used to, or because of the unhealthy action of the media…, and who only knows how to complain: ‘Nothing can be done here’” 26 . Or like that of the “localist, who is concerned only with the interests of his parish, who lives wrapped up in his little work, as if the Church were exhausted in his parish, or in his city, province or country” 27 . If a seminarian, if a priest, if a brother or novice ‘settles in,’ that is, builds his nest in things that are not God (his comfort, how well he does in this or that office, the experience accumulated in this or that apostolate, all the people he moves because ‘he is in charge,’ and so many other things we could mention), that religious stops vibrating for the ideal of dying in order to see Christ in all things: such a one seeks himself. If a religious does not fervently seek to advance in the spiritual life, if he settles for the least instead of the most, he is a religious –if the name even fits him– “who shies away from the missionary adventure.” That is, he is not moved by the same criteria as Christ -whose concern is to save men-; he does not go in search of the sheep; it seems to him that the minimum he does is enough; he perhaps hides behind his age, the lack of time or of means… and so he ends up neglecting the souls entrusted to him, imposing ridiculous bureaucratic obstacles on them, or blaming how bad the times are, etc.… Dear all: to be a missionary religious of the Incarnate Word “means all that is most noble, most perfect and heroic in the imitation of Our Lord; consequently, everything that opposes this ideal does harm and wounds the spirit” 28 . That is why we must not only live the life of Christ ourselves, seeking God in all things, but also spread the life of Christ in others 29 . This is, and this has always been, the spirit of our dear Institute: all generosity, zeal and charity. That is why may God preserve us from this spirit being lowered or diminished through our laziness or pettiness. May nothing in us obscure, even in the slightest, the brilliant and wholly evangelical ideal of the missionary life, as the Institute understands and carries it out, and which, together with our own personal sanctification, constitutes our whole purpose. To conclude, I would like to read you a good night talk that St. Luigi Orione gave to his sons and which I believe applies very well to our case. It is entitled: “The dynamite of Charity,” and it goes like this: “There are the Benedictine religious, who have their purpose; the Franciscans with theirs, the Dominicans; there are the Jesuits with their very special purpose. And we too have our exclusive purpose (…) Our nature, a characteristic that must distinguish us from all the other Congregations. And if you ask me what that characteristic is that must distinguish us from all the other Congregations, I tell you that it is THE DYNAMITE OF CHARITY. In charity toward the humblest and most abandoned of our brothers we must be dynamic and not marmots. (…) Our Congregation must be dynamic, and not necessarily numerous. I never dreamed of a numerous Congregation. When St. Aloysius Gonzaga learned that the Jesuits had reached 20,000, he began to weep (…) Quantity is not what matters. It is not, it is not at all. During the First World War, when almost all of ours were under arms, we did not close a single house. We multiplied ourselves by seven and the Lord assisted us spiritually and materially. We were like four poor walnuts in a drawer… When there are many, little or nothing gets done: little or nothing. When there are many, time is wasted, there is criticism, grumbling, and one always ends up doing something unbecoming to the religious spirit. (…) Do not drag along, or go in tow. Now in Italy they have imposed the Roman step: and our step, what will it be? Everyone must get it well into his head that we will march at an apostolic pace. Not only a Christian pace, but an apostolic pace. Whoever does not feel the force of charity, its flaming force, the force of apostolicity, should have stayed at home, in his village, not with us. Perhaps he could be a holy Trappist… But whoever remains here must be a true agitator of charity. Whoever does not have this strong will to go all the way, in love of God and of neighbor, let him leave: we can be good friends, but there is no need for us to be many. Few! Few! So that it may not have to be said: «Multiplicasti gentem et non magnificasti laetitiam» (You multiplied the nation and did not increase the joy – according to the Vulgate, Is 9:3). (…) Ours must not be a congregation of slackers, or worse still, of effeminate men; it must be a manly and strong congregation, not an invertebrate one; to such a point that, if one day a persecution were to break out (…), a bloody persecution, our Congregation should fall entire, like the Theban legion, and die as martyrs. That is how the seed of Christians is multiplied: «sanguis martyrum semen est christianorum». Exactly so! Our Congregation has to be prepared for the hardest trials; in defense of the faith and of the Church, of the Pope, and also of the Fatherland; because we must never separate the sacred loves of faith and fatherland. But if we do not form ourselves, if Jesus Christ is not in us, if our breast is not on fire with love of God, we will never be prepared for such a great undertaking” 30 . To be a religious of the Incarnate Word is “to immolate each day our whole person and all our activity to honor his Blood with our blood” 31 , as St. Gregory Nazianzen said. Only thus can we be the chalices that pour out his superabundance upon others. With the hymn to Our Lady of Sorrows we ask her to preserve in us, and to make grow mightily in our souls with waves of charity, apostolic fervor and the joy of evangelizing 32 . Preparing to be a victim

House of Formation of Our Lady of Sheshan – Philippines Beginning of the 2017 academic year [ Exordium] Dear Fathers, seminarians and novices, First of all, I would like to say that I am very happy to be here. It is the first time I have come to the Seminary (at least in this place; I visited it in the beginning, when you were in another place) and it is certainly a joy to meet all of you. I must say that it is a joy for me to see that the call of Christ is bearing fruit in your hearts, and I give thanks to the Lord and to Our Lady for the gift of the vocation of each one of you to our Institute. I also want to thank Fr. Diego for inviting me to preside at the Mass and preach on this occasion of the beginning of the academic year. The beginning of a new academic year in the seminary –and in reality, in any of our houses of formation– means another opportunity to “configure ourselves to Christ.” Because that is what every seminarian and every member of the Institute of the Incarnate Word is called to be –even from the Novitiate–: “to imitate Jesus Christ as perfectly as possible” 1 ; to put on Christ 2 , configuring oneself to Him 3 , as we read in our Directory of Spirituality . And if we are called to be “other Christs” –as we proudly confess in our Constitutions– we must imitate our Lord, who came to die so that others –and that includes you and me– might have life. Seminarians often say: “I am studying to be a priest.” But how many times does a seminarian say, or even think: “I am studying to be a priest and a victim”?… and yet, that is what we do. Because, if we are called to imitate the Incarnate Word, that is precisely what we seek to imitate: Him who was Sacerdos-Victima . He united in Himself the priesthood and the condition of victim, and we cannot conceive of our priesthood without becoming victims in pursuit of our specific end: the prolongation of His Incarnation. Our Directory of Spirituality , speaking of the earthly life of our Savior, goes on to say: “He offered himself without restriction as a victim to the Father; he sacrificed himself in expiation; he gave himself to the Father without reserve” 4 . And it continues: “Such must be the priestly attitude of all the members of our little Religious Family” 5 . Hence the beginning of this new academic year means a new opportunity to configure ourselves to the Incarnate Word as Priest-Victim. That is why, in this homily, I would like to speak to you –even if only briefly– about what we mean when we say that the Incarnate Word is Priest-Victim and about how we must imitate Him. 1. First, the Incarnate Word is Priest-Victim The texts of our Constitutions and Directories contain much material on this subject, which I encourage you to read. Nevertheless, let us begin by saying that our Lord differs from all the other priests –pagan and Jewish– of the Old Testament. All the other priests offered a victim distinct from themselves; for example, a goat, a lamb, an ox; but Christ offered Himself as the victim. He offered Himself without blemish to God, a spiritual and eternal sacrifice 6 , writes St. Paul. All others who have come into this world came to live; He came to die. A sacrificial death was the goal of his life, the gold he was seeking: I have a baptism with which I must be baptized, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished! 7 . Now, pay attention to this: our Lord was always Priest and Victim, from his Incarnation. Not only a priest, nor only a victim. Christ was numbered among sinners because he was the Victim for their sins. But he was separated from sinners because he was a sinless priest. He ate and mingled with sinners, he shared their nature and looked upon their sins. But he was separated from them by his innocence. “Jesus was at the same time priest and victim of his own sacrifice” 8 . He is at once the Offerer and the Offering; the Priest and the Victim. And although the Incarnate Word did not speak of this profound secret of the Suffering Servant to the crowds, he reserved it for his disciples and future priests, whom he called Friends 9 . To them alone he unveiled the prophecy of Isaiah 53, and to them alone he interpreted his death as a ransom for sinners 10 . And he wants to entrust the same to you, through the moments of prayer and in the various aspects of formation. As Priest he was sinless, and Sacred Scripture has more than enough material to prove it. The Archangel Gabriel proclaims it at the Annunciation: The angel answered: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the one to be born will be holy and will be called Son of God” 11 . He himself said it when he asked the Jews: “ Which of you can prove that I am a sinner?” 12 And later he said to his apostles: “ I will no longer speak much with you, for the Prince of this world is coming. He has no power over me 13 . Even the devil confessed it: “ What have we to do with you, Jesus of Nazareth? Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are: the Holy One of God.” 14 As Victim he identified himself with sinners: “Him who knew no sin he made sin for us, so that we might become the justice of God in him.” 15 . As Priest , he was holy with the Holiness of God; as Victim, he was made sin . As Priest he was “ set apart” from the world; as Victim he entered into it to fight against the Devil, the Prince of the world. Look at the beautiful Crucifix you have here: on the Cross, he stood upright as Priest; on the Cross, he lay prostrate as Victim. As Priest, he interceded for us before the Father; as Victim, he mediated for the sins of men. Before Pilate, he spoke seven times as Priest-Shepherd; before Pilate, he was silent seven times as Victim-Lamb. As Priest he had dignity; as Victim he suffered indignity. As Priest he begged the Father to let the Chalice pass; as Victim he drank it to the dregs. When his ministry reached its culminating moment, he insisted more and more that victory over the principalities and powers had to come through his sacrifice and his death. And although he was personally free from sin, he was considered guilty. Christ was innocent of sin, says St. Paul, and yet “Him who knew no sin he made sin for us, so that we might become the justice of God in Him.” 16 . He died in our place because he loved us and, in doing so, “ reconciled the world to himself, not counting men’s transgressions against them, but entrusting to us the word of reconciliation ” 17 . “What [Christ] is by nature we are by communication; He is so in fullness, we are so by participation; He is the Son of God by generation, we are so by adoption.” 18 Here is the key to the victimal priesthood of Christ and of all of us who are called to be priests. As priests, we must be holy. It is not that by our priesthood we are bound to the world; by the priesthood we are bound to God the Father! Yet as victims, we take the place of sinners, assuming their guilt and their poverty and interceding for them. Thus, just as Christ is a Priest-Victim, we –who aspire to be “other Christs”– must follow the same path. Our seminarians and novices are preparing not only to be preachers but also “sin-bearers,” not only to be offerers but also to be offered, not only to attend to the needs of men as social workers do, but also as redeemers. And as the Capitular Fathers remind us: “If we do not form religious who are deeply convinced of this, we will not form religious of the Incarnate Word.” 19 Being victims means feeling the guilt and sin of the world as if they were one’s own, and, through constant union with Christ, seeking to reconcile all humanity with Him. 2. So now the obvious question arises: How do we prepare ourselves to be priest-victims? a. In the profession of our vows we can clearly see this aspect of victimhood of which we have been speaking, as we make ourselves voluntary victims in order “to accept death to this world so as to be united totally to Christ and to share in his kingdom” 20 . Indeed, our “religious profession constitutes a true holocaust of oneself, since we offer ourselves and all our goods totally and without reserve to God ” 21 . Notice that we have said: totally and without reserve . We, like Christ, freely enter religious life in order to die to ourselves, completely. And like Christ, who was always priest and victim, we do not want to turn back. Our self-giving is forever, that is, to the very end. St. John Paul II wrote: “Those who are preparing for the priesthood must realize that their whole priestly life will have value to the extent that they are able to give themselves to Christ and, through Christ, to the Father” 22 . And this brings me to the second element that helps us prepare ourselves to be priest-victims. b. Because the profession of our vows demands of us: fidelity . Fidelity means, of course, that we are faithful to the nature and the demands of our call, that we live a life of integrity flowing from the interior conviction of who we are in the eyes of God, that we fully carry out the duties associated with our vocation, that we are men of our word, who can be counted on to do what we say and to live as we profess. Fidelity is the essential thing in the whole life of a man who desires to be, or who already is, configured to Christ in the depths of his being through the sacrament of orders. Our houses of formation must be that “family atmosphere” where our religious are formed in this virtue: fidelity. Fidelity to the commitment to Christ and his Church through the three vows, fidelity to one’s own vocation, fidelity to the command of Christ: Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature 23 . And as our Directory points out, “a true religious is faithful and shows great love not only for his religious life, but also for his own Institute, which includes in a very particular way its Founder and its Constitutions.” Then, quoting Vita Consecrata , it says: “ fidelity to the founding charism and to the subsequent spiritual heritage of each Institute is necessary. It is precisely in this fidelity to the inspiration of the founders, an inspiration which is itself a gift of the Holy Spirit, that the essential elements of consecrated life can be more readily discerned and put into practice with greater fervor.” 24 Why? Because it is our “charism that will lead us to belong entirely to God, to speak with God or about God in every situation. Because it will also foster an intimate and joyful communion of life with the Incarnate Word, in the school of his generous service to God and neighbor. And so we will be conformed to Christ progressively” 25 . Learn to be faithful. Make it a habit. So that later in life, when the “external structures” of seminary life are removed, you will persevere in your fidelity. Fidelity to your life of prayer, where the Lord himself will whisper in the depths of your souls what it means to be a victim. Fidelity to your studies, to your apostolates, to the duties assigned to you, to the timetable, to the traditions of our Institute… Not like robots, not only outwardly, but deeply convinced that this is God’s will for you. Be faithful even if you do not have the best means, or in the face of exterior difficulties and interior trials, because that is when you best show that you are authentic religious of the Incarnate Word, that is, when you “work in utmost docility to the Holy Spirit and following the example of the Virgin Mary so that Jesus Christ may be Lord, even in the most difficult situations and in the most adverse conditions”, 26 as our charism says. Fidelity in action springs from a trusting, grateful and humble awareness of our vocation. Be faithful to Christ who has called you. In the end, everything else is spiritual commentary. And not only be faithful—be joyfully faithful! That is –as you know– one of the non-negotiable points of our charism: joy! It is not that you must force yourselves to fake laughter at every moment; that would be ridiculous. But rejoice in the fact that, even in difficult situations, God helps you to do what is best for you. God chose suffering to redeem us. So, if suffering is “borne with patience, accepted as coming from God, and sanctified by uniting it to the pain of Christ” 27 , you will save countless souls. c . Third, the So that “you may grasp the ‘style’ of our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, his attitudes and sentiments. [Discipline is the fundamental attitude of the disciple. It is a submission to the rules of life so that the truth may become flesh in the life of the disciple. For us, the truth is Christ, and to be docile to discipline means to let Him be our Lord” 28 . Always keep this in mind. d. Fourth, study . We cannot love what we do not know. That is why, if we do not study, if we do not read Scripture, if we do not immerse ourselves in the study of the teachings of the Church, how can we give reasons for our faith to others? For it must not happen that someone becomes “an empty preacher of the word of God to others, without hearing the word of God in his own heart” 29 , says John Paul II, quoting St. Augustine. e. Finally, perseverance . As we have been saying: ours is a formation aimed at configuring us to Christ Priest-Victim, which necessarily points to the Cross in our life. Therefore, we cannot conceive of a priesthood without the cross, without enemies, without trials. All of that is nothing but fine, individual opportunities to make our life more like that of Christ. Yes, the priesthood is a great dignity, which brings with it the glorious suffering of ignominy for the sake of Christ. And that makes perseverance all the more necessary. “The value of good works lies in perseverance,” said St. Gregory the Great. Your preparation as priest-victims here in these houses of formation means that you are preparing to be witnesses. In Scripture, witness means martyrdom 30 . But even if none of you sheds his blood for the sake of Christ, witness always implies separation from the world. You must be the salt of the earth: by your works bringing people to God, by the proclamation of the truth denouncing the spirit of the world, etc. That is why you must always remember what our rule says: “‘Being in the world’ only makes sense when it depends on ‘not being of the world.’ [Which is exactly what our Lord, Priest and Victim, did]. Only thus can one truly be salt of the earth and light of the world (Mt 5:13ff)” 31 . Again: this will necessarily bring the cross into your lives. Therefore, you must expect to share in his Passion: ridicule, mockery, persecution, ingratitude, etc. But you must persevere. Our disposition must be that of a martyr. Keep this in mind as you advance through this academic year. St. Isaac Jogues, one of the North American martyrs, after many years in his mission, having suffered much at the hands of the natives and feeling that he was not really advancing toward this configuration with Christ Priest and Victim, once wrote to his superior: “ Dear Father, when shall I begin to serve and to love him whose love for us had no beginning? When shall I begin to give myself completely to him who has given himself to me without reserve? Although I am extremely wretched and have misused the graces Our Lord has given me in this country, still I do not lose courage . He takes the trouble to help me do better ; he still provides me with new opportunities to die to myself and to unite myself inseparably to him .” And he added –listen carefully–: “ My trust is placed in God, who does not need our help to accomplish his designs. The only thing we have to do is try to be faithful to him and not spoil his work with our defects .” How important it is that we live by that! [Dear brother priests, seminarians and novices: It is my wish for all of you that this new academic year you are now beginning may be an opportunity to configure yourselves to the Incarnate Word, Priest and Victim. You too are called to imitate Him who, as Priest, was holy with the holiness of God, “through the holiness of your lives” 32 ; to imitate Him as Victim, who was “made sin,” through the “holocaust of yourselves” in the faithful living of the religious vows. You too are called to imitate Him as the Priest “set apart” from the world who came to fight with the Prince of this world, by giving public witness to your consecration through the way you live, which “includes detachment from the world” 33 , and by “becoming a fool before the world in order to convert that same world by the foolishness of your preaching” 34 . Know that you too are called to imitate the Incarnate Word who, as Priest, asked the Father to let the chalice pass , but who, as Victim, drank it to the full, “loving the living cross of labors, humiliations, insults, tortures, pains, persecutions, misunderstandings, annoyances, contempt, shame, calumnies, death… and being able to say with St. Paul: I die every day in order to nail into their hearts Him who was nailed to the cross for you” 35 . In fact, we call ourselves ‘co-redeemers’!” 36 . I encourage you all not to skimp on any activity, any lesson, any task as you strive to attain this sublime Ideal. He came to you first. Let yourselves be formed by Him. Value and be grateful for the magnificent call you have received, that of being “other Christs,” through your fidelity to it. May our Most Holy Mother, Mother of Christ Priest and Victim, educate you with her maternal love, so that the authentic image of her Son may be reflected in you. To her I entrust you and all who will come after you to study in her house, the House of Formation of Our Lady of Sheshan. God bless you all! A missionary to proclaim Jesus Christ

Homily for the 20th Anniversary of the Major Seminary “St. Joseph of Anchieta” – Brazil [ Exordium ] To celebrate the great apostle of Brazil, St. Joseph of Anchieta, patron of this beloved Major Seminary, is already reason for a great feast. To celebrate today, as well, the twentieth anniversary of its foundation, and to say that this is currently the largest major seminary of the Institute 1 , makes this feast take on limitless dimensions of happiness and, therefore, of heartfelt gratitude to the Incarnate Word and to his Most Holy Mother, from whom all gifts come to us. Touches of the merciful Providence of our Lord that must not go unnoticed. Moved by the sublime example of this great missionary, in this sermon, which I wish to dedicate very especially to our major seminarians who will be future missionaries, I would like us to reflect on one aspect of the life of “that humble man named Joseph Anchieta,” as a poet called him 2 , and who was one of the greatest missionaries ever to set foot in America. Life as a student Joseph of Anchieta was born, as you know, on the feast of St. Joseph in the year 1534, the same year in which Ignatius of Loyola was gathering his first companions in Paris. At the age of 14 he was sent to study Philosophy at the University of Coimbra, Portugal. Having finished those three years of Philosophy, he entered the Ignatian order on May 1, 1551 (a day on which St. Joseph is also celebrated today). And as soon as he had finished his novitiate, at the age of 19, he was sent to the Mission of Brazil with the third expedition of Jesuits, which set out from Lisbon precisely on a May 8, 1553 (the day of Our Lady of Luján). He was at that time the youngest missionary in the New World. The great miracle of the Apostle of Brazil was his life. It was humanly impossible for him to survive no less than 44 years with his double tuberculosis 3 , which he contracted while in the novitiate; but he, without “shying away from the missionary adventure” 4 , despite his illness and the absolute lack of resources, went to a mission that was just beginning and there he displayed a most fruitful apostolic activity. To the point that today he is venerated not only as the apostle of Brazil, but as the founder of São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro; author of the First Tupi-Guarani Grammar; creator of Brazilian literature and theater; first historian of the minerals, of the flora and fauna, and of the ecology and anthropology of Brazil. But let us begin at the beginning: on arriving in Brazil in 1553, this young religious, without experience, a stranger to the customs of the place, and sick, was sent to the south of Brazil, to São Vicente, where the Jesuits had a school and where some vocations had arisen. The only one who could teach Latin was Anchieta, so there he went. And, sick as he was, he gave three different classes daily from morning until night, having to write out by hand the texts for his students and preparing his classes during the nights. That was his life as a student, his life as a seminarian. In a letter, which perhaps you know, addressed to Fr. Diego Laínez, Superior General of the Society of Jesus, dated June 1, 1560, Joseph of Anchieta wrote word for word: “For this reason, without letting ourselves be intimidated by the great heat, the storms, the rains, the torrential and impetuous currents of the rivers, we strive without rest to visit all the villages and towns, both of the Indians and of the Portuguese, and even at night we go to the sick, crossing dark forests at the cost of great fatigue, both because of the roughness of the paths and because of the bad weather.” And describing even more openly the conditions of those who, with him and like him, devoted themselves to the sublime work of evangelization, he reveals still more deeply the greatness of his love and of his spirit of sacrifice when he says: “But nothing is difficult for those who cherish in their heart, and have as their only end, the glory of God and the salvation of souls, for whom they do not hesitate to give their life.” Hence St. John Paul II, in the homily of a Mass celebrated here in São Paulo in the year 1980, affirmed that Joseph of Anchieta did not come here as a conqueror in search of treasures and glory, but “came as a missionary , to proclaim Jesus Christ, to spread the Gospel. He came with the sole aim of leading men to Christ, transmitting to them the life of children of God, destined for eternal life. He came without demanding anything for himself ; on the contrary, ready to give his life for them” 5 . Perhaps we could point out here that Joseph of Anchieta was very young, that he had a high level of education for the time, that he certainly had European customs and that, for that reason, practically everything, from the food to the smells, the local language and the extreme poverty, was a cause of self-denial for him. Not to mention the six or seven months without confession or Mass, or having to meditate not in a comfortable little corner –as he says– but in the midst of the wickedness of the Indians 6 . All this already speaks of an “admirable” 7 seminarian whom God wanted to make very holy. However, there is something else I would like to emphasize, and it is the great forgetfulness of self , and the love for souls and for his Congregation, that he showed from the very beginning. For there is a letter he writes to the sick in Coimbra, with whom he had even shared the infirmary, in which he tells them that he was basically cured by teaching classes. He tells them that even though he taught practically all day and therefore had almost no time to rest like any sick person, even though the food there was very poor –in fact, he recounts that he ate “boiled mustard leaves and other vegetables of the land and other delicacies that you over there cannot imagine” 8 –, and even though he had fasted the whole of Lent, he was practically cured in the mission. And in that letter he reveals an important detail; the saint says: “as soon as I acted as if I were not sick, I soon began to be healthy.” There you have the forgetfulness of self that God blessed so superabundantly. That is why he goes on to tell his companions back in Coimbra: “if the Father Master wished to send here all of you who are poorly and half sick, half well, the land is very good, the air very healthy, the medicines are labors, and all the better the more they conform us to Christ .” And he goes on to say, pay attention: “I also tell you, my dearest ones, that it is not enough to leave Coimbra with just any sort of fervor , which withers right away before crossing the line [of the Equator], or cools afterward with desires to return to Portugal. It is necessary, brothers, to bring your saddlebags full , so that they last until the end of the journey, because without a doubt the labors that the Society has here are great, and virtue is needed in each one, so that the honor of the Society may be entrusted to him” 9 . That is to say, it is not enough to jump about singing “Verbo Encarnado,” or to say in words that one loves the Institute; it is not enough to have read the Constitutions at some point; it is not enough just to say “we are essentially missionary and Marian” 10 , nor even to be a good student in the seminary, to make of us a thorough missionary of the Incarnate Word. All of that, even though good, if it is not with conviction, if it does not have deep roots in the soul, belongs to those kinds of fervor the saint speaks of, which wither right away and grow cold and make one want to turn back. Because, as St. Ignatius taught very well –and we meditate on this every year when we make the exercises– “ love ought to be put more in deeds than in words ” 11 . Do you understand me? St. Joseph of Anchieta had understood this well; that is why he tells his companions that one must have one’s saddlebags full of fervor , of the fervor that withstands the great waves of trial that will undoubtedly come upon the missionary; saddlebags full of “ apostolic charity ” 12 –as our Proper Law asks of us– that make the missionary forget himself in order to work “even in the most difficult places and in the most adverse conditions” 13 , and this not in just any way, but with great zeal for the good of souls and the expansion of the Church of Christ; full of the fervor that makes the missionary –even when he no longer has the spiritual consolations he once had “and which one day God withdraws completely” 14 , and stripped also of “the supports and assurances regarding the state of his soul” 15 – nevertheless trust “with unshakable firmness that even the most adverse events, and those most opposed to his natural view, are ordered by God for his good” 16 . Conditions for the mission For this reason the Directory of Missions Ad Gentes establishes as a most important condition for the mission that capacity to deny oneself, to renounce that selfish attitude that makes us seek our own interests, our own comfort, in order to work with zeal in the place and in the office that the Institute entrusts to us for the greater glory of God. The directory says: “The missionary is asked ‘to renounce himself and everything he had until then and to become all things to all’: in the poverty that leaves him free for the Gospel; in detachment from the persons and goods of his own milieu , so as to become thus a brother to those to whom he is sent and to bring them to Christ the Savior” 17 . Notice what it says: to renounce himself and everything he had until then… detachment from the persons and goods of his own milieu… this is part of the program of all who wish to be missionaries in the Institute, and they must begin to exercise themselves in it from now on. That is why St. Joseph of Anchieta adds in his letter: “I say no more to you, except that you prepare yourselves with great interior fortitude and great desires to suffer, so that, even though the labors be many, they may seem few to you” 18 . To which I add here other virtues that our Proper Law mentions for us: “Those who in our houses of formation are preparing to carry out great works for the glory of God in the missions to which they will be sent [notice that it is speaking directly to you], so as not to deceive themselves with vain fantasies, should cultivate a great love for the virtues of humility , charity and docility to superiors .” Then our Proper Law continues: “‘It is not enough that nothing negative be found in our candidates; it is not enough that they be sufficiently diligent in study and exterior discipline. One must study their character, measure the fervor of their spirit , the absolute submission of the will, generosity in sacrifice, the spirit of initiative, fidelity to duty’ 19 . Those types of personality that ‘know everything,’ ‘get along badly with everyone,’ find fault with everything, argue about everything, or neither listen to nor obey anyone except when others agree with what they think, will hardly be suited for the mission. The reason why such characters will not be able to bear fruit is that God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (1 Pet 5:5). And if God resists a missionary, what will he be able to do?” 20 . All this makes “evident that a great part of the formative effectiveness [for our seminarians] depends on the mature and strong personality of the formators from the human and evangelical point of view” 21 . Thus far our Proper Law. Joseph of Anchieta was in the Captaincy of São Vicente, today the state of São Paulo, for 12 years, from where he left for the north, to Bahia, to be ordained a priest the following year, in 1566. His companions were ordained at 23 or 24 years of age. He, at 32. Did this delay trouble him? Not for a moment. Another trial that he knew how to bear with faith. He would be a priest when God so disposed. His part was to wait. Later on, when he was Provincial, he was conversing in Rio de Janeiro with other Fathers and Brothers on the subject of the conformity that every Jesuit must have with his office in order to preserve interior peace. Joseph confessed with the greatest simplicity: “When I was a brother, it never entered my imagination that I could be a priest. And when I least expected it, I found myself with orders. When I was a priest, it never crossed my mind that I could be professed or a superior… here you see me as Provincial” 22 . He was provincial superior for ten years. [ Peroratio ] Dear seminarians: Our mission is marvelous, sublime I would say, and at the same time challenging. Consider yourselves, then, the favorites of the Incarnate Word, whom He himself has called to be his missionaries. Having embraced this vocation, know that you have at the same time taken on the mission; therefore you must feel responsible for your personal preparation . The superiors and the formators are here to help, certainly, but continual growth in the spiritual, intellectual, human and pastoral dimensions depends on you, on the awareness of your duty 23 as religious of the Incarnate Word. The Holy Patron of this beloved seminary gave us a magnificent example of this very thing throughout his thirteen years of preparation for the priesthood. Christ needs the contribution of all in order to bring to other hearts the word that not all can understand 24 , the word that the Word became flesh . Are you ready?… then put that love into practice and strive to acquire that interior fortitude and that longing to suffer for Christ which made Joseph of Anchieta an “authentic missionary, a true priest” 25 . That is my message. And now, to conclude, I would like to renew my gratitude, my trust and my affection to all of you, to all the priests who in one way or another are involved in your formation, and I encourage you to keep going, always forward!, giving the best of yourselves for the glory of God and the expansion of the Institute. To the Most Holy Virgin of Aparecida I entrust the intentions of all of you, and I ask Her to take under her maternal protection the present and future vocations of this seminary and to make them “tireless evangelizers” 26 . May the Mother of the Incarnate Word and of the Church always accompany your steps, and may the Holy Spirit continue to raise up numerous Brazilian vocations. A very happy anniversary! Children in one same Family

[ Exordium ] Our Constitutions , in number 20, say that “in the name of Christ we want to constitute a Religious Family… loving one another in such a way because we are children of the same Father.” That is to say, Christ has called us individually, certainly, but in order to form a family, a particular family, the Religious Family of the Incarnate Word. This is an aspect on which St. John Paul II insisted a great deal every time he spoke to religious. Thus, for example, in ’86 (perhaps you had not even been born yet) he said: “The preparation of candidates for religious life is not limited only to imparting knowledge. It is above all the delicate task of leading them to give a deep and personal response to God’s call… with a generous and sincere love for their own Religious Family ” 1 . This is key. 1. Love for the Religious Family What does it mean to have love for one’s own Religious Family? Our Proper Law says it very clearly: a true religious keeps fidelity and shows a great love not only when he appreciates the gift of religious life but also when he loves and defends his own Institute, which includes in a particular way the founder and the Constitutions. That is in the Directory of Consecrated Life 2 . This love for the Religious Family is key for our mission. Because it is what will make us soak up the spirit of our beloved Institute, in such a way that its interests are our interests, its projects are my projects; if the Institute is attacked, I am attacked. Do you understand? Moreover, if there is charity among us, if there is unity, that gives our religious witness a power that nothing and no one else can give it. No matter how many popular missions we preach, no matter how pure our doctrine, no matter how much we expand into many countries of the world, if there is no charity and unity among us, our efforts are in vain because, as John Paul the Great also says, “division among brothers, among sisters, is a stumbling block for evangelization” 3 . Word for word. On the other hand, if we are solidly united in love for our Religious Family, that is a constant, intelligent preaching, even without words, of the message of Christ, which is none other than a message of charity. And this love for the Religious Family –which naturally includes our brothers in this Family– is also key for the future of the Institute. It is in the seminary that one begins to live the spirit of priestly fraternity 4 . For notice what our Spiritual Father says: prayer and the apostolate –it is true– help us to grow in charity, but “even more important for a deep spirit of brotherhood is ‘ the unity of soul and heart ,’ which is strengthened by your shared commitment to holiness, your common charism and your lifelong commitment to follow Christ by observing the Gospel and the Constitutions of your Institute ” 5 . All the holy founders placed great emphasis on the love that religious must profess for their Institute. I quote here two examples, just to illustrate: St. John of the Cross, for example, gave the following counsel to a religious: “By no means desire to know anything except how you will better serve God and better keep the things of your Institute” 6 . St. Peter Julian Eymard, for his part, calls his Congregation “mother” and tells his religious that “the first duty you have toward her is to love her with filial love” 7 . And he adds the following: “The rule is for you what the gospel is for the Church” –notice how important– therefore be careful, because “some come who say: If this were modified, if that were added…, it would be better if things were done this other way… It may be that such men have talent, experience and influence, but I tell you [–says the saint–] that, willingly or not, they are traitors to the first grace, to the grace of the foundation, to the ideas of the Founder, and that whoever listens to them will ruin the Institute” 8 . Let us be, then, good children of our beloved “mother,” the Congregation, which is the place where God the Father has called us to consecrate our existence to the greater honor and glory of his Name. 2. The servant religious – the son religious St. Luigi Orione, founder of the Sons of Divine Providence, insisted a great deal that his congregation live in an authentic family spirit, in which the bond of love for the Incarnate Word would be the secret of harmony and mutual collaboration. But of course, he realized that not everyone loved the congregation as they should; that is why he distinguishes “two different types of religious: there is the servant religious and the son religious” 9 , and in a fantastic good night talk before a profession of vows he explains them. Let us see what it is about. The saint begins by clarifying that these are not two categories of his own religious, but that he is referring to religious in general, according to the love they have for their mother, the Congregation. And therefore what he teaches here applies to us as well. “I have traveled a great deal,” says Don Orione, “I have visited many religious congregations; I know many religious; I know the Trappists, the black Benedictines, the white Benedictines, the Olivetans, I know the Lateran canons, the various Franciscan families, the Jesuits, the Piarists; I know the religious of this part of the world and also of the other part of the world…; the Salesians of Italy and the Salesians of America, the Philippines, the Somascans 10 , etc. Well, among religious there are ‘servant’ religious and ‘son’ religious: two types of religious” 11 . “What is the ‘servant’ religious like? [Pay attention] He is the one who seeks his own interests in everything, who takes advantage of the Congregation to achieve his personal ends . He is the one who obeys his Congregation only with fear and out of fear. The ‘servant’ religious is the religious who serves the Congregation and works with indifference and reluctance. One could say that piety and love for his mother, the Congregation, are not in his heart . He lives in the schools, in the convents, in the abbeys, in the educational institutes, in the communities, more as a stranger than as a brother. His soul seems closed toward his superiors; the ‘servant’ religious always has a closed heart . He is like a book open only in part, with many parts still untouched, in which the superior cannot read how and when he wishes. The ‘servant’ religious,” Don Orione goes on to say, “as soon as the superior turns his eyes away, feels free. The first thing he does in the morning is to find out whether the superior will be at home or will go out. When the ‘servant’ religious has occasion to go out, if he is away from home, he never finds the moment to return to his religious house. He enjoys living his own life : he acts like lay people. His conversations are mainly worldly, rather than the conversations of a good religious. He is inclined to criticism ; among the brothers, always criticism; for him all the brothers have a weakness; even in the best he knows how to find the weak side, and he always takes care to point it out. In his judgments he always leans to the left and never to the right. He is always with the most lukewarm, with the professional jokers. The superior, before making even the slightest observation to him, must make the sign of the cross three times, for fear of a bad reception. When it comes to giving him an assignment, the superior has to examine: will he accept or not? And when he is in that house to assist, to say Mass, to preach, how will he behave? Will he behave like a good religious or like a ‘servant’ religious? And above all, when it comes to working, to tiring himself out, the ‘servant’ religious does this much (he stretches out his hand as if to measure a span) and nothing more. The ‘servant’ religious has his scheme, his confidants. Even at table one must be careful with one’s words, because the ‘servant’ religious makes public the most confidential news of his religious family . Love for the Congregation is not in his heart . If he speaks outside his Congregation, it is a lot if he does not throw stones at it. If he knows that the Congregation has enemies outside, setbacks, he remains apathetic, he remains indifferent; on the contrary, he behaves in a way that even seems as if he were inwardly enjoying it” 12 . How sad, isn’t it? Let us now see how Don Orione describes the religious who knows himself to be a ‘son’ of his religious family. “There are also, thanks be to God, the ‘son’ religious, who feel themselves to be ‘sons’; nothing is dearer to them, after God, than their Congregation . He desires nothing other than to see it prosper, to see it spread its tents over the face of the earth for the greater glory of God. He sees in the Congregation his mother and, after holy things, nothing is dearer than she. He prays, suffers, works, wears himself out for his Congregation . Who are religious like this? They are the ‘sons’… Whatever the office in which they are occupied, the ‘son’ religious is always content. Whether you tell him to work as a nurse, or put him in the school, or in an agricultural colony, he is always content; he is content to serve, with love, in any office of his Congregation. [Moreover,] he strives to perfect himself in the performance of his duties, and he does not squander his health with imprudence in work, but works with moderation and constancy without always thinking about his health. He takes care to nourish himself in order to live and to do good; he does not eat much, so as not to feel unwell: if he needs something, he goes with an open heart to the superior; he does not abandon himself to the sense of pessimism and melancholy that does so much harm to the Congregation… Who are religious like these? …They are the ‘son’ religious. If at some time the superior of the ‘son’ religious says or does something that is not to his liking, thus leading him to renounce himself, well then, the ‘son’ religious blesses God in holy joy; because he knows that the ‘son’ religious must above all deny himself … and so he takes up his cross and follows Jesus to Calvary… Unlike the ‘servant’ religious, the religious who knows himself a son of his congregation is like a book open to his superiors, in which one can read whenever one wishes.” Then Don Orione concludes with the following exhortation: “Dear sons, the ranks of the Congregation are growing in number, and the hour has come for us to understand each other well, because I know that you are on the eve of making or renewing your vows. If you feel yourselves to be ‘son’ religious, go forward!, but rather than be ‘servant’ religious, it is better to stop. Because Christ told us: I will no longer call you servants, but friends and sons .” And here I want to paraphrase what Don Orione says: “Let whoever is not clear about being a son [of the Incarnate Word] know that it is not Paul or Apollos whom he serves, but the Incarnate Word; he serves the Congregation, and the Congregation belongs to no one but the Incarnate Word” 13 . [ Peroratio ] That is why tonight, with the hymn to Our Lady, while we thank her for all the Brazilian vocations she has been pleased to call to grow and be nourished in the lap of this mother, our beloved Congregation, we ask her very especially for two graces: That in all our houses, especially in the houses of formation 14 , a family atmosphere may always be lived, with a family spirit. So that, just as a “family is a community of persons in love, a communion in love, our houses may be communities of charity, to such a degree that it may be said that Christ himself lives in them” 15 . That in this beloved major seminary religious may be formed who know themselves to be ‘sons’ of our beloved mother, the Congregation. Religious who venerate her, who are available for the service of God in the Congregation, religious who are holily proud of her, who defend her, and who desire to spread to countless souls this marvelous spirit with which God has blessed us. So be it. And may God always bless you. Homily at the Major Seminary in Argentina

1 Kgs 19:16b, 19-21/Gal 5:1, 13-18/Lk 9:51-62 [ Exordium ] All the readings we have just heard can make us feel a little uncomfortable. All the details we read in them are profoundly countercultural, against the current. So, for example, in the first reading we heard the call of Elisha, whom Elijah chooses as his successor. That is to say, this reading from the book of Kings has to do with following one’s vocation. Now, when we speak of finding our own path in life, we set a very high price on ʽour own judgmentʼ about what suits us or does not suit us to do with our life –for us it is like a fundamental right–: ʽnobody is going to come and tell me what I should do with my lifeʼ, ʽI decideʼ what to do with ʽ my lifeʼ. Well, that may be our perspective, our way of thinking in today’s culture, but it was definitely not the biblical perspective. Notice that Scripture does not suggest that Elijah and Elisha knew each other. Suddenly Elijah appears, passing by him while he is plowing, and just like that, without consulting him, without asking his permission, without any discussion, without preparations, Elijah simply throws his mantle over him, and Elisha follows him. Choosing your own path? Deciding what to do with your life? It does not seem to be the biblical way. Let us also note the change Elisha has to make in accepting his call. Elisha was in the field plowing with twelve yoke of oxen , that is, he was a wealthy person for the time, or at least of ‘high society’; twelve yoke of oxen is a lot of animals, and besides, he had sophisticated machinery, the plow; only people of the upper class of society could have such possessions. It is as if today we were to say that Elisha was driving his Lamborghini. What does Elisha do? Immediately, he took a yoke of oxen, slaughtered them, and with the oxen’s gear he cooked their meat and gave it to the people; then he arose, followed Elijah and became his servant . This is equivalent to saying ‘he sold his whole business’, ‘he gave away all his money’, ‘he gave away his house’. Just imagine! A person who is rich, who has people working for him, who has a big house, a very sophisticated way of life, suddenly leaves it all, gives it away. Throughout the centuries we have seen many who, like Elisha, spontaneously, following God’s initiative, left everything to follow our Lord. Let us think, for example, of St. Anthony the Abbot, who one day went ‘by chance’ into a church and heard the Gospel where Jesus says to the rich young man: go and sell all that you have, give it to the poor and follow me . And he did it! even though he was rich. He spent the rest of his life living in the simplicity and austerity of the desert. Think of St. Francis of Assisi, who was the son of a very rich merchant; he gave it all away and even gave his father the clothes he was wearing and walked naked into the forest. Let us think of St. Katharine Drexel, an American saint, the sole heiress of an immense fortune, who in order to follow God’s call left everything. Radical self-giving I imagine that by now you are thinking: ‘ well, we have in some way, more or less, already done that ’; ‘we have left the comfort of our homes, our money –little or much–, our studies…’. However, and this is the point, as religious of the Incarnate Word we are called to a radical self-giving that does not end on the day of the profession of temporary vows, nor on the day of perpetual vows, nor on the day of our priestly ordination; we must “aspire to live with all radicality the demands of the Incarnation and of the Cross” 1 always , that is, “to live poverty in the maximum and absolute degree in order better and more radically to imitate the poor Christ” 2 . And the major seminary must be a school in that sense. Poor in the material sense, one can say that you already are… here I would rather refer to that degree of poverty of which our proper law speaks and which invites us to conquer “total detachment, not only from material goods –the proper object of the virtue of poverty– but from everything that is not God Himself, which presupposes the perfection of charity and complete and consummate holiness” 3 . This is very important for our life as missionaries. Here you do not have twelve oxen, or a Lamborghini, but you are indeed surrounded by a great many consolations. If you stop to look, you have the good fortune of being surrounded by very good priests to whom you can turn whenever you want; you have access to the sacraments daily; you are surrounded by a great many brother seminarians; none of you –not even the one who lives at the end of the last block– has to walk kilometers to go to church; and we could go on listing many very consoling details. Careful! I am not saying those things are bad, all right? On the contrary, all those things are very good, extremely good, because they are conducive to formation. But one must be attentive and not set one’s heart on those things, because one day God is going to ask you, too, for a radical change, as He did Elisha, and God is fully within His rights. It is the deal we made when we took our vows in this Institute. That is why one has to be prepared for it. It happened, for example, to St. Junípero Serra. At 56 years of age, and with the sole experience of having been a professor of Theology, very comfortable in the seminary, he had to leave for a mission that seemed impossible in the new world. He left his comfort zone and off he went. He founded 9 of the 15 missions that today give their names to cities in California. Was it hard for him? Of course it was hard for him. He was asthmatic and had a wound in his leg that never healed, and yet he walked the whole way (38,000 km). “ Always forward, never back ”, he used to say. It also happened to St. José de Anchieta: having barely finished the novitiate, and while still sick with tuberculosis, he was sent to the mission in Brazil, which had just begun, with all the hardships that implied at that time. He did his seminary in the mission. His companions were ordained at 24 or 25; he at 32. But before God’s call they did not shrink back, they did not look back; they threw themselves into what God was asking of them. That is why, notice that the Directory of Missions Ad Gentes establishes as a most important condition for the mission that capacity to deny oneself, to renounce that selfish attitude that makes us seek our own interests, our own comfort, in order to work with zeal in the place and in the office that the Institute entrusts to us for the greater glory of God. The directory says: “The missionary is asked ‘ to renounce himself and everything he had up to then and to make himself all things to all’: in the poverty that leaves him free for the Gospel; in detachment from the people and goods of his own milieu , so as to become a brother to those to whom he is sent and bring them to Christ the Savior” 4 . Notice what it says: to renounce himself and everything he had up to then… detachment from the people and goods of his own milieu… that is part of the program of all who want to be missionaries in the Institute, and you must begin to exercise yourselves in it from now on. Let it be well understood that the missionary, in order to truly be one, must give himself entirely, and must give himself forever. This, and nothing else, is the apostolic ideal always promoted in the Institute from its very foundation 5 . Nothing is given to the Lord by halves; nothing is measured out to the Lord. What we can offer Him is already so little! So, not to give oneself forever is not to give oneself entirely. Once St. Peter Julian Eymard was giving a sermon to those who were professing for the first time, and he asks them: “For how long are you signing this contract? Out of prudence the rule orders you to sign it only for a few years, one or three. Are you going to say on that account: Fine! I give myself for this time, but afterward we shall see? Certainly not! In your hearts you must act as if you were making perpetual vows. Because if you do not want to belong to God forever, you are not worthy to be His for one year. Stay here, the saint tells them, do not take one more step, because where God is concerned one does not make trial runs 6 . However, there are souls who, as soon as a difficulty arises, when they have some clash in the apostolate, when they experience some rejection –like the disciples in the Gospel when they were not received–, when they are given a correction, when they hear some criticism of the Institute, immediately call into question the following of Christ, to the point that at times they behave as enemies of the cross of Christ 7 , as St. Paul says; they look back, as the Gospel we heard says. Sometimes, to avoid a renunciation, so as not to deny themselves, out of fear of sacrifice, they miss out on great graces. They are afraid that by giving something they will be left with nothing. Tell me something: why cling to a match when we can have the sun? “Cowards –says our proper law– die many times before their death” 8 . Nothing could be further from us. That is why we read in another of our documents: “The religious vocation is to leave everything in order to obtain everything; it is to leave the things of this world in order to cling to the All, which is God. St. Teresa said: ‘This King does not give Himself except to the one who gives himself entirely to Him’ 9 . Far from lamenting what we leave behind, we should consider the goodness of God who wishes to give Himself to us” 10 . In this sense the witness of one of the North American martyrs, Noël Chabanel, is truly exemplary; he belonged to the same group as St. Jean de Brébeuf, Isaac Jogues… who are perhaps the best known. The point is that Fr. Chabanel was a successful professor in France, but he fervently desired to be a missionary in New France (Canada) and prayed that his martyrdom would be accepted, that is, his offer to go to those lands as a missionary. The fact is that when at last he was sent and arrived at the mission, once he had contact with the Indians and had the opportunity to experience in his own flesh the difficulties of the mission, he felt like running away, like going back to the comforts and securities of France, like looking back. They say that of all the Jesuits who went to New France, he was the one for whom the mission was hardest. He found the language incomprehensible and the way of life repugnant, and naturally all this saddened him. However, and here is the heroism that prepared him for martyrdom, even though his superiors gave him permission to return to France, he made a vow to remain firm in the mission no matter what happened. Why? Because he was fully aware of the words we hear the Incarnate Word pronounce today in the Gospel: Whoever puts his hand to the plow and looks back is not fit for the Kingdom of God 11 . And do you know what? God took him at his word. He was the one who stayed longest in the mission, because he was the last to be martyred. One night, as he was fleeing from some warrior Indians and trying to reach the central mission post the Jesuits had, he came upon a very deep river that could not be forded, and while he was thinking how he would manage to cross, an Indian –in fact a Christian apostate– approached him and offered to take him across in his canoe. But halfway across, the man killed Fr. Chabanel, stole what he was carrying and threw his body into the river. The man took two years to confess what he had done, saying that he had acted out of hatred for the missionaries and for the faith. Do you see? If he had gone back to the comforts and securities of France, if he had gone back to his comfort zone, he would have missed the palm of martyrdom and eternal beatitude. That is why it is important now, while you are in formation, that you load your saddlebags full of fervor , the fervor that withstands the great waves of trial that will undoubtedly come upon the missionary; that you load your saddlebags full of “ apostolic charity ” 12 –as our proper law asks of us– which makes the missionary forget himself in order to work “even in the most difficult places and in the most adverse conditions” 13 , and this not in just any way, but with great zeal for the good of souls and the expansion of the Church of Christ; and that you be filled with that courage which makes the missionary –even though he no longer has the spiritual consolations he had before “and which one day God withdraws completely” 14 , and stripped also of “the supports and securities regarding the state of his soul” 15 – nevertheless trust “with unshakable firmness that even the most adverse events, those most opposed to his natural outlook, are ordained by God for his good” 16 . That genius St. Alberto Hurtado used to say: “In life there are no difficulties, there are only circumstances. God directs everything, and He directs everything well. There is nothing to do but abandon oneself, and serve at every moment as far as possible”. Looking forward Therefore, listen to me carefully: there have been and there always will be difficulties; criticism, threats, crosses of every kind are not lacking and will not be lacking, because God does not want them to be lacking, either here or anywhere else. However, we have to look forward ; we must put out into the deep , trusting in the word of Christ: Duc in altum! Jesus Himself warns us: Whoever puts his hand to the plow and looks back is not fit for the Kingdom of God 17 . In the cause of the Kingdom there is no time to look back, much less to let oneself be carried away by sloth. Much is expected of us: nothing more and nothing less than the sublime task of “claiming for Jesus Christ the lordship of all that is authentically human, even in the most difficult situations and in the most adverse conditions” 18 . We must act with generosity 19 , with resolve 20 , “working always against the temptation of delay, against the fear of sacrifice and of total self-giving, and against the temptation to take back what we have given by seeking compensations or by settling down, making a ‘nest’ in things that are not God” 21 . It is the example of Christ Himself in today’s Gospel, which says that Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem 22 . And in that “attitude one must live permanently, without diminishing or retracting, without reservations or conditions, without subterfuges or delays, without retreats or sluggishness” 23 . For “he who is not capable of setting fire to his ships when he lands is not capable of building empires” 24 . [ Peroration ] Let us ask in this Holy Mass for the grace that from this beloved house of formation may go forth missionaries who live lordship over themselves, over men, over the world and over the devil; who enjoy the ‘freedom’ of the children of God… who are courageous , who are accustomed to discipline , who know how to give each thing its value , and in hierarchical order; who love the Institute by living its proper charism; missionaries who say, with all the radicality and commitment that it implies: Lord, I will follow you wherever you go! 25 . We ask this of the Incarnate Word through the intercession of the Most Blessed Virgin Mary.
