Model of every mission

[ Exordium] “In a special way, we will dedicate ourselves to the preaching of the Word of God in all its forms,” one of them being “the carrying out of popular missions,” says number 16 of our Constitutions . Ours is a vocation particularly destined for the missions. “God willed that the world should be saved by means of missionaries,” says our Directory of Popular Missions 1 . And thus, throughout the whole history of the Church, God in His infinite mercy has associated countless men and women with Himself to cultivate His vineyard, “since ‘it is only through the missions that souls attain their eternal salvation’” 2 . So great is the importance of preaching and of the missions that the Church points out that among the principal duties of the priest is obviously the proclamation of the Gospel, but also, if they are pastors, the organizing of popular missions at certain times 3 . The end of the popular mission follows from the missionary mandate 4 and is, as you know, the “renewal of Christianity in believers” 5 and “the conversion of sinners” 6 . Now, the paradigm of every mission lies in the first mission of the disciples, narrated in St. Luke in the Gospel we have just heard. The evangelist says: … the Lord appointed seventy-two others. It is God who appoints and chooses His missionaries. As He did before with the seventy-two disciples, He continues to do so now through His Church. Bishops and religious Superiors choose missionaries in His name and with His authority 7 . And in case anyone thinks this is something of the past, let me tell you that, by the grace of God, the Institute is today on mission in more than 103 jurisdictions in 45 countries. And at present we are on mission in 16 European countries, in 13 Asian countries, in only 10 countries in the Americas, in 3 countries in Africa and in another 3 in Oceania. What is more, as of today we have at least some 164 requests for foundations –both for monasteries and for parishes– awaiting realization. I send you The Gospel goes on to say: … and sent them. The Lord not only chooses, but also sends. A sending that is in the likeness of the sending of the Son by the Father: As the Father has sent Me, so I send you 8 . A sending that formally constitutes the mission 9 . But He does not send them in just any way; St. Luke carefully specifies that He sent them two by two… “Our Lord must have had His reasons for acting this way, and in fact many continue to proceed in the same manner. St. Gregory the Great said: ‘He sent them in this way because the precepts of charity are two: love of God and love of neighbor; and with fewer than two there cannot be charity: this indicates to us that whoever does not have charity toward his brothers should not take up the office of preacher’ 10 . And in this sense we read in our Constitutions : ‘it is also very true that, if in mathematics one plus one is two, one man plus another man is two thousand. One man together with another grows in courage and in strength, fear disappears, and he escapes any trap’ 11 ” 12 . By the grace of God, at present very few of our men are alone, and although from the very beginning the intention was that they should not be alone, sending a companion has not been easy. For example, the priest who is in the Solomon Islands has been waiting a long time for another father to arrive, but certain difficulties with visas at the beginning, and then the pandemic, have made it impossible for the priest assigned there to arrive. Only this month are they going to open the borders, and God willing the other father will be able to go. However, we can say that the immense majority of the foundations made in these last 6 years have always been made in pairs, except in exceptional cases in which it was seen necessary for one to take up the mission first until the other arrived. St. Luke goes on to say that Christ sent the missionaries ahead of Him to every town and place where He was to go . That is, He sends them to the magnificent task of preparing the way by which He Himself will reach souls. This is the great consolation of the authentic missionary: the certainty of being sent by Him and for Him who is the one who must come to men. Hence the unshakable confidence in the inexhaustible power of the mission for the conversion of men. It is Jesus Christ Himself who wants to come to them 13 . Now notice that it says to every town and place… That is why the Proper Law explicitly tells us: “There is no place where there is a soul that is forbidden to the missionary. To the humblest huts, to the highest heights, to the most rugged ravines, to where there are fewer people, where less fruit is expected, where the people are more unruly, where there are more difficulties… there the missionary must go, staff in hand, by car, by plane, on foot or on horseback, by sulky or by boat… because that is his vocation and that is where obedience sends him” 14 . One of the requests for foundations we have, for example, is to work with the Native Americans in South Dakota in the United States; another is to found in two more cities in Uzbekistan… We, as members of the Institute, cannot reject a place a priori . We have to be ready to go anywhere, to every town and place where He wants to go . We are His ambassadors, as St. Paul said: We are, then, ambassadors for Christ, as if God were exhorting through us 15 . And wherever we go, our mission is always to bring Christ: “There is no true evangelization as long as the name, the teaching, the life, the promises, the Kingdom, the mystery of Jesus of Nazareth, Son of God, are not proclaimed” 16 . People are not interested in hearing about politics, about soccer players, about celebrity gossip; what people want to hear from the missionary is precisely about Christ, without cuts, without watering down His teaching, but rather that His truth be preached with all authenticity and vigor. And for that one must prepare, one must study, one must be well formed. Not long ago I was reading some statistics from the Fides agency 17 which said that the number of priests in the world is 414,336, which means there is 1 priest for every 14,853 people in the world. Likewise, the number of major seminarians in the world has decreased and currently stands at 114,058 (68,609 diocesan and 45,449 religious), almost 2,000 fewer seminarians than the previous year. That is why it is not surprising that today too Christ says to us: The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few. Pray, therefore, the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into His harvest . The apostolic work is enormous; that is why we must stop our ears when someone, contradicting the words of the Lord, says there are many vocations. The laborers will always be few and the harvest will always be plentiful. Only thieves and robbers 18 , only the hireling shepherd 19 , can be so criminal as to divert, discourage, fail to work for, or oppose vocations. We must always pray, asking God to send laborers into His harvest. But we must also work for missionary vocations, and one of the means we have to promote vocations is precisely the popular mission 20 . How many of our members came to know the Institute through popular missions! So far, so good. Christ sends us, we go two by two, we go everywhere… but that does not mean there will be no difficulties. Christ does not deceive us; He is very explicit when He tells us: Go! Behold, I send you as lambs in the midst of wolves . Our Lord insists: Go! , as if saying, do not fail to go, although He warns us of the dangers we will face. We are unarmed prophets (that is, defenseless), weaponless; we have only spiritual weapons. That is why the Proper Law, quoting the great and experienced apostle Paul, gives us the following exhortation: Put on the armor of God so that you may be able to withstand the snares of the devil. For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the rulers of this dark world, against the spirits of evil in the heights. Therefore, take up the armor of God, so that you may be able to resist on the evil day and, having overcome everything, to stand firm. Stand, then, with your waist girded with truth and clothed with justice as a breastplate, your feet shod with zeal for the Gospel of peace, always holding up the shield of faith, so that with it you may extinguish all the flaming darts of the Evil One. Take, also, the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God; always in prayer and supplication, praying on every occasion in the Spirit, keeping watch together with perseverance and interceding for all the saints… 21 . Pastoral work is a cross You have heard it many times, and you will have experienced it many times too: “Pastoral work is a cross, difficulties, dangers, sufferings: it is not taking advantage of the milk, the meat or the wool of the sheep. Those who empty out the cross empty out pastoral work. Hence so many strident and resounding pastoral failures. Keep in mind that the sheep will not follow a stranger; rather, they will flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers 22 ” 23 . Then Christ gives us the following recommendation: Carry no purse, no bag, no sandals . What does this mean? The Proper Law, when it explains this instruction of the Incarnate Word, says that “it does not mean that our Lord wants us to do without all of that, but rather it teaches the spirit of poverty that the missionary must have. That is, we must not be attached to what is unnecessary . We must trust in Providence without limit, while putting the means” 24 . Now it is interesting that Christ says: And greet no one on the road . Does He perhaps command us to be unfriendly or impatient? No! What our Lord indicates to us here is that “the task is urgent; we must not waste time, nor opportunities to do good: ‘opportunity is like iron, you have to hammer it while it’s hot’ 25 ” 26 , as the Martín Fierro says. Therefore, we must make the most of all the opportunities God gives us to do apostolate. One day many of you will very probably be in some parish, and you will realize how important it is that the priest be at the door at the end of Mass or at the end of any celebration, greeting the people, listening attentively, without hurry, without anxiety, to whoever approaches him. The immense majority of people go to Mass only on Sundays; if on that day you do not attend to them well, if you do not give them due attention, the people will go looking for help elsewhere or will stop coming, and you will have lost the beautiful opportunity of performing a great act of charity. Pastoral charity is indispensable for carrying out the priestly ministry effectively. Always keep this in mind. But “nowadays it is not enough to call people to come to the Church. We must go out to meet people!” 27 . “We must go where people live, to their environments, to their workplaces” 28 . Jesus Himself visited many houses and reminds us of this apostolate in today’s Gospel: Into whatever house you enter, first say: “Peace to this house.” St. John Paul II gave great importance to this apostolate of visits. That is why it is told that once, when he visited a parish in Rome, he said to them: “I come to your parish to carry out in it the principal apostolic ministry : the ministry of visiting” 29 . Let us note, moreover, that Christ establishes peace as the end of the mission, peace in souls, because what the mission seeks is precisely to reconcile souls with God. “That is why it is so important that in the personal visit everyone be invited to be in the grace of God. Hence one must guide the conversation with people, without getting caught up in superficial or less important topics, but aiming at conversion” 30 . That visit to homes, so highly recommended by the Proper Law and by Christ Himself, “must not be a ‘doctor’s visit,’” a short one; “nor hurried, as if taking a census” 31 . At times more importance is given to the number of houses visited than to the spiritual fruits, and it should not be so. One must take all the time necessary to be able to detect the spiritual needs of the family, its difficulties, to be able to deal with their questions, answer their doubts, dismantle the sophisms against the faith, etc.” 32 The Gospel goes on to say that the seventy-two returned rejoicing… “Always, inevitably, the missionary returns from the mission with immense joy. Perhaps there is no man more joyful than the authentic missionary. What the Lord promised will always be fulfilled: Blessed are those who work for peace… 33 ” 34 . Every week, when we watch the little video of ¡Viva la misión! , we have the opportunity to see the joy of our missionaries, even though they are in very adverse places. For “the characteristic of every authentic missionary life is interior joy, which comes from faith” 35 . Now, what does it mean when it says: Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name , and Christ answers them: “I saw Satan fall from heaven like lightning” ? Well, there the effect of a mission well done is declared: the fall of the devil, unable to trap souls in sin. And that is the reason for missionary joy. Christ goes on to say: Behold, I have given you the power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you… That is why, even if all the forces of hell come together, they will have no power over the missionary, since his powers come to him from Christ. Nothing can harm one who is a true disciple of the Lord. St. Francis Xavier, in one of his letters, speaks of the dangers of the mission, but stresses that in the mission there are dangers greater than poison and violent death, and these are the loss of hope and of trust in God, when one sees oneself threatened, when the apostolate seems to bear no fruit. Then the saint says: “if it is important for His greater service, God will protect us from all the dangers of this life, and without His permission and His authorization, the demons and their ministers can do us no harm. That is why our security lies in the word of the Lord: Whoever loves his life, according to this world, will lose it, and whoever loses it for God will find it 36 . And in this other similar one: Whoever puts his hand to the plow and looks back is not fit for the Kingdom of God” 37 . The Gospel concludes by saying: but do not rejoice that the spirits are subject to you; rejoice that your names are written in heaven . “The greatest reason for the missionary’s joy is to have been chosen by the Lord to preach His Gospel; a choice and a mission that will not go unrewarded: let him know that whoever brings back a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of his sins 38 ” 39 . [ Peroratio ] I conclude by making my own the words of Blessed Paolo Manna: “We need a veritable army of superior men, filled with the Spirit of God, capable of founding and organizing new Christian communities and Churches, capable, moreover, of suffering much: not mere soldiers, but leaders; not hirelings or amateurs, but true Pastors of souls in the most sublime sense of the word, who know how to form Jesus Christ in souls from the overflowing of their treasure of grace and virtue” 40 . Let us ask the Most Holy Virgin, Queen of the Apostles, in this Holy Mass, for the grace never to diminish, for any reason, our missionary identity, nor to forget the exact purpose of the ministry and of the apostolic service to which we have been called: may we be, today and always, essentially missionary 41 . Joy and eutrapelia according to the spirit of the IVE

1. In our spirituality It is remarkable how our Constitutions speak of the virtue of eutrapelia, which shows that the practice of this virtue is not incidental for us. Fr. Buela uses very strong words when he refers to participation in the moments of rest for the soul: “the rest of the soul is delight, so this must be the remedy against weariness of the soul, interrupting the tension of the spirit. Hence it is necessary to procure this rest for the soul through games and festivities, the moderation of which belongs to the virtue of eutrapelia, practiced in the moments of recreation” 1 . But not only is it recommended in this way; even much more, in number 214 of the Directory of Spirituality we read: “Whoever does not practice the virtue of eutrapelia gladly will hardly persevere,” and it even warns us: “one must be very wary of those who, under the cloak of virtue, do not want to practice the virtue of eutrapelia; they are generally driven by their selfishness, fail in charity toward their neighbor, and are harsh in judgment. The worst thing is that they go against the truth of man, who, because he is intelligent, has to know how to be playful.” When community life is spoken of, in the part on discipline, the first point dealt with is that of recreation: “In this order, the time dedicated to recreation or eutrapelia deserves special mention… Above all in the smaller communities no one should be excused from participating in it,” and it says: “generally, if one of our members does not participate cordially in recreation, after correcting him, if he does not change, let him be told charitably that he does not have the spirit for our Institute, and let him be separated” 2 . 2. Joy in the Christian life Joy is essential in the Christian life, since it is a necessary fruit of the virtue of charity, that is, of love of God and neighbor lived in fullness. As charity grows, joy will necessarily grow. On the contrary, faults against joy are in turn faults against the virtue of charity. It can be said that if one lives the Christian life well, he must necessarily live the peace and joy that spring from the paschal mystery of Jesus Christ. “Joy, which is the gigantic secret of the Christian, is spiritual and supernatural and is born from considering the mystery of the Incarnate Word: Rejoice, be glad, the angel Gabriel said to Mary; She would later say My spirit exults with joy (Lk 1:47), having moments before testified to Elizabeth the child in my womb leapt for joy (Lk 1:44); and then the angel to the shepherds: I announce to you a great joy, which is for all the people (Lk 2:10); and it is born from acknowledging the mystery of the resurrection of the Lord: filled … w ith great joy (Mt 28:8); like the disciples of Emmaus: they still did not believe because of their joy and amazement (Lk 24:41), they returned… with great joy (Lk 24:52); the disciples rejoiced on seeing the Lord (Jn 20:20). That is why St. Paul insists: Rejoice, I say it to you again, rejoice (Phil 4:4)” 3 . And this is the foundation of our joy; joy presupposes a foundation, something to rejoice about. In our Constitutions Fr. Buela quotes a phrase of Pieper taken from the book Una teoría de la fiesta which says that to rejoice is “the response of a lover to whom what he loves has fallen to his lot” 4 . Someone rejoices because he possesses the good that is suitable to him, either in reality or in hope. And this is our case: since we possess Jesus Christ and follow Him in the most perfect way that a man can follow Him on this earth, “what we love has fallen to our lot.” The loss of this good is precisely sadness. That is why, from the Incarnation of the Word to the fulfillment of the paschal mystery, the Gospel is the great reason for joy and festivity for all Christians. After the triumph of Christ on Easter Sunday, there is no room for sadness or for pessimism. Because we know well that not only has He conquered, but He has made us sharers in His victory. That is why a spiritual author said: “all our difficulties, all our tribulations, all our desolations and spiritual dramas, lapse before this proclamation: Christ my hope is risen.” That is why we must always be joyful, in everything: in the virtues, in sufferings, in ourselves and in others, in our community and in the Church. 3. Temptations against joy That is why we must be very careful that the devil does not draw us out of this natural state of Christianity: the kingdom of God is joy, love and peace in the spirit, says the letter to the Romans. And therefore, if we lose this joy, love and peace, we lose something essential in the Christian life, and with much greater reason in religious life. Moreover, it is an Achilles’ heel in the soul that wants to make progress; if the devil does not leave us in peace, if we live sad and weighed down, we know well that we cannot work on our spiritual life that way. – That is why we must flee from all sadness or melancholy as from the plague: “That is why the Christian must rejoice always and in everything: the Kingdom of God… is joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom 14:17); may the God of hope fill you with complete joy (Rom 15:13); coming to you with joy (Rom 15:32); rejoice (2 Cor 13:11); rejoice in the Lord (Phil 3:1); be always joyful (1 Thess 5:16)” 5 . Be careful, then: when there is sadness in the soul, one must ask oneself why and rationally seek the remedy. Don Bosco, when he saw a sad boy in the oratory, would immediately call him and ask him: “what is wrong?” A sad Christianity is inconceivable. If we play sadness’s game, the only one who wins is the devil. – One must know how to carry on through desolations : which can and must come to the soul. And not be distressed by that. We seek the God of consolations and not the consolations of God. Even more, to the soul that wants to progress in the spiritual life, it matters little whether it is in consolation or desolation; the important thing is to keep going. Quindi , one must know how to act correctly in these moments: The fifth rule of St. Ignatius: “In time of desolation never make a change, but remain firm and constant in the resolutions and determination in which one was on the day preceding such desolation, or in the determination in which one was in the preceding consolation. Because, just as in consolation the good spirit guides and counsels us more, so in desolation the evil spirit does, with whose counsels we cannot take a path to get things right.” Do not do as so many do… In such times one cannot make decisions… – Let neither our tribulations be a cause of desolation, nor our sins , nor our failings , nor our failures : “He must also rejoice in sufferings: I overflow with joy in all our tribulations (2 Cor 7:4); as sorrowful yet always rejoicing (2 Cor 6:10); I rejoice in my sufferings (Col 1:24)” 6 . That is why, even when something fails, act rationally, correct any error there may be on our part, and keep going. And on the contrary, the more there are, try to be all the happier, like St. John Bosco. – Nor must we lose our joy over the goods of others . This is a typical temptation of the devil, against which one must positively fight, striving to consider others as our superiors and to admire God who has given them such gifts: “He must also rejoice in the community of the followers of the Risen One: I rejoice in you (Rom 16:19); my joy is also yours (2 Cor 2:3); we want to contribute to your joy through your firmness in the faith (2 Cor 1:24); always, in all my prayers, I pray with joy for you (Phil 1:4); Brothers… my joy and my crown (Phil 4:1); you are our glory and our joy (1 Thess 2:20)” 7 . – We must be very careful that crosses do not become a reason for taking away our joy. On the contrary, we should consider ourselves happy, like the apostles, to be worthy of suffering something for Jesus Christ. Any cross, however heavy, must not take away one gram of our joy, but on the contrary must fill us with gladness. Whatever it may be and however hard it may be, embrace it and kiss it as a preferential gift of God and rejoice in it. It is a temptation against which one must positively practice agere contra . The cross cannot take away our spiritual joy. “Those who relish the cross of Christ our Lord find rest living in these labors, and die when they flee from them or find themselves outside them,” said St. Francis Xavier. Just because we were scolded, we must not think that everything is falling apart. No! Correct and keep going. Just because we were humiliated, we must not give up; on the contrary, we must take advantage of the grace to grow. “ whoever gives −St. Paul says to the Corinthians− let him do it with joy” . It is the only characteristic that is mentioned. That is why we must rejoice in all our spiritual efforts: “He must rejoice in the virtues: whoever practices mercy, let him do it with joy (Rom 12:8); joyful in hope (Rom 12:12); strength­ened in every virtue according to the might of His glory, in all patience and long­suffering, with joy (Col 1:11)” 8 . 4. Essential remedies For all these reasons, whenever we have the temptation of sadness, or of not wanting to do something as it should be done, it is necessary to seek an urgent remedy; we know well that we cannot go on like this and that, therefore, we are going backward in the spiritual life. Three remedies are suggested, then: – To be rational, not sentimental or melancholic. To act with the strength of reason, looking for where the error lies. As a matter of principle we have no reasons to be sad, and quindi it is a temptation of the devil. Therefore, rationally seek the appropriate remedy. If we have been humiliated, accept it with humility. If we have offended someone, ask for forgiveness. If crosses overwhelm us, embrace the cross of Christ with love. If it is a temptation, reject it with all energy and without hesitation. Let us remember that there are three causes of desolation: 1. it is because we are tepid, lazy or negligent in our spiritual exercises, and so through our faults spiritual consolation withdraws from us; 2. to test us, to see what we are like and how far we extend ourselves in His service and praise without so much payment of consolations and increased graces; 3. to give us true knowledge and understanding so that we may interiorly feel that it is not ours to bring about or to hold such increased devotion. – The agere contra , when there is no cause: the sixth rule of St. Ignatius: “Given that in desolation we must not change our former resolutions, it helps greatly to change ourselves intensely against the desolation itself, such as by insisting more on prayer, meditation, on much examination, and on extending ourselves in some suitable way of doing penance,” and the seventh: “let the one who is in desolation consider how the Lord has left him to be tested in his natural powers, so that he may resist the various agitations and temptations of the enemy; for he can do so with the divine help, which always remains with him, even though he does not clearly feel it. because the Lord has withdrawn from him his great fervor, increased love and intense grace, leaving him. nevertheless, sufficient grace for eternal salvation.” – The affective and effective practice of the virtue of charity: St. John Chrysostom said: “Where charity rejoices, there is festivity” 9 . Our Constitutions say that “joy is a fruit of the Holy Spirit and an effect of charity; one must try by every means that ‘no one be disturbed or saddened in the house of God’ 10 ” 11 . And they add: “For this it is absolutely indispensable to live fraternal charity: ‘That is: let them hold others as more worthy (Rom 12:10); let them bear with boundless patience their weaknesses, both bodily and spiritual; let them put all their effort into obeying one another; let all seek the good of others rather than their own; let them put into practice a sincere fraternal love; let them live always in the fear and love of God; let them love their Abbot [Superior] with a sincere and humble charity; let them prefer absolutely nothing to Christ, and may He bring us all together to eternal life’ 12 ” 13 . May Our Lady grant us the grace to live and preserve the joy that she lived. Trust in God

Homily preached on Good Shepherd Sunday [Exordium] Dear brothers and sisters. How the words we have just heard in the Gospel of this Sunday of Eastertide must resound in our ears! How much trust they must inspire in us! How much security for our life! Many times in the Gospel our Lord expresses Himself in these terms, giving us consolation, inspiring trust in us, encouraging us to keep going, not to lose heart, never to despair. These sentiments are, without a doubt, parts of the truth of the Gospel, of the message of salvation that Christ came to bring to men. That is why let us always remember and meditate on these words, on the strength they have and the security they offer us; let us think of the greatness they contain: My sheep hear my voice .. I know them and they follow me. And further on, with all that this means: I give them eternal life and they shall never perish, because no one shall snatch them out of my hand. And to give proof of all this, it is the Father who has given them to me, and He is greater than all … He is greater than all. Who, then, can doubt the value of these statements? From words so firm and clear, spoken by the Incarnate Word, spring all Christian peace and joy. Peace and joy that are founded on the most beautiful promises given by God to His followers, to His sheep. Before such great and concrete assurances, how can we not live in peace, how can we not be happy in this life, even in the midst of so many tribulations and sorrows… No one shall snatch them out of my hand… I will give them eternal life 1 … These very beautiful words of today’s Gospel constitute the end of the parable of the good shepherd; the Church always places a passage of this Gospel on this day on which the World Day of Prayer for priestly and religious vocations is celebrated, asking God that, in accordance with that text of Jeremiah, He grant us shepherds after His own heart 2 . 1. To be a sheep of Christ In the first place, then −and it is the basis of everything for making ourselves worthy of these blessings of the Lord− it is necessary, before all else, as the only indispensable condition asked of us, to strive with all our strength, as the greatest of our longings, to be a sheep of Jesus Christ… to belong to Him… to possess His spirit. Since these words are addressed to and fulfilled in my sheep 3 , it is therefore necessary, in order to be worthy of the consolation and the immeasurable good they contain … to belong, no matter what, to the flock of Jesus Christ. And this is our struggle and this is our combat in life: to belong to Jesus Christ. Every other aspiration should be subordinated to this one. We must always strive for, and ask God for, that inestimable grace which is to be a sheep of His flock, a member of His body which is the Church, the grace −in the words of St. Ignatius− to “serve as a soldier under His standard” 4 . We must ask for the grace to be faithful to Him, not to be deaf to His calls, but to be docile to His sighs of mercy. To be faithful to His teachings, to the demands of His way of life, to His spirit of conquest; to be faithful in keeping His commandments, in the frequent reception and love of His Sacraments (particularly the Eucharist and Confession); to be faithful to the impetus and the fire of Pentecost in our life; to have the spirit that the apostles and the saints had. To be a sheep of Christ… there is our greatest aspiration, our only goal. Why is this so? Because only in this way will we too be sharers in His victory, in the paschal victory which we celebrated with so much joy on Easter Sunday, in Easter week, and during these fifty days that we live until the celebration of Pentecost. To achieve it, on our part −and this too is interesting− we are only asked to want to be faithful … to want it effectively … and consequently to strive to achieve it. That is all; the rest is God’s work. Certainly the help of our Lord for this will never be lacking to us, if it is precisely He who wants all of us to be sheep of His flock, it is precisely He who wants there to be one flock and one shepherd 5 … Sacred Scripture bears eloquent witness to this: God wants all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth 6 … God gives His grace to all 7 … God does not want the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live 8 … To all of us He says: “Let them only stretch out their hand to me and I will lead them” 9 . That is why my yoke is easy and my burden is light 10 … You do not have to weep much, sinner 11 , says Isaiah, even a single teardrop is enough to set in motion all the love of a God eager to find you… Whoever comes to me I will not cast out 12 . Let us think of all the biblical texts that speak of this; let us think of God seeking Adam in paradise; let us think of God forgiving the people for the betrayal at Sinai; let us think of the parables of mercy, of the love of the father for the prodigal son, of the tenderness of the good shepherd who finds the lost sheep, of the charity of the good Samaritan, eager to help and to heal the one who is sick. This truth is impressive: God seeks us more than we seek Him. It is not much that we have to do to be a sheep of Christ; even more, we must do only one thing, and it is this: be faithful. 2. We must trust in Him It is to His sheep, then, that Jesus promises the most beautiful consolations, even in this life. We must think a great deal about this. About the greatness and the content of these promises. About what is at stake in our Christian life. The world has not heard and will never hear such words; no one is capable of expressing himself like this. That is why we must be attentive. Let us always think of, and let there always resound in our ears, in our daily life, those texts of Sacred Scripture that speak of the goods that will be given to the sheep of Jesus Christ. Whoever comes to me will never hunger, and whoever believes in me will never thirst 13 … I am the resurrecti o n and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he dies, will live 14 … I am the bread of life; whoever eats of this bread will live forever 15 . .. Whoever is baptized will be saved 16 … Your joy will be complete 17 … Life does not end but is transformed 18 … To those who follow me I will give a hundredfold in this life and afterward eternal life 19 … I will not leave you orphans; I will always be with you 20 … I will give them eternal life and they shall never perish 21 … Who in the history of mankind has had the daring and the boldness to express himself like this? Who has had the courage to die for these truths and to give his life on the cross so that men, convinced of his extreme love, might turn back to him? How well the first Christians understood this; how well the apostles understood it: St. Paul affirms in one of his letters: God is faithful and will not fail those whom He called to communi o n with His Son Jesus Christ 22 . The author of the Letter to the Hebrews affirms that God says: I will never leave you, I will never abandon you 23 . St. Peter expresses this unfathomable mystery with unexpected words: by His divine power, He has granted us everything that pertains to life, making us sharers in the divine nature and escaping from the corrupti o n that is in the world 24 . St. James counsels us forcefully: Happy the man who endures trial! Because, having passed the test, he will receive the crown of life that the Lord has promised to those who love Him 25 . St. John makes us notice the love God has for us: See what love the Father has had for us, that we should be called children of God 26 … This is the message… God has given us eternal life 27 . 3. Trust in God How, then, in the face of these great truths, can we not abandon ourselves to God , to His divine providence, to His merciful love, to His boundless tenderness, to His desire to save us! In the face of words such as those of today’s Gospel, my sheep hear my voice 28 … I will give them eternal life… they shall never perish 29 … how can we not attain peace within ourselves, how can we not realize that this world passes away, with its sorrows, its tears and its tribulations; and that even in the midst of them we must have great interior peace, great tranquility, that we must be authentically happy, because an eternal weight of incalculable glory awaits us. How can we not be joyful : rejoice always in the Lord; again I say to you, rejoice 30 . .. There is no greater joy than this: to know that we live in the truth 31 … That is why it has rightly been said that a Christianity without joy is inconceivable. Sadness, as such, is foreign to the Christian spirit. That is why, in the face of our tribulations, let us always remember the words of today’s Gospel… my sheep, no one shall snatch them out of my hand; I will give them life, and eternal life 32 . How can we not be optimistic : if the glory of this world passes away. Hence the words of our Lord in the Gospel: do not fear, I have overcome the world 33 . If we have been promised life, and life forever. Who can promise something like that? Who can grant us such a gift? And yet it has been granted to us in Jesus Christ, the only name through which we can be saved 34 ; the only one who has words of eternal life 35 . How can we not find strength to keep going: how can we not be ready to fight, not to collapse, to keep going, to redouble our strength. There will always be trials in our life, and it is necessary that it be so, but in the words of Scripture we must find the strength to keep going and to pass with a firm step through the midst of them. Happy the man who endures trial! 36 . That is why the same St. James said: count it the greatest happiness to have to endure various trials; you know that when our faith is tested we learn to be steadfast 37 . And St. Peter: In this rejoice, even though for a while you may have to endure some trials. Your faith will come out of them tested like gold that passes through the fire 38 … Rejoice in sharing in the sufferings of Christ 39 … Since, as the Letter to the Corinthians teaches: God will not allow you to be tempted beyond your strength 40 . How can we not abandon ourselves forever into the hands of God , who loves us and protects us; who will never allow us to lack anything we need for our salvation. For, as St. Teresa said: “the Lord never abandons those who venture out for Him alone.” If we are faithful to Him, He will never leave us, He will never abandon us, and He will always help us. How well Don Orione exclaimed: “O Divine Providence, there is nothing more lovable and more adorable than you, who in a motherly way feed the birds of the sky and the flowers of the field: the rich and the poor! In you is all our trust, O Holy Providence of the Lord, because you love us, and love us more than we love ourselves. No, with your help, I never want to pry into you, I do not want to tie your hands, I never want to hinder you; I only want to abandon myself into your arms, serene and calm. Grant that I may always be before you with the simplicity of a child in its mother’s arms.” [Peroratio] That is why let us ask God that in this Easter season we may find that trust in Him which the victory of the Lord’s resurrection inspires in us, since, if we are faithful to Him, nothing and no one will be able to take away from us the peace and joy we carry within. As the apostle St. Paul said −words we should always think about− with challenging questions: What then shall we say to this? If God is with us, who is against us? He who gave us His own Son, how will He not give us all things with Him? Who will accuse God’s chosen ones, knowing that it is He who makes them just? Who will condemn them? Will it perhaps be Christ Jesus, He who di e d, even more, He who ros e and is at the right hand of God interceding for us? Who will separate us from the love of Christ? tribulati o n? anguish? persecuti o n? hunger? nakedness? dangers? the sword? 41 … And he himself answers: in all this we come out victorious thanks to Him who lov e d us. And he concludes: for I am sure that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God made manifest in Christ Jesus our Lord 42 . May the Blessed Virgin grant us the grace to possess this firmness and this unshakable trust in God our Lord. May it be so.
