The scandal of evil

If God the Father Almighty, Creator of an ordered and good world, takes care of all His creatures, why does evil exist? It is a question as pressing as it is inevitable, as painful as it is mysterious, to which no simple answer can be given. Only the whole of the Christian faith constitutes the compelling answer to such a question: the goodness of creation, the drama of sin, the patient love of God who comes to meet man with His covenants, with the redemptive Incarnation of His Son, with the gift of the Spirit, with the redemptive Consecration, with the power of the sacraments, with the call to a blessed life which creatures are invited to accept freely, but which, also freely, by a terrible mystery, they can refuse to reject. An author says: There is not a single feature of the Christian message that is not in part an answer to the questi o n of evil. But why did God not create a world so perfect that no evil could exist in it? St. Thomas teaches that God, in His infinite power, could always create something better. But, as the Catechism of the Catholic Church says, God in His infinite wisdom and goodness willed to create a world in a state of journeying toward its ultimate perfection. In God’s plan this becoming brings with it, together with the appearance of certain beings, the disappearance of others; together with the more perfect, the less perfect; together with the constructions of nature, also its destructions. That is, together with physical good –as St. Thomas says in the Contra Gentiles – there therefore also exists physical evil. There is no getting around it: angels and men, intelligent and free creatures, must journey toward their ultimate destiny by free choice and a love of preference. That is why they can go astray, and in fact that is how moral evil entered the world, incomparably more serious than physical evil. That is why God is in no way, neither directly nor indirectly, the cause of moral evil; nevertheless He permits it, respecting the freedom of His creature, and mysteriously knows how to draw good from it; as St. Augustine repeated so many times: For Almighty God, because He is supremely good, would never allow any evil to exist in His works if He were not powerful and good enough to bring good out of evil itself. And so it is that, with time, one can discover that God, in His almighty providence, can draw a good from the consequences of an evil, even a moral evil, caused by His creatures: It was not you, says Joseph to his brothers, who sent me here , but God … although you meant to do me harm, God meant it for good, to keep alive a numerous people 1 . From the greatest moral evil ever committed, the rejection and death of the Son of God, caused by the sins of all men, God, by the superabundance of His grace 2 , drew the greatest of goods: the glorification of Christ and our redemption. All things work together for the good of those who love God 3 , St. Paul teaches the Romans. The testimony of the saints confirms this truth: – Thus St. Catherine of Siena says to those who are scandalized and rebel against what happens to them: “ Everything proceeds from love; everything is ordered to the salvation of man; God does nothing except for this end .” – And St. Thomas More, shortly before his martyrdom, consoles his daughter: “ Nothing can happen to me that God does not will. And everything He wills, however bad it may seem to us, is in reality what is best .” – And Julian of Norwich 4 : “ I understood, then, by the grace of God, that I had to hold firmly to the faith and believe no less firmly that all things will turn out for good .” We Christians firmly believe that God is the Lord of the world and of history. But we also confess that the ways of His providence are often unknown to us. And only at the end, when our partial knowledge comes to an end, when we see God face to face, will we fully know the ways by which, even through the dramas of evil and sin, God will have led His creation to the rest of that definitive glory for the sake of which He created heaven and earth. Notes 1 Gen 50:19-20. 2 Cf. Rom 5:20. 3 Rom 8:28. 4 English mystic of the 4th century.
The Virgin Mary, example for the religious

The religious has two mothers: one in the flesh, the other in the spirit; one on earth, and one in heaven. Much more is known about the first; much more has been written about the second. Our Lady, Mirror of holiness The life of Our Lady must always be for us a mirror in which to look at ourselves, in such a way that her actions too may be our example; the acts and deeds of Our Lady must help us to make our life an image of her life; it is she whom we must imitate. Just as Mary’s spiritual motherhood was not a privilege separate from her humanity, neither will it be a privilege of the religious to dispense with zeal for souls. Mary, going in haste over the hill country at the Visitation , revealed how she, the handmaid of the Lord, became the handmaid of Elizabeth. She is now the example for the religious that Christ within him must bring about dedication to souls and to all those who need us. Like Our Lady, we must know how to hurry; nothing demands such speed as the need of others. Just as Mary’s visit sanctified souls, so too through our prayers we must sanctify all those who need it . The religious feels a deep love for Mary, not only in his best moments, but in his failures; he trusts in her intercession to combat his weaknesses. So he always turns to her with special attention, knowing that the child who falls most often will be the one who gets the most kisses from his mother. In the loss and finding of Jesus in the Temple we must take an example of knowing how to rise up truly from our weaknesses; she too lost Christ. Mary and the weak religious suffer together, but in different ways. She felt the darkness of losing God when the Child Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem without her knowing it. It was at this moment that Mary became the Refuge of Sinners. She understood what sin was, since, being a creature, she experientially lost the Creator. She lost the Son only in the mystical darkness of the soul, whereas the religious who falls feels the moral blackness of an ungrateful heart; but Mary found the Child. At the feast of the Wedding at Cana , Mary teaches the religious how much he belongs to the Church, and how little to himself. At this time during the feast she is called “Mother of Jesus.” At the end, however, she becomes “woman.” What happened here is like what happened when Christ was lost for three days. Mary had said then, “ your father and I” , and our Lord had immediately reminded her of His heavenly Father, thinking of the mystery of the Annunciation and the fact that Joseph was only His putative father. From that moment Joseph disappears from Sacred Scripture: nothing more is heard of him. At Cana the Mother of Jesus asks her Son for a manifestation of His messianic power and of His Divinity: Our Lord tells her that the moment He works a miracle and begins His public life, He is going toward His hour, toward the cross. Once the water is turned into wine before the divine gaze, she becomes woman. Just as Joseph disappears in the Temple, so Mary as the mother of Jesus now disappears in Sacred Scripture to become the mother of all those whom He will redeem. She never speaks again in Sacred Scripture; she has uttered her last words, with a beautiful farewell: Whatever He tells you, do it . Universal Mother She is the universal mother, the woman with more seed than the sands of the sea. In the Passion Our Lady teaches us religious compassion: the saints who were least indulgent with themselves are those who were most indulgent with others. That is why the religious who leads an easy life, without mortifications, cannot speak the language of those who suffer. So to speak, the one who stands upright above need cannot draw near to console; and if he does so, it is out of condescension and not out of compassion. The good religious, on the contrary, sees Mary in the dust of human lives; she lives among the miseries of men, bodily and spiritual. She is, in a most particular way, Mother of Sinners; the Immaculate is with the stained: the Sinless One with the sinner. In the Passion Our Lady feels neither resentment nor bitterness, but only pity, pity that they do not see or do not know how to love that Love which they are sending to death. A man can become so obsessed with his sin that he refuses to ask God for His forgiveness, but he cannot turn away and fail to invoke the intercession of the Mother of God. In the mystery of Our Lady at the foot of the cross, the religious must know how to find strength to overcome all crosses. If the good and Holy Mother Mary, who never deserved to feel evil, could nevertheless, in the special providence of her Son, have a cross, then how can we, who do not deserve to be placed at her level, expect to escape encountering the cross? That is why, in the face of our tribulations, we must desire that there never be a complaint against God for sending us a cross, and that we have enough wisdom to see that Mary is there making it lighter, sweeter, making it her own. Mary, as Universal Mother, gives us a true sense of the Church; every misfortune, every wound in the world, is ours as religious. As long as there is an innocent religious in jail, I am in prison. As long as a missionary is without a roof over his head, I am homeless. That is compassion. The religious will never sit back and watch the world’s enmity against our Lord, knowing that Mary’s cooperation was so real and active that she stood at the foot of the cross. In every depiction of the Crucifixion, Magdalene is prostrate, almost always at the feet of Our Lord, but Mary is standing. The religious, who by his juridical state of perfection occupies a prominent place in the Church, must also stand out for his deep and heartfelt devotion to Mary. He must carry her not only in the depths of his heart, but also on his lips, so that he may always appear before the faithful as an ardent promoter of the cult of and devotion to Mary. May our lips continually repeat these words: “Jesus” and “Mary.” And, as St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort said, may Mary be the mold in which we are sculpted. Notes 1 Based on a writing of Ven. Fulton Sheen.
Fidelity to the Constitutions

Pope John XXII used to say: “give me a religious who has been faithful all his life to his rule and constitutions and I will canonize him without further examination.” Hence we must constantly examine ourselves on this, since it is essential to our religious life. There is no clearer sign that one is progressing in the spiritual life than affective and effective regular observance, of both the letter and the spirit of what is written. We may have the greatest successes (apostolic successes, great constellations, enjoying a certain peace, etc.), but if there is no faithful fulfillment of the rule, it is of no use. That is why we must always have great confidence in our religious life and also great fidelity in fulfilling it. Confidence in the rule Certainly it is God who gives graces to religious, but it is from God through the rule that the religious must hope for everything: holiness and perseverance until death. This is the precious way we have of attaining holiness. – Certainty that we are on the right path : And this is a great grace: to sanctify ourselves, it is enough for us to keep our rule carefully and lovingly. It is a path so straight and sure that going astray is impossible. For holiness consists in nothing other than the full conformity of our will with the divine will; and the religious who is faithful to his rule does nothing other than fulfill at every moment the will of God expressed and contained in it. His whole life is transformed into a continual exercise of obedience and love for the will of God. – Certainty of perseverance : it is the best guarantee that we will persevere and remain in religious life. If we are faithful to the teachings of the founder, we can be sure that we will attain the threefold perseverance: perseverance in grace: because incorruptible fidelity to one’s rule and constitutions presupposes in the faithful religious an exquisite delicacy of conscience and a profound spirit of prayer. One could say that it is impossible to sin if one does not depart from the fulfillment of one’s rule. perseverance in the vocation: because this is the best way to become rooted in the vocation. One who tries to be faithful even in the smallest things of the rules will hardly feel tempted to betray the vows he has professed. There is no firmer guarantee of perseverance in the vocation than the exact and meticulous practice of one’s own rule and constitutions. final perseverance, since the rule is for the religious “the key to paradise,” and given that one dies as one lives, the practice of most faithful fulfillment of the rule is a sure guarantee that the religious will die faithful to the vows he has made. “Everyone who dies kissing the habit of his order dies with the clearest and most unmistakable sign of the predestined.” The risks of non-observance While it is true that we must hope for everything from the faithful fulfillment of the rule, at the same time we must fear everything from its non-observance, which, if habitual and prolonged, can become a stumbling block for others and an occasion of ruin for ourselves. These are the main risks that are usually pointed out: – Mediocrity of life : generally, God treats us as we treat Him. “God gives Himself wholly only to the one who gives himself wholly to Him,” said St. Teresa. And objectively, stepping outside the rule, acting by one’s own spirit (even in small things), holding a private judgment about its application, is objectively to place oneself outside the providential order and to withdraw from the influence of the Holy Spirit. God called us to holiness in a religious family and under its rule. If one lets oneself go, the consequences will be inevitable: languor of soul, the weakening of the virtues and an exhausted spiritual life. less grace, less sap, and therefore fewer flowers and less fruit. “Without water and without sun, the soul becomes dry and parched earth, with little and stunted vegetation. This is the explanation of many religious lives, neither good nor bad, but simply insubstantial. It is the triumph of moral insipidity. No bursts of enthusiasm, not a single impulse to rise toward the ideal. A continuous and endless march along the track of mediocrity, a perennial spiritual drowsiness and somnolence, as if sleeping sickness had taken hold of the soul. What the moth is to clothing and the slug to flowers, that is what repeated faults of observance are to fervor.” – Lukewarmness : the frequent, unjustified violation of the rule or constitutions, without a purpose of amendment, brings with it habitual venial sin, that is, lukewarmness. The one who practices regular observance only when it suits his taste, who with full deliberation and frequently disregards silence, dispenses himself from some exercises or community acts, judges and criticizes his superiors, sows discord with malicious or imprudent gossip, neglects the prescribed delicacies regarding poverty and modesty, is without any doubt a religious who has fallen into lukewarmness. A terrible sin, abominable in the eyes of God: “ I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot. Would that you were cold or hot! But because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I am about to vomit you out of my mouth ” (Rev 3:15-16). From here to falling into mortal sin there is only one step, and some take it. – Mortal sin: if it is an enormous misfortune for a Christian, mortal sin is a true catastrophe for a religious. Normally religious do not fall into it; however, just as a good religious who suffers such a misfortune rises quickly, the same does not happen to those who little by little let themselves fall irremediably into lukewarmness. “In the moral order, as in the physical, sudden deaths are an exception. The normal thing is to end one’s life through illness or worn out by old age. The soul almost always dies a victim of lukewarmness.” Anemia. The habitual violation of the rule engenders lukewarmness, which is to the soul what tuberculosis is to the body: it weakens the organism, drains its strength and turns life into a slow spiritual agony. Contempt of the law. St. Thomas teaches it: “the frequency of sin disposes to contempt of the law,” and formal contempt of the law constitutes grave sin. Illusion of conscience. Lukewarmness darkens judgment and falsifies the conscience. From slight infractions one passes little by little to more important faults, and even grave ones, ending up without realizing it in enormous infidelities. “With the dividing line between mortal and venial sin hesitant and blurred, one rides along this slack rope cheerfully and dangerously.” A doubtful rule is formed in the intellect that works at the whim of the transgressor. Delicacies of conscience appear as “scruples” and “narrow-mindedness.” And so little by little, almost without realizing it, one begins to come crashing down. Scandal of others. Few things spread so easily in a religious community as the bad example of one of its members. And so the fact of one being falsely lax leads the others and the whole community to break basic points of observance. Divine punishment. It will be enough to neglect just one of those precautions to find oneself in a compromising situation or for a most grave temptation to arise which, by God’s just punishment, one does not manage to resist l How many deep and scandalous falls could have been avoided with a little more care and respect for the most holy prescriptions of the rule! Deus non deserit nisi prius deseratur says the Council of Trent: “God abandons no one unless we first abandon Him.” – Loss of vocation: An exceptional grace—the greatest of all after redemption and baptism, according to St. Alphonsus—the religious vocation can be lost through one’s own fault. It is true that not all religious who leave religious life are guilty of infidelity to their vocation. There may be entirely blameless causes that authorize and advise a return to secular life. But the usual thing is the reverse: generally the return to the world implies a true disloyalty toward God. The phrase of St. Paul in the letter to the Romans will always be true: “ the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable .” – Eternal damnation: the religious who have fallen into hell have been damned, without any exception, through the fault of their non-observance. For if fidelity to the rule down to its smallest details is one of the clearest signs of predestination and an infallible pledge of salvation, the spirit of irregularity constitutes, on the contrary, one of the most fearsome signs of eternal damnation. It must be repeated many times: consecrated souls do not hurl themselves headlong into the abyss in one leap; they slip and fall into it gently and imperceptibly … Conclusion Let us always strive to have great fidelity to our constitutions, to their letter and to their spirit, which we, by a particular grace, have had the grace of drinking in from the founder himself, whom we have known, with whom we have lived. I think greater ease is impossible. And even in the smallest things, which is no mere detail. Don Orione spoke to his religious of the utmost care they had to take in preserving the spirit, even in the smallest details. St. Augustine said: “What is small is small, but to be faithful in small things is a very great thing.” Like St. Thérèse of the Child Jesus, of whom it was said that she had “a stubborn and tremendous obstinacy in fulfilling her duty in the smallest things out of love for the Beloved.” To this exquisite fidelity in small things it is owed that she is, in the words of St. Pius X, “the greatest saint of modern times.”
The only person foretold

Sermon for the First Sunday of Advent Today we Christians celebrate the season of Advent, that season in which we prepare ourselves in a special way to celebrate the feast of Christmas in a Christian manner. That is why it is a time in which one should try in a particular way to grow in prayer, in the Christian life, so that when that day comes, one more year, one may have a renewed heart and be able to fill it with the coming of the Savior. Advent as preparation for the coming of the Messiah That is why we must await the birth of Christ, await His coming and prepare ourselves for that day, in the same way that the world in its time prepared itself for the coming of the Messiah. Or better said, as God prepared the coming of His Son. Reason tells us that if God really decided to become incarnate, the least God could have done to support His claim would have been to announce His coming beforehand. If God sent someone on His own behalf, or if He Himself came with a message of vital importance for all men, it seems reasonable that He should first let men know when His messenger would come, when he would be born, where he would live, the doctrine he would teach, the enemies he would stir up, the program he would adopt for the future and the kind of death destined for him. According to the measure in which the messenger conformed to these announcements, one could judge the validity of his claims. Moreover, reason assures us that if God did not do such a thing, nothing could prevent some impostor from appearing in history and saying: “ I come from God ,” or “ an angel appeared to me and told me to announce this ,” as happens nowadays with so many sects and visionaries who appear day after day wanting to claim to be divine envoys. If a foreigner arrived in San Rafael and said he was a diplomat of some country , the least he would be asked for are his documents, that is, the credentials attesting that he does in fact represent a certain government. And if this is necessary for the delegates of other countries, with how much greater reason is it asked when someone claims to be a divine envoy. In this Christ accredits His mission more than anyone. Socrates had no one to foretell his birth. Buddha had no one to announce beforehand his coming and his message. Every founder of some sect appeared in history without anyone expecting him; no one ever heard of them until propaganda spread their name. But the case of Christ was different. Because of the prophecies contained in the Old Testament, His coming was not an unexpected event. There were no predictions about Buddha, Confucius, Muhammad or anyone else who may be going around, but there were about Christ. Others came and simply said: “ Here I am, believe in me ” . These, therefore, were only men in the midst of men, and not an incarnate God. Awaited by all Christ was the only one who stood out from this line, saying: “search the scriptures of the Jewish people; they speak of me.” Christ was not a chance occurrence in history; rather, the world was waiting for Him. I. The Jews were waiting for Him : it is true that the beautiful prophecies of the Old Testament can be better understood in the light of their fulfillment. But one need only read the prophets: it can never be doubted that these predictions point to Christ and the kingdom He established. In the Old Testament it is prophesied that through them all the nations of the earth would be blessed (as indeed happened); that the tribe of Judah would have preeminence over the other Hebrew tribes (and from this tribe Christ was born); in the Old Testament is prophesied the virginal birth of the Messiah, the accounts of the Man of sorrows are plainly there, which announced the death of the Savior, that He would be born in Bethlehem , that He would be humble and despised. In whom but Christ did these prophecies find their fulfillment? That is why in Christ there is a singularity that sets Him apart from all the other founders of world religions. He was the only person foretold. II. But note that not only the Jews awaited Christ, but also the pagans ; that is, without knowing divine revelation, the world had a certain thirst for the Incarnation, for God to become man. Tacitus , a Roman writer, said: “ People were generally persuaded ,” on the basis of the ancient prophecies, “ that the East was to prevail, and that from Judea would come the Master and Sovereign of the world .” Suetonius said: “ There was throughout the East an ancient and constant belief that, with the support of prophecies undoubtedly certain, the Jews were to attain supreme power ” . How is all this to be explained? In China writings are found in which the same state of expectation is shown, but because it was on the other side of the world, it believed that the great Sage was to be born in the West. The annals of the Celestial Empire contain the following account: “ In the 24th year of Chao Wang, on the 8th day of the fourth moon, a light appeared on the southwest side that illuminated the king’s palace. The monarch, surprised by the brightness, questioned the wise men. They showed him books in which it was indicated that this prodigy signified the appearance of the great Holy One of the West, whose religion was to be introduced into their country .” Even the Greeks, without knowing it, were awaiting Christ, since Aeschylus in his Prometheus, six centuries before His coming, wrote: “ Do not expect an end to come to this curse until God comes to take upon His head the pains of your own sins, by way of expiation .” And if not, how did the Magi from the East know that one day He was to come? Certainly, not only the Jews awaited the birth of a great king, a sage and a savior, but also Plato and Socrates spoke of the Word and of the universal sage “ who was to come .” Confucius spoke of the Holy One . Aeschylus of a Savior and Redeemer who would free man from the original curse. All these persons stood on the side of expectation on the part of the pagans. What separates Christ from all men, what distinguishes Him, is that above all He was awaited ; even the Gentiles felt a longing for a liberator or redeemer. This fact alone already distinguishes Him from any impostor who might wish to proclaim himself a religious leader. *** In short, the world awaits Christ; the Jews await Him and so do the pagans; He is the most important Being in history; we cannot be the ones who remain indifferent before such an event . Quite the contrary, we must dispose ourselves so that there may also be a Christmas in our hearts, that they may be filled with God. May we find in this preparation the occasion to take up Christianity seriously, with renewed enthusiasm, so that God may be all in all .So that at Christmas the feast may be complete, because unlike many who know neither whom nor why they are celebrating, may we know how to rejoice at the birth of Jesus. Above all we must imitate Our Lady. In Peru there is an image that is very striking; it is found in the Church of the Jesuit Fathers in Lima, and the Peruvians call it the Virgin of the O; it is Our Lady of the Expectation, and it is an image that commemorates the immense joy of the moments before the birth of Jesus. May she grant us the grace to prepare ourselves fittingly for this new Christmas that is approaching.
Holy baptism and religious life

St. Thomas teaches that Christ in His Baptism plunges into the waters, burying the old man in them (for He had the flesh of sin), and purifying the waters so that they might have the power to sanctify. That is why we, in our Holy Baptism, die with Christ to the old man and rise with Him to the new life of grace. The letter to the Romans says: we were, through baptism, buried with Christ into death, so that as Christ was raised from the dead … so we too might walk in newness of life . That is, through Baptism we Christians are configured to Christ; we receive from Him the enormous grace of sharing in the divine life and of being able to be called, properly speaking, Children of God. That is why the Baptism of Christ is celebrated with such solemnity in the Christian liturgy; St. Thomas himself says that on the day of the baptism the fact that the heavens were opened allegorically represents the fact that on that day too the gates of heaven were opened for all men . That is why, through baptism, we are Sons in the Son and temples of the Holy Spirit. Now, by the grace of God, we too are consecrated, and if in baptism we already gave ourselves to God by the renunciation of Satan and the profession of the faith of the Church—that is, we belong to God, we are God’s, and in some way we are God, insofar as we have the divine life and are one spirit with Him —in religious consecration we do something similar, insofar as in it we wish to give ourselves totally to the things of God; but there is something more in the self-giving we make when we take our vows. Relationship of baptism with religious life Baptism has an intimate relationship with religious life, for strictly speaking religious life is nothing other than an attempt to achieve a perfect development of Holy Baptism. It is to carry death to the world and life in God to their ultimate consequences. This is what the Catechism of the Catholic Church teaches: The religious state thus appears as one of the ways of living a more intimate consecration “which is rooted in baptism and is totally dedicated to God. In consecrated life, the faithful, under the movement of the Holy Spirit, propose to follow Christ more closely, to give themselves to God loved above all things, and, pursuing the perfection of charity in the service of the Kingdom, to signify and announce in the Church the glory of the world to come.” . The Second Vatican Council already affirmed this in Perfectae Caritatis : “ Let the members of any institute remember above all that, by the profession of the evangelical counsels, they responded to a divine call, so that, not only dead to sin but also renouncing the world, they might live for God alone. They have indeed handed over their whole life to the service of God, which undoubtedly constitutes a special consecration, which is intimately rooted in the consecration of baptism and expresses it more fully .” Hence this continual union, to such a point that the Christian tradition is in perfect agreement that religious profession constitutes, as it were, a second baptism. The number of Holy Fathers—both Eastern and Western—and of theologians of all schools who use the formula secundum baptismus is overwhelming; nor is it merely as a simple renewal of the promises of baptism, nor even because of its sanctifying effect: what is proper and characteristic of religious profession as a second baptism consists in this, that through it the demands of baptism are carried to their utmost fullness and perfection. Those same baptismal demands—death to the world and life for God—are ratified and affirmed so fully and so consummately in religious profession that this ratification not only produces in the soul of the one who makes it the same effects as baptism—remission of the guilt and of the punishment due for previous sins —but also constitutes him in a state of perfection, something that the simple reception of the first baptism did not produce. A second baptism—says a theologian (S. Aguilar C.M.F.)—insofar as in profession the sacrament of baptism is administered and received in the whole integrity of its baptismal being; this is a grace granted by the Church and voluntarily accepted by the Christian as a means of entering entirely into the kingdom of God without voluntary attachments to this world that would diminish the perfection of his new life as a child of God. Religious life fulfills these demands, that is, death to the world and life for God, and this because, as the Church teaches: Religious profession, as a state of perfection, includes the voluntary commitment, under vow, to live the evangelical counsels with the aim of truly living death to the world and giving oneself totally to the things of God; thus the Council says: Therefore religious, faithful to their profession, leaving all things for Christ, must follow Him as the one thing necessary, listening to His words and devoting themselves with solicitude to the interests of Christ. Religious profession is a second baptism because it can have the same effect as baptism of renewal to a new life of perfection, precisely because the will of the one professing constitutes an act of perfect charity which produces—here ex opere operantis (that is, not as in baptism, whose effects are produced ex opere operato , by the very fact, whether Peter baptizes or Judas baptizes; but ex opere operantis means that the effect is produced according to the efforts put forth by the one making the profession)—produces the same effect as baptism: total remission of the guilt and of the punishment of all past sins. Hence St. Thomas teaches: If a man can make satisfaction for his sins by almsgiving, according to that word of Sacred Scripture, redeem your sins with alms , how much more does he make satisfaction for all his sins who gives himself totally to divine things by entering religious life, which exceeds every kind of satisfaction, ... just as the holocaust exceeds the sacrifice, as St. Gregory says. Thus is understood what the fathers say, that those who enter religion obtain the same grace as the baptized. Thus a religious—however great a sinner he may have been—can become, through profession and vows, holy and innocent before God. Consecration to Our Lady This intimate relationship and this splendid communication found between the effects of baptism and those of religious profession is also found in something very much our own and very dear to us, which is our fourth vow of consecration to Our Lady. This consecration is intimately united to Holy Baptism. St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort teaches this in the Treatise on True Devotion , saying that it is precisely for this that we make the present devotion, for through it we renounce the devil, the world, sin and ourselves, and we consecrate ourselves totally to Jesus Christ ; it is simply that we add to baptism not only that we do it voluntarily, offering even the value of our good actions , but also that we expressly consecrate ourselves to our Lord through the hands of Mary . To say that we want to be one with Jesus Christ, to say that we want to live to their ultimate consequences the promises of our baptism in order to belong more fully to Jesus—in short, to say that we wish to do this with total perfection—means to say that we want to be faithful to God in religious life, because in it the ends of baptism are fulfilled in an admirable way, by which we are united to God and sanctify our souls through the renunciation of sin and participation in a new life. Today, as we celebrate the baptism of the Lord, all of us must recall with joy the day of our baptism and that of our perpetual vows, and in the case of those of you who have not yet made them, look with hope to that day when you will give yourselves totally to God, so as to obtain in fullness the effects of holy baptism. That is why the apostle St. Andrew, when the executioner wanted to make him deny Jesus Christ, answered him: Oh, if you knew the mystery of the cross! If you knew the love that Jesus Christ showed you by dying on the cross to save you, you would not weary yourself trying to persuade me to deny Him, but you yourself would abandon all you have in order to consecrate yourself entirely to the love of Jesus Christ. How much they will console us at the hour of death if during life we meditate on them assiduously with love! The Kempis said: “ Nothing is so profitable as to meditate on the Passion of the Lord .” When we see the crucifix and the bleeding face of Jesus, may we know how to say: “ Lord, how much You have loved me, and how small is the poor love I return to You .” The Incarnation was the greatest work of God’s love; let us ask today for the grace to return to God, day by day, something of the love God had and has for us. May we know how to sing the love of God, as St. Augustine said, with our love. Since God has given us the grace to suffer for Christ. Or even more, as St. Francis of Assisi asked: “may I die for love of Your love, since for love of my love, You deigned to die .”
The most beautiful of the religious vows

We may ask ourselves, as St. Thomas Aquinas does: which is the greatest of the religious vows, the one that far surpasses the others? It is the vow of obedience. St. Gregory the Great, in his work Moralia , says that the religious vows are equivalent to holocausts, and he adds: “Obedience is rightly preferred to sacrifices, because in sacrifice the flesh of others is offered, whereas in obedience one’s own will is immolated.” In obedience a more perfect holocaust is offered: what is most intimate, what is most our own. St. Luigi Orione said: “Obedience is the fragrance of sacrifice” 1 . For three reasons this vow is the most perfect: 1. Because in it a greater good is offered to God Our own will is offered, which is superior to one’s own body, offered to God through chastity, and to external goods, offered through the vow of poverty. We have said many times that religious life is a martyrdom, a holocaust; and that holocaust is more perfect when what is most one’s own and the best one has is offered. This is the reason why what is fulfilled through obedience is more beautiful and more meritorious for the soul than what is done according to one’s own will. It is very important to be clear about this; otherwise, religious life is distorted. If one thinks that being poor is more important than being obedient, one does not understand the core of religious life. The three vows are important, but the principal one—the one that best manifests the holocaust and the sacrifice of the religious oblation—is obedience. That is why, saving the essence of the other vows (which does not mean that they need not be kept), obedience comes first. One could not, for example, under the pretext of poverty, do something contrary to obedience, such as giving away things belonging to the community. To go against obedience is to go against the very essence of religious life and against all the other vows at the same time. Such is the admonition of St. Jerome to Rusticus, a monk: “My words are meant to teach you not to trust your own judgment.” And he adds: “Do not do what you want; eat what you have been ordered; accept what has been granted you; wear the habits you have been given.” St. Thomas Aquinas adds: “Not even fasting is pleasing to God if it is done by one’s own will,” as is evident from the words of the prophet Isaiah, who showed the complaint of the people: “Why do we fast and You do not see it? Why do we mortify ourselves and You do not know it?” (cf. Is 58:3). 2. Because the vow of obedience embraces the other two The religious, even though bound by special vows to chastity and poverty, lives these under the form of obedience, “which embraces many other things along with it.” Obedience informs and orders the other vows. 3. Because it is ordered directly to the end of religious life The vow of obedience properly extends to the acts closest to the end of religious life. The more proper a thing is to the end, the better it is. That is why the vow of obedience is the most essential to the religious state. If someone—should the case arise—observed poverty and chastity, even under vow, and did not observe obedience, let him know that he is not a religious. Obedience is preferred even to virginity, as St. Augustine of Hippo affirms: “No one, as far as I know, has ever dared to prefer virginity to the monastic life of obedience” 2 . This doctrine is very important and also very beautiful. Just as among the theological virtues charity is the most excellent, so too among the religious vows that of obedience is the most precious, the one with which—so to speak—we must most fall in love and strive to live well. It must be the watchword of our religious life. St. Ignatius of Loyola says: “And although I desire for you all perfection in all the virtues and spiritual graces, it is true—as you will have heard from me at other times—that I desire it more particularly in obedience than in any other… because obedience is a virtue which alone implants the other virtues in the soul and, once they are impressed there, preserves them (St. Gregory); and as long as it flourishes, all the others will be seen to flourish and bear the fruit that I desire in your souls and that is asked by Him who redeemed through obedience the world lost through the lack of it: made obedient unto death, even death on a cross (cf. Phil 2:8).” “In other religious orders we can bear to be surpassed in fasts, vigils and other austerities; but in the purity and perfection of obedience, with the true resignation of our wills and the abnegation of our judgments, those who serve God our Lord in this Society must distinguish themselves, never looking at the person whom one obeys, but at Christ our Lord, for whose sake one obeys.” He adds the fundamental principle: “Not because the Superior is very prudent, nor very good, nor very well endowed with other gifts, but because he holds His place and authority, he must be obeyed, for the eternal Truth says: He who hears you hears me; and he who despises you despises me (cf. Lk 10:16).” And quoting St. Paul the Apostle: Servants, obey your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in simplicity of heart, as to Christ (Eph 6:5). Whatever you do, do it willingly, as one who serves the Lord and not men (Col 3:23-24). St. Bernard of Clairvaux also says: “Whether it be God, or man, His vicar, who gives any command, it must be obeyed with equal care, when the man does not command things against God” 3 . For his part, St. John Bosco affirmed: “If you practice obedience in the way indicated, I can assure you, in the name of the Lord, that you will spend a peaceful and happy life in the congregation. But from the day that, setting obedience aside, you act only according to your whim, you will begin to feel regret for your state” 4 . And St. Francis de Sales said: “Everything is safe in obedience; everything is suspect outside of it” 5 . Finally, the Virgin Mary is our perfect model of obedience. She always obeyed with submission of judgment, joy of heart and promptness in execution. She obeyed St. Joseph, whom she saw as the head of the home and the representative of God’s authority. She did not argue with his orders nor contradict his directions. She never considered small the things commanded by obedience. She called herself the handmaid of the Lord (cf. Lk 1:38). Let whoever has made a vow of obedience see what he has bound himself to. There is no other way of fulfilling it than to live totally surrendered—in freedom, will and one’s own opinion—to legitimate authority. In imitation of Mary, he must not stop to examine the reasons for what is commanded, but know whether it is commanded or not, and act without delay. Make a careful examination on this point: analyze your obedience, compare it with Mary’s, and deduce from it what you must do. Notes 1 Spiritual letter on obedience . 2 St. Augustine, De sancta virginitate . 3 Sermons . 4 Spiritual Letters . 5 Introduction to the Devout Life .
The disciples of Emmaus

THE ENCOUNTER WITH THE LIVING JESUS CHRIST Dear brothers and sisters: In the account we have just read, Luke describes in a beautiful way one of the encounters our Lord had with His disciples after He had risen. I – EMMAUS This account holds a most important teaching for our lives, since in these disciples we must know how to see ourselves. In them the evangelist reveals three states or moments: Before contact with the risen Christ : Cleopas, with his sad face , said to Him: are you the only one who does not know what has happened in these days? ….. We had hoped that He would be the one to set Israel free... And our Lord would reproach them: Men slow of understanding, how hard it is for you to believe all that the prophets announced. They were sad, discouraged, and this because their faith was as if dead (it seemed to have died with Jesus Christ on Golgotha); and so they had no hope; before the cross they had despaired of Jesus Christ. And that is why they were returning as if defeated to Jerusalem. The encounter: It took place in a way similar to how it happens in our lives, under the veil of Faith. Certainly in a different way, but a similar one: … Jesus Himself drew near and went on walking with them… but something kept their eyes from recognizing Him. In fact they will recognize Him by effects proper to Jesus Christ, by two things that only Jesus Christ could do in that way: make hearts burn with His words, and break the bread. John Paul II: “There is no doubt that St. Luke, in narrating this episode, especially the decisive moment in which the two disciples recognize Jesus, makes an explicit allusion to the accounts of the institution of the Eucharist, that is, to the way Jesus acted at the Last Supper (cf. Lk 24:30). The evangelist, to relate what the disciples of Emmaus tell the Eleven, uses an expression which in the nascent Church had a precise Eucharistic meaning: They had known Him in the breaking of the bread (Lk 24:35)” ( Ecclesia in America ). What remained in their souls: Joy: at that very moment (before, they had said it was late and the day was ending) they returned to Jerusalem. Spiritual consolation: were not our hearts burning while He explained the Scriptures to us? II – EMMAUS IN THE TIMES OF THE CHURCH How can we repeat that experience of the disciples of Emmaus? John Paul II: (explain in my own words) “ The Church is the place where men, encountering Jesus , can discover the love of the Father: indeed, whoever has seen Jesus has seen the Father (cf. Jn 14:9). Jesus, after His ascension into heaven, acts through the powerful action of the Paraclete (cf. Jn 16:7), who transforms believers by giving them new life. In this way they begin to be capable of loving with the very love of God, which has been poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom 5:5). Divine grace, moreover, prepares Christians to be agents of the transformation of the world, establishing in it a new civilization, which my predecessor Paul VI rightly called the ‘civilization of love.’” So that the search for Christ present in His Church may not be reduced to something merely abstract, it is necessary to show the concrete places and moments in which, within the Church, it is possible to encounter Him. 1- In the first place, “Sacred Scripture read in the light of Tradition, of the Fathers and of the Magisterium, deepened in meditation and prayer.” That is why we must seek knowledge of the Gospels, in which is proclaimed, in words easily accessible to all, the way Jesus lived among men. The reading of these sacred texts, when it is listened to with the same attention with which the crowds listened to Jesus on the slope of the mount of the Beatitudes or on the shore of the Lake of Tiberias as He preached from the boat, produces true fruits of conversion of heart. Sacred Scripture, even the Old Testament ( beginning from Moses and going through the prophets … all that had been said about Him ). “Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Jesus Christ” (St. Jerome). How many times our world complains of the silence of God … and yet it leaves in oblivion the revealed Word of God, in which God teaches us the fundamental mysteries of our existence. 2- A second place for the encounter with Jesus is the Sacred Liturgy. To the Second Vatican Council we owe a very rich exposition of the multiple presences of Christ in the Liturgy (SC 7): Christ is present in the celebrant who renews on the altar the same and unique sacrifice of the Cross; He is present in the Sacraments, in which His efficacious power acts. When His word is proclaimed, it is He Himself who speaks to us. He is present moreover in the community, by virtue of His promise: Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them (Mt 18:20). He is present “above all under the Eucharistic species.” My predecessor Paul VI thought it necessary to explain the uniqueness of the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, which “is called ‘real’ not by exclusion, as if the other presences were not ‘real,’ but par excellence, because it is substantial.” Under the species of bread and wine, “Christ whole and entire is present in His ‘physical reality,’ even bodily.” (St. Paul VI, Mysterium fidei) 3- Scripture and the Eucharist, as places of encounter with Christ, are suggested in the account of the appearance of the Risen One to the two disciples of Emmaus. Moreover, the text of the Gospel on the last judgment (cf. Mt 25:31-46), in which it is affirmed that we will be judged on our love for those in need, in whom the Lord Jesus is mysteriously present, indicates that a third place of encounter with Christ must not be neglected: “Persons, especially the poor, with whom Christ identifies Himself” (29). As Pope Paul VI recalled at the closing of the Second Vatican Council, “in the face of every man, especially if it has become transparent through his tears and his sorrows, we can and must recognize the face of Christ (cf. Mt 25:40), the Son of man.” III – CONCLUSION Dear brothers and sisters, we must strive to encounter the risen Christ as those disciples did. Christ lives; He is our contemporary, and to the extent that we unite ourselves to Him we will have eternal life and therefore also the true joy of the soul. However, John Paul II says: “The Lord’s invitation always respects the freedom of those He calls. There are cases in which man, on encountering Jesus, closes himself to the change of life to which He invites him. There were numerous cases of contemporaries of Jesus who saw and heard Him and yet did not open themselves to His word. The Gospel of St. John points to sin as the cause that prevents the human being from opening himself to the light that is Christ: The light came into the world and men loved darkness rather than light, because their works were evil (Jn 3:19). The Gospel texts teach that attachment to riches is an obstacle to welcoming the call to a generous and full following of Jesus. Typical in this respect is the case of the rich young man (cf. Mt 19:16-22; Mk 10:17-22; Lk 18:18-23).” That is why it is not enough to encounter Christ; He also asks that we seek the things that are above, so that one day He may call us from death to life. If you believe that you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above ; or as St. Peter says: So that your faith and hope may be set on God . Let us ask this grace of the Most Blessed Virgin, she who will always give us Jesus Christ when we ask her for Him; for that was, is and will be her vocation: to give Jesus Christ to the world.
“And blessed is he who finds no scandal in me”

[Exordium] Dear brothers and sisters: As last Sunday, the Church continues to present to us—as she does every year—in this season of Advent the figure of St. John the Baptist, the precursor. Last Sunday we read the Gospel of John’s preaching in Judea, a preaching of conversion in view of the coming of Christ; a conversion that we must know how to listen to in a particular way, we who look forward with longing to the feast of Christmas, so that the coming of the Lord may find us with a well-disposed heart. That is why Advent is a time of conversion, a strong season in the life of the Church, for drawing closer to God, for deepening and examining how our spiritual life is going, how our sacramental life is going. Last Sunday John bore witness to Christ: repent, for the Kingdom of Heaven has come. This is the one of whom the prophet Isaiah speaks … the one who comes after me is greater than I 1 . In this Gospel, the one we have just read, it is Christ who bears witness, first to Himself and then to John, saying: truly I say to you, among those born of woman there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist… 2 He is Elijah who was to come 3 . Very beautiful is that description by Christ: Whom did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet 4 . I believe that throughout these 12 verses we have just read—full of content, to be sure—there is a theme we can bring to light which I consider very profitable to consider in the heart of Advent. And it is the demand of the Gospel: what it implies, the work it entails. We are in Advent; it is good to reflect on this. This Gospel has three parts. 1. Christ’s testimony about Himself John, the Gospel says, was imprisoned in jail; from that gloom John would go forth to the glory of martyrdom at the episode of Herod and the dance of Salome, the daughter of Herodias. It was from that cellar of Herod’s palace that John closed his mission by handing over the rest of his disciples—he had already sent others—to that Jesus who from Capernaum was going about the lake, the villages and the hills working miracles. The disciples came to Jesus and asked Him: Are you the one who is to come, or must we wait for another? 5 And Jesus answered in an apologetic way— the works bear witness to me —and answered with scripture: Go and tell John what you have seen and heard: the blind see and the lame walk, lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, the dead are raised and the Good News is proclaimed to the poor 6 . A forceful answer: those who heard Him could not doubt the truthfulness of His testimony. For Jesus summed up in that brief answer the wonder-working prophecies of Isaiah—from the songs 29, 35, 61, 13, 26 and above all from song 5, of which two literal phrases are here, and which were applied to the Messiah—as if to say: “this is what was announced; well, this is what you are seeing.” But we want to speak about the demand of the Gospel. And there is a phrase in Jesus’ answer on which I believe we must reflect—an enigmatic phrase, as one of the holy fathers says—and it is when Jesus, after telling John’s envoys that the miracles testify that I am He, says the following: “go also and tell John not to be scandalized by me,” literally blessed is he who finds no scandal in me 7 . There is a mystery in the whole Gospel. John was the greatest of those born of woman; John is a lamp that burns and gives light 8 , says the fourth Gospel; John had faithfully fulfilled his mission and with great humility had announced the precursor; yet John was in prison in a cellar of Herod’s palace, suffering chains and very close to death. Tell John not to be scandalized by me : from this phrase we must learn that whoever wants to follow Jesus in this life must carry his cross, fulfilling his duty. Such a one will be great in the eyes of God. Blessed is he who is not scandalized by me , that is, “blessed are those who do not stumble over me, because on encountering Christ, one either believes, or stumbles and is scandalized.” 2. Christ’s testimony about John the Baptist Then in the Gospel we see that Christ bears witness to John the Baptist. Those disciples of John had come to the place where Our Lord was working miracles; they had asked Him the question whether He was the one or whether they should wait for another. Jesus had answered and many had heard Him; among them were many who had previously heard John. Christ now bore witness to him, showing the worth of John’s life, and said: What did you go out into the desert to see? A reed shaken by the wind? What did you go out to see, if not a man elegantly dressed? No! Those who dress elegantly are in the palaces of kings. Then what did you go out for? To see a prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet —the precursor. This is the one of whom it is written: behold, I send my messenger before me … Truly I say to you, among those born of woman there has not arisen one greater than John the Baptist 9 . These words are also very interesting because in a certain way they mark the spirit of Christianity. The vigor, the firmness and the manliness they contain paint a full-length portrait of the greatness of that man who was John the Baptist. An upright man, who practiced what he preached; who asked for conversion and penance and himself dressed in camel’s hide and ate locusts and wild honey. Christ’s phrase is challenging. Christianity was not made for pampering oneself in this life but for those who demand much of themselves. John was one of them. It also shows the manliness contained in the Christian spirit. Certainly our religion was not made for the weak (in spirit) but for those who want to demand much of themselves wholeheartedly, for those who want to be rigorous with themselves, who know how to master their passions and practice virtue—which will always be difficult—and who know how to be faithful to God even to martyrdom, of which we have had so many examples in the History of the Church. Whom did you go out to see? 10 Not just anyone, but a grown man in every sense, faithful to himself and faithful to God. The greatest among the sons of woman 11 . 3. The verse that culminates the Gospel The third and last part I would like to point out are the verses with which the Gospel culminates. Also enigmatic is the phrase when Jesus says: the Kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and only the violent take it by force 12 . Jesus had just canonized John, that man who had fulfilled with such rigor the mission entrusted to him; He had also said that, nevertheless, even the least in His kingdom is greater than he. Now He also declares that to reach His kingdom it will be necessary to work to attain it. Only those who do violence to themselves attain it 13 ; even more, the text, if we have been attentive, says take it by force, as if giving strength to the expression. Therefore, the proposition is clear: to reach heaven it is necessary to make an effort, it is necessary to work. This is perceived throughout the whole of Sacred Scripture when man’s life on earth is presented as a warfare, as a combat that must be won—against what enemies? Our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against the spirits of the air 14 , St. Paul will say. A struggle against the devil, against the world and against the flesh; for to overcome them we will have to do violence to ourselves. Violence to reject temptations, to fulfill the commandments perfectly, to be faithful to what God asks of us each day and at every moment. The kingdom of heaven suffers violence and only the violent take it by force 15 . We must arrive in heaven weary. The path of this life will not always be one of roses; there will also be thorns, and before them it is necessary to be faithful, it is necessary to do violence to oneself. And it is necessary to work, then, to win that great heaven that Jesus has promised us, where—in the words of St. Paul— eye has not seen nor ear heard what God has prepared for those who love Him 16 ; and—in the words of St. Peter—where there awaits us an eternal weight of incalculable glory 17 ; because—as the canon of the Mass for the dead says—“there God will wipe away the tears from our eyes and there will be no more grief or pain.” [Peroratio] Dear brothers and sisters, the Gospel account we have heard is deeper, because it ultimately reveals how we must walk through this life. Let us know, then, how to listen to the words of Jesus: not to be scandalized by Him in the face of the difficulties that may arise and will arise along the way; to be faithful like John, a man of integrity, faithful to his mission; and to work doing violence to ourselves, that is, demanding much of ourselves in order to enter Heaven, where Jesus awaits us. As St. Alphonsus Maria de Liguori said: “everything is little, not to say everything is nothing, so long as we attain paradise.” Remember always what the Gospel of St. John says: your sadness will be turned into joy 18 ; “consequently let us lift our eyes to heaven and always console ourselves with the hope of paradise … there the saints await us, the Most Blessed Virgin and Jesus Christ Himself with the crown to make us kings of that heavenly kingdom.” Notes 1 Mt 3:2-3;11. 2 Lk 7:28 3 Mt 11:14. 4 Mt 11:9. 5 Lk 7:19. 6 Lk 2:22. 7 Mt 11:6. 8 Jn 5:35. 9 Mt 11:7-11. 10 Mt 11:8. 11 Mt 11:11. 12 Mt 11:12. 13 Ibidem . 14 Eph 6:12. 15 Mt 11:12. 16 1 Cor 2:9. 17 2 Cor 4:17. 18 Jn 16:20.
The parables of the Kingdom

[Exordium] Dear brothers and sisters, we have heard in the Gospel we have just read three of the parables known as the parables of the kingdom, which Jesus spoke in His preaching through the Decapolis, that is, through the cities near the Sea of Galilee. In these parables is narrated, in a very simple but very beautiful way, the truth of our Christian life: how it is born, how it must grow and, still more, how it must culminate. And if we go deep, these parables are ultimately teaching the truth of human life, its beginning, its end, where we come from, where we are going. 1. In the first place we have heard the parable of the weeds . The kingdom of heaven, then, is like a sower who sowed good seed in the field. This parable in the Gospel of Matthew is related immediately after the parable of the Sower, which we read last Sunday. Jesus will better clarify the meaning of this parable, saying: it is the Son of man who sows the good seed; the field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom (those who are faithful, those who will make the good seed bear fruit). The weeds are the children of the evil one, and it is the devil who sows them. Both must grow together, and the good seed must persevere so as not to let itself be choked by the weeds, because one day—and we all know that it will be so (it is dogma of faith)—the time of harvest will come; the harvest is the end of the world , says the Gospel. The reapers will be the angels, and just as the weeds are gathered and thrown into the fire, so will it be at the end of the world . As graphic as it is dramatic: just as the chaff, the bad, dry weed that has borne no fruit, is thrown into the fire, so will it happen to the wicked on the day of the last judgment. The Christian life is no joke, nor is human life on earth; there is an end and an eternal destiny: either eternal happiness for those who were faithful, or a sad, horrifying and eternal end for those who are damned; His angels will gather out of His kingdom all causes of scandal and all evildoers, and throw them into the furnace of fire, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth . For the faithful, on the other hand, quite the opposite: the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father . An eternal end: eternal happiness or eternal damnation. That is the drama the Gospel sets forth; that is the drama of human life, of which we are invited today to become aware, and therefore to act accordingly. Not for nothing did St. Jerome say in his life, considering these realities: “ territus terreo ,” “terrified, I terrify.” 2. In the second place, more briefly but no less eloquently, we have the parable of the mustard seed , that tiny seed that is cultivated in Jerusalem, especially in the area of Bethany, which can barely be seen because it is a tiny black speck; yet it is destined to grow, and if it grows and overcomes the difficulties that all growth has, its dignity is very great: and though it is the smallest of all seeds, when it has grown it is the largest of all garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and nest in its branches . The kingdom of heaven—to which we all aspire—is a seed that is destined to grow. 3. In the third place, very similar to the previous one, we have the parable of the dough and the leaven . Once again, it is a little leaven that ferments everything, that grows, that bears fruit. Very simply, but in a very clear and forceful way, the drama of man is set forth. God has given to man, He has given grace (the Gospel says this in many ways: He has given some talents, He has given us the vineyard to care for, He has leased us His field, etc.), and that treasure which is grace has been given to us so that it may grow, so that it may bear fruit, and it is we who must make it grow. In the end, if we are aware, that is the only work in our life; that is what God created us for: that you may go and bear fruit, and that your fruit may be abundant and lasting . We could summarize the teachings of the Gospel in three great truths, of which the Church invites us to become aware this Sunday: a. The seed of grace The Christian life is like a seed. It is a seed that God our good father placed in our souls on the day of our baptism. A very great treasure. We do not have time here to speak of all that grace means in a soul, of the value a soul in grace has (whose value is greater than that of the whole world). The gift of baptism is a very great one (that is why the Church insists so much that children be baptized when they are little, and the sooner the better, because something very great happens in each baptism; if parents truly want the best for their children, it is incomprehensible that they should deprive them of becoming Christians as soon as possible). Grace is a very great gift of God that makes us children of God and heirs of heaven (if things are going well, speak a little more about grace). Well, this so great treasure is given to us on the day of baptism as a seed, which has to grow, which has to struggle. When we baptize children (and also adults) we always perform that rite which is the clothing with the white garment: “ may this garment be a sign of your dignity, and with the help of the example of your family may you keep it pure until the day of your burial ,” and when the paschal candle is handed over, the children being very little, the parents and godparents are given the mission of helping that light to grow: “ to you, parents and godparents, is entrusted the mission of increasing this light .” The Christian life is a seed that has to grow, that must always grow. Spiritual authors rightly say that “in the Christian life, whoever does not advance goes backward.” The first truth of which we must become aware, then, is that we have a mission in our life, and it is to make the life of grace in the soul grow and bear fruit. The ancients used to say it: “I have a God to serve, I have a soul to save, I have a mission to fulfill in this life.” b. The struggle The second truth of which we must become aware—and it is another great truth revealed in the Gospel—is that we must struggle. In the Lord’s vineyard, where our seed must bear fruit, there will also be struggle. The good God sows the seed, but He also permits another truth: the enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away . And then the weeds grew and there had to be a struggle. The Gospel is very clear: where do the weeds come from? And He answered him: “ an enemy has done this . There are, then, enemies; we must know it; we must not deceive ourselves. And all the more care, since the weeds are the children of the evil one and the one who sows them is the devil . The Christian life is no joke. Whoever wants to be a good Christian, whoever wants to fulfill God’s design and make the seed bear fruit, will necessarily have to struggle. My son —says the book of Proverbs— if you decide to devote yourself to the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation . St. Paul often speaks of a struggle, and he will say forcefully: our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against the spirits of the air . Certainly whoever wants to be victorious in life will have to conquer those three great and powerful enemies of human life, which are: the devil , with all his pomps and deceits, Father of lies, and his fallacies that envelop us; the world , with its illusions and its passing pleasures of the moment, like—says Scripture—a feather carried off by the wind; and the flesh , with its passions that want to impose themselves over the rule of reason. All the saints and good Christians have had to fight, as St. Paul said, the good fight . Militia est vita hominis super terra , says the book of Job, the life of man on earth is a warfare . But before such strong and powerful enemies we have divine help and the divine promises that if we are faithful we will conquer, and if not we will perish. Christ said it to St. Paul when he complained of the din of the Christian struggle; Our Lord answered him: my grace is sufficient for you . Let us ask God for this grace, so that we may say as St. Francis Xavier said when he was dying on the shores of India: “I have confessed You to the end, with firmness and without shame; never, Lord, did I put the light under the bushel; anguish and sufferings hemmed me in with rigor, but in my discouragement I conquered, Lord, with determination; You gave me five talents and I return to You five more.” c. The glory The third and last great truth of the parables of the kingdom that we highlight today and that we must never forget. It is that truth which increases our hope and whose promise makes us always vigorous and constant in the fight, and it is heaven. The unfaithful, those who despised the mercy of God and are damned, will go to hell forever (if it goes well, speak about the eternity of hell); the righteous, on the other hand, will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father ; they will go to heaven, to that great heaven that Jesus has promised us and that will crown the victory of His faithful ones. Where—in the words of St. Paul— eye has not seen, nor ear heard, what God has prepared for those who love Him , because—as St. Peter said— there awaits us an eternal weight of incalculable glory . St. Alphonsus rightly said: “all suffering is little, all pain is nothing, so long as we gain paradise.” Life without end, life forever, eternal joy. I count as nothing the sufferings of the present life, so long as I gain paradise . Always—every day of our life—we must ask God for this grace, what the fathers of the Church called the gratia gratiarum , the grace of graces, which is the grace of dying in the grace of God. Of being faithful until the last moment of our life. Always very beautiful is the example of St. Mary of Egypt and of the bishop St. Zosimus when he came to give her her last communion… how had she been able to bear so many sufferings?… With the hope of heaven. [Peroratio] Dear brothers and sisters, we could say much more; may these considerations serve to consider in depth the value of human life, the value of the Christian life. On the day of our baptism, God placed an immense treasure in the soul which, like a seed, like the mustard seed or the leaven in the dough, is destined to grow and to produce fruit, to become a leafy and fruitful tree where the birds of the air may make their nests. May the Most Blessed Virgin, Mother of Victories, grant us the grace of fidelity, of knowing how to struggle and to conquer. So be it.
The saints spur us on to seek the city that is to come

Pier Giorgio Frassati Novitiate (Italy) [Exordium] Dear Fr. Jesús, dear novices: first of all, I thank you very much for the invitation to celebrate this Holy Mass with you on the day on which we commemorate the 30th anniversary of the beatification of Pier Giorgio Frassatti, Patron of this novitiate. If all the saints “impel us to seek the city that is to come… perfect union with Christ, that is, holiness” 1 , certainly the example of the holy patron of the Novitiate, “fascinated by the beauty of the Gospel of the Beatitudes” 2 , becomes particularly relevant for all the novices of this house, since as members of the Institute they are called to bear “witness that the world cannot be transformed and offered to God without the spirit of the beatitudes” 3 , as the Constitutions ask of us. The life of Blessed Pier Giorgio Frassatti “was entirely enveloped by grace and by the love of God, and it was consumed, with serenity and joy, in passionate service to Christ and to his brothers. Young like you, he lived his Christian formation with great commitment and gave a simple and effective witness of faith” 4 . That is to say, Pier Giorgio was consistent between what he believed and the way he behaved. By his example, he teaches us that “the life lived in the Spirit of Christ, the Spirit of the Beatitudes, is ‘blessed,’ and that only the one who becomes a ‘man of the Beatitudes’ succeeds in communicating love and peace to others. He affirms that it is worth sacrificing everything to serve the Lord” 5 . That is why today I want to give you three thoughts of the Blessed, in the hope that they may serve to enkindle in you the great impetus toward holiness that must prevail in every member of the Institute, already from the novitiate. 1 st Thought – Pier Giorgio said: “ We must hold on tightly to faith ; without it, what would our whole life be? Nothing; it would pass by uselessly. The faith that Baptism gave me tells me with a sure voice: alone you will do nothing, but if you have God as the center of all your actions, you will reach the end ” 6 . “This is the principal occupation of the novice: to seek God, the God revealed by faith” 7 . “We must live by faith” 8 , our Proper Law tells us; that is why we must ask for and strive “to have a faith that is living, firm, intrepid, eminent and heroic” 9 . Holiness does not consist in “acquiring the manners and behavior of others; nor in carrying out exterior works to perfection” 10 . Careful! “these things are not bad; what is bad is to neglect seeking God with faith in prayer and to be content with simply ‘doing things well’” 11 . “Doing things well −while it is important and very good− comes in second place and will be the consequence of the love of God” 12 that moves us interiorly. That is why St. John Paul II, on the day of Pier Giorgio’s beatification, highlighted precisely this: Pier Giorgio was an “‘interior’ man” 13 , a man of faith who manifested by his works the faith that animated him interiorly. Thus, for example, he would keep night vigils before the Blessed Sacrament, he helped the poor… but, as our Spiritual Father pointed out: it was faith in God and love of God, the “true driving forces of his life, [that] made him an active worker” 14 . So faith, the interior life, our love of God, comes first. Otherwise it may happen that outwardly “one gradually puts on the clothing of a religious, but inwardly remains still immature” 15 . Hence one of the first points of our Constitutions emphasizes “the primacy of the spiritual in all our thinking, feeling and acting” 16 and how “we must put nothing before his love” 17 . In other words, if you will accept a piece of advice as you begin religious life, it is this: always give priority to everything that concerns the interior life. 2 nd Thought – Taken from a letter of Pier Giorgio: “ The end for which we have been created points out the way to us, strewn, if you will, with many thorns, but in no way sad. It is joyful , even through suffering ” 18 . That is why the Directory of Novitiates says: “All those of simple and upright heart who seek God and live in his grace must always be full of joy, and with joy possess the divine peace that surpasses all understanding” 19 . “It is in eutrapelia that generosity is seen and good spirit is verified; not in amusement in itself, which can be the fruit of human enthusiasm, but insofar as it is supernatural joy, which can exist even in the company of trials or interior dryness” 20 . In this sense, the more charity one puts into participating in community activities and in eutrapelia, the more of God’s goods one will receive: and it can be seen that those who are most generous in recreation are the ones who perform best in their other activities 21 , as our Proper Law points out, particularly for novices. Several times in the beatification homily John Paul II highlighted Pier Giorgio’s joy, for example: “in the serene acceptance of the difficulties of life, including those of his family, and in the sacrifice of chastity lived as a joyful discipline” 22 . A great example for all the members of the Institute, because crosses will not be lacking, nor does God want them to be lacking, but joy is one of the characteristics of the Christian (it is his gigantic secret, as Chesterton said) and, even more, one of the non-negotiable elements attached to our charism. That is why it is important to cultivate, that is, to strive to acquire, interior joy, which does not depend on temperament, nor necessarily on external events, but on knowing oneself loved, chosen and sought by God. The joy that comes from a life well lived. The more deeply we are imbued with this thought, the more joyful and the more at peace we will be. One must even find what is called the joy of the Cross, which comes with the science of the Cross of Christ. 3 rd Thought – “ Always remember what the Lord said: The good you do to the poor is the good you do to me. Around the sick, the wretched, around the unfortunate, I see a special light that we do not have ,” Pier Giorgio told a friend. Thus our Constitutions teach: “care for the poor, the sick and the needy of every kind must be given priority: the charity of Christ urges us 23 , practicing charity concretely, as a witness, in the first place, to all the members of our Institutes that ‘charity, only charity will save the world. Blessed are those who have the grace to be victims of charity!’ 24 . It must be very clear to all the novices and to all the members of the Institute that “charity is indispensable for evangelizing 25 and the principal business of our life. In the life of Pier Giorgio “faith was fused with charity: he was firm in faith and active in charity, because faith without works is dead ” 26 . No less is asked of us. Pier Giorgio was a champion of charity and, as such, he is a precious model to imitate. May God grant us the grace to have a great heart like that of Pier Giorgio… a heart conformed to the heart of Christ. [Peroratio] Finally, Verso l’alto , your holy Patron used to say: the goal must be set very high, the ideal very noble; do not be petty when it comes to resolutions of holiness 27 , and do not become discouraged, because if holiness is possible, it is because it is above all the work of God. May Most Holy Mary, whom Pier Giorgio Frassati loved so much, guide you and protect you so that you may always advance with perseverance in the struggle to attain holiness. We ask her this in this Holy Mass. Notes 1 Directory of Spirituality , 256; op. cit.
