Spiritual formation must prevail

Spiritual formation must prevail [ Exordium ] On this day I would like us to reflect on a very short sentence of our Constitutions , which says: “In the novitiate spiritual formation must prevail”. It is in number 245 of the Constitutions . This sentence, which so often goes unnoticed, is of great importance, because we “have wanted to give an absolute preponderance to the spiritual aspect, because we understand that this is what our charism demands” 1 . What does this mean? First of all, we must say that you have not entered religious life “to train yourselves for the apostolate” 2 the way someone learns the trade of a mechanic; you have not entered to learn languages and travel the world, nor to study philosophy or to live for free… but you have entered principally –listen carefully– in order “to seek God” 3 ; that is the principal occupation of the novice 4 . That does not mean that one should not do apostolate, or should not put ʽgritʼ into one’s study, or should not learn other things, because “it is true that we must serve God with the talents He gives us, but all those things are only means to a higher end, and our end is God Himself” 5 . Is that clear? All the activities carried out in the novitiate and, in fact, from now on and throughout the whole of religious life, “are means to find God” 6 . That is why one should not even set perfection in action as the goal 7 : “may the food never get burned on me”, “may I never fail a subject”, “may I be the best organized in the apostolate”… all those things are very good –careful!– I am not telling you to be lazy, to say ‘anything goes!’, not to organize anything, no! Everything God asks us to do –an office, sports, study… whatever it may be– must be done in the best possible way, but that alone is not enough ; that alone would be nothing more than an exterior ornament 8 , and the end we seek is principally interior, namely: to know and love the Incarnate Word 9 , and not to stop until we attain a “holy familiarity” 10 with Him. That is also why we must not be discouraged when things do not turn out well for us, or do not turn out as perfectly as we would have liked; it is not as though we are out of the championship because of it, because the main thing for us is to love God, “to unite ourselves to His Person” 11 , and very probably the humiliation that this mistake, this carelessness, this fault brings me is a beautiful occasion to unite myself to God. “Jesus –says St. Thérèse– has no need of our works, but only of our love” 12 (and this is in the Directory of Spirituality , 220). Notice that this is so important that the Constitutions , in their first pages, point out to us that “in our lives and actions there must have primacy ‘ the name, the teaching, the life, the promises, the Kingdom, the mystery of Jesus of Nazareth, Son of God ʼ , lived in such a way that we put nothing before His love ” 13 . That is why our proper law emphasizes that in the novitiate spiritual formation must prevail, because no one is born knowing these things; one has to learn them, and the sooner one learns them the better. The primacy of Christ is key in our spirituality as religious of the Institute, because our religious life according to the charism of the Institute is Christocentric, and that Christocentric stamp must be branded into us and into our apostolate 14 . Now, this spiritual formation is imparted in the novitiate in many ways. To look no further, the Holy Mass itself is catechetical in itself, and one has to learn to participate in it –as our Founder and the Constitutions themselves say– “ever more consciously, more actively and more fruitfully” 15 ; there it is Christ Himself who teaches in the secret of the soul, and the Mass is, as you know, “the principal thing, the most important thing we must do each day” 16 . The subjects you take also have a clearly spiritual tint 17 , and that is why one must know how to make good use of the time of study and of spiritual reading, because that opens doors for us; it helps us to find the path to finding God. Two specific ways But there are two ways clearly specified in the Directory of Novitiates by which the novice of the Institute of the Incarnate Word must seek God: “ prayer and penance , in the atmosphere of fraternal charity in which one must live” 18 . These are “two wings of that search” 19 . Interesting, isn’t it? Regarding prayer: one must learn to pray well. Sometimes some religious think that because they wear the cassock they already know how to pray, or they are embarrassed to ask if they have difficulties, if they experience temptations, if they feel reluctant to pray. So the first thing is to be willing to let oneself be taught; one has to accept that one does not know everything, that perhaps the way one used to pray when one was in the youth group ʽdoes not work anymoreʼ now that I am a religious; therefore, one simply has to know how to ask and let oneself be guided with humility. What should the prayer of a novice of the Incarnate Word be like? It must be “ unceasing prayer ” 20 . It does not mean that one is in the chapel all day, or that one is with hands joined in silence in a corner while the others play sports. It means that whatever one does, one always keeps one’s soul recollected in God, for which it often helps to say a prayer beforehand, to set one’s thoughts on God. When I was a novice, we were always taught to pray before beginning an activity, so that the remembrance of Christ would never depart from us. That is also why the prayer of the novice, especially that of adoration, must be a “ remaining with God in prayer” 21 , because prayer does not consist “in thinking much, but in loving much” 22 . Remember that. Regarding penance in community life: anyone who lives a few months in community learns very soon that “community life is the greatest penance” 23 , and this is an excellent means of finding God. Because life in community implies a certain denial of oneself in order to help the other, to encourage him, to ʽbear with himʼ, not to go around looking at the defects of others… that is part of the life of any family. One has to deny oneself many times in order to keep the schedule, to come back tired from the apostolate and still do one’s service with a smile, to eat quietly the food that did not turn out well for one’s companion, to know how to keep silent even when one is right and let the others win… but in all these occasions of ʽpenanceʼ one has to find wings to reach God. For these are the occasions that most allow us to imitate the self-emptying of Christ. Because you should know that ours is neither command nor honors, but humble service, generous self-giving, the gratuitous gift of oneself through love to the end 24 . Be convinced, then, that charity is the essence of holiness, and take advantage of all the opportunities that community life gives you to practice this virtue. St. John of the Cross, who was a master of novices, has some brief counsels that he gives to a religious who asks him for advice about how to attain perfection (and which I recommend you read). There the saint tells him: “And all these mortifications and annoyances he must suffer with interior patience , keeping silent for the love of God , understanding that he did not come to the Religious Order for anything else but to be worked upon in this way and so become worthy of heaven. For if it were not for this, there would be no reason to come to the Religious Order, but rather to stay in the world seeking one’s own comfort, honor, reputation and ease… [therefore] let him always try to bear them [those annoyances of community life] with patience and conformity to the will of God, and not bear them in such a way that, instead of God proving him to his profit in this trial, He comes to reject him for not having been willing to carry the Cross of Christ with patience” 25 . So far St. John of the Cross. Now, this is not easy; that is why one must be well grounded, spiritually speaking, in our Lord Jesus Christ and in the spirit of our Institute. In this Religious Family we have to be ready to live with all radicality the demands of the Incarnation and of the Cross –our proper law says it very clearly–; that is why we cannot expect a life with folded arms, where everything is ʽdrifting aboutʼ, where everything is consolation… our spirituality is the robust spirituality of the Incarnation, where there is self-emptying, where there is humiliation, where there are sacrifices… All that is part of the program. Since our call, as our founder says, “is not a call to have a good time, but to have a hard time” 26 . But pay attention to this: the Incarnate Word does not leave alone any of those He has called, but always accompanies them and, through the action of the Holy Spirit, predisposes them for the mission for which He destines them. That is why, from now on, look always with confidence to Christ, who has called you to follow Him in our beloved Institute. There is a sentence of our proper law that I find very consoling, and I like to repeat it especially when I visit the houses of formation; it says: “holiness is attainable because it is, above all, the work of God” 27 . Therefore, one must abandon oneself into the hands of God. Think of that when study is hard for you, when praying is hard for you, when obeying is hard for you, when you experience difficulties of any kind, or after you commit some fault, some mistake. Repeat to yourselves again and again: “holiness is attainable because it is, above all, the work of God; I only have to be docile to what God disposes for me, which will always be the best”, and keep going forward with hope ! [ Peroration ] That is why, I repeat, spiritual formation is so important, because one must become accustomed from now on to discern and to decide in the light of supernatural motives, that is, always seeking the greater glory of God, and also, and above all, to act and to live as faithful religious, never tiring of doing good, like the Incarnate Word. May the Most Blessed Virgin obtain this grace for us from her Divine Son. Notes 1 Constitutions , 46 . 2 Directory of Novitiates , 17. 3 Ibidem. 4 Cf. Living in a climate of festive joy

One of the healthy traditions we have in the Institute is Friday pizzas. Generally on Fridays, after the traditional fast at midday, the pizzas at night are a treat. And Friday nights are also nights of eutrapelia, when there is a somewhat longer recreation, and they are usually great fun. This, which seems a simple custom, a simple detail of our life, has much to teach us, and it is fitting that we learn it well; it is what Venerable Fulton Sheen (an American archbishop who died only in 1979) calls the “philosophy of pleasure.” If we are asked whether we want to be happy, we will all say yes. And right away someone may imagine that being happy is something like an endless belly laugh, or eating ice cream forever and ever, or seeing one’s soccer team always winning (that wouldn’t be bad)… however, Fulton Sheen says that there are three laws by which that pleasure associated with happiness is obtained much more easily. First law The first of these laws is that, if we intend to have a good time, we cannot plan our life only with “good moments,” fun and relaxed ones. Pleasure is like beauty; it is conditioned by contrast. Fireworks, for example, would not delight us if they were set off at noon; they are appreciated precisely because they are set off at night. If a woman wants to show off her black dress, and she is intelligent, she will not stand in front of a black curtain, but in front of a white one. That is, contrast is necessary to help us see each thing vividly. Pleasure, fun, delight, according to the same principle, are best enjoyed when they come to us as ‘a little treat,’ a gift, a rest, in contrast with experiences that are less pleasant or that require greater effort: fasting, study and the work of a long week… do you understand? We would make a great mistake if every night were a party night. No one would enjoy pizzas so much if he ate pizzas every night; no one would enjoy the fireworks at Christmas and New Year if we had fireworks every night. What is funny, the enjoyment of a funny situation, stands out by contrast against something that is not funny. If, for example, a distracted master of ceremonies put a bishop’s miter on sticking out to one side (instead of nice and straight), we would laugh; but it would not strike us as funny at all that all bishops always wear the miter. That is why when a priest, for example, who never dresses up in costume appears in costume, we die laughing; but if he were always in costume, it would no longer surprise us and would not strike us as funny. That is why we enjoy life more if we include that spiritual requirement of including a certain mortification and self-denial in our lives. That keeps us from getting fed up with fun things; it is as if it preserves the freshness and the joy of living. Self-discipline, interior penance, self-denial make one enjoy much more afterwards any simple thing that Providence offers us. Second law The second law is very simple and consists in this: what is pleasant is more pleasant after we have survived a moment of tedium or of pain, and this makes any small pleasure we may have –having reached the top of the mountain, winning a game, passing an exam, seeing people receive the sacraments in the popular mission, etc.– last us a great while. And for that one has to make an effort in whatever we are asked to do and not abandon it at the first difficulty. You will have experienced it on the outings or the excursions: one begins to enjoy the climb once one has gotten past those first moments of feeling exhausted. Or one enjoys and begins to take an interest in the job after having overcome that impulse to drop everything. Third law The third law of pleasure is the following; pay attention: pleasure, fun, delight is a by-product (a secondary product), not an objective. Happiness in this world should be like our bridesmaid, not like our bride. Many people in the world –and it can happen to us too– make the grave mistake of aiming directly at attaining pleasure in this life, forgetting that pleasure comes from the fulfillment of a duty or from obedience; because every man must inevitably obey the laws of nature, just as one obeys the law of gravity. We enjoy having an ice cream because in some way we are fulfilling that obligation or that duty imposed by our nature, which is eating. But if we eat more ice cream than our body can handle, there is no longer pleasure; there is a stomachache. That is why seeking pleasure, fun, enjoyment, while forgetting obedience and one’s own duty, is to lose it, not to enjoy it. I mention this to you because, as you well know, joy is “essential in our spirituality” 1 , as is also “the practice of penance” 2 , above all interior penance –our Proper Law clarifies– that is, the penance that comes from the silent sacrifice of fulfilling one’s own duty, from the practice of generous charity, from the penance that daily life together brings with it… do you understand me? That is why Fulton Sheen said that if joy is not common nowadays, it is because there are timid souls who do not have the courage to forget themselves and sacrifice themselves for their neighbor. Do you see the relation between joy and sacrifice? Hence the Directory of Spirituality reminds us that we are called to the practice of apparently opposite virtues That is why the joy that must characterize us is a spiritual joy, and therefore it can be experienced both in prosperity and in adversity, in pleasant moments as well as in the hardest moments. If it is in prosperity, our joy does not consist in delighting in the goods we enjoy but in those eternal goods we hope for, which are those that the moth cannot eat, nor rust corrupt, nor thieves steal from us. And even in adversity, in trial, in difficulties, this joy can be experienced, knowing that Christ died on the cross as the condition for his Resurrection and recognizing that, as our Proper Law says, “his triumph is our triumph, his victory is our victory” and “there is no reason for greater joy” 3 , and with that always moving forward, ‘putting a brave face’ –as we say– on every trial. That is the joy that allows us to live with festive joy 4 . **** With the hymn to the Virgin, Cause of our joy, we ask her for the grace to live like her in permanent joy 5 , to know how to rejoice together 6 , and not to spare ourselves sacrifices so that we ourselves may be a cause of joy for others, without being discouraged by trials or by crosses, but on the contrary learning to engrave in our hearts the joy of the cross. Directory of Spirituality , 212. 6 Cf. Directory of Fraternal Life , 42.
The trial of Joseph: the virginity of Mary

Sermon for the Fourth Sunday of Advent Dear brothers and sisters: The passage of the Gospel we have just read is known as the Gospel that narrates “the trial of Joseph.” The verse that follows the passage we have read already tells of the birth of Jesus; the account of that central event the Church reserves for Christmas Day. For now she leaves us only here, with the expectation, with the enthusiasm, with the longing: He did not know her until she gave birth to a son. It is logical: we find ourselves already—practically—on the eve of the great celebration of the birth; the path of Advent (of intense prayer, of penance and purple vestments) is coming to its end. It is therefore the moment to meditate on and consider the moments before the birth of Christ. The Church proposes to us—in the cycle of readings of the current year—the dream of Joseph, and more still: what is hidden behind the narrative of the dream, and what lies latent beneath the whole account we have heard and also beneath the first readings—let us recall the words of Isaiah and the beginning of St. Paul’s letter to the Romans—is the gospel of the virginity of Mary, our Mother. A precious dogma of Mariology and therefore a constitutive part of our faith: The Most Blessed Virgin was a virgin before, during and after childbirth; that is why we speak of the perpetual virginity of Mary, the Most Pure, the Immaculate Conception. Let us consider this truth a little today in this homily; it is necessary, because today as always—as already happened in the first centuries of the preaching of the apostles—there are those who openly and brazenly deny it. And this right beside us: think of the Jehovah’s Witnesses, think of the evangelicals, sects of the twentieth century. It is, however, one of the most beautiful dogmas of our faith: Christ was born of a Virgin mother. 1. The Gospel we have read We have heard, then, the revelation made to Joseph. The simplicity of the Gospel account we have heard does not, however, fail to show a violent tension: the fact is that Joseph must assume the legal paternity of Jesus and that Mary is a Virgin Mother, for she has conceived by the work of the Holy Spirit. That is why it is called the Gospel of the trial of Joseph. Perhaps for us, in a world so distant from the Hebrew world and as carnal as ours, it is hard to understand what this meant. In the Gospel account, Mary was the betrothed wife of St. Joseph. Betrothal—according to the custom of the Hebrew people—entailed a real commitment, such that the bridegroom, already from the betrothal itself, was called “husband” and could break the betrothal only with a formal repudiation. Mary was found with child by the work of the Holy Spirit, and Joseph, who was just and did not want to repudiate her, decides to divorce her in secret. Joseph’s justice consists in the fact that, convinced of Mary’s virtue, he refuses to hand over this fact—which he does not understand—to the legal procedure, which was most rigorous. The law in fact prescribed—according to the book of Deuteronomy—that if, when the time of the marriage came, the young woman was not found in a state of virginity, Deuteronomy says, They shall bring her out to the entrance of her father’s house and the people of her city shall stone her so that she dies, because she has committed a great infamy (Dt 22:21). To repudiate the woman with legal repudiation was to expose her to defamation and also to death. 2. Mary was a virgin before childbirth Mary conceived not by the work of a man, but by the work of the Holy Spirit. We have heard it in the Gospel we have just read; a Gospel that ratifies with all the authority proper to it the prophecy of Isaiah that we heard in the first reading: it is the prophecy of Emmanuel applied to Mary. They ask the prophet for a sign of when this will happen, and Isaiah says: Hear, House of David ! The Lord Himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son who shall be called Emmanuel, God with us. St. Matthew, as we have heard, announces the supernatural conception of the Messiah and says: All this took place to fulfill what the Lord had announced through the prophet, who says: Behold, the virgin shall conceive and give birth… and he repeats the prophecy of Isaiah. We also heard it in the first verse we read today: The conception of Jesus Christ took place in this way: when Mary, His Mother, was betrothed to Joseph, before they lived together, she was found to have conceived by the Holy Spirit. And what was happening was not foreign to the Scriptures nor to the hope of the people (today we read Isaiah); with such a conception the beautiful prophecy of Ezekiel was fulfilled: The gate shall remain shut. It shall not be opened, nor shall any man enter by it, because the Lord, the God of Israel, has entered by it (Ez 44:2). 3. Mary was a Virgin during childbirth A French theologian explains it very well when he says: “Just as the light of the sun bathes the glass without breaking it, and with impalpable subtlety passes through its solidity and does not break it when it enters, nor destroy it when it leaves, so the Word of God, the splendor of the Father, entered the virginal dwelling and came forth from there, the virginal cloister remaining closed; for the purity of Mary is a most spotless mirror, which is neither broken by the reflection of the light nor wounded by its rays” 1 . And Fray Luis de León says: “What was conceived in the holy womb, as the months went by, came forth from it without causing it pain and leaving it holy and intact. And as the one who was being born was, according to His divinity, a ray and a radiance flowing with purity and simplicity from the light of His Father, He also gave His humanity the properties of light, and came forth from His mother as the ray of the sun passes through the windowpane without harm, and we saw an admirable mixture: flesh with the properties of God and God with the properties of flesh, and divinity and humanity together, and man and God born of father and mother, and without father and without mother—without mother in heaven and without father on earth” 2 . 4. Mary was a Virgin after childbirth That is why we speak of the perpetual virginity of Mary. This is what many modern sects deny (Jehovah’s Witnesses, Mormons, etc.). It is nothing to be alarmed about; it is not a new error, it is always there. Already the Ebionites and Cerinthus in the first centuries taught that Christ was conceived like everyone else … heretics. St. Thomas himself, speaking of the perpetual virginity of Mary, warns: “Without any doubt whatsoever we must reject the error of Helvidius Priscus (who was a Stoic philosopher and Roman statesman who lived in the first century A.D.), who dared to say that the Mother of Christ, after His birth, had lived with St. Joseph and had other children by him. This cannot be admitted in any way.” And he says that to admit this is not only heresy but also blasphemous, because: It is offensive to Christ , for being the Only Son of God, it was fitting that He also be the only son of His mother. It is offensive to God the Holy Spirit , whose sanctuary was the virginal womb of Mary, where He formed Christ, and it was not fitting that it be profaned by any man. It is offensive to the dignity and holiness of Mary , who would prove most ungrateful if she were not content with such a Son and consented to lose her virginity, which had been so miraculously preserved for her. It is offensive to St. Joseph himself, who would have incurred a most grave rashness had he attempted to defile her whom he knew to have conceived by the work of the Holy Spirit. That is why we Catholic Christians, as good children, defend today and always the perpetual virginity of Mary: before, during and after childbirth. Mother and Virgin, as had been announced —you shall conceive and bear a son—. The sects deny this truth by arguing through a false and private interpretation of the scriptures, and by this means they deceive many people… and they will bring up the matter of the firstborn, the brothers of Jesus and who knows how many other things…. they may know the Bible, but it is a relative knowledge, for they err abruptly in its interpretation… for their study, far from being a scientific study, is tendentious… that is why they do not develop a body of thought, much less a theology. Let us always, before them and before anyone, defend this, one of the most beautiful dogmas of our faith. Mother and Virgin. And with a vow of perpetual virginity; that is why, when the angel of God set about asking a maiden of Galilee to lend her nature for the Incarnation of the Word, the answer that was heard was: how can this be, since I do not know man? *** Dear brothers and sisters: Now on the threshold of the feast of Christmas, of the celebration of the birth of Christ, the Church presents His Mother to us. And contemplating His Mother as the Dawn that precedes the rising Sun, let us also foretaste even now the greatness of the birth we are going to admire this coming 25th. Advent draws to its close looking at the Most Blessed Virgin; under the enraptured gaze of the mystery of the Virgin Mother, let us too await with longing the birth of the redeemer. So be it. Homily at the St. John the Apostle Minor Seminary

Holy Mass at the first Minor Seminary of the Institute [Exordium] Dear Fathers, prefects, and dearest minor seminarians: I am extremely pleased, and it is truly a great joy and a beautiful consolation to have come here, to the first Minor Seminary of the Institute, which this year is celebrating its 30th anniversary. And even more, to come and meet these [#] souls who have decided to follow our Lord, dedicating to him from now on the best years of their life! The flower of life! Giving God the best! I thank you very much for the joy you have given me and for the possibility of celebrating this Holy Mass with you. In the first reading, taken from the Prophet Nehemiah, we have heard how three times Scripture says: Do not be sad 1 . That is why I wanted, in this Holy Mass and now that we are gathered around him who is the very Fountain of Joy, to reflect together with you on this characteristic so proper to the Minor Seminary, which is joy 2 , and which goes hand in hand with the family atmosphere that must reign in this house 3 . Everyone here has perhaps heard or read how St. John Bosco greeted his boys, saying to them: “Be joyful.” And why? Because this attitude of joy is rooted above all in a profound sense of faith in which the presence of the Lord as someone who loves and saves always dominates and stands out 4 . Hence our joy is founded on the mystery of the Incarnation 5 . Rejoice, the archangel St. Gabriel said to Most Holy Mary at the Annunciation. And when the Child had been born, the angels also said to the shepherds: I announce to you a great joy . Christ is our Friend, who wants only our good and, in fact, the greatest good possible. How can we not be filled with joy! This attitude of joy is also rooted in the fact that God, being our Father, takes care of all our affairs, and that is why, as Christians, we must “rejoice always and in everything” 6 . And know how to flee, as from a serpentine temptation, from everything that threatens joy: discouragement because of difficulties –whatever they may be: in study, in prayer, in living together with the other seminarians–, entertaining thoughts about what we have left behind, worries about family, and anything else that makes you less happy, because that is not from God. On the other hand, also avoid being oneself the cause of sadness to others: ‘let no one be disturbed or saddened in the house of God’” 7 , said St. Benedict. I say the same to you. Also know how to open your soul to your spiritual director with the greatest confidence when any of these or other things trouble your soul. Because that is how it is: we all need help in the struggle… But even more, cultivate and promote joy with endless initiatives. And for that, here in the Minor Seminary, you have a thousand opportunities! In recreation, in games, in competitions, in the floral games, in the conviviums , the feasts of the saints… all, all of that must not only be done, but must fire us up with joy. In such a way that the soul is soaked in that joy, which is ultimately a gift of God, and that this very joy may serve as our motivation to face the struggle with a magnanimous spirit and generosity. You will know the life of the martyr José Sánchez del Río, who is the patron of our Minor Seminary in the United States. When they took him prisoner, knowing that they were going to kill him, he wrote a letter to his mother which reads as follows: “ My dear mom: I was taken prisoner in combat today. I believe that at this moment I am going to die, but it does not matter at all, mom. Resign yourself to the will of God; I die very happy , because I die in the ranks of our God. Do not worry about my death, which is what troubles me. Rather, tell my two other brothers to follow the example of their youngest brother, and you do the will of God. Have courage and send me your blessing together with my father's. Greet everyone for me for the last time, and finally receive the heart of your son, who loves you so much and wished to see you before dying. José Sánchez del Río .” Note that supernatural and spiritual joy of which we spoke at the beginning in the life of this martyr (he was barely 14 years old). I die very happy… With that same joy we should all face the crosses that God sends us. Because Christ not only helps us with his grace, but with his Resurrection he has already won the victory for us. Always keep that very much in mind, especially in moments of trial, of difficulty. Nothing whatsoever should make you lose your joy. The very Patron of this Seminary, James the Less, wrote in his letter: rejoice deeply when you find yourselves subjected to any kind of trials 8 . Because God is above everything! So he is above everything that makes me suffer. And thus truth is above falsehood, good above evil, beauty above ugliness, love above hatred, peace above war, mercy above vengeance, life above death, grace above sin; in short, being above nothingness, Our Lady above Satan, Christ above the Antichrist, God above all 9 . Because “God is infinite joy” 10 , as St. Teresa of the Andes said. That is why we must celebrate, since the reason for celebration is joy. The Prophet Nehemiah goes on to say: Go and eat splendidly, drink sweet drinks, and send something to those who have nothing 11 . In the Minor Seminary, too, there must be celebration. Mainly on Sunday –which is the prolongation of the Paschal Mystery– and at the same time a sign and foretaste of the true Feast with a capital F, which will be Paradise 12 . And the best way to do this is with the celebration of Holy Mass, with active participation, ever more conscious and more fruitful 13 . And also, of course, with the other feasts… They say that St. Mary Mazzarello was so interested, and so continually, in the joy of the girls that, in imitation of Don Bosco, she always asked them: “Are you happy?” For she considered the joy of her daughters to be the principal proof of their holiness 14 . If her daughters were happy, then she was doing things well. This joy is also asked of those whose principal apostolate is the work of forming the Minor Seminarians. Note that our Proper Law tells us: “Everything must contribute to the joy ‘which must be the atmosphere of every center of education’” 15 . It is necessary, then, to know how to create the atmosphere in which celebration and joy are lived, without fear of spending on everything that contributes to the festivities 16 . May the boys always be happy! That will also be our joy. Let us walk, then, on the pilgrimage of this life always rejoicing 17 , as St. Paul says, since, as we heard in the first reading: joy in the Lord is our strength 18 . [Peroration] To the parents of these children and young people who are here, and to those who for various reasons cannot be here today: my most sincere gratitude and my best wishes. I know that God will not leave you without reward in this life and in the next for the great gift of your sons to the Church. May you know how to appreciate the predilection he has shown you in calling one or several of your sons to so high a vocation. For you who are here, and for the parents who are farther away, especially those who are sick or going through some difficulty, we pray in this Holy Mass. To Most Holy Mary, who is the Cause of our joy, I entrust you all. May she always take care of you and be pleased to see you always joyful. To her we also give thanks for all the priestly, contemplative and missionary vocations that have come from this blessed St. John the Apostle Seminary. For many, many more vocations we also ask her in this Holy Mass. God bless you all. In the Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. School of filial love for Mary

For the minor seminarians [ Exordium] Dear Fathers, prefects, and my dear minor seminarians, it gives me great joy to be able to be with you on the day we celebrate the Immaculate Heart of Mary. This gives us the occasion to ponder that phrase of the Directory of Minor Seminaries which says: “The Minor Seminary must be a school of filial and deep love for the Most Holy Virgin Mary” 1 . All of us here, by the simple fact of being Christians, have the Virgin Mary as our Mother. Because “just as in the natural order every child must have a father and a mother, so in the order of grace every true child of the Church must have God as Father and Mary as Mother” 2 . But even more, being members of the Institute, we belong to the Virgin with an irrevocable belonging: we profess ourselves to be essentially Marian. And therefore our houses, and especially the minor seminary, where the figure of a mother is so necessary, are houses of the Virgin. The maternal presence of the Mother of God is what makes our ‘houses’ a true home, where there is familiarity 3 , where there is trust, where there is security because the Mother who watches over us is there, where there is joy because one feels loved 4 ; in a word, she is the one who allows us to live in a warm family atmosphere 5 . Filial and deep love Hence, then, the seminary must be a school of filial and deep love for the Virgin, who has a Heart so very, very great that, as St. Louis Marie says, the Virgin “loves her children with tenderness, but with a tenderness greater than that of all mothers put together. Gather together, if you can, –says the saint– all the natural love that all the mothers of the world have for their children into the heart of a single mother for her only son: certainly this mother would love that son very much. Mary, however, truly loves her children more tenderly than this mother would love hers” 6 . That is why, right from the start of the day, the minor seminarian must begin by praying the three Hail Marys, which will allow him to greet her –as a son gives his mother a kiss on getting up– and to begin the day in honor of the Virgin 7 . And at night the same: those Hail Marys are like a good-night kiss to the Mother. Throughout the whole day there are many moments in which one can show affection to the Virgin, whether by praying the Angelus 8 , or praying the rosary 9 , renewing one’s consecration to her after Communion, kissing her mantle during a visit to the Blessed Sacrament, and of course invoking her help in the face of any difficulty, any danger, any temptation; whatever the situation, we must always be quick to have recourse to this tender and kind Mother. Many of you, I believe all of you, wear the scapular of Our Lady of Luján. In your fears, or if you ever experience loneliness, feel on your chest the embrace of the Virgin who comforts, who heals, who accompanies you night and day through this valley of tears. And whenever you can, at least once a year, try to read some book about the Mother of God that will help you deepen your devotion to the Virgin. St. Louis Marie, as he himself says, read all the books that dealt with devotion to the Most Holy Virgin 10 Angello Giuseppe Roncalli That is why today I wanted to propose to you as an example Angello Giuseppe Roncalli, who later became Pope and is today St. John XXIII. He, as you will know, entered the Seminary of Bergamo when he was only 11 years old. There, at 14, he began to write some spiritual notes that accompanied him, in one form or another, throughout his life, and that were gathered in what is known today as the “ Journal of a Soul .” There one reads of the spiritual struggles Angello went through in his life as a minor seminarian: his distractions in prayer 11 , his failures to keep his resolutions 12 , his efforts to guard purity 13 , his struggles to master his tongue and not be so quick to answer impatiently 14 , even a toothache that would not let him pray 15 , etc. However, Angelo, far from being discouraged by the difficulties or by thinking that he was not advancing enough in virtue, would say: “I entrust this to the Virgin, and onward!” 16 , “with her help I am sure I will be able to get through” 17 . His great and tender devotion to the Virgin kept growing over the years. And he himself recommended it and resolved to teach it to everyone: “I am going to do the best I can on my part to teach others this truth: that the most direct way to go to Jesus is Mary. In a word, I will be all for Mary in order to be all Jesus’s ” 18 . And that is the motto I would like you to treasure in your hearts. Love our Heavenly Mother filially, that is, with the greatest trust, and deeply. May you be able to repeat in the depths of your souls each day as it begins: I will be all for Mary in order to be all Jesus’s. When Angello was 18 and was already finishing minor seminary, he wrote: “O Immaculate Mary, you know my needs, my faults, my great need to remain in the background, to humble myself, to be despised; and with all these faults you also know my desire to love you and to become a saint. So you must humble me, you must watch over me, you must sanctify me ” 19 . The struggles, the falls, the difficulties always continued, even as a priest and even as Pope, but the maternal help of the Most Holy Virgin never left his side. For Angello had one day asked the Virgin: “O Virgin of the Rosary, bind me with your rosary to Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament” 20 . And so it was. As a major seminarian, at the beginning of the month of May, one reads the following entry in his Journal : “The faithful begin the month of May to honor the Incarnate Word. I too come to your feet with love, like a child, to offer you my life and my acts and to ask you for the grace to love Jesus more ardently each day .” And so that we may be persuaded that the saints did not become saints overnight, but that acts of virtue cost them and they made efforts and, of course, asked the Virgin for help so that she might obtain grace for them and they might come out victorious, Angelo wrote: “A few more words to keep your name in my heart, to offer you flowers, praises and my good deeds, to please you and to ask your help. What will please you most this month will be for me to make continual efforts, though without strain, to fulfill my duty in a perfect, serene and cheerful way, without getting angry and without reluctance. Mary! you who have begotten me, make my soul, my thoughts and my acts resemble yours.” Do you see? He knows that on his own he will not be able to offer the Virgin anything that pleases her; that is why he asks her for help. When he was made a bishop, the future Pontiff took up the custom of praying the rosary in the chapel after supper with the staff of his house. And later, as Successor of Peter, he published an encyclical, Grata Recordatio , on the rosary, written with filial ardor for his Mother, the Virgin Mary. He died on the evening of June 3, 1963, in a profound spirit of abandonment to Jesus, longing for his embrace. [ Peroratio] My dear Minor Seminarians: it is my fervent prayer for each one of you on this day of the Immaculate Heart that, in imitation of St. John XXIII, you may always want to be all Most Holy Mary’s in order to be all Jesus’s . I repeat to you again: love the Virgin very much, constantly, tenderly, always striving to give her joy. Do not fail to entrust yourselves to her by praying the Rosary and the three Hail Marys. And take heart! because, as the Directory of Minor Seminaries says: “holiness is attainable because it is, above all, the work of God” 21 and of the Virgin. The distinctive joy of Minor Seminarians

[ Exordium ] What a joy and what a blessing to be able to be in the largest minor seminary of the Institute! How much I wanted to be here! Thank you very much for the invitation. It is truly a great consolation. When I was thinking about what to speak to you about in this goodnight talk, what message I wanted to leave you, there immediately came to mind that phrase of the Directory of Minor Seminaries which says: “Every Christian must be joyful; for the child [or for the young person] in particular, this is his life” 1 . And it seemed to me very important to highlight it, because it is not only one of the non-negotiable elements of the Institute, that is, something that must characterize all of us, but it must especially stand out in the minor seminarians. This joy 2 , which must be distinctive of the minor seminarians, goes hand in hand with the family atmosphere that must reign in this house 3 . Our Proper Law says it explicitly: “another characteristic of this house must be youthful joy” 4 . Many here have perhaps heard or read how St. John Bosco greeted his boys by saying to them: “Be joyful.” That is the watchword for all the minor seminarians of the Institute. But let us make clear that it is not just any joy; it is not the euphoric joy of having won a match (although that also makes us happy, of course), nor is it the ‘joy’ that one was chosen for something nice and the other was not; that cannot even be called joy. However, there are certain characteristics or concrete manifestations of what this joy must be like. 1. An affectionate and joyful family atmosphere The first mark of joy reads as follows: life in the “Minor Seminary must unfold in an affectionate and joyful family atmosphere : the seminarian learns to love his companions as true brothers and his Superiors as true fathers” 5 . That is, this joy we are speaking about is born of charity, of charity toward the other seminarians, of charity toward the superiors, toward the prefect… Feeling loved always brings joy. That is why, in the same way that each one of us likes to experience that we are loved and appreciated by others, we have to love and appreciate others. This is not a boarding school. This is the house where the youngest members of our Religious Family live, and therefore the family spirit must reign; this means that there must be familiarity with one another, and, as in every family, this is a house where we know each other well –with our virtues and defects– and even so we love each other, and love each other very much; we trust each other and know how to appreciate and value the gifts and the efforts of others, and we also know how to accept their corrections, their miseries… And because we are a family, we take care of one another, we respect one another and avoid by every means harming a companion, as can happen, for example, when we mercilessly criticize another seminarian, or leave him out, or do not want to share with some, or cruelly ridicule them… That damages the family spirit, and if we act that way we are opening the doors to sadness. Do you understand me? You have to be promoters of joy, loving the superiors as your fathers –and therefore speaking with them with complete trust–, and loving the other minor seminarians as your brothers: defending them, taking care of them, helping them in everything you can, being a support for them. And at the same time as we strive to be a cause of joy for others, we must avoid being the cause of sadness for others: that ‘no one be disturbed or saddened in the house of God’” 6 , said St. Benedict. I say the same to you. That is why, if we want there to be joy in our house, the first thing is that there be charity. If this is lacking, however beautiful a house we may have, even if we eat ice cream every Friday and get the highest grades, we are not going to be happy. 2. A spiritual joy Another very important characteristic of this joy is that it is a spiritual joy . St. Tarcisius died a martyr for Jesus, that is, he sacrificed his life to console Jesus; it is not that he spent his time playing, or going on outings and singing songs. Because this joy is rooted above all in a deep sense of faith, in which the presence of the Lord as one who loves and saves always dominates and stands out 7 . Christ is our Friend, who only wants our good, and in fact the greatest good possible. How could we not be filled with joy! This does not mean that we will not have setbacks, difficulties, sufferings, temptations or sorrows… but rather that, since our joy is supernatural (it is supported by and anchored in God), all those sufferings and sorrows are borne with a smile, or I would almost say while forgetting that they are sorrows or sacrifices. Because, since God is our Father, we know that He takes care of all our affairs, and that is why, not only as seminarians but as simple Christians, we must “rejoice always and in everything” 8 . At the same time we must know how to flee, as from a serpent’s temptation, from everything that threatens joy: discouragement because of difficulties –whatever they may be: in study, in prayer, in living together with the other seminarians–, entertaining thoughts about what we have left behind, worries about family, and anything else that makes you less happy, because that is not from God. And if it ever happens to you that thoughts of sadness come to you, or you are worried, or you experience some pain or sorrow, you must know how to open your soul to your spiritual director or to the Father Rector with complete trust, because we all need help in the struggle… A very beautiful example of this spiritual joy is given to us by the martyr St. José Sánchez del Río, who is the patron of our Minor Seminary in the United States. When they took him prisoner, knowing that they were going to kill him, he wrote a letter to his mother which reads as follows: “ My dear Mom: I was taken prisoner in combat today. I believe that at this moment I am going to die, but it does not matter, Mom. Resign yourself to the will of God; I die very happy , because I die in the ranks of our God. Do not worry about my death, which is what pains me. Rather, tell my two other brothers to follow the example of their youngest brother, and you do the will of God. Have courage and send me your blessing together with my father’s. Greet everyone for me for the last time, and you receive, finally, the heart of your son who loves you so much and wished to see you before dying. José Sánchez del Río .” Notice the supernatural and spiritual joy in the words of this martyr, who was barely 14 years old! I die very happy… The technological society in which many young people live has multiplied, perhaps, the occasions of pleasure and comfort, but it finds it very difficult to generate joy. Have you noticed? And that is because true joy is spiritual. 3. Cultivating and promoting joy Finally, our Proper Law, in a very fatherly way, also invites us to cultivate and promote joy . And for that, here in the Minor Seminary, you have thousands of opportunities! In recreation, in games, in competitions, in the floral games, in the conviviums , in the feasts of the saints, in the feasts of the Religious Family… all of that must not only be done, but must fire us up with joy. I remember when I was a prefect in the minor seminary in Argentina, I would see the minor seminarians on the weekends getting up with more energy than ever, and it was because on those days they could play soccer; you would look at them and get the impression that they wanted to play more than they wanted to live. And afterward they were exhausted, but happy, and many times, if during the week there had been some friction or disagreement between seminarians, in the game they forgot everything and were the best teammates. And that joy of playing and jumping and shouting over a game stayed soaked into their souls and served them as motivation to face the daily struggle in school, in their duties, and in everything they had to do, so as to do it with a magnanimous spirit and generosity. I think they spent their time waiting for the weekend to experience that delight again and recharge the batteries of joy that lasted them the whole week. The news of the Religious Family around the world is also an occasion for rejoicing. Now we have the ‘missionary adventure’ videos that come out weekly, and it is always a reason for joy to see all the good that the other members are doing in other parts of the world. “ Everything must contribute to joy ” 9 , says the Directory of Minor Seminaries . Whether I study, whether I work, whether I am on duty, whether I am an altar server, whether we go on some outing together… everything must contribute to making joy reign not only in my soul or in my community, but in our dear Religious Family and in the Church herself. That is how Christ rejoices: seeing that we strive to be joyful, to cultivate joy by doing good to others, fulfilling His most holy Will. They say that St. Mary Mazzarello was so interested, and so continually, in the joy of the girls that, in imitation of Don Bosco, she always asked them: “Are you happy?” For she considered the joy of her daughters the principal proof of their holiness 10 . If her daughters were happy, then she was doing things well. The same rule applies to us. That is why this joy is also asked of those whose main apostolate is working in the formation of the Minor Seminarians. For if those under them perceive self-denial and true joy in their formators, they will feel moved to imitate them. But it must also be said that it is the responsibility of the formators to create the atmosphere so that festivity and joy may be lived, without fearing to spend money on everything that contributes to the celebration 11 . May the boys always be happy! That will also be our joy. [ Peroratio ] With the hymn to Our Lady, who is the Cause of our joy, we ask her to increase our joy through the concrete practice of charity and our union with Christ. And at the same time, let us give thanks to God for the beautiful vocations of minor seminarians with which He has blessed the Institute in this dear country. And I especially ask Our Lady to always take care of you and to be consoled in seeing you always joyful. God bless you! The Queen who won the heart of God

Coronation of Our Lady Monastery of Velletri – Segni, [Exordium] Dear Mother and Sisters: first of all, I would like to thank you very much for the invitation you have extended to me. I am very happy to have been able to come and celebrate Holy Mass with you, here in the Chapel of this Monastery, and even more so on the beautiful occasion of the Coronation of the image of Our Lady, Madonna delle Grazie . The Coronation of Our Lady is without a doubt an occasion of singular importance for a community. For, in doing so, you proclaim the reign of Mary in particular over your hearts and the hearts of the children of this diocese, who are honored to have her as their Mother. But you also commit yourselves to serving her with filial submission. To act in this way is nothing other than to render homage of adoration to God, who is the Father, Son and Spouse of Mary, because it is He who has constituted her Queen of the whole universe. That is why this coronation is also what is called “a public oath of fealty.” That is, we show our bond of fidelity and total dependence on so most worthy a Queen, because in calling us one day here to Velletri to live in her house, she made herself our Sovereign, and very particularly yours. Finally, this Coronation of Our Lady which we will carry out today -by the grace of God- is without a doubt a tribute of gratitude and filial love, justly owed to this most tender Mother and most merciful Patroness of this diocese and of the monastery. Here, then, are the three points that I would like to touch on briefly in this homily, begging the intercession of the Mother of Divine Grace herself. 1. Homage to God Let us begin with the first: our homage of adoration to God in venerating his Mother. It belongs to the supreme Goodness and the unfathomable designs of God to have created a multitude of men and women and destined them to an eternal happiness by virtue of the Incarnate Word and through the mediation of the Mother of God. Now, in the great procession of humanity She rises up, blessed among all women ; she is the great woman par excellence: the Most Holy Virgin Mary. She alone is a great miracle: “ Magnum miraculum ” 1 , said St. John Chrysostom, because She alone surpassed and exceeded in excellence and dignity all the earth and all the heavens. For her dignity as Mother of God is quasi-infinite , according to the expression of the Angelic Doctor. That is why an author said that the Most Holy Virgin “alone among all creatures rose, on the foundation of her humility, to form in a singular and marvelous way the exterior complement of the Trinity itself, she alone also giving it the greatest accidental glory” 2 . And he went on to say: “In her, the Father, who eternally had only the Divine Son, came to have in time the Daughter he lacked; the Son, who was eternally begotten by the Father without a Mother, had one in Her; and the Spirit of God, who is charity, eternal love, I mean the Holy Spirit, likewise came to obtain in Her the Divine Spouse who was fitting for him and whom he had loved from all eternity” 3 . That is why, dear sisters, the Coronation of Our Lady –if you will allow me the expression– is like the payment of a debt owed by God himself to Her. It is as if Christ, on entering in triumph and sitting at the right hand of the Father, “missed” the presence of his Mother, and that is why God himself raises her to heaven to be exalted by the Eternal King himself and to be worthily crowned. This is what the Magisterium of the Church teaches us, saying: “The Immaculate Virgin, preserved free from every stain of original sin, when the course of her life on earth was finished, was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory, and was exalted by the Lord as Queen of the universe, so that she might be more fully conformed to her Son, Lord of lords (cf. Rev 19:16) and conqueror of sin and death” 4 . Yes, Most Holy Mary triumphed by her virtues and triumphed by the most pure flesh that she freely offered in her chaste womb to her Divine Son. That is why the Incarnate Word himself crowns her, saying to her, and I quote here the Song of Songs: Come from Lebanon, my Bride, come from Lebanon, come, you shall be crowned 5 . And it is as if the whole universe ought to second the honors offered by God to the Divine Queen. Because, although adoration is due to God alone, God himself wants all the creatures of heaven and earth, for the honor and worship of God himself, to honor this Most Sweet Mother. And so, when in a moment we crown Our Lady as Queen, we are doing nothing other than rendering the just homage of adoration to the Trinity itself, which displays itself so great and splendid in her who is its Daughter, Mother and Spouse. So the rite of coronation signifies, beyond the acknowledgment of the glorification of Our Lady, thanksgiving to God because he chose her as the virginal Mother of his Son, because Mary was entirely faithful even to the cross, because Jesus gave her to us as Mother and She received us as children. And in her lap we are sheltered from every storm. 2. Oath of fealty This coronation that we are about to carry out in a moment –a replica of the Coronation of the Mother of God by the Trinity itself– is also, in our case, an act of surrender and dependence on this Precious Mother, in deference to and respect for her majesty and sovereignty 6 . How many are the immense favors she grants us! And this is truly our intention, because we want to acknowledge and venerate her as who she is: our Sweet Sovereign. By making her Queen of the monastery and of the hearts of all those who live here now and will live here in the future, we establish the Kindest of all Mothers as the Abbess who “knows how to have compassion on the misery of her daughters” 7 and in her most gentle providence grants them all graces. And She is established as the Mistress who, with loving affection but also “with a sure hand, guides her daughters to perfection” 8 . Since She is the Queen, She will be the one who presides over all your activities, your prayers, your moments of eutrapelia, and everything you do. This brings with it the ineffable grace of living in the light of her smile, in the warmth of her heart and sustained by her hand. What is more, by crowning her we express that we want her to reign not only within these walls, but in each of the hearts that beat here, so that through “fidelity to the one Love, which is manifested and strengthened in the humility of a hidden life, in the acceptance of sufferings in order to complete in one’s own flesh what is lacking in the tribulations of Christ (Col 1:24), in silent sacrifice, in abandonment to the holy will of God, in serene fidelity even in the face of the decline of one’s strength and of one’s own influence” 9 , there may be born the fervent desire for oblative self-giving out of love for one’s neighbor, and so her reign may spread to the ends of the earth. And we do so with the utmost confidence and without reserve, because we know that this august Lady “will not allow us to honor her with respect without repaying us a hundredfold” 10 . 3. Tribute of gratitude and filial love The coronation expresses our gratitude for Mary’s maternal care, our joy at her exaltation as Queen, our confidence in her protection in dangers. Finally, this coronation is a sign of the tribute of gratitude and filial love owed to the Maddona delle Grazie . For one day She welcomed us into this blessed diocese of Velletri‑Segni, and under her virginal mantle she willed to shelter you in this monastery –which is her house– for a very special mission: to pray for priests. That is why in this simple and welcoming chapel, like another Nazareth, which serves as a dwelling for the Lord of lords and King of kings 11 , we want to make her Queen, since we are certain that, like Queen Esther, the Immaculate Virgin, who won the heart of God and in whom the Almighty did great things 12 , will not fail to grant the petitions that you, her daughters, raise to her unceasingly. It is in this sense that our Directory of Consecrated Life , quoting St. Anthony Mary Claret, says: “the pleas and prayers of a small number of good souls hold back the wrath of God so that he does not let his arm fall upon a people and even upon a nation” 13 . That is why, while I thank you very much for the prayers you offer for us and encourage you to continue doing so with great fervor, I too ask our Mother that this crown which today I am very pleased to place on her precious brow may be a figure of your souls. Because good children are the crown of their parents, and not only the children but also the children’s children. That is why in this Mass we also pray very especially for you, for your families, and for the fruits of the most worthy mission to which Our Lady herself seems to have called you, so that, thanks to the fidelity of each one of you, an immense multitude of souls may weave the crown of the Most Pure and ever Virgin Maddona delle Grazie . It is my wish that, just as Our Lady holds the Child Jesus in her lap, She may hold you and bring you closer each day to the Incarnate Word. May Our Lady bless you. Notes 1 In Brevi. Rom. Dom. Spouse of the Virgin, protector of the Incarnate Word and true servant of God

Solemnity of St. Joseph, Spouse of Mary March 19, 2019 Mt 1:16. 18-21. 24 [ Exordium] Dear brothers and sisters, today we contemplate the figure, so dear and close to the heart of all of us and of the Church herself, of St. Joseph, spouse of the Virgin, protector of the Incarnate Word and true servant of God. Inspired by the words of our dear St. John Paul II, who said that reflecting on the participation of the Spouse of Mary in the divine mystery will help us to find our identity within the redemptive plan 1 , it seemed to me that it may be useful for each Servant sister, but also for the Institute of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará as a whole, to reflect on three attributes of St. Joseph: as spouse, as father and as servant, since each of them contains a cluster of virtues which, exercised as he did in the domestic setting of our religious life, can help us -and a great deal- to attain perfection and, in the end, bring us to “our home,” which is heaven. 1. Spouse St. Joseph was in all truth the spouse of Mary. In fact, it seems as though the evangelists delight in referring to him as the spouse of the Virgin of Nazareth. We heard it a moment ago in the Gospel of St. Matthew: Jacob begot Joseph, the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ 2 . St. Luke for his part speaks of Mary as a virgin betrothed to a man named Joseph 3 . And the angel Gabriel himself says to this just man: Do not be afraid to take Mary your wife into your home, for what has been conceived in her is the work of the Holy Spirit. She will give birth to a son, whom you shall name Jesus, because he will save the people from their sins 4 . These last words of the angel to Joseph are what is known as the ‘annunciation’ of St. Joseph, in which he hears not only the divine truth about the ineffable vocation of his spouse, but also the truth about his own vocation 5 . The Gospel goes on to say that St. Joseph did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him 6 . And I would like to dwell on that, because such must also be the attitude of each Servant sister: “the attitude proper to the ‘third class of persons,’” 7 which gives itself entirely to God and to his plan –as our Directory of Spirituality says, and these are words that must be weighed– without diminutions or retractions, without reservations or conditions, without subterfuges or delays, without retreats or sluggishness 8 . The Magisterium of the Church teaches that “the just man of Nazareth possessed above all the characteristics proper to a husband” 9 and, as the evangelist says, he was a good husband 10 , with all that this entails, which I would like to sum up with that saying of St. John of the Cross: “Whoever is truly in love at once lets himself lose everything else in order to gain more in what he loves” 11 . For at the cost of no small personal sacrifices St. Joseph knew how to be the pillar of his family, the defender of the greatest treasures a man could possess on this earth, absolutely devoted to his family, for there was nothing that could distract him from the eminent and prior place that his family held in his mind and in his heart. And St. Joseph did all this, as the Mystical Doctor of Fontiveros says, “without seeking gain or reward, but only to lose everything and himself in his will for love of them” 12 . St. Joseph made –and I want to emphasize this– a complete oblation of himself, of his life, of his work, of his heart, of all his talents, in order to place them at the service of his family. And so he let himself lose everything else in order to gain in what he loved most: the Incarnate Word and his Most Holy Mother. Because –we know it– love, if it is true, has nothing to do with calculations. How instructive, then, is the example of St. Joseph for all the members of our Religious Family, called like him to “live always through Jesus and through Mary, with Jesus and with Mary, in Jesus and in Mary, for Jesus and for Mary” 13 . Certainly St. Joseph was the first to bow before the Virgin of Nazareth when She became the Mother of God and the Queen of this world. But it is no less true that St. Joseph exercised over the Blessed Virgin the sweet and gentle authority of a husband solicitous for her well-being and happiness, and therefore his Most Sweet Spouse was not only subject to him in everything, but with attentive and provident love took care of him (what is more, we can say that She was the first devotee of St. Joseph). In the intimacy of the house of Nazareth, she who is –in the words of St. Louis Marie– “the reflection of eternal light, the spotless mirror of the majesty of God and the image of his goodness” 14 , with great affection was always ready to serve him with all the deference and delicacy of a wife, to attend to his needs whatever they might be, to listen to him attentively, to respect him in his role as head of the family, to follow his directions. Though She was the Mother of God, it never occurred to her to have a plan different from that of her husband, or to go another way, or as we would say today, ‘to have a different agenda.” Simply because the Virgin recognized in her husband “the one whom the heavenly Father willed to make, on earth, the man of his confidence” 15 , her protector and the “governor of Incarnate Wisdom” 16 . Both knew themselves to be united, though in different roles, to the same and single plan of redemption. That is why an author says that the Most Holy Spouse of St. Joseph, with her ineffable sweetness, was the one who inflamed the heart of her most chaste spouse with holy ardor, who enlightened his mind and gave strength to his arm. For his part, St. Joseph also knew that he could always go to Her in search of relief for his soul, in search of genuine and enthusiastic help for his labor and his struggles, of refreshment on his pilgrimage, of fortitude and courage in adversity, and of someone with whom to share his joy in his achievements. All with great confidence, knowing themselves to be members of one same family with a common project. How can we fail to see in the example of the Blessed Virgin and St. Joseph the great models to imitate in the joint work of our Institutes as parts of “one same Family with an identical specific end” 17 , which is none other than “to love and serve, and to make Jesus Christ loved and served” 18 , precisely as they did. Because our union, dear sisters, is not reduced to the Constitutions and the Directories : we have a common plan, a mission entrusted by God to both Institutes as members of one single Religious Family within his Church. It follows, therefore, that our union must be complete, constant and unalterable if we truly want to be faithful and to render Him some service effectively; knowing how to immolate ourselves in a real way each day 19 in order to attain the ideal of our Religious Family, which is none other than that He reign 20 . And this brings me to the second attribute of St. Joseph. 2. Guardian of the Incarnate Word “The Incarnate Word remained hidden for 30 years: he hid himself in the shadow of Joseph” 21 . Truly St. Joseph consecrated his life to caring, with the deep affection of a father, for the Son of God born of Mary. And to caring for him in every sense: education, food, clothing, in his piety, teaching him a trade, forming him in the virtues. But St. Joseph was also his guardian, his staunchest defender, and that is why he did not fear to leave behind everything familiar and journey to an unknown country to protect him. For that reason St. Bernardine of Siena goes so far as to call St. Joseph “savior of our Savior,” “teacher of Incarnate Wisdom” 22 . In other words, what I mean is that St. Joseph knew how to place the exercise of his fatherhood at the service and in the guardianship of the person and mission of the Incarnate Word. And are we not called to do the same when we are invited, as missionaries, to forge that love of a father and of a mother that devotes itself without reserve and without looking back to the service of Jesus Christ 23 ? We may even think that St. Joseph will be very pleased because on this day we want to ask the Lord for all the Servants and, to tell the truth, for every member of our Religious Family, the grace of that maternal wisdom that instills that wholly provident affection which goes ahead to meet the unspoken needs of one’s own (and when I say one’s own I also mean the priests of the IVE); which carries charity into the smallest detail; which makes its hidden and silent service to one’s own a luminous and joyful sacrifice; which defends one’s own even with a look; which knows how to spare them sorrow and work by putting itself at their disposal; which receives with a strong heart the worries and annoyances that cloud their faces; which never keeps a tally of the things it did for those it loves, because the happiness of every Servant must lie in giving herself “without measure, to the extreme, until she can give no more, to the end” 24 . Because seeking the limelight, thinking ourselves self-sufficient, multiplying demands, lack of docility, pretending that attacks on our Institutes do not affect oneself, not taking a genuine and effective interest in the needs of each Institute, that is, of our one Religious Family — none of this has anything to do with the example of St. Joseph, much less with the spirit of our Religious Family. Always keep in mind that each one of you, like St. Joseph, is called to “live for the Incarnate Word and to let yourselves be guided by Him” 25 . Therefore, says our Proper Law, “you must be zealous for the honor and glory of the Word” 26 . That is the humble and mature way in which the Servants serve; that is how they “participate” in the economy of salvation, precisely as the adoptive father of Jesus did. 3. Servant of the Incarnate Word Lastly, the third attribute with which the Church honors St. Joseph is that of having been the faithful and prudent servant of the very Son of God. Indeed, St. Joseph possessed an “absolute availability to serve faithfully the saving will of God” 27 and in all truth “gave himself entirely to serving the Incarnate Word” 28 with heroic fidelity to the commitments assumed before God. In a few minutes we will say the Prayer over the Offerings , which asks precisely that we be granted the same love and purity of heart that St. Joseph had in serving Jesus. And what prayer could be more fitting to pronounce here with all fervor together with you, who bear the honorable name of “Servants of the Lord.” If a true Servant must love and give herself to the point of the heroism of self-giving without reserve 29 , then what is proper to the Servants is to give all of themselves, and their very life with it, for the greater glory and service of the Incarnate Word and, according to the order of charity, to those of the Religious Family in the first place. This requires on your part “not a halfway self-giving; not a self-giving only in some places or in some things; not a self-giving at some moments; but a total and full self-giving, in whatever place and time it may be” 30 , just as Joseph of Nazareth did. Since, then, “the oblation of oneself” 31 is the characteristic that must stand out most in the Servants, how the exhortation you have received from the very beginning must resound in you!: “None of so much selfishness, so much pettiness, so much calculation! We must go for total self-giving!” 32 . In that spirit must live, and in that spirit must be formed, the many vocations that, through the intercession of the glorious Patriarch, we trust will come to be part of the Institute of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará. And yet, how often we ourselves obstruct this perfect love for the Incarnate Word, fearful that in having Him we will be left with nothing else. We hesitate to venture out and risk everything for God; we fear losing something if we follow his plan, without realizing that with Him we have everything! That is not the example of the spouse of Mary. Giving oneself entirely and out of love to the Family will never be to the detriment either of oneself or of one’s own Institute. On the contrary! It will increase in us forgetfulness of self, the spirit of faith, detachment from our own judgment and our own plans, even detachment from our own goods, now placed at the service of the common project; all of which must redound in fidelity to the intention of the Founder, in joy and deep peace, because then we will be doing what God asks of us, and in the way He asks it of us. All of this will contribute to the fullness and fruitfulness of our religious life, and I believe it will be the greatest contribution we can make to the cause of the evangelization of culture. And at this point I want to take the opportunity to thank all the Sisters who, throughout the length and breadth of this world, silently, simply, render us countless services. Which, let me tell you, in many cases represents an irreplaceable support for many of us priests. Like St. Joseph and like the First Servant, always hold high the magnificent title of Servants . Being aware that to be a Servant implies living in the “more” and in the “above and beyond” 33 . Do not be afraid when love becomes demanding. Do not be afraid when love asks for sacrifices. Do not be afraid of the cross of Christ. Because the cross is the source of all joy and peace 34 and the only way to reach the “most high embrace” 35 of union with God, which is given, as St. John of the Cross says, “to those already exercised and tested in the service of the Bridegroom” 36 . Take this thought home with you today: All the wealth of a Servant consists in giving herself to the Word 37 , and that is and must always be your “particular style of sanctification and apostolate” 38 . [ Peroratio] So then, through the intercession of St. Joseph, today I invite you to join me in asking the Lord for the whole Institute of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará, in addition to the graces I have already mentioned, these three graces: 1) the grace to excel in “humble service and generous self-giving, that is, in the gratuitous gift of yourselves through a love to the extreme” 39 on behalf of the ideals of the Religious Family. 2) The fatherly and provident protection of the Foster Father of the Incarnate Word for all the Sisters in all their missions. 3) The grace of many vocations –active and contemplative– who, in imitation of the First Servant and of St. Joseph, want to live and die in the joyful and solicitous service of the Incarnate Word. We ask Jesus to grant them to us through the glorious Patriarch St. Joseph and his Most Holy Spouse and our Mother, the Virgin of Luján. Notes 1 Cf.
