Counsels of St. John of the Cross

St. Paul Monastery – Tuscania, June 10, 2017 [Exordium] Dear Mothers and Sisters: First of all, I want to tell you that I am very grateful for the invitation you have extended to me to come and visit you and share this “good afternoon” talk here with you. It is sincerely a joy for me, since a monastery is -as St. John of the Cross said- “a land very well suited for serving God” 1 , and I am sure that here He is served in abundance. Today, as we celebrate the great solemnity of the Most Holy Trinity, a mystery to which “we must have a ‘deep and deep-rooted devotion,’ since it is the active principle of the Incarnation” 2 , I would like –if you will allow me– to reflect with you on the most singular call that each one of us has received to live “a transfigured existence” 3 , through which –as we say in our formula of profession– we want “to be a concrete imprint that the Trinity leaves in history” 4 . 1. The p rimacy of the spiritual Our spirituality undoubtedly has an “intensely Christological and Trinitarian” character 5 . If you notice, already from the first paragraph of our Constitutions the Trinity is mentioned. What is more, in the very introduction and in what refers specifically to our Spirituality, we read that from this devotion to the One and Triune God there derives something that gives our spirituality a special stamp, namely (verbatim quote): “the primacy of the spiritual in all our thinking, feeling and acting, since God is the one who works in us both to will and to work according to his will (cf. Phil 2:13), and because the teaching of the Incarnate Word is most clear: Seek first the Kingdom and its justice, and all these things will be given you besides (Mt 6:33)” 6 . And this endeavor –which must be firm and resolute– to configure our existences to that of Christ, imitating all the attitudes this entails, we must live in our Religious Family “with a particular style” 7 –as the Directory of Consecrated Life says–, which implies on our part a “ serious, not sentimental, spirituality ” 8 (which, as you know, is one of the non-negotiable elements attached to our charism). That is, it is a distinctive and most noble characteristic of our spirituality “to transcend the merely sensible, and to be ready to pass through the dark nights” 9 in order to attain this divine transformation. This non-negotiable element attached to our charism, that of a “serious spirituality,” is non-negotiable precisely because it is what sets us apart against the world, and although it has often generated and still generates rejection, it is what has allowed us to present a living Christianity and has been a source of abundant spiritual fruits and of vocations (and also of numerous crosses and persecutions, since it is in frank opposition to a sentimental or, even more, an empty spirituality). And, therefore, everything that does not correspond to it, everything that tries to diminish its decisive force or draws us away from it, must be set aside as something foreign to our charism. To put it positively: it is because of this distinctive and most singular note of our charism that, for example, we practice the Spiritual Exercises and that we are formed –as our Constitutions wisely and clearly indicate– “with the doctrine of the great masters of the spiritual life, especially: St. Augustine, St. Thomas Aquinas, St. John of the Cross, St. Teresa of Jesus, St. Ignatius of Loyola, St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort, St. Thérèse of the Child Jesus, and of all the saints of all times whom the Church proposes as exemplars so that we may imitate their virtues” 10 . That is, always seeking to be formed in the school of the great mystics and doctors of the Church. Within this framework, today I would like to highlight the figure of St. John of the Cross (and I have chosen him because, as you know, this year marks the 475th anniversary of his birth), since his doctrine is explicitly quoted nine times in our Constitutions and Directory of Spirituality , and as many more times in the rest of our Proper Law 11 . From this we have more than enough elements to infer that the doctrine of this Holy Doctor of the Church is a most certain guide for finding and uniting oneself to the Triune God –which is not a sensible reality but a purely spiritual one, and requires a great faith which is purified in the tribulations or nights of the soul–. We can sum up his doctrine on this point in a well-known quotation of St. John of the Cross, in which he says that “to enter into this divine union, everything that lives in the soul must die, little and much, small and great, and the soul must remain without craving for all of it and as detached as if it did not exist for the soul nor the soul for it” 12 . Without this, he clarifies elsewhere, there cannot be the “true and total transformation of the soul in the three Persons of the Most Holy Trinity” 13 , and therefore we could not speak of the “transfigured existence” we mentioned at the beginning. Such a transfiguration is certainly a grace of God, but like all graces, it must be implored with prayer and sacrifice, and one must likewise dispose oneself to receive it, “keeping oneself in solitude for God” 14 , says St. John of the Cross. Therefore, it will not be given unless we have intimacy and familiarity with God, which is acquired, exercised and nourished principally in prayer, in contact with Christ in the soul. It is very important for everyone (for those who have been in religious life for a short time as well as for those of us who have already been in it for some years) to read and reread the doctrine of St. John of the Cross and to become steeped in his teachings in such a way that they come, as it were, to govern our life of prayer; to illuminate our nights; to serve us as a criterion for interpreting God’s action in our souls (and even in the souls of others, should it fall to us by office or by charity to do so); that his teachings may help us to moderate our spirits in consolations; even serve as an incentive in the practice of charity in community life –hence that “where there is no love, put love, and you will draw out love” 15 – and in everything “help us to work at stripping ourselves of all that is not God for love of God” 16 . You who by vocation “dedicate yourselves to God alone in solitude and silence” 17 must –and here I quote words of the Holy Doctor taken from our Proper Law–: “Live as if there were in this world nothing but God and [your soul], so that your heart may not be detained by any human thing” 18 . But rather leave everything, even “your skin and all the rest for Christ” 19 . Because what is greater and nobler than God? It is precisely from this doctrine of St. John of the Cross that the wise and most practical teaching contained in number 68 of our Constitutions derives, where it deals with the vow of poverty, which invites us not to be concerned: “with the esteem and good opinion of men, with health and bodily strength, with the posts or offices that may be given to us or taken away from us, with the prosperous or adverse events that may befall us, with dying young or old.” But rather to have our center, our “nest” 20 , in God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit. An author says, commenting on the drawing of the Mount of Perfection made by the Saint: “If we foolishly entertain ourselves with the goods of earth, which is what usually happens; or foolishly entertain ourselves with the goods of Heaven, we are wasting our time. We do not arrive where we ought to arrive, ‘because when you dwell upon something, you cease to reach the all.’ This fits perfectly with what Jesus wants of us, as we have seen in the two standards: supreme spiritual poverty, enduring reproaches and contempt, in order to arrive at supreme humility. For the one who truly seeks this: ‘Nothing wearies him from above and nothing oppresses him from below, because he is at the center of his humility.’” He goes on to say: “If we were capable of forming religious women who truly love the Cross, the world could change. But as long as we do not have souls who really follow Christ crucified and want to be crucified with Christ, we will do things, often external things, which may have some value. But we will not do the most important of what we have to do, which is to attain holiness and spread the holiness of Christ throughout the whole world.” 2. Four spiritual counsels For this, St. John of the Cross gives four spiritual counsels (or pieces of advice) 21 , which we can summarize in four words: a. Resignation : “living in the monastery as if no other person lived there. That is, without meddling either in word or in thought in the affairs of others; and even if the world should collapse, not wanting to notice it or interfere in it, in order to keep the tranquility of the soul.” This is what we mean when we say “avoid worrying uselessly about things that are none of my concern.” Avoiding frivolous thoughts, thoughts of the past, judging one’s neighbor, etc., which only serve to interrupt the interior silence that must reign in the soul. Notice, then, how important it is to keep the peace of the soul and the vigilance we must have in this regard, because this is a sign that one is struggling to eliminate contrary loves and it is a sign of self-possession 22 . b. Mortification : knowing “that we have come to the convent for no other reason than to be worked upon and exercised in virtue.” In this regard an author says that one must avoid “seeking heaven without putting the things of earth in order, always going about seeking consolations, seeking to be understood, or in prayer seeking to feel good. Claiming securities that cannot be had here; trying to understand mysteries that exceed our capacity.” c. The exercise of virtue : “for which it is fitting to have constancy in carrying out the things of your Religious Order and of obedience, without any human respect, but solely for God. And for this never set your eyes on liking or disliking, but do it solely for God.” This is what St. Ignatius calls “holy indifference.” That is why you should never fail to do anything because you dislike it, but do it because it is the Will of God and you only want to please Him. d. Finally, solitude : by which “it is fitting for you to consider all the things of the world as finished.” By which, the Saint himself clarifies, “it is not meant that for this reason one should fail to do the office one has, or any other that obedience may command, with all the solicitude possible and that may be necessary, but that one should do it in such a way that no fault clings to one in it, because neither God nor obedience wants this.” And after these four counsels, the Holy Doctor concludes by saying: “Try to be continual in prayer… and go about always desiring God and with your heart set on Him, for which it is required not to leave the soul to any thought that is not directed to God, and in forgetfulness of all the things that are and happen in this miserable and brief life. In no way, says St. John of the Cross, seek to know anything except only how you will better serve God and better keep the things of your Institute.” And since it could not be lacking in a “serious and not sentimental spirituality” and in this disposing oneself to attain a “transfigured existence,” devotion to Most Holy Mary, the tender and filial love we owe her, occupies a preponderant place and must be renewed daily –as St. John Paul II said– according to one’s own traditions, through a “spiritual union with the Virgin Mary, going through with her the mysteries of the Son, particularly with the praying of the Holy Rosary” 23 . Dear Sisters: as St. John of the Cross wrote in one of his letters: Rejoice and trust in God! 24 “On this road one must always keep walking in order to arrive, which means always removing desires, not sustaining them. And if they are not completely removed, one does not completely arrive… and so the soul will not be transformed in God” 25 . “And this transformation must not be held to be impossible,” because nothing is impossible for God, and “because it is precisely so that we might reach this transformation that God created us in his image and likeness ” 26 . The cross is the program of life of the Servants

Solemnity of the Exaltation of the Cross [ Exordium ] Dear Mothers and Sisters, it is a grace for me, and certainly a great joy, to celebrate this Mass with you, which I gladly offer together with the priests present here in thanksgiving for all the Servants who throughout the world live to the full “the radicality of the Cross” 1 ; and asking at the same time for the grace that “we may never lack the Cross” , but that it may be the “most beautiful program of life that [all] those who take pride in bearing the name of Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará strive to attain” 2 . From the very beginning the Servants have been associated with the cross. In fact, they were born from the cross and they carry everywhere the emblem of the Cross of Matará that distinguishes them, and it is precisely the cross that is the platform from which they must always launch themselves “ boldly to restore all things in Christ ” 3 . It is as if a Servant cannot be understood without the cross and, I do not think I am mistaken when I say, that it is precisely the cross that draws them to itself. That is why, if you allow me, I would like to point out some elements that show how the Servants have been –and must always continue to be– bound to the cross. 1. Name One of the elements that clearly shows us the association of the Servants with the cross is found in the very founding act of the Institute of the Servants, where it is explained how the sisters had wanted to be called “slaves,” and how some thought they should be called “daughters,” but that it was the Bishop, Msgr. León Kruk, who decided that they should be called “Servants,” according to the account of St. Luke which speaks of some women… Mary Magdalene, Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Susanna and many others, who served the Lord while He went through cities and villages, preaching 4 . Later, our Founder would add that they are called Servants because the sisters must resemble those holy women who stood by the cross , because of what the evangelists say: there were many women there […] among whom were… 5 , by the Cross of Jesus …: Mary, his Mother 6 ; Mary Magdalene , Mary Salome , Mary of Clopas , and many others 7 . And so these women, having gone up with Him to Jerusalem , contemplated the sacrifice of the cross 8 . That is why these words are explicitly addressed to the Servants: “ You must be among them . The holy women are the first servants there have been in the history of the Church, and from them you receive your name” 9 . Therefore it is a most special vocation of the Servants to imitate the Incarnate Word in his self-emptying, as we heard in the second reading. A vocation to self-emptying that implies the cross: the cross of becoming a servant 10 , of humiliation 11 , of obedience even to accepting death 12 for the love of God. What is more, the Directory of Consecrated Life states very clearly that it is the task of the Servants to give special witness to the Incarnate Word through “humility, in disinterested service and, in particular, in merciful love” 13 . For “one of the characteristics of woman is to make herself a gift . Precisely in ‘the following of Christ, expressed in service’ 14 , [a service which] often implies sacrifice. For to make oneself a gift is to give one’s own life to the other, so that the other may decide what he wants to do with the giver. It is a total service accompanied by a high degree of forgetfulness of self, in order thus to be totally free in the service of the other” 15 . You must always keep this in mind, since to act otherwise would be to betray the very reason for the existence of the Servants. 2. Cross of Matará Another element that very especially manifests the indissoluble union between our dear Sisters and the Cross is found in the fact that they are called “Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará” because they identify themselves with the Cross of Matará, “on which are carved the central mysteries of our spirituality: the Incarnation, the Passion, the Eucharist, etc.” 16 , and we can add: “Because the Lord is crucified there and we want to know nothing but Jesus Christ and Jesus Christ crucified 17 , through whom the world is crucified to me and I to the world , as St. Paul says” 18 . And because at the foot of the cross stood the most compassionate First Servant, who must always remind them “not only of why [they are so called], but of the place , the role and the mission of the Servants.” Likewise we must say that the Cross of Matará, being the oldest in America, had a clear catechetical purpose, becoming for us “a most beautiful example of the evangelization of culture, which is precisely the specific end of our Institutes” 19 , and it is its doctrine, that is, the doctrine of the cross, that we must go about preaching throughout the world: Jesus Christ crucified, a scandal to the Jews and folly to the Greeks 20 . And to do this without timidity, but boldly, as we said at the beginning, because our trust must always be in Him who by the power of his cross conquered the world. 3. The Habit and the Cross of Matará Another element that plainly reveals the firm association of the Servants with the cross is that from the very beginning the religious habit our sisters wore (perhaps you have seen it in photos) bore as part of the tunic the tau cross in blue, a symbol of the religious sister’s espousal with the cross of our Lord. Today, the habit our sisters wear bears as an integral part and distinctive sign the Cross of Matará, which shines on the blue background of the scapular to announce to the world that they are not of the world 21 and that they have been “espoused to Christ under the sign of the cross” 22 . Even more: the cross they always wear on their breast reminds them and proclaims to the world that the sisters hold as their most sublime office “to live with Him the demands of God’s plan and to set out courageously on the way of the cross” 23 , because “Jesus is loved and served on the Cross and crucified with Him, and in no other way” 24 , and only thus do they understand that they are to be fruitful, begetting many spiritual children for God. Therefore, a true Servant of Christ “must never be turned in on herself, but must be open like the arms of Christ on the Cross, whose arms were wrenched out of joint from opening them so wide out of love.” 25 4. Feast of the Exaltation As a consequence of all we have been saying, and without going any further, from the very beginning this same feast of the Exaltation of the Cross which we celebrate today has been and is the proper and principal feast of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará; “because of the most lofty significance of the Cross,” says the founding act. So much so that among us this feast has become synonymous with the feast of the Servants. For in it we are reminded –as we heard in today’s Gospel– that God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish, but may have eternal life 26 . That is, it speaks to us of the redeeming love of Christ, who called them to religious life precisely “only to deal in love with Jesus Christ” 27 . But we must also know how to read in this marvelous feast the longing we must have to participate actively in the redemptive action of Christ and to bring that saving love to all peoples, even to the most difficult places (those where no one wants to go) 28 and even in the most adverse situations 29 , striving to conform our life to that of Christ Crucified through “humble service and generous dedication, in the free gift of oneself through a love to the very end” 30 , as our Proper Law asks. That is why this feast gives us the occasion to celebrate and give thanks together for the vocation and mission of our dear Sister Servants, which is none other than to raise high the Cross of Christ throughout the length and breadth of this world (as in fact they already do very well in the 35 countries where they are present, and very particularly here, in this beloved country of Ecuador). [ Peroratio ] Finally, my dear Mothers and Sisters: you know well that what is proper to us is “neither Jesus without the Cross, nor the Cross without Jesus” 31 , and that it is one of the healthy traditions of our beloved Religious Family to place at the foot of the cross a sign that says: “ This is how one loves .” Because, as we have heard so many times: “The cross makes fruitful whatever it touches […] The cross is the pulse of love, and to know how to suffer, one must know how to love” 32 . That is why on this day, on which with great joy we celebrate the Exaltation of the Cross, which is the same as saying the exaltation of God’s love for men, I invite you to know how to respond to that love with the only possible measure, that is, with radicality . Far be it from you to become discouraged or troubled before the cross. Far be it from you to make excuses or complain about the cross. Rather, overcoming the fears so proper to our nature and pride, go forward with a firm spirit to embrace the cross with generosity and joy. “The Cross is God’s most beautiful gift.” And so Jesus made it known to St. Gemma: “See, my daughter, the greatest gift I can grant to a soul loved by me is the gift of suffering” 33 . That is why we ask in this Holy Mass: “that you may always know how to embrace, love and never come down from the Cross,” “that you may truly follow Christ Crucified and want to be crucified with Him,” because that is “to attain holiness and to spread the holiness of Christ throughout the whole world” 34 . I raise this same prayer today for each and every one of you, invoking the intercession of Most Holy Mary, who is the Model of love to the end. 50th Anniversary of the Cross of Matará

Exaltation of the Holy Cross Homily on the occasion of the 50th anniversary of the ‘discovery’ of the Cross of Matará [Exordium] Dear Mother and Sisters: The solemnity we celebrate today has an altogether particular character for all Christians and very especially for the Servants. It is the mystery of “the cross of Christ the Bridegroom” 1 , as St. John of the Cross calls it. And, incidentally, while I was preparing this sermon, I was pleased to see that six times the Monastic Rule of the Servants calls Christ: Bridegroom. For each contemplative nun enters monastic life precisely “to share the solitude of [her] Bridegroom, who through the Eternal Spirit offered himself to the Father” 2 on the Cross. Therefore, if the Cross is coextensive with the Christian life, it is all the more so for a bride of Christ, since the Cross is the “spirit” of one who consecrates herself to God , and that is also her path: that of the Cross, that is, of self-denial. “Whoever takes any account of himself neither denies himself nor follows Christ” 3 , wrote St. John of the Cross with his usual radicality. This is one of the causes, if not the principal one, why today so many Christians and religious live deceived [examples] and think “that any manner of withdrawal and reformation in things is enough; and others [who] are content with practicing the virtues in some manner and continuing in prayer and pursuing mortification, but do not arrive at the nakedness and poverty, or detachment or spiritual purity” 4 ; “and they think that this and that will be enough for them to come to union” 5 . To these the Mystical Doctor gave warning, saying that this “is beating about the bush” 6 , it is “fleeing from imitating Christ” 7 , and therefore they will not make progress in perfection. Ours, what is truly Christian, is this: to walk the way of the Cross of Christ the Bridegroom 8 . Today, moreover, this solemnity shines with a special light because it marks 50 years since the ‘discovery’ –so to speak– of the Cross of Matará, and 40 years since the Argentine Episcopal Conference reproduced the “carved Cross of Matará” on its cover. I say ‘discovery’ to refer to the finding, by the researchers Martínez Moreno, of the Cross of Matará, which was in the possession of the Sosa Ruiz family in Santiago del Estero 9 , and which allowed the world to come to know the Cross of Matará. There is a part of the Cross of Matará to which perhaps we rarely pay attention. It is the figure at the base of the Cross of Matará, a figure that researchers think “could be an indigenous chief, or cacique” 10 . Speaking of this figure, Martínez Moreno says in his work Cruces Catequísticas de Santiago del Estero that “its position in an attitude of supplication, with the arms crossed over the breast, and at the base or beginning of the work [that is, at the base of the cross], would indicate the following: The cacique implores the intercession of Most Holy Mary… through the martyrdom of Christ” 11 for his people, which is what is centrally represented on the Cross. That is why in that supplicant figure, in a certain way, I seem to see represented the mission of the contemplative sisters and religious of our Religious Family, and therefore your mission. Because you, too, are at the base, at the beginning, in the vanguard of the work of evangelization of the Institute. And because you too have been called to intercede before our heavenly Mother for all souls, but especially for the members of our Religious Family 12 . This is how we must always be, like the cacique, at the feet of Jesus and of the Most Holy Virgin of Sorrows, very close to the cross! That is our vocation! This is what our Proper Law says, quoting St. Teresa: “For this [to implore Mary’s intercession before the throne of God] Christ has gathered you here; this is your vocation and your desire, this is the reason for your tears and your prayers… The day your prayers, disciplines, longings and fasts are not devoted to this which I have told you, you will not attain –know it well– the end for which the Lord has gathered us here” 13 . This is supremely important! Crucial! Because to the prayers and holiness of life of each one of you our Religious Family is entrusted in a particular way, with all its patrimony, with all that magnificent spirit our Founder has bequeathed to us, with all its missions… And since the purpose of the contemplative life is to plead for our Family before the merciful Heart of the Mother of God, it is your responsibility, and it is the noble office God has assigned you, to contribute by your holocaust to keeping our Religious Family unscathed and to gladden it with the fruits of a loving faith. That is no small task! It is no trifling vocation! That is the mission God has been pleased to grant you, as to the cacique on the Cross of Matará, and one must be faithful. And as with his, so too in us, the authenticity of prayer is verified when it is closely united to the cross of Christ and to the Virgin of Sorrows at the foot of the cross. You all know well that witness means martyr, and the Church is faithful in martyrdom, in witness. I tell you this because when the mystery of the Cross touches our lives, with its nights and its aridities, to the point that the soul “comes to believe that all its blessings are ended forever” 14 , you must feel yourselves privileged missionaries of our Lord. Particularly when fidelity to one’s vocation becomes difficult or becomes a Cross, and therefore prayer itself is crucified. We know well that God has placed great power in the joined hands of those who suffer. We see it in the very mystery of Christ that we contemplate today: Christ annihilated on the Cross, “annihilated in his soul without any consolation or relief” 15 . But in this moment “of the greatest abandonment,” “he accomplished the greatest work of his whole life,” which was “to reconcile and unite the human race with God through grace” 16 . Analogously, the contemplative nun, in union with Christ Crucified, when she denies herself, when it falls to her to suffer something, by her prayers and her sacrifices, can do more for the Church, for the mission of our Institute, for all souls, than others who carry out missions and tasks of great importance. This is how the mystery of the Cross that we contemplate today takes shape, becomes reality in our lives. St. John of the Cross, in his writings, identifies the “cross” and “love.” And both with the following of Jesus. Love is denial of self, inasmuch as it is the affirmation of the other as the reason and center of one’s own life. And this denial, “in which the pure spiritual cross consists” 17 , “must be a death and annihilation” 18 . That is why, paraphrasing two texts of the Gospel of St. John, he will say that “whoever wishes to possess something or seek it for himself, that one will lose it [his life, his soul].” Whereas “whoever renounces for Christ all that he can desire and enjoy, choosing what most resembles the cross … that one will gain it” 19 . “Knowing how to lose one’s life means acting in communion with the whole community, through sincere obedience and mutual solidarity. It means adhering to Christ with an undivided spirit in the offering to Him of one’s body and soul; it also means placing greater trust in poverty than in riches, without concerning ourselves with anything other than serving God and others” 20 . And sometimes, when we see that several years of religious life have already gone by and we still seem to be just beginning, we ask ourselves: will I be able to do that? We do not know. The love and the science of the Cross is an enormous grace, but above all ‘it is a grace’ that we must ask of Jesus insistently, convinced that it is the greatest of graces and the one that in some way brings about the perfection of our vocation, even when it seems totally to surpass our strength. It is then that, with all humility and trust, we can repeat the Prayer of the Enamored Soul with our arms crossed over our breast like the cacique of the Cross of Matará, and say: “Lord God, my beloved! If you still remember my sins, and for that reason do not do what I keep asking of you, do your will in them, my God, for that is what I most desire, and exercise your goodness and mercy, and you will be known in them. And if you are waiting for my works in order by that means to grant my request, give them to me yourself and work them in me, and the sufferings you would be willing to accept, and let it be done. And if you are not waiting for my works, what are you waiting for, my most merciful Lord? Why do you delay? For if, after all, it must be grace and mercy that I ask of you in your Son, take my little copper coin 21 , since you want it, and give me this good, since you also want it. Who can free himself from lowly ways and limits if you do not lift him up to yourself in purity of love, my God? How will man, begotten and reared in lowliness, rise up to you, if you do not raise him, Lord, with the hand that made him? You will not take from me, my God, what you once gave me in your only Son Jesus Christ, in whom you gave me all that I desire. Therefore I will rejoice that you will not delay if I wait.” [Peroratio] The Cross on which the Lord and the Virgin of Matará appear constitutes a most beautiful program of life which we must strive to attain, with the grace of God, which is never lacking if one does what must be done 22 , as our Founder wrote. Likewise, it is the mission of each Servant to project to the new generations the lofty ideals expressed in this Cross, so that throughout the length and breadth of this world the Gospel of Jesus Christ may resound: I have overcome the world 23 . May the Most Holy Virgin, the Madonna delle Grazie, always console us in our daily labors and nourish our hopes. To conclude, it may be useful to recall one of the counsels that the Master of Fontiveros gave to Mother Ana de Jesús: “Meanwhile, now… occupy yourself in exercising the virtues of mortification and patience, desiring to become in suffering somewhat like this great God of ours, humbled and crucified; for this life, if it is not for imitating him, is not good ” 24 . The beatitudes of the contemplative life

[Exordium] We have just heard one of the Gospel passages that has most moved the world down through the centuries: the eight beatitudes of the Sermon on the Mount. Many years ago now, Pope St. Paul VI spoke of this passage, presenting it as “one of the most surprising and most positively revolutionary texts: Who, in the course of history, would have dared to proclaim ‘blessed’ the poor in spirit, the afflicted, the meek, the hungry, those who thirst for justice, the merciful, the pure of heart, the peacemakers, the persecuted, the insulted…? Those words, sown in a society based on force, on power, on wealth, on violence, on abuse, could have been interpreted as a program of baseness and apathy unworthy of man; and yet they were proclamations of a new ‘civilization of love’” 1 . The Gospel program of the beatitudes is transcendental for the life of the Christian. It is certainly a lofty and demanding program, but at the same time it is fascinating. This is the program of life followed by all the saints whom we celebrate today. That is the narrow path along which they walked. Our beloved John Paul II said that “each of the eight beatitudes points to that goal beyond time [holiness, the heaven to which we are called]. But at the same time each of the beatitudes affects man directly and fully in his earthly and temporal existence. All the situations that make up the whole of human destiny and of man’s conduct are concretely included, by their own name, in the beatitudes. These point out and guide in particular the conduct of the disciples of Christ, of his witnesses” 2 . That is why today we are going to reflect on the beatitudes of the contemplative life. For whoever has understood the eight beatitudes proposed by the Incarnate Word and resolves to practice them has understood the whole Gospel and can make it a reality; that is, can attain holiness. The Church has always repeated them and does so now as well, addressing them above all to contemplative souls, of whom the whole world has great need. Listen well. 1. The beatitudes of the contemplative life Jesus proclaims: Blessed are those who mourn : that is, the afflicted, those who feel physical suffering or moral sorrow, those who go through terrible solitudes and dark nights; for they shall be comforted. That is why the Monastic Rule of the Contemplative Branch says that contemplatives consecrate themselves in a particular way to penance and consider it a special gift of their vocation to share voluntarily in the redemptive suffering of Christ 3 . Why? Because “in suffering there is concealed a particular power that draws a person interiorly close to Christ” 4 . This is the consolation of those who mourn. And so, says St. John of Ávila, “The song and the laughter of the religious woman must be to weep for her betrothed, Jesus Christ. In the choir, in the garden, in the refectory, in the cell and everywhere, she must go about sighing for her Spouse Jesus Christ; and this must be her office and this must be her song, and when she is singing in choir with the sweetest melody, her heart must be sighing with an inner and very deep sigh for her most beloved Spouse, whose memory and desire must never depart from her heart. With this she must fall asleep, and of this she must dream while sleeping, and this must be the first thing to come to her mind on waking; her heart always melting in love for him, and her memory occupied with nothing else but her beloved Spouse” 5 . Blessed are the pure of heart . Jesus assures us that those who practice this beatitude shall see God. For “There is no holiness without purity of soul: ‘holiness means purity’ 6 ” 7 says our Directory of Spirituality . And it is “here −in the contemplative life− that one acquires those eyes whose serene gaze wounds the Spouse with love and whose purity makes it possible to see God” 8 . Blessed are the merciful for they shall obtain mercy . St. Edith Stein −that marvelous contemplative− who left the cloister only to be martyred, wrote this beautiful paragraph: “Do you hear the groaning of the wounded on the battlefields of the East and the West? You are not a doctor, nor a nurse, and you cannot bind their wounds. You are enclosed in your cell and cannot reach them. Do you hear the agonized cry of the dying? You would like to be a priest and be at their side. Are you moved by the weeping of widows and orphans? You would like to be a consoling angel and help them. Look at the Crucified One. If you are united to him as a bride in the authentic fulfillment of your holy vows, your blood is his precious Blood. United to him you are omnipresent as he is. You can help like the doctor, the nurse or the priest, here or there. In the power of the Cross you can be on every front, in every place of affliction; your merciful love will carry you everywhere, the love of the divine Heart, which everywhere pours out its most precious Blood, Blood that soothes, sanctifies and saves” 9 . How important and how necessary is the office of souls like yours, who implore mercy for the other members of the Institute and for the whole world! Never abandon your post… the Lord rewards the merciful with mercy itself, with joy, with peace. Blessed are the peaceful , the peacemakers . This is an exceptional category of men and women whom Jesus proclaims blessed. And in this contemplatives have a role without equal, since they consecrate their prayer and sacrifice to the great concerns and intentions of the Church, especially for those gifts which no merit, but only prayer and penance, can obtain from God. In their prayers, in their hearts, in their hands −I would say− they carry the lot and the destinies of the Church and of the whole world. Blessed are the meek . These words that came from the mouth of the “good Word of the good Father” 10 , who, preaching the kingdom of God, also said to his disciples: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart 11 , must resound in the contemplative soul with singular power. This is what John Paul II teaches us when he says: “Love him as befits your spousal condition: taking on his very sentiments; sharing his way of life, made up of humility and meekness , of love and mercy, of service and joyful availability, of tireless zeal for the glory of the Father and the salvation of the human race” 12 . Such must be the meekness of a contemplative soul, to the point that one should be able to apply to it that paragraph of the Directory of Spirituality which says: “Look at the fools! Stones are thrown at them and they kiss the hand that throws them; people laugh at them and mock them and they laugh too, like children who do not understand; they are beaten, persecuted and martyred, but they give thanks to God who found them worthy” 13 . Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice . A thirst for justice that translates into a thirst for holiness. Jesus has called you to the consecrated life and especially to the contemplative life precisely so that you may be “deiform” 14 , as St. John of the Cross says. And if that must be the principal work [in which] every Christian [is employed], all the more so for one who glories in being called a monk 15 . But the personal work of holiness is necessarily joined to the ‘thirst for souls’, which makes the contemplative soul offer itself to God so that through it all the members of the Church may grow in holiness. Blessed are the poor in spirit . This is the first of the eight beatitudes that Jesus proclaimed in the Sermon on the Mount. “The poverty embraced by Christ increases the freedom of spirit and the princely spirit that the religious must possess by his consecration” 16 . That is why here I would like to repeat the counsel the Mystical Doctor gives to a Carmelite nun, which says: “God wants the religious to be a religious in such a way that he has done with everything and everything is done with for him; because he himself is the one who wants to be his wealth, consolation and delightful glory” 17 . The poor in spirit are those who are most open to God and to the “wonders of God.” Hearts open to God are, for that very reason, more open to men. They are ready to help selflessly. Ready to share what they have. And what is the reward of the poor monk? Jesus tells us: to the poor in spirit belongs the kingdom of heaven . This is the reward that Jesus promises them. More cannot be promised. Together with the first, I now want to cite the last beatitude, the one concerning those who suffer persecution for the sake of justice , those who are persecuted for bearing witness to the faith: these are authentic poor in spirit, and that is why Jesus also says that theirs is the kingdom of heaven. How many monasteries, how many contemplative souls guarded the deposit of faith entrusted to them in the midst of the bloodiest persecutions, and shored up the sound doctrine of the Church in the face of a multitude of errors and confusions 18 ! A task that is not foreign to you . And particularly in these times the need to pray and do penance for the members of the persecuted Church becomes urgent; for the conversion of sinners, above all of consecrated souls and of the persecutors of the Church . [Peroratio] These eight beatitudes are the precious pearl for which all the saints whom we celebrate today left everything. If you want to be happy in the contemplative life, seek identification with Christ. It is true that the beatitudes are not commandments. But they are certainly all contained in the commandment of love, which is the ‘first’ and the ‘greatest.’ The beatitudes are like the portrait of Christ, a summary of his life, and that is why they are also presented as a “program of life” for each one of us. Love your vocation very much. And from here, from the silence of the cloister and the hidden life, proclaim the preeminence of the Lord over all reality; make manifest in your life and with your life the full relevance of the beatitudes; be ‘the revolutionaries’ of the civilization of love, as St. Paul VI said. May the Virgin, Queen of all saints, help you to be very holy, since it is for that end that the Lord has gathered you together, as St. Teresa said 19 . From His fullness we have all received grace upon grace

From his fullness we have all received grace upon grace [Exordium] Dear brothers and sisters, as we reach the end of the year and look back on everything that has happened in our lives, in the life of the Institute, in the Church, we see how, if we try to have a real view of things, all the events of history, and particularly those that happen in our own lives, are interwoven with one another as if forming a golden chain that always leads us unfailingly toward God, from whom all good proceeds 1 . We must always be very aware of this, because it is, in the final analysis, the truth of life and of existence… of our life and of our existence. And that is why, finally, we must conclude the year saying, and marveling at, how many graces we have to be thankful for. And we must be very aware that, even though some of the things that have happened have been adverse to us, they have been ordained by God for our good –because that is what is most fitting for all of us– and therefore we can truly say with the Evangelist: From his fullness we have all received grace upon grace 2 . It is important, I would say fundamental, to keep this clearly present and well illuminated in the soul. We may suffer persecutions, great misunderstandings, apostolic tribulations that truly grind down the soul, unfounded suspicions, senseless accusations… and thousands of other trials. And this not only on a personal level but also at the level of the Institute. Notice that every tribulation, and especially persecution, in order to be blessed –says the Directory of Spirituality – must necessarily fulfill two requirements: that we be “reviled for the sake of Christ,” and that “what is said against us be false” 3 . As long as that is the case, on our part we must rejoice that God tests us in that way. That is why, when some say “the IVE has problems,” we should smile and feel sorry for whoever says it, because in reality we have the happiness of ‘suffering something’ out of loyalty to God 4 , and that is an enormous grace, which –as our Proper Law also teaches– implies “the full and total rejection of the evil world” 5 . At times we might ask ourselves: why do we have ‘problems’? (if indeed they can be called problems). We have ‘problems’ for defending the truth, for not being tributaries 6 , for defending the Patrimony of the Institute 7 , for being Thomists, for living forgetful of ourselves in order to spend ourselves and wear ourselves out in the care of those who are so often forgotten or rejected by their own families or by the State and who depend on us to live, for proclaiming the truth of Catholic dogma and morals with our efforts and our lives, and for so many other things… How can anyone think we are not going to have problems? It would be worrying if we did not have them, and God save us from not having them… We might think that those who cause us problems (let us realize this too) are in general those who do not love these things, those who do not love religious life (that is why they attack it or abandon it), those who do not love the perennial philosophy, nor the poor and the needy, nor the missions or the new foundations, nor formation in Thomism, nor the increase and perseverance of so many young vocations. That is why our Proper Law warns us very clearly “to be very careful not to turn over and over our ills” 8 , that is, never to let the fatalistic and negative thought that ‘we have problems’ settle in among us, because in reality what we have, the so-called ‘problems,’ are great blessings for which to rejoice and which move us to love God even more. Paraphrasing St. Edith Stein, we too can and must say that from crosses (or from ‘problems,’ if you like) we always come out renewed and strengthened. * * * So the truth is what it always is (and these are principles to which we must cling): it does not matter much what happens in our lives, but rather how one reacts to it. That is why, in view of the new year that is beginning, I wanted to offer you three considerations on divine providence (which are very well known, but which it is good always to have engraved in the soul) in the hope that they may help to reaffirm the firm hope we must always have in God and the conviction that everything that happens, happens for our good. So that –as St. Paul says– the God of hope may fill you with complete joy 9 . First consideration 1. We must always keep in mind that everything that happens has been foreseen and known by God from all eternity and has been willed by God, or at least permitted by Him. It is healthy to think about this. And it is also very important. God’s knowledge does not increase like ours, which passes from ignorance to wisdom. He knows everything and everything is present before His eyes. The fall of Adam and Eve in Paradise, so to speak, did not catch God taking a nap. God is Knowledge, He is not a scientist: God knows everything, He learns nothing by experience, as we do. Put another way, He does not look at us the way we look at an anthill, watching us go in and out of the house, going to work, and then telling a secretary angel to note down that we were unkind to the sister we just passed. One author asked: Why is it that we always think God looks only at the bad things we do and never at the good ones? And he answered: God does not keep a file of all the acts we perform. We keep the accounts of all of them in our own books. Our conscience takes down the dictation we give it. God knows all things not because He looks at us from up there, but because He looks within Himself, as the Cause of all things. God never tries to read over our shoulder. An architect can tell you how many rooms the house will have and the exact size of each one long before the house is built, because he is the ‘cause’ of that house being made. God is the cause of the being of all things. He knows them before they happen. Like those old film reels that contained the whole story of the movie before it was projected on the screen. The same happens with God: He knows everything before the events take place on the stage of life. What one must not think is that because God knows everything, He has predestined some to go to heaven or to hell independently of their merits and overriding the freedom of each person. That is why the study of freedom is so important. For the knowledge that someone is going to act in a certain way is not the immediate cause of our acting. The fact that you now know you are seated is not the cause of your being seated, nor does it prevent you from standing up. The Blessed Virgin could have refused to be the Mother of God, and Judas could have resisted the temptation of betrayal. The fact that God knew how each one would act did not make them act the way each one did. Now, since in God there is no future, the fact that He knows beforehand what is going to happen does not mean that He pre-causes it. You could be standing on the roof of this house and see a person approaching the house. You know that before entering, he has to pass through the garden gate, go under such-and-such a tree, walk along a path, knock on the door, etc. You see all those possibilities, but you are not the cause of that person going through all those areas. That is why, when a person asks us: “If God knew I was going to be damned, why did He create me?” The answer is: “God did not create you so that you would be damned. You do that yourself.” The universe is moral and therefore conditional: Behold, I stand at the door and knock 10 . God does not break doors down. The latch is on our side, not on God’s side. This is the first thing one must know in any circumstance of life. Now, the second. Second consideration 2. God allows or permits evil, but always for a greater good related to His love and to the salvation of souls. This is extremely important. The doctrine of evil, of providence and of predestination, far from being a subject to avoid, was of great profit for him to consider. And truly it is. God permits evil. Let us remember that our Lord said to Judas: This is your hour 11 . Evil has its hour, but God has His day, Bishop Fulton Sheen used to say. When some evil befalls us, we must always remember that God can draw good out of evil, because while the power to do evil lies with men, the effects of our evil acts are beyond our control and therefore in the hands of God. Joseph’s brothers were free to throw him into the pit, but from that moment on Joseph was in the hands of God. You meant to do me harm, but God disposed it for good, in order to preserve the life of many people . We must never judge the evil that God permits by its immediate effects but rather by its final effects. To complain, to become sad or downcast in the face of these evils is foolish and is a failure to realize the hand of God in all things. It is failing to realize that our miniature minds cannot grasp God’s plan. A doctor would not allow an operation if he could not restore the patient’s health through it, and God would not permit an evil if He could not draw a good from it. One must never forget this. Third consideration 3. We must do everything in our power to fulfill the will of God as it is made known to us through the Church, the commandments, the Constitutions, our legitimate superiors and the obligations of our state of life. And everything that is beyond our power we must surrender and submit to the will of God. Another truth that, in my view, is fundamental. One must clearly note the distinction between what is within our power and what is beyond our power . We must never have a fatalistic attitude. Some things are indeed under our control. The one who is negative in the face of evils fails to recognize that –within certain limits– his will can affect the events of life. It is God’s will that men have free will to use it under His subordination and thus to be happy, always, whatever happens. But here we want to deal with those things that are beyond our reach (which is most of what happens to us), for example, illnesses, false accusations, the death of a loved one, a sickness, the contradictions one does not expect to have, and you can continue mentally adding your own examples. God could have prevented all these events, could He not? But if He did not, we must always know (because it is the truth of things) that it is for a higher reason. And therefore we must learn to say with Our Lady: Fiat. We must learn to be docile and to submit to the will of God…and everything will be ours. Even the most irritating things of this life can be stepping stones to our salvation, and a cause of joy for our souls. We must never complain, still less lament, but see providence and the hand of God in everything. Everything that happens, happens for our good (and it is good to give due weight to each of these words). A saint used to say that one act of thanksgiving when things do not go as we like is worth far more than a thousand acts of gratitude when things go according to our will. * * * [Peroration] That is why, on this beautiful day, the eve of the Solemnity of the Mother of God, who is our most sublime example of what humility is and of the most perfect fulfillment of the will of God, I would like to read you what St. Luigi Orione used to say to his own: “ Fiat! Pronounce this gentle word, O my sons and friends, pronounce it with every breath, with every heartbeat, with every movement of the lips. God will always understand it in the way in which you want Him to understand it, now as a prayer , now as an act of faith in doubt, as an act of hope in fear, and always as an act of love. Fiat! Into your hands, then, into your hands, O my God!… Work, work this clay, O my God, give it a shape and then break it to pieces again; it is yours and belongs to the one who takes your place, and it will never again have anything to say… Suffering, raised up, brought low, useful for something or useless to all, I will always adore you and I will always be yours, O my God! No one will separate me from you! In joys and in sorrows I will always be yours, O my sweetest love, Jesus. Solitary and unknown like the flower of the desert, wandering like the bird without a nest, always, always, Lord and most gentle love of my soul, there will come from my lips the submissive word of her whom you gave me as Mother: Fiat! Fiat! Be it done unto me according to your word! ” 12 . In view of all the events of this year that is now ending, knowing how to have a supernatural outlook on all of them, but also clothing ourselves with a deep vision of faith to begin this new year, the invitation is this: to live in our lives the mystery of the Incarnation; that, after all, is our charism. That is to say: like Our Lady, to give our whole heart to God as if we no longer possessed ourselves –because in truth that is how it is–; our will is ours only to do His. Let us always pray, not that God may change His will, but that He may change ours. Let us not measure the Goodness of God by His readiness to do our will (that would be a very grave error, almost a blasphemy). Let us always trust in God, who makes all things work together for good. We call God Father every day when we pray the Our Father, and do we not believe that He wants the best for His children? Let us beware of always thinking that we could do more good for souls if we were not sick, if we had another position, if we had the opportunities, if we had the gifts another person has, or if what happens to us did not happen, or if people did not speak ill of us… What matters in life is not where we are, but whether we are doing the will of God. The holy abandonment the saints and mystics speak of. It is worth recalling here, it seems to me, the counsel St. John of the Cross gave to a nun: “[Remain] well forgetful of all things so as to be able to enjoy God well in solitude, not caring that they do with you what they will for the love of God, since you are not your own but God’s” 13 . It is always edifying to read that passage of St. Louis Marie which speaks of how God always exalts the humble, and that is why He made Mary sovereign of heaven and earth, treasurer of His riches, dispenser of His graces, worker of His wonders, mediatrix of men, exterminator of the enemies of God and faithful companion of His greatness and His triumphs 14 . Certainly all the graces received during this year have passed through the precious hands of our Most Pure Mother, and we must not forget that. This, as our Constitutions say, “makes manifest the dominion and maternal providence that Mary has over all things, but especially over faithful souls” 15 . May this very thing be one more motive of hope and confident courage for the year that is beginning. May the Mother of God grant all of us, today and always, to live each day rejoicing in hope 16 . Perfect model of the consecrated woman

Perfect model of a consecrated woman [Exordium] Dear Mothers and Sisters, first of all, I would like to thank you for the invitation to celebrate this Eucharist with you on this Saturday traditionally dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary. Since we are essentially Marian 1 , and since our Proper Law has indicated in several of its documents the principal and preponderant role Our Lady has in our spirituality and missionary activity, we cannot fail to consider and go deeper into the example of our Most Holy Mother. In fact, our Proper Law presents her to us as the “perfect model of a consecrated person, whom every religious must always contemplate and imitate” 2 . That is why today I would like to highlight some aspects, or rather attitudes, of our Mother which, although they challenge every Christian, are –in my view– essential in a Servant. 1. Service And the first attitude or quality that stands out in Our Lady is precisely that of service. Many times we have read in the Gospel that passage from the account of the Visitation which says: In those days Mary set out for the hill country… 3 . The words of the Gospel account make us see with the eyes of the heart the young Virgin of Nazareth on her way to the town of Judah where her cousin lived, in order to offer her services. Analogously, each Servant sister, because she is a missionary –which is another essential aspect in us– is or will be sent to another town to offer her services. This implies availability, forgetfulness of self in order to serve others, humility, zeal for souls… However, what strikes us above all in Mary is her attentiveness, full of tenderness ,toward her elderly cousin. It is a concrete love , which is not limited to words of understanding, but commits itself personally to genuine assistance. Our Lady does not simply give her cousin something that belongs to her; she gives herself , without asking for anything in return. She has understood perfectly that the gift received from God, rather than a privilege , is a duty that commits her in favor of others with the gratuitousness proper to love. That is why the quality that must stand out in each Servant sister must be precisely an attitude of service. If a sister does not serve others, she is of no service. It is a contradiction. Because what is proper to every Servant is precisely to serve, with humility, with concrete acts of service toward the members of her own community, toward the poor who come each day to the door of the convent, toward the priests, the seminarians –members of our own Family– and of course toward the souls that have been entrusted to her. You must be convinced that you have consecrated your lives to the service of the Incarnate Word. That is not something abstract, a vague idea, or something utopian; it becomes concrete “in humble service and generous self-giving, in the gratuitous gift of yourselves through a love to the end” 4 in the service of your neighbor. And saying gratuitous gift means without expecting reward, without expecting recognition, without expecting consolations, without demands… It is, moreover, a constant service; it is not something sporadic, but, following the example of Mary Most Holy, it is a self-giving that fills everything and every day. If a Servant says she wants to be humble, or believes she is humble, but does not serve others, no matter how many resolutions she makes and prayers she raises to heaven, she is beating around the bush. That is why the virtue that, intrinsically associated with service, must most distinguish the Servants is humility. And from there follows a second quality, which is: 2. Joy Each day at Vespers we pray the canticle of the Magnificat, which says: my soul proclaims the greatness of the Lord and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior, for he has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid . It is precisely from that readiness to serve, from knowing herself to be the ‘servant of the Lord,’ that the joy of the Blessed Virgin springs. Similarly, if each Servant is ready to proclaim her fiat to the will of God –without reluctance, without slowness, without reservations– then she will be able to proclaim her magnificat and live her consecration to the full. The joy of Our Lady springs from knowing that she is looked upon by God, despite her lowliness 5 ; it springs from the ‘service’ she is able to render, thanks to the wonders the Almighty works in Her. It is interesting to note that the Magisterium of the Church says that “woman cannot find herself except by giving love to others” 6 and therefore she will not find her joy, her fulfillment, except by giving herself. Which I –by my poor lights– understand as giving everything that love asks of us, with total availability, immediately, unconditionally, without asking anything in return, with joy and wishing to be asked for even more. For this what is needed –among other things, and in my view– is to ask for the grace of maternal wisdom, which instills that wholly provident affection that anticipates and satisfies the unspoken needs of one’s own; which carries charity down to the detail; which makes of its hidden and silent service to one’s own a luminous and joyful sacrifice; which defends one’s own even with a glance; which knows how to spare them pain and toil; which receives with a strong heart the worries and annoyances that cloud their faces; which never keeps a tally of the things it has done for those it loves, because its happiness lies in giving itself “without measure, to the extreme, until it can give no more, to the end.” Notice that after the Magnificat came those three months of service to her cousin Elizabeth, about which the Gospel says nothing. Or perhaps it tells us the most important thing: good makes no noise ; the strength of love is shown in the serene discretion of daily service. And that is a great lesson for all of us who so often seek offices and conspicuous apostolates that attract human glory to us. Our Lady served in silence. 3. Intercession Finally, a third quality that we should see reproduced in each Servant is that of being an intercessor. We see it in the dialogue between Our Lady and the Incarnate Word at the wedding at Cana. She is sensitive to the needs of others 7 and intercedes before Christ. She is the one who asks for graces and favors from heaven for us. St. Louis Marie says that there is no grace of God that does not pass through the hands of Mary. That is why the Blessed Virgin is the Woman who intercedes. Likewise, each Servant must implore, with her sacrifices and prayers, favors from heaven for all souls, especially for the Institute, for the whole Religious Family and of course for all souls. Our Proper Law tells us so explicitly: “we must have recourse to her merciful intercession” 8 and ask for all the graces we need to be faithful to our consecration 9 , as our formula of profession of vows says, a grace that must be asked not only for ourselves but for all the members of our Institutes. In this sense “it befits the Servants… to direct everyone toward heaven by the example of their lives and by their intercession”; that is why you must pray for every grace for yourselves, for the Institute, for sinners … and especially now, when these are not easy times for the Church [and for the Institute], is when one must ask the most. The intercession of Mary Most Holy does not fail. Because as a good Mother she is not distant from our worries, our problems or our struggles; rather, with maternal solicitude She seeks to help us, protect us, defend us, give us what She knows is good for us to be happy in time and in eternity… That is why I invite and encourage you to pray fervently for our own, for our own Religious Family, that it may always remain united and rooted in the precious charism that has been bequeathed to us. And when some cross comes upon you, some sacrifice you must make –God willing– be so good as to offer it –following the example of our heavenly Mother– for the good of our Family. [Peroration] In short, dear sisters, the exemplary holiness of Our Lady must always move us to lift our eyes toward Her. That is why let us ask in this Holy Mass that the contemplation of the virtues of our Most Holy Mother –especially her readiness to serve, her joy and her dedication to intercessory prayer– may adorn our souls, and that we may reproduce them in concrete acts in daily life. For thus, only thus, will we be behaving as true devoted children of Our Lady and fulfilling our purpose of being essentially Marian. May Our Lady bless you. Notes 1 Cf. To serve our neighbor like Mary

[ Exordium] Dear Mothers and Sisters, first of all, thank you very much for the invitation to celebrate this Holy Mass with you. It is a joy to see that the sisters have increased in number (it seems to me) and accompany very closely the apostolate of the fathers here in Chile. That is why in this Holy Mass I invite you to give thanks to God for all these years of apostolate as a Family (with a capital F). Now that we are among family, I would like us to reflect together on a very simple but very profound line of our Directory of Spirituality , which says: “To serve one’s neighbor, even, like Mary, in the simplest tasks”. It is in number 84 of the directory, where it explains what Jesus taught us when He was enclosed for nine months in the womb of Our Lady. Well, one of the things He taught us is precisely that: to serve our neighbor even in the simplest tasks. The logic of the world vs. the logic of the Incarnation Many of you here have the privilege of serving the poor directly, the most forgotten or most despised men and women, the children who often do not have access to the enjoyments that children elsewhere have; however, I believe that this is the visible part of the road to God. Yes, because the poor lead to the heart of God! The Incarnate Word Himself, poor among the poor, revealed a great mystery when He told us: “ whatever you did to one of the least of these my brothers, you did to Me 1 ; [that is why] serving the needy is the way to attend to Christ in His flesh” 2 . Hence it seems very clear to me that the path of sanctification of the Servants throughout the world, but especially here, because of the work you carry out, passes very much through gestures of kindness and service to the poor, which is indeed a gift of God that fits squarely with the purpose of our Religious Family, which includes precisely “living with all radicality the demands of the Incarnation and of the Cross” 3 and seeing Christ especially in the poor 4 . The logic of the world invites to selfish greed for material things without giving anything in return, and even incites to greed for interior satisfactions or consolations without any sacrifice, or at most, to giving, but always expecting to receive something in return. The logic of the Incarnation, which is the logic of the Son of God, who emptied Himself, taking the condition of a servant 5 , is quite the opposite. According to the logic of the Incarnate Word, “to love means to give, to give everything that love asks of us, to give immediately, without complaining, with joy, and wishing to be asked for even more” 6 . That is the program; that is how the Most Blessed Virgin Mary served her Son and her spouse St. Joseph, and that is how we must serve our neighbor. This is a sentence of a Polish blessed, foundress of the Sisters of St. Felix of Cantalice, Blessed Maria Angela Truszkowska 7 , which seems to me to sum up the principal marks of how the service of a Servant should be. Qualities of the service of a Servant Let us look briefly at each of the qualities of this service. First, it says that the service is a loving service, because “ to love means to give ”. Ours is not a social assistance service, like someone who gives alms but does not get involved with the good of that person’s soul; you know that better than I do. Ours is not a merely technical service of distribution, but that of well-ordered love of neighbor 8 , by which we fulfill the command received from our Lord to love our neighbor as ourselves; if it were not so, the apostle James could ask us: What good is it if one of you, on seeing a brother or sister naked or lacking the necessary food, says to them: ‘Go in peace, keep warm and eat’, and does not give them what they need for their body? 9 . That is why charity toward our neighbor is an exercise of faith that leads us to God. Do you understand me? Secondly, it says: “ to give everything that love asks of us ”. And in this sense our proper law points out the following: “It is not enough to give to the poor; one must give oneself” 10 , like those who exercise a motherly office, forgetful of themselves. Even more, our Directory of Spirituality , speaking of the Servants, says –pay attention– that “all their wealth consists in giving themselves to the Word” 11 . And how do the Servants give themselves to the Word? “even in the simplest tasks” 12 , which is what we were saying at the beginning. That is, going out to beg in the market, serving food, cleaning the church, playing with the kids, teaching catechism, visiting families… Doing everything that love asks of us, even in those things that according to the logic of the world are unimportant, and that some might even consider demeaning; but we follow the logic of the Incarnation, which implies self-denial, sacrifice, humiliation. And, thirdly, the service of a Servant implies “ giving immediately, without complaining, with joy, and wishing to be asked for even more ”. It is interesting to note that the Directory of Spirituality , among the things it mentions that the Incarnate Word taught us in the womb of Our Lady, includes precisely that of “doing the things of God promptly” 13 , “because ‘slow calculations are foreign to the grace of the Holy Spirit’ 14 ” 15 . That is why the Servants must be “docile and prompt in carrying out what the Holy Spirit asks of them, like Our Lady, who quickly set out on her way 16 ” 17 ; and serve with joy, without complaining, “working always against the temptation of delay, against the fear of sacrifice and of total self-giving, and against the temptation to take back what we have given by seeking compensations” 18 . I know that you here in Chile carry out a magnificent work of charity in all the apostolates you have, and I encourage you to keep working and always doing more and better in this sense, because, as you know very well, “charity is indispensable to evangelize the culture” 19 , and even the most modest gestures can speak of Jesus Christ. [Peroration] May the Most Blessed Virgin of Mount Carmel, Patroness of Chile, who holds the Child Jesus in her arms, always remind you that you are called to serve the Incarnate Word in the person of your neighbor, to carry the burden of the needy, of the weakest. And in this self-sacrificing service –as is the service of all mothers– may God fill you with joy, and may the unsearchable riches of Christ 20 superabound in your souls. A grace that we implore from our Lord through the intercession of Our Lady in this Holy Mass. May God bless you today and always.
