The wedding dress

[ Exordium ] My dear friends:Today we find ourselves in the Church of the mother house of the Institute to celebrate this Holy Mass in which several religious of the Institute of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará will take the habit. A celebration that is already in itself spiritually overwhelming and joyful, and which today, being the day of the Immaculate Heart of Mary, takes on even greater dimensions. Today’s liturgy presents to us the heart of the Mother, first in search, as the Gospel we have just heard says: they went back to Jerusalem looking for him . And once He was found, the heart of the Mother becomes a tabernacle: his mother kept all these things in her heart . So too the novices who are going to receive the habit today, after going in search of the Beloved and having now found Him, must treasure Him in their hearts, like one who takes refuge within, under the veil of love. You are already beginning to sense how lovingly provident God has been with us, having prepared even the smallest detail of this celebration. 1. Sign of their consecration For today these dear sisters of ours will put on the holy habit for the first time, a habit that is not only a “sign of belonging to a particular religious family” 1 , our beloved Family of the Incarnate Word, but which, moreover, as our Constitutions say, “is a sign of their consecration and a witness of their poverty” 2 . “St. Thomas teaches that religion is a state of penance and of contempt for worldly glory; for this reason, lowliness of dress befits religious, and this for two reasons –the saint affirms–: first, for their own humiliation; second, as an example to others, ‘he who preaches penance wears the habit of penance’ 3 . Therefore, we religious of the Incarnate Word bear witness with the religious habit to our total consecration to God” 4 . It is interesting to note that “the use of the religious habit implies, on the one hand, the laying aside of secular clothing, [that is, setting aside the clothing they wore until now in the world]. Such abandonment concretely expresses our not being of the world 5 , our separation from everything that is not God, and it becomes ‘the means of constantly reminding ourselves of our commitment, which contrasts with the spirit of the world’ 6 . But also, and more importantly still, it entails the aspect of being clothed. Hence the imposition of the religious habit: – speaks of a consecration , that is, of a self-giving to God [as we were just saying. Because it is an evident sign of total consecration to the ideals of the kingdom of heaven]. – signifies the change of life and of mentality (the metanoia of the New Testament), total surrender to God, wholehearted, effective and irrevocable adherence to the Catholic religious tradition, [it is the assimilation of the style of the Incarnate Word]. – signifies also the renunciation of the world , [that is, a definitive separation from merely human and earthly interests] and also a renunciation of material goods [that is why wearing the habit, the cassock, bears witness to a life of poverty joyfully lived and loved in trusting abandonment to the provident action of God]. [And finally, also] it implies that one wishes to strive for the perfection of the Christian life, that one denies oneself, takes up one’s cross, and dies with Jesus Christ a mystical death” 7 . All these realities are implied, contained, supernaturally imprinted in the habit that you will wear from now on. 2. The wearing of the holy habit You who receive the habit today for the first time, and all of us who have already been wearing it for some years, must be aware that the wearing of the holy habit “is a silent but eloquent witness before others; it is a sign that our secularized world needs to encounter on its way, and which is, moreover, the sign that many Christians desire’” 8 . We ourselves must be ever more deeply convinced of this. How many people think of God, of Our Lady, simply by seeing religious in their habit; how many are moved to pray, or at least to ask how to pray; for how many souls are religious, identified by their holy habit, a point of reference in terms of goodness, of sound doctrine, in short, of consistency of life. That is why I dare to say that the wearing of the holy habit that you will receive today renders, in some way, an ecclesial service. Indeed, our Constitutions , citing St. Francis of Assisi, say that the mere presence of the religious dressed in his holy habit already preaches 9 . The Spiritual Father of our Institutes, St. John Paul II, also repeated insistently that “we religious, not only by our life in common, or by our way of behaving, but even by our way of dressing –which must always distinguish us as religious– are in the midst of the world a constant and intelligent preaching, even without words, of the Gospel message; and in this way, we religious become not mere signs of the times, but signs of eternal life in today’s world” 10 . And this is so because the religious habit, in its simplicity and modesty, attracts the poor and quietly challenges the powerful, preaching to them without words about the very way of life of the Incarnate Word. Silently, a religious in his holy habit challenges others with the message that “this world cannot be transformed without the spirit of the beatitudes” 11 . He points out to them the transience of earthly things and speaks to them of a supernatural reality, infinitely abundant and eternal. Let us realize, then, the importance of wearing it in these times: “Signs must be used now more than ever, –say the Constitutions – ‘above all in today’s world, which shows itself so sensitive to the language of images… where the sense of the sacred has been so terribly weakened, people also need these reminders of God, which cannot be neglected without a certain impoverishment of our priestly’ 12 or religious ‘service’, we could also say. The value of the habit, dear novices, comes “not only from the fact that it contributes to the propriety of the religious [or of the priest] in her external behavior or in the exercise of her ministry, but above all because it makes evident within the ecclesial community the public witness that every priest or religious is called to give of his or her own identity and special belonging to God” 13 . Let us never be ashamed of this most worthy identity! 3. Wedding dress The religious habit is, moreover, for you who are novices, like a wedding dress. Consecrated virginity –which for today’s world is madness– but whose dignity is confirmed in the image of the Virgin of Nazareth and is completely founded on the radicalism of the ideal that the Incarnate Word proposes to whoever is willing to understand , is the ideal of exclusive dedication to the Incarnate Word, analogously to the way a wife dedicates herself to her husband and her children. Therefore, consecrated virginity, which you have embraced, is founded in particular on a profound and constant yes in the nuptial order; on the gift of yourselves out of love, totally and without reserve. Evidently virginity in its evangelical meaning entails the renunciation of marriage and therefore of physical motherhood. But this renunciation does not cause frustration –as many think, even members of our own families– because virginity opens one’s whole being to a motherhood according to the spirit; to a spiritual motherhood which is expressed in many ways. Let it be well understood: virginity does not deprive a woman of her proper characteristics: the spousal love which she nourishes for Christ makes her open to each and every person. The Magisterium of the Church in Lumen Gentium has expressed this truth perfectly; pay attention: “And let no one think that religious, by their consecration, become strangers to men or useless to earthly society. For, although in some cases they do not directly serve their contemporaries (like contemplatives), they nevertheless keep them present in a more intimate way in the heart of Christ and cooperate spiritually with them” 14 . Therefore, dear sisters, this sublime vocation, which is at once maternal, nuptial and virginal, you must learn to live in the school of the Immaculate Heart of Most Holy Mary. Your identity from now on is that of consecrated women, and this identity is illuminated and enriched in the light of the teachings of this Kind Mother, who wants us, her children, also to be seekers of God, lovers of God, happy to live separated from the world, yet solicitous toward our brothers and sisters who live in the world and united to them through the bond of charity in Christ, happy to live in the ‘house of God’ as in a family, rooted in obedience and in charity. Many times the Polish Pope pointed out that we religious are “a living sign of the world to come ” 15 –and he added– “a sign that takes root by means of the habit” 16 . In such a way that the religious habit becomes a consistent and serene, but also courageous, witness to that for which we live. That is, “to imitate the Incarnate Word, chaste, poor, obedient and son of Mary” 17 ; it speaks of our mission, which “is founded on the conviction that He must reign ” 18 ; it speaks of the fact that “all our wealth consists in giving ourselves to the Word” 19 because, as St. John of the Cross says, “all the best of here below, compared with those eternal goods for which we were created, is ugly and bitter” 20 , and thus, by means of all this, we wish to attain the highest end, which is union with God. That is why the taking of the habit is in some way a celebration that carries us into the future, which begins, yes, here today, but which extends throughout our whole life and points toward eternity, toward that new heaven and new earth 21 that will not pass away. Our Constitutions , with accents of the gentlest paternal charity, which contain at once a fervent longing of the heart and a loving precept, ask us to “love, then, the habit, which must become our very skin” 22 . May this be our fervent desire today and always. ***** [ Peroratio ] To conclude, I would like to tell you, with the words St. Clare of Assisi once wrote, that: “Among the other benefits we have received and receive each day from our Giver, the Father of Mercies, for which we are bound to glorify Him with lively thanksgiving, great is that of our vocation” 23 . Always remember that the gifts and the call of God are irrevocable 24 and if we are unfaithful, He remains faithful 25 . Strive to bear witness all together to the power of grace, and show by deeds the generosity, even to the point of heroism, that can be born of a heart conquered by the love of Christ and that prefers nothing to this love. Keep your hearts always open to the Church and make yourselves available, as true Servants, to the action of God through your self-giving to Him. May the Mother of the Incarnate Word make you –as St. Paul said– blameless in His presence, in love 26 . We also pray with gratitude for the parents of these novices, that God may reward with abundant blessings the generous, selfless offering of their daughters that they make with great faith. St. Joseph Most Valiant

Homily preached on the occasion of the 35th anniversary of the founding of the SSVM [Exordium] We find ourselves here today, under the shelter of the Immaculate Heart of Mary, to celebrate the beautiful feast of St. Joseph, her most chaste Spouse; an occasion that becomes even more festive as we also celebrate the 35th anniversary of the founding of our sisters, the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará. Among the many titles with which we invoke St. Joseph, adoptive father of the Incarnate Word, are the titles of Guardian of the Redeemer, Servant of Christ, Minister of salvation, Support in difficulties, Patron of exiles, Patron of the afflicted, Patron of the poor (which are the litany titles added by Pope Francis in May 2021). Each of them reveals in some way a ‘mission’ of this great Saint. However, there are other titles that reveal to us the heroism of his virtues precisely so that we may imitate him and invoke him when we ourselves are in need of practicing that virtue. Thus, then, we have the litany invocations that honor St. Joseph by calling him: Joseph, most just; Joseph, most chaste; Joseph, most prudent; Joseph, most valiant; Joseph, most faithful. In this homily −if you will allow me− I would like to invite you to reflect on the title of Joseph, most valiant. Strong men and women The Latin text of the litany of St. Joseph uses the expression Joseph fortisimo , which refers to the physical strength that the young spouse of the Virgin Mary must have had. Just imagine: he walked on foot from Israel to Egypt. But the title Joseph fortisimo does not refer only to that, but rather to the spiritual dimension that this title evokes, to the cardinal virtue of fortitude on which courage rests . The translation of this invocation as Joseph most valiant takes us to the root of the word, which is valens , meaning strong, robust, the one who has no fear. The valiant man is the one who loves the good more than he fears evil and suffering. When one thinks of a strong man, of a valiant man, perhaps someone may call to mind a soldier who defends his homeland, exposing himself to danger in the midst of a war. And, yes, that soldier is valiant. But it is also true, as the great Patriarch St. Joseph shows us, that in time of peace we also need fortitude. In fact, a great witness of fortitude or of courage is given to us by someone who risks his own life to save someone who is about to drown, for example, or by a firefighter who does not hesitate to throw himself into the flames to rescue a person, or by the men who lend their help in natural disasters, as we have seen on television during the earthquake in Syria and in Iraq. Truly, there are many examples of courage that occur even in the everyday reality of our lives. I think, for example, of a woman, mother of an already large family, whom many “advise” to eliminate the new life conceived in her womb and to undergo an “operation” to put an end to motherhood; and she answers firmly: “No!” Of course she realizes all the difficulty that this “no” means: difficulty for her, for her husband, for the whole family; and yet, she answers: “No.” For the baby she carries in her womb is something too great, too “sacred,” to give in to such pressures. Another example might be that of the man who is promised freedom and even a good career and an even better salary, on condition that he renounce his principles or approve something contrary to his honesty toward others. And he too answers “no,” even in spite of threats on the one hand and flattery on the other. That is a valiant man! According to the doctrine of St. Thomas, the cardinal virtue of fortitude is what lies at the basis of the practice of courage. And this is found in the man: – who is ready to face dangers; – who is ready to endure adversities for a just cause, for the truth, for justice, for fidelity to one’s given word, and so on. That is why courage always requires a certain overcoming of human weakness and, above all, of fear. Because we, by nature, spontaneously fear danger, unpleasantness and suffering, the unknown. To be truly valiant men and women we must “surpass” ourselves, overcome our own limitations, even running the “risk” of finding ourselves in a difficult, unknown situation; it further implies not being afraid to take the risk of being looked down upon, the risk of exposing oneself to unpleasant consequences, to insults, to demotions, to material losses, and perhaps even to the risk of going to prison or suffering merciless persecutions. To attain such fortitude, such courage, the man/the woman must be sustained by a great love for the truth and for the good to which he or she is devoted. Because, as St. John Paul II rightly said, “the virtue of fortitude walks in step with the capacity to sacrifice oneself ” 1 . And for those of us who are religious of our beloved Religious Family of the Incarnate Word this is very important and reminds us of that line of the Directory of Spirituality that says: “This is the resounding idea: to sacrifice oneself” 2 . Which is the same as saying: Be valiant! Be strong! St. Joseph’s example of courage Let us look, then, at St. Joseph’s example of courage. St. Joseph was not only strong or valiant, but he was so to a heroic and superlative degree: most strong, most valiant. Why? Because St. Joseph was not only valiant or strong on certain occasions, which we know from the passages of his life narrated in the Gospels, but also in that part of his life which we do not know he led a heroic life over many years, with determination −whatever it might cost−, with courage for the struggle, with great constancy and endurance to carry the effort through to the end without laying down his arms in the midst of combat 3 . He was the man of the duc in altum , because he was a man called “to accomplish great works, extraordinary undertakings” 4 . For example: St. Joseph always showed himself strong in self-mastery, living a life of singular chastity and showing great fidelity in fulfilling his promises. When he was young, the just Joseph asked Sts. Anne and Joachim, her parents, for the hand of the Virgin Mary in order to marry her, and this alone, nowadays, can be considered an act of courage, because his desire was to love his wife forever and he wished to do so rightly before God and before men. When she was later found to be with child, St. Joseph suffered great uncertainty, but he did not draw back and chose once again to love the Mother of Jesus, and what is more, moved by a true purity of heart, he received the Virgin Mary into his home. “He had the courage to assume the legal paternity of Jesus, to whom he gave the name revealed to him by the angel: You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins 5 ” 6 . Shortly afterward the spouses had to travel to Bethlehem, with all the insecurity of not having a place to stay in that city, and with the hour of the birth very near. Yet St. Joseph carried his worries alone ; he kept them in his heart, wishing not to trouble the Mother. But, I believe, the episode in which St. Joseph’s courage stands out most was when they had to set out for Egypt. As you know, it was in the middle of the night that Joseph received from the angel the order to leave in order to protect the Child Jesus from Herod. We can imagine Joseph waking the Virgin in the middle of the night to tell her the news… Bl. Anne Catherine Emmerich in her book relates that “then [after giving Mary the warning] Joseph went into a stall (stable) where he kept the donkey and passed into a room where there were various objects, and he arranged everything for a prompt departure. Mary, for her part, got up and dressed for the journey.” “For those holy persons the will of God came first,” St. Catherine continues in her account, and although “they were very moved and grieved, they did not let themselves be carried away by sadness and prepared what was necessary for the journey. Mary took almost nothing of what they had brought from Bethlehem.” Let us imagine how painful was the farewell between the Holy Spouses and the parents of the Virgin, with whom they were living, for they did not know whether they would see each other again. It was still night when they set off. They say that the Virgin wrapped the Child in her mantle to protect Him from the cold, and they began to walk; it was a long, uncertain road; serpents appeared to them, fierce animals, even robbers… they suffered all kinds of privations, they suffered thirst −in fact at times they had to beg for water−, they suffered great fatigue and they were sad. At times, too, they got lost, because they had to take out-of-the-way paths and avoid villages and public inns, since they were fleeing. Anne Catherine Emmerich says that “Mary was very afflicted and wept.” And yet, led by the hand of St. Joseph most valiant, they pressed on. Imagine what it was for the Holy Family to settle in a completely unknown country, deprived of all human help. They say that they went to live in the ruins of a building to which Joseph added a wooden structure. There the Virgin sewed and wove while St. Joseph, outside in the courtyard, worked the wood with the few tools he had been able to bring. They endured many humiliations and many hardships among unknown, pagan people, with a culture and traditions entirely foreign to their own. How much patience and serenity of spirit St. Joseph showed in the face of all the sorrows and adversities that besieged them, seeing himself persecuted by the powerful, unknown to all, without human resources, in a life so full of privations, and with those two beings so dear to him threatened by the bitterness of danger. How many times must St. Joseph have felt that the task was beyond him, as he tried to fulfill as best he could his role as foster father of the Son of the Heavenly Father. And then he had to return to Nazareth! And make the same journey. And once “back in his own land, he lived a hidden life in the small and unknown village of Nazareth, in Galilee −from where, it was said, no prophet arises and nothing good can come 7 −, far from Bethlehem, his city of origin, and from Jerusalem, where the temple was” 8 . Nevertheless, there, in that place insignificant in the eyes of the world, he persevered in the loving care of his most beloved Spouse and of her Son, the Incarnate Word. How many times, in the intimacy of the family, must they have spoken about the Passion, because they recognized that the birth of Emmanuel, the God-with-us prophesied by Isaiah, had been fulfilled in them, and they anticipated in faith the fulfillment of what had been announced about the Suffering Servant, the Man of Sorrows. Nevertheless, we can say that it was from St. Joseph that Jesus learned the courage to face His hour , the hour of the Passion. How many deaths the heart of Jesus’ adoptive father suffered thinking of the sufferings that awaited the Son entrusted to him. And there, in the intimate familiarity and serenity of the hidden life in Nazareth, the Guardian of the Redeemer renewed daily his yes to the Lord, living only “for Jesus and for Mary” 9 and doing everything “for Jesus and for Mary” 10 . Let us think of the affliction that must have pierced the heart of St. Joseph when the Child was lost during the pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Let us imagine the grief of this father, so protective of his family. Yet in all adverse and difficult situations, the carpenter of Nazareth knew how to turn the problem into an opportunity, always putting trust in Providence first. “Joseph was not a man who passively resigned himself. He was a courageous and strong protagonist” 11 ; he had a “creative courage,” as Pope Francis points out. “This creative courage arises especially when we encounter difficulties. In fact, when we face a problem we can stop and give up, or we can find some way around it. Sometimes difficulties are precisely what bring out resources in each of us that we did not even think we had. […] If at times it seems that God is not helping us, that does not mean He has abandoned us, but that He trusts in us, in what we can plan, invent, find” 12 . [Peroratio] From St. Joseph, then, we learn that the truly valiant man does not present himself presumptuously; he does not raise his voice or shout in order to humiliate others; he does not have a haughty look nor present himself with the arrogant attitude of a ‘winner,’ but knows how to master his temper; he does not exalt himself, but rather avoids imposing himself on others. St. John of the Cross said that “to go about losing, and to let everyone get the better of us, belongs to valiant spirits, to generous hearts” 13 . The truly valiant one, who knows how to put out into the deep , also knows how to recognize in humility that his strength comes from the grace of God and, following the example of St. Joseph, “constantly keeps his soul ready for whatever God may dispose” 14 , without reserve, without conditions, only to please Jesus and the Most Holy Virgin, even when this means a continual dying to self so that God may be loved and served. St. Joseph was prudent in making his decisions, but he never retraced his steps, because wherever he discerned the will of God, there he went without delay and with confidence, keeping everything in his most chaste heart. It was the immense love he kept there for the Incarnate Word and His Most Holy Mother that gave him the strength to bear courageously the “most difficult situations” 15 and to live in “the most adverse conditions.” In short, St. Joseph most valiant teaches us that without love one cannot be truly valiant. Let us ask today that his powerful intercession grant us a stronger love, so that we may learn to be, like him, most valiant. Being a mother is a life choice

[Exordium] Today God grants us the grace of meeting in this place to celebrate the august memorial of St. Gianna Beretta Molla. A celebration made even more beautiful and moving by the presence of her daughter Gianna Emanuela. It is not every day that one has the opportunity to celebrate Mass in the company of the saint’s immediate family; that is why this is a special grace. In a general audience a few years ago, the Holy Father said: “being a mother does not only mean bringing a child into the world, but it is also a choice of life” 1 . And “to give one’s life,” the Pope goes on to say, is “to have a spirit of martyrdom; it is to give it in duty, in silence, in prayer, in the honest fulfillment of duty; in that silence of daily life, […] it is to bear witness always, even in the worst moments, to tenderness, to self-giving, to moral strength.” If this is said of every mother, how much more can these words be applied to St. Gianna. A heroic and exemplary choice To this woman, wife and mother who made a monumental choice, a heroic and exemplary option, and who will bear witness down through the centuries –as John Paul the Great said– “that only the one who has the courage to give himself totally to God and to his brothers fulfills himself.” An option that speaks of many previous options, perhaps smaller, but definitely laden with true love and therefore sacrificial. I am pleased to quote at this point her own husband, Pietro Molla, who, speaking of the choice made by his beloved wife, said: “hers is certainly a heroic witness of maternal love. Her choice of love was extremely difficult considering that she was a mother who loved her other three children intensely and who loved life itself. Her choice cannot be properly understood and appreciated except in the light of Gianna’s firm convictions, of her conscience as a mother, of her unshakable trust in Providence. […] It was certainly a dramatic choice […] a tremendous sacrifice, and one that makes manifest her trust in Providence” 2 . Our options In the same way, each one of us here present is called to make our options daily, small and great, some more dramatic than others, but always faithful to our convictions, to the faith we profess; making of our lives “an unceasing worship of divine Providence” 3 . Certain that God, who sees in secret, will reward us 4 . For it is from these small fidelities that great holiness is born 5 , which will spur many others to follow the Incarnate Word carrying their own cross. St. Gianna said: “ The secret of happiness is to live moment by moment and to thank God for everything that he, in his goodness, sends us day after day .” That is trusting in Providence! That is why, for me, in my modest opinion, the magnificent example of St. Gianna clearly teaches us a great truth of life, namely that the option for the good –the true exercise of our freedom– so very often brings with it suffering and the cross. Suffering that must be borne with serene acceptance, with trust in the Providence that knows how to draw good out of evil. And a cross that must be carried every day, whatever our vocation or our occupation in life may be. Because, as the life of St. Gianna shows, it is in the oblation of oneself that one becomes fruitful, that one bears fruit. Hence the heroic example of love and fidelity of St. Gianna speaks eloquently to every person living in our tumultuous and confused age. As a daughter and sister in a family, she was a model of service and diligence in study. When she was young, she was kind, cheerful and sociable, but entirely devout and very active in the Catholic faith that she professed with such clarity. As a successful doctor, she showed how medical science serves the dignity of human life. As a wife and mother, she made Jesus the heart of the home, the strength of the family, the goal they were to reach. She also knew how to balance her busy schedule as a working mother while maintaining an ardent life of prayer, especially through daily Mass and Communion and the praying of her Rosary, also daily. In short, St. Gianna tells us: “When one fulfills one’s own duty, one must not worry, because God’s help will not be lacking.” The luminous example of this wife and mother reminds us that “love is a light –in the end, the only one– that constantly illuminates a darkened world and gives us the strength to live and act” 6 . Let us always keep it in mind in our choices. [Peroratio] St. Gianna was the last saint canonized by St. John Paul II. At the end of his canonization homily the Holy Father asked: “ Let not your hearts be troubled or afraid 7 . The earthly vicissitudes through which the saint passed spur us to persevere on our way, trusting in God’s help and in the maternal protection of Mary” 8 . A request that we renew today before her mortal remains. We ask her to watch over each one of us from heaven and to sustain us with her powerful intercession so that we may always and everywhere choose the good, love, the Supreme Good. A happy feast of St. Gianna Beretta Molla to all! Notes 1 Wednesday, January 7, 2015. 2 Cf. Pietro Molla & Elio Guerreiro, Saint Gianna Molla: Wife, Mother and Doctor , Part II, 5. [Translated from the English] 3 Constitutions , 63 . 4 Mt 6:6. 5 Cf. Blessed Paolo Manna, Virtudes Apostólicas , Circular Letter no. 19, Milan, December 15, 1932. 6 Deus Caritas Est , 6; 39. 7 Jn 14:28. 8 Homily of Canonization , May 16, 2004.
The religious as bride

[Exordium] In yesterday’s homily we considered and contemplated that profound and ineffable gift that Christ has given to every consecrated soul, particularly to women religious, which is that of having called them to the dignity of brides, He Himself becoming, in the fullest sense, the Divine Bridegroom of that soul. Already in this life, thus anticipating −by an ineffable choice of love− the mystical espousals of eternal heaven. Christ, bridegroom of virgins. Let us now look, in today’s homily, at this same truth but from the other angle, from the perspective of the bride. More concretely, at what this ineffable reality entails for every soul that has been chosen to travel through this life as bride of the Word, … intimately united to Him, precisely in spousal love. 1. THE RELIGIOUS AS BRIDE What we considered yesterday is certainly to be admired: what Christ does for that soul whom He chooses to become, by a special title, His divine bride. We have seen His love of election, by which He chose her among so many (this is a great truth); His love of self-giving, by which in some way He gave Himself up for her, giving Himself in a mystical surrender of love; His exclusive love, since t here is no greater love than this , spousal love. Let us pause for a moment to consider what this means for each of the religious souls whom Our Lord has wished to honor with so sublime a title. To become a bride −even on the natural level, how much more on the supernatural− requires a whole disposition of the heart. While it presupposes a choice on the part of the lover, it also implies, on the part of the beloved, a correspondence of love in self-giving. Hence the bride, so to speak, moved by the gift of love that has been shown, must dispose herself to return love for love. If God has given Himself to her and has declared Himself to her in everything, it is also necessary, for there to be an authentic espousal, that the bride too give herself totally to that love: St. John Chrysostom reminded virgins: “consider that He has given Himself to you without reserve”; do the same yourselves. In the first place, I consider that there are three characteristics with which the bride must correspond to the love of the bridegroom: A. It must be a love that is one , which implies: In the first place, to be souls of a single love. Every religious must know that, by that divine union of love, she must cancel all other loves in order to live for Him alone (as wives do). And since His love was sublime, they must dispose themselves to live with a sublime love, alone for Him. They must live as if only their Divine Bridegroom existed. She must be for Him alone, as good wives are with their husbands. There is nothing else that should matter, there is nothing else she should think about, and even less −if the love is true− is there any other love that should be put before Him. For Him alone; that is why St. John of Ávila said that it belongs to the religious, by virtue of her divine espousal, to sigh for the Bridegroom: “To be the bride of Jesus Christ she must be a dove. The bride of this Lord must also be a turtledove. Why a turtledove? Because its song is a moan. The song and laughter of the nun must be weeping for her betrothed, Christ. In the choir, in the garden, in the refectory, in the cell and everywhere, she must go about sighing for her bridegroom Jesus Christ, and this must be her office and this must be her song, and when she is singing in her choir with the sweetest melody, her heart must be sighing with an interior and very deep sigh for her most beloved Bridegroom, whose memory and desire must never depart from her heart. With this she must go to sleep, and of this she must dream while sleeping, and this must be the first thing that comes to her memory on waking; her heart always melted in His love, and her memory occupied with nothing other than her beloved Bridegroom” 1 . It is the same St. John of Ávila who says that only one thing belongs to the bride, and that is to look after the honor of the Bridegroom; he writes it in a very beautiful dialogue. “See also that you must take great care, as good brides, of the honor of your bridegroom. Do you know what is the first thing the bridegroom says to his bride, especially if he is jealous? He says to her: ‘My bride, see that my honor is in your hands, and that all my honor depends on you. For the sake of the one God, I ask you to look after me (these are words that each one of us must feel addressed to himself).’” What will the bride say to this, if she is good? “I will look after your honor; I will never do wrong to your honor.” Especially if the bridegroom were to say to her: “My bride, see that the one who is pursuing you does not do so out of love he has for you, but out of hatred he has for me, so that by dishonoring you he may dishonor me.” What will the bride answer when someone wishes to deceive her with some other love: “Away, traitor, for you are not pursuing me because you love me, but to dishonor my bridegroom … if I looked only at myself, perhaps I would consent to the temptation, but by this you want to dishonor my bridegroom, and that is why you will take nothing from here, but you will go away defeated by the favor of my bridegroom, because where you thought to dishonor him and me, you are the one left dishonored, and my bridegroom is left with the honor, for I owe it to him.” Very beautifully said: it belongs to the religious to look after the honor of her Divine Bridegroom. Her love must never be soiled by another love; it must be unique. St. Francis of Assisi said that the bride should say: “You are my honor, my fortune and my delights: You are everything to me.” St. Paul declared it: “ The virgin con s ecrated to God thinks o f nothing but God and of be ing wholly God’s” (1 Car 7:3 4 -3 5 ). In the second place, a love that is one also implies being souls who are united by love, who take on each other’s likeness through love. This too is required of every bride, and in a particular way of the bride of the Word. Spousal love necessarily demands unity, and intimate unity: they are no lo nger two but one flesh , says Genesis. Bridegroom and bride are made one in love; they are one in their love. That is why the same John of Ávila teaches that the bride and the bridegroom must be of the same condition; this is her obligation, to become like the bridegroom: “What more is there to do, ladies, brides of Jesus Christ, than that you have the qualities of your Bridegroom, so that you may be one with Him.” This is an imperative of spousal love; we see it in the world too… a marriage is stable when they are one, or, as is commonly said, when one is for the other, or when they are a match in being one. For St. John of Ávila says: “There is nothing more foolish than for two people of very different qualities to be joined into one.” So then, ladies, to be what you ought to be, since you are brides of Jesus Christ, you must imitate Him in His qualities, so that you may be conformed to Him, as it is right that the bride be to the bridegroom, and to such a bridegroom as the one you have, ladies.” That is why there is so much insistence that the life of the religious must be like that of Christ; it must be like another humanity of His, in which no division can be found. Just as one cannot conceive of a wife who does not unite herself with her husband, one cannot conceive of a bride who does not have a love affair with Jesus Christ. Why? Because the love is spousal; that is why they must be one with Him… like wives … otherwise they are not brides. B. It must b e an indissoluble love … Like that of spouses. Such must be the unity forged between the spouses that there can be nothing that wounds the love or shows any symptom of dissolubility. If there is dissolubility, it is because the love is cold, it is wounded. That is why in the spousal love of the soul with God −as Sacred Scripture recalls so many times− there must necessarily be involved a resolute hatred of sin, of disordered affections, of false loves, in a word, of everything that could threaten the dissolution of love. This is very beautiful, and it is very consoling to think about. He is the most faithful of all bridegrooms; if −God forbid− there were a dissolution, that dissolution would be because of our fidelity. If we are faithful, then it is a love that can never be broken. The Bridegroom is the most faithful of all; if the love between a bride of Christ breaks down, it will always be because of the infidelity of the bride, because in some way she is betraying that love, and worse still, she is despising that love. The dissolubility of marriage implies an infidelity to love; this occurs on the part of one of the spouses, but it can never occur on the part of Jesus Christ, since He is faithful. St. Paul emphasizes this truth forcefully when he writes: This statement is certain: if we have died with Him, we shall also live with Him; if we remain firm, we shall also reign with Him; if we deny Him, He too will deny us; if we are unfaithful, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself (2 Tim 2:11-13). The religious bride must therefore dispose herself −like every bride− to give herself in a love of fidelity, as faithful as is the love the bridegroom offers her. That is why the letter to the Hebrews rightly recommends: Of the one who is called, what is asked of him is that he be faithful. C. It must be a love for ever: God chose you for an eternal love, not only indissoluble but also irrevocable. Vocations, like the gifts of God, a re i rr evoca ble, the letter to the Hebrews also teaches. “ If He chose you, be sure that it is neither a f alse ch o ice nor a fragile choice; it is an e ternal choice .” That is why women religious are very rightly called brides of the new and eternal covenant. And this name is full of meaning, even though we cannot develop it here in its full extent. To be brides of the new covenant means to be brides forever. Your vocation is e ternal , says the prophet Hosea. Such is the religious vocation; it has, then, resonances of eternity. That is why the brides of the Word, because they are brides of the New Testament (not like those of the Old), are brides forever; this is their vocation, a vocation guaranteed by the most stable fidelity. The spousal union between God and His people in the Old Testament (in the old covenant) proved fragile; the unfaithful people destroyed it and broke the covenant, as the prophet Jeremiah declares (they destroyed my covenant). In the New Testament it is not so; the covenant between God and His people was made decisively with the precious seal of the Blood of Christ; it is solid, stable and therefore eternal. Women religious, brides of the Word, are religious of this covenant. “A covenant full of love, since it was achieved thanks to the fact that the Divine Bridegroom penetrated so deeply into the interior of the bride that He changed her heart so that she would be His forever.” To be brides of the new covenant means to be brides of the berit olam , that is, brides forever. I found the one wh om my so ul loves; mine he is and I will not let him go (Song 3:4). 2. THE PECULIARITIES O F BEING A BRIDE OF THE WORD In the second place, I also want to say that in the spousal love between each religious and the Incarnate Word there are certain sublime peculiarities that cannot be left aside. Rather, it is necessary to know them very well, to keep them very much in mind, in order to realize all the purity this love signifies, to know all that it implies, and also to come to know all the delights it holds. Of all these peculiarities I want to set forth only four, which characterize very well the greatness of the bridegroom’s love: A. The religious is a bride through faith and i n faith. The mystical espousal is made through faith and in faith in the Son of God. The Lord says it through the prophet Hosea: I will make you my bride through faith (Hos 2:10). This implies very sublime and profound considerations. The spousal knowledge between the bridegroom and the bride will be constituted by the sublime knowledge of faith, the highest of all, the most spiritual of all, the purest, the deepest and the most complete, the most solid and secure, since it rests on the very knowledge that God has of Himself. To this He calls you. In some way, by this spousal union and by this choice of love, the bride is invited to know more of the depths of God than any other soul. Her union is mystical and spiritual, not banal and carnal. The deepest of unions, the union of intentions, of soul and of heart, is the union that nothing and no one will be able to break. Such is the union, such is the love. That is why every religious, however alone she may sometimes be, however far away she may be, however afflicted or tormented she may be in martyrdom, must have an imperturbable security and peace. Why? Because her Bridegroom will always be beside her. This guarantees and seals the union in a deep, stable and lasting way. It is the purest love because it is spiritual, not conditioned by anything carnal; it is the deepest and most profound purity of the notion of love; and that is also why its joys are ineffable. For this it is enough to read the writings of any of the great women mystics when they speak of the delights of the spiritual marriage: St. Catherine of Siena, St. Teresa of Jesus or Sister Elizabeth of the Trinity. Hence the imperative requirement to grow in the life of prayer, which is precisely where the union of love in this divine marriage takes place. It is there that the delights with the Bridegroom must be found; it is there that they must experience the joys of this sublime love. Pope John Paul II said it in that well-known Wednesday audience: “Among all the values present in feminine consecrated life, first place must always be given to prayer. It is the principal form of carrying out and expressing intimacy with the Divine Bridegroom. All women religious are called to be women of prayer, women of piety, women of interior life, of ‘a life of prayer.’ B . F e cundity through the cross: The world thinks that when a virgin consecrates herself, she renounces being a mother, but it is very mistake To accept being a bride of the Incarnate Word is to dispose oneself for the very opposite; it is to dispose oneself to be the most fruitful of all mothers. Her fruitfulness will be all the greater −as with every bride− the greater the unity she keeps with her Divine Bridegroom, He who accomplished the most fruitful work the world has ever beheld, since He made the redemption of men fruitful through the tree of the cross. “Hence appears the dimension of fruitfulness proper to consecrated virginity, inasmuch as there is a deeper participation in the sacrifice of Christ for the redemption of the world.” That is why the unity of fruitfulness with the Divine Bridegroom must be realized by embracing Him on the cross. The bridegroom and the bride must be of the same condition in order to be fruitful; that is why she must love the cross as Christ loved it; on it she must meet Him and on it she must rejoice with Him. Fr. Buela rightly said in one of his homilies that women religious are brides of blood. The cross is the bed of love, for it is on the cross and in the fruitfulness of the cross that they were espoused with a passionate love of God for being a soul, a passionate love of Jesus for His virgin brides. That is why St. Alphonsus says that: “although it is true that Jesus Christ died for all, He died especially for virgins, His brides.” And that is why St. Magdalene de’ Pazzi rightly says that, the religious having been called to be the Bride of the Crucified, she must look at nothing in her whole life and in all her actions except Jesus Crucified, and must occupy herself with nothing except considering the great love that her Divine Bridegroom had for her. And St. John of Ávila: “The life of the bride must be like that of her Bridegroom. What was His life? You know it well: labors, tears, poverty, humility and, finally, so great a love for His bride that for love of her He shed His blood, to make beautiful His bride, who had been disfigured, and He died on the cross to give her life, because she was dead… Look, ladies, at who your Bridegroom is and how great is the love He has for you and with which He loves you. Has there ever been a bridegroom in the world who drew blood from his veins to make perfume for his bride? It has never been seen. Well, see it here. You have a Bridegroom, ladies, who broke open His veins, who opened His side, to make a perfume to beautify you and a medicine with which you might be healed of your illnesses and wounds. Do you see here the life of your Bridegroom and the love He has for you? Well then, your life, ladies, must be like this: tears, poverty, humility, contempt, obedience, and the more of this you have, the more like your Bridegroom you will be, and likewise the more beloved of His you will be, because you are more like Him; and you must love Him so much that you would shed your Blood for Him, if need be, and lay down your life for whatever concerns His honor”… and he continues: “blood you must shed, ladies, for love of your Bridegroom” […]. And so it is fitting that, since your Bridegroom went by this road, she would not be a good bride who did not go by it.” How well St. Alphonsus put it when he said: “The crucified bridegroom wants crucified brides.” C. Spiritual motherhood. If fruitful, then mothers. For women religious, together with the Divine Bridegroom, beget through their sorrows and their sufferings, through their intimate union with the Bridegroom by means of prayer and of the cross with Him, souls for eternal life, souls for the life of grace. As motherhood goes, there is no motherhood greater or more sublime than this: to beget for eternal life. Physical motherhood, which begets children for death, bears not even a shadow of comparison; spiritual motherhood, on the other hand, begets children for eternity. That is why women religious are made like, in a most particular way, to the Blessed Virgin, who was mother of grace, she who begot us to a life much greater and more perfect and beautiful than the one to which our natural mothers begot us. Not to realize this is not to understand the greatness of consecrated virginity, which, far from renouncing fruitfulness, entails a disposition to become mothers in a much fuller and more perfect sen se… like the Blessed Virgin Mary. The Pope said it: “Virginity entails a renunciation of physical motherhood, but in order to be translated, according to the divine plan, into a motherhood of a higher order, upon which shines the light of the motherhood of the Virgin Mary. All consecrated virginity is destined to receive from the Lord a gift that reproduces in a certain measure the characteristics of the universality and spiritual fruitfulness of Mary’s motherhood. I suppose you know this, but do you realize what it means? The world does not understand; it comes to think that it means a failure … it is not to under stand at all what it means for a soul to be a bride of the Word.” D . Finally , a peculiarity of the bride of the Word mus t be her joy. From all that has been said there follows, then, the source of joy that the mystical espousals of the cros signify. Here too there is much to think about and much to say, but we cannot say it here. How poor is the joy that a married woman in this world can attain compared with that sublime joy, of a higher and spiritual order, which belongs to the one who is called to be a bride of Jesus Christ. To the bride of the Word −says St. Alphonsus− belong the greatest delights and the greatest joys. “Oh, my ladies, brides of Jesus Christ, who could tell you of the endearments and conversations, so gentle and loving, that pass between the bride who thus leaves everything to occupy herself with her bridegroom alone! Who could tell you of the gentle music that such a bride hears from the cross of her beloved, the embraces so loving, the gifts so truly those of a bridegroom that pass between these two beloved ones! You, ladies, as people through whom this will have passed and will pass each day, could better inform those of us who do not know of this matter. Yours is this office, and to you it belongs to know this; and whoever does not know this does not yet fully know how to be a true bride …. Do you remember, ladies, what I said here on another occasion. That God did not give the sweet food of manna to the people of Israel until the flour of Egypt had run out for them? So, then, your Bridegroom will not give you the manna of His consolation and delight if first the flour of the delight that we ourselves seek does not run out for us, and if first the consolation of Egypt, the consolation we had on earth, does not run out.” Only by giving yourselves to Him “will you be good brides and appear beautiful before His eyes.” In short, there is no bridegroom who can make his bride happier, with the most sublime of his joys, than the Divine Bridegroom. [Peroratio] Finally, to conclude for today, each religious must feel in her heart the question that Christ asked Peter and the other disciples at the Last Supper after having washed their feet: ¿ Scitis quid facerim vo bi s? “Do you understand what I have done to you?” We can say the same now, and −I continue with St. John of Ávila− “your beloved bridegroom Jesus Christ can say to you: do you understand what I have done to you? Do you understand the favors the Lord has done you in setting you apart from the world and choosing you as His brides? Do you understand it, ladies? Do you comprehend what He has done with you? Then have it well understood. That before you were born, or even conceived, and long before −what am I saying, long!−, infinitely before the world was made, God already had all of you who are here inscribed in His breast to be His brides… God had chosen all of you from among so many thousands of people, not only so that you might know Him by faith, like other Christians, but precisely from among the other Christians He chose you for a vocation as sublime as that of being His brides.” Understand it well… Then have it well understood. Notes 1 St. John of Ávila, Pláticas a monjas , n. 15, pt. 7, 884.
You are my altar and you will also be my victim

Memorial of Blessed Concepción Cabrera de Armida [Exordium] Today we celebrate the memorial of a great woman, the memorial of Blessed Concepción Cabrera de Armida. She was born in San Luis Potosí, Mexico, in 1862 and died in Mexico City (DF) in 1937. She was a daughter, fiancée, wife, mother, widow, grandmother, foundress, mystic, writer, tireless apostle of Jesus Christ, and, by a special indult of St. Pius X, without ever leaving her family setting, she even died canonically a religious, in the arms of her children. She was declared Venerable by St. John Paul II on December 20, 1999, in Rome, and was beatified on May 4, 2019 (just 6 years ago) in the Basilica of Guadalupe. Wife and mother From her childhood she felt drawn to Jesus; later to Jesus Crucified , but in an original, unprecedented way: by the interior sufferings of Christ, Priest and Host , Priest and Victim in His least actions, from His “ Ecce venio” to His “ Consumatum es t” upon the Cross. And so, little by little, this woman, simple in her outward appearance, married, and the mother of nine children, became identified with Christ. All who knew her declare that she was the most normal woman in the world. One of her daughters stated: “She always seemed to me the most normal woman in the world. She had to admonish me many times. We never saw her in ecstasy.” And the youngest of her children said: “She was very affectionate, but she reprimanded firmly when one misbehaved.” Yet she lived her daily life transfigured. And although nothing in her outward appearance betrayed the wealth of her interior life, reading her diary or her writings reveals to us a mystic of the highest caliber. It is beautiful to read, for example, the resolutions she made in her spiritual exercises—very concrete, very practical. Let me read you a few: “ With my husband: I will take care not to lose his trust, but rather to win it more and more; informing myself about his business affairs, I will ask God for light to counsel him rightly. I will strive that he always find in me holy consolation, sweetness and complete self-denial.” “ With my children : I will exercise special care and vigilance. I will not weary them by loading them with prayers and making piety burdensome to them; quite the contrary, I will try to make it pleasant in their eyes, so that they seek it naturally, beginning to give wings to the soul with little ejaculatory prayers.” That is why her message, the example of her life, is for everyone: for lay people, for religious, for priests themselves. Just think: at 10 she received her First Communion; at 22 she married Pancho, as she affectionately called her husband, Mr. Francisco Armida; at 35 she already experienced spiritual marriage with Christ; at 39 she was widowed; at 44 she received the extraordinary grace of the mystical incarnation. This young married woman, overflowing with love for her husband and her children, had an irresistible desire to love Christ, Master of her heart and supreme rule of all her loves. But for Conchita her desire to imitate Christ was not a utopia, a dream up in the air, but something very concrete in her daily life: “I must reproduce Jesus in myself by means of the transforming virtues, that is, by means of the Cross, which is what most likens us to Him . What Jesus wants of me is not a Christ in the poverty of Bethlehem… Not a Christ in the hiddenness of Nazareth, not a Christ in the course of His public life, but a Christ in the ignominies, abandonments and crucifixions of Calvary and of the Eucharist. I must therefore reproduce in myself Christ Crucified” 1 . She has a phrase that our founder always liked to repeat, especially when someone was going through times of particular difficulty: “The cross makes fruitful everything it touches! ” And he would say it as a prelude of good omen, as if something good were about to happen, as if much fruit were going to be gained… The mystical incarnation Well then, one March 24, Jesus said to Conchita: “I want you to be mine…, to belong to Me entirely; I want all your affections to be for Me; I want that place of my rest to be clean of all dust: your heart,” and He granted her the extraordinary grace of the mystical incarnation. Although it is an infrequent grace, it is a grace of transformation in Christ received in seed at baptism and to which all of us are called, as St. John of the Cross, for example, repeats in his works: that God has called us to be deiform, to be “God by participation,” etc., for which it is necessary to pass through the nights, through the purifications of the cross. Her soul being now purified, our Lord said to Conchita: “The Word became incarnate, and becomes mystically incarnate in souls, only in order to be sacrificed. That is the end of all mystical incarnations… Your Word has just become mystically incarnate in your heart… in order to be sacrificed constantly on an altar, not of stone, but in a living temple of the Holy Spirit[…]. The Father wills that I, united with your victim soul, should bring you to sacrifice and immolate Me with that same love of His on behalf of a world that needs a shock and a grace of this kind in order to come to its senses, embrace the Cross and be saved ” 2 . This extraordinary grace of the mystical incarnation made her aware of her priestly character in a singular way, and Jesus Himself taught her: “You are altar and priest at the same time , for you have with you the sacrosanct Victim of Calvary and of the Eucharist, whom you can offer constantly to the Eternal Father for the salvation of the world. This is the most precious fruit of the great favor I have worked in you by becoming incarnate in your heart… You are my altar and you will also be my victim : in union with Me, offer yourself and offer Me at every moment to the Eternal Father for the most noble end of saving souls and giving Him glory . Forget everything, even yourself, and let this be your constant occupation . You have a sublime mission: the mission of the priest; look upon my goodness and be grateful for it, for without your knowing it, it has given you what you so longed for, and even more: the power to be a priest, not holding Me in your hands, but in your heart, and without ever separating Me from it. But fulfill the magnificent end of this grace, which, as you see, is not only for you but universal, obliging you to be, with all the purity that can exist, at once altar and victim, which consumes in whatever holocaust may please Him the other Victim, the Only One who can save the world” 3 . Blessed Conchita received this extraordinary grace, but all of us too—religious, lay people and priests—are called to offer on the altar of our lives, of our hearts, a sacrifice pleasing to God. In this sense the Second Vatican Council teaches: « for all their works, prayers and apostolic undertakings, their married and family life, their daily work, their rest of soul and body, if they are carried out in the Spirit, and even the hardships of life if they are patiently borne, become ‘ spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ’ (1 Pet 2:5)” 4 . Conchita, very humbly, asked Christ to teach her how to make use of that grace, to which Jesus replied: “The principal end of that grace is transformation , uniting your desires to mine, your will to mine, your immolation to mine. You must, all pure and sacrificed in your body and in your soul, offer yourself and offer Me to the heavenly Father at every moment, with every breath if possible, on behalf first of all of my priests and of my Church, …of the whole world, of the good and of the wicked. You must be transformed into charity, that is, into Me, who am all charity, putting to death the old man and having with Me a single heart and mind. […] Reproduce my life in you , but with the tint of sacrifice, being a living holocaust for my glory. Alone you are worth nothing, but in union with Me you will fulfill your mission on earth, saving souls in the secret holocaust that God alone sees” 5 . And He adds: “ I want you to be my host and to renew your intention many times, night and day, of offering yourself in union with Me on all the patens of the earth: so that, transformed into Me by suffering, by love and by the virtues, this cry of your soul may rise to heaven in union with Me: ‘ This is my Body, this is my Blood ’” 6 . [Peroratio] And that, in the end, is our program. The marvelous and most noble office to which God has called us who are religious, and those who, like Blessed Concepción Cabrera, are lay people in His Church: to make of our lives and our deaths a holocaust pleasing to God. To fuse our life into that of the Incarnate Word, or put another way, to empty ourselves completely of ourselves so that the Word Himself may pour Himself into us and transform us into Him. And that is the grace that today, in this Holy Mass, we ask of our Lord through the intercession of Blessed Concepcion Cabrera de Armida. Delicacy in observance

We find ourselves on the shores of the Sea of Galilee. Jesus has chosen the Twelve; He has spent the night in prayer; He wanted to speak to His own, but a multitude appeared, so He went up a mountain and began to proclaim the beatitudes, thus beginning the Sermon or Discourse on the Mount. The Christian spirit in the interpretation of the law Jesus Christ is about to purify the law and give the true meaning to the messianic promises. From now on He will set things forth in harmony with the beatitudes He has declared. He is going to purify the law; He is going to declare the Christian spirit in the interpretation of the law: you have heard that it was said to you … but I say to you 1 . He has not come to abolish it but to bring it to its fullness. But before this, what is it that we will hear in the Gospels of tomorrow and the day after? For the moment He pauses only to emphasize two things: – first, the validity of the law, which is not abolished but purified – and second, delicacy in fulfillment, in observance. And this second point is curious, and it is what I want to speak about, because Jesus highlights in minute detail how the observance of our duty must be. The Gospel speaks insistently of the obligation to be delicate in fulfilling the law, in such a way that not one iota nor one comma of the Law will pass away 2 , and He insists: Whoever does not keep the least of these commandments, and teaches others to do the same, will be considered the least in the Kingdom of Heaven 3 . Having emphasized this, He will begin to set out the plan of utmost demand: You have heard that it was said: “You shall love your neighbor” and hate your enemy. But I say to you: Love your enemies, pray for those who persecute you 4 ; You have heard that it was said: “You shall not commit adultery.” But I say to you: Whoever looks at a woman with desire has already committed adultery with her in his heart 5 . Our Lord is very strict in His statements. That is why it is good for us to pause today to consider this aspect of the fulfillment of our obligations, which is thoroughness: not one dot, not one iota , down to the smallest thing; what some spiritual authors call the delicacies of observance. Jesus Christ made this clear before purifying the law. There are many ways of doing what is asked of us, even while being dutiful; thus one can speak of infinite degrees and shades in observance. Alongside an ideal of punctual, meticulous, joyful and persevering observance, many middling, lax, slack observances can be mixed in, full of cracks and leaks. Every religious who tries to live the demands of the Gospel must make the unbreakable resolution to be extremely careful in keeping the schedules and obligations required of him. Characteristics of fidelity to the duty of one’s state There are three main characteristics of fidelity to the duty of one’s state, of exact fidelity to our obligations: 1. The perfect and finished manner . Generally it is not enough to do materially what is commanded; rather, everything asked of us must be carried out in a perfect and finished way. We must pay homage to the finished thing. How many religious do things haphazardly, however they turn out, however they cost the least effort! They attend prayer bodily, but with their soul absent and distracted; they rush through the breviary, half-pronouncing the words; they carry out their duties reluctantly and sluggishly. And they forget the words of the prophet Jeremiah: cursed is he who does the work of the Lord negligently 6 . Of the Curé of Ars his biographer tells us: “He said nothing and did nothing that could have been said or done better.” 2. Love of detail : “What is small is small—said St. Augustine—but to be faithful in small things is a very great thing.” In terms of fidelity, what is asked of us is to go down to the last detail. In a certain sense it is necessary to pay more attention to small things than to great ones, and this for several reasons: great things present themselves rarely, small things at every moment; great things draw everyone’s attention, small things go almost unnoticed even by ourselves; fidelity in small things is the best guarantee of fidelity in great ones (Le 16:10); he who despises small things will little by little fall in great ones (Sir 19:1). St. Thérèse of the Child Jesus, for example—the Doctor of the Church—was called by some authors the saint of detail. She did not do strange or extraordinary things, but she always had, as someone has said, “a stubborn and tremendous obstinacy in fulfilling her duty in the smallest things out of love for the Beloved.” To that exquisite fidelity! in small things it is owed that she is, in the words of St. Pius X, “the greatest saint of modern times.” 3. Exact punctuality . The third characteristic of perfect observance is exactness. Doing everything at the appointed hour, neither before nor after. Not disrupting the various occupations. Always being in the place where obedience calls us. Avoiding any voluntary delay, however small. At the sound of the bell, obeying at once. These may be trifles. But it is these trifles that distinguish the saints from those who are not. Or, as one author rightly says: “holiness does not consist in that, but it is manifested in that.” Pope John XXII used to say: “Give me a religious who has always been meticulously faithful to his obligations and I will canonize him without further examination.” Jesus Christ, before clarifying and making explicit the spiritual summit that He set forth in the beatitudes, paused to speak of fidelity down to the perfect, the finished, down to the iota, down to the dot, down to each one of these least commandments. Let us ask Him for the grace to have this spirit in fulfilling the new law, since whoever keeps them and teaches others to keep them in this way will be considered great in the kingdom of heaven 7 . Notes 1 Cf. Mt 5:21, 27, 33, 38, 43. 2 Mt 5:18. 3 Mt 5:19. 4 Mt 5:43. 5 Mt 5:27-28. 6 Jer 48:10. 7 Mt 5:19.
A single whole, a compact block

[ Exordium ] In 1982 the spiritual father of our Religious Family visited Spain, and there, before more than a thousand religious of different congregations, he said to them: “The religious is not called to work as an isolated person or on his own. Today more than ever it is necessary to live and work united , first within each religious family and then collaborating with other consecrated persons and members of the Church” 1 . Since today I have the joy of celebrating this Mass together with all the members of the Religious Family in this beloved country, it seems important to me –above all because of the special circumstances we are going through– that those words of St. John Paul II find an echo in the depths of our souls: Today more than ever it is necessary to live and work united , first –says the Holy Father– within each Religious Family . Working united This, although it is a watchword common to all religious, is something fundamental for us. Because we have been conceived in the Church and for the Church as a Religious Family. And how is it manifested that we form a Religious Family? The Constitutions say it very clearly: in that “we profess public vows and live fraternal life in common” 2 ; that is at the level of each Institute. But in turn, both the Institute of the Servants and the Institute of the Incarnate Word form one and the same Religious Family within the Church 3 . And therefore, although our Institutes are juridically independent, they have the same spirit, the same charism, the same Constitutions, the same founder, the same mission in the Church. That is why they are “indissolubly united” 4 , as the Constitutions themselves express very well. Moreover, this includes the lay people of the Third Order who live according to the genuine spirit of our Religious Family. Hence anyone who seeks to sow division –whether from outside or from within– and in whatever way, attacks one of the fundamental marks of our Institutes and, consequently, blows up all the potential, or at least seriously hinders the whole evangelizing force that could be had by working united. Because we were conceived to function as a Family. God took us out of our families, but He planted us in another Family, and that Family is made up of the priests of the Incarnate Word and the Servant Sisters. It is what the Pope said: no one has been called to work as an isolated person or on his own. And what is said of a religious, individually speaking, applies analogously to our Institutes. That is why, if division is a great obstacle to evangelization, working in unity gives our mission a strength, a vitality, an effectiveness it would not otherwise have. In my visits to the various missions I have verified that, even though adequate means may be lacking, even though progress may come in very small steps, even though all the work may be very sacrificial, even though the place where one is assigned to do missionary work may be very adverse… if one works in unity, according to the spirit of the Institute, that already bears incalculable fruit, and one can say with complete certainty that a great work of evangelization is being done, even if perhaps the fruits are not as palpably noticeable as we would like. But certainly the Gospel of Christ is being preached to others –and with great eloquence– even without preaching. And that is what I have been able to see here. When we accepted our Lord’s call and decided to consecrate ourselves in our Institutes, we not only took the charism and the spirituality as our own, but we accepted our Religious Family as the framework in which our life offered to God and our mission would unfold. It is part of the deal we made when we took our vows, so to speak. We are children of this beloved Religious Family of the Incarnate Word, and founded on Him we form “ a single whole, a compact bloc ” 5 , as our proper law expresses very well. And it is necessary to maintain that unity, to foster it, to defend it and to know how to make the most of it. We will fulfill our mission much better if we are imbued with this filial spirit toward the Institute and this fraternal spirit among ourselves. Fraternal charity, the distinctive mark of our identity In the world in which we live, afflicted by indifference, by divisions, by conflicts in families, unity among brothers, rooted and founded in charity, is an eloquent example for all, which silently preaches the charity of Christ. What attracts many people to our Religious Family is precisely that: the family spirit. “To live fraternal charity is an imperative of the Incarnate Word; He it was who raised fraternal love to a sublime degree when He left us the commandment of love as His testament: I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you 6 ; this is my precept, that you love one another as I have loved you 7 ” 8 . If one makes the effort to accept one another and strives to overcome the typical difficulties of heterogeneous communities, by that very fact one is showing the transcendence of the motive that has brought us together, that is, God. “In the community –in the mission– we are together not because we have chosen one another, but because we have been chosen by Christ” 9 . This commandment of charity that Christ left us, although it is common to all Christians, is very important for us as religious of the Incarnate Word, and even for the laity: “it is on this point that one’s identity as a member of the Religious Family of the Incarnate Word is at stake in a most particular way, because only through the effective practice of charity can they be called disciples of Him who said: by this they will know that you are my disciples: if you have love for one another 10 ” 11 . “Without charity we are nothing; we may build buildings, schools, colleges, orphanages, we may even form great groups and movements, but if the genuine spirit of Christian charity is lacking in these works, all of them would be in vain, and in time they would end up collapsing like a house of cards, and they would be worth nothing” 12 , because charity is the life of the soul, and therefore we are dead if we are not led by the love of God, which is identified with love for our brothers . And that is why, where there is charity, even if one is lost in an insignificant little town, even if apparently no one notices our good works, even if one barely manages to get support, even if everything is rowing against the current and in time weariness begins to make itself felt, everything bears much fruit, very much fruit. “For there is no better witness than that of Christian charity. In fact, a fraternal life lived as it should be necessarily attracts well-disposed people, and it is very likely that God will bless that witness with even unexpected fruits” 13 . And that shows. It shows in the kind way people treat you; it shows in the fact that people support the initiatives of the Institute as far as they are able; it shows in that they turn to the religious to tell them their hardships; it shows also in that the apostolate keeps growing, and there is more joy in the religious and more fervor in everyone… and there is a longing to do more and better. And all of this is very good, and I congratulate you. Perhaps here you do not realize it, you take it for granted, but this does not happen everywhere, and it is beautiful to see how over these years the mission of the Religious Family has been growing more solid here in Chile, because there is growth in charity, in fidelity to the charism of the Institute, and so vocations are arising, and families and young people are drawing near… truly a grace of God. Notice that the Constitutions and the Directory of Spirituality name some 5 things that are indispensable for us: the help of Our Lady for evangelization; to unite oneself to the adorable Person of Christ; that for persecution to be blessed it has to be for Christ’s sake, and what is said about us must be false; but also two of those 5 things refer to charity: thus, when speaking of joy, one reads in the Constitutions : “it is absolutely indispensable to live fraternal charity” 14 , and when speaking of the apostolate it says: “charity is indispensable to evangelize the culture” 15 . This charity, it is understood, is not only that which is practiced by the fathers who work in the home, nor is it limited only to when food is distributed, but, as our proper law says in one of its documents: “True charity [is that] which seeks the good of the other even at the cost of one’s own harm, which sees to it that others are well before one’s own good, which tries to make others happy more than oneself, which has its eyes set more on one’s neighbor, in whom it contemplates the presence of God, than on personal comforts” 16 . And that is something we can all practice, every day. [ Peroration ] That is why I encourage you to continue always working united, taking special care of charity among yourselves, which is a treasure. May your communities always be an oasis of peace and welcome, without anyone being marginalized, generously accepting the daily renunciations, helping one another to carry your burdens. Which means, as St. John Paul II said, “to accept with benevolence the real or apparent defects of others, even when they are annoying, and to accept gladly all the sacrifices imposed by living with those whose mentality and temperament do not fully agree with our own way of seeing or judging” 17 . All that charity, practiced in silence, firmly founded on charity toward Christ, before which nothing is to be preferred, is then translated into great strength for the apostolate, into a defense for the very vocation of each one of you, and into a great consolation for the Heart of Christ. Let us ask the Incarnate Word in this Holy Mass to grant these three graces to the Religious Family: That of always living and working united; That of conducting ourselves with esprit de corps, that is, as “a single whole, a compact bloc”; The increase in us of the charity that makes us give ourselves more each day in the apostolate. We ask this through the intercession of the Most Blessed Virgin of Mount Carmel, patroness of the Chilean people.
