Homily at the pilgrimage of the Homes of Mercy to Valle Grande

Homily preached on the occasion of the pilgrimage of the Religious Family to the Virgin of Valle Grande – Argentina [Exordium] My dear all, what joy and what consolation it is to be able to celebrate this Holy Mass here with you at the feet of our Most Holy Mother. I know that it has been no small sacrifice to get here, and I am sure that our Mother in Heaven looks with pleasure upon all the efforts you have made to come and honor her today, on the day when the Church commemorates our Mother under the title of Our Lady of the Rosary. “To go on pilgrimage is to project oneself, or to set out on the way to Heaven, through self-denial” 1 . That is why this pilgrimage, although it has its penitential character, also speaks to us of the immeasurable consolation the soul will experience upon reaching Heaven and meeting, as today, our Most Holy Mother with her arms outstretched and her infinitely tender heart. But even more: the Virgin Mary not only awaits us at the end of the road, but she herself guides us and accompanies us all along the pilgrimage. She is always a cause of consolation and hope, because “she shines forth before her pilgrim children on this earth as a sign of sure hope and consolation until the day of the Lord comes” 2 . That is to say, the most pure Virgin also makes the pilgrimage with us. Her pilgrimage began at the Annunciation, because that was the starting point of her journey toward God 3 . And on that journey toward God she met with many sorrows: such as the foretelling of the sword that would pierce her soul 4 , the tortuous paths of the exile in Egypt and of interior darkness, when she ‘did not understand’ Jesus’ attitude at the age of twelve in the temple, arriving later at the summit of her pilgrimage on Golgotha, when she sees her Son die 5 . That is to say, our beloved Mother is a mother who knows the sorrows of this life, and although she already enjoys the eternal reward, she does not forget her children who are still on pilgrimage, weighed down by this world. That is why ‘this valley of tears’ –as we say in that most beautiful prayer, the Salve Regina– is transformed into a valley of hope, of sweetness, of joy through her consoling presence. This merciful Mother walks with us, because it is proper to mothers to suffer with their children and to want to share their trials, their sadness and their sufferings. And it is well known that our most tender Mother has never failed to come to the aid of any child who has invoked her help. But we too must walk with Mary, as we committed ourselves to do when we made the fourth vow of Marian consecration. That is, to accept ‘the companionship (of Mary) and (to act according to) the model that must guide “all our intentions, actions and operations”’ 6 , as our Constitutions say. 1. Accepting her companionship Accepting her companionship means being constantly at home with our Mother. I mean that this walking with Mary implies having a serious spiritual life, not a sentimental one; applying oneself to prayer; being ready to pass through “the purifications of the senses and of the spirit, active and passive” 7 . For an “intense spiritual life” is the duty of every Christian, but it is “the first and principal duty of all religious” 8 . But not only of them. In fact, St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort wrote: “I personally believe that no one can attain intimate union with Our Lord and perfect fidelity to the Holy Spirit without a very close union with the Most Blessed Virgin and a true dependence on her help” 9 . A filial and tender relationship with the Mother of God is, for every Christian, the privileged path to fidelity to the vocation received –whatever it may be– and a most effective help to advance in it and live it to the full, that is, to attain holiness 10 . “There is, then, no interior life or spiritual action possible that does not depend on her” 11 . To the dear religious men and women who work in our houses of mercy, striving to show the fatherly face of God and the motherly face of the Church 12 : it is by being grounded in an intense spiritual life, one that sinks its roots into the mystery of the Incarnate Word and has as its fundamental pillar a filial and tender relationship with the Mother of God, that we will be able to carry out an authentic Catholic pastoral work 13 . It is with Mary that one learns to found all apostolic enthusiasm 14 solely on the Rock which is Christ 15 . Not on our poor physical strength, not on our organizational ability, not on the little or much money we may have at our disposal. For that would be to shut ourselves up within human horizons. From our Most Holy Mother, who praised the Lord for knowing herself ‘looked upon’ by Him, despite her ‘lowliness’, her littleness 16 , we learn that for the works of God the most important thing is to abandon oneself with full confidence to His Providence. And the fathers and sisters who work in our homes know this very well… It is with Mary that one learns “to do the things of God promptly 17 . To serve one’s neighbor even in the simplest tasks” 18 . Everything –whatever the task may be– has a higher sanctifying efficacy if one always acts with Mary. Always keep this in mind. 2. Acting according to the Model: Mary Now, this walking with Mary on the pilgrimage of this life also implies acting with her. Not only sometimes, not intermittently, but always. In fact, our proper law explicitly points us to “doing everything with Mary” 19 . And this acting with Mary in everything “is to take the Most Blessed Virgin as the perfect Model of Christian conduct” 20 . Therefore, the Virgin Mary, besides being our Mother, who delights in our company, is also our Model. The Virgin Mary is above all the Model of those theological virtues that are characteristic of the Christian: faith, hope and love 21 . Model of that faithful perseverance in the Gospel that allows us to travel with her “the pilgrimage of faith”. Model of an apostolic self-giving that allows us to cooperate in the spreading of the Gospel and in the growth of the Church 22 . Model of a life committed to God and to men, to the designs of salvation and to fidelity to her children. Mary is also the Model of “fortitude in exile 23 and in sorrow 24 . Sublime Model of poverty borne with dignity and trust in the Lord 25 . Exemplary Model of watchful care for her Son, from the humility of the crib to the ignominy of the Cross 26 . Model at once of virginal purity 27 and of strong and chaste spousal love” 28 . That is why there is no Christian who cannot have this beloved Mother as Model. Moreover, St. Paul VI affirmed that “with these virtues the children will be adorned who, with steadfast purpose, contemplate the example of their Mother in order to reproduce them in their own lives” 29 . By invoking her with the words of the angel and by going over her Gospel life in the praying of the Holy Rosary, all will always have before their eyes the perfect model of the Christian 30 , which is Most Holy Mary. *** [Peroration] My dear all: Behold your Mother, Christ told us before dying. I too repeat it today to all of you who have come here to venerate our most beloved Mother, the Virgin of Valle Grande. Open the doors of your souls and of your lives to the Mother of God. Accept her companionship and follow her as Model. She will teach you the paths of the Gospel. She will make you know Christ and love the Church. She will show you the way of life and encourage you in difficulties. To all the sick and to the young people and children who are with us today: know that you are the favorites of Our Lady. Love her with tender and simple devotion and make others, too, love our Mother dearly. On this day when the whole Church venerates the Virgin Mary under the title of Our Lady of the Rosary, I invite you, at the end of this Holy Mass, to pray the Holy Rosary as a family and for the family , here at the feet of the Mother of the Incarnate Word, who is also our Mother. Of her we must ask, for all the members of our Religious Family, the grace of an ever greater and more convinced fidelity to our charism. Together with the grace –like her– “to strive with all our strength always to advance in virtue” 31 and “to preserve and cultivate spiritual fervor and the joy of evangelizing, even when we must sow in tears” 32 . My dear all: may we live today and always “through Jesus and through Mary, with Jesus and with Mary, in Jesus and in Mary, for Jesus and for Mary” 33 . May Our Lady bless you. Homily in a contemplative Monastery of the Servants, June 2019

Homily in a Contemplative Monastery of the Servants [Exordium] Dear Sisters: First of all, I would like to thank you very much for the invitation to celebrate Holy Mass. It truly gives me great pleasure to be able to do so. On this occasion I would simply like to reflect with you on one line of our Directory of Spirituality , in number 52. There, speaking of women religious as spouses of Christ, it says that: all her wealth –that of the religious sister– consists in giving herself to the Word. And I would like to place the emphasis on that giving herself in the sentence. Notice that it is a reflexive verb, that is, it applies to oneself. Therefore, it is not only a matter of giving something exterior or accessory, such as handing over goods or academic degrees, leaving one’s own country, or doing some exterior work without greater commitment, etc. It is rather a matter of giving yourselves . And this giving yourselves is a giving with all the powers of body and soul, with all the finitude of one’s own being, with all the affections that lie in the folds of the heart, with all one’s past, present and future, with all one’s talents, and with all one’s miseries too. And to do this with all one’s strength, with all one’s mind, with all one’s heart, with all enthusiasm, with all trust, with all generosity and promptness, and with a great joy founded on the faith that does not disappoint. And to do this once and for all, without seeking to recover what has been given by looking for compensations or settling down and making a “nest” in things that are not God 1 . Even more, one must want to “live permanently” in this attitude, “without diminutions or retractions, without reservations or conditions , without subterfuges or delays, without withdrawals or sluggishness,” as the same Directory says in number 73. That is, this giving of oneself is emptying oneself into the hands of Christ. Let Him dispose, let Him decide, let Him protect, let Him mold the soul as He pleases, let Him use us as He wishes, because it will always be –beyond all doubt– for the good of our soul. Put in other words, that giving oneself to the Word is to empty oneself of self in order to be filled with Him. It is to have nothing in order to have everything in Him (as St. John of the Cross teaches). That is, the religious empties herself of her frailty to find in Him all her strength; she empties herself of her weakness to be filled with his omnipotence; she empties herself of her ignorance to be filled with his immeasurable wisdom; she empties herself of her disorders to be filled with his peace; she empties herself of her misery to be filled with his infinite riches; she empties herself of human horizons to be filled with supernatural life; she empties herself of attachments of the heart in order to run without obstacles to the divine union. And to do it only out of love for Him. Because the religious gives herself in spousal love to the Incarnate Word, to no one else. And without that love , which is the theological virtue of charity and which must permeate all her acts, they are –as St. Paul says– like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal 2 . That giving oneself to the Word is to live in the attitude that the great doctor of the Church, St. Teresa of Jesus, declares in her poem, saying: Behold here my heart, I place it in your palm; my body, my life and soul, my inmost being and my love. Sweet spouse and redemption, since I offered myself as yours, what do you bid be done with me? Notice that the Saint says what do you bid be done with me? Because, since love must be placed more in deeds than in words 3 , as we meditate each year in our Spiritual Exercises, one must give oneself to the Word by giving oneself to others . That is, in the concrete practice of charity, living in permanent availability for whatever God asks. Because love of God and love of neighbor cannot be separated! The two “merge into each other” 4 ; they are inseparable 5 . Our Directory of Works of Mercy has a magnificent paragraph, taken from the “ Encyclical Deus Caritas Est” , which reads: “If in life attention to the other is omitted altogether, wishing only to be “pious” and to fulfill one’s “religious duties,” then the relationship with God also withers. It will be merely a “correct” relationship, but without love. Only readiness to help one’s neighbor, to show him love , makes us sensitive to God as well. Only service of neighbor opens our eyes to what God does for us and to how much he loves us” 6 . And then further on it goes on to say: “Love grows through love.” Therefore, my dear sisters, to serve one’s brothers and sisters –all of humanity from the cloister, as well as the sister who lives with me or the people who come to the parlor– is to serve Christ himself. And it is by giving yourselves to your brothers and sisters that you give yourselves to Christ himself. One cannot say “I give myself entirely to the Incarnate Word” without giving oneself to others. Rather, out of love for God one must give oneself to one’s brothers and sisters. Which is nothing other than imitating Christ, who came into the world for all men 7 . Our Proper Law explicitly commands us “to love in deed and in truth the concrete man who is in need” 8 . Understand here not only the poor man who comes to the monastery door looking for food, but also those whom we always have with us… look at one another, at those of your own family, at the priests, the seminarians… How can our “existence be a concrete trace that the Trinity leaves in history” 9 without loving and serving those who share history with us? How could we “be like another incarnation of the Word” 10 if we do not cherish in our heart his same sentiments of compassion toward our brothers and sisters? How could a Servant say that she loves the Incarnate Word and not be available for generous and disinterested service? We must love as Christ loved us: that is, to the end 11 , to the point of giving his life for us 12 , making himself a servant 13 ; submitting even to death, and death on a cross 14 ; being light 15 among men (not sowing darkness); praying to the Father for us 16 ; walking the extra mile 17 and giving us even what we do not know how to ask for . 18 You, who are women –and contemplatives!– make use of the fine sensitivity God has given you to lavish that charity in a thousand delicate gestures and details. Look, I have always liked very much the example of St. Catherine Labouré. She entered the convent and as a novice –nine days after entering the novitiate– the Blessed Virgin appeared to her, and she spoke with her for two hours kneeling at her feet, resting her hands on the lap of Our Lady, who was seated in the chapel. Then, in another apparition, Our Lady asked her to have made what we know today as the Miraculous Medal. That happened when she was 24 years old. St. Catherine died at 70. During 46 years of religious life no one (except her spiritual director) knew that she had seen Our Lady and that she had been entrusted with having the miraculous medal made, which worked so many wonders. What did she do her whole life? Take care of old people!, mend their clothes, wash them, feed them, supervise their recreation, scold them when they misbehaved, deal with the kitchen… She rose at dawn and was the last to go to bed, only to give herself to the Word , concretely, by giving herself to others without restrictions, without conditions… It is not your lot to take care of old people, but it is your lot to pray and immolate yourselves silently for fallen humanity, and to do so hiddenly and in the face of the incomprehension of so many, only to give yourselves to the Word. Do you want an even more sublime example? Look at the most beautiful example of the True Servant of the Lord who was our Most Holy Mother. With her heart and soul wholly set on God, she sensed within herself the needs of others and sought with maternal wisdom to attend to them promptly, generously, without trying to be noticed, without seeking herself. She did not limit herself to words of understanding, but committed herself personally to authentic assistance. “Our Lady’s service is marked principally by her humility” 19 . So too must be the service of every Servant. The Virgin Mary rendered her service without becoming irritated by fatigue. In fact, on arriving at the house of her cousin Elizabeth after a long journey on foot, the Blessed Virgin intoned the Magnificat! Our Lady rejoices in the service she can render. Therefore, from our Mother, the Model of every Servant, you too must learn to serve with joy, with deep serenity –because in the end the work is God’s–, seeking always to be instruments of peace, of concord, each from the post God has assigned her. Without fear of sacrifice, with total availability, with all “spiritual fervor and joy, even if it falls to you to sow in tears” 20 , as our Proper Law says. Because the sacrifice of the spouse of a Crucified Christ must be a sacrifice of love without restrictions, without withdrawals, but rather a holocaust. You who have the immense grace of living in the cloister have concrete, very concrete opportunities to distinguish yourselves by service to others, especially to the Religious Family. St. Peter Julian Eymard told his religious: “love your brothers above all. But you must love them out of pure love of God, and love them in God, and not for the gratitude and response you expect from them. Render them all the services you can within due order. And whenever you render them, do it for that motive alone. Then you will not complain that they do not respond; since you did not act for men but for God, you have no need of human gratitude. To try to draw personal profit from what was done out of duty is to destroy charity and deprive God of his glory. I am inclined to say -says the saint- that you should take excessive displays of gratitude as an insult. To render a service is to fulfill a duty ” 21 . And if the Saint says this to his religious, who were adorers of the Blessed Sacrament, how much more must it be said of those who bear the name Servants . Only by giving yourselves to others out of love for Christ will you find all wealth . That is, only thus will you come to be those “chalices full of Christ that pour out their superabundance upon others” 22 of which our Constitutions speak. Only thus will you be able to show with your lives that Christ lives 23 . [Peroratio] My dear Sisters, I know that you already do so, but I want to entrust to you very especially the task of praying for our beloved Religious Family, for its protection, for its unity, for its fidelity to the very rich patrimony it has received. Pray also that we may be ever more faithful to the vows we have pronounced. That is, that “we may carry out with greater perfection the service of God and of men,” that is, “with an ever more sincere and intense love,” and so “prolong the Incarnation of the Word ‘in every man, in the whole man and in all the manifestations of man’” 24 , for to all this we committed ourselves when we recited our formula of profession before God. May our Heavenly Mother, the Servant of the Lord par excellence, to whom I entrust you with all my heart, obtain this grace for us. In the Name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Homily for the monks on Christmas Eve 2018

Christmas Eve Mass, December 24, 2018 Lk 2:1-14 – Preface of Christmas In the first reading we have just heard, the Prophet Isaiah speaks to us of a people that walked in darkness … [that bore a] heavy yoke, and whose shoulders were wounded by a rod 1 . And that people, with all its darkness and its pain, on a night like this one, saw a great light and its joy was made great 2 . So it is: to a depressed, despairing and distrustful world God came 3 . And he came to order men and the world according to God, to order not only their hearts and their souls but also their business dealings, their family life, their governments and everything. How did he do it? God solved the social, political, family and economic problems of the world not by promulgating a new economic system; not by showing us a mountain of papers with the results of his research revealing new aspects of the problem; he did not do it with wars. He saved the world from its evils by being born as a Child in the insignificant village of Bethlehem. That apparently trivial incident, so common and so ordinary, in which –as we heard in the Gospel– the owners of the inn turned the Holy Family away, simply telling them that there was no room for them in the inn , is the event that turned the order of the world upside down and the solution that gave it its peace. The Evangelist tells us that his Mother sought refuge in a manger and laid the newborn Child on the ground of this world. And this Child –whose birth we celebrate today– like another Samson shook the pillars of the world from its very roots, pulled down the edifice that was already collapsing and built the Temple of the living God, where men will once again be able to sing because they have found their God. But someone may ask: what does the birth of God as a Child have to do with the social, political and economic conditions of his time and of our time? What relationship can there be between the Child lying on the straw of a manger and Caesar on his golden throne? The answer is this: the birth of the Son of God in the flesh was the introduction into the historical world order of a new life; it was the proclamation to the world that the rebuilding of society has to do with its spiritual regeneration; that nations can be saved only when men are reborn to God as God is born tonight to men. By becoming man, God enters the created order, becomes part of its history, draws close to us and gives us a strength that comes from on high. Our Proper Law cites in this regard a phrase of St. John Paul II that says: “God was never so close to man -and man was never so close to God- as precisely at that moment” 4 . Put in other words, “The Savior… willed to become Son of Man so that we might become children of God” 5 . That is why Christ is born as a Child: to teach us that liberation from all the economic, social and political chaos can be achieved only by a birth. Humanity was mentally weary and spiritually exhausted; for four thousand years it had been conducting the experiment of humanism, and it found itself like a sick man who cannot cure himself. It was in a state like that of our world, which since the days of the Renaissance has tried to build a civilization on the self-sufficiency of man without God. Let us realize that humanity, left thus to itself, sinks and becomes little more than a beast. We have sufficient proof that people of an advanced culture can end up as a savage culture… (if not, watch the news every night). Without supernatural help, society goes from bad to worse until its deterioration becomes universal. Not evolution, but regression is the law of man without God, just as it is the law of the sunflower without the sun. Humanity left to itself cannot even tie its own shoelaces. With all the knowledge man has today about chemistry, about genetics… we cannot make a human life in a laboratory, because we lack the life-giving principle that is the soul, which comes only from God. Life is not a push from below, but a gift from above. It is not the result of man’s necessary ascent, but of God’s descent. It is not ‘progress”; it is the fruit of the Incarnation. Therefore, like that world into which Christ was born, the world of today also needs not a mixture of old ideas touched up, not a new economic system, not a new monetary system –it needs a New Birth. It needs the entry into its order of a new life and a new spirit, which only God can give. We cannot give ourselves that New Birth, just as none of us can be born again naturally. If we are to be reborn to this new life, the principle of regeneration must come from heaven, and that is precisely the meaning of the Incarnation: the introduction into the world, at the level of human life, of the Life of God, who came not to judge the world but to save it. And that is why I say that the Incarnate Word solved our problems by being born as a Child, because the regeneration of society has to do with being born, being born to the life of grace and growing according to it. What God did to his individual human nature –which he took from the Blessed Virgin Mary– is what he wishes to do, in no lesser degree, to every human nature in the world; that is, to make us partakers of the divine life. The Incarnate Word, who is from all eternity, willed to be born in Bethlehem on a night like tonight; he wants us, and all the men and women out there, who were born of our earthly parents, to be born to the eternity of our Heavenly Father, made new creatures, possessed by the new life of his grace and members of his Kingdom. The same divine life that came into the world two thousand eighteen years ago must return once again into the course of the world. And unless the world is reborn to the new life, it will perish. And hence the most important and leading role of our monastic branch, of the monks of the Institute of the Incarnate Word: to implore heaven that there may descend upon souls –as the dew descends every morning upon the field– that divine life which makes souls fruitful. That is why the monastic rule says that our contemplatives: “Will pray and offer penances for the souls in Purgatory, for ecumenism, for the life of the Church, for human promotion, and for other problems that pertain to the realization of the temporal order according to God and to the establishment of the Kingdom of God in souls ” 6 . This is the great need. “At present there is a great famine in the land, a famine not of bread, because we have already had too much of that and our luxury has made us forget God; a famine not of gold, because the glitter of so much of it has blinded us to the meaning of the twinkling of the stars; but a much more serious famine, and one that threatens almost every country in the world: the famine of truly great men. In other words, the world of today is suffering the terrible nemesis of mediocrity. We are dying of commonness; we are perishing through our pettiness. The greatest need of the world is for great men, someone who understands that there is no greater conquest than victory over oneself; someone who realizes that real worth is attained not so much through activity as through silence; someone who seeks the Kingdom of God and his justice, and puts into practice the law that only by dying to the life of the body do we live for the life of the spirit; someone who will defy the mockery of Good Friday in order to win the joy of Easter Sunday; who, like a flash of lightning, will burn through the bonds of those feeble interests that tie up the energies of the world; who, with a fearless voice, like another John the Baptist, will rouse our weakened nature from that elegant sleep of cowardly repose; the need of someone who will win victories not by coming down from the Cross and compromising with the world, but who will suffer in order to conquer the world” 7 . This Christmas, in a word, what we need are holy (monks), because saints are the truly great men the world needs to obtain for us the precious divine gift of his grace and mercy. Monks who are –as today’s second reading says– fervently devoted to doing good 8 . Monks who show us that grace which has been manifested to the world and which is Jesus himself, born of the Virgin Mary, true God and true man; who has come into our history to free us from darkness and give us light 9 . Monks who, in short, make us experience that great joy which the shepherds experienced on having found Jesus, who is Love made flesh. We ask this grace of the Mother of the Incarnate Word, who contemplated the Messiah in her Son wrapped in swaddling clothes . Notes 1 Cf. Is 9:2; 4. 2 Cf. Is 9:3. 3 From here on I quote freely Ven. Homily in St. Peter’s Basilica

Homily during the Mass at the altar of the Chair in St. Peter’s Basilica, with the participants of the International Meeting of the IVE in Rome Vatican, Today we are gathered here around the altar raised over the very place that treasures the remains of the Prince of the Apostles, as members of one single Religious Family united in one same love for God and for his Church. A love in which we always want to stand out, clearly showing by the witness of our life that for us love for the Incarnate Word and love for his Church are one and the same. Because we firmly believe and are convinced that the Mystical Body of Christ is Jesus Christ himself “continued, spread and communicated” 1 . Therefore, we are not speaking of two distinct loves or services; rather, our love and service of Jesus Christ are one with our love and service of the Church. And just as Christ loved the Church and gave himself up for her 2 , so we too “want to love and serve, and to make Jesus Christ loved and served… both the physical Body of Christ in the Eucharist and the Mystical Body of Christ, which is the Church” 3 . Now, “Jesus is loved and served on the Cross and crucified with Him, and in no other way” 4 . And we can say the same with regard to the Church as the Mystical Body of Christ: the Church is loved and served on the Cross and crucified with her, and in no other way. This has practical consequences in our life, as we see in the life and in the teachings of the Apostle St. Peter himself in his letters. Simon, son of Jonah, after his confession of Christ as the Son of the living God , was scandalized by the cross that following Christ implied, and as soon as our Lord tells him that he will have to suffer much and be condemned to death, Peter tries to prevent it, to keep Him away from the cross, saying: Far be it from you, Lord! This shall not happen to you 5 . To which the Incarnate Word responds by calling him Satan 6 . Because keeping us away from the cross will always be the devil’s business. Peter was scandalized by the cross. Like so many Christians today who abandon the church with the excuse that “they will never be able to become anything with a cross on their backs.” And like so many others who keep their faith behind closed doors because of the commitment that friendship with Christ demands. However, Peter learned the lesson, and we too must learn it today. That is why in one of his letters he beautifully warns us: Resist, firm in the faith 7 ; arm yourselves also with the same disposition as Christ to suffer 8 . Serve one another, each with the gift you have received, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God 9 . And he clearly counsels us not to be ashamed of being Christians and of suffering something for Christ 10 ; that is, not to be ashamed of carrying our cross held high. For this reason, the mission of the laity of the Incarnate Word cannot be reduced to the pure and simple example of honesty, competence and faithfulness to duty. All of that is presupposed. Rather, there must also shine forth in you “an authentic witness of Christian life” 11 , a bold and firm witness to Christ, primarily through the radiance of faith, hope and charity 12 . From you, the Church and the Institute itself expect “a living and burning witness of Christ alive in his Church; they expect you to speak and act by example , to stand out before others by the effective practice of the Christian virtues, as men and women who carry Jesus and Mary in their blood; they expect you to strive to fill your domestic, social and professional activity with Christian magnanimity ” 13 . That is, to be a lay member of the IVE is to be someone who truly loves and serves the Church, working hard for his personal sanctification, striving to be ‘another Christ’ 14 . This translates into following the poor Jesus, without being dejected by scarcity or puffed up by wealth; imitating the humble Christ without craving vain glories, but in everything seeking to please God rather than men, always ready to leave everything for Christ; and even to suffer persecution for justice’s sake, always remembering the words of the Lord: if anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross and follow me 15 . That will always be the best service you can offer the Church. Because –my dear brothers and sisters– words move, but examples draw others along 16 ; as St. Peter himself experienced, who died crucified head downward in this very place. It is true that these are not easy times in which to live and practice our faith. It is not easy for parents to raise their children in a Christian way in a world that seeks to eradicate God. It is not easy for young people to live chastely in a world that preaches a sexual life without responsibility. It is not easy for professionals who strive for the primacy of Christ in society when their colleagues think that fraud is part of business, and greed the engine of society. Nevertheless, what is proper to our laity is to bear witness to Christ in all circumstances and situations. A witness that must be free of all fear. We must not be surprised at the violence that has been unleashed against you to put you to the test, as if something extraordinary were happening to you 17 , the Apostle Peter warns us in his first letter. For note that “one of the most interesting observations made by our Lord concerning His Mystical Body was that it would be hated by the world, as He Himself was. The world loves the things of the world, but hates what is divine …but because you are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you 18 ” 19 . But in that very thing, says the Prince of the Apostles, we must rejoice: Rejoice insofar as you are able to share in the sufferings of Christ. Thus, when his glory is revealed, you too will overflow with gladness and joy. Blessed are you if you are insulted for the name of Christ, because the Spirit of glory, the Spirit of God, rests upon you 20 . Notice that the apostle mentions sufferings, insults… all of that is part of the program. That is why today St. Peter tells us again, with all the power of the divine truth that abides in his word: Who can harm you if you devote yourselves to doing good? Blessed are you if you have to suffer for justice’s sake. Do not fear and do not be troubled; on the contrary, glorify Christ the Lord in your hearts. Always be ready to give a defense before anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that you have. But do it with gentleness and respect, and with a clear conscience. Thus all those who defame you will be put to shame for their slanders, because you conduct yourselves as servants of Christ . It is better to suffer for doing good, if that is the will of God, than for doing evil 21 . We have been begotten for an inheritance that cannot perish, nor be defiled, nor fade away, and that is reserved in heaven for us 22 . That is why, with our gaze fixed on Christ, we must launch ourselves into the epic mission of transforming the world for Christ. * * * * * My dear all: “The law of the Body is the law of the Head: Crucifixion and Empty Tomb. […] Now Christianity is under attack. But that means that these are wonderful days to be alive . It is easy to drift with the current. Corpses drift downriver. But it takes living bodies to resist the current. […] True Catholic life is not made up of routine acts of piety, but of a crisis that sets a great choice before us […] That is why these are splendid days in which to live . We can make decisions that will echo in eternity” 23 . We entrust ourselves to Mary, Mother of the Church, and to the prayers of the Apostle St. Peter, over whose tomb we celebrate this Holy Mass. Inauguration of the 2017-2018 Academic Year at Fossanova

Votive Mass of St. Thomas Aquinas [Exordium] Dear all: today we have the immense grace –which brings with it so much happiness!– of celebrating Holy Mass in this place, in the Abbey of Fossanova, thus marking the beginning of the academic year of our houses of formation in Italy. Fossanova is a historic place, a sacred place and, we must also admit, a very significant place for all of us. – It is a sacred place! Through this place passed the direct disciples of St. Benedict, who in the year 529 (let us remember that St. Benedict died on March 21 of the year 547) founded the first monastery here upon the remains of an ancient Roman villa (some of whose ruins can still be seen in the square, as one leaves the Church). – St. Bernard also passed through here, and left a group of monks to found in this place the first convent of the Cistercian order in Italy; they were French Cistercians who came from the abbey of Hautecombe in France. It was Pope Innocent II who in the year 1135 granted them this place, strategically located on the road that led from Rome to Naples, from where countless monks would set out to ‘colonize’ –we might say– all of central Italy 1 (let us remember that St. Bernard died in the year 1153). It was these same monks who 28 years later began the construction of this most beautiful Church, which was consecrated after 55 years of work, in the year 1208. – That is why this church, where the Incarnate Word has gathered us today, has a very rich history, in which it is also worth mentioning that it has been distinguished by the presence of –at least– two successors of Peter: once, by Pope Innocent III (Lotario dei Conti di Segni, born in Gavignano, in the territory of our dear Segni… the pope of the Fourth Crusade and of the Crusade against the Albigensian heretics), who came to this place to consecrate this temple… the temple where we are today! The other presence was that of Pope Gregory IV 2 , for he was a monk here in the 9th century, before being Pope. – And to add even more to the great significance this place has for us, we must say that these walls, magnificent in their architecture, one day sheltered St. Thomas Aquinas, who, feeling ill when he had already set out to attend the Council of Lyon, stayed in the guesthouse of the Abbey, where on March 7, 1274, he was called by our Lord to enjoy definitive union with him as a reward for all his labors. – It was here, in this very abbey, that with heartfelt emotion the Holy Doctor wished to make his profession, on his knees before the Eucharist that would be his Viaticum to eternal life, saying: “Now I receive You, my Jesus, who paid with your blood the price of the redemption of my soul. All the teachings I have written manifest my faith in Jesus Christ and my love for the Holy Catholic Church, of whom I profess myself an obedient son.” It was here, on his deathbed, that he produced his posthumous work, commenting on the Song of Songs for the monks 3 . – And it was also here that Divine Providence determined that his remains should rest at the foot of this high altar, and that there should be carried out in 1321 what was called the Second Process of canonization of St. Thomas, devoted exclusively to the miracles worked by him after his death 4 . Today, 743 years after the death of him who was “the Prince and Master of all the scholastic doctors” 5 , by divine grace and providence, our Institute comes to this place… we have come here! On a day that from now on will also be historic for our religious family, on this occasion, to begin a new academic year. 1. The importance of good formation It is always worthwhile at the beginning of the year to reflect on the importance of our formation; for it is a reality… a fact… that many aspects of what our students in formation will do in the future, as religious and missionaries, in the various posts where God calls them to serve him –whether in the cloister or in mission lands–, will be marked in some way by the seriousness, the integrity, the solidity and the depth of the formation that today, with the celebration of this Holy Mass, begins again. That is why I would like briefly on this occasion to highlight the great importance for our times, because of the heavenly fruits it produces, of the study of the doctrine of St. Thomas, which in the words of Pope Urban V is “truthful and Catholic” 6 and which “has above the others –Innocent VI added– propriety of words, order in its matters, truth in its judgments, in such a way that those who follow it will never be seen to stray from the path of truth, and whoever attacks it will always be suspect of error” 7 . A doctrine that becomes key when it comes to evangelizing the modern world, and which –as we have just said in the lectio brevis – shows itself more necessary and timely than ever for the times in which we have to live. 2. The world we are called to evangelize The world in which we live… The Venerable Servant of God, Archbishop Fulton Sheen, in the prologue of his book “ Religión sin Dios ,” describes with clairvoyance the religious panorama we face today… the religious panorama of the contemporary world. He says there, for example, that in today's world “the word ‘God’ is still used by certain thinkers, but it is emptied of all its content and left watered-down and diffuse, so that it can be made to signify any idea, however volatile, or any kind of insubstantial fantasy.” He characterizes modern thought as a thought in which “God has been dethroned, the heavens have been abandoned, and man has been put in the place of God[…].” Thus the Venerable Archbishop formulated the same thing that our Cornelio Fabro would later denounce systematically and brilliantly in his studies, in his courses and in his books: namely, the primacy of immanence and its fatal consequence, atheism, a world without God. Bishop Fulton Sheen continues his “description” of our world, saying that: “The problems that formerly centered on God are now solved with reference to man, and those that formerly referred to man are now merged with the whole universe. […] God is humanized, and man naturalized. Physical science […] comes to tell us what God is and what man is.” And he goes on to say: “Man now not only imagines himself to be God, but actually believes he is beginning to be so. And thus man, raised to this state which they call ‘supernatural,’ needs no redeemer; just as in the natural state he does not need God. As a result of this philosophy of self-sufficiency there arises the bizarre phenomenon proper to our times, of a religion without God and a Christianity without Jesus Christ.” The general principle implicit in all this is, in the end, the denial of the transcendent and the affirmation of the immanent 8 . From this follow the nefarious errors with which we have to live. And so –I continue quoting the venerable Archbishop– preeminence is given “to man instead of God… to love of neighbor instead of love of God… [one speaks of] a social message instead of a message of salvation… of openness to the world instead of the Cross… of the truth of the times instead of absolute truth” 9 ; “faith is diluted into the rational, the sacred becomes profane” 10 , and so there is an attempt to accommodate the Church to the modern world, to group Catholicism with Protestantism; theology and philosophy are finally confused with sociology and psychology 11 , and there is no longer any talk of the slavery of sin, of the reality of hell, etc., all of which is consistent with immanence , since thus, under these presuppositions, as Fr. Cornelio Fabro said, “without hell, existence becomes a country outing” 12 . 3. Our preparation to evangelize the world in which we live Our Proper Law says that it is to this world that God sends us as lambs among wolves in order to transform – “the wolves themselves into lambs” 13 ; to seek and know how to identify the “seeds of the Word” through which the Holy Spirit continues to act in the heart of man 14 . To be the salt and light of the world 15 . This magnificent undertaking requires of us –who are essentially missionaries– a competent philosophical preparation, which above all gives us “a solid and coherent knowledge of man, of the world and of God” 16 , for it represents “an indispensable help for deepening the understanding of the faith and communicating the truth of the Gospel to those who do not yet know it” 17 . It is in this sense that our Constitutions highlight the urgency of its study 18 , since it is sound philosophy, the metaphysics of being, that gives us a “certainty of the truth,” and “without it there is no basis for a total personal self-giving to Jesus and to the Church, since ‘if one is not sure of the truth, how can we stake our own life and have the strength to seriously challenge the lives of others?’” 19 Let us strive, then, to acquire what our Proper Law –making use of an expression of Fr. Cornelio Fabro– calls “essential Thomism.” In such a way that, well imbued with the doctrine of the Angelic Doctor, we may be capable of thinking from him; and, “from him, enter into dialogue and debate with contemporary problems and thinkers” –as our specific end asks of us and our Proper Law commands us–. Only thus will we be able to discern what corresponds to the Gospel, in order to accept it, and what does not, in order to reject it. This obviously entails an active judgment on human thought and on Thomism itself in relation to modern thought 20 . That is why today we are asked that, taking into account the philosophical research of modern times, especially that which most influences the life of nations and the progress of the sciences, we come to know well the character of the age in which we have to live, so as to be prepared for dialogue with our contemporaries 21 . And in this way to seek the solution of human problems in the light of Revelation; and to know how to apply the eternal truths to the changing condition of human affairs, and of course, to communicate them in an appropriate manner to the souls entrusted to us 22 . That is why today, as we begin this new academic year, in this place that witnessed the passing to eternal life of him who made “a full submission of mind and heart to divine revelation” 23 (as our St. John Paul II says), I would like to quote here, by way of conclusion, the wise counsel set out in our Directory of Intellectual Formation : “Without the discipline and habit of study, the future priest will not be able to be the wise man according to the Gospel who, in season and out of season, exhorts with the word of God, convinces with the truth and frees from error. The priest is called to be a teacher of the Christian faith and must therefore be capable of giving a reason for the faith he preaches and teaches. Dedication to study must be undertaken with this pastoral perspective ” 24 , and the same can be applied to women religious. That is why I told you at the beginning that many aspects of all that we do in the future depend –with the help of God's grace– on the seriousness, solidity and depth of our formation. The philosophy of St. Thomas is the philosophy of being, that is, of the ‘ actus essendi’ , whose transcendental value is the most direct path for rising to the knowledge of subsistent Being and pure Act, which is God. And only by rediscovering in its fullness being and the first principles of being and of thought can man validly ascend to Subsistent Being itself, his beginning and end, and the supreme guarantor of his inalienable freedom. 25 Let us remember that each one of us is a disciple of Him who one day presented himself to the disciples saying I am 26 . So we too must be priests, religious and missionaries of ‘being.’ This implies: “being pioneers, ready to take the first steps for Christ, to commit oneself totally to God, trusting in his Word, in his power and in his mercy. It also implies being men of transcendence, not confined or trapped in the temporal sphere of the principle of immanence, but rather knowing how to rise up through created things so as to reach also beyond the limited horizons of this world” 27 . It implies launching out – with a genuinely catholic spirit – to help with the needs of the whole Church, with a spirit ready to kindle the light of the Gospel everywhere. 28 [Peroration] We can, then, on this day, implore of the Mother of the Incarnate Word, through the intercession of that giant who was St. Thomas Aquinas, the same graces that Archbishop Fulton Sheen asked for on the eve of his priestly ordination, and which were two: “I begged that these two graces be granted me –he writes in his autobiography–: the first, to know very well what the thinking of the modern world is; and the second, to know how to refute the errors of modern thought in the light of the philosophy of St. Thomas Aquinas” 29 May the Mother of God, who is Teacher by the holiness of her example, educate us with maternal wisdom to conform our lives to that of the Incarnate Word. On the Cross in the thought of Padre Pio

On the Cross in the thought of Padre Pio Sermon delivered by Rev. Fr. Carlos Miguel Buela in the Parish of “Our Lady of Sorrows,” on September 14, 2001, on the occasion of the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross Today we celebrate the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, and on this day several of the Servants of the Lord and the Virgin of Matará are making their perpetual vows. The great St. Thomas Aquinas compares the consecration proper to religious life to nothing less than the greatest sacrifice there is, which is the holocaust, that is, the total offering of oneself as a victim to God 1 . It seemed to me that for this occasion it might be profitable to put together what we may call a sort of florilegium of the Cross, following the thought of that great crucified man of the last century, Padre Pio, who, as some of you well know, has sublime thoughts on the Cross. Pleasing God The Cross is a pleasing of God: «To love God is to please Him, and it is not worth worrying about the rest, knowing that God will take care of us more than can be said or imagined». Chosen He treats each one of us, and in a special way consecrated souls, as chosen ones: «Open your heart to the heavenly physician of souls and abandon yourself with confidence into His arms. He treats you as one of His chosen and invites you to follow Him closely up the slope of Calvary». Climbing Calvary This is what consecrated life is about: climbing Calvary, and it is a climbing of Calvary every day, as is the life of the priest who, in going up to the altar each day, climbs a little further up Calvary. Padre Pio says: «Yes, let us take comfort when we see ourselves more and more oppressed by afflictions; let us give thanks to the divine mercy that makes us sharers in the Passion and death of our divine Master, and until it can be said of us “this Christian is another Christ,” let us not stop until we have climbed Calvary». His love This is the fruit of His love: «If God subjects us to a very heavy Cross, and gives us the strength needed to bear it with merit, these are unmistakable and unique signs of His love for us». That very heavy Cross may at times be health problems, family problems; it may also be misunderstandings, temptations, or tribulations of various kinds… We must ask for those crosses. Let us think about this: «they are unmistakable and unique signs of His love for us». Being crucified The fact is that we must be crucified, as our divine Head is. «Let us follow the divine Master along the slope of Calvary carrying our Cross, and when He sees fit to nail us to the Cross, let us thank Him and consider ourselves fortunate for so great an honor granted to us, knowing that to be crucified with Jesus is a far more perfect act than simply contemplating Jesus on the Cross». Not being frightened by the Cross That is why we must not be frightened by the Cross. There are souls that do not advance in the spiritual life out of fear of the Cross. What is more, there are souls that go backward; there are even souls that abandon Christ because they are afraid of the Cross. «Do not let the Cross frighten you. The greatest proof of love consists in suffering for the beloved; and if God, out of so much love, suffered so much pain, the pain suffered for Him becomes lovable by reason of love» Jesus and the Cross: bridegroom and bride indissolubly united And things are so arranged that there is no Jesus without the Cross, nor the Cross without Jesus. Jesus the bridegroom, the Cross the bride, indissolubly united. «Jesus is never without the Cross, but the Cross is never without Jesus». The Cross does not crush And because Jesus and the Cross, the Cross and Jesus, are thus united, the Cross never crushes, even though that is the impression it sometimes gives us when we have to suffer great difficulties; but the Cross does not crush. «Do not let the Cross crush you. If its weight makes you stagger, its power sustains you». It seems that the weight makes us succumb, but at the same time it is this very weight that makes us stand firm in the combat, in the spiritual struggle that lies before us. With the Cross on our shoulders That is why we must climb Calvary with the Cross on our shoulders: «Let us climb Calvary with the Cross on our shoulders. Let us not hesitate. Our ascent will end with the heavenly vision of the most sweet Savior». Life is Calvary For life is Calvary: «Life is a calvary. It is fitting to climb it joyfully». The Cross is a banner And the Cross is a banner: «The Cross is the banner of the chosen. Let us not separate ourselves from it, and we shall sing victory in every battle». The harder, the more merit And the harder, the heavier the Cross, the more merit we will have: «The harder the trial God sends His chosen ones, the more abundantly He comforts them during the oppression and exalts them after the struggle», Love and suffering It is the mystery that always goes together: love and suffering, suffering and love. The more suffering, the more love. The more love, the more suffering: «Whoever begins to love must be prepared to suffer». Suffering and happiness «The life of the Christian is nothing but a continual struggle against oneself. Happiness is not attained except by means of suffering». That is why on this day, dear brothers and sisters, let us ask the Lord, through His Mother, the Blessed Virgin Mary, that we may come to have within us the science of the Cross; for it is a grace of God to have the wisdom of the Cross. And when we have the wisdom of the Cross we will have that other great thing which only the Cross gives: the joy of the Cross. We ask this of Our Lord, who was the first to suffer it for our sake, and of His Mother, who was the second, suffering spiritually all the sorrows that her Son suffered out of love for us. May we always be friends of the Cross, may we never flee from it, because whoever flees from the Cross flees from Jesus, and whoever flees from Jesus will never find happiness. __________________________________ Words before the blessing What a contrast between the terrifying images of the catastrophe of the Twin Towers, which we have seen in these last days and which has shaken every man and woman of good will in every part of the world, and a beautiful ceremony like this one, where, in peace and with great joy, young women fully aware of what they are doing consecrate themselves for their whole life to the Lord of all creation. I congratulate these sisters, and I congratulate in a special way all their relatives, friends and acquaintances, and also all those who have prayed to make it possible for these young women to consecrate themselves totally to God. I also congratulate their superiors, and the fathers and priests who have accompanied them spiritually. I hope that this may truly be a sign of a better world for all, a more human world, a less cruel world, a world where the love of God truly shines for all men. Notes 1 Cf. ST. THOMAS AQUINAS, S. Th . II-II, 186, 1.
Review of the Roman Missal

Roman Missal Spanish Episcopal Conference, Madrid (Spain), 2016, pp. 1382. In my more than 45 years of Masses celebrated in Spanish, for the first time!, I come across a Missal in Spanish of great quality, of such editorial excellence that it adds glory to the heritage of Spain and of its Episcopate. I will make use of the sheet of recommendations that comes with the text and the indications given on the envelope containing the three CDs (Compact Disks) on music and singing in the Eucharistic liturgy 1 , which accompany the Missal. «Recommendations for the care and preservation of this liturgical book» 2 Its qualities The Roman Missal you hold in your hands has been manufactured in keeping with the dignity proper to a liturgical book; from the choice of paper and of the various materials, which are acid- and chlorine-free, to the various production processes: a) Printing: with environmentally friendly ink. b)Binding: each process has been carefully chosen to provide maximum durability together with good opening: – sewn with vegetable thread; – the spine of the blocks lined with a special reinforcing paper to give the book greater firmness; – endpapers of ecological card stock to improve the joining of the pages to the cover of the book; – the ribbon markers are cut with a heat technique to prevent fraying, and are made from two different ribbons, which allows a better grip. c) Manufacture of the cover: using an ecological material for the cover that imitates leather, made of polyurethane 3 and thermo-turning 4 . The stamping has been pressed deeply into the material, which makes it less subject to wear from handling and friction. All the materials used in this book hold the certificates of quality and environmental respect, for the sustainable management of forests, required by the current laws of the European Union, as do the printing and binding processes. Its use The following practices for the care of the book are recommended so that it may remain in optimal condition for as long as possible: a) In the way of picking up the book: always try to do so with the book closed, never by a single cover or by a group of pages; hold it with both hands or rest it on a lectern. b)In the way of opening the book: open it as you normally would and use the tabs (thumb indexes) to turn the pages one by one; do not try to open the book by using the tabs. c) In the way of storing it: after using it, close the book; when the celebration is over, do not leave it on the lectern or on the altar, but put it in its box. To store it, it is preferable to do so horizontally (not vertically, as is customary) so as not to put too much strain on the binding of the book. It is also important, whenever possible, to keep it in a dark room or in a cupboard. d)In the way of cleaning it: normally do so with a soft, dry cloth, although, if necessary, dampen the cloth a little and pass it gently over the surface of the cover. Tests have been carried out by putting the cover material in contact with different substances used in liturgical celebrations, such as wine, water, lemon juice and olive oil, and it has been verified that the material is highly resistant to this kind of liquid and to stains in general. «Sound illustration of the texts set to music in the Roman Missal» Special mention is due to the place given in the Missal to Sacred Music, reminding us: «The Apostle exhorts the faithful who gather together awaiting the coming of their Lord to sing together psalms, hymns and inspired songs (cf. Col3:16). Singing is a sign of the heart’s exultation (cf. Acts2:46). Hence St. Augustine rightly says: «Singing belongs to one who loves»; and from very ancient times comes the famous proverb: «He who sings well prays twice» 5 . Music in the new edition of the Roman Missal In this new edition of the Roman Missal in Spanish a real effort has been made to include an abundant musical appendix, not only the Ordinary, but also other texts, as well as one hundred and three prefaces; all of this to facilitate and encourage the primacy of the solemn liturgy: «Liturgical action takes on a nobler form when the divine offices are celebrated solemnly with song» 6 . The musical differences in comparison with other earlier editions of the Missal are not very numerous, but they are significant, above all because of the changes in some texts, which have meant slight alterations to the existing melodies or even the need to create some new ones. This novelty will undoubtedly require an effort to learn it correctly, as well as an important pastoral work to help the faithful become acquainted with the music of the Missal and thus to foster their participation in liturgical actions. For this reason the material we present in triple-CD format has been prepared. On the musical content l. The «Amen» of the greeting, of the prayers, of the doxology, etc., which has become popular in our communities is no longer the Gregorian one (sol-sol-la). For this reason it has been proposed that the «Amens» incorporated into the Ordinary be those the people already sing with only two notes: sol-la. Moreover, it is a way of making the criterion uniform, since some current liturgical books include the Gregorian model, others the popular model, and in one and the same liturgical book we may even find both. 2. The musical setting of the three formulas of the Penitential Act has been included. 3. In the Liturgy of the Word three simple melodic models have been included for singing the readings (first, second and Gospel). These models are not intended to replace the traditional «Gregorian tones for the singing of the readings», but to serve as a help for communities that are not proficient in Gregorian chant, so that they may, in a simple way, sing the Liturgy of the Word for greater solemnity. The criterion has been to use melodic elements in a graduated way through the «mediant cadence» in the first and second readings, and to incorporate in the Gospel the melodic formula for the «highlighted words» of Christ (la-do-ti-sol-ti-la), creating an ornamental progression whose melody evokes the account of the institution of the Eucharist, thus establishing a musical parallel between the summit of the Liturgy of the Word (Gospel) and that of the Eucharistic liturgy (consecration). The same has been done with the acclamation to the Gospel (The Word of the Lord) and its response (Glory to You, Lord Jesus). A new acclamation «in imitation» is proposed, in such a way that the faithful will be able to answer the deacon or priest who sings the Gospel with ease. For this new acclamation the final formula of the response to the acclamation «This is the Mystery of faith» (do-ti-sol-la) has been taken. Thus the assembly responds by singing with the same melodic formula to the Gospel as to the Mysterium fidei. 4. Eight models have been included for the sung response of the prayer of the faithful . 5. This new edition of the Missal includes the melody for singing Eucharistic Prayers I, II, III and IV from the epiclesis onward. 6. At the consecration the appropriate musical adaptation has been made in view of the change in the following text: «which will be poured out for you and for many». 7. The acclamations and responses of the consecration , which have changed in accordance with the new translation criteria, have been adapted musically. Three formulas remain: a. In the first there are no changes in the acclamation or in the response; only the order of the first and second option varies: «This is the Mystery of faith», or else: «This is the Sacrament of our faith». b. The second, which is new, is: «Let us acclaim the Mystery of faith», instead of «Acclaim the Mystery of redemption». The response remains the same as in earlier editions. c. The third, also new, changes in its acclamation and in its response: «Let us proclaim the Mystery of faith». «Save us, Savior of the world, who have set us free by your cross and resurrection». 8. Two models are offered for singing the Our Father : the one that has already become popular (A) and another adapted from the Gregorian Pater noster (B). 9. In the concluding rite the musical setting of the simple blessing, the episcopal blessing and two melodic models for the solemn blessings (A and B) have been added. One more popular (A) and another adapted from the Gregorian (B). 10. Finally, the 103 prefaces found in the Missal are included, each individually set to music. With the publication of this new edition of the Roman Missal, LIBROS LITÚRGICOS, the publishing imprint of the Spanish Episcopal Conference, maintains its commitment to editorial excellence, and to the dignity and veneration deserved by the books used to proclaim the liturgical texts, in order to move pastors and faithful to greater reverence for the Word of God and for sacred things. Its price: € 84.- We said years ago that the Roman Missal: «Is truly a veritable monument of Castilian, Spanish and Spanish-American literature, which perhaps the Royal Spanish Academy of the Language and its counterparts in the Spanish-speaking countries ought to take more into account» 7 , and in this most painstaking edition it reaches its summit. With the appropriate care and correct handling that liturgical books require, as we have indicated here, you will be able to use this volume for many years. The materials hold all the certificates of quality and environmental respect, as do the printing and binding processes. Its texts have also been studied by a member of the prestigious Royal Academy of the Spanish Language. For all these reasons we foresee a qualitative leap in the ars celebrandi and in the ars participandi of the Holy Sacrifice . We are before a liturgical jewel, after many years of liturgical vulgarities, frivolities and pettiness. Let us hope that this example of liturgical dignity may be imitated by many in Spanish America and wherever Mass is celebrated in the «language of the angels», as Don Marcelino Menéndez y Pelayo put it! Notes 1 This recording was made between June and August 2016 at the Major Seminary of Santiago de Compostela. 2 Ed. Libros Litúrgicos, Spanish Episcopal Conference. 3 The term polyurethane (PU) designates a vast family of polymers in which the polymer chain is made up of urethane bonds -NH-(CO)-O-. 4 Thermo-turning polyurethane is particularly versatile, perfectly suited to the hot printing process. 5 General Instruction of the Roman Missal, n. 39. 6 Second Vatican Council, Dogmatic Constitution Sacrosanctum Concilium on the Sacred Liturgy, 113. 7 Series of Spiritual Exercises over the Internet, Series 3, Redemption in the Roman Missal.
Prologue to the book “El Progresismo Cristiano”

Reading the table of contents of this somewhat uneven and disorderly collection of lectures, articles and sermons from very different periods of Fr. Julio Meinvielle, what Gilbert Keith Chesterton said about St. Thomas Aquinas comes to mind: “he thought pugnaciously… (which) does not mean bitterly or contemptuously, without charity, but combatively.” Like St. Thomas, to whom he knew himself indebted, Fr. Julio thought pugnaciously, as is plainly evident. (The talented Cornelio Fabro admired his polemical “vis.”) Ramiro de Maeztu maintains that: “Culture is polemical. I know of no work and no life that has left a mark on the history of culture that has not been a work and a life of polemics.” Fr. Julio used to say: “To fight is a grace.” And if, undaunted, for almost fifty years, he stood firm in the breach 1 , that is, always prepared and ready to fight the battles of God, it is because his soul was nourished assiduously in the contemplation of Jesus Christ, the Logos made flesh: in Himself, in His Church, in the Eucharist, in every man. If someone, in order to restrain his unbending fortitude, had advised him to content himself with saying Mass, he would have answered as Fray Francisco de Paula Castañeda did: “it is precisely the Mass that sets me on fire, and drives me on, and compels me to unceasing struggle.” Hence he was able to detect and denounce from the housetops 2 the progressive avalanche of the 1960s, a task that reaches its fullness, in my view, in his masterwork “ De la Cábala al progresismo ” (Ed. Calchaquí, Salta, 1.970, 470 pp.). It was impossible for him not to notice and warn us about the deviations of neo-modernism, because its principal end, like that of all the errors concerning the truths the Church professes, is “to diminish Christ in His dignity” 3 . The liberal progressives diminish the dignity of Christ, since they do not want the reign of Christ the King over society, over politics, economics, culture, nations and states. All the progressives diminish the dignity of Christ, since they do not affirm the absolute necessity of grace for the solution of man’s problems -even temporal problems- Unless God guards the city, in vain do the watchmen keep vigil 4 ; thus frustrating the coming of the Son of God in the flesh: Grace and truth come through Jesus Christ 5 . The Marxist progressives diminish the dignity of Christ, since they seek to put Christ and His Church at the service of the revolution, emptying them of their supernatural content. They attack the dignity of Christ by attacking the faith and morals taught by Christ. Read the Declarations of the Sacred Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith: “to safeguard from some recent errors faith in the mysteries of the Incarnation and of the Most Holy Trinity” (21/2/1972), “on Catholic doctrine concerning the Church, to defend it from some present-day errors” (24/6/1973), “on certain questions concerning eschatology” (17/5/79), “on abortion” (18/11/1974), “on certain questions of sexual ethics” (premarital relations, homosexuality, masturbation, etc. 29/12/1975), “on the admission of women to the ministerial priesthood” (15/10/1976), the very recent one of 6/8/1983 “on certain questions concerning the Minister of the Eucharist”: does this not indicate that some have at times come to oppose Catholic faith and morals, even in fundamental matters? Did not the Credo of the People of God (30/6/1968) come out to confront those who were tearing down truths of Christian doctrine, like some Catholics “captive to a certain desire to change and innovate”? The doctrinal errors about the Eucharist, which merited the Encyclical Mysterium Fidei of His Holiness Paul VI, are manifestly repugnant to the dignity of Christ, just as so much vulgar, crude, kitschy and tasteless “liturgy,” which destroys the “ sacrum ” of the mystery, degrades the dignity of Christ 6 . And must we not speak here of the internationally orchestrated campaign against the celibacy of the ministers of the Eucharist, which occasioned the encyclical Sacerdotalis Caelibatus (24/6/1967)? Will it be necessary to highlight “the Christological significance of celibacy” 7 ? Everything that lowers the dignity of His Most Holy Mother, the Virgin Mary, lowers the dignity of Christ. Paul VI did not hesitate to recall the doctrine of the cult of the Blessed Virgin in texts “to which it will not be useless to return in order to dispel doubts” 8 . A pastoral expert went so far as to state publicly that it was necessary to tear down the Marian shrines “because they were hotbeds of superstition” (sic). Those who do not accept -in fact or in principle- the true and only visible head of the Church, the Pope, attempt to undo Christ, seeking to diminish Him in His dignity, because they patently dissolve the unity of the Mystical Body: it could not be one single Body if it did not have one single Head; nor one single community if it did not have one single leader, as its Founder taught: one flock and one shepherd 9 . Recall, for example, the deviations of Hans Küng and of so many others, and, following an apparently opposite path, the experience of Ecône, and, in its exacerbation, those of El Palmar de Troya, etc. See likewise, to give two very visible examples, the progressives’ lack of obedience to the only visible head of the only Church founded by Christ, in the desacralizing tampering with the liturgy and in not wearing ecclesiastical dress. The progressives seek to diminish the dignity of Christ by preventing the development of His life in new human beings, by being against the transmission of human life, hence the need for the Encyclical Humanae Vitae (27/5/1968), and against the transmission of divine life, hence the need for Evangelii Nuntiandi and for treating at the next Synod, among other things, the irreplaceable importance of the sacrament of Confession. We have also read that “the sacraments are the dead weight of the Church” (sic), when in truth they are what drive the ship of the Church forward with impetuous and unstoppable vigor, with force, strength, resolution and onrushing energy, since they are, in the words of St. Thomas, “separated instruments of the Divinity” and “like divine relics of the Incarnation.” They diminish the dignity of Christ by trying to baptize so-called modern philosophy -which connotes not a chronological reason but an ontological one-, inasmuch as it is closed to transcendence and therefore denies a priori the divinity of Our Lord Jesus Christ, “thus creating a new gnosis” 10 . The progressives lower the dignity of Christ by plunging into the temporal while forgetting the eternal; by not bringing adequate solutions to the pressing temporal problems of lack of justice, of peace, of bread and of shelter; by keeping silent and not denouncing the true enemies of the progress and development of men and of peoples; when priests dilute their sacramental charism, which identifies them with Christ the Priest, by invading fields that belong exclusively to the laity; by not having the vigor to take a clear, firm and wise position in the face of modern culture; by not teaching that everything -culture, politics, economics, work, family, etc.- must be subordinated, while respecting legitimate autonomies, to the lordship of the one King of kings and Lord of lords. John Paul II cries out: “Open, indeed, open wide the doors to Christ! Open to His saving power the doors of States, economic and political systems, the vast fields of culture, of civilization and of development.” In years now past, the cooling of missionary zeal, the emptying and liquidation of seminaries and novitiates, the abandonment of generous self-giving in so many consecrated souls, the absence of great converts, were unmistakable signs of the sterility and destruction that characterize the progressive phenomenon, as a just retribution for experimenting in an attempt to derogate from the dignity of Christ. They have sought the dissolution of Christ by spreading errors in faith and morals that caused -and cause- a great many spiritual deaths, since “The Son of God by His Incarnation has united Himself in some way with every man” 11 . In short, they diminish the dignity of Christ by hindering the true progress, material and spiritual, of man, the image of Christ. For a soul contemplative of the mystery of the Incarnate Word, as Fr. Julio was, it was absurd to excuse himself from bearing witness, behaving like a dumb dog 12 before those who lower the majesty of Jesus Christ. He had the gift of thinking pugnaciously because he defended the dignity of Jesus Christ, and this as a fruit of charity. I heard someone say with a certain sarcasm: “What must he have said if he ran into Maritain in heaven!” I immediately thought: “He must have rejoiced exceedingly!” He loved his enemies and, because he wanted the eternal salvation of all, he hated error. He taught us that “love covers a multitude of sins” 13 and that we must pray and do penance for those who are in error and for those who persecute us, forgiving them from the heart: Lord, do not hold this sin against them 14 . Finally, in fact, we owe them a great deal, since, in spite of themselves, they work for our good, if we truly love God: E v e rything works together for the good of those who love God 15 ; and we must be grateful to them, since their errors are an occasion for us to clarify and deepen our faith, and their unjust persecution makes it possible for us to live the eighth beatitude, makes us gain many merits for eternal life and obtains for us an unsuspected supernatural fruitfulness. In a similar way, those who lower the dignity of Christ will thank us for not having let them carry out, with greater freedom and to a greater extent, their work in favor of error and deceit. Therefore, as the Virgin of Fatima asked, we must always pray and do penance, especially in this time, for those who despise lordship and blaspheme the glories… feeding themselves; they are clouds without water carried along by the winds; autumn trees without fruit, twice dead, uprooted; wild waves of the sea, casting up the foam of their impurities; wandering stars for whom the gloom of darkness is reserved forever 16 . For them we say with St. Luigi Orione: “Place me, Lord, upon the mouth of hell, so that by Your mercy I may close it,” as Meinvielle lived it and as anyone who does not diminish the dignity of the love of Christ fully understands it. On his tomb was engraved: He loved the Truth 17 , because he lived it in the strictest sense of the word. He loved the truth reflected in every particle of the universe, as a spark of the infinite Truth, which is God. He loved the truth, and for that reason he studied problems, even temporal ones, in order to arrive at solutions that would lead us to a better world for our Homeland and for all of suffering and anguished humanity; he knew that “truth is the first and fundamental condition of social renewal 18 . He loved the truth taught by the Catholic Church: “ Sine illa peritur! ,” as Blessed John Paul I recalled. He loved Jesus Christ, the Truth, and out of love for the Truth he argued against the grumblers, the malcontents, who live according to their passions, whose mouths speak arrogantly, who flatter people for the sake of gain 19 , seeking their salvation, snatching them out of the fire 20 by refuting their errors, so that they might not diminish Jesus Christ, who is the Only One who has words of eternal life 21 .
