Our Lady of Guadalupe IV – The Image I

Sermon belonging to the series of sermons on Our Lady of Guadalupe preached for the first time at the priests’ gathering of the Province “Madonna di Loreto,” in Val d’Aosta, from August 20 to 30, 2006 We can now describe the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe as it is imprinted on the tilma of St. Juan Diego, highlighting only some of the most beautiful or striking aspects it contains. She is clothed with the sun, like the woman of the Apocalypse (12:1); like her, she also has the moon under her feet, and a little angel beneath her as well, who holds in his hands the tunic and the mantle of the Virgin. Let us highlight some important elements of this image, which has been studied so very much over the centuries. 1. Christ Our Lord is indicated in the image of the Guadalupana. On the womb of Most Holy Mary there is a four-petaled jasmine ( Philadelphus mexicanus ), a stylization of the center of the sun stone, which in the Nahuatl culture symbolizes fullness (the nahui ollin ). The Virgin is with child, and holds the Son of God in her womb. We do not grasp it because we are not indigenous, but for them the message was very clear. That is also why the area of Mary’s Womb is the most illuminated of the whole image, more so than Mary’s face itself. 2. The Virgin From the first moment the face reflects the attitude of the Virgin, which is one of deep prayer: the lowered gaze, the seriousness, and the drooping of the eyelids, the very sweetness and peace she radiates. The shape of the face is oval, and the complexion dark. It is a mestizo face. The Virgin, who is an evangelizer, wants to win over the indigenous people, who were extremely harsh. They were terribly bloodthirsty. If at sunset they saw that the sky was red, they understood that they had to offer blood to the sun god, and they carried out veritable hecatombs of children from the subjugated tribes. More or less as is done today with abortion, with the difference that now they are offered to the god of sex. There was very great corruption: homosexuality, incest, cannibalism, all mixed with great cruelty. That is why evangelization was not advancing. The Franciscans themselves could not find the vein, a vein that opened only with the apparition of the Virgin. And she even made up for the great poverty of means the missionaries suffered. They did not even have oils for the chrismations (later the pettifoggers of the day came along and said that all the baptisms they had performed had been invalid; thank goodness the Holy See sided with the Franciscans). They were so poor that later the rumor spread that they had changed the color of their habit and made it blue, whereas in reality it was because they had no other habit nor brown dye, and with successive washings it kept fading and degenerating into an old bluish color. Returning to the face of the image. As we have also pointed out, the skin tone varies in each photograph. In the description of the Nican Mopohua it is said to be “tobacco-colored, or of dark corn.” Others have described it as “just slightly darker than pearl” (Miguel Cabrera, 18th c.) and, in our day, as “olive.” Her eyebrows are very fine and well defined, more similar to European features; her eyelids are full and the eyes almond-shaped. The nose is fine and straight in form, not of indigenous characteristics. Her mouth is located right over a defect (a tear) in the tilma, and yet it looks delicate and anatomically perfect, sketching moreover a sweet smile. Beneath the graceful chin a long, strong neck can be glimpsed. Her hair, parted down the middle, is dark mahogany in color. The face of the Virgin is fresh, young, tender, clean and with well-defined features. Feminine qualities of gentleness and firmness can be observed. Not for nothing did they describe her in Nahuatl as “she who is perfectly looking in every direction.” The hands joined in prayer have a beautiful particularity that the Virgin willed: the left hand is an indigenous hand, dark, plump; while the right is Spanish, slender and white. The scholars we have already cited (Callahan and Smith) say that the pigments with which the hands are colored, like those of the face, are unknown and inexplicable. Her garments are full of details charged with symbolism, of clear meaning for the indigenous people. The color of the tunic is an indefinite ochre, ranging from pale pink, almost white, to dark shades of the same color. The golden stars of the mantle (46 in all) represent the constellations visible in Mexico in December, the month of the apparitions. The flowers that appear on the dress and on the mantle, and which, in the manner of indigenous painting, do not follow the folds of the garment (as if they were on a flat surface), are all from the area of the apparition. The belt is in a high position, indicating that she is awaiting the birth of the Savior. In addition, there are some details that enhance the delicacy of the Image represented and the rank of “Lady” of the Virgin, such as the golden brooch at her neck (with a black cross inside it), what appear to be two golden bracelets, and in her hair, what could be a comb or an accessory to hold the mantle. 3. The angel Besides the moon, the Virgin has an angel as the throne of her sacred feet. Just as Jesus Christ, Son of God, and the most perfect creature, who is Mary, are present, so the angelic order is represented in the image. At first sight the colorful wings catch the eye; they follow the anatomical shape of the wings of the eagle, but their colors follow those of another bird of Mexico, called the tzindzcan . The angel has a reddish tunic similar to the shirt the Indians used in the early days of evangelization, which replaced the loincloth. He has a brooch on which, according to experts, some letters can be made out: JU, at that time the abbreviation of “Juan”; and a D with a drawing that looks like a little pot, which according to studies could well be the abbreviation of Diego, “Do.” The angel, moreover, has his hair cut in the style of the “macehuales,” or common men among the indigenous people, the class to which Juan Diego belonged. 4. The Indians, her children The image is full of references to the culture and customs of the Indians, healed and elevated by the Gospel. This can be seen in the very presence of the angel with its probable reference to Juan Diego (or with the angel almost identifying himself with him), and also in the fact that he is grasping and, as it were, covering himself with the mantle of the Virgin. The image is an icon of great transparency and of unsurpassable catechetical value for the evangelization of the indigenous Mexicans. They saw themselves present there in every symbol, in every detail, in the very features of the Virgin. They felt identified. But we must not forget, and the Indians understood it so, that there are also the details that refer to the great Spanish (Greco-Roman) civilization through which the Gospel reached them. Thus the Indians learned to grasp the Virgin as Lady, both of themselves and of the Spaniards, and they knew her to be their Mother. And even today it is so for all the peoples of Spanish America. It is a prototype of the evangelization of culture. We who have as the end of our Religious Family the evangelization of culture must learn from her, and learn from those great men who were the Franciscans of all times, who did those stupendous works, among which is the evangelization of America. Of the 250,000 missionaries who went to America over five centuries, most of whom were sent by Spain, 70 percent were Franciscans, that is, 180,000 missionaries. Even today Spain has more than 23,000 missionaries in America. And they, the Franciscans, have great glories. One of them is the evangelization of America. Another of them, perhaps even greater, is that they always defended and spread devotion to the Immaculate Conception, until it was finally declared a dogma of faith. And the other great thing about the Franciscans, which must be remembered, is the Custody of the Holy Land, entrusted to them by the kings of Spain, Spain being the one that paid all the costs and expenses it entailed. The Custody of the Holy Land at that time covered Cyprus, Turkey, Egypt, the Holy Land, Jordan, Iraq, Iran, and reached as far as China, where Fray John of Montecorvino, a Franciscan, arrived among the first and established himself there for more than 30 years, in what was at that time called Cathay, today Beijing. That is why, looking at the Virgin, we must kindle in our hearts enthusiasm for evangelization, which is indeed the new evangelization, but which is the evangelization of always, and which needs well-disposed men, with light in their heads, with enthusiasm in their hearts and with great courage so as not to lose heart.
Meditation for Christmas

“The Heavens are distilling joys of honey” One of the mysteries of the life of our Lord Jesus Christ that is sweetest, most devout, and most full of wonders and teachings is this one of His glorious birth. “On this day, the heavens are distilling drops of honey over all the world.” Let us look upon Jesus, brothers and sisters! Not only with the crown with which God the Father begot Him from all eternity, but with the one with which His Mother crowned Him when she gave birth to Him and clothed Him with our humanity. Come and see God! no longer in the bosom of the Father, but in the arms of His Mother; not amid the choirs of angels, but amid lowly animals; not seated at the right hand of the Majesty, but laid in His poor manger; not thundering and flashing lightning in the heavens, but weeping and trembling with cold in a humble stable. Come and see the Christ of God! That hour has come which was so desired by all peoples, so awaited in all ages, so promised in all times, so sung and celebrated in all the divine Scriptures. Come and see the Son consubstantial with the Father! That hour has come on which depends the salvation of the world, the restoration of heaven, the victory over the devil, the triumph over death and sin, the hour for which all the saints wept and sighed. It was midnight, far brighter than midday, when all things were in silence and enjoyed the calm and repose of the still night. At that blessed hour the Only-begotten Son of God comes forth from the virginal womb of the Blessed Virgin. Let us contemplate Him! At that most blessed hour, that Omnipotent word of God, the Eternal Word, the Divine Son, having come down from heaven, appeared clothed in our flesh, like us in all things but sin. Let us look upon the Sweet Child! He already knows good and evil, He knows weeping, He knows sorrows, He knows tears, He knows hardships, pains and groans; and He goes through all this out of love for us. Let us marvel at the Holy Manger! The goodness, the mercy and the love of God toward men went so far that He exchanged His Holy Temple for the stable and heaven for the Manger, out of love for us: works full of love which the very ones for whom He did them regarded as madness: “ the preaching of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing; but to those who are being saved -to us- it is the power of God ” (Cor 1:18). Let us learn by looking at the Divine Infant! Here He condemns greed, the root of all evils. From the cradle of the manger, from that heavenly chair, this is the firm lesson He gives us. O glorious manger, where the word of God, struck dumb, speaks all the more clearly the more silently it warns! Look, brother, do not depart from this stable where the word of God, keeping silent, weeps; but this weeping is sweeter than all the words of men and even than all the music of the angels of heaven. Let us rejoice in seeing the Merciful Child! It is a sweet thing to contemplate Him, and not only sweet, but powerful and effective for healing our wounds. He was in glory and I in misery. He admirable and I miserable; but He bowed the heavens, came down to earth and drew me out of vanity, and washed me and clothed me and restored me and strengthened me. He gave me His hand when He was born, He drew me out when He preached, He washed me when He died, He clothed me when He rose again, He restored me when He ascended to heaven, He strengthened me when He sent the Holy Spirit. But who is this one, so high and so low, so great and so small? Small in the flesh… manger… stable, but great in heaven, where the stars served Him; great in the air, where the angels sang; great on earth, where Herod and Jerusalem were afraid. Be enraptured by the humility and greatness of Jesus! It is great humility for God to be conceived, but greater glory to be conceived of the Holy Spirit. It is great humility to be born of a woman, but great glory to be born of a Virgin, and such a one as Mary. It is great humility to be born in a stable, but great glory to be announced by a star. It is great humility to be among animals, but great glory to be sung and praised by the angels. It is great humility to be circumcised, but great glory is the name of Savior given Him there. All this was so that we might know what He came for. If you look at who He was, all glory and all honor befitted Him, because He was the Son of God; but if you look at what He came for, all humility and all poverty befitted Him, because He came to heal our pride. With the one He confirms our faith, with the other He builds up our conduct. Let us look upon Jesus! We will learn humility of heart, contempt for the glories of the world, the nakedness and poverty of spirit so celebrated in the Gospel. Let us look upon Him! He is most beautiful in heaven and most beautiful in the stable, most beautiful on the throne of His Church and most beautiful in the manger of Bethlehem, most beautiful amid the choirs of angels and most beautiful between the little donkey and the ox.
What is an oratory for?

Interview with Fr. Carlos Buela conducted by the young people of the Press Workshop of the Festive Oratory Blessed Pier Giorgio Frassati. We take the interview from the bulletin “Chispas” no. 1, publication of the Oratory. For what purposes is the Festive Oratory carried out? -The Festive Oratory has several specific purposes: it is so that young people can meet one another, enjoy themselves, be instructed and help one another. How do you define the Oratory? -It is very difficult to define, because it is something that embraces religious aspects, cultural aspects, musical aspects. St. John Bosco defines it, in a way, by saying: “it is a church, a school, a home (as a family home), and a playground (in the sense of a place of recreation, of fun).” It is difficult to define; it is described. What does the “spirit of the Oratory” consist of? -The spirit of the Oratory is a spirit of great joy, and in joy to find the meaning of life, why we are here in this world, and to learn to direct ourselves toward the other life. What importance does the Oratory have? -The Oratory is so important because, as St. John Bosco says, “to change a town you have to have an Oratory” ; that is why, in fact, there should be an Oratory in every parish, so that young people could meet one another, because many times it is not that young people do not want to, but that they are not given the opportunity. What qualities should those who work in an Oratory have? -Simply to want to do good. For whom is the Oratory carried out? The Oratory is for every young person, boy or girl, whether in early adolescence, in late adolescence, or already fully into youth. As long as one has good will, it is for everyone. In the spirit of which saint is this Oratory carried out? -The Oratory begins with someone the 350th anniversary of whose death was celebrated not long ago: St. Philip Neri. He was a very joyful saint; he was a Florentine but lived in Rome. Over time, following his custom, Oratories continued to be held. In the last century it was Don Bosco who took up the idea of the Oratory, but transformed it, making something very particular, very personal to him, which is what we try to do here. So I think these are the two great saints who mark out what an Oratory must be: St. Philip Neri and St. John Bosco. Tell us a little about St. John Bosco. -St. John Bosco has been named patron of youth because from his earliest days as a priest he began to work with young people, and for that he also knew how to gather around him those who had a vocation to work with young people, and for that purpose he founded the Salesian Congregation, which is dedicated especially to the education of youth in schools and which also continues the custom of the Oratory, sometimes with greater skill and other times with less, because it turns out that it is not easy nowadays to run Oratories for young people; for us it is easy because we have many young seminarians: there are some who are capable in painting, others in music, others who like journalism, others who know how to do impressions, others who sing… So we can run an Oratory more easily, because one of the necessary things -since attendance at the Oratory is voluntary- is that the activities of the Oratory have to have a hook, for if they have no hook or are a bore, you don’t go. If a priest is alone it is very difficult to organize an Oratory today, because many people have to be involved. That is why I think that because of this very special situation, that we have such a large Seminary with so many young men, we can run an Oratory more easily, something that is more difficult to do elsewhere. -In what way is the family integrated into the Festive Oratory? How can it take part? -I think we must seek to have the family integrated as much as possible, both in accompanying the liturgical participation and also in the recreational part or when the campfire is held. That is why your dads and moms often come, because they want to see; it strikes them that you are enthusiastic about something, because today it is a serious problem that there are many young people who are not enthusiastic about anything. It is as if their arms were hanging down. It is terrible, but it is so. I see that families must be integrated, although the older people have more problems than the young. We have the difficulty in schools -at least I had it in Buenos Aires- that the problem was not with the young people but with the parents; many times the young person still has fine ideals and yet it is the grown-ups who discourage them. -Why did you decide to form an Oratory when there was already another one in San Rafael? -Because, as I said before, there should be an Oratory in every parish. It is not that it is an Oratory for this city. Just as there are many parishes, there should be many Oratories. In what way can the community help? -The community can help in many ways, by making transportation possible and other things that are needed to make the Oratory different each day. A successor of Don Bosco used to say that “every Sunday the Oratory has to put on its festive clothes .” In this way the young person feels at home, and putting on festive clothes is not difficult: it is a very simple thing!
Good Night I

The Constitutions and the Incarnate Word Recalling the thought of our Founder During the Novena of the Annunciation On the first day of the novena, on which we pray specifically for our faith in the preexistence of the Word from all eternity in the bosom of the Most Holy Trinity , we call to mind Fr. Buela’s thought on the subject, taken from his book “ El Señor es mi Pastor. Memoria y Profecía .” The Constitutions and the Incarnate Word T he first part, “Our Path,” was surely written between May 3 and August 1981, because in August we held the first meeting to report on what we wanted to do. There (in “Our Path”) is a first great development of what the Mystery of the Incarnate Word is. A development that in some way reaches its summit in “El Arte del Padre.” I drew my inspiration first and foremost from all the passages of Sacred Scripture where the Incarnate Word is spoken of (e.g. the Hymn of the Kenosis, the prologue of St. John…). And in the Magisterium of the Church, there is a formula there that is fantastic. There are many citations of the Council, but there is one I like most: “Council of Ephesus,” D 111, St. Leo the Great, Dz 143, 144. And here comes, for me, the most important text: Dz 148, Council of Chalcedon: “… one only and the same Jesus Christ, without division, in a single hypostasis, one only and the same Only Son…”. Ephesus in 431. St. Leo the Great 449. Chalcedon 451. “Hence the Magisterium of the Church has always defended the Catholic truth about the Incarnate Word: «Dogma says that in Christ there is only one person, namely, the divine person of the Logos, and two natures, both subsisting in one and the same divine person. The human nature has been assumed into the unity and dominion of the divine person, so that it is the divine person who acts in the human nature and through the human nature as through an organ of His own. The Third ecumenical Council of Ephesus (431) confirmed the twelve anathematisms of St. Cyril of Alexandria, but without formally defining them. Later they were recognized by the popes and the councils as an expression of the genuine doctrine of the Church. Here, in condensed form, are their main points: a) Christ with His own flesh is a single being, that is, one single person. He is God and man at the same time ( 2 and 6). b) The Logos-God is united to the flesh by an intrinsic, physical or substantial union ( An . 2 and 3). Christ is not a bearer of God, but truly God ( An . 5). c) The human and divine properties of which Sacred Scripture and the holy fathers speak to us must not be divided between two persons or hypostases (the Man-Christ and the Logos-God), but must be referred to the one Christ, the incarnate Logos ( An . 4). It was the divine Logos who suffered in the flesh and was crucified, died and rose again ( An . 12). d) The Blessed Virgin Mary is Mother of God, because she gave birth according to the flesh to the incarnate Logos-God ( An . 1). The Council of Chalcedon (451) defined that the two natures of Christ are united “in one single person and one single hypostasis” (DZ 148)». And leaping across the centuries we come to His Holiness Paul VI, in his Solemn Profession of Faith, on June 30, 1968, who once again confesses the now twice-millennial faith of the Catholic Church in the divinity of Jesus Christ: «We believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the Son of God. He is the eternal Word, born of the Father before all ages and consubstantial with the Father, homooúsios to Patri , and through whom all things were made. He became incarnate by the work of the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin Mary and was made man: equal therefore to the Father according to the divinity and inferior to the Father according to the humanity, and one in Himself, not by an impossible confusion of the natures, but by the unity of the person» With the approval of the same Pontiff, the Sacred Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, on February 21, 1972, published a very important «Declaration to safeguard the faith from certain recent errors concerning the mysteries of the Incarnation and of the Trinity». Among the Christological errors the Declaration points out three principal ones: 1) The denial of the preexistence of the person of the Son subsisting as distinct from the Father and the Holy Spirit from all eternity; 2) The abandonment of the notion of the one person of Christ; and 3) The denial of the assumption of the human nature of Christ by the Second Person of the Most Holy Trinity, asserting instead that it would exist in itself as a human person. The paragraph concludes with this lapidary sentence: «Those who think in this way are far from the true faith in Christ, even when they affirm that the singular presence of God in Jesus makes Him become the supreme and definitive summit of divine revelation; nor do they recover the true faith in the divinity of Christ when they add that Jesus can be called God because God is supremely present in what they call His human nature». [With the hymn to the Virgin we ask her to obtain for us the grace we are asking for on this day of the novena and to keep us from erroneous doctrines about the mystery of the Incarnation]
Good Night II

The reality of the Incarnation Recalling the thought of our Founder During the Novena of the Annunciation On the second day of the novena, on which we pray specifically for our faith in the mystery of the Incarnation , we call to mind Fr. Buela’s thought on the subject, taken from his book “ El Arte del Padre .” The reality of the Incarnation T he fact of the Incarnation of the Word is known through God’s revelation, and to recognize it is a grace of God: «flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven» (Mt 16:17). «The first and fundamental mystery of Jesus Christ [is] the mystery of the Incarnation of the Son of God». And «God was never so close to man –and man was never so close to God– as precisely at that moment: At the instant of the mystery of the Incarnation !». It is a supernatural mystery « quoad substantiam » which, even after being revealed –given the limitation of our intellect– leaves its intrinsic elements in a zone beyond the horizon of mere human reason. God teaches the Incarnation of His Son in various passages of Sacred Scripture. We will recall some: – The angel Gabriel announces to Joseph that: «what has been begotten in her is of the Holy Spirit» (Mt 1:20). – The angel reveals to the Blessed Virgin: «you will conceive in your womb and bear a son» (Lk 1:31). – St. John expresses it in a concise and sublime way: «And the Word became flesh» (Jn 1:14). – The apostle St. Paul does so by saying simply, with enormous force and richness of content, that Christ Jesus «emptied Himself» (Phil 2:7). – In Heb 1:6: «when He brings His Firstborn into», about which St. Thomas explains that «he calls the Incarnation an introduction into the world». Tradition confessed this august mystery under various names: economy (as a disposition or ordering of God), susception, assumption, inhumanation, incorporation, convention, exinanition, union, self-emptying, incarnation ( sarkosis , of clearly biblical origin, which prevailed in the Creeds: «He emptied Himself», or «He became incarnate»). We consider that the eloquence of these texts is such, and of such impact, that they are more than enough for our purpose: Sacred Scripture and Tradition teach, clearly and categorically, the Incarnation of the Word, and the Magisterium of the Church has always confessed it as an immutable dogma of faith. One cannot fail to recall how St. Peter of Alcantara would be enraptured when asking himself: «That God became incarnate? That God became man? That God came to take flesh? That God took human flesh?…» and he would enter into the sweetest ecstasies. Not even the angels themselves know some things concerning the mystery of the Incarnation . In addition, there are the things Jesus took together with human nature, which relate fundamentally to four realities: grace ( S. Th., III, q. 7-8), truth (III, q. 9-12), power (III, q. 13) and imperfections (III, q. 14-15), that is, the perfections and the defects assumed. Perfections assumed in the soul: a) in its very essence; b) in its intellect; and c) in its will; and d) the imperfections of body and soul, which do not imply any moral defect. […] Today people do not want to accept the truth and the reality of the Incarnation: – the action of the Holy Spirit; – the divine maternity; – the hypostatic union; – perpetual virginity. These are all things that speak of God’s lordship over men. But many today do not even want to hear about these things. That is how things go for men. St. John Paul II recalled it: «Man, from the beginning, is tempted to want to be like God (cf. Gen 3:5)… but without God! Without the mystery of the Incarnation . Without the night of Bethlehem». I believe that on this point the ultimate reason for this rejection is the hatred some progressives have for what is genuinely Catholic. It is not a misunderstanding, it is not a passing distraction, it is not an unconscious oversight; there is a theological reason in their persecution. Hence: – We are the backward ones; they the forward ones. – We the retrograde; they the advanced. – We the ones of the past; they the ones of the future. – We the conservatives; they the progressives. – We the medieval ones; they the ones of the coming century. – We the closed; they the open. – We the obscurantists; they the enlightened. – We the cave-dwellers; they in spaceships, but they only repeat very old errors. – Everything negative is ours; everything positive is theirs. – They the good; we the bad. – No vocations in diocese ‘X’? It is our fault. – Priests apostatize? It is our fault. – The sects advance? It is our fault. – Fewer and fewer people at their Masses? It is our fault. We are the mangy sheep to blame for everything. «But fear not, little flock: it has pleased the Father to give you the Kingdom!» (Lk 12:32). For all this, and in order to be faithful to God today and always, we must renew ourselves in the charism of our religious family. In a particular way in the face of the enormous graces of the Holy Spirit which are the new foundations, the new conversions, the new vocations and the new missions. First, by renewing in ourselves the urgency of the witness to the Incarnation of the Word: «We must bear witness that the message of the mystery of the Incarnation retains all its vigor, which wants all men to be children of God and in solidarity with the lot of their brothers». «… the Church, willed and founded by Jesus on Peter, the Apostles and their successors, has as its end the proclamation of the incarnation of the divine Word, who came into the world to reveal the truth and to save all men». Second, by remembering that living this truth must be palpable in our lives: «we are in the world, but we are not of the world» (Jn 15:18-19). Trying not to fall into the falsehood of those who: – are not in it but are of it: «angelism» (they are not in reality). – are in it and are of it: «temporalism» (they have nothing to give the world). – are neither in it nor of it: «fence-sitters» (« because you are neither cold nor hot …»; Rev 3:16). – are not, but pretend to be: religious in disguise. Mary is the living emblem of what the Christian must be, the synthesis of two humanly irreconcilable grandeurs: motherhood and virginity: she is the certificate of the truth of the Incarnation. [We sing to her, renewing the intention of this day of the novena]
Good Night III

«But who do you say that I am?» Recalling the thought of our Founder During the Novena of the Annunciation On the third day of the novena, on which we pray specifically for our faith in Jesus Christ, true God , we call to mind Fr. Buela’s thought on the subject, taken from his book “ El Arte del Padre .” «But who do you say that I am?» V ery different is the impression made on us by the judgments about Jesus pronounced by those who were His Apostles and disciples, and by their successors. Here everything is unity, clarity, joyful certainty, truth, homogeneous development, consideration of all aspects without silencing or denying any of them. It is the calm sea of faith, the clear sky of evangelical simplicity, the firmness of the rock, the solidity of good foundations; in short, light after darkness. – «This is the Son of God » (Jn 1:34), confesses St. John the Baptist, and he evidently means a sonship by nature, because if it were by mere adoption it would express nothing singular, since all the Jews knew themselves to be adopted children of God. – «The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, Son of God », St. Mark sets down at the start of his account (1:1). – St. John begins his Gospel directly by affirming: «In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God and the Word was God », by which he affirms the preexistence of the Second Person of the Most Holy Trinity, His distinction from the Father and His divinity. And in his first epistle he declares that Jesus Christ «is the true God and eternal Life» (5:20). – St. Thomas the apostle, falling prostrate, adores Him, saying: «My Lord and my God » (Jn 20:28). – «I believe that you are the Messiah, the Son of God » (Jn 11:27), exclaims St. Martha. – St. Paul speaks to us of his «hope in the glorious manifestation of our great God and Savior, Christ Jesus» (Titus 2:13), of that Christ «who is above all things, God blessed forever» (Rom 9:5)77. Let us now turn to the Prince of the Apostles, as the Lord Himself did: «Who do you say that I am?» St. Peter answers: «You are the Christ, the Son of the living God » (Mt 16:16). Glorious confession, in which the Catholic Church begins and on which she is built! And what do the successors of Peter and Vicars of Christ tell us? The Fathers gathered at the First Ecumenical Council, at Nicaea, in the year 325, proclaimed the faith of the Church «in one Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God … God from God and Light from Light, true God from true God , begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father ( homooúsios tõ Patri ), through whom all things were made…» (Dz. 54). As Hermann Josef Sieben says: «No Council, either before or since, has made, even remotely, a dogmatic decision so fundamental and so important in its consequences». The « homooúsios » is the key word, the term a thousand times blessed that should sound to us like heavenly music, the watchword of Catholic orthodoxy forever and ever. It expresses the unity of substance, numerically one, between the Father and the Son, and therefore that the one is as much God as the other. […] And leaping across the centuries we come to St. Paul VI, in his Solemn Profession of Faith , on June 30, 1968, who once again confesses the now twice-millennial faith of the Catholic Church in the divinity of Jesus Christ: «We believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God . He is the eternal Word, born of the Father before all ages and consubstantial with the Father, or homooúsios tõ Patri , through whom all things were made. And He became incarnate by the work of the Holy Spirit, of Mary the Virgin, and was made man: equal, therefore, to the Father according to the divinity, less than the Father according to the humanity, entirely one, not by confusion (which cannot be) of substance, but by unity of person». […] The Catechism of the Catholic Church , promulgated by St. John Paul II on October 11, 1992, also affirms clearly and unequivocally faith in the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ, as well as in His sacred humanity and in the mystery of the hypostatic union. This is the faith of the Church! The same Great Pope approved «with certain knowledge and by his apostolic authority», in the heart of the Year of the Great Jubilee, a fundamental document on the Christological faith of the Church and the salvific unicity and universality of Jesus Christ, issued by the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith: the declaration Dominus Iesus . Against many present-day errors this great document also reaffirms faith in the definitive and complete character of God’s revelation in Jesus Christ; the personal unity between the eternal Word and Jesus of Nazareth; the unity between the economy of the Incarnate Word and the action of the Holy Spirit; the salvific unicity and universality of the mystery of Jesus Christ; etc… Hence we, counting on the backing of the ecclesiastical Magisterium of all times, in spite of our nothingness and sin, confess with all the strength of our soul and of our heart the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ , who is «one single person in two natures» (Dz. 429), and we do so not without a certain belligerence, «as if giving heresy a wet willy,» as Ignacio B. Anzoátegui put it, with the holy pride of the children of God who know that «flesh and blood did not reveal this to them, but the Father who is in heaven» (Mt 16:17), and that it is a truth by which we live and for which we are ready to die. [We sing to the Virgin, asking for this grace.]
Good Night IV

The humanity of Christ is our happiness Recalling the thought of our Founder During the Novena of the Annunciation On the fourth day of the novena, on which we pray specifically for our faith in Jesus Christ, true man , we call to mind Fr. Buela’s thought on the subject, taken from one of his sermons entitled: The humanity of Christ is our happiness T he humanity of Christ is our happiness». It is a phrase of St. Thomas Aquinas found at the beginning of the part of the Summa Theologiae in which he speaks of Jesus. […] St. Anthony of Padua [for his part] begins a homily by saying: «Christmas: behold paradise». When, two thousand years ago, Mary gave birth in Bethlehem: behold paradise. Happiness that ceases to be a promise, an expectation, a hope, that is no longer glimpsed from afar. Happiness made flesh was present. It was visible. When He came forth from His mother’s womb, visibly happiness, that is, paradise, the supreme delight (as Dante says: «and thus may the supreme delight unfold to him»), the supreme delight had Himself come out to meet man: behold paradise. […] The Incarnation Two thousand years ago, then, happiness came: behold paradise. Happiness came: it ceased to be a promise, it ceased to be pointed to as the end of the human journey. Happiness came, paradise came. It came in the flesh so that it might be seen, so that it might be touched, so that it might be embraced. So that St. Augustine can say: «I knew that happiness was God, but I did not enjoy You [because one does not enjoy knowing; one enjoys when one is embraced], but I did not enjoy You until, humble, I embraced my humble God Jesus». This is the experience of happiness on earth: humbly to embrace my humble God Jesus. Not God as a distant destination, but God made a child , a tiny little child: thus paradise, happiness, came to meet us; thus happiness drew near, thus it came within reach of our gaze, within reach of our heart, within reach of our hands, of the hands that can embrace it. Paradise on earth is He: […] God is faithful, by whom you have been called into the fellowship of His Son Jesus Christ, our Lord (1 Cor 1:9). The fellowship is with His Son Jesus Christ, our Lord […]. Jesus Christ is the happiness of man. It is that man, in His singularity, I would say in His individuality: that man. The fellowship of His Son Jesus Christ, our Lord. […] I wish to read a passage which, in my opinion, is one of the most beautiful and most comprehensive of Giussani 1 , in which he says what this humble relationship with the humble Jesus is, this humble embrace with the humble Jesus, this humble embrace with happiness here on earth, this fellowship of the Son of God, this possibility of familiarity with His Son Jesus Christ. Giussani says: «Your relationship with Christ does not have to be already developed, experienced, mature, for your personality to be born from it and for you, starting from that, to know how to create a companionship [to know how to love. When we are loved gratuitously we can freely, that is, gratuitously, love]. It is enough -how shall I put it- the surprise that John and Andrew had [who were the first two who, at the beginning of His public life, met Him], who understood nothing [who understood nothing and yet had understood everything, for Andrew meets his brother Peter and says to him: We have found the Messiah (Jn 1:41). What they were waiting for, they had found, and therefore they had found everything, because what the heart waits for is everything; consequently they had understood everything. It is enough, the surprise that John and Andrew had, who understood nothing]; the surprise is enough, an initial devotion is enough, wonder is enough. More precisely: it is enough to ask for it.» […] Giussani goes on to say: «More precisely, it is enough to ask for it [because wonder is what makes you ask for it], that embryonic perception of what He is is enough, which makes you beg for it, because of which you ask for it». To begin the experience of happiness on earth, to embrace happiness on earth, to embrace, humble, my humble Jesus, that embryonic perception because of which you ask for it is enough, that embryonic wonder, that embryonic sweetness because of which you beg for it. This is enough to begin to embrace happiness on earth. […] I end by reading a passage of St. Augustine [says Fr. Buela] on the beauty of Jesus: «For us believers, the Word of God appears beautiful everywhere / pulcher Deus, Verbum apud Deum , / beautiful as the Word with God, / pulcher in utero virginis , / beautiful in the womb of the Virgin, where He did not lose His divinity and took on humanity ; beautiful born a child, because even while He was very small, nursing, being carried in arms, the heavens spoke, the angels paid Him tribute of praise, the star guided the Magi, He was adored in the manger, and at all times He was the food of the meek. So He is beautiful in heaven and beautiful on earth; beautiful in the womb, beautiful in the arms of His parents [of Mary and Joseph], beautiful in His miracles, beautiful in the scourging. [Yes, also in the scourging, because -Augustine says- in the scourging, when He was all disfigured, let us think why He was like that, why He had let Himself be beaten like that by the scourges; let us think of the mercy that made Him come to this for you, for love of you; He was beautiful even in the scourging]. When Mary took Him dead in her arms beneath the cross (« vidit suum dulcem natum moriendo desolatum / she saw her sweet newborn, her sweet Son, die alone, alone on the cross»), when she took Him in her arms, there was nothing more beautiful than her Son, that disfigured Son. When the good thief said to Him: Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom (Lk 23:42), he had never in his whole life found anything more beautiful than that moment, at the moment of death, when Jesus answered him: Today you will be with me in paradise (Lk 23:43)]. Beautiful in His miracles, beautiful in the scourging, beautiful inviting us to follow Him, beautiful not concerning Himself with death, beautiful giving His life, beautiful rising again / pulcher in ligno, pulcher in sepulcro, pulcher in coelo / beautiful on the cross, beautiful in the tomb and beautiful in heaven». [To Mary, Mother of the Incarnate Word, we ask the grace humbly to embrace this God who counted it as nothing to empty Himself so that we might begin to embrace happiness already here on earth.] Notes 1 Luigi Giussani, El atractivo de Jesucristo , Ediciones Encuentro, Madrid 2000, 166.
Good Night V

The unity of Christ Recalling the thought of our Founder During the Novena of the Annunciation On the fifth day of the novena, on which we pray specifically for our faith in the union of both natures , we call to mind Fr. Buela’s thought on the subject, taken from his book “ El Arte del Padre .” The unity of Christ So that, irrefutably, according to Sacred Scripture, the following four truths […] are certain: Christ is a single being, one single Person, true God and true man at the same time. The Word is united to the flesh by an intrinsic, physical and substantial union . He is not a bearer of God, but truly God. The divine and human properties of Christ are not divided between two persons, but are referred to the «one Lord Jesus Christ» (1 Cor 8:6). The Virgin Mary is Mother of God. «We have been redeemed only if Jesus Christ shares in His person the full divine life». «In saying that “we believe in one God,” that “Jesus is Lord” (1 Cor 12:3; Rom 10:9; Jn 20:28), we break with everything else that claims to set itself up as absolute, and we destroy the idols of money, of power, of sex, those that hide in ideologies, “lay religions” with totalitarian ambition». From this central truth of our faith derive enormous consequences that concern not only the spirituality of man, but the very civilization of humanity. It is curious, for example, what can be seen in Taiwan. The Museum of Taipei, in Taiwan, has a very large hall where the history of mankind is presented in charts, in photographs and in various other ways, and in which Chinese culture is compared with Western culture. There one can clearly see that Chinese art did not evolve with respect to the human figure, whereas Western art and Eastern Christian art did, particularly after the Incarnation of the Word. In short, Christ is one beyond compare, in eight ways, as Nicholas of Gorran says very well: «It must be noted that Christ is one beyond compare, in many ways: – Nature of God: In the first place, God is one alone because of the divine nature; hence, no one is God but God alone. – One sole Almighty Creator: In the second place, He is one sole creator because of His infinite power: “One is the Most High, creator of all things” (Sir 1:8). – Holiness of the Incarnate Word: In the third place, He is unique as man because of the singular eminence of His holiness. “There is none who does good…” (Ps 13:1); “it is fitting that one man die for the people” (Jn 11:50). – Government of the world: In the fourth place, He is one sole Lord because of His governance of preeminence: “One Lord, one faith…” (Eph 4:5). And in this way there is one sole Lord, Jesus Christ. – One sole Teacher: In the fifth place, one sole teacher because of the infusion of knowledge: “Call no one teacher, for your only Teacher is the Christ” (Mt 23:10). – One sole Father: In the sixth place, one sole Father because of the production of all things: “One is your Father who is in Heaven” (Mt 23:9)38. – One sole Shepherd: In the seventh place, one sole Shepherd because of His common care of the faithful people: “Let there be one flock and one shepherd” (Jn 10:16). – One sole Victim: In the eighth place, one sole victim because of the singular price of our Redemption: “For by a single offering He consecrated forever those who are sanctified” (Heb 10:14). The unity of Jesus Christ is a barrier against all false oppositions and divisions, for example, against the separation of the Word and Christ, of Christ and the Kingdom, of the Christ of faith and the Christ of history… In short, «God willed to unify all things, both natural and supernatural, in Christ Jesus, “so that He may have first place in all things” (Col 1:18)». Consequences of the hypostatic union Here are some consequences that derive from the hypostatic union in Christ, set out schematically: The person of Christ is of infinite dignity , since He is a divine person, the second of the Trinity. All that Jesus Christ does and all that He possesses, whether as man or as God, must be attributed to God the Son, because it is always God the Son who does it and who possesses it. Thus His words, His sufferings, His blood, His heart, His wounds, are those of the Son of God: consequently, all these things are divine . All the actions of Jesus Christ are of infinite dignity, because actions are attributed to the person, and therefore they are divine actions, actions of God, and are, for that very reason, of infinite value and merit . They are of «a superabundant grace for infinite worlds, if they exist». All the actions of Jesus Christ are infinitely holy . Everything that belongs to Christ, humanity, flesh, blood, heart, is divine and as such adorable . There is no room for any «co-adoration». Being the only Son of God, He is infinitely pleasing to God the Father . His humanity is filled with all the gifts of God, that is, with the fullness of grace –personal grace and capital grace– and of truth –beatific knowledge, infused knowledge and acquired or experiential knowledge–, and of His fullness we have all received . Therefore: «Everything that has been truly said belongs to us Christians» (St. Justin); «Let every good Christian understand that any truth, wherever it may be, belongs to his Lord» (St. Augustine); «Every truth, by whomever it is spoken, proceeds from the Holy Spirit» (St. Ambrose). And St. Thomas: «no one can say anything true unless moved by the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of Truth»; «there is no knowledge of the truth except in the Holy Spirit, who works in the intellect and preserves it»46; «everything good and everything true is from the Holy Spirit». «Every truth, spoken by whomever, comes from the Holy Spirit». To the one Person are attributed divine and human properties . This is what is called the «communication of idioms» (from the Greek ίδιος, which means proper , property , what belongs to one ). Jesus Christ is the natural Son of God the Father even as man; only we mere creatures are adopted children. […] Let us always ask for the grace to be always great contemplators of the Incarnate mystery, that we may know how to present it courageously to our brothers and, in a special way, that we ourselves may live it in its fullness, confessing the same and only Lord Jesus Christ as true God and true man. [We ask this of the Virgin, Mother of the Incarnate Word, with the hymn.]
Good Night VI

A knot of relationships Recalling the thought of our Founder During the Novena of the Annunciation On the sixth day of the novena, on which we pray specifically for our faith in the priesthood of Christ , we recall what Fr. Buela wrote in his book “ Sacerdotes para siempre .” A knot of relationships The priesthood is, essentially, communion. That is why the priesthood is a knot of relationships. A knot made of bonds that tighten and close in such a way that it is almost impossible to untie them, and the more they are pulled, the tighter they become. A knot of many and manifold relationships. Hence living the priesthood as a mystery of communion is something never attained in total perfection. […] Relationship with the Incarnate Word The Second Person of the Most Holy Trinity made man: with all the mysteries of His life, Passion, Death and Resurrection. With what He did and taught. In a particular way with the Eucharist, as sacrificial sacrament and as sacramental sacrifice. Sacramental root «Through sacramental ordination, conferred by the imposition of hands and the consecratory prayer of the bishop, there is established in the presbyter “a specific ontological bond, which unites the priest to Christ, High Priest and Good Shepherd.” The identity of the priest, then, derives from the specific participation in the priesthood of Christ , whereby the one ordained is transformed, in the Church and for the Church, into a real, living and transparent image of Christ the Priest: “a sacramental representation of Jesus Christ, Head and Shepherd.” Through consecration, the priest “receives as a gift a spiritual power, which is a participation in the authority with which Jesus, through His Spirit, guides the Church.” This sacramental identification with the High and Eternal Priest specifically inserts the presbyter into the Trinitarian mystery and, through the mystery of Christ, into the ministerial communion of the Church, in order to serve the People of God». Specific identity «The Christological dimension −like the Trinitarian− arises directly from the sacrament, which configures one ontologically to Christ the Priest, Teacher, Sanctifier and Shepherd of His People. To those faithful who −while remaining grafted into the common priesthood− are chosen and constituted in the ministerial priesthood, there is given an indelible participation in the same and one priesthood of Christ , in the public dimension of mediation and authority, as regards the sanctification, the teaching and the guidance of the whole people of God. Thus, if on the one hand the common priesthood of the faithful and the ministerial or hierarchical priesthood are necessarily ordered to one another −for each, in its own way, participates in the one priesthood of Christ −, on the other hand they differ essentially from one another46. In this sense, the identity of the priest is new with respect to that of all Christians, who, through Baptism, participate together in the one priesthood of Christ and are called to bear witness to Him throughout the earth47. The specificity of the ministerial priesthood stands in relation to the need that all the faithful have to adhere to the mediation and lordship of Christ, made visible by the exercise of the ministerial priesthood. In his particular Christological identity, the priest must be aware that his life is a mystery inserted totally into the mystery of Christ in a new and specific way, and this commits him totally to pastoral activity and fulfills him». Relationship with Our Lady «There exists an “essential relationship… between the Mother of Jesus and the priesthood of the ministers of the Son,” which derives from the relationship between the divine maternity of Mary and the priesthood of Christ . In this relationship is rooted the Marian spirituality of every presbyter. Priestly spirituality cannot be considered complete unless it takes seriously into consideration the testament of Christ crucified, who willed to entrust His Mother to the beloved disciple and, through him, to all priests, who have been called to continue His work of redemption. As to John at the foot of the Cross, so Mary is entrusted to each presbyter as Mother in a special way. Priests, who are numbered among the disciples most loved by Jesus crucified and risen, must welcome Mary into their life as their Mother: she will therefore be the object of their continual attentions and of their prayers. The Ever-Virgin is for priests the Mother who leads them to Christ, while at the same time making them authentically love the Church and guiding them to the Kingdom of Heaven. Every presbyter knows that Mary, because she is Mother, is the eminent formator of his priesthood: since she is the one who knows how to mold the priestly heart; the Virgin, then, knows how and wants to protect priests from dangers, weariness and discouragement: she watches, with maternal solicitude, so that the presbyter may grow in wisdom, age and grace before God and men. Those who do not know how to imitate the virtues of the Mother will not be devoted sons. The presbyter, therefore, must look to Mary if he wants to be a humble, obedient and chaste minister, who can bear witness to charity through total self-giving to the Lord and to the Church. Masterpiece of the priestly Sacrifice of Christ, the Virgin represents the Church in the purest way, without spot or wrinkle , wholly holy and immaculate (cf. Eph 5:27). The contemplation of the Blessed Virgin always places before the eyes of the presbyter the ideal toward which he must strive in his ministry on behalf of his own community, so that it too may be a wholly glorious Church through the priestly gift of his own life». Love for Mary is visibly manifested in praying the Holy Rosary. […] May Mary Immaculate obtain for us the grace to be faithful to the mystery of communion that we represent.
Good Night VII

The humanity of Christ – The living monument of God’s love Recalling the thought of our Founder During the Novena of the Annunciation On the seventh day of the novena, on which we pray specifically for our faith in the motive of the Incarnation , we call to mind Fr. Buela’s thought on the subject, taken from his books “ El Arte del Padre ” and “ Las Servidoras V .” The humanity of Christ The end of the Incarnation was the redemption from sins : «The principal cause of the divine Incarnation is the expiation of sins»; it is «to save sinners» (1 Tim 1:15), it is the «restoration of human nature»; in other words, «He came into the world so that men might exchange the love of earthly things for that of spiritual things». In Lumen Gentium 55 we are taught for what purpose the Son of God took human nature from the Virgin: «in order to free man from sin through the mysteries of His humanity». [In accordance with which, Fr. Buela declares in Las Servidoras V :] The living monument of God’s love Out of love God sent His Son into the world so that He might give His life for us on the Cross: God so loved the world that He gave it His only-begotten Son… (Jn 3:16), in such a way that: The love of God toward us was made manifest in this, that God sent His only-begotten Son into the world … In this is love, not that we have loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as propitiation for our sins (1 Jn 4:9-10). Love, then, which is manifested in the Incarnation of the Word, and in the Redemption, by dying as propitiation for the sins of all. A love that goes first, because God takes the lead. He takes the initiative. He has the primacy in love: He loved us first (1 Jn 4:19). A love that has its origin in Him: … charity comes from God (1 Jn 4:7); He is the inexhaustible source of all true love, and every little spark of love springs from that burning bonfire of charity which is the love of God. It is a greater love: No one has greater love than this, to give one’s life for one’s friends (Jn 15:13). It is a love of election: You did not choose me, but I chose you… (Jn 15:16). It is a fruitful, full, abiding love: …and I have appointed you that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain… ( ibidem ). Well then, this love of God is not only manifested by the fact that the Word became flesh (Jn 1:14), it is not only manifested by His Passion and Death on the Cross: Father, forgive them… (Lk 23:34), but, in addition, He has left a living, perpetual, efficacious, supreme monument of His love: the Eucharist! Having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the end (Jn 13:1); He loved them to the limit of His strength, He loved them to the extreme, He loved them to the point of remaining under the bread and under the wine. He loved us even to the Eucharist! The great school of Christian love is the Mass. It opens its doors every day, and will open them until the end of the world, until He comes (1 Cor 11:26). For everyone who wants to learn to love as Christ loves, it is a solicitous teacher, who teaches not only with words but, what is much more, with the deed itself. In the Mass, by learning to love, we show ourselves to be children of God: everyone who loves is born of God (1 Jn 4:7); we come to know Him more: everyone who loves knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, for God is love (1 Jn 4:7-8); we come to have life through Him: … so that we might live through Him (1 Jn 4:9). In the Mass, with the Eucharistic bread, God teaches us, in the mill of His heart, to let ourselves be ground like the grain of wheat. Truly, truly I say to you, if the grain of wheat does not fall into the earth and die, it remains alone; but if it dies, it will bear much fruit (Jn 12:24), until He teaches us to love with His own love. By loving us He teaches us to love, since love is repaid with love. He teaches us to love God: God is love, and whoever lives in love abides in God, and God in him (1 Jn 4:16), this is the love of God: that we keep His commandments (1 Jn 5:3); and He teaches us to love our neighbor: … let us love one another; if God loved us in this way, we too must love one another … if we love one another, God abides in us and His love is perfected in us… whoever loves God must also love his brother (1 Jn 4:7.11-12.21). […] In the Mass, Christ Himself forms us in the school of His love. On the table of the altar He kneads our heart together with His own, made into white wheat flour, and He teaches us, with the delicacy of a Teacher, with the affection of a Father, with the nobility of a King, with the strength of a Lion, with the meekness of a Lamb, with the sureness of the Way, with the lavishness of a Savior, with the sharing of a Companion, with the closeness of a Brother, with the majesty of a Lord, with the confidence of a Friend, that if I do not have love, I am nothing… not having love, nothing profits me… Love is patient and ready to serve. Love does not envy; it does not brag; it is not puffed up; it is not discourteous; it does not seek its own advantage; it does not get irritated; it keeps no account of evil; it does not take delight in injustice. Love delights in the truth. Love excuses everything. Love believes everything. Love hopes everything. Love bears everything. Love will never die (cf. 1 Cor 13:2-8). Having loved His own He loved them to the end, to the point of keeping no secret in His heart, to the point of teaching us to love with the love of His own heart, to the point of making us «living victims for the praise of His glory» . […] The crisis in participation in Sunday Mass, which in some places is growing worse, is due to the general crisis of faith, but above all its cause is the crisis of love in which the contemporary world is struggling, which makes us recall that saying of Jesus: …the charity of many will grow cold (Mt 24:12). The soul that loves God cannot abandon Holy Mass. The fact that the Mass is a work of love and that it requires love as a response makes it difficult to teach participation in it by means of rules, as St. Basil the Great says: «The love of God is not something that can be learned by rules and precepts. Just as no one has taught us to enjoy the light, to love life, to love our parents and teachers, so too, and with greater reason, the love of God is not something that can be taught; rather, from the moment this living being we call man begins to exist, a spiritual force is placed in him, in the manner of a seed, which contains within itself the capacity and the tendency to love. This seminal force is diligently cultivated and wisely nourished in the school of the divine precepts, and thus, with God’s help, it reaches its perfection» . [We ask the Blessed Virgin, Mother of the Redeemer and our Mother, for the grace that the virtue of charity may increase in us, by which we immolate ourselves spiritually in each Holy Mass by uniting ourselves to the one sacrifice of the Incarnate Word.]
Good Night VIII

The Virgin Mary Is the Mother of God Recalling the thought of our Founder During the Novena of the Annunciation On the eighth day of the novena, in which we pray specifically for our faith in Mary as Mother of the Incarnate Word , we recall Fr. Buela's thought on this subject, taken from his book “ El Arte del Padre ”. The Virgin Mary Is the Mother of God If someone is called the son of such-and-such a mother, it is because he has taken his body from her, even though his soul does not come to him from his mother, but from outside. But the body of that man was taken from the Virgin Mother; and we have also seen that the body of that man was the body of the natural Son of God, that is, of the Word of God. Therefore it is fittingly said that the blessed Virgin is mother of the Word of God, and also of God, even though the divinity is not taken from the mother, for it is not necessary that the son take from the mother everything that belongs to his substance, but only the body. Moreover, the Apostle says: “God sent his Son, made of a woman” (Gal 4:4), by which words it is shown how the mission of the Son of God is to be understood, since he is said to be sent inasmuch as he is made of a woman. And this could not be true if the Son of God had not existed before being made of a woman, since what is sent to something necessarily exists before being in that to which it is sent. But that man, the adoptive son, according to Nestorius, did not exist before being born of a woman. Therefore the saying “God sent his Son” cannot be understood of the adoptive Son, but must be understood of the natural Son, that is, of God, the Word of God. But if one is made of a woman, he is called the son of a woman. Therefore God, the Word of God, is the son of a woman. But perhaps someone will say that the Apostle's expression should not be understood as if the Son of God had been sent in order to be made of a woman, but as if the Son of God, who was made of a woman and under the law, had been sent to redeem “those who were under the law” (Gal 4:5). And according to this, the statement “his Son” would not need to be understood of the natural son, but of that man who is a son by adoption. But such a sense is rejected by the very words of the Apostle. For only he who is above the law, who is the author of the law, can free from the law. Now, the law was laid down by God. Therefore it belongs to God to free from the law. And yet the Apostle attributes this to the Son of God of whom he speaks. Therefore the Son of God of whom he speaks is the natural Son. Consequently, it is true to say that the natural Son of God, that is, God, the Word of God, was made of a woman. This is also made evident by the fact that in the Psalms the redemption of the human race is attributed to God himself: “You have ransomed me, O Lord, God of truth” (Ps 31:6). The adoption of sons of God is brought about by the Holy Spirit, according to what is said: “You have received the spirit of adoption as sons” (Rom 8:15). But the Holy Spirit is not a gift of man, but of God. Therefore the adoption of sons is not caused by man, but by God. It is caused, then, by the Son of God, sent from God and made of a woman; which seems clear from what the Apostle adds: “So that we might receive the adoption of sons” (Rom 8:15). Consequently, the Apostle's word must be understood as said of the natural Son of God. Therefore God, the Word of God, was made of a woman, that is, of the Virgin Mother. St. John says: “The Word became flesh.” Now, he cannot have flesh except from a woman. Therefore the Word was made of a woman, that is, of the Virgin Mother. The Virgin, then, is mother of the Son of God. The Apostle also says: “Christ comes from the patriarchs according to the flesh, he who is above all things, God blessed forever” (Rom 9:5). Now, he does not come from the patriarchs except through the Virgin. Therefore God, who is above all things, comes from the Virgin according to the flesh. Consequently, the Virgin is Mother of God according to the flesh. [In accordance with this, Fr. Buela said in a good-night talk 1 :] To be ignorant of this is to be ignorant of the most elementary things, and the worst of it is that it sows confusion, even in consecrated souls, because afterwards I had the case of a seminarian who came to ask me the same question: [“Can God really have a mother?”], exactly the same question. When such outrageous notions enter a consecrated soul, that soul will not remain consecrated for long, because if it does not know that Jesus Christ is true God and true man, and is One alone because both natures are united in the One Person of the Word, what sense does religious life have, what sense does virginity have, what sense does poverty have, what sense does obedience have, what sense do the sacraments have? If the one we see on the cross does not have a human nature hypostatically united to a divine Person, no one paid for our sins, because he would be a mere man; neither would baptism wash you of your sins, nor confession, nor would the Eucharist be the Body and Blood of the Lord, together with his soul and his divinity. All the sacraments fall, the Church falls. That is why we are as we are, that is why there are so many priests who have devoted themselves to temporal matters, and some seem to have stopped believing in the eternal truths. That is why we must always go deeper into these truths of faith, because it is these truths of faith that are capable of moving our heart to imitate the Lord. And to know them in such a way as to be able to respond when someone comes out with something like that. Because, as John Paul I said: “Of the faith we only have what we are capable of defending.” If there is something of the faith that we are not capable of defending, it is because we do not have faith, because we do not have the faith we ought to have. That is why tonight let us ask the Blessed Virgin, to whom we are going to sing in a few minutes, for the grace to defend with the greatest possible strength the truth of the Word who became flesh. The Person of the Word after the Incarnation A misunderstanding of the august mystery of the Incarnate Word logically leads to a misunderstanding of the mystery of the Church, since the Church is nothing other than the Incarnate Word “extended and communicated.” It is not surprising, then, that a Christological Nestorianism should lead to an ecclesiological Nestorianism. By denying –as some sedevacantists and some progressives do– that there is a single head in the Church, they seek to destroy the unity of the Mystical Body –just as they seek to destroy the unity of the Incarnate Word– since there cannot be a single Body if there were not a single Head, nor a single Church if there were not a single Chief, as the Incarnate Word himself teaches us: “There will be one flock and one Shepherd” (Jn 10:16). The “chanta”

Reflection of the Founder on the occasion of the feast of St. Louis Marie The Lord says: “Whoever loves me will be faithful…” (Jn 14:23) One of the forms of lack of fidelity into which people very often fall is the one proper to the “chanta.” The “chantas” are among those chiefly responsible for the mediocrity of communities. And in some, “chantism” is an attitude of life. We will look at: First: What is it? Second: Its remedies. * * * 1. What is it? Popular speech calls certain people “chantapufi,” which comes from the Genoese “ciantapufi” = one who does not pay his debts or keep his promises. The shortened form chanta is common with the same meaning, as are the augmentative chantún and the superlative chantumazo. He is a mixture of show-off, conceited fellow and braggart. The show-off is the one who pretends to be different from what he is. The conceited fellow is the one fond of giving himself importance. The braggart is the one who makes a manifest display of what he is not. The chanta is a combination of all of them, identical in their essential inauthenticity. His essence: he seems, but he is not. He is concerned with what people will say; that is why he needs an audience to look at him and admire him, and before which he acts according to his own poses. There have been famous ones: – Tartarin of Tarascon… imagines himself to be what he is not. – The master of Lazarillo de Tormes… appears before others in a way that does not correspond to reality. … he is the one who nods with a knowing look without having the slightest idea. … he is the one who makes impossible or simply fantastical plans. … if he is a cook, he over-salts the food on several occasions. … when it is time to work, they always find an excuse. … during study time he gets up for any reason at all. … at adoration, he always leaves for physiological needs. … he commits himself to something, and then disappears… … intellectually, he talks a lot and says nothing. – He carries around under his arm every book he finds. – He never finishes reading any of them. – He does not go deeply into any subject. – He is full of plans, to write in the future. – He is never on time to hand in the monthly paper on the set day, nor does he make it to the Thomistic Conferences. He always asks for an extension. He acts as if he were interested in a subject, but the only thing that interests him is to appear and be noticed. … he improvises everything and expects to “pull rabbits out of the hat” – e.g., there is half an hour left before the triduum and only then does he remember the prayers… he has to lead the singing… and he chooses the songs on the fly… 2. Remedies Reject appearances. Show ourselves as we are, with simplicity, without hypocrisy, but without the impertinent brashness that confuses authenticity with spontaneity… killing can be spontaneous… Be humble, acknowledge our limitations. Be “faithful” to the Word of Christ, to the Will of Christ. * * * Dear brothers, in one way or another we are all more or less chantas. All of us… except the saints. We are chantas to the extent of our own inauthenticity. Let us imitate St. Louis Marie. In him there was nothing of the chanta. That is why they persecuted him. That is why they hated him. That is why he was a saint. Let us ask him to obtain for us the grace of authenticity.
THE EUCHARIST DELIGHTS

Homily preached by Rev. Fr. Carlos Miguel Buela on Sunday, June 18, at the Holy Mass of the Solemnity of Corpus Christi I “Eat, friends, drink, O beloved, be drunk!” (Song 5:1). St. Thomas applies this verse of the Song of Songs to the Eucharist 1 . This is one of the effects of the Eucharist: TO DELIGHT. (“Delectat,” says St. Thomas 2 ). Just as material food delights the body, this spiritual food delights the soul. That is why: “Eat, friends, drink, O beloved, be drunk!” (Song 5:1). This sacrament spiritually gives grace together with charity. Hence St. John Damascene compares it to the burning coal that the prophet Isaiah saw: “Just as the coal is not simply wood, but wood with fire, so the bread of communion is not ordinary bread, but bread united to the divinity” 3 . O miraculous thing! The banquet and the one who invites are one and the same 4 . II “Eat, friends, drink, O beloved, be drunk!” (Song 5:1). St. Gregory the Great teaches that “the love of God is not idle, but, when it is possessed, it works great things” 5 ; it follows that this sacrament has of itself the efficacy not only to give the habit of grace and of virtue –especially of charity– but also to stir up the act of charity, because, as St. Paul says, “the love of Christ urges us on” (2 Cor 5:14). With the love of Christ “the soul is strengthened, spiritually delights, and in some way becomes inebriated with the sweetness of the divine goodness,” teaches St. Thomas 6 . The soul… “delights and in some way becomes inebriated!” Hence: “Eat, friends, drink, O beloved, be drunk!” (Song 5:1). That is why we exclaim in the “Anima Christi”: “Blood of Christ, inebriate us!” O miraculous thing! The banquet and the one who invites are one and the same. III St. Thomas calls this delight the actual effect or actual charity 7 , and also fervor, because it implies actuality, and a tense actuality. The grace of the Eucharist, which theologians call nourishing grace, among other things actually produces the sustaining of the spiritual life, its increase, its development, the repairing of the strength that is lost, giving greater habitual grace and greater habitual charity. But beyond the actuality of the habit there is the actuality of the act into which the possessed habit bursts forth. The Eucharist produces love of God in souls. That is why, when we are at Mass, we love more; that is why the Mass does us good, because it teaches us to love our neighbor more by teaching us to love God more. This delight produced by the Eucharist is also called joy, because it comes from the actual perception of the good that one possesses –nothing less than Christ!– for which there must be no distraction in the reception –sacramental or spiritual– of the Eucharist. Many souls lose the actual delight of the Eucharist… because they are distracted at Mass or at Adoration! Set aside foolish distractions!: “Eat, friends, drink, O beloved, be drunk!” (Song 5:1). IV The delight produced by the Eucharist is not necessarily sensible, nor is it a sensible affection either. It is a spiritual joy, a deep joy of the soul, a supernatural joy that comes from the appreciation of the great good that is received: the Lord, Jesus Christ!, with all that he is and with all that he has. That is why Don Miguel de Cervantes Savedra says, in a poem: O miraculous thing! The banquet and the one who invites are one and the same. The delight consists substantially in the promptness of the will for the virtuous works of the Christian life. Besides actual distractions, that is, at the moment of communion, what other things impede the delight of the Eucharist? Venial sins. Actual venial faults impede the actual effect of the Eucharist; not the habitual effect, but certainly the actual one. The spiritual sweetness is infallible on the part of the sacrament, but actual attachment to venial faults or actual distraction at the moment of Communion –sacramental or spiritual– impede the effect of actual joy, of spiritual fervor, of delight or of actual love, which are all the same thing. V “Eat, friends, drink, O beloved, be drunk!” (Song 5:1). Urban IV said of the Eucharist: an admirable and stupendous memorial, delightful, sweet… in which every delight and every sweetness of flavor is tasted, and the very sweetness of God is savored…” 8 And Leo XIII: “it pours into (souls) the sweetest joys, which far exceed anything that men can understand and appreciate in this matter” 9 . That is why: Dear friends, “Eat, …drink, …be drunk!” (Song 5:1). O miraculous thing! The banquet and the one who invites are one and the same. Panem de coelo praestitisti eis. Omne delectamentum in se habentem. You gave us, Lord, bread from heaven. Containing in itself every delight! Notes 1 S.Th. III, 79, 1, ad 2. 2 S.Th. III, 79, 1 c. 3 De fide orthod. l. 4, c.13. 4 Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra, «La Sagrada Eucaristía» 5 In Evang. l. 2, Homily 30. 6 Same as note 1. 7 S.Th. III, 79, 1, ad 2; a. 4 c; a. 8. 8 Const. Transiturus, 1364. 9 Encyclical Mirae caritatis, March 28, 1902.
