For example, since they have to deal with young people (and they are all decrepit, all with arthritis, with rheumatism), they get the idea of wearing a toupee, dyeing their hair, wearing blue jeans, having… and they do not realize that this very thing is repulsive to young people, because, after all, for a person to grow old is the most normal thing there is, since the same thing happens to all of us. To pretend otherwise, being a religious, is no longer so interesting. That is why we must always ask Jesus Christ for the grace of fidelity to him, which takes concrete form in fidelity to the living Magisterium of the Church −what Peter teaches− and ask him for the grace not to fall into that labyrinth which is progressivism, manifested in a thousand forms and a thousand different ways. I have always asked for the grace to maintain, preserve and increase the authentic Catholic faith. And in the midst of all that havoc, God glories in raising up holiness and works great things. For example, what World Youth Day in Manila (Philippines) was. For the first time in the history of the world −since the world has been the world, since man has walked the planet earth− for the first time, for a religious event, the number of people gathered that gathered in Manila. According to L’Osservatore Romano , which is not given to exaggeration, five million people attended!, that is, five times the number of people who gathered in Buenos Aires when the Pope came to Argentina. Never has any politician, never ever, been able to gather such a number of people. And it was a man who called them together, a weak man who falls getting out of the shower, who trips over his cassock and fractures his shoulder, who was once shot, a weak man… but one to whom Jesus Christ promised, in the person of Peter, that the gates of hell would not prevail against the Church founded upon him. That man called them together, the man who continues to preach an unpopular doctrine, because to say nowadays that divorce is wrong is unpopular, to say that abortion is wrong is unpopular, to say that premarital relations are wrong is unpopular, to say that spouses in marriage must perform the act open to life is unpopular. Nevertheless, one sees that in the depths of the conscience of humanity, in the depths of the conscience of Christians, the thirst for truth still beats, even for truth in the moral order, even though it may be hard for one to live up to it. We have this example, unique in the present-day world. There is not a single leader in the present-day world of the spiritual and moral caliber, of the leadership that John Paul II exercises, and this because he is faithful to Jesus Christ and because he is a true Son and Slave of the Blessed Virgin. Let us ask her to know how to imitate, in spite of our limitations, in the place where God puts us, this giant whom God has raised up, this “Viking of God,” as they called him on the trip he made to Mexico in ’79, so as not to give in before all the confusion of Christian progressivism, which is ravaging the Church. Let us sing to Our Lady.”
Purity

Homily preached by Fr. Carlos Miguel Buela to the students of the “Isabel la Católica” school on the occasion of the feast of their co-patroness St. Edith Stein, on August 9, 1999 On this very special day on which we celebrate this great woman who was St. Edith Stein, I want to leave you a lesson in a beautiful, artistic way, with a beautiful fable that Fr. Leonardo Castellani gives in his famous book Camperas. It is a fable that illustrates an enormous truth, a truth that the saint we celebrate today illuminated with her life. The fable is called “The Mire,” and it is about purity. A boy is talking with his dad: “ – Dad, can I go to the marsh? -No. -Why? -Because I said no. -I'm not going to drown. Don't you know the saying: How deep could the marsh be, if a cat crossed it at a gallop? It doesn't even come up to my knee.” Then the dad begins to tell this boy the story of an Englishman, the manager of the “Los Tilos” sugar mill, who one day went into the marsh, broke the wing of a white heron, and went in to look for it. A white heron was worth 200 pesos back then. And this Englishman thought he knew all the secrets. The secrets of the woods, perhaps, “but the secrets of the marsh, the secrets of the mire, nobody knows to the bottom. They have no bottom. The farmhand he took with him was also an outsider. And they said: ‘The water comes up to our knees at most.’” (That is the first lie of the marsh. It will go no further; the water comes up to the knee.) “The wounded heron went flapping its wings further and further in, further and further in. How wide is the marsh? Who can know? In the dry season it may be half a league or perhaps one. But in the rainy season the whole lowland floods. And when, on top of that, the Amores River overflows, who can know the leagues of water and mud that stretch beneath the green and lying mantle of water hyacinth that covers it? It all fills with rushes and bulrushes, so that it looks like a field of oats. A lovely field. In the peace of the quiet afternoon, the sun varnishes it and the wind gently ripples it. Up above, everything is beauty and charm. The white and purple flowers. The pink flamingos, which also look like great living flowers. The ducks, the gray herons, the jabirus. A red-breasted bird that rises chirping and flies in joyful circles. A little blue puddle here and there, where the sky is painted. And beneath all that beauty, the mud, stinking, who knows how many meters of mud. That is what vice is like. That is what a vice is like, one that you do not know yet. But the Englishman was wearing high boots, and the heron was close by, tempting his greed. How lovely the little white heron, delicate and graceful! The Englishman, who was stubborn, set his heart on it. And on and on they go, at times in two spans of mud, and at times over almost dry ground, which reassured them. That is how it is: that is the diabolical lie of the swamp. That is how it also goes…” with vice. (It is the lie: yes, one sinks a little at times, but then one gets out. One goes to confession, it seems one is safe. But one remains in the occasion of sin.) “-Did they catch it, Dad, the little heron? -I don't know. What does that matter? Suddenly they came to a patch of reeds and there they stepped on firm ground and looked around. The farmhand said: -Let's go back, boss. And the Englishman said: -What is that group of trees over there in front of us? Isn't it the bed of the Amores? -It seems to me it must be, said the other. -We have to cross the marsh and get over there, said the Englishman. It's close. When the Englishman said ‘We have to,’ there was no turning him around. It's close! Haven't you seen what happens on the pampa, a little hut or some trees that seem to be very close, and one walks and walks and never gets there? That is the other lie of the swamp. (It is the lie of thinking that one will soon get out. It is another lie of the swamp.) Happiness is just over there, and one looks and longs, and runs and runs, and never, never gets there. And their legs sank deeper and deeper, and the mud was thinner and stickier. -Let's go back, boss. But the Englishman cursed and kept going. The trees were right there. Try to always step on top of the bulrushes. Careful, splash… A hidden pool, no need to be frightened, just a soaking… although even the cartridges in the cartridge belt have gotten wet, damn it. Now a detour; there is a dead cow over there, and an unbearable stench… Let's go back, boss. Go back, yes. The boss's face was somber and bathed in sweat: but was going back still possible? (There comes a point, when one is in the swamp, when it seems that one is closer to getting out than to going back.) Night was rushing down upon them, and it was better to make a superhuman effort and reach, even if half-dead, the banks over there, which were now much closer than the ones back here. The decision was desperate, but no other could be thought of anymore, if indeed those heads, upon which Terror had already cast its trembling and treacherous shadows, were now in any state to think. And indeed, the dreadful thing happened. They fell into a mud pit and sank up to their hips, and night fell upon them. The moon with its immense mantle of shimmering silver, and the stars that gaze at themselves in the waters as in a mirror of steel, watched impassively the flailing, the plunging, the falling sideways and face-down in the mud, the snapping of the vines they clung to, the despair of those who feel the ground give way inch by inch, the agony of living bodies swallowed by the slimy and fatal mouth of the lagoon. And they heard cries of horror and desperate curses. -Kill me, boss. Do you have a cartridge left? Shoot me, please. Then the cries ceased. The marsh is evil and treacherous and an enemy of the human race. No one can understand the agony of that night. Suddenly, in the midst of the funereal splendor of the full moon, a voice abruptly began to sing: it was the farmhand Benito. He had gone mad. And then the diabolical marsh began to sing too. It sang perversely, with its thousands of crickets, of toads, of frogs, of whispering rushes, of moaning waters, with the voice of the thousands of suckers of mud that swallow. Glug, glu, glu, said the marsh. Haven't you seen mad Benito, the poor old man, how he howls every night of the full moon, feeling inside his brain the horrible song of triumph of the marsh? He says he heard it sing, that it said Glu, glu, that it laughed. And it is true that he heard it sing. -How did he get out, Dad? -He got out on his own. Nobody knows how he got out. From the swamp, if one does not get out on one's own –and it is a miracle of God–, no one else can get him out; you can't go on horseback or on foot, you can't go by boat… -And the Englishman? -And there we were, searching for them in the woods! We could never have imagined that they were in the marsh, after so many warnings… Until we heard the shot of the Englishman's Martini rifle, which had a powerful voice, it never occurred to us that… -Dad, but what became of the Englishman? -Look, do you see that rusty rifle in the corner? Once, three or four years later, there was a great flood of the Amores. Floating islands of water hyacinth were coming down the river, full of snakes, rushes and rubbish. On one of them (I found it) came that rifle, and beside it a skull split by a bullet. The rest of the Englishman, even his bones, the swamp had swallowed. -Dad! –said the Gurí , turning his eyes away and shuddering all over–. How horrible! Why did you keep it? -To show it to my children and tell them: all those who go deliberately into the swamp of lust have always said: I'll only go as far as there. The mud doesn't come up any higher than my knee.” (That is the great lie of the swamp.) That is how it is with you. How many good girls! How many good young women I have known in my life! “Only as far as there.” First, not giving importance to knowingly entertaining bad thoughts, to watching bad television programs. Then, sometimes pushed by their own mothers, having a little boyfriend. The caresses begin, the kisses, the bad dances. Then they ask her for the proof of love. She becomes pregnant. Sometimes they force her to have an abortion. It is like the swamp. And it does not all happen at once, but little by little. And at some point they find themselves stepping on firm ground because they went to confession, and then they think that, well, now they are all right. But they remain in the swamp. And the swamp swallows everything. That is why you should ask St. Edith Stein, your patroness, on this her feast day, for the grace to know how to defend that beautiful virtue, the most beautiful virtue of purity. And know how to defend it “now,” from now on and always! Above all with the difficulties that abound in this world in which we have to live, that beautiful –most beautiful!– virtue. Do not let yourselves be deceived by the flowers on top of the swamp. Yes, the pretty things… Ah, what a cute little nose he has… Oh, light-colored eyes! What a handsome boy! But the mud below… Don't be foolish. Think of your children. Think that you must know how to form honest families. Think that you must be young women with a sense of your own dignity. That you must not let yourselves be taken as objects, that you are persons and not things, and respect yourselves. Beware of the swamp. Once one goes in, only one can get oneself out, and only by a miracle. Because there is no help that avails, neither from your mother, nor from a priest, nor from the Sisters, nor from anyone. When one goes in, one thinks one will get out easily, and many times one never gets out again. We also ask this grace of the Blessed Virgin.
Seminaries!, not semi-asinaries

Good-night talk given by Fr. Carlos Miguel Buela on April 28, 1998, on the occasion of the feast of St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort, at the “Marcelo Javier Morsella” Novitiate It occurred to me to give a good-night talk on a special topic, as we generally do on the day of St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort. In a special way for me, because precisely in these days I was thinking about how God does things, how God has gone about forming one. It is not by chance that whatever happens happens, that we have whatever we have. And for me the most important thing we have is the Major Seminary. It is the “goose that lays the golden eggs” of the Congregation. That is why the topic I want to address in this good-night talk is that of priestly formation, because I personally think that the most important thing we have in our congregation, as I already said, is precisely the Major Seminary. To develop the topic, I will first recount some seminary experiences that I think will be useful, and then I will give some points of what I think is important to bear in mind in order to have a good seminary. I. SEMINARY EXPERIENCES In seminary X, I had a classmate who did not believe in virginity. I gave him Pius XII's encyclical “ Sacra Virginitas ,” and he laughed. I mention it to a spiritual director, and he answers me: –“That was a very weak encyclical that Pius XII wrote.” I thought: “They are of the same family,” as Castellani says in the story of the Quillotana. It is a most beautiful encyclical! Among my classmates I had men who had been Marxist trade unionists, who were no longer trade unionists but were still Marxists; also a Freudian psychologist, a diplomat… All of these left. But it was a tremendous thing. Thank goodness that, by the grace of God, when I was a member of Catholic Action I had studied from a manual of apologetics by Naguemela, from Hilaire, from Olgiati, etc., which taught the central notions of the faith with great clarity. There were points of the faith that these classmates did not believe simply because they had not studied them. I remember that once –it was the time of the Council– a seminarian was running and shouting through the halls of the Seminary with the magazine “Criterio” in his hand: “…priests have to marry, priests have to marry!” The general atmosphere of the Seminary was hostile to celibacy. So much so that for a week, in prayer, I was asking God for light to see what I had to do. The proposal some were making was that it would be obligatory for priests to marry. I was aware that there was no power on earth that could oblige me to marry if I did not want to. But I asked myself: if they give permission to marry, what am I doing in the seminary? Because if I am thinking of marrying, I have to patch things up with the girlfriend I left, I have to start looking for work and housing, because to marry one has to have the means of support… So I said to myself: “God gave me the charism of giving myself to him totally, and I am going to give myself to him totally, with his grace.” I remember that in my little room I had a window that looked out onto a terrace. From there one could see those who passed by, who were the kind who never study. One of those days one of them says to me: – “So? How are you doing?” –“Very well, happy…” – “Ha, ha! It'll pass. What's happening is that you're on your honeymoon now.” In another seminary… From one day to the next thirty-five seminarians left. Thirty-five! In one theology class only six of us remained. Of those who left, many were admirable: virtuous, upright, pious, joyful… Of the professors I had, the one I remember most (it stayed etched in my mind) was the one who denied the bodily resurrection of Our Lord Jesus Christ. Incredible! But there were also other kinds of professors. For example, one whose material for teaching his class fit on a little piece of paper the size of a tram ticket. Then he would say: “In class we are going to cover three points: point one, blah, blah, blah.” At the end of the class we would ask: –“And the second and third points?”; the answer was: –“I already covered them.” And so he taught the class badly, and who knew what he had covered. Another, if he taught Deo Uno , one barely got to learn that God was one, and if he taught Deo Trino , one never got to the trinity of persons. Twelve of those professors left the priesthood. One December 8 we were in a neighborhood where we had gone to take part in a First Communion Mass. At one point, a Seminary professor was standing next to a priest who was Galician. The priest said to the First Communion children: –“Well, that business of loving God, that was before. Now you have to love your neighbor, because God is very far away. How are you going to say that you love God?” First, does not the first commandment of the law of God say that one must “love God above all things”? Second, God is not far away; he is more interior to us than we are to ourselves; he is in heaven, on earth, everywhere. And the professor, instead of correcting the priest, on the contrary, was laughing. So one had to study the subjects twice: once to take the exam and again to see what the doctrine of the Church was. Fr. Ángel Mancuso, when he was a seminarian, had to take an exam but did not want to study from the notes given by the professor of Deo Creante : “This is heresy; I'm not going to study from this.” So in the exam he presented what he understood to be the Catholic faith. And the professor failed him because he had not studied according to what had been taught in class. For the second exam he said to himself: “I am going to present what the professor said, but God knows that I don't believe any of this, so what I am going to say is simply to pass the exam.” He took the exam according to what the professor had taught in class, and the professor failed him as a heretic. In his simplicity, he had drawn the conclusions to which such principles led. Something the professor did not do! Another seminary… The room of one of the seminarians: there was a picture of a finger writing on the sand: “ I love you .” Next to the picture, a prayer of Teilhard de Chardin about the world. In the middle of the room, a stereo system with all the music of the moment. … At that time the spiritual director used the “Medellín Documents” for spiritual direction. How can one teach Spirituality from the “Medellín Documents”? It is a mystery. One seminarian put little labels on his flowerpots, took care of them, watered them, got up half an hour early to tend his little flowerpots… The seminarians, with their own keys, go out, come and go, come in, and all at whatever hour. The philosophy students with girlfriends. They are given Freud, Hegel, Rahner to study, as if they were something good. In another seminary, the rectors came to remain in office for fifteen days, or a month, at most three months. With the aggravating factor that one of them, besides being rector of the Seminary, was pastor of the Cathedral, which is located kilometers away. Sometimes, even in Seminaries that we suppose to be good, one can notice that they fall into the crassest, coarsest formalism. At bottom they fall into pastoral Jansenism, where what prevails is the supposed letter of the supposed law, rather than the spirit that should reign in the heart of a priest ready to give his life for others. The main shortcomings occur, in my view, in different areas: disciplinary, doctrinal, intellectual, pastoral. Even charity disappears. Discipline grows lax: getting up in the morning at a fixed time is questioned; the fact that everyone has to get up at the same time is a coercion, because if someone had stayed up at night praying (generally it was daydreaming), then in the morning he could get up later, etc. Therefore Mass and meditation, which was only half an hour, were optional. There was a certain piety, but properly speaking it was a pietism without content, without strength. Without forming men who eagerly seek the principle and foundation, who seek to reach God, who use the means in spite of their sins, their miseries. But no, they did not see that relationship with the heavenly Father. In seminaries like that, the one who realizes it may well ask himself whether he is not the only one who has faith. When the case of the one who denied the bodily resurrection of Christ was put to the rector of the seminary, he answered: “What a thing! Some say that Christ did not rise bodily, but well, don't worry about it. There are many who hold that at most there are three miracles in Sacred Scripture.” The rector of the seminary! Those who ought to be specialists in priestly formation! There was not much preaching; rather, there was little, and all very superficial. It was an insisting “on love, on love, affection, unity…” They preached unity and love, but among themselves they were all divided. “Pastoral, pastoral, pastoral.” Pastoral was nothing more than methods, without effective practical application: pastoral work was reduced entirely to method alone and it was a failure. Pastoral work consisted in seeking the latest novelty and in settling in at people's homes. They went for that and they failed. I was able to work with modern methods –such as those of “discussion groups,” and Phillips 66– with much success. The point is to apply the good methods but giving them a religious sense; and not to fill them with contents of another kind, foreign to the Gospel. From the intellectual point of view, a great, total void. Not a single topic could be discussed in depth. The “ disputatio ” was unknown, and the vast majority did not even know St. Thomas. From the doctrinal point of view, they did not know the elementary things we had learned when we were aspirants of Catholic Action, such as the commandments of the law of God, the precepts of the Church, the works of mercy. They were not known, and they were not studied. Finally, the most serious thing of all was that charity was not lived in concrete terms. And a great many other things. In conclusion: all this bad priestly formation –together with the lack of creativity and of respect for individualities– inevitably leads to weariness, to a lack of joy, to a permanent questioning of what the priest is. It leads to a profound identity crisis, to holding superficially every topic under discussion, and even the truths and articles of the faith. II. WHAT IS NEEDED FOR THERE TO BE A GOOD SEMINARY The lesson of this, my particular and non-transferable experience, is that one must reflect in order to find a solution. By the grace of God, that is what we have tried to do, are doing, and are trying to do. To have a good Seminary two fundamental things are required: 1. A homogeneous team of formators What does homogeneous mean? That they have the same essential criteria regarding priestly formation, that they work united, that they know that the work of forming a seminary is a work that requires much sacrifice, that many times the fruits are not seen, that many times there are several pastoral failures. 2. The seminarians This is because the Seminary is not made by the formators alone. Nor is it made by the seminarians alone. But if one has a very good team of formators but does not have seminarians who have “the right stuff,” who seriously want to seek holiness, who want to be formed (to the extent of each one's possibilities), one does not have a Seminary. This year I am particularly happy because I believe we have a good team of formators in the Seminary. Perhaps as we have never had before. I believe that the reinforcements we have made, and the fact that there are more priests who can dedicate themselves full time to the Seminary, is very important. There is no action at a distance, nor is it written in souls with a pen alone, as Plato said. Nor is it written in the soul of the seminarian with a pen alone. The seminarian has to see the priest –even with the mistakes we have, so as not to commit them–. There has to be closeness. And realize that these are the two essential things for having a good Seminary. III. ELEMENTS NECESSARY FOR A GOOD FORMATION IN THE SEMINARY Formation must not be a formation that is merely orthodox in doctrine –which is already a great deal. That is not enough. Formation in the seminary for the future priest must be integral . No empty spaces must be left. That is, the whole soul of the seminarian must be evangelized, because if we leave something unevangelized, then later that unevangelized something is going to turn against him, and that can be a cause of misfortune, of problems, of giving up, even from the human point of view. Hence the irreplaceable importance of the camps in Bariloche, to give one example. Seminarians must be formed who practice sports, as should normally be done; who work –like the work of the cooks, which is an admirable thing. Eutrapelia must be practiced and fostered; that is, they should be normal men who are clear about the true meaning of festivity, who are joyful. One of the things that has most struck me in seminaries is that they are all stressed out by study: “Well… it's because they study a lot.” As far as I know, none of them has distinguished himself in anything, none of them has published any book. Another very important aspect is that of music. That must always be watched over, because when some seminarian begins to like bad music, it is a bad sign. It is a sign that spiritually he is declining, because evidently “the style is the man.” If there is a man who likes stupid music, not on the occasion of having fun, or in order to have fun, but who gets hooked on that music, it means that spiritually he is going about in foolishness. “The style is the man.” In a monastery there was a Christ made out of twine, all twisted –poor Christ–. When a brother was asked: “–And what is this? How can this be?” he answered: – “Well, but it's just a detail.” It is a detail, yes, but life is a sum of details. Formation must be integral; men with their own engine must be formed. That was a great longing, and in part I feel very gratified because after years we have managed to have young men who think, who study philosophy in depth, seeking to have a metaphysical mind. This preparation is extremely important in order to be capable afterwards of knowing, seeking and finding solutions to the extremely complex problems that present themselves today. Solutions do not come out just like that, like an air plant. Solutions are years of thinking, of seeing, of deciding, of weighing pros and cons, of studying. Deep intellectual formation in metaphysics must give the most complete knowledge possible of St. Thomas (this must surely be one of the greatest graces we have had in the seminary and that we continue to have). What has been done is not enough. The new generations must continue carrying out, as Pius XI said, an “ite ad Tomas” (go to St. Thomas). One must go and get to know not only the Summa Theologiae, but all the rest of his brilliant output, and the more and more, the better. The sense of beauty must be formed; that is, young men must be formed whose stomachs turn viscerally when they are faced with something ugly, in bad taste. May there become incarnate in them what Alexander Solzhenitsyn repeats (although in reality it is a phrase of Fyodor Dostoevsky): “Beauty will save the world.” Fidelity to the Magisterium of the Church: who could think of teaching something outside the Magisterium of the Church? Christ promised only to Peter, and in the person of Peter to his successors, “upon this rock I will build my Church” ( Mt 16:18). Spirituality must be robust, not mere sentimentality. The life of discipline. Another of the graces I believe we have is that there is a climate of great joy, a climate that seems to me to be one of great interior freedom, but nevertheless there is seriousness, discipline. Pastoral life. This means pastoral work in concrete terms; one must not do as those who talk and talk about pastoral work and remain in pure theories. Pastoral work must be a concrete accomplishment. That is why I believe it is also a grace that our men are taught what popular missions are, how to carry them out in concrete terms. A realistic and true pastoral work includes the Spiritual Exercises, vocational ministry, spiritual direction, sacred oratory, youth ministry, catechesis, concrete work with the poor. Regarding this last point, I want to recommend that you never abandon the poor. If you have the poor with you, then you will have God with you. Never abandon the poor or the sick, who are poor in health. IV. CONCLUSION I want to recall these things that I think are fundamental, because the test, the great test of priestly formation, you do not have now in the seminary. The test of priestly formation is outside. When it falls to you to do mission work in the Amazon jungle, there the true test will come. It is gratifying to see the maturity and the acquisition of supernatural criteria in newly ordained priests who are in mission territory. It is a very interesting thing to see that maturing that is reached later in the priesthood, because when one is a seminarian one does not know what it is to be a priest. One has the theory about what the priest is, but one does not know, because one does not experience what it is to be a priest. One knows what it is to be a priest when one is a priest, when one celebrates Mass, when one hears confessions, when one preaches, when one gives spiritual direction. Only then does one know what the priest is. Because before, you see the priest “from the outside.” Therefore, with renewed enthusiasm, let us continue our task, asking in a special way of the Blessed Virgin, and on this day also of St. Louis Marie, the grace to form great priests: priests according to the Heart of Jesus, slaves of the Blessed Virgin, abounding in spirit, ready to set alight this world that is dying of cold because it is atheist, Marxist, secularist, to set it ablaze with the faith and with the charity of Christ.
Pharisaism, the cancer of religion

Homily of Rev. Fr. Carlos M. Buela, V.E., preached at the Sunday Holy Mass to the young people of the “Blessed Pier Giorgio Frassati” festive oratory, in November 1995 In the Gospel we have just heard, we are told the famous parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector. The Pharisee –who thought himself righteous– enters the temple all full of pride, and speaks to God as one equal to another: “O God! I thank you that I am not like other men, thieves, unjust, adulterers, nor even like this tax collector” (Lk 18:11). The tax collector, on the contrary –who considered himself a sinner because he was the collector of taxes– had stayed at the back of the temple. Unlike the Pharisee, he takes on a profoundly humble attitude. He keeps his distance, he does not even dare to raise his eyes to heaven, he strikes his breast –as when we pray the “I confess,” as a sign that we consider ourselves sinners and that we are repentant–. He says from the back of the temple: “O God! Have compassion on me, for I am a sinner!” (Lk 18:13). The Pharisees were a group of men who had certain characteristics that we are going to analyze. In man, each organ has its own disease: the disease of the eyes is called conjunctivitis; that of the stomach, gastritis; that of the liver, hepatitis; that of the bronchi, bronchitis. In animals the same thing happens: the most common disease in dogs is called rabies, in cows foot-and-mouth disease, and so we could go on with countless examples. In religion, the disease proper to it is Pharisaism. It is, as it were, the cancer of religion, the syphilis of religion. Our Lord Jesus Christ fought tooth and nail against the Pharisees of his time –against the Pharisees of all times– who are the ones who finally brought him to death. And how does Jesus characterize Pharisaism? He characterizes it perfectly in the twenty-third chapter of the Gospel of St. Matthew. There he describes everything these men did. Let us base ourselves, then, on this chapter to describe the fundamental elements of Pharisaism. First characteristic: hypocrisy. On the outside, they pretended to be religious, but on the inside they were not. They wore phylacteries hanging on their cloaks, and on their foreheads inscriptions of the Law, of the Torah and of the commandments, because it is written: “…the commandments (of Yahweh) …shall be as a sign between your eyes…” (Dt 6:1.8). But what about the inside? Inside, interiorly, they were corrupt, putrid. That is why Jesus compares them to whitewashed tombs. For them, it was a sin to touch tombs; that is why they whitened them with lime: so that their presence would be noticed and no one would walk on them. From the outside, they looked clean because of the whiteness of the lime, but inside there was only rottenness. Such were the Pharisees, and such are the Pharisees of all times, in our time as well. I always say that the seminary is the factory of priests, because that is what it is. But if there is no good formation, it becomes a factory of Pharisees! Because it is very easy to put the emphasis of religion on external things and forget that the main thing is in the interior. That is why Jesus says in the Gospel of St. Matthew: “They say, and do not do ” (Mt 23:3). They said many things, they had hundreds of precepts, which they themselves invented, but they did not keep them. For example, to see the absurdity rabbinic legislation reached, it is enough to consider what the topics of their disputes were: they argued among themselves –in the time of Our Lord– over whether it was lawful to eat the egg that a hen laid on the Sabbath , because in laying the egg, it worked, and on the Sabbath –according to Pharisaic law– one cannot work. Ridiculous! Second characteristic: ostentation. They wanted to show others their goodness, their piety, their religiosity. “…they make their phylacteries very broad and the tassels of their cloaks very long, they want the first place at banquets and the first seats in the synagogues…” (Mt 23:5-6). It is religion turned into ostentation, an external thing. Third characteristic: contempt for one's neighbor. It is the case of the Pharisee in the temple: “I am not like other men, thieves, unjust, adulterers, nor even like that tax collector.” They consider others inferior. That is why they are like parsley: they get into everything (in my day parsley was used in every meal; now I think it is no longer used). In conversations they only talk about themselves, about their things, about their problems, about what they did, about what they are going to do, about what they think… They only talk about themselves, and they do not listen to others. Why? Because they despise them, because for them the most important ones are themselves. At bottom, they are the center of the world. They think they are the center of the world! They despise their neighbor above all if he is ignorant, poor or a sinner. “This man eats with scribes and tax collectors” (Mt 9:11), they said of Jesus. Fourth characteristic: a false delicate conscience. In some things they are strict, exaggeratedly strict, and in others lax, exaggeratedly lax. As sometimes happens with some, who demand of people things that people cannot do. And they fail to do what they have to do, such as providing the means for them to have Mass on Sunday! Jesus said it in a marvelous way: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who pay the tithe of mint, anise and cumin –some plants that grew in their gardens– and neglect the most important things of the Law: justice, mercy and faith! These are what you should have practiced, without neglecting the others. Blind guides, who strain out the gnat and swallow the camel!” (Mt 23:23-24). The law dictated that they could not eat the animal, yet they did eat roast camel, which is a very tasty meat, although it was forbidden by the law. They strained out the gnat, but swallowed the camel! Fifth characteristic: disguise. It is those people who have a smile at every moment, but since you already know them, you are waiting for them to plunge the dagger into your back. On the outside, they wear sheep's clothing; on the inside, they are wolves. They are “wolves in sheep's clothing,” as Our Lord said. They hide their lack of mercy toward their neighbor under the cloak of a false religion. And so it is that the Pharisees bring about the crucifixion of Our Lord Jesus Christ on the pretext that he healed on the Sabbath. They kill the Only Son of God, the Incarnate Word. Why? Because he did not keep an external precept of their religion. And this, dear brothers –I take this opportunity to say it especially to the young people–, is something that happens today, unfortunately! Many Christians, many Catholics, are Pharisees; they are Catholics in name only, on the outside. Sometimes without fault, because no one has taught them; but sometimes, in some cases, it happens because they fall into this evil, into this deep vice of the religious man, which is to make religion something merely exterior. Hence also the seriousness of this evil, as Our Lord points out. What is the greatest seriousness of the Pharisee? The greatest seriousness is religion without love. The Pharisees are those who neither enter nor let others enter. That is why many times in our groups –of young people or adults– there are people who would like to enter, but do not, because there are Pharisees who do not enter but do not let others enter either. As Our Lord Jesus Christ also said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the Kingdom of Heaven to men! You certainly do not enter; and those who are entering you do not allow to enter” (Mt 23:13). What are the remedies? In the first place, to study the virtues of Our Lord Jesus Christ: patience, humility, love, the spirit of service, self-giving to others. All the virtues of Our Lord, in order to imitate them. These virtues are diametrically opposed to the vices of the old Pharisees. Our Lord taught an eminently interior religion, which is also manifested exteriorly, but is not mainly exterior, but mainly interior. And the most important thing of what he came to bring is the New Law, which is faith working through charity in our heart, and that is interior, it is infused. In the second place, we must manifest with our life, with our works, with our words, evangelical truth and simplicity, against Pharisaic falsehood. In the third place, we must be humble, as Our Lord teaches: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted.” And against Pharisaic pride, he teaches: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Lk 14:11). In the fourth place, finally, to the contempt that the Pharisees have for the poor, for the ignorant and for sinners, we must oppose the love of Jesus Christ. If he shed his Blood on the Cross for them, we certainly can and must sacrifice ourselves for that most needy part of humanity. That is why we must do as the tax collector did, who, without raising his eyes to heaven, strikes his breast, saying: “Have mercy, Lord, for I am a sinner.” This is the religion that Jesus Christ taught us. And I believe that young people understand this language, because they are looking precisely for that Lord who never fails, for the One who dies no more because he has risen, for the One who has the words of eternal life. Let us ask Our Lady for this grace.
Craftiness

(astutia, sollertia, calliditas) St. Thomas studies craftiness as a vice opposed to prudence, but one that has a certain likeness to it. The crafty man is the prudent one, the one who thinks, the politician, the “clever” one. The crafty man is intelligent. But although he is intelligent, he is not of upright intelligence. He uses his intelligence to achieve his objective, whatever the means used. For St. Paul, craftiness is opposed to the clear manifestation of the truth. Crafty is the apostle who does not preach the truth, who falsifies the word of God: “Therefore, invested with this ministry of the mercy of God, we do not lose heart, of which we have been the object, we do not lose heart, nor with craftiness nor falsifying the word of God, we manifest the truth…” (2 Cor 4:1-3). In his commentary on the text, St. Thomas teaches us that craftiness goes against rectitude of intention. For there can be an outwardly evil work. “In the intention evil is avoided if the intention is upright, and for this reason he says NOT WALKING IN CRAFTINESS, that is, with craftiness, simulation, hypocrisy, like those who act falsely, aiming at one thing outwardly while inwardly they seek another” ( In II Cor 4:3). Being a vice of the intention, it has a particular seriousness: it is hidden and interior. And therefore more difficult to see and to correct. But it is not only hidden. There are other hidden vices: pride, despair, for example. Rather, its very essence is to hide, not to manifest. Hence St. Thomas relates it to simulation, hypocrisy, falsehood. It is the duplicity of which Scripture speaks: “I hate duplicity and I love your law.” (Ps 119:113) There are people who have a great capacity for concealment. It is typical of traitors. Let us think of Judas: how he must have hidden his plan from Christ and the Apostles. Even his very way of betraying him is hidden: “with a kiss…”. The gesture of love hides the inner contempt. In the Old Testament we find the case of the high priest Onias, murdered by the crafty Andronicus: “Andronicus came to Onias and, trusting in craftiness, clasping his hand and giving him his right hand with an oath, persuaded Onias, although the latter was not without suspicions, to come out of his refuge, and immediately put him to death, with no regard whatsoever for justice” (2 Mac 4:34). Among us, a bad intention can be hidden beneath a pious gesture, a kindly face, a smile. Also beneath tears, which make the adversary lower his guard and feel sorry. That is why the Martín Fierro said: “I believe neither in a dog's limp nor in a woman's tears.” It is best to concede nothing to the crafty man, for if a partial truth is conceded to him, he will easily use it to argue and to deduce from it, with great intelligence, erroneous, bad or less good conclusions. One must stand up to him, as St. Ignatius teaches with the example of the bad woman: “… it is proper to a woman, when she quarrels with a man, to lose heart and take flight when the man shows her a firm face; and, on the contrary, if the man begins to flee, losing heart, the anger, vengeance and ferocity of the woman grow very great and without measure…” (S.E. 325). Craftiness is opposed to simplicity. Simple is the one who is one, not two: the one outside and the one inside. The enemies of the Faith, says St. Paul, use craftiness : “…so that we may no longer be children, tossed about and carried along by every wind of doctrine through the deceitful game of men, who, to seduce, craftily employ the devices of error; but rather, embracing the truth, may we grow in all things in charity…” (Eph 4:14). It is proper to the crafty man to “play” with people. He is “agile”: he advances or retreats, he laughs or cries, he gets angry or asks for forgiveness, he acts the friend or acts offended, he pressures or feigns docility… all of this is a deceitful game to get people to think well of him, to tell him what he wants to hear, to give him that permission he is asking for. “Seducing” is proper to him (and in this woman is a specialist). Seduce comes from se-ducere : that is, to lead the other along with oneself; it is the art of bringing the other to my will, employing “the devices of error.” And how many devices it is possible to use. We can say with St. Louis Marie: “I would never finish if I wanted to describe here the twists and turns of nature…” ( Letter to the Friends of the Cross , n. 48). But in the same text St. Paul gives us the means to resist the crafty: “Embracing the truth.” Note the force of the expression, for a timid and superficial adherence is not enough when strong winds blow hard. Firm adherence to dogma. But not only to dogma. Firm adherence to spiritual truths, to the doctrine of the saints. Nor only that. Firm adherence to the concrete command of the superior. Summing up a little, we can say that two acts belong to the crafty man: scheming and deceiving. Scheming (excogitare) is the act by which he thinks, imagines, remembers what means to use to achieve his objective. Here the cogitative power, experience of people, intuition play a large part. In this sense, not everyone who wants to be crafty can be. He isn't even up to that, and so he “trips himself up,” “digs his own grave,” acts rashly. “There are fools who do not even know how to do evil,” says Scripture (Eccl 19:20). Deceiving is the exterior act. It is the execution of what was schemed. In this too, not everyone who wants to can. In the execution, the first means is the word, “for it holds the principal place among the signs by which man signifies something to another.” Hence guile is principally attributed to speech. However, one can also deceive by deeds. Hence the care we must have in our words. It is very common to distinguish between “what I said” and “what I meant to say.” This shows the little value we give to words. We empty them of rational content in order to fill them with affective content. May we be able to say: “Righteous are all the words of my mouth; there is nothing crafty or crooked in them” (Prov 8:8). Craftiness is also exercised through deeds: “There is one who goes about bent over and in mourning, but inside he is full of deceit. He keeps his head down and pretends to be deaf, but when you least expect it he is upon you” (Eccl 19:23-24). Craftiness is what is proper to the devil. That is why he is represented by the serpent, “the craftiest of all the animals” (Gen 3:1), for, like the serpent, the crafty man advances silently, knows how to hide and conceal himself among the foliage, knows how to wait for the opportune moment, attacks suddenly, is hard to catch, and is flexible and slippery. In this regard, St. Paul wrote to the Corinthians: “But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve with its craftiness, your minds may be corrupted, turning away from sincerity toward Christ” (2 Cor 11:3). Craftiness, among us, can be exercised between superiors and subjects. Cassian says that the ABC of monks was to give an account of every evil thought and temptation to their superiors. St. Ignatius says something similar: “it is greatly fitting that subjects make themselves fully known to their superiors” (Const. 34,4). This openness of conscience is what is most opposed to craftiness, for through it our interior is revealed, our intentions, good or bad. In religious life, craftiness is the means to achieve two opposite things at once: to obey the superior and to do my own will. And how do I do it? Simply by making the superior command what I want to do, so that he comes over to my will. And this is not obedience, though it may seem to be. Superiors too can act with craftiness, with a certain duplicity. With subjects we must be as transparent as we expect them to be with us. But this does not mean that the superior may not keep things, reasons, to himself, when it is for the good of the community. Let us proceed, then, in our life, as Christ himself did, “always embracing the truth.”

Prayer to Our Lady of Luján

Beloved Mother! Prayer in honor of the Queen and Patroness of our Institute, Our Lady of Luján Most Holy Virgin Mary of Luján, Daughter of God the Father, Mother of God the Son and Spouse of God the Holy Spirit, Heart of the Trinity! At the beginning of time, God gathered all the waters and called them: sea; when the fullness of time came He gathered all the graces and called them: Mary¹, Full of grace! So much so, that one sigh of yours for a soul has more power than all the prayers of the other saints together², Suppliant Omnipotence! At that very moment God created an irreconcilable enmity that will last forever between You, Immaculate Virgin, and Satan: “… I put enmity between you and the woman, between your offspring and her offspring…” (Gen 3:14-15). You are terrible as an army set in battle array! You ever abhor evil! You are the Virgin par excellence, you are the singular Virgin who introduced perfect virginity without any prior example and who brought forth, by your virginizing power in those who love and serve you, a constellation of virgins, men and women, over twenty centuries, with a force as unbending as a tectonic plate, against every advance of pansexualism, remaining “in any case mystically effective”³ even in the midst of devastating eroticism⁴. Enclosed garden! Sealed fountain! “Miracle of miracles”⁵! You are the Woman of truest renown in all humanity: “Blessed are you among women!” (Lk 1:42), “From now on all generations will call me blessed, for the Mighty One has done great things for me” (Lk 1:48-49)⁶. In the fullness of time you united to yourself not only the Son of God, by giving Him flesh and blood as Head of the Mystical Body, but also all of us, the members of that Head, Mother of God! Mother of the Church! Neck that joins the Head to the members and the members to the Head! During your life in this world you had much to suffer, Panoply of 7 swords! At the foot of the cross, as you stood there, what had taken place at the Incarnation was publicly manifested, when the Son entrusted you to all the men and women of the world, in the person of St. John: “Woman, behold your son” (Jn 19:26), Genome of all redeemed humanity! To be your devotee, Mary, is a “ Charta libertatis ”⁷. Flame of fire and wind! Assumed: a woman's body is in Heaven! Queen! Former of the saints of the latter times, Tsunami of graces! That will be when you are better known than ever⁸. Amen of amens!⁹. You know who we are and that we need you. We are your slaves in a maternal slavery of love, who wish to do everything “through Mary, with Mary, in Mary and for Mary.” You who stayed beside the river of Luján, stay today and always deep within our hearts¹⁰. Amen. NOTES ¹ Cf. St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort, Treatise on True Devotion , 23. ² Cf. Prayer for the renewal of religious vows

Monthly renewal of religious vows (To be prayed on the 25th of each month) O Father, who have called us to be “the unconditional ones of God” 1 ! O Jesus, who came “as the inflexible vanquisher of error and the gentle champion of love”! 2 O Jesus, “than whom nothing better exists” 3 !, who have freely wrapped us “in the inextricable 4 nets of grace” 5 and who have chosen us to reproduce in our life your form of life: chaste, poor, obedient and Marian; therefore we now renew our four vows as a witness to the life that You lived, and your Most Holy Mother, and the Twelve Apostles, and which we wish to imitate. O Jesus, “the good Word of the good Father” 6 , who “proclaim us victors at the Supper”! 7 O Holy Spirit, who appeared in tongues of fire, “so that a law of fire might be preached by tongues of fire” 8 , make us “the salt of the earth” (Mt 5:13) and not honey! Mary, Daughter of God the Father, Mother of God the Son and Spouse of God the Holy Spirit! obtain for us these gifts: to be unconditional ones of the Trinity, inextricably embraced by grace, faithful to the four vows, victors in the Mass, and with tongues of fire to live and preach the New Law of love established by your Son. Amen. Notes 1 Origen, On Prayer, 13: PG 457. 2 William of Saint-Thierry, On Contemplating God, 10: SC 61,93. 3 St. Ignatius of Antioch, Letter to the Magnesians, ch. 6,1: Funk 195. 4 That cannot be disentangled. 5 St. Basil the Great, Letter 161,1 to Bishop Amphilochius: PG 32, 630. 6 St. Athanasius of Alexandria, Against the Pagans, Sermon 40: PG 75,79. 7 Nicholas Cabasilas, On the Life in Christ, bk 1: PG 150,515. 8 Peter of Blois, Sermon 25: PL 635.
Thirty-day prayer to St. Joseph

O most lovable Patriarch St. Joseph! From the abyss of my littleness and misery I contemplate you, with emotion and joy of soul, on your throne in heaven, as the glory and delight of the blessed, but also as father of orphans on earth, consoler of the sorrowful, protector of the helpless, helper of the Angels and Saints before the throne of God, of your Jesus and of your holy Spouse. Therefore I, poor, helpless, sorrowful and needy, direct to you today and always my tears and sorrows, the pleas and cries of my soul, my repentance and my hopes; and today especially I bring before your altar and your image a sorrow for you to console, an ill for you to remedy, a misfortune for you to prevent, a need for you to relieve, a grace for you to obtain for me and for my loved ones. And to move you and oblige you to hear me and obtain it for me, I will ask and entreat you for thirty consecutive days, in reverence for the thirty years you lived on earth with Jesus and Mary; and I will ask you urgently and confidently, invoking all the titles you have to take pity on me, and all the reasons I have to hope that you will not delay in hearing my petition and remedying my need; my faith in your goodness and power being so certain that, on feeling it, you will also feel obliged to obtain and give me even more than I ask and desire. I ask it of you by the divine goodness that moved the Eternal Word to become incarnate and be born in poor human nature, as Son of God, God-man and God of man. I beseech it of you by your immense anxiety when you felt obliged to leave your holy Spouse. I beg it of you by your most sorrowful resignation in seeking a stable and a manger as palace and cradle for God born among men. I implore it of you by the painful and humiliating circumcision of your Jesus, and by the holy, glorious and most sweet Name that you gave Him by command of the Eternal One. I entreat it of you by your alarm on hearing from the angel of the death decreed against your Divine Son, by your most obedient flight into Egypt, by the hardships and dangers of the journey, by the extreme poverty of the exile, and by your anxieties on returning from Egypt to Nazareth. I ask it of you by your most sorrowful affliction of three days on losing your Son, and by your most sweet consolation on finding Him in the Temple, and by your ineffable happiness during the thirty years you lived in Nazareth with Jesus and Mary, subject to your authority and providence. I beg and hope for it by the heroic sacrifice with which you offered the victim, your Jesus, to the Eternal God for the Cross and for death for our sins and our Redemption. I entreat it of you by the sorrowful foreknowledge that made you contemplate every day those infant hands later pierced on the cross by sharp nails; that head, which rested so sweetly on your breast, crowned with thorns; that divine body, which you pressed to your heart, naked, bloodied and stretched out upon the arms of the cross; that last moment in which you saw Him breathe His last and die. I ask it of you by your most sweet passing from this life in the arms of Jesus and Mary, and your entrance into the limbo of the just and at last into heaven. I beseech it of you by your joy and your glory when you beheld the Resurrection of your Jesus, His ascent and entrance into the heavens, and His throne as immortal King of the ages. I entreat it of you by your ineffable bliss when you saw your most holy Spouse come forth risen from the tomb and be taken up into heaven by the Angels and crowned by the Eternal One and enthroned on a seat beside your own. I ask it of you, and beg, and confidently hope for it, by your labors, hardships and sacrifices on earth, and by your triumphs and glories and happy beatitude in Heaven with your Son Jesus and your spouse Holy Mary. O my good St. Joseph! I, inspired by the teachings of Holy Church and of her doctors and theologians, and by the universal sense of the Christian people, feel within me a mysterious strength that encourages and compels me to ask you, to beseech you, and to hope that you will obtain for me from God the great and extraordinary grace that I am about to place before your image and before your throne of goodness and power in heaven. (Here, lifting up the heart on high, ask the Saint with loving insistence for the grace desired). Obtain also for my own, and for those who have asked me to pray for them, all that they desire and that is good for them. St. Joseph, pray for us, that we may be made worthy of the promises of Our Lord Jesus Christ. Prayer: O God, who in your ineffable providence deigned to choose blessed Joseph as Spouse of your most holy Mother, grant that, as we venerate him as our protector on earth, we may deserve to have him as our intercessor in heaven. O God, who live and reign for ever and ever. Sts. Philip and James, Apostles

See Missal Feast of Saints Philip and James, apostles. Philip, who, like Peter and Andrew, had been born in Bethsaida and was a disciple of John the Baptist, was called by the Lord to follow him. James, for his part, was the son of Alphaeus, surnamed “the Just,” regarded in the West as the kinsman of the Lord; he was the first to govern the Church of Jerusalem, and when the controversy over circumcision arose, he sided with the opinion of Peter, so that that ancient yoke would not be imposed on the disciples who had come from the Gentiles. Very soon he crowned his apostolate with martyrdom (1st c.). Proper Law Directory of Spirituality Ecclesial communion is at once invisible and visible. As an invisible reality, it is the communion of each man, on the one hand, with the Father through Christ in the Holy Spirit and, on the other, with other men, who are also sharers in sanctifying grace, in the Passion of Christ, in the same faith, in the same Spirit. All these realities are intimately related to the visible communion founded on the teaching of the Apostles , on the sacraments and on the hierarchical order. This relationship between the visible and the invisible in ecclesial communion is constitutive of the Church as “universal Sacrament of salvation” Founder “Who is meeker than Jesus? Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter: «He was led like a sheep to the slaughter; and like a lamb, silent before its shearer, so He does not open his mouth. In his humiliation justice was denied him; who can tell of his descendants? For his life was taken from the earth». The eunuch asked Philip : « Please tell me, of whom does the prophet say this: of himself or of someone else? Then Philip , beginning from this text of Scripture, proclaimed to him the Good News of Jesus » (Acts 8:32-35): « Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth as their Inheritance » (Mt 5:4)” (Excerpt from “Mi Parroquia. Cristo Vecino”).
The liturgical texts

Download PDF Our Proper Law states with complete clarity that “the books used for proclaiming the liturgical texts in the vernacular, with the people or for their benefit, must possess such dignity that their outward appearance moves the faithful to greater reverence for the Word of God and for sacred things. Therefore, it is necessary to move beyond, as soon as possible, the provisional stage of sheets and leaflets, wherever this occurs. All books intended for the liturgical use of celebrating priests or deacons must be of a size large enough to distinguish them from the books for the personal use of the faithful” 1 . That is, when dignified and fitting liturgical books are available, one should avoid missals or lectionaries that are coming apart (detached from the cover), with frayed ribbons, so small that a magnifying glass is needed to read them, leaflets or ring binders with loose sheets, or tablets (or a digital missal), etc. What is more, our Founder advised: “ Never proclaim the Word of God from hand missals or loose sheets” 2 and added: “Do not treat the lectionary as if it were a novel” 3 . So, even though people may have ‘little missals’ or apps on their phones to take part in the Mass, the celebrant should not use them to read the readings, much less to celebrate the Mass from them. For, as Sacramentum Caritatis points out: “The ars celebrandi should foster a sense of the sacred and the use of outward forms that educate us in it” 4 . In this sense, the General Instruction of the Roman Missal commands: “ Special care must be taken that the liturgical books, especially the Book of the Gospels and the Lectionary , which are intended for the proclamation of the Word of God and therefore enjoy special veneration, truly be in the liturgical action signs and symbols of supernatural realities, and hence be truly worthy, beautiful and fitting ” 5 . Moreover, Fr. Buela always recommended to us that, in addition to the Lectionary and the Roman Missal, we should have the Missal and Lectionary of the Blessed Virgin, the Missal of the Holy Land, and that all the liturgical books be of the best editions. He placed special emphasis on our sacristies never lacking a beautiful Book of the Gospels. Regarding the use of the liturgical books employed at Mass, we recall here that: The Lectionary must be placed on the ambo, open and marked at the corresponding reading 6 . That is, the Lectionary is not carried in the entrance procession 7 . The Missal must be marked before Mass. Fr. Buela taught us to mark the proper (prayers, rites, introductions, universal prayer), the Preface and the chosen Eucharistic Prayer. Furthermore, the Missal, once marked, should be placed “next to the priest’s chair” 8 . However, once the universal prayer is over, everyone sits and the offertory chant begins, the acolyte or another lay minister places the Missal on the altar 9 . The Book of the Gospels may be set out on the altar, facing the faithful, before Mass begins 10 . But when there is an entrance procession, let the Book of the Gospels also be prepared, and once the altar is reached: “it is praiseworthy to place the Book of the Gospels on the altar” 11 . During the Liturgy of the Word, “if the Book of the Gospels is on the altar, he takes it and, preceded by the lay ministers, who may carry the thurible and the candles, goes to the ambo, carrying the Book of the Gospels slightly elevated” 12 . The Book of the Gospels is incensed with three swings of the thurible 13 . The Book of the Gospels (like the altar) is also venerated with a kiss. “In more solemn celebrations the Bishop, as circumstances suggest, imparts the blessing to the people with the Book of the Gospels. Finally, the Book of the Gospels may be carried to the credence table or to another suitable and dignified place” 14 . In short, as the Directory of Parishes rightly says: “there is a wealth of liturgical signs that should be made use of with a view to an ever more fruitful active participation” 15 , and this concerns all of us, whether parish priests or not. Consecration of the Parish to Our Lady of Guadalupe

Consecration of the Parish of St. Louis King of France (Ecuador) O Most Holy Virgin of Guadalupe, Mother of the True God through whom one lives 1 , moved by your maternal tenderness and the incomparable beauty of your face, today we gather before your throne to express our love for you and to honor you as good children do with their mothers. Holy Virgin of Guadalupe! Most beautiful Lady, Heavenly Empress of Christian America 2 . On this solemn day on which we celebrate your Immaculate Conception, inspired by the most sweet gentleness with which you bend down toward us, we, these your faithful of the Parish of St. Louis King of France, draw near to You, and in the presence of the Archbishop and of our Superiors and before the whole heavenly court we wish to consecrate to you in perpetuity our entire Parish, with all its families, with all our children and young people, with all its married couples, with all its elderly and sick, with all its priests and women religious, with all the religious and priestly vocations that through your intercession and for You we would like to see flourish among us, with all its poor and its professionals, and all its good enterprises and institutions, present and future. Mother of God, Immaculate Virgin Mary, You who one day said to St. Juan Diego: ‘Am I not here, I who am your Mother? Are you not under my shadow? Are you not, perchance, in my lap?’ 3 and who delight in being the Compassionate Mother of those who honor you by trusting in your intercession 4 : Look upon us, Beloved Mother; behold your children. Be our Queen, Most Pure Lady. Receive us under your mantle as your humblest servants. Through You , Most Sweet Lady, with you , in full union with your intentions and for You , we, these your children of the Parish of St. Louis King of France, wish from this day forward to live to honor and glorify you, and so fulfill the most sweet duty of loving you in time and for all eternity. O Virgin of Guadalupe, you of the eyes of infinite tenderness, keep within your suppliant hands all the souls here present, those who are no longer with us and those who will come after us. We beseech you, Virgin Queen of our Parish and of our lives: convert sinners, dry the tears of those who suffer, relieve the poor, help families wounded by violence, lies and selfishness; guard the flower of purity of these your children and young people; increase the love of spouses, so that they may always walk in the light of your Son; strengthen in faith the catechists and the laity of our parish so that they may be ever more committed and available for the service of the Gospel; raise up among us abundant vocations to the priesthood and to consecrated life, who will hold as their most sublime office the guiding of many other souls to the love of your Divine Son; may all the priests who pass through here always be “true servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God” 5 . And finally, Beloved Mother, grant that all of us together, under the protection of your precious help and example, may work united and without rest to implant the Gospel of the beatitudes, and that we may be authentic apostles of the evangelization of culture. Here we are, Most Holy Virgin of Guadalupe; from today and forever all the faithful of the Parish of St. Louis King of France are your blessed servants. To You we belong irrevocably. Heavenly Missionary of the New World, bless us and bless all our works of apostolate and all the projects that, for the glory of the Incarnate Word and through your intercession, we trust we may be able to carry out. † A. Vow to St. Thomas Aquinas

Vow to St. Thomas Aquinas Offering of a Votive Lamp at Fossanova Make vows to the Lord your God, and fulfill them 1 , says the psalm. That is why, on this magnificent and solemn occasion of the 744th anniversary of the death of the Angelic Doctor, we gather to make a promise under vow to St. Thomas Aquinas. He himself taught us that “by a promise, [men] ordain what they are to do for the good of others ” 2 . For “a promise proceeds from the purpose of doing something. And purpose requires prior deliberation, since it is an act of the deliberate will” 3 . And so, today we wish to offer this votive lamp to the one who was acclaimed “Light of the Church and of the whole world” 4 , that it may hang above the altar of this chapel, built precisely on the spot that divine Providence chose for the Saint's passage to true life, and as a vow for the realization and the fruits of our Center of Higher Studies . May this votive lamp remind us all, and serve as a testimony before others, that it is our purpose to work with untiring effort and in perfect harmony so that this Center of Higher Studies may be a place in which “each discipline is cultivated according to its own principles, its own methods and the freedom proper to scientific research, in such a way that the understanding of these disciplines may grow deeper each day, and that, by considering with all attention the problems and discoveries of recent times, it may be seen more exactly how faith and reason move harmoniously toward the truth, which is one, following the teachings of the doctors of the Church, but above all through the scientific study of the Angelic Doctor” 5 . For it is our deliberate intention “to face the challenges of the modern world in the light of essential Thomism” and thus to offer “a positive and effective answer to the great challenges, or even dramas, of man” 6 today. For we are convinced that the Gospel which the Incarnate Word came to bring us “was not meant to be kept hidden. [Rather,] it must be set on the lampstand, so that people may see its light and praise our heavenly Father (cf. Mt 5:15-16)” 7 . We ourselves are to work “not like the hireling who wants his wages after each day of work, nor like a servant who works for pay for a while in order later to secure an independent position, but serving Christ and the cause of the Gospel without pledges, without days off, without days of rest, without consolation and without glory. Like the candle that loves and is consumed before the Sacred Host without noise and without interruption, leaving behind not even ashes” 8 . Thomas died here to become a greater light for the world, so that Fossanova might thus be a lampstand, a place renowned for this burning lamp that is not hidden. From now on may it be said that here St. Thomas dwells as in his own home 9 . That is why today we light this votive lamp: so that the light of the Sun of Aquino 10 , who enlightened the Church of God more than any other doctor 11 , may radiate all its splendor from our house of studies; that it may make the light of the truth that the Incarnate Word came to teach us shine in souls (for He Himself told us: teach them to observe all that I have commanded you 12 ) and may kindle in hearts the spark of ardent apostolic zeal (so necessary for the new evangelization), so that those who are formed here may go forth with the impetus of apostolic charity to carry the torch of the good news into every sphere of humanity and, by its influence, transform humanity itself from within 13 . It is our fervent desire that, from now on, all the priests of the Institute of the Incarnate Word who offer the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass on this altar and in the light of this votive lamp do so for this twofold intention: First, in thanksgiving for the immense grace of Thomism , which was bequeathed in its integrity, and as an integral part of the charism of the Institute, to all the members of the Religious Family of the Incarnate Word. Likewise, we desire that our priests, in celebrating Holy Mass, ask, through the intercession of St. Thomas Aquinas, who loved the Incarnate Word in the Eucharist so exquisitely, that Our Lord may be pleased to protect, accompany and bring to a successful conclusion all the efforts that are being made, and that thanks to his intercession will continue to be made, by the future members of the Institute, so that what is today the project of the Center of Higher Studies may soon become reality, be consolidated, grow and expand, for the glory of God and the good of souls. Furthermore, since, as our Proper Law says, “after Jesus Christ no one does as much for the evangelization of culture as our Mother in heaven” 14 , from whom we trust to obtain the “indispensable help to prolong the Incarnation in all things” 15 , we commit ourselves to offer to the main Church of the Abbey an image of the Blessed Virgin Mary . And another image, that of the master of thought 16 and doctor St. Thomas Aquinas , who loved the Truth disinterestedly, sought it wherever it might be manifested, and highlighted its universality 17 , allowing us to reach Him who perfects all things 18 . So that, interposing before God the most efficacious patronage of the Mother of the Incarnate Word and of the apostle of truth 19 , both may guard and keep unharmed our fidelity and loving veneration for the Supreme Truth, which is God Himself. For the world needs the God who became incarnate in the most pure womb of Mary and whom St. Thomas knew, loved and adored 20 . May the Eternal Lord of all things accept this offering which, under vow, we His children of the Institute of the Incarnate Word, with His favor and help, before His infinite goodness and before our glorious Mother, and through the intercession of the august doctor St. Thomas Aquinas, present today as a pledge of our unending commitment to work with esprit de corps so that the Center of Higher Studies may be distinguished by solidity and thoroughness in the “scientific study of St. Thomas Aquinas, as theologian, philosopher and exegete, without forgetting or neglecting all the legitimate developments contributed by later theologians, philosophers and exegetes and, especially, the developments contributed with great clear-sightedness by the Roman See” 21 , remaining constantly “open to every particle of truth wherever it may be found” 22 and always with the purpose of making “the Gospel penetrate the fabric of society, transforming people's hearts and the structures of society, in order to create a civilization of true justice and love” 23 and making Christ reign 24 . For, as the Aquinate affirms: “He Himself is the whole good of the Church, and there is no greater good than He, nor are all together greater than He alone” 25 . May the Incarnate Word Himself, who is at once the inspiration, motive and model of so colossal an undertaking, present our vow before the Eternal Father and help us to be faithful in the work that He Himself has begun.
