Relying on these words St. John Paul II affirmed that culture is a “characteristic of human life as such” 12 ; “it is a specific way of man's ‘existing’ and ‘being’”; only man –because he transcends matter by virtue of the life of his spirit– “is the only ontic subject of culture” and is “also its only object and its end.” That is, culture is of man, by man and for man. It embraces the whole activity of man, his intellect and affectivity, his search for meaning, his customs and his ethical resources. Culture is so connatural to man that his nature does not attain its full expression except through culture. Therefore, “culture is that through which man, as man, becomes more man, ‘is’ more, has more access to ‘being’” 13 . 7. The teaching of the Church in recent times, and more particularly in Gaudium et spes 14 , has left us a clear teaching about culture and its essence: “It is proper to the person to arrive at true and full humanity through culture, that is, through the cultivation of the goods and values of nature.” That is, man must, by means of a process –culture–, come to be man in fullness, with all his corresponding good or perfection. This includes man's activity in its different dimensions, through which he is integrally perfected: “The word culture in its general sense indicates everything whereby man refines and develops the manifold gifts of his soul and body.” This process or development necessarily implies a repercussion in the social order; and hence in the same document this other dimension or sense of culture is also affirmed: “man strives to bring the world under his control by knowledge and labor; he renders social life more human, both in the family and in the whole civic community, through the progress of customs and institutions.” In this way there is constituted what we may call the cultural patrimony of the human race in its various manifestations: “and finally, throughout the course of time, he expresses in his works his deepest spiritual experiences and aspirations, communicates them and preserves them, so that they may be of advantage to many, and even to the whole human race” 15 . 8. It is from this “historical and social aspect” of culture that we can speak of a “plurality of cultures”: “for from the different ways of using things, of working and of expressing oneself, of practicing religion and of shaping customs, of establishing laws and juridical institutions, of fostering the sciences and the arts and of cultivating beauty, there arise different conditions of common life and various ways of combining the values of life” 16 . Thus we have the diverse cultural patrimonies proper to each people, from which man learns the values he receives by tradition. 9. Finally, we may point out, on the basis of all that has been said, the decisive influence of culture on the life and perfecting of men. Culture is a fundamental dimension of the person and of human communities. Since culture is the result of the life and activity of a human group, the persons who belong to that group are formed, to a great extent, by the culture in which they live. As persons and societies change, the culture also changes with them. When culture is transformed, it likewise transforms persons and societies 17 . From this it is easy to deduce the fundamental importance, together with the decisiveness, of carrying out an evangelization that deeply penetrates the cultures of men and of peoples. 2. Foundations of culture 10 . We have said that culture is the activity man carries out in order to perfect himself. But not everything he does truly contributes to his perfecting, and therefore not all his activities are truly “culture.” Hence the importance of establishing the true foundations so as to be able, on their basis, to discern which manifestations of man are truly culture and which are not. The foundation must be maintained principally on the philosophical plane and in a threefold domain: metaphysical, anthropological and ethical, for in this way we reach what is essential –what endures– above the vicissitudes of history and of the various cultural creations. a) Metaphysical foundation 11. It is metaphysical reflection that provides the necessary openness for all true thought and on which all true thought must rest. If human knowledge were strictly limited to the world of sense experience, that is, without a true metaphysical horizon, it could never find the ultimate meaning of things and of man himself. St. John Paul II expressed it thus: “It is not possible to stop at experience alone; even when experience expresses and makes manifest the interiority of man and his spirituality, speculative reflection must reach his spiritual nature and the foundation on which it rests” 18 . Therefore, not every philosophical reflection grounds a true human culture, since there are many currents of thought widespread today whose errors lead to the distortion of any culture that rests upon them. By way of example, we cite some, following St. John Paul II in Fides et ratio . In the first place, eclecticism , which accepts the different ideas that come from the different philosophical currents without discerning the portion of truth each of them may have. Historicism , which in a similar way considers that each philosophy has its truth, but only provided it is seen within the historical period and purpose in which it was formulated. Scientism , which admits as true only the knowledge of the positive sciences. Nihilism, which denies the humanity of man and his very identity, since it denies being and therefore all objective truth. These and other currents of thought show the need to ground culture in a true metaphysics, which can be none other than the metaphysics of being. For it is the metaphysics of being, and only the metaphysics of being, that can restore to man the true place he occupies in society and provide the true foundations on which man must build his culture. And this is so because it is the philosophy of being that allows a full and comprehensive openness to the whole of reality, surpassing every limit and making it possible to reach Him who brings all things to perfection 19 . The philosophies we have described, and all those that are not grounded in the act of being, are far from satisfying the deepest aspirations of man. They are far from providing man with “an absolute capable of giving an answer and meaning to all his searching. Something ultimate and the foundation of everything else. […] Hypotheses may be fascinating, but they do not satisfy” 20 . For there are many systems that speak of God, that affirm the existence of God, but it is not the God we men need and whom the Christian faith proclaims 21 . It is from a philosophy of being that man can find his true foundation, which is being, and can find his ultimate end, which is Being by Essence, and also find his depth, which is freedom. In this way he will be able to discover the true cultural values. For ultimately, all cultural values –of science, of art, of laws and customs, etc.–, insofar as they are objective expressions of beauty, truth and goodness, are grounded in the act of being 22 . 12. The pastoral care of culture will be able to offer a positive and effective response to the great challenges or even dramas of “postmodern” man, principally from the metaphysical level, through the philosophy of being. For the nihilist position, the present horizon of many philosophies that have strayed from the sense of being, denies all objective truth and, consequently, that which grounds human dignity and freedom 23 . Hence the urgency of recovering the metaphysics of being, a dynamic philosophy that allows full and comprehensive openness toward the whole of reality, until reaching Him who brings all things to perfection 24 . b) Anthropological foundation 13. The anthropological conception is decisive in the consideration of culture, for man is the author and at the same time the recipient of culture. Culture is grounded in human nature, in particular in its spiritual openness to the universal and to transcendence. The nature of man constitutes the measure of culture 25 . 14. Therefore, it is necessary to preserve an integral view of man, one that overcomes a partial and reductionist reading, capable of including his different aspects and dimensions as they are given in reality, that is, united in that unique and unrepeatable subject, at once corporeal and spiritual, that each man is. Pope St. John Paul II affirmed: “This fundamental dimension is man, man in his integrity, man who lives at the same time in the sphere of material values and in that of spiritual values” 26 . 15. From the perspective of an integral reading of man, we have in the first place the culture of material values, which correspond to the human being in his bodily dimension. 16. So then, an authentically human culture requires the values of human work and of technology ordered to the production of material goods, economic and political relations, the sciences directed toward health and natural prosperity, etc.; that is, everything necessary for the material aspect of human and earthly life, and in conformity with the dignity of the human being. 17. We have, in the second place, the culture of spiritual values, corresponding to the spiritual dimension of the human being. 18. Man, by reason of his spiritual dimension, exercises a series of activities that transcend matter, for the soul, by reason of its immateriality, is “in a certain way all things.” Here is found the foundation of man's transcendence; for by his spirituality he is open to all beings and, therefore, to the divine Being. This is what Grabmann affirms: “St. Thomas has grounded psychologically the meaning and value of the bodily, and the right as well as the duty of earthly culture, in his doctrine of the spiritual human soul as the formal principle of the body… but at the same time, and I would not want to omit this, he has also pointed out the transcendent and the ordering of this earthly life toward an eternal existence of the richest and purest spiritual life, by demonstrating that the human soul is a subsistent essence according to its nature, spiritual and personally immortal” 27 . From the spiritual dimension of man and his consequent openness to the universal and to transcendence, there emerges the culture of spiritual and universal values related to beauty, truth and goodness, ultimately to God. 19. The bodily and spiritual dimensions of the human being, as we were saying, must be considered from the perspective of an integral and, at the same time, unitary view of the human person; although different, both dimensions form a single subject, at once material and spiritual. 20. Consequently, an authentically human culture must always strive to achieve and maintain this synthesis of spirit and matter: “Man is always in his totality: in the integral whole of his spiritual and material subjectivity; in culture one must always seek the integral man, the whole man, in the whole truth of his spiritual and bodily subjectivity; this is a sufficient basis for not superimposing on culture –an authentically human system, a splendid synthesis of spirit and body– preconceived divisions and oppositions. Indeed, neither an absolutization of matter in the structure of the human subject nor, inversely, an absolutization of spirit in that same structure expresses the truth about man or renders any service to his culture” 28 . 21. Benedict XVI, in the context of eros and human love, affirms: “Man is truly himself when his body and soul are intimately united; the challenge of eros can be said to be truly overcome when this unification is achieved. Should man aspire to be pure spirit and to reject the flesh as pertaining to his animal nature alone, then spirit and body would both lose their dignity. On the other hand, should he deny the spirit and consider matter, the body, as the only reality, he would likewise lose his greatness. The epicure Gassendi used to offer Descartes the humorous greeting: ‘O Soul!’ And Descartes would reply: ‘O Flesh!’ Yet it is neither the spirit alone nor the body alone that loves: it is man, the person, a unified creature composed of body and soul, who loves. Only when both dimensions are truly united does man attain his full stature” 29 . 22. On the basis of this integral and, at the same time, unitary view of the human being, in his bodily and at once spiritual dimension, it is necessary to affirm, finally, the supremacy of the spirit over the body and, therefore, of the culture of spiritual goods over the culture of material goods, and the ordering of the one to the other. The body exists for the soul, since the soul is its form; therefore material goods are subordinate to spiritual ones. The body is limited by matter, to the immediacy of the here and now; the soul, on the other hand, being spiritual, is in a certain way unlimited and infinite, open to all being. For this reason St. John Paul II urged us to “mobilize all the forces that channel the spiritual dimension of human existence, that bear witness to the primacy of the spiritual in man, of what corresponds to the dignity of his intellect, his will and his heart” 30 . 23. For this reason he defines culture as “that through which man, as man, becomes more man, ‘is’ more, has more access to Being” 31 . 24. From this there also follows the primacy of being over having, which is restricted to the field of material goods. 25. For this reason, “culture is always situated in an essential and necessary relationship to what man is, whereas its relationship to what man has, to his ‘having,’ is not only secondary but entirely relative; and it is a factor of culture only when man, by means of his ‘having,’ can at the same time ‘be’ more fully as man, become more fully man in all the dimensions of his existence, in everything that characterizes his humanity.” Therefore, the Holy Father concludes: “Culture is thought of and spoken of principally in relation to the nature of man; and then only in a secondary and indirect way in relation to the world of his products” 32 . 26. We can conclude by pointing out that what is at stake in a pastoral care of culture is to restore to man his condition as a creature “in the image and likeness of God” 33 . That is, it consists in the anthropological grounding of culture through a view of man as that single subject, at once bodily and spiritual, open to the universal and to transcendence. Furthermore, in a Christian anthropological view, one must emphasize the fundamental truth of Jesus Christ as the fullness of man and of every authentically human culture 34 . c) Ethical foundation 27. Man, starting from the foundation of his human nature, through the dynamism of his acts in conformity with the truth of the good, must tend toward his full realization. St. John Paul II said that “in order to perfect himself in his specific order, the person must do good and avoid evil, safeguard the transmission and preservation of life, improve and develop the riches of the sensible world, cultivate social life, seek the truth, practice the good, contemplate beauty (cf. Th ., I-II, 94, 2)” 35 . That is why “there is no doubt either that the first and fundamental dimension of culture is sound morality: moral culture” 36 . 28. One speaks of perfecting oneself in one's specific order because one starts from the nature common to all, that is, the human nature that each one possesses singularly. On the contrary, establishing a separation between freedom, which expresses the whole domain of man's activity, and human nature, “as a certain current of contemporary philosophy would have it, obscures reason's perception of the universality of the moral law” 37 . 29. It must be pointed out that we are witnessing a disorientation of man's ethical conscience, or moral subjectivism, which derives principally from the crisis concerning the truth about the good. In this way man, by means of his conscience, grants himself the privilege of fixing autonomously the criteria of good and evil, and of acting accordingly 38 . Man, then, must orient himself to the truth of the good, which presupposes a philosophical anthropology and a metaphysics of the good. The present challenge regarding the ethical grounding of cultural values lies in defending and interpreting the values rooted in the very nature of the human being 39 . 30. We must affirm that there exists something permanent that transcends all concrete cultures and that grounds their reason for being, and that “something is precisely the nature of man: precisely this nature is the measure of culture and is the condition for man not to be the prisoner of any of his cultures, but to defend his personal dignity by living in accordance with the profound truth of his being” 40 . On the other hand, it is this nature of man, common to all, that alone justifies the natural law, which constitutes the universal “grammar” by which a fruitful dialogue can be established between cultures and religions, a dialogue ordered to the search for truth within the framework of respect and mutual love. 31. In summary, man, as the image of God, is an “artisan.” For although God alone is the Creator, the one who gives being itself to things, drawing them out of nothing – ex nihilo sui et subiecti –, nevertheless man too, precisely because he is the image of God, has the task of subduing the earth (cf. Gen 1:27), using something already existing and giving it form and meaning 41 . He carries out this task, above all, by being the artisan of his own life, of which he must make a “masterpiece.” “The human person is the author of his own acts and responsible for their moral value” 42 . Man must form his own personality and realize himself, and he accomplishes this in the process of his “life” through free decisions that must be directed toward truth and goodness: “The way in which man establishes his own relationship with being, with truth and with goodness, is by living and working” 43 . 32. [Conclusion] By way of conclusion to this chapter devoted to the foundations of culture, we can say that at present there is a “crisis of meaning,” for human thought shuts itself up within the limits of its own immanence, without any reference to the transcendent. Therefore, in the first place, Philosophy must renew the awareness of ultimate values and give a foundation to the sense of man's ultimate end 44 . In the second place, man's capacity to attain knowledge of objective truth must be affirmed 45 . These two requirements entail the third: the need for a Philosophy of genuinely metaphysical range, capable of transcending empirical data in order to reach, in its search for truth, something absolute, ultimate and foundational. A great challenge facing us at the end of this millennium is to know how to make the passage from phenomenon to foundation . The metaphysical element is the necessary path for overcoming the situation of crisis that today affects large sectors of Philosophy and thus for correcting certain erroneous forms of behavior widespread in our society 46 . 3. Spheres of culture and hierarchy of cultural values 33. From what was said in the preceding chapter we can deduce the various spheres found in culture and the just hierarchy of cultural values. For on the basis of the different dimensions or formalities of man and of his moral dynamism, we have the different spheres of culture. These cultural values possess a just hierarchy and ordering that corresponds to the hierarchy existing among the various formalities of man. a) Cultural spheres 34. We have, in the first place, everything that refers to the sphere of the “culture of making,” that is, the activity of man directed to material things in order to transform them into useful goods. This is the dimension proper to human work and to the technology it uses as an instrument. Here too belongs artistic making, the art of man that transforms material things, making them beautiful. This dimension of “human making,” although directed to the immediate perfection of things external to man, nevertheless starts from man himself and is ordered to him. It is man who possesses –because he is spiritual– that intelligent dominion over things and who has in himself those habits –or skills– by which he transforms them. The human person is always the subject, center and end of all human activity. 35. In the second place, we have the cultural sphere ordered directly to the perfection of man himself: “physical culture,” which perfects his body (for example, by means of diet or gymnastics), and, above all, the “culture of acting,” which refers to the perfection of the human soul, or better, of man insofar as he is man. That is, intellectual activity ordered to the search for and acquisition of truth, and the activity of the will which, by means of the moral virtues, tends toward the perfection of man in the possession of his true good. In this way man attains his moral perfection and becomes morally good. This moral dimension constitutes the decisive dimension of human culture, as St. John Paul II affirmed: “there is no doubt either that the first and fundamental dimension of culture is sound morality: moral culture” 47 . 36. Hence the fundamental importance in the life of man of the exercise of his free will, for, as St. Thomas says, “everyone who has a will is called good insofar as he has a good will, because by the will we use all the things that are in us. Hence a man is called good not because he has a good intellect, but because he has a good will” 48 . “A good will makes a man good ( bonum simpliciter ); and for this reason the virtue (of the appetitive part of the soul) by which the will is good is the one that makes the virtuous man truly good ( simpliciter bonum )” 49 . 37. Why is man good, that is, why does he attain his perfection, especially through the unfolding of his will? Because the will looks to the good as its proper object; it is not simply a matter of the particular good of some power, for example the good of being an artist or of knowing the natural sciences, of handling technology, etc., but of the good of man considered integrally, in all his powers. This is the sphere of the will, which moves itself and all the other powers of man, leading him to his good simpliciter 38. [Transcendent dimension of culture] We have pointed out that the moral dimension of human culture constitutes its first and fundamental dimension. But this moral dimension has its foundation and ultimate end in God; that is, the moral dimension, in order to be fully such, necessarily includes the transcendent-religious dimension of the human person; it is, therefore, an ethical-religious dimension. The culminating point of man's ascent to “being more” is reached in the possession of God, which is why St. Thomas sums up the whole of human morality as “the movement of the rational creature toward God” 50 . 39. Man is essentially a religious being, which is why the transcendent dimension constitutes the heart of culture. “Every culture is an effort to ponder the mystery of the world and in particular of man: it is a way of giving expression to the transcendent dimension of human life. The heart of every culture is its approach to the greatest of all mysteries: the mystery of God” 51 . The great cultural challenge of today lies in the sphere of man's openness to truth and goodness, ultimately to transcendence and to the mystery of God. Man's “ontological” dependence on God is the ultimate foundation of the full development of human freedom and life, as well as of respect for the dignity and life of every human being. For this reason the central place in every culture is occupied by the attitude man takes before the mystery of God 52 . 40. We may further point out that values are not simply pure creations of the human spirit. St. John Paul II noted: “in some currents of modern thought freedom has come to be exalted to the point of being considered an absolute, which would be the source of values” 53 . 41. Cultural values, insofar as and to the extent that they constitute authentic and objective expressions of beauty, truth and goodness, are grounded in and related to being, and ultimately to God, Being by Essence, first Truth and supreme Good, ultimate foundation and first Cause of being by participation, of its truth and goodness. 42. On the other hand, man, through his spirit, remains open to the universal and the transcendent, to the divine being insofar as it is the highest reality and the supreme Good. 43. As St. Thomas explains, the object or reality toward which man's will is directed is the universal good, as the object of the intellect is universal truth. “Hence nothing can bring rest to man's will except the universal good, which is not found in anything created, but only in God, because every creature has participated goodness” 54 . 44. In this way, the perfection and perfect happiness of man is found only in God, inasmuch as He, as infinite and perfect good, “can fill man's will” 55 . 45. This is the profound meaning of what our Lord Jesus Christ answered the rich young man (Mt 19:16ff.). He asks Jesus: Teacher, what must I do to gain eternal life? “For the young man, rather than a question about rules to be followed, it is a question of full meaning for life . That is, this question is ultimately an appeal to the absolute Good which attracts us and beckons us; it is the echo of a call from God, who is the origin and goal of man's life” 56 . 46. What does Jesus answer him? That God alone is good: One alone is the Good (Mt 19:17) 57 . For God alone is good by essence and the source of all participated goodness. Jesus Christ with His answer goes straight to what is fundamental: “indeed, to ask about the good ultimately means to turn toward God, the fullness of goodness” 58 . Ultimately, one can speak of goodness, and more particularly of morally good actions, in relation to God, supreme Goodness, source and end of all participated goodness. Hence the fundamental importance of the transcendent dimension of the human being and of every culture: “Jesus relates –said St. John Paul II– the question of morally good action to its religious roots, to the acknowledgment of God, who alone is goodness, fullness of life, the final end of human activity, and perfect happiness” 59 . b) Hierarchy of values and subordination 47. We have, then, the different spheres of cultural values, which must be considered according to a just hierarchy dependent on the various formalities of the human being and, in particular, on the subordination of man's material and instinctive dimension to his spiritual and interior dimension. This is what the philosopher Aristotle already taught in antiquity: the choice or possession of natural goods, goods of the body, riches, friends and other things, will be good if they help us to contemplate God. It is fitting –that is, good– for man to act in accordance with his determined nature 60 . Thus it is natural for him –man is a social animal– to live in society, for, not being self-sufficient, he needs the help of others. Man, insofar as he possesses a certain animality, naturally disposes of lower things for the needs of his life. Furthermore, man has –as something proper to him– rationality, and, according to the nature of his being, man has a body for the sake of the soul, and the lower powers of the soul for the sake of reason; and therefore it is fitting that the body help the soul, and the lower powers help the higher powers of the soul, it being thus “naturally right that man should look after his body and the intimate tendencies of the soul in such a way that the act of reason and its good are in no way hindered… Finally, the good of reason, which is virtue, culminates in the possession of God: those things are naturally fitting to each one by which he tends to his natural end; since man is naturally ordered to God as his end, it follows that all those things that lead man to the knowledge and love of God are naturally right” 61 . 48. To the extent that men do or do not live this subordination of goods in a just hierarchy of values, we will have the different forms of cultures or, on the contrary, of “anticultures.” Therefore, explains Fr. Meinvielle, man “can rise, then, from the lowest reality to God by participation; or he can be content with being only man, as happened in the rationalism of the classical age; or he can become an animal, as happens in the men of the nineteenth century; or he can be simply a ‘thing,’ as the proletarian dictatorship strives to make him” 62 . 49. That is, in man there are found four formalities: that of reality or thing, that of animal, that of rational being and, finally, the supernatural or divine; these formalities explain the four possible stages of a cultural cycle. In a normal culture, these four formalities must be articulated in a hierarchical ordering that ensures their unity of dynamism. “And thus man is something in order to feel as an animal, he feels as an animal in order to reason and understand as a man, he reasons and understands as a man in order to love God as God. For this reason, just as there is no culture ‘more anticultural’ than the atheistic one, there can be no culture more cultural (of greater cultural density) than one that stands under the sign of holiness” 63 . 50. [Conclusion] In the just hierarchy of cultural values, and decisively in the emergence of the ethical-religious dimension of man, the destiny of the life and culture of men, and of each man, is at stake. The Holy Father John Paul II ended his address at the UN with this exhortation: “Consciences must be moralized! The efforts of human consciences must be increased in proportion to the tension between good and evil to which men are subjected at the end of the twentieth century. We must be convinced of the priority of ethics over technology, of the primacy of the person over things, of the superiority of spirit over matter 64 . The cause of man will be served if science allies itself with conscience. The man of science will truly help humanity if he preserves ‘the sense of man's transcendence over the world and of God's over man’” 65 . 51. On the contrary, when the impossibility of knowing the truth is upheld and the search for the transcendent and absolute is abandoned, then man's reason is placed as an instrument at the service of utilitarian ends, of pleasure or of power. In this way, for example, scientific research, deprived of all ethical reference, yields to the temptation of demiurgic power over nature and over the human being himself; and what man produces, in particular the products that contain a special portion of his genius, can turn, indirectly but radically, against man himself, as for example everything related to nuclear weapons or to dominion over human life through the new techniques in the field of bioethics 66 . 52. Therefore, this effort to recover in men's consciences the need to respect the just hierarchy and subordination of cultural values and the primacy of the moral and transcendent dimension of the human person does not constitute a peripheral and useless effort, but on the contrary the essential and most urgent task for responding positively to the challenges of the present and to the deepest aspirations of every human heart. 53. Let us conclude with a text of St. Thomas: “The whole man exists for the sake of his ultimate end, which transcends him, namely, for the sake of the possession of God… rational creatures, besides this image of the divine Goodness, are directed to God as their ultimate end in a special way, inasmuch as by their activity, by their knowledge and love, they can attain God” 67 . Evangelization of cultures 1. Its essence 54. Having seen what culture is, its foundations, its spheres and its hierarchy of values, we now go on to consider what it means to evangelize cultures. a) Gospel 55. To speak of evangelization, the first thing required is to clarify the notion of the Gospel. Etymologically it means “Good News.” The newness brought by our Lord, the Word made flesh. The New Law consists principally in the grace of the Holy Spirit infused into the heart of man. St. Thomas says: “the New Law is principally the very grace of the Holy Spirit, which is given to the faithful of Christ” 68 . St. Paul calls it the law of faith (Rom 3:27), the spiritual law (Rom 7:14) and explicitly the law of the spirit of life (Rom 8:2). A New Law which, secondarily, is written in the book of the New Testament. This written law has no other reason for being than to be ordered to grace: whether as a disposition, containing all that our intellect must know for faith and what the love of our will must despise so that man may be capable of grace; or by teaching everything relating to the use of grace, such as the works of the virtues and the reception of the sacraments. 56. This New Law, or grace of the Holy Spirit, is the only thing that saves man: I am not ashamed of the Gospel, which is the power of God for the salvation of everyone who believes (Rom 1:16). It saves because it justifies man through the forgiveness of sins, healing his wounded nature and elevating it to a participation in the very divine nature, making men children of God. For this reason, in all truth, “the good of grace in one person is greater than the natural good of the whole universe” 69 . b) Evangelization 57. Evangelization is a rich, complex and dynamic reality, and “means for the Church bringing the Good News into all the strata of humanity” 70 . Therefore, to evangelize consists principally in bringing the grace of God to all men, making a new humanity, that is, of new men created according to God in true justice and holiness (Eph 4:23-24). In this sense, the end toward which evangelization tends is “this interior change, and if it had to be expressed in one sentence the best way of stating it would be to say that the Church evangelizes when she seeks to convert, solely through the divine power of the message she proclaims (cf. Rom 1:16), both the personal and collective consciences of people, the activities in which they engage, and the lives and concrete milieux which are theirs” 71 . 58. Evangelization is carried out, as the same document explains, by means of: 59. – The witness of life: “through this wordless witness these Christians stir up irresistible questions in the hearts of those who see how they live: Why are they like this? Why do they live in this way? What or who is it that inspires them? Why are they in our midst? Such a witness is already a silent proclamation of the Good News and a very powerful and effective one. Here we have an initial act of evangelization… all Christians are called to this witness, and in this way they can be real evangelizers” 72 . 60. – The explicit proclamation of “the name, the teaching, the life, the promises, the Kingdom and the mystery of Jesus of Nazareth, the Son of God, which is so necessary and important in evangelization that it is often taken for the whole, although it is no more than one aspect” 73 . 61.– Finally, and this is the most important, the vital adherence to the program of life –a life in fact already transformed– that He proposes. It is a matter of adherence… to a new way of being, of living, of living in community, which the Gospel inaugurates 74 . 62. For this reason, authentic evangelization must lead to and culminate in the worthy reception of the sacraments, for through them the grace of the Holy Spirit is communicated in the ordinary way. “One cannot sufficiently stress the fact that evangelization does not consist only of the preaching and teaching of a doctrine. For evangelization must touch life: the natural life to which it gives a new meaning, thanks to the evangelical perspectives that it reveals; and the supernatural life, which is not the negation but the purification and elevation of the natural life. This supernatural life finds its living expression in the seven sacraments and in the admirable radiation of grace and holiness which they contain” 75 . Therefore, through the word and the sacraments, the Church brings the Gospel to men, that is, she offers them and communicates to them instrumentally divine grace, making men new creatures vitally united to Christ and to the Church. Finally, it must be pointed out that, together with the proclamation of the Word and the administration of the sacraments, the service of charity also forms part of the essential spheres of evangelization 76 . c) Meaning of evangelization of cultures 63. We come to the central point: the question of the meaning of the evangelization of cultures. St. Paul VI, in Evangelii nuntiandi , specifies that evangelization bears upon the culture and cultures of man, thereby making explicit the whole content and force that evangelization virtually contains. “All this could be expressed in the following words: what matters is to evangelize man's culture and cultures –not in a purely decorative way, as it were by applying a thin veneer, but in a vital way, in depth and right to their very roots– in the wide and rich sense which these terms have in Gaudium et spes , 50” 77 . 64. Therefore, one must evangelize not superficially but in a radical way, incarnating the Gospel in the heart of cultures, that is, in the life and cultural values of men. Gaudium et spes devotes a point to the relationship of culture with faith, inasmuch as culture “can serve as a preparation for the reception of the message of the Gospel, and thus be informed with divine charity by Him who came to save the world. In this sense, by means of culture, the soul of man, freer from servitude to things, is led without obstacles to the worship and contemplation of his Creator. And even more, under the impulse of grace, it is disposed to know the Word of God, who was already in the world as the true light that enlightens every man (Jn 1:9-10)” 78 . Therefore, culture disposes the human spirit to receive the Gospel message and, at the same time, constitutes a resource for “spreading and explaining the message of Christ. For its part, the Gospel message can enter into true communion with the various forms of culture. The Gospel, in this way, from within, makes fruitful, defends, perfects and restores in Christ, with its own heavenly riches, the spiritual riches and characteristics of each people and age” 79 . 65. This is precisely, following the analogy with the mystery of the Incarnate Word, what has come to be called the “inculturation of the Gospel,” or the incarnation of the divine message in the heart of cultures. The evangelization of culture, or inculturation, as Redemptoris missio teaches, “means the intimate transformation of authentic cultural values through their integration in Christianity and the insertion of Christianity in the various human cultures… Through inculturation the Church makes the Gospel incarnate in different cultures and at the same time introduces peoples, together with their cultures, into her own community. She transmits to them her own values, at the same time taking the good elements that already exist in them and renewing them from within” 80 . This is what Evangelii nuntiandi clearly teaches: “For the Church it is a question not only of preaching the Gospel in ever wider geographic areas or to ever greater numbers of people, but also of affecting and as it were upsetting, through the power of the Gospel, mankind's criteria of judgment, determining values, points of interest, lines of thought, sources of inspiration and models of life, which are in contrast with the Word of God and the plan of salvation.” All this means “to evangelize man's culture and cultures… always taking the person as one's starting-point and always coming back to the relationships of people among themselves and with God” 81 . 66. We may emphasize, finally, the fundamental influence of culture on each man and, consequently, the need to inculturate the Gospel. That is, since culture is a fundamental dimension of the person and of human communities, it is also the privileged place of encounter with the message of Christ. So much so that evangelization itself is at stake here, for “a faith that does not become culture is a faith not fully received, not thoroughly thought through, not faithfully lived” 82 . For their part, cultures, to the extent that they are rooted in all that is authentically human, remain open and tend toward their perfection in Jesus Christ. 2. The mystery of Christ and the evangelization of cultures 67. We have already briefly considered the meaning of the evangelization of cultures. Now we shall refer to its foundation and to the different aspects of this single process of inculturation. a) The Incarnation as the foundation of inculturation 68. [Gospel and culture] We must point out, in the first place, that Gospel and culture are two distinct and therefore autonomous realities. The Gospel is the revelation that God makes to man through Jesus Christ, the Word made flesh, who comes to bring to humanity “truth” and “grace”: grace and truth have come to us through Jesus Christ (Jn 1:17). Culture, on the other hand, “flows immediately from the rational and social nature of man” 83 . In this sense, “the Gospel, and therefore evangelization, are certainly not identical with culture, and they are independent in regard to all cultures” 84 . The Gospel message transcends every culture. For this reason, “at the same time, sent to all peoples of every time and place, the Church is not bound exclusively and indissolubly to any race or nation, to any particular way of life, to any customary practices, ancient or modern” 85 . 69. But, in the second place, it must be pointed out that, although distinct and legitimately autonomous, in analogy with the mystery of the Incarnate Word –two really distinct natures, the human and the divine, but united in the one divine Person of the Word–, culture and the Gospel are called to enter into communion, forming a positive and fruitful synthesis. That is, the Gospel must become incarnate in the culture and cultures of man in order to make them fruitful with its divine power and, at the same time, be enriched with new cultural expressions. This bond between the Good News of Christ and human culture takes its origin in divine revelation itself, “for God, revealing Himself to His people to the extent of a full manifestation of Himself in His Incarnate Son, has spoken according to the culture proper to each epoch” 86 . The Church, in her mission of evangelizing all peoples, has continued this same process, making use of the “language” of the different cultures she has encountered in order to transmit the message of Christ. 70. [Foundation] One must, then, carry out a profound evangelization that “incarnates” the Gospel in the heart of cultures. The foundation of this inculturation is the mystery of the Incarnate Word: “From this derives, at its root, one of the principal elements of our spirituality. […] through the Incarnation, nothing authentically human is foreign to us. Therefore, we must work to prolong the Incarnation in all reality, specifically by evangelizing the culture, because ‘no human activity is foreign to the Gospel’” 87 . 71. In this sense St. John Paul II taught: “the term acculturation or inculturation, neologism though it may be, expresses very well one of the elements of the great mystery of the Incarnation” 88 . 72. St. John Paul II himself, in Pastores dabo vobis , refers to the “Catholic principles” of “inculturation” and points out that these principles “are linked to the mystery of the Incarnation of the Word of God and to Christian anthropology, and they illumine the authentic meaning of inculturation” 89 . 73. The foundation and model of inculturation is the mystery of the Incarnation of the Word of God, because in this mystery the divine nature and the human nature are safeguarded, each with its respective autonomy, and at the same time there is manifested the unique bond that places them in mutual relationship without confusion 90 . Analogously, through the task of inculturation, “the Gospel penetrates vitally into cultures, becomes incarnate in them” 91 . That is, the Gospel, through inculturation, enters into profound communion with cultures, through a mutual relationship which, without confusion and with respect for their respective autonomy, at the same time assumes and transforms with its divine power all the authentically human values present in cultures, thus achieving a unique bond and a vital synthesis that enriches and perfects cultures and at the same time the Church as well, through new cultural expressions of her one Gospel message. 74. We may further point out that just as the Word assumed human nature in His one divine Person –a union of assumption that leaves the human nature of Christ intact while elevating it to the dignity of being the human nature of the divine Person of the Word–, in an analogous way the Gospel assumes the cultures that are to be evangelized, which, remaining intact in their own cultural values, are at the same time consolidated, renewed and perfected with the riches of the grace of Christ and of the Good News of the Gospel. “A mere union is not enough for us, nor is merely putting a nominalist label on reality, for it to be truly ruled by Christ” 92 ; rather, the Gospel must penetrate into the heart of culture 93 ; “what matters is to evangelize man's cultures –not in a purely decorative way, as it were by applying a thin veneer, but in a vital way, in depth and right to their very roots” 94 . It is a matter of bringing the Good News to men following the style of the Incarnation: penetrating and transforming human culture “from within” 95 . 75. In conclusion, on the basis of the foundation, and in analogy with the mystery of the Incarnation, the Church in her mission of evangelizing all peoples must strive in the task of inculturation, that is, of the insertion of the Gospel and of the Church into men, their values and their ways of living, in a word, into the heart of cultures 96 . b) The process of inculturation: assumption, purification and divinization 76. Inculturation constitutes a single process of assumption, purification and perfection of cultures, in analogy with the mystery of the Incarnation. Let us see what each of these stages means, and what it implies both for the mission of the Church and, particularly, for cultures. Assumption 77. In the process of inculturation we have, in the first place, the task of the assumption, on the part of the Church and of the Gospel, of the authentically human values present in cultures. That is, evangelization must assume all the elements of truth and goodness present in cultures, which reflect all that is authentically human; in particular, the human openness to transcendence in the groping search for the Absolute that is expressed in religious traditions, which constitute a principal part of human cultures. That is, one must assume the “seeds of the Word,” which constitute a preparation for the Gospel and find their perfect fulfillment in Jesus Christ. 78. This does not consist in a mere “adaptation or accommodation,” but in a true assumption of all that is authentically human. “The proclamation of the Church is not afraid to make use of contemporary cultural expressions. Indeed, these, by a certain analogy with the humanity of Christ, are called, so to speak, to participate in the dignity of the divine Word” 97 . 79. This is what Evangelii nuntiandi calls “permeation”: the Gospel, “independent in regard to cultures… not necessarily incompatible with them, but capable of permeating them all” 98 . 80. It must be emphasized that if the Church in her evangelizing mission does not manage to assume the authentically cultural values of the peoples with whom she comes into contact, then such cultures will in fact remain, and be considered, separate from and foreign to the faith. On the contrary, through this ever-renewed process of assuming authentically human values, the Church “becomes a more intelligible sign of what she is, and a more effective instrument of mission” 99 . That is, by speaking a cultural language intelligible to the men of different peoples and cultures and by assuming their authentically human values and customs, they will be able to discover that the Gospel is not only not something foreign and strange, but above all constitutes the definitive answer that sustains and gives ultimate meaning to all those values, and, ultimately, the Good News that all men, in the depths of their hearts, long to hear. For we must not forget that those values or seeds of the Word constitute a preparation for the Gospel and find their perfect fulfillment in Jesus Christ. That is, cultures, to the extent that they are rooted in what is authentically human, “tend” toward their perfection in Jesus Christ, toward their full realization through the reception of the Gospel. 81. We may also emphasize the need and urgency of the assumption of cultures in the evangelizing mission of the Church, recalling once again that culture is a fundamental dimension of the person and of peoples and, therefore, the “privileged place of encounter” with the Good News of the Gospel. In this sense St. John Paul II taught, for example, that missionaries must “learn the language of the region in which they work, become familiar with the most important expressions of the local culture, and discover its values through direct experience,” for “only if they have this kind of awareness will they be able to bring to people the knowledge of the hidden mystery in a credible and fruitful way” 100 . In this same sense the Pope said in Cameroon: “on the other hand, it is true that the Christian faith must be good news for each of the peoples; therefore it must respond to the noblest expectations of their hearts, it must prove capable of being assimilated in their language, of finding an application in the age-old traditions that their own wisdom would have gradually elaborated to guarantee social cohesion and the maintenance of physical and moral health” 101 . 82. Furthermore, only through this process of assumption can the purification and transformation of cultures be accomplished, because what is not assumed is not redeemed 102 . “Through inculturation the Church makes the Gospel incarnate in different cultures. She transmits to them her own values, at the same time taking the good elements that already exist in them and renewing them from within” 103 . 83. In summary, this assuming, on the part of the Gospel and of the Church, of the cultural elements of truth and goodness in order to transform them with its divine power consists in discovering with joy and respect the seeds of the Word scattered in the national and religious traditions of the different peoples 104 and, at the same time, in continuing the requirement that “has marked her whole historical journey but which today is particularly acute and urgent” 105 . Purification 84. In the process of inculturation we have, in the second place, the task of the purification of cultures. The Magisterium emphasizes that in the process of inculturation all that is truly human and, therefore, good must be assumed 106 . All that is not human, and even more, anti-human, analogously to what happens in the mystery of the Incarnation, cannot be assumed. This is one of the two principles that St. John Paul II establishes as fundamental in the process of inculturation: “compatibility with the Gospel of the various cultures to be assumed, and communion with the universal Church” 107 . 85. Just as the divine Word assumed human flesh, like us in all things but sin, thereby assuming all and only what is human, in an analogous way the Gospel must assume all that is truly human –the values found in cultures– and in no way error and sin, the anti-values that do not belong to human nature as such but only in fact, by reason of its sinful condition. We must not forget that culture is “a product of man and, consequently, marked by sin. In the work of inculturation, discernment must be exercised, since there is the risk of passing uncritically from a sort of alienation from culture to an overvaluation of it. For culture too must be ‘purified, elevated and perfected’” 108 . 86. Furthermore, just as the divine Word, in becoming incarnate, came to destroy the old man and his concupiscences (cf. Eph 4:22), analogously the Gospel –and essentially grace– must heal wounded human nature together with all its perverse consequences in the life of men. The Church, through her evangelizing mission, offers her contribution and collaborates in the purification and overcoming of all that is contrary to the dignity, freedom and fulfillment of the human person. 87. That is why “we must go to the culture and cultures of man not to be converted to them, but to heal and elevate them with the power of the Gospel, doing, analogously, what Christ did: ‘He suppressed what was diabolical, assumed what was human and communicated to it what is divine’” 109 . 88. On the one hand, “nothing authentically human must be rejected, since Christ assumed an integral human nature” 110 ; but, on the other hand, we must always remember that “only what has dignity or necessity can be assumed. Neither the inhuman, nor the anti-human, nor the infra-human can be assumed. The irrational, the absurd and all their derivatives cannot be assumed” 111 . 89. Whatever has malice is not assumed –that is impossible–; on the contrary, it is redeemed, purified. The teaching of the Church on this point is very clear and constant. St. John Paul II taught that in the process of incarnating the Gospel message in cultures, referring specifically to the catechetical task, one must always remember that “the power of the Gospel everywhere transforms and regenerates. When that power enters into a culture, it is no surprise that it rectifies many of its elements. There would be no catechesis if it were the Gospel that had to change when it came into contact with the cultures.” And he goes on to list certain risks that follow from misunderstanding this incarnation of the Gospel in cultures, such as allowing catechesis to be impoverished “through a renunciation or obscuring of its message, by adaptations, even in language, that would endanger the precious deposit of the faith (cf. 2 Tim 1:14), or by concessions in matters of faith or morals”; on the contrary, “true catechesis eventually enriches these cultures by helping them to go beyond the defective or even inhuman features in them…” 112 . 90. The Second Vatican Council already taught: “The good news of Christ constantly renews the life and culture of fallen man; it combats and removes the errors and evils resulting from the permanent allurement of sin. It never ceases to purify and elevate the morality of peoples” 113 . 91. We can sum up this aspect of the purification of cultures with what St. John Paul II teaches in Pastores dabo vobis : “This obedience (to preach the Gospel to the whole world) does not mean syncretism, nor a simple adaptation of the Gospel proclamation; rather, the Gospel penetrates vitally into cultures, becomes incarnate in them, overcoming those cultural elements that are incompatible with the faith and with Christian living” 114 . 92. Without this task of purification, if “everything” were assumed without discerning values from what are not values, one would simply bring about a contradictory and pernicious syncretism, which would deprive cultures of the possibility of overcoming the defective or even inhuman features in them –the fruit of sin–, and which would at the same time prevent the transformation and regeneration of cultures through the communication of the fullness of Christ to their legitimately human values. In this way one would bring about what St. Paul calls emptying the cross of Christ (1 Cor 1:17). Elevation and divinization 93. Lastly, in the third place, in this process of inculturation we have the task of the elevation or divinization of culture. Through inculturation an intimate transformation and renewal of cultures takes place 115 . That is, the Good News of Christ not only purifies but at the same time elevates and perfects the cultural values of peoples 116 . The Word took flesh and elevated human nature to the dignity of His one divine Person. In this way, by a certain analogy with the humanity of Christ, cultures are called, so to speak, to participate in the dignity of the divine Word 117 . 94. In this sense, the culture of man transcends the purely human plane, reaching the supernatural level that corresponds to the children of God. Human culture in relation to the Gospel is autonomous, but it is also theonomous; that is, it is assumed by the Gospel in order to be divinized, attaining at the same time its own human fullness. For Jesus Christ brings about the fullness of human existence, as Gaudium et spes teaches: “The truth is that only in the mystery of the Incarnate Word does the mystery of man take on light. Christ… fully reveals man to man himself and makes his supreme calling clear.” This vocation in Christ is a supernatural vocation, and all men without exception are called to participate in it: “Christ died for all, and the ultimate vocation of man is in fact one, and divine” 118 . Therefore, the Church, through inculturation, transmits the values proper to the Gospel, perfecting cultures and giving them a new impulse and new possibilities. The Good News of Christ enriches cultures, communicating to their legitimate values the “fullness of Christ” 119 . Christ, through grace, heals and elevates human nature; for their part, man and his cultures “tend” toward their fullness in Jesus Christ. 95. This can never be stressed enough. Men need Jesus Christ, for He alone grounds in all its fullness the good of man, authentic humanism. For every human being “is, in a certain sense, a stranger to himself. Jesus Christ not only reveals God, but fully reveals man to man himself” 120 . That is, the Son of God, by becoming man, has introduced into the history of humanity all the evangelical riches of truth, goodness and beauty, establishing at the same time concern for man and his destiny. The Incarnation constitutes “God's valuing of man” 121 . 96. For this reason the presence of the laity in the privileged places of culture “is intended not only for the recognition and eventual purification of the elements of the existing culture, critically weighed, but also for their elevation through the original riches of the Gospel and of the Christian faith” 122 . In this way “the good news of Christ constantly purifies and elevates the morality of peoples” 123 . The Gospel, on coming into contact with cultures, produces a transformation; it “becomes incarnate in them, overcoming those cultural elements that are incompatible with the faith and with Christian living and raising their values to the mystery of salvation which comes from Christ” 124 . 97. By way of summary, regarding the meaning of this single process of inculturation, we may conclude by quoting Gaudium et spes : “The Good News of Christ continually renews the life and culture of fallen man; it combats and removes the errors and evils resulting from the permanent allurement of sin. It never ceases to purify and elevate the morality of peoples. By riches coming from above, it makes fruitful, as it were from within, the spiritual qualities and traditions of every people of every age. It strengthens, perfects and restores them in Christ” 125 . c) The organic bond between faith and cultures 98. We have dealt with the foundation and the process of inculturation, with its aims of assumption, purification and elevation of cultures. We now try to go a little more deeply into the bond between the Good News of Jesus Christ and the cultures of peoples, also in the light of the problems that arise today in the field of inculturation. History of inculturation 99. The Church, in her evangelizing mission of incarnating the Gospel in the heart of cultures, enters into dialogue with them and establishes a vital communion that enriches cultures from within and, at the same time, enriches the Church through new and inspired expressions of the one mystery of Christ. In fact, this has been the historical path of the Church in her universal task of evangelizing all peoples. 100. It is enough just to review briefly the history of inculturation to verify the historical effort of the Church to incarnate the Gospel in the heart of cultures 126 . 101. We may recall the figure of St. Benedict (480-547), whose monasteries –through the cultivation of the fields and the copying of manuscripts– were the first cultural centers of Europe; he was declared patron of Europe by St. Paul VI in 1964 127 . Sts. Cyril and Methodius (885), evangelizers of the Slavic world, considering that in Great Moravia the Mass celebrated in the Roman rite was not very successful, translated the liturgy into the Slavic language, thereby inviting the people “to be aware of their national and cultural identity” 128 ; St. John Paul II named them co-patrons of Europe and devoted his fourth Encyclical to them: Slavorum Apostoli . We may also recall the work of Matteo Ricci (1532-1610) in China, notable for his desire to respect the Chinese rites 129 . And the luminous example, in the work of evangelizing America, offered to us by the pastoral labor exercised by the Jesuits in the Guaraní reductions. 102. From the very beginning the Gospel was proclaimed to all peoples, and Christians lived their faith within the framework of their own culture, as the Letter to Diognetus testifies: “Christians are distinguished from other men neither by country, nor language, nor customs… their manner of life has nothing singular about it… they conform to local usages in dress, food and the rest of life, while at the same time displaying the extraordinary and truly paradoxical laws of their way of living.” They live, therefore, according to the customs of their own cultures, but elevated by the divine power of the Gospel: “they are in the flesh, but they do not live according to the flesh. They pass their days on earth, but they are citizens of heaven. They obey the established laws, and their way of living surpasses the laws” 130 . 103. Pope Alexander VII (1659), giving directives to the first missionaries in Asia, urged them: “do not make any attempt, and do not in any way seek to persuade those peoples to change their customs, their way of life, their usages, when they are not manifestly contrary to religion and morals. There is nothing more absurd than to want to bring France, or Spain, or Italy, or any other part of Europe into China. Bring none of that, but the faith, a faith that does not reject or offend the way of life and usages of any people, when it is not a question of evil things. On the contrary, the faith wants these things to be preserved and protected” 131 . 104. This is, in a special way, the thought of the Church in the twentieth century, which has been progressively clarified. Benedict XV, in Maximum illud (30/11/1919), cautions that in evangelization the characteristics of each people be taken into account, that a native clergy be established capable of understanding the inner life of the peoples, and, for the same reason, that foreign clergy know the languages of the peoples to be evangelized. Pius XI, in Rerum Ecclesiae (28/2/1926) 132 , insists on the formation of a native clergy. For the mission has as its purpose “to found and naturalize the Church of Jesus Christ in those beloved regions,” and the native clergy better understands the soul of its people, their traditions, customs and language. Pius XII, in Evangelii praecones (2/6/1951), exhorts missionaries to acquire the formation necessary to understand the country where they are going to work, including medicine, agriculture, history, ethnography and geography; he also insists on a proper hierarchy and the formation of a native clergy, and says that “it is necessary to follow the very prudent norm that, once peoples embrace the Gospel, nothing should be ruined or destroyed of what is good, honest and beautiful in their character and their own genius.” Better still, such customs –as he likewise affirms in Summi Pontificatus (20/10/1939)–, if they are not indissolubly bound up with superstition or errors, should as far as possible be “preserved intact” 133 . Gospel and evangelized cultures 105. Nevertheless, at present some insist on emphasizing that in the past the evangelizing mission of the Church did not always respect the cultural and religious values of the evangelized peoples and that, on some occasions, it even imposed a sort of “cultural-religious colonialism.” Certainly, in the task of bringing the Gospel to all cultures, one cannot simply impose a particular culture on the peoples being evangelized. For the Gospel is one reality and the culture in which it becomes incarnate is another. No culture is essential to the Gospel, as we have already pointed out: “the Church does not identify herself with any culture, not even with Western culture, notwithstanding that she has been bound to it by history” 134 . 106. What is more, evangelization must incarnate the Gospel in the culture and “take as its starting point, with prudence and discernment, elements –religious or otherwise– that form part of the cultural patrimony of a human group, in order to help people to understand better the integrity of the Christian mystery” 135 . 107. However, this does not mean that in this task of inculturation the Gospel message must simply be completely isolated from the cultures in which it has historically been inserted and expressed. St. John Paul II says in this regard: “the Gospel message cannot be purely and simply isolated from the culture in which it was first inserted (the biblical world or, more concretely, the cultural milieu in which Jesus of Nazareth lived), nor, without serious loss, from the cultures in which it has already been expressed down through the centuries” 136 . Therefore, one must discern and appreciate the values of the cultures that are being evangelized; but, at the same time, one must preserve and duly value those cultural milieux in which the Gospel has in fact been inserted and expressed from its very beginnings. “This message does not spring spontaneously from any cultural ‘humus’; it has always been transmitted by means of an apostolic dialogue which inevitably becomes part of a certain dialogue of cultures” 137 . 108. We find an example of this in the evangelizing work of Sts. Cyril and Methodius, who carried out a true inculturation or “Incarnation of the Gospel in native cultures.” For “by creating, in an original and inspired way, an alphabet for the Slavic language, they made a fundamental contribution to the culture and literature of all the Slavic nations.” But “the brothers from Thessalonica were heirs not only of the faith but also of the culture of ancient Greece, continued by Byzantium.” The Holy Father, in saying this, refers not only to the verification of a fact but, above all, to the positive character of it: “everyone knows the importance of this heritage for the whole of European culture and, directly or indirectly, for universal culture” 138 . 109. Therefore, the Church cannot simply isolate or leave behind all that she has already acquired so brilliantly through the inculturation of her Gospel message in Greco-Latin culture and in other cultures, “without serious loss” 139 . This principle is also valid for the Church of tomorrow, which will be enriched by new contributions arising from her contact with other cultures in which the Gospel has not yet become incarnate. That is, the evangelizing mission first encountered Greek Philosophy, but this does not exclude other approaches. New tasks continually open up for inculturation 140 . Some difficulties 110. We have already pointed out some difficulties relating to the dialogue between Gospel and cultures. But, more profoundly, in this field serious objections arise today. In this sense, some even postulate the need for a revision of the contents concerning the definitive character and fullness of divine revelation in Christ and the unique and universal value of His saving mediation, which would allow the recognition of a plurality of saving mediations parallel to and autonomous from that of Christ, while being complementary to one another. At the basis of this position there is evident the cultural orientation of relativism that prevails today in the West 141 , and the philosophical position of “historicism” regarding the question of truth. 111. Consequently, these authors maintain that no historical religion –Christianity included– can receive and express fully and definitively the truth or manifestation of God. In the same sense, no particular historical event –including that of Christ– can claim to express in principle a unique and universal saving content. Christ, as a historical particular, would have a necessarily contingent and limited significance. To justify this position, some attempt to introduce a separation –contrary to the faith– between Jesus and the Word of God 142 . 112. In this same perspective, with respect to cultures, the legitimate claim to the specificity and originality of the thought of a cultural heritage is asserted –for example, Hinduism, or the great cultures of China, etc.–, while at the same time maintaining that each cultural tradition must shut itself up within its own difference 143 . 113. As a consequence, there is an attempt to reduce the mission of the Church to a task solely of the temporal order and to a dialogue consisting in an exchange of opinions –without the intention of going deeper and attaining a common and universal truth, which would be impossible!–, in opposition to the proclamation of the Gospel. 114. In relation to these serious difficulties, St. Paul VI already pointed out in Evangelii nuntiandi that “many, even generous Christians who are sensitive to the dramatic questions involved in the problem of liberation, in their wish to commit the Church to the liberation effort are frequently tempted to reduce her mission to the dimensions of a simply temporal project. They would reduce her aims to a man-centered goal; the salvation of which she is the messenger would be reduced to material well-being. Her activity, forgetful of all spiritual and religious preoccupation, would become initiatives of the political or social order. But if this were so, the Church would lose her fundamental meaning. That is why we wished to emphasize, in the same address at the opening of the Synod, ‘the need to restate clearly the specifically religious finality of evangelization. This latter would lose its reason for existence if it were to diverge from the religious axis that guides it: the kingdom of God, before anything else, in its fully theological meaning’” 144 . 115. St. John Paul II, in this regard, in his magnificent Encyclical Redemptoris missio , presents with complete clarity the principal points of the present problematic surrounding the evangelizing mission of the Church, especially in the field of inculturation and interreligious dialogue, also indicating the principles for its solution. “Nevertheless, also as a result of the modern changes and the spread of new theological ideas, some people ask: Is missionary work among non-Christians still relevant? Has it not been replaced by interreligious dialogue? Is not human development an adequate goal of the Church's mission? Does not respect for conscience and for freedom exclude all efforts at conversion? Is it not possible to attain salvation in any religion? Why then should there be missionary activity?” 145 . 116. He shows, furthermore, that at the basis of this problematic there emerge certain incorrect theological views that maintain the salvific equality of religions 146 and that therefore affect authentic faith in Christ, the only Savior, with all its negative consequences for the whole of missionary activity 147 . 117. Therefore, an undifferentiated cultural and religious pluralism is proposed, which places all positions on the same level. But in this perspective every possibility of establishing a dialogue as a search for truth is closed off. That is, one accepts the contradiction of identifying the essence of cultural and religious values with those that are not values, given the impossibility of verifying and distinguishing in a culture and in a religion what is positive –elements of truth and goodness in an objective and universal sense– from what is, on the contrary, negative, that is, error and superstition, the fruit of sin. 118. Concretely, from this perspective, in relation to inculturation, the path to establishing a dialogue between Gospel and cultures would be closed. For it would not be possible to discern the authentic values present in cultures and religions from those elements that are, on the contrary, the fruit of sin. That is, the different cultural forms would always constitute –in principle– “valid” and at the same time “contingent” expressions, that is, expressions valid 148 for their own cultures in a given context, but not in a universal sense. Therefore, cultures would remain in principle closed to dialogue –understood as a search for truth– with other cultures and closed to the Gospel. Moreover, it would be unnecessary and useless to offer a Gospel that is valid for “Christian cultures” but foreign to other cultures, and moreover contingent, since its revelation would not be definitive and the salvation it offers not universal. As a result, the Church would have to limit herself to a dialogue –set in opposition to proclamation– that tends to be identified in practice with a human development reduced to the merely horizontal dimension of human life. Therefore, in the field of the task of inculturation –and of interreligious dialogue– it is urgent to renew awareness of the universal character of the content of the faith, in particular of faith in Jesus Christ, the “only” Savior, which lies at the basis of the evangelizing mission 149 . 119. Cultures, for their part, also contain a universal value in their different expressions “proper” to “objective and universal truth.” Cultures manifest in themselves the typical openness of man to the universal and to transcendence, and in this sense they “tend” toward their fulfillment. Therefore, it is “possible” for cultures to receive divine revelation. Cultures, in their objective elements of truth, of goodness, of groping search for the unknown God, “tend” toward their perfection in Jesus Christ 150 . 120. St. Paul VI affirmed in Evangelii nuntiandi that “only a Church which preserves the awareness of her universality and shows that she is in fact universal is capable of having a message which can be heard by all, regardless of regional frontiers” 151 . 121. In this perspective of universality, St. John Paul II indicates the criteria to be followed in inculturation: a) The universality of the human spirit, whose basic needs and aspirations are the same in the most disparate cultures. b) When the Church enters into contact with great cultures not yet evangelized, she cannot leave behind what she has gained from her inculturation in the world of Greco-Latin thought. This criterion is valid also for the Church of the future. c) In the third place, one must not confuse the legitimate defense of the specificity of a cultural tradition with the idea that it must shut itself up within its difference and affirm itself by opposing other traditions, which is contrary to the very nature of the human spirit 152 . 122. [Conclusion] Gospel and culture are called to a fruitful communion, which allows culture to attain its authentically human fullness in Jesus Christ. Between them “there exists an organic and constitutive link” 153 , to which Christian Europe bears special witness 154 . Therefore, although a culture is not the criterion of truth with regard to the revelation of God, nevertheless the Gospel is not contrary to any culture. On the contrary, the Gospel proclamation leads cultures to their real liberation and to full truth. 123. In the process of inculturation, the Church transmits her truths and values, renewing cultures from within, while also drawing from them the positive elements already present. In this way, the Church brings about “an intimate transformation of authentic cultural values through their integration in Christianity and the insertion of Christianity in the various human cultures” 155 . In turn, the particular churches will be able to express and translate their own Christian experience and the treasure of the faith in an original way, in accordance with their own cultural traditions and in the legitimate variety of their expressions 156 . That is, the various cultures, when purified and renewed in the light of the Gospel, can become true expressions of the one Christian faith. 124. In this way, the Church establishes a fruitful dialogue with the cultural and religious values of the different peoples. When she knows and understands these various aspects of culture, she can begin the dialogue of salvation, offering the Good News of the Redemption 157 . Orientations of present-day culture 125. We have considered the essential aspects of culture and of the meaning of its evangelization. We now go on to reflect on the principal characteristics of present-day culture. 126. [Introduction] In order to evangelize the culture it is indispensable to know present-day culture sufficiently in its major lines of thought and orientations, in order to discern its positive aspects and also its shadows and imbalances. 127. All the more so in a world that has undergone profound changes, as Gaudium et spes observes: “the living conditions of modern man have been so profoundly changed in their social and cultural aspects, that we can speak of a new age in human history” 158 . In the same sense Pope St. John Paul II, in Dives in misericordia , pointed out that our generation “is aware of the approach of the third millennium and profoundly feels the change that is occurring in history” 159 . 128. What is happening in the world is also experienced –in another order– in the Church, which is inserted in it. There is “such an upheaval of religious and social situations that it is difficult to apply concretely certain ecclesial distinctions and categories to which we had grown accustomed. Even before the Council it was said that some Christian cities and countries had become mission territories. The situation has certainly not improved in the years since” 160 . 129. Present-day culture has certain characteristics that we can describe following the Magisterium of the Second Vatican Council and of the recent Popes. 1. Positive aspects 130. There has been a true “growth of the natural and human sciences, including the social sciences,” as well as “progress in technology” and “advances in the use and organization of the means of communication” 161 . The heritage of knowledge and wisdom has been enriched in various fields: Logic, the Philosophy of language, Epistemology, the Philosophy of nature, Anthropology, the in-depth analysis of the affective ways of knowledge, the existential approach to the analysis of freedom 162 . So much so that man, through his intellect and work, has “brought about profound changes, both in the domain of science and technology and in social and cultural life.
