Man has extended his power over nature; he has acquired a deeper knowledge of the laws of his social behavior” 163 . 131. This progress has benefited man with a series of advantages. The great advances of science and technology have succeeded in extending man's power over nature and in providing new material goods 164 . But not only new material goods, for, for example, the growth of the positive sciences “sharpens critical judgment to the utmost, and studies in psychology explain human activity more profoundly” 165 . That is, all these new acquisitions of the human sciences –biological, psychological or social– will help “man to penetrate better into the riches of his own being” 166 . These advances offer the men of our time new opportunities for education, “above all through the wider diffusion of books and of the new instruments of cultural and social communication” 167 . In particular, the development of information technology “will allow access to the intellectual and cultural riches of other peoples. The new communication techniques will foster greater participation in events and a growing exchange of ideas” 168 . These new conditions of life and progress, characteristic of present-day culture, favor a more universal culture, as the Second Vatican Council foresaw: “a more universal form of human culture is being prepared, which will be all the more apt to foster and express the unity of the human race the more it respects the particularities of each cultural unit” 169 . A more universal culture that can collaborate in the creation of a culture of greater “solidarity”: “The present generation feels privileged because progress offers it so many possibilities, undreamed of only a few decades ago. […] It has seen the obstacles and distances that separate men and nations collapse or lessen, through an increased sense of the universal, through a clearer awareness of the unity of the human race, through the acceptance of mutual dependence within an authentic solidarity, and finally through the desire –and the possibility– to come into contact with its brothers and sisters beyond the artificial divisions of geography or national or racial frontiers” 170 . 132. There is, then, at present a growing sense of solidarity among peoples 171 , as Benedict XVI describes it in the Encyclical Deus caritas est : “Today the means of mass communication have made our planet smaller, rapidly narrowing the distance between different peoples and cultures. This ‘togetherness’ at times gives rise to misunderstandings and tensions, yet our ability to know almost instantly about the needs of others challenges us to share their situation and their difficulties. […] At the same time, one notes that there are innumerable means today of offering humanitarian assistance to our brothers and sisters in need, not least in modern systems of distributing food and clothing, and of providing housing and care. Concern for our neighbor transcends the confines of national communities and has increasingly broadened its horizon to the whole world” 172 . 133. In summary, the Church recognizes and gladly welcomes the authentic values of the culture of our time, which we can sum up in the enormous advances of scientific knowledge and technological development, and in a new awareness of human rights, of religious freedom and of solidarity. 2. Shadows and imbalances 134. But alongside these positive aspects, there also exist great shadows and imbalances in the culture of our time, which we must identify, uniting our efforts in order to overcome them. Imbalances that are connected with that other fundamental imbalance rooted in the human heart 173 , and that are related to “the profound response that man knows he must give” 174 . That is, there is a profound imbalance between the very rapid growth of technology and the much slower growth of moral resources. 135. We must not forget that all human life is marked by sin, as “an integral part of the truth about man” 175 . St. John Paul II pointed out that “the panorama of the contemporary world also presents shadows and imbalances that are not always superficial” 176 and, referring to the statement of Gaudium et spes about “the imbalances under which the modern world labors” 177 , he asked himself: “In the course of these fifteen years since the conclusion of the Second Vatican Council, has that picture of tensions and threats that mark our epoch become less disquieting? It seems not. On the contrary, the tensions and threats that in the Council document seemed only to be outlined and not to manifest in depth all the danger hidden within them have revealed themselves more fully in the space of these years; they have in a different way confirmed that danger, and do not permit us to cherish the illusions of the past” 178 . 136. There are in present-day culture multiple antinomies that require a solution: a) The increase of exchange between cultures, which in itself can favor a fruitful dialogue, also contains the possibility of disturbing the life of communities –and in fact it sometimes gives rise to misunderstandings and tensions–, of overthrowing traditional wisdom and of endangering the character proper to peoples 179 . b) The culture that arises from the progress of science and technology, and from the ever more fragmented study of particular disciplines, carries with it the risk of not harmonizing with the cultivation of the spirit that is nourished by classical studies according to the different traditions, and with the need to arrive at a synthesis of them 180 , preserving the faculties of contemplation and wonder that lead to wisdom 181 . Furthermore, the one-sided development of the sciences and of technology, which by themselves are “incapable of penetrating to the intimate essence of things, when their method is unreasonably considered the supreme norm for the search for truth, fosters a certain phenomenalism and agnosticism; and, together with this, when man trusts ‘too much’ in these kinds of discoveries, he runs the danger of believing himself ‘self-sufficient’ and of no longer seeking higher realities” 182 . c) Hence the third antinomy, which goes to the heart of the modern drama: “the legitimate autonomy of culture may seek to extend itself into the undue and harmful claim of a purely earthly humanism, and even one opposed to religion” 183 . 137. In this sense, St. John Paul II describes secularism as “a movement of ideas and customs which advocates a humanism totally without God, completely centered upon the cult of action and production and caught up in the heady enthusiasm of consumerism and pleasure” 184 . 138. Consequently –and this aspect must be emphasized among the shadows and challenges of our age– there is the phenomenon of a true eclipse of conscience. “It is a matter of a true overturning or collapse of moral values, and the problem is not only one of ignorance of Christian ethics, but rather of the sense of the foundations and criteria of the moral attitude” 185 . We are witnessing, in this sense, “the decline of so many fundamental values that constitute an unquestionable good not only of Christian morality but simply of human morality, of moral culture, such as respect for human life from the moment of conception, respect for marriage in its indissoluble unity, respect for the stability of the family. […] Linked to this are the crisis of truth in human relationships, the lack of responsibility in speech, the purely utilitarian relationship of man with man, the diminished sense of the authentic common good and the ease with which it is alienated. Finally, there is the desacralization that at times turns into ‘dehumanization’: the man and the society for whom nothing is ‘sacred’ are in moral decline, despite appearances” 186 . 139. This dehumanization is experienced above all in the multiplication and intensification of threats to the life of persons and of peoples, with the new prospects opened up by scientific and technological progress, and in a new cultural situation that justifies attacks on human life in the name of the rights of individual freedom, even obtaining the authorization of the State and the cooperation of the health-care system. With the dramatic result of the elimination of so many human lives at their beginning or close to their end, and the “no less serious” fact that conscience itself finds it ever more difficult to perceive the distinction between good and evil in what concerns the very fundamental value of human life 187 . 140. Benedict XVI describes in a few strokes the central points and the dangers contained in the culture predominant in the West: “From this there derives a new wave of enlightenment and secularism, according to which only what can be experienced and calculated would be rationally valid, while in practice individual freedom is set up as the fundamental value to which all others must be subjected. Thus God is excluded from culture and from public life, and faith in Him becomes more difficult, among other reasons because we live in a world that almost always presents itself as our own work, in which, so to speak, God no longer appears directly; He seems already superfluous, indeed foreign. In close connection with all this, there takes place a radical reduction of man, considered a mere product of nature, as such not really free, and who in himself may be treated like any other animal. Thus there occurs a genuine overturning of the starting point of this culture, which was a claim to the centrality of man and his freedom. Along the same lines, ethics is placed within the confines of relativism and utilitarianism, excluding any moral principle that is valid and binding in itself. […] Furthermore, the insufficiency of a rationality closed in on itself and of an overly individualistic ethics is felt ever more clearly; concretely, the seriousness of the danger of being cut off from the Christian roots of our civilization is perceived” 188 . 3. Atheism 141. The fundamental concern regarding the dark side of present-day culture, profoundly evident, and the root of the problem, emerges in the sphere of contemporary nihilism-atheism. “How can we fail to think of the persistent spread of religious indifference and atheism in its more varied forms, particularly in its perhaps most widespread form of secularism ? Inebriated by the prodigious conquests of a continuous scientific-technological development and fascinated above all by the oldest and ever new temptation of wanting to become like God (cf. Gen 3:5) through the use of a liberty without bounds, man cuts the religious roots that are in his heart: he forgets God, or considers Him without significance for his own existence, or rejects Him, putting himself to adore the most diverse ‘idols’” 189 . 142. “The present-day phenomenon of secularism is truly serious; and it affects not only individuals, but in some way entire communities, as the Council already observed: ‘Growing numbers of people are abandoning religion in practice.’ At other times I myself have recalled the phenomenon of de-Christianization which strikes long-standing Christian peoples and which continually calls for a re-evangelization” 190 . 143. This entails serious consequences for man. For the reality we experience is not the absolute; God alone is the absolute; therefore, every illusion of autonomy that ignores essential dependence on God leads to dramatic situations that destroy the meaning of human existence 191 . In this sense, “when not acknowledged and loved in his dignity as the living image of God (cf. Gen 1:26), the human being is exposed to more humiliating and degrading forms of ‘manipulation’ that most assuredly reduce him to a slave of the strongest. And ‘the strongest’ can take the names of an ideology, economic power, political and inhumane systems, scientific technocracy or the intrusiveness of the mass media . Once again we find ourselves before many persons, our sisters and brothers, whose fundamental rights are being violated, owing also to the excessive tolerance and even the patent injustice of certain civil laws: the right to life and to integrity, the right to a home and to work, the right to a family and responsible parenthood, the right to participation in public and political life, the right to freedom of conscience and the practice of religion” 192 . 144. We are, once again, before “the drama of man of all times, which is also the drama of man today: ‘his Babel-like character,’ that is, opting for the merely horizontal dimension of work and social life, paying no attention to the vertical dimension by which they would have found themselves rooted in God, their Creator and Lord, and oriented toward Him as the ultimate end of their journey” 193 . If we try to discover the philosophical root of the great present-day problems concerning man, we can find it in the common horizon of the nihilist position. Modern philosophy has concentrated its search on human knowledge, highlighting its limits and conditioning, and leaving aside the radical question of the truth about the person, about being and about God 194 . Modern philosophical thought gradually distanced itself from revelation and explicitly opposed it. Different forms of atheistic humanism arose that presented faith as harmful and alienating. In scientific research a positivist mentality has gradually prevailed that forgets every relation to the metaphysical and moral vision; nihilism, with the primacy of the ephemeral, has gained ground 195 . The nihilist position seems to constitute the common horizon of many philosophies that have strayed from the sense of being. This forgetfulness of being inevitably entails the loss of contact with objective truth and, consequently, with the foundation on which the dignity of man rests. The humanity of man and his identity are denied 196 . 145. In summary, certain currents of thought related to “postmodernity” maintain that the time of certainties has irremediably passed; man would have to learn to live in a perspective of total absence of meaning, characterized by the provisional and fleeting 197 . In summary, the root is evident in the present philosophical situation, in its forgetfulness of being and of the search for an objective truth –the foundation on which the dignity of man rests–, in a perspective of total absence of meaning and of affirmation of the ephemeral, with all its tragic consequences. 146. This is what constitutes contemporary nihilism-atheism 198 . Nihilism, or radical atheism, as the denial of the transcendent, of the existence of “a metaphysical world that transcends the sensible world” 199 . Modern philosophy, under the influence of Hegel, with the –contradictory and dialectical– identification of being and non-being, has “forgotten being as foundation and has brought about the collapse of speculative thought, to such a point that one cannot even speak of weak thought… because to anchor oneself in nothingness is not to think: nothingness, in fact, is the absence of everything, total privation, irrecoverable flight, irremediable defeat” 200 . 147. In “this dialectical interchange… of being and non-being, contemporary nihilism-atheism stands at the door as the point of arrival; although one should rather speak of a blocking of the spirit within itself and of a slipping or closing-in of thought because of the unstoppable advance of nothingness. The human spirit, closed in on itself, no longer opens itself to the real –to the act of being– and, therefore, to God, and so it becomes incapable of expressing the truth and of grounding freedom” 201 . Evangelization of cultures and our specific end 148. Our Religious Family has as its specific end “to inculturate the Gospel” 202 , the singular end of “dedicating ourselves to the evangelization of culture” 203 . Inculturation is an intrinsic requirement of evangelization, but in present circumstances it takes on, in addition, a special urgency, for present-day culture, together with its positive aspects, presents at the same time profound imbalances. This culture has progressively distanced itself from and set itself against the Gospel. In this sense, the Second Vatican Council points out that “the split between the faith which many profess and their daily lives deserves to be counted among the more serious errors of our age” 204 . In the same way, Evangelii nuntiandi affirms that “the split between the Gospel and culture is without a doubt the drama of our time, just as it was of other times” 205 . Therefore, since we find ourselves “before the development of a culture that is taking shape as cut off not only from the Christian faith but even from human values themselves, as well as before a certain scientific and technological culture powerless to respond to the pressing demand for truth and goodness that burns in the hearts of men, the Church is fully aware of the pastoral urgency of reserving a very special attention for culture” 206 . “This is a requirement that has marked her whole historical journey, but today it is particularly acute and urgent” 207 . We must, then, “make every effort with a view to a generous evangelization of culture, or more correctly of cultures” 208 . 149. Put briefly: faith must become culture. That is, faith must become incarnate in the life and culture of men, for otherwise, in the case of a faith that does not become culture, it must be said that “it is a faith ‘not fully received, not thoroughly thought through, not faithfully lived’” 209 . For this task of inculturation, on the one hand, we have the advantages offered to us by present-day culture, which we must take advantage of as a starting point in order to build from there a new culture purified and elevated by the Gospel; on the other hand, there appear alongside this –or better still, within this very thing– shadows and profound imbalances that cause well-founded concern and that challenge us to offer positive and long-term solutions. The Church must respond, above all, with an evangelization –or, as the case may be, a new evangelization– that reaches the heart of cultures in order to transform them in Jesus Christ. Our Institute must also collaborate in this work of the Church, all the more so as it has as its specific end the evangelization of cultures. 150. We now go on to consider, in the first place, what the cultural contribution of our Institute must be according to our charism and specific end. In the second place, we shall reflect on our proper apostolates and the selection of ministries with a view to a more effective inculturation. 1. The contribution of religious life in relation to our specific end 151. [Introduction] In the field of inculturation new answers must be worked out for the new problems of today's world, acting with boldness in the respective fields of one's own founding charism 210 . If we try to point out some characteristics of our apostolates in their relationship with the charism and specific end of our Institute, perhaps the first thing that appears is their breadth and variety, which is in conformity with our specific end of evangelizing the culture. For everything authentically human –technology, art, intellectual and moral life, the contemplation of divine things– forms part of culture and, therefore, can and must be evangelized, since “no human activity is foreign to the Gospel” 211 . The evangelization of culture consists in “prolonging the Incarnation in every man, in the whole man and in all the manifestations of man” 212 , in imbuing all human activity with the Gospel 213 . Therefore, everything that concerns man, both in his body and in his soul, in his individual and also in his social life, can and must be purified and elevated by the grace of Christ; and consequently we can affirm that every form of apostolic activity is in conformity with our specific end, although in a hierarchical way. 152. In this sense, our Constitutions mention a great variety of apostolates, such as the preaching of the Spiritual Exercises and spiritual direction 214 , priestly formation in seminaries, education at all levels, the formation of lay leaders, the means of social communication 215 , help to parishes through preaching and the administration of the sacrament of Reconciliation, popular missions in all their forms, the running of parishes especially in mission areas 216 , the concrete practice of charity 217 , and the care of the Second and Third Order 218 . Our Constitutions also point out our charism of prolonging Christ in “families, in education, in the media, in men of thought and in every other legitimate manifestation of the life of man” 219 . 153. Analogously, the plurality of our Institutes –the First, Second and Third Order, with their active, contemplative and lay branches in their three levels of consecration– harmonizes perfectly with our specific end, inasmuch as they constitute different calls, according to the vocation of each one, to collaborate in the evangelization of culture, which is a work of all the members of the Church. a) Specific cultural contribution of consecrated life 154. More specifically, it must be affirmed that consecrated life itself, when it is lived authentically, can offer an original contribution to the challenges of inculturation. The evangelical style of life is an important source for proposing a new cultural model 220 . 155. [Witness of charity] This original contribution is specified, in the first place, in the sphere of the promotion of charity through the preferential option for those who find themselves in a situation of greater weakness and, therefore, of more serious need. That is, it is specified in the sphere of charity toward the poor, which leads one to live like them 221 ; in the care of the sick and of those who suffer, contributing significantly to the mission of the Church 222 . 156. For this reason, in the variety of apostolates of our Institutes a preferential place must be reserved for charitable work, which is an essential component of the evangelizing mission of the Church and an indispensable element for the evangelization of culture. “Likewise, priority must be given to the care of the poor, the sick and the needy of every kind: the love of Christ urges us (2 Cor 5:14), concretely practicing charity as a witness […] that charity is indispensable for evangelizing the culture, as the end of the one who acts and as the end of the work. Otherwise, ‘the civilization of love’ will not be attained” 223 . For this reason too, “those who devote themselves to the works of mercy are the key pieces of the apostolic endeavor of our Institute” 224 . Benedict XVI describes the path of evangelization in the first centuries, saying: “The strong union between faith that is friendly to the intelligence and a practice of life characterized by mutual love and attentive care for the poor and suffering made possible the first great missionary expansion of Christianity in the Hellenistic-Roman world”; and this “remains the royal road for evangelization” 225 . 157. [Witness to the primacy of God] In the second place, this cultural contribution of consecrated life is specified in its prophetic witness to the primacy of God and of Gospel values 226 . More concretely, the profession of chastity, poverty and obedience, while affirming the value of created goods, relativizes them, presenting God as the absolute good. In this way, they present a spiritual therapy for humanity, for they reject the idolatry of creatures and make the living God visible 227 . In this there are clearly manifested both the eminently cultural character and contribution that consecrated life offers and the consistency of its response to present-day cultural challenges. For the transcendent dimension of human life, openness to and approach toward the mystery of God, constitutes the “heart” of every culture. In this way, it is also understood why the consecrated person is always “on mission.” This witness to the primacy of God as the only absolute good, through an authentic religious life faithful to its commitments, constitutes the principal apostolate of religious, also and in a particular way in the task of inculturation. Our Directory of Spirituality says: “we want to base our spirituality on the absoluteness of God, before whom everything is as nothing . […] We want in everything and through everything to give primacy to the spiritual and to give ourselves in holy abandonment to the will of God's good pleasure” 228 . In this sense, the branches of contemplative life give eloquent witness to this principal dimension of human culture, a witness therefore particularly necessary in the work of the evangelization of cultures, as can be verified historically, for example, in the decisive collaboration the Benedictine monks offered in the building of European culture. St. Paul VI pointed out that “the Church and the world… need… a small ideal society where there reign, as their end, love, obedience, innocence, freedom from things and the art of using them well, the prevalence of the spirit, peace, in a word, the Gospel” 229 . b) Need for ongoing formation 160. On the other hand, since the witness to the primacy of God and of charity, through an authentic consecrated life, constitutes the first apostolate of consecrated persons and their principal contribution to the evangelization of cultures, it is fundamental to preserve the quality of this witness, giving the greatest importance to the periods of formation and to ongoing formation in its different dimensions. Our Directory of Spirituality says: “No less weight for our spirituality has the example of Jesus in His hidden life. Hence every time of preparation must be very important for us […] the future of our brothers in religious life and, therefore, of the Institute depends fundamentally on the formation given to them in the times of preparation: postulancy, novitiate, seminary, subsequent further training, ongoing formation” 230 . Our Directory also emphasizes that our apostolic commitment to evangelize the culture requires of us a spirituality with particular nuances, which consists, as St. John Paul II teaches, in “a faith enlightened by continual reflection that measures itself against the sources of the Church's message, and a constant spiritual discernment pursued in prayer” 231 . That is, it requires ongoing spiritual and cultural formation, capable of sustaining the quality of the witness of religious life, and also a pastoral care of culture that can respond positively and convincingly to the great challenges of present-day culture. 161. In this sense, consecrated life, as St. John Paul II emphasizes, needs within itself a renewed love for cultural commitment. A decline in concern for study can have serious consequences in the apostolate as well, generating a sense of marginalization and inferiority, or fostering superficiality and rashness in initiatives 232 . This cultural commitment appears even more urgent and necessary if one considers our specific end of the evangelization of culture. 162. Furthermore, the task of inculturation also requires constant formation in the spiritual dimension, for it is precisely the imitation of Christ's attitude of humility and love in the mystery of the Incarnation that fosters in consecrated souls the best dispositions for the difficult and urgent task of inculturation: “Relying on the charism of their founders and foundresses, many consecrated persons have been able to approach different cultures with the attitude of Jesus, who emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil 2:7), and, with a bold and patient effort of dialogue, they have established fruitful contacts with the most diverse peoples, proclaiming to all the way of salvation. […] A genuine inculturation requires an attitude like that of the Lord, who when He became incarnate came among us with love and humility. In this sense consecrated life prepares persons to face the complex and arduous task of inculturation, because it accustoms them to detachment from things, including many aspects of their own culture. Applying themselves with these attitudes to the study and understanding of cultures, consecrated persons can better discern in them the authentic values and the way in which they can be accepted and perfected, with the help of their own charism” 233 . c) Key pieces in our apostolic endeavor 163. We must also mention those members of our Institutes –“the sick and the elderly –together with the members of the contemplative branches–, the coadjutor brothers and those who devote themselves to the works of mercy”– who “are the key pieces of the apostolic endeavor of our Institute” 234 , precisely because of their greater participation in and imitation of the radical self-emptying of the Word of God, who out of love for man became a servant obedient unto death on the Cross in order to give His life for many (cf. Mt 20:28), and in this way transfigure the world. 164. [Laity] Finally, since “inculturation must involve the whole people of God, and not just a few experts” 235 , we point out the specific contribution of the lay branches to the evangelization of cultures. The laity, whose proper and particular characteristic is their secular character, which is rooted in the mystery of the Incarnate Word, evangelize the culture through their own vocation “to seek the Kingdom of God by engaging in temporal affairs and ordering them according to the plan of God” 236 . They live “in each and in all of the secular professions and occupations, and in the ordinary circumstances of family and social life, being led by the spirit of the Gospel in all of this so that, from within, like leaven, they may contribute to the sanctification of the world, and in this way, radiating faith, hope and charity, above all by the witness of their life, they may make Christ known to others” 237 . Therefore: “in their existence there cannot be two parallel lives: on the one hand, the so-called ‘spiritual’ life, with its values and demands; and on the other, the so-called ‘secular’ life, that is, life in a family, at work, in social relationships, in the responsibilities of public life and in culture. Every activity, every situation, every concrete endeavor –as, for example, skill and solidarity in work, love and dedication in the family and the education of children, service to society and public life, and the promotion of truth in the area of culture– are the occasions ordained by Providence for a ‘continuous exercise of faith, hope and charity’” 238 . 165. In a particular way, they will collaborate, in a common work, with the apostolate carried out by the priests and the men and women religious of the Family of the Incarnate Word. 166. Let us remember that in order to carry out our apostolate “we wish to achieve the most filial and fraternal relationship with the Pontifical Council for Culture, so as to achieve a greater and better concrete realization of the purpose of the Institute” 239 . 2. Turning points of culture 167. We have already pointed out the characteristic plurality and variety of our apostolates, in conformity with our specific end of evangelizing the culture. But, at the same time, one must emphasize the need to make a selection of ministries, working principally at the turning points of culture. 168. In order to offer our contribution to the Church's mission of inculturating the Gospel, one can never insist enough on the priority of the life of the spirit and of the qualified witness of religious life, as well as on the concrete practice of charity and on the need to carry out our proper apostolates with discernment and competence, working especially in the places of greatest cultural influence. Our Constitutions say: “The Institute of the Incarnate Word will take on the apostolates most conducive to the inculturation of the Gospel” 240 . 169. St. Thomas teaches that “acts that have as their object the spiritual good of the soul are more useful to one's neighbor than those ordered to bodily good, and are a greater service of God, which is why no sacrifice is more pleasing than zeal for souls” 241 . 170. All the more so when that spiritual good reaches many: “it is better to teach sacred doctrine, and more meritorious, if it is done with a good intention, than to attend to the particular care of the salvation of this or that person… the same reason shows that it is better to teach the things that pertain to salvation to those who can profit both for themselves and for others than to the simple, who can profit only for themselves” 242 . For this reason, “those who devote themselves to theological, philosophical, scientific, cultural research, etc., must be very clear that, although it may seem more remote, this intellectual work is not only for the greater glory of God, but also for the greater good of souls, and falls fully within the charism of our Institute” 243 . In this field of the intellectual apostolate, emphasis must be placed above all on “publications, since what is written endures and spreads further” 244 . 171. Concretely, one must “work on the turning points of culture, namely: families, education –especially seminary, university and tertiary education–, the means of social communication and men of thought or ‘intellectuals’” 245 . 172. The turning points of culture are the milieux and places existing in society in which culture has its proximate source –where culture is “created”– and through which culture is transmitted in a privileged way, whether in an integral and profound manner, for example in the family and in the field of education –especially university education and research settings–, or in a massive manner, as for example in the modern means of communication. 173. It is these turning points that we must give priority to in our work of incarnating the Gospel in modern societies, since “concretely, it is only from within and through culture that the Christian faith becomes a part of history and the creator of history. Therefore, it is necessary to intensify the presence of the Church and of the laity in the privileged places of culture, such as the world of schools and universities, the settings of scientific and technical research, the places of artistic creativity and of humanistic reflection. Also in the instruments of social communication, which today constitute the privileged path for the creation and transmission of culture” 246 . We now go on, then, to consider the nature and importance of the turning points of culture. a) The family 174. God is the creator of the family –the original cell of society–, to which He has given its proper goods, ordering it to the mutual and fruitful love of the spouses, a fruitfulness begun through procreation and prolonged in the integral and Christian education of the children 247 . The family constitutes the “fundamental cell of society” and the “primary place of humanization” of the person and of societies; therefore, “as experience shows, the civilization and cohesion of peoples depend above all on the human quality of their families. […] The Church is profoundly convinced of this, knowing perfectly well that ‘the future of humanity passes by way of the family’” 248 . 175. [The family and education] Parents are the first and principal educators of their children, in such a way that their education is the foundation of all other education and exerts a decisive influence. The Document Gravissimum educationis teaches that parents, since they have given life to their children, “are bound by the most serious obligation to educate their offspring and therefore must be recognized as the primary and principal educators. This role in education is so important that only with difficulty can it be supplied where it is lacking. Parents are the ones who must create a family atmosphere animated by love and respect for God and man, in which the well-rounded personal and social education of children is fostered. Hence the family is the first school of the social virtues that every society needs” 249 . In the family, “from infancy one can learn moral values, one begins to honor God and to make good use of freedom” 250 . 176. The family has an analogous efficacy in the transmission of Gospel values. The family, as a domestic church, must be “a place where the Gospel is transmitted and from which the Gospel radiates. This transmission takes place from parents to children and vice versa: the parents not only communicate the Gospel to their children, but can in turn receive from them this same Gospel as deeply lived by them; and it is also transmitted beyond the sphere of one's own family, for such a family becomes the evangelizer of many other families and of the neighborhood of which it forms part” 251 . In this way, through Christian families, the Church finds “her cradle and the place where she can bring about her own entry into the human generations, and where these in their turn can enter the Church” 252 . In places where de-Christianization, secularism and even anti-religious legislation prevail, “the domestic church remains the one place where children and young people can receive an authentic catechesis” 253 . In summary, “Christian marriage and the Christian family build up the Church: for in the family the human person is not only brought into being and progressively introduced by means of education into the human community, but by means of the rebirth of Baptism and education in the faith the child is also introduced into God's family, which is the Church” 254 . 177. Therefore, this evangelization in families is also in some way irreplaceable and decisive: “family catechesis has a unique character and is in a sense irreplaceable; and it is exercised principally by an everyday life lived in accordance with the Gospel. This transmission of the faith in the family setting will often allow it to leave a decisive mark on children for their whole lives” 255 . 178. Consequently, because of its fundamental and decisive influence on the human and evangelical growth of human generations, we must give great importance to every kind of apostolic endeavor directed toward promoting, strengthening and multiplying Christian families in their various goods and ends. St. John Paul II, speaking of inculturation, affirmed that “study… and pastoral effort must be continued so that this ‘inculturation’ of the Christian faith may be carried out ever more extensively, also in the area of marriage and the family” 256 . 179. [The family and the culture of life] In the second place, in relation to the challenges arising from present-day culture in the field of respect for human life, we can point out the essential relationship between the family and the culture of life 257 . Man has been created in the image of God, who is a mystery of communion among the divine persons. God created the human being in His image and likeness, and created him male and female, to live the communion of persons and to become complementarily a mutual gift, as husband and wife –in a mutual and total, unique and indissoluble relationship–, and in the depth of that mutual love to become father and mother. In this sense, the family is organically related to the civilization of love; it is its heart and center. 180. However, the crisis of truth leads to a civilization of production and of use, a civilization of things and not of persons, in which persons are used in the same way as things. It leads to a consumerist civilization with an anti-birth mentality. The civilization of love, on the contrary, evokes the joy of life, the joy that a human being comes into this world and that spouses become parents. If the family is so important for building the civilization of love, it is because of its particular closeness and the intensity of the bonds that exist between persons and generations within it 258 . That is to say, the family, founded on marriage, is a community of life and love whose mission is “to guard, reveal and communicate love” 259 . Parents are the co-workers and interpreters of God’s own love in the transmission of life and in its education. In the family each person is recognized, respected and honored because he is a person. The family is the setting in which life can be welcomed and protected, and can develop according to the demands of authentic human growth. For this reason, the role of the family in building the culture of life is decisive and irreplaceable 260 . 181. Therefore, the pastoral care of the family is very necessary, all the more so at a moment in history that is witnessing a widespread and radical crisis of this fundamental institution. The family is being attacked as never before and is undergoing the most acute crisis in all of history 261 . It is urgent that families offer a convincing witness to the possibility of a marriage lived in a way fully in accordance with God’s plan and with the true demands of the human person: of the spouses and, above all, of the more fragile persons, the children 262 . 182. In a particular way, a cultural change in favor of life must be promoted beginning from families, first of all within the Christian communities themselves 263 . For this, what is needed is the formation of the moral conscience regarding the inviolable value of human life and the rediscovery of the constitutive link between freedom and truth 264 . Furthermore, educational work is indispensable so that young people may understand and live sexuality and love according to their true meaning and in their intimate interrelation 265 . And the formation of spouses for responsible procreation is required 266 . 183. In summary, cultural change demands of everyone the courage to adopt a new lifestyle within the framework of the primacy of being over having, of the person over things. This new lifestyle also implies passing from indifference to concern for the other, and from rejection to acceptance. In this task everyone has an important role to play: teachers and educators; intellectuals; those responsible for the social communications media 267 ; women, who are called to bear witness to the meaning of authentic love, that gift of oneself and that acceptance of the other, since the experience of motherhood fosters a keen sensitivity toward other persons 268 . b) Education 184. The most grave obligation of education, which belongs first and foremost to parents, requires the collaboration of society, and, furthermore, this duty of educating also belongs to the Church. “Above all, because the Church has the duty of proclaiming to all men the way of salvation, of communicating the life of Christ to believers, and of helping them with unceasing concern so that they may attain the fullness of this life” 269 . 185. All men, since they are endowed with the dignity of persons, have the inalienable right to an education “that corresponds to their own end, their own character, their different sex, and that is adapted to the culture and traditions of their country and, at the same time, open to fraternal relations with other peoples”; and ordered to man’s ultimate end and to the common good of society, for “true education aims at the formation of the human person in view of his ultimate end and of the good of societies” 270 . 186. Specifically, education must help children and adolescents “to develop harmoniously their physical, moral and intellectual endowments, so that they may gradually acquire a more perfect sense of responsibility in the proper development of their own lives, through continual effort and the acquisition of true freedom; likewise, that they be encouraged to value moral values with an upright conscience and to give them their personal adherence, and also that they be prompted to know and love God more” 271 . That is to say, the intellect must be formed, but without neglecting the formation of freedom, of the courage to make definitive decisions, and of the capacity to love through the sincere and selfless gift of oneself to others. 187. For their part, Christians, by reason of their condition as new creatures –born of water and the Holy Spirit– and as children of God, have a right to a Christian education, which “does not merely pursue the maturity of the human person, but seeks that the baptized… be disposed to live according to the new man in justice and holiness of truth (Eph 4:22-24), and so attain to the perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of Christ (cf. Eph 4:13), and collaborate in the growth of the Mystical Body. Helping, moreover, toward the Christian shaping of the world” 272 . 188. Given the importance of education in the human and Christian transformation of men and of societies, the Church exhorts her children “to give their help generously in the whole field of education” 273 ; and she “reminds pastors of souls of their most grave obligation to arrange everything so that the faithful may enjoy a Christian education, and above all the young, who are the hope of the Church” 274 . St. John Paul II reminded religious of the need for a renewed commitment in the field of education, taking up the educational mission with renewed dedication, with schools of every kind and level, with universities and institutes of higher learning 275 . Catholic schools 189. Among all the means of education, “the school has a special importance. For, while it cultivates the intellectual faculties with unremitting care, it develops the capacity for right judgment, introduces students to the cultural heritage won by past generations, promotes a sense of values, prepares for professional life, fosters friendly relations among students of diverse character and background, and contributes to mutual understanding” 276 . 190. The presence of the Church in the field of schooling is shown above all through Catholic schools; these, in addition to fostering, to no lesser degree, all the goods mentioned concerning the cultural and human formation of students, have as their “distinctive note” to help “adolescents, in the development of their own personality, to grow at the same time according to the new creature they have been made by Baptism, and, finally, to order all human culture to the message of salvation, so that the knowledge the students are gradually acquiring of the world, of life and of man may be illumined by faith, educating their students to pursue the good of the earthly city and… to serve the spread of the Kingdom of God” 277 . 191. Hence the Catholic school retains “its transcendent importance also at the present time” 278 , and the work of educators is of “the utmost importance” 279 . 192. In accordance with the right of the Church and in order to carry out our specific end, we must strive “to establish and freely direct schools of every order and grade” 280 , favoring “primary and secondary schools, which constitute the foundation of education, and also those required by present conditions: such as professional and technical schools, institutes for adult education, for social assistance, for the handicapped, and those in which teachers are prepared for religious education and for other forms of education” 281 . 193. Furthermore, bearing in mind that education must aim at the integral perfection of the human person, that is, at “cultivating the mind in such a way as to promote the capacity for wonder, for intuition, for contemplation and for forming a personal judgment, as well as for cultivating a religious, moral and social sense” 282 , and not only at providing practical training in the sciences and in the various technical skills, it is very fitting that, wherever possible, our Institute establish and develop Catholic humanistic schools. Finally, in the sphere of educational work in schools as a turning point of culture, and without losing sight of its ultimate purpose of building the civilization of love, we can never forget “to attend to the needs of the poor, of those who are deprived of the help and affection of a family, or who do not share in the gift of faith” 283 . Seminaries 194. Our Constitutions say that we wish to work in “education –especially in seminaries, universities and tertiary education–” 284 . 195. We must devote a great part of our best efforts and concerns to the formation of the seminarians of our Institute and also, to the extent of our possibilities, collaborate in other seminaries that ask for our help. For “the religious and moral condition of peoples depends in great part on the priest” 285 , and likewise “the longed-for renewal of the whole Church depends in great part on the ministry of priests” 286 ; in turn, having priests who effectively change and transform societies with the power of the Gospel “depends on the formation received in the seminary” 287 . Hence the Second Vatican Council “proclaims the very great importance of priestly formation” 288 , which is indispensable to such a degree that Pius XI exhorted the bishops of the whole world: “give your colleges the best priests; do not regret withdrawing them from tasks that are apparently more important, but which cannot be compared with this capital and irreplaceable work” 289 . It is our desire “that God might give us the gift of being able to discover and guide so many vocations that we could fill all the good seminaries and novitiates of the whole world” 290 . This demands vocational ministry, into which the best energies must be invested, with appropriate dedication to youth ministry 291 . That is to say, priestly and religious vocations must be promoted, above all through the faithful and joyful witness of consecrated life, while at the same time carrying out with competence and generosity our proper apostolates: Spiritual Exercises, oratories, formation courses, spiritual direction, etc.; and working in fraternal collaboration. Faculties and universities 196. In order that the Gospel may become incarnate in the heart of cultures, the presence of the Church in the world of the universities, that is, of thought and research in their various fields, is “essential.” That is why the Church takes the greatest care of institutions of higher learning, above all of universities and faculties 292 . Since “the destiny of society and of the Church herself is intimately connected with the progress of young people dedicated to higher studies,” the Second Vatican Council exhorts pastors to be solicitous in caring for university students –both of Catholic universities and also of non-Catholic ones–, providing “permanent spiritual and intellectual help to university youth” 293 . 197. The Second Vatican Council clearly indicated the principal objective of every university and faculty that depends on the Church, an objective that shows all its timeliness and urgency: “that each discipline be cultivated according to its own principles, its own methods and the freedom proper to scientific research, in such a way that the understanding of these disciplines may become ever deeper, and that, by considering with all attention the problems and discoveries of recent times, it may be seen more exactly how faith and reason move harmoniously toward the truth, which is one, following the teachings of the Doctors of the Church, above all of St. Thomas Aquinas” 294 . 198. In this way, “the presence of Christian thought must become, as it were, public, stable and universal in the endeavor to promote higher culture, and the students of these institutes must be formed as men outstanding for their learning, prepared to carry out the most important functions in society and to be witnesses of the faith in the world” 295 . 199. In this regard, St. John Paul II teaches in the Encyclical Letter Fides et ratio that the principal task of the university is the effort to achieve a new synthesis between reason and faith, and to recover Philosophy as a unified knowledge. The separation between faith and reason impoverishes and weakens both. Faith, deprived of reason, has stressed feeling and experience, and runs the risk of being reduced to “myth” or superstition. Reason, deprived of the contribution of revelation, runs the danger of losing sight of its final goal. A reason that does not have an adult faith before it is not motivated to turn its gaze toward “the newness and radicality of being. Hence the pressing need to recover the profound unity between faith and Philosophy while respecting their reciprocal autonomy 296 . 200. Connected with this, the conviction that man is capable of attaining a unified and organic vision of knowledge is one of the tasks that Christian thought will have to take up in the course of the next millennium of the Christian era. The fragmentation of knowledge, insofar as it implies a partial approach to the truth, hinders the interior unity of contemporary man 297 . 201. In a special way, starting from the metaphysics of being, a convincing response must be given to the challenges coming from the various philosophical currents, which deserve appropriate attention; for example, eclecticism 298 ; historicism, which establishes the truth of a Philosophy on the basis of its suitability to a particular period and a particular historical purpose, implicitly denying the perennial validity of truth 299 ; scientism, which does not admit as valid any forms of knowledge other than those proper to the positive sciences, relegating religious and theological knowledge and ethical and aesthetic understanding to the borders of the imagination, while at the same time turning values into mere products of emotion and setting aside the notion of being in order to make room for the pure and simple fact 300 ; pragmatism, as the mental attitude of one who, in making his choices, excludes recourse to theoretical reflection or to judgments based on ethical principles 301 . In summary, special attention must be paid to the cultural challenge of the loss of the sense of being, which constitutes the common horizon of many philosophies and which leads to a nihilistic attitude 302 . 202. Furthermore, we must continue to deepen our understanding of the meaning and universal value of the natural law, of the relationship between the positive sciences and faith, between freedom and truth, between bioethics and ethics, etc.; above all in the contemporary context, which seems to grant primacy to an artificial intelligence ever more subject to experimental technique, forgetting that all science must safeguard the human being and promote his inclination toward authentic good 303 . 203. Given the importance of Catholic and ecclesiastical universities and faculties in the field of education and evangelization, the Institutes that direct them must be very conscious of their responsibility, ensuring that in them, while engaging in active dialogue with present-day culture, the Catholic character that is proper to them is preserved, in full fidelity to the Magisterium of the Church 304 . In this last sense, it is necessary to remain on guard against the constant temptation to “be in fashion” and to seek the consensus of common opinion. On the contrary, a permanent disposition of obedience to the truth must be cultivated 305 . 204. Finally, “the Church also expects much from the Faculties of sacred sciences. For she entrusts to them the most serious task of forming their students not only for the priestly ministry but, above all, for teaching in centers of higher ecclesiastical studies, for scientific research, or for carrying out the most arduous functions of the intellectual apostolate” 306 . 205. [Dialogue between faith and reason] 307 It seems fitting to us to examine this question more deeply, since it is also central to the task of inculturation, following the main points of the magnificent address that Benedict XVI gave at the University of Regensburg on the theme of faith and reason 308 . In the first place, Benedict XVI affirms the intrinsic necessity of the encounter between biblical faith and Greek thought, since there is an essential relationship between the two. The Holy Father quotes a sentence that the Byzantine emperor Manuel II Palaeologus addressed to his Persian interlocutor: “not to act according to reason is contrary to the nature of God.” In this conviction of the emperor “the profound harmony between what is Greek in its best sense and what is faith in God according to the Bible becomes manifest.” That is to say, “God acts ‘σὺν λόγω’, with Logos.” Therefore, “the encounter between the biblical message and Greek thought was not a mere coincidence. St. Paul’s vision: ‘Come over to Macedonia and help us’ (cf. Acts 16:6-10), can be interpreted as a condensed expression of the intrinsic necessity of a rapprochement between biblical faith and Greek philosophizing.” A rapprochement that had begun long before: “the mysterious name of God uttered from the burning bush… which affirms of Him simply ‘I am,’ His being, stands in contrast to myth, and bears a close analogy to Socrates’ attempt to defeat and overcome myth itself.” “At bottom, it is a matter of the encounter between faith and reason, between authentic enlightenment and religion” 309 . Hence the faith of the Church “has always held to the conviction that between God and us, between His eternal creating Spirit and our created reason, there exists a true analogy, in which certainly –as the Fourth Lateran Council said in 1215– the dissimilarities are infinitely greater than the similarities, yet not to the point of abolishing analogy and its language” 310 . 206. On the contrary, for Muslim doctrine “God is absolutely transcendent. His will is not bound to any of our categories, not even that of rationality.” Within the Church it is necessary to mention certain theological tendencies that break this synthesis: “In contrast to so-called Augustinian and Thomist intellectualism, John Duns Scotus introduced a voluntarist approach which, after successive developments, finally led to the claim that we know of God only the voluntas ordinata . Beyond this there would be the Freedom of God, by virtue of which He could have created and done even the opposite of everything He has actually done. […] Here positions emerge which… could even lead to an image of a capricious God, who is not bound even to truth and goodness. God’s transcendence and otherness are emphasized in so exaggerated a way that even our reason, our sense of the true and the good, cease to be an authentic mirror of God, whose abysmal possibilities remain eternally inaccessible to us and hidden behind His actual decisions” 311 . Therefore, it is precisely the encounter between faith and reason, and the analogy between Being by essence and being by participation, that opens access to the possibility of knowing and expressing truly, though with limits, the biblical God, the God of faith; and at the same time of overcoming the irrational and absurd notion of a capricious God who is not bound even to truth and goodness. And it is also this encounter that makes it possible to ground truth and goodness metaphysically, overcoming the contradiction of affirming a God who is not bound to truth and goodness and who could, if He wished, make it lawful even to practice idolatry. 207. In fact, the historical process of separation between faith and reason, or the process of the dehellenization of Christianity –“which has increasingly dominated theological discussions since the beginning of the modern age”–, already in its first stage confined and reduced the sphere of faith “to practical reason”: “Dehellenization first emerges in connection with the postulates of the Reformation of the sixteenth century. […] Thus faith no longer appeared as a living historical word but as one element inserted into the structure of a philosophical system. The principle of sola Scriptura , by contrast, seeks the pure primordial form of faith, as it is originally found in the biblical Word. Metaphysics appears as a presupposition derived from another source, from which faith must be freed so that it may once again be entirely itself. Kant, with his assertion that he had had to give up thinking in order to make room for faith, carried this program forward with a radicalism the Reformers had not foreseen. In this way he anchored faith exclusively in practical reason, denying it access to reality as a whole” 312 . 208. Then comes the second stage of dehellenization, with liberal theology, which reduced the figure of Jesus to a mere man with a moral message: “The liberal theology of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries represented a second stage in the program of dehellenization, whose most prominent representative is Adolf von Harnack. […] Harnack’s central idea was simply to return to the man Jesus and to his simple message, prior to all the elaborations of theology and, precisely, also of hellenization. […] In the end, Jesus was presented as the father of a humanitarian moral message” 313 . We may point out that this doctrine continues to exert a wide influence on certain present-day theologies of religious pluralism, which even go so far as to present the figure of Jesus Christ as a “myth” or as a –“gnostic”– manifestation, one among many, of the “inexpressible and unknowable” divinity. 209. Continuing with Benedict XVI’s address, it is very important to point out that this process of dehellenization –of separation between faith and reason– “coincides” with and adapts itself to the process of modern reason; and that in fact it not only substantially impoverishes the theological field of faith, but at the same time reduces the proper sphere of reason, which progressively loses –dangerously for man– all interest in the most properly human questions that belong to the ethical and transcendent dimension of the human being. “At bottom, Harnack’s aim was to bring Christianity into harmony with modern reason, freeing it precisely from seemingly philosophical and theological elements, such as faith in the Divinity of Christ and in the Trinity of God. In this sense, historical-critical exegesis of the New Testament, in his view, restored to Theology its place in the cosmos of the university: for Harnack, Theology is something essentially historical and therefore strictly scientific. […] Underlying all this is the modern self-limitation of reason, classically expressed in Kant’s ‘critiques,’ but further radicalized in the meantime by the thinking of the natural sciences. This modern concept of reason is based, to put it briefly, on a synthesis between Platonism (Cartesianism) and empiricism, a synthesis confirmed by the success of technology. […] This implies two fundamental orientations, decisive for our question. Only the kind of certainty that derives from the synergy of mathematics and the empirical method can be considered scientific. Anything that claims to be science must conform to this criterion. The human sciences too, such as History, Psychology, Sociology and Philosophy, have attempted to approximate this canon of scientific value. Furthermore, it is important for our reflections to note that this method as such excludes the question of God, presenting it as an unscientific or pre-scientific question. But in this way we find ourselves facing a reduction of the sphere of science and of reason that must be called into question. I will return to this argument later. For the moment it suffices to bear in mind that, from this perspective, any attempt to maintain Theology as a ‘scientific’ discipline would leave of Christianity only a tiny fragment. But we must add more: if science as a whole is only this, then man himself would suffer a reduction, for the specifically human questions, that is, where he comes from and where he is going, the questions of religion and of ethics, cannot find a place within the space of common reason described by ‘science’ understood in this way, and must be relegated to the realm of the subjective. […] The situation thus created is dangerous for humanity, as can be seen in the pathologies that threaten religion and reason, pathologies that necessarily erupt when reason is reduced to the point that the questions of religion and ethics no longer concern it” 314 . 210. Finally, Benedict XVI refers to the third stage of dehellenization, which is currently spreading: “in view of the encounter among many cultures, it is often said today that the synthesis with Hellenism in the early Church was a first inculturation, which ought not to be binding on other cultures. These, it is said, should have the right to go back to the point prior to that inculturation, in order to discover the pure message of the New Testament and inculturate it anew in their respective settings. […] However, the fundamental decisions that concern precisely the relationship between faith and the search of human reason are part of the faith itself, and are a development consonant with its own nature” 315 . 211. In conclusion, Benedict XVI proposes to acknowledge “what is positive in the modern development of the spirit” and “to broaden our concept of reason and of its use.” Because we also see the dangers that arise from the new possibilities, it is necessary to ask how to avoid them: “We will succeed in doing so only if reason and faith come together in a new way, if we overcome the self-imposed limitation of reason to what can be verified by experiment, and once again open up its horizon in all its breadth. In this sense, Theology, not only as a historical discipline and human science, but as genuine Theology, that is, as a science that inquires into the reason of faith, must find a place in the university and in the wide dialogue of the sciences. […] The West has long been threatened by this aversion to the fundamental questions of its reason, and can only suffer great loss as a result. The courage to open oneself to the breadth of reason, and not the denial of its grandeur, is the program with which a Theology committed to reflection on biblical faith enters the debate of our time. ‘Not to act according to reason, not to act with logos , is contrary to the nature of God,’ said Manuel II, starting from his Christian image of God, in answer to his Persian interlocutor. In the dialogue of cultures we invite our interlocutors to this great logos , to this breadth of reason. To rediscover it constantly for ourselves is the great task of the university” 316 . c) Intellectuals 212. What we may call the intellectual class deserves a chapter of its own. Among the turning points of culture are “men of thought, or intellectuals,” whom we must help “with regard to the initiation and calling, development, discernment, formation, consolidation, accompaniment and subsequent exercise of the vocation to the intellectual apostolate” 317 . 213. St. John Paul II, speaking “of the privileged places of culture,” besides mentioning the “world of the school and the university,” also refers explicitly to “the settings of scientific and technical research, the places of artistic creation and of humanistic reflection” 318 . Here we find ourselves in the sphere par excellence of the “creation” of culture. Intellectuals, who devote themselves to research and reflection in the various branches of human knowledge, are the principal “creators” of culture, since they have an incisive influence on the behavior and cultural models of men and of societies. It is they, above all, who present to society “the criteria of judgment, the determining values, the points of interest, the lines of thought, the sources of inspiration, the models of life of humanity” 319 . 214. As St. Thomas teaches –referring specifically to the Church–, intellectuals are –analogously– what architects are in the construction of a building: “the doctors of Theology are as principal craftsmen, who investigate and teach how others ought to procure salvation” 320 . 215. Therefore, those who have greater intellectual capacity should, as far as possible, be provided with the means and time necessary to devote themselves to scientific research in their respective disciplines. 216. As the Second Vatican Council counsels: “young men of greater talent… who show aptitude for teaching and research must be carefully prepared and incorporated into teaching” 321 . 217. Moreover, the level and future of our seminaries and also of our universities depend particularly on having professors who devote themselves seriously and with distinction to scientific research. 218. Finally, in the sphere of the intellectual apostolate and of scientific research, priority must be given to “publications, since what is written endures and spreads further,” and therefore “special emphasis will be placed on the spread of the Gospel through articles in scholarly or popular journals, monographs, books and other levels of publication” 322 . d) The culture of “making” 219. God has entrusted to man, created in His image and likeness, the task of having dominion over the earth, first of all “by shaping the wonderful ‘material’ of his own humanity and then by exercising creative dominion over the universe that surrounds him” 323 . This second aspect represents the proper sphere of the culture of “making.” Human work 220. In this sense, we have, in the first place, everything that concerns human work and technology and, in the second place, artistic activity. Although this activity directly perfects things exterior to man –making them useful or beautiful–, nevertheless man and his dignity are always the principle that must illumine and guide the sphere of “making.” The human person is and must always be the subject, the center and the end of all human activity and of every social institution. Consequently, the man who works is much more important than the product of his work, since this product derives from man –through the actualization of the skills and capacities inscribed in his nature– and is destined for his benefit and for the promotion of his dignity and of his good considered integrally. 221. We may also point out, in relation to the dimension of human work, but within the broader sphere of the social and political order whose soul is justice, the task of the Church to proclaim the social doctrine of the Church. That is, the task of purifying reason and of ethical formation, so that the demands of justice may be understood and put into practice 324 . For the Church, with her social doctrine, which argues on the basis of what is in accordance with the nature of every human being, helps to make it possible for what is just to be effectively recognized and then also carried out. In this sense, we may highlight the effort of the Magisterium, above all in the twentieth century, to read social reality in the light of the Gospel and to offer its own contribution to the solution of the social question 325 . 222. The Gospel must also penetrate, purify and transform the economic, social and political order. That is why “the new evangelization, which the modern world urgently needs and on which I have insisted on more than one occasion –said St. John Paul II–, must include among its essential elements the proclamation of the social doctrine of the Church” 326 . “Today special attention and extraordinary commitment are required by the great challenges in which vast sectors of the human family are in greatest danger: wars and terrorism, hunger and thirst, and certain terrible epidemics. But it is also necessary to confront, with the same determination and clarity of purpose, the danger of political and legislative choices that contradict fundamental values and anthropological and ethical principles rooted in the nature of the human being, in particular with regard to the defense of human life at all its stages, from conception to natural death, and to the promotion of the family founded on marriage, avoiding the introduction into public law of other forms of union which would contribute to destabilizing it, obscuring its particular character and its irreplaceable social role” 327 . 223. This is the sphere of the laity, whose proper vocation is to seek the Kingdom of God by engaging in temporal affairs, ordering them according to God and informing them with the spirit of the Gospel 328 . The ethical and social aspect is an indispensable dimension of Christian life and witness: “The temptation to a hidden and individualistic spirituality must be rejected, one that has little to do with the demands of charity, or with the logic of the Incarnation and, in the end, with the very eschatological tension of Christianity” 329 . Artistic activity 224. In the culture of making we have, in the second place, the sphere of artistic activity. This consists in giving aesthetic form to the ideas conceived in the mind. Just as in the dimension of work, in this task of producing “beautiful works” it is man who has primacy, not only because he is their author but also, in particular, because “in shaping a work the artist expresses himself to the point that his production is a unique reflection of his very being, of what he is and of how he is” 330 . Artistic activity occupies an important place in human culture, in particular because of its proper and peculiar relationship with beauty, “which is, in a certain sense, the visible expression of the good, just as the good is the metaphysical condition of beauty” 331 . For this reason, the artistic vocation is a social service for the benefit of the common good, which “in its own way contributes to the life and the rebirth of a people” 332 . 225. Moreover, the historical development of beauty has found profound inspiration in the mystery of the Son of God made visible. “Indeed, the Son of God, in becoming man… has also revealed a new dimension of beauty, of which the Gospel message is full. […] The biblical Word has countless times become image, music or poetry, evoking in the language of art the mystery of the ‘Word made flesh’” 333 . 226. If we try to specify the cultural contribution of artistic creation in its proper relationship with beauty, we can say that it consists in the concrete effort to express and interpret “beautifully” the mystery hidden in reality. “Every authentic form of art is, in its own way, a path of access to the deepest reality of man and of the world” 334 . In this sense, art has an intimate affinity with the world of faith. “As a search for beauty, the fruit of an imagination that goes beyond the everyday, it is by its nature a kind of call to mystery” 335 . For this reason, the activity of artists constitutes a “noble ministry,” “when their works are able to reflect in some way the infinite beauty of God and to direct the thoughts of men toward Him. They are, in their own way, true theological ‘places’” 336 . In this sense, St. Paul VI pointed out that “Theology and Philosophy have another relationship with beauty, which consists in this: beauty, lending to doctrine its vesture and ornament, with the sweetness of song and the visibility of figurative and plastic art, opens the way for its precious teachings to be taught to many. Lofty disquisitions and subtle reasoning are inaccessible to many; yet they are able to grasp, to feel and to appreciate the influence of beauty, and more easily, by means of it, truth shows itself to them in splendor and nourishes them” 337 . 227. Consequently, the Church needs art in order to transmit the Gospel message, that is, to make the world of the spirit, of the invisible and of God “perceptible” and, as far as possible, “fascinating.” For art “possesses that particular capacity to reflect one or another aspect of the message, translating it into colors, forms or sounds that assist the intuition of the one who contemplates and listens. All this without depriving the message itself of its transcendent value and its halo of mystery. The Church, in particular, needs literary and figurative art, musicians, architects, etc.” 338 . In turn, artists, in their search for the hidden meaning of things and in their longing to express the world of the ineffable, find abundant inspiration in religious themes, which in fact are those most treated by artists of all ages. Above all in Christianity, since it, “by virtue of the central dogma of the Incarnation of the Word of God, offers the artist a particularly rich horizon of motifs of inspiration. How impoverished art would be if it abandoned the inexhaustible vein of the Gospel!” 339 . “Beauty is a key to mystery and a call to the transcendent. It is an invitation to savor life and to dream of the future” 340 . e) The social communications media 228. Finally, we have, as a most important turning point of culture, the social communications media, which we must also evangelize. 229. They are instruments, “technical inventions which are directed principally to the human spirit and which have opened new ways of communicating with extraordinary ease news, ideas and doctrines of every kind” 341 . In our age, thanks to the progress of technology, they have been perfected in an admirable way. 230. Among them stand out “those media which by their nature can reach and move not only individual men but also the multitudes and the whole of human society, such as the press, cinema, radio, television and the like, which therefore can rightly be called the media of social communication” 342 . 231. Since they communicate news and ideas with great ease and speed, and reach the multitudes –the whole world–, their influence on present-day culture is evident; they in fact exercise an “influence, at once planetary and capillary, on the formation of mentalities and customs” 343 . 232. These instruments, if they are used rightly, “provide valuable help to the human race, since they contribute effectively to the relaxation and cultivation of minds and to the spread and strengthening of the Kingdom of God” 344 . 233. These media constitute “at present the privileged path for the creation and transmission of culture, and present themselves as a new frontier for the mission of the Church” 345 . 234. The Areopagus of Athens, to which St. Paul addressed himself, represented the center of the culture of the Athenian people; today “the first Areopagus of the modern age is the world of communications, which is unifying humanity and turning it –as the saying goes– into ‘a global village.’” These media have come to have such importance that “for many they are the chief means of information and formation, of guidance and inspiration for individual, family and social behavior. The new generations above all grow up in a world conditioned by these media” 346 . 235. The evangelization of the social communications media is therefore urgent; otherwise the Church and the Gospel will remain completely foreign to what constitutes “the first Areopagus of the modern age,” with grave losses for the task of inculturation, since, as St. John Paul II affirmed, “the very evangelization of modern culture depends in great part on their influence” 347 . For this reason the Church exhorts that “they be used, without the least delay and with the utmost effort, in the most varied forms of apostolate, as the reality and the circumstances of our time demand. This task is urgent for the lay faithful and also for the members of the clergy: let the sacred pastors, therefore, hasten to fulfill their mission in this field, which is intimately linked with their ordinary duty of preaching” 348 . 236. Pastoral work in the media must have as its objective not only “to multiply the proclamation” and “to spread the Christian message,” but especially “to integrate the message itself into this ‘new culture’ created by modern communications” 349 . 237. That is to say, through these instruments of social communication human and Gospel values must be transmitted in a new synthesis.
