Phil 1:8). 141. What kind of love is this? It is much more than that of a teacher; it is the love of a father; and even more, that of a mother (cf. 1 Thess 2:7.11; 1 Cor 4:15; Gal 4:19). Such is the love that the Lord expects from every preacher of the Gospel, from every builder of the Church. 142. A sign of love will be the desire to offer the truth and to lead to unity. A sign of love will likewise be to devote oneself without reserve and without looking back to the proclamation of Jesus Christ. Other signs of this love will be: a) Respect for the religious and spiritual situation of the person being evangelized. Respect for his pace, which must not be forced too much; respect for his conscience and his convictions, which must not be treated harshly. b) Care not to wound others, especially if they are weak in their faith (cf. 1 Cor 8:9-13; Rom 14:15), with statements that may be clear to the faithful but that can be a source of bewilderment or scandal to the newly initiated, inflicting a wound on their souls. c) The effort made to transmit to Christians solid certainties based on the Word of God, and not doubts or uncertainties born of poorly assimilated erudition. The faithful need these certainties in their Christian life; they have a right to them inasmuch as they are children of God who, placing themselves in his arms, abandon themselves totally to the demands of love. With the fervor of the Saints 76 143. We must proclaim the Gospel with the fervor and enthusiasm of the saints, even in moments of difficulty and persecution in a de-Christianized and atheistic world. The saints are a most eloquent sign of the Church's vitality; they have always transformed the world. They have been the true reformers of the world and of the Church. They are the finest members of the Mystical Body of Christ. They are the greatest and most complete fruit of the Incarnation and the Redemption. The saints have been the eminent witnesses and guardians of the divine Tradition of the Church; that is, by their lives they recall and pass on the very breath of the Church. They knew how to overcome all the obstacles that stood in the way of evangelization, and therefore they are models to be followed and to whom we must turn in this work. 144. We must preserve, cultivate and ask God for spiritual fervor , the joy of evangelizing, even when we have to sow in tears. “May it mean for us—as it did for John the Baptist, for Peter and Paul, for the other Apostles, and for a multitude of splendid evangelizers all through the Church's history—an interior enthusiasm that nobody and nothing can quench. May it be the great joy of our consecrated lives. And may the world of our time, which is searching, sometimes with anguish, sometimes with hope, be enabled to receive the Good News not from evangelizers who are dejected, discouraged, impatient or anxious, but from ministers of the Gospel whose lives glow with fervor, who have first received the joy of Christ, and who are willing to risk their lives so that the Kingdom may be proclaimed and the Church established in the midst of the world” 77 . g) Missionaries ad vitam and missionary cooperation A special vocation 145. The existence of missionaries in the Church has been emphasized by the Second Vatican Council: “Although the task of spreading the faith, according to his state, falls upon every disciple of Christ, Christ the Lord always calls from among his disciples those whom he wills, so that they may be with him and so that he may send them to preach to the nations” 78 . 146. It is, then, a “special vocation” which has as its model that of the Apostles: it is manifested in a total commitment to the service of evangelization; it is a self-giving that involves the missionary's whole person and whole life, demanding of him a limitless gift of energy and time. 147. “The special vocation of missionaries ad vitam retains all its validity: it is the model of the Church's missionary commitment, which always stands in need of radical and total self-giving, of new and bold endeavors. Therefore the men and women missionaries who have devoted their whole lives to bearing witness to the risen Lord among the nations must not allow themselves to be daunted by doubts, misunderstanding, rejection or persecution. They should revive the grace of their specific charism and courageously continue on their way, preferring—in a spirit of faith, obedience and communion with their Pastors—the humblest and most difficult places” 79 . 148. Given the missionary character of our Institute, we must use all the necessary resources, our experience and creativity, in fidelity to the original charism, to prepare ourselves adequately and so that there may be no lack of missionaries, thus ensuring the renewal of the spiritual, moral and physical energies of our members. Each according to his condition and ability 149. Our priests are impelled by the sacrament of Holy Orders: “The spiritual gift which priests have received in ordination prepares them, not for any narrow and limited mission, but for the most universal and all-embracing mission of salvation ‘to the end of the earth,’ for every priestly ministry shares in the universal scope of the mission entrusted by Christ to his Apostles” 80 . 150. Our members of contemplative life will respond to the invitation of the Second Vatican Council, repeated by St. John Paul II, to establish communities in the young Churches, so as to give “splendid witness among non-Christians to the majesty and love of God, as well as to unity in Christ” 81 . 151. For our members of active life immense spaces open up for charity, the proclamation of the Gospel, Christian education, culture, and solidarity with the poor, the discriminated against, the marginalized and the oppressed. 152. Our missionary religious brothers will translate their consecration of poverty, chastity and obedience for the sake of the Kingdom into manifold fruits of paternity according to the Spirit. Precisely the mission ad gentes offers them a vast field in which to give themselves with a total and undivided love. 153. The members of the Third Order , in their own measure, are not excluded from the missionary urgency. The mission belongs to the whole People of God. The participation of the laity in the spread of the faith is clearly evident from the earliest days of Christianity, through the efforts of individual faithful and families, and also of the entire community. They therefore have the general obligation, and enjoy the right, both individually and in association, to work so that the divine message of salvation may be known and received by all people throughout the world. Moreover, given their own secular character, they have the specific vocation “to seek the Kingdom of God by engaging in temporal affairs and ordering them according to the plan of God” 82 . As circumstances permit, let consideration be given to the possibility of inviting members of the Third Order to take part, for a set period of time, in the missions ad gentes that have been entrusted to the Institute. 154. In this way all the members of our Institutes, by virtue of Baptism, share responsibility for missionary activity . “The Council invites all to a profound interior renewal, so that, having a lively awareness of their own responsibility for the spreading of the Gospel, they may accept their share in missionary work among the nations” 83 . Missionary cooperation and animation 155. Among the forms of participation, first place belongs to spiritual cooperation : prayer, sacrifice and the witness of Christian life. The sacrifice of the missionary must be shared and supported by that of all the faithful. For this reason, we urge those who exercise their pastoral ministry among the sick to instruct them on the value of suffering, encouraging them to offer it to God for missionaries. 156. Cooperation is also shown in promoting missionary vocations within one's family and surroundings. It is striking that several nations, while increasing their monetary donations, show an ever lower rate of missionary vocations, which reflect the true dimension of self-giving to one's brothers. Vocations to the priesthood and to consecrated life are a sure sign of the vitality of a Church. 157. The material and financial needs of the missions are many: not only for founding the Church with minimal structures (chapels, schools for catechists and seminarians, housing), but also for supporting works of charity, education and human promotion—an immense field of action, especially in poor countries. The missionary Church gives what she receives; she distributes to the poor what her children who are better off in material resources generously place at her disposal. 158. In our parishes, therefore, missionary animation must be included as a primary element of ordinary pastoral care, in associations as well as in groups, especially youth groups. To achieve this end, information through the missionary press and the various audiovisual media is valuable above all. Animation activities must always be directed toward their specific goals: to inform and form the People of God for the universal mission of the Church; to promote vocations ad gentes ; to foster cooperation in the work of evangelization. Indeed, one cannot give a reductive picture of missionary activity, as if it were principally help to the poor, a contribution to the liberation of the oppressed, the promotion of development, or the defense of human rights. The missionary Church is also involved on these fronts, but her primary task lies elsewhere: the poor are hungry for God, and not just for bread and freedom; missionary activity must first of all bear witness to and proclaim salvation in Christ, establishing local Churches which then become instruments of liberation in every sense. 159. We will carry out all our missionary undertakings in communion with the Church , aware that it belongs to the missionary Dicastery to direct and coordinate throughout the world the work of the evangelization of peoples and missionary cooperation. h) A proper spirituality 160. Missionary activity demands a specific spirituality , which applies in particular to those whom God has called to be missionaries. 161. “This spirituality is expressed first of all by a life of complete docility to the Spirit; it commits us to being molded from within by him, so that we may become ever more like Christ. Docility to the Spirit also commits us to welcoming the gifts of fortitude and discernment, which are essential elements of missionary spirituality” 84 . 162. “An essential characteristic of missionary spirituality is intimate communion with Christ : we cannot understand or carry out the mission except in reference to Christ, sent by the Father to evangelize (cf. Lk 4:18.21). Paul describes his attitudes: Have among yourselves the same mind that was in Christ: who, though he was in the form of God, did not cling greedily to being equal with God, but emptied Himself, taking the condition of a servant, becoming like men and appearing in his bearing as a man; and he humbled Himself, being obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Phil 2:5-8)” 85 . 163. “The missionary is required ‘to renounce himself and everything that up to this point he considered as his own, and to make himself everything to everyone’: in a poverty which sets him free for the Gospel; in detachment from the people and things of his own surroundings, so as to become a brother to those to whom he is sent and bring them Christ the Savior. This is the goal of missionary spirituality: I became weak with the weak… I have become all things to all, so as to save some at all costs. And I do all this for the sake of the Gospel (1 Cor 9:22-23)” 86 . 164. “Missionary spirituality is also marked by apostolic charity, the charity of Christ who came to gather into one the children of God who were scattered (Jn 11:52)” 87 . 165. “The missionary is moved by ‘zeal for souls,’ a zeal inspired by Christ's own charity, which takes the form of attentiveness, tenderness, compassion, openness, availability, and interest in people's problems. Jesus' love is very deep: he who knew what was in man (Jn 2:25) loved everyone by offering them redemption, and he suffered when it was rejected” 88 . 166. “The missionary is a person of charity: in order to be able to proclaim to every person that he is loved by God and is himself capable of loving, he must bear witness to charity toward all, spending his life for his neighbor. […] Like Christ, he must love the Church: Christ loved the Church and gave Himself up for her (Eph 5:25). […] For every missionary and every community, fidelity to Christ cannot be separated from fidelity to his Church” 89 . 167. The call to mission derives, of its nature, from the call to holiness. The universal vocation to holiness is closely linked to the universal vocation to mission. Every member of the faithful is called to holiness and to mission. The missionary spirituality of the Church is a journey toward holiness. 168. “The renewed impulse to the mission ad gentes demands holy missionaries. It is not enough to update pastoral techniques, organize and coordinate ecclesial resources, or delve more deeply into the biblical and theological foundations of faith: what is needed is the encouragement of a new ‘ardor for holiness’ among missionaries and throughout the Christian community, especially among those who work most closely with missionaries” 90 . “The missionary must be a ‘contemplative in action’ who finds answers to problems in the light of the Word of God through personal and community prayer” 91 . 169. “The missionary is a person of the Beatitudes. Before sending out the Twelve to evangelize, Jesus instructs them, pointing out to them the paths of mission: poverty, meekness, acceptance of suffering and persecution, the desire for justice and peace, charity—in other words, he points out to them precisely the Beatitudes, practiced in the apostolic life (cf. Mt 5:1-12). By living the Beatitudes, the missionary experiences and shows concretely that the Kingdom of God has already come and that he has accepted it. The characteristic of every authentic missionary life is the inner joy that comes from faith. In a world tormented and oppressed by so many problems, a world tempted to pessimism, the one who proclaims the ‘Good News’ must be a person who has found true hope in Christ” 92 . 6. Mary, model of the missionary 170. The Most Blessed Virgin Mary occupies a privileged place in the work of man's Redemption accomplished by her Son: “With him and in dependence on him, she placed herself, by the grace of almighty God, at the service of the mystery of Redemption” 93 . In this way she is, for the Church, Mother and model in the mission which the Church received from the Savior. 171. Indeed, Mary, according to the divine good pleasure, even after her glorification in heaven, has continued to show, in her various apparitions to the men and women of every age and place, what the attitude of the Lord's disciples ought to be in the work of Redemption. She has drawn near to the humblest and has simply adapted herself to the language and the capacity of reception of her sons and daughters, even in the outward appearance of her face. All this with one sole aim: to form, in the school of prayer and penance and of the following of Jesus in the various states of life, true disciples who actively participate in the redemptive task with her same attitude: “that maternal love by which all who join in the Church's apostolic mission for the regeneration of men should be animated” 94 . 172. The Church, missionary by her very essence, finds in Mary an eminent model to follow in her task of inculturating the Gospel, especially when she is sent by Christ ad gentes . Throughout the centuries her finest sons and daughters have known how to respond to the Lord's calls by entrusting their lives and their various apostolic tasks entirely to the protection of the Mother of God. 173. Countless are the concrete examples of missionary saints who entrusted to Mary their efforts, their difficulties and their daily joys in the task of reaching every person and every culture in order to offer the Gospel of Redemption. On many occasions they placed under the patronage of the Blessed Virgin, invoked under one of her many titles, the mission in territories and among cultures where the proclamation was being made for the first time. 174. Mary's example is particularly illuminating when she proclaims at one and the same time “the greatness of the Lord” and the “lowliness of his handmaid,” showing—centuries ahead of false controversies—that the proclamation of Jesus Christ is not arrogance, but a work of justice and charity. 175. May the first missionary after her Son Jesus Christ give us that soul and that heart as great as the world, which is the heart that the missionary must have. Conclusion At the beginning of the third millennium of the Redemption, “God is preparing a great springtime for Christianity, and we can already see its first signs. In fact, both in the non-Christian world and in the world of ancient Christian tradition, people are gradually drawing closer to Gospel ideals and values, a development which the Church seeks to encourage. Today in fact there is a new consensus among peoples about these values: the rejection of violence and war; respect for the human person and for human rights; the desire for freedom, justice and brotherhood; the surmounting of different forms of racism and nationalism; the affirmation of the dignity and role of women. Christian hope sustains us in committing ourselves fully to the new evangelization and to the worldwide mission, and leads us to pray as Jesus taught us: Thy Kingdom come, Thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven (Mt 6:10). […] We cannot be content when we consider the millions of our brothers and sisters, who like us have been redeemed by the blood of Christ but who live in ignorance of the love of God. For each believer, as for the entire Church, the missionary task must remain foremost, for it concerns the eternal destiny of humanity and corresponds to God's mysterious and merciful plan” 95 . ***** Notes 1 Cf.
