The religious, to the extent that he fully submits his soul to God, reaches a state of indifference and detachment from the things of the world, which does not mean impotence but on the contrary, a masterful and free will, capable of dedicating itself to things without letting itself be dominated by them. b) Lordship over men: to the extent that the religious gives himself generously to the service of Jesus Christ, the only King who deserves to be served, he acquires an effective, though spiritual, kingship over men, even over those who have power and authority, and even over those who abuse it. Because they take upon themselves the burden of their sins and their sorrows, through a humble and serving love that goes as far as the sacrifice of oneself. c) Lordship over the world, in two ways: – One, by collaborating with the world of creation through work and with the world of Redemption through the apostolate. For this kingship to be effective, it will be necessary that, together with dedication to things, there be at the same time a detachment and disengagement from them: It remains that those who have wives live as though they had none; those who weep as though they were not weeping; those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing; those who buy as though they did not possess, and those who enjoy the world as though they were not enjoying it, for the outward form of this world is passing away (1 Cor 7:29ff.). – The other, by rejecting the world, whether out of loyalty to the world itself, which must be held as a means and not as an end, or out of loyalty to God, resisting the concupiscences, temptations and sins of the world; being independent in the face of the maxims, mockeries and persecutions of the world, depending only on our right conscience enlightened by faith; ready for martyrdom out of loyalty to God, which constitutes the full and total rejection of the evil world. The greatest grace that God can grant our tiny Religious Family is persecution, especially that which reaches martyrdom 53 : “Long live Jesus Christ, who gives us strength to bear all trials for love of him. The works of God have always been opposed, for the greater splendor of the divine magnificence” 54 . We must always remember that, for persecution to be blessed, it must necessarily meet two requirements: that we be “insulted for the sake of Christ,” and that “what is said against us be false” 55 ; and we must take great care not to turn our troubles over and over, entertaining ourselves with delicate self-satisfaction in them, or falling into “that Luciferian belief that we are something great” 56 , that we are suffering a great deal. Our pride leads us to “regard blades of grass as beams, pinpricks as wounds, mice as elephants” 57 . d) Lordship over the devil: We need religious convinced not only that by the grace of God they have power to resist the devil, but also power to exorcise him. – Living as risen ones: seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your minds on the things that are above, not on those of the earth (Col 3:1); in the freedom of the children of God , who do not let themselves be enslaved: – neither under the elements of the world (Gal 4:3), – nor under the letter that kills 58 , – nor under the spirit of the world 59 , because we must not submit to the yoke of slavery… (otherwise) Christ would profit us nothing 60 . We must be so docile to the Spirit that we can say: “My glory is to live as free / as a bird in the sky; / I make no nest upon this ground…”; owing nothing to the flesh, because all flesh is like grass and all its glory like the flower of grass (1 Pet 1:24), and if we live by the Spirit, let us also walk by the Spirit (Gal 5:25), since what is born of the flesh is flesh; but what is born of the Spirit is Spirit (Jn 3:6). That is to have a princely spirit 61 : it is to direct the soul toward great acts… it is to be concerned with great things… it is to accomplish great works in every virtue. It is to be noble. And what is it to be noble?… That is felt and not said. It is a man of heart. It is a man who has something for himself and for others. They are those born to command. They are those capable of punishing themselves and of punishing. They are those who have put style into their conduct. They are those who ask not for freedom but for hierarchy. They are those who set laws for themselves and keep them… They are those who feel honor as they feel life. Those who, because they possess themselves, can give themselves. They are those who know at every instant the things for which one must die. Those capable of giving things that no one obliges and of abstaining from things that no one forbids. They are those who always consider themselves beginners: let us always consider ourselves beginners, never ceasing to aspire to a holier and more perfect life, never stopping. So that we may be firmly resolved to attain holiness. A religious who is not willing to pass through the second and the third conversion, or who does nothing concrete to achieve it, even if he is with us in body, does not belong to our spiritual family. We must have “a great and very resolute determination not to stop until reaching it (holiness), come what may, happen what may, whatever the toil, whoever may murmur, whether one gets there, or dies on the way, or has no heart for the labors along it, even if the world should sink…” 62 . What matters is to take a step, one more step; it is always the same step beginning again. Through Baptism, through the practice of the virtues and by reason of religious profession, “which is intimately rooted in the consecration of Baptism and expresses it more fully” 63 , we want to imitate more closely and represent perpetually in the Church that form of life which the Son of God chose when he became incarnate 64 . We want to imitate Jesus Christ as perfectly as possible, since he teaches us: I have given you an example (Jn 13:15), and St. Paul exhorts: Have the same sentiments that were in Christ Jesus… (Phil 2:5), in such a way that we may be the good fragrance of Christ (2 Cor 2:15), ambassadors for Christ (2 Cor 5:20) … of the mystery of the Gospel (Eph 6:19), a letter of Christ (2 Cor 3:3), clothed with Christ (Gal 3:27), firmly convinced that we are predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Rom 8:29), reproducing him 65 , becoming like him 66 , configuring ourselves to him 67 , knowing that we reflect the very image (2 Cor 3:18) of the Only Son of God. We want to imitate him until we can truly say to others: Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Cor 11:1), it is no longer I who live, it is Christ who lives in me (Gal 2:20). The fact that the Word assumed a human nature must move us to the practice of the virtues of self-emptying: humility, poverty, suffering, obedience, self-denial, mercy and love for all men. From the very fact of becoming man without ceasing to be God, we must learn to be in the world 68 “without being of the world” 69 . We must go to the world to convert it and not to blend in with it. We must go to the culture and to the cultures of man not to be converted into them, but to heal them and elevate them with the power of the Gospel, doing, analogously, what Christ did: “He suppressed the diabolical, assumed the human and communicated the divine to it” 70 . Just as Christ became like us in all things except sin (Heb 4:15), so for us sin, error and all their derivatives cannot be assumed. Before baptizing one must exorcise; without conversion reconciliation is impossible; without renouncing evil there is no Redemption. There can be no unity at the expense of truth. There is no holiness without purity of soul: “holiness means purity” 71 . Only what has dignity or necessity can be assumed. Neither the inhuman, nor the anti-human, nor the subhuman can be assumed. The irrational, the absurd and all their derivatives cannot be assumed. But nothing authentically human must be rejected, since Christ assumed a complete human nature. We must assume everything human, since “what was not assumed was not redeemed either” 72 , and what is human and is not assumed “sets itself up as a new idol with an old malice” 73 . And this assuming of what is human must not be merely apparent, but real. This assumption is only real when it truly transforms what is human in Christ, elevating it, dignifying it, perfecting it. What is left merely on the human level has only apparently been assumed. What has been said applies, in a particular way, to the evangelization of culture, which demands of us a spirituality with particular nuances: “this calls for a new way of approaching cultures, attitudes and behaviors, in order to enter into deep dialogue with cultural milieus and to make their encounter with the message of Christ fruitful. And on the part of responsible Christians, this work demands a faith enlightened by continual reflection that is confronted with the sources of the Church’s message, and a constant spiritual discernment sought in prayer” 74 , never forgetting that “true inculturation is from within : it consists, ultimately, in a renewal of life under the influence of grace” 75 . Furthermore, we must attend spiritually to religious sisters, because of the very dignity of their consecration, which makes them “spouses of the Word.” In a certain way, religious sisters resemble the human nature of Christ, which: – is totally stripped of itself, without even having its own personhood; – is united to the Word with an intimate and most perfect union; – is a most docile instrument of the Word; – all its wealth consists in giving itself to the Word. The religious sister who truly longs to be a spouse of the Word must, out of love for this divine Spouse 76 : – “abandon everything”: through the three vows she separates herself from everything that might hinder perfect union with Jesus Christ; – “in order to unite herself with all her strength to the Word”: through charity and through a stable, firm and constant fidelity to the will of Jesus Christ: “in the Church, in the cloister, in the cell, in the refectory, at recreation, they must go about sighing for Jesus Christ” 77 ; – “to live for him and let herself be guided by him”: they must be zealous for the honor and glory of the Word, their Spouse, and must be able to say with St. Paul: it is no longer I who live, it is Christ who lives in me (Gal 2:20); – “to conceive of the Word what she must bring forth for the Word”: since through the Holy Spirit all her acts must be supernatural, fruitful and meritorious. c) The union of both natures The whole august mystery of the Incarnate Word must be a motive of constant inspiration for our life: “The Father begot the Son as uttering himself, equal to him in all things; for he would not have expressed himself completely and perfectly if in his Word there were anything more or less than what is in him. There we recognize in the highest degree the yes, yes; no, no (Mt 5:37). And that is why this Word is truly the Truth” 78 . The Word, in the Incarnation, anoints with a most holy anointing each and every one of the cells of the body of Jesus, and the whole soul in its essence and in its faculties. There is nothing in Christ that is not thrice holy, and therefore infinitely adorable . Everything in him is transparency, authenticity, sincerity, coherence, truth: I am… the Truth (Jn 14:6). He is the Amen (Rev 3:14). All the promises of God find their Yes in him; and through him we say Amen, to the glory of God (2 Cor 1:20); in him dwells the fullness of the divinity bodily (Col 2:9). In him there is nothing empty, hollow, or not hypostatically assumed. There is nothing of veneer or shell. Nothing simulated or camouflaged. Nothing of lies, falsehood, insecurity, concealment or hypocrisy. He is One Alone 79 –the Word– in two distinct natures, both perfect, complete and hypostatically united. For this very reason Christ is one beyond comparison, and “this is said of Christ in many ways: – In the first place, God is one alone because of the divine nature; hence, thus, no one is God but one alone. – In the second place, he is one Creator alone because of his infinite power: One is the Most High, Creator of all things (Eccl 1:8). – In the third place, he is unique as man, because of the singular eminen­ce of his holiness: there is none who does good (Ps 14:1); it is expedient that one man die for the people (Jn 11:50). – In the fourth place, he is one Lord alone, because of his government of preeminence: one Lord, one faith (Eph 4:5). In this way there is one Lord alone, Jesus Christ. – In the fifth place, one Teacher alone, because of the infusion of knowledge: call no one teacher, for you have but one Teacher: the Christ (Mt 23:10). – In the sixth place, one Father alone, because of the production of all things: one is your Father who is in heaven (Mt 23:9). – In the seventh place, one Shepherd alone, because of the common care of the faithful people: there shall be one flock and one Shepherd (Jn 10:16). – In the eighth place, one Victim alone, because of the singular price of our Redemption: for by a single offering he has consecrated forever those who are sanctified (Heb 10:14)” 80 . We confess our Only Master and Lord Jesus Christ (Jude 4), and that in him a reference to all creatures is contained. He is the point of union and meeting of the comprehensor and the wayfarer; of the Master 81 and of the slave 82 ; of this age and of the age to come; of the universe and of the atom; of the from now on of salvation and of the until now of the promises; of the not yet of what we hope for and of the already accomplished; he is the point of union and meeting of God and man; of the eschatological and of the incarnate; of sidereal distances and of the millimeter. That is why nothing escapes Christ: neither space travel, nor the world of electronics and computers, of the most current science or the most advanced technology, nor recent discoveries, nor the family, work, culture, the economic-political sphere, etc. That is why we want to live the exhortation of St. Ignatius of Antioch: “Stop your ears when you hear anyone speak of anything that does not have Christ Jesus as its foundation…” 83 . There is one Lord Jesus Christ (1 Cor 8:6); that is why we do not want “to leave anything untried so that the love of Christ may have supreme primacy in the Church and in society” 84 . Because Christ is one, we want to work with all our strength to build our life in union with the legitimate Pastors, and most especially with a heartfelt adherence to the Bishop of Rome, thus showing the Church as one: – So that all Christians may reach perfect unity in order that the promise and prophecy of the Lord may be fulfilled: There shall be one flock and one Shepherd (Jn 10:16), and that his prayer may bear fruit: Father, that all may be one (Jn 17:21). This is the ecumenical work. – So that all men may confess the adorable Name of the Lord Jesus, fulfilling his commandment: Go into the whole world and preach the Gospel to every creature (Mk 16:15). This is the missionary work. Not forgetting that: “it is truth, more than anything else, that builds unity: the communion of minds is easily transformed into a union of hearts…” 85 . Only in the truth will we be able to live the ineffable reality that St. John Eudes expresses: “All that is his is yours: the Spirit, the heart, the body, the soul and all his faculties… all that is in you must be grafted onto him… he must be your spirit, your heart, your love, your life and all that is yours” 86 . The two natures, complete and perfect, of the Incarnate Word remind us of the twofold reality, supernatural and natural, of created things, and therefore of the real distinction between grace and nature, faith and reason, Church and world, which must not be confused, nor changed, nor mixed, nor absorbed, nor subsumed. One must not mix the human with the divine, which is a kind of mixture that no Christian understanding should wear. They move us, furthermore, to the practice of apparently opposed virtues, respecting their essences and avoiding every false gnostic monism; for example, justice and love, firmness and gentleness, fortitude and meekness, holy anger and patience, purity and great affection, magnanimity and humility, prudence and courage, joy and penance, etc. Lofty holiness is the eminent union of all the virtues, even the most diverse. Both natures, preserving their properties, are substantially united in the person of the Word; therefore, they leave no room for false dualisms or destructive dialectics that seek to divide, separate and oppose grace and nature, faith and reason, Church and world, realities that must not be destructively opposed, but united in an orderly way. They also move us not to dialecticize either our spiritual life or our pastoral life, not emphasizing one element against another, avoiding every duality, permeating our whole life with the Truth, being an “amen” of the Amen (Rev 3:14). Care must also be taken never to fall into Manichean views of reality or into Jansenist reductionisms, preventing the legitimate and just autonomy of the temporal and of the spiritual from degenerating into independence from God: “The creature without the Creator vanishes” 87 . Atheism is “the most serious phenomenon of our time” 88 . Certainly it is God who assumes a human nature and not the other way around. And so it must be in our whole life, in which we must always give primacy to God over the world, to grace over nature, to faith over reason: “in the priority of ethics over technology, in the primacy of the person over things, in the superiority of spirit over matter” 89 . Just as in Christ there is an order between his two natures, so in all of reality there must be a hierarchical subordination between the supernatural and natural orders. He is the one who gives us the law that governs the relations between both orders. It is God who heals and elevates man, not the other way around; it is faith that purifies and perfects reason, not the other way around; it is the Church that heals and saves the world and not the other way around. The inversion of values that affects modern culture is another of the problems of our time. One must give more importance to what has it, and one must seek first what counts first: Seek first the Kingdom and its justice, and all the rest will be given to you besides (Mt 6:33). Nor is the mystery of the Incarnation a mere union of the divine nature with the human nature; rather, it is a union of assumption 90 . Not just any mode of union between God and the creature is enough for us to recapitulate all things in Christ (Eph 1:10); rather, analogously to the mystery of the Incarnation, it must be an assumption, that is, there must be an action and a passion that express the becoming and not only the final result, and that bear a distinct reference to each of the terms, of departure and of arrival. Cultures must be “assumed,” purifying them and elevating them starting from Christ and his Gospel, understood “in the Church” 91 . A mere union is not enough for us, nor is merely putting a nominalist label on reality so that it may truly be made subject to the lordship of Christ. “Being in the world” only makes sense for us when it depends on “not being of the world.” Only thus can one truly be salt of the earth and light of the world (Mt 5:13ff.). Otherwise we would become salt that has lost its savor and a light under the bushel basket. d) On the end of the Incarnation The ultimate and absolute end of the Incarnation is the glory of God; the mediate end is the exaltation and glory of Christ, redeemer of man; and the immediate end is the Redemption of the human race. Hence in everything and through everything we want always to seek the glory of God, the ultimate end of the whole universe; in a particular way, in the search for, investigation, proclamation and celebration of the truth, because we follow the Word who says: I am the Truth (Jn 14:6), since that very thing is “the ultimate end of the universe… the truth” 92 , and because it was for this that Jesus Christ became incarnate: For this I have come into the world, to bear witness to the truth (Jn 18:37). It is first of all the truth that gives clear knowledge, with praise, of God. A particular way of giving glory to God is to trust without limit in His Providence, grounded in His plan of salvation, which is manifested in a most eminent way in the Incarnation. We must learn to look upon everything as coming from Him who does not forget even a little sparrow… and who has numbered even the hairs of our head 93 . That is why St. Paul teaches that all things work together for the good of those who love God (Rom 8:28). In saying all things , he excepts nothing. Therefore everything is included here: all events, prosperous or adverse, whatever concerns the good of the soul, the goods of fortune, reputation, all the conditions of human life (family, studies, talents, etc.), all the interior states we pass through (joys, gladness, privations, dryness, displeasures, weariness, temptations, etc.), even our faults and our very sins. Everything, absolutely everything. In saying work together for the good , it is understood that they cooperate, contribute and come about for our spiritual good. We must have this view, and not that of the carnal or worldly man. We must see everything in the light of the loving designs of God's Providence, which only the spiritual man discovers: the spiritual man judges all things (1 Cor 2:15). We must believe with unshakable firmness that even the most adverse events, those most opposed to our natural outlook, are ordained by God for our good, even though we do not understand His designs and do not know the goal to which He wishes to lead us. But on our part we must fulfill one condition for this to come about, and that is why he adds of those who love God , that is, those whose will is united and submissive to God's, who seek above all the interests and the glory of God, who are ready to sacrifice everything without reserve, persuaded that nothing is so advantageous as abandoning oneself into the hands of God in all that it may please Him to ordain, as Jesus gave us to understand: if anyone serves me, the Father will honor him (Jn 12:26). He alone knows everything, even our soul, our feelings, our character, the secret springs that must be moved to bring us to heaven, the effects that this or that thing will produce in us, and He has all means at His disposal. If we love God, it is impossible that there should be anything in the world that does not concur and contribute to our good. And we wish to tend toward the sanctification and salvation of men, our brothers. Jesus Christ came into the world "for us men"; therefore "every man, the whole man and all men" 94 –without discrimination–, and preferentially the most needy, must be the object of our love and of our service. In the likeness of the Incarnate and crucified Word we must have a "thirst for souls." We must love in deed and in truth the concrete man who is in need –of material or spiritual goods–, and never use him as demagogic propaganda. We follow Him who, inspiring St. John, said of Himself: God is love (1 Jn 4:8). Article 2: His Earthly Life The whole life of Christ must be for us a source of spirituality: "He willed to prefigure us in His body, in His own body" 95 . a) In becoming incarnate When the Father brings His Firstborn into the world (Heb 1:6), the sublime priestly consecration of Jesus Christ takes place, by which He is marked and anointed forever: God, your God, has anointed you, O God, with the oil of gladness above your companions (Heb 1:9); High and Eternal Priest 96 , sole Mediator between heaven and earth. In that instant, His soul contemplated the infinite majesty of the Father and experienced "the incomprehensible immensity of His abundance" 97 , and at the same time contemplated the immense offense done to God –in a certain way infinite– by the sins of all men of all times, and the insufficiency of the victims offered up to that moment; and He experienced that the Father had made Him Priest and Victim –for which He had to assume matter–, and the impulse of His unspeakable love made a supremely priestly act in giving Himself entirely to His Will 98 . That first priestly act of the most holy soul of Christ, in the very instant of His Incarnation and priestly ordination, was never bent, never retracted, and remains forever in His priestly heart. It is present during His infancy, His hidden and public life, at the Supper and on Calvary, in His Resurrection and Ascension, and the five precious wounds recall it to Him permanently in the heavenly Jerusalem. That priestly act was the prelude to His redemptive sacrifice on the Cross and to all the acts of His heavenly priesthood: coming into the world He says: a body you have prepared for me… Here I am!… (Heb 10:5-7). He acknowledges the supreme dominion of the Father; He offers Himself to Him without restriction; He makes an oblation of Himself as victim; He immolates Himself in expiation; He gives Himself to the Father without reserve. Such must be the priestly attitude of every member of our little Religious Family. Through Baptism all are built up as a spiritual house for a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ (1 Pet 2:5). All, even our lay brothers and sisters, are a royal priesthood (1 Pet 2:9), because "they are united to Him and to His sacrifice" 99 ; so too are those who by religious vows must give themselves totally to God by another title; and so must be those who, in addition, through Holy Orders exercise the ministerial priesthood. All the members of the Institute must perfect themselves by being in Christ "an eternal offering to God" 100 , "a living and perfect victim for the praise of your glory" 101 . It is the priestly attitude proper to the "third class of men" of the Spiritual Exercises of St. Ignatius of Loyola 102 . It is man's response to God's revelation: "By faith man gives himself entirely and freely to God" 103 . An attitude that must be lived permanently, without diminutions or retractions, without reservations or conditions, without subterfuges or delays, without retreats or slackness. Both in the undertakings of the inner life and in the high undertakings of history: he who is not capable of setting fire to his ships when he lands is not capable of building empires. In this sublime instant of the Incarnation He gives us a signal example of the practice of the mortifying virtues to an abysmal degree, since without ceasing to be infinite God, He became finite man, showing us an infinite humility, poverty, obedience and love. It is an example of humility, since Christ, being in the form of God, did not cling greedily to being equal with God… He humbled Himself… (Phil 2:6-8) in assuming the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men (Phil 2:7); without ceasing to be God, He manifests a supreme lowering – He emptied Himself (2:7)– even as man, an immeasurable abasement, in His inner and outward judgment; His humanity knew that it had everything from God. Seeing such great humility, we must learn to regard one another as superiors, each one seeking not his own interest, but that of others (Phil 2:4) 104 . We must never cease to consider the whole inexhaustible treasure of virtues of the hypostatic Heart of Jesus. To contemplate that richest of veins and not to want to leave it must be the badge of honor, the distinctive sign, of our Institute. There, in the Incarnation, we must also take example from the Blessed Virgin. In the first place, from her faith: Blessed is she who believed… (Lk 1:45); we must live by faith 105 and have a faith that is living, firm, intrepid, eminent, heroic; a faith convinced that God would not be God if we were capable of encompassing Him with our limited intelligence, if we understood all His judgments and ways; a faith in absolute harmony with the doctrine proposed by the Catholic Church, even in the smallest details, kneaded in the strictest docility to the directives and teachings of the Pope; a faith full of promptness in rejecting error perceived even under the faintest appearances, full of ardent zeal in spreading it, but without bitterness or harshness; a penetrating faith that sees all things in the light of revelation, sub specie aeternitatis , raising the soul to the supernatural plans of God, so that we must consider ourselves "deserving of all afflictions" 106 ; a heroic faith like that of the saints of the Old Testament 107 , which triumphs over the world and evil 108 , which builds great things, which illumines life and gives it meaning, which strengthens, encourages, comforts and casts out fear: Do not be afraid! It is I (Mk 6:50). Cowards die many times before their death. From the Virgin Mary we must take example, moreover, of her humility: she was troubled at hearing these words (Lk 1:29), and she proclaimed herself lowly 109 : and He has exalted the lowly (Lk 1:52); of her prudence: she pondered what this greeting might mean (Lk 1:29); of her purity: How can this be, since I do not know man? (Lk 1:34); of her abandonment to God: Behold the handmaid of the Lord… (Lk 1:38). In Mary we must find strength to rediscover permanently the Christian and priestly life as fidelity to the religion of mystery and miracle, of martyrdom and mercy, of the Magnificat and of magnanimity. Of mystery, because there the Trinity is revealed: the Lord God… Son of the Most High… the Holy Spirit… (Lk 1:32-35), and the Incarnate Word is revealed: Be it done unto me according to your word (Lk 1:38). Of miracle: a virgin… you will conceive in your womb and bear a son (Lk 1:27.31). Of martyrdom: set for the fall and the rising… and for a sign of contradiction… and a sword will pierce your heart… (Lk 2:34-35). Of mercy: God so loved the world that He gave His only-begotten Son (Jn 3:16); whom you shall name Jesus (Lk 1:31), because He will save His people from their sins (Mt 1:21), and His mercy is poured out from generation to generation… forever (Lk 1:50-51). Of the Magnificat : My soul proclaims the greatness of the Lord (Lk 1:46), and the angels praise God saying: Glory to God in the highest… (Lk 2:14). Of magnanimity: the Mighty One has done great things for me (Lk 1:49). We could say that our spirituality must be that of the "Hail Mary," that of the "Angelus" and that of the hymn of the k enosis 110 , that of the "Magnificat" and that of the "Gloria." b) In the womb of the Virgin We must learn to see ourselves enclosed with Christ in the womb of Mary. There, at the moment of His becoming incarnate, we were included in Him: Christ assumes, morally, the flesh of all. In Mary's womb He took physically His own flesh and morally the flesh of all of us, in such a way that we were conceived in the most pure womb of Mary, and that is why she is our true and proper spiritual Mother: "We have been born from the womb of the Virgin, in the manner of a body united to its head" 111 . We will never insist enough on this mysterious and ineffable reality of our incorporation into Christ by the principle of koinonia , solidarity or communion, by which we are recapitulated and as it were concentrated in Him, since He took upon Himself the representation, the responsibility and the destiny of all men. By this intimate interpenetration and identification of Christ with each one of us, at the moment of the Incarnation we are made –in root– children of God, forming with the Incarnate Word a single whole, a compact block: we are sons in the Son, filii in Filio . "The Savior… willed to become Son of man so that we might become sons of God" 112 . "Together with Him they form one single mystical person" 113 . And not only men. In the Word made flesh all things converge, gather, join hands, interlock, are summed up and are epitomized… recapitulating all things… in the Alpha and the Omega 114 . For nine months the Virgin was the tabernacle that sheltered Jesus, just as for almost two thousand years she has been the monstrance that shows Him to the world, and the one task is no less important than the other. There God was taking human form; that is why St. Augustine calls the Virgin " forma Dei " 115 , and in the likeness of Jesus we, consecrating ourselves as slaves of the Virgin, wish "to enter into our Mother's womb and be born again" 116 . To consecrate ourselves to Jesus through Mary is to follow the path that He followed, that He continues to use and that He will use to come into the world 117 . There Jesus taught us to depend totally and in every way on God through Mary. There He taught us the evangelical ministry of visiting. Like Mary, "carrying Him who carried her" 118 , He taught us to found all our apostolic enthusiasm on Him. To carry out the things of God quickly 119 . To serve our neighbor, even, like Mary, in the simplest tasks. To praise and give thanks, to sing and rejoice in God who is Mighty, Holy, Merciful, Savior and Faithful, like Mary, because He "looked upon" her and did "great things" in her (the Incarnation), displaying His power, scattering the proud, casting down the mighty, filling the hungry, exalting the lowly, protecting His servants, forever. c) Infancy The birth of the Incarnate Word urges us, among other things, to live holy poverty strictly, for he who has God is extremely rich. And to live in joy, fruit of the Holy Spirit and consequence of the Incarnation, as the angel announced to the shepherds: I bring you good news, a great joy that is for all the people (Lk 2:10); it is the joy of the Virgin Mary, "cause of our joy": Rejoice, Mary… (Lk 1:28), the angel Gabriel said to her, and she, most docile, sang: my spirit exults with joy in God, my Savior (Lk 1:47), and that is why all generations have called her and will call her blessed (Lk 1:48), happy in the highest degree. It also urges us to work in the most difficult places (those where no one wants to go), and when it is no longer possible to continue there, after praying over it for a night before Jesus in the Blessed Sacrament, to ask the bishop to send us to a worse place. From the Epiphany we must draw light to commit our whole life to manifesting Christ to the world, so that He may be recognized not only by the poor but also by the rich, not only by the ignorant but also by the wise, not only by those of our own homeland but also by those of other peoples. We must not get trapped in false reductionist dialectics in which others are excluded (for example, the rich, intellectuals, foreigners or outsiders, etc.), in which one is concerned exclusively with some people or some place –narcissistic localism–, because the Spirit blows where it wills (Jn 3:8). The field of our action has no limits of horizon; it is the wide world: go into the whole world… (Mk 16:15), said Jesus. From the loss and finding of Jesus we wish to learn to be firm and faithful to the call, to our vocation, above any other claim of this earth: I must be about my Father's business (Lk 2:49). And to fulfill the will of God ever better, that is, in a manner: – more universal in its object : in all the forms in which it can be manifested, whether when God commands –commandments, precepts, laws, etc.–, or when He counsels –inspirations, vocation, evangelical counsels, etc.–, or when He manifests Himself through events –signified will–; – more exact in its execution , not contenting ourselves only with what is substantial but also attending to the details (God has refinements of love, and we must respond to those refinements); – more supernatural in its motives , with our intention being purer, doing things only because God wills them; – more perfect in the dispositions with which we fulfill it, not doing the will of God out of worldly fear or out of selfish or temporal interest, but out of pure love, showing Him in this way that we love Him and that we want nothing but to please Him. His example also moves us to have love for theological science, to have the true sense of the dialogue of salvation: "Apostolic dialogue starts from faith and presupposes a firm Christian identity" 120 , to be occupied with the Father and to have a profound spirit of piety. d) Hidden life No less weight for our spirituality has the example of Jesus in His hidden life. Hence every time of preparation must be very important for us; it is not lost time when it is put to good use, it is not a time to be gotten through as quickly as possible, it is not a necessary evil; the future of our brothers in religious life and, therefore, of the Institute, depends fundamentally on the formation given to them in the times of preparation: postulancy, novitiate, seminary, subsequent further training, ongoing formation. For this, good doctrine alone is not enough; in addition, "masters" are needed who have much spirit and a clear intention of making a most rigorous selection; this is capital for maintaining the good spirit. Knowing that in selecting it is better to err by excess than by defect. In the likeness of Jesus, particularly in the times of formation, there must stand out in the candidates the yearning to grow , love for fruitful silence, a dauntless dedication to intellectual and manual work (fulfilling the duty of one's state perfectly to the end), being subject 121 with responsibility, promptness and maturity, and living in a climate of festive 122 joy. Silence is a need of the soul, to express in the most profound way that, in the presence of God, there is nothing more to say. It is a means for attaining union with God and, therefore, must lead to the summit of prayer. He who seeks to keep silent will do so in order to converse only with God, who leads the soul into the desert to speak to its heart 123 . Also in the likeness of the Word, who willed to live in the silence of Nazareth for thirty years, some of our members consecrate themselves to Him in the state of contemplative life. They wish to dedicate themselves to the one thing necessary; they have chosen the better part 124 . "How precious is the contemplative life in the eyes of God and of the Church! It constitutes one of the fundamental structures of holy Church; it has been present in all the phases of her two-thousand-year history, always fruitful in solid virtues, always endowed with a mysterious and powerful attraction over the most elevated and noble souls" 125 . For that very reason, these members are in the vanguard of all the apostolic works of the Institute, since by their life of prayer and penance they obtain from the Lord the graces necessary for the salvation of many souls: "Institutes of contemplative life have the greatest importance in the conversion of souls by their prayers, works of penance and tribulations, because it is God who, through prayer, sends laborers into His harvest, opens the souls of non-Christians to hear the Gospel and makes the word of salvation fruitful in their hearts" 126 . To them apply these words of St. Teresa: "For this (the salvation of souls) He has gathered you here; this is your vocation and your desire, this is the reason for your tears and your prayers… On the day when your prayers, disciplines, longings and fasts are not dedicated to this that I have told you, you will not attain –know it well– the end for which the Lord has gathered us here" 127 . Our monasteries of contemplative life must be magnets of God's grace and lightning rods of His wrath. Would that we could multiply them throughout the whole world! "The Church and the world… need… a small ideal society where there reign, as its end, love, obedience, innocence, freedom from things and the art of using them well, the prevalence of the spirit, peace, in a word, the Gospel" 128 . e) Public life It is impossible to summarize all that Jesus Christ teaches us by His life and His doctrine, which is the source of all Christian spirituality. By way of example –not as an exhaustive list– we wish to point out some aspects of the spirituality of our little Religious Family inspired by the signal examples of our Savior and Redeemer. The Baptism Christ was baptized by John in order to consecrate Baptism 129 ; hence the whole theological depth of our baptismal birth and of our religious profession, which "is intimately rooted in the consecration of Baptism and expresses it more fully" 130 , can only be grasped in the light of the Baptism of the Lord. It reminds us that we must give ourselves unceasingly to the Father, who in the Son has said to us: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased (Mt 3:17); to the Son, whose disciples we are made and from whom we are called Christians 131 ; and to the Holy Spirit, who descended upon us in the Son – in bodily form, like a dove upon Him (Lk 3:22)–; and all this was worked in us sacramentally on the day of our Baptism. It reminds us of the grave obligation to remain faithful to the promises of holy Baptism, by which we commit ourselves to renounce the devil and to confess the holy Catholic faith, and to the promises of religious profession. It must also be a spur to live the virtue of humility in its fullness, since Christ was not afraid to pass for one more sinner, because He wished "to purify the waters so that, cleansed by contact with the flesh of Christ, which knew no sin, they might have the power to baptize" 132 , and "to leave them sanctified for those who were afterwards to be baptized" 133 ; likewise, He left us an example of the exercise of the virtue of justice: it is fitting that we fulfill all justice (Mt 3:15). The fast The practice of penance is essential to the Christian life, and therefore it must be so in our spirituality: Unless you do penance, you will all likewise perish (Lk 13:3). Above all interior penance, metanoia 134 , that is, the intimate and total change and renewal of the whole man in all his feeling, judging and disposing. In Christ we recognize the holiness of God and the gravity of sin 135 ; by His word we are invited to conversion and to receive the forgiveness of sins, gifts which we receive in their fullness in Baptism and which we must "incarnate" by denying ourselves, taking up our own cross and sharing in the sufferings of Christ. For our tiny Religious Family, the holy sacrament of Reconciliation or Penance occupies a most important place in the spiritual life, so much so that we consider it advisable to receive it weekly. We must have devotion to frequent confession, since many are the fruits that follow from it: "genuine self-knowledge increases, Christian humility grows, bad habits are uprooted, spiritual tepidity and indolence are resisted, the conscience is purified, the will is strengthened, the salutary direction of consciences is carried out, and grace increases by virtue of the sacrament" 136 . But we must also hold exterior penance in the highest esteem: regarding eating and drinking, regarding the manner of sleeping, "giving sensible pain" 137 to the flesh by means of hair shirts 138 , disciplines, etc. The preferentially interior and religious character of penance does not in any way exclude or lessen the external practice of this virtue; on the contrary, it demands its necessity with special urgency. The norms given by St. Ignatius must regulate its practice 139 . We must always give priority to the penitential seasons –Advent and Lent– and penitential days, according to the precept of our Holy Mother Church 140 , in which we must dedicate ourselves in a special way to prayer, to the practice of charity and piety, to self-denial, to fulfilling better the obligations of our state, etc. The example of our Lord in withdrawing for forty days must lead us to value to the highest degree the practice of the Spiritual Exercises, especially according to the method of St. Ignatius of Loyola, and the customary thirty-day Exercises toward the end of the novitiate and every ten years. Likewise, making annual eight-day Exercises is altogether praiseworthy. We also believe that the monthly retreat is very important. This clear awareness of the irreplaceable value of the Spiritual Exercises for the renewal of the Christian life, teaching one to conquer oneself and to order one's own life according to God, must lead us to know them in depth, to prepare ourselves to preach them fruitfully, and to have the necessary availability so as not to let any opportunity of preaching them pass by, as occasion offers. The temptations The example of the Lord in undergoing the assaults of the devil in the desert will always be an inexhaustible source of encouragement for religious. For He willed to give us strength against temptations: He conquered "our temptations by His own" 141 ; so that no one, however holy he may be, should consider himself free from being tempted: My son, if you come to serve God, prepare your soul for temptation (Eccl 2:1); to teach us with what promptness and firmness, and with what justice, the temptations of the devil must be overcome: "the Devil is not to be conquered by force, but by justice" 142 ; so that we may trust more in His mercy: For we do not have a High Priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin (Heb 4:15). Above all, because just as in the three temptations is found "the matter of all sins" 143 , religious, by the three vows, are diametrically opposed to all sins and to all the temptations that push toward sin and that can, in some way, be reduced to the three that our Lord underwent. And by the fourth vow we oppose sin by yet another title, since by being slaves of the Virgin we clearly take sides in that enmity created by God: I will put perpetual enmity between you (the devil) and the woman, and between your seed and hers; he shall crush your head… (Gen 3:15). It is not a good sign to be frightened at having great and grave temptations, and to give them excessive importance, for two reasons: a) "The Whole Christ was tempted by the devil, since in Him you were tempted… Recognize yourself tempted in Him and recognize yourself also victorious in Him… our progress is accomplished by means of temptation, and no one can know himself unless he is tempted, nor can he be crowned unless he has conquered, nor can he conquer unless he has fought, nor can he fight if he lacks an enemy and temptations" 144 ; b) No temptation has overtaken you that is not human, and God is faithful, who will not let you be tempted beyond your strength; rather, with the temptation He will also provide the way out, so that you may be able to resist it (1 Cor 10:13). Worthy of note are some of the most common temptations that we observe in ourselves, damaging our spiritual and pastoral life. Among these states are the self-centered priest , who seeks human glory, that is, who seeks to please men rather than God 145 , cares only about what affects him personally, and is hyper-jealous, above all if the younger priests have more gifts than he; the functionary , with the spirit of a bureaucratic civil servant, with multiplied demands on the people, whom he sees as clients, who thinks himself "obedient" because he fulfills the formalities but neither burns others nor is burned with the fire of the Holy Spirit, who knows nothing of venturing out for Christ, is not creative, does not undertake new apostolates, does not "make the road by walking," does not realize that the priest must be a poet, a craftsman; the one who sows sparingly , doing as little as possible on the excuse of not falling into activism, or because the times are bad, or because the family does not form as it used to, or because of the unhealthy influence of the mass media…; he only knows how to lament: "nothing can be done here"; the inconstant one , who begins many things but never finishes any, who lacks follow-through; the boring one : some are as orthodox as they are boring; they have the rare ability to make the truth tedious; deep down they do not love: "The soul that walks in love neither tires others nor grows tired" 146 ; the improviser , who does everything without foreseeing anything, does not prepare his sermons, does not set goals and, if he does, does not know how to use the means, does not think about how a thing ought to be done, is incapable of planning pastoral work, is disorderly, is not master of himself, ends up being irresponsible, does not fulfill what he promises, does not know how to choose his ministries; the frivolous one , who trivializes everything; everything is superficiality; he thinks himself clever, does not respect essences, handles everything carelessly, lacks nobility of bearing and ignores hierarchies, delights in being "smooth," especially with young women, and is incurably childish and superficial; the uptight one , all seriousness, always distant, inaccessible, tense; he does not know how to laugh, every healthy recreation seems to him levity, an ill-sounding word is for him a grave sin; for such men it seems that eutrapelia is not a virtue; in looking at the tree they forget the existence of the forest; they tend to make storms in teacups; the mediocre one , who takes shelter under a false balance, considers himself "middle of the road"; all magnanimity seems to him pride, all heroism seems to him extremism, all generosity seems to him exaggeration; he makes everything mediocre: retreats, camps, popular missions, catechesis, his own spiritual life, etc.; the localist , who cares only about parish-pump interests, lives engrossed in his little work, has a ghetto spirit; it seems as if the Church were exhausted in his parish, city, province or country; if he is of the diocesan clergy it seems to him a sin if some young man he knows wants to be a religious; if he is a religious, he suffers if someone wants to enter a congregation other than his own; he does not understand what it means that the Church is "missionary by her very nature" 147 ; his problems are exhausted in the assistant pastor, or some little old lady, or the neighboring pastor, or his own bishop, and he does not see as problems either the "invasion of the sects" 148 , or militant atheism, or the de-Christianization of culture…; the affected one , all elegant and clean, a perfect little gem, but all outward shine; he stays in the details and that is his world; the sacrum of the liturgy slips through his fingers; he lacks grit, fortitude and worldly experience in the non-pejorative sense of the word; the avaricious one , who chooses apostolates according to their financial yield, more interested in stipends than in the salvation of souls; the expenses of popular missions, Spiritual Exercises, etc., seem to him an unpardonable waste; he does not invest in pastoral work but in finance companies; all the poor who knock at his door are freeloaders; he does not understand that we must make for ourselves purses that do not wear out (Lk 12:33); the ill-humored one , always impatient, sullen, approachable only when he is in a good mood; he is sterile, sees everything as black, is not a celibate but an old bachelor, and in practice ignores that one milligram of grace weighs more than all the sins of the world, even these raised to the nth power; the laicized one , who is lay in his customs, life and spirituality; he seems not to have the sacrament of Holy Orders; he is known by his lay manner of dressing, by his way of dealing with people, by the number of hours he spends watching television, by his worldly criteria, etc.; the fearful one , worried about what people will say, who mistrusts everything, interprets the simplest gesture as if it were a grave disqualification, makes up stories that feed his phobias; he lacks the intrepidity of the Holy Spirit; the timid one is a milder variant of the previous one; he thinks only that he is not worthy, that he does not know how to preach, that people make fun of him; he does not deal with cultured people, is faint-hearted, falls into false humility, and does little or nothing to conquer himself; the climber , who sidles up to authority, flattering it in order to rise; he sees the priesthood as a career ladder, takes great care of his image, tends to be of an effeminate psychology and therefore a schemer; he is incapable "of blooming where he has been planted"; he wants to be in flowerpots set out on balconies; the loner , who acts according to his own spirit, is incapable of joining others for a common task, does not integrate, and ends up that way; the ubiquitous one , who is everywhere except where he has to be, who goes up, comes down, comes and goes, confuses the pilgrim Church with a nomadic Church, does not know how "to restrain vain steps" 149 , and therefore does little and wastes much time. In short, this is enough as a sample and to point out that what is needed are holy priests and religious who are poets, metaphysicians and soldiers, who sing, contemplate and fight. Teaching and works Jesus did and taught (Acts 1:1). Therefore, in our spirituality, we must never dialectically separate teaching from doing, nor doing from teaching. We must always unite integrity of doctrine with uprightness of life, orthodoxy and orthopraxis. In all of revelation, word and deed, dabar and bara , are inseparably united. The lines of the spirituality of teaching must also be inspired by the examples of our blessed Savior. Above all in this time of revitalization of evangelization and catechesis. We think that the fundamental characteristics of the eloquence of Jesus are: originality, authority, serenity and universality. The members of our Institute dedicated to teaching –and in some way all must be– must grasp these characteristics very deeply in prayer so as then to be able to transmit them to others. We must have the firmest conviction that only in the strictest fidelity to the doctrine of Jesus as understood in the Church is the strongest, most living, freshest and most graceful originality to be found: No man ever spoke like this man (Jn 7:46), His hearers said of Jesus. Everything that departs from Jesus is outdated, grows old quickly and, sadly, will be a boring refrain. Here that ancient counsel also applies: "do not love singularities" 150 . Being convinced of the truth contemplated makes one teach with conviction and –according to its degree of theological certainty– with an authority, which is nothing other than a participation in the authority of Christ, such that it astonishes: They were astonished at His teaching, for He taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes (Mk 1:21). To teach one's own doctrines, to demand undue assent, to emphasize the accidental, to have a doubtful attitude about everything, to remain in insinuations or approximations, to problematize the simplest things, to obscure what is clear and not clarify what is obscure, to seek oneself in teaching, to prefer chaos to order, to be padded instead of sober, opaque instead of transparent, confused instead of precise, verbose instead of concise, to stir up the waters so that others may think they are deep… this is not to have the spirit of Christ, who said: Let your word be yes, yes; no, no; anything beyond this comes from the Evil One (Mt 5:37). Serenity and gentleness are another characteristic of evangelical teaching, which are not at odds with, but rather required even in, the lively reply, intelligent polemic, effective refutation, academic or apologetic discussion. One must never lose spiritual peace, moderation, affability, unction. Likewise, one must know how to let oneself be penetrated by the universality of Christ's teaching. Intellectual "sectarianism" is neither evangelical nor intellectual. Those who are incapable of making themselves understood by simple people, because they are compartmentalized, do not grasp the universality of the message of Jesus. Only the contemplative and the authentic intellectual do not forget that "there exists a fundamental unity that is prior to all pluralism, and that is the only thing that allows pluralism to be not only legitimate but desirable and fruitful" 151 . We must be impatient to preach the Word in every way, following the counsel of St. Paul: preach the word, be insistent in season and out of season, reprove, rebuke, exhort… (2 Tim 4:2). We must not be dumb dogs, unable to bark (Is 56:10). We must seek out the sheep, use the method of dialogue, of witness and of solidarity 152 , correct sinners, teach doctrine: faith comes through hearing (Rom 10:17), visit the sick, bring souls to the sacrament of Reconciliation. "Show by the depth of your convictions and by the coherence of your conduct that Jesus Christ is our contemporary" 153 . Works Our Lord not only spoke, but "did"; in particular, He became flesh (Jn 1:14) in the Incarnation, and He became sin 154 in dying on the Cross in sacrifice for our sins. So numerous are the things that Jesus "did" that St. John says that if they were written one by one, I think this world could not contain the books that would be written (Jn 21:25). What is common to all the works of Christ is that He did nothing of Himself, but only what He sees the Father doing; for whatever He does, the Son does likewise (Jn 5:19), and this is what constitutes the essential work of Jesus: My food is to do the will of Him who sent me (Jn 4:34), so much so that He says of Himself: I can do nothing of myself… I do not seek my own will, but the will of Him who sent me (Jn 5:30). And here lies the true greatness of the Christian and religious vocation: union with God. The will of the Father has a first fundamental concrete form: the Kingdom… He has made us a Kingdom (Rev 1:6). Hence it must be our first concern: Seek first the Kingdom… (Mt 6:33). To build the Kingdom He called men in order to make them disciples: He was making more disciples… (Jn 4:1), and He formed them by teaching them, above all by example, so that they would do the same as He: For I have given you an example, that you also should do as I have done (Jn 13:15). In a similar way, as an integral element of our spirituality, we must know how to call, teach, direct, accompany and select priestly, diaconal, religious, missionary and secular vocations. Knowing that "the vocation is present in germ in the majority of Christians" 155 , we must fulfill the Pope's mandate: "with passion and discretion, be awakeners of vocations" 156 , knowing how to detect the action of the Holy Spirit in the soul, which drives it to irresistible demands of sacrifice for love of Christ, which is at the same time an act of integral faith and total self-giving, with the formal decision not to make pacts, not to compromise, not to capitulate, not to negotiate, not to make concessions, nor to come to terms with the spirit of the world. The letter of this Directory will be a dead letter if we do not know how to form young men of great spirit who know how to transmit to the new generations of our Religious Family the charism that the Holy Spirit granted to the Founder. The Incarnate Word also taught us to work for purification and renewal: making a whip of cords, He drove them all out of the temple (Jn 2:15); for reconciliation: He made the two peoples one (Eph 2:14); for not losing sight of the eminently supernatural character of the faith and of the Christian life, for which He did works that no one else has done (Jn 15:24); for attaining the oblative and Eucharistic attitude, imitating our Lord who did this once for all (Heb 7:27); for trying to do things as well as possible and not just any old way, since Jesus has done all things well (Mk 7:37), and as the good thief confessed: He has done nothing wrong (Lk 23:41). The miracles worked by our Lord are irrefutable proof of the credibility of our holy religion and a most eloquent manifestation of the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ, God from God and Light from Light. He worked miracles over all the beings of creation: over the angels (good and bad), over the heavenly bodies, over men and over irrational creatures; as proof and argument of the faith He taught, that He freed men from the power of the demons, that He was the one who saved men, that He was the Master and Lord of all creation. In this way He raised up the Kingdom on solid and indestructible foundations. And on that solidity our spirituality must be founded, which must be steeled by trials, refined by tribulations, perfected by persecutions, unshakable before all the unleashed furies of hell, even should it fall to us to live in the times of the Antichrist… we follow Him who today, as yesterday, has all power, and therefore there is no room for any fear, and nothing can move us to renounce revealed truth and the love of Christ 157 . The miracle of the Transfiguration, by which He showed His disciples the glory and beauty of His body, must not only encourage us, through the brief contemplation of eternal joy, to bear difficulties, but must also remind us of the specific end of our very little Religious Family: to evangelize the culture , that is, to transfigure it in Christ. Therefore, on August 6, the feast of the Transfiguration of the Lord, we will always commemorate with solemnity that which constitutes us and must distinguish us among the various religious families of the Church. f) The priesthood of Christ By reason of the union of the Word with human nature and of the grace of headship, Jesus Christ is constituted true High and Eternal Priest. No one is so truly Priest as He; the others are in His image. No one is more High Priest than He, in whom the others participate by derivation. No one is Eternal Priest as He is, who will perpetuate His sacrifice on the altars until the end of the ages and will consummate His priesthood in heaven: You are a priest forever… (Ps 110:4), High Priest (Heb 4:14), Priest forever (Heb 6:20). He was, at the same time, priest and victim of His own sacrifice: He gave Himself up for us to God as an offering and sacrifice… (Eph 5:2). His priesthood has superabundant power to expiate all the sins of men: by His wounds we have been healed (Is 53:5). He is the most perfect mediator between God and men: For there is one God, and one mediator also between God and men… (1 Tim 2:5); He is mediator of a more excellent covenant (Heb 8:6). In fact, Jesus Christ communicates His own priesthood to His disciples, in diverse degrees, making them participate in it truly and really. It is in the liturgy that the Mystical Body of Christ, that is, "the Head and the members, exercises the whole of public worship. Consequently… it is a sacred action par excellence, whose efficacy, by the same title and to the same degree, is equaled by no other action of the Church" 158 . In the liturgy, the Incarnate Word prays for us –He is our Priest–, He prays in us –He is our Head–, and we pray to Him –He is our God–. We must recognize our voice in Him and His voice in us. We must pray with Him, since He prays with us; pray in Him, since He prays in us 159 . This participation in the priesthood of Christ is the essence of the sacramental character, which begins with Baptism, is perfected with Confirmation, and reaches its maximum fullness in Holy Orders. a) The baptismal character empowers us to receive the other sacraments, and empowers the ordinary faithful to act as the proper ministers in the sacrament of Matrimony (this is the highest realization of the common priesthood). How we ought to nourish our soul with the reality of our Baptism! How we ought to teach this reality to the lay Christian faithful! b) The baptismal character empowers every baptized person to offer the Eucharistic Sacrifice. We must teach this grand and impressive prerogative insistently to all the members of our Institutes who are not ministerial priests. The baptized participate in the oblation of the Victim of the altar to the Father –without themselves performing the liturgical rite– in two ways: first, they offer the sacrifice through the visible priest, since he offers in the name of all the members when acting in the person of Christ as Head and Shepherd; and second, together with the visible priest , by uniting their prayers of praise, of petition and of expiation. c) The character of Confirmation empowers one to confess the faith of Christ with courage and fortitude, by giving strengthening or corroborating grace, defending the faith against its adversaries with greater ease and as if by office. d) The character of Holy Orders configures one to Christ the Head, giving the ministerial priest power over the physical Body of Christ and over His Mystical Body. It enables him to act " in persona Christi " 160 , his principal act being the immolation and oblation of the sacrifice of the Mass 161 , and, in addition, blessing, presiding, preaching, baptizing, hearing confessions, etc. The members of our Institute who are ministerial priests must return again and again to this ineffable reality, which produced in them an ontological change by making them like Christ the Head, and no lay spirituality should diminish their priestly spirituality. Article 3: His Departure from this world a) Passion According to the plan of the Most Holy Trinity it was necessary that Jesus Christ suffer in order to save all men: Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in Him may not perish, but have eternal life (Jn 3:14-15); Was it not necessary that the Messiah should suffer these things and enter into His glory? (Lk 24:26); He began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things… and be killed and rise again after three days (Mk 8:31). If in the present economy of salvation the Passion of Christ was necessary, our suffering will also be necessary. If there were another way to go to heaven, Jesus Christ would have followed it and, what is more, would have taught it. But it is not so: Christ went by the royal road of the holy Cross and taught us to go by it: If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross daily and follow me (Lk 9:23). St. Cyril of Jerusalem teaches: "Jesus, who had in no way sinned, was crucified for you; and you, will you not crucify yourself for Him, who was nailed to the Cross for love of you?" 162 . The cross in our life Therefore we must love the living cross of labors, humiliations, affronts, torments, pains, persecutions, misunderstandings, setbacks, disgraces, slights, insults, calumnies, death… and be able to say with St. Paul: I die every day (1 Cor 15:31), so as to nail in our heart Him who for us was nailed to the Cross 163 . We must vehemently desire the cross: "that I may die for love of your love, since for love of my love you deigned to die" 164 . It is a grace that must be asked for in prayer: God has given you the grace… of suffering for Christ (Phil 1:29). In a special way we must ask for the grace of the science of the cross and of the joy of the cross, which are attained only in the school of Jesus Christ. Love of the cross That is why we must have a very great devotion to the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ: "Everything is in the Passion. It is there that the science of the saints is learned" 165 . The love that is not born of the Cross of Christ is weak: "from whatever side we look at it, whether from the side of the person who suffers, or of the things He suffers, or of the end for which He suffers them, it is the highest and most divine and secret thing that has happened in the world since God created it, nor will anything like it happen until its end" 166 . The Cross "was the chair from which He taught, the altar on which He immolated Himself, the temple of His prayer, the arena where He fought, and as it were the forge from which so many wonders came forth" 167 . This devotion must take concrete form in knowledge and love of the Gospel accounts of the Passion (Mt 26-27; Mk 14-15; Lk 22-23; Jn 18-19), in the theology of the Passion and Redemption, in the contemplation of the holy places of Jerusalem, of crucifixes, of the Way of the Cross, of the beautiful texts of the Imitation of Christ on this subject 168 , of the Eucharist as the perpetuation of the Passion and Cross and second act of the one drama of the Redemption, of the cross in our life so well taught in the Circular Letter to the Friends of the Cross of St. Louis Marie Grignion de Montfort, and finally, in fervor to bring the grace of the Redemption to all of reality: to man, to the whole man and to all men, to marriage and the family, to culture, to political, economic and social life, to the international life of peoples with special reference to the question of peace, that is, to all the great contemporary problems analyzed by the Pastoral Constitution Gaudium et Spes in its second part 169 . In Sacred Scripture we are taught that many men conduct themselves as enemies of the cross of Christ (Phil 3:18). This is because they reject it: He who does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me (Mt 10:38); they cut it down 170 , they lower it: let him come down from the cross and we will believe in Him (Mt 27:42); they avoid being persecuted on account of the cross of Christ (Gal 6:12); they do not preach the whole message: if I still preach circumcision… then the scandal of the cross is done away with! (Gal 5:11). The Incarnate Word Himself teaches us to love the cross: deny yourself, take up your cross every day and follow me (Lk 9:23). Of this the saints give us an example, who bore in their bodies the sufferings of Jesus 171 , completing in us what is lacking in the Passion of Christ 172 . We must not wish to know anything except Jesus Christ and Jesus Christ crucified (1 Cor 2:2). This doctrine of the cross 173 must be what we preach: the folly of preaching… of Jesus Christ crucified, a scandal to the Jews and folly to the Greeks (1 Cor 1:21-23). It is in this cross that we must glory, in imitation of the Apostle: I will glory only in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to me, as I am to the world (Gal 6:14). This cross prepares for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure (2 Cor 4:17), for the sufferings of the present time are nothing in comparison with the glory that is to be revealed in us (Rom 8:18). Hence the Lord himself encourages us: Blessed will you be when they insult you and persecute you and falsely say every kind of evil against you because of me. Rejoice and be glad, for great will be your reward in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets who were be­fore you (Mt 5:11-12). There is no other school but the Cross, in which Jesus Christ teaches his disciples how they must be: It is “for us the supreme Chair of the truth of God and of man” 174 . Hence “in the school of the Incarnate Word we understand that it is divine wisdom to accept his cross with love: the cross of the humility of reason before the mystery; the cross of the will in the faithful fulfillment of the whole moral law, natural and revealed; the cross of one’s own duty, at times arduous and unrewarding; the cross of patience in sickness and in the difficulties of every day; the cross of tireless effort to respond to one’s own vocation; and the cross of the struggle against the passions and the snares of evil” 175 . And it is a Chair because in It “the glory of the Love that is ready for everything has been revealed” 176 . The cross is the only way of life, the sign of the predestined, the scepter of the kingdom of holiness; “it is the source of every blessing, the origin of every grace; through It, believers receive strength from weakness, glory from shame, and life from death” 177 . The saints of all times, true words of God 178 , show us the necessity of the cross in our lives: “Rightly is he glorified with Christ who, suffering for Him, truly suffers with Him” 179 . “Whoever wishes to lead a perfect life need do nothing else but despise what Christ despised on the Cross and love what Christ loved on it” 180 . “Jesus is loved and served on the Cross and crucified with Him, and in no other way” 181 . They themselves burned with desire for the cross: “If the Head is crowned with thorns, shall the members be crowned with roses? If the Head is mocked and covered with mud on the way to Calvary, shall the members wish to live perfumed upon a throne of glory?” 182 . “Those who relish the Cross of Christ our Lord find rest living in these labors, and die when they flee from them or find themselves without them” 183 . “To suffer or to die” 184 . “I want and choose poverty with Christ poor rather than riches, insults with Christ laden with them rather than honors, and I desire more to be esteemed as worthless and a fool for Christ, who was first held to be such, than as wise or prudent in this world” 185 . “I know well what is good for me… Let fire, the cross, packs of wild beasts, lacerations, amputations, dislocation of bones, severing of limbs, the crushing of my whole body, all the cruel torments of the devil come upon me, provided only that this may serve me to attain to Chris­t” 186 . “Allow me to imitate the Passion of my God” 187 . In a word, “neither Jesus without the Cross, nor the Cross without Jesus” 188 . And the saints remind us of the joy that is the fruit of this cross: “I have reached the point of not being able to suffer, for all suffering is sweet to me” 189 . We must hope in such a way that every sorrow gives us consolation. It “is the fulcrum, upon which leverage is applied to serve man, as well as to transmit to so very many others the immense joy of being Christians” 190 . The Cross of Christ demands of us a generous response: “(the Passion and the Cross)… are a persevering and unbending aspiration and a cry: an immense cry of hearts” 191 . “Jesus, who had sinned in nothing, was crucified for you; and will you not crucify yourself for Him, who was nailed to the cross out of love for you?” 192 . Hence it is also –because of the imitation of Christ that it implies– “a crown, not a disgrace” 193 . This is the resounding idea: to sacrifice oneself. Thus is history directed, even silently and hiddenly. Fittingness Of the many advantages that Christ’s redeeming us by his Passion has brought us, we must discover: a) How much God loves us and, therefore, how much we must love Him: God proved his love for us in that, while we were sinners, Christ died for us (Rom 5:8); I live by faith in the Son of God who loved me and gave himself up for me (Gal 2:20). b) The example he gave us of so many virtues necessary for human salvation, such as obedience, humility, constancy, justice, contempt for worldly things… Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example that you should follow in his steps (1 Pet 2:21). c) Not only how he redeemed us from sin, but the greatness of sanctifying grace and of the eternal glory that he merited for us. d) The greater need to keep ourselves free from sin: You have been bought at a great price! (1 Cor 6:20). e) The greater dignity of man, for although he was conquered by the devil, the devil was conquered by man: Thanks be to God who gave us the victory through Christ! (1 Cor 15:57). In short, we find a thousand mysteries in the Passion of the Lord, so that its abundance is inexhaustible. We must also consider attentively that Christ freely willed to suffer all the bitter sorrows of his Passion and Death; he did not prevent them though he could have prevented them: I lay down my life… No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself. I have power to lay it down and power to take it up again (Jn 10:17-18). And showing that he kept all the vigor of his bodily nature until the last moment, crying out with a loud cry, in a loud voice he said: Father, into your hands I commend my spirit. Having said this he breathed his last (Lk 23:46). And he freely subjected himself to obedience in order to fulfill his Father’s command: By the obedience of one many will be made righteous (Rom 5:19). It is true that obedience is better than sacrifice (1 Sam 15:22), but sacrifice offered out of obedience is the highest perfection. Hence we must learn to live the vow of obedience freely and never fall into the destructive dialectic of opposing freedom to obedience or freedom to authority, and vice versa. So that, everything well considered, in the Passion is manifested the severity of God, who did not wish to forgive without fitting satisfaction: he did not spare his own Son ; and his infinite goodness: he delivered him up for us all ; from which there must spring up in us a boundless confidence in the overflowing generosity of the Father: How will he not give us all things with Him? (Rom 8:32). Example This is his second great abasement: the kenosis of the Passion. His humility shines forth in it and we must imitate it: in humility regard one another as superior (Phil 2:3). In this regard St. Thomas Aquinas teaches that in man two things can be considered: what there is of God in him, that is, everything that pertains to salvation and perfection; and what is proper to man, that is, everything that pertains to defect. And since humility properly refers to the reverence by which man subjects himself to God, it follows that every man, according to what is his own, must subject himself to every neighbor, as regards what is of God in him. In this subjection humility shines forth 194 . Modes Contemplating the different ways in which the Passion of the Lord attains its end, that is, the Salvation of men, leads us to admire his infinite Wisdom, who has done all things well (Mk 7:37); the delicacy of his love: he loved them to the end (Jn 13:1); the magnanimity and generosity of his action: where sin abounded grace superabounded (Rom 5:20). This so marvelous and exuberant work of art of the Savior gives rise to the most absolute certainty in the Salvation brought about by Him, by way of merit, of satisfaction, of sacrifice, of redemption and of efficacy. These five modes of causality of the redemptive work, far from dismembering it, make us see it with greater force and greater unity, like the fingers that perfect the hand. Thus Christ merited for all men of all times all the graces that they receive or will receive, without any exception whatsoever; a merit that is universal: He is the propitiation for our sins. And not only for ours, but for those of the whole world (1 Jn 2:2), superabundant, infinite and of strict justice. Thus Christ made satisfaction for the sins of all men by offering the Father a universal, superabundant reparation in strict justice. He bore the sins of all upon himself (Is 53:12); him who knew no sin, [God] made sin for us so that we might become the righteousness of God in Him (2 Cor 5:21); he became a curse for us (Gal 3:13), paying for all: Christ Jesus… gave himself as a Redemption for all (1 Tim 2:6). Thus Christ saves us by the sacrifice of the Cross, which is a unique oblation: we are sanctified by the offering of the Body of Christ, made once for all (Heb 10:10); it is a definitive sacrifice: instituted… according to the power of an indestructible life (Heb 7:16); it is an eternal sacrifice, since he holds a perpetual priesthood because he remains forever (Heb 7:24), and the Victim is perfect: and he is able to save perfectly (Heb 7:25), since he was at once a host for sin, a peace offering and a holocaust: he loved us and gave himself up for us as an offering and sacrifice of fragrant and pleasing odor (Eph 5:2). Should we not recall here that those are called religious who consecrate themselves totally to the service of God, offering themselves to Him as a holocaust? 195 .
