Thus Christ redeems us from all slaveries, since he came to give his life as a Redemption for many (Mt 20:28), as a Redemption for all (1 Tim 2:6); he gave himself for us to ransom us from all iniquity (Titus 2:14), freeing us from all the slaveries of sin, of the punishment of sin, of death, of the power of the devil and of the Mosaic law. Thus Christ is the efficient cause both of the objective Redemption, accomplished by Him on Calvary, and of the application to us of the fruits of the Redemption –the so-called subjective Redemption– through faith and the sacraments. He is the most efficient cause of our salvation because he is God, the Word of God, and because his humanity is the conjoined instrument of the divinity; hence all the actions and sufferings of Christ work, instrumentally, the salvation of the human race. Effects And if it is an abyss to consider the modes by which Jesus Christ saves us, the effects of his Passion are an abyss as well: a) it frees us from sin: he washed us from our sins in his blood (Rev 1:5); b) it frees us from the power of the devil: now the prince of this world will be cast out (Jn 12:31); c) it frees us from the punishment of sin: he took upon himself our infirmities and bore our sorrows (Is 53:4); d) it reconciled us with God: we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Rom 5:10); e) it opened to us the gates of heaven: having firm confidence to enter the sanctuary by virtue of the blood of Jesus (Heb 10:19); f) it grants him exaltation: therefore God exalted him (Phil 2:9). We must still treat of an aspect already hinted at but which we now wish to make explicit: I complete in my flesh what is lacking in the Passion of Christ (Col 1:24), teaches St. Paul. Certainly we add nothing substantial to the sacrifice of Christ, but in the order of operation we complete it in some way. In his sacrifice, Christ the Head offered to the Father his own sufferings and those of all the members of his Mystical Body; he took upon himself not only the sins of all men but all their sorrows, the sufferings that his members would have to suffer for love of him, since they would be persecuted because they served Him 196 . Christ “suffered as our Head, and continues to suffer in his members, that is, in us” 197 . That is why “Christ will be in agony until the end of the world,” since “the total measure of the sufferings of all men will not be filled up until the end of the world” 198 . Suffering Suffering is something precious and of incalculable value, since it was chosen by God to redeem us, when it is borne with patience, accepted as coming from God and sanctified by uniting it to that of Christ. Here is the deepest reason for our apostolate with the sick, which will always be a verification of our Christian authenticity. They must always be our favorites! All our sufferings had entered into the heart of Christ on Calvary. Those sufferings, offered beforehand by Christ, Priest and Victim, remained to be fulfilled in our flesh. The sacrifice of Christ, complete in his prophetic thought, will be totally fulfilled in reality when the number of the elect is complete. We are co-redeemers! All the co-redemptive efficacy of our sufferings depends on their union with the Cross, and in the measure and degree of that union. We live from the sacrifice of Christ: no act of virtue has value if it was not offered by our Head on the Cross; no sin is forgiven if Christ did not plead for mercy for it on Golgotha; no suffering is redemptive if it is not united to the Passion of Christ. If we do not learn to be victims with the Victim, all our sufferings are useless. We must learn to complete what is lacking in the Passion of Christ 199 with a reparation that is affective –through prayer and love–, effective –the fulfillment of the duties of one’s state, apostolate, etc.–, and afflictive –sanctified suffering–, for our own benefit and that of the whole Mystical Body. That is why the great benefactors of our Institutes are their sick members, whom we must consider privileged members, for whom we must be ready to sell “the chalices” 200 if it were necessary for their good. b) Death on the Cross and Burial Christ by his death kills death: Death has been swallowed up in victory; where, O death, is your victory? (cf. 1 Cor 15:54-55); and that is why his death gives life: it is the passage to his resurrection and to ours, both spiritual and bodily. That is why true Christians consider: if we have died with Him, we shall also live with Him (2 Tim 2:11). In Baptism we die, and that death assures us of the resurrection: If we have been grafted into Him by the likeness of his death, we shall be so also by that of his resurrection (Rom 6:5), offering with Him our daily sufferings, sharing in his sufferings, being conformed to Him in his death (Phil 3:10), until we can exclaim: for me to live is Christ and to die is gain (Phil 1:21). That is why it is “necessary to live dying” 201 , or as the poet sings: “He who does not know how to die / while he lives, is vain and foolish: / to die a little every hour / is the way to live […]/ from death I receive / new life, and if I live, / I live from so much dying”. This is the secret of all supernatural fruitfulness! Everything lies in knowing how to die! That is the great science! Unless the grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies it will bear much fruit. Whoever loves his soul loses it; but whoever hates his soul in this world will keep it for eternal life (Jn 12:24-25). But the Cross offers us another magnificent lesson. Just as all of us men had sinned and perished in solidarity in Adam, since through one man sin entered the world… inasmuch as all had sinned (Rom 5:12), so, in Christ, the new Adam, by that principle of communion ( koinonia ), we all find salvation and life: those who receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness will reign in life through the one man, Jesus Christ (Rom 5:17). Jesus Christ takes upon himself the representation of all men: “he suffered for me, paid for me and died for me” 202 . In Him we are recapitulated and, as it were, concentrated. This so intimate and mysterious interpenetration and, as it were, identification of Christ with each one of us is what caused Christ to take on our sins, to make them his own: he became sin 203 . Now then, not only did he die representing us, but all of us also died, represented and contained in Him. He and we, we and He, form a single whole, a compact block: you are all one in Christ Jesus (Gal 3:28). That is why we too die on the Cross, by the moral interpenetration or mystical identification of persons. By that mysterious solidarity or ineffable communion of men with Christ, at the root , we have died in Christ. Because Christ truly died representing all men, it was necessary that all of us, in some way, should die in Him and with Him: if one died for all, then all died (2 Cor 5:14), that is, all of us have died in Him. For all to die because the one dies presupposes that all are in the one and that the one and all are the same: we are all one… We must carry out in fact what was accomplished on the Cross at the root : we must die, in fact, to the old man, to sin, to sinful affections, even to the very appearance of evil. We must die totally to our own self. There are three moments in perfect self-denial: Christian mortification, the spirit of sacrifice, and total death to one’s own self. It is very difficult to rise to this third moment. It is achieved through perennial work. It is a matter of dying in order to live : you have died and your life is hidden with Christ in God (Col 3:3). The life of Christ was a continual death, whose last act and consummation was the Cross. Through various degrees of death the mystical life of Christ is established in us: – death to sins, even the slightest, and to the least imperfections; – death to the world and to all exterior things; – death to the senses and to immoderate care of one’s own body; – death to one’s temperament and natural defects: not speaking or acting according to one’s own mood or whim, always remaining at peace and in possession of oneself; – death to one’s own will and one’s own spirit: subjecting the will to reason, not letting oneself be carried away by whim or fancies, not being obstinate in one’s own judgment, knowing how to listen, always being joyful with what God gives us; – death to self-esteem and self-love: to amour-propre; – death to spiritual consolations, which one day God withdraws completely, and then everything bothers the soul, everything annoys it, everything wearies it; nature cries out, complains, becomes en­raged; – death to supports and securities regarding the state of our soul: experiencing abandonment by God…; – death to all ownership in what concerns holiness: complete nakedness. One no longer sees one’s gifts or virtues, only one’s sins, one’s own nothingness. We must learn to discover ourselves, and others, in the Heart and in the wounds of Christ, and thus we will understand what we ask of Him when we say: “within your wounds, hide us” 204 , since “we have been made Christ” 205 . Folly of the Cross But we must take into account yet one more thing: the folly of the Cross, which is the folly of God, wiser than the wisdom of men (1 Cor 1:23.25). This folly consists in living in the more and in the beyond , that is, where all balancing acts, all calculation, all “I give so that you may give to me” cease. This folly begins where one no longer counts, nor calculates, nor weighs, nor measures. Do you love only the one who loves you? Do you give only to the one who can give it back to you? Do you do favors only for those who thank you? What importance does all that have? Do not the pagans do the same? (Mt 5:47). The folly of the cross consists in living the beatitudes. Blessed are the fools for Christ! They will be pushed from here to there, people will laugh at them and consider them clumsy, backward and even feeble-minded: theirs is the Kingdom of Heaven. Blessed are the fools for Christ! For they have stripped themselves and stand before God in all their guilelessness. Blessed are these fools for Christ! No wisdom of the world will ever be able to deceive them. It is the folly of love without limits or measure. It is to bless those who curse us 206 , it is not to repay evil for evil (Rom 12:17). When the world says to us: Look at the fools! stones are thrown at them and they kiss the hand that throws them; people laugh at them and mock them and they laugh too, like children who do not understand; they are beaten, persecuted and martyred, but they give thanks to God who found them worthy. When the world says that, it is a sign that we are on the right path. Folly of love! But a folly that the folly of the Cross makes wiser than the wisdom of all men (1 Cor 1:25). c) The Descent into Hell St. Peter teaches that Christ went to preach to the spirits who were in prison (1 Pet 3:19), and he adds, the Gospel was proclaimed to the dead (1 Pet 4:6). The kenosis of the Incarnation of the Word is prolonged in his Passion and Death, and reaches its fullness when he descends into hell, so that, if we ceased to consider this truth of our faith, we would be diminishing somewhat the reality of the Incarnation. There Christ showed the fruit of his Passion to the saints of the Old Testament, to the Patriarchs and Prophets, to St. Joseph and St. John the Baptist, to the Holy Innocent Martyrs, to the good thief… and he communicated to them glorious beatitude. He also consoled the souls in purgatory, bringing out from there those who were sufficiently purified. In our preferential option for the poor we must always keep these blessed souls in mind, so as to offer suffrages for them. Article 4: His glorious Life a) Resurrection The Fact The fact of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ is a Mystery and a double miracle. It is a theological miracle that surpasses the capacity of every created intellect, so that, if Christ has not risen, vain is our preaching, vain also is your faith (1 Cor 15:14). But, in turn, it is an apologetic miracle, since, through the empty tomb and the appearances, the prophecies are ful­filled and the truth of the divinity of Jesus Christ is certified. He is the firstborn of the dead (Col 1:18) , the firstfruits of those who die (1 Cor 15:20), that is, the first to rise in a glorious way to an immortal life. He is the principle of the new creation or re-creation of the world, infinitely superior to the first creation. Effects The Resurrection of our Lord brought us two principal benefits: our future bodily resurrection and our present spiritual resurrection. That is why we are taught, on the one hand: as death came through a man, so also through a man came the resurrection of the dead (1 Cor 15:21); and, on the other: Christ was handed over for our sins and was raised for our justification (Rom 4:25); it is evident that justification is the resurrection of souls, spiritually dead through sin, to the life of grace. That is why St. Thomas teaches: “The good of grace of one individual is greater than the good of nature of the whole universe” 207 . It is in the Resurrection of the Lord that the importance of grace in the saving economy of the New Covenant is best seen, and why it is the “sole formal cause” 208 of our salvation. Sanctifying grace is what makes us partakers of his divine nature (2 Pet 1:4); it is, as theologians say, a physical and formal, though analogous, participation in the divine nature itself. With Him we have been raised! (Eph 2:6), coming “to be by grace what He is by na­ture” 209 : children of God (cf. Rom 8:16), brothers of Christ, the Firstborn among many brothers (Rom 8:29) and, therefore, co-heirs with Him, heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ (Rom 8:17). Together with grace we are given the infused virtues and the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Sending of the Holy Spirit: the New Law On the very Sunday of his Resurrection, privately, Jesus Christ did what he would later do publicly on the day of Pentecost, sending the Holy Spirit: he breathed on them and said to them: receive the Holy Spirit (Jn 20:22), who constitutes the principal element of the New Law, or New Covenant, or Gospel, that is, the life, and life in abundance (Jn 10:10) that Christ came to bring to the earth. It is the law of Christ (Gal 6:2), it is the law of faith (Rom 3:27), a spiritual law 210 , the perfect law (Jas 1:25), the law of freedom (Jas 2:12), the law of the Spirit (Rom 8:2), the Gospel of grace (Acts 20:24). It is the infused law –poured into the heart– prophesied by Jeremiah: I will put my law within them and write it on their heart (Jer 31:33). It is “that in which all its power lies… in the very grace of the Holy Spirit, which is given through faith in Christ…” 211 . Only this law justifies and saves man: the Gospel… is the power of God for the salvation of everyone who believes… (Rom 1:16). Only insofar as it is infused, that is, insofar as it is communicated interiorly, does the new law, the Gospel, save and justify; insofar as it is secondarily written, it does not. That is why St. Paul says that the letter kills, the Spirit gives life (2 Cor 3:6), and by letter is to be understood anything or any writing that is outside of man, even if it concerns spiritual and heavenly things, such as those contained in the Gospels, “whereby even the letter of the Gospel would kill if it did not have the interior grace of faith, which heals” 212 . If this holds for the Holy Gospels, whose Principal Author is the Holy Spirit, how much more does it hold for this Directory! Without faith in Christ, without the Holy Spirit, without the love of God, without sanctifying grace, all these wri­tings would kill souls, since they would remain merely exterior things. To live according to the new law is to live in accordance with this reality: The love of God has been poured into our hearts by the power of the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us (Rom 5:5). It is to live according to faith that works through charity (Gal 5:6). And charity will never die! (1 Cor 13:8). Freedom Through the Resurrection and the sending of the Holy Spirit we understand that we have been called to freedom 213 , since for us to enjoy freedom, Christ has set us free (Gal 5:1). Freedom implies “building up a communion and a participation… on three inseparable planes: – man’s relationship with the world, as lord; – with persons, as brother; – and with God, as son” 214 . “Today the range of abuses of freedom has spread greatly, and this leads to new forms of slavery, very dangerous ones, because they are disguised under the appearance of freedom. This is the paradox, the profound drama of our time: in the name of freedom, slavery is imposed” 215 . Against these abuses St. Peter already warned, exhorting the faithful to be truly free and not as one who uses freedom as a cover for wickedness (1 Pet 2:16), and St. Paul, who admonished us not to take freedom as a pretext for serving the flesh 216 . Authentic freedom is identified with holiness, with the New Law, with the Christian faith, with charity; it is the freedom… of the children of God (Rom 8:21). It has truth as its foundation, as our Lord showed when he taught us that the truth will make you free (Jn 8:32). It is proper to those who let themselves be guided by the Holy Spirit: The Lord is Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom (2 Cor 3:17). That is why St. Augustine teaches: “Love and do what you will” 217 , and St. John of the Cross places at the summit of the mount of perfection: “Here there is no longer any path, for for the just man there is no law” 218 . Christian freedom “is being able to avoid sin and to do meritorious works, without anyone having the power to prevent one from attaining the last end” 219 . We must be, and must know how to form, men and women who are: “Free… free… free… free… free… free with your freedom… who will go everywhere with… the holy Gospel on their lips and the holy rosary in their hand, to bark like do­gs, to burn like live coals and to illumine the darkness of the world like suns” 220 . St. Thomas himself teaches: “He is free who is the cause of his own acting; he is a servant who has his master as the cause of his acting. Therefore, whoever acts by his own decision acts freely; whoever does so moved by another does not act freely. Thus, he who avoids evil, not because it is evil, but because God commands it, is not free; but he who avoids evil because it is evil, he is free. This is done by the Holy Spirit, who interiorly perfects the soul through a good habit, in such a way that it abstains from evil out of love, as if the divine law commanded it; and therefore it is called free, not because it does not submit to the divine law, but because it is inclined by good habits to do what the divine law commands” 221 . The New Man It is this New Law that brings forth the new man, who, by essence, is Jesus Christ himself: so as to create in himself one new man out of the two (Eph 2:15), and, by participation, all those who are incorporated into Jesus Christ by grace: put on the new man, created according to God in true righteousness and holiness (Eph 4:24). The new man is opposed to the old man, corrupted by seductive desires (Eph 4:22) 222 , of whom the Apostle prophesied: they will not endure sound doctrine; rather, with itching ears, they will heap up teachers in accordance with their passions (2 Tim 4:3). The new man is the interior man, powerfully strengthened … by the action of his Spirit (Eph 3:16 223 ). The new man is identified with the spiritual man (1 Cor 2:15). He is the man who sings the new song, “a song… that only new men can learn, renewed from their former condition by the work of grace and already belonging to the New Testament, which is the Kingdom of Heaven. For it all our love sighs, and it sings the new song. But it is our life more than our voice that must sing the new song … Each one asks himself how he will sing to God. Sing to Him, but do it well. He does not accept a song that offends his ears… When will you be able to set yourself to sing with such art and mastery that you in no way displease such perfect ears? But see, He himself suggests to you the way you are to sing to Him: do not worry about the words, as if these were capable of expressing what delights God. Sing with jubilation. This is the song that pleases God, the one that is done with jubilation… (that is), to realize that we cannot express in words what the heart feels… This way of singing is the most fitting when it concerns the ineffable God. For if He is ineffable, He cannot be translated into words. And… on the other hand you are not permitted to remain silent, so the only thing you can do is sing with jubilation. In this way the heart rejoices without words, and the immensity of the joy is not limited by syllables” 224 . The supreme and eternal new man is Jesus Christ, who wants us to assimilate his doctrine, imitate his examples, unite ourselves in heart to his Person and frequent his sacraments. Modern immanentist conceptions abhor Him, proposing a “new man” who is nothing but a human wreck, since they deny him the supernatural dimension of grace. The only authentically new thing that there has been, is and will be in the world is Jesus Christ, who “in giving himself, has given newness to all things” 225 . The new man who is the Christian intones his own song: “song springs from joy, and, if we look at it carefully, it is born of love: to act is proper to love . He, then, who knows how to love the new life also knows how to sing the new song” 226 , “because singing and chanting psalms is the business of those who love” 227 . The Christian pilgrimage must be accompanied by song, by expressions of joy: “let us sing, then, now, brothers; not for the delight of rest but for the relief of our labor. As travelers are accustomed to do, you too sing and walk. Relieve your weariness as a traveler with song. Do not let sloth overcome you; sing and walk. What does walk mean? Always advance in the good. For there is no lack of those who go backward, going from bad to worse, as the Apostle says (2 Tim 3:13). If you progress and go forward, you walk; but progress in the good, progress in faith, do not turn back, do not stop” 228 . Joy From here too, from the Resurrection of the Lord, there arises an element that must be essential in our spirituality –and in every Christian spirituality–: joy, which, in our case, must be manifested in a special way in the celebration of the Lord’s day, Sunday; in the sense of feast; and in recreation, which we call eutrapelia. Joy, which is the gigantic secret of the Christian, is spiritual and supernatural, and is born from considering the mystery of the Incarnate Word. Rejoice , be glad, the angel Gabriel said to Mary; She would say later: my spirit exults with jubilation (Lk 1:47), Elizabeth having testified moments before: the child in my womb leaped for joy (Lk 1:44); and the angel had said to the shepherds: I announce to you a great joy, which is for all the people (Lk 2:10). It is born from verifying the mystery of the Resurrection of the Lord: filled… with great joy (Mt 28:­8); like the disciples of Emmaus: Were not our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us on the way? (Lk 24:32); they still did not believe for sheer joy and amazement (Lk 24:41); they returned… with great joy (Lk 24:52); the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord (Jn 20:20). That is why St. Paul insists: Rejoice, I say it again, rejoice (Phil 4:4). That is why the Christian must rejoice always and in everything: the Kingdom of God… is joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom 14:17); may the God of hope fill you with complete joy (Rom 15:13); coming to you with joy (Rom 15:32); rejoice (2 Cor 13:11); rejoice in the Lord (Phil 3:1); be always joyful (1 Thess 5:16). He must rejoice in the virtues: whoever practices mercy, let him do it with joy (Rom 12:8); joyful in hope (Rom 12:12); strengthened in every virtue according to the might of his glory, in all patience and long-suffering, with joy (Col 1:11). He must rejoice also in sufferings: I overflow with joy in all our tribulations (2 Cor 7:4); as sorrowful yet always rejoicing (2 Cor 6:10); I rejoice in my sufferings (Col 1:24). He must rejoice also in the community of the followers of the Risen One: I rejoice over you (Rom 16:19); my joy is also yours (2 Cor 2:3); we wish to contribute to your joy through your firmness in the faith (2 Cor 1:24); always, in all my prayers, I pray with joy for you (Phil 1:4); Brothers… my joy and my crown (Phil 4:1); you are our glory and our joy (1 Thess 2:20). He must rejoice with Christ proclaimed: that Christ is proclaimed, in this I rejoice and will rejoice (Phil 1:18); I will remain with you for your progress and joy in the faith (Phil 1:25); make my joy complete (Phil 2:2); receiving the word with joy in the Holy Spirit (1 Thess 1:6). At bottom, joy springs from considering that God is 229 , that Christ is: Take courage, I am (Mk 6:50); that truth prevails over falsehood, good over evil, beauty over ugliness, love over hatred, peace over war, mercy over vengeance, life over death, grace over sin, and finally, being over nothingness, Our Lady over Satan, Christ over the Antichrist, God over all. “God is infinite joy” 230 . Sunday From the Paschal Mystery and from the Lord’s day –Sunday–, which is the feast day par excellence, our feasts must be born, since the authentic feast must be born from worship, that is, from the praise rendered to the Creator for the goodness of existence, since on the seventh day God saw that everything was good… and he rested (Gen 1:31; 2:2-3). And, as St. Augustine teaches, worship takes place through “the offering of praise and thanksgiving” 231 , and since the prin­ci­pal act of worship is sacrifice, sacrifice thus becomes the soul of the feast. How much more meaning this has in the light of the Resurrection of the Lord and of the perpetuation of his Sacrifice on the altars! Indeed, through the Incarnation of the Word and his Paschal Mystery, man is raised to a supereminent plane, the plane of grace, which absolutely exceeds the order of nature. Therefore it is the Paschal Mystery, and Sunday, which is its prolongation, that is the source of the authentic fea­st, where we celebrate both the goodness of this higher existence that the Word brought us, for grace and truth have come to us through Jesus Christ (Jn 1:17), and the hope of being able finally to enter into eternal Beatitude, the true Feast, of which the Paschal Mystery and Sunday are a sign and a foretaste. The very name by which Christian tradition calls the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass refers to this thanksgiving: “Eucharist”. And it is already an entering into the true feast, that of eternity: for us who live here, our feasts are an open access to that life. We go from feast to feast toward the Feast 232 . Feast Every other feast also takes part in the Resurrection of the Lord and in Sunday, since the motive of a feast is joy: “A feast is joy and nothing more” 233 . But joy presupposes a foundation, something to rejoice in: it is the response of a lover to whom what he loves has been granted. Someone rejoices because he possesses the good that is fitting for him, whether really, or in hope, or at least in memory. And only he truly rejoices who rejoices in love: “Where charity rejoices, there is festivity” 234 . That is why there is no greater motive for joy than the Resurrection of the Lord, because his triumph is our triumph, his victory is our victory. The Paschal Mystery is the manifestation par excellence of God’s love for men: he loved them to the end (Jn 13:1). That is why we must rejoice in this mystery, and our joy must be permanent. Hence in our Institutes the great solemnities must be celebrated fittingly, especially the Octave of Easter, Sundays, and the days of the Apostles and of Our Lady. Likewise there is, as it were, another feast in miniature, which is recreation, in which the virtue of eutrapelia must be practiced. The soul, like the body, grows tired and must rest. The rest of the soul is delight, so that delight must be the remedy against the weariness of the soul, interrupting the tension of the spirit. Hence it is necessary to procure this rest for the soul through games and feasts, whose moderation belongs to the virtue of eutrapelia, practiced in times of recreation. Whoever does not practice the virtue of eutrapelia gladly will hardly persevere. One must be very wary of those who, under the cloak of virtue, do not wish to practice the virtue of eutrapelia; generally they are carried away by their selfishness, fail in charity toward their neighbor and are harsh in judgment. The worst is that they go against the truth of man, who, because he is intelligent, must know how to be playful. Sending and Mission The risen Christ, as the four evangelists indicate, gives us the mandate of the mission: As the Father has sent me, so I send you (Jn 20:21); in which we must bear witness: You will bear witness to this (Lk 24:48); by the power of the Lord, addressing all nations, of the whole world: Go and teach all nations (Mt 28:19), throughout the whole world (Mk 16:15); to preach the Gospel, teaching them to observe what He commanded us, baptizing in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that whoever believes will be saved; Christ accompanying us until the consummation of the world (Mt 28:20). In order not to shy away from the missionary adventure 235 , and to move many others to it, one must have something of the poet, since peoples have been moved by none but poets, and what greater poet than Jesus Christ! And what greater poetry than his crying out to us: Put out into the deep! Duc in altum! (Lk 5:4). A profound word, of very profound content, of deep mystical resonances, which impels to great ideals, understood by those who are men of action, of broad vision, of resolute and generous heart, who because of the nobility of their soul smile with joy on knowing that it is Jesus himself who says to them Duc in altum! It is an invitation to carry out great works, extraordi­nary undertakings in which there is much of adventure, of vertigo, of danger, where the waves toss the boat, the salt water splashes the face, the prow cuts its way for the first time, where there are no tracks and the only points of reference are the stars, where the keel is tossed by opposing whirlpools, the unfurled sails receive the fury of the wind, the masts creak… and the soul trembles… Into the deep! far from the shore and from the solid ground of merely human, calculating and cold thoughts… where the water seethes, the heart beats fast, where the soul knows heavenly inebriations and fascinating joys. To put out into the deep is to take seriously, thoroughly, the demands of the Gospel: go, sell all that you have… (Mt 19:21); it is the longing of our restless heart, which yearns to possess the Infinite; it is the impetus of the Saints and the Martyrs, who gave everything for God. It is what is proper to fishermen: humble, hardworking men, who do not fear dangers, watchful, patient in prolonged vigils, constant in repeating their outings to sea, prudent in hauling in the fish, weathered by salt and sun. It is to make oneself ready to die, like the grain of wheat, in order to see Christ in all things. For this reason, we make our own the ardent words of St. Luigi Orione: “Whoever does not want to be an apostle, let him leave the Congregation: today, whoever is not an apostle of Jesus Christ and of the Church is an apostate ” 236 . b) Ascension The Ascension of Christ into heaven, among other things, moves us always to seek the essential things, which are invisible to the eyes of the body, and which are those things that do not pass away and do not die: Aspire to the things above, where Christ is… relish the things above, not those of the earth (Col 3:1-2). In these times of crude temporalism, in which many contemporaries are infected by secularism, we must give clear witness of being men who are not absorbed in the horizons of this world, not even in the unavoidable commitment to promote justice. Likewise, the Ascension of the Lord must fill us with unshakable hope, since he assured us: In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places… I am going to prepare a place for you… I will come again and take you with me, so that where I am you also may be (Jn 14:2-3). “It is necessary that the members follow wherever the Head goes before them” 237 . His Ascension is the cause of ours. “He with us is one single thing” 238 . All with Christ “form one single Christ” 239 . We are citizens of heaven! (Phil 3:20). They were looking at the sky, their gaze fixed on Him… (Acts 1:10). We will always have a preferential place in our Institute for the contemplative branches. Contemplative life, as St. John Paul II teaches, is “the core from which you prepare to give full meaning to your religious life, as ambassadors of Christ 240 in the midst of this world” 241 . And the reason for this lies in the fact that contemplative life implies a permanent dedication to God and to the consideration and love of his mystery and of his plan of salvation for all men, according to that saying of St. Paul: Seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God… You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God (Col 3:1.3). That is why St. John Paul II says: “To dedicate oneself to God is… the noblest and highest form of activity of the human being, inasmuch as he concentrates himself entirely on the adoration of the Infinite Being, who wills the salvation of all humanity… Here, then, is the precise form of collaboration that… you offer to the Church for the good of souls” 242 . In this sense St. John of the Cross says: “Let those, then, who are very active, who think to encircle the world with their preaching and exterior works, take note here that they would bring much more profit to the Church and be much more pleasing to God if they spent even half the time being with God in prayer. Certainly then they would do more, and with less labor… otherwise it is all hammering away and doing little more than nothing, and at times even harm” 243 . And likewise St. Thérèse of the Child Jesus: “Only this does Jesus ask of us. He has no need of our works, but only of our love” 244 . And thanks to the prayer and sacrifice of those who consecrate themselves to God in contemplative life, the Lord raises up preachers, confessors, spiritual directors, etc., who transmit the truth to men, so that it can truly be said that others transmit what they contemplate. c) At the Right Hand of the Father He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high (Heb 1:3): according to St. John Damascene, this refers to “the glory and honor of the divinity” 245 , that is, it means that Christ reigns together with the Father and, moreover, has judicial power over the living and the dead. Knowing that the Lord is with the Father must make our confidence in Him grow immeasurably: I can do all things in him who strengthens me (Phil 4:13), in keeping with that other magnificent expression of total confidence: I know in whom I have placed my trust! (2 Tim 1:12). d) Kingship of Christ The Lord is King of all humanity in the strict, literal and proper sense, since he received from the Father authority, power and the Kingdom (Dan 7:13), and that is why he is King of kings and Lord of lords (Rev 19:16). The foundation of this kingship is fourfold: in the first place, it belongs to him because he is God, the Incarnate Word, and thus St. Cyril of Alexandria says: “Christ obtains dominion over all creatures, not seized by force nor taken for any other reason, but by his very essence and nature” 246 ; in the second place, it belongs to him by virtue of the Redemption, by right of conquest, since he bought us with his blood: You were not ransomed… with perishable gold or silver, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet 1:18-19); in the third place, because he is Head of the Church, by the fullness of grace: full of grace and truth (Jn 1:14); in the fourth place, by right of inheritance: whom he appointed heir of all things (Heb 1:2). His royal authority includes the fullness of the threefold power: legislative, judicial and executive. The sphere of his kingship is twofold, personal and social. He reigns over intellects because he is the Truth, “and it is necessary that men receive the truth from Him with obedience” 247 ; he reigns over wills because he is Goodness, “in such a way that he inflames us toward the noblest things” 248 ; and he reigns over hearts because he is Love. And he also reigns socially, since “there is no difference between individuals and civil society, because individuals, united in society, are not for that reason any less under the power of Christ than each of them is separately. He is the source of private and public well-being” 249 . Certainly His is not a temporal or earthly kingdom: my Kingdom is not of this world (Jn 18:36), but rather it is an eternal Kingdom: his Kingdom will have no end (Lk 1:33), and it is universal: to him was given all power in heaven and on earth (Mt 28:18); a Kingdom of truth and life, of holiness and grace, of jus­tice, love and peace 250 . All missionary and apostolic work is founded on the conviction that He must reign (1 Cor 15:25). Article 5: His mystical Life a) The Church, Mystical Body From his Resurrection and forever, the sacred humanity of Jesus Christ lives a glorious and immortal Life, which since the moment of the Ascension is in heaven and which will return when his second Coming takes place. But, in the span of the centuries between the Ascension and the Parousia, he lives his mystical Life here on earth. Indeed, just as the Word assumed a human nature to fulfill the design of salvation, so, to prolong that design throughout the ages, he chooses other human natures so that salvation may reach all men of all times. The Church is Jesus Christ continued, diffused and communicated; she is like the prolongation of the redemptive Incarnation, continuing the threefold function: prophetic, priestly and royal; she is the new People of God; “she is in Christ like a sacrament or sign and instrument of intimate union with God and of the unity of the whole human race” 251 ; she is an organically structured community 252 , “a people gathered by the unity of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” 253 . The Church is mystery, communion and mission 254 . Our belonging to Her, through faith and Baptism, must be our badge of honor. The Church always, in the light of the Word of God, celebrates the mysteries of Christ for the salvation of the world 255 . b) Her “history” The reality of the Church-mystery precedes the creation of the world, as St. Clement of Rome says: “the Church is not of now, but of before” 256 , and the Shepherd of Hermas: “she was created… before all things… for her sake the world was set in order” 257 . She was, in a mediate way, “prepared in a remarkable way in the history of the people of Israel and in the Old Testament” 258 ; in an immediate way, “established in the last times” 259 by Jesus Christ, who gave her doctrine, the sacraments and the hierarchy, in a special way in Peter, through whom her constitution begins when he confesses, and is told: You are Peter and upon this rock I will build my Church (Mt 16:18); her preparation culminates on the summit of Calvary, when blood and water flow from the wounded side of the crucified Jesus Christ, and “as often as the sacrifice of the Cross, in which Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed (1 Cor 5:7), is renewed on the altar, the work of our Redemption is carried out” 260 ; she was publicly “manifested by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit” 261 , both in the Pentecost of the Jews 262 and in the Pentecost of the pagans 263 ; and “she will be gloriously perfected at the end of time” 264 , when all the just “from Abel the just to the last of the elect” 265 will be united before the Father in a Universal Church. We must always consider this so as not to fall into the temptation of thinking that the Church begins with us. On our shoulders there are not only 2000 years of history, but the past of the world and all its future. c) Her “soul”: the Holy Spirit In the Church the Holy Spirit plays a fundamental, essential role, constitutive of the Church herself. Indeed, it is He who brings about our incorporation into the Mystical Body of Christ, of which we are members by virtue of Baptism, since it is necessary to be reborn of water and the Spirit 266 : we have been baptized in one Spirit to form one body (1 Cor 12:13). The Holy Spirit had already been revealed in the Old Testament, although not as a Divine Person, under different aspects related both to the life of the People of Israel and to that of its members. Thus he intervenes in creation 267 ; he is a source of life: I will pour out my Spirit upon your offspring… and they will grow as willows grow among the grass, beside flowing streams of water (Is 44:3-4); his action is directive, both of Israel: The Lord came down in the cloud and spoke to Moses, and taking some of the Spirit that was in him, he poured it upon the seventy men (Num 11:25), and, prophetically, of the Messiah: The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon Him, a spirit of wisdom and understanding, a spirit of counsel and fortitude, a spirit of knowledge and piety, and he shall be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Is 11:2-3), upon Him I have poured out my Spirit (Is 42:1); by his action the prophets speak: and as soon as the Spirit rested upon them, they began to prophesy (Num 11:25); his action renews, purifies the heart, sanctifies: do not take your holy spirit from me… create in me, O God, a pure heart… sprinkle me, and I shall be purified; you will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow (Ps 51:9.12.13). In the New Testament all these aspects are taken up again and acquire a new meaning in the light of the revelation, made by Jesus Christ, of the Holy Spirit as a Divine Person. And in the very life of the Incarnate Word, the Holy Spirit is present in a most particular way. He is the author of the hypostatic union, which is called the “grace of union” 268 , so that He brings about the Incarnation: the Holy Spirit will come upon you (Lk 1:35). Hence Christ “is the supreme marvel accomplished by the Holy Spirit” 269 , and we confess in the Creed that he “was conceived by the work and grace of the Holy Spirit” 270 , that is, “by the power of the Spirit” 271 . It is this same Spirit who is the author of the holiness of Jesus: therefore what will be born of you will be Holy (Lk 1:35). Even the response of the Blessed Virgin, from which the Incarnation followed, is the fruit of the action of the Holy Spirit in her soul 272 , who establishes a most personal, spousal, nuptial relationship with Her, a union that is a model for us 273 , since the Spirit dwells in you (1 Cor 3:16), for he dwells in every soul in grace. He is also present in the messianic prayer and preaching of Jesus; Christ applies to himself the fulfillment of the prophecy of Is 61:1: the Spirit of the Lord is upon Me because He has anointed me; He has sent me to bring the Good News to the poor, to proclaim liberty to captives and sight to the blind, to set the oppressed free, to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor (Lk 4:18ff.); he is the source of Christ’s joy: In that hour he thrilled with joy in the Holy Spirit (Lk 10:21); from Him Christ has the power to cast out demons: If it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, it is evident that the kingdom of God has come upon you (Mt 12:28). He is present in his redemptive Sacrifice, which Jesus calls a “Baptism”: Can you drink the cup that I must drink and receive the Baptism that I must receive? (Mk 10:38); I came to bring fire upon the earth, and what am I to desire but that it be kindled! I have a Baptism with which to be baptized, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished! (Lk 12:49). John the Baptist had already announced that he who comes after me… will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire (Mt 3:11), and we are taught that through his eternal Spirit he offered Himself without blemish to God (Heb 9:14). Finally, the Holy Spirit is the author of the Resurrection of Christ: he was put to death in the flesh, but called to life by the Spirit (1 Pet 3:18). And in this he is manifested as the Vivifier, “Lord and giver of life” 274 , as we profess in the Creed. Precisely, the Gospel, the New Law, consists in the grace of the Holy Spirit, which is why it is the “law of life”: The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and death (Rom 8:2). This same Spirit, after the Resurrection and Ascension of Jesus into heaven, is sent to the Church, according to the Lord’s own promise: when the Intercessor comes, whom I will send you from the Father, the Spirit of Truth, who proceeds from the Father, He will bear witness to Me (Jn 15:26). “Once the Lord Jesus had been exalted on the Cross and glorified, he poured out the Spirit he had promised, through whom he called and gathered together in unity of faith, hope and charity the People of the New Testament, which is the Church” 275 . This sending was fulfilled on the day of Pentecost: they were all filled with the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:1-4). Therefore the Holy Spirit is a gift given by God to the Church: you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit (Acts 2:38), a gift that at the same time gives her life: If you knew the gift of God and who it is that says to you, “give me a drink,” you would have asked Him and He would have given you living water (Jn 4:10), and gives her life to such a degree that he is rightly called the “Soul of the Church,” for “he so vivifies, unifies and moves the whole body that his operation could be compared by the Holy Fathers to the service performed by the principle of life, or soul, in the human body” 276 . Therefore the Holy Spirit is the source of the unity of the Church: we were baptized in one Spirit, to be one body (1 Cor 12:13), a unity that is based on charity, which is also the fruit of the action of the Spirit: The love of God has been poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom 5:5). Rightly, then, did St. Augustine call the Holy Spirit the “Kiss, Love, Bond of union between the Father and the Son” 277 . Consequently the Spirit is also the source of the holiness of the Church, since He himself is Holy: Spirit of holiness (Rom 1:4) and, therefore, works sanctification: God has chosen you… through the sanctification of the Spirit (2 Thess 2:13). He works this sanctification interiorly in our hearts, since the Spirit of God dwells in you (1 Cor 3:16), and by this renewing presence he transforms us, making us children of God: and because you are sons, God sent into our hearts the Spirit of his Son, who cries “Abba, Father!” So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, also an heir, by the favor of God (Gal 4:6-7); those who are moved by the Spirit of God, these are children of God (Rom 8:14ff.). He renews us, makes us new creatures, built up by God: You are being built together in the Spirit into a dwelling place of God (Eph 2:22), and through this renewal and purification, and in Him, we can have access to the Father: both of us have access to the Father in one Spirit (Eph 2:18). Therefore, he is the pledge of eternal life: the Spirit of the promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance (Eph 1:13-14), and who already here teaches us all things, because he searches everything (cf. 1 Cor 2:10-11); He will teach you all things (Jn 14:26) because he is the Spirit of Truth (Jn 14:17); he helps us, since the Spirit comes to the aid of our weakness, for we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings (Rom 8:26); he enriches the Church with the diversity of his gifts: all these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills (1 Cor 12:11). We must, then, always ask the Lord to grant us his Holy Spirit, and docility to Him, so that we may belong ever more to Christ, and therefore to his Mystical Body, since if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ (Rom 8:9). God never denies this most precious gift, in which the whole New Law consists, and therefore all our salvation: If you, who are evil, know how to give good things to your children, how much more will the Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him! (Lk 11:13). We must, then, understand that the Kingdom of God is… justice, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom 14:17). The Word of God The Holy Spirit is the Principal Author of Sacred Scripture, because he willed that we might be nourished abundantly at “the table of the Word” 278 . “The Holy Spirit made Sacred Scripture fruitful with a truth more abundant than men can comprehend” 279 . The Bible is closely united to the mystery of the Incarnate Word: “just as the substantial word of God became like us in all things except sin, so the words of God expressed in human languages have become like human language in all things, except error” 280 . The richness of this heavenly treasure 281 of the Word of God is seen, among other things, in the fact that it is: – contained in the Holy Books, – celebrated in the Sacred Liturgy, – commented on by the Holy Fathers, – witnessed to by the Martyrs, – deepened by the Doctors, – authentically interpreted by the Magisterium of the Church, – and lived by the saints of all times. The Word of God must be “deepened in the Church” 282 , that is, with the same Spirit with which it was written 283 , and it is truly the strength of our Institute, “as is its supreme sacramental proclamation in the Eucharistic Sacrifice” 284 . Sacred Scripture must be the soul of our soul, of our spirituality, theology, preaching, catechesis and pastoral work. It should be possible to say of us what St. Jerome said of a person he knew: “Through daily reading and meditation of Scripture, he has made of his heart a library of Christ” 285 , for to us “the Word of God represents nothing less than the Body of Christ” 286 . d) One Church “This is the one Church of Christ, which in the Creed we confess to be One, Holy, Catholic and Apostolic” 287 . The Church of Christ is One and unique. The idea of koinonia (communion) adequately expresses the profound core of the Mystery of the Church, since this is the mystery of the personal union of each man with the Most Holy Trinity and with other men, begun by faith and Baptism. This common union implies the vertical dimension, that is, communion with God, and the horizontal dimension, that is, communion among men. This unity is a gift of God, the fruit of the divine initiative accomplished in the Paschal Mystery. Ecclesial communion is at the same time invisible and visible. As an invisible reality it is the communion of each man, on the one hand, with the Father through Christ in the Holy Spirit and, on the other, with other men, who also share in sanctifying grace 288 , in the Passion of Christ 289 , in the same faith 290 , in the same Spirit 291 . All these are realities that bear an intimate relationship with the visible communion founded on the teaching of the Apostles, on the sacraments and on the hierarchical order. This relationship between the visible and the invisible aspects of ecclesial communion is constitutive of the Church as the “universal Sacrament of salvation” 292 . This reality, at once hierarchical and mystical, visible and spiritual, earthly and heavenly, canonical and charismatic, human and divine, by a profound analogy “resembles the Mystery of the Incarnate Word” 293 , since “Christ himself is Incarnate in his Body, the Church” 294 . Therefore we, who take pride in calling ourselves religious “of the Incarnate Word,” would most gravely betray our charism if we did not work to have an authentic ecclesial spirituality, which incorporates us fully into the Church of the Incarnate Word. And we want to know nothing outside of Her. The most solid unity goes together with a diversification that does not hinder unity, but rather makes it communion. The universality of the Church, “within the unity of faith and the one divine constitution of the Church” 295 , accepts the plurality of ministries, charisms, forms of life and of apostolate, diverse liturgical and cultural, theological, spiritual and disciplinary traditions. This reality “admirably shows the undivided catholicity of the Church” 296 . We must be fervent promoters “of the unity that does not hinder diversity, as well as… of a diversity that does not hinder unity but enriches it” 297 . We are called to build up, respect and safeguard this unity in diversity each day, above all through that love which is the bond of perfection (Col 3:14). As the Angelic Doctor says: “The Church is one… by the unity of charity, because all are united by the love of God, and among themselves by mutual love” 298 . An expression of this unity in diversity are the religious institutes, among which we wish to be counted, which, although they do not belong to the hierarchical structure of the Church, belong “indisputably to her life and holiness” 299 . When they have a supra-diocesan character, rooted in the Petrine ministry, they are also elements at the service of communion among the various particular Churches. This is an important fact for our spirituality, as we already experience. Being of One Mind We aspire, in accordance with the words of St. Paul, to be of one mind (2 Cor 13:11) in the Lord (Phil 4:2). This unanimity or concord that we seek means unity in the judgment of reason about what must be done, and unity of wills so that all want the same thing. Thus, this concord is born of the same faith, through which we know what we must do, and of charity, through which we all love the same goods and share the labors as good soldiers of Christ Jesus 300 . This union exists because all think alike about God , that is, because wisdom reigns among all, which is that savory knowledge of divine things, a wisdom that is not of this age… a divine, mysterious, hidden wisdom (1 Cor 2:6-7), which only Jesus Christ crucified can grant, the power and wisdom of God for those who are called (1 Cor 1:24). In this unanimity of feelings toward one another (Rom 12:16) the Kingdom of God becomes present, since “the nature of the Kingdom is the communion of all human beings among themselves and with God” 301 . This presupposes that each of the members of our Religious Family not only rejoices in the good he possesses: joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom 14:17), but also tends unceasingly toward greater perfection: Forgetting what lies behind, I strain forward to what lies ahead, looking toward the goal (Phil 3:13-14). And it also presupposes setting aside everything that may hinder or distort this unanimity of mind. In the first place, pride, by which we inordinately seek our own excellence and do not wish to submit to others or to recognize the excellence of others; and therefore where there is pride, only discord dwells: Among the proud there are always insults (Prov 13:10). Another obstacle is the presumption of wisdom, by which we do not accept the teachings of others, believing ourselves sufficient, contrary to the example of St. Paul: I set before them the Gospel that I preach among the Gentiles… to know whether I was running or had run in vain (Gal 2:2). The Holy Spirit poured into our hearts, who is the New Law, is the one who makes us preserve the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace (Eph 4:3). He it is who, through love, makes us come out of selfishness, of particularism, of the spirit of opposition and distrust, of the spirit of reserve, of non-participation, of non-agreement with others. On the contrary, the Spirit of Christ is a Spirit of communion: strive to have unanimity of feelings toward one another (Rom 12:16), so that we truly care for others, that all the members may be equally concerned for one another (1 Cor 12:25). Hence in our communities, which must be a unity among persons, a body full of members who think, no one should behave as a closed and solitary whole, like a self-sufficient nomad; rather we must learn to act as the parts or members of a whole. The concord we seek is also destroyed both by obsequiousness and by servility, which sacrifice the truth and one’s own conscience in an attempt to maintain a false peace, not to cross a friend, to avoid some problem or, at times, to gain an advantage through silence or applause. Those who do such things resemble those Jews who believed in Him, but because of the Pharisees did not confess him, fearing to be expelled from the synagogue, for they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God (Jn 12:42-43). The fruit of this common mind in the Lord is precisely peace: the fruit of justice is sown in peace for those who make peace (Jas 3:18). True peace, given by Christ 302 , is the tranquility of order. It arises naturally when all, through faith and charity, are ordered to God. And together with peace, another effect of this unanimity of mind toward one another according to Christ Jesus (Rom 15:5) is the unity that reigns among all, even in the least details of daily life or of any decision. This can happen because each one has the certainty that in everything we do we seek the glory of God, having for this one heart and one soul 303 . e) Holy Church The Church is the “Communion of saints” 304 . It is the common union through the visible sharing of holy goods, especially the Eucharist, which is the root of the invisible common union of those who share in them, that is, of the saints. There is a spiritual koinonia among the members of the same Body, which leads to an effective union in charity and in prayer. Not only among those of us who are still pilgrims on earth, but also between these and all those who have reached the end and are in heaven or on their way to it, in purgatory. There is a mutual relationship among the various states of the one Church, because, being members of Christ (cf. 1 Cor 12:12-27), in whom the fullness of grace resides (cf. Jn 1:16), in Him we also are members of one another (Rom 12:5) and benefit spiritually from one another. Hence the importance of being aware of Christ’s intercession for us: he always lives to make intercession for us (Heb 7:25); of the intercession of the saints, who “are intimately united to us” 305 ; of their examples, which “impel us to seek the city to come… perfect union with Christ, that is, holiness” 306 ; and, eminently among the saints, of the intercession of the Blessed Virgin Mary, “to whose protection the faithful have recourse with their supplications in all their dangers and needs” 307 . Hence the depth of devotion to the saints corresponds to the reality of the Church as a mystery of communion. The saints are a most eloquent sign of the vitality of the Church, and therefore they have an apologetic value for the truth of our faith, by concretely realizing the mark of the holiness of the Church. They are the best members of the Mystical Body of Christ and the greatest and most complete fruit of the Incarnation and the Redemption. And thanks to this they are the ones who transform the world by their example and by the power of their intercession. They constantly commend to us heaven, eternal life, the reward of merits, God! That is why in honoring them we honor God himself, for the saints are his masterpiece, and in “crowning their merits the Lord crowns his own gifts” 308 . Even after their death they fulfill posthumous missions, pushing entire generations to the heroism of following Jesus Christ, being not only for the young but also for the great majority of the nation… an example of nobility and a memorial of virtue (2 Macc 6:31). That is why there is no history more complete, more magnificent and more profitable than the Litany of all the saints; it evokes and invokes all the great spirits who have illustrated the planet and who have made humanity advance by their virtues. Likewise we must venerate their relics, which do not cease to work. Therefore, for our part, we must do everything possible so that the face of the Church may be without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but holy and blameless (Eph 5:27), always remembering the irreplaceable importance of sanctifying grace, given to us by the sacraments worthily received, which are “like divine relics of the Incarnation” 309 . f) Catholic Church The Church of Christ is the universal community of the disciples of the Lord which extends to all times, to all places, to all races, languages and cultures; that is, it is catholic, it is universal. The Church is catholic also in doctrine. Some emphasize more the teachings of St. John, others those of St. Paul, etc.; there is a variety of theological schools, there are different and venerable liturgical rites. In this regard it is our desire to be able to have in our Institute an eastern branch in order to help our brothers of the Eastern Churches, since they form part “of the undivided patrimony of the Universal Church” 310 . From this it follows that we must not fall into particularisms, reductionisms, partialities or one-sided approaches that offend against catholicity. The Catholic Church breathes with two lungs: “one cannot breathe as a Christian, I would say more, as a Catholic, with only one lung; one must have two lungs, that is, the eastern and the western” 311 . The universal Church is the “Body of the Churches” 312 , and is, therefore, a communion of particular Churches. These are “parts… of the one Church of Christ” 313 ; they are constituted “in the image of the universal Church” 314 ; in them “the Church of Christ, which is One, Holy, Catholic and Apostolic, is truly found and operates” 315 ; and, therefore, they have with the universal Church a peculiar relationship of “mutual interiority” 316 . The universal Church, in her essential mystery, is a reality ontologically and temporally prior to every concrete particular Church. The Church-mystery is the mother of the particular Churches, which are her daughters. We do not belong to the universal Church in a mediate way, through a particular Church. Through faith and Baptism we are immediately incorporated into the One, Holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church, although entry into and life in the universal Church necessarily take place in a particular Church. That is why in the Church no one is a foreigner 317 ; whoever belongs to a particular Church belongs to all the Churches –without blurring canonical dependence 318 – since belonging to the Communion, as belonging to the Church, is never merely particular, but by its very nature is always universal: “He who is in Rome knows that the Indians are his members” 319 . A Missionary and Ecumenical Church Because the Church is the “universal Sacrament of salvation” 320 , she is open to the missionary and ecumenical dynamic, and not folded in upon herself, since she has been sent to proclaim and bear witness to, to make present and extend, the mystery of communion that constitutes her; to gather all people and all things together in Christ 321 . That is why, in the image of the Church, our small Religious Family must never be folded in upon itself, but must be open like the arms of Christ on the Cross, whose arms were dislocated from so much opening them out of love. The Holy Spirit, present and active in every time and place, acts “in the heart of man, through the ‘seeds of the Word,’ even in religious initiatives, in the efforts of human activity directed toward truth, toward the good and toward God” 322 . It is our mission, therefore, to discover them, with joy and respect, in order to seek that men may awaken to a more ardent desire for truth and charity 323 , since “the Holy Spirit offers to all the possibility of being associated, in a way known only to God, with this Paschal Mystery” 324 . This presence of the Spirit “affects not only individuals, but also society, history, peoples, cultures and religions… It is also the Spirit who sows the ‘seeds of the Word’ present in rites and cultures, and prepares them for their maturity in Christ” 325 , for the Holy Spirit was already at work in the world before Christ was glorified 326 . This work of the Holy Spirit has the role of a preparation for the Gospel and “cannot but be referred to Christ, the Word made flesh by the power of the Spirit” 327 , so that “it must not be separated… from the special action which he carries out in the Body of Christ, which is the Church” 328 . That is why the teaching of St. Ambrose will always be for us like a torch illuminating our action: “Everything true, by whomever it is said, comes from the Holy Spirit” 329 . So the saints affirmed and believed: “all that has been said truly belongs to us Christians” 330 ; “let every good Christian understand that any truth, wherever it may be, belongs to his Lord” 331 ; “no one can say anything true unless moved by the Holy Spirit, who is the Spirit of Truth” 332 ; “there is no knowledge of the truth except in the Holy Spirit, who works in the intellect and preserves it” 333 ; “everything good and everything true is from the Holy Spirit” 334 . Thanks to the teaching of Christ, we know that there exists a humanity opposed to faith and to the gift of grace, which the Lord himself calls the “world” 335 . Faced with the world, into which Christ sends us like sheep in the midst of wolves (Mt 10:16), St. Paul admonishes: Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind (Rom 12:2). However, this difference cannot be translated into fear or contempt 336 , since if one is conscious of what the Lord wants, one also perceives the duty of evangelization and the urgency of the mission. For this a merely conservative attitude is not enough; rather, what is also necessary is the spreading and proclamation of the deposit of faith, according to the command of Christ himself. And “this interior impulse of charity” 337 is called dialogue . This dialogue, which is a spiritual communication, has its transcendent origin in God himself, whose intention is to establish “a dialogue in which the Word of God expresses himself in the Incarnation” 338 . Such a dialogue of God with men is born of divine love and is addressed to all men, without doing violence to anyone. It is necessary to know and “to share common customs” 339 , without succumbing to the danger of attenuating or diminishing the truth, since “irenicism and syncretism are at bottom forms of skepticism regarding the power and content of the Word of God that we wish to preach” 340 , certain that “only he who lives the Christian vocation in its fullness can be immunized against the contagion of the errors with which he comes into contact” 341 . Of particular importance is preaching, which must be done “always practical in language and skilled in method, assiduous in exercise, backed by the witness of true virtues, eager to progress and to lead hearers to the security of faith” 342 . Although this dialogue embraces all men, nevertheless, taking into account the concrete positions of humanity, four spheres or “circles” are distinguished in which this spiritual communication takes place: – In the first place is the circle of those with whom we share human values, in order to raise them to the supernatural and Christian level 343 . In this sphere the problem of atheism stands out in a singular way, founded on false theories and consisting not in “a liberation but (in) a drama that tries to stifle the light of the living God” 344 . In these circumstances dialogue is especially difficult, and one must be “very cautious in judging and… effective in refuting” 345 , knowing that many situations are occasions for such an attitude. – In the second place, we find the worshippers of the one God, among whom are the Jews, the Muslims and the faithful of Afro-Asian religions. Conscious that the true religion is the Christian one, and longing that all who seek God may recognize it as such, it is necessary to recognize the many spiritual and moral values that they possess and the ideals that can be promoted and defended in common 346 . – In the third place is the circle of those who bear the name of Christ, with whom it is necessary to emphasize, above all, what unites us, and then what divides us. It is necessary to show how those elements of the Church that appear as an obstacle to union are the fruit of the will of Christ for the benefit, unity and freedom of all. In particular, the Primacy of Peter, perpetuated in the Pope, cannot be considered an obstacle, both “because without the Pope the Catholic Church would no longer be such” 347 , and because without the Roman Pontiff “as many schisms would be formed in the Church as there are priests” 348 . – And, finally, dialogue takes place with the Catholic faithful, children of the house of God. This dialogue “does not suppress the exercise of the proper function of authority, on the one hand, and of submission, on the other” 349 , but presupposes it, for “by obedience directed toward dialogue we understand the exercise of authority, entirely imbued with the awareness of being a service and ministry of truth and charity” 350 . In order to become men of authentic dialogue we must learn to practice the following virtues: “ clarity above all: dialogue presupposes and demands intelligibility; it is an exchange of thought… Then, affability : dialogue is not proud, it is not hurtful, it is not offensive. Its authority is intrinsic, through the truth it sets forth, the clarity it spreads, the example it proposes; it is not a command or an imposition… Confidence , both in the value of one’s own word and in the disposition of the interlocutor to receive it; it promotes familiarity and friendship… Finally, pedagogical prudence , which takes careful account of the psychological and moral conditions of the hearer 351 … and strives to know his sensibility and to adapt reasonably and modify the forms of one’s own presentation so as not to be annoying and incomprehensible to him” 352 . Moreover, “it shows, on the part of the one who initiates it, an intention of correctness, of esteem, of sympathy and of goodness; it excludes a priori condemnation, offensive and habitual polemics, the vanity of useless conversation… it respects his dignity and his freedom, it seeks… his benefit and would wish to dispose him to a fuller communion of sentiments and convictions… it presupposes in us… the state of mind of one who feels within himself the weight of the apostolic mandate” 353 . Likewise we must embrace the holy cause of ecumenism; at stake is a promise-prophecy of the Lord: There will be one flock and one shepherd (Jn 10:16), and a prayer of the Lord: That all may be one (Jn 17:21). We must strive by prayer, penance, study, dialogue and collaboration to attain full communion in the unity of the Church “which Christ granted to his Church from the beginning, and which we believe subsists indefectibly in the Catholic Church, and which we hope will grow until the consummation of the ages” 354 , so that “in a renewed conversion to the Lord it may become possible for all to recognize the permanence of the Primacy of Peter in his successors, the Bishops of Rome, and to see the Petrine ministry carried out, as it is understood by the Lord, as a universal apostolic service, present in all the Churches from within them, and which, its substance as a divine institution being preserved, can be expressed in diverse ways…” 355 . The ecumenical commitment is “to pray and work for reconciliation and for ecclesial unity according to the mind and heart of our Savior Jesus Christ” 356 . g) Apostolic Church Another of the awe-inspiring realities of the immeasurable mystery of the Church of the Incarnate Word is her apostolicity, that is, the fact of being founded on the Apostles and perpetuated by apostolic succession. Communion among the particular Churches in the universal Church is founded –besides faith, Baptism and the Eucharist– on the Episcopate. The unity of the Church is rooted, also, in the unity of the Episcopate: “In order that the Episcopate itself might be one and undivided, he placed blessed Peter over the other Apostles, and established in him the visible principle and perpetual foundation of the unity of faith and communion” 357 . “Each Bishop is the visible principle and foundation of unity in his own (particular) Church, formed in the image of the universal Church” 358 . But for this to be so, the supreme authority of the Church must be present in the particular Church as a proper element: the episcopal College “together with its Head the Roman Pontiff, and never without it” 359 . The Primacy of the Bishop of Rome and the episcopal College are proper elements of the universal Church, not derived from the particular Churches, but interior to each particular Church. “In the Pope we see Jesus Christ, we follow Jesus Christ, we love Jesus Christ. And in the Bishops? In the Bishops we see, follow, venerate and love the Successors of the Apostles…” 360 . Each of the members of our Religious Family “wish to be something entirely of the Pope, of the Bishops and of the Church: rags, servants and most obedient children of the Church, of the Bishops and of the Pope, in humility, with fidelity, with love without limits…” 361 . That is why we must have a gaze of faith in order always to recognize those whom the Holy Spirit has appointed bishops to shepherd the Church of God (Acts 20:28). We must make our own the counsel of St. Ignatius of Antioch: “Nothing without the Bishop and the priests” 362 , and much less against them. St. Luigi Orione also counseled: “The state of the Bishop is the most perfect of all, even more than the religious state; to him belongs the fullness of the priesthood; to him above all others, the spirit of faith, of wisdom and of fortitude… The Bishop knows no enemies of his own; for him there are only children, and the littlest, the humblest, the most unhappy are dearest to him. For all he prays, for all he has words of eternal life, for all he goes up to the altar and offers the Blood of the immaculate Lamb who takes away the sins of the world… The Bishop is the Good Shepherd, who watches, feeds and evangelizes; who knows how to suffer in silence and knows how to give his life for his sheep” 363 . The history of the Church offers us abundant examples of glorious figures of the Episcopate: bishops who evangelized and founded nations, defended and organized peoples, guarded the deposit of faith entrusted to them 364 in the midst of the bloodiest persecutions, and shored up the sound doctrine of the Church against a multitude of errors and confusions. That is why: “… let us love the Bishops!” 365 . Not only is communion with the bishop necessary, but also, “… under the authority of the Bishop” 366 , who is God’s steward (Titus 1:7), communion must be sought with the other priests, a communion that constitutes a single presbyterate founded on the common participation in the priesthood of Christ: “By virtue of their common sacred ordination and common mission, all priests are united among themselves in an intimate fraternity, which must be manifested in spontaneous and willing mutual help, both spiritual and material, both pastoral and personal…” 367 . Unity with the other priests, both of the diocesan and of the religious clergy, takes place above all in “intimate sacramental fraternity” 368 , and from there we also wish to establish close collaboration in pastoral work, since priests, “… although they devote themselves to diverse offices, nevertheless exercise a single priestly ministry on behalf of men” 369 . Therefore, “between the secular clergy and religious communities a renewed fraternity and a bond of cooperation must be fostered; let them hold in great esteem certain forms of mutual help and certain contacts… which help so much toward mutual trust, apostolic unanimity and fraternal concord…” 370 . This unity and cooperation with the other members of the presbyterate, which we wish to establish insofar as we are able, aims at our all preaching Jesus Christ by word and by the example of our life without there being divisions 371 , conscious of being ministers of a new Covenant, not of the letter, but of the Spirit… (2 Cor 3:6) and, therefore, that in so grave an office we must bear one another’s burdens (Gal 6:2). Paraphrasing the Apostle 372 , we always wish, as we have the opportunity, to do good to all, especially to our brothers in the priesthood, received through the imposition of hands 373 . The marvelous gift of God that consecrated life signifies, as do vocations to the priesthood, the diaconate, religious life, the missions or consecrated secularity, “affects the whole Church in one of her fundamental marks, which is that of her apostolicity” 374 . The foundation of this essentially supernatural work lies in God’s own choice and call: You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit (Jn 15:16); likewise, when the Lord chooses the twelve, it is said: He went up a mountain and calling those whom he wanted, they came to Him (Mk 3:13), since they are God’s property: I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom You gave me; for they are yours, and all that is mine is yours and what is yours is mine (Jn 17:9-10). We would like God to give us the gift of being able to discover and guide so many vocations that we could fill all the good seminaries and novitiates of the whole world, according to the Pope’s recommendation: “God calls whom he wills, by the free initiative of his love. But he wishes to call through our persons… There must be no fear in proposing directly to a young person, or a less young one, the calls of the Lord” 375 . That is why work with vocations must be active, constant, full of drive and vitality, committed and urged on by the charity of Christ 376 , and necessarily opposed to a mentality of “ordinary administration or bureaucratic slowness” 377 , which negligently waits for vocations to knock at the door. God sows the seeds of vocation by grace with full hands 378 . The vitality of a community and of the Church herself can be measured by the vocations that God raises up in it, and to this fostering of vocations the right formation of those chosen is inseparably joined. Hence the importance of “making intense efforts to foster vocations and to provide the best possible priestly formation in seminaries. An abundance of vocations and an effective formation of seminarians: here are two proofs of the vitality of the Church” 379 . This task of discovering and guiding vocations is not carried out only through pastoral action –an enthusiastic pastoral ministry–. Essential, above all, is prayer: Ask the master of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest (Mt 9:38), for I planted, Apollos watered; but it was God who gave the growth (1 Cor 3:6).
